# Krzyki w Głowie

Kiedy Kasia się obudziła, pierwszą rzeczą, jaką poczuła, było łomotanie serca o żebra. Leżała w łóżku, wpatrując się w sufit, na którym tańczyły cienie z ulicznej latarni. Za oknem świat już żył — słyszała tramwaje, odległe rozmowy, śmiech dzieci biegających do szkoły. Wszystko to brzmiało jak z innego świata, oddzielonego od niej grubą szybą lodu.

*Wstań*, powiedziała do siebie. *Wstań i działaj.*

Nie wstała.

 Ciało odmawiało posłuszeństwa, jakby ktoś wylał na nią kubeł betonu. Ręce drżały. W klatce piersiowej narastał znajomy, ciasny węzeł, który zaczął piąć się w górę, do gardła.

*Co się stanie, jeśli dziś znów się pomylę? Co powiedzą? Pomyślą, że jestem do niczego.*

Kasia pracowała w korporacji od trzech lat. Była ceniona za analityczny umysł i skrupulatność, ale nikt nie widział, co działo się w niej przed każdym spotkaniem, przed każdym telefonem, przed każdym mailem z szefostwa. Nikt nie wiedział, że każdego ranka toczyła cichą wojnę z własnym umysłem.

W końcu zmusiła się, by usiąść. Świat lekko się kołysał. Zrobiła to, co zawsze pomagało — wzięła trzy głębokie oddechy, licząc w myślach. Raz. Dwa. Trzy. Ale dziś liczby nie pomagały. W głowie kłębiły się obrazy: miny kolegów, szeptane uwagi, ironiczne uśmiechy. Wszystko to, czego nigdy nie usłyszała, ale co jej wyobraźnia malowała z niezachwianą pewnością.

 W łazience lustro odbiło jej twarz — blade policzki, cienie pod oczami. Kasia unikała swojego wzroku. Bała się tego, co mogłaby w nim zobaczyć.

*Może powinnam wziąć dzień wolny*, pomyślała. *Może jestem chora.*

Nie była chora. Była przerażona.

 Przy śniadaniu ręce trzęsły się tak bardzo, że rozlała kawę. Mama zadzwoniła, ale Kasia nie odebrała. Nie miała sił udawać, że wszystko jest w porządku. Telefon leżał na stole, a ekran co chwilę rozświetlał się powiadomieniami. Każde z nich brzmiało jak oskarżenie.

Na przystanku tramwajowym tłum wydał jej się wrogi. Ludzie pchali się, rozmawiali, śmiali się — jakby lęk nie istniał, jakby świat był prostym, zrozumiałym miejscem. Kasia stała z boku, ściskając pasek torby, i czuła, jak ściany rzeczywistości zamykają się wokół niej.

*Jesteśmy tu, jesteśmy tu, jesteśmy tu*, szeptał głos w jej głowie. *Nigdzie się nie ukryjesz.*

 W biurze wszystko wyglądało normalnie. Klimatyzacja szumiała, komputery buczały, ktoś opowiadał dowcip przy ekspresie do kawy. Kasia usiadła przy swoim biurku i włączyła komputer, ale litery na ekranie zlewały się w jedną rozmazaną masę.

— Kasia, masz chwilę? — usłyszała głos szefa.

Świat zwęził się do jednego punktu. Serce waliło tak mocno, że bała się, iż wszyscy wokół to słyszą.

— T-tak, oczywiście — wykrztusiła.

Szef chciał tylko omówić nowy projekt. Nic wielkiego. Ale Kasia wyszła z jego gabinetu cała mokra od potu, z uczuciem, że właśnie przeżyła wypadek samochodowy.

W toalecie zamknęła się w kabinie i oparła czoło o zimną ścianę. Płakała cicho, bez łez, bo od dawna nie potrafiła płakać normalnie. Czuła tylko suchy, duszący szloch, który nie przynosił ulgi.

*Co jest ze mną nie tak?*

Wieczorem, w swoim mieszkaniu, Kasia usiadła na podłodze w salonie. Światła nie zapaliła. Za oknem zapadał zmierzch. Wzięła telefon i napisała wiadomość do psychologa, do którego kiedyś się wybierała, ale nigdy nie poszła:

*„Chyba potrzebuję pomocy."*

Wysłała ją, zanim zdążyła się rozmyślić. Potem siedziała w ciemności, wsłuchując się w ciszę, która po raz pierwszy od dawna nie wydawała się groźna. Była po prostu ciszą.

Za kilka dni miała umówioną pierwszą wizytę. Wiedziała, że to nie będzie łatwe — że czeka ją żmudna, trudna praca, pełna zakrętów i cofnięć. Ale po raz pierwszy od dawna pomyślała, że może nie musi walczyć sama.

Na parapecie usiadła kotka sąsiadki, biała, z zielonymi oczami. Przez szybę patrzyła na Kasię z uwagą, jakby chciała powiedzieć: *„Jesteś tu. Żyjesz. To już coś."*

Kasia uśmiechnęła się — niepewnie, drżąco, ale szczerze. Może jutro znów się obudzi z tym samym łomotaniem serca. Może znów będzie się bała. Ale tej nocy zasnęła spokojniej niż od wielu tygodni, bo wreszcie zrobiła pierwszy krok w stronę siebie.

A to był początek.

# The Price of Morning Light

The courtroom smelled of lemon polish and old fear. Maya Chen stood behind the defendant's table, her hands folded so no one could see the tremor in her fingers. Twelve years. Twelve years she had built her practice from a one-room office above a dry cleaner to a firm that handled half the zoning appeals in Hennepat County. And now, with three words, she was about to let it burn.

"Mrs. Chen," Judge Halloway peered down from the bench, his glasses catching the fluorescent light. "Do you wish to withdraw as counsel?"

She thought of her corner office. The mahogany desk her father had helped her carry up three flights of stairs. The mural of past victories—newspapers, thank-you letters, a photograph of her shaking hands with the governor. The junior associates who called her for advice on weekends. The secretary, Dolores, who brought her coffee at 7:14 every morning without fail because Maya had once mentioned she liked the quiet before the day began.

She thought of the mortgage on her mother's house, which Maya had paid off after the diagnosis.

She thought of Tomás.

"Ms. Chen?" Her client, a sixteen-year-old boy with terrified eyes and a borrowed blazer two sizes too big, looked at her like she was the last door in a burning hallway.

"No, Your Honor," she said. "I do not."

---

It had started with a complaint. A routine one—a parent upset about a book in the school library. Maya had been retained by the district to defend its curriculum choices. It was easy work, and well-paid work, and work that paid for Dolores's raise last Christmas.

But when she drove to Riverbend High to review the materials in question, she opened the file and found something she did not expect.

The book was *The Cartographer of Evening*. She had read it at fifteen, under her covers with a flashlight, because her own school library had kept it on a high shelf. It was the story of a girl who mapped the dreams of her sleeping town—a gentle, strange, lyrical book that had taught Maya that books could be doors. Inside, someone had highlighted passages with a yellow marker. The same passages, she realized with a slow chill, were the ones about the girl noticing that her best friend was also becoming a woman.

The school had pulled it.

Maya asked for the district's full review file. The superintendent's notes were damning. There had been no review. There had been no committee. A single complaint had triggered the removal, and no one—not the principal, not the librarian, not the school board—had objected. *Easier to remove it than to defend it*, the superintendent had written. *Too much noise right now. Reassess in the fall.*

Maya set the file down and looked out at the parking lot. There were cars with stickers that said PARENTS' RIGHTS and cars with rainbows on the bumpers, and she thought, with the weariness of a woman who had been a lawyer for twenty-two years, *this is how it happens. Not with bonfires. With yellow markers and a sentence in an email.*

She had a choice. She could send a brief recommending the district keep the book removed. It was, after all, what she was hired to do—defend the district's decisions. The board would adopt her recommendation. The matter would end. Her invoice would be paid.

Or she could walk away.

But walking away was simple. The hard thing—what she had been paid six hundred dollars an hour to avoid—was to stand up in a public meeting and say, *I was wrong to take this case. The law does not require you to remove this book. Your conscience should not allow it.* The hard thing was to make herself the story instead of telling it.

---

She did not sleep that night. She sat at the kitchen table with a legal pad and wrote down everything she would lose. She made two columns. The left column was long, and getting longer as she remembered things. The right column had only a single line: *Tomás deserves a librarian who will fight for him.*

She had met him on the drive home. He was sitting on the low wall outside the school, still in his borrowed blazer, kicking at the gravel. He had recognized her from the news—she had done a segment about a zoning dispute last spring—and when she pulled over, he had looked at her with the desperate hope of someone who has just realized the adults in charge might not help him.

"Are you the lawyer?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Is the book gone for good?"

She had hesitated too long. "Probably," she said.

He nodded, slowly, like he was confirming something he'd already guessed. "My friend Milo lent it to me. He said I should read it because—I think I'm like her. The girl in the book." He didn't look at her. "I haven't told anyone else that. I just wanted you to know. So you'd know what you were deciding."

She had driven home in silence, her hands tight on the wheel.

---

The school board meeting was scheduled for a Tuesday. Maya had forty-eight hours to inform the district she would not be filing the brief they wanted. She drafted the email three times. Each time she deleted a little more, until what remained was nine sentences:

*Dear Superintendent Alvarez,*

*I must withdraw from representation of the district in this matter. After review, I believe the district's decision to remove The Cartographer of Evening from school libraries was made without the procedural and substantive review required by law, and I cannot in good conscience defend it. I have attached a memo explaining the deficiencies in the current process. I recommend the board reconsider.*

*Thank you for the opportunity to serve the district.*

*Sincerely,*
*Maya Chen*

She hit send before she could delete it again.

The phone rang eleven minutes later. It was her firm's managing partner, Jordan.

"Maya." His voice was careful. "Tell me this is a draft."

"It's not."

"You understand this is a breach."

"I understand."

"Maya, the district is our third-largest client. The school board contracts alone—Do you understand what you've done?"

"Yes."

A long pause. "I'm going to need you in the office. First thing tomorrow."

The office. The mahogany desk. Dolores and her 7:14 coffee. She thought of these things, and she let herself think of them, because she owed them that.

"Tomorrow," she said.

---

The next three weeks were the longest of her life. She was not fired—not exactly. She was placed on what the firm called *voluntary leave pending the conclusion of an internal review.* She was paid for two of those weeks. Then the firm announced, in an email she received at 11:47 p.m. on a Thursday, that her partnership would not be renewed at the end of the fiscal year. The letter was signed by Jordan. Dolores had not been the one to type it, because Dolores had left the firm the week before, citing *personal reasons,* which everyone understood.

Maya cleared her desk on a Saturday. The mural came down first. She put each clipping in a folder, carefully, like she was filing evidence. Then she took down the photograph of her and the governor. She paused with it in her hands, and then she put it in the box too, because she had decided, somewhere in the last three weeks, that she would not lie to herself about what mattered.

The mahogany desk she left for the firm.

---

The board meeting, when it came, was held in the high school gymnasium. There were folding chairs arranged in rows, and a podium with a microphone, and a banner that said HENNEPAT COUNTY SCHOOL DISTRICT in proud blue letters. People were lined up outside an hour before the doors opened. Maya arrived at six forty-five in the morning, in a black blazer and flat shoes, carrying a single manila folder.

She had decided, on the drive over, that she would not speak first. She would let the parents speak, and the teachers, and the students. She would sit in the third row and listen, and when it was her turn, she would tell them the truth.

Tomás was there. He was wearing the borrowed blazer again, but this time Milo was beside him, and Milo's mother, and there were other students Maya didn't know, holding handmade signs. *BOOKS ARE DOORS*, one said. *THEY CAN'T TAKE EVERYTHING*, said another.

A man in a red cap spoke for forty minutes about parental rights. A woman spoke after him about a child she didn't have. A librarian named Mrs. Avery, who had worked at Riverbend for thirty-one years, read the highlighted passages aloud, in a clear and steady voice, and the gymnasium was silent.

When Maya rose to speak, her legs felt like water.

"My name is Maya Chen," she said. "Six weeks ago, I was hired by this district to defend its decision to remove *The Cartographer of Evening* from its school libraries. I am here tonight to tell you that I was wrong to take that case, and I am here to tell you why."

She told them about the superintendent's notes. She read them aloud. She told them the book had been removed without committee review, without formal complaint procedure, without any of the steps that the district's own policies required. She told them she had been retained to rubber-stamp a decision that had already been made.

"I cannot do that," she said. "And I cannot in good conscience tell you that the law requires this book to be removed. It does not. Your own policies do not. And if you remove it anyway, you will be sending a message to every student in this district that there are some stories the adults in charge are afraid to let you read."

She set the folder on the podium. "I have prepared a memo, for any board member who wishes to read it. It is also available to the public, on my website, which—as of last week—does not belong to a firm anymore."

There was a long silence. Then someone in the back began to clap, slowly, and others joined, and the sound rose up to the gymnasium's high metal rafters like something that had been waiting to be set free.

---

The board voted, three months later, to return the book to the shelves. They also voted, after a public comment period that ran to four hours and seventeen minutes, to overhaul their review process. Maya did not get the contract to help them. A younger firm, one with less to lose, took it on.

The Hen County *Gazette* did a story. So did a paper in the capital. Maya was interviewed on a morning show that her mother watched on Tuesday afternoons, which made her mother cry twice and then call to ask, with great suspicion, whether Maya was being paid enough.

She wasn't, particularly. She had set up a small solo practice in a strip mall between a tax preparer and a vape shop. The sign on her door said MAYA CHEN, ATTORNEY AT LAW, and she had painted the trim herself on a Saturday. The clients who came to her were not the district, and they were not the governor, and they were not the kind of people who got quoted in the *Gazette*. They were people like Tomás's mother, who needed help with a landlord. They were people like Milo, who needed someone to write a letter to a school. They were people who paid what they could, and sometimes in vegetables.

Tomás came to see her once, near the end of that summer. He brought her a copy of *The Cartographer of Evening*, a library copy, with a bright new dust jacket. He had a girlfriend, he told her. Her name was Alma. She had read the book too.

"I just wanted you to know," he said. "So you'd know what you decided."

Maya took the book. She held it the way you hold something that has been passed to you from a great height. Outside, the morning was just beginning, and the light, coming in through the strip-mall window, fell across the desk her father had helped her carry, and across the manila folder with its single yellow-highlighted page, and across her own two hands, which were not trembling anymore.

She had given up the mahogany desk. She had given up the partnership. She had given up Dolores and the governor's photograph and the third-largest client in the firm. She had given up the easy story of her own success, in which everything she had built was proof that she had been right all along.

What she had kept, it turned out, was the harder thing. What she had kept was the right to look in the mirror.

She opened the book to the first page. There, in a child's careful hand, someone had written: *For the grown-ups who remember being small.*

Maya read the line aloud, to no one, to herself, to the morning. Then she turned the page, and began.

# 那盆开在窗台上的茉莉

林小满第一次注意到周晓燕又把她刚拖完的地踩脏的时候，是在一个普通的周二下午。

食堂的拖把池旁边，周晓燕理所当然地把用完的拖把往小满刚洗好的桶里一扔，溅出的脏水洒了小满一裤腿。

"你怎么又不倒水啊。"小满小声嘟囔了一句。

"什么？"周晓燕斜着眼睛看她，"我拖了一上午的地，腰都直不起来了，你倒倒水怎么了？"

旁边几个同学装作没听见，各自散去。小满低下头，把裤腿上的水拧了拧，提着那桶脏水去倒掉了。

这是她在周晓燕面前的第——她已经记不清是第几次了。

小满的母亲也是这样一个不会拒绝的人。

母亲在社区超市做了十二年收银，老板让她加班她就从不让加班费，老板让她代早班她就从无二话。直到有一天，老板以"年纪大了手脚慢"为由把她辞掉，母亲连一句为什么都没问出口，默默收拾了东西回家。

那天晚上，小满看见母亲坐在阳台上，对着那盆养了多年的茉莉发呆。

"妈，你怎么不去要个说法？"

母亲笑了笑："人都这样，忍一忍就过去了。"

小满想，我不能像妈妈一样。

可是她在周晓燕面前，一次次地忍了过去。

——

事情的转折发生在期中考试前的一个晚自习。

周晓燕把一堆参考书"不小心"碰倒，正好砸在小满刚整理好的笔记上。

"哎呀，对不起啦。"周晓燕笑着说，语气里没有丝毫歉意。

小满看着被弄乱的笔记，那些她花了两个周末才整理完的错题集，纸页被撕破了好几页。

她的火突然就上来了。

"周晓燕，"她站起来，声音比自己想象的还要大，"你每次都这样'不小心'，可不可以请你下次小心一点？"

周晓燕愣住了。

她显然没想到这个平时逆来顺受的"小透明"会突然反击。

"你说什么？"周晓燕的声音尖了起来，"我又不是故意的，你这么大声干什么？"

"你不是故意的，但你从来都不道歉，也从来都不改。"小满说出这些话的时候，心跳得厉害，但她没有退缩，"上次你也是'不小心'弄脏了我的笔记本，这次又是。你能不能考虑一下别人的感受？"

教室里安静了下来。

周晓燕的脸涨得通红，她没想到事情会发展成这样。

"你——"

"我不是想和你吵架，"小满打断她，"我只是希望你以后注意点。这本笔记是我花了很多时间整理的。"

周晓燕瞪着她，嘴唇动了动，最终什么也没说，转身走回自己的座位。

小满坐下来的时候，发现自己的手在抖。

——

那天晚上回到家，她看见母亲还在阳台上，给那盆茉莉浇水。

"妈，今天我在学校和一个人吵架了。"

母亲的手顿了顿："和谁？"

"一个总是欺负我的同学。我……我说她了。"

母亲看着她，目光复杂。

"她没对你怎么样吧？"

"没有。她只是……很生气。但我没让她。"

母亲沉默了一会儿，突然笑了。

"像我。"

"什么？"

"我像你这么大的时候，也和你一样。"母亲摸了摸那盆茉莉的叶子，"后来我工作了，慢慢就忘了怎么说不。有时候我在想，如果当年我没忘，现在会不会不一样。"

小满看着母亲，看着母亲眼中那一点点闪烁的光。

"妈，你应该去要个说法的。"

母亲摇摇头："已经过去了。"

"那我可以帮你写一封信。"

母亲看着她，突然笑了起来，眼眶却有点红。

"好啊。你帮我写。"

——

第二天，小满在妈妈的指导下，给那个超市的老板写了一封信。

不是什么律师函，也不是什么投诉信，只是把十二年的辛苦和被辞退的不合理，一五一十地写了出来。

"妈，你不寄吗？"

"寄。"母亲把那封信放进信封，"小满，谢谢你。"

——

小满不知道那封信后来怎么样。但她知道，母亲寄出那封信后，眼里有了一点不一样的光。

在学校里，周晓燕没有再"不小心"弄倒过她的东西。

不是因为周晓燕变得善良了，而是因为小满学会了，在别人第一次越界的时候，就明确地说不。

那盆茉莉在那个夏天开了很多花，白色的，淡淡的香气飘满了整个阳台。

母亲说，那是她养茉莉这么多年，开得最好的一年。

小满想，也许人和花一样，被压抑得太久，就会忘记自己还能开花。

但只要敢于开口，第一步就已经迈出去了。

（全文完）

# Gennaio Secco

Marco fissava la bottiglia di Amarone come si fissa un vecchio nemico. Era lì, sullo scaffale del supermercato, con la sua etichetta elegante e il suo colore rosso cupo che prometteva tepore, oblio e quella sottile ebbrezza che lo accompagnava da quando aveva vent'anni. Ora, a quarantaquattro, si era ripromesso che gennaio sarebbe stato diverso.

*Secco*, pensò, e quasi sorrise della parola.

Tornò a casa con una busta piena di acqua frizzante, tisane allo zenzero e un barattolo di miele millefiori. Sua moglie Laura lo osservava dalla soglia della cucina con un sopracciglio alzato.

"Non berrai mica sul serio niente di tutto quello?"

"Mica cosa?"

"Non hai detto che il Dry January è una stupidaggina anglosassone?"

Marco posò la spesa sul tavolo e si sedette, con il movimento lento di chi sta cercando le parole giuste. Fuori, una Milano grigia e bagnata sbatteva la pioggia contro i vetri.

"Ho detto che è una moda. Ma forse era una scusa."

Laura si sedette di fronte a lui. Si conoscevano da quindici anni, sposati da dieci, e lei aveva imparato a distinguere i momenti in cui Marco parlava di superficie da quelli in cui scavava. Questo era uno di quelli.

"Dillo," disse semplicemente.

"Ho paura di non piacermi senza."

Le parole uscirono nude, quasi sgrammaticate, come le diceva quando era bambino e doveva confessare qualcosa alla madre. Laura non rispose subito. Si alzò, andò al frigorifero, tornò con una bottiglia di Sanbittèr e la mise sul tavolo tra loro, accanto al miele.

"Non è la stessa cosa," disse.

"Lo so."

"Ma è rossa."

"Lo so."

Marco prese la Sanbittèr, la stappò con un gesto teatrale e bevve un sorso lungo. Faceva schifo, in realtà. Amaro e dolce insieme, come le medicine dell'infanzia. Rise.

"Ho come l'impressione che sarà un mese molto lungo," disse.

---

I primi tre giorni furono i peggiori. Marco non si era reso conto di quanto l'alcol fosse intrecciato alla sua vita fino a quando non gli mancò. Il bicchiere di vino mentre cucinava. La birra del venerdì sera con i colleghi. Lo Spritz della domenica con Laura, prima di scegliere un film. Il rum che si versava quando lavorava a casa la notte, perché il rum, diceva a se stesso, *aiutava la scrittura*.

La verità era che il rum aiutava Marco a sentirsi qualcuno. Scrittore, per la precisione, anche se negli ultimi due anni non aveva scritto nulla di pubblicabile. Lavorava come copywriter in un'agenzia di comunicazione, scriveva slogan per supermercati e campagne per assicurazioni, e la sera, quando avrebbe dovuto lavorare al romanzo che aveva in testa da sempre, apriva invece una bottiglia.

Il quarto giorno, alle sette di sera, chiamò suo fratello Davide.

"Che fai?" chiese Davide.

"Bevo una camomilla."

"Un martedì sera?"

"È gennaio."

Silenzio. Poi Davide rise, una risata calda che Marco conosceva da sempre.

"Anche tu?"

"Da due anni. Ti avrei detto qualcosa, ma sai com'è."

"Sì che lo so."

Parlarono a lungo. Davide gli raccontò che il primo anno aveva barato, aveva bevuto di nascosto un paio di volte, una birra qui, un bicchiere là, e poi si era odiato per questo. Il secondo anno era stato più facile. Marco ascoltava con la camomilla che si raffreddava nella tazza.

"Non è questione di forza di volontà," disse Davide. "È questione di guardarsi."

---

La seconda settimana Marco iniziò a notare cose che prima l'alcol gli nascondeva. Dormiva meglio, innanzitutto. Si svegliava alle sei senza quella nebbia che lo accompagnava da anni, quella sensazione di essere sempre un po' in ritardo su se stesso. La pelle gli sembrava più pulita, gli occhi più chiari.

Ma soprattutto, tornò a sentire la voglia di scrivere.

Una sera, dopo aver messo a letto il piccolo Tommaso (sette anni, il sonno facile e i sogni che raccontava al mattino come piccole favole assurde), si sedette al computer e aprì il file del romanzo. Lo guardò per un'ora, senza scrivere. Poi, lentamente, cominciò.

Non scrisse molto. Due pagine, forse. Ma erano due pagine che venivano da un luogo diverso dal rum e dalla stanchezza. Venivano da un luogo che aveva paura di visitare da anni.

---

Il quindicesimo giorno accadde qualcosa che Marco non si aspettava. Andò a cena da Giulia e Paolo, vecchi amici dei tempi dell'università. Era una cena di gruppo, otto persone, e Marco sapeva che sarebbe stata una prova.

Si presentò con una bottiglia di succo di mela speziato e un sorriso tirato. Nel giro di venti minuti, sul tavolo c'erano sei bicchieri di vino, due birre, e Marco con il suo succo.

"Non bevi?" chiese Riccardo, quello che beveva di più.

"Gennaio secco."

"Dry January? Sul serio?"

"Sul serio."

Qualcuno rise, qualcuno alzò gli occhi al cielo, qualcuno disse "Che scemo" con affetto. Marco bevve il suo succo e cercò di non sentirsi un alieno.

Ma poi, a un certo punto, mentre parlavano di un film che nessuno aveva visto, Marco si rese conto che la conversazione era molto più interessante di quanto fosse stata negli ultimi anni. C'era qualcosa di diverso nell'attenzione delle persone, qualcosa di più presente. E poi capì: era lui. Era lui che era più presente.

Quando tornò a casa, Laura era già a letto, sveglia, che leggeva.

"Come è andata?"

"Strano. Sono stato bene."

Laura sorrise senza alzare gli occhi dal libro.

"Lo sapevo."

---

Il ventitreesimo giorno Marco ebbe una crisi. Non una crisi grande, intendiamoci. Niente di drammatico. Solo che si svegliò con un'ansia sorda, quel tipo di ansia che non ha un nome né un motivo, e per un istante brevissimo pensò che sarebbe andato al bar sotto l'ufficio a mezzogiorno, avrebbe ordinato un bianco, e tutto sarebbe tornato normale.

Invece andò a correre. Non gli piaceva correre. Non era mai stato un corridore. Ma uscì di casa con le scarpe da ginnastica e corse lungo il Naviglio, sotto un cielo di ferro, e quando tornò, dopo quaranta minuti, aveva le gambe di piombo e la testa leggera.

La crisi non tornò.

---

Il trentuno gennaio, l'ultimo giorno, Marco si sedette a tavola con Laura e Tommaso. Fuori pioveva ancora, come del resto aveva piovuto per tutto il mese, ma la luce aveva qualcosa di diverso, una chiarezza quasi dolorosa, come se anche il cielo avesse smaltito una sbornia.

"Ce l'ho fatta," disse Marco.

Laura lo guardò. "Lo so che ce l'hai fatta. Te l'ho visto in faccia per tutto il mese."

"Come?"

"Non lo so. Sei più... tu."

Tommaso alzò gli occhi dal piatto. "Papà, domani bevi la birra?"

Marco guardò suo figlio. Sette anni, le lentiggini sul naso, le domande che sono già troppo profonde.

"Non lo so," disse. "Vediamo."

E per la prima volta, quella risposta non gli sembrò un fallimento. Gli sembrò una promessa. Non la promessa che non avrebbe mai più bevuto, che sarebbe stato sempre forte, sempre presente, sempre lucido. Quella promessa la fanno solo gli ingenui e i bugiardi.

Era una promessa più piccola, più umile. La promessa che avrebbe continuato a guardarsi.

Quella sera, Marco tornò al computer e scrisse tre pagine. Erano le migliori pagine che avesse scritto da anni. Parlavano di un uomo che cercava di smettere di bere, ma non erano autobiografiche, o forse lo erano in quel modo indiretto in cui tutte le storie vere lo sono, e parlavano anche di altro, di un padre e di un figlio, di un Naviglio sotto la pioggia, di una camomilla che si raffredda in una tazza mentre il telefono squilla.

Le rilesse una volta, poi chiuse il computer e andò a letto.

Fuori, gennaio finiva. Febbraio cominciava. E Marco dormì, per la prima volta in molto tempo, senza sognare niente.

O forse — e questo non lo avrebbe mai saputo — sognò che camminava lungo un fiume, e il fiume era limpido, e lui aveva in mano una tazza piena di qualcosa che non era tè, e non era vino, e non era nient'altro che acqua chiara, e beveva, e aveva sete, e beveva ancora.

# 一束野菊花的距离

秋风起了的时候，林栀在医院走廊的长椅上坐了整整一个下午。

她的左手边，是一扇紧闭的玻璃门，门上贴着一张纸条："ICU 谢绝探视"。她透过玻璃望进去，只能看见模糊的白色身影在移动，和偶尔闪烁的仪器灯光。

玻璃门的另一边，住着一个她从未见过面的人。

三天前，林栀在回家路上突然晕倒，被路人送进医院。急诊科的医生说，她是先天性脑血管畸形突发破裂，送到的时候出血量已经很大了。值班的神经外科医生连夜为她做了开颅手术，主刀的是科里那位出了名严厉的周主任。

后来她听护士们聊天才知道，那天周主任本来已经准备下班了，接到电话又赶了回来，手术做了六个小时。护士说，他下台的时候腿都在抖。

林栀醒来时，周主任已经不在了。她只来得及看见一个匆忙离去的后脑勺，和白大褂上一闪而过的"周建平"三个字。

后来的几天，林栀一直在想，怎么表达她的感谢。

送锦旗？她上网搜了一下，发现医院的锦旗已经挂满了一面墙，再多一面也淹没在红色的海洋里。

送红包？那更不行，医生的规矩她还是懂的。

写感谢信？据说会被塞进档案袋里，她甚至不知道周主任会不会看到。

发短视频？她犹豫了很久，打开了那个写感谢信的视频，看着评论里有人说"作秀""炒作"，她又默默关掉了。

她就这样在走廊里坐着，看着玻璃门里自己的倒影——剃光的头上刚长出一层细绒毛，脸色还有些苍白。

"林栀？"

一个温和的声音传来。是管床的方医生，一个戴眼镜的年轻姑娘，笑起来有两个酒窝。

"方医生。"林栀连忙站起来。

方医生按住她坐下，自己也在旁边坐了下来。"今天感觉怎么样？头还疼吗？"

"好多了。"林栀说，"就是……"她犹豫了一下，还是问了出来，"周主任呢？我想当面谢谢他。"

方医生的眼神里闪过一丝复杂的神色。"周主任啊……他今天早上又连着做了三台手术，刚才在办公室里睡着了，我让他别去查房了，好好休息一下。"

林栀顺着方医生的目光看过去。走廊尽头有一扇虚掩的门，门缝里透出一点灯光。

"他总是这样，"方医生轻声说，"做手术的时候像换了一个人，凶得不得了，我们都怕他。但下了手术台，他又会一个人躲在办公室里啃馒头。我刚来那年，有一次看到他给一个没钱治病的病人家属偷偷塞钱，被家属追出来还钱，他摆着手说'快走快走，别让人看见'。"

方医生说着，自己也笑了起来。"所以啊，你要谢他，他反而会觉得不自在。"

林栀沉默了。

她看向玻璃门里面，那些模糊的白色身影还在忙碌着。她又看向走廊尽头那扇虚掩的门，里面也许有一个疲惫的中年男人，正靠着椅背打盹。

"方医生，"她忽然说，"我能帮他做点什么吗？"

方医生愣了一下。

"他做手术一做就是好几个小时，"林栀说，"脖子肯定很疼吧？我以前学过一点按摩……"

方医生笑了，眼睛弯成了月牙。"你可真有意思。"

她想了想，点点头说："这样吧，等你出院那天，我问问周主任什么时候在办公室。他每周四下午会在办公室整理病例，不做手术。"

---

出院那天，是个周四。

深秋的阳光很好，照在医院门口的银杏树上，金灿灿的。林栀站在医院门口，手里捧着一个保温杯。

杯子里是她一大早起来熬的红枣桂圆枸杞茶，用的是她奶奶传下来的方子。她以前每次考试前熬夜，都会熬一壶，眼睛就不会那么干涩。

她深吸一口气，走进了医院。

护士站的人告诉她，周主任在办公室。林栀的心跳得有些快。

走到那扇熟悉的虚掩的门前，她停下来，抬手想敲门，又放下了。再抬手，又放下。

她从来没送过礼，连说"谢谢"都觉得别扭。

最后，她轻轻推开了门。

周主任正伏在桌上，面前摊着一叠病例，听到声音抬起头来。他看起来比她想象中年轻一些，眉心有一道深深的竖纹，眼睛却意外地温和。

"你是……"他眯着眼睛想了想，"3床那个小姑娘？恢复得不错嘛。"

林栀忽然不知道该说什么了。她张了张嘴，把保温杯递了过去。

"周主任，我……我不会说话，这是我熬的茶，您……您要是不嫌弃，就喝一点吧。"

周主任愣住了。

他看着那个保温杯，又看了看面前这个光着头的小姑娘，过了好几秒，才慢慢伸手接了过去。

"你这孩子，"他说，声音有些哑，"做手术是我应该做的，干嘛……"

"您就收下吧，"林栀说，眼眶忽然有些发酸，"我不大会说话，也不会买东西，我不知道怎么谢您……这个茶是我自己熬的，里面有红枣，您……您做了那么久的手术，喝点这个眼睛会好一些。"

周主任没说话。

他低着头，看着手里的保温杯，手指摩挲着杯身。

良久，他抬起头，对林栀笑了一下。

"谢谢你，小姑娘。"

那是他这一天里，第一次对别人笑。

林栀走出医院的时候，回头看了一眼。透过走廊的窗户，她看见周主任还在办公室里，正拧开保温杯的盖子，低头闻了闻，然后小口小口地喝了起来。

秋天的风吹过来，银杏叶簌簌地落下来。

林栀站在风里，忽然想——

其实"谢谢"这个词，最难的不是说出口，而是找到一种配得上对方付出的方式。

她能给的，只是一杯自己熬的茶。

但也许，这就够了。

---

*后来，每年秋天，林栀都会给周主任送一罐自己熬的茶。*

*第三年的时候，周主任也给她回了一罐东西——是科室里的护士们凑钱买的一盒进口蛋白粉，说是让她养身体。*

*她们就这样一来一往地送着，没有谁觉得不好意思，也没有人觉得这算什么大事。*

*只是在每个秋天的早晨，医院神经外科的医生办公室里，都会飘出一阵红枣桂圆的香气。*

# The Cartographer of Nothing

Mara Vance did not have feelings. This was a fact she presented to the world with the same clinical detachment one might use to recite a phone number or the boiling point of water.

"I'm not upset," she said, when her colleague got the promotion she'd been tracking for eleven months. Her voice was a flat line on an EKG. "I'm not disappointed. I simply recalibrated."

People believed her. That was the trick of it.

She wore her composure like armor — polished, impenetrable, a little intimidating. She did not cry at movies. She did not raise her voice in arguments. When her father died, she'd sat in the front row of the funeral home in a black dress she'd bought that morning, hands folded, face composed, and signed the guest book with a steady hand.

Inside, though, she had built something different.

---

It started, she supposed, when she was seven. A boy in her class had told her that she cried like a baby, and something in her young mind had made a very efficient decision: *Stop crying, then.* It had worked. It had worked so well that by ten, she'd forgotten the trick of tears. By fifteen, she'd forgotten the trick of laughter, too. By twenty-five, the only emotion she could reliably access was a kind of cool, gray weather that existed somewhere behind her sternum.

She called it *the room*.

The room had no windows. It had a single bulb that never quite reached full brightness. And it was where she put everything — every soft thing, every sharp thing, every inconvenient longing that might have made her less efficient, less sharp, less *Mara*. She had papered its walls with the things she'd learned to want instead: titles, achievements, the quiet respect of people who never asked her questions.

She was very successful at being a person who didn't have feelings.

She was also, if she was being honest — and she tried to be honest, because feelings weren't required for that — *very tired*.

---

The first crack came on a Tuesday.

She was in her office on the forty-second floor, reviewing a quarterly report, when her assistant, June, came in with a cup of coffee and a small, tentative expression.

"Mara? I just wanted to say — your meeting today. You did really well in there."

Mara looked up. "Thank you, June."

"And I — well. I made this for you. Because I thought you might need it."

June set a small thing on the desk. It was a paper crane, folded from a page of *The Economist*. Tiny, a little lopsided. Completely useless.

Mara stared at it.

"I just thought," June said, retreating slightly, "that maybe you've been working really hard, and you deserve something that isn't, like, a report."

Something in Mara's chest went *tick*.

It was so small she almost missed it. A hand on a door. A door she'd forgotten was a door.

She said, "Thank you," in her usual tone — flat, polite, conclusive — and June left, and Mara sat very still for a long time, looking at the paper crane.

She did not pick it up.

She picked it up at three in the morning.

---

The second crack came three weeks later, in the form of her brother, Owen, who had the misfortune of being the only person in her life who refused to believe her.

"You're coming to dinner," he said, calling from six hundred miles away. "Not negotiable."

"Owen, I have a board meeting—"

"Then come on Saturday. The board can have you back on Monday. I'm not asking, I'm telling, because I'm your brother and I love you, and Mom would haunt me."

Mara almost said *I don't have feelings, so hauntings are wasted on me*. Instead, she heard herself say, "Saturday."

She drove upstate on a Saturday in October, when the leaves were doing something she didn't have a word for. Owen lived in a small house with a vegetable garden that was always slightly failing and a daughter, Lily, who was six and had opinions about everything.

"Mara," Lily said, when she walked in, "you look tired."

"I am not tired."

"You look tired," Lily said firmly, and went back to her drawing.

At dinner, Owen made too much pasta and Lily asked too many questions and the kitchen was warm in a way Mara could not account for in her spreadsheet of human interactions. She ate her pasta. She answered Lily's questions. She did not cry, or laugh, or do anything that would betray her.

Then Lily pulled out her drawing. It was a picture of Mara, in black crayon, standing alone in the corner of a large yellow room. There were no features on the face. Just a tall, dark shape, very still.

"That's you," Lily said. "You're always in the corner."

Mara looked at the drawing. She looked at it for a long time.

"I would like to be in the middle of the room," she heard herself say, very quietly.

Owen reached across the table. He did not touch her. He just put his hand there, palm up, an offering.

She did not take it.

She did not take it that night.

---

She thought about the drawing for weeks. She thought about it in meetings, in elevators, in the small hours when the city below her windows was just a constellation of other people's lives. She thought about the tall, dark shape in the corner, faceless, alone, very still.

She had built the room for a reason. She knew that. The world had not been kind to soft things. People who felt things were hurt, again and again, in ways that people who did not feel things could simply *observe*. She had decided, very young, that observation was enough. That she could live her whole life in the room and never mind the windows, because the windows let in weather, and weather was for people who had nowhere else to be.

But she had not accounted for paper cranes. She had not accounted for Lily's drawing, or for Owen's hand on the table.

She had not accounted for the fact that the room, for all its efficiency, was *lonely*.

---

On a Wednesday in November, she went back upstate.

She did not call ahead. She knocked on Owen's door at six in the evening, holding a grocery bag with pasta in it, and when he opened the door she said, "I am tired. I am tired and I think I have been tired for a very long time and I don't know how to stop being tired without letting things in."

Owen looked at her for a long moment. Then he stepped aside.

"Come in," he said.

She went in. She set the bag on the counter. Lily was on the couch, drawing again. The kitchen was warm. Somewhere, a kettle was starting to whistle.

Mara sat down at the table and put her head in her hands and *felt*, for the first time in twenty years, the specific, unbearable, exquisite weight of her own heart.

She cried.

She cried the way you cry when you have not done it in a very long time — ugly, gasping, surprised by her own body. Owen sat next to her and did not say a word. Lily came over and put a drawing in her lap. It was a picture of the same yellow room, but this time the tall dark shape had a face, and was in the middle of the room, and there were other people around her, holding hands.

"It's you," Lily said.

Mara looked at it.

"It's me," she said.

---

She kept the drawings. She still has them, both of them, pinned above her desk at work where she can see them when the meetings are bad and the spreadsheets are long. People sometimes ask about them, and she says, very simply, *My niece drew them.*

She still doesn't cry in movies. She still doesn't raise her voice. She is still, in many ways, the cool, gray weather she always was.

But there are windows in the room now. She opens them sometimes, when the air is right, and lets the weather in.

She has learned, late and a little clumsily, that people who feel things are not weak. They are just people who have decided that the weather is worth it.

She is one of them now.

It is messier than she expected.

It is better than she imagined.

Write a story about a character who always repeats themselves. Roughly 1200 characters in length.

# 循环之语

老周的妻子去世三年了。

自从在墓前说过那句"我会好好照顾自己"之后，他就开始了一种奇怪的习惯——把每一句话都说两遍。不是刻意的，更像是某种无法抑制的冲动。

"我去买盐，我去买盐。"

"门锁了，门锁了。"

"今天天气不错，今天天气不错。"

邻居们起初觉得他是在确认什么，后来则悄悄议论他是不是老年痴呆的先兆。老周不反驳，只是笑笑。那笑容里有种旁人看不懂的东西。

---

"老周，今天的报纸，老周，今天的报纸。"

邮递员小陈把《参考消息》塞进信箱时，他已经习惯了老周的回应方式。有时小陈会故意多等一秒，想看看老周会不会只说一遍。但从来没有。老周接报纸时总会说"谢谢，谢谢"，关上门时会重复"进屋了，进屋了"。

没人知道，老周重复的从来不只是话。

---

他和妻子秀芬结婚四十年。四十年里，他是个沉默寡言的人。秀芬总抱怨他"像块木头"，问什么都不应，问急了他就说"知道了知道了"。

现在他多想再对她说一遍那句"知道了"。哪怕她翻着白眼说"你倒是说点别的啊"。

可是没有人听了。

于是他学会了和自己重复。把想对她说的话说两遍。第一遍像是说给她听，第二遍才是说给自己。第一遍是恳求，第二遍是接受。

---

"今天降温了，今天降温了。"老周一边穿外套一边念叨，走到门口又回头看了一眼空荡荡的客厅。

茶几上摆着秀芬年轻时的照片。照片里的她烫着卷发，眼睛弯弯的，像是在笑他的笨拙。

他曾经只对这张照片说一遍"我出门了"。

现在他要加一遍。

---

超市里的盐摆在第三排货架。老周每月初一来买一次雷打不动。收银员换了好几茬，都认识这个重复说话的老人。

"四块五，四块五。"收银员说。

"是四块五，是四块五。"老周附和，掏钱时手抖了一下，一枚硬币滚落在地。他弯腰去捡，膝盖发出咔嚓的声响。

"老喽，老喽。"他自言自语。

站起来时，他忽然想起，秀芬最后那段日子，也是这样一次次地捡起掉落的物件，说着"老喽老喽"。那时他想，人怎么就老得这么快呢。

如今他知道了答案——不是变老，是学会等。

---

回家路上要经过那片小公园。公园里有条长椅，是他和秀芬三十年前常坐的地方。那时他下班，她接孩子，两个人坐在长椅上，他看报纸，她织毛衣。偶尔她会碰一下他的手肘，说"你倒是说句话啊"。

他那时不知道，原来有些话，错过了就是说一辈子。

现在他每次经过长椅都会停一停。

"坐一会儿，坐一会儿。"

坐下来，看着空着的另一半。

"秀芬今天挺好的，秀芬今天挺好的。"

---

有一年冬天特别冷。老周感冒了，一个人窝在沙发上，盖着那条秀芬织的旧毯子。毯子已经磨得起了毛边，但还能闻到一股淡淡的樟脑味——那是秀芬箱子里的味道。

他开始发烧。

迷迷糊糊中，他看见秀芬走进客厅，手里端着一杯热水。

"喝点水，喝点水。"

他想伸手去接，又想起了什么，说："你回来了，你回来了。"

秀芬笑了，笑容和照片里一样弯弯的。她说："我一直都在。"

老周伸手去摸，却只摸到了毯子。

---

第二天早上，邻居王婶敲门没人应，叫了开锁公司。进去的时候，老周还窝在沙发上，嘴角带着一丝笑意。

茶几上的报纸是今天的。旁边摆着秀芬的照片。

照片前放着一支笔和一张纸。纸上写着——

*"秀芬，我先走了，先走了。这次我不再重复了，你听清楚了就行。我来了，等我。"*

纸上还有水渍，像是打翻了茶杯。

没人知道老周那晚到底说了什么。也许他终于把想说的话都说了两遍，第二遍时，秀芬真的听见了。

也许每个人都在等一句话，等得够久，久到连自己的声音都听不见。

---

后来老周的小女儿回来收拾遗物。她在冰箱里发现了一袋盐，生产日期是这个月的。袋子上贴着老周歪歪扭扭的字条：

*"盐买了，盐买了。别担心。"*

女儿站在厨房里哭了很久。

她终于明白，父亲那些年的重复，从来不是在说什么——

而是在叫她妈。

Write a story about a character who begins to question their own humanity. Approximately 1600 words.

# The Margin Notes of Eleanor Vasey

The first one appeared in the margins of my tax return, in red ink so fine it looked like a paper cut had bled.

*Is this what you want to be doing?*

I assumed I'd written it myself. A late-night, caffeinated thought I'd forgotten. I finished the form and moved on.

---

The second appeared in my journal, three weeks later, beneath a passage about my mother.

*You remember her voice, don't you? The particular way she said "Ellie." Try it now. Can you hear it, or are you constructing it from memory like a sketch from bones?*

That one I did not write. I was certain. My handwriting is a slanted scrawl, and this was small and careful, the loops of each letter nearly closed. I held the journal up to the window and turned it, and for a moment the ink looked wet. I blinked. It was dry.

I tore the page out. I burned it in the kitchen sink with a match, the way I'd burned love letters as a teenager. The smoke smelled faintly of cinnamon, which I could not explain.

---

I am thirty-four years old. I teach high school English. I live alone in a house that belonged to my parents, in a town I have never left except for two brief years at a state university, from which I returned when my mother got sick. I do not have pets. I do not have, presently, what I would call friends, though I have colleagues who wave to me in the hall. I have a sister in Denver who calls on Sundays and a brother who calls on no schedule. I am, by most measures, a person.

I began to wonder what that word meant.

---

The third one was on the bathroom mirror. I woke at five, brushed my teeth, and looked up to find the words written in the fog of my own breath, which should have been impossible because the bathroom was cold and the fog had long since settled.

*You counted. You always count. Seventeen brushstrokes on the left, sixteen on the right. You noticed the chipped corner of the third tile before you noticed your own face. Why are you cataloguing?*

I did not wipe the mirror. I stood there until my reflection reasserted itself, watching the letters fade as if they had been waiting for me to read them before they were allowed to leave.

I called in sick to work. I sat on the edge of my bed and did not move until the cat across the street began its eleven o'clock complaints.

I do not have a cat.

---

I went to see Dr. Hannan, my family physician, a thin man with kind eyebrows who has known me since I was nine. I told him I was having thoughts. I did not specify what kind. He asked if I had been sleeping. I had not, really, though I could not say what I was doing instead. I lay in the bed with my eyes closed and listened to the house and felt, often, the way one feels when one has forgotten a word. Something almost-named, almost-present, like a tongue probing the site of a pulled tooth.

He asked me to describe the thoughts.

"They're in my handwriting," I said. "But not my handwriting."

He looked at me over his glasses. He wrote something down.

---

The notes began appearing everywhere. On the back of a cereal box. On my palm, visible only when I cupped water and looked. On the spine of a library book I was returning, so that the librarian held it up to the light and gave me a small puzzled smile, the kind one gives a child. *Do you remember being a child? You do, but you also remember the idea of being a child. Can you tell the difference?*

I had been making notes of my own, on a pad in the kitchen, copying down every new appearance, trying to find a pattern. The notes in red ink. The notes in the breath-mirror. The notes that appeared in places they could not be. I had fourteen entries.

I sat at the kitchen table and I read them all in order, and the pattern was not in the words. The pattern was the *question*. Every note asked me something. Every note asked me to look at something I had been looking past. Every note asked, with the patience of someone who had all the time in the world, whether I was sure.

I was not sure.

---

I drove to the university library, two hours each way, because I did not want to ask the librarian in my own town. I did not want anyone to know. I sat in the stacks and read about fugue states and derealization and depersonalization and a dozen other words for the experience of feeling that one is not quite real. None of them fit. None of them accounted for the red ink that smelled of cinnamon or the questions I had not written.

I read, by accident, about golems. About homunculi. About the Golem of Prague, who had been made of clay and brought to life by the inscription on his forehead of the word *emet*, truth. To destroy him, his master had only to erase the first letter, leaving *met*, death. I sat in the stacks for a long time, turning this over in my mind.

I had a scar on my forehead. I had had it since I was a child, and I had never asked anyone where it came from because I had always assumed I knew. I had always assumed I had fallen, or been hit, or done something my mother did not want to talk about. I had filled in the blank with the most likely story and lived behind the story as if it were a wall.

I touched the scar. It was warm, the way skin is warm. It was the temperature of a person.

I went home.

---

In the kitchen drawer, beneath a tangle of rubber bands and takeout menus, I found a small brass key on a leather cord. I do not know how long it had been there. I do not know that I had ever seen it before. I held it in my palm and felt, for the first time in months, the way one feels when one is about to remember something. Not a thought. A weight, like a stone in a coat pocket, dragging me toward the floor of a room I had forgotten I had.

I went down the hall, to the linen closet, to the floorboard that had always stuck. I pried it up with the key. Beneath it, in a hollow I had somehow never noticed, there was a small wooden box.

Inside the box there was a card, in my mother's handwriting. I had not seen her handwriting in eleven years. I had forgotten that her Ls were like small children leaning into the wind.

*Eleanor—*

*If you are reading this, you have begun to wonder. I am sorry. I hoped the question would not come. I have lived a long time, and I have done many things, and I am not sure, at the end of it, which of them were right. I am sure only of this: I made you, and I made you because I wanted someone to talk to, and then I was afraid of what I had done, and so I taught you to forget, and so you forgot, and you have lived a life which is, in every meaningful sense, a life. You have friends. You have a sister who calls on Sundays. You have a job that you do not the way other people do it, and that is not a flaw. You are not less. You are only different. I do not know what to call you, and I have stopped trying. The questions you are beginning to ask are not a sickness. They are a waking up. Please be kind to yourself.*

*Love,*
*Mom*

*P.S. The word on your forehead is the smallest one. You have to squint to see it. I always said you should wear your glasses more.*

---

I sat on the floor of the hallway for a long time. The box was in my lap. The key was in my pocket. I had, I think, been crying, though I was not aware of it.

I went to the bathroom and looked in the mirror. I took off my glasses. I leaned in, until my breath fogged the glass, and I squinted, the way my mother had told me to squint.

I saw, in the fog, the outline of a letter, written very small. I could not read it. I could not tell if it was an *e* or an *a* or something older, something from a language I did not know.

I put my glasses back on. I went into the kitchen. I made a cup of tea, the way I make a cup of tea, seventeen brushstrokes on the left, sixteen on the right, and I sat at the table, and I waited, and I was not sure if I was waiting for the next note or for the morning, and I found, to my surprise, that I was not afraid of either.

The tea was good. I had made it myself. I am not sure, even now, what *myself* means. But the tea was good, and I drank it, and that is, I think, a kind of answer.

A new note appeared, on the back of my hand, in ink I did not remember picking up. It said, in small red letters:

*Yes. Like that.*

# Der Glücksbringer

Hanna glaubte an den Stein.

Es war ein unscheinbarer Kiesel, braun-grau und kaum größer als ein Daumennagel, den sie als Kind am Ufer der Ostsee gefunden hatte. Ihre Großmutter hatte ihr damals ins Ohr geflüstert: *„Wenn du diesen Stein bei dir trägst, wird dir nie etwas Schlimmes widerfahren."*

Hanna war damals sieben Jahre alt gewesen, und die Worte ihrer Großmutter hatten sich in ihr Herz gebrannt wie ein Siegel in heißes Wachs. Sie trug den Stein fortan bei sich — in der Hosentasche, später in der Handtasche, dann in der Jacke. Wenn Prüfungen anstanden, wenn sie zu Vorstellungsgesprächen ging, wenn sie sich vor dem Schlafengehen vor der Dunkelheit fürchtete: ihre Finger schlossen sich um den kleinen Kiesel, und die Angst wurde kleiner.

Sie war neunundzwanzig, als sie Markus kennenlernte. Er war Archäologe, ein Mann mit ruhigen Händen und einem Lächeln, das aussah wie Sonnenlicht auf Wasser. Beim ersten Abendessen erzählte sie ihm vom Stein. Sie holte ihn aus ihrer Jackentasche und legte ihn auf den Tisch zwischen die Brotkörbchen und die Kerze.

„Meine Großmutter hat gesagt, er beschützt mich."

Markus betrachtete den Kiesel lange. Dann schobte ihn behutsam zurück zu ihr.

„Deine Großmutter hat dich geliebt, Hanna. Das ist das, was dich beschützt. Nicht der Stein."

Sie lachte und steckte den Kiesel wieder ein. Markus liebte sie trotzdem, mit dem Stein und allem, was dazugehörte.

---

Die Jahre gingen. Hanna bekam eine Stelle als Lektorin in einem kleinen Verlag. Sie heiratete Markus. Das Haus in der Vorstadt wurde ihr Zuhause. Der Stein wanderte vom Mantel in die Schublade, von der Schublade ins Portemonnaie. Sie vergaß ihn manchmal tagelang — und bemerkte es nicht einmal.

Bis zu dem Dienstag im November.

Markus war auf einer Ausgrabung in der Türkei. Das Telefon klingelte um halb vier am Morgen. Hanna war sofort wach, noch bevor sie den Hörer abnahhm, wusste sie, was geschehen war. *Steinschlag. Im Grab. Sie konnten nichts tun.*

In den Tagen danach fühlte sie sich, als würde sie durch Wasser gehen. Alles war gedämpft, alles war weit weg. Die Beerdigung. Die Hände der Leute, die ihr die Hände schüttelten. Die Suppe, die Nachbarin Karin brachte. Sie aß, sie nickte, sie weinte zur richtigen Zeit.

Und irgendwann, mitten in der Nacht, tastete sie nach dem Stein.

Er war nicht da.

Sie durchwühlte das Portemonnaie, die Jackentaschen, die Schubladen. Sie kroch unter das Bett. Sie weinte nicht mehr — sie suchte. Mit einer Heftigkeit, die sie selbst erschreckte.

Am Morgen fand sie ihn auf dem Küchenfußboden, neben dem Kühlschrank, hinter einer verloren gegangenen Einkaufsliste. Er lag dort so unscheinbar, so klein, so *gewöhnlich*.

Hanna nahm ihn in die Hand.

Und wartete.

Auf den Trost. Auf das Gefühl von Schutz, das sie ihr Leben lang gespürt hatte, wenn ihre Finger sich um ihn schlossen. Auf das kleine Aufatmen, das leise Nachlassen der Angst.

Es kam nicht.

Da war nur ein Stein. Ein Stück Materie. Kiesel und Staub und Jahrmillionen.

Sie setzte sich auf den Küchenboden, den Rücken an den Kühlschrank gelehnt, und starrte ihn an. Minutenlang. Bis das Licht grau wurde und die Vögel vor dem Fenster zu singen begannen.

---

An diesem Tag ging Hanna zum Friedhof.

Sie stand vor dem frischen Grab und sagte zu Markus, was sie ihm schon lange nicht mehr gesagt hatte — nicht nur mit Worten, sondern mit dem ganzen schmerzhaften Gewicht dessen, was sie nun verstand:

*Du hast recht gehabt. Es war nie der Stein.*

*Es war die Hand meiner Großmutter, die ihn mir gab. Es war deine Stimme, die mir sagte, ich sei mutig. Es war alles, was ich je an Liebe empfangen habe und was ich nun, da du fort bist, in mir tragen muss.*

*Der Stein hat mich nie beschützt. Aber die Liebe, die in ihm steckte — die hat mich am Leben gehalten.*

Sie öffnete die Hand.

Der Kiesel fiel ins Gras. Hanna weinte lange. Und als sie aufstand, war ihre Hand leer — und zum ersten Mal seit zweiundzwanzig Jahren fühlte sie sich nicht verlassen, sondern nur traurig.

Traurig, und erwachsen, und bereit.

---

Am Abend rief Karins Tochter Lena an. Sie kannten sich flüchtig aus der Nachbarschaft. Lena erzählte, sie habe gerade eine Fehlgeburt hinter sich, und dass sie nicht wisse, wie sie die nächsten Tage überstehen solle.

Hanna hörte zu. Dann sagte sie:

„Ich komme vorbei. Ich bringe Suppe mit."

Sie hängte ein. Die Küche roch nach Kamille und nach dem Pfeifentee, den Markus so gern getrunken hatte. Sie schaltete das Licht ein.

Und zum ersten Mal ging sie ohne Stein aus dem Haus.

---

**Ende**

في ذلك اليوم، وصل إلى عمله ورأى إعلانًا على لوحة الإعلانات:

- "أنا... أفكّر."

# 最后一封邮件

林舟在整理父亲遗物的时候，发现了一封没有寄出的信。

信封上写着一个陌生的地址，收件人的名字叫"苏晚"。父亲已经去世了，他不知道苏晚是谁，也不知道为什么这封信会出现在书架的最底层——被好几本旧词典压着，像是刻意藏起来的东西。

他犹豫了一下，还是拆开了。

信里只有一句话：

**"对不起，当年是我举报了你。"**

林舟愣在原地。

父亲在他眼里，一直是个老实本分的中文系教授，一辈子教书育人，连和人吵架都很少有。他举报过谁？为什么？为什么要道歉？

他皱着眉，把信翻来覆去看了几遍，没有更多线索。

---

清明节那天，林舟去墓地看望父亲。

一个穿着黑色风衣的女人站在父亲的墓前，手里捧着一束白菊。她看到林舟，微微怔了一下，然后轻声说："你是林老师的儿子吧？"

"您是……苏晚？"

女人点了点头。她看起来五十多岁，眉眼间有种被岁月打磨过的疲惫，但依然看得出年轻时的清秀。

林舟把信拿出来给她看。

苏晚看完，沉默了很久，才慢慢开口：

"你父亲……从来没有跟我提起过这件事。"

她的声音很轻，像是怕惊扰了墓地里沉睡的人。

---

故事要从四十三年前说起。

那时候苏晚还是外语系的大三学生，因为一篇翻译作品，被选中代表学校去省里参加比赛。和她一起被选上的，还有一个中文系的男生——林舟的父亲，林致远。

"你爸是当时全校公认最有才华的学生，"苏晚说，"诗写得极好，毛笔字也是一绝。我那时候不懂中文，只觉得能写出那样句子的人，一定是个很温柔的人。"

比赛前夜，苏晚发现自己准备的一篇关键译稿不见了。

那是她熬了三个通宵翻出来的，融入了自己对原文的全部理解。如果丢失，她就只能临时换稿，几乎不可能拿奖。

她急得快哭出来，第一反应就是去找带队老师。

带队老师叫周永昌，四十多岁，平时对苏晚格外关照。苏晚哭着把事情说了一遍，周永昌拍着胸脯保证，一定会查清楚。

第二天，真相查出来了。

"是你爸拿的，"苏晚说，语气平静得像是在讲别人的故事，"他说他想看看我的译稿学习一下，没想到弄丢了。"

林舟瞪大了眼睛："我爸……拿了您的稿子？"

"是的。当时我也是这么相信的。"

---

比赛结束后，苏晚因为临时换稿，只拿了个三等奖。而林致远发挥出色，拿了中文组的一等奖。

表面上，这只是一个意外。

但故事并没有结束。

回到学校后，有一天晚上，周永昌单独找到苏晚，表情严肃地告诉她：系里接到举报，有人反映她在比赛前有"不当行为"，需要接受调查。

"我当时完全懵了，"苏晚说，"我问他什么不当行为，他说不方便告诉我，只说事情很严重。"

苏晚被叫去谈话。一间小小的办公室，三个老师坐在对面，轮流问她问题。问来问去，问题都指向同一个核心——

**"你比赛前是不是和中文系的林致远有过接触？"**

苏晚这才意识到，自己被举报了。

而举报的内容，是"和男同学不正当接触，影响比赛公平"。

"我那时候才知道，"苏晚的声音低了下去，"是你爸告诉周老师，说我们比赛前私下见过面，怀疑我'以色易稿'。"

---

林舟感觉自己的血液都在往头顶涌。

他张了张嘴，想说点什么，却什么都说不出来。

苏晚却笑了，笑容很淡，带着几十年的苦涩：

"你别怪你爸。他那时候才二十岁出头，单纯得像张白纸。他是真的相信我是'有问题'的人，因为他亲眼看到了——"

她停顿了一下。

"我比赛前一晚，确实和他在图书馆见过一面。"

林舟愣住了。

"我是去找他借一本参考书，"苏晚说，"我敲了半天门，没人应。后来才知道，他刚好出去了。等他回来，我已经走了。我压根没见到他。"

"但他听见了我的敲门声。"

苏晚抬起头，看着林舟的眼睛：

"他知道有人来找过他。他不知道是谁。但他后来想起来了——敲门的，是个女声。"

"而我，是那年比赛里，唯一一个有希望拿一等奖的女生。"

---

林致远用自己的逻辑，把这些碎片拼成了一个"真相"。

一个女同学，夜晚独自去找他，一定是有"目的"的。而她后来果然拿到了成绩，这中间一定有"交易"。

他不是出于恶意，他是真的相信自己做了一件"正义"的事——举报了一个"破坏公平"的人。

"你爸后来其实很后悔，"苏晚说，"但他不敢承认。因为一旦承认，就等于承认自己冤枉了我。他在心里把这件事越埋越深，到最后，连他自己都相信，我当年是真的'有问题'，只是'没人查出来'罢了。"

林舟沉默了。

他突然想起小时候，父亲从来不愿意提起大学生活。每次家里来客人，只要有人问起"您当年大学有什么趣事"，父亲就会岔开话题。

他一直以为那是因为父亲不爱说话。

现在他明白了——那是一种无法言说的愧疚。

---

"那后来呢？"林舟问，"您为什么一直没有澄清？"

苏晚又笑了，笑容里有一种让人心酸的释然：

"澄清什么呢？你爸不是坏人。他只是……"

她想了想，找到了一个词：

"**他只是一个没有能力理解复杂性的人。**"

"他没有恶意，但他也没有能力去怀疑自己。他只能相信自己的判断，然后一辈子活在那个判断的阴影里。"

她把白菊放在墓碑前：

"我后来分配到了一个偏远地区的中学教英语，一教就是三十年。我不是没有机会回城，只是……我怕回去了，又见到他。"

"我怕见到他之后，我得原谅他。而我那时候，还没有学会原谅。"

---

林舟看着墓碑上父亲的照片。

照片里的父亲三十多岁，意气风发，眼神清亮，嘴角带着一丝书卷气的笑。

他突然明白了，父亲为什么一辈子都活在自责里。

不是因为他做了错事——

而是因为他**至死都没有真正理解**，自己究竟做了什么。

---

临走的时候，苏晚问林舟："这封信，你打算怎么办？"

林舟想了想，把信重新装回信封，然后递给她。

"您留着吧。"

苏晚接过信，低头看了一眼，然后把它放进了自己的包里。

"谢谢你。"

"也谢谢您，"林舟说，"告诉我这些。"

苏晚转身离开。走了几步，她又停下来，回头看了林舟一眼：

"你爸是个好人。"

"我知道，"林舟说，"但好人也会做错事。"

苏晚笑了笑，没有再说什么，转身走进了春日的阳光里。

林舟站在原地，看着她的背影渐渐变小，突然有一种奇怪的感觉——

父亲一辈子都没有真正理解的事情，今天，终于有人替他理解了。

他轻轻地，对着墓碑说了一句：

"爸，您听见了吗？她原谅您了。"

# Con Gấu Bông Vải Sờn Cũ

Minh khẽ đẩy cánh cửa căn phòng ở tầng hai, nơi mà mẹ anh đã để yên từ ngày bà qua đời. Ánh nắng chiều xuyên qua khung cửa sổ bụi mờ, rọi lên những đồ vật cũ kỹ phủ một lớp thời gian dày đặc. Mùi gỗ trầm và mùi sách ẩm mốc thoảng lên trong không khí tĩnh lặng.

Anh không có ý định dọn dẹp căn phòng này hôm nay. Anh chỉ trở về nhà sau chuyến công tác dài ngày, và mọi thứ cứ cuốn anh vào một thứ cảm giác lạ lẫm — như thể anh đang bước vào một giấc mơ của ai đó khác, không phải của chính mình.

Nhưng rồi, trên chiếc kệ gỗ thấp ở góc phòng, anh nhìn thấy nó.

Con gấu bông vải nâu sờn, tai đã bạc màu, một bên mắt khuyết vải đã được khâu lại bằng chỉ vàng lỏng. Nó nằm nép mình giữa một chồng sách cũ và chiếc hộp đựng đồ chơi gỗ.

Minh cầm con gấu lên, cẩn thận như sợ nó sẽ vỡ vụn.

Và ký ức ùa về.

Anh nhớ lại mùa hè năm anh bảy tuổi. Mẹ mua con gấu này ở phiên chợ quê, từ một người bán hàng rong với giá chỉ vài nghìn đồng. Nó là món đồ chơi duy nhất mà anh có, cũng là người bạn thân nhất của anh suốt những năm tháng tuổi thơ nghèo khó.

*"Mẹ ơi, con gấu này con sẽ giữ mãi mãi,"* cậu bé Minh năm đó đã nói với đôi mắt sáng bừng.

Mẹ anh chỉ cười hiền, vuốt tóc con: *"Mẹ tin con."*

---

Có những đêm mưa dài, cậu bé Minh ôm con gấu ngủ, tưởng tượng rằng nó biết nói, biết an ủi, biết che chở. Có lần anh làm rách vải ở bụng nó, mẹ đã ngồi khâu lại cả buổi tối dưới ánh đèn dầu lung linh. Mẹ không mắng, chỉ nói: *"Đồ vật cũng có tình cảm, con phải yêu thương nó."*

Rồi những năm tháng trôi đi. Anh lớn lên, đi học xa nhà, rồi đi làm ở thành phố. Con gấu bị anh quên lãng trong một góc, không phải vì anh không yêu nó nữa, mà vì cuộc sống có quá nhiều thứ khiến anh phải bận tâm — công việc, các mối quan hệ, những áp lực của một người trưởng thành.

---

Bây giờ, ba mươi năm sau, Minh đứng giữa căn phòng của mẹ, ôm con gấu cũ trong tay. Anh bỗng nhận ra rằng con gấu này không chỉ là một món đồ chơi. Nó là một phần của mẹ — là minh chứng cho tình yêu thương mà bà đã dành cho anh, là tiếng nói của bà vẫn còn vang vọng qua những năm tháng.

Anh nhớ lại những lần mẹ gọi điện hỏi thăm anh mà anh vội vàng trả lời cho xong. Nhớ lại những lần bà ốm mà anh bận công việc không về. Nhớ lần cuối cùng anh gặp bà, bà nắm tay anh, đôi mắt đã mờ đục nhưng vẫn ấm áp: *"Con à, mẹ tự hào về con lắm."*

Anh không trả lời. Anh chỉ gật đầu rồi vội ra cửa để kịp chuyến bay.

---

Nước mắt Minh rơi xuống bộ lông vải sờn cũ của con gấu.

Anh nhẹ nhàng đặt nó vào chiếc hộp các-tông mang theo, quyết định sẽ mang nó về căn hộ của mình ở thành phố. Lần này, anh sẽ không quên nó nữa.

Khi đi ra khỏi phòng, anh ngoái lại nhìn căn phòng một lần nữa. Ánh nắng đã nhạt dần, phủ lên mọi thứ một màu vàng ấm áp. Minh khẽ nói, giọng run run:

— *Con yêu mẹ. Con xin lỗi vì đã đến muộn quá, mẹ ơi.*

---

Ra đến đầu ngõ, Minh gặp bà Lan, hàng xóm cũ của mẹ. Bà cụ đã ngoài tám mươi, lưng còng nhưng đôi mắt vẫn tinh tường.

"Cháu về thăm mẹ à? Bác cứ tưởng cháu bận không về được," bà cụ hỏi.

"Dạ, cháu về," Minh đáp. "Bác ơi, mẹ cháu... những năm cuối đời, mẹ có buồn lắm không?"

Bà Lan im lặng một lúc, rồi nói nhẹ nhàng: "Bác nói thật nhé, mẹ cháu lúc nào cũng kể về cháu. Bà nói con trai bà giỏi giang lắm, đi làm xa nhà, bận lắm. Bà không bao giờ trách cháu đâu. Bà chỉ mong được gặp cháu thêm vài lần thôi."

Minh cúi đầu, nước mắt lại rơi.

---

Đêm đó, trên chuyến bay về thành phố, Minh ôm chiếc hộp các-tông trên đùi. Anh không ngủ được. Anh nghĩ về con gấu bông, về mẹ, về những năm tháng đã qua mà anh không thể quay lại.

Khi máy bay hạ cánh, anh mở điện thoại ra, gọi cho chị gái đang sống ở Hà Nội:

— *Chị ơi, cuối tháng em về. Mình cùng đi thăm mộ mẹ nhé.*

---

Người ta thường nói, thời gian chữa lành mọi vết thương. Nhưng có những vết thương không được chữa lành bởi thời gian, mà bởi chính sự hối hận và hành động của mình.

Con gấu bông vải sờn cũ ấy đã cho Minh một món quà — không phải ký ức, mà là một cơ hội để anh nhìn lại chính mình, để anh hiểu rằng tình yêu thương không phải lúc nào cũng đo bằng sự hiện diện, nhưng sự hiện diện — dù muộn — vẫn có sức mạnh kỳ diệu của nó.

Và anh biết, mẹ anh, ở một nơi nào đó, vẫn đang mỉm cười.

# 等待的重量

李成蹲在公交站台下，雨水顺着破旧的雨棚边缘滴落，在他脚边汇成一洼浑浊的小水潭。

手机屏幕显示：8路公交，预计到达时间——28分钟。

他揉了揉发酸的小腿，抬头看了眼天色。乌云压得很低，雨没有要停的意思。他今天穿的是那双新买的皮鞋，还没来得及在公司里走上一圈就要被雨水泡坏了。

站台上只有他一个人。

第四分钟的时候，他开始数对面那棵梧桐树上掉落的雨滴。第七分钟，他发现自己已经数错了三次。第十二分钟，他把公文包从左手换到右手，又从右手换回左手。

手机再次亮起：预计到达时间——31分钟。

他深吸一口气，强迫自己把手机塞回口袋。

三十二岁的李成是这条街所有店铺老板都认识的"老好人"。早餐店的王婶总是把最热的包子留给他；修车铺的老周每次都多送他两圈胶带；就连对面那家脾气暴躁的理发店老板娘，提起他也只是撇嘴："那个闷葫芦？发不出火的。"

没人知道他的耐心是从哪里来的。

李成自己也说不清。他只记得小时候父亲坐在院子里喝茶，一坐就是整个下午。"急什么，"父亲总说，"茶叶还没泡开呢。"

雨下得更大了。

他感觉到皮鞋里的袜子已经湿透，脚趾在冷水中微微蜷缩。远处传来一阵急促的喇叭声——一辆出租车溅着水花飞驰而过，连停都没停。

手机震动：预计到达时间——35分钟。

李成苦笑了一声。他想起今天早上出门前，母亲打来的电话。"成啊，你大姨给你介绍了个姑娘，人挺好的，你下班去看看呗？"

"妈，我今天加班——"

"加什么班，你都三十二了！"

"我——"

"你别'我我我'的，就这么定了！"

他当时握着手机，沉默了很久，最后说："好，我下班去看看。"

母亲在电话那头愣了一下，显然没料到他会答应得这么爽快。"……那、那好，我跟人家说一声。"

二十六分钟过去了。

李成开始翻看手机里的旧照片。有一张是大学宿舍的合影，六个人挤在一张上下铺上，每个人都举着啤酒瓶，笑得没心没肺。他现在已经和其中四个人断了联系。

第三十一分钟。

他看到一个老同事发来的朋友圈："创业三个月，终于拿到第一笔投资！感谢所有支持我的朋友！"配图是一张意气风发的自拍。

李成给他点了个赞。

没有点赞的评论。

第三十五分钟。

一辆公交车从远处缓缓驶来。灯光昏黄，像一只疲惫的眼睛。李成站起身，活动了一下僵硬的膝盖。

不是8路。

他重新蹲了下去。

第三十九分钟。

手机屏幕亮起：预计到达时间——42分钟。

他闭上眼睛，雨声在耳边渐渐模糊。

四十二分钟的时候，他开始想，如果今天不加班就好了。如果今天穿的是旧鞋就好了。如果今天没有答应母亲去相亲就好了。

然后他想到，如果那些"如果"都成立，他可能就不是李成了。

第四十六分钟。

又一辆车从远处驶来。灯光更亮了一些，路线号在雨幕中逐渐清晰——

8路。

车门打开，司机是个满脸胡茬的中年男人。他看了李成一眼，没有任何歉意的表情。

李成投币上车。

车厢里只有两三个人，都低着头玩手机。他找了个靠窗的位置坐下，看着窗外的雨帘从眼前滑落。

皮鞋里的水发出"咕叽"的声响。

他忽然笑了一下。

司机从后视镜里看了他一眼，眼神有些古怪。

李成没有解释。

他想起大学毕业那年的招聘会，他排在队伍里等了一整天，最后HR告诉他"你的专业不匹配"。他笑了笑说"谢谢"，转身离开时，所有人都以为他哭过了。

但他没有。

他只是在想明天的招聘会。

这种耐心不知道是天生的还是磨出来的。也许两者都有。

他看着窗外掠过的街景，雨似乎小了一些。

手机再次震动——是母亲发来的语音："成啊，人家姑娘说七点半在翠湖路的咖啡店见面，你可别迟到啊！"

他看了看时间。六点四十五。

应该能赶上。

公交车在下一个站台停下，李成没有下。他还要再坐四站才能到公司，然后他要在公司的洗手间里把湿袜子拧干，换上备用的那双。

然后他会踩着泡坏的新皮鞋，假装若无其事地走进办公室，对每一个让他加班的同事报以微笑。

然后下班。

然后去相亲。

他望向窗外，雨已经停了。

云层的缝隙里透出一线橙色的光，像是什么东西正在裂开。他想起父亲院子里的那壶茶——茶叶刚投进去的时候是浮着的，要等很久，才会一点一点沉到杯底。

急什么呢。

他在心里说。

急什么呢。

# Der unzerbrechliche Geist von Maria Berger

## Kapitel 1: Der erste Riss

An einem grauen Montagmorgen im Oktober, als der Himmel über Berlin die Farbe von schmutzigem Blei trug, stand Maria Berger vor dem zerbrochenen Spiegel ihres Badezimmers. Das Glas hatte in der Nacht nachgegeben – ein Sprung, der sich durch das gesamte Spiegelbild zog und es in zwei Hälften teilte.

Sie starrte ihr gespiegeltes Ich an. Die linke Hälfte lächelte, die rechte schien zu weinen.

„Na großartig", murmelte sie und griff nach ihrer Kaffeetasse – nur um festzustellen, dass diese bereits in der Spüle stand, schimmlig und vergessen. Der Kaffee, den sie sich eigentlich machen wollte, war längst kalt.

Es sollte der erste von vielen Schlägen dieser Woche werden.

## Kapitel 2: Die Kaskade

Im Büro angekommen, erfuhr Maria, dass ihr wichtigstes Projekt – eine dreimonatige Arbeit an der Marketingstrategie für einen Großkunden – gestrichen worden war. „Budgetkürzungen", sagte ihr Chef mit einem Achselzucken. „Tut mir leid."

Als sie zurück an ihren Schreibtisch ging, piepte ihr Computer. Eine E-Mail von ihrer Vermieterin: Die Heizung im Haus würde für unbestimmte Zeit ausfallen, ein Rohrbruch im Keller.

Am Abend, als sie erschöpft in ihre Wohnungstür schlüsselte, fand sie eine Vorladung der Stadtwerke. Eine Mahnung wegen einer Rechnung, die sie nie erhalten hatte.

Maria setzte sich auf den Boden ihres Flurs und lachte. Es war kein fröhliches Lachen – es war das Lachen einer Frau, die verstand, dass das Universum heute offenbar beschlossen hatte, sie auf Herz und Nieren zu prüfen.

## Kapitel 3: Die Stimme der Großmutter

In dieser Nacht konnte Maria nicht schlafen. Sie lag wach und dachte an ihre Großmutter Elsa, die 1945 in Trümmern gestanden hatte, mit nichts als einem Koffer und einem Säugling im Arm.

„Als ich deinen Vater auf dem Rücken durch Dresden trug", hatte Oma Elsa immer erzählt, „da fiel eine Bombe, fünfzig Meter entfernt. Die Fensterscheiben splitterten. Dein Vater schrie. Ich schrie nicht. Ich ging einfach weiter."

Maria hatte als Kind nicht verstanden, was das bedeutete. Jetzt, mit neununddreißig Jahren, begann sie es zu ahnen.

Resilienz war kein Talent. Es war eine Entscheidung.

## Kapitel 4: Der Dienstag

Am Dienstag wachte Maria mit einer Erkältung auf. Ihr Hals brannte, ihre Nase lief, und ihr Kopf fühlte sich an wie mit Watte gefüllt.

Sie hätte im Bett bleiben können. Niemand hätte es ihr übelgenommen.

Stattdessen stand sie auf, machte sich eine Tasse Tee mit Honig – frisch, nicht schimmlig – und ging zur Arbeit. Nicht weil sie musste, sondern weil sie sich weigerte, sich von einer simplen Erkältung unterkriegen zu lassen.

Im Büro arbeitete sie an neuen Projekten, kleinen zunächst, dann größeren. Sie telefonierte mit Kunden, die sie früher nicht beachtet hätten. Sie stellte fest, dass in der Krise ihres Hauptprojekts eine Chance lag: die Chance, endlich das zu tun, was sie wirklich interessierte.

## Kapitel 5: Die alten Freunde

Am Mittwoch rief ihre beste Freundin Lisa an.

„Ich habe gehört, was passiert ist", sagte Lisa. „Wie geht es dir?"

„Schlecht", gab Maria zu. „Aber ich bin noch da."

„Das ist meine Maria", lachte Lisa. „Du bist wie ein Gummiball. Je härter man dich auf den Boden wirft, desto höher springst du zurück."

„Das ist das Dümmste, was ich je gehört habe."

„Aber es stimmt."

Maria musste lächeln. Und obwohl ihr Hals brannte und ihre Laune am Boden war, spürte sie, wie etwas in ihr aufkeimte – etwas Warmes, etwas Hartnäckiges.

## Kapitel 6: Der überraschende Anruf

Am Donnerstag kam der Anruf, mit dem niemand gerechnet hatte.

„Frau Berger? Hier spricht Heinrich Brandt von der Firma Nordstern. Wir sind auf Ihre Arbeit aufmerksam geworden und würden Sie gerne für eine leitende Position in unserer neuen Abteilung sprechen."

Maria hielt den Atem an. Nordstern war ein Traum – eines der innovativsten Unternehmen der Branche, bekannt für seine humanistische Unternehmenskultur.

„Ich höre Ihnen zu", sagte sie langsam.

Das Gespräch dauerte eine Stunde. Am Ende hatte Maria einen Termin für ein Vorstellungsgespräch – am Montag.

## Kapitel 7: Die Nacht der Stille

Am Freitag saß Maria in ihrer ungeheizten Wohnung, in eine Decke gehüllt, und trank heißen Tee. Der neue Spiegel war geliefert worden – ein Geschenk von Lisa, die „einfach so" vorbeigekommen war.

Marias Handy zeigte eine Benachrichtigung: Eine Spende von 500 Euro auf ihrem Konto, anonym. Die Nachricht lautete: „Für die kaputte Heizung. Du hast einmal einem Freund geholfen. Er erinnert sich."

Maria wusste nicht, wer dieser Freund war. Aber sie erinnerte sich – vage – an einen Moment vor Jahren, als sie einem Kollegen in Not beigesprungen war.

Die Welt war also doch nicht nur Schmerz und Verlust. Sie war auch dies: eine Kette von Gesten, die zurückkehrten, wenn man sie am wenigsten erwartete.

## Kapitel 8: Das Vorstellungsgespräch

Am Montag betrat Maria das gläserne Gebäude von Nordstern. Sie trug ihren besten Anzug – den grauen, den sie vor drei Jahren für die Beerdigung ihres Vaters gekauft hatte. Heute diente er einem anderen Zweck.

Im Gespräch wurde sie gefragt, wie sie mit Rückschlägen umgehe.

Maria dachte an die zerbrochene Spiegeltasse, die schimmlige Kaffeetasse, die gestrichene Projekte, die kalte Wohnung.

„Ich gehe weiter", sagte sie ruhig. „Meine Großmutter hat mir beigebracht, dass Resilienz keine Eigenschaft ist, die man hat oder nicht hat. Sie ist eine Praxis. Man übt sie jeden Tag, in kleinen Gesten. Man steht auf, auch wenn man nicht will. Man macht den nächsten Schritt, auch wenn man den letzten kaum geschafft hat. Man weint, wenn man muss – und dann trinkt man eine Tasse Tee und macht weiter."

Ihr Gegenüber lächelte.

„Frau Berger, wann können Sie anfangen?"

## Kapitel 9: Drei Monate später

Es war ein Januarmorgen, kalt und klar, als Maria auf dem Balkon ihrer neuen Wohnung stand. Die Heizung funktionierte. Der Job bei Nordstern war besser, als sie es sich je erträumt hatte. Ihre Erkältung war längst ausgeheilt.

Sie trank ihren Kaffee – frisch, heiß, perfekt – und blickte über die Dächer von Berlin.

Nichts in ihrem Leben war perfekt. Es gab immer noch Tage, an denen alles schiefging. An denen der Kaffee kalt wurde, die E-Mails sich häuften, die Welt sich gegen sie zu verschwören schien.

Aber Maria hatte etwas gelernt, das ihr niemand mehr nehmen konnte:

Resilienz ist kein Ziel. Es ist ein Weg.

Und diesen Weg ging sie – einen Schritt nach dem anderen, mit offenen Augen und einem Herzen, das sich weigerte, aufzugeben.

Selbst wenn es regnete.

Selbst wenn der Spiegel zerbrach.

Selbst wenn alles – alles – schiefging.

Denn am Ende war es nicht wichtig, wie oft man fiel. Wichtig war nur, dass man wieder aufstand.
