**The Long Road Home**

The bell above the door of Murphy's Garage hadn't rung in three years.

Mara O'Connell stood in the doorway of the bay, staring at the layers of dust on the cement floor, at the empty tool racks, at the faded outline on the wall where her father's lucky wrench used to hang. The place smelled like old oil and forgotten things.

Forty-two years old. Three ex-husbands. A failed restaurant, a failed marriage, and now this—this inheritance of rust and regret.

She almost walked away.

Almost.

Instead, she pulled her sleeves up and got to work.

---

The first month was the hardest. Not because of the work, though the work was brutal—her hands cracked and bled from unfamiliar labor. The hardest part was the town.

Sullivan, Missouri had watched Mara leave at eighteen, trailing clouds of big-city dreams and older boyfriends. They had watched her come back three times, each time a little more broken. By now, they had her filed away in the cabinet of local disappointments, right next to the meth lab on Route 9 and the Henderson boy's pumpkin-smashing incident of '07.

"Opening a garage, are you?" old Hank Briggs said at the gas station, his grin all teeth and pity. "That'll last about as long as your catering business."

Mara just nodded and paid for her gas. The money in her account was enough for maybe six months. Probably less.

---

She got her first real customer on a Tuesday in April. A woman with a flat tire and a baby screaming in the backseat, the kind of crying that suggested she'd been driving for hours with nowhere else to go.

"I don't have much," the woman said, clutching her wallet like a life preserver. "I can pay you half now, half next week—"

"Twenty bucks," Mara said. "And the next time you need an oil change, you come see me."

The woman looked at her like she'd offered her the moon.

Word spread, the way it does in small towns—not through advertising, but through whispered conversations between women at the post office, at the school pickup, at the diner counter. *She helped me when I had nothing. She didn't charge me what she should have.*

---

The second year, Mara hired a kid named Theo—nineteen, fresh out of the youth home, skittish as a wild horse. He knew nothing about cars, but he had the kind of hands that could feel when a bolt was about to strip.

"You're gonna ruin your reputation hiring *him*," Hank told her at the gas station.

"Hank," she said, "if I cared about my reputation, I'd have stayed in St. Louis."

Theo learned fast. He also kept coming back, which was more than anyone expected.

---

The third year, a regional parts distributor offered to buy her out. A nice check, enough to live comfortably for a long time. The buyer sat in her tiny office and laid out spreadsheets showing her how much easier her life could be.

"Why would you want to keep grinding like this?" he asked. "You're not getting any younger."

Mara looked past him, through the window, to where Theo was teaching a girl—maybe sixteen, maybe younger—how to check tire pressure. The girl had the same skittish look Theo had worn when they'd met.

"Because grinding is the only thing that ever worked for me," she said.

The buyer left without a deal.

---

The fifth year, a regional magazine did a piece on "Small Town Success Stories." They wanted to photograph her for the cover. Mara declined twice before they wore her down.

The picture that ran was simple: Mara, in coveralls, with Theo and the girl—her apprentice now, her name was June—standing in front of Murphy's Garage. The sign out front had been repainted, but it still read *Murphy's*, because she'd decided that was who she really was. Not Mara the failure. Not Mara the thrice-divorced. Not Mara the town joke.

Just someone who showed up every morning and did the work.

---

On the tenth anniversary of the day she inherited the garage, Mara closed early. She drove out to the edge of town, to the cemetery where her father was buried.

His headstone read: *Patrick Murphy — He Fixed Things.*

"I tried, Dad," she said out loud, to the wind and the weeds and the indifferent sky. "I tried to fix things."

When she got back to the garage, Theo was waiting with a key to a brand-new tool chest. June had made a cake. Hank Briggs, eighty-three now and mostly retired, was sitting on an overturned bucket, holding a bottle of something that wasn't from the gas station.

"To Murphy's," he said, raising the bottle.

"To Murphy's," Mara said, and meant it.

---

The bell above the door rang every day now. Sometimes it rang before she'd even had her coffee. Sometimes it kept ringing long after she'd gone home.

But it rang.

And that was enough.

# Bayangan di Balik Layar

## 1

Pagi itu, hujan masih turun dengan malas di atas kota Jakarta. Di sudut lantai empat sebuah kantor berita *Harian Nusantara*, Rangga Pratama duduk di balik meja kecilnya—meja yang nyaris tersembunyi di balik tumpukan map dan kabel ethernet yang kusut. Tidak ada name tag di mejanya. Tidak ada plakat. Hanya secangkir kopi sachet yang sudah dingin.

Semua orang mengenal nama Darmawan Salim, redaktur senior yang wajahnya nyaris setiap hari muncul di layar kaca. Namanya harum, kalimatnya dikutip, pendapatnya didengar di meja-meja kekuasaan. Namun tidak ada yang tahu bahwa setiap kata yang keluar dari mulut Darmawan Salim di televisi—setiap kalimat berani, setiap sindiran tajam—sebenarnya ditulis oleh tangan seorang pemuda berusia dua puluh tujuh tahun yang tak pernah muncul di layar.

Rangga adalah penulis bayangan. *Ghostwriter* yang tidak menulis buku, melainkan menuliskan nurani orang lain.

## 2

Sore itu, seperti biasa, Rangga menerima amplop cokelat dari asisten Darmawan. Di dalamnya, secarik kertas dengan instruksi: *“Tentang banjir di Tangerang Selatan. Sudut pandang: kegagalan tata kelola, bukan bencana alam. Nada: pedas tapi intelektual. Panjang: cukup untuk tujuh menit tayang.”*

Rangga membaca instruksi itu tiga kali. Lalu ia membuka laptopnya dan mulai bekerja. Di balik nama besar Darmawan Salim, Rangga menulis tentang anak-anak yang bermain di genangan air tercemar, tentang ibu-ibu yang menggendong电视机 sambil berenang ke posko, tentang angka-angka yang sengaja disembunyikan agar proyek-proyek mercusuar tampak berhasil. Ia menulis dengan kemarahan yang ia simpan bertahun-tahun—kemarahan atas keadilan yang dijual murah di pasar politik.

Satu jam kemudian, enam ratus kata telah lahir. Ia mengirimnya ke nomor pribadi Darmawan. Balasan datang cepat: *“Cepat dan tajam seperti biasa. Kau aset yang tak ternilai.”*

Rangga tersenyum tipis, lalu mematikan laptopnya.

## 3

Di meja makan sederhana di rumah kontrakan kecilnya di Bekasi, Rangga makan bersama ibunya yang sudah lanjut usia. Ibunya pernah bertanya, “Apa yang sebenarnya kau kerjakan di kota, Rangga?”

Ia menjawab, “Aku jadi penulis, Bu. Di kantor berita.”

Ibunya mengangguk bangga. “Syukur. Jangan seperti Darmawan Salim di televisi itu. Orang sombong.”

Rangga tertawa pelan. “Iya, Bu. Aku tidak akan sombong.”

Ironi itu hanya ia simpan sendiri. Ia bekerja untuk orang yang dianggap sombong oleh ibunya, dan ibunya bangga padanya tanpa tahu bahwa tulisan-tulisan itu keluar dari jari-jari yang sama dengan tangan yang kini mengaduk sayur di piring.

## 4

Malam itu, di kedai kopi dekat kantor, Rangga duduk bersama Hana, sahabatnya satu-satunya di Jakarta. Hana bekerja di bagian riset, perempuan yang punya idealismis tinggi dan rambut selalu diikat asal.

“Kamu pernah kepikiran,” kata Hana suatu malam, meniup asap kopinya, “bahwa tulisan-tulisanmu itu sebenarnya mengubah opini jutaan orang?”

Rangga menggeleng. “Bukan tulisan Darmawan saja tanpa kontroversi. Ia berani, ia konsisten, ia…”

“Braver?” potong Hana. “Atau hanya lebih vokal karena ia berdiri di bahumu?”

Hening sejenak.

“Kau yang memilih kata-katanya,” lanjut Hana. “Kau yang menentukan sudut pandangnya. Kau yang memilih fakta mana yang diangkat dan mana yang dikubur. Kau lebih berpengaruh dari yang kau sadar.”

Rangga menatap kopinya. “Tapi aku tidak pernah berdiri di depan publik. Aku tidak pernah menanggung risikonya. Ketika esok hari ada pihak yang marah, yang terima ancaman bukan aku. Yang dikutip media bukan aku. Yang diingat sejarah bukan aku.”

Hana mengangguk pelan. “Itu yang aku maksud. Kau punya pengaruh tanpa nama. Dan itu, Rangga, lebih berbahaya dari sekedar tidak dikenal.”

## 5

Krisis datang di bulan Juni.

Darmawan memutuskan mengangkat kasus penggusuran sebuah kampung di pesisir utara Jakarta. Instruksinya datang seperti biasa, tapi kali ini nadanya lebih agresif: “Buat lebih keras. Aku mau ini viral.”

Rangga menulis. Ia menulis tentang nenek-nenek yang rumahnya dihancurkan di depan mata, tentang anak-anak yang kehilangan sekolah, tentang suap yang mengalir dari kontraktor ke pejabat. Ia menulis dengan segala api yang ia punya—karena ia juga pernah hampir kehilangan rumah waktu kecil ketika proyek jalan tol merobohkan pemukiman di desanya.

Tapi kali ini, ada yang berbeda. Rangga menyelipkan satu kalimat di paragraf keempat—kalimat yang biasanya tidak akan pernah ia tulis untuk Darmawan: *“Mereka yang menandatangani surat perintah penggusuran tinggal di rumah-rumah yang dibeli dengan uang rakyat, sementara mereka yang digusur tidur di bawah jembatan.”*

Ia tahu kalimat itu akan membuat Darmawan marah. Tapi ia tidak bisa menghapus kebenarannya.

## 6

Tayangan itu viral. Memang. Tapi bukan karena alasan yang Rangga harapkan.

Darmawan dipanggil oleh petinggi partainya. Sumber internal kantor berita bilang, tekanan datang dari atas: *“Kau sudah kelewat batas.”* Artikel Rangga telah menyentuh nama-nama yang tidak seharusnya disentuh.

Darmawan punya dua pilihan: mengakui bahwa tulisannya dibuat oleh orang lain—yang akan mengakhiri kariernya—atau melempar Rangga ke bawah bus.

Ia memilih yang kedua.

Ketika Rangga datang ke kantor keesokan harinya, security sudah menunggu di pintu. Di tangannya, surat pemutusan hubungan kerja: *“Batas waktu kontrak berakhir. Tidak diperpanjang.”*

Tidak ada penjelasan. Tidak ada ucapan terima kasih.

Hanya di ujung surat, satu kalimat dari tangan Darmawan sendiri: *“Maaf, Rangga. Kau tahu resikonya.”*

 ## 7

Rangga duduk di trotoar depan kantor berita, memandangi tumpukan map di dalam ranselnya. Ia tidak sedih. Tidak marah. Hanya lelah.

Ia teringat ibunya yang bertanya kapan ia pulang. Teringat Hana yang bilang ia lebih berpengaruh dari yang ia sadar. Teringat Darmawan yang selalu bilang ia “aset yang tak ternilai”—dan sekarang membuangnya seperti kertas bekas.

Di dalam map itu, masih ada tulisan-tulisan yang belum dipublikasikan. Tulisan-tulisan yang lebih keras dari yang pernah ditulis Darmawan. Tulisan-tulisan yang selama ini ia simpan karena terlalu berbahaya, terlalu jujur, terlalu dekat dengan kebenaran-kebenaran yang tidak ingin didengar oleh siapa pun.

Rangga tersenyum tipis. Mungkin sudah tiba waktunya tulisan-tulisan itu lahir di bawah namanya sendiri.

## 8

Tiga bulan kemudian, muncul akun media sosial bernama **@RanggaMenulis**. Tidak ada wajah. Hanya tulisan-tulisan panjang yang ditulis dengan presisi yang tajam dan hati yang terluka. Dalam hitungan minggu, pengikutnya menembus angka yang tidak pernah ia bayangkan.

Ia menulis tentang penggusuran. Tentang kebijakan yang lahir di balik pintu tertutup. Tentang pejabat-pejabat yang tidur nyenyak di atas mimpi-mimpi orang kecil. Ia menulis dengan nada yang ia kembangkan sendiri—bukan lagi meniru suara Darmawan Salim, melainkan suaranya sendiri yang selama ini tertindas.

Satu tulisan buatannya viral: berjudul **“Siapa Sebenarnya yang Menulis Indonesia?”** Ia mengisahkan—tanpa menyebut nama—tentang bagaimana seorang redaktur terkenal di televisi ternyata tak pernah menulis satu pun kalimatnya sendiri. Tulisan itu jadi perdebatan nasional. Diskusi panjang di Twitter, di grup-grup Whatsapp, di meja-meja redaksi seluruh Indonesia.

Dan di suatu sore, Darmawan Salim membaca tulisan itu sambil duduk di ruang kerjanya. Ia meletakkan teleponnya dengan tangan gemetar.

Ia tidak bisa melawan kebenaran yang ditulis oleh tangan yang pernah ia gunakan.

## 9

Rangga tidak pernah menjadi terkenal. Tidak seperti Darmawan. Tidak masuk daftar Forbes. Tidak pernah tampil di layar televisi.

Tapi di gang sempit di belakang pasar Minggu, seorang ibu pedagang kaki lima menyalin tulisan-tulisannya ke buku tulis dan membacanya kepada anak-anaknya yang sedang belajar. Di warung kopi di Yogya, seorang mahasiswa mengutip satu paragraf dari tulisannya dalam tugas akhir tentang kebijakan publik. Di Aceh, seorang jurnalis muda menempelkan kutipan Rangga di dinding kamarnya: *“Mereka yang menulis tanpa nama, menulis untuk semua nama.”*

Rangga hidup dengan sederhana. Ia mengajar menulis di sebuah komunitas kecil di akhir pekan. Ia tetap tinggal di rumah kontrakan. Ia masih makan di meja yang sama dengan ibunya, yang sekarang sudah tahu segalanya.

Ibunya tidak marah. “Syukurlah,” katanya. “Akhirnya kau menulis untuk dirimu sendiri.”

Rangga tersenyum, dan untuk pertama kalinya dalam bertahun-tahun, ia merasa tulisan-tulisan itu benar-benar miliknya.

## 10

Di sebuah sore yang tenang, Rangga duduk di balkon rumahnya, menulis di laptop tua yang baterainya sudah lemah. Hana datang dengan dua gelas teh.

“Kau bahagia?” tanya Hana.

Rangga tidak menjawab segera. Ia menatap langit Jakarta yang mulai beranjak sore—langit yang sama dengan langit yang dilihat Darmawan dari lantai atas gedung kantornya, tapi dari tempat yang berbeda.

“Dulu,” kata Rangga pelan, “aku menulis untuk membuat orang lain terlihat besar. Sekarang aku menulis untuk membuat kebenaran terlihat jelas. Dan kurasa, itu cukup.”

Hana mengangguk. Mereka tidak berkata-kata lagi.

Di bawah langit yang mulai memerah, Rangga melanjutkan menulis. Tidak ada nama besar yang menunggui di kursi sampingnya. Tidak ada amplop cokelat berisi instruksi. Hanya layar kosong dan suara jiwanya sendiri yang akhirnya berani bicara.

Dan di tempat lain di kota ini, jutaan orang membaca tulisannya tanpa tahu siapa dia.

Tapi Rangga tidak butuh nama. Ia hanya butuh tahu bahwa kebenaran yang ia tuliskan menyentuh satu hati saja—maka ia sudah menjadi pahlawan. Walau tak pernah ada yang menyanyikan lagunya.

# The Night We Crossed the Line

---

## **Maya**

The music thrummed through the floorboards, a low pulse that vibrated in my molars. I pressed my back against the kitchen wall and tried to make myself invisible. Twenty minutes. I had twenty minutes before Mom noticed the car was gone and twenty years before I'd stop feeling like the world was ending.

Sophie grabbed my wrist. "Stop looking at the door. You're going to give yourself away."

"I just—" I swallowed. "I keep thinking about what Dad said. About us not being the kind of family that—"

"He was talking about *himself*." Sophie tilted her chin up, defiant in that way she got, the way that made me want to follow her anywhere. "He doesn't get to decide that. Not tonight."

The screen door banged open. Behind us, in the dark yard, a car engine idled.

"Alright, ladies?" Jason's voice, warm and low, with the laugh woven through it.

Sophie pulled me toward the door. I let her.

---

## **Jason**

I saw them come out of the house before they saw me.

Maya was half-hidden behind Sophie, her shoulders hunched, and I thought: *she's going to bolt.* I recognized that posture. I'd worn it the year Dad came back from deployment and didn't recognize me, and I'd worn it the week Mom stopped coming home at all.

I revved the engine a little—not loud, just enough. A hello.

"Alright, ladies?"

Sophie smiled like I'd handed her something. Maya didn't smile, but she came closer. That was enough.

I had the windows down. The air smelled like cut grass and somebody's grill three streets over. I was thinking about how I'd driven past this house a hundred times and never stopped, and how tonight I was going to, and how that mattered in some way I couldn't name.

"Pile in," I said. "We're burning moonlight."

---

## **Priya**

I almost didn't come.

I had my calculus textbook open on the kitchen table. I had a study plan with color-coded tabs. I had a mother who would ask questions, and an acceptance letter I hadn't told anyone about, and the very specific terror that if I stepped even slightly outside the lines I'd drawn for myself, I'd lose the thing I'd been working toward for three years.

Then Jason texted: *Maya's going. Come.*

I closed the textbook.

I told myself it was just a ride. I told myself I'd stay in the car. I told myself a lot of things, standing in the hallway with my jacket half-on, watching the front door.

What I didn't tell myself—what I refused to even think—was that I was tired. So tired of being the responsible one. Of being the example. Of carrying around the quiet fear that if I ever, *ever* relaxed, the whole thing would come apart.

When I slid into the backseat, Maya looked up at me in the rearview mirror. Her eyes were wet.

"Hey," I said softly.

"Hey."

I sat down beside her and didn't say anything else. She leaned her shoulder against mine. A small, deliberate weight.

---

## **Connor**

I met them at the gas station on Route 9.

I was late because I couldn't find my good lighter, the one Dad gave me before he moved to Tucson. I'd searched every drawer, every jacket pocket, and finally found it in the freezer, of all places, buried under a bag of peas I'd forgotten about.

When I pulled up behind Jason's Civic, the girls were inside, laughing at something. I could see Maya through the window, and she looked—

She looked like herself. Not the version of herself she'd been wearing for months. The real one.

I got out. The night was huge and warm, and the fluorescent lights made everyone look a little sick. I bought a Slurpee and a pack of gum and walked over.

"You're late," Sophie said.

"I'm here now."

"Being here now isn't the same as being on time."

"Sophie."

"What?"

"Nothing. Hi."

She smiled, finally. "Hi."

We all climbed into the Civic. It smelled like old french fries and Jason's deodorant. Priya was in the middle seat, knees pulled up, reading something on her phone. Maya had the window down and her hair was getting everywhere.

"Where are we going?" I asked.

No one answered.

"Literally nowhere?"

"We're going to the lake," Sophie said. "We're going to sit on the dock. We're going to do nothing. That's the entire plan."

"Okay."

"Don't sound so suspicious."

"I'm not suspicious. I'm—"

"You are. You always are." She turned around in her seat and looked at me, and her face was very close, and she was right.

---

## **Sophie**

We parked at the trailhead and walked in the dark.

I led because I always led, and I was good at it, and I was terrified of it. Maya stayed close to me. Priya stayed close to Maya. Connor drifted at the back, hands in his pockets, occasionally breaking twigs with his foot.

The dock was old and creaky and the water was black and there were frogs or something screaming in the cattails. I sat at the very end and let my legs hang over.

One by one, they sat beside me.

I wanted to say something. I'd been wanting to say something all night, since I'd talked Maya out of the house, since I'd decided that this was the night we would do something real. I had a speech, sort of. About how we were seniors. About how this was the last summer. About how I didn't want to be the friend who only ever drove everyone around—I wanted to be the friend who actually went somewhere.

But when I opened my mouth, none of it came out.

Connor put his hand on my back.

"Are you okay?" he asked.

"I'm fine."

"You don't have to be fine."

I started crying, which was mortifying, and Maya put her arm around me, and Priya said, very quietly, "Me too." And then we were all kind of crying, or close to it, sitting on this stupid dock in the middle of nowhere at 1 a.m., and the frogs kept screaming, and nobody said *what are we even doing out here,* because we all knew.

We were saying goodbye without saying it.

We were saying: *I love you and I'm scared and I don't know what happens next.*

We were saying: *I am here.*

---

## **Maya**

On the way back, I sat in the front seat.

I don't remember deciding to. One moment I was in the back, and the next I was climbing over the console, and Jason just lifted his arm like a tollbooth to let me through.

The highway was empty. The streetlights made stripes across the dashboard. I watched Jason's hands on the wheel—steady, sure, the way I'd always wanted my own hands to be.

"You okay?" he asked, low enough that the others couldn't hear.

"I think so."

"Yeah?"

"Yeah." I paused. "Thanks for coming to get me."

"Always."

We drove in silence for a while. Behind us, I could hear Connor saying something quiet to Sophie, and Priya humming a little, off-key, under her breath.

I thought about my dad, and the way his voice had sounded earlier—*we're not that kind of family, Maya*—and I thought about my mom, asleep right now in her chair with the TV on, and I thought about tomorrow, when I'd have to explain where the car was, and whether I'd be grounded, and whether any of it mattered.

It mattered. All of it mattered.

"Same time next week?" I asked.

Jason glanced at me. Grinned.

"Same time next week."

---

## **Priya**

When they dropped me off, the porch light was on.

I sat in the backseat for a moment, gathering myself. Maya had already gone inside—she lived closer. Sophie and Connor were next, in that order or the reverse, I didn't remember. It was just me now, standing in my own driveway, the key cold in my hand.

I went inside.

The kitchen light was off, but there was a glow from the living room. Mom was still up, of course. She always was, when I was out late, even though she never said a word about it.

"How was it?" she asked, without looking up from her book.

"Good."

"Good?"

"Yeah." I stood in the doorway. "Mom."

"Mm?"

"I love you."

She looked up then. Her glasses were sliding down her nose. She looked tired. She looked like someone who had waited up for me without complaint, every single time, for seventeen years.

"I love you too, baby. Go sleep."

I went.

In my room, I opened my laptop and looked at the acceptance letter again. I read it all the way through. Then I closed it and lay in the dark and thought about the dock, and the water, and the way Maya had leaned on me, and how I'd let her.

I'd never let anyone lean on me before.

It felt like the first thing I'd done in years that was actually mine.

---

## **Connor**

I didn't sleep.

I sat at my desk with the window open and watched the sky start to lighten, and I thought about all the things I'd been too cool, too scared, too male to say in the car.

*I'm scared too.*

*I'm scared we'll lose each other.*

*I'm scared that next year, when we're at four different schools, we'll be polite strangers exchanging Christmas cards.*

I thought about Sophie, crying on the dock, the way her shoulders had shaken. I thought about Maya, white-knuckled, coming out of her house. I thought about Priya, finally, *finally*, putting down the textbook.

I thought about Jason, who was the best of us, and the most patient, and the most overlooked.

I took out a notebook and started writing them all letters. Real ones, on paper. I'd mail them in September, when we were all somewhere else, so they'd arrive like a small surprise, like proof that a night like tonight had actually happened.

*Dear Sophie,* I wrote first. *Thank you for not letting me be late. Thank you for letting me be late. I'm sorry I said "are you okay" when you obviously weren't and obviously didn't want to be asked. You looked beautiful on the dock. I'm not going to send that part.*

I laughed at myself, alone, in the dark.

Then I kept writing.

---

**THE END**

# The Weight of Doorways

The taxi smelled of stale cigarettes and pine air freshener, a combination that belonged to no real place, and Eleanor pressed her forehead against the cool window glass as the suburbs of her childhood unraveled outside. Strip malls she didn't recognize had risen where fields had been. The drive-through coffee shop had replaced the diner where her grandfather had taught her to order coffee—black, one sugar—though she hadn't thought about that in twenty years.

The driver glanced at her in the mirror. "You okay, miss?"

"Fine," she said. "Just been a long time."

Three weeks since the call. Three weeks since her mother's voice on the phone, thin and strange with grief, had asked her to come sort through the house. *Come home,* she'd said, as if Eleanor still had one.

The taxi turned onto Maple Street, and there it was—the house at the end, smaller than memory insisted. The porch swing was gone. The shutters, once a defiant green, had been painted a quiet gray. Someone had let the lilacs grow wild.

"Here works," Eleanor said, and paid too much.

She stood on the sidewalk for a long time before walking up the path. The key still worked, though she had to jiggle it twice. The door opened onto the smell of old carpet and her mother's perfume, something floral that hadn't quite faded, and Eleanor felt something crack open in her chest that she had been keeping sealed for years.

Her mother was in the kitchen, and for a moment they just looked at each other across the linoleum.

"You kept it," Eleanor said finally, nodding at the kettle on the stove, the one shaped like a cat, the one she'd broken at sixteen and hidden in the garbage.

Her mother smiled, watery and small. "I kept everything, Ellie. That's the problem."

---

They spent the first afternoon not sorting anything. They sat at the kitchen table with cups of tea and talked about nothing in particular—the weather, a neighbor's new dog, the strange quality of the autumn light. Eleanor learned that the pear tree in the backyard had died two winters ago, that her mother had started attending a book club, that she sometimes couldn't sleep until four in the morning.

"I should have come sooner," Eleanor said, though she'd said it before, and the words had worn thin.

Her mother reached across the table and squeezed her hand. "You're here now."

That night, lying in her old childhood bed, beneath the ceiling she'd stared at through so many teenage afternoons, Eleanor couldn't sleep. The house settled around her with its familiar noises—pipes in the walls, the tick of the hallway clock, a branch somewhere tapping at a window. She had lived in four cities since leaving this room. She'd unpacked her boxes in each one, always carefully, never quite believing she would stay. Her lease in Portland had ended the day she got the call. She hadn't renewed it.

In the morning, her mother was already at the table, paging through a photo album Eleanor hadn't seen in years. There was Eleanor at seven, missing her two front teeth. Eleanor at twelve, all knobby elbows and self-conscious smile. Eleanor at twenty-two, the day she'd graduated college, standing between her parents with a face that already belonged to someone Eleanor barely recognized.

"I look happy there," Eleanor said.

Her mother looked up. "You were."

---

The sorting was harder than Eleanor had expected. Every box in the attic contained a small archaeology of who she'd been. A box of letters from a boy named David, whose face she couldn't picture. A diary from the year she was fifteen, its pages dense with the catastrophic importance of ordinary days. A drawing she'd made in second grade, of a horse with too many legs, that her mother had framed and kept on the fridge for an entire year.

"Throw it away," Eleanor said, holding the letters.

Her mother hesitated. "Are you sure?"

"I'm sure."

But when her mother wasn't looking, Eleanor slipped the diary into her suitcase. She didn't know why.

On the third day, they found her father's shirts in the back of the closet, still wrapped in dry-cleaner plastic. He had been dead eleven years. Her mother had never given them away.

"He was a difficult man," her mother said, almost to herself. "But he had good shirts."

Eleanor laughed—a real laugh, surprising them both.

That evening, they drove to the cemetery. It was smaller than Eleanor remembered, the headstones weathered and leaning. Her father was near the back, under a maple that had grown enormous. Eleanor laid the stone she'd brought on the grass, and they stood together without speaking, and the late afternoon sun made everything gold.

"I don't know if I believe in any of it anymore," Eleanor said finally. "Heaven. Souls. Any of it."

Her mother put her arm through Eleanor's. "I don't, either, most days. But I like visiting him."

They stood a little longer. A bird sang somewhere in the maple. Then they walked back to the car, slowly, and went home.

---

The decision came on the fifth morning.

Eleanor was in the attic, holding a coffee mug she'd painted in art class, when she heard her mother on the stairs. She appeared at the top of the hatch, slightly out of breath, and looked around at the cardboard towers, the half-filled boxes, the dust motes turning in the slanted light.

"I'm thinking of selling the house," her mother said.

Eleanor set the mug down carefully. "Okay."

"I've been thinking about it for years. I just didn't want to do it alone."

"You won't," Eleanor said. "You won't do it alone."

They sat on the floor of the attic, among the boxes, and made a list. Things to keep. Things to give away. Things to throw out. Eleanor's handwriting and her mother's, side by side on the same yellow legal pad. It was, she realized, the first time in many years they had made anything together.

---

The house sold in the spring, to a young couple who wanted to start a family there.

Eleanor helped her mother pack the things she would take to the apartment—a smaller place, with a garden, in a town thirty miles north. On the last day, they walked through every room. Eleanor trailed her hand along the hallway wall, the place where she had measured her height each birthday until she was twelve, the small pencil marks climbing the wallpaper like a slow ascent.

"I have to tell you something," her mother said, in the doorway of Eleanor's old room.

Eleanor waited.

"I was angry at you. For a long time. For leaving."

"I know."

"But I'm not anymore." She paused. "I'm glad you lived everywhere you needed to live. I'm glad you found your own life."

"Mom."

"And I'm glad you came back. Even if it was just for this."

Eleanor crossed the room and put her arms around her mother, who was smaller than she had been at sixteen, when Eleanor had last stood this close. They held each other for a long time, in the quiet of the empty house, and then they locked the door and walked out to the car.

The lilacs were blooming in the yard. The neighbor's dog barked once and stopped.

---

In the rearview mirror, the house grew smaller, then smaller, then disappeared around a bend, and Eleanor felt the strange double pull of leaving a place you are leaving and have already left, both at once, forever.

Her mother reached over and squeezed her knee.

"Same time next month?" Eleanor asked.

"Same time next month," her mother said.

The road opened up ahead of them, unfamiliar and known at the same time, and they drove on.

Write a story about someone finding acceptance. Roughly 1900 words in length.

# The Weight of Wings

The butterfly had been dead for three days before Mira found it.

She noticed it first by the kitchen window, pressed against the glass as if trying to reach the garden it could never touch. Its wings were the color of dried lavender—faded now, edges crumbling like old paper—and its body curled inward in that final, universal posture of surrender.

She should have swept it away. There were chores to finish, bills to sort, a thesis chapter that had been stalled for six weeks. Instead, Mira fetched a small box from the craft drawer, lined it with a scrap of cotton, and laid the butterfly inside.

"You don't have to be beautiful today," she whispered.

No one heard her. That was the point.

---

Mira was twenty-six years old and had spent exactly twenty-three of those years trying to be the right kind of girl.

She had been the right kind of daughter: quiet, helpful, never raising her voice even when her father's moods darkened the house like a storm. She had been the right kind of student: the one teachers praised in conferences, the one who never caused trouble, the one who edited her personality down to something smooth and acceptable. She had been the right kind of friend, mostly—loyal in the ways that didn't ask for too much, present in the ways that never made anyone uncomfortable.

What she had never been was seen.

Her mother, before the cancer took her, had come close. "You're too good, Mira," she'd said once, with the particular exhaustion of someone who recognized a performance. "Too good. It's going to exhaust you someday."

Mira had been too busy being good to listen.

---

She named the butterfly after a week.

This was not strange behavior, she told herself, though she said it to no one. Entomologists named specimens. Scientists labeled their discoveries. There was nothing odd about a graduate student naming a dead moth in a shoebox.

"Lila," she decided. Because of the color. Because the name meant *play* in some language she couldn't quite remember.

She placed the box on her desk, beside the laptop and the cold cup of tea and the stack of articles she was supposed to be reading. Lila watched her work with patient, empty eyes.

"I think I'm broken," Mira told her one evening, after a particularly brutal meeting with her advisor. "He said my research question was 'diffuse.' He said I needed to 'find a spine.' As if spines were things you could just *acquire*."

The butterfly said nothing. This was, Mira found, exactly what she needed.

---

The trouble with acceptance, Mira was beginning to understand, was that it required a person to *be* someone. You couldn't be accepted if there was no you to accept.

She had spent so long being what others needed that she had stopped asking what she herself required. Food, mostly. Shelter. A path through each day that involved as little friction as possible. Beyond the basics, she was a blank—a polite absence, a comfortable silence, a shape that moved when prodded and stopped when ignored.

Her therapist, the one she had started seeing three months ago after a panic attack on the subway, called this *fawning*. "You're a chronic appeaser," Dr. Reyes had said, not unkindly. "You learned early that your survival depended on keeping the peace."

Mira had nodded. She always nodded.

"What did you want to be, before you learned that?" Dr. Reyes asked.

Mira couldn't remember. She had tried, in the weeks after, to reach back to some earlier version of herself—a Mira before the lessons, before the careful editing—but there was only fog there. A pleasant, featureless gray.

---

She started talking to Lila more often.

Not in a way that worried her, exactly. Lila was a research subject, that's all. A prompt for self-reflection. Mira kept a notebook now, and in it she wrote down things she told the butterfly:

*Today I wanted to say no and I said yes.*
*Today I laughed at a joke that wasn't funny.*
*Today I wore the blue sweater because she likes blue, not because I do.*

The notebook filled up. She bought a second one.

"She" was Priya. Priya from the writing seminar, who sat next to Mira and laughed at everything Mira said with a delight that felt, at first, like sunlight on Mira's skin. It took Mira four months to realize that the delight was conditional—that Priya preferred the quiet, agreeable Mira, the one who nodded along to her opinions, who deferred to her choices of restaurants and films and weekend plans.

When Mira disagreed with her, just once—just *once*, about whether a particular character in a novel was sympathetic—Priya's face did something complicated and then smoothed itself into a smile that didn't reach her eyes.

"Oh," Priya said lightly. "I didn't know you had opinions about things."

The sentence landed like a stone in water. Mira felt the ripples for days.

---

She stopped seeing Priya after that.

Not dramatically. She simply stopped answering texts as quickly. Stopped inventing reasons to be available. She let the friendship thin out, the way a lake dries in summer, until one day she realized she hadn't thought about Priya in a week.

The emptiness where the friendship had been felt, at first, like failure.

Then it felt like relief.

---

Dr. Reyes was pleased. "You're starting to have boundaries," she said. "That's a big step."

Mira wasn't sure *boundaries* was the right word. Boundaries suggested she knew what her edges were, what she was protecting. She felt more like someone who had accidentally walked out of a building and was now standing in an unfamiliar street, blinking.

"What do you want, Mira?"

She didn't know. She had been working on this question for months, and she still didn't know. She had tried the exercises Dr. Reyes suggested—the lists, the visualizations, the body scans. She had tried to imagine a future self who was confident and whole. But every time she reached for it, her mind went blank. She could not picture a Mira who wanted things, because the wanting felt dangerous, and the danger felt like death.

Not real death. Something worse.

The death of being liked.

---

The thesis was due in six weeks.

Mira sat at her desk and stared at the document, the cursor blinking in the empty space where her introduction should have been. Lila watched from her box. The lavender wings had faded further; they were nearly gray now.

*What are you even studying?* Mira thought, and for the first time the question felt urgent.

She was getting a PhD in organizational psychology. She had chosen it, years ago, because her undergraduate advisor had said she was good at understanding people. She had taken it as a recommendation and built a life around it—the internships, the research assistantships, the fellowship that paid her rent and not much else. She was good at it. Everyone said so.

But *good at* and *called to* were different things.

She closed the laptop. She went to bed. She lay in the dark and listened to the city breathing outside her window.

---

The next morning, something strange happened.

She was making coffee, and she dropped the bag of grounds on the floor, and the sound of it—the small, ridiculous impact—made her laugh. Not a polite laugh, not a social laugh. A real one, surprised out of her.

She laughed until she cried.

She cried on the kitchen floor for an hour, and somewhere in the middle of it she understood what was happening. She had been carrying something for so long that she had forgotten she was carrying it. The weight of being acceptable. The weight of being small enough to fit through any door. The weight of never once, in twenty-six years, taking up the space she actually occupied.

It was a small grief. It was a huge one.

She didn't know yet that it would pass.

---

She called Dr. Reyes that afternoon and canceled her appointment.

"No," she said, when Dr. Reyes asked why. "I'm not canceling forever. I just need to be alone for a while. I need to figure something out."

"Mira—"

"I spent my whole life being what other people needed me to be. I think I need to find out if there's anything underneath that."

There was a long pause on the other end of the line. Then, softly, Dr. Reyes laughed.

"You're going to be fine," she said.

Mira wasn't sure that was true. But she thought, maybe, she would let herself find out.

---

That week, she took Lila out of her box.

The butterfly was so fragile now that Mira was afraid to touch it. The wings crumbled at the edges. The body had stiffened. She carried it carefully to the window where she had first found it, and she set it on the sill.

"Goodbye," she said.

She didn't know what Lila had been, in the last weeks of her brief life. She didn't know what Lila had wanted, or whether butterflies wanted anything at all. She only knew that Lila had been beautiful, in her own small way, without ever trying to be.

The next morning, Lila was gone. A breeze had taken her, or a bird, or nothing at all. Only a faint dust of lavender remained.

Mira opened the window. She let the cold air in.

---

She did not finish her thesis on time.

She did, eventually, finish it. Six months late, with a new introduction that she wrote in three feverish days, that her advisor called "finally specific, finally *yours*." She did not know, exactly, what that meant. But she thought she was beginning to.

She defended her dissertation on a Tuesday in May, in a room full of people she did not try to impress. She answered questions honestly, even when the honest answers were uncertain. She did not pretend to know things she did not know.

She passed.

Afterward, in the hallway, her advisor put a hand on her shoulder. "You've changed," he said. "For the better."

Mira nodded. She did not say thank you. She did not say *I'm sorry it took so long*. She just stood there, in her own skin, and let the moment be what it was.

---

Years later, when she had a job she mostly liked and an apartment full of plants she had chosen on purpose and friendships that did not require her to disappear, Mira would sometimes think of the butterfly.

She would think of how she had found it, already dead, trying to get through a window.

She would think of how she had kept it, and talked to it, and let it go.

She had been afraid, for so long, that if she stopped being the right kind of person, there would be nothing underneath. That she would crumble like old paper, that the people who loved her would look at what remained and turn away.

What she had found, instead, was this: she was not a performance. She was not a kindness. She was not the absence of trouble.

She was just a person. Specific. Ordinary. Hers.

And that, she was learning, was enough.

---

**The end.**

# Życie Pożyczone

Halina zawsze wiedziała, że to, co przeżywała, nie do końca należało do niej.

W szkole podstawowej, gdy inne dzieci opowiadały o wakacjach nad morzem, o dziadku łowiącym ryby w niedzielne poranki, o zapachach ciasta drożdżowego unoszących się z kuchni babci – Halina milczała. Nie dlatego, że nie miała nic do powiedzenia. Po prostu nauczyła się, że jej historie nikogo nie interesują.

Jej matka pracowała na dwóch etatach. Ojciec wyjechał, kiedy miała trzy lata – podobno do Niemiec, podobno na zawsze. Halina dorastała w mieszkaniu, które pachniało proszkiem do prania i zmęczeniem.

## I

Wszystko zaczęło się od Ewy.

Ewa przeprowadziła się do ich bloku w październiku, kiedy Halina miała czternaście lat. Nowa klasa, nowi ludzie – to Halina wiedziała o niej na początku. Potem zaczęły się rozmowy. Przy automacie z napojami w szkolnym korytarzu, przy oknie w czasie przerw, na przystanku tramwajowym numer pięć.

Ewa mówiła, a Halina słuchała.

Opowiadała o ojcu, który rano w niedzielę przygotowywał naleśniki dla całej rodziny. O siostrze, która uczyła się gry na pianinie i ćwiczyła godzinami, aż palce czerwieniały. O matce, która wieczorami siadała z nimi przy stole i opowiadała o swoim dniu, śmiejąc się z własnych historii.

– A ty? – zapytała kiedyś Ewa. – Opowiedz coś o swojej rodzinie.

Halina otworzyła usta i nic z nich nie wyszło. Pomyślała o matce, która wracała o dziewiątej wieczorem, zdejmując buty w przedpokoju z taką miną, jakby każdy krok kosztował ją więcej, niż mogła zapłacić. O braku ojca. O ciszy, która wypełniała mieszkanie po powrocie mamy ze zmiany.

– To nie jest ciekawe – powiedziała w końcu.

Ewa spojrzała na nią uważnie, tym specyficznym wzrokiem, który miała – nie współczującym, nie ciekawskim, tylko jakby widzącym rzeczy, których inni nie widzieli.

– Każda historia jest ciekawa – odparła. – Trzeba tylko umieć ją opowiedzieć.

## II

Halina zaczęła żyć życiem Ewy po cichu, niepostrzeżenie, tak jak rosnące drzewa w filmach przyrodniczych – nikt nie widzi momentu, w którym zmieniają kształt.

Kiedy Ewa mówiła, że jej ojciec czyta jej wieczorami, Halina wyobrażała sobie ciepły głos, niski i spokojny, i książkę z dużymi literami. Kiedy Ewa wspominała, że jej babcia hoduje pomidory na balkonie – czerwone, mięsiste, pachnące latem – Halina zamykała oczy i czuła zapach ziemi.

Z czasem zaczęła zapożyczać szczegóły. W zeszycie, który trzymała w szufladzie pod bielizną, zapisywała zdania, które usłyszała od Ewy. Nie dosłownie – przetwarzała je, dodawała coś od siebie. *Moja babcia ma balkon pełen pomidorów, ale najbardziej lubię te zielone, bo kiedy dojrzewają, jest w nich coś obiecującego*. To było jej zdanie. Ale materiał – materiał należał do Ewy.

Pewnego dnia, na lekcji polskiego, nauczycielka zapytała, kto chce opowiedzieć o swoich rodzinnych tradycjach. Halina podniosła rękę.

Opowiedziała o naleśnikach. O pianinie. O pomidorach na balkonie.

Nauczycielka się uśmiechnęła. Klasę zainteresowała ta inna Halina – ta, która miała ojca, siostrę, babcię, balkon pełen lata.

Ewa, która siedziała trzy ławki dalej, patrzyła na nią długo, z tym swoim wzrokiem-widzeniem.

## III

Po liceum ich drogi się rozeszły. Ewa wyjechała do Krakowa, na studia. Halina została w mieście, pracowała w biurze ubezpieczeniowym, potem w księgowości małej firmy budowlanej.

Ale nie przestała słuchać.

Była Marta z marketingu, która opowiadała o podróżach po Azji. Był Tomek z działu IT, który miał brata bliźniaka i rodziców, którzy wciąż się kochali, choć po trzydziestu latach małżeństwa. Była Kasia, sąsiadka z piętra wyżej, która trenowała taniec i miała kota o imieniu Kapitan.

Halina słuchała i zbierała. Składała z tych historii coś swojego – mozaikę, która wyglądała jak życie, choć nim nie była.

Na portalach społecznościowych prowadziła konto. Prawdziwe imię, fałszywe życie. Zdjęcia z cudzych wakacji – *moja podróż do Włoch*, podpisywała pod fotografiami znalezionymi w internecie. Historie o rodzinnych obiadach, których nigdy nie było. Facet o imieniu Bartek, który istniał tylko w jej wyobraźni, ale na zdjęciach wyglądał jak prawdziwy chłopak – brodaty, z tatuażem, w okularach.

Miała tysiące obserwujących. Pisali do niej: *Jak Ty to robisz, że masz takie ciekawe życie?*

Halina odpowiadała: *Trzeba tylko umieć je opowiedzieć*.

## IV

Matka umarła w październiku, kiedy Halina miała trzydzieści dwa lata. Rak trzustki – szybki, bezlitosny, taki, który nie daje czasu na pożegnanie.

Halina siedziała w pustym mieszkaniu. Matka nie zostawiła po sobie prawie nic. Ubrania w szafie, kilka książek, pudełko ze starymi zdjęciami – na większości matka sama, bez ojca, z Haliną jako dzieckiem, z Haliną jako nastolatką.

Na dnie pudełka Halina znalazła list. Napisany przez matkę, ale nie do niej – do ojca Haliny, tego, który wyjechał.

*Wiem, że nie wrócisz. Ale Halinka rośnie. Codziennie staje się bardziej podobna do Ciebie. Ma Twoje oczy, Twój upór, Twój sposób na patrzenie na świat. Nie mogę jej dać tego, co moglibyśmy razem. Nie mogę jej dać rodziny, o jakiej marzyłam. Więc pozwalam jej wymyślać. Niech sobie wyobraża. Niech opowiada historie, których nie było. Może to jedno, co mogę dla niej zrobić.*

Halina siedziała na podłodze i trzymała list w rękach. Czuła, jak podłoga pod nią się trzęsie, choć wiedziała, że to niemożliwe.

Jej matka wiedziała. Od zawsze wiedziała.

## V

Halina zamknęła konto w mediach społecznościowych. Wyrzuciła zeszyt z zapisanymi historiami. Przestała słuchać.

To było trudniejsze niż myślała. Przez tyle lat żyła cudzymi słowami, że jej własne wydały się jej obce. Kiedy ktoś pytał ją o życie, o przeszłość, o rodzinę – nie miała nic do powiedzenia.

Zaczęła pisać.

Nie posty, nie historie na blogu. Nie cudze życie, nie skradzione wspomnienia. Własne. Takie, jakie były – puste, ciche, samotne.

Pisała o matce, która wracała o dziewiątej wieczorem. O braku ojca. O proszku do prania i zmęczeniu w powietrzu. O sobotach spędzonych samotnie w pustym mieszkaniu.

O tym, jak bardzo kochała matkę, choć nigdy jej tego nie powiedziała.

Pierwszy tekst wysłała do małego literackiego pisma internetowego. Redaktorka odpisała: *To jest surowe i bolesne i prawdziwe. Proszę, pisz więcej.*

Halina pisała. Z każdym tekstem czuła, jakby oddawała coś, co przez lata w niej zalegało. Cudze historie wychodziły z niej powoli, ustępując miejsca jej własnym.

## VI

Na zjazd absolwentów Ewa nie przyjechała. Halina dowiedziała się od kogoś, że mieszka teraz w Berlinie, pracuje w jakiejś fundacji, ma męża Hiszpana i dwójkę dzieci.

To było jej życie – prawdziwe, nie pożyczone.

Halina nie czuła zazdrości. Dawniej czułaby. Teraz czuła coś innego – spokój, może nawet wdzięczność. Ewa nie wiedziała, że przez te wszystkie lata była dla Haliny oknem na świat. Nie wiedziała, że Halina ukradła jej ojca, siostrę, babcię, balkon pełen pomidorów. Nie wiedziała, że te skradzione historie pomogły Halinie przetrwać.

I nie musiała wiedzieć.

## VII

Halina ma teraz czterdzieści pięć lat. Mieszka sama. Prowadzi warsztaty pisarskie dla nastolatków z domów dziecka – tych, które nie mają historii do opowiedzenia, albo mają ich za dużo, albo wstydzą się tych, które mają.

Mówi im: *Każda historia jest ciekawa. Trzeba tylko umieć ją opowiedzieć*.

Nie mówi im, że przez lata żyła cudzym życiem. Nie mówi im, że jej własne było puste, ciche, samotne. Nie mówi im, że musiała wymyślić sobie ojca, siostrę, babcię, balkon pełen lata.

Mówi im tylko, żeby pisały prawdę. Tyle, ile potrafią w danym momencie. Tyle, ile są gotowe oddać.

A jeśli nie są gotowe na prawdę – niech piszą cokolwiek. Niech wymyślają. Niech kradną szczegóły z cudzych opowieści, jeśli to im pomoże przetrwać.

Niech żyją pożyczonym życiem, dopóki nie będą gotowe na własne.

Ale niech w końcu napiszą swoje.

Na dnie szuflady, w której kiedyś trzymała zeszyt z cudzymi historiami, Halina trzyma teraz list od matki. Czyta go czasem, kiedy jest ciężko. Kiedy pustka w niej jest zbyt duża, kiedy cisza zbyt głośna.

I za każdym razem myśli to samo: *Mamo, może mnie nie zrozumiałaś. Może nie pozwalałaś mi wymyślać dla mnie samej. Może pozwalałaś mi wymyślać, bo wiedziałaś, że inaczej nie przeżyję.*

*Może właśnie dlatego teraz jestem tutaj.*

Write a story about someone trying to paint (or otherwise create) a self-portrait. In total around 1200 words.

The Mirror Lies

The face in the mirror was wrong.

Marlene pressed her thumb against the canvas, smearing ochre into the hollow of a cheek that wasn't quite hollow enough. She leaned back on her stool, stretched her neck, and looked again.

The woman in the glass looked back. Mid-fifties. Gray threaded through dark hair pulled into a knot that was slowly unraveling. Eyes the color of weak tea, set deeper than they had been last year, or the year before. A mouth that had smiled more in the past six months than in the previous decade combined.

The woman on the canvas was none of these things.

Her subject—she could not bring herself to think *herself*—sat in three-quarter profile with one hand raised to her chin, a gesture Marlene had copied from a Renaissance print she'd found in a book at the library. The eyes were too large. The nose too straight. There was a quality to the painted mouth that suggested sensuality, or cruelty, or some private joke the subject was keeping from the artist. The whole thing had the smug composure of a woman who knew she was being watched and enjoyed it.

"You look like her," Marlene's daughter had said last summer, pointing at Marlene's first attempt, the one now leaning against the back of the closet behind a tower of moving boxes. "Like the lady in that painting. The one with the weird smile."

She had meant the *Mona Lisa*, and Marlene had laughed. But she hadn't been able to shake the observation, and she hadn't been able to throw the painting away. She had started another instead.

That one was wrong too, but wrong in a different way. The chin was too soft. The neck was a column. The expression had frozen somewhere between surprise and indigestion.

This was her third attempt. She had bought the mirror at a thrift store on Main Street, a heavy oak-framed rectangle that smelled faintly of cigarettes and someone else's grandmother. She'd set it on an easel across from her work stool, angling it to catch the late-morning light from the kitchen window. She had taken to sitting in front of it for a few minutes each morning before she began, as if she could study the woman who lived inside the glass and learn her habits.

"You're not a painting," she told the reflection once, in a moment of irritation. "Stop posing."

The reflection had, of course, posed more.

She mixed a darker tone into the corner of her palette, a burnt umber with a touch of cadmium red, and began work on the shadow beneath the painted jaw. As she painted, she thought about her mother, who had died the previous winter in a hospice room in Bend, the curtains half-drawn against a rain that had not stopped for three days. Her mother had been a beautiful woman once. Marlene had inherited none of it. She had inherited, instead, her father's heavy brow and the small mole on her left cheek that she had learned, by age twelve, to hide with makeup.

"You could be an actress," her father had said once, drunk, looking at her across a kitchen table lit by a single bulb. It had not been a compliment.

She had not become an actress. She had become an accountant, then a bookkeeper, then a wife, then a mother, then a widow, then a grandmother, then a woman who lived alone in a house that was too big and tried, very late, to paint.

Her neighbor Nora had suggested the painting. "You should do something," Nora had said, in the gentle, clipped way people spoke to the recently bereaved. "A project. My sister took up pottery after her husband passed and she made the most wonderful—"

"No," Marlene had said. Then, after a pause: "Maybe painting."

She did not know why she had said painting. She had not painted anything since high school, where she had received a B-minus in Art and a note from the teacher that her self-portrait showed *unusual emotional depth but poor technical execution*. She had taken this as a verdict on her entire self.

But she had bought the cheap paints at the hardware store, and a few brushes, and some pre-stretched canvases. She had set up the easel in the front room where the light was best. And she had begun.

The first attempt had been a disaster, but a useful disaster. She had learned that her own face, viewed straight-on, was a thing she could not bear. There was too much to see, and none of it arranged in any pleasing way. The second attempt, in profile, had been easier and therefore worse. She had flattered the subject without meaning to, sanding down the angles of her grief.

This third one she had positioned in three-quarter view, a compromise, but the hand she had raised to the painted chin now belonged to a younger woman. The eyes still looked out from the canvas with an amused, knowing intelligence that Marlene did not possess and had never possessed.

She stepped back. She sighed.

She poured herself a cup of coffee, which had gone cold an hour ago, and drank it anyway, standing at the window and looking out at the yard. The lilacs were blooming. The neighbor's cat was sleeping on the low stone wall. A child was laughing somewhere down the block.

She had not painted for a week after her mother died. Then she had painted badly for a month. Then she had started again, and here she was, on a Tuesday morning in May, failing to capture her own face for the third time.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. Her daughter, sending a photograph of her granddaughter at a school play, dressed as a tree. *She's the best oak*, the caption read.

Marlene typed back a string of small, delighted emojis, then set the phone down and turned back to her work.

She sat on the stool. She looked in the mirror.

The mirror looked back.

"You," Marlene said, very softly, "are not what I look like."

The reflection waited.

"But you're not *not* what I look like, either. You're just the closest I can get to looking at myself without flinching."

She picked up a brush. She looked at the canvas. She thought about her mother, who had refused to be photographed in her last year and had drawn the curtains when Marlene tried to sketch her. She thought about her father, who had looked at her once across a kitchen table and seen someone other than who she was. She thought about her husband, dead six years now, who had never once seen her clearly and had loved her anyway.

She began to paint.

She painted the shadows under the eyes a little deeper. She softened the line of the brow. She made the mouth smaller, less amused, more uncertain. She added, at the corner of the painted mouth, a tiny upward turn that was not quite a smile.

It was, she decided, the best of the three. It was also the saddest. There was a quality to the painted face that she could not name, a kind of weariness and a kind of stubborn, surprised tenderness. It was not her. It was not *not* her.

It would have to do.

She set down her brush and went to make a fresh pot of coffee, and the woman in the mirror watched her go with the patience of someone who had all the time in the world, and intended to use it.

Write a story about someone walking through a park on a spring evening, told only through internal monologue. Length: about 900 characters.

# 暮春行

石板路上的影子已经拉得很长了。我该往哪走？这条路我走了二十年，闭着眼都不会错，可今天不知怎么，脚步就是慢了下来。

风从湖面吹过来，带着一点腥，一点甜。是水草的味道，混着不知哪棵树的花香。槐花？不对，槐花要再过一个月。那是……迎春？也不对，早谢了。我懒得想了，反正春天什么花都有，什么味道都混在一起，醉醺醺地往人鼻子里钻。

左边那条长椅上坐着两个老太太。我认得她们，一个姓陈，一个姓孙，每天傍晚都来，就坐这张椅子，聊些我听不见的事。她们有时候笑，声音尖细，像麻雀打架；有时候又不说话，各自看着湖面，好像在想心事。我有时候羡慕她们。两个人，能说这么久的话，又能在不说话的时候也不觉得尴尬。这是什么境界？

我往前走。脚下咯吱一声，踩碎了一片干枯的落叶。这很奇怪——春天怎么会有落叶？我低头看，是去年的法国梧桐叶，卷曲着，发黄，藏在石板缝里，躲过了所有清洁工的扫帚。它在这里躺了整整一个冬天，等着被一个无聊的行人踩碎。我有种奇怪的内疚。

前面有个小男孩在追泡泡。他爸——或者爷爷——站在后面，手里举着泡泡瓶，一次一次地蘸，一次一次地吹。小男孩跑得跌跌撞撞，泡泡在夕阳里变成金色，又变成橙色，又变成我找不到名字的颜色。啪，一个破了。小男孩不哭，接着追下一个。

我忽然想起我小时候。什么小时候的事？我抓不住。好像也是这样的傍晚，也是这样的金光，也是这样追着什么跑，追不上，又不甘心。到底是什么？我想不起来了。算了。

湖面上有几只野鸭。真的假的？我眨了眨眼。三只。不，是四只。不，三只，可能有一只是我的影子。它们一动不动地浮着，脖子弯成一个问号。我小时候以为鸭子睡觉是睁着眼睛的，后来知道是错的，可此刻我又希望是真的——那样它们就能看见这个傍晚，看见天边那条橘红和淡紫交接的线，看见对岸的柳树是怎么把枝条垂进水里，洗一洗，晾一晾。

我今天为什么出来散步？我也说不清。可能是家里闷。可能是吃多了。可能是想一个人待一会儿，又不想真的一个人，所以来这种到处都是人、又没有一个人认识我的地方。陌生人真好啊。他们不跟你说话，不问你为什么看起来不开心，不劝你回家。他们就存在着，像树，像椅子，像湖里的鸭子，存在本身就是一种陪伴。

前面那棵树开花了。我停下来，凑近看。是海棠。粉的，一簇一簇，压得枝条都弯了腰。有一只蜜蜂嗡嗡地飞过来，停在我鼻尖前面，又飞走了。它大概觉得我是个没用的东西，不产蜜。

我笑了一下。

太阳又矮了一点。我的影子变得更长了，长到快要够着湖面。再过半小时，天就全黑了，灯会亮起来，那些灯白天看丑丑的，晚上却温柔得要命。到时候那条路上的情侣会更多，散步的、遛狗的、推婴儿车的，人声和虫声会混在一起，乱糟糟的，却让人安心。

可是我现在还不想回家。我就这么走着。一步，再一步。踩着落叶，躲着泡泡，闻着花香，听着风。

就这样吧。

Write a story about someone who believes they are an extremely good judge of character. Approximately 1500 words.

# The Eye

Marcus Webb considered himself a connoisseur of people. In thirty-four years of life, he had never been fooled by a lie, never surprised by a betrayal, never caught off-guard by a hidden motive. He could walk into a room and, within the hour, tell you who was trustworthy, who was desperate, who was pretending to be something they weren't. It was a gift, really. Perhaps even a calling.

His friends joked about it. "Ask Marcus," they'd say when a new boyfriend seemed too charming, when a business partner's handshake lingered a beat too long. Marcus would tilt his head, study the person with his pale green eyes, and deliver his verdict with the calm certainty of a doctor reading a scan.

"He'll disappoint you," Marcus would say. Or: "She's exactly what she appears to be." Or: "There's something hollow in him. Watch your back."

He was always right.

---

The new tenant moved into the downstairs apartment on a Thursday. Marcus heard her from his balcony—the scrape of furniture, the particular rhythm of someone organizing a small life into a new space. When he went down to help with a heavy box, he saw her for the first time.

Eleanor Vance. Late twenties, maybe early thirties. Dark hair pulled back, a smudge of dirt on her cheekbone, reading glasses pushed up on her forehead. She thanked him three times for carrying the box and then apologized for the inconvenience of her moving.

"Practiced gratitude," Marcus noted to himself. "Performs politeness for strangers. Slightly anxious—probably lonely, probably something to prove. Mid-level administrative work, judging by the calluses on her fingers and the way she scans for systems. Divorced recently. The ring tan is still there, but she's scrubbed the skin raw."

He smiled warmly and invited her to the building's monthly potluck.

"She's harmless," he told his roommate Devon later. "A little performative, but genuine underneath. The kind of person who would help you move but never ask you to help her."

Devon raised an eyebrow. "You're already writing her biography?"

"I'm observing. There's a difference."

"Sure, man."

---

Within two months, Marcus knew Eleanor's rhythms. She worked from home Tuesdays through Thursdays, left early on Mondays, came back late on Fridays. She had a sister in Portland she called every Sunday. She drank her coffee black but saved the cream for her cat, a fat orange tabby named Chairman. She hummed when she was happy and went silent when she wasn't.

He had diagnosed her with what he privately called *the Eleanor condition*: a deep need to be perceived as kind, combined with a terror of being seen as needy. She'd overextend herself for others and then feel embarrassed about it. She'd ask for nothing and want everything.

He recognized the pattern because he'd seen it a hundred times. People were, in his experience, deeply legible. They were puzzles with only a few pieces.

"She's one of the good ones," he told his sister at Thanksgiving. "Next door. Quiet. Keeps to herself but would give you the shirt off her back."

"You've talked to her, what, twice?"

"I don't need to talk to her. I can see her."

His sister, who knew him better than most, said nothing. She just sipped her wine and looked at him with an expression he couldn't quite read.

---

The problem began, as these problems often do, with a kindness.

Eleanor left a note on his door one morning in March. *Heard your alarm at 4 AM—is everything okay? Made too much soup, if you want some. E.*

He stared at the note for a long time. Something about the handwriting—rounded, slightly oversized, the lowercase e's all identical loops—made him pause. Then he laughed at himself. It was soup. Just soup.

But when he went down to thank her, he found himself studying her more intently than usual. The way she held her body slightly turned away from him, even while smiling. The way she asked about his day without quite looking at him. The way she filled silences with unnecessary information.

*She's lonely*, he thought. *More than I thought. The kindness is a reflex—she's trying to build a bridge to someone, anyone, before the loneliness swallows her whole.*

"Would you like to come up for coffee sometime?" he heard himself say. The words felt foreign in his mouth.

Her face did something complicated. "I'd like that."

---

They became friends. Real friends, he told himself—the kind where you actually know someone, not the kind where you just observe them from a polite distance. They watched bad movies on Fridays. She made him tea when he worked late. He helped her fix the leaky faucet she'd been ignoring for weeks.

And Marcus, to his own surprise, found his readings of her growing less certain.

She'd say something that seemed, on the surface, simple and kind, and he'd find himself wondering, hours later, whether there had been another layer. She'd cancel plans with vague excuses, and he couldn't tell if she was protecting her privacy or hiding something. Once, he saw her laugh on the phone with her sister, and the laugh sounded different from her usual laugh—older, somehow—and he realized he'd never heard her truly unguarded.

"She performs for you," he muttered to himself one night, annoyed. "Even now. Even after all this time. She's still performing."

But then he thought: *Maybe I'm the one performing. Maybe this whole friendship is just me playing the role of the good neighbor, the perceptive friend, while never actually showing her who I am.*

He didn't like that thought. He set it aside.

---

The revelation came in April, on a night when neither of them could sleep.

They'd been drinking wine on his balcony, watching the city lights smudge against the horizon. The conversation had wandered, as late-night conversations do, into dangerous territory. She'd asked him, out of nowhere, "Do you ever feel like you don't actually know the people you think you know?"

"Meaning?"

"Meaning... I spent eight years married to someone. I thought I had him figured out. I thought I knew what made him tick, what he wanted, what he was afraid of. And then one day I realized I'd been so busy reading him that I'd never actually asked him."

Marcus said nothing.

"You do that too," she said, turning to look at him. Her eyes were steady in the dim light. "You read people. You're brilliant at it. But Marcus—you never ask. You just decide."

"That's not—"

"Let me finish. You decided I was lonely the first week we met. You decided I was kind but needy. You decided I was performing for you. And some of those things are true. But some of them aren't. And the ones that aren't—you never noticed. Because you weren't curious. You were just... certain."

The city hummed below them. Somewhere, a car alarm went off and then stopped.

"I think," she said softly, "you've never actually seen me. You've seen your reading of me. And you've mistaken it for me."

Marcus opened his mouth to argue. To explain that his gift wasn't arrogance—it was perception, it was careful, it was *kind* in its own way because it spared people the indignity of having to explain themselves. He knew people. He saw people. He was the person who saw.

But he stopped.

Because he thought of all the friendships he'd ended because he'd decided, early on, what someone was. The jobs he'd left because he'd diagnosed a boss as a narcissist before giving them a chance. The romances that had flickered out because he'd already written the ending in his head.

He thought of his sister, at Thanksgiving, looking at him with that unreadable expression. He thought, with a small cold shock, that he had never once tried to read her expression. He had simply decided she disapproved of him, and left it at that.

"Eleanor," he said. His voice sounded strange to him. Quieter than usual.

"Yeah?"

"What am I missing? About you. What have I decided that isn't true?"

She was quiet for a long time. Then she smiled—a real smile, he thought, the kind she usually kept hidden.

"Ask me again sometime," she said. "When you're ready to actually hear the answer."

---

Marcus sat with his wine long after she'd gone downstairs. The city lights blurred and sharpened, blurred and sharpened.

He thought about the certainty he had always carried like a coin in his pocket—always there, always ready, always shiny. He thought about how he'd mistaken it for wisdom. How he'd mistaken observation for connection. How he'd mistaken the quick verdict for the slow, difficult, unending work of actually knowing another person.

He thought about all the people he had seen and never met.

And for the first time in his life, Marcus Webb felt himself standing at the edge of someone—a real someone, a whole and hidden and irreducible someone—and understood that the edge was not a failure of perception.

It was the beginning of one.

Write a story about someone who decides to confront their fears head-on. Around 1300 words.

# The Edge of the Pier

The lighthouse at Cape Moray had been Eleanor's nemesis since she was seven years old. Not the structure itself—she actually found the white tower beautiful, especially at sunset when it bled gold against the bruised sky. It was the climb. The 137 steps spiraling up through the center, the catwalk at the top with its wrought-iron railing, and the dizzying view of the Atlantic crashing against the rocks far below.

For twenty-three years, Eleanor had avoided that lighthouse the way other people avoided tax collectors or exes with grudges. She'd drive fifteen minutes out of her way to reach the coastal trail. She'd invent headaches when her brother suggested a family climb. She'd told a white lie to her therapist about having "made peace with it" just to end the conversation.

She had not made peace with it.

The fear had burrowed into her life in ways she was only beginning to admit. She avoided heights of any kind—second-floor balconies made her hands sweat, and she had once hyperventilated on a step stool changing a light bulb. She couldn't watch movies with high-flying scenes without pressing her face into a pillow. Her partner, Daniel, had learned not to point out scenic overlooks on road trips.

It was Daniel, actually, who finally said the thing that cracked her open.

"We can't keep pretending this isn't running your life, Elle."

They were sitting on their porch on a Tuesday evening, drinking wine, watching the summer sun sink toward the sea. She'd just declined, for the fourth time, an invitation to a friend's rooftop wedding.

"It's just a wedding," he said gently. "It's just a building. It's just *height*, Eleanor. And it's eating you alive."

She wanted to argue. She wanted to point out all the things she *did* do, all the ways she was brave. But the words stuck somewhere in her throat, because he was right.

The next morning, she drove to Cape Moray.

---

The parking lot was nearly empty. A lone fisherman was baiting hooks at the edge of the pier, and an elderly woman walked a terrier along the coastal path. Otherwise, Eleanor had the lighthouse to herself, which was how she wanted it. She couldn't bear the thought of someone witnessing her possible humiliation.

She sat in her car for a long time, hands on the steering wheel at ten and two, the way her father had taught her decades ago. Her father, who had died when she was twelve, three months before he was supposed to take her up the lighthouse for her birthday. The trip had been planned. The fear had been waiting.

*Get out of the car, Eleanor.*

She got out of the car.

The wind hit her immediately, salt-heavy and insistent, tugging at her hair, her jacket. She walked toward the entrance, and with each step, her pulse climbed. By the time she reached the heavy wooden door, her heart was slamming against her ribs like something caged.

She pushed the door open.

The smell hit her first—old stone, dust, the faint metallic tang of the ocean below. Then the spiral staircase, narrow and rising away from her into the dimness above. She counted the steps as she climbed, her breath coming faster with each turn.

*Twenty. Thirty. Forty.*

At fifty-two, she had to stop. She pressed her forehead against the cool stone wall and closed her eyes. The lighthouse seemed to sway, though she knew it didn't. Her legs had gone soft beneath her. The old horror was there, patient and familiar, whispering all the things it always whispered.

*You can't. You're not the kind of person who can. Sit down. Go back. No one will know.*

A tear slid down her cheek.

She kept climbing.

---

The catwalk was exactly as bad as she remembered—or as she had imagined, all those years of avoiding it. The railing was chest-high, solid enough, but beyond it: the sky, the wheeling gulls, the sea spread out like hammered tin, and the rocks far, far below.

Eleanor gripped the railing with both hands. She could feel the metal trembling, though she told herself it was her, not the structure. The wind pulled at her clothes. She was certain, absolutely certain, that if she let go she would be lifted up and tossed over the edge like a scrap of paper.

*This is the moment*, she thought. *This is the test.*

She didn't know how long she stood there. Five minutes. Twenty. The fisherman on the pier had gone; she hadn't noticed him leave. The elderly woman with the terrier had gone too. The sun had slipped lower, painting everything in honey and rose.

And then, very slowly, Eleanor loosened her grip.

She didn't let go. Not entirely. But she loosened her fingers until she was only barely touching the railing, only resting her palms against it, and she stood there, in the wind, on the edge of the highest place she had ever been.

She was shaking. She was terrified. She was also, unexpectedly, furious—not at herself, but at the years she had given back to this fear. The weddings skipped. The vacations avoided. The step stools and the second floors and the silly, small humiliations that had piled up like the rocks below.

"I'm here," she said out loud, to no one, to herself. "I'm *here*."

The lighthouse keeper had long since been replaced by automation, but Eleanor liked to imagine he was somewhere in the tower with her, the old man who had climbed these steps ten thousand times, who had known the smell of the salt and the squeal of the gulls and the way the light felt in his bones when he lit it.

She stayed at the top until the sun touched the horizon.

Then she walked down the 137 steps, and she did not count them, and she did not hold the railing.

---

In the car, on the drive home, Eleanor's hands were still trembling. She pulled over at a turnout overlooking the cove, and she sat there for a long time, watching the last light fade.

Her phone buzzed. Daniel.

*How did it go?*

She thought about how to answer. The truth was complicated. She hadn't conquered anything—not really. The fear was still there, humming in her blood. She doubted she would ever stand on a balcony and feel nothing. She doubted the lighthouse would ever feel safe.

But she had stood on it. She had stayed.

She typed back: *I went up.*

Three dots. Then: *Proud of you, Elle.*

She started the car. Behind her, the lighthouse stood against the darkening sky, its light just beginning to wake, sweeping out across the water in slow, patient arcs.

She drove home.

---

That night, Eleanor dreamed of the lighthouse for the first time in years. In the dream, she was not climbing it. She was sitting at the top, cross-legged on the catwalk, the railing nowhere in sight. Below her, the sea was perfectly still, and the gulls were suspended in the air like paper cutouts. The sky was the color of a robin's egg.

She wasn't afraid.

When she woke, the feeling lingered for a few precious minutes—the dream-fearlessness, the sense that she had been somewhere high and holy and had not fallen. She knew it wouldn't last. The old voices would come back. The next wedding invitation might still feel like a small defeat.

But something had shifted. A stone had been dislodged. Somewhere in the architecture of her fear, there was now a crack, and through the crack, light.

Eleanor got out of bed. She made coffee. She looked out her kitchen window at the ordinary morning sky.

Then she opened her laptop and RSVP'd yes to the rooftop wedding.
