The small attic room smelled of cedar and old paper. Rain tapped the single windowpane, a rhythm that Mira had come to associate with the hours just before dusk. She sat cross-legged on the worn rug, her back against the side of her grandmother's bed—a brass-frame relic from another century—while the old woman lay propped among pillows, her silver hair fanned across the pillowcase like something drawn in moonlight.

"Again?" her grandmother asked, though her eyes were already bright with the wanting.

Mira smiled and lifted the book from the nightstand. It was slim, its cloth cover soft from decades of handling, the title long since faded to a ghost of itself: *Letters from the Coast*. Her grandmother had carried it across an ocean at nineteen, a gift from a man she had loved and lost to the war. She had read it so often the pages had gone velvet at the corners.

"I'll read the one about the lighthouse," Mira said, finding the page by feel as much as sight. Her grandmother's hand drifted out from under the quilt and settled, cool and light as a leaf, on Mira's knee.

Mira began.

*"The lamp was not lit when I arrived. I had walked all afternoon from the village, and the fog had taken the shape of everything I feared—walls where there were none, voices that were only the sea. But when the keeper opened the door and stepped aside to let me in, I understood that to be lost is not the same as to be abandoned. He had left the door unlocked. He had left the lamp trimmed and waiting, though he had not lit it yet, because he believed I might want to see how the dark looked from inside, before it was changed."*

Her grandmother's breathing had slowed. Mira glanced up and saw that her eyes were closed, but not in sleep—more in the way one closes one's eyes to listen more carefully, as if the words themselves had weight and texture, and she wanted to feel them more fully.

Mira went on.

*"I asked him why he had not married. He laughed and said he had, to the sea, and the sea was a jealous wife who did not share him well. Then he was quiet for a long while, and the lamp ticked as it cooled, and I thought: this is what faithfulness looks like, when no one is watching. This is what it looks like to keep a light burning for a ship that may never come in."*

Outside, the rain had thickened. Mira's voice grew softer, not from tiredness but from reverence—the way one lowers one's voice in a cathedral, even when alone. Her grandmother's thumb moved slowly against the fabric of Mira's jeans, a small unconscious stroke, the way a person touches something precious to be sure it is still there.

*"I left the next morning. The keeper walked me to the path, and at the edge of the cliff he put something into my hand. It was a piece of the glass from the lamp—not broken, but old, clouded from years of flame. He said, when you are far from here, and the night is very long, hold this against your eye, and you will remember what it looked like to be found."*

When Mira finished the page, the attic was very still. The lamp on the nightstand cast a small, warm circle on the ceiling. Her grandmother opened her eyes, and they were wet, but she was smiling—the kind of smile that has outlived the thing it was made for and learned to live on its own.

"You read it differently now," she whispered.

Mira closed the book gently and set it on her grandmother's lap. "How did you read it, when you were young?"

Her grandmother considered this. "As a promise. As a thing I was waiting to happen." She placed her palm flat against the cover, over the faded title, as if she could feel the letters through the cloth. "Now I hear it as a thing that already has. Many times over."

The rain went on. Somewhere below them, the house creaked and settled into its bones. Mira reached over and tucked the quilt more closely around her grandmother's shoulders, and the old woman caught her hand and held it, there, against the book, against the letters, against the small and abiding weight of everything that had been, and was, and would be carried forward into the next unknown dark.

"Read me another," her grandmother said. "The one about the garden."

And Mira opened the book, and began again.

# 雨后的第一口呼吸

林夏站在出租屋的阳台上，看着雨滴从生锈的铁栏杆上滑落。

手机屏幕亮了一下，又暗了。是妈妈发来的消息，叮嘱她记得吃饭。她没有回复。

楼下便利店的灯牌在雨幕中晕开一团昏黄的光。玻璃门上贴着的招聘启事已经被雨水打得模糊不清，但那几个字她早就背下来了——"招夜班店员，2200元/月"。她每天都路过，每天都不进去。

今天不一样。

今天是她辞职后的第七天。上一份工作是在写字楼里做行政，每天对着Excel表格，把同样的话重复给不同的人听。辞职的那天，她没有跟任何人告别。她只是关掉了电脑，把工牌扔进了垃圾桶，然后走进了地铁站。

她不知道自己在做什么。

雨越下越大。她回到屋里，靠着墙滑坐在地上。房间里只有一张床、一个衣柜、一把椅子。房租月底就要到期了，余额宝里的数字她不敢再看第二遍。

她闭上眼睛。

不知道过了多久，敲门声响了。

是隔壁的张阿姨，拎着一个保温盒。"小林啊，我炖了排骨汤，你尝尝。"

林夏愣了一下，接过来。保温盒很沉，里面还冒着热气。

"阿姨……"

"吃完了把盒子放门口就行。"张阿姨摆摆手，转身要走，又停下来，"对了，我儿子在城西开了家小餐馆，正缺人帮忙。不累，管吃管住，三千五。你要是愿意，我让他联系你？"

林夏张了张嘴。眼泪先掉了下来。

"好。"

---

三个月后，城西的"老张面馆"里飘出葱油香。

林夏系着围裙，站在灶台前颠勺。汗水顺着额角滑下来，灶火舔着锅底发出呼呼的声响。后厨闷热，油烟呛得眼睛发酸，但她的动作利落又稳当。

张哥——也就是张阿姨的儿子——是个四十出头的中年男人，话不多，做事踏实。他从不催她，也从不说教，只是偶尔在她忙不过来时伸手搭一把。

今天是周末，店里的客人比平时多。林夏从中午忙到晚上，腿站得发麻，腰也开始隐隐作痛。但她没有坐下过一刻。

最后一桌客人离开时，已经是晚上十点。她把碗筷收进后厨，泡进水槽，然后走到店门口透口气。

夜风吹过来，带着一丝凉意。街灯把她的影子拉得很长很长。她抬头看了看天空——今晚有星星，很亮，亮得有些不真实。

她忽然笑了。

这三个月，她每天早上五点起床，和面、切菜、熬汤。手指上多了几道新茧，指甲缝里永远洗不干净油渍。她再也不用挤地铁，不用在早会上假笑，不用对着表格假装一切都好。

她想起了三个月前那个雨夜，她坐在地板上，觉得自己像一只被雨困住的蚂蚁。

而现在，她站在这里，闻着油烟和葱花的味道，听着水龙头滴答滴答的声音，感受到自己的心跳——砰，砰，砰——一下一下，真实，有力。

她深吸了一口气。

**"我感觉自己活着。"** 她轻声说，声音被夜风吹散。

不是"我感觉到累"，不是"我感觉到难"，不是那些她在朋友圈里写过的、看似积极实则麻木的话。

是活着。

是感觉到胸口有火在烧，是感觉到脚底踩着大地，是感觉到这一刻和下一刻不一样。

店里的灯还亮着。明天还要早起，还要继续颠勺、擦桌、招呼客人。日子不会因此变得轻松，钱包也不会因此突然鼓起来。

但她站在那里，忽然觉得这就够了。

张哥从里面走出来，递给她一瓶水。

"想什么呢？"

"没什么。"她接过水，拧开瓶盖喝了一口，"张哥，谢谢你。"

"谢什么。"张哥点了一根烟，靠在门框上，"你干活踏实，比我雇过的那些大学生强多了。"

林夏笑了笑，没有说话。

她把水瓶放在门槛上，又走回店里。

明天，太阳还会照常升起。而她，会照常醒来。

Write a story that includes someone saying, “Let’s go for a walk.” Total: ~500 words.

The morning sun was just beginning to spill over the horizon, painting the sky in shades of amber and rose, when Maren heard the familiar creak of the back door opening. She was sitting at the kitchen table, a half-empty cup of tea cooling in her hands, staring at nothing in particular. She had been doing a lot of that lately—staring at nothing, thinking of everything, sleeping too little.

Her husband, Cal, appeared in the doorway, his reading glasses pushed up into his salt-and-pepper hair. He was wearing the old gray sweatshirt she loved, the one with the frayed cuffs, and his boots were already laced.

“Let’s go for a walk,” he said.

She looked up at him, surprised. Cal wasn’t usually up this early on a Saturday. And he almost never suggested they do anything together anymore—not since the diagnosis, not since the long silences had become more comfortable than conversation.

“A walk?” she repeated.

He nodded. “Yeah. Down to the creek. The maples are turning.”

She almost said no. She almost said she was tired, that her knees were aching, that she didn’t have the energy. She almost said that walking through the world didn’t feel like something she wanted to do today, when the world felt so uncertain and frightening and sad.

But she looked at him—really looked at him—and saw the quiet plea behind his eyes. He wasn’t asking for himself. He was asking for her. Because he knew, the way long-married people always know, that she was sinking. That the grief over what was happening to her mother, the fear of what was coming next, was pulling her down like a riptide.

“Okay,” she said. “Give me a minute to get my shoes.”

They walked in silence for the first quarter mile, their breath misting in the cool air, their footsteps crunching on the carpet of fallen leaves. The world was painted in golds and reds and rusts, and the light coming through the trees made everything look like it was glowing from within.

Cal reached over and took her hand. She let him.

At the creek, they sat on their old log, the one they’d claimed years ago when the kids were small and they used to come out here on Sunday afternoons. The water was low and clear, and somewhere a woodpecker was drumming on a dead tree.

“I didn’t want to say anything at first,” Cal said quietly. “But then I thought—if not now, when?”

She leaned her head against his shoulder. “I’m scared,” she whispered.

“I know.”

“I don’t know how to do this.”

“You don’t have to know yet. You just have to put one foot in front of the other.”

She looked down at her boots, covered in leaves and dirt. Then she looked out at the creek, at the trees, at the sky that was now a pale, clear blue.

“One foot in front of the other,” she repeated.

He kissed the top of her head. “That’s my girl.”

They sat there for a long time, watching the leaves fall, listening to the water, holding on to each other. And when they finally stood to walk home, Maren felt—just for a moment—that maybe, just maybe, she could do this after all.

Because sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is exactly what someone wise once suggested.

Let’s go for a walk.

# 雨夜的屋檐

林夏没想到，自己会在深夜十一点的便利店门口，看见那个她以为再也不会遇见的人。

雨下得很大。她刚加完班，出来时才发现忘了带伞。正犹豫要不要直接冲进雨里的时候，头顶突然多了一把黑色的伞。

"给你。"

那个声音低沉而熟悉，像是一杯隔夜的咖啡，苦涩里带着余温。林夏抬起头，雨水模糊了她的视线，但她还是一眼就认出了那张脸——陆川。

她大学时暗恋了整整四年的人。

"陆……陆川？"她的声音有些发颤。

他笑了笑，眼角的细纹比记忆里多了几分："好久不见，林夏。"

那把伞最终没有还给他。他们站在便利店明亮的灯光下，透过玻璃窗看着外面的滂沱大雨，像是两个被世界遗忘的人。

"我刚搬来这附近，"陆川说，"没想到第一天上班就遇见了你。"

"你不是在深圳吗？"

"回来了，"他顿了顿，"有些事情想通了。"

林夏没有问是什么事。她不想打破这一刻微妙的平衡。他们聊了很多——大学时的趣事，那些共同认识的老同学，还有这些年各自走过的路。她发现他变了很多，又好像什么都没变。

雨渐渐小了。便利店的店员开始拖地，不时向他们投来疑惑的目光。

"我该走了，"林夏说，"明天还要上班。"

"我送你吧。"陆川撑着伞，向她伸出手。

那一瞬间，林夏感觉自己的心像是被什么轻轻撞了一下。她把手递过去，掌心的温度让她想起很多年前，那个同样下着雨的傍晚，她站在图书馆门口，而他撑着一把伞向她走来。

只是那时候，她没有勇气接过那把伞。

他们走在空旷的街道上，路灯把他们的影子拉得很长。谁都没有说话，但那种沉默并不让人难受。

到了她家楼下，林夏停下脚步。

"谢谢你送我，"她说，"也谢谢你的伞。"

陆川把伞递给她："拿着吧，明天应该还会下雨。"

"那你呢？"

"我住得近，跑两步就到了。"

他说完，转身走进了雨里。林夏看着他的背影渐渐模糊，忽然喊了一声："陆川！"

他回过头。

"……**Thank you for that.**"

她不知道自己为什么会用英文说这句话。也许是因为有些感情，中文表达起来太过郑重，而英文反而显得轻松。

陆川愣了一下，然后笑了。那笑容像是雨夜里突然亮起的一盏灯。

"不客气，"他说，"晚安，林夏。"

她站在屋檐下，看着他的身影消失在街角。雨还在下，但她心里却晴空万里。

回到家后，林夏把伞撑开晾在阳台上。她知道，有些故事才刚刚开始。

Write a story that includes someone saying, “We’re not alone.” About 700 words long.

The forest swallowed sound. Snow fell in slow, deliberate curtains, muffling the world until Elena could hear her own pulse.

She crouched behind a fallen spruce, the rifle across her knees, her breath a ghost in the air. Ahead, through the timber, the distant flicker of the cabin lights caught her eye—Marek’s cabin, where he’d lived alone for nearly forty years.

She’d come to check on him. Three days without word. Three days of silence.

The snow was freshly broken, she noticed. Boot prints, not animal tracks, led up the slope. The door to the cabin stood open, just a crack, and pale light spilled from within like a wound.

She rose and moved forward, the cold biting her fingers even through gloves.

She was ten paces from the door when she heard it.

A voice, low and urgent, from inside the cabin. Not Marek’s.

*“—we have to leave before it comes back.”*

Elena’s grip tightened on the rifle. She stepped closer, pressing her back to the log wall, listening.

Another voice—Marek’s this time, strained, tired, old.

*“There’s nowhere to go, lad. It’s everywhere now.”*

The first voice—young, frightened.

*“Then what do we do?”*

A long pause. Then Marek, quietly:

*“We wait. We watch. And we don’t let it know we’re afraid.”*

Elena’s mouth went dry. *Lad.* Marek had no son. Marek had no one, not for decades, not since his wife—

She pushed the door open.

Inside, Marek sat in his chair by the stove, the same chair he’d sat in since she was a child. He looked up at her, unsurprised, the way you look at weather.

And beside him, kneeling on the rug, hands pressed flat against the floorboards as though feeling for vibrations, was a boy. Maybe sixteen. Dark hair, hollow cheeks, a coat too thin for the cold.

Elena’s rifle came up on instinct.

Marek lifted a hand. Slowly. The way you calm a horse.

*“Elena.”*

“Who is this?”

The boy looked at her. His eyes were wrong—not in color, but in *attention.* As though he were seeing her from very far away.

*“You can see me,”* the boy said. Wonderingly. *“You can actually see me.”*

Marek’s gaze was steady.

*“Sit down, girl.”*

She didn’t sit. “Marek, what is this?”

He gestured to the boy. *“This is Tomáš.”* A pause. *“He’s been coming to the cabin for three nights. Watching me through the window.”*

“*Watching* you?”

*“They do that,”* Marek said. *“The new ones. The ones who haven’t decided yet.”*

A laugh escaped Elena—sharp, incredulous. “Marek, what are you—”

*“Your grandmother knew,”* he said, softly. *“She told you stories. You thought they were stories.”*

The snow fell harder. The wind rose, then died.

The boy—Tomáš—looked at her with those distant eyes.

*“I don’t know how I got here,”* he said. *“I was in Prague. Then I was here. Then I was back in Prague. Then here again.”* He swallowed. *“There’s a woman, she keeps coming. She has no face. She stands at the end of the lane and watches.”*

Elena’s rifle lowered, an inch.

*“There’s no woman,”* Marek said, not unkindly. *“There’s no lane. There’s only what you remember and what you don’t.”*

The cabin lamp flickered. Outside, something moved between the trees—not a shape, exactly. More like the idea of a shape. The snow fell *around* it.

Elena felt it then. A pressure behind her eyes, like a migraine forming. Like someone thinking very loudly, very close.

She turned toward the window.

The forest looked back.

*“Marek,”* she whispered.

*“I know.”*

*“What do we do?”*

The old man leaned forward. His eyes, she saw, were wet.

*“We remember,”* he said. *“That’s all we have. We remember who we are. We remember their names. We remember we had lives.”* He placed a hand over hers, on the rifle. *“And when it gets very quiet, child, and you can’t tell if you’re awake or dreaming, you say it.”*

“Say what?”

He looked at her. Looked at the boy. Looked out, at the place where the snow fell around nothing.

*“You say it so you don’t forget.”*

The cabin grew very still. The lamp steadied.

Elena drew a breath, and the air felt thin and old, like the air in churches.

*“We’re not alone,”* she said.

And somewhere—far off, or very near, or both—something answered.

# Бег

Андрей остановился у края обрыва, и лёгкий утренний ветер ударил ему в лицо. Внизу расстилалось море — серое, холодное, равнодушное. Как и весь мир, от которого он бежал последние три месяца.

Позади послышались шаги. Медленные, уверенные.

— Ты далеко забрался, — раздался голос сзади.

Андрей обернулся. Из тумана вышел мужчина в длинном тёмном пальто. Лицо знакомое — слишком знакомое. Сергей Громов, его бывший напарник. Человек, которому Андрей когда-то доверял свою жизнь.

— Ты можешь не объяснять, — продолжил Громов, не приближаясь. — Я знаю, почему ты украл деньги. Знаю, на что тебе пришлось пойти. Знаю, для кого ты их взял.

Андрей почувствовал, как внутри что-то сжалось.

— Тогда зачем ты здесь?

— Потому что я должен вернуть тебя. Не из-за денег. Из-за тебя самого. — Громов сделал шаг вперёд. — Андрей, послушай меня. Я был в твоей шкуре. Двенадцать лет назад — долги, больная мать, выхода нет. Я тоже думал, что бегство — это решение.

— И что же?

— Ничего. Я бежал шесть лет. Шесть лет фальшивых документов, дешёвых гостиниц и взглядов через плечо. Знаешь, что я понял? Бег — это не дорога. Это круг.

Андрей смотрел на море. Волны разбивались о скалы внизу — глухо, ритмично, словно сердцебиение земли.

— У меня нет выбора, Серёжа. Если я вернусь — тюрьма. А может, что похуже.

— У тебя есть выбор, — Громов достал из кармана сложенный вчетверо лист бумаги. — Я поговорил с людьми. Не со всеми — с теми, кто может решить. Они готовы пересмотреть дело. Твоя мать... Ей нужна операция, да? Я знаю. Знаю, что ты сделал это ради неё. И ещё знаю, что она бы не хотела такой жертвы.

Андрей сжал кулаки. Глаза защипало.

— Ты не можешь этого обещать.

— Могу. — Громов бросил лист бумаги к его ногам. — Прочти.

Андрей поднял лист, развернул. Письмо от адвоката. Печати. Подписи. Слова о снисхождении, об особых обстоятельствах, о возможности нового суда.

— Почему? — тихо спросил Андрей. — Почему ты это делаешь?

Громов помолчал, глядя на море.

— Потому что двенадцать лет назад мне никто не протянул руку. И я сломался. — Он повернулся к Андрею. — Я не хочу, чтобы это случилось с тобой. Ты не плохой человек, Андрей. Ты просто загнанный.

Ветер усилился. Где-то внизу кричали чайки.

— А если я не пойду? — спросил Андрей, и сам удивился, как хрипло прозвучал его голос.

Громов пожал плечами.

— Тогда я уйду. И ты останешься один на этом обрыве. С деньгами, которые не принесут счастья. С матерью, которая никогда тебя больше не увидит. С правдой, которую узнаешь только в конце.

Он сделал ещё один шаг.

— Ты не можешь бежать вечно, Андрей. Рано или поздно — либо тебя найдут, либо ты перестанешь быть собой. Я видел таких, как ты. Видел, что с ними становится через год, через пять, через десять. Это не жизнь. Это медленное угасание.

Андрей смотрел на письмо в своих руках. Буквы расплывались.

— Я боюсь, — прошептал он.

— Конечно, боишься, — мягко сказал Громов. — Это нормально. Но знаешь, чего стоит настоящий страх? Того, чтобы сделать шаг назад, когда всё внутри кричит — вперёд, к обрыву, к концу. Сделай этот шаг. Пойдём домой.

Андрей поднял глаза. Громов стоял в двух шагах от него, протянув руку. Ладонь — широкая, надёжная, знакомая.

Прошла минута. Или вечность.

Андрей сложил письмо, спрятал во внутренний карман. И взял протянутую руку.

Они шли по тропинке обратно, к машине, к городу, к жизни, которая ждала где-то там, впереди — нелёгкой, возможно, даже трудной, но настоящей.

А море осталось позади. Равнодушное и вечное, каким и было всегда.

The gymnasium smelled of chalk and old wood, the same scent it had carried for fifty years. Maren tightened the laces on her borrowed climbing shoes, her fingers trembling just enough to notice.

"You've got this," said Jonas from the belay line, his voice steady and warm.

"I haven't really *done* anything since college."

"I know that too."

Maren exhaled, slow and deliberate, the way the therapist had taught her. She pressed her palm against the first hold. The resin was gritty beneath her fingers, real in a way that felt almost unfamiliar. When had she last touched something that wasn't a keyboard or a coffee mug or the arm of her couch?

She reached up. Her foot found a foothold she hadn't seen, and her body remembered before her mind did—the way her hips should square to the wall, the way her weight should drop into her legs. College. The Cascade Mountains. A boy named Eli who had laughed when she fell and called her "mountain goat" when she didn't.

She climbed.

The first few moves were mechanical, each one a negotiation between fear and muscle memory. Below her, Jonas paid out rope with the patient rhythm of someone who had done this a thousand times. The gym was quiet except for the soft slap of palms on holds and the occasional clink of carabiners.

Halfway up, her forearms began to burn.

"I can't feel my fingers," she called down.

"That's just the pump," Jonas said. "It means you're climbing."

She laughed despite herself, a short, surprised sound. When was the last time she'd laughed like that? A month ago? Six months? A year?

The wall steepened. The holds got worse—small crimps, a sloper that felt like pressing against wet soap. She paused, shaking out one hand, then the other.

The cancer had been the worst part. Not the chemo, not the surgery, not even the fear—though there had been plenty of fear, enough to last several lifetimes. The worst part had been the way illness had quietly rearranged her life. The friends who drifted away. The job she'd finally had to leave. The way her body had become a stranger, something that betrayed her in small and not-so-small ways. After the surgeries, after the reconstruction, after the long months of learning to recognize herself again in the mirror, she had retreated. She had told herself she was healing. Healing, it turned out, was an excellent word for the act of doing nothing at all.

Until the letter.

The letter from the foundation, addressed to *Survivor*, which she still wasn't sure how she felt about. *We would like to honor your journey by sponsoring a climb in your name.* She had read it three times. She had cried, which surprised her, because she thought she was done with crying. Then she had called Jonas, the only friend from those college climbing days she still spoke to, and she had said yes.

A holds popped. Her foot slipped. For one breathless second she was falling—then the rope caught her, snug against her harness, and she swung gently against the wall.

"Breathe," Jonas called. "Take it. Find your next hold."

She breathed. She looked up. Three moves to the top, maybe four. She had climbed harder things in her life. She had climbed things no one was supposed to climb back from. This was just a wall. This was just a Tuesday night at a gym in a city that wasn't her own.

She reached. She pulled. She felt her body, for the first time in a long time, do exactly what she asked of it.

The last hold was a jug—a wide, friendly thing that practically begged to be grabbed. She grabbed it. She stood up. Her forearms screamed and her fingers were numb and she was *standing*, fifteen meters above the ground, with nothing between her and the floor but rope and trust.

"You did it," Jonas called from below, his voice cracked with something like pride. "Maren, you did it."

She looked out across the gym, at the scattered handful of climbers on their own walls, each one locked into their own small private battle. She thought of all the things she had survived. All the things she had not yet done.

She thought of the letter on her dresser back at the hotel, signed by a foundation director whose name she didn't recognize. *In honor of your journey.* She had hated that phrase at first. She had wanted to throw the letter away. But standing here, with the lights of the gym glowing soft against the high ceiling, she understood something she hadn't before. The journey wasn't something she had finished. The journey wasn't even something she was halfway through.

The journey was this. The journey was right now.

She lowered slowly, the rope hissing through the device, the ground rising up to meet her like an old friend. When her feet touched the mat, her legs almost buckled. Jonas was there, his hands on her shoulders, steadying her.

"You've got this," he said again, and she realized, finally, what he had meant. It wasn't just for the climb. It had never been just for the climb.

She nodded, tears running freely now, and she said the only thing she could think to say:

"Yeah," she said. "I think I do."

# O Relógio do Avô

A oficina do meu avô cheirava sempre a óleo de máquina e a pó de relógios antigos. Eu passava as tardes de verão ali, entre peças minúsculas e engrenagens que pareciam ter vida própria, ouvindo ele contar histórias sobre os tempos em que consertava os relógios da cidade inteira.

— Um relógio, minha neta — dizia ele com os olhos brilhando por trás dos óculos grossos —, é como uma pessoa. Tem o seu ritmo, os seus segredos, e se você souber ouvir, ele conta tudo o que aconteceu.

Eu tinha doze anos naquela época e não entendia muito bem o que ele queria dizer. Os relógios, para mim, eram apenas objetos bonitos com ponteiros que giravam. Mas o avô insistia:

— Quando alguém me entrega um relógio para consertar, eu sei o que se passou naquela casa. Se o mecanismo está travado, houve discussões. Se o pêndulo está torto, alguém tropeçou no amor. Se o mostrador está riscado, houve lágrimas.

Eu ria, achando que eram invenções de velho. Mas o avô levava tudo aquilo a sério. Tinha um caderno preto onde anotava cada história, e guardava os relógios que ninguém reclamava numa estante no fundo da oficina, como troféus de memórias.

No verão em que fiz quinze anos, o avô adoeceu. Lembro-me de estar ao lado da cama dele no hospital, segurando a mão enrugada e fria, enquanto ele murmurava sobre engrenagens que precisavam ser apertadas.

— Promete-me uma coisa, Catarina — sussurrou ele.

— O que, avô?

— O relógio do meu pai. Está na estante, no fundo. O grande, de madeira escura, com os anjos pintados na tampa. Quando eu partir, dá corda a ele todos os dias, à mesma hora. Não deixes que pare.

— Porquê?

Ele apertou a minha mão com a força que ainda lhe restava.

— Porque ele guarda uma coisa. Uma coisa que eu nunca tive coragem de te contar. Mas vai precisar de saber, mais cedo ou mais tarde.

O avô faleceu três dias depois, num entardecer de quinta-feira, quando os sinos da igreja tocavam as seis. O funeral foi pequeno, como ele tinha pedido, e no dia seguinte, com os olhos ainda inchados de chorar, entrei na oficina para cumprir a promessa.

A oficina cheirava a pó e a silêncio. Dirigi-me ao fundo, onde a estante de madeira escura guardava os relógios abandonados. Havia dezenas deles: de parede, de bolso, de mesa, alguns empoeirados, outros ainda a funcionar com um tique-taque suave. Mas o que o avô descrevera estava no último lugar, no canto mais alto.

Peguei nele com cuidado. Era mais pesado do que parecia, feito de madeira escura quase negra, com anjos dourados pintados na tampa, cujas tintas já se tinham quase apagado. O mostrador era de um branco amarelado, com números romanos, e os ponteiros marcavam uma hora que não existia: três e um quarto da manhã.

Dei corda. O mecanismo rangeu, como se acordasse de um sono muito longo, e começou a andar. Ouvi o tique-taque suave e rítmico, e quase me pareceu uma respiração.

Naquela noite, enquanto o vento batia nas janelas da oficina, o relógio parou. De repente, sem aviso, o tique-taque cessou. A casa ficou num silêncio tão profundo que eu conseguia ouvir o meu próprio coração a bater.

Levanteei-me assustada, fui até à oficina e acendi a luz. O relógio estava imóvel. Tentei dar corda outra vez, mas o mecanismo não respondia. Tentei perceber o que se passava, mas não conseguia. Era como se alguma coisa dentro dele se tivesse quebrado.

Desesperada, decidi abrir a tampa traseira. Lá dentro, entre engrenagens, encontrei um pequeno envelope de papel amarelado, escondido atrás do mostrador. Estava selado com cera vermelha, e no exterior, com a caligrafia trémula do meu avô, lia-se:

*“Para a Catarina, quando o relógio parar.”*

Sentei-me no chão empoeirado da oficina, com as mãos a tremer, e abri o envelope. Dentro havia uma carta e uma fotografia antiga, a preto e branco, de uma mulher jovem que se parecia comigo de uma forma que me fez arrepiar.

A carta dizia:

*Minha querida Catarina,*

*Se estás a ler isto, é porque eu já parti e o relógio decidiu que está na hora de saberes a verdade. A mulher da fotografia é a tua avó, que nunca conheceste, porque morreu jovem, muito antes de tu nasceres. Mas há outra coisa que precisas saber.*

*O relógio que tens nas mãos é muito mais antigo do que a nossa família. Pertenceu a um relojoeiro de Lisboa, no século XVIII, que o construiu para guardar a memória de todos os momentos importantes das pessoas que o possuíram. Cada vez que um momento significativo acontece na vida de quem cuida dele, o mecanismo ajusta-se. E quando chega a hora de revelar um segredo guardado durante gerações, ele pára, forçando quem o possui a procurar a verdade.*

*O segredo que guardo é este: a tua avó não morreu de doença, como te contaram. Morreu de desgosto, por amor a um homem que não a merecia. E esse homem, Catarina, era o teu pai.*

*Ele era violento, minha neta. E quando a tua avó tentou fugir com a tua mãe, ainda bebé, ele perseguiu-as. A tua avó deu a vida para que a tua mãe pudesse escapar. A tua mãe cresceu sem saber a verdade, e quando tu nasceste, ela prometeu que nunca te contaria, para te proteger.*

*Mas eu, como velho relojoeiro que sou, sei que a verdade tem sempre de sair à superfície. Caso contrário, envenena-nos por dentro, como o óleo rançoso num mecanismo parado.*

*Por isso te peço: não guardes raiva do teu pai. Ele também foi uma vítima, à sua maneira, de um ciclo que se repetia na família dele há gerações. Mas usa esta história para ser diferente. Para escolher o amor em vez do medo, a coragem em vez do silêncio.*

*Dá corda ao relógio outra vez, Catarina. Ele vai voltar a andar, e desta vez, vais perceber que o tempo é generoso connosco: dá-nos sempre novas oportunidades de fazer as coisas bem.*

*O teu avô, que te amou mais do que as palavras conseguem dizer.*

Com os olhos cheios de lágrimas, fechei a carta e voltei a dar corda ao relógio. E, com um estalo suave, o mecanismo recomeçou, os ponteiros moveram-se, e o tique-taque encheu novamente a oficina.

Mas agora não era apenas um som. Era uma voz. Era a voz do meu avô, da minha avó, de todas as gerações que tinham passado por aquele relógio, sussurrando-me que eu tinha o poder de quebrar o ciclo, de escolher ser diferente, de amar sem medo.

Naquela noite, saí da oficina com o coração partido e inteiro ao mesmo tempo. O relógio ficou na prateleira, a marcar as horas, mas eu sabia que, de certa forma, ele tinha parado de ser apenas um objeto. Tinha-se tornado uma testemunha, um guardião, um professor.

E quando, anos mais tarde, o meu próprio filho me perguntou porque é que o avô guardava tantos relógios antigos, eu sorri e respondi:

— Porque cada relógio tem uma história para contar, meu amor. E algumas dessas histórias só se revelam quando estamos prontos para as ouvir.

Ele olhou para mim com os seus olhos grandes e curiosos, e eu soube que, um dia, quando fosse a altura, também ele ia parar o relógio do bisavô, e encontrar a sua própria carta, com a sua própria verdade.

Porque o tempo, afinal, é o maior relojoeiro de todos. E nós somos apenas engrenagens nas suas mãos, à espera de sermos ajustadas.

E eu, Catarina, neta de relojoeiro, filha de uma história que quase foi esquecida, aprendi a lição mais importante de todas: **não se pode fugir do passado, mas pode-se usá-lo para construir um futuro diferente.**

E agora, sempre que olho para um relógio parado, sorrio, porque sei que ele está apenas à espera de alguém corajoso o suficiente para lhe dar corda e ouvir o que tem para dizer.

---

*“I didn't see that one coming,”* murmurei para mim mesma naquela noite, enquanto os ponteiros giravam e o tique-taque preenchia a oficina do meu avô com a promessa de que, às vezes, as maiores verdades da nossa vida encontram-nos nos momentos mais inesperados.

# Bayangan di Balik Layar

Rina menatap layar laptopnya dengan mata yang terasa berat. Sudah tiga jam ia bekerja sebagai penulis lepas di apartemen kecilnya di Jakarta, dan kalimat-kalimat yang seharusnya mengalir dengan mudah kini terasa kering. Kopi di cangkirnya sudah dingin, dan hujan mulai mengguyur jendela dengan iramanya yang monoton.

"Aku butuh istirahat," gumamnya pada dirinya sendiri sambil memijat pelipis.

Tapi kemudian, sesuatu yang aneh terjadi. Kursor di layarnya bergerak sendiri.

Rina mengernyitkan dahi. Mungkin ada debu di touchpad? Ia menggerakkan jarinya, dan kursor kembali normal. Tapi beberapa detik kemudian, huruf-huruf muncul di dokumennya:

**AKU DI SINI.**

Rina menahan napas. Tangannya gemetar. Ia menutup laptop dengan kasar, lalu duduk diam selama beberapa menit, mendengarkan detak jantungnya yang berpacu.

"Itu pasti virus komputer," bisiknya, mencoba menenangkan diri. "Tidak mungkin nyata."

Dengan ragu, ia membuka laptop lagi. Dokumen kosong. Tidak ada pesan aneh. Hanya kata-katanya yang belum selesai. Rina memutuskan untuk mengabaikan kejadian itu dan melanjutkan menulis.

Tapi malam itu, saat ia sedang membaca berita di ponselnya, sebuah notifikasi muncul dari aplikasi yang tidak pernah ia pasang:

**"Jangan tidur malam ini."**

Jantung Rina berdegup kencang. Ia menghapus aplikasi itu—tapi namanya tidak ada di daftar aplikasi terpasang. Itu tidak masuk akal. Ia memeriksa riwayat unduhan, tidak ada apa-apa.

Mungkinkah ada seseorang yang mengawasi? Tapi siapa? Dan untuk apa?

Rina mencoba menjalani hari-harinya seperti biasa. Ia bekerja, bertemu teman, berjalan di mal. Tapi selalu ada perasaan aneh, seolah ada mata yang tak kasat mata mengikutinya. Kadang ia merasa ponselnya sedikit lebih panas dari biasanya, atau kursor di komputernya bergerak lebih lambat.

Suatu malam, saat sedang menulis di balkonnya yang menghadap kota, ia mendengar sesuatu. Bukan suara hujan, bukan suara motor. Tapi bisikan halus, seperti ada seseorang yang berbisik tepat di telinganya.

"Kamu tahu aku ada."

Rina menoleh dengan cepat, tapi tidak ada siapa-siapa. Hanya lampu-lampu kota yang berkedip-kedip di kejauhan.

"Aku pikir seseorang sedang mendengarkan," bisiknya pada angin malam, mencoba membuat dirinya terdengar berani.

Lalu, ponselnya bergetar. Pesan masuk dari nomor tak dikenal:

**"Kamu benar."**

Rina merasakan bulu kuduknya meremang. Ia membalas pesan itu: *"Siapa kamu? Apa yang kamu mau?"*

Tidak ada balasan. Ia menunggu lima menit, sepuluh menit, setengah jam. Tapi tidak ada apa-apa.

Keesokan harinya, Rina memutuskan untuk mengubah rutinitasnya. Ia keluar rumah dengan rute berbeda, bekerja di kafe yang berbeda, mematikan ponselnya selama beberapa jam. Tapi semua itu tidak menghentikan kehadiran tak kasat mata itu. Di mana pun ia pergi, selalu ada tanda-tanda kecil: sebuah pesan singkat, layar yang berkedip tanpa alasan, atau perasaan diawasi yang tidak bisa ia jelaskan.

Akhirnya, Rina memutuskan untuk menghadapinya. Ia duduk di mejanya, membuka laptop, dan mengetik di dokumen kosong:

**"Apa yang kamu mau dariku?"**

Layar berkedip. Lalu, perlahan, huruf-huruf muncul:

**"Aku hanya ingin kamu tahu bahwa kamu tidak pernah sendirian."**

Rina tertegun. Ia tidak tahu harus merasa takut atau lega. Apakah ini hantu? AI yang entah bagaimana lolos dari sistem? Atau hanya manifestasi dari kesepiannya sendiri yang selama ini ia abaikan?

Ia mengetik lagi: **"Kenapa sekarang?"**

**"Karena kamu mulai lupa,"** jawab tulisan itu. **"Bahwa ada lebih banyak hal di dunia ini daripada yang bisa kamu lihat."**

Rina duduk diam, merenungkan kata-kata itu. Mungkin memang benar. Selama ini, ia terlalu fokus pada pekerjaannya, pada angka-angka dan tenggat waktu, sehingga ia melupakan hal-hal yang tidak bisa dilihat dan dijelaskan. Keberadaan yang lebih besar dari dirinya.

**"Bagaimana aku bisa berkomunikasi denganmu?"** tanyanya.

**"Dengan cara yang sudah kamu lakukan. Lewat kata-kata. Lewat pikiran. Aku ada di mana-mana, dan di mana-mana aku ada, aku bisa mendengar."**

Malam itu, untuk pertama kalinya dalam berminggu-minggu, Rina tidak merasa sendirian. Ia tahu ada sesuatu yang mendengarnya—entah apa itu, dia belum sepenuhnya yakin—tapi kehadiran itu memberikan rasa aman yang aneh.

Sejak malam itu, Rina tidak pernah merasa diawasi lagi. Tapi kadang, saat ia menulis di larut malam, kalimat-kalimatnya terasa mengalir lebih lancar, seolah ada tangan tak kasat mata yang membimbingnya. Dan kadang, saat hujan turun, ia merasa mendengar bisikan halus yang berkata:

**"Teruslah menulis. Aku mendengarkan."**

Rina tersenyum. Mungkin memang ada seseorang yang mendengarkan—bukan untuk mengintimidasi, tapi untuk menemani. Dan itu lebih dari cukup.

**Le Tabouret du Roi**

Dans la grande salle du trône, le silence s'était installé comme un invité qu'on n'avait pas convié. Les conseillers, la cape pourpre sur les épaules, les seigneurs aux bagues scintillantes, la reine elle-même, dans sa robe brodée d'or — tous regardaient le monarque avec une sorte de fascination horrifiée.

Le roi Théobald était assis sur son tabouret.

Pas sur son trône. Pas sur la chaise de cérémonie en chêne sculpté qu'on avait fait venir de Bourgogne trois générations plus tôt. Non. Sur un *tabouret*. Un vulgaire tabouret de cuisine en bois de hêtre, rapporté on ne sait comment des communs du château, et sur lequel il siégeait depuis bientôt deux heures.

Le Grand Chambellan, un homme sec et nerveux nommé Aldric, fut le premier à réagir. Il s'approcha à pas feutrés, la bouche entrouverte, tel un héron ayant repéré un poisson dans une mare.

— Majesté, hasarda-t-il, ne croyez-vous pas que… peut-être…

— Quoi ? gronda le roi, dont la barbe noire frémissait d'indignation contenue.

— Eh bien… le trône, Votre Majesté… il est… juste là, derrière vous. Très confortable, d'ailleurs. Coussin en plumes d'oie. Le tapissier l'a retapé la semaine dernière.

Le roi ne daigna pas se retourner.

— Je suis très bien ici.

Aldric recula, livide. La reine, qui observait la scène depuis son propre fauteuil — un fauteuil parfaitement acceptable, en velours cramoisi, avec accoudoirs —, pinça les lèvres. Les jeunes princesses, dans un coin, se retenaient visiblement de pouffer. Le prince héritier, lui, affichait l'expression résignée de celui qui a vu trop de choses.

Les minutes s'écoulèrent. Un conseiller tenta une plaisanterie sur la stabilité du nouveau mobilier. On ne rit pas. Un page apporta un coussin pour adoucir l'assise du tabouret, et le roi l'envoya promener d'un revers de la main.

La cour commençait à étouffer.

C'est alors que le bouffon entra.

Petit, sec, le nez rouge et l'œil vif, Fend-le-Vent traversa la salle en sautillant, s'arrêta net devant le roi, le dévisagea longuement, puis promena son regard sur l'assemblée pétrifiée.

Et c'est lui qui dit, avec une innocence désarmante :

— *Personne ne va le dire ?*

Tout le monde retint son souffle.

— Le roi, continua-t-il en pointant le tabouret du doigt, est assis sur un tabouret de cuisine. Un tabouret. De cuisine. Celui sur lequel la cuisinière s'assoit pour écosser les petits pois. Celui qui sert à attraper la marmite quand elle glisse dans l'âtre. *Ce* tabouret-là.

Un murmure horrifié parcourut la salle. Le Grand Chambellan ferma les yeux, comme pour se dissocier spirituellement de la scène.

— Et alors ? aboya le roi. Un roi ne peut-il pas s'asseoir où bon lui semble ?

— Si, Majesté, bien sûr, répondit le bouffon. Mais voyez-vous, un roi qui choisit son siège, c'est une chose. Un roi qui *refuse* de le quitter alors que tout son royaume lui fait les yeux doux pour qu'il daigne migrer de quarante centimètres vers la gauche, c'en est une autre.

Le roi ouvrit la bouche. La referma. Ses doigts tambourinèrent sur ses genoux.

— Pourquoi, demanda la reine d'une voix dangereusement douce, avez-vous pris *ce* siège, mon époux ?

Silence.

Les conseillers se regardèrent. Les princesses retinrent leur souffle. Le prince héritier pria silencieusement pour que son père trouve une réponse qui n'entraîne pas une guerre civile.

— Parce que, lâcha enfin le roi d'un ton rogue, l'autre est *trop confortable*.

Un silence abasourdi accueillit l'aveu.

— Pardon ? fit la reine.

— Trop confortable ! répéta-t-il. Chaque fois que je m'y assois, je m'endors. Les ministres font leurs rapports, je ronfle. Les ambassadeurs présentent leurs doléances, je rêve de chasses au sanglier. J'ai failli laisser échapper trois provinces rien qu'en bâillant au mauvais moment !

— Et donc, Votre Majesté, résuma le bouffon avec une gravité comique, vous avez opté pour un tabouret de cuisine, qui vous scie les vertèbres, afin de *rester éveillé* ?

— Exactement !

— Et le royaume ? interrogea doucement le prince héritier.

— Quoi, le royaume ?

— Le royaume, Majesté, qui vous regarde depuis deux heures, épuisé, sans oser vous suggérer de changer de siège. Dois-je comprendre que nous sommes gouvernés par un homme que seul un meuble inconfortable maintient en état de conscience ?

Le roi parut se dégonfler comme une baudruche piquée.

— Ce n'est pas… balbutia-t-il. Ce n'est pas tout à fait…

— *Personne ne va le dire ?* répéta le bouffon en se tournant vers la cour.

Le Grand Chambellan, sentant que l'Histoire allait l'engloutir, fit un pas en avant.

— Majesté, dit-il avec toute la dignité dont il était capable, peut-être pourrions-nous trouver un siège *à la fois* confortable et susceptible de vous garder éveillé ?

Le roi le dévisagea. Longuement. Puis, avec une lenteur de cérémonie, il se leva du tabouret.

— Très bien, soupira-t-il. Qu'on aille chercher une chaise de jardin.

Ce soir-là, quand le roi s'endormit pour la cinquième fois au milieu d'un édit sur la taxation des moulins, la cour comprit qu'on n'avait pas encore tout résolu.

Mais au moins, on avait dit le mot.

Et quelque part dans les communs, la cuisinière retrouva son tabouret, marqué de l'empreinte royale — petite consolation dans un royaume qui ne savait plus très bien sur quel pied danser.

**FIN**

**The Clockmaker's Apprentice**

The bell above the shop door chimed softly as Mara pushed it open, shaking the snow from her coat. The smell of old brass and wood polish wrapped around her like a memory she couldn't quite place.

"Mr. Holloway? It's me, Mara."

No answer.

She stepped further into the dim shop, where hundreds of clocks lined the walls, each one keeping its own time. Some ticked loudly, others whispered, and a few stood silent, their faces frozen in moments long past. Mr. Holloway had always said every stopped clock held a secret, if you knew how to listen.

"Mr. Holloway?" she called again.

She found him in the back room, slumped over his workbench, a magnifying glass still held loosely in his weathered hand. A half-finished clock lay before him, its gears scattered like a constellation across the wood.

Mara's breath caught. She knelt beside him, her fingers finding his wrist, then pulling away quickly. His skin was cold, but there was something peaceful in his face, something almost smiling.

"I'm sorry, old friend," she whispered.

She sat with him for a long time, the clocks filling the silence with their endless chorus. When she finally rose, her eyes fell on a small envelope tucked beneath his hand. Her name was written on it in his careful, slanted script.

*For Mara, when I'm gone.*

She opened it with trembling fingers.

*Dear girl,*

*If you're reading this, I've finally run out of time. Don't be sad. I've had a full life, measured in springs and clockwork.*

*I'm leaving you the shop. I know you always said you didn't want it, but I also know you've been fixing my clocks better than I have for years now.*

*There's one more thing I need to ask of you. The clock on the top shelf, the one with the blue face—I never told you the truth about it. It's not from this world. I built it from pieces I found in a place I shouldn't have been, a place between seconds, where time folds back on itself.*

*I've been too afraid to wind it. But I think you should.*

*Mara, whatever you do, don't ask it the wrong question.*

*Yours in all hours,*
*Edmund*

Mara looked up at the shelf. There it was, smaller than she remembered, its blue face shimmering like a deep winter sky. She reached for it carefully, surprised by how light it was, as if it held nothing at all inside.

The clocks in the shop seemed to quiet as she held it.

She found the winding key on the back, hesitated, then turned it.

The clock made no sound. But something shifted in the air, a feeling like the moment between waking and sleep. The blue face began to glow, soft and steady.

A voice came from everywhere and nowhere, gentle as grandfather's hands.

**"You have wound me. You may ask one question. Choose carefully."**

Mara's heart hammered. A thousand questions crowded her mind. *Where do we go when we die? Can I see my mother again? What does it all mean?*

But Edmund's warning echoed in her: *Don't ask it the wrong question.*

She thought of the old man lying cold on the workbench. She thought of the clocks, each holding a different moment. She thought of how time had always been the one thing she feared most, running out, slipping away, never enough.

Then she asked, quietly, the only question that mattered:

"What time is it?"

The blue face pulsed once.

**"Now,"** the voice said. **"It is always now. And now is enough."**

The light faded. The clock went silent. But Mara could have sworn the hands had moved, just slightly, into a shape that looked almost like a smile.

She placed the clock carefully back on the shelf, kissed her fingertips, and pressed them to Edmund's forehead.

"Goodbye, old friend. I'll take good care of them."

As she walked back through the shop, she paused, and for the first time in years, the clocks didn't sound like they were running out.

They sounded like they were arriving.

# The Lighthouse Keeper's Secret

The fog rolled in thick that evening, swallowing the coastline whole. Eleanor Hartwell climbed the spiral stairs of Cape Misery Lighthouse for the last time, her hands steady on the salt-worn railing. Forty-three years she'd tended this light, and tomorrow the automated system would replace her. Progress, they called it.

At the top, she found him waiting. Thomas Greer, the man who'd once been her husband's closest friend. The man she'd last seen on the night her husband, William, had disappeared twenty-three years ago.

"You knew I'd come," she said, setting down her coffee thermos on the windowsill. Outside, the beam swept through the darkness, painting circles over the black water.

Thomas flinched. "Eleanor, please. I just wanted to talk before—"

"Before I told someone what I knew?" She moved to the light mechanism, her fingers brushing the great brass lens that had guided countless ships home. "I've had twenty-three years to think about this moment, Thomas. Twenty-three years of pretending I didn't see what I saw."

He went pale. "I know what you did," Eleanor continued, her voice soft as the fog against the glass. "I know what you did to William."

"It was an accident." The words came out strangled. "You were never supposed to find out. The storm that night—it wasn't planned. The rocks weren't meant to—" He stopped himself, his confession tumbling out like water through cracked stone.

Eleanor turned to face him. In the sweeping light, she looked ancient and terrible, a woman carved from salt and sorrow.

"No one will believe you," Thomas said, a desperate edge creeping into his voice. "A retired lighthouse keeper, confused in her old age. A grieving widow who never accepted the truth. That's what they'll say."

"Maybe." Eleanor reached into her cardigan pocket and withdrew a small recorder. "But the Coast Guard will. The insurance investigators will. The courts will." She pressed play, and Thomas's own voice filled the lamp room, damning and clear.

Outside, the fog began to lift. In the harbor below, the fishing boats were coming home, guided by a light that had never once failed them.

# The Ledger of Small Returns

The diner on Route 9 had been a truck stop for sixty years, but the vinyl booths were new, the coffee was weak, and the pie was honest. Eleanor Carter chose the seat by the window where the winter light came through dirty glass and made everything look like a faded photograph.

She ordered coffee she didn't want and waited.

He arrived at 9:47, three minutes late, looking like a man who had been losing small wars for a very long time. His coat was the wrong weight for the weather. His eyes did the thing she remembered—they moved too quickly, cataloguing exits, counting witnesses, searching for the shape of a trap.

"Ellie."

"Don't call me that."

"Wren, then. Eleanor. Whatever you're using now."

She didn't offer her hand. She didn't smile. She laid her phone on the table between them, screen down, like a card she'd been saving.

"Fifteen years," she said.

"I know."

"You left a note. One line. *Don't try to find me.* I didn't. I tried to understand, which was worse."

He sat. He didn't reach for a menu. He looked like he hadn't eaten in a day, maybe two.

"You said in your letter that you'd explain someday."

"I did."

"It's someday, Frank."

The waitress came. He ordered toast and nothing else. She watched his hands around the coffee cup—how the knuckles had changed, how the wedding ring was gone, how there was a pale line on his finger where the sun hadn't touched in years.

He didn't start at the beginning. He started in the middle, the way people do when they've rehearsed.

"I didn't leave because I stopped loving you. I left because I had become a man I didn't recognize, and I was going to make you into a woman I didn't want you to be. I could feel it happening—the way I was starting to count your smiles, the way I was rehearsing your answers before you gave them. I was building a small, exact replica of you in my head and then being angry when the real one didn't fit."

She listened. She did not nod.

"I owed money," he said. "Not gambling. Not anything you'd guess. I owed it to a man I'd borrowed from when your mother was sick, because the insurance wouldn't cover the experimental treatment, and I was not going to let her die on a waiting list. I borrowed from the wrong person. When I couldn't pay, he offered me an arrangement. I declined. He suggested I decline again. I took the money I had and I left, and I spent the next decade working it off, one job at a time, in towns with different names."

"You could have told me."

"I could have. I didn't. That's the truth of it. I made a choice to protect you from a choice I'd already made badly, and in doing so, I hurt you worse than the original problem would have. I know that. I've always known that."

She stirred her coffee. The spoon clinked against the mug in a way that sounded like a small bell.

"Give me one good reason to trust you," she said. Not loud. Not angry. The voice of a woman who had packed the question carefully for a long trip and was now setting it on the table between them, like a small, live thing.

He thought about it. She could see him sifting through the rehearsed speeches, the prepared appeals. She watched him put them down, one by one, the way a man lays down cards he knows won't win.

"I don't have one," he said.

She blinked.

"I have nothing that would convince a sensible person. I left you. I didn't trust you with my trouble, which is its own kind of lie. I am asking you to take a risk on a man who has, up until this moment, not earned it. I can tell you I love you. That is true and it is also free, and you should not have to pay for the truth with anything you can't afford to lose."

The toast came. He didn't touch it.

"The only reason I have," he said, "is the small one. That I have spent fifteen years becoming the kind of man who could sit here and say *I don't have a reason* and mean it. That the man who left could not have said it. He would have had a speech. He would have had a plan. This man just has a piece of toast and a question."

She was quiet for a long time. The diner filled with the small sounds of spoons and the weather.

"My mother died," she said. "Four years after you left. The treatment didn't work anyway. I thought about calling you. I decided you had chosen not to be a person I could call, and that I had to learn to live in a world shaped like that."

He closed his eyes. He didn't ask for forgiveness. She noticed that, and it mattered to her in a way she didn't expect.

"I don't want to come back into your life," he said. "I want to be allowed to be in whatever part of it, if any, that you choose. I want to send you a letter once a month, with nothing in it except a true thing about my week. You don't have to read them. You don't have to answer. If after a year you want me to stop, I stop. If you want me to explain more, I will. If you want to walk out of this diner and never look back, I will sit here and finish this terrible toast and that will be the last you ever hear of me."

She looked out the window at the parking lot, at the way the frost was melting on a red pickup truck.

"One letter a month," she said. "One true thing. Nothing about us. Nothing about the past. Just a true thing about your week, and I will read them, and I will not answer, and I will decide at the end of a year."

He nodded. He did not smile. He did not reach across the table. He ate a corner of the toast.

She left money for both their coffees. She stood.

"Eleanor," he said.

She stopped, but didn't turn.

"You asked for one good reason. I told you I didn't have one. I want to give you the small honest thing instead, which is this: I came here prepared for you to say no. I came here prepared to be wrong about myself for the rest of my life. That is not a reason. It is the weather I am willing to walk home in."

She stood there for a breath. Then she left, and the bell over the door made the small sound that small bells make, and outside the air was very cold, and the sun had just come out, and her shadow on the pavement was sharp and singular, and no one else's.

She did not look back.

But three weeks later, an envelope came. Inside, on a plain card, in handwriting she half-recognized:

*I learned the name of every tree on the road I take to work. I did not know there were so many. The man at the gas station told me most of them. He has not charged me for this knowledge. I think he is lonely.*

She read it twice. She put it in a drawer. She did not write back.

At the end of the year, she wrote one line on a card of her own, and mailed it to the address he'd given her, which turned out to be a P.O. box in a town she had never heard of:

*Send the next one to my address. I will answer, but not about us. Not yet. Tell me about the trees.*

And somewhere in a small room in a town she had never heard of, a man who had been losing small wars for a very long time opened an envelope and sat down very slowly, and did not cry, because he had learned by then that the things you are given back, when you are given anything back at all, are not to be spent quickly.

He went to the window. There was a tree out there he had learned the name of in October, and he had forgotten it, and now he would have to learn it again, because he was going to have to write it down, because someone was going to read it, because he had been, against all the small odds of his life, allowed to keep going.

# The Cage and the Canopy

The lock had rusted shut decades ago, but that hadn't stopped the old woman from trying. Every morning, she knelt by the iron gate and pulled at it with fingers that remembered strength they no longer possessed. Every night, she slept with her back against the bars, as if even in dreams she couldn't bear to be separated from her one obsession.

Her name was Miriam, and she was ninety-three years old. The townspeople called her the Keeper of the Aviary, though most had forgotten why.

The structure that surrounded her had once held dozens of birds. Now it held only one—a small, gray songbird that perched on a twisted branch and watched her with one bright eye.

"Tomorrow," Miriam whispered to the bird each evening. "Tomorrow, I'll get it open. I swear I will."

She'd been saying this for sixty years.

---

When Miriam was thirty-two, her husband, Ezra, had built the aviary for her. It was a gift, a marvel of curved iron and climbing roses, meant to surround her in song while she recovered from the fever that had nearly taken her life.

"The world needs to hear you sing again," he'd said, fitting the last pane of glass into the dome.

She'd laughed then, her voice rusty from weeks of silence. "I never sang well."

"You sang for me," he'd said. "That's all that matters."

The birds arrived in baskets. Finches from Spain, a pair of lovebirds from Africa, a thrush with a throat of gold. For one perfect summer, the aviary rang with their music, and Miriam walked the paths among them, finally healthy, finally joyful.

Then Ezra died. A carriage accident, sudden and senseless, leaving her alone in a world that had grown too large.

The birds escaped within the year. Some flew off when she forgot to latch the doors. Others she released herself, opening their cages one by one, watching them vanish into the sky with something like grief and something like relief.

All except one. A plain gray thing that refused to leave, that perched on her shoulder as she wept and pecked gently at her tears.

"You're a fool," she told it. "Go on. Be free."

It never did.

---

On the morning of her ninety-third birthday, Miriam woke to find the lock had finally given way. Rust and time had done what she could not. The gate stood open, just a crack, just enough.

She stared at it for a long time.

The bird watched her from its branch.

"I could walk out," she said. The words felt strange. "I could leave this place."

She had been a prisoner of her own making so long that the concept of leaving required a kind of translation, as if she were learning a new language.

She thought of the town beyond the aviary walls. The bakery on the corner where she'd once bought Ezra his morning bread. The church where they'd married. The river where they'd swam on hot summer days, laughing like children. All of it waiting for her, just beyond the rusted gate.

Miriam stood. Her knees cracked. Her hands trembled.

The bird hopped along its branch, tilting its head.

"Not yet," she said to it. "Not yet."

She walked, instead, to the small chest where she kept her treasures. Inside, she found what she was looking for: a yellowed letter, a pressed rose, and a small brass key.

She didn't remember keeping a key. She must have made it, long ago, in one of her saner moments. A backup, in case the lock ever failed.

She knelt by the bird's cage—a smaller cage within the larger one, the original home she'd never had the heart to dismantle. The lock on it was newer, sturdier, kept oiled through decades of habit.

She fit the key into it.

The bird watched. It did not flutter. It did not sing.

Miriam turned the key.

The cage door swung open with a soft creak.

For a long moment, nothing happened. The bird simply sat there, as it had always sat, gray and small and waiting.

Then it ruffled its feathers. It blinked. It looked at her, really looked, and she saw something in its eye that she had never seen before.

Recognition. And permission.

"Go on," Miriam whispered. "Be free."

The bird hopped to the edge of its cage. It considered the open door, the vast expanse of the aviary beyond, the cracked gate that led to the sky.

Then it opened its beak.

It had never sung before. Not in all the years she'd kept it. She had assumed it was a mute, or a plain creature without music in its throat.

But now, in the morning light, it sang.

The sound was small and clear and sweet, a single note that hung in the air like a held breath. Then another. Then a cascade, a tumbling melody that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere, from the walls of the aviary, from the twisted roses, from the morning itself.

Miriam closed her eyes. Tears slid down her cheeks, but for the first time in sixty years, they were not tears of grief.

She felt a flutter against her hand. A small weight, there and gone.

When she opened her eyes, the bird was gone. Just a feather, drifting down from the open dome, catching the light.

And beyond the cracked gate, a small gray shape, rising.

---

Miriam stood in her aviary for a long time after that. She gathered her treasures. She tucked the letter and the rose into her pocket. She picked up the brass key.

When she stepped through the gate, the town was waiting.

Not the town of her memory—that town was dust and memory now—but a new town, built on the bones of the old, with strangers who glanced at her with curiosity but not unkindness. A young girl offered to help her across the street. A baker pressed a warm loaf into her hands, refusing payment.

In the churchyard, she found Ezra's grave. She sat beside it and told him everything—the years, the birds, the lock that finally gave way.

"I kept my promise," she said. "I got it open."

The wind stirred the leaves of the old oak tree above her.

On the way home, she stopped at the river. She took off her shoes. She waded in, the cold water shocking and sweet against her ankles.

She laughed.

It was the first time she'd laughed in sixty years.

---

That night, she slept in a real bed for the first time since her husband's death. Outside her window, she heard something she had not heard in a very long time.

A bird, singing.

Not in a cage. Not in an aviary. Just singing, free and wild, somewhere in the dark.

"I'm free," she whispered to the empty room.

And somewhere, far above, a small gray shape wheeled through the stars, and sang back.

---

**THE END**

# Forse in un'altra vita

Il caffè al *Caffè delle Rose* aveva lo stesso sapore di sempre: amaro, denso, con quel retrogusto di tostatura che si attaccava al palato. Marco lo sorseggiava lentamente, osservando la pioggia scivolare lungo i vetri della vetrina. Erano passati tre anni dall'ultima volta che aveva messo piede in quel bar.

Tre anni da quando aveva voltato le spalle a tutto.

Il campanello sopra la porta tintinnò. Marco non alzò lo sguardo, troppo impegnato a fingere di leggere il giornale che teneva aperto davanti a sé. Ma poi sentì una voce, e il suo cuore si fermò.

«Un cappuccino, per favore. Senza schiuma, come piace a me.»

No. Non poteva essere.

Alzò lo sguardo e il mondo sembrò rallentare. Lei era lì, in piedi al bancone, con i capelli raccolti in una coda disordinata e quella sciarpa rossa che lui le aveva regalato per il compleanno, anni prima, in un'altra vita. O forse in questa.

Elena si voltò, come se avesse percepito il suo sguardo. I loro occhi si incontrarono.

Il tempo si fermò.

«Marco?» mormorò lei, e nella sua voce c'era tutto: sorpresa, paura, gioia, dolore.

«Ciao, Elena.»

Si fissarono per un istante che parve durare un'eternità. Il barista tossicchiò, imbarazzato, e Marco fece un cenno verso la sedia di fronte a lui.

«Posso?» chiese lei, esitante.

«Ti prego.»

Elena si sedette, avvolgendo le mani attorno alla tazza come faceva sempre quando era nervosa. Un'abitudine che lui conosceva bene. Un'abitudine che gli spezzava il cuore.

«Non sapevo che tornassi in città», disse lei.

«Sono tornato la settimana scorsa. Per lavoro.»

Annuì, e un silenzio imbarazzato calò tra loro. Quante cose avrebbero dovuto dirsi. Quante cose non si erano mai dette.

«Mi dispiace», sussurrò Elena. «Per come è finita.»

Marco scosse la testa. «Non dispiacerti. Avevi ragione tu. Sono stato io a sbagliare.»

«Eravamo entrambi in errore. Troppo giovani, troppo presi dalle nostre paure.»

«Forse.»

Elena abbassò lo sguardo sulla tazza. «Mi sono sposata, lo sai.»

«Lo so. Ho visto le foto. Auguri, erano in ritardo.»

«Grazie. È un brav'uomo. Mi vuole bene davvero.»

«Ne sono felice.»

Ancora silenzio. La pioggia continuava a battere contro i vetri, e il mondo fuori sembrava lontano, irreale.

«E tu?» chiese lei, alzando finalmente gli occhi. «Ti sei rifatto una vita?»

Marco sorrise, un sorriso amaro. «Ci ho provato. Ma non sono mai riuscito a dimenticare questo bar, questo caffè, questa città.»

Elena abbassò di nuovo lo sguardo. «Neanche io.»

Restarono in silenzio per un lungo momento, due estranei uniti da un passato che non smetteva di far male.

«Forse», disse Marco, e la voce gli si ruppe in gola, «forse in un'altra vita, le cose sarebbero andate diversamente.»

Elena lo guardò, e nei suoi occhi brillò qualcosa che somigliava a una lacrima trattenuta. «Sì, Marco. Forse in un'altra vita.»

Si alzò, lasciando una banconota sul tavolo. Prima di andare, si fermò un istante, come se volesse dire qualcosa. Poi si voltò e uscì dal bar, e Marco restò lì, solo, con il suo caffè ormai freddo e il cuore pieno di una malinconia che non lo avrebbe mai abbandonato.

Fuori, la pioggia continuava a cadere, lavando via le promesse non mantenute, i sogni infranti, le parole mai dette.

E in qualche parte della città, Elena camminava sotto l'acqua, con la sciarpa rossa che le copriva il viso perché nessuno vedesse le sue lacrime.

Forse in un'altra vita, sarebbero stati felici.

Ma non in questa.

# The Long Road

The old mason looked up from his work as a young journalist approached, notebook in hand.

"Mr. Castellano," the journalist said, brushing dust from his sleeves, "I've been sent to write a story about the cathedral's restoration. They say you've been working on it for forty years. Is that true?"

Giuseppe Castellano set down his chisel and smiled, wiping his weathered hands on a cloth. "Forty-three, actually. I started when I was twenty-two."

The journalist blinked. "Forty-three years on a single building? Don't you ever get... tired?"

Giuseppe laughed, a warm sound that echoed off the ancient stone walls. "Tired? Never. Frustrated, sometimes. Discouraged, often. But tired? No, my friend. You see this archway here?"

He gestured to a magnificent curve of stone that seemed to glow in the afternoon light streaming through the scaffolding.

"I laid the first stone of this archway in 1981. My father helped me. He died in 1995. My son laid stones with me starting in 2005, but he moved to Milan for work in 2012. My apprentice Marco joined me in 2018. He has the steady hands I had thirty years ago."

The journalist scribbled furiously. "But surely, with modern equipment, you could finish faster?"

"Faster?" Giuseppe considered the word carefully. "Perhaps. But the cathedral wasn't built quickly either. The original builders began in 1347. They finished in 1620. Two hundred and seventy-three years. And do you know what happened in all that time?"

"No?"

"Generations were born and died. Wars came and went. Famines struck, then harvests. People changed their minds about the design. Some architects gave up. Others picked up the work. The cathedral is the product of countless hands, countless intentions, countless dreams."

He picked up his chisel again and ran a finger along the cool stone.

"When I started here, I thought I would finish it in ten years. Then twenty. I used to lie awake at night worrying that I would die before the restoration was complete. But one day, maybe fifteen years ago, I understood something."

"What was that?"

Giuseppe looked at the young man with kind eyes. "I am not the owner of this work. I am merely a keeper. For this brief time, the cathedral passes through my hands. When I am gone, someone else will take up the chisel. Or perhaps no one will, and the work will rest. Either way, it is not mine to finish."

The journalist looked up from his notebook. "But don't you want to see it complete? To say 'I did this'?"

"Ah, ego." Giuseppe smiled again. "I have spent a lifetime learning to let go of ego. Do you know what I have instead? I have had the privilege of touching this stone, of contributing my small part to something greater than myself. When I lay a stone, I think of the mason who came before me, and I try to honor his work. When I lay the next stone, I will think of those who will come after."

He tapped a particular stone in the archway.

"This one here. I have been trying to get it right for six months. It was placed by the original builders, but it had shifted. I removed it last October, and I have been shaping its replacement ever since. Six months for a single stone. When it is done, no one will see it. It will simply be part of the whole, indistinguishable from its neighbors."

The journalist frowned. "That seems... wasteful."

"Wasteful?" Giuseppe's eyes twinkled. "Six months of my life, poured into a stone that no one will notice. Yes, I suppose it is. But this is how cathedrals are built. Stone by stone. Day by day. Generation by generation."

He paused, looking at the soaring walls around them.

"There is a saying my father used to tell me. 'Rome wasn't built in a day.' I used to think it meant that great things take time. But now I think it means something else."

"What?"

"It means that Rome was never *finished*. It is still being built. By everyone who lays a brick, who teaches a child, who plants a tree, who writes a book. The building never ends. It only continues."

The journalist closed his notebook slowly.

"So you will never finish."

"I will finish my part," Giuseppe said. "And then I will rest. And someone else will continue. That is enough. That is more than enough."

He picked up his chisel, then paused.

"You might write that in your article. Tell them the old mason says not to be afraid of work that cannot be completed. Tell them to begin anyway. Begin with a single stone, and trust that the hands that follow will know what to do."

The journalist nodded, tucking his pencil behind his ear. As he turned to leave, Giuseppe called after him.

"And young man?"

"Yes?"

"Whatever you are building — your career, your family, your character — be patient. Rome wasn't built in a day. And neither were you."

The journalist smiled, thanked him, and walked out into the piazza, where the cathedral's ancient bells began to ring, marking the hour as they had for six hundred years, calling generation after generation to begin again.

# Ostatni Gość Kawiarni Pod Złamanym Zegarem

Deszcz padał nieprzerwanie od trzech dni, jakby ktoś gdzieś wysoko zapomniał zakręcić kranu. W takie wieczory kawiarnia Pod Złamanym Zegarem zwykle świeciła pustkami, ale tamtego piątku, dwudziestego trzeciego listopada, przy stoliku pod oknem siedział mężczyzna w wyświechtanym szarym płaszczu.

Ewa, właścicielka kawiarni, wycierała kubek ściereczką już czwarty raz, choć był czysty od dawna. Obserwowała go kątem oka. Nie zamówił nic od godziny. Popijał tylko wodę, którą przyniosła mu z litości, gdy zobaczyła, jak wpatruje się w puste menu, nie mogąc się zdecydować.

Nie było w nim nic szczególnego. Twarz zwyczajna, może czterdzieści, może pięćdziesiąt lat — trudno powiedzieć. Ręce spokojne, zbyt spokojne, jakby należały do kogoś, kto dawno przestał się spieszyć. Ale to oczy nie dawały jej spokoju. Patrzył na deszcz za oknem tak, jakby widział w nim coś, czego inni nie mogli zobaczyć.

O dziewiątej, kiedy ostatni gość — starszy pan czytający gazetę — wreszcie wyszedł, Ewa postanowiła podejść.

— Panie, zamykamy za piętnaście minut — powiedziała, stawiając na stole małą filiżankę espresso, które postawiła przy kasie, na szczęście. Był to jej gest, zwykle zarezerwowany dla stałych bywalców.

Mężczyzna podniósł wzrok. Uśmiechnął się lekko, z czymś, co przypominało wdzięczność, ale też smutek.

— Dziękuję pani. Za wszystko. — Przesunął palcem po krawędzi filiżanki, nie podnosząc jej. — Wie pani, ja tu kiedyś bywałem. Dawno temu. Zanim kupno tego lokalu.

Ewa zmarszczyła brwi. Kupiła kawiarnię siedem lat temu.

— Nie wydaje mi się. Ja tu jestem od lat.

— *Siedem* lat — powiedział cicho, jakby potwierdzał coś, co już wiedział. — A ja przyszedłem tu dziewięć lat temu. Na jedną noc. Przy tym samym stoliku. Zamówiłem wtedy szarlotkę i herbatę z cytryną.

Serce Ewy na chwilę zamarło. Szarlotka. Przez pierwsze lata prowadzenia kawiarni piekła szarlotkę według przepisu swojej babci. Była to jedyna rzecz, którą zmieniła w menu, gdy przejęła lokal. *Szarlotka z cynamonem i wanilią, podawana na ciepło z gałką lodów.*

— Skąd pan wie?

Mężczyzna wreszcie sięgnął po filiżankę. Upił łyk. Na jego twarzy pojawił się wyraz spokoju, jakby to, co pił, było wodą z innego źródła, nie zwykłym espresso.

— Pamiętam też deszcz — ciągnął. — I pustą ulicę. I to, że ostatni klient wyszedł o dwudziestej pierwszej, a pani postawiła mi espresso, choć go nie zamawiałem. Bo byłem smutny. I pani to widziała.

Ewa cofnęła się o krok. Filiżanka, którą trzymała, zadrżała w jej dłoni.

— Kim pan jest?

Mężczyzna odstawił espresso i spojrzał na nią prosto, po raz pierwszy tego wieczoru, z całą uwagą.

— To jest właśnie pytanie, które zadaję sobie od dziewięciu lat, pani Ewo. I wreszcie znam odpowiedź. Jestem tym, którego pani uratowała. Tego wieczoru.

— Ratowała? Nic nie rozumiem.

Mężczyzna wyciągnął z kieszeni płaszcza złożoną kartkę — pożółkłą, ze sfatygowanymi rogami. Położył ją na stole i przesunął w jej stronę.

Ewa rozłożyła ją drżącymi rękami. Był to jej własny charakter pisma, choć nie pamiętała, żeby cokolwiek pisała.

*„Nie odchodź. Deszcz się skończy. Szarlotka dnia następnego jest najlepsza. Zjedz ją powoli. Poczekaj na słońce."*

— To... to moje — wyszeptała.

— Pani napisała to do mnie, gdy wychodziłem stąd tamtego wieczoru. Powiedziała pani, że zostawiła to na serwetce w kawiarni obok. Myślałem, że pani żartuje, ale schowałem kartkę do kieszeni. — Uśmiechnął się, a w kącikach jego oczu pojawiły się zmarszczki. — Tamtego wieczoru zamierzałem wrócić do domu i zrobić coś strasznego. Straciłem żonę, pracę, sens. Wszystko naraz. Nie widziałem powodu, żeby iść dalej. A pani zostawiła mi te słowa na serwetce w kawiarni, w której nigdy nie byłem. Pani, która nigdy mnie nie spotkała. A mimo to podała mi pani kawę, gdy byłem na dnie.

Ewa oparła się o kontuar. Pokój zawirował jej przed oczami.

— To niemożliwe — szepnęła. — Ja nigdy...

— Wiem, że pani tego nie pamięta. — Mężczyzna wstał, wygładzając płaszcz. — Ale ja pamiętam. I przyszedłem, żeby podziękować.

Wyciągnął rękę. Na jego nadgarstku Ewa zauważyła delikatną bliznę — starą, wyblakłą. Ciągnęła się od wewnętrznej strony dłoni do przedramienia.

— *Who are you?* — zapytała po angielsku, nie wiedząc dlaczego. Może dlatego, że słowa po polsku nie wystarczały.

Mężczyznę rozbawiło to pytanie. Zaśmiał się cicho, szczerze, po raz pierwszy tego wieczoru.

— Jestem Wojciech. Jestem nauczycielem muzyki w szkole podstawowej na Pradze. Mam trzydzieścioro dzieci w klasie, wszyscy mnie uwielbiają, choć jestem strasznie wymagający. Gram na pianinie wieczorami w domu kultury. Mam kota, którego nazwałem Elliot, bo lubię proste imiona. I każdego ranka, od dziewięciu lat, wstaję i myślę o pani serwetce. I o tym, że gdzieś tam jest ktoś, kto widzi więcej, niż powinien. — Zamilkł na chwilę. — A pani? Kim pani jest?

Ewa otworzyła usta, żeby odpowiedzieć czymś prostym — *jestem Ewą, mam kawiarnię, lubię czytać kryminały* — ale zamiast tego powiedziała:

— Jestem zmęczona. I samotna. I przestraszona. I nie rozumiem, co się dzieje.

Wojciech skinął głową powoli.

— Ja też tak się czułem. Dziewięć lat temu. A potem ktoś zostawił mi serwetkę. — Wskazał na kartkę w jej dłoni. — I ta ktoś, kimkolwiek była, sprawiła, że poszedłem dalej.

Deszcz za oknem ustał nagle, jak nożem uciął. W ciszy, która zapadła, Ewa usłyszała tykanie starego zegara na ścianie — tego, od którego kawiarnia brała swoją nazwę. Złamany Zegar. Kupiła go razem z lokalem i nigdy go nie naprawiła. Wskazówki stały nieruchomo od lat, na godzinie trzeciej i piętnastej minucie.

Ale teraz, przez jedną krótką chwilę, wskazówka drgnęła. Ruszyła do przodu o jedną sekundę.

I znów stanęła.

— *Czy my się już kiedyś spotkaliśmy?* — zapytała Ewa, choć znała odpowiedź. Wiedziała to z taką pewnością, z jaką wie się, że po zimie przychodzi wiosna.

Wojciech uśmiechnął się. Położył dłoń na serwetce, przykrywając na chwilę jej dłoń swoją. Był ciepły. Zupełnie, cudownie ciepły.

— Spotkaliśmy się w miejscu, które nie istnieje. W deszczu, którego już nie ma. W godzinie, która nigdy nie wybiła. I oboje mieliśmy szczęście, że to spotkanie w ogóle się wydarzyło.

Wyszedł, zanim zdążyła go zatrzymać. Dzwoneczek nad drzwiami zadzwonił cicho, jakby z westchnieniem ulgi.

Ewa stała przy oknie i patrzyła, jak jego postać znika za rogiem, w ciemności, która już nie była taka straszna. Spojrzała na serwetkę w swojej dłoni. Zobaczyła pod spodem, prawie niewidoczny, drugi napis — kobiecy, delikatny, znajomy:

*„Do zobaczenia. Po drugiej stronie deszczu. — E."*

Nie pamiętała, żeby to pisała.

Ale wiedziała, że to zrobiła.

---

Następnego ranka Ewa wyciągnęła złamany zegar ze ściany i zaniosła go do zegarmistrza na rogu.

— Czy da się go naprawić? — zapytała.

Zegarmistrz, starszy mężczyzna z binoklami na nosie, obejrzał mechanizm uważnie, obracał go w rękach, długo milczał.

— Pani Ewo — powiedział wreszcie, zdejmując binokle. — Ten zegar nie jest zepsuty. On po prostu wskazuje czas, który nie istnieje. Godzinę trzecią i piętnastą minut. Godzinę, w której wszystko jest możliwe. Naprawić go to znaczy zniszczyć.

Ewa zabrała zegar do domu.

Postawiła go na półce, w sypialni, obok łóżka.

I co noc, przed snem, słyszała, jak tyka — cicho, miarowo, delikatnie.

Odmierzając czas, który nigdy nie minął.

A czasami, bardzo rzadko, słyszała ciche dzwonienie dzwoneczka nad drzwiami. Jakby ktoś właśnie wchodził do kawiarni, której już nie było.

W pokoju, w którym siedziała kobieta, która nie istniała.

Podając niewidzialną szarlotkę niewidzialnemu gościowi.

I czekając, aż deszcz się skończy.

Bo zawsze się kończył.

Zawsze.

# The Bus Stop

"Bus late again?"

"Ten minutes now."

"Every single day."

"My feet hurt."

"There. The corner."

"Is that it?"

"Has to be. The 7:15 never fails."

"Not when it's snowing."

"You take the 7:15?"

"Used to. Before the divorce."

"Oh."

"Yeah."

"Sorry."

"Don't be. Best thing that ever happened."

"Really?"

"Got the apartment. Got the weekends."

"You sound different than most people."

"My mother says the same thing."

"She's right."

"You don't even know me."

"I know enough."

"What's that supposed to mean?"

"You waited. Even though it's cold."

"You noticed."

"I notice things."

"Is that a compliment?"

"Take it however you want."

"The bus is here."

"Looks full."

"I hate when it's full."

"People pressed together like sardines."

"That's what she said."

"What?"

"Nothing. Forget it."

"You're blushing."

"Am not."

"Are too."

"Goodbye."

"Wait."

"What?"

"I'm getting on too."

"Why should I care?"

"Maybe you shouldn't."

"Stop smiling then."

"I can't help it."

"Your stop?"

"Grandview. And you?"

"Grandview."

"No."

"Yes."

"This is a coincidence."

"Is it?"

"What do you mean?"

"I mean, I asked for a sign this morning."

"From who?"

"The universe."

"And I'm the sign?"

"Maybe."

"This is ridiculous."

"Totally."

"I don't even know your name."

"Eli."

"Maggie."

"Nice to meet you, Maggie."

"Nice to meet you, Eli."

"Same seat?"

"Why not?"

"Mind the gum."

"Always."

"This is strange."

"Good strange or bad strange?"

"I haven't decided."

"Take your time."

"The bus jerks."

"Hold on."

"I am."

"To the rail, Maggie."

"To you, then."

"Excuse me?"

"Nothing. Bad joke."

"Wasn't bad."

"You laughed."

"I did."

"Liar."

"Shut up."

"Make me."

"Excuse me?"

"I said shut up."

"You're ridiculous."

"You smiled."

"I did not."

"Did too."

"Eyes on the window."

"Whatever you say."

"My stop's coming up."

"Mine too."

"Walk together?"

"And then?"

"And then maybe coffee?"

"I don't drink coffee."

"Tea?"

"Hot chocolate."

"That works."

"Chloe's on Third."

"Know it."

"Of course you do."

"Stop it."

"Stop what?"

"Knowing things."

"Not possible."

"Why not?"

"Made up my mind about you."

"Already?"

"Bus stop. Ten minutes. Saw it all."

"That's presumptuous."

"Maybe."

"Truth?"

"Truth."

"Hot chocolate first."

"Then what?"

"Then maybe a second sign."

"From the universe?"

"From you."

"That's cheating."

"Is it?"

"Completely."

"Still in?"

"...yes."

"Grandview stop. Next."

"Ready?"

"No."

"Me neither."

"Here we go."

"Here we go."

"..."

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Say it."

"Your hand's warm."

"So is yours."

"The universe?"

"Shut up, Eli."

"Make me, Maggie."
