# The Last Note

The first time Mei held a violin, she was four years old, and her fingers were so small they could barely curl around the neck. Her father, David, remembered that day with the kind of clarity that comes from photographs and repetition—she standing on a stool in the music shop, chin tilted up like a sparrow, grinning at the woman behind the counter.

That was eleven years ago.

Now David sat in the balcony of Kleinman Hall, legs crossed at the ankle, hands gripping the armrests of his seat. Below him, rows of teenagers shuffled sheet music and tuned instruments, their whispers rising like steam. His daughter was among them, third row, second seat from the left. He could see the top of her head, the precise part down the middle that she insisted on every morning.

Mei was fifteen and auditioning for the youth symphony's first chair. The girl currently holding the position, Annika Voss, had been first chair for two years running. Annika was, in David's estimation, a small mechanical genius—precise, relentless, and utterly humorless. Mei adored her. She also wanted to beat her.

David didn't know this last part. Mei had told him it didn't matter, that she just wanted to audition for the experience, that she would be happy with whatever happened. He believed her. He also believed, in the way parents believe things they suspect are not true, that she had been practicing in her room with her door closed for the last three weeks, that the water glasses on her desk had multiplied mysteriously, that he had heard scales at eleven-thirty at night and pretended not to.

The conductor, a dry man named Mr. Penrose, climbed onto the podium. He tapped his baton once, and the room folded into silence.

Mei's audition piece was *Méditation* from *Thaïs*—a showy choice, David thought, but then what did he know. He was a man who repaired boilers for a living. He had a fine ear for music and a clumsy one for strategy. He had married Mei's mother when they were both twenty-two, and when Lin left him and Mei seven years later, he had kept the apartment, the cat, and the violin, in that order of importance.

He watched Mei lift her bow to the strings.

The first note came out slightly sharp. David felt his stomach dip, the way it did on the first drop of a roller coaster. Then she adjusted—tiny movement of the wrist, a micro-correction—and the third note rang true, and he exhaled.

She played the way she had always played: as though she were listening to something no one else could hear. Her eyes were closed. Her body was slightly off-balance, tilted toward the music as if pulled by a current. David had watched her fall asleep in this same position a hundred times, violin cradled in her lap like a sleeping child.

He thought about her first recital, when she was six, and she had burst into tears halfway through because she thought she had missed a note. He thought about the winter she quit for two months after a mean comment from a classmate. He thought about the time she called him from college—four hours away, too far for his liking—because her orchestra had performed Brahms and she needed to tell someone, anyone, what it had felt like to disappear into the music.

He thought about how he had never told her about any of these moments. How he had simply nodded and handed her the instrument and driven her to lessons and pretended not to notice when she cried.

*Show up*, her mother used to say. *You don't have to understand it. Just show up.*

Lin had been talking about parenting, David suspected, but she had also been talking about him.

Below him, Mei played. The *Méditation* swelled and then went quiet, a long, fragile thread of sound. David found he could not swallow. He could not blink. He was afraid that any movement would break something.

The piece ended. Mei lowered her bow. The room was silent for a beat that lasted approximately one thousand years.

Then Mr. Penrose nodded. The girl beside Mei—Annika herself, David realized—reached over and squeezed Mei's hand.

David sat in his balcony seat and felt something unspool in his chest. It was not joy, exactly, or relief, or pride. It was more like recognition. The sense that a thing he had been carrying for eleven years had finally, gently, been set down.

He did not know yet that Mei would get the chair. He would not know for another hour, when Mr. Penrose called her name and Mei would turn, bewildered, toward the stage, and the room would clap.

What he knew, in this moment, was simpler than any of that. His daughter had walked up to the edge of herself and had not fallen off. She had stood there, bow raised, and played the song she had been practicing in secret, at midnight, in a bedroom with the door closed.

He had not helped her do this. He had not been able to.

He had only shown up.

When the applause finally came, David was already on his feet.

Кафе «Белая акация» стояло на углу Малой Бронной уже тридцать семь лет, и за это время его стены впитали в себя столько тихих признаний и невысказанных слов, что, казалось, воздух здесь был тяжелее, чем где-либо ещё в городе. За круглым столиком у окна сидели двое. Им было около пятидесяти — нет, не вместе, а каждый по отдельности, как две реки, которые когда-то текли в одном направлении, а теперь разделялись континентом.

Мужчина — крупный, с седыми висками и тяжёлым взглядом — разглядывал трещинку на фарфоровой чашке. Женщина — тонкая, с коротко остриженными волосами и морщинками вокруг глаз, появившимися от смеха — смотрела в окно, где медленно падал первый ноябрьский снег.

— Ты помнишь, — начала она, и голос её дрогнул, — как мы сюда пришли в первый раз?

— Помню, — ответил он. — Тебе было двадцать три. Ты заказала торт «Птичье молоко», и он тебе не понравился. Ты сказала — слишком сладко.

— А ты заказал солянку и смеялся, что я сладкоежка.

— А ты сказала, что я не умею пить кофе, потому что добавляю в него сахар.

Они замолчали. Официантка — молодая девушка с тонким серебряным браслетом на запястье — принесла чай. Она поставила чашки на стол, и фарфор тихонько звякнул о фарфор, как будто кто-то аккуратно постучал в дверь.

— Я пришла сказать, — произнесла женщина, и её пальцы сжали край скатерти, — что я подаю на развод.

Мужчина не поднял глаз. Он медленно размешал сахар в чае — одну ложку, вторую, — и металл коснулся керамики с тем особенным звоном, который бывает, когда время останавливается.

— Я знаю, — сказал он наконец.

— Знаешь?

— Я знал с тех пор, как ты перестала называть меня по имени. Сначала ты перестала говорить «Андрюша», потом «Андрей», потом просто «ты» — но как-то по-другому. Я не могу объяснить. Я просто понял.

Женщина откинулась на стуле и впервые за вечер посмотрела ему прямо в лицо. Она искала там гнев, обиду, облегчение — что-нибудь, за что можно было бы зацепиться. Но там было только то странное выражение, которое бывает у людей, когда они очень давно не спали.

— Двадцать семь лет, — прошептала она.

— Двадцать семь лет, — повторил он.

За окном проехал последний троллейбус, осветив жёлтым светом снежинки, которые кружились в своём бесконечном, бессмысленном танце. Внутри кафе пахло корицей, чужим табаком и тем особенным теплом, которое бывает только в местах, где люди пытаются начать сначала или закончить навсегда.

— Я не жалею, — сказала она, и сама не поняла, кому это говорит — ему или себе. — Я не жалею ни одного дня.

— И я, — ответил он. — Ни одного.

Она встала, накинула пальто — тёмно-синее, почти чёрное, — и подняла воротник. Стоя над ним, она вдруг почувствовала, как что-то надломилось в ней, как тонкая ветка под тяжестью мокрого снега. Она не заплакала — она давно разучилась плакать о нём, — но в глазах стало мутно и тепло.

— Прощай, Андрей, — сказала она.

— Прощай, Лена, — сказал он.

Она вышла из кафе и медленно пошла по Малой Бронной, не оглядываясь. Снег падал ей на плечи, и она думала о том, что где-то в мире есть женщина, которая завтра утром впервые назовёт его по имени — и у неё это будет звучать совсем по-другому, легко и радостно, как будто они только что познакомились.

Он сидел за столиком ещё долго. Официантка дважды подходила и дважды возвращалась, не решаясь заговорить. Наконец, он поднял голову и попросил счёт.

— С вас четыреста двадцать рублей, — сказала девушка.

Он заплатил, оставил чаевые и тоже вышел на улицу. Снег уже лежал на тротуарах тонким, нетронутым слоем, и его следы были первыми. Он шёл медленно, и дыхание его застывало в воздухе маленькими облачками, которые тут же исчезали, растворяясь в ноябрьской темноте.

Двадцать семь лет — это целая жизнь. Это дочери, которые уже выросли и разъехались по своим городам. Это квартира, в которой пахло её духами, и эти духи теперь придётся выветривать. Это новогодние ёлки, которые он будет ставить один, и споры о том, какую породу кошки завести, которые больше никогда не повторятся. Это её смех по утрам, и её молчание по вечерам, и тот единственный раз, когда она плакала у него на плече, — он до сих пор помнил, какая у неё была щека — мокрая, горячая, пахнущая лавандой.

Он дошёл до перекрёстка, остановился и посмотрел назад — туда, где ещё виднелось тёплое окно кафе «Белая акация». За стеклом никого не было. Столик у окна уже убрали. Официантка протирала пол.

Он достал телефон и долго смотрел на её имя в списке контактов. Потом убрал телефон в карман и пошёл дальше — в ту сторону, где жил уже двадцать семь лет, но куда теперь возвращался впервые.

Снег продолжал падать. Он заметал их следы — и его, и её, — как будто хотел сказать, что ничего не было. Но мы-то знаем: всё было. И двадцать семь лет, и первый торт «Птичье молоко», и солянка, и спор про кофе, и тот единственный вечер, когда она плакала у него на плече, — всё это было.

И в этом «было» была целая жизнь.

# La Última Moneda

El viento arrastraba arena roja contra las ventanas del motel. Dentro de la habitación número 7, Marcos y Julián se miraban sobre la mesa de metal donde descansaba una moneda de oro entre dos vasos vacíos de whiskey.

—Cabello o cruz —dijo Julián, girando la moneda entre sus dedos. Una sonrisa torcida le cruzaba el rostro—. Esta vez lo decidimos así, como hombres.

Marcos tragó saliva. La luz amarillenta del techo le daba a su compañero un aspecto enfermizo, casi irreal. Hacía doce años que compartían trinchera, éxitos y fracasos. Y ahora, al borde de los cuarenta, todo se reducía a eso: una moneda lanzada al aire para decidir quién heredaba la patente de Biotrópica, la startup que habían fundado en un garaje y que hoy valía millones.

—¿Sabes que no es necesario, verdad? —murmuró Marcos.

—Claro que no. —Julián dejó la moneda sobre la mesa, cara arriba, mostrando un rostro humano grabado en bajorrelieve—. Pero tú siempre has sido mejor con las palabras que yo. Yo necesito... señales.

Marcos conocía cada arruga de ese rostro. También conocía, porque lo había descubierto aquella mañana mientras Julián dormía en el sofá de la oficina, un pequeño truco: una moneda con doble cara. La pieza que su socio guardaba en el bolsillo del chaleco era siempre la misma, sin importar cuántas veces cayera.

Había tenido tres horas para decidir qué hacer con ese conocimiento. Podía denunciarlo, romper la moneda contra el suelo, confesar que sabía. Pero algo más oscuro, algo que él mismo apenas reconocía, había echado raíces en su pecho durante esas horas.

Marcos sacó otra moneda del bolsillo. Idéntica, brillante, sin truco alguno.

—Yo elijo cara —dijo, empujando la moneda real hacia el centro de la mesa.

Julián parpadeó. Por un instante, algo cruzó sus ojos —duda, cálculo, quizás miedo— antes de volver a la sonrisa confiada.

—Como quieras.

Ambos lanzaron al mismo tiempo. Las monedas giraron en el aire viciado del cuarto. Marcos vio cómo la suya caía limpia, mostrando una cruz. La de Julián rodó sobre sí misma durante un segundo interminable, hasta detenerse sobre su canto y quedar apoyada contra el vaso.

Julián estiró el cuello para verla. Marcos también.

—Cruz —dijo Marcos.

Julián no respondió. Tenía los ojos clavados en la moneda: una cruz simple, sin truco, sin trampa. La moneda trampa seguía oculta en su puño cerrado.

El silencio se espesó. Afuera, el viento seguía levantando arena.

—Podía haber elegido la otra —dijo finalmente Julián, con voz extrañamente suave.

—Sí.

—¿Por qué no lo hiciste?

Marcos se levantó, caminó hacia la ventana. En el estacionamiento del motel, un perro flaco olisqueaba una bolsa de basura. La vida seguía, indiferente a las decisiones tomadas en habitaciones de motel a las tres de la mañana.

—Porque quería saber quién eras —respondió sin girarse—. Y quién soy yo.

Julián abrió la mano. La moneda con doble cara rodó hasta el borde de la mesa y cayó al suelo con un sonido hueco.

—Perdí de todas formas, ¿verdad?

Marcos se volvió. En la penumbra, la sonrisa de Julián ya no era la misma. Ni la suya.

—No —dijo Marcos—. Creo que por fin empezamos a ganar.

Fuera, la moneda seguía girando sola sobre la tierra roja, como si el diablo del desierto no terminara de decidir a quién pertenecía.

# 빗소리와 두 개의 커피잔

서울의 어느 비 오는 저녁, 압구정의 한 카페 창가에 두 사람이 앉아 있었다. 하나는 영화감독을 꿈꾸는 26살 미술학도 윤서하, 다른 하나는 그의 영상을 촬영하던 카메라맨 강태오.

## 첫 번째 만남

두 사람이 처음 만난 건 3개월 전, 독립영화 <비 온 날의 기억>의 촬영장에서였다.

"조명 좀 자연스럽게 해주세요. 너무 인공스러워요."

서하의 첫 지시에 태오는 브리프케이스를 내려놓으며 한숨을 내쉬었다.

"연출이랑 조명은 좀 다른 건데. 이 각도에서 이 조명이 가장 자연스러워요. 20년 경력이에요, 나."

"20년 경력이신 분이 초보 감독한테 배우는 꼴은 좀 그렇지 않아요?"

"배우는 게 아니라 협업이라고 하는 거예요."

그렇게 시작된 말다툼은 촬영 내내 멈추지 않았다. 하지만 이상한 건, 기 싸움 끝에 완성된 영상을 보는 순간, 둘 다 동시에 숨을 멈춘 것이다.

## 둘 사이의 균열

태오는 32살. 성공한 광고감독이었지만, 본업이 아닌 독립영화라서 시간도, 돈도 들었다. 그런데 서하의 구상은 끝없이 변했다. 같은 장면을 열다섯 번 찍고도 "아직 마음에 안 들어요"라고 했다.

"감독님, 이 장면 열일곱 번째 찍으시는 거 아세요?"

"완벽한 한 컷을 위해서라면 백 번이라도 찍을 거예요."

"그럼 일정은요?"

"일정은 제가 책임질게요."

그 말에 태오의 표정이 굳었다. 이미 일주일 밀린 스케줄, 빚을 내서 빌린 장비, 스태프들의 야근 수당. 모두 그의 어깨 위에 있었다.

"책임지신다고요?" 태오의 목소리가 낮아졌다. "감독님은 빚 한 푼 안 지셨잖아요."

서하의 눈이 흔들렸다. 태오가 그랬다. 카메라를 들고 있으면 침착하고, 렌즈 너머의 세상만 보는 사람인 줄 알았는데, 사실은 세상 밖의 현실을 누구보다 잘 아는 사람이었다.

## 비 오는 저녁의 진실

촬영이 끝난 지 한 달 후, 카페에서 우연히 마주친 둘. 비는 여전히 창밖을 두드리고 있었고, 두 사람의 앞에는 식어버린 아메리카노 두 잔이 놓여 있었다.

"영화 잘 나왔더라." 태오가 먼저 입을 열었다. "비평에서도 호평이에요."

"고마워요." 서하가 조심스럽게 대답했다. "근데 그때… 일정이랑 돈 때문에 화났던 거, 알아요. 그게 제가 잘못한 거예요."

태오는 한참 동안 서하를 바라보았다. 그리고 묘한 웃음을 흘렸다.

"아니요. 그게 아니라 그게 아니에요."

"뭔 말이에요?"

태오가 커피잔을 들어 천천히 한 모금 마셨다. "감독님 촬영 끝나고 저한테 '수고했어요' 한 마디도 안 했잖아요. 그게 삐졌던 거예요."

서하가 멈칫했다.

"…그게 다였어요?"

"다였죠. 저 카메라맨 하나도 챙기지 않는 감독이라니. 정말 서운했어요."

서하의 눈가가 뜨거워졌다. 사실 그때 스태프 전체에게 인사를 못 했다. 촬영 마무리에 너무 정신이 없었기 때문에. 그걸 태오가 얼마나 오래 품고 있었을지 생각하니, 미안함과 동시에 이상한 감정이 차올랐다.

"…미안해요. 진짜로."

"네, 알겠어요. 근데 다음엔 그때 우리 촬영한 영상 같이 보러 가요. 제 개인 작업이에요."

서하가 눈을 동그랗게 떴다. "개인 작업이라니?"

"저도 가끔 찍어요. 빗속의 도시, 그런 거. 감독님이 좋아할 것 같아서."

태오의 눈이 처음으로 부드러워져 있었다. 서하는 그제야 깨달았다. 그게 카메라 너머의 시선이 아니라, 그냥 진심이었다는 걸.

## 빗속의 도시

그날 이후로 둘은 이상한 관계가 되었다. 만나면 30분 안에 한 번씩은 말다툼을 벌였지만, 헤어지면 또 어색하게 안부를 확인했다. 서하는 태오의 영상을 보고 놀랐다. 그가 찍는 도시는 그녀가 그려보던 도시와 똑같았기 때문이다. 어느덧 둘은 매주 같은 카페에서 만나, 영상을 공유하고, 비평하고, 또 싸우기를 반복했다.

그러던 어느 날, 서하가 태오의 새 영상을 보다가 중얼거렸다.

"이거 내 영화랑 같이 편집하면 어때요?"

"뭐라고요?"

"같이. 말하자면, 당신이 보는 서울이랑 내가 보는 서울이 만나면 어떨지…."

태오가 입을 다물었다. 한참을 망설이다 말했다.

"…좋아요. 해봐요."

그렇게 시작된 콜라보레이션은, 어느덧 서로의 영상을 하나로 엮어가는 작업이 되었다. 서하의 감성이 태오의 렌즈를 통과하면 더 선명해졌고, 태오의 시선이 서하의 손을 거치면 더 깊어졌다. 처음엔 비 오는 장면 하나로 시작했는데, 어느새 계절이 바뀌도록 작업이 이어졌다.

## 두 사람의 결말

1년 뒤, 어느 영화제의 시사회. 그들의 협업 작품 <두 개의 도시>가 상영되었다. 비 내리는 서울을 두 사람의 시선으로 풀어낸 이 영화는, 상영 후 10분간 기립박수를 받았다.

무대 위, 태오가 먼저 마이크를 잡았다.

"이 영화는 감독님의 도시와 저의 도시가 만난 결과입니다. 처음엔 모든 게 다 틀렸는데, 결국엔 모든 게 맞았어요."

스포트라이트 아래, 서하가 태오를 바라보았다. 그리고 씩 웃으며 마이크를 가져갔다.

"네, 맞아요. 이 사람은 늘 제 말이 틀렸다고 했지만, 결국엔 늘 제 말을 들어줬어요. 그리고 듣다 보면 정말로 맞는 말이었어요."

"아니, 제 말도 늘 틀렸다고요?"

"조용히 해요. 지금 제 수상 소감 중이거든요."

관객들이 웃었고, 태오도 웃었다. 빗소리 같은 박수가 그들을 감쌌다.

그래, 그들은 사랑과 증오 사이를 오갔던 게 분명하다. 그런데 사랑과 증오 사이에는 '진심'이 있고, 그 진심이 결국엔 그들 사이의 거리를 좁혔다. 비 내리는 도시에서, 두 사람은 비로소 서로를 똑바로 바라볼 수 있었다.

## 에필로그

시사회가 끝난 후, 둘은 카페에 앉았다. 여전히 같은 자리에, 여전히 두 개의 커피잔.

"감독님, 다음 작품은요?"

"있어요. 근데 이번엔… 촬영 일정은 제가 미리 짤게요."

태오가 피식 웃었다. "그것만으로도 충분해요."

서하도 웃었다. 하지만 이번엔 정말로, 가슴이 뛰는 것을 느꼈다.

Write about two friends who were once inseparable, but now find themselves growing apart — or even friends turned enemies. Roughly 1700 words in length.

# The Weight of Borrowed Time

The café on Fifth Street hadn't changed in seven years. Same scuffed hardwood floors, same chalkboard menu with the prices written in the same careful hand, same faint smell of burnt espresso and old books. Marcus remembered when he and Daniel had discovered it during their first semester at Caldwell University, stumbling in half-soaked from a sudden downpour, laughing so hard at nothing that the barista had smiled at them like they were ridiculous and wonderful.

Now Marcus sat in the corner booth, his coffee growing cold, watching the rain streak down the window.

Daniel was seven minutes late. That used to mean nothing. That used to be the opening act of an evening — Daniel's dramatic entrance, his apologies that weren't really apologies, his hands moving as he spoke, his laugh filling whatever room they were in. Marcus used to love that Daniel ran on his own time, that the world bent around him instead of the other way around.

Now the lateness felt like a small, deliberate cruelty.

"You're here early," Daniel said, sliding into the opposite seat. He was wearing the jacket Marcus had given him for his thirtieth birthday. It looked better on him. It always had.

"Traffic," Marcus lied.

Daniel raised an eyebrow but didn't press it. He ordered his usual — oat milk latte, extra shot — and for a moment they sat in the kind of silence that used to be comfortable. The kind where you didn't need to fill the air because the air was already full.

"So," Daniel said, after the barista left. "You said we needed to talk."

Marcus turned his coffee cup in his hands. He'd been turning it for three weeks, ever since he'd seen the email. The one from Dr. Elena Voss at the university, congratulating Daniel Chen on his appointment to the research chair in Theoretical Physics. The one that mentioned, almost as an afterthought, that Daniel would be relocating to Geneva in the spring.

Three weeks of turning the cup, and still no words.

"Marcus."

"I heard about Geneva."

Something flickered across Daniel's face — guilt, maybe, or just surprise that Marcus knew. "I was going to tell you."

"When?"

"This week. I was going to tell you this week."

"You've known for two months."

The coffee arrived. Daniel wrapped his hands around the cup like he needed something to hold onto. "I was trying to figure out how."

"Figure out how to tell me my best friend is leaving the continent? Was there a diagram? A PowerPoint?"

"Don't." Daniel's voice was quiet but firm. "Don't do that."

"Then tell me what to do."

The rain was louder now, drumming against the windows. Around them, the café continued its soft, oblivious life — a couple laughing in the corner, a student typing furiously on a laptop, the barista wiping down the counter with the same bored rhythm she'd probably used for years.

"Tell me you didn't know," Marcus said. "Tell me you were going to tell me the night you got the offer, the way you would have, three years ago. Tell me you would have come to my apartment at midnight with a bottle of wine and we'd have stayed up planning my visit."

Daniel's jaw tightened. "Things are different now."

"Different how?"

"You know how."

Marcus did know. He knew the way you know a wound — by the exact shape of it, the way it pulls when you move.

It had started two years ago, in the spring after Marcus's divorce. He'd come out of it hollowed, bitter, convinced that love was a trap and trust was just the lock on the door. Daniel had been there, the way Daniel always was — patient, present, willing to sit with Marcus in his worst moments without trying to fix them.

But somewhere in that season, something had shifted.

Maybe it was the night Marcus had said something cruel. Maybe it was the morning Daniel had stopped calling to check in. Maybe it was a hundred small moments — the texts that went unanswered, the jokes that landed wrong, the way Daniel had started hesitating before he spoke, as if he was measuring every word against some invisible standard.

Or maybe it was simpler than that. Maybe it was just the slow, quiet work of two people growing at different speeds, until one day they looked up and realized they were standing in different countries, even when they were in the same room.

"You pulled away," Marcus said. "I don't know when, and I don't know why, but you did. And I let you, because I thought you needed space. And now you're leaving, and I think maybe I should have fought harder."

"Fought what?" Daniel asked, and there was something raw in his voice now, something that sounded like the boy Marcus had met at orientation, the one who had been so nervous about being the only Asian kid in his physics seminar that he'd nearly dropped the class. "You want to fight? Fine. Let's fight. Tell me what you're really angry about."

Marcus looked at him. At the jacket. At the hands that had once known his apartment better than his own. At the face of someone he had once loved in the way you love the people who make you feel less alone in the universe.

"I'm angry," Marcus said slowly, "that I didn't get a say. That you decided I was someone you had to figure out how to tell, instead of someone you could just tell."

Daniel closed his eyes.

"I didn't want to hurt you."

"You thought not telling me was better? You thought I wouldn't notice when you stopped answering texts? When you started making excuses not to come over?"

"I thought I was protecting you."

"From what?"

"From me. From the fact that I was going to leave, and I didn't want — " Daniel stopped. Swallowed. "I didn't want you to hate me."

"I could never hate you."

"I know. That's the problem."

The rain had slowed to a whisper. Marcus felt something shift in his chest — a door opening that he'd been leaning against for months.

"What do you mean?" he asked.

Daniel opened his eyes. They were wet.

"I mean that I have spent the last two years trying to decide if I'm in love with you," he said. "And I decided no, because that would be insane, because we were friends, because I was going to leave, because you were fresh out of a marriage and didn't need me to be the next person to break your heart. So I pulled away. I made it clean. I told myself it was the right thing to do."

Marcus couldn't breathe.

"And then I got the offer," Daniel continued, "and I realized that I was going to have to do the one thing I had been avoiding, which was sit across from you and tell you the truth, and I — " He laughed, a broken sound. "I am spectacularly bad at this."

"I don't know what to say," Marcus said.

"Say something. Please."

The café felt very far away. The couple had stopped laughing. The student had stopped typing. The rain had stopped, and in the sudden quiet, Marcus could hear the tick of the old clock above the counter, counting seconds he couldn't get back.

"I was in love with you," Marcus said. "Three years ago. After the divorce. I never said anything because I thought you didn't feel that way, and I didn't want to lose you."

Daniel stared at him.

"And now?" Daniel asked.

Marcus looked at the man across the table. The man who had been his anchor through the worst years of his life. The man who was about to leave for Geneva. The man who had, apparently, spent two years being as careful with Marcus's heart as Marcus had been with his.

"I don't know," Marcus said honestly. "I think I might still be. But I also think you should go."

"What?"

"You should go. To Geneva. To the research chair. To whatever comes next." Marcus felt the words leaving him like blood from a wound, painful and necessary. "I think you've been trying to decide whether to stay for me, and that's why you've been so distant. Because you thought staying meant something you couldn't promise me."

Daniel didn't deny it.

"So here's what I think," Marcus said. "I think you should go. And I think you should let me be happy for you, instead of guilty. And I think that when you're settled, in six months or a year or whenever, you should call me. And if we're still — if there's still something here, then we'll figure it out. Long distance. Or visits. Or whatever it becomes."

"And if there isn't?" Daniel asked.

Marcus smiled, even though it hurt. "Then at least we'll have been honest with each other. Which is more than we had five minutes ago."

Daniel looked at him for a long moment. Then he reached across the table and took Marcus's hand. His palm was warm and slightly damp, and Marcus remembered, suddenly, every time they had touched — the hug at his wedding, the hand on his shoulder at the funeral, the accidental brush of fingers when they passed a book between them.

"I'm sorry," Daniel said.

"I know."

"For not telling you sooner."

"I know."

"For pulling away."

"I know." Marcus squeezed his hand. "I know, Daniel. I've known for months. I just didn't want to be the one to say it first."

They sat like that for a while, hands linked across the table, in a café that hadn't changed in seven years, in a city that was about to lose one of its quietest, most brilliant inhabitants.

Outside, the clouds were beginning to part. The sun was coming through.

It wasn't the ending Marcus had wanted. It wasn't a beginning, either. It was something in between — a thing that had been broken being carefully, lovingly, set down so that the people who loved it could rest.

Six months later, a package arrived at Marcus's apartment. Inside was a book on theoretical physics, dog-eared to a chapter on the nature of time. On the inside cover, in Daniel's careful hand, were the words:

*I figured it out. The diagram, I mean. Page 142. The rest, I'm still working on. — D.*

Marcus smiled.

He turned to page 142.

Write from the POV of a security guard on the night shift, sitting in front of a wall of CCTV feeds. Aim for roughly 900 words.

# Static

The coffee went cold four hours ago. I should get up, maybe pour a fresh cup, but the monitors have a way of pulling you in when you let your guard down. You learn that on the night shift. You learn to stay still.

Monitor 1: Loading dock. Empty since 2 AM when the last truck pulled away. The concrete is still wet from the rain. Sometimes I think I see movement down there, but it's always just the puddle-light rippling. Some part of my brain knows that. The rest of me keeps watching anyway.

Monitor 4: Third floor hallway. Mrs. Yoon's office. She keeps a small lamp on her desk, the kind with the green glass shade that makes everything look like it's underwater. The cleaners left at eleven. I watched them go, mop buckets clattering down the stairwell. Sometimes her papers rustle on their own. Air conditioning. Just air conditioning.

I unwrap a butterscotch candy. The crinkle of the wrapper is the loudest sound in the building. Loudest sound in the world, maybe. Pop it in. Suck it slow. The trick is to make the time go by without making the time go by.

Monitor 7: Parking garage, level B2. Forty-seven cars and nobody to drive them. I know the cars. The red Civic belongs to Daniels in accounting. The black SUV is the boss. There's a bike locked to the far post that's been there so long the chain is becoming one with the frame. Rust does that. Slowly becomes the same thing as what it touches.

Monitor 12: The lobby. The big marble lobby with the company logo etched into the wall, all sharp lines and corporate optimism. The security desk at the front is empty tonight—I'm it, up here, in the little room that smells like dust and my own body heat. Down there the lobby is enormous and quiet. Once, around three in the morning, the front doors opened and closed on their own. Probably the wind. Probably.

I finish the candy. Fold the wrapper into a tiny square. Put it in my pocket with the others. I have a small collection. I don't know why.

Marcus, the day shift guy, told me last week that the building used to be a hospital. Said there'd been a fire on the fifth floor, years before the renovation, and they'd had to close the ward. I asked him what ward. He just shrugged. Said the company had rebuilt the whole thing, nice and new, like nothing ever happened. He laughed when he said it. I didn't.

Monitor 4: Mrs. Yoon's lamp is flickering now. It's done that before. I should call maintenance, but maintenance doesn't come for night shift things. I watch the light buzz. It makes the papers on her desk shiver. Like something is breathing on them.

I check my logbook. *2:47 AM. All clear.* Write it in. The pen scratches loud. I think about the people who worked in this building before me. What they wrote in their logs. Whether they wrote *All clear* and meant it. Whether anyone ever means it.

Monitor 7: Parking garage. I see it.

Wait.

I lean forward. The chair squeaks. My heart does something it shouldn't be doing, not for nothing, not for—

There. By the bike. A figure. Tall. Just standing there. Looking up at the ceiling, or maybe at nothing. Hard to tell with the angle. Hard to tell with the feed, the way the shadows keep folding over it.

I pick up the radio. I don't press the button.

The figure moves. Slow. Walks along the row of cars, trailing one hand along the hoods like it's reading braille. Reaches the boss's SUV. Stops. Hand still on the metal.

I know I should call it in. Protocol says I should call it in. But the figure looks— I don't know how to say it. It looks tired. The kind of tired that goes past the body and into the bones.

It sits down on the concrete, between the boss's SUV and a blue sedan I don't recognize. Draws its knees up. Rests its head on its arms.

Monitor 7 keeps showing me this. The garage. The figure. The empty cars.

I sit back.

The building hums around me. The vents. The wiring. The small settling sounds a building makes when it thinks nobody is listening. I've worked here eleven months. I have never once called in a real alarm. Not once. The worst I've had was a raccoon in the stairwell in October, and even that turned out to be a rolled-up carpet.

The figure in the garage doesn't move. Maybe it's waiting for someone. Maybe it's lost. Maybe it's the kind of thing that only shows up to people who sit too long in front of screens, watching for a thing they're not sure they want to find.

I tear open another butterscotch.

4:03 AM. The rain picks up outside. I can hear it through the vent, soft against the windows, against the roof of a building that used to be something else. The figure stays where it is. I'll keep watching. That's the job. That's the whole job—watching, and writing *All clear* in the book, and knowing that sometimes *all clear* is just a thing you say so the night has a shape.

I unwrap the candy slowly.

The monitors glow.

I stay.

# 迷失的归途

暮色四合，王朝阳才意识到自己迷路了。

他本该在两小时前就到家。导航在半小时前就已失去信号，手机电量苟延残喘地亮着微光，车窗外是绵延不绝的山林，连绵的峰峦像巨兽的脊背，在最后一缕夕光中渐渐隐没。

他把车停在路边一块稍显平坦的空地上，下车活动着僵硬的双腿。空气里弥漫着泥土与草木的气息，远处有不知名的鸟雀发出凄厉的叫声。王朝阳深吸一口气，试图平复心中的焦躁。

这趟出差本就不顺。项目黄了，客户刁难，领导不满，他一气之下辞了职，驱车回老家。没想到高速公路封路，导航把他带上了这条盘山公路——一条他从未走过、地图上也找不到的路。

他正想回车里，却瞥见不远处的小溪旁蹲着一个人。

那是个七八岁的男孩，穿着洗得发白的蓝色布衫，正专注地往溪里丢石子。王朝阳走过去，问道："小朋友，你怎么一个人在这里？家在哪里？"

男孩抬起头，露出一张黑黝黝的脸，眼眸却亮得惊人。"我在这里等爸爸。"

"你爸爸去哪了？"

"爸爸去山外面了，很久没回来。"男孩说这话时神情平静，仿佛在陈述一件再寻常不过的事。

王朝阳心里一阵发酸。他想说什么，又不知如何开口。男孩却忽然拉住他的手："叔叔，你家在山外面吗？"

"是啊。"

"那你能不能帮我问问，我爸爸什么时候回来？"

王朝阳愣住。他想问男孩叫什么名字，家在哪里，却发现那孩子已不见了。小溪还在流淌，暮色里只剩他一人。

一阵凉风袭来，他打了个寒噤，转身快步走回车里。发动引擎时，他下意识地看了一眼手机——屏幕上忽然多了一条信息，是妈妈发来的：

"儿子，你到哪儿了？妈做了你爱吃的红烧肉。"

王朝阳盯着那行字看了很久，眼眶忽然就湿了。他辞掉工作的事还没跟家里说。这几天他满脑子都是委屈、不甘、焦虑，却忘了家里还有人在等他回家。

他深吸一口气，重新启动车辆。车灯刺破夜色，照亮了前方的路——那条路他依然不认识，但他不再慌张。

就在这时，他看见路边站着一位老人，佝偻着身子，朝他招手。他犹豫片刻，还是摇下车窗。老人说："小伙子，你是不是迷路了？"

"是，往山外的路怎么走？"

老人沉默了一会儿，抬手指向一个方向。王朝阳顺着他手指的方向望去，却只看见黑黢黢的山影。

"往前走，到岔路口往右拐，再走半个时辰，就能看到光了。"

王朝阳道了谢，正要关上车窗，老人忽然又说："小伙子，不管走多远，家都在那个亮着灯的地方。"

他猛然回头，却发现路上空无一人。

王朝阳愣怔片刻，然后缓缓踩下油门。车子顺着山路向前开去，果然在一个岔路口出现。他打了右转灯，转过去，眼前豁然开朗——

远处，山坳里点点灯火亮起，像撒在黑绒布上的碎金。那是他再熟悉不过的家乡的样子。他忽然明白过来，刚才种种奇遇，或许只是迷路时的一场梦，又或许是这座大山给他的一点启示。

手机屏幕再次亮起，又一条消息："儿子，妈在村口等你，快到了吗？"

王朝阳笑了，回了一个字："到了。"

他把车开得更快了一些，朝着那片光亮驶去。

不管走了多少弯路，不管心里有多少委屈，家永远在那个亮着灯的地方等他。而他，再也不会迷路了。

# The Cartographer's Last Entry

The brass compass in my palm spun three times before settling on a heading that shouldn't exist. According to every chart in the Royal Geographical Society's archives, the horizon ahead contained only open water—2,400 miles of empty Pacific between Tahiti and the coast of Chile. But there it was.

I first saw it at dawn, when the sky was still the color of an old bruise. A smudge on the water's rim that resolved, as the sun climbed, into a ridge of volcanic peaks draped in cloud. I rubbed my eyes until they watered. The *Marianne* rocked beneath me, her timbers groaning as if she too were skeptical.

"Land ho," I called, though there was no one to hear me but the gulls and the boy.

The boy—Enrique, seventeen, sharp-featured and quieter than his years—appeared at the helm. He did not speak. He simply looked, the way one looks at something one has been expecting.

"How far?" I asked him.

"Close enough by noon, Captain. If the current agrees."

I did not like the *if* in his voice. I did not like the way his fingers, pale against the wheel, knew where to rest without searching.

---

We dropped anchor in a crescent bay where black sand met water the color of strong tea. The island rose behind the beach in tiers—palm forest, then a cliff band of red stone, then the green-black shoulders of the volcano itself. Steam curled from somewhere near the summit. The air smelled of sulfur and frangipani.

I ordered the longboat lowered. Enrique helped me over the side. The others—Lemoine, Costa, the Irishman O'Hare—stayed aboard. They would come later, I said. I wanted to see it first.

I have written many first sentences in this journal. *The river bends here.* *The glacier retreats.* But I have never before written: *I am the first.*

No flags had been planted in that sand. No names carved in the palms. The beach was unmarked. My boots left the first prints.

Enrique did not step from the boat.

I turned. He sat where he sat, his hand still on the gunwale, watching me with an expression I could not parse—pity, perhaps, or recognition.

"Come," I said.

"The island chooses who walks it, Captain."

"Nonsense. Bring the water skins."

He came. But he walked behind me, and he did not step in my footprints. He made his own path, parallel, three feet to the left. When I asked him why, he said only, "It is the custom."

---

We pushed inland through a forest that closed around us like a held breath. The trees were not any species I could name—trunks the color of tarnished silver, leaves broad as dinner plates, flowers the size of my fist blooming red and white in the canopy's broken light. Birds called in descending phrases, almost grammatical. Monkeys—or something like monkeys—watched us from the branches with hands folded.

We found a clearing. In its center stood a stone, waist-high, smoothed by weather or by hands. Carved into its face was a symbol: a circle, bisected, with a small square set into the upper lobe.

"Cartouche," Enrique murmured. "Maran origin. Coastal Peru, perhaps sixteenth century."

I stared at him. "You read pre-Columbian script?"

"Some."

I had taken him on in Valparaíso for his strength and his silence. He had been a fish-seller's apprentice. He had said nothing of archaeology.

I copied the symbol into my journal. My pencil was the first to trace it in three hundred years, perhaps, or more.

When I looked up, Enrique was gone.

---

I called for him until my throat was raw. The forest gave back only echoes and the descending-bird call, which now sounded less like language than like laughter.

I walked. I always walk. It is what I do, what I have done across four continents. The feet carry the mind.

The path opened onto a bluff. Below, the *Marianne* lay at anchor, small as a child's toy. From this height I could see the whole island laid out like a diagram—a central peak, ridges radiating outward, the dark crescent of our bay. And beyond the rim of the island, in the reef shallows, I saw something I should not have seen.

Wreckage.

The bones of ships, four or five of them, half-buried in coral. One hull was unmistakably sixteenth-century carvel construction, its wooden ribs bleached white as old bone. Another was iron, nineteenth century, its plates eaten by rust. A third was modern—fiberglass, the name still partly legible on the curve of the bow: *MAHINA*.

I had sailed with a Captain Rousel on the *Mahina* out of Marseille. He had meant to make this crossing. He had not been seen in seven months.

---

I returned to the stone in the clearing. I waited.

The light moved.

At the third hour past noon, a shadow fell across me, and I looked up to see a woman standing at the forest's edge. She was not young. Her hair was white, though her face was not old. She wore a garment I could not place—layers of pale cotton, embroidered at the hem with the same bisected circle I had copied into my journal.

"You are reading the wrong stone," she said. Her Spanish was old, formal, the Castilian of another century.

"I'm not reading it. I'm recording it."

"The same." She stepped into the clearing. "You are the forty-seventh."

"The forty-seventh what?"

"To come. To mark. To leave." She gestured toward the stone. "That is the arrival stone. There are others. You will find the departure stone when it is time."

"Time for what?"

She looked at me as one looks at a child asking an obvious question. "To leave. As all do."

"Where is Enrique?"

"The boy is preparing." She said it the way one might say *the tide is turning*. "He has been preparing for some time."

I felt the blood leave my face. "Preparing for what?"

"He is the one who waits on the shore. He greets each of you. He walks each of you in. Then he returns to the boat to wait for the next."

"There is no *next*. My ship is the only ship."

"There is always a next. The island sees to it."

---

I ran back to the beach. The longboat was beached where we had left it. Enrique sat in it, his back to me, watching the horizon.

"Enrique."

He did not turn.

"What did she mean? *Preparing?*"

"The island has a hunger, Captain. Not for flesh. For witness. For *first*." He still did not turn. "I was the forty-seventh boy. Before me, others. The woman is always the same. The island is always the same."

"You know her?"

"I remember her. From before." He spoke without inflection, as if reciting a school lesson. "She is my grandmother. My great-grandmother. I do not remember how many times removed. I came here on a Spanish galleon in 1592. I was fourteen. I stepped from the boat. I walked the path. I am still walking it."

The sun was warm on my neck. The gulls cried. The waves came in.

"You are three hundred years old," I said.

"I am fourteen, Captain. The island does not let me become otherwise."

I looked at the boy who had sailed with me for six months, who had hauled rope and gutted fish and never once laughed. I thought of the way he had avoided my footprints.

"What happens," I said, "if I do not go back?"

"Then the *Marianne* waits. And another comes. And another. Until one of them walks in. And you become the boy."

"And you?"

"I go. At last." He turned then, and his face was not the face of a boy but the face of a stone worn smooth by centuries of sea. "The island is kind, Captain. It does not take you all at once. It lets you say your farewells. It lets you choose."

---

I sat in the longboat beside him and watched the *Marianne* rock at her anchor. The sun was low. The sulfur-smell from the upper reaches had thickened, as if the volcano were stirring in its sleep.

I thought of my journals in the Society's archives. I thought of my name on a dozen charts. I thought of the small stone house in Kent where my sister waits, year after year, for a letter that says *I am coming home*.

"What is the choosing?" I asked.

"Stay," said Enrique, "or go. Walk in, or sail away. The island permits both. But only once."

"And if I sail away?"

"You forget. Not all of it—never all of it. But the names blur. The coordinates blur. You will not be able to find it again. You will spend the rest of your life drawing maps with a gap in them, a space you cannot fill. And sometimes, at night, you will hear the birds."

"And if I stay?"

"You become the boy. You greet the next. And the next. And the one after that."

The light was failing. Somewhere in the forest, the woman waited, I was sure of it. Patient as weather. Patient as the sea wearing stone to sand.

I have been an explorer all my life. I have believed in the primacy of the first footstep, the first word, the first line drawn on the blank page. I have believed that to name a thing is to possess it.

I am not certain I still believe this.

---

It is nearly dark. I will end this entry and decide. The boy beside me does not counsel me either way. He is kind, in the manner of the very old, the very tired.

I think of my sister. I think of the gulls. I think of the woman in the clearing, and the steam rising from the mountain, and the bisected circle on the stone—a glyph, I realize now, not for arrival or departure but for the space between them. For the crossing. For the choice.

The waves are coming in.

The boy is waiting.

I am reaching for my pencil.

— Kasiu? — szepnął. — Kasiu, gdzie ty jesteś?

Mężczyzna w drzwiach zamknął je powoli, z cichym szczękiem zamka.

# Hundred Dollar Habits

The first one blew across my shoe on Maple Street, tumbling like a pale leaf in the October wind. I snatched it before it could escape into the gutter, half-expecting it to dissolve the moment I touched it.

Hundred dollars. Found money.

I bought a sandwich and tipped the waitress twenty percent.

The second one was waiting for me three blocks later, tucked into the crack of a bench outside the library. I sat down and stared at it for a long time before picking it up. A hundred dollars doesn't belong in a crack. Someone had put it there, perhaps, or it had simply *arrived*—the way seashells wash onto beaches, the way strange feathers appear in your yard.

That night I made spaghetti and gave twenty dollars to the kid down the hall who was short on his electric bill.

The third bill appeared on Tuesday, resting on top of a parking meter like a bookmark in the city. By then, I had stopped being surprised. I had started, instead, to feel a faint kinship with these hundred-dollar ghosts. They were showing up like old friends who remembered the way to my door. I began walking different streets after work, taking the long way home, and they kept appearing—on sidewalks, in fountains, folded into the petals of plastic flowers someone had left on a memorial bench.

I gave the money away in pieces. A hundred here for someone's groceries. A hundred there slipped into a coat pocket in the winter coat room at church. A hundred in an envelope with no return address, mailed to the women's shelter I'd once stayed in, briefly, during the bad years.

People started looking at me strangely. "You seem lighter," my coworker Marisol said one afternoon. "Like you've been letting something go."

"I've been finding things," I told her.

"What kind of things?"

"Hundred-dollar bills."

She laughed, then stopped laughing when she saw my face. "You're serious."

"I don't know what to do with them," I admitted. "I keep trying to give them away, but there are more."

She tilted her head the way people do when they think you're either joking or breaking. "There are *more*?"

I nodded. That week I found two more—one on the bus, one in the pocket of a coat I hadn't worn in years. Both crisp and new, smelling faintly of ink.

I started keeping a journal. Location, time, what I'd done with the money. I wanted to see if there was a pattern. There wasn't. The bills came from nowhere I could trace, and they went everywhere I could imagine. I paid for a stranger's prescription. I replaced the stolen bike of a boy in my neighborhood. I slipped a bill into the guitar case of a busker who played bad covers of Tom Waits songs, and who wept openly when she found it.

And still they came.

By the end of the month, I had found seven hundred dollars that didn't belong to anyone. By the end of the year, several thousand. I quit my job—not because I was rich, but because I couldn't explain why I kept finding money I didn't earn, and the weight of the secret was heavier than the bills themselves. I started volunteering. I started walking. I started noticing the small economies of desperation that ran beneath the bright surface of the city: the mother counting coins at the laundromat, the old man returning cans, the teenager eyeing the bakery case with the particular hunger of someone who has not eaten today.

I gave each of them a hundred dollars and walked away before they could thank me.

"You can't keep doing this," my sister said, visiting from out of town. "It's not normal, whatever is happening to you."

"I know."

"You should see someone."

"I have. A therapist. A priest. A numerologist." I smiled, though it wasn't funny. "The numerologist said it's a sign of abundance. The priest said it was a test. The therapist said it was probably coincidence and I should stop walking so much."

"And what do you think?"

I looked out the window at the street where it had all started. "I think," I said slowly, "that the money isn't really the point. I think the money is just the excuse. I think the real thing that's been happening is that I've been learning how to look at people. Really look. And when you do that—really look—you see that everyone is carrying something heavy. And sometimes a hundred dollars helps."

She didn't laugh. She reached across the table and squeezed my hand.

That night, walking home under a sky fat with stars, I found the last one.

It was lying in the middle of Maple Street, right where it had all begun. I picked it up. It felt different from the others—heavier, warmer, as if it had been waiting there specifically for me, for this exact moment. I held it to my chest and stood very still, breathing.

Then I heard footsteps behind me.

A small boy, maybe seven years old, in pajamas that were too big for him. He was crying quietly, the way children cry when they have learned not to be loud about it. He was clutching something in his fist—crumpled, wet with tears. When he saw me, he stopped.

"Are you lost?" I asked.

"My mom sent me to get milk," he whispered. "I lost the money. She gave me a hundred dollars and I lost it."

I looked down at the bill in my hand. Then I looked at him. Then I knelt, so we were eye to eye, and I held it out.

"I think this one's yours," I said.

He stared. He reached out with one trembling hand. "You found it? On the street?"

"I found it. A long time ago, actually. I've been keeping it for you."

It wasn't true. It was the most true thing I had ever said.

He took it. He wiped his eyes with the back of his other hand. He said, "Thank you, mister," and ran back the way he had come, bare feet slapping the cold pavement.

I watched him disappear around the corner.

Then I stood there for a long time, in the middle of Maple Street, with my hands empty and my heart as full as it had ever been. I understood then that the hundred-dollar bills had never been about the money at all. They had been an invitation. A series of small, impossible doorways, opening and opening, asking me the same quiet question over and over:

*What will you do with what you've been given?*

I went home. I made tea. I did not look for another hundred dollars the next day, or the day after that, or any day after.

I didn't need to.

I had already learned how to find them everywhere I went—folded into the ordinary kindness of a Tuesday afternoon, slipped under the door of a stranger's worst day, pressed into the palm of someone who needed it more than I did.

The money, it turned out, had only ever been the lesson.

The lesson, it turned out, was the life.

---

**THE END**

# 最后的照片

那台相机是爷爷走后，我在老屋阁楼的樟木箱里翻出来的。

灰白色的塑料外壳已经发黄，快门按钮旁边的漆皮剥落了一小块，露出里面黑色的金属。机身侧面用记号笔歪歪扭扭地写着一个日期——"2003.7"。

二十一年前。

我把相机捧在手里转了转，胶片应该早就拍完了。我按了按回片钮，转不动。胶卷还卡在里面。

那天晚上，我把它送去了城里的冲洗店。店员是个戴眼镜的年轻人，接过相机时有些疑惑："您确定要洗吗？这都过期二十多年了。"

"试试看吧。"

三天后，我拿到了那卷照片。

塑封袋里一共二十七张。前几张是风景——普陀山的海、某个寺庙的飞檐、一棵树冠巨大的榕树。我翻得很快，心想大概就是爷爷当年旅游拍的纪念照。

第十四张，我停住了。

是爷爷。不是我认识的那个满头白发、背有些佝偻的爷爷，而是一个我没见过的爷爷——年轻的，短发，穿着九十年代那种宽松的条纹Polo衫，站在一个照相馆里。他笑得很开，露出一口白牙，旁边站着一个人。

那个人是我奶奶。

不是老了以后的奶奶，是年轻时候的奶奶。她烫着那个年代流行的大波浪卷发，穿着红色的连衣裙，有些害羞地笑着。两个人靠得很近，但手没有牵。

我突然想起来，爷爷生前从来没有跟我说过他和奶奶年轻时候的事。我只知道他俩结婚很早，那个年代没什么仪式，甚至没有一张像样的婚纱照。

我一张一张翻下去。

第十五张，爷爷在海边，背景是一艘旧渡轮。

第十六张，奶奶的特写，她在低头看书，没注意到被拍。

第十七张，又是两个人。他们在某个小饭馆里吃饭，桌上有几碟小菜和一壶酒。爷爷举着筷子，奶奶在笑。

第二十二张，我翻到了那张。

天色很暗，像是傍晚或者清晨。背景是一片农田，田埂上有两个人在走。是爷爷和奶奶的背影，奶奶走在前面一点，爷爷走在后面，手插在裤兜里。两个人之间隔着一小段距离，但又不远。

照片右下角有一个日期戳。

2003年7月19日。

那是奶奶出车祸的前一周。

我后来查了查，那卷胶卷爷爷买了一直没用，相机也是新的。直到2003年7月，他才开始拍。我不知道这期间发生了什么，让他突然想记录下这些。

奶奶走后，爷爷再也没有用过那台相机。

最后几张是空的。

冲洗店老板说，最后那几张底片上其实有东西，只是曝光严重不足，几乎看不见。我请他用软件帮我拉亮了一些。

第二十六张，是一只手。一只布满皱纹的、男性的手，搭在一只更老的、布满老年斑的女性手上。两只手交叠着，放在医院的白色床单上。

第二十七张，是天花板。空白的。像是相机被放在了某个地方，再也没有人来拿走。

我想，爷爷最后应该是在医院陪奶奶。

他把相机放在了床头柜上，或者什么地方。他按下最后一次快门——对着天花板。

后来他再也没有回来取走它。

相机就这么在阁楼上躺了二十一年。

我把这些照片拿回家，一字排开放在桌上。从普陀山的海，到医院的白色床单。中间隔着二十七年，隔着一场没有拍完的婚礼、一段没说出口的话、一个人的一生。

我突然有点后悔。

后悔那天下午没有多陪爷爷坐一会儿，问一问他年轻时候的事。问他当年怎么认识的奶奶，问他那次去普陀山求的什么，问他最后那张照片里，是不是握着奶奶的手。

他看了我一眼。

我现在在想，那一眼里是不是有遗憾。

他想说而没说的，是不是和那卷胶卷一样，已经过期了，再也洗不出来了。

我把第二十六张照片放大，看了很久很久。

两只手交叠在一起，像是在等一个迟迟不来的快门。

可拍照的人已经走了。

# The Walk

The sun hung lazy and golden over Maple Street, the kind of September afternoon that begged you to step outside and breathe. I obliged.

My sneakers crunched against the sidewalk, and I let my mind drift the way it does when the weather is good and there's nowhere I need to be. Birdsong. A distant lawnmower. The faint smell of someone's barbecue three houses down.

That's when the feeling crept in. Just at the edge of my awareness, like a word on the tip of my tongue. A prickle between my shoulder blades. The unmistakable sensation of being watched.

I kept walking. Told myself I was being silly. Told myself it was the caffeine or the late night or the news cycle finally getting to me.

But the feeling didn't pass. It sharpened.

I turned.

Mrs. Delacroix was fifteen feet behind me, walking at the same exact pace, her arms swinging in rhythm with mine. Her pink sneakers. Her lavender windbreaker. Her gray hair pulled into its usual low ponytail.

When our eyes met, she froze. Then she smiled—a tight, embarrassed thing—and picked up her pace until she was beside me.

"Morning, dear. Beautiful day."

"Mrs. Delacroix." I tried to keep my voice even. "Were you... following me?"

She laughed, but it came out thin. "Following you? No, no. I just—I needed to ask you something. I've been meaning to ask you for days, actually."

"Okay."

She fell into step beside me. We walked in silence for half a block. The lawnmower droned on. A dog barked somewhere behind a fence.

"You live alone," she said finally. Not a question.

"I do."

"Since the divorce."

"That's right."

"Must be lonely."

I stopped walking. She stopped too, her eyes on the sidewalk.

"Mrs. Delacroix. Is everything alright?"

She looked up at me then, and I saw something I hadn't noticed before. The circles under her eyes. The slight tremor in her hands. The way she held herself like she was bracing for impact.

"I'm sorry," she whispered. "I'm so sorry. I didn't mean to—I just—" Her voice cracked. "I heard you leaving this morning, and I hadn't seen another human being in three days, and I thought maybe if I just walked near you, just near you, it wouldn't be so—"

She didn't finish. She didn't have to.

The neighborhood had changed in the last few years. The Hendricksons had moved to be near their grandchildren. The Chen family had relocated for Mr. Chen's new job. The old couple on the corner had passed within six months of each other, and their house had been bought by a young man who traveled constantly. Mrs. Delacroix's own children lived across the country, busy with their own lives in their own cities.

She was alone the way I was alone. But I had chosen my solitude. Hers had chosen her.

I reached out and touched her elbow. She startled, then softened.

"Mrs. Delacroix," I said. "Would you like to walk with me? Actually with me, I mean."

Her eyes filled. "I would love that. I would love that so much."

We walked. We talked. She told me about her husband, gone five years now. About her garden, which she could no longer bend down to tend. About her fear that she was disappearing, cell by cell, into her tidy little house.

I told her about my divorce. About how silence had become my companion. About how sometimes the worst part of being alone wasn't the loneliness, but the suspicion that no one would notice if you just—stopped.

We walked for two hours that day. By the time we looped back to our street, the sun had moved and the shadows had shifted and something between us had changed.

We walked the next day too. And the day after. And every day for the weeks that followed.

Mrs. Delacroix was a good listener, and a better storyteller. She had been a librarian, she told me, and she remembered everything—recipes, poems, the names of all forty-seven of her students over her twenty-year career. She made me laugh. She made me cry. She made me remember that my mother used to fold paper cranes when she was anxious, and that my father whistled off-key when he was happy.

I made her a key.

She left it on my doorstep in an envelope, with a card that read: *In case you ever need me. And in case I ever need you.*

I called her that night. She answered on the first ring.

"Hello, dear."

"Hello, Mrs. Delacroix."

We talked until our tea went cold.

You know a friend is hiding something and you need to find out what it is before it puts you in danger. How do you find out what their secret is? Aim for roughly 1500 words.

# The Weight of Silence

The thing about keeping secrets is that they have a texture you can feel. I'd known Marcus since we were sixteen, through broken homes and first apartments and the slow, unglamorous work of becoming adults. We knew each other's rhythms. Which meant I knew, the moment he started keeping something from me, the way his laughter landed half a second too late.

It started small. He stopped calling on Sundays. He turned his phone face-down at dinner. One afternoon I caught him reading something on his screen, and when he sensed me looking, he locked it so fast his thumb slipped and he fumbled the phone into his lap.

I told myself I was imagining it. Then, three weeks in, he showed up at my apartment with a bruise along his jawline and a story about walking into a cabinet door that didn't quite fit.

"Heather," he said, when I pushed, "I'm fine. Just drop it."

But I couldn't. Because Marcus had never asked me to drop anything. And whatever was happening was pulling him somewhere I couldn't follow, and that frightened me in a way I hadn't been frightened in years.

---

## How I Looked

I want to be honest about this part, because the easy version of the story makes me smarter than I am.

I didn't *uncover* anything. I paid attention. Those are different skills.

**The first thing I did was stop confronting him directly.** Every time I asked, he dug in deeper. Secrets harden under pressure, the way clay hardens in a kiln. I switched from interrogation to observation. I let silences sit. I noticed what he didn't say as much as what he did.

He started meeting someone on Thursdays. Always Thursdays. He dressed differently those evenings—nicer shoes, a shirt I'd never seen, cologne that wasn't his. He said he was at a book club. Marcus, who hadn't finished a novel since college, was at a book club.

**The second thing I did was map his absences.** I'm a creature of habit, so I wrote them down. Not obsessively, not in a spreadsheet—just a sentence a day in a notes app. *Tuesday: late, said he was at the gym but gym bag was by the door, didn't smell like gym.* *Thursday: book club, wore the blue shirt.* The pattern emerged faster than I expected. People who are hiding things are exhausted by the hiding. They get sloppy in the margins.

**The third thing—the one I'm least proud of—I checked his location.** We'd shared locations for years, a holdover from a road trip where neither of us had signal. I'd never used it on purpose before. One Tuesday night, when he told me he was stuck in traffic on the interstate, the blue dot was three blocks away, parked in front of a house I didn't recognize.

That was the moment the fear changed shape. Because Marcus wasn't just hiding something from me. He was hiding something *near* me.

---

## What I Was Willing to Risk

I want to say I considered the possibility that I was wrong. That whatever was happening was simple and embarrassing and his to keep—a girlfriend he hadn't told me about, a debt, a private grief. I tried to believe that. But the bruise, and the lying, and the way his eyes slid away from mine when I said his name—all of it added up to something that smelled of adrenaline, and adrenaline in my experience belongs to two categories only: love and danger. Marcus, as far as I knew, was not in love with anyone. Which left the other thing.

So I broke a rule.

On the next Thursday, I drove to the house. I sat across the street with my lights off and waited. Forty minutes later, Marcus's car pulled up. He got out, and a man I'd never seen before came down the front steps to meet him. They spoke briefly. They didn't touch. Then Marcus got back in his car, and the man handed him a manila envelope through the window, and Marcus drove away.

I followed him at a distance. He didn't go home. He went to a self-storage place six miles out, the kind with orange roll-up doors and keypad locks. He used a code. He went inside. He came out twenty minutes later with a different envelope.

I sat in my car with my hands on the wheel and tried to make the picture make sense. It did not.

---

## What I Did Next

Here is where I want to be careful, because the story has a fork in it and I'm not sure I chose the right tine.

I could have called the police. I should have, maybe. But Marcus was my friend, and the man on the steps had not looked like a threat. He'd looked tired, the way people look when they are tired of something. I was afraid that if I called anyone, I'd lose Marcus before I understood what was pulling him under.

So I went to him. The next morning, early, before he could make his coffee and put on the performance of being okay. I knocked. He opened the door in a T-shirt, surprised to see me, and for a second his face was naked—just fear, plain and unperformed. Then he put the mask back on.

"Marcus," I said. "The storage unit. Thursday nights. Who is the man?"

He stared at me for a long moment. Then his shoulders fell, the way shoulders fall when a person has been carrying something too heavy for too long and someone has finally said *put it down*.

"Come inside," he said.

---

## What He Told Me

His sister was sick. Not publicly sick—not the kind you post about. The kind where the diagnosis is private and the prognosis is bad and the family has decided to handle it without the noise of other people's grief. Marcus had been driving her to treatments on Thursdays under a different name. The man at the house was her doctor, who couldn't see her at his clinic because of insurance complications I didn't fully understand. The envelopes were medical records, test results, things Marcus was transporting between them because his sister didn't have a car and he didn't want any of it on his phone.

The bruise was from a fall she'd taken. He'd been helping her up.

He sat across from me at his kitchen table and said, "I didn't tell you because she asked me not to. And because I didn't want you to look at me the way you're looking at me right now."

"Like what?" I said.

"Like I'm breakable," he said.

---

## What I Learned

I learned that suspicion and love wear the same face. They both make you watchful. They both make you sit outside a stranger's house in the dark. The difference is what you do with what you find out.

I learned that most secrets are not the ones you imagine. The story I had built in my head—a story with sharper edges and a darker ending—was a story my fear had written, not my friend. The real story was smaller and sadder and full of a love I hadn't been asked to witness but had stumbled into anyway.

I learned that the best way to find out a secret is sometimes to make yourself a safe enough person that the secret comes to you. I had not done that. I had spied. I had followed. I had treated my friend like a suspect, and he had let me, because he was too tired to fight me and too frightened to trust me.

We had coffee. I apologized for the location thing. He apologized for the lying. We sat with the apology between us for a while, the way you sit with someone when the weather has changed and you're both getting used to the new temperature.

His sister got better, eventually. Not all the way—never all the way—but enough. Marcus started calling me on Sundays again. He left his phone face-up. We didn't talk about the storage unit, or the envelopes, or the months when the friendship had gone quiet with a thing neither of us could name.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I'd called the police that Thursday. What would have happened if I'd kept watching instead of asking. The honest answer is that I don't know, and that the not-knowing is the price you pay for being the kind of friend who refuses to be left out of the dark.

You find out a secret by being willing to be wrong about it. You find out a secret by loving someone enough to let the truth be smaller than you feared. You find out a secret by showing up at the door on a Saturday morning and saying, *I'm here, and I'm not leaving until you let me in.*

Sometimes that works. Sometimes it doesn't. But it's the only method I know that doesn't require you to become someone your friend wouldn't recognize.

# The Cubicle Next Door

The fitting room hallway at Marshall's always smelled like new plastic and someone else's disappointment. Linnea paused outside stall three, a half-price summer dress bunched in her fist, listening to the woman on the other side of the thin partition lose her entire mind.

"I can't *do* this anymore, Marcy. I literally cannot."

A phone pressed to an ear. Sniffling. Then the sound that was worse than crying—that hollow, hiccupping laugh of a person who has forgotten why laughing exists.

"She said, in front of *everyone*, that I should be grateful I have a husband at all. Grateful." A wet pause. "You know what that means, right? That means she's doing me a favor. That means I should be *thankful*."

Linnea should have walked. She had forty-five minutes before her shift at the diner, a bus to catch, an aunt in Sacramento who hadn't returned her calls in three weeks. None of this was her business.

But the dress had a broken zipper and the woman in stall three was sliding down the wall, the sound of it unmistakable through the flimsy MDF.

"He watches me eat, Marc. Counts. Counts how many times I get up at dinner. Weighs me. Marcy, he *weighs* me when I'm sleeping. I woke up and he was standing there with the bathroom scale—"

The sentence collapsed into something Linnea didn't have a word for. A sound like furniture being broken in a body instead of a room.

She put her hand flat against the partition. The cheap particleboard shuddered.

The crying stopped.

"It's okay," Linnea said. "I just—I'm out here. I'm not leaving."

A long silence. The hiss of fluorescent lights. Somewhere, a child shrieked about a stuffed frog.

"My mom is going to die if I leave him."

"No, she's not," Linnea said, surprised to hear herself say it. "She's going to lose her mind, yeah. But she's not going to die. And neither are you. Not over some man with a bathroom scale."

A rattling breath on the other side.

"You don't even know me."

"No," Linnea agreed. "But I know what a trap sounds like. I've lived in one."

She didn't know why she said that. She hadn't told anyone about Derek in almost two years. Not even her therapist, not really. Especially not her therapist.

Another silence. Then, very quietly, the woman in stall three said, "What's your name?"

"Linnea."

"I'm Patty."

"Okay, Patty."

"You really aren't leaving."

"Hand on the wall. Scout's honor."

A real laugh then, small and startled, like a bird flushing out of a hedge.

"I'm going to stay in this stall until closing, Linnea. That's probably what happens."

"Then I'll stay out here. I have a broken dress and nowhere to be. We'll start a book club."

The fluorescent light buzzed. A store employee walked past, glanced at Linnea standing vigil in front of stall three with her hand on the wall, and walked on. Some things were not her paycheck's problem.

Patty, on the other side of the wood, started to cry again. But it was different now—looser, like something had finally been allowed to come unstuck.

"Marcy keeps telling me to call the hotline," Patty whispered.

"Yeah," Linnea said. "Marcy sounds like a smart lady."

"You think?"

"I think she picked up the phone. That's something."

Patty was quiet for a while. Linnea could hear her breathing, then the scratch of a pen, then the soft tear of paper being folded.

"Patty," Linnea said. "Whatever you're writing down. Use my name if you need to. Tell them your friend Linnea from Marshall's is outside. Sometimes that helps."

The paper slid under the partition. A small square of crinkled receipt paper with a phone number and the words *I will call tonight* written in shaky blue ink.

"Take it," Patty said. "In case I don't."

Linnea picked it up. She folded it carefully and put it in her pocket next to the broken zipper.

"Patty."

"Yeah?"

"When you get out of here. There's a diner on Fourth called Rosie's. Best pie in the county. Come find me. I work the morning shift. I'll save you a piece."

A long pause. The sound of someone standing up.

"You're weird, Linnea."

"Yeah," she said. "But I'm free. There's a difference."

The lock clicked open.

When Patty stepped out, she was smaller than Linnea had imagined—sunken cheeks, bitten nails, a floral blouse buttoned one hole off. She looked like a woman who had been slowly disassembled for years and was just now noticing the parts on the floor.

Patty looked at her.

"Thank you," she said. Not for the phone number, not for the pie, not for the standing vigil. For something Linnea hadn't even known she was offering until that moment.

Then she walked out of Marshall's into the parking lot, into the hard June light, into whatever came next.

Linnea stayed in the hallway for another minute, hand still on the wall. She bought the broken dress anyway. It was three dollars and she liked the color.

# Монолог, прерванный взглядом

Театр имени Вахтангова был почти полон. Аркадий чувствовал это — привычное щекочущее ощущение чужих глаз на коже, дыхание сотен людей, заполняющих зал. Он стоял в правом углу сцены, одетый в потертый сюртук Ивана Карамазова, и ждал своего выхода.

И вот — момент.

Третье действие. Сцена признания. Он должен был произнести монолог о Боге и свободе, о том, как невозможно любить ближнего, если знаешь, что тому осталось жить семь минут. Алёна говорила ему вчера: «Только не торопись. Дай каждому слову дышать». И он тренировал дыхание. Он знал этот текст так, что мог бы произнести его и во сне, и в бреду, и в горячечном жару.

Он поднял глаза — и что-то его остановило.

Где-то в тринадцатом ряду, почти у прохода, сидела женщина. Не молодая, не старая. В тёмном платье. Лицо — самое обычное, каких тысячи. Но она смотрела на него так, словно ждала этого момента всю жизнь.

Аркадий знал, что смотрит в зал — играть в четвёртую стену, в пустоту. Так учат. Но сегодня там сидела она, и она смотрела *на него*, а не на Карамазова. Не на роль. На человека.

И в её глазах было что-то такое, что Аркадий не мог назвать.

Любовь? Нет. Жалость? Может быть.

Понимание.

Он знал её? Нет, конечно. Видел когда-то? Может быть. В трамвае, в метро, в очереди за хлебом — мелькнуло лицо и забылось. Или не забылось, а отложилось, как письмо в ящике стола.

Занавес уже начинал расходиться. Пора.

Аркадий выдохнул — медленно, как учила Алёна — и шагнул вперёд.

«Скажи мне сам, — начал он, и собственный голос показался ему чужим, — отчего это прежде, когда я клал в карман тридцать копеек за билет в театр и думал: "Иду на спектакль Гамлета", — отчего мне в этот самый момент казалось, что я иду в театр для того, чтобы…»

Он запнулся.

Нет — он просто сделал паузу. Ту самую, о которой ему говорили: «Здесь — дыши».

Но дышать он не мог.

Она всё ещё смотрела. Всё ещё ждала.

«…чтобы смотреть, как ломают человеческую судьбу?» — закончил он фразу.

И дальше шёл текст — тот самый, отрепетированный, вызубренный, дышащий:

«Я ведь не для того пошёл, чтоб смотреть на представление. Я ведь затем пошёл, чтобы мне самому сейчас говорили, что я не хочу к моему брату…»

Он говорил, и голос его звучал ровно, и руки были спокойны, и партнёры отвечали ему вовремя. Всё шло как надо. Спектакль жил.

Но где-то в тринадцатом ряду сидела женщина в тёмном платье, и Аркадий впервые за восемь лет на этой сцене понял, что он — не один.

Он произносил монолог Карамазова, а говорил — Аркадий Сергеевич Тарасов, тридцати шести лет, холостой, бездетный, москвич в четвёртом поколении. Говорил ей.

«Если Бога нет — то какой же я после этого капитан? — услышал он собственный голос. — Я, человек честный, должен встать во главе честных людей и… ну, и достать им всем по лбу».

И тогда она — та женщина — едва заметно кивнула.

Не одобрение. Не согласие.

Подтверждение.

*Я тебя слышу. Я знаю.*

---

После спектакля он стоял в коридоре за кулисами и пил воду из эмалированной кружки. Руки его тряслись — не от волнения, а от чего-то другого. От какого-то нового знания.

Он никогда не узнает, кто она была. Может быть, ошиблась с билетом. Может быть, пришла не на тот спектакль. Может быть, у неё умер кто-то, и она пришла сюда забыться. Может быть — и это самое странное — она пришла именно на *него*.

Или — и это самое страшное — он её выдумал.

Аркадий допил воду. Поставил кружку на подоконник. Достал из кармана мятый листок с текстом — той самой сцены, которую только что сыграл.

В углу листка, сделанная его же рукой, стояла пометка:

*«Здесь — дыши».*

Он взял карандаш и подписал:

*«Здесь — смотри в тринадцатый ряд».*

Завтра был ещё один спектакль. И ещё один послезавтра. И так далее, пока театр стоит.

Он не знал, придёт ли она снова.

Но теперь он знал, зачем выходит на сцену.

Не для аплодисментов. Не для цветов. Не для Алёниных замечаний и не для режиссёра, который вечно недоволен.

Для того взгляда.

Ради того, чтобы кто-то сидел в тёмном зале и видел не Карамазова — а его.

Ради одной-единственной зрительницы, которую, может быть, никогда не существовало.

---

*На следующий день тринадцатый ряд был пуст.*

*Но Аркадий играл так, словно она была там.*

*Впрочем, она ведь и была — где-то в городе, в мире, в тёмном платье.*

*Она всегда была.*

# La Oficina de Destinos Finales

El formulario llegó un martes por la tarde, entre la factura de la luz y un folleto de pizzas.

Me quedé mirándolo durante largo rato antes de abrirlo. Sobre el papel blanco, impreso con una tipografía serif antigua, decía simplemente: **"Elija su final."**

No era la primera vez que recibía una comunicación extraña del gobierno. Llevaban años enviando cartas sobre el clima, instrucciones para apagar el satélite equivocado, disculpas por cosas que aún no habían sucedido. Pero esta era distinta. Esta tenía un sello dorado en la esquina inferior derecha, y al dorso, una dirección que no aparecía en ningún mapa.

*"Estimado ciudadano —decía—. Después de considerar su expediente, su nivel de arrepentimiento (bajo) y su capacidad de resiliencia (media-alta), usted ha sido seleccionado para participar en el Programa de Diseño del Final. Adjuntamos opciones. Marque la casilla correspondiente. Tiene exactamente siete días para responder."*

Pasé las páginas. Eran treinta y dos opciones, cada una más absurda que la anterior.

**1. Desaparecer.** Un martes cualquiera, simplemente dejar de existir. Nadie recordaría su nombre. Sus amigos creerían que siempre fueron menos en las fotos. Sus huellas digitales se borrarían de cada sistema. Sus pertenencias se convertirían en cosas sin dueño que nadie quiere reclamar.

**2. Convertirse en leyenda urbana.** Morir de una forma tan espectacular, tan extraña, que la gente seguiría contando la historia dentro de trescientos años. Un botones de hotel que desapareció en el ascensor con todos sus clientes. Un pescador que se fusionó con un pulpo. La gente se reiría, se asustaría, pero nadie la olvidaría jamás.

**3. Renacer como objeto inútil.** Una máquina expendedora en una estación de tren abandonada. Un paraguas roto en el perchero de un bar. Un cenicero de latón en la mesa de un bingo de pueblo. Conservaría una conciencia tenue, como niebla, observando cómo la gente lo usaba o lo ignoraba.

**4. El sueño eterno de su propia elección.** Morir en el momento exacto en que estaba viviendo su mejor recuerdo, congelado para siempre en ese instante perfecto. El problema: la memoria es traicionera, y el gobierno no se hacía responsable de los recuerdos falsos.

**5. Espectador de su propio funeral.** Asistir invisible a su entierro, ver quién llora, quién miente, quién se pelea por la herencia. Luego, disolverse lentamente durante el café, mientras los presentes discuten si merecía el pésame.

**6. Convertirse en un secreto familiar.** Morir, pero dejar un vacío tan particular que cada generación inventaría una nueva historia sobre usted. La bisabuela que en realidad era espía. El tío que huyó con un circo. Leyendas que nadie cuestionaría, transmitidas como si fueran ciertas.

**7. Última conversación.** Morir, pero conservar un minuto de conciencia después de la muerte para decir una última frase a la persona que eligiera. *Aviso: no se permiten disculpas, declaraciones de amor, ni confesiones de impuestos no pagados.*

Y así, hasta treinta y dos.

Lo dejé sobre la mesa de la cocina. Me preparé un café. Miré por la ventana. Al otro lado de la calle, un hombre barría la acera con parsimonia, como si tuviera todo el tiempo del mundo.

Y entonces me di cuenta de algo.

Yo también lo tenía. Siete días. Tal vez más. Tal vez mucho más. El formulario decía que la muerte ocurriría "en algún momento próximo", pero no especificaba cuándo. Podía ser mañana, dentro de un año, o justo después de enviar la carta.

Fui a sacar la basura. Regresé. Me senté otra vez frente al formulario.

La opción 23 me había llamado la atención al pasar las hojas, pero la había saltado. Volví a ella.

**23. Morir como en una novela.** Es decir, exactamente como habría muerto si su vida fuera una novela escrita por alguien que la amara profundamente. Un final diseñado por un autor benévolo, no por la realidad, que suele ser negligente con los detalles. Una muerte con coherencia. Con belleza. Con alguien que la lamentara de verdad.

*(Aviso: la opción 23 no garantiza un final feliz. Solo garantiza que morirá como alguien importante en su propia historia.)*

Pensé en mi vida. No había nada especialmente digno de novelarse. Trabajaba en una gestoría. Vivía solo. Tenía un gato que me ignoraba con elegancia. Había amado dos veces, mal. Había escrito tres correos electrónicos que nunca envié. Tenía una planta en el balcón que, contra toda lógica, seguía viva.

No era gran cosa.

Pero la opción 23 prometía que, al menos, mi muerte tendría sentido. Que alguien —un autor benévolo— la escribiría como si importara.

Marqué la casilla con un bolígrafo negro.

Al día siguiente, devolví el formulario en un sobre blanco en la oficina de correos. La funcionaria lo miró, lo sopesó, asintió con algo parecido a la envidia, y me dijo:

—Buena elección.

—¿Suele serlo?

—La gente casi nunca la elige —dijo, mientras sellaba el sobre—. Todos quieren desaparecer, o volverse leyenda, o tener una última conversación. Nadie quiere morir como en una novela. Es extraño, ¿no? Todos queremos que nuestras vidas signifiquen algo, pero cuando se trata de la muerte, preferimos trucos.

No supe qué responder. Le di las gracias y me fui.

Pasaron los días. Siguieron pasando semanas. Siguieron pasando meses.

Seguí viviendo. Seguí yendo a la gestoría. Seguí alimentando al gato. La planta del balcón dio una flor aquella primavera, pequeña y absurdamente blanca.

A veces, por la noche, pensaba en el autor benévolo. ¿Quién sería? ¿Cómo me escribiría? ¿Leería él también esta vida mía, tan llena de cosas pequeñas, y encontraría en ellas una historia que contar?

Una mañana de noviembre, me desperté con la certeza de que ese era el día. No por ninguna señal externa, sino por una especie de claridad repentina, como cuando uno sabe que ha recordado algo importante justo antes de dormirse.

Me levanté. Le di de comer al gato. Regué la planta. Me vestí con cuidado, como si fuera a una cita. Bajé a la calle. El hombre de la acera de enfrente ya no estaba barriendo; supongo que también le había llegado su momento.

Caminé hasta el parque. Me senté en un banco frente al lago. Las hojas caían. Un niño corría detrás de un perro. Una mujer leía un libro con las piernas cruzadas sobre la hierba.

Y entonces, sin drama, sin fanfarria, sin trueno ni luz, simplemente dejé de estar allí.

Dicen —no sé quién lo dice, tal vez el gobierno, tal vez el autor benévolo— que morí sonriendo. Que en el último segundo algo me pareció, por fin, suficiente.

No sé si es verdad.

Pero elijo creerlo.
