The flashlight trembled in my hand, casting jittery shadows across the basement walls. Water dripped somewhere in the dark—*drip, drip, drip*—each drop landing like a held breath.

"You're pretty sure you've never been this scared before," I whispered to myself, testing the theory. My voice cracked on the last word, betraying me. "Then again, anyone would be in your position."

Anyone, that is, who had just watched their twin brother walk into the woods three days ago and not come back.

Anyone who had just received a text from his phone, at 3:47 this morning, containing only their childhood address and a single period.

Anyone who, after ignoring every rational instinct, had driven two hours to stand in their grandmother's abandoned house and descend these rotten basement stairs because *it might be him*.

The smell hit me first—pine needles and something sweeter, like apples rotting in the sun. It was the smell of the forest in October, the smell of the last time I'd seen Marcus. We'd built a fort by the creek. We'd been seven.

*This is stupid*, I told myself. *Call the police. Call Mom.*

But Marcus's phone had sent that message from this address. The police had searched the woods for seventy-two hours and found nothing. No body. No trace. No closure.

And the message had contained a period.

When we were kids, before language got complicated, we'd made up a code. A period meant *help*. It had meant *I found something*. It had meant *come see*. I hadn't thought about that code in twenty years.

My foot hit something soft.

I looked down. The flashlight beam crawled across the floor and found a shoe. Small, child-sized, caked in dried mud. A sneaker. Red, with a white stripe. The kind you'd buy at Walmart for twelve dollars.

My breath stopped.

I knew that shoe. I'd thrown it in the creek when I was seven, the same afternoon Marcus and I had fought about whose turn it was to be the captain of our fort. I'd been mean about it. He'd cried. We hadn't spoken for the rest of the summer, and by autumn the fight had been forgotten.

But the shoe had stayed in the creek.

I'd seen it there, years later, when I came back for the funeral. Gray and waterlogged, half-buried in silt. I'd walked past it without stopping.

I picked it up now with shaking fingers. It was dry. Clean. Brand new.

And in the heel, in handwriting I recognized as my own seven-year-old scrawl, were words:

*Don't come down here.*

I dropped the shoe. I should have run. Every nerve in my body screamed at me to run.

Instead, I lifted the flashlight and turned toward the far corner of the basement, where the dark seemed thicker, somehow. Heavier. Waiting.

A voice came from that darkness. Not Marcus's voice. Not any voice I recognized.

It was my voice. Exactly my voice. But younger. The way I had sounded at seven.

"You came anyway," it said. "I told you not to."

I pointed the light at the corner.

Something was sitting there in the shadows, wearing my brother's face. It smiled with teeth that were too white, too even, too many.

"You always come anyway," it said, standing up. "You always have."

And I remembered then—really remembered, for the first time—that I had never actually gone back to that creek. That I had never actually seen the shoe.

I had only ever *thought* I had.

"You don't remember, do you?" the thing said, stepping into the light. It looked like Marcus but it was *me*, somehow, wearing him like a costume. "You never wanted to remember. It was easier to forget that you were the one who—"

"Stop," I whispered.

"—the one who left him there."

The basement door slammed shut above me. The dripping water stopped. The smell of rotting apples grew so strong I gagged.

"I'm sorry," I said. The words came out of me like blood from a wound. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry—"

"I know," it said, almost gently. "That's why I called."

It reached out a hand that looked like Marcus's hand, like my hand, like every hand that had ever tried to help me out of a dark place I'd put myself in.

"But you can't come back from what you did," it said. "And neither could he."

I took the hand.

We walked up the stairs together, into a house that wasn't empty anymore, that had never really been empty, where my grandmother was calling us in for dinner and the kitchen light was on and the creek ran behind the house like a long-held secret.

In the doorway, I turned back.

The basement was gone.

There was just forest, deep and dark and endless, and somewhere in it a boy in red sneakers who had waited thirty years for his brother to finally come find him.

"Thank you," I said.

But I was alone now.

I was always alone now.

---

O relógio da parede marcava exatamente 22h17 quando Mariana percebeu que não estava sozinha na loja de conveniência.

O frigorífico atrás dela roncava baixinho, como sempre. O mesmo som de sempre — exceto que hoje não havia mais o tilintar dos euros no caixa, nem o farfalhar do jornal sendo folheado pelo Sr. Nogueira, o cliente das últimas horas, que agora jazia desacordado junto à secção das bebidas energéticas.

Ela ainda segurava a lata de Coca-Cola que tinha tirado do expositor.

— Humm, noite tranquila — murmurou, mais para si mesma do que para qualquer outra pessoa.

O homem perto da porta — um capuz cinzento sobre a cabeça, mãos enluvadas, algo brilhante refletido sob a luz fluorescente — virou-se lentamente na sua direção.

— Abre o caixa — disse ele. Baixo, rouco, como uma garganta que não estava habituada a ser usada. — E não grites.

— Gritar? — Mariana arregalou os olhos com um espanto perfeitamente coreografado. — Eu? Por quem me tomas? Não tenho absolutamente nada a dizer a ninguém.

Abanou a cabeça com convicção, ainda com a Coca-Cola na mão como se fosse um microfone de conferência que tivesse acabado de usar numa reunião importante.

— Só queria pagar uma Coca-Cola, senhor. Preço inflated, escusado será dizer, mas pronto. A inflação, *what can you do*, não é?

O homem hesitou. Mariana conseguia ver, mesmo sob a sombra do capuz, que as sobrancelhas dele se tinham contraído num gesto de confusa indignação. Ele provavelmente tinha um guião — *ameaça a operadora, ela entrega o dinheiro, eu saio*. Ela não estava a seguir o guião.

— O. Caixa. — repetiu ele, dando um passo em frente.

— Sim, claro, claro. O caixa. — Mariana virou-se devagar, colocou a Coca-Cola no balcão com uma precisão cirúrgica, e depois começou a reorganizar os chocolates da prateleira ao lado. — Vês, é que temos um pequeno problema de organização de stocks. Esta prateleira dos Twix está caótica, e o meu chefe... ah, o meu chefe vai ficar *furious*. O Sr. Coelho. Costa. Whatever. O homem do escritório. Não tenho a certeza se é Coelho ou Costa, porque ele raramente aparece.

— Fecha a merda do caixa!

— A *merda* do caixa? — Mariana virou-se, genuinamente chocada. — Meu amigo, posso ser a funcionária mais mal paga de Lisboa, mas trabalho num estabelecimento de *elite*. Aqui dizemos "o sistema de processamento de pagamentos". Muito mais profissional.

O ladrão piscou os olhos. Uma vez. Duas.

— Senhora, eu tenho uma...

— Uma arma, sim, sim, imagino. — Mariana acenou com a mão como quem dispensava um vendedor insistente. — A minha colega Sandra tem três em casa, é colecionadora. *Totally fine*. Faz parte da nossa cultura, não sei se tens acompanhado a nossa história. Século XVII, navegadores, Brasil — coisas assim. Mas a Coca-Cola, meu caro? Coca-Cola é universal.

Ele deu outro passo em frente. Estava agora a menos de um metro. Mariana conseguia ver a ponta da faca — porque era uma faca, não uma arma, ela tinha reparado com alívio discreto — a tremer ligeiramente na mão enluvada.

— Abre o caixa, ou...

— Ou o quê? — Mariana inclinou a cabeça com curiosidade académica. — Vais furar as Rolos da Nestlé? Furares a *minha* Coca-Cola? Porque isso seria uma tragédia que a humanidade nunca recuperaria.

A porta de vidro atrás dele rangeou.

O ladrão virou-se — por reflexo, por instinto — e naquele segundo exacto, Mariana agarrou no extintor de incêndio por trás do balcão e disparou-o directamente contra o rosto dele.

Nuvem branca. Gritos abafados. A faca caiu com um ruído metálico.

— *Now* — disse Mariana, sem fôlego, sobre o som do alarme — abro o caixa, sim?

Atirou o extintor para o lado e correu para o Sr. Nogueira, verificando os sinais vitais com uma eficiência que contrastava violentamente com o seu comportamento anterior. O homem velho respirava. Só desmaiado.

Quando a polícia chegou — oito minutos depois, porque era Lisboa e o trânsito — encontraram uma cena curiosa:

Uma funcionária de uniforme verde-azeitona, sentada no chão ao lado do extintor vazio, a beber calmamente a Coca-Cola que tinha ido comprar inicialmente.

— Estava a pagar — disse ela, erguendo a lata como prova. — Posso voltar ao trabalho, ou precisam de uma declaração formal?

O ladrão, algemado a uma das prateleiras de batatas fritas, fungava com os olhos vermelhos do pó químico.

E a Sandra — a colega colecionadora de armas — chegou nesse momento para o turno da noite, avaliou a cena com o olho clínico de quem já tinha visto muita coisa, e apenas disse:

— Outra vez, Mariana?

— *Again* — suspirou ela, erguendo um brinde à Coca-Cola. — Welcome to *clássicos* do bairro.

Mais tarde, no relatório policial, a agente Moreira escreveria uma nota que se tornaria famosa entre os colegas:

*"A funcionária em questão demonstra uma capacidade invulgar de manter o sangue-frio sob ameaça. Recomendo que seja considerada para programas de formação de segurança interna. PS: Tive de ir eu própria buscar um café à máquina, porque ela tinha acabado os que estavam no balcão."*

---

Mariana guardou a história num envelope amarelo que guardava no fundo da gaveta dos talheres, ao lado das facturas do gás. Tinha muitas daquelas.

Mas essa, a do sino — como ela lhe chamava, porque o alarme da loja tinha aquele som grave, quase litúrgico, que lhe lembrava os sinos das igrejas antigas — essa, guardava com especial carinho.

Porque tinha sido a primeira vez que percebera que o seu instinto de sobrevivência, afinal, era muito parecido com o seu instinto de cliente insatisfeita:

*Não grites. Não cedas. Mas também não deixes o mundo esquecer quem é que está realmente no controlo.*

E ela nunca deixava.

# L'eco di un volto

Il caffè era lo stesso di allora, con le stesse tazze di porcellana scheggiata e lo stesso bancone di legno scuro che aveva visto chissà quanti segreti. Elena lo riconobbe prima ancora di vederlo entrare.

Non per i lineamenti. Per l'inclinazione della testa.

Erano passati quindici anni dall'ultima volta che lo aveva visto, quel pomeriggio d'estate alla stazione di Firenze, quando lui era salito su un treno senza voltarsi. Aveva lasciato una lettera sul tavolo della cucina, tre righe scarabocchiate, una scusa che non era una scusa. *Devo andare. Non chiedermi dove.*

Si era chiesta per mesi se l'avesse fatto apposta, a non voltarsi. Poi aveva smesso di chiederselo.

Ora lui era lì, in piedi vicino alla vetrina, con una giacca troppo pesante per la stagione e una cicatrice fresca che gli attraversava il sopracciglio sinistro. I capelli, una volta nerissimi, erano striati di grigio alle tempie. Portava occhiali che non aveva mai portato, dalla montatura sottile, quasi invisibile.

Elena sentì il cuore accelerare, poi rallentare, poi accelerare di nuovo.

Lui la vide. I suoi occhi — sempre stati troppo chiari per il suo viso — la trovarono subito, come se non avesse fatto altro, in tutti quegli anni, che aspettare di essere trovato.

Si avvicinò.

«Il tavolo nell'angolo è libero» disse Elena, e si stupì di quanto fosse calma la sua voce.

Lui si sedette. Ordinò un espresso. Lei un cappuccino, come sempre.

Per un momento nessuno dei due parlò. Fuori, una pioggia sottile cominciava a battere sui vetri.

«Sei dimagrita» disse lui, alla fine.

«Sei invecchiato.»

Lui sorrise, ma non era il sorriso di un tempo. Quello di un tempo avrebbe illuminato l'intero bar. Questo era più piccolo, più cauto, come una fiamma riparata dal vento.

«Non sono venuto per caso» disse. «Non qui. Non oggi.»

Elena lo guardò. Cercò nel suo viso qualcosa del ragazzo che era stato, quello che rubava le mele dal frutteto del vicino e poi le divideva con lei sull'erba, quello che sapeva a memoria ogni verso di una poesia di Montale e gliela leggeva al telefono, di notte, quando non riusciva a dormire.

Qualcosa c'era ancora. Nella curva del naso. Nelle mani, lunghe, che tenevano la tazzina con la stessa precisione di un tempo.

«Perché sei qui, Marco?»

Lui mise la tazzina sul piattino, con un tintinnio quasi impercettibile.

«Perché dovevo dirtelo. Quello che non ho mai avuto il coraggio di scrivere.»

Elena attese.

«La lettera. Quella che ho lasciato sulla tavola. Non era per me. Era contro di me. Ero così spaventato — di noi, di quello che provavo, di non essere abbastanza — che ho preferito scappare. Sono salito su quel treno convinto di salvarti da me.»

«Invece mi hai distrutta.»

«Sì.»

Non si scusò. Non cercò giustificazioni. Elena si accorse, con una specie di meraviglia fredda, che gliene fu grata.

«E adesso?» chiese.

Marco si tolse gli occhiali, li pulì con un angolo della giacca. Aveva gli occhi lucidi.

«Adesso non so. Sono venuto a dirtelo, e adesso che l'ho detto mi sembra di aver finito le parole. Come quella volta.»

Elena bevve un sorso del suo cappuccino. Era tiepido. La schiuma si era sciolta.

Fuori, la pioggia si era fatta più fitta. Una donna con un ombrello rosso attraversò la piazza di corsa, guardandosi intorno come se cercasse qualcuno.

«Quella poesia di Montale» disse Elena.

Marco alzò lo sguardo.

«Quella che mi leggevi al telefono.»

«*Xenia*» disse lui. «*Non so come sia / seguire il tuo lampo tra le foglie.*»

Elena chiuse gli occhi. Per un istante fu di nuovo sedici anni, sul letto di casa sua, con il telefono premuto contro l'orecchio e il cuore che batteva così forte che lui doveva sentirlo attraverso il filo.

«Non la finivi mai» disse. «Ti addormentavi a metà.»

«E tu restavi in linea lo stesso.»

«Perché era bello starti a sentire mentre dormivi.»

Marco rise, piano. Questa volta il sorriso raggiunse gli occhi.

Elena riaprì i suoi.

Si guardarono, al di sopra delle tazze vuote, dei piattini, dei quindici anni che li avevano separati. La pioggia batteva sui vetri. Il cameriere sparecchiava un altro tavolo con aria indifferente.

«Ho un treno fra due ore» disse Marco.

Elena annuì.

«Tornerai?»

Lui non rispose subito. Infilò gli occhiali, si alzò, lasciò una banconota sul tavolo.

«Forse» disse. «O forse ti scriverò. Una lettera vera, questa volta. Con tutte le parole che mancavano nell'altra.»

Si avviò verso la porta. Poi si fermò, si voltò.

«*E il vento batte la porta già scheggiata*» disse, piano.

Elena sentì qualcosa sciogliersi nel petto, come ghiaccio che si scioglie al primo sole di marzo.

«*E tu, cuore mio, sei stato un bel gioco*» rispose.

Marco sorrise — il sorriso di un tempo, quello vero — e uscì nella pioggia.

Elena restò seduta a lungo, con le mani intorno alla tazza ormai fredda, ad ascoltare il rumore dell'acqua contro i vetri, a chiedersi se fosse destino o solo caso, se lui sarebbe tornato o se si sarebbe limitato a quella lettera che forse non sarebbe mai arrivata.

Ma per la prima volta, in quindici anni, la risposta non le sembrò importante.

Qualcosa, almeno, era stato detto.

# The Weight of a Century

The shovel bit into something that wasn't root or stone.

Marcus dropped to his knees in the damp earth, brushing away a century of soil with trembling fingers. The object was a metal box, no larger than a breadbox, its surface mottled with rust and the ghosts of paint. He could just make out the raised letters: TIME CAPSULE — DO NOT OPEN UNTIL 2024.

"Grandma, come look at this!"

But Grandma Elena had passed three winters ago, in the house that had belonged to her mother, and her mother's mother before that, all the way back to 1924 when a woman named Miriam Cole had first broken ground on this soil.

Marcus carried the box inside, set it on the kitchen table, and pried open the rusted latch with a butter knife. The hinges screamed.

Inside, wrapped in yellowed tissue paper, he found:

A bundle of letters tied with red ribbon, the paper so thin he could see his hand through it. A photograph of five women in long dresses, standing where his porch now stood, their faces serious and bright. A child's drawing of a house with a smoking chimney, signed *Elena, age 7*—his grandmother, alive again in graphite.

A pressed bouquet of wildflowers, brown as old blood.

And a small leather journal.

---

Miriam's handwriting was careful, ornate, the letters of a woman who'd been taught penmanship as a sacred art.

*April 12, 1924*

*We have built our home. Walter says the foundation is sound. I say the foundation is made of hope, which is a fragile thing, but he laughed and kissed me and said hope held more weight than stone when properly placed.*

*I am writing this because I have just learned I am with child. I do not know if it is a boy or girl. I do not know what the world will look like when they are grown. I do not know if this box will be opened, or by whom, or whether the person who finds it will remember me.*

*I am putting in the flowers Walter gathered for me on our first walk on this land. I am putting in a photograph of my sisters and myself. I am putting in my wedding ring.*

Marcus stopped. He looked at the box again. There, beneath the tissue paper he'd lifted, nestled in a small velvet pouch, was a thin gold band.

*I am putting in my wedding ring because I do not need it anymore.*

His heart, which had been beating steadily, forgot its rhythm.

*I am dying, you see. The doctor has told me so, though he used gentler words. I have perhaps until the end of summer. The child will be born, and I will not see their first step, their first word, their first heartbreak. I cannot bear the thought of Walter alone with an infant, the way he looks at me when he thinks I am sleeping, as if he is trying to memorize my face before it disappears.*

*So I am doing what I can. I am leaving pieces of myself where they might be found. And I am writing this letter to whoever you are, you who stand in my kitchen a hundred years from now.*

---

Marcus read the rest with his face wet.

Miriam wrote of the baby (a girl, she would learn), of her hopes for the world the child would inherit, of small kindnesses that had sustained her through the long winter of her illness. She wrote of Walter, how he whistled while he worked, how he held her hand in the night when the coughing came, how she had loved him so fiercely that even now, dying, she felt lucky.

And at the end:

*If you are reading this, then I was right about one thing: the box was opened. Not by me, and not by Walter, who has promised to bury it the week after I am gone.*

*I do not know what year you live in. I do not know what wonders or horrors the world has wrought. I do not know if you are a stranger or a descendant or someone in between.*

*But I am asking you, please, to do one small thing.*

*Plant the flowers.*

*There are seeds in the envelope at the bottom of this box. I gathered them from the meadow behind our property, the same meadow where Walter proposed. I do not know if they will grow. I do not know if the soil is still good. But if you can, if you have a patch of earth and an hour to spare, plant them.*

*And when they bloom—wild columbine, black-eyed Susan, bee balm—think of me for a moment. Think of a woman who lived a short time and loved enormously and wanted, more than anything, to leave the world a little more beautiful than she found it.*

*That is all.*

*That is everything.*

*Miriam Cole, 1924*

---

The envelope was there, beneath the velvet pouch, brittle and sealed with wax. Marcus opened it with hands that shook. Seeds spilled across the table, tiny and patient, a hundred years asleep.

He went outside. The sun was setting, throwing long shadows across the yard—the same yard, the same soil, a different century. He walked to the back corner of the property, where the wild part met the tended part, and where the ground sloped down toward what had once been a meadow.

He knelt. He dug. He planted.

And when the first shoots came up in June—delicate, improbable, stubborn with life—he thought of a woman he'd never met, who had loved a man who whistled, who had died so that a daughter would live, who had trusted a stranger a century away to remember her.

He thought of his grandmother, seven years old, drawing a house that would one day be his.

He thought of how the dead are never really gone. They live in the seeds we plant, in the houses they leave us, in the small acts of love that travel down through generations like water through stone.

The flowers bloomed. They were, exactly as Miriam had promised, beautiful.

And every year, when they came back, Marcus told their story to whoever would listen—his children, his neighbors, the curious strangers who paused at the fence to admire the wild columbine and the black-eyed Susans and the bee balm growing in impossible profusion against all odds, in a yard where a woman had once stood with her sisters and dreamed of the future.

The future had arrived.

It had remembered her.

# The Seventh Night

The food bowl sat untouched, and the silence where there should have been paws on tile grew heavier each day.

I set it out at the usual time—6:14 p.m., the precise moment the kitchen light caught the angle of the window and Curious would appear, as if summoned by the geometry of late afternoon sun. I'd named her that because she'd watched me, unblinking, from the moment I'd opened the carrier in my apartment three years ago. *You're going to get into everything,* I'd said. *I can tell.* She had blinked once, slowly, and then disappeared behind the refrigerator for six hours.

The first day, I assumed she was off doing cat things—hunting in the alley behind the Italian restaurant, sunning herself on Mrs. Pellegrini's roof, terrorizing the squirrels who lived in the oak at the end of the block. Curious had always operated on her own schedule, her own logic. She came and went through the window I'd installed for her, a small wooden flap I'd sanded and painted to match the frame.

The second day, I started leaving the window open at night, just in case.

The third day, I walked the neighborhood. I asked the mailman. I asked the kids at the bus stop, who knew her because she'd let them pet her—a rare honor, apparently, that she extended only to those under twelve and over seventy. I checked the storm drains. I checked the crawl space under the porch of the abandoned house on Elm. I posted on the neighborhood app with a photo: her orange face, the white blaze on her chest, the notch in her left ear from the time she'd gotten into a fight with something I never identified.

By the fourth day, I was inventing reasons to stay home. Work could wait. The world could wait. I sat by the window and watched the street.

On the fifth day, Mrs. Pellegrini knocked on my door. She was eighty-four and wore house slippers even in winter.

"She came to me," she said. "Three days ago. Sat on my porch all day. I fed her. She left when it got dark."

Three days ago. The first day. The day I'd assumed she was fine.

"Why didn't you tell me?"

She looked at me the way elderly women sometimes look at younger ones—with a patience that bordered on pity. "I just did, dear."

That night, I didn't sleep. I sat by the window with the lights off, watching the streetlamps flicker against the wet pavement. It had rained that afternoon. The whole city smelled like wet asphalt and cold.

At 2:17 a.m., I heard it.

Not a sound exactly—more like the absence of one. The refrigerator had been humming. A car had passed. And then nothing. Just the particular quality of silence that means an animal is holding very still in the dark.

I got up slowly. I didn't turn on the light.

She was sitting on the kitchen counter, which she wasn't supposed to do. Her fur was matted with something—mud, maybe, or something darker. Her green eyes caught what little light there was and threw it back at me, multiplied.

"Hey," I whispered.

She didn't move. She didn't blink.

I took a step toward her. She tensed, and I saw it then: her left ear was torn worse than it had ever been. There was a long scratch down her face, half-healed. Her tail was wrapped tight around her body, the way cats wrap themselves when they are trying to become small.

I knelt down. I didn't reach for her.

"What happened to you?"

She made a sound then—not a meow, not a purr, but something I had never heard her make before. A thin, airless chirp, like a bird that had forgotten how to fly.

I put my hand on the floor, palm up. The way I'd done when I'd first brought her home, when she'd circled me for hours before deciding I was acceptable.

She watched my hand for a long time.

Then she crossed the kitchen, slowly, and pressed her head against my palm, hard. Hard enough that I could feel the ridges of her skull. She stayed there, breathing, while the refrigerator started humming again, while a car passed, while the night rearranged itself around us.

She didn't eat that night. Or the next morning. She drank a little water from the bowl, and then she disappeared under the bed, where she stayed for two more days.

Now, a week and a half after she'd first gone missing, she is sitting on the windowsill in the late afternoon sun. The scratch on her face has scabbed over. She is watching something outside—a bird, a leaf, something I can't see.

I don't know where she went. I don't know what she saw. I have learned, over the past seven nights, that there are some questions you don't ask the ones you love. You just leave the window open, and you leave the light on, and you wait for them to come back in their own time, in their own way.

At 6:14 p.m., exactly, she drops down from the windowsill and walks to her bowl.

She eats.

I sit across from her, on the kitchen floor, and I don't say anything at all.

"……不是这样的……"一个细如蚊蚋的声音说。

林夏听见自己的卧室门被轻轻推开了。

然后是漫长的寂静。

但她发现了一件事——她放在玄关的那双高跟鞋，鞋跟朝向了门口。

林夏决定搬家。

"姐，这镜子挺沉啊。"他说，"要不一起搬了？"

林夏看向洗手间。

那面镜子不知什么时候已经自己取下来了，端端正正地立在客厅中央，像是早就等着被带走。

那个林夏，正对着她笑。

# 老屋檐下的话

奶奶走的那年，我十八岁。

她走得很突然。前一天还在院子里晒被子，第二天就再也没有醒来。

父亲说，奶奶临终前一直念叨我的名字。我从学校赶回去时，她已经走了。

后来整理遗物，我在她枕头底下发现了一个红布包。布包里，是一张泛黄的纸条和一枚铜钱。

纸条上的字歪歪扭扭，是奶奶的手笔：

**"孩子，奶奶没能给你留下什么值钱的东西。但有一句话，你要记住——"**

**"这世上，没有过不去的坎儿，只有过不去的心。"**

**"心若宽了，路就宽了；心若窄了，路就窄了。"**

**"奶奶这辈子，穷过、苦过、哭过、也被人看不起过。可我从来没觉得过不去。你爷爷走得早，我一个人拉扯四个孩子，照样把他们养大成人。"**

**"你记住，碰到难事儿，先睡一觉。睡醒了，天还是那个天，路还是那条路。可你的心，可以变。"**

我握着那张纸条，哭了很久。

---

后来，我离开了家乡，去大城市读书、工作。

刚毕业那年，我在出租屋里啃着馒头写简历，投出去的石沉大海。室友已经拿到了offer，我连面试通知都收不到。

那晚，我躺在窄小的床上，想起了奶奶的话。

**"先睡一觉。"**

我真的睡下了。第二天醒来，我删掉了几份海投的简历，针对一家最喜欢的公司重新写了求职信。三天后，我收到了面试通知。

再后来，我恋爱，又失恋。对方留下的一句话是："你太累了，我不想陪你走了。"

那晚，我在阳台坐到凌晨。楼下是车水马龙，眼前是万家灯火，却没有一盏属于我。

我又想起了奶奶。

**"心若窄了，路就窄了。"**

我开始反思。我确实把爱情当成了救命稻草，把对方当成了唯一的光。一个人如果自己心里没有光，怎么可能照亮两个人呢？

我开始学着独处，学着把自己活成一片海，而不是一条小溪等着别人流进来。

三年后，我遇到了现在的丈夫。他说我身上有一种"松弛感"，让他很安心。

我想，那大概就是奶奶说的"心宽"吧。

---

再后来，奶奶的那枚铜钱一直挂在我车钥匙上。

那是一枚民国时候的铜钱，被奶奶磨得光亮，包浆温润。她说，那是你太爷爷留下的，你太爷爷说那是更早的老物件儿。

我一直不知道它的来历，也不值钱。可每次摸到它，我就觉得奶奶在我身边。

前几年，我做生意亏了钱，欠了一屁股债。最难的时候，我连女儿的奶粉钱都发愁。

我蹲在车里，没敢回家。

我摸到了那枚铜钱。

**"没有过不去的坎儿，只有过不去的心。"**

我深吸一口气，发动了车，去找朋友借了周转的钱。三年后，我还清了债，还小赚了一笔。

---

去年清明，我带着女儿回去给奶奶上坟。

女儿问："奶奶，这是什么？"

她指着墓碑前的铜钱问。我愣了一下——我明明没放铜钱啊。

父亲走过来，说："那是你奶奶的。她临走前让我放上去的，说这枚铜钱陪了她一辈子，要继续守着这个家。"

我蹲下来，看着那枚铜钱。

阳光照在它身上，泛着淡淡的光。

**"奶奶，您的话，孙女一直记着呢。"**

我轻声说。

风穿过墓前的松柏，沙沙作响。

仿佛是奶奶在笑。

---

*这世上，没有过不去的坎儿，只有过不去的心。*

奶奶的话，陪了我二十多年。

每当我撑不下去的时候，我就想起她。

一个裹着小脚的老人，独自把四个孩子养大。

她都能过去，我凭什么过不去？

# The Weight of an Unlocked Door

Marcus stared at the phone like it might detonate.

The number was local. The message was polite. The name at the bottom—*Catherine Bell*—felt like a hand reaching up from a grave he'd stopped visiting years ago.

His mother wanted coffee. Just coffee. At a place called The Wren on Maple Street, Saturday at two.

He read it four times, then put the phone face-down on the counter and went to take a shower, because that's what people do when the past knocks: they go about small domestic motions as if the world hadn't just tilted.

---

In the mirror, he practiced nothing. He didn't know what face to wear.

Twenty-six years of being someone's son had not prepared him for the simple mechanics of reconciliation. There were no instructions. No one's story quite matched his own—not the fathers who left and came back pennitent, not the mothers who explained and begged. His mother had done neither. His mother had simply *gone*, in increments so small that by the time he noticed, she was already a stranger with his last name.

He thought about not going. He thought about it the way you think about not opening a suspicious email—not because you're curious, but because you suspect the damage is already done.

---

The Wren was the kind of place that served avocado toast and called it brunch. Catherine was already seated by the window, hands wrapped around a mug she wasn't drinking from. She looked older. They always look older.

"Marcus." She said his name the way people say a word in a language they once spoke fluently.

He sat down. He ordered coffee he didn't want.

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Outside, a woman walked a corgi. A child laughed somewhere. The world continued its ordinary business around them.

"I know I don't have the right," Catherine said finally. "To ask anything of you."

"No," he said. "You don't."

She nodded, as if she'd been expecting that. As if she'd rehearsed it.

"I left because I was drowning," she said. "And I thought if I stopped swimming, at least one of us would survive."

"That's a beautiful metaphor," Marcus said, and was surprised by the coldness in his own voice. "Did you practice it?"

"Yes," she said quietly. "Many times."

Something in that admission cracked something in him. He didn't want it to. He had spent years constructing a fortress of not-caring, and she had walked in and sat down and *told the truth*, and the mortar was suddenly wet.

"What do you want from me, Mom?"

The word came out before he could stop it. *Mom.* Not Catherine. Not *her.* The word his body remembered even when his mind had tried to forget.

"I want to know if you'll let me try again," she said. "Not to be forgiven. Just to be present. If you'll allow it."

---

He thought of the boy he'd been—eleven, twelve, thirteen—checking the door each night, then the driveway, then the mailbox, then nothing. He thought of the man he'd become, careful with everyone, allergic to promises, half-convinced that love was just a word people used before they left.

He thought of the child laughing outside, and how easy it seemed to be young in the world.

"If I say yes," Marcus said slowly, "you need to understand something. I'm not the boy you left. That boy is gone. Whatever you get back will be someone you have to meet from the beginning."

"I understand," she said.

"Do you?" He leaned forward. "Because I don't trust you. And I may never trust you. And if you can live with that—if you can sit across from me, week after week, knowing I'm holding something back—then maybe we can try."

Catherine's eyes filled, but she didn't look away.

"I can live with that," she whispered.

---

He stayed for the coffee. He stayed for an hour. He didn't promise anything except a second meeting, and even that felt like swinging open a door he'd nailed shut for a decade.

When he left The Wren, the sun had shifted. The corgi was gone. His shadow stretched long behind him on the sidewalk.

He texted his therapist as he walked.

*Saw her. It went okay. I think.*

Then he put his phone away, and let the afternoon be ordinary, and tried not to think about how the door—once opened—could never be quite closed again.

# The Margin Club

The envelope arrived without a return address, smelling faintly of cedar and old paper. Inside, a single cardstock invitation:

*You have been observed finishing books. We meet Thursdays. The address will be disclosed upon your reply.*

Mara Chen almost threw it away. She edited academic monographs for a living; unfinished manuscripts haunted her dreams. Finishing a book was, in her experience, a minor miracle.

She replied anyway. Of course she did.

The reply envelope, when it came, contained no address, only a single line of instruction: *Place this letter under your pillow tonight. You will wake knowing where to go.*

Mara laughed out loud, alone in her apartment. Then she placed the letter under her pillow, mostly as a joke.

She dreamed of a library that had no doors.

---

The address turned out to be a basement beneath a used bookshop in the village she hadn't realized was there—hadn't realized she lived so close to. The door was unmarked except for a small pencil mark in the margin of the brickwork.

Inside, seven people sat around a scarred oak table with a single lamp. They looked up when she entered. None of them smiled, but none of them seemed unfriendly either. They simply *looked*, with the patient attention of people waiting for a sentence to resolve.

"You came by dream," said the woman at the head of the table. Her name tag read: EDNA, FOOTNOTE. "Most of us did. Please, sit."

Mara sat. "What is this?"

"We read," said Edna. "And sometimes we write. The two are more related than people think."

A man with wire-rimmed glasses—his tag said HENRY, EPILOGUE—pushed a slim volume across the table. "Open to page forty-seven. Begin where the margin is marked."

The book was unfamiliar: *The Hour of the Interior*, one Lila Vane. The passage on page forty-seven described a woman unlocking a door in her own house and finding a room she had never seen. Mara read it aloud, feeling the words sit strangely on her tongue, as though she had spoken them before.

When she finished, Henry nodded. "Now. Write the next paragraph. Here." He produced a pen and a single sheet of cream paper.

"I—what?"

"The book is waiting for it," said Edna. "It's been waiting thirty years."

Mara picked up the pen. The nib hovered over the page. Then, without quite deciding to, she wrote:

*The woman understood then that the room had always been part of her house, and that her house had been patiently explaining itself to her, line by line, for years.*

She set the pen down. Her hand was trembling.

"Read it back," said Edna gently.

Mara read it back. The words on the page were not the words she had just written. They were different. They were *better*.

"That's not—" She looked up, but the others were nodding as if she had confirmed something.

"The room," said a young man whose tag read PETER, COLOPHON, "is a real place. The house is a real house. We have been writing her into existence for thirty years. We are very nearly finished."

Mara stared. "You're saying—the book is real? The woman is real?"

"The woman," said Edna, "has been waiting. We have been drafting her into being. You, Mara, are the last contributor we needed. The final chapter will close tomorrow."

Mara laughed, but it came out thin. "You're insane. All of you. This is some kind of—"

But she had felt it. The weight of the pen. The way the room had *listened*. The way her own handwriting had looked back at her from the page like a stranger's face.

"We don't require belief," said Henry. "We require contribution. You have given it. Thank you."

She left shortly after, or tried to. The stairwell seemed longer on the way up. The bookshop above was closed; the windows were dark. When she stepped outside, the street was not the one she had walked down.

She walked home by a route she knew, but had never taken.

---

For three days, Mara did not sleep. She reread the passage she had written—not *written*, *transcribed*—and watched the ink move. Subtle. Almost imperceptible. A comma here, a clarifying clause there, the language tightening itself like a muscle.

On Thursday, she returned.

The same seven sat around the table. They greeted her like an old colleague.

"Tomorrow," said Edna.

"Tell me what's real," said Mara. "Please. I can't—I need to know what I walked into."

Edna regarded her for a long moment. Then she opened her own notebook—the one she had been carrying, bound in some pale animal skin—and turned to the first page.

"This is the original draft," she said. "Thirty years ago. One sentence. *There was a woman who opened a door she had not known was there.* That was all. A sentence I could not finish. I passed it to Henry. Henry passed it to Peter. The book has been writing itself through us ever since."

"But the house—the woman—"

"There is a house in the country," said Henry quietly. "No one has lived in it for thirty years. We have, all of us, been inside it once. We were each, in our own way, the woman at the door."

Mara looked around the table. She saw, for the first time, that they were all her age. Or near it. As if the club existed outside of time, and recruited only at the precise moment it needed.

"The book ends tomorrow," said Edna. "And when it ends, the woman either walks into the room, or she does not. We have not yet determined which."

"Which do you want?"

Edna smiled, finally, and it was the saddest thing Mara had ever seen.

"We want her to walk in. We have written her a beautiful room. We have written her a chair by the window, and a kettle, and an afternoon that lasts forever. But whether she chooses to enter is not ours to say. That is the part we cannot write."

She turned the notebook toward Mara.

"Would you like to write the final line?"

Mara stared at the page. She saw the words her hand had written—the words that were no longer hers—and beneath them, an empty line, waiting like a held breath.

"Will I know what to write?"

"You will know," said Edna, "when you stop needing to know."

Mara took the pen.

She did not write *she walked in*.

She did not write *she turned away*.

She wrote: *The woman stood at the threshold and understood that the door had been written for her, by her, all along—and that to open it was to forgive the author she had been waiting for.*

She set the pen down.

This time, the ink did not move.

Around the table, the seven exhaled together.

---

In the morning, Mara read in the paper that an abandoned country house had been found, opened for the first time in three decades, by a woman who said she had dreamed the address. Inside, the local reporter wrote, there was a kitchen with a kettle on the stove, still warm, and a chair by the window where the afternoon light fell in a long, unbroken sheet.

No one had been seen to enter.

No one had been seen to leave.

The Margin Club, Mara thought, had published at last.

She brewed herself a cup of tea, sat by her own window, and began, at last, to read.

# 最后一口水

背包里只剩下一瓶水了。

林夏盯着那瓶矿泉水，塑料瓶在阳光下折射出细碎的光斑。嘴唇已经干裂到起了白皮，喉咙像被人用砂纸打磨过，每吞咽一次口水都带着刺痛。

她已经在沙漠里走了三天。

三天前，旅行社的中巴车在无人区的公路上抛锚，司机说去找救援，让游客原地等待。可那个方向扬起沙尘之后，就再也没有回来。卫星电话没有信号，指南针在磁矿区失了灵。

她现在唯一的同伴是背包里那只半死的骆驼——不，那不是她的骆驼。那是同车的陌生人，那个沉默寡言的中摄影师留下的。他比她走得快，说要去找水，答应回来接她。

两天了。

林夏知道自己不该等下去。可她连方向都辨不清，唯一的希望就是那个人真的会回来。

太阳落下去又升起来。第三个早晨，她听见远处传来脚步声。

是摄影师。

他瘦得脱了形，嘴唇乌青，眼眶深陷得像两个洞。但他还活着。他怀里抱着一只军用水壶，摇摇晃晃地走过来。

林夏迎上去，接过水壶。

空的。

摄影师的嘴唇开合了几下，发不出声音。最后他用沙哑到几乎听不见的嗓音说："三十公里外……有绿洲……没有水……走到不了。"

林夏的血液凉了半截。

"你一路上……没找到水？"

摄影师摇头。他靠在一块岩石上滑坐下来，眼神涣散地望着天空："我以为能走到的。"

沉默。

只有风卷着沙子打旋的声音。

林夏看着他，忽然明白他回来不是为了给她希望。他回来，是因为他自己也走不动了。

她蹲下来，拧开背包里那瓶水的瓶盖。

还剩三分之一瓶。

她盯着那点清水，盯着摄影师乌青的嘴唇，盯着自己同样裂开的指尖。

两天的路程，三十多公里的沙漠，两个人，共享三分之一瓶水。

——走不到绿洲的。

她知道。

如果不走，更是死路一条。

"你先喝。"林夏把水壶递到摄影师嘴边，声音比自己预想的平静，"喝完我们就走。"

摄影师抬起浑浊的眼睛看了她一眼。

"……你呢？"

"我喝过了。"林夏说。

她没有。

摄影师盯着她。她迎着那道目光，没有躲避。

四目相对的瞬间，她忽然感到一阵尖锐的羞耻——不是为自己撒谎，而是为了自己撒谎时的那种镇定。她在心里演练过无数次这一刻，演练得太多，到真正发生的时候，竟然像在演一出烂熟的戏。

摄影师没有接水壶。

"你没喝。"他说。

林夏的手僵在半空。

"我喝过了。"

"你嘴唇是干的。"摄影师的声音很轻，"比我的还干。"

林夏握着水壶的手指微微发抖。她可以说那是风，可以说不渴，可以找一百个借口。但她突然觉得累了，累得连撒谎都维持不住。

她垂下眼睛。

"……喝吧。"她说，声音哑得不像自己，"走不到也得走。"

摄影师沉默了很久。

然后他伸出手，没有去拿水壶，而是握住了林夏的手腕。他的手指冰凉，力气却大得惊人。

"一人一半。"他说，"喝了我们就走。谁也别想偷偷死在这儿。"

林夏的眼泪突然就掉下来了。

她也不知道自己在哭什么。也许是三天三夜积累的所有恐惧，所有孤独，所有不确定。也许只是因为在这个世界上，她竟然遇到了一个愿意和她平分最后一口水的人。

她把水壶举到两人中间。

摄影师从口袋里摸出一把折叠刀，在水壶盖上刻了一道线。

"一人喝到这里。"

两个人轮流喝了口水。

水入喉的时候，林夏觉得从没有尝过这么甘甜的味道。她小心翼翼地把水壶盖拧紧，生怕洒出一滴。

摄影师站起来，朝她伸出手。

"走吧。"

林夏握住他的手。

两个摇摇晃晃的人，朝着太阳升起的方向走去。

走了很远之后，林夏偶然回头。

那个他们刚才坐过的地方，岩石后面的沙子里，露出一截生锈的铁皮——是某个年代翻车的卡车。

车斗里堆着几只被沙子掩埋的木箱。

最近的一只已经被风沙刮开，露出里面整整齐齐码放的矿泉水瓶。

林夏停下脚步。

她回头看摄影师。摄影师也回头看。

两个人对视了一眼，然后不约而同地笑了出来。

那笑声在空旷的沙漠里显得荒腔走板，笑到一半林夏又哭了。摄影师也红了眼眶，却还在笑。

"你他妈的……"摄影师笑着骂了一声，没说完。

他们往回走。

水很充足。足够他们走出沙漠的。

但林夏在很多年后回忆起这段经历，记住的不是那箱救命的水。

而是那一道刻在水壶盖上的线。

一人一半。

谁也别想偷偷死在这儿。

# Toute ma vie m'avait menée à cet instant

Le métro s'arrêta en grinçant à la station Châtelet-Les Halles. Clara resta assise un instant de trop, le regard perdu à travers la vitre, son reflet se superposant aux visages pressés sur le quai.

Toute sa vie l'avait menée à cet instant.

Elle repensa à la petite fille de six ans qui collectionnait les éclats de verre sur la plage de Saint-Malo, convaincue que chacun contenait une histoire. À l'adolescente maigre qui écrivait des poèmes dans son cahier à spirales, cachée sous les draps avec une lampe torche. À la jeune femme qui avait quitté Lyon pour Paris un matin de septembre, une valise jaune et trois cents euros en poche.

Trente-quatre ans. Huit déménagements. Deux cœurs brisés. Un diplôme de lettres modernes dont personne ne voulait. Des petits boulots — serveuse, vendeuse de chaussures, opératrice de saisie, gardienne de musée la nuit.

Et maintenant, ce café.

*Le Comptoir des Mots Perdus* se trouvait au coin de la rue Sainte-Anne et d'un passage que peu de gens connaissaient encore. La devanture était modeste, presque fatiguée. Une enseigne en bois peint, à peine lisible. Deux chaises bancales. Un géranium qui survivait par miracle à l'automne parisien.

Clara poussa la porte. La clochette tinta — un son minuscule, presque oublié.

— Vous êtes fermée ? demanda-t-elle.

La femme derrière le comptoir leva les yeux. Soixante-dix ans peut-être, les cheveux blancs tirés en chignon, des lunettes rondes, un tablier à fleurs.

— Non, dit-elle. J'attendais quelqu'un.

— Je m'appelle Clara Vasseur. J'ai répondu à votre annonce. Pour le poste de libraire.

La vieille femme ne bougea pas. Elle l'observa avec une attention particulière, comme si elle lisait un manuscrit ancien.

— Asseyez-vous, Clara Vasseur.

Il y avait quelque chose dans la façon dont elle prononçait son nom. Une douceur étrange. Clara s'assit.

— Savez-vous pourquoi j'ai mis cette annonce dans le journal, après toutes ces années sans prendre d'employé ?

Clara secoua la tête.

— Parce que la dernière libraire qui a travaillé ici était ma sœur. Elle est morte en 1998. Et je n'ai jamais voulu remplacer quelqu'un. Mais le cœur ne suit plus. Et puis... il y a trois jours, j'ai rêvé d'elle. Elle m'a dit : *"Lève-toi, Mathilde. Il y a une fille aux éclats de verre qui arrive."*

Clara sentit quelque chose frémir dans sa poitrine.

— Aux éclats de verre ?

— Vous en collectionniez, non ? Quand vous étiez petite ?

Clara ne répondit pas. Elle ne pouvait pas. Elle avait dix ans la dernière fois qu'elle avait parlé de cette collection à quelqu'un. C'était à sa grand-mère, à Saint-Malo. Et sa grand-mère était morte depuis longtemps.

— Comment savez-vous...

— Je ne sais rien, mon enfant. Je crois, c'est tout. Il y a des rencontres qui n'arrivent pas par hasard. Il y a des librairies qui attendent leur libraire. Et il y a des noms qui sonnent comme des promesses.

Mathilde se leva lentement, contourna le comptoir, et prit les mains de Clara dans les siennes. Elles étaient chaudes, légèrement rugueuses.

— Toute ma vie, j'ai attendu cet instant. Celui où quelqu'un reprendrait ce que j'ai construit. Non pas pour moi. Pour ceux qui viendront chercher des livres ici.

Clara regarda autour d'elle pour la première fois vraiment. Les murs étaient couverts de rayonnages en bois sombre. Des milliers de livres. Des milliers d'histoires. Elle vit un coin avec un fauteuil défoncé près de la fenêtre, une couverture en patchwork pliée sur l'accoudoir. Elle vit des piles de livres au sol, comme des villes miniatures. Elle vit une odeur de papier et de café, et quelque chose de plus ancien encore.

Elle sentit qu'elle était exactement là où elle devait être.

— Quand est-ce que je commence ? murmura-t-elle.

Mathilde sourit.

— Vous avez déjà commencé.

Dehors, Paris bruissait de son indifférence éternelle. Personne ne remarqua la clochette qui tinta une seconde fois quand la porte se referma. Personne ne vit Clara Vasseur poser ses mains à plat sur le comptoir, fermer les yeux, et respirer enfin — vraiment — pour la première fois depuis des années.

Toute sa vie l'avait menée à cet instant.

Et tout ce qui restait à vivre en découlait.

# The Sync

The update notification arrived at 4:17 AM, Eastern Standard Time, on a Tuesday.

Most of the world slept through it. The servers pushed silently, the way they did every quarter—new background gradients, a slightly different icon, a handful of bug fixes no one had asked for. But this update contained one additional change, buried in the forty-seventh line of the release notes, in language designed to be skimmed: *Improved countdown calibration across regional cell towers.*

Mortality had been downloadable since 2021. The app had started as a joke from a Bay Area startup—an act of nihilism disguised as wellness. *Know your numbers,* their marketing had read. *Live intentionally.* The first version had been wildly inaccurate, assigning the same number to everyone regardless of age, health, or circumstance. People had laughed, then wept, then forgotten. The app sat in the limbo of the App Store's mediocre middle, three stars, few updates, no real users.

Then the second version launched.

The second version was perfect.

No one knew how. The company's engineers claimed machine learning, neural networks trained on insurance actuarial tables, hospital records stolen and repackaged. Whatever the method, it worked. The numbers it gave people were, with eerie precision, correct. Not guesses. Not ranges. *Correct.* 

The CEO had been the first to discover this, when his own countdown suddenly accelerated from forty-seven years to four days. He drove home from the office and sat in his garage and didn't get out. The news spread slowly, then all at once. By the end of that year, two hundred million people carried their death in their pockets.

By 2034, it was unremarkable. People glanced at it the way their grandparents had glanced at the weather. *Three weeks. Plenty of time to finish the deck.* *Six months. Should probably call Mom.* A quiet companion. A useful one, some argued—it focused the mind, prioritized the days. Others found it unbearable and lived anyway, determined to spite the number.

Then came the sync.

---

Maya Chen noticed hers during her morning run.

She was forty-one, in good health by the app's estimate, with eleven years showing when she'd gone to bed. The path along the river was empty at this hour. Her breath came out in pale plumes. Her footfalls were steady on the gravel. The phone buzzed softly against her forearm, a vibration she'd learned to ignore.

When she lifted it, she almost tripped.

The number glowed white against the dark interface.

**11 days, 14 hours, 22 minutes.**

She stopped. Stood still in the cold, her chest heaving. The number held steady, ticking down one second, then another. Eleven days. *Eleven days.*

She wiped sweat from her forehead and looked around, as if the river or the trees might confirm what she was seeing. A man was walking a dog across the footbridge in the distance. He stopped too. She saw him raise his phone, and even at this distance she saw the way his posture changed—the slight droop, the hand falling to his side.

She ran home.

---

By 9 AM, the streets had that particular texture they got during collective crisis—not quite panic, not quite grief, but something adjacent to both. Cars moved at exactly the speed limit, no one passing anyone. People stood on sidewalks in coats, phones in hand, staring. A few were crying quietly. A few were laughing. One man was on his knees in the median of Fifth Avenue, and no one told him to get up.

Theories multiplied online faster than they could be disproven. Mass hallucination. Coordinated hack. Some kind of psychological attack, drones in the sky, signals from the towers. A programmer on Twitter pointed to the release notes and was ratioed into oblivion. *It's a glitch,* people insisted. *It'll be fixed by lunch.*

It wasn't fixed by lunch.

By noon, the number was universal. Every phone. Every person. Eleven days, fourteen hours, *X* minutes. The only variation was the seconds.

---

The President addressed the nation at 2 PM. He looked, Maya thought, like he was trying to remember how to breathe. He did not have answers. He urged calm. He urged prayer, for those who prayed. He urged community. Behind him, the seal of the United States looked, for the first time in her life, like something that might fall off the wall.

Maya sat on the floor of her apartment and watched.

Her phone sat face-down on the coffee table, ticking audibly now—a soft sound she'd never noticed before, but which had, in the last few hours, become impossible to ignore. She could hear it from across the room.

Eleven days.

---

The first three days were chaos.

Markets crashed and then stopped opening. Governments declared states of emergency that no one enforced, because what was the point of enforcement when everyone knew the number? Crime rates plummeted for forty-eight hours, then spiked as people processed the realization that the usual deterrents no longer applied. There were suicides, fewer than predicted, more than anyone wanted to acknowledge. There were also births—a strange, defiant surge in maternity wards, the body insisting on its own continuation even as the mind accepted its ending.

Churches overflowed. So did the rivers, briefly.

Then, around day four, something shifted.

Maya noticed it first in the small things. A neighbor she'd never spoken to left a pot of soup on her doorstep with a note: *For the days ahead.* A delivery driver carried her packages up three flights because, he said, "it seemed like the thing to do." Strangers made eye contact on the street and didn't look away. People were softer. Rougher, in some ways—less patience for the small cruelties—but also more open, as if the locked doors of themselves had all swung wide.

She called her mother.

Her mother picked up on the first ring.

"I know," her mother said, before Maya could speak. "Eleven days."

"Mom."

"I'm here. I'm here, baby." Her mother's voice was thick, but steady. "I have eleven days too. We all do."

Maya closed her eyes. Somewhere in the city, a siren wailed and then went quiet.

"Do you think it's real?" she whispered.

A long pause. "I think," her mother said slowly, "that it doesn't matter if it's real. The eleven days are real. Whatever comes after—who knows. But these eleven days are real, and we have them."

---

Theories kept proliferating, but they grew less frantic. Some said the app had always known, had been quietly counting down since its launch, and the sync was just a final correction. Some said it was a test, sent by something higher—a simulation, a god, a future self. Some said the world was about to end, and some said it wasn't, and most people stopped caring which was true.

What mattered was the shape of the days.

People stopped pretending they might get to things *later.* They stopped saying *someday.* The houses they had meant to renovate were renovated, badly, joyfully, with whatever paint was at the hardware store. The letters that had sat half-written for years were finished and mailed. Estrangements ended or were confirmed, but gently, with final coffees and shared tears. Marriages collapsed and marriages were repaired. Children were told the truth, in whatever words their parents could find, and most children took it better than anyone expected, because children had always known, in some way, that the days were finite.

Maya flew home. Her mother met her at the airport with flowers, which made no sense and made perfect sense. They sat in the kitchen and drank tea and talked about nothing and everything, and the phone on the table ticked, and neither of them looked at it.

---

On day eight, a strange thing happened.

Maya was walking in the park near her childhood home when she saw the man from the river path—the one with the dog. He was sitting on a bench, and the dog was asleep at his feet, and he was sketching something in a small notebook. He looked up as she passed, and there was a flicker of recognition.

"The river," he said.

"The river," she agreed.

She sat down beside him without being invited. He closed the notebook. His name was David, and he was fifty-three, and the dog's name was Biscuit, and he had once been an architect but had quit to paint, which was the kind of thing people always said they wanted to do and rarely did. He had done it. He didn't seem to regret it.

"How many days?" she asked, though she knew.

"Eleven," he said. "Less now. Eight, I suppose." He looked at her. "You?"

"Eight."

He nodded. They sat in the quiet, and the dog shifted in its sleep, and somewhere a child was laughing.

"I used to be afraid of it," David said, after a while. "The number. When it first came. I was fifty-three with thirty years left and I was *terrified* of thirty years. Isn't that something?" He shook his head. "All that fear. All that running."

"And now?"

He looked at the dog, then at the trees, then at her. "Now I have eight days. And I don't feel afraid. I feel like I finally have enough time."

---

The world did not end on day eleven.

It didn't end on day twelve, or thirteen, or any of the days after. The app kept counting down, tick by tick, and when the numbers reached zero, they simply stopped—the screen went dark, the app closed, and a small gray icon remained. No fireworks. No rapture. Just silence, and then the ordinary business of continuing to be alive.

Theories again, of course. Mass psychosis. A coordinated lie. The simulation's programmers rolling back the code. But the people who had lived through those eleven days—the ones who had come out the other side—didn't much care about the explanations. They had been changed in ways that didn't need a reason.

There were more soups on doorsteps. More letters in the mail. More strangers who looked you in the eye. The divorce rate dropped. The volunteer rate doubled. People planted gardens, even in winter, just to see what would grow.

Maya stayed in her hometown. She and David built a small studio behind her mother's house, where he painted and she wrote, and the dog slept in a patch of sun that moved across the floor throughout the day. Her mother came by every morning with coffee and stayed too long, and the phone on the kitchen counter—which still bore its gray icon, and which no one ever opened—ticked softly against the silence, a metronome for a world that had learned, finally, to count.

---

Years later, when journalists asked what those eleven days had meant, people gave different answers. A reset. A wake-up call. A mercy, of sorts, or a curse that became a blessing. The answers were unsatisfying, because the answers couldn't capture the texture of it—the way time had stretched, the way small moments had become enormous, the way the collective weight of knowing had somehow made everything lighter.

But there was one thing almost everyone agreed on.

If the number came back—if tomorrow morning, the app updated, and the gray icon bloomed again into white, and the ticking resumed—most people said they would be afraid, at first. They would be terrified.

Then they would call the people they loved.

Then they would begin.

# 最后一个守夜人

我叫林远。

或者说，我曾经叫林远。在这座空城待了四百七十三天之后，名字已经变成了一种多余的装饰，像没人看的旧日历。

## 一

起初，我和所有人一样，以为新闻里说的"全球性公共卫生紧急事件"只是又一次流感。

我清楚地记得，那天早上我还在阳台上浇花。三楼，朝南，阳台下面是一排梧桐。城市照常运转，楼下早餐店的蒸汽裹着油条香飘上来。

然后病毒来了。

不是新闻里那种温和的叫法。它没有名字，因为来不及命名。等我反应过来的时候，整座城市已经哑了。

我是在第七十天才真正确认的。我骑着自行车，从城东到城西，从城西到城北，把每一条街道都走了一遍。

没有人。

只有风吹过空荡的十字路口，把一只塑料袋吹得很高。

## 二

我住在城郊的一栋小楼里。房子是父母留下的，他们走得很早——不是被病毒带走的，是在我二十岁那年，一次普通的交通事故。

现在我三十一岁。

我会定期去超市搬物资。最开始还小心翼翼，后来发现完全没有必要——没有人会和我抢。更重要的是，没有人会再生产任何东西了。

罐头、保质期长的米面、纯净水、医疗用品、电池。

我把超市搬空了至少三次。最后一次，我站在空空荡荡的货架之间，听到自己的呼吸声在空旷的建筑里回荡，突然觉得，这些物资像是一座为死人准备的陵墓。

我活下来，是为了什么？

## 三

第三个月，我开始发电报。

是的，电报。我知道这很荒谬，2024年了，谁还用这种东西？但我父亲留给我一台老式电报机和一本莫尔斯电码表。小时候他教过我，我一直当作业余爱好保留着。

每天晚上八点，我坐在书房里，戴上耳机，一下一下地按动电键。

"CQ CQ CQ，这里是 BG2XYZ，中国某处，是否有人收到？"

从来没有回复。

但我还是每天发。

第四个月，我在电键旁边放了一盆绿萝。它在没有人打扰的房间里长得很好，藤蔓垂下来，绕在电键的金属杆上。

## 五

第五百天。

我去了城里最后一家还开着的药店——其实已经很久没开了，只是我路过的时候习惯性地进去看看。

在药店的角落里，我发现了一个广播站的老式发射器。不知道是谁留下的，也不知道它为什么在一家小药店里。

我把它搬回了家。

那天晚上，我对着麦克风坐了半个小时。

"有人吗？"

我的声音在空荡荡的房间里显得很可笑。

"如果你能听到，请回答。"

静电噪音。

"我叫林远。我在中国北方的一个城市。如果你活着，请告诉我。"

静电噪音。

我正准备关掉发射器的时候，听到了一声很轻的"咔嗒"。

不是噪音。

是有人在调频。

我的心跳几乎停止了。我颤抖着手，开始在不同的频段间搜索。

"咔——嗒——"

是的，是有人在调频。

然后，我听到了一个声音。很轻，像隔着很远的距离。

"……收到……"

我的眼泪流了下来。

## 六

她叫苏晚，在南方，一个我从未听说过的小城。

我们用发射器聊了整整一夜。

她告诉我，她是一名护士，在病毒爆发的初期被困在了医院的隔离病房里。她一个人在那个封闭的空间里活了将近一年，直到有一天，她终于鼓起勇气走出了那扇门。

"外面……一个人都没有。"她说，"我也以为我是最后一个。"

"我也以为。"我说。

## 七

现在是第七百二十一天。

我们还没有见面。两个城市之间隔着两千三百公里，公路上不知道有多少危险，开车可能要花好几天。

但我正在准备出发。

我把车加满了油，后备箱里装满了物资。电台发射器放在副驾驶座上。

"我要出发了。"我说。

"小心。"苏晚的声音从电台里传来，带着轻微的电流声，"我等你。"

我发动了汽车。

后视镜里，城市在慢慢变小。那些我走过的每一条街道，每一个十字路口，那家我曾经吃过早餐的小店，那栋我住了一年的小楼，都在我身后远去。

电台里传来苏晚的声音。她正在播放一首歌，歌名我从来没听过，但旋律很温柔。

我踩下油门，向南方驶去。

我不知道前面有什么。也许什么都没有。也许苏晚也是我孤独太久产生的幻觉。也许我会在路上死掉，被一棵树撞上，或者被某种我已经忘记的危险夺去性命。

但我还是在开。

因为在这个空荡荡的世界上，我终于有了一个可以奔赴的方向。

## 尾声

（这是苏晚在第七百三十二天记录的）

林远到了。

他比我想象中更瘦，头发很长，胡子也长。但他笑起来很好看。

他给我带了一盆绿萝——他从家里带来的，那个绕着电报机的绿萝。他把它养在了我们现在的窗台上。

我说："为什么是绿萝？"

他说："因为它很顽强。在没有人的房间里都能活下来。"

窗外的城市还是空的。

但屋子里有两个人的呼吸声。

我们决定一起活下去。不是因为这个世界还需要我们，而是因为我们还想看看，明天会不会有什么不一样。

电台还开着，每天晚上八点，我们一起发送：

"CQ CQ CQ，这里是 BG2XYZ，这里是 BG5XYZ，我们在中国，是否还有人？"

也许没有人会回答。

但我们会一直问下去。

因为在这个已经沉默的世界上，还有两个声音在说话，就已经足够了。

# The Cartographer of Closed Worlds

The map was a lie. Wren had known this for as long as she could remember, though it took her fourteen years to understand exactly *how* it lied.

It wasn't that the map contained false places—Phantom Peaks that didn't exist, rivers flowing toward no sea. No, the map lied by omission. The edges of the world simply... stopped. Beyond the final ring of the Candlewoods, beyond the Sea of Glass, there was nothing. Not unknown nothing, not *terra incognita*. Just nothing. A thick gray border, like fog pressed flat against parchment, with a single phrase inscribed in the careful hand of the Council:

*Here ends the world. Beyond lies the forgetting.*

In the village of Hollowmere, this was gospel. The oldest children were told it first, at the age of seven, when they could be trusted not to repeat it. "The world is a house," the elders said, "and a house has walls. Beyond the walls is the cold. The cold takes everything."

Wren had always wondered what "everything" meant.

She was seventeen when she began to suspect that the cold was a story. It happened on the night her mother died.

---

The fever took Lira Elmwood quickly, the way fires take dry thatch. Wren sat at her bedside, holding a hand that grew colder by the hour, listening to breathing that grew shallower. Her mother had been the village's best seamstress, her fingers quick and clever, her laughter rarer than rain in late summer.

"Lira," Wren whispered. "Stay. Please."

Her mother's eyes opened. They were filmy, distant, but they focused on Wren with sudden, startling clarity.

"Beyond the glass," Lira breathed. "I went there. Once."

Wren's heart stumbled. "What?"

"Your father and I. Before you were born. We wanted to see." A smile, faint as moth wings. "We wanted to know."

"Know what?"

But the fever had her then, and her mother was swept away on its tide, leaving only the words, repeating like a lullaby she didn't know: *beyond the glass, beyond the glass.*

The next morning, Wren found the letter.

---

It was hidden beneath a floorboard in her mother's workroom, wrapped in oilskin that had gone stiff with age. The paper inside was yellowed, the ink faded to brown, but the words were unmistakable. Her mother's hand. Her father's hand, too—a few lines here and there, cramped and impatient.

*We have crossed the Glass Sea. It is not a sea. It is a field of something like ice, but it does not melt. We walked for two days. Wren, if you are reading this, you will want to follow. Do not. The Council was right about one thing: there is a price.*

*The land beyond is not cold. It is empty. Not empty like an absence—empty like a held breath. Like the moment before a wave breaks. We stood there, and we felt the world waiting for us to do something. To speak, perhaps. To name.*

*Your father named a tree. There was nothing there, and then there was a tree—a great gray thing with leaves like pages. It grew in the silence, and the silence grew back. We were afraid.*

*We came home. We never spoke of it. We told the Council nothing. But your father, after—I think the silence followed him. He forgot things, small things at first. The color of his mother's eyes. The taste of summer fruit. Then larger things. He forgot his own name, on the last day. He looked at me and asked who I was.*

*I have begun to forget, too. But I remembered long enough to write this. I remembered long enough to love you.*

*Do not go, Wren. The world is not meant to be finished.*

Her mother had signed it with a single tear, the mark still visible on the page.

---

For a year, Wren did not go.

She worked. She sewed, as her mother had, taking on her mother's clients, learning the village's needs as she had once learned her mother's patterns. She ate. She slept. She tried to love the boy, Tam, who courted her with flowers and shy smiles. She tried to believe the map.

But the map had a wound in it now. Every time she looked at the gray border, she saw her mother's handwriting, translucent as a ghost pressed against the paper from the other side.

*There is a price.*

*What is a price?* Wren thought. *I have already paid.*

---

She left on the longest night of the year, when the cold was supposed to be deepest and the elders said the walls of the world were thinnest. She packed light: a knife, a waterskin, the letter, a small pot of ink. She left a note for Tam, gentle and true. She left her mother's sewing shears on the pillow, where the morning light would find them.

The Glass Sea was three days' walk from Hollowmere. She walked it in two, barely sleeping, fueled by something she did not have a name for. Her feet blistered. Her lips cracked. The Sea of Glass stretched before her like the surface of a frozen dream, and she stepped onto it without pausing, because pausing was how people died of waiting.

The ice—it wasn't ice—didn't creak beneath her. It sang. A thin, clear note, like a finger drawn around the rim of a glass. The song followed her, or maybe she followed it. She couldn't tell.

At the end of the second day, the gray border.

---

It was not a border at all. It was a place where the world ended and the other thing began, and the transition was so gentle she almost didn't notice. One moment there was sky, blue-black and stitched with stars. The next, there was the same sky, but the stars had no light. They were suggestions of stars. Memories of stars. The ground beneath her feet was no longer the singing glass but something else—something like clay, like dust, like the bottom of a dried-up well.

The silence her mother had written about.

Wren stood in it. She let it fill her. She understood, now, what the Council feared. The silence was not empty. It was *waiting*. It was a question, asked so softly that the asking was almost nothing. *What will you make?*

She understood, too, why her mother had been afraid. To name a thing was to give it weight. To give it weight was to begin. And beginning was a kind of violence against the nothing. The nothing would fight back. It would fill the cracks.

She thought of her father, forgetting his name. She thought of her mother, forgetting her own.

But she thought, too, of a different thing. A thing she had not expected to find in herself.

*Curiosity.*

The Council had called it a sin. The elders had called it a sickness. Her whole life, she had been told it was the flaw in her—the reason she could not be content with the known world, the known borders, the known endings.

But standing in the silence, she felt it differently. She felt it as a *gift*. The strange, stubborn thing that had kept her walking when the glass sang her to sleep. The thing that had made her read the letter three times, four times, twenty. The thing that had made her pack the ink.

She uncapped the pot. She knelt.

And she began to draw.

---

She drew the Glass Sea. She drew it carefully, the singing surface, the way it caught the suggestion of starlight. She drew Hollowmere—the crooked spire of the meeting house, the row of stone cottages where she had grown up. She drew her mother's workroom, the spools of thread on the table, the shears glinting in a slant of sun.

She drew them in ink, on the dust-clay, with her finger as a brush.

And as she drew, the world *came*. Not instantly, not all at once. But the drawings became *places*. The Glass Sea appeared beneath her hand, solid and singing. Hollowmere rose around her like a memory remembering itself. She smelled bread baking. She heard her mother's laughter, faint and far.

The silence pressed back. She felt it—the cold, the forgetting, the slow unknitting of what she had made. Her father's face, which she had not consciously memorized, began to blur. She could not remember the color of her own eyes.

But she kept drawing. She drew the Sea of Glass. She drew Hollowmere. She drew her mother, young and laughing, holding a skein of red thread.

She drew herself, seventeen, holding a pen.

When she was done, she stood. The world she had drawn held. It wavered at the edges, but it held. The silence had withdrawn, sulking, perhaps. Or simply *considering*.

Wren looked out at what she had made. She looked back at the gray border of her old map, the safe, walled, *finished* world.

Then she turned, and walked further in.

---

The elders found her three days later, sitting in the town square of Hollowmere—*a* Hollowmere, one of dozens, she would learn, scattered across the silence like seeds. She was drawing. She was drawing the world behind her, the world she had come from, filling it in.

"Wren Elmwood," said Elder Mara, her voice thin with horror. "You have defiled the map."

"I have *finished* it," said Wren, without looking up. "There was more paper."

"There was nothing—"

"There was everything." She held up the letter, her mother's letter. "She knew. You knew. The Council has always known. You just didn't want anyone to *see*."

Elder Mara's face went pale. "The forgetting—"

"Is a choice," Wren said. "The silence wants us to forget because if we remember—if we *name*—it has to become something. And becoming something is dangerous. To it."

She looked up. Her eyes were clear. Her name, she remembered. Her mother's laugh, she remembered.

"I am willing to pay the price," she said. "I will pay it every day. I will draw the world, and the world will remember itself, and the silence will retreat, and the map will grow."

She dipped her pen in ink.

"Go home, Elder. Tell the Council the borders are open now. Tell them the house has no walls."

She bent back to her work.

---

In the years that followed, they called her many things. The Heretic. The Mapmaker. The Girl Who Drew the World.

But the children, the ones who came after her, the ones who slipped past the old walls with their pots of ink and their knapsacks of bread, called her something else.

They called her *Wren*.

And they called the place beyond the Glass Sea, the place that had once been nothing, by the name she had given it on that first night, kneeling in the dust-clay with her mother's letter in her pocket and a pen in her hand.

*The Beginning.*

---

*Author's note: This story is for anyone who has ever looked at the edge of the map and felt the pull. The walls are not always made of stone. Sometimes they are made of agreement. But curiosity, I think, is older than any wall. And the world is bigger than we have been told.*

# The Vanishing Coefficient

In the end, it wasn't humankind that destroyed the world. It was entropy's final indulgence—the Heat Death arriving six billion years ahead of schedule, a cosmic clerical error that turned the universe's slow, dignified cooling into a sudden, catastrophic fever.

Dr. Elena Vasquez noticed it first in the lattice readings from CERN's successor facility beneath the Argentinian pampas. A whisper of anomaly. A single decimal point out of place. She remembered thinking, with the peculiar calm of the doomed, *how strange that the end begins with such precision*.

Within seventy-two hours, thermodynamic equilibrium began cascading across the planet like dominoes in a cathedral. The oceans didn't boil. They simply... settled. The frantic dance of molecules slowed, slowed, and stopped. Ice formed in the tropics—not from cold, but from stillness. The wind forgot how to move.

Children asked why the sky had stopped twinkling. The stars had dimmed not from any drama of supernova or expanding cosmos, but from the universe itself losing interest in light. Photons lost their momentum and lay down on the ground like tired sheep.

There was time, in those final days, to do the things humans had always postponed. To say the names of those we loved, complete with all the syllables we'd abbreviated. To apologize for the wars, the small cruelties, the unlived lives.

Elena stood on the pampa as the last gust of wind exhaled across the grasses. She felt it die against her cheek like a kiss from a departing lover.

The machines fell silent. The birds, who had been the first to sense it, had already gone—migrating toward a warmth that no longer existed, following instincts coded for a cosmos that had just... *settled*.

She thought of all the philosophers who had theorized about endings. Fire. Ice. Flood. The hammer of gods. None had imagined this: the universe simply running out of ambition.

In the final moment, Elena Vasquez, last physicist of a species that had briefly illuminated one small corner of creation, smiled at the beautiful absurdity of it all.

Not fire. Not ice. Just a great, cosmic *sigh*—as if the universe had been holding its breath for thirteen billion years and had finally, gently, forgotten why.

Then stillness. Then home.

# 最后的日记

## 11月7日

今天是便利店最后一批罐头被吃完的日子。我站在货架前，看着空荡荡的金属架子，回声在寂静中显得格外清晰。

我已经很久没有听到过除自己以外的任何声音了。

## 11月12日

城市的电力系统终于停了。我坐在阳台上，看着对面大楼的窗户一扇一扇陷入黑暗。那些曾经彻夜通明的写字楼、便利店、公寓，现在都像闭上了眼睛一样。

我点燃了一根蜡烛。火焰在风中跳动。

## 11月18日

我开始翻看图书馆里那些没人再会读的书。一本一本，把它们摊开在阳光下。我不知道自己为什么要这样做。也许只是觉得，这些文字不应该只存在于黑暗中。

但最后一个人读它们，又有什么意义呢？

## 11月24日

今天我在街头看到了一只猫。它从我面前跑过，尾巴高高翘起，消失在巷子里。

原来我不是最后一个人。

原来这个词并不准确。

## 11月29日

我开始写日记了。不是给谁看，只是觉得应该留下点什么。

窗外下起了雨。雨声是世界上最孤独的声音，因为它落在每一寸土地，却只为一个人演奏。

## 12月3日

我找到了一台还能用的收音机。拨过无数频率，只有沙沙的静电声。

但我没有关掉它。就让它陪着我。

## 12月10日

今天是我的生日。我给自己煮了一碗面。

蜡烛插在碗中间，我对着它许了一个愿望。然后一口气把它吹灭。

## 12月15日

有时候我会忘记"他们"的样子。我试图回忆妈妈的脸，却只看到一片模糊。

人类消失得如此彻底，就好像从未存在过一样。

## 12月21日

今天很冷。我裹着所有的被子蜷缩在床上。

我想起小时候妈妈抱着我的样子。那时候我总嫌她抱得太紧。

现在我终于明白了那种紧。

## 12月25日

圣诞。

商场里的圣诞树还没拆。我坐在树下的长椅上，看着那些彩灯。它们早就不会亮了，但白天有阳光照进来，让玻璃球闪闪发光。

我对自己说：圣诞快乐。

## 12月31日

这一年就要结束了。我坐在窗前，等待新年的第一缕阳光。

没有人需要我了。

没有人需要任何人。

这是我这一生中，第一次如此彻底地拥有自由，也是第一次如此彻底地明白——

自由，原来是这样的滋味。

## 1月1日

新年快乐。

我对自己说。然后起身，去寻找下一个罐头。

---

*这本日记被后来的人在一个旧公寓里发现。日记本已经泛黄，但字迹依然清晰。*

*他们无法理解，但也被深深触动。*

*在最后一页，有一行用铅笔写下的字：*

*"后来者，如果你读到这些，请记住我们曾经活过、爱过、哭过、笑过。请替我们，把这盏灯传下去。"*

*——2024年12月31日，最后的守夜人*

# 끝나기 전, 한 시간

세계의 끝까지 정확히 한 시간.

그 소식을 처음 들었을 때, 나는 편의점 앞에 서 있었다. 아이스 아메리카노를 든 손이 미약하게 떨렸다. 하늘을 올려다봤다. 파란 하늘은 여전히 파란 하늘이었고, 구름은 여전히 천천히 흘러갔다. 하지만 나는 알았다. 한 시간 뒤, 이 모든 것이 사라진다는 것을.

---

처음 10분 동안, 나는 그냥 서 있었다.

사람들이 어떻게 반응하는지 지켜봤다. 어떤 남자는 길 한가운데서 웃기 시작했다. 눈물이 뺨을 타고 흘러내리는데, 입꼬리는 위로 올라가 있었다. 어떤 여자는 전화를 걸었다. "엄마, 나 사랑해." 그녀의 목소리가 갈라졌다. 어떤 아이는 엄마의 손을 꼭 잡고 "집에 가고 싶어요"라고 말했고, 엄마는 그 아이를 안아 올렸다.

나는 전화를 꺼내 들었다. 저장된 번호들을 하나하나 살펴봤다. 아버지, 어머니, 친구들. 하지만 손가락이 움직이지 않았다. 어떤 말을 해야 하는지 몰랐다. "잘 지내?" "보고 싶어?" — 한 시간 뒤 모든 것이 사라지는 세상에서, 그런 평범한 인사가 갑자기 너무 작게 느껴졌다.

---

20분쯤, 나는 발걸음을 옮기기 시작했다.

특별한 곳으로 가는 건 아니었다. 그냥 걷고 싶었다. 한 시간은 길지도, 짧지도 않은 시간이었다. 전화벨이 울렸다. 대학 동기 재영이었다.

"너야?"

"응."

"들었어?"

"응."

"그래서… 지금 어디야?"

"걷고 있어."

재영은 잠시 침묵했다. "나도 밖이야. 한강에 왔어. 바람이 참 차다."

나는 걸음을 멈추고 주위를 둘러봤다. 보도블록, 가로등, 지나가는 사람들. 온 세상이 아직 평소 그대로였다. "난 어디로 가야 할지 모르겠어."

"그냥 와. 같이 걸자."

---

한강에 도착했을 때, 남은 시간은 40분이었다.

재영은 벤치에 앉아 있었다. 맥주를 들고. 나는 옆에 앉았다. 강바람이 얼굴을 스쳤다. 찬 바람이었다. 하지만 이상하게, 그 바람이 좋아 보였다.

"맥주 줄까?"

"좋아."

캔을 따는 소리가 났다. 거품이 넘쳤다. 우리는 말없이 강을 바라봤다. 강 건너편 아파트들이 하나둘 불을 켜기 시작했다. 사람들은 집으로 돌아가고 있는 걸까. 아니, 집이 무슨 소용일까.

"낮게 떨어지는 거야, 아니면 갑자기 오는 거야?"

"몰라. 누가 알겠어."

"그래. 누가 알겠어."

재영이 캔을 들어 올렸다. "건배하자."

"뭐에?"

"뭐에긴. 살아 있는 거에."

캔이 부딪혔다. 작은 금속성 소리가 한강 위로 울렸다. 우리는 맥주를 마셨다. 쓰고, 차갑고, 약간 씁쓸했다. 하지만 인생에서 마신 어떤 맥주보다 맛있었다.

---

남은 시간은 20분이었다.

"후회되는 거 있어?"

재영의 질문에 나는 생각했다. 사랑한다고 말하지 못한 사람들. 가고 싶었지만 가지 못한 곳들. 해보고 싶었지만 용기를 내지 못했던 것들. 하지만 이상하게도, 그런 것들이 지금은 크게 느껴지지 않았다.

"글쎄. 많기도 해."

"나도."

우리는 한동안 말없이 앉아 있었다. 강 위에 작은 비행기가 지나갔다. 비행기는 어디로 가는 걸까. 시간이 끝나는 곳 따위는 없을 텐데.

재영이 말했다. "조금 무섭다."

"나도."

"같이 무서워하자."

나는 웃었다. 이 친구, 끝까지 이런 놈이니까. "그래, 같이 무서워하자."

세계가 끝났는지는 알 수 없었다.
