# السقوط

سقطت ورقة شجر ببطء شديد في ذلك الصباح الخريفي.

كانت الشمس تتسلل بخيوطها الذهبية المائلة بين أغصان شجرة الدلب العتيقة التي تقف وحيدة في ساحة بيت عائلة "ناصر" المُهمل منذ سنوات. كانت الورقة تدور حول نفسها كراقصة تائهة، تبحث عن مكان تستقر فيه، لكنها في الحقيقة كانت تبحث عن شيء آخر — عن معنى.

من نافذة الطابق العلوي، راقبت "ليلى" ذلك المشهد بعينين ثقيلتين من السهر. كانت قد أمضت الليل كله تتصفح أوراقاً أخرى — أوراقاً صفراء باهتة، مكتوبة بخط يد والدها المتعب الذي رحل قبل عشرين عاماً. عشرون عاماً وهي تحتفظ برسائله في صندوق خشبي قديم، تخبّئها عن أعين الجميع، خاصة عن عيني أمها التي فضّلت النسيان.

همست ليلى للورقة التي سقطت: "إلى أين تذهبين أيتها المسكينة؟"

كأن الورقة سمعتها، فاستدارت في الهواء دورة أخيرة، ثم استقرت على حافة النافذة، قريبة جداً من يدها المرتجفة. مدّت ليلى أصابعها ولمستها بحذر. كانت باردة، رطبة بندى الصباح، لكنها كانت تحمل في عروقها الدقيقة ذكرى كل ربيع عاشته تلك الشجرة.

تذكرت ليلى آخر رسالة قرأتها الليلة الماضية، رسالة لم تفهمها إلا بعد كل هذه السنوات:

*"يا ليلى، حين تكبرين، ستعرفين أن بعض الأوراق يجب أن تسقط حتى تحيا الشجرة. لا تحزني عليّ، فأنا لم أمت. أنا فقط غيّرت مكاني."*

لم يكن والدها قد مات كما أخبروها. كان قد اختار الرحيل — ليس بالموت، بل بالحياة. كان قد ذهب ليبحث عن ابنه الأكبر "سامح" الذي ضاع في زحمة الحرب الأهلية ذات ليلة مظلمة، ولم يعد.

نظرت ليلى إلى الورقة في يدها، ثم إلى الساحة المقفرة. فجأة، فهمت لماذا تحتفظ أمها بكل شيء كما هو في هذا البيت — الأثاث، والستائر، وحتى ذلك الكرسي الخشبي المهترئ في الزاوية. كانت أمها تنتظر أيضاً. تنتظر عودة من لن يعود.

لكن ليلى قررت شيئاً ذلك الصباح.

قررت أن تُسقط أوراقها هي أيضاً. ستترك البيت، ستترك الذاكرة المقيّدة، وستبحث عن أخيها الذي ربما لا يزال حياً في مكان ما من هذا العالم الواسع.

أمسكت حقيبتها، ونظرت نظرة أخيرة إلى رسائل والدها. لم تأخذها معها هذه المرة، لكنها تركت ورقة واحدة على الطاولة، بخط يدها:

*"سأعود يا أبي. وحين أعود، سأكون أنا الورقة التي لم تسقط، بل طارت."*

فتحت الباب، وخطت إلى الخارج. كانت الشمس قد ارتفعت قليلاً، والشجرة العتيقة تتمايل بأغصانها كأموات يودعون بحّاراً مسافراً.

وفي مكان ما على الأرض، كانت ورقة أخرى تستعد للسقوط.

# A Colheita Perdida

O vento frio de outubro varria os campos secos de Santo André, levantando poeira onde antes deveriam estar os trigais dourados. Raimundo Caminha observava a extensão morta de suas terras, os olhos fundos de quem não dormia há muitas noites. Os cereais que deveriam encher os celeiros não passaram de palha quebradiça, e as vinhas que normalmente pingavam cachos suculentos estavam mirradas, como se alguma mão invisível tivesse sugado toda a seiva da terra.

O padre Bento havia benzido os campos. A curandeira Adelaide tinha queimado ervas e rezado aos santos antigos. Nada funcionara. O que quer que estivesse acontecendo, escapava ao entendimento dos homens.

Foi numa madrugada cinzenta que o Conselho dos Anciãos se reuniu na sala ampla da taverna de Seu Aprígio, a única construção que ainda mantinha as paredes inteiras na vila. O cheiro de cachaça misturava-se ao do medo.

— Precisamos saber se outras vilas estão sofrendo o mesmo — disse Raimundo, sua voz rouca ecoando entre as vigas de madeira. — Se o mal é só nosso, lutamos sozinhos. Se é geral, talvez seja castigo divino.

— Ou coisa do demo — murmurou Adelaide, apertando entre os dedos o rosário gasto.

Raimundo foi designado para a missão. Montou o cavalo baio antes do sol nascer, levando apenas uma garrafa de água, pão duro e a bússola que pertencera a seu pai. Seu destino: as vilas de São Miguel, Três Pontes e Várzea Grande, que se estendiam ao longo do rio numa distância de três dias a cavalo.

---

A primeira parada foi São Miguel. Raimundo chegou ao entardecer, quando as sombras já se adensavam sobre a igreja matriz. O que encontrou gelou-lhe o sangue: as ruas desertas, as portas cerradas, um silêncio de sepulcro. Bateu na primeira casa que viu luz.

Uma mulher magra e de olhos assustados abriu uma fresta.

— Não há ninguém — sussurrou ela. — Foram todos embora. Partiram antes da colheita, quando viram que nada vingava. Os homens foram para as bandas do sul, buscar trabalho nas fazendas de café. As mulheres e crianças, para a cidade grande. Dizem que a terra aqui está morta.

— E ninguém sabe por quê?

A mulher balançou a cabeça, os lábios tremendo.

— Uns falam que é o rio. Outros, que são as nuvens que não chovem. Mas meu avô dizia que nestas terras houve outrora uma maldição. Quando os primeiros povoadores chegaram, expulsaram os nativos que aqui viviam. Talvez seja isso.

Raimundo agradeceu e seguiu viagem. Naquela noite, dormiu sob uma árvore, e o sono foi perturbado por sonhos com figuras escuras correndo pelos campos.

---

Em Três Pontes, no dia seguinte, a cena era diferente, mas igualmente devastadora. Aqui os povoadores tinham ficado, mas a fome já se instalara. Raimundo viu crianças de barrigas inchadas, homens de olhar vazio sentado em frente a casas que mais pareciam tumbas. O chefe da vila, um senhor de barbas brancas chamado Joaquim Pimentel, recebeu-o com lágrimas nos olhos.

— Tudo secou — disse ele, conduzindo Raimundo aos campos. — Milho, feijão, mandioca, nada. As sementes que plantamos na primavera brotam, mas murcham antes de dar fruto. É como se a terra estivesse ferida.

— E não há explicação?

Joaquim hesitou. Olhou para os lados, como se temesse ser ouvido até pelos pássaros.

— Há uma coisa — disse por fim. — Meu neto, que é caçador, disse ter visto estranhas luzes na mata, perto da nascente do rio. Disse que ouviu vozes também. Eu disse que eram imaginações dele, mas...

Raimundo anotou mentalmente a informação. A nascente do rio. Ali perto de sua própria vila. Pediu mais detalhes, mas Joaquim já parecia ter medo de falar demais.

---

Foi ao terceiro dia que Raimundo chegou a Várzea Grande, a vila mais distante e a maior das três. Ali, para sua surpresa, encontrou uma cena completamente diferente. Os campos estavam verdes, as árvores carregadas de frutos, os celeiros cheios.

O líder local, um homem corpulento chamado Coronel Estácio, recebeu-o com desconfiança.

— O que o traz por aqui, irmãozinho? — perguntou, os olhos pequenos perscrutando Raimundo.

Raimundo explicou a situação. Estácio ouviu em silêncio, tamborilando os dedos na mesa.

— Pois bem — disse finalmente. — Aqui as coisas vão bem. E não, não temos solução para os males dos outros.

Mas Raimundo notou algo estranho. Enquanto caminhava pela vila, percebeu que vários rostos se viravam ao seu encontro com expressões que misturavam curiosidade e hostilidade. E quando perguntou sobre a nascente do rio, o sorriso de Estácio gelou.

— Não sei do que está falando — disse ele, mas seus olhos disseram outra coisa.

Naquela noite, Raimundo dormiu na taverna da vila, mas permaneceu alerta. E foi bem mais da meia-noite, quando ouviu passos suspeitos do lado de fora. Viu sombras movendo-se pela janela. Preparou-se para o pior, mas os passos se afastaram.

Pela madrugada, deixou Várzea Grande com a sensação de que ali havia segredos que não queriam ser revelados.

---

A viagem de volta durou outros três dias. Quando Raimundo finalmente viu as casas de Santo André no horizonte, sentiu um peso no peito. O que diria aos anciãos? Que duas vilas estavam morrendo e a terceira prosperava sem explicação?

Desmontou do cavalo já cansado e foi direto à taverna de Seu Aprígio, onde o conselho o aguardava. Contou tudo — as vilas abandonadas, os campos secos, as luzes na mata, a hostilidade de Várzea Grande.

Quando terminou, houve um longo silêncio.

— Então é uma praga — disse Adelaide por fim. — Algo que se espalha pela terra.

— Ou algo que alguém espalha — disse Raimundo, lembrando-se dos olhos de Estácio.

O padre Bento, que até então permanecera calmo, levantou-se com expressão grave.

— Meu filho — disse ele —, há coisas que a Igreja prefere não revelar, mas que um padre tem o dever de conhecer. Vou consultar os livros antigos da paróquia. Há registros de fatos semelhantes nestas terras, e talvez lá encontremos respostas.

Raimundo concordou. Antes de se retirar, Adelaide o puxou pelo braço.

— As luzes na mata — sussurrou ela. — Se são o que penso, tenha cuidado. Há forças antigas que os homens brancos esqueceram, mas que os antigos deste povo conheciam bem.

Naquela noite, sozinho em sua casa, Raimundo olhou pela janela para os campos secos e prometeu a si mesmo que descobriria a verdade, mesmo que isso o levasse às profundezas da mata ou aos segredos mais sombrios de seus vizinhos.

A colheita daquele ano estava perdida. Mas a esperança, essa ele ainda guardava — dura e teimosa como as raízes de um velho ipê que resiste às piores tempestades.

---

# The Cartographer of Autumn

Theodore Finch had measured his life in leaves.

For sixty-three years, he had lived in the same gray stone cottage at the edge of the village of Aldermere, and for sixty-three years, he had watched the copper beech tree in his front yard shed its leaves each autumn. As a boy, he had gathered them into piles and leapt into them with the abandon of someone who had not yet learned that joy was a finite resource. As a young man, he had pressed them between the pages of books, preserving their shapes like small green prayers. As an old man, he simply watched them fall, and counted.

Seventeen thousand, four hundred and sixty-two leaves. He had been counting since he was nine.

His wife, Marguerite, had called him foolish for this. *Theodore,* she would say, her voice warm with the particular exasperation of someone who loved a man she did not fully understand, *you cannot count leaves. There are too many. You will go mad.*

But he had not gone mad. He had gone something else.

He noticed things others did not. That the first leaf to fall each year was always from the highest branch, always on a Tuesday, and always exactly nine days after the first wood pigeon had called from the churchyard. He noticed that the beech leaves fell in spirals when the wind came from the east, and in straight lines when it came from the west. He noticed that the air smelled of woodsmoke and wet earth on the same three days each October, and that those days were always followed by a frost.

He kept a notebook. He had kept one every year since 1947.

---

The first September of his marriage, Marguerite had laughed when she found his notebooks. Hundreds of them, lined up on the shelf in his study, each one a record of a single year.

"You've made a science of melancholy," she said, and kissed his temple.

He had not corrected her. He did not think of it as melancholy. He thought of it as *attention*. The world was always leaving, he believed. The leaves fell. The light shifted. The cold came. And if you did not watch carefully, if you did not mark each departure, then you might miss the leaving altogether. You might wake up one morning and find yourself sixty years old and not know how you had arrived there.

Marguerite died in March, when the snowdrops were pushing through the last of the frost. She had been unwell for a long time. Theodore held her hand as she went, and afterward, he did not go into the garden for many weeks. The crocuses came and went without him. The daffodils opened and dropped their heads. He sat in his chair by the window and watched the beech tree bud and leaf and become green without him.

When he finally went outside, in late April, he stood beneath the tree and looked up at the new leaves, trembling in the breeze. They were small and bright and did not know yet what they were for.

*Hello,* he thought. *I'm still here.*

---

The years after Marguerite's death were strange ones. Theodore aged in the way that old men do, gradually and then suddenly. His knees began to pain him. His hearing faded. The village children, who had once waved to him from the schoolyard, grew up and moved away to cities, and new children arrived who did not know his name.

But every autumn, he still counted the leaves.

In his sixty-seventh year, he climbed a ladder to clean the gutters, fell, and broke his wrist. From the ground, staring up at the sky through the branches, he had laughed. The leaves had fallen on his face like green rain, and he had thought, *this is how it will end one day. Under this tree.*

In his seventy-first year, he made friends with a stray tabby cat he called October. The cat lived in his shed and caught mice and sat on his lap in the evenings, purring. Theodore talked to her about the leaves, about the weather, about the slow turning of the earth.

"You understand," he told her, "that it's all the same thing, don't you? The falling and the rising. The coming and the going. The cat and the leaf."

October blinked at him, slowly, and he took this as agreement.

---

On the morning of his seventy-fourth birthday, Theodore woke to find the beech tree bare.

It was early for it. Usually the leaves held until late October, sometimes into November. But there had been a hard frost the night before, the first real one, and when he drew back the curtain, the tree stood skeletal against a sky the color of tin, every leaf dropped in a single night as if it had been waiting for the right permission.

He dressed and went outside. The lawn was thick with copper. He knelt, slowly, his joints protesting, and gathered up a handful of leaves. They were cool and dry and smelled of nothing at all.

He thought of his father, dead these forty years, who had first taught him to look. *Pay attention, Theo,* his father had said, *the world is always talking. Most people just don't listen.*

He thought of Marguerite, who had listened to him even when she didn't understand.

He thought of October, who was probably asleep in the shed, dreaming of mice.

He thought, *this is the last autumn I will see.*

He didn't know how he knew this. There was no reason for it. He was healthy, for seventy-four. But he felt it in his bones the way he felt the change in the weather, the way he knew when the first wood pigeon would call. The leaves had told him. They always told him.

---

He spent that autumn differently.

He went into the village and spoke to people he hadn't spoken to in years. He gave the woman at the post office a jar of his wife's old quince jelly, still good, still sweet. He invited his neighbor, a young man named Will who had recently lost his wife, to come for Sunday dinner. Will came, and they ate lamb and talked about nothing important, and afterward Will shook his hand and said, "Thank you, Mr. Finch. I didn't know I needed that."

He went to the school and asked if he might read to the children. They let him, and he read them a story about a tree that lost its leaves every year and grew them back again, and at the end one of the small girls raised her hand and said, "But why does it bother? It knows they'll come back, doesn't it?"

"Yes," Theodore said. "But it still feels the leaving."

He sat with his notebooks and read through them, year by year, the long record of his attention. The first ones were in his boyhood handwriting, careful and precise. The later ones were shaky, the entries shorter, some just a single line: *Wind from the east. Sixteen leaves today.* But each one was true. Each one had been seen.

On the last day of October, he climbed the hill above the village, from which you could see the whole valley—the church, the cottages, the river, the woods turning red and gold. The beech tree was a small dark shape in the distance, but he could see it. He could always see it.

He stood in the wind and let it blow through him.

---

He did not die that winter, or the next spring, or even the following summer, though he was frail and tired and moved through his days like a man wading through deep water. He had been wrong, he realized. Or perhaps not wrong, just early. The leaves had not been predicting his death. They had been predicting something else.

On the morning of his seventy-fifth birthday, he woke and went to the window. The beech tree was in bud, the first small green of spring pushing through the gray bark.

He sat down in his chair and wept, though he did not know why.

October jumped into his lap and began to purr, and outside, the first wood pigeon called from the churchyard.

---

He kept counting.

He could not help it. It was what he was for. To stand at the window with his cup of tea and watch the leaves turn, to mark the day the first one fell, to know that the world was always leaving and always returning and that someone, at least, was paying attention.

The leaves fell. The leaves rose. The years turned.

Theodore Finch watched, and recorded, and was grateful.

# Panen di Lerah Kakek

Matahari pagi belum sepenuhnya naik ketika Pak Marno sudah berdiri di beranda rumahnya, secangkir kopi hitam mengepul di tangan. Embun masih menempel di ujung-ujung rumput, dan udara dingin menyusup lewat celah-celah kain yang melingkar di bahunya. Di kejauhan, sawah Lerah Kakek terbentang seperti permadani hijau yang dijahit dengan benang emas.

"Tahun ini cukup baik," gumamnya, menatap deretan padi yang mulai menundukkan kepalanya. Bulir-bulirnya padat, kuning mengkilap, bergoyang pelan ditiup angin.

Ini musim tanam yang ke-37 baginya. Pak Marno mulai mengenal tanah ini sejak usianya lima belas tahun, diajari oleh ayahnya, yang juga diajari oleh kakeknya. Garis keturunan yang tak terputus, mengalir bersama air irigasi dan keringat yang meresap ke dalam bumi.

---

Di rumah, Bu Marni sudah sibuk di dapur. Aroma sambal terasi dan ikan asin mulai memenuhi ruangan. Sebagai istri yang telah menemaninya lebih dari tiga puluh tahun, ia tahu persis bahwa suaminya akan pulang dengan lapar yang luar biasa setelah seharian bekerja di sawah.

"Anak-anak sudah pulang semua?" tanya Pak Marno, mengintip ke dalam.

"Sudah. Dani sedang menyiapkan traktor kecil, dan Rina sudah siapkan tampah-tampah di pendopo," jawab Bu Marni tanpa berhenti menumbuk bumbu. "Kalau mau panen hari ini, semua sudah siap."

Pak Marno mengangguk. Ia berjalan ke belakang rumah, ke tempat dua anaknya sudah menunggu. Dani, anak laki-laki sulungnya yang kini berusia tiga puluh dua tahun, memeriksa mesin perontok portable warisan mendiang ayahnya. Rina, putri bungsunya yang berambut panjang diikat ke belakang, sedang menyusun anyaman bambu untuk menjemur gabah.

"Pagi, Pak," sapa Dani.

"Pagi, Nak."

Mereka bertiga berjalan berdampingan menyusuri pematang sawah. Pak Marno di depan, anak-anaknya di belakang—seperti barisan pendek yang menolak untuk putus.

---

Pekerjaan dimulai saat matahari sudah sepenuhnya terbit. Traktor mini meraung pelan, bergerak dari satu sisi sawah ke sisi lain, merontokkan bulir-bulir padi yang sudah matang. Dani mengemudikannya dengan hati-hati, sementara Pak Marno dan Rina mengikuti dari belakang, mengarahkan bulir-bulir yang tercecer, memastikan tak ada yang terbuang percuma.

"Rina, lihat sana—ada yang masih hijau," seru Pak Marno, menunjuk sepetak kecil di ujung sawah.

Rina mengangguk dan berjalan ke sana, tangannya cekatan memisahkan bulir yang belum matang.

"Hei, Pa," panggil Dani dari atas traktor, "tahun ini hasilnya lebih bagus dari tahun lalu, ya?"

"Kalau hujan di awal musim tanamnya tidak telat, ya memang bagus," jawab Pak Marno. "Kakekmu dulu bilang, padi itu seperti manusia—kalau masa pertumbuhannya dijaga dengan benar, hasilnya akan bicara sendiri."

Rina tersenyum. Ia selalu menyukai cara ayahnya bercerita—tenang, tapi penuh makna yang tersembunyi.

---

Jam dua siang, mereka istirahat sejenak di bawah pohon beringin yang rindang di tepi sawah. Bu Marni datang membawa rantang berisi nasi, lauk pauk, dan air teh dalam botol kaca. Mereka makan bersama, di atas tikar pandan, di bawah naungan daun-daun yang bergoyang.

"Pa," kata Rina setelah menelan suapannya, "aku mau tanya sesuatu."

"Apa?"

"Kalau suatu hari Dani dan aku tidak mau lagi jadi petani, Bapak marah?"

Pak Marno berhenti mengunyah. Wajahnya tidak berubah, tapi matanya bergerak pelan ke arah sawah di belakangnya. Padi-padi yang sudah dirontokkan terlihat seperti tumpukan emas kecil di bawah terik matahari.

"Mari," katanya pelan.

Anak-anaknya menatapnya bingung.

"Mari lihat sini," ulangnya.

Mereka bangun dan mengikuti Pak Marno ke tengah sawah. Di sana, di antara jejak-jejak kaki dan sisa-sisa batang padi, tumbuh rumpun kecil padi liar. Tidak dipanen, tidak dijaga, tapi tetap hidup.

"Lihat itu?" tanya Pak Marno, menunjuk. "Itu juga tanah. Juga air. Juga matahari. Tapi tidak ada yang merawatnya. Hasilnya? Biji yang kecil-kecil, separuh kosong, dimakan burung sebelum sempat matang."

Ia berbalik menghadap anak-anaknya.

"Tanah tidak memilih siapa yang mengurusnya. Tapi kalau ada yang memilih mengurusnya—memilih untuk bangun pagi, untuk memastikan airnya cukup, untuk menjaga dari hama—maka tanah itu akan memberikan yang terbaik. Itu bukan soal generasi. Itu soal pilihan."

Rina menelan ludah. Dani memegang tangan ayahnya.

"Kami tidak akan meninggalkan tanah ini, Pa," kata Dani.

Pak Marno tersenyum tipis—senyum yang sama yang pernah diberikan ayahnya dulu, ketika suatu sore ia pertama kali diizinkan memegang cangkul kecil di pematang sawah.

---

Sore itu, ketika matahari mulai turun dan cahaya jingga membasahi sawah, tiga orang itu berdiri di beranda rumah, memandang tumpukan gabah yang sudah dikumpulkan di pendopo. Aromanya—segar, sedikit manis, seperti memori—mengalir ke seluruh ruangan.

"Ini cukup untuk setahun?" tanya Rina.

"Cukup," jawab Pak Marno. "Lebih dari cukup. Kita punya tetangga yang juga butuh."

Ia menoleh ke barat, di mana langit berubah warna dari jingga menjadi ungu.

"Tahukah kalian, kenapa kakek kalian dulu memberi nama sawah ini 'Lerah Kakek'?"

Anak-anaknya menggeleng.

"Karena beliau bilang, tanah ini akan merawat cucu-cucunya, asalkan cucu-cucunya juga merawatnya. Sebuah perjanjian yang tidak tertulis, tapi selalu ditepati."

Hening sejenak. Cicit jangkrik mulai terdengar dari semak-semak.

"Mari kita syukuri panen tahun ini," kata Pak Marno, tangannya terangkat ke langit yang mulai berbintang. "Dan mari kita bersiap untuk musim tanam berikutnya."

Di bawah langit yang mulai gelap, di atas tanah yang tak pernah ingkar janji, sebuah keluarga kecil berdiri bersama—menjaga warisan yang jauh lebih tua dari diri mereka sendiri, dan jauh lebih muda dari generasi yang akan datang.

# 那条遗失的围巾

深秋的风已经带上了冬天的味道。

苏瑾站在地铁站的出口，看着眼前川流不息的人群，下意识地把脖子往衣领里缩了缩。她忽然想起了什么，伸手往肩头一摸——空的。

那条围巾不见了。

那是一条绛红色的羊绒围巾，是外婆亲手织的。细细的绒线里藏着岁月的温度，外婆的手指已经不太灵活了，织到收尾的时候针脚有些参差不齐，但苏瑾每次戴上都觉得格外安心。

她开始回忆——

早上出门时还在，进地铁站的时候也在，过安检的时候……她皱了皱眉。好像过安检的时候取下来过一次？她记不清了。

苏瑾转身往回走。

地铁站里人来人往，谁会注意到一条旧围巾呢？她问询了安检处的工作人员，得到的回答是"捡到东西要交到失物招领中心"。

失物招领中心在站台尽头的一个小房间里。苏瑾推门进去，里面只有一个中年男人坐在桌后，戴着眼镜看报纸。

"您好，我想问一下，有没有捡到一条绛红色的围巾？"

男人抬起头，从柜台下面拿出一个塑料袋："是这个吗？"

苏瑾一眼就认出了那条围巾。它被叠得整整齐齐，装在透明的袋子里。她接过来，心里松了一口气："太感谢了，是我的。"

"是一个小姑娘送来的，"男人推了推眼镜，"说是看到围巾掉在安检的传送带旁边，怕被人踩脏了，就送过来了。"

"小姑娘？"苏瑾有些疑惑，"她人呢？"

"走了，放下就走了，"男人重新拿起报纸，"大概十六七岁的样子，扎着马尾辫。"

苏瑾走出失物招领中心，把围巾从袋子里取出来，绕在脖子上。熟悉的柔软触感贴上皮肤，像是外婆的手轻轻拂过她的脸颊。

她低头看着围巾末端那个不太平整的收尾，忽然想起外婆织这条围巾时的样子——坐在窗边的藤椅上，老花镜架在鼻梁上，一针一线地慢慢织着。阳光照在她花白的头发上，温暖而宁静。

外婆已经走了三年了。

苏瑾站在站台里，看着来来往往的乘客，忽然有些想哭。她想，外婆如果还在，一定会笑着责备她粗心大意。

列车呼啸而来，苏瑾转身走进去，找了一个靠窗的位置坐下。

窗外的城市在后退，高楼、行人、红绿灯，一切都一闪而过。她把脸埋进围巾里，闻到了一股淡淡的樟脑丸的味道——那是外婆衣柜的味道。

那一刻，她仿佛又回到了那个老房子里，回到了外婆的身边。

---

回到家，苏瑾把围巾叠好，放进了衣柜最里层。她想着，明年冬天一定要小心一些，不要再弄丢了。

因为那条围巾里，不只是羊绒和绒线，还有一个老人对孙女永远的爱。

# 第一场秋色

小满是从南方来的。

她在海南岛出生、长大，二十三年里，头顶永远是那种化不开的浓郁绿意。椰子树、芒果树、榕树、三角梅——所有的植物都像是约好了似的，一年到三季都铆足了劲地绿着，没人肯先褪色。

所以当她第一次踏上北方的土地，正赶上九月，导师让她去植物园报到时，她甚至不知道该看什么。

"小满，明天带你去看看银杏大道。"导师笑着说，"再过几天就该黄了。"

"黄了？"她不解，"叶子不是一直是绿的吗？"

导师愣了一下，然后哈哈大笑："来了就知道了。"

那天下午，她一个人先去探了路。

九月中旬的北京，阳光还带着夏天的余温。银杏大道两侧，一排排古老的树木挺立着，枝叶层层叠叠，密密麻麻。叶子还是绿的——至少在小满眼里，全是绿。

她有点失望。

回宿舍的路上，她路过一条小巷。巷口有一棵她叫不出名字的树，半人高的枝条探出墙来，挂着些心形的叶子。她路过时，余光瞥见了一点不一样的颜色。

她停下脚步。

那点颜色很淡，像是谁在浓绿的画布上小心地点了一笔——只有一片叶子，边缘开始泛出微微的黄，像是日落时分天边最初的那一抹金。

她凑近了看。

那片叶子孤零零地挂在枝头，周围还是一片浓绿。它小小的、薄薄的，脉络清晰，像一只刚刚睁开眼睛的蝴蝶。她从来没见过这样的颜色。不是凋零的枯黄，而是——像是某种正在发生的变化，某种生命里她从未见过的时刻。

她站在那里，看了很久很久。

第二天，她一大早就跑去那条巷子。那片叶子还在那里，黄得更深了一些。

第三天，第四天，第五天……

她每天都去看。起初只是看那一片叶子，后来那棵树上开始出现第二片、第三片、第十片。然后，不仅仅是那一棵树，整条街、整条巷、整座城市的树，都开始响应某种她看不见的信号。

每天早上推开门，空气都不一样了。

那些绿色开始松动、开始稀释、开始酝酿。浅黄、橙黄、金黄、褐黄——她从没见过这么多种"黄"。有些是温柔的，像是把阳光揉碎了塞进叶子里；有些是激烈的，红得像在燃烧；有些干脆变成深沉的紫，像是天空在傍晚留下的最后一口气。

她想起小时候，奶奶给她讲过的故事。

奶奶说，人是有颜色的。你笑的时候是什么颜色，哭的时候是什么颜色，思念一个人的时候又是什么颜色。小时候她不信，觉得奶奶是老糊涂了。

现在她站在银杏树下，仰头看满树金黄——那些叶子在阳光里闪闪发光，像是挂了满树的小太阳。风一吹，无数金色的"小太阳"纷纷扬扬地落下来，落在她头发上、肩膀上、掌心。

她捧起一片叶子，贴近脸颊。

它是温的。

那一刻，她忽然明白了奶奶的话。

她想，如果思念有颜色，那一定是此刻满地的金黄——是每一个清晨推开门时心里那一点点小期待，是小心翼翼地收藏着每一场变化时的那种郑重，是终于懂得"变化本身也是一种完整"的释然。

她从来不知道，原来告别也可以这么美。

原来一片叶子从绿变黄，不是死去，是去赴一场漫长的、与自己相遇的约。

那天晚上，她给奶奶打了个电话。

"奶奶，"她说，"我看到叶子换衣服了。"

电话那头沉默了一下，然后传来奶奶轻轻的笑声。

"好看吗？"

"好看。"

"那就多看两眼，"奶奶说，"这样的颜色，一年只有一次。"

挂了电话，小满站在窗前。窗外，月光下的银杏大道像是一条铺满碎金的河。

她想，她要在这里等到十一月，等到银杏叶全部落完。她要把每一片叶子都认认真真地看一遍，看它们是怎么从绿到黄，从黄到金，从金到褐，最后轻轻地落回大地的怀里。

然后她要在春天的时候，再来看它们一次——看新绿是怎么从枝头冒出来的。

她要看完一整年。

她要看明白，原来生命是这样，一年又一年，循环往复，却每次都不一样。

她终于明白了，为什么奶奶每年秋天都要去一趟北方。

不是为了看叶子，是为了——

# 土地的呼吸

## 第一天

清晨五点，我就醒了。

不是被闹钟叫醒的，是被光叫醒的。九月末的日出来得越来越晚，但当第一缕橘红色的光线从窗帘缝隙钻进来时，我的眼睛自动睁开，像那些埋在地里的南瓜也感应到了阳光。

我裹上那件洗得发白的卡其色夹克，推开后门。空气冰凉，呼出的气在面前凝成一团白雾。院子里那棵老槐树落了一地黄叶，我踩上去，发出酥脆的声响。

然后我走向那片土地。

十二亩地，从我父亲手里传下来，又从我手里准备传给儿子——如果他愿意回来的话。地里躺满了南瓜，橙的、绿的、灰白的、奇形怪状的。它们安安静静地趴在那里，像是土地呼出的一个个饱满的气泡。

我蹲下来，把手放在一个南瓜上。表皮冰凉，带着细微的霜意。

"早上好啊。"我轻声说。

这是我每年秋天的第一天必做的事。说给南瓜听，也说给自己听。说给这片土地听。

三十年前我第一次站在这里时，还是个毛头小子，跟着父亲学习怎么分辨熟透的南瓜。父亲说："你敲敲它，如果声音是闷的，就是好的；如果声音是空的，就让它再长长。"我当时不懂，为什么空心的反而不好。多年以后我才明白，土地和人一样，饱满的才是好的，虚空的只会塌陷。

我站起身，望向远处。山脊线被晨雾染成淡蓝色，几只乌鸦从麦田里飞起，发出沙哑的叫声。风从北边吹来，带着一丝枯草和冷霜的味道——那是秋天第一天的味道，我闻了三十年，从来没有认错过。

今天会有很多人来。带着孩子的父母，手牵手的年轻人，拄着拐杖的老人。他们会在南瓜间走来走去，挑挑拣拣，拍照，尖叫，笑着。然后他们会选一个最完美的南瓜，带回家，在万圣节前夜挖空它，点上一支蜡烛。

他们不会知道，为了这个"完美"，我在过去九十天里付出了多少。

春天播种，夏天灌溉，整个八月我几乎睡在田边，看着它们从绿色慢慢转成橙色，看着藤蔓一寸一寸枯萎，看着每一片叶子掉落。每掉一片叶子，我都觉得心被揪了一下。但父亲说过："叶子掉了，果实才甜。"

我把所有的心思都放在了这里。

但今天早上，我心里却有一丝隐秘的空洞。

儿子上周打来电话，说他今年还是不回来了。纽约的项目正值关键期，他说，"爸，真的很抱歉。"我说没关系，语气平淡得像在说天气。挂掉电话后，我在门廊上坐了很久，看那片南瓜地。

他小时候最爱这片地。会在南瓜堆里打滚，会骑着自行车从藤蔓间穿过，会用小刀在还没熟的南瓜上刻下自己的名字。我总骂他，说他会毁了那些南瓜。但我心里是高兴的。

现在他在曼哈顿的一间公寓里，做着我不明白的工作，吃着我叫不出名字的食物。他说他爱上了那个城市，那里有博物馆，有歌剧院，有二十四小时营业的便利店。

我替他高兴。我真的替他高兴。

只是这片土地，今年又会少一个人来分享。

太阳升起来了。我把这种感觉压回心底，戴上那顶旧草帽，走向田边的小木屋。今天要做的第一件事，是把昨天没收完的南瓜搬到木屋前的桌子上。昨晚风大，吹倒了几十个。

我弯腰抱起一个巨大的"阿特拉斯"，它沉甸甸的，像抱着一个熟睡的孩子。

"今年也要加油啊。"我对它说。

它没有回答。但我感觉到它在我怀里，微微地、温热地呼吸着。

## 最后一天

下雪了。

十一月底的雪，来得比往年早。我站在门口，看着雪花落在南瓜地上。那片曾经生机勃勃的橙黄色，现在只剩下残破的藤蔓和零星几个被我故意留下的南瓜。

雪很轻，像盐，像面粉，像时间本身。

我慢慢地走进雪里。脚下的土地已经冻得硬邦邦的，踩上去发出沉闷的声响，不像九月时那样酥软。

走到田中央，我停下来。

南瓜地空了。

这个"空"，是慢慢发生的。从十月中旬万圣节前夜开始，人们蜂拥而至，把最漂亮的南瓜都挑走了。然后是感恩节，又走了一批。最后这几天，零零星星的，只剩下几个歪瓜裂枣，或者故意留着的——留给我的老顾客，他们喜欢奇形怪状的东西。

昨晚最后一个客人来的时候，天已经黑了。一对年轻夫妻，孩子才两三岁，走路还跌跌撞撞的。他们挑了很久，最后选了一个很小、形状很奇怪的南瓜，像个歪嘴的葫芦。

"这个多少钱？"男人问。

我看着那个南瓜，想起它是怎么长出来的——被藤蔓压着，石头硌着，歪歪扭扭地长成了这个样子。但它活了下来，并且成熟了。

"送你们了。"我说。

女人惊讶地抬起头："真的？"

"真的。它等了一整个秋天，就为了遇见你们。"

他们道了谢，抱着那个小南瓜离开了。我看着他们的背影消失在夜色里，看见小孩的头靠在父亲的肩膀上，心里突然涌起一种奇怪的感觉。

是安慰。

今天早上我醒来时，天地之间已经是一片银白。我没有急着出门，在屋里喝了杯咖啡，又喝了杯。然后我穿上那件最厚的棉衣，走到这片空地上来。

雪越下越大。

我突然想起父亲。

他在最后那年的秋天，也是这样站在这里。只不过他站的位置更靠近那棵老槐树。他当时已经病得很重了，但还是坚持要来看看南瓜。他站在那里，看了很久，然后对我说：

"这块地啊，会呼吸。"

我那时以为他在说胡话。但现在我懂了。

是的，这块地会呼吸。春天它吸气，把所有的种子和雨水都吞下去；夏天它屏息，把所有的阳光都转化成糖分；秋天它呼气，把所有的果实都吐出来；而冬天，它要休息了。

我深吸一口气。

冷得刺骨，但也清醒。

我想到很多事情。想到儿子今年还是没有回来，但他在电话里说，明年春天想来看看我播种——"如果那个时候项目结了的话，爸。"想到我的妻子，已经去世五年了，但她最喜欢的那个位置，那块稍微高一点的台地，每年长出来的南瓜总是最甜的。想到我的老顾客们，有些已经搬走了，有些已经不在了，但他们的孩子还会带着自己的孩子来。

想到我自己。

我已经六十二岁了。还能种几年呢？

这个问题我以前不敢想。但今天站在雪地里，我突然觉得可以想了。

也许五年。也许十年。也许明年就不行了——膝盖越来越不好，去年冬天摔了一跤，躺了两个月。

但那又怎样呢？

这块地不会因为我不在就不呼吸了。它已经呼吸了几百年，会继续呼吸下去。会有别的人来种它，会有别的南瓜在这里成熟，会有别的父亲带着别的儿子在这里打滚。

而我留下的那些南瓜——那些被挑走的，被雕刻的，被摆在窗台上的，被遗忘在角落里慢慢腐烂的——它们也完成了自己的使命。

它们的种子，明年还会发芽。

我蹲下来，用手扒开一层雪。雪下面是泥土，黑色的、潮湿的、带着一种特有的腥气。我抓了一把在手里。

冷，但活着。

"明年见。"我对土地说。

雪落在我花白的头发上，落在我的肩膀上，落在整片空旷的南瓜地上。

我站起来，往回走。身后，我的脚印在雪地里留下了一串清晰的痕迹，很快又被新雪覆盖。

但我知道，明天早上，那片土地又会呼吸的。

它只是闭着眼睛，做一个长长的、关于春天的梦。

# The Last Pumpkin Spice Latte of Autumn

The line at Brewed Awakening stretched out the door and curled around the corner, a familiar sight on the first truly cold morning of October. Eleanor adjusted her scarf and stared at her increasingly dim phone screen. 4%. The email she'd been waiting on from the gallery—about her exhibition, her future, her everything—could come at any moment, and her battery was dying.

She was next in line when she smelled it. That heady perfume of cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, and espresso—that unmistakable signal that autumn had truly arrived. The barista, a young woman with rings in her nose and a smile that suggested she was either very kind or very caffeinated, was holding out a cup.

"Pumpkin spice latte for Eleanor?"

Eleanor blinked. She hadn't ordered yet. "I didn't—"

"The woman in front of you paid for it. Said to make sure you got it." The barista gestured vaguely toward the door, but when Eleanor turned, she saw only a blur of scarves and coats disappearing into the gray morning.

She accepted the cup with murmured thanks, warmth seeping into her cold fingers. No name was written on the side, only a small "E." painted in careful script.

Eleanor found a small table by the window and set her phone on it, willing it to hold on a little longer. She took her first sip, and the sweet, spiced warmth flooded through her like a remembered embrace. Her grandmother had made pumpkin spice everything every October—pumpkin pancakes, pumpkin cookies, pumpkin soup. She'd passed away in March, and Eleanor had spent the summer avoiding everything that reminded her of her.

Until now.

She took another sip, longer this time, and let the taste bring her back to her grandmother's kitchen, the soft yellow walls, the old wooden table where they'd shell peas and Eleanor would draw pictures with her colored pencils. *You have a gift, Ellie-bird. Don't let anyone tell you it's small.*

Her phone buzzed.

**1%.**

She lunged for it, fumbling, and the latte wobbled. The cup tilted, splashing a slow, warm cascade across her grandmother's old wool coat—the one she'd inherited, the one she'd worn every day since March as if it were a hug.

"No, no, no—"

She watched in horror as the latte bled into the gray wool, forming a stain shaped like a small, defeated heart.

And then her phone died.

Eleanor sat very still. The gallery was waiting for her to confirm the exhibition by noon. Without her phone, she couldn't check her email. She didn't have a laptop. She lived alone. Her grandmother was gone.

The morning light was making the latte stain glow.

She looked down at the cup and noticed something she hadn't before. On the other side, beneath the cardboard sleeve, someone had written in tiny letters: *Call your sister.*

Eleanor didn't have a sister.

She picked up the cup and turned it in her hands, certain she was imagining things. But no—there it was, in the same careful script as the "E." on the other side: *Call your sister. You have one. She has you.*

Her hands were shaking now. She thought of all the family secrets her grandmother had kept, all the stories that had been interrupted by Alzheimer's in her last years, all the questions Eleanor had never thought to ask. Her grandmother had come to America from Poland at nineteen, alone, the only one of her family to survive. Or so the story went.

What if the story was a story?

Eleanor looked up at the barista, who was watching her with that same strange smile.

"The woman who paid for this," Eleanor said. "Did you see her? Was she—"

"Old?" The barista's smile deepened. "Polish? Wearing a yellow coat and a hat with a feather?"

Eleanor's breath caught.

"She said to tell you she's sorry she couldn't stay. And that the stain will come out if you use cold water and a little vinegar." The barista winked. "She also said to tell you she loved the painting you did of her kitchen. The one with the yellow walls. She said it was the most seen she'd ever felt in her whole life."

Eleanor didn't remember standing up, but she was outside now, in the cold October air, holding the stained coat and the empty cup. She walked for a long time without direction, thinking of all the things she didn't know, all the secrets buried in her grandmother's silence.

Finally, she found a payphone—yes, a payphone, because some things in Brooklyn refused to die—and called information. Then she called a number in Warsaw. A woman answered, and when Eleanor said her grandmother's name, the line went quiet for so long Eleanor thought they'd been disconnected.

Then, in Polish so accented Eleanor could barely understand it, the woman said: *"My sister. You sound like my sister."*

Eleanor sat down on the wet sidewalk, the phone receiver pressed to her ear, and laughed until she cried.

The latte had gone cold long ago. The stain on her coat had set. But Eleanor—Eleanor had finally come home.

---

*Years later, when she was preparing for her first gallery show, Eleanor would title her centerpiece "The Last Pumpkin Spice Latte of Autumn." It would depict a cup with a slow spill, and a woman walking away in a yellow coat. Critics would call it a meditation on memory and loss.*

*Eleanor would only ever tell one person what it really meant.*

*And every October, without fail, she would order a pumpkin spice latte and leave it on a certain grave, untouched, still warm in the cold morning air.*

I hate fall, but I love autumn.

It was a distinction only Eleanor Whitfield seemed to understand, and she had long stopped trying to explain it to anyone. Fall was what happened to people—gravity's slow victory, the body's betrayal, the small surrenders that accumulated over decades until you found yourself stooped and cautious, watching your step. Autumn was something else entirely. Autumn was the trees deciding, collectively, to burn.

At seventy-three, Eleanor walked the path behind her cottage each morning, counting the maples as they turned. She had been counting them for forty-one years, ever since she'd moved to this house in the Vermont hills with a husband who was now ash in a box on the mantel and a daughter who called on Sundays and meant well but lived in another time zone of understanding.

The first tree to change was always the sugar maple by the stone wall. It had turned the week before the equinox this year, the earliest she could remember. Eleanor stood before it now, wrapped in her wool coat, her breath making small ghosts in the cold.

"Early," she said aloud, to no one.

The leaves were that particular orange that exists for perhaps three days each year—too bright to be called mere color, too transient to be called anything but a warning. *Look*, the trees seemed to be saying. *This is what beauty costs. Watch it happen and then watch it leave.*

She remembered being young and thinking autumn was melancholy. Now she understood it was the opposite. Melancholy was a gray thing, a thing of fog and resignation. Autumn was fire. Autumn was the world giving one last magnificent performance before the long hush of winter, and every year Eleanor felt the same quiet astonishment that she was still alive to witness it.

She walked on. The path curved through birches that had gone gold at their crowns, down past the old apple orchard where the gnarled trees still produced a few stubborn fruit each year. She picked one up from the ground—wounded, bruised, leaking sweetness onto her palm. She bit into it anyway. The wasps were mostly gone now, drowsing in the crevices of the bark. There was less competition for the fallen things.

Her grandmother had lived to ninety-six, sharp as a tack until the final six months, and Eleanor had inherited her stubbornness if not her certainty that God was watching. Her mother had died at fifty-eight, young and unjust and leaving behind a box of recipes Eleanor still hadn't opened. Her father had faded at seventy, the way men sometimes did, just dimming one evening and never quite relighting.

She had expected, at various points in her life, to die young. She had expected to die in childbirth (she hadn't had children after Margaret, the difficult one, the daughter who was difficult because Eleanor had been difficult first). She had expected to die of her smoking habit (she'd quit at fifty, gasping and furious with herself). She had expected to die of heartbreak (Harold's death had almost done it, the first year). And now here she was, walking through her own private cathedral of light, utterly unprepared to have lived this long.

*Fall*, she thought. *I am in my fall.*

But the trees, the trees were in their autumn. And autumn was not an ending. Autumn was a decision, a conscious act of letting go performed with tremendous artistry. The trees did not fall. They released. They let go of their green and reached for something else, something more honest, more precise, something that cost them chlorophyll but gave them, briefly, the appearance of being on fire.

She turned toward home. The cottage, small and gray-shingled, sat in a clearing surrounded by her congregation of trees. She had lived here longer than anywhere else in her life. Harold had built the porch swing himself, badly, so that it groaned when you sat in it. She had never had it repaired.

Inside, she made tea and sat at the kitchen window with her notebook. For twenty years she had kept a record of the first frost dates, the peak color days, the strange arrivals and departures of birds. It was not science. It was something closer to devotion.

Her phone buzzed. Margaret, asking if she needed anything delivered for the weekend.

*No*, she typed. *Just watching the trees.*

*You're so weird, Mom*, came the reply, with a laughing emoji.

Eleanor smiled. Margaret loved her in the way that daughters love their mothers—part admiration, part bewilderment, part relief at the geographical distance. She was a good daughter. She was a busy daughter. She was a daughter who had been, Eleanor sometimes thought, mostly raised by the answering machine and the neighbor woman, because Eleanor had been busy too, working, grieving, surviving.

She had done her best. She thought this often now, as the end approached, not with regret but with a kind of clinical assessment. She had done her best. It had been, by most measures, insufficient. And yet here she was, still drinking tea, still watching light, still counting the maples.

In the afternoon, a knock at the door. Eleanor wasn't expecting anyone. She opened it to find a young man she didn't recognize, mid-twenties maybe, with a red beard and tired eyes. He held a clipboard.

"Sorry to bother you, ma'am. I'm doing a survey for the forestry service. We're tracking the spread of the hemlock woolly adelgid."

Eleanor studied him. She thought of all the things she could say. She thought of how strange it was to be interrupted at seventy-three by someone who hadn't yet been born when she moved here. She thought of the hemlocks along the north ridge, the ones that had been her husband's particular pride, how their loss would diminish the view.

"Come in," she said. "I'll show you."

She made him coffee. He sat at her kitchen table, looking uncomfortable in the way young men often did in old women's kitchens, unsure whether to be kind or to escape. She took him out to the north ridge, pointing out the affected trees, the white fuzz beneath the needles, the slow death that had begun.

"My husband planted these," she said. "Forty-one years ago."

The young man was gentle with the clipboard. He wrote things down.

"Beautiful property," he said. "How long have you been here?"

"Since before you were born, I imagine."

He smiled politely. He did not believe her.

When he left, Eleanor returned to her porch swing and sat in the groaning wood and watched the light change. The maples were at their peak now, that impossible orange, that borrowed flame. She thought of Harold, who had planted the hemlocks without knowing why, only that he wanted to, only that the world should contain more green things.

She thought of Margaret, who would inherit this place and probably sell it, who would not understand why Eleanor had never moved closer to town, why she had never downsized, why she had stayed here with her dead husband and her notebooks and her apples.

She thought of herself as a young woman, which seemed increasingly like a different person. That young woman had been terrified of falling. Falling in love, falling behind, falling ill, falling apart. She had spent her whole life bracing.

Now, finally, she thought: *Let it come.*

The leaves let go. One drifted down and landed in her lap, orange as a coal, orange as a heart, orange as the last good thing.

She picked it up. She looked at it. She put it in her notebook, between the pages marked September.

Outside, the world burned on.

Sempre considerei-me um homem de talentos variados. Sei tocar três acordes de violão, improvisar uma rima quando pedem, e até já troquei o vedante da torneira da cozinha sem inundar a casa — uma proeza que a minha esposa, Helena, ainda hoje reconhece com um misto de admiração e espanto. Cozinhar, porém, nunca foi o meu forte. Talvez por isso, quando o meu vizinho Joaquim elogiou publicamente o meu “talento culinário” durante um churrasco de bairro, eu tenha levado a peito o desafio de provar que ele tinha razão.

O disparate começou com uma abóbora.

Era uma abóbora enorme, alaranjada, quase grotesca na sua perfeição. Tinha-a ganho numa feira rural, depois de uma discussão amigável com um senhor que insistia que era a maior da região. Não sei por que razão a trouxe para casa. Talvez porque o meu filho mais novo, o Tomás, de sete anos, tenha feito aqueles olhos enormes quando a viu — os mesmos olhos que o meu pai descrevia como “a expressão de um gato diante de um pepino”. Ou talvez porque eu seja, no fundo, um homem incapaz de recusar um desafio.

Helí encontrou-me na cozinha, três dias depois, com a abóbora aberta ao meio sobre a bancada e um ar de cirurgião iniciante.

— Vais cozinhá-la? — perguntou ela, com aquele tom que pode significar tanto “que amor” como “vais mesmo fazer isto?”.

— Vou fazer uma tarte de abóbora — anunciei, com uma gravidade que não condizia com a situação.

— Uma tarte de abóbora? Tu? — Ela cruzou os braços, encostou-se à ombreira da porta. — Tu mal sabes ferver um ovo.

— Pois, mas é precisamente por isso que é um desafio — respondi, convicto. — O Joaquim disse que eu era um cozinheiro nato. É altura de provar isso.

Helí ficou em silêncio durante uns segundos, como quem avalia a situação clínica de um paciente. Depois, suspirou.

— Vou estar no quarto do Tomás a ajudá-lo com os trabalhos de casa. Se ouvires um barulho estranho vindo da cozinha... ignora. Se a casa pegar fogo... não ignora.

Retirou-se. Eu fiquei a olhar para a abóbora com a determinação de um general antes da batalha.

A receita, encontrei-a num livro antigo da minha mãe. As páginas estavam amarelecidas, algumas com manchas de gordura que sugeriam que ela própria tinha experimentado o feito. Havia mesmo uma nota rabiscada a lápis na margem: “Não uses esta receita para impressionar sogras. Não vale a pena.” Ri-me sozinho. A minha sogra já tinha falecido, felizmente. Toquei de azar eliminado.

A primeira etapa era simples: cortar a abóbora em pedaços e cozê-la em água com sal. Eu, que sempre achei que a faca era um instrumento subestimado, ataquei a abóbora com um facão que só usava para abrir cartas. A abóbora, teimosa como uma rocha, resistiu com estoicismo. Bati com ela na bancada, fiz força com os pés, e finalmente ela cedeu — mas não sem antes me fazer um corte no polegar que me fez derramar mais sangue do que uma novela das nove.

Enfaixei o dedo com um guardanapo de Natal — o único pano limpo que encontrei — e continuei. Cozi os pedaços durante quarenta minutos, como a receita mandava. O cheiro, devo admitir, era agradável. Pela primeira vez, senti uma onda de otimismo. Talvez o Joaquim tivesse razão.

Depois de escorrer a água e triturar a abóbora — operação esta que realizei com um Passatudo que parecia ter sido inventado na Idade Média —, adicionei os restantes ingredientes: leite condensado, ovos, canela, noz-moscada. Foi aqui que tudo começou a correr mal.

Confundi uma colher de sopa com uma de sobremesa. Erro fatal. A canela, generosa como um avô num Natal, inundou a mistura com uma quantidade que mais parecia própria para aromatizar uma loja de perfumes. Provei. Era como comer um pudim com um travesseiro de especiarias dentro.

— Vai ficar bom depois de ir ao forno — murmurei para mim mesmo, com uma fé inabalável.

O forno estava regulado para 180 graus, como a receita indicava. Mas o meu forno, um eletrodoméstico tão antigo como a minha sogra (descanse em paz), tem a particularidade de aquecer mais de um lado do que do outro. Coloquei a tarte na prateleira do meio, fechei a porta e sentei-me no sofá a ver televisão com a Helena, que entretanto descera do quarto do Tomás.

— Cheira bem — disse ela, com honestidade.

— Obrigado — respondi, orgulhoso.

— Cheira a canela.

— É suposto cheirar a canela. É tarte de abóbora.

— Cheira... só a canela.

O relógio da cozinha avançou. O Tomás desceu para ver o que era aquela coisa enorme no forno. A minha filha, a Inês, de vinte anos, apareceu misteriosamente como sempre que há comida em preparação — uma bússola interna que a guia para a cozinha. Até o gato se aproximou, farejando o ar com desconfiança felina.

Quando abri o forno, vinte minutos depois, a tarte estava irreconhecível. Não no bom sentido. A superfície estava tostada, sim, mas de um tom que mais parecia couro curtido. As bordas tinham subido como uma cordilheira em miniatura, e havia uma fissura no centro que mais parecia uma cratera lunar.

— Hmm — disse a Helena, com diplomacia.

O Tomás aproximou-se, com o otimismo da infância.

— Posso provar?

— Espera — respondi, tirando a tarte do forno com luvas que pareciam feitas de amianto e má vontade. Coloquei-a sobre a bancada. Ela tilintou. Sim, tilintou. Como se o recheio tivesse decidido tornar-se num mineral.

— Isso não parece tarte — observou ela.

— Tinha uma quantidade excessiva de canela — confessei.

— Eu provei o recheio antes — admitiu o Tomás, com uma careta que me confirmou o pior.

A Inês, sempre prática, pegou numa colher e tirou uma amostra do centro da tarte. Mastigou durante cinco segundos com uma expressão neutra. Depois, engoliu com dificuldade.

— Pai — disse ela, com cuidado —, isto é... uma experiência.

— Uma experiência boa? — perguntei, com esperança.

— Uma experiência.

Pusemos a tarte na mesa de jantar, como manda a tradição, na noite desse mesmo dia. A Helena cortou-a com dificuldade — a faca rangeu como se estivesse a abrir caminho numa mina — e serviu quatro fatias. O Tomás lambeu a dela uma vez, fez uma careta, e empurrou-a para o lado. A Inês, educada, deu duas dentadas antes de declarar que já estava saciada. A Helena comeu metade da fatia com uma expressão de sofrimento estoico. Eu, o autor da desgraça, comi a minha inteira — por orgulho, mas sobretudo porque não sabia o que fazer com ela.

Às onze da noite, a tarte estava quase intacta na mesa. O gato aproximou-se, farejou-a, e saiu com um ar de indignação. Até o gato a rejeitou.

— Amanhã deito-a fora — disse a Helena, com ternura.

— Não. Vou comê-la ao pequeno-almoço — respondi, teimoso.

— António.

— Vou comê-la!

Comi-a ao pequeno-almoço. E ao almoço. E ao jantar. A cada refeição, repetia para mim mesmo que ia ficar melhor, que era uma questão de tempo até o meu paladar se adaptar àquela obra-prima de canela. Não ficou.

Na manhã do quarto dia, olhei para a tarte com a honestidade brutal de quem finalmente aceita a derrota. Havia ainda um quarto dela, encrostada na forma como uma peça de arte contemporânea que ninguém quer comprar. Levantei-me da mesa, peguei nela com as duas mãos, e levei-a até ao caixote do lixo. Hesitei um segundo. Depois, com uma pontada de remorso e alívio, larguei-a.

Quando voltei à cozinha, a Helena estava encostada à bancada, com um sorriso sereno.

— Pronto?

— Pronto — admiti, suspirando.

Ela aproximou-se, beijou-me na bochecha, e disse:

— Para a próxima, ofereces chocolates. É mais seguro.

Anuí. O Joaquim, quando soube do sucedido, riu-se durante uma semana inteira. O Tomás, sempre poético, descreveu a tarte como “uma almofada de canela que queria ser comida, mas não conseguiu”. A Inês, pragmática, sugeriu que eu me concentrasse em pratos que não envolvessem fornos.

Hoje, quando alguém me pergunta se sei cozinhar, respondo com sinceridade: “Sei ferver água. Com cautela.” E quando vejo uma abóbora numa montra, olho para o outro lado e caminho mais depressa. Já tive a minha dose.

E esta foi a primeira e última vez que tentei fazer uma tarte de abóbora.

Write about a character driving in the rain. In total around 400 words.

The rain came down in sheets, hammering the windshield with a ferocity that turned the world beyond the glass into a blur of smeared lights and shadow. Eleanor gripped the steering wheel tighter, her knuckles pale against the dark leather, and let out a breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding.

The wipers swept across the glass in a frantic rhythm—*thump, thump, thump*—each pass buying her only a half-second of clarity before the water swallowed the road again. She should have waited. She'd known the storm was coming, had watched the forecast turn from bad to worse on her phone while finishing her coffee that morning. But waiting meant staying, and staying meant facing the questions still hanging in the air between her and Daniel.

So she had packed a bag. So she had left.

The headlights of an oncoming truck loomed suddenly in her mirror, too bright, too close, and she eased her foot onto the accelerator just enough to feel the car surge forward. The truck roared past, sending a wall of spray across her lane that made her heart lurch. She blinked hard, once, twice, and the road reappeared—a dark ribbon unspooling through nothing.

She didn't know where she was going. That was the strange part. She'd pulled out of the driveway with such certainty, such righteous momentum, but forty minutes into the drive the certainty had curdled into something else. The anger was still there, banked low in her chest like coals, but beside it now sat a quieter, more uncomfortable thing. A question.

*Was she wrong?*

The defroster hummed. The rain kept falling. Somewhere behind her, the city she'd left was going about its evening—lights in high windows, brake lights on wet pavement, people moving through their small dramas without her. She tried to imagine Daniel in the house now, the silence of it, the way he would have stood in the doorway looking at the empty space where her car had been. Would he have called? She glanced at her phone on the passenger seat, dark and silent, and hated herself for looking.

A mile marker flashed past. *Route 9. 12 miles to Thornfield.* She'd never been to Thornfield. Had only seen the sign once or twice in her life, on drives she didn't remember now. But her hands had taken the exit anyway, the way hands do when the mind has given up making decisions.

The wipers beat on. The tires hissed against the asphalt. And Eleanor drove, and drove, and drove, the storm keeping pace with her like something that knew her name.

# Mùa Táo Vàng

Nắng sớm thu tràn qua tán lá, rải những vệt vàng lung linh trên mặt đất. Mai ngồi trên chiếc xe lăn, đôi mắt nâu long lanh ngước nhìn những trái táo đỏ mọng treo lủng lẳng trên cành. Bên cạnh cô, Khoa đang cười tươi, tay xách hai chiếc giỏ tre đan bằng tay nghệ nhân.

"Hôm nay trời đẹp quá, Mai," Khoa nói, giọng ấm áp như nắng thu. "Mình hái táo ở vườn ông Bảy nhé. Ông ấy hứa cho mình chọn bất kỳ cây nào mình thích."

Mai gật đầu, khoé môi cong lên. Cô không nói được nhiều từ sau cơn tai biến năm ngoái, nhưng đôi mắt cô luôn biết cách kể câu chuyện của riêng mình. Và Khoa, người bạn thân từ thuở nhỏ, là người hiểu cô nhất.

Đường đến vườn táo ngoằn ngoèo qua con dốc đá ong. Mai bám vào tay vịn xe lăn, Khoa nhẹ nhàng đẩy cô từ phía sau, tránh từng viên sỏi nhỏ. Hai người đã quen với nhịp điệu này - sự kiên nhẫn, nhẹ nhàng, và tình bạn không cần nói quá nhiều.

"Ông Bảy ơi!" Khoa gọi to khi đến cổng vườn.

Một ông lão với khuôn mặt nhăn nheo nhưng nụ cười hiền hậu bước ra từ căn chòi nhỏ. "Cháu đến rồi hả? Táo năm nay ngọt lắm, đỏ như son. Cháu gái đây là Mai phải không? Lớn rồi, đẹp quá!"

Ông Bảy dẫn hai người vào vườn. Hàng trăm cây táo trải dài như một tấm thảm xanh điểm tô những quả cầu đỏ. Mùi táo chín thơm ngọt hoà quyện với mùi cỏ tươi và đất ẩm, tạo nên một bản giao hưởng của mùa thu.

"Cây này nè," ông Bảy chỉ vào một cây táo ở giữa vườn, cành thấp, trái sai trĩu. "Hai đứa cứ thoải mái hái. Không cần trả tiền đâu, coi như ông cho."

Khoa cảm ơn ông rối rít, rồi quay sang Mai. "Mình thử cây này nha, Mai. Cành thấp, em có thể với tới."

Nhưng Mai lại chỉ tay về phía một cây táo ở xa hơn, nơi có những trái táo to nhất, đỏ nhất. Khoa nhìn theo hướng tay cô, rồi cười hiểu ý.

"Được rồi, mình hái cây đó. Em đợi ở đây nhé, anh sẽ lấy cho em những quả đẹp nhất."

Mai lắc đầu. Cô chỉ tay vào mình, rồi chỉ vào cây táo xa kia, cuối cùng khoát tay ra hiệu: "Em muốn đi cùng anh."

Khoa do dự một lúc, rồi gật đầu. Anh đẩy xe lăn của Mai qua lối đi hẹp giữa hai hàng cây. Bánh xe lăn nghiến nhẹ trên đất mềm, và những chiếc lá vàng rơi xuống như mưa.

Khi đến dưới gốc cây táo đẹp nhất vườn, cả hai cùng ngước lên. Những trái táo đỏ ửng treo trên cành như những chiếc đèn lồng nhỏ, tỏa sáng dưới ánh nắng thu trong vắt.

"Đẹp quá, Mai à!" Khoa thì thầm.

Mai mỉm cười, đôi mắt long lanh. Cô chỉ vào một trái táo ở vị trí thấp nhất, vừa tầm tay cô. Khoa hiểu ý, nhẹ nhàng đưa tay cô đến gần cành cây. Ngón tay Mai run run chạm vào trái táo, rồi từ từ nắm lấy. Cô kéo nhẹ, và trái táo rời cành, rơi vào lòng bàn tay cô.

Tiếng cười trong trẻo của Mai vang lên, khiến Khoa cũng bật cười theo. Trong khoảnh khắc ấy, Mai không phải là cô gái ngồi xe lăn, không phải là người bị giới hạn bởi cơ thể. Cô chỉ đơn giản là một cô gái đang hái táo, đang tận hưởng mùa thu, đang sống một ngày bình thường và hạnh phúc.

Hai người cùng nhau hái táo suốt buổi sáng. Có lúc Khoa bế Mai lên cao để với những trái trên cành cao, có lúc Mai cầm giỏ đựng táo cho Khoa. Họ không nói nhiều, nhưng giữa họ là sự hiểu nhau đã được tích luỹ suốt hai mươi năm kể từ ngày hai đứa trẻ nghịch bùn cùng nhau ở con hẻm nhỏ.

Khi giỏ táo đã đầy, cả hai ngồi nghỉ dưới gốc cây. Khoa lấy ra hai ổ bánh mì sandwich mẹ Khoa chuẩn bị sẵn, cùng một hộp sữa tươi. Họ chia nhau bữa trưa đơn giản, giữa vườn táo rộng lớn và tiếng chim ríu rít.

"Mai," Khoa nói bỗng dưng, giọng nghiêm túc hơn. "Anh muốn hỏi em một chuyện."

Mai ngước lên, đôi mắt thắc mắc.

"Tháng sau, anh sẽ lên thành phố học. Anh đã được nhận vào trường đại học rồi." Khoa dừng lại, nuốt nước bọt. "Anh lo cho em. Ai sẽ đưa em đi dạo, ai sẽ đọc sách cho em nghe, ai sẽ..."

Mai đặt tay lên tay Khoa, ngắt lời anh. Đôi mắt cô dịu dàng nhưng kiên định. Cô chỉ vào ngực mình, rồi chỉ vào ngực Khoa, cuối cùng nắm tay lại, đặt hai bàn tay lên ngực mình - cử chỉ mà họ đã từng làm từ nhỏ, có nghĩa là: "Chúng ta sẽ ổn thôi."

Khoa hiểu. Dù xa cách, dù cuộc sống có thay đổi, tình bạn của họ sẽ không bao giờ phai nhạt. Mai có gia đình, có hàng xóm tốt bụng, và cả bản thân cô - mạnh mẽ hơn bất kỳ ai nghĩ.

Hai người cùng nhìn lên bầu trời xanh trong vắt, nơi mây trắng lững lờ trôi. Mùi táo chín ngọt ngào lan toả trong không khí.

"Giờ mình về thôi," Khoa nói, đứng dậy. "Anh sẽ làm bánh táo cho em ăn tối nay. Bí mật của mẹ anh đấy."

Mai cười, ánh mắt lấp lánh. Cô đưa tay ra, và Khoa nắm lấy, nhẹ nhàng đỡ cô vào xe lăn.

Trên đường về, chiếc giỏ táo đầy ắp nằm trên đùi Mai. Cô ôm lấy giỏ táo, áp má vào những trái táo mát lạnh. Nắng chiều thu dịu dàng phủ lên hai bóng người - một cao, một thấp, một bước chân vững chãi, một chiếc xe lăn lăn bánh nhẹ nhàng.

Mùa thu năm ấy, Mai đã học được rằng: cuộc sống vẫn đẹp, vẫn ngọt ngào như những trái táo chín, miễn là ta biết trân trọng từng khoảnh khắc bên những người mình yêu thương.

Và cô sẽ luôn nhớ mùa thu này - mùa thu của những trái táo vàng, của tình bạn không phai, và của một buổi sáng đẹp đẽ trong vườn táo ông Bảy.

# La Hoja y el Tiempo

El otoño había llegado a Viña del Mar con una melancolía que olía a sal y a hojas secas. Camila caminaba por el sendero del Castillo Wulff, pateando distraídamente las hojas caídas de los plátanos orientales que bordeaban el camino. El viento frío le enrojecía las mejillas, pero ella no se inmutaba; necesitaba caminar, pensar, poner en orden sus pensamientos después de la larga jornada en la galería de arte.

Fue entonces cuando una hoja particularmente grande, de un tono cobrizo casi dorado, se desprendió de una rama baja y cayó frente a sus pies, girando en el aire como una bailarina ebria antes de posarse sobre la tierra húmeda. Un impulso la llevó a agacharse y recogerla. No sabía por qué; simplemente lo hizo.

Cuando la levantó, algo brilló debajo. Algo que no pertenecía a ese lugar, algo que no debería estar ahí.

Camila frotó el objeto contra su chaqueta para quitarle el polvo y la tierra. Era una pequeña llave de latón, antigua, con una forma peculiar: no era plana como las llaves modernas, sino que tenía un cilindro diminuto y una guardas decorada con volutas que recordaban a las llaves de los muebles coloniales del siglo XIX. En el extremo superior, grabado con una caligrafía elegante, podía leerse un número: **1847**.

—No puede ser —murmuró Camila, sintiendo cómo el corazón le daba un vuelco.

Su tía Marta le había contado una historia mil veces, una que ella consideraba solo un cuento familiar para niños. La historia de un amor imposible entre un capitán de barco portugués y una joven aristócrata porteña, en los tiempos en que Valparaíso era apenas un puerto menor. Según la leyenda, el capitán, llamado Henrique Ferreira, había escondido una carta y un pequeño cofre de madera de olivo en algún lugar del castillo, antes de zarpar hacia Lisboa y no regresar jamás. La carta era para su amada, Esperanza Bravo, quien murió esperando su regreso sin saber nunca que él había dejado un mensaje para ella. La familia guardó la llave durante generaciones, pero se perdió en un incendio que destruyó la casona familiar en 1923.

Camila siempre había pensado que era una fantasía, algo bonito para contar en las noches de invierno. Pero ahora tenía la llave entre sus manos, fría, real, con un peso que iba más allá de lo físico.

Caminó lentamente hasta el mirador del castillo. El Pacífico se extendía infinito frente a ella, gris y tumultuoso como su propio corazón. Recordó las palabras de su tía Marta, fallecida el invierno pasado: *"Si algún día encuentras la llave, no la uses para abrir un cofre. Úsala para abrir un recuerdo. Los objetos guardan la memoria de quienes los tocaron, y a veces, si tienes paciencia, te la muestran"*.

Camila cerró los ojos, apretó la llave contra su pecho y respiró hondo, dejando que el viento le llenara los pulmones. No esperaba nada racional. No buscaba un tesoro. Solo quería... sentir.

Y entonces lo sintió.

Un aroma a naranjas y canela, un perfume que jamás había olido pero que reconoció de inmediato, como si llevara toda la vida buscándolo. Vio, con los ojos cerrados, el destello de un vestido de seda verde esmeralda, el sonido lejano de una risa de mujer, el rasgueo de un violín. Percibió una mano cálida rozando la suya, una voz grave con acento portugués susurrando algo en un idioma que entendió sin saberlo: *"Esperanza, volveré antes de que caigan las hojas del próximo otoño"*.

Camila abrió los ojos. Las lágrimas corrían por sus mejillas sin que pudiera detenerlas. No sabía cuánto tiempo había permanecido allí, pero el sol se había puesto y el mar se había teñido de violeta. La llave seguía en su mano, pero ya no estaba fría. Estaba tibia, casi caliente, como si alguien acabara de devolverla al mundo de los vivos.

Se levantó despacio, guardó la llave en el bolsillo interno de su chaqueta, cerca del corazón, y emprendió el camino de regreso. Sabía que no buscaría el cofre. Sabía que la carta, si existía, no era para ella. Pero ahora entendía algo que nunca había comprendido del todo: que el amor verdadero no muere cuando muere el cuerpo. Que hay promesas que desafían al tiempo, que hay objetos que son cápsulas de memoria, puentes entre los que fueron y los que somos.

Esa noche, en su departamento del barrio Puerto, Camila sacó la llave y la colocó sobre su mesa de trabajo, junto a los pinceles y las pinturas. Luego tomó un lienzo pequeño y empezó a pintar, casi sin pensarlo: un puerto antiguo, una mujer de vestido verde mirando hacia el horizonte, y un barco que se alejaba dejando una estela de plata sobre un mar de nácar.

Al día siguiente, cuando llevó el cuadro a la galería, la dueña lo miró durante largo rato, en silencio.

—¿Quién es ella? —preguntó finalmente.

Camila sonrió.

—Se llama Esperanza —dijo—. Y ha estado esperando mucho tiempo a que alguien la recordara.

---

*La llave permanece hoy en una pequeña vitrina de la galería, junto al cuadro, con una nota que dice únicamente: "No abrir. El recuerdo ya ha sido liberado."*

# Kolorowy Śnieg

Dziesięć centymetrów śniegu spadło nocą, dokładnie tak, jak zapowiedział meteorolog. Wszystko zgadzało się co do joty — temperatura, wilgotność, kierunek wiatru. Jedno tylko nie pasowało.

Śnieg nie był biały.

Kiedy Marek wyszedł rano na ganek ze swoją filiżanką kawy, zamarł w pół kroku. Podwórko, dach starej stodoły, gałęzie jabłoni — wszystko pokryte było delikatną, różową warstwą. Nie bladoróżową. Nie przybrudzoną. Głęboko, wyraziście różową, jak wnętrze dojrzałego arbuza.

— Chryste Panie — szepnął.

Łyżeczka wypadła mu z ręki i zniknęła w puszystej masie. Marek stał tak przez dobrą minutę, wsłuchując się w absolutną ciszę zimowego poranka. Nigdzie żadnego ptaka. Żadnego szczekania psów u sąsiadów. Jakby cała okolica wstrzymała oddech.

Wszedł do domu i włączył telewizor. Na wszystkich kanałach to samo — prezenterzy w studiu wyglądali na równie zdezorientowanych. Na monitorach za ich plecami leciały zdjęcia z całej Polski. Różowy śnieg w Zakopanem. Różowy śnieg w Gdańsku. Różowy śnieg na Podlasiu.

— *Naukowcy uspokajają* — mówił spiker poważnym tonem. — *Najprawdopodobniej mamy do czynienia z piaskiem saharyjskim, który przyniósł ze sobą prąd strumieniowy...*

Marek wyłączył telewizor. Miał piaszczyste burze pustynne kojarzyły się z czymś żółtawym, może pomarańczowym. Nigdy z takim nasyconym różem.

Wyszedł ponownie na dwór, tym razem w kaloszach i starej kurtce ojca. Zszedł z ganku i ukucnął przy rabacie kwiatowej, gdzie śnieg był najgrubszy. Wziął garść w rękawice.

Był zimny. Był mokry. I kiedy go ścisnął, na rękawicy zostały ślady, które wyglądały jak resztkowy makijaż.

Marek rozejrzał się po podwórku. Wszystko wyglądało niezwykle pięknie w tym dziwnym świetle — jakby ktoś oblał świat landrynkową polewą. Stara stodoła wyglądała jak domek z piernika. Jabłoń wyglądała jak eksplozja waty cukrowej.

Zrobił kilka kroków i zatrzymał się gwałtownie.

Na środku podwórka, tam, gdzie zawsze rosła jedyna kępka trawy, której żaden kosiarz nie potrafił zwalczyć, stało coś. Coś, czego wczoraj nie było.

Drzewo.

Małe drzewo, mniej więcej metr wysokości, z korą koloru zwykłego brązu, ale z liśćmi — wszystkie liście bez wyjątku — były różowe. Dokładnie takim samym odcieniem jak śnieg.

Marek obszedł je dookoła. Korzenie wyraźnie wyrastały ze śniegu, jakby drzewo wyrosło w ciągu jednej nocy. Bo wyrosło. Marek pamiętał doskonale — wczoraj po południu kosił trawę w tym miejscu.

Poczuł dziwne ukłucie gdzieś pod żebrami. Nie strach. Raczej coś w rodzaju rozpoznania. Jakby czekał na to drzewo całe swoje pięćdziesiąt lat, nie wiedząc, że czeka.

Wszedł do domu i zadzwonił do brata, Wojciecha, który mieszkał w mieście.

— Wojtek, przyjedź. Musisz coś zobaczyć.

— Marek, jest siódma rano.

— Właśnie. Przyjedź, zanim to coś zniknie.

Wojciech przyjechał po dwóch godzinach, z termosem kawy i siatką rogalików. Stał teraz na środku podwórka, z rogalikiem w jednej ręce i telefonem w drugiej, próbując zrobić drzewu zdjęcie, które wyglądałoby wiarygodnie.

— Marek — powiedział w końcu, chowając telefon — czy ty wiesz, że to drzewo wygląda jak... jak klony?

— Klony?

— Tak. Te rośliny z *Pokémonów*. Snivy. Ta cała seria. Ten odcień liści to jest jeden do jeden.

Marek nie grał w *Pokemony*, ale skinął głową.

— I co z tego?

Wojciech wzruszył ramionami.

— Nic. Tylko że moje dziecko oszalałoby ze szczęścia, gdyby to zobaczyło.

Przez chwilę stali obaj, patrząc na drzewo. Śnieg dookoła nich delikatnie różowiał w bladym zimowym słońcu.

— Myślisz, że to coś z tych wszystkich satelitów? — zapytał w końcu Wojciech. — Słyszałem, że Starlink robi jakieś dziwne rzeczy z pogodą.

— Wojtek. — Marek pokręcił głową. — Czy ja ci kiedykolwiek powiedziałem, że jako dziecko miałem drzewo?

— Jakie drzewo?

— Takie. Różowe. Za domem dziadka, w Sadlinkach. Miałem wtedy pięć lat, może sześć. Mama mnie zabrała, bo ojciec pił. Zostaliśmy u babci przez lato. Za stodołą było takie jedno drzewo, inne niż wszystkie. Liście różowe, jak landrynki. Siadałem pod nim i rysowałem. Babcia mówiła, że to odmiana ozdobna, ale nigdy nie widziałem takiego gdzie indziej.

Wojciech odstawił rogalika na śnieg.

— I co się z nim stało?

— Nic. Wróciliśmy do domu. Następnego lata ojciec się nie zmienił. Mama nie pozwalała mi już tam jeździć. Potem babcia umarła, a dom sprzedano. Nigdy więcej go nie widziałem.

— A teraz masz pięćdziesiąt lat i ono cię znalazło.

Marek roześmiał się krótko, bez wesołości.

— Coś w tym stylu.

Nie rozmawiali o tym więcej. Wojciech pojechał do domu, obiecując, że wróci z dzieckiem w weekend. Marek wrócił do środka, ale nie mógł usiedzieć na miejscu. Co kilka minut wychodził na ganek.

Drzewo rosło.

To było niemożliwe, ale Marek nie potrafił tego dłużej ignorować. Kiedy wyszedł po południu zrobić sobie herbatę, miał pewność, że drzewo jest wyższe o dobre trzydzieści centymetrów. Kiedy wrócił godzinę później, było wyższe o kolejne piętnaście.

O zachodzie słońca sięgało mu do pasa.

Marek stał w drzwiach ganku i patrzył, jak gałęzie drzewa powoli, majestatycznie obracają się w stronę domu. Jakby drzewo sprawdzało, gdzie jest właściciel.

Poczuł, jak jeżą mu się włosy na karku. Nie ze strachu. Z czegoś innego. Z uczucia, którego nie umiał nazwać.

Wszedł do środka, zamknął drzwi na klucz i oparł się o framugę.

— Nie — powiedział do pustego przedpokoju. — Nie wiem, co ty jesteś. Ale nie wpuszczę cię do domu.

Za oknem śnieg delikatnie różowił się w zapadającym zmroku. Marek stał tak długo, aż zobaczył, że w gałęziach drzewa zapaliły się małe, ciepłe światła — jak gdyby ktoś powiesił na nim girlandę choinkową.

Światła migały powoli, w jakimś regularnym rytmie.

Marek zamknął oczy.

Kiedy je otworzył, drzewa już nie było. Tylko różowy śnieg na trawie, który teraz, w ciemności, jarzył się delikatnie własnym, ciepłym światłem.

Marek patrzył na to przez okno bardzo długo.

Rano śnieg był biały. Biały jak śnieg. Wszystko wyglądało normalnie. Jedyną rzeczą, która zniknęła, było drzewo. I kępka trawy, która od lat nie dawała się wykosić.

Marek poszedł do sklepu, kupił zapas kawy i chleba, i wrócił do domu. Zamknął drzwi. Zaciągnął zasłony. Usiadł przy stole w kuchni i wziął do ręki ołówek.

Nie rysował od czterdziestu lat. Ale kiedy pochylił się nad kartką, jego ręka sama pamiętała, jak to się robi. Narysował dom. Narysował stodołę. Narysował jabłoń. I na końcu, na środku kartki, narysował drzewo.

Różowe jak landrynka.

Za oknem wiatr kołysał gałęziami jabłoni, strącając z nich ostatnie płatki różowego śniegu, który miał już nigdy więcej nie spaść.

# 千年打工人的日常

## 第一章：又是周一

我承认，被困在这个铜灯里三千年，偶尔是会有些无聊的。

但我万万没想到，"无聊"这个词有一天会变成一种奢侈。

"出来吧，瓶中精灵！"

一阵刺眼的蓝光闪过，我揉了揉眼睛，从铜瓶里慢悠悠地飘了出来。按照流程，我应该摆一个威严的姿态，喷两团烟雾，念一句"遵命，我的召唤者"之类的台词。

但我已经懒得喷烟了。

"呃……您好。"我打量着面前这个穿着连帽衫、手里举着我那瓶子晃来晃去的年轻人，"请问您想要……"

"天哪！"他尖叫着往后退了三步，"你、你怎么就直接出来了！我还没说第三句咒语呢！"

"因为您第一句念对了，"我耐心地解释，"咒语内容其实是'摩诃摩里无量至圣精灵'，后面那句'出来吧'只是礼貌用语，不念也行。"

他愣住了，手里的笔记本掉在地上。我瞥了一眼，上面密密麻麻地写着：

> **召唤精灵完整版（务必背熟）：**
> 1. 摩诃摩里无量至圣精灵（必须正确发音）
> 2. 我以真主的名义命令你
> 3. 出来吧，瓶中精灵（可省略）

"我练习了三个月！"他几乎要哭了，"三个月！就为了能完美地说出这三个句子！"

"感动，"我点点头，"那么，您需要什么？"

他从地上捡起笔记本，翻到后面："我想要……呃……"他皱眉，"等等，我忘了我想要什么了。"

我叹了口气。

---

## 第二章：典型案例

三千年来，我服务过的召唤者包括：苏丹、皇帝、法老、海盗、教皇、首相、总统，以及——近些年越来越多了——大学生。

我的KPI考核表（是的，精灵也有KPI，是精灵管理局强制要求的）显示，2024年我的"愿望满意度"评分为4.2分（满分5分），而"召唤者智商预估"平均分仅为87。

这是个令人沮丧的数据。

我曾试图向管理局申请调岗，比如去做北极光，或者去当沙漠里的海市蜃楼。但他们说："你就认命吧，阿布杜尔，你是黄金级精灵，不能浪费在低价值任务上。"

黄金级。我苦笑。曾经的我是可以让所罗门王都忌惮三分的存在，如今却要满足一个十六岁男孩想要"让所有人都觉得我酷"的愿望。

"等等！"那个年轻人突然一拍脑袋，"我想起来了！我想要无限的钱！"

"好的，"我点点头，"根据《精灵服务条例》第37条第4款，'无限'不在可实现愿望范围内。我可以为您提供一千万美元，或者等值的其他货币、黄金、数字货币。"

"那不行！"他激动地说，"我就要无限！无限！懂吗？"

"我懂，"我平静地说，"但条例不允许。"

"那你就不是真正的精灵！"

"我是的，"我说，"要不您看看我的工作证？"我从长袍里掏出一张塑封卡片，上面印着我的照片、名字和一个闪闪发光的金色徽章。

他接过去翻来覆去看了半天，表情从怀疑变成了尴尬，最后变成了羞愧。

"对不起，"他小声说，"我没想到……精灵也有……体制。"

"我们也有工会，"我说，"去年还闹过一次罢工，要求改善油灯的通风条件。"

---

## 第三章：前辈的忠告

我第一次被召唤时，我的师傅——一个困在银壶里五千年的老精灵——曾经给我留下过忠告：

> "孩子，你即将开始一段漫长的服务生涯。你会遇到各种各样的人类。他们有的睿智，有的愚蠢；有的慷慨，有的贪婪。但无论如何，请记住一点——"

> "永远不要让他们看到你的本体。"

我当时不懂他的意思。

现在我懂了。

上个月，一个召唤者看到我的真身后——那是一团由纯粹能量构成的、不断变换的几何图形——她尖叫着拨打了精神病院的电话。我花了整整六个小时解释自己没有传染病，也没有想要占据她的肉体。

更糟糕的是，她把整个过程拍成了短视频，发到了某个视频平台上。

"破亿了，"我的同事，一个困在戒指里的精灵，幸灾乐祸地对我说，"恭喜你啊阿布杜尔，你火了。"

我甚至不敢去看那条视频下面的评论。

---

## 第四章：今日份的召唤

"那个，"年轻人弱弱地开口，"一千万美元……也行。但是我想要现金，要美钞，不要连号的。"

"好的，"我打了个响指，"它们现在在您床底下。"

他冲到卧室，趴在地上往床底看，然后发出一声尖叫："天哪！这么多！"

"您可以分批存入银行，"我说，"建议不要一次性存入，以免触发反洗钱系统。"

"你怎么这么专业？"

"这是我们入职培训的内容，"我面无表情地说，"第三章第七节，'如何帮助召唤者避免因实现愿望而入狱'。"

他呆呆地看着我，半晌才回过神来："那……愿望结束了？你要回瓶子里了？"

"理论上是的，"我说，"但在我回去之前，我需要您签署这份文件。"

我递过去一张羊皮纸。

> **《愿望履行确认书》**
>
> 召唤者：杰森·米勒
> 精灵：阿布杜尔·伊本·哈桑（三级黄金精灵）
> 愿望内容：现金（等值1000万美元）
> 履行状态：已完成
> 召唤者满意度：________
> 
> 请注意：满意度低于3分将影响精灵的年终绩效。请高抬贵手。

他看到最后一行，嘴角抽了抽："你们……精灵也要写年终总结？"

"是的，还要做PPT。"

"……"

他签了名，给了我一个满分5分。

"谢谢您，"我真心实意地说，"祝您生活愉快。"

然后我钻进了瓶子里，盖上了盖子。

---

## 第五章：瓶中世界

瓶子里其实挺舒服的。

有一间小公寓，两室一厅，家具齐全（精灵风格的），还有wifi。

我瘫在沙发上，打开精灵内网，开始写今日的工作日志。

> **2025年1月15日 工作日志**
>
> 召唤者：杰森·米勒，16岁
> 愿望：现金
> 履行结果：已交付
> 备注：此人为"准备型召唤者"，耗时3个月准备咒语，但未能清晰表达需求。建议下次准备一份《召唤精灵需求文档》。
>
> 附加说明：今日绩效+5分（满分满意度）。感谢杰森。

写完日志，我看了看墙上的日历。

下一个召唤，要等到……

"叮——"

手机响了。是精灵管理局发来的提醒：

> **【召唤警报】**
> 您有一笔新的预约召唤，将在3小时12分钟后生效。
> 召唤者：玛格丽特·布朗，67岁
> 愿望内容：（未知）
> 备注：此召唤者信用评级为A+，请认真对待。

我叹了口气，起身去泡了杯茶。

又是平凡的一天呢。

---

## 尾声

三千年来，我见过无数人的贪婪、愚蠢、自私、虚荣。

但我也见过有人许愿让失明的孩子重见光明，有人许愿让战争中的村庄得到庇护，有人许愿只是为了给去世的母亲写一封信。

我曾以为自己被困在瓶中，是最大的不幸。

但后来我发现，真正困住我的，从来不是铜瓶。

是那些年复一年、日复一日的召唤，让我忘记了自己曾经是谁。

不过没关系。

三小时后，又会有一个召唤者打开瓶盖。

届时，我会整理好长袍，喷两团烟雾（今天心情好，就喷两团），用威严的声音说：

"遵命，我的召唤者。"

这就是精灵的命。

也是我的命。

——阿布杜尔·伊本·哈桑，困于瓶中第3007年，写于一个普通的周二晚上

"我看见她了，"老人哽咽着说，"她穿着那条白裙子，站在河边上冲我笑……"

视频播放量一夜之间破了十亿。

紧接着，各大糖果厂纷纷投入研发。从"初恋"到"初雪"，从"童年的院子"到"外婆的手心"，每一种口味都对应着一段特定的记忆。官方宣称绝对安全——你只是在旁观，像看一部以自己为主角的电影，不会对当下的大脑造成任何损伤。

苏晚知道，这些都是真的。

因为发明这款糖的，是她的父亲。

---

"下一个！"

店员的声音把苏晚从思绪里拉回来。队伍终于挪动了一大截，轮到她了。

推开那扇玻璃门，冷气扑面而来。店内的装潢很简约，浅木色的货架上整整齐齐地摆着一排排玻璃罐，每一只罐子里都盛着不同颜色的糖。"春日樱花"是淡粉色的，"初雪"是银白色的，"深海"是一种深邃的蓝，像是把一片汪洋压缩进了方寸之间。

"您好，请问需要什么？"店员是个年轻的小姑娘，戴着印有糖果logo的围裙，眼睛弯弯的。

"深海。"苏晚说。

店员愣了一下，随即露出一个了然的微笑："您是苏先生的家属吧？这是他生前最后一款作品，我们一直保留着。今天刚好是周年祭，所以特别调配了一批。"

苏晚点了点头，没有说话。

店员小心翼翼地从柜台下面取出一只深蓝色的玻璃罐，打开盖子，一股咸湿的气息飘了出来——像是海风，又像是泪水。

"一共九颗，"店员轻声说，"第一颗免费，是苏先生生前留下的，附了一封信给您。"

---

回到家，苏晚坐在窗边，一直坐到太阳落山。

玻璃罐放在桌上，那颗"第一颗"静静躺在罐子最上面，旁边是一封泛黄的信封。她认得那个字迹，是父亲的。

信封上只写了两个字：**晚晚**。

她拆开信，展开那张薄薄的纸。

> 晚晚：
> 
> 见信如晤。
> 
> 如果你读到这封信，说明我已经不在了。也说明，我终于可以跟你说说那件事了。
> 
> 你八岁那年的夏天，妈妈带你去了海边。那是我最后一次见她笑。后来她走了，我一直不知道该怎么跟你解释。直到你渐渐长大，我才明白——有些伤口，与其揭开，不如让它留在海里。
> 
> 这颗糖，是我为你做的。
> 
> 它不是用来让你回忆的，是用来让你**告别**的。
> 
> 等你准备好的时候，吃下它。它会让你回到那一天，但这一次，你可以对她说话。你可以说那些来不及说的话，也可以什么都不说，就看着她，看她穿着那条白裙子，站在海风里。
> 
> 然后，你会知道她有多爱你。
> 
> 多想我。
> 
> ——爸爸

苏晚的视线模糊了。

窗外，最后一抹霞光慢慢沉入地平线。她拿起那颗深蓝色的糖，在手心里握了很久。

---

她没有立刻吃。

她把糖放回玻璃罐，把玻璃罐放在床头柜上。每天睡前看一眼，每天醒来再看一眼。

一个月后的某个雨夜，她终于拿起了那颗糖。

窗外雨声淅沥，像是海浪拍打礁石的声音。她把糖放入口中，闭上眼睛。

---

咸的。

她睁开眼，发现自己站在一片金色的沙滩上。

阳光很好，风很轻，海水蓝得像一块被揉皱的绸缎。远处，一个穿着白裙子的女人正蹲在沙滩上，用树枝画着什么。

那女人听见脚步声，回过头来。

是妈妈。

二十几岁的妈妈，眼睛弯弯的，像两弯新月。她看见小小的苏晚，笑了，伸手揉了揉她的头发：

"晚晚，来，看妈妈画的这是什么？"

小苏晚跑过去，蹲在她身边。沙滩上画的是一只小海龟，旁边还有一串歪歪扭扭的字：**妈妈爱晚晚**。

苏晚站在"现在的自己"里，看着这一幕，眼泪无声地落了下来。

她终于明白那颗糖为什么叫"深海"。

不是让你沉入深海，是让你在深海里，找到那颗最亮的珠母。

她没有走过去。她只是站在那里，看着妈妈抱着小小的自己，在海风里笑啊笑啊，笑得眼睛里有星星。

然后，慢慢地，画面淡去。

---

苏晚睁开眼睛。

窗外，雨不知道什么时候停了。一轮明月挂在天空，清辉如水。

床头柜上的玻璃罐里，还剩八颗糖。

她把罐子重新盖上，轻轻笑了笑。

不需要了。

那一次，已经足够。

# Les Géants du Cœur

---

## Chapitre 1 — Le casting

Le bureau de production sentait le café froid et l'ambition. Sur les murs, des affiches de précédentes émissions : *Célébrités sous pression*, *Stars en cuisine*, *Le loft des people*. Mais rien qui ressemblât à ce que préparait désormais Blanche Vermeer, productrice exécutive connue pour flairer les concepts avant tout le monde.

— On cherche des géants, avait-elle dit à son équipe.

— Des géants ? avaient répondu les assistants, incrédules.

— Pas au sens figuré. Au sens propre.

---

## Chapitre 2 — Les participants

Il y avait six candidats.

**Adrien Morel**, 2,12 mètres, ancien basketteur reconverti en comédien de second rôle. Il portait des chaussures orthopédiques et une mélancolie tenace depuis qu'un chirurgien lui avait annoncé qu'il cesserait de grandir.

**Mireille Tshilumba**, 1,98 mètre, mannequin à la retraite, qui avait marqué les podiums parisiens avant qu'une maladie auto-immune ne la contraigne au repos.

**Léon Bronstein**, 2,04 mètres, ancien mineur reconverti en conteur public, fils d'immigrés ukrainiens, dont la voix grave remplissait les salles municipales du Nord.

**Inès Achterberg**, 2,21 mètres, professeure des écoles en Allemagne, la plus grande femme d'Europe, qui avait publié un livre sur la vie à hauteur d'homme.

**Tomás Reyes**, 1,95 mètre, boxeur mexicain dont la carrière avait été interrompue par une blessure à la colonne.

**Fatou Sène**, 2,08 mètres, ancienne basketteuse sénégalaise devenue entraîneuse.

Tous avaient entre quarante et soixante-dix ans. Tous avaient connu la gloire, puis son lent reflux.

---

## Chapitre 3 — La règle du jeu

Le concept était simple, presque cruel.

Six anciens géants. Une maison normande aux plafonds rehaussés pour l'occasion. Vingt-et-un jours. Une seule caméra, qui les suivrait partout.

Et chaque soir, un tirage au sort désignerait celui ou celle qui devrait quitter la maison.

Le présentateur — un jeune animateur à l'humour acerbe, choisi précisément pour sa petitesse — demanda devant les caméras :

— Pourquoi avoir accepté, vous qui avez déjà tout vécu ?

Léon répondit le premier :

— Parce qu'on m'a toujours vu avant de m'entendre.

Inès ajouta :

— Parce qu'on m'a demandé mille fois combien je mesurais, et jamais comment je pensais.

---

## Chapitre 4 — Premier soir

Le premier tirage désigna Mireille.

Elle resta debout, immobile, dans la grande salle aux poutres apparentes. Puis elle s'avança vers la porte, et comme elle dut se baisser pour passer sous le linteau, elle rit — un rire profond, inesperado, qui contamina toute la pièce.

— Vous voyez, dit-elle. Même partir, c'est se plier.

Dehors, elle laissa ses empreintes dans la terre meuble du jardin. Le réalisateur cadra ses chaussures : du 47, légèrement usées, avec une petite fleur brodée sur le côté, un travail qu'elle avait fait elle-même.

---

## Chapitre 5 — Les jours suivants

Les éliminations se poursuivirent. Tomás le quatrième soir. Fatou le septième.

Restèrent : Adrien, Léon, Inès.

La production, qui cherchait du spectaculaire, fut déçue. Aucun clash. Aucune romance. Juste des conversations à hauteur de lustres, des parties d'échecs jouées sur un immense plateau rapporté pour eux, et de longues promenades dans le verger, où les pommes semblaient avoir été cultivées par des nains.

Léon lisait à voix haute chaque matin. Inès corrigeait la prononciation d'Adrien. Adrien, qui n'avait jamais appris à cuisiner pour des quantités normales, finit par préparer un repas pour trente personnes.

Le jeune animateur, dépité, dit en off à la production :

— Mais ils sont gentils. C'est insupportable, ils sont gentils.

---

## Chapitre 6 — La finale

Le dernier tirage désigna Adrien.

Il ne dit rien pendant un long moment. Puis il s'assit sur le sol, parce que les sièges étaient trop bas pour lui. Inès s'assit à côté. Léon resta debout, comme pour les protéger tous les deux du monde extérieur.

— C'est étrange, dit Adrien. Je suis venu ici pour qu'on me regarde. Et c'est la première fois qu'on me voit.

— Non, dit Inès. C'est la première fois que tu acceptes d'être vu.

---

## Chapitre 7 — L'après

L'émission ne fit pas d'audience convenable. Blanche Vermeer fut renvoyée. Le jeune animateur rebondit sur une chaîne cryptée.

Mais quelque chose demeura.

Adrien publia un roman. Mireille ouvrit un atelier de couture pour personnes de grande taille. Inès créa un réseau international d'écoles inclusives. Léon se produisit dans les Ehpad du Nord, où ses histoires calmaient ceux que l'âge rapetissait.

Et chaque année, le vingt-et-unième jour du vingt-et-unième mois, les six anciens candidats se retrouvaient dans la maison normande — vide, silencieuse, sans caméras — pour partager un repas trop copieux et rire, ensemble, du plafond qu'ils n'avaient plus besoin de baisser.

---

## Épilogue

Sur le mur du salon, on avait laissé un cadre. Dedans, la photo du premier jour : six géants, debout, serrés les uns contre les autres, souriant à un monde qui les avait enfin regardés en face.

Sous la photo, une inscription manuscrite :

*« On mesure la taille des hommes à la hauteur de leurs cœurs. »*

---
