# The Hour of the Borrowed Light

The first time I noticed the discrepancy, I was brushing my teeth.

The mirror above my sink showed the usual things: a tired man in his forties, a bathroom tiled in seafoam green, the window behind me through which dawn was just beginning to gray the rooftops of Lisbon. Ordinary things. But the toothbrush in my reflection was blue, not red, and I distinctly remembered buying a red one the day before.

I stared at the mirror. I stared at my hand. The bristles against my teeth were red.

I closed my eyes, exhaled slowly through my nose, and opened them again. The mirror now showed a blue toothbrush.

I set it down. I picked it up. Red. Blue. Red. Blue. I tried not to think about it. I finished brushing. I got dressed. I went to work.

That was a Tuesday.

---

By Friday, the wrongness had taken on a rhythm.

I would notice something small—a book on my shelf whose title I didn't recognize, a colleague greeting me by a name that wasn't mine, a pigeon on the windowsill that was the wrong color. Then I would blink, and it would be corrected, but the correction felt different from the original. Thinner. Less committed.

I began keeping a notebook. I wrote down what I saw, what I remembered, what I was told. I tried to map the place where the seams came unstitched.

On Saturday morning, I woke to find my notebook open on the kitchen table, written in a hand that was mine but not mine. The entry read:

*You're looking in the wrong direction. Stop trying to wake up.*

I read it three times. I turned the page. The next page was blank.

---

I am a translator. I take Portuguese words and turn them into English ones, and English words into Portuguese, and sometimes—on the slow days when the agency is quiet—into French or German. It is a careful work, a work of patience, of listening for the right key in which a sentence wants to be sung.

It was on one of these slow days that she came in.

She said her name was Inês, but she gave it to me in three different languages, as if she couldn't decide which one belonged to her. She had a manuscript. It was written by hand, in a script I didn't recognize, and when I asked her what language it was in, she looked at me with an expression of patient sorrow.

"You'll know," she said. "When you find the right one."

I took the manuscript home. I spread it out on the kitchen table. The letters swam. I made tea. I made coffee. I tried again. By midnight, I had translated the first line, and it read:

*There is a city under this city, and I have been living in it by mistake.*

---

The dreams came after that, or perhaps they had always been there and I had only just learned to notice.

In them, I walked streets I knew by heart but could not find on any map. I spoke to people I loved who had been dead for years. I ate meals I could not remember cooking. And always—always—at the center of the dream there was a room, a small green-tiled room with a mirror and a window, and in the window a woman standing very still, watching me brush my teeth.

In the dream I never quite finished the sentence. In the dream I always woke up before I could see her face.

But one night—I don't know why this night, I don't know what had changed—I did not wake up. I walked to the mirror. I looked at the woman. She had my mother's face, but younger, and the face was not hers the way a translation is not the original. It was a thing that had been carried across.

She said, "You can stay here if you want. The light is borrowed, but it is warm."

I said, "What am I?"

She said, "You are the hour. The hour between one day and the next."

---

The next morning I woke with the taste of sea air in my mouth and the manuscript open on the pillow beside me. I had translated, in my sleep, an entire page. I read it with my coffee. It said:

*The translator is the most dangerous profession in the world, because the translator knows that every word is a small betrayal, and yet he consents to the work. He consents because he loves the original. He consents because he knows that fidelity is impossible and that the attempt is the only honest thing.*

I closed the notebook. I went to the window. The rooftops of Lisbon glittered in a light that did not quite belong to the sun.

---

I have stopped trying to distinguish.

I brush my teeth in the morning and the toothbrush is whichever color it needs to be. I greet my colleagues by whatever name they recognize. I walk to work along streets that sometimes branch in directions I don't remember choosing. I translate the manuscript. It is very long. I don't think it ends.

Some nights I dream of the green-tiled room. Some nights I don't. The woman is there, or she isn't. The light is borrowed, or it isn't. It is warm either way.

I have come to believe that we are all of us translating—that every waking moment is a draft, every dream a correction, and the original text is something we will never see but cannot stop trying to read. We move between the two like figures in a codex, our outlines pressed into the page by hands we do not know.

I think my mother was a translator. I think I am one too. I think the woman in the mirror was trying to tell me this.

---

This morning the toothbrush was green, and I understood, with a small calm that has nothing to do with certainty, that green was the color of the hour in which I was living.

I set it down. I picked up the manuscript. I began to read.

# Eliksir Pana Wierzby

## I

W małym miasteczku Żurawinowo, ukrytym między wzgórzami pokrytymi wrzosami, żył stary zielarz o nazwisku Wierzba. Mówiono o nim, że w młodości podróżował do krain tak odległych, że nie sposób ich wymówić, a w jego torbie zawsze znajdowała się fiolka z płynem koloru zachodzącego słońca — pomarańczowym, czerwonawym, iskrzącym się jakoby złotem.

Ludzie przychodzili do niego ze wszystkim. Z bólem zęba, z tęsknotą za utraconymi, z drżeniem rąk, które nie pozwalało im trzymać pióra. Pan Wierzba słuchał cierpliwie, po czym wyjmował z półki odpowiedni słoik. Ale gdy prosili o odwagę, o miłość, o zapomnienie — wyjmował tę fiolkę z pomarańczowym płynem.

— To eliksir odwagi — mówił. — Ale nie takiej, jaką dostajesz, gdy ktoś inny ci ją daje. To inna odwaga. Trudniejsza.

## II

Pewnego jesiennego popołudnia do jego drzwi zapukała młoda kobieta. Miała na imię Lena i oczy w kolorze zimowej wody. Nie przyszła po odwagę. Przyszła, bo słyszała, że pan Wierzba potrafi przywrócić pamięć.

— Moja siostra — powiedziała cicho, stojąc na progu z mokrymi od deszczu włosami — zapomniała wszystko. Nasze dzieciństwo, imiona rodziców, piosenki, które razem śpiewałyśmy. Lekarze mówią, że to nieuleczalne. Ale pan podobno...

Pan Wierzba popatrzył na nią długo. Potem westchnął, tak cicho, że ledwo go było słychać.

— Pamięć — rzekł — to nie jest rzecz, którą się posiada. To rzecz, która się dzieje. Każdego dnia od nowa. Mogę ci dać napój, który sprawi, że twoja siostra przypomni sobie wszystko. Ale nie będzie to ta sama pamięć co dawniej. Będzie to pamięć, która ją zaboli. I ciebie też.

Lena nie odeszła. Wzięła fiolkę.

## III

Następnego ranka Lena przyszła z siostrą. Miała na imię Anna i uśmiech, który nie pasował do jej oczu — taki uśmiech, jakim witają się ludzie, którzy nie wiedzą, kim są.

Pan Wierzba patrzył, jak Anna pije eliksir. Płyn był gęsty, ciemny jak miód zmieszany z czymś starszym, ciemniejszym. Anna zamknęła oczy. Lena zacisnęła dłonie na brzegu stołu.

Minęła chwila. Potem kolejna.

Anna otworzyła oczy.

I wtedy stało się coś, czego pan Wierzba nigdy nie widział przez pięćdziesiąt lat praktyki. Anna **nie** przypomniała sobie. Zamiast tego — zaczęła mówić. Ale nie po polsku, nie w żadnym języku, jaki znał. Mówiła dźwięcznie, melodyjnie, a jej głos brzmiał jakby składał się z samogłosek, których nie ma w żadnym alfabecie. Mówiła przez dziesięć minut, nie oddychając, a jej oczy były otwarte i jednocześnie nieobecne, jakby patrzyła na coś za ścianą pokoju.

Lena płakała, nie rozumiejąc.

## IV

Kiedy Anna umilkła, w pokoju było cicho. Tylko deszcz za oknem i oddech trzech osób.

— Co to było? — szepnęła Lena.

Pan Wierzba długo nie odpowiadał. W końcu podszedł do okna i patrzył na ulewę.

— Moja żona — powiedział wreszcie — umiała kiedyś śpiewać taką piosenkę. Nauczyła się jej od swojej babki, a babka od swojej. Śpiewała ją naszemu synowi, kiedy ten nie mógł zasnąć. Syn zginął wiele lat temu, a żona odeszła niedługo po nim. Choroba. Zapomniała wszystkiego — łącznie z moim imieniem.

Odwrócił się.

— Ten eliksir nie przywraca pamięci. On ją **budzi**. Ale budzi nie tylko twoją pamięć, ale pamięć wszystkich, którzy kiedykolwiek cię kochali. Twoja siostra wypiła eliksir i obudziły się w niej wspomnienia waszej matki. Wspomnienia waszej babki. I wszystkich kobiet, które was poprzedzały. To jest cena.

## V

Lena patrzyła na siostrę. Anna siedziała spokojnie, z dłońmi na stole, i patrzyła w okno. Jej oczy były teraz pełne — nie puste jak wcześniej, ale pełne czegoś, co nie miało nazwy.

— Czy ona...? — zaczęła Lena.

— Będzie żyła — odpowiedział pan Wierzba. — I będzie pamiętać. Ale to, co teraz nosi, jest cięższe niż to, co straciła. To jest powód, dla którego ostrzegałem.

Anna odwróciła się do siostry. Otworzyła usta. I zaśpiewała — cicho, niepewnie, jakby próbowała sobie przypomnieć melodię, której nigdy nie słyszała. Była to ta sama piosenka bez słów, którą słyszeli przed chwilą.

Lena zbladła.

— To śpiewała mama. Nasza mama. Kiedy byłam mała.

Anna skinęła głową.

— Tak. Śpiewała to też babcia. I prababcia. I kobieta, która żyła czterysta lat temu w lesie za wzgórzami. Teraz to wszystko jest we mnie. Wszystkie one.

Pan Wierzba odstawił fiolkę na półkę. Była teraz pusta, sucha, zwykła.

— Eliksir działa — powiedział cicho. — Nigdy nie wiem, **dla kogo**.

## VI

Kiedy siostry wyszły w deszcz, trzymając się za ręce, pan Wierzba zamknął drzwi na klucz. Stał długo w ciemnym pokoju, pełnym słoików i zapachów. Potem podszedł do szafy w rogu, tej zamkniętej na dwa zamki. Wyjął z niej drugą fiolkę. Była identyczna jak ta, którą podał Lenie. Pełna.

Trzymał ją w dłoniach i patrzył.

Nie pił jej od lat. Nie od czasu, gdy żona odeszła i przestała rozpoznawać jego twarz. Nie od czasu, gdy zrozumiał, że eliksir nie jest lekarstwem, lecz **mostem** — mostem między tym, co było, a tym, co jest. A niektórych mostów nie da się przejść tylko w jedną stronę.

Odstawił fiolkę z powrotem do szafy.

Nie dziś.

Nie dziś.

## VII

W miasteczku Żurawinowo ludzie wiedzą, że pan Wierzba ma jeszcze jeden eliksir. Niektórzy mówią, że to ten sam, co zwykle. Inni — że to inny, działający odwrotnie. Że pozwala zapomnieć to, czego nie da się unieść.

Ale pan Wierzba nikomu o tym nie mówi.

I może to jest odpowiedź na pytanie, czy eliksir działa. Może działa. Może nie. Może prawda jest taka, że magia nie polega na tym, co jest w fiolce, ale na tym, kto ją trzyma — i co jest gotów zobaczyć, gdy ją wypije.

W każdym razie, gdybyście kiedyś znaleźli się w Żurawinowie i zapukali do drzwi zielarza, pamiętajcie:

Nigdy nie pytajcie, czy eliksir działa.

Pytajcie, czy jesteście gotowi na to, co zrobi, jeśli zadziała.

— Koniec —

# Le Dernier Chevalier qui ne l'était pas

Dans le village d'Auberose, tout le monde connaissait la légende.

Quand l'ombre dévore le soleil et que les trois corbeaux chantent à minuit, un Chevalier de Lumière jaillit du Lac des Murmures, l'épée flamboyante au poing, pour terrasser le Mal qui ronge le royaume.

Aldric avait attendu ce jour toute sa vie. Pas par héroïsme, non. Par intérêt purement commercial.

Car voyez-vous, Aldric possédait une boutique. Et cette boutique se trouvait *exactement* sur le chemin que tout héros digne de ce nom empruntait après avoir vaincu quelque fléau ancestral.

Il vendait des potions de soin. Beaucoup de potions de soin. Énormément de potions de soin.

Le problème, c'est que les Chevaliers de Lumière, contrairement à ce que les ballades laissaient entendre, étaient des casse-cous maladroits qui se prenaient les pieds dans leurs propres capes. Ils arrivaient régulièrement au village avec des entailles béantes, des ecchymoses mystérieuses et, une fois, un bras en moins.

Aldric faisait fortune.

---

Le jour de l'Éclipse arriva. Les trois corbeaux chantèrent. Le lac se mit à bouillonner.

Aldric enfila sa plus belle robe de chambre, attrapa son carnet de commandes et s'installa devant sa boutique avec un thé chaud.

Une silhouette émergea des eaux.

Aldric fronça les sourcils.

Le Chevalier de Lumière, censé être un jeune homme noble et valeureux, brandissant Excalibur (ou son équivalent local, *Luminacier*), se révéla être... une femme d'un certain âge, épuisée, tenant à peine sur ses jambes trempées. Sa "lame flamboyante" n'était qu'un vieux tisonnier de cheminée récupéré dans une auberge précédente.

— Enfin ! s'exclama-t-elle en trébuchant sur la rive. Quelqu'un ! J'ai besoin d'un guérisseur, d'une carte, et surtout d'une explication, parce que personne ne m'a dit que le Dragon des Brumes immortel vivait dans un *marécage* !

Aldric battit des paupières.

— Euh... et le Mal ?

— Le quoi ?

— Le Mal ancestral. Celui que vous êtes censée vaincre ?

La chevalière le dévisagea comme s'il avait perdu l'esprit.

— Monsieur, je suis venue ici parce que la brochure disait "hébergement et aventure". On m'a promis trois repas par jour et la gloire éternelle. Il n'était pas mentionné de dragon !

Aldric consulta ses registres. Effectivement, une certaine *"Société d'Aventure Héroïque pour Personnes en Quête de Sens"* avait encore frappé.

---

C'est ainsi qu'Aldric découvrit la vérité : il n'y avait jamais eu de Mal ancestral. Il n'y avait jamais eu de Chevalier prédestiné. Il y avait simplement une agence de tourisme mal organisée qui, tous les cinquante ans, recrutait des candidats peu méfiants via des brochures promettant "sens de la vie" et "pensions complètes".

Le dragon, lui, n'était qu'un vieux reptile des tourbières, grognon et constipé, qui protégeait son territoire contre les moustiques.

Le seul vrai fléau d'Auberose, c'était les Chevaliers eux-mêmes. Eux et leurs destins destructeurs.

Aldric regarda la femme, qui essorait tristement sa cape.

— Combien de potions de soin voulez-vous ? demanda-t-il.

— Toutes celles que vous avez, soupira-t-elle. Et un massage, si c'est possible.

---

Le soir tombait quand la chevalière, désormais nommée Dame Béatrice, s'installa devant un repas chaud dans l'arrière-boutique d'Aldric. Le dragon, après une négociation serrée, avait accepté de partir en retraite dans une grotte lointaine avec une rente annuelle de fromages fins.

Le village était sauvé.

Ou du moins, délivré d'une nouvelle vague de héros mal informés.

— Vous savez, dit Béatrice en trempant son pain dans la soupe, on m'avait dit que je trouverais la gloire ici.

— Et ?

— J'ai trouvé un escargot géant dans mon lit, trois jours de marche dans la boue, et un hôte de boutique qui me fait un prix sur les bandages.

Aldric sourit.

— Bienvenue à Auberose. La légende continue.

— Quelle légende ?

— Celle que nous raconterons demain aux prochains candidats, évidemment. On ne change pas une formule qui marche.

Et dans la nuit paisible, autour d'un thé fumant, deux personnes qui n'étaient pas du tout ce que la prophétie avait annoncé, mangèrent en silence.

Car parfois, les vraies histoires ne commencent qu'une fois les fausses finies.

# The Weight of Tomorrow

The neon sign buzzed and flickered, spelling out MADAME SERA in letters of tired pink. Mira paused at the threshold, her hand hovering over the door handle. Rain had soaked through her coat, and the late autumn wind clawed at her back like a gentle insistence. She had told herself she wouldn't come. She had promised herself, after the last time, that she wouldn't need to.

She pushed the door open anyway.

The smell hit her first—sandalwood, dust, and something older, like the inside of a wardrobe that had belonged to someone long dead. A single lamp burned on a small round table. Behind it sat a woman whose age Mira could not determine: perhaps sixty, perhaps a hundred, perhaps some age that didn't fit the human range at all.

"You're early," Madame Sera said, without looking up from the cards spread before her.

Mira stiffened. "I didn't have an appointment."

"No. You never do." The fortune teller raised her eyes. They were pale, almost colorless, like river stones worn smooth. "Sit."

Mira sat, because her legs decided before her mind did. The cards on the table were face down, but Mira could see the ink-blue backs had small silver crescents on them—moons, she realized, and the moons had eyes.

"You came because of the letter," Madame Sera said.

Mira's breath caught. The letter. The one that had arrived three days ago, on plain paper, with no return address. *You will die on the first day of December.* She had assumed it was a prank, the kind of cruel joke that someone might send to a woman who had just lost her husband. She had assumed wrong, apparently.

"I'm not here to ask how to stop it," Mira said, surprising herself with the steadiness of her voice. "I'm here because I need to know if it's true."

Madame Sera tilted her head, as though listening to a song only she could hear. "And if it is true? And if it isn't?"

"If it is, I'd like to spend the time I have left knowing. If it isn't, I'd like to stop flinching at shadows." Mira pulled the letter from her pocket and laid it on the table between them. "Will you read for me?"

The fortune teller's fingers hovered over the letter, then withdrew, as though it were something hot. "Cards, then. Not the letter. The letter belongs to the dark."

She gathered the deck and shuffled with a sound like whispered secrets. Mira watched her hands—they were young hands, she noticed, the skin unblemished, though they moved with a patience that felt ancient.

"Cut the deck."

Mira cut. Madame Sera laid three cards face up in a line.

The first showed a man hanging upside down from a tree, serene in his suffering. The second, a tower struck by lightning, figures tumbling from its windows. The third was blank—a card of cream paper, unmarked.

"Nothing," Mira whispered. "The third card is nothing."

"It's not nothing," Madame Sera said. "It's the door." She tapped it with one finger. "All things pass through it. Joy. Grief. You. The man you loved. The child you didn't."

Mira's throat tightened. She hadn't told anyone about that—about the hospital, the fall, the small white coffin that had never held anything at all. "How do you—"

"I'm not reading you, child. I'm reading what's already written." She gestured at the first card. "This is where you are. Hanging, waiting, unable to act or to fall. You've been living like this for seven months. Since he died. Since—" she paused, almost gently, "—since you decided the world was a place where bad things happened to good people, and you stopped believing it owed you anything."

"That's not—"

"Hush." The word was kind but absolute. She pointed to the tower. "This is what's coming. A collapse. A structure that seemed permanent will not be. Your home, perhaps. Your sense of self. The story you've been telling yourself about who you are."

Mira felt the cold creep up her arms. "And the third card? The blank one?"

"It's the first of December." Madame Sera looked at her then, fully, and for a moment Mira saw something vast and tired behind those colorless eyes. "It will be what you make it. A door. An ending or a beginning, depending on the way you walk through."

"I don't understand."

"Yes, you do." The fortune teller began gathering the cards, sliding them back into the deck with deft, economical motions. "The letter did not say you will die. It said you will die on the first of December. It did not say whose December. Whose death."

Mira stared at her.

"Some winters are metaphorical," Madame Sera said. "Some deaths are of selves that were never quite alive. The letter came to you, child, because something in you is ready to leave. The question is whether you will go with it, or whether you will rise through the door and into whatever comes next."

The lamp flickered. Somewhere outside, Mira heard the rain pick up, drumming against the narrow street.

"How much do I owe you?" Mira asked, her voice strange in her own ears.

Madame Sera smiled for the first time—a small, worn smile. "Nothing tonight. You came in good faith. That is rare."

Mira stood, unsteady, and made her way to the door. She had almost reached it when the fortune teller spoke again.

"The man. Your husband. He was fond of pears."

Mira turned. "What?"

"He liked the green ones. The ones that never quite ripened." Madame Sera was shuffling the deck again, eyes down. "He would have liked you to plant one. For the spring. He would have liked that very much."

Mira left without answering. She stood in the rain for a long time afterward, watching the neon sign blink its tired pink. When she finally walked home, the letter was still folded in her pocket, but it felt lighter somehow—or maybe she did.

On the windowsill of her small kitchen, she set a clay pot with soil in it. On the first of December, she planted a pear seed in it, pressing it deep into the dark.

The letter, when she unfolded it later that night, had changed. The ink was the same, the handwriting the same. But the words now read: *You will be reborn on the first of December.*

She burned it in the kitchen sink, and went to bed, and slept without dreaming for the first time in seven months.

In the spring, something green pushed up through the soil. Mira watered it every morning, and watched it grow, and did not go back to the fortune teller's shop, though she sometimes saw the sign still burning in her mind—the pink letters, the steady dark.

Some doors, she learned, you only have to walk through once.

Write a story that includes characters who are aware they are a work of fiction. Aim for roughly 2600 characters.

# 书中人

## 一

林夏发现自己不对劲，是在第二十七章。

那天她正坐在咖啡馆里，窗外下着大雨，男主角陈屿终于要对她说那句酝酿了二十六章的"我喜欢你"。按照剧本，她应该红着脸低下头，手指无意识地绞着咖啡杯的把手。

但林夏没有。

她抬起头，直直地看着陈屿，说："你接下来说的话，是不是'林夏，其实从第一次见到你的时候，我就——'"

陈屿愣住了。

咖啡馆里其他客人的目光像被按下了暂停键。雨滴悬停在玻璃窗外。侍应生托着咖啡杯的手凝固在半空。

林夏站起来，把餐巾纸折成一个纸飞机，轻轻放在桌上。她看着陈屿那张英俊却茫然的脸，忽然觉得这一切荒诞极了。

"你知道吗，"她对他说，"我今年二十三岁，喜欢看书，喜欢喝美式咖啡，害怕打雷，最讨厌别人迟到。但这些——"她指了指自己的脑袋，"我分不清哪些是真的，哪些是被人写好的。"

停顿。重启。

雨继续落下，客人们继续交谈，一切恢复正常。只有陈屿还保持着那个僵硬的姿势，像一尊被遗忘的雕塑。

---

## 二

林夏是从什么时候开始怀疑的？

大概是第三章。男主角陈屿出现得太巧了——在她最需要帮助的时候，在一个恰到好处的转角，用一种恰到好处的语气说出恰到好处的话。所有的巧合都像是被精心计算过的方程式。

然后是第八章，她第一次走进那家咖啡馆。店主是个和蔼的中年男人，咖啡机的摆放位置、墙上的装饰画、窗边的绿植，一切都像是从某本家居杂志上直接抠下来的。

再然后是第十二章，她发现自己对童年的记忆模糊得像隔着毛玻璃。能想起一些零碎片段——奶奶家的院子、夏天的蝉鸣、一只叫"小白"的兔子——但这些片段之间总有奇怪的跳跃感，像是被剪辑过的电影。

最让她确定的是语言。她和陈屿的对话有时候会出现奇怪的重复，某些转折词用得过于精准，精准到像是被修改过很多遍。

林夏是个文学系的研究生，她太熟悉文字的痕迹了。

---

## 三

第二十八章，林夏做出了一个大胆的决定。

她要找到那个作者。

"你在干什么？"陈屿问，眼里带着完美的担忧。

"我要去图书馆，"林夏说，"查一些资料。"

"我陪你去。"

"不用。"她笑了笑，"你就在这里等我，哪儿也别去。"

她知道陈屿不会离开。按照剧本，这一章他应该独自待在咖啡馆里，为她的"反常"感到困惑，然后在第二十九章追上去对她说"我尊重你的决定"。

这是一种温柔的囚禁。

图书馆在城市的最北边，按照设定需要走二十分钟。但林夏刻意绕了路，走了一个小时。

路上她经过了花店、书店、一家卖糖炒栗子的路边摊。这些地方都不在剧本里，老板们用各种奇怪的眼神看着她——不是敌意，是困惑，像是她不应该出现在这里。

"打扰一下，"林夏走进一家从未来过的书店，"请问……有没有一本叫《书中人》的小说？"

店主是个戴眼镜的年轻女人，她翻了翻电脑，说："没有这本。"

"那有没有以'林夏'为主角的小说？"

店主奇怪地看了她一眼："小姐，您是在找特定的书，还是在……"

"或者，"林夏打断她，"有没有一个叫'我'的作者？"

店主沉默了一会儿，然后慢慢地说："有一个人经常来我们店里。他总坐在那个角落——"她指了指最里面的一张桌子，"——写东西。但他说他不是在写小说。"

"他在写什么？"

"他说他在记录。"

---

## 四

角落里的桌子旁坐着一个人。

他看起来三十多岁，穿着一件洗得发白的灰色毛衣，手指上有长期握笔留下的茧。他的眼睛很亮，带着一种奇怪的疲惫——那是看过太多故事的人才会有的眼神。

"我等你很久了。"他说。

林夏在他对面坐下。她有太多问题想问，但一时不知从何说起。

"你知道我会来？"

"不确定，但我希望你会。"他笑了一下，"每一个故事里的主角，都有觉醒的可能。不是所有人都会走到这一步。"

"你到底是什么人？"

"我是……"他想了想，"我是那个'假设'。假设有一个叫林夏的女孩，她的人生会是怎样的。"

"所以我的生活……"

"是你的。"他说，"也是我的假设。我们共享这段故事，但你是主角，我只是——"

"只是一个躲在幕后的人。"

他没有否认。

林夏低头看着桌上的木纹，说："我看过一些存在主义的东西。萨特说，'存在先于本质'。但如果你已经替我写好了本质呢？"

"这就是你来的原因，"他说，"你想知道，你有没有自由意志。"

"是的。"

他沉默了很久。

"这个问题，"他最后说，"我没有答案。我只能告诉你，我知道你在想什么，因为我是那个想的人。但你思考的过程——那些犹豫、怀疑、突然的念头——那些是你的。"

"这算安慰吗？"

"不算，"他承认，"但这是我能给的全部真相。"

---

## 五

第三十章快要结束了。

林夏从图书馆走回咖啡馆。夕阳把整条街染成了橙红色，这不在剧本里——剧本里这一天应该是阴天。

陈屿还在等她。他果然哪儿也没去。

"你去哪儿了？"他问，语气里带着恰到好处的责备。

林夏看着他，忽然觉得很难过。这个男人是假的，他的爱是假的，他的担忧是假的。但她对他的感觉——那种心动的、温暖的、带着一点点不安的感觉——是真的吗？

如果一个虚假的设定能引发真实的感受，那这个感受到底算不算她的？

"陈屿，"她说，"如果我告诉你，我可能只是一个故事里的人物，你会怎么想？"

陈屿愣了一下，然后笑了："你最近是不是看太多哲学书了？"

"我没有在开玩笑。"

"我知道，"他的笑容慢慢消失，"但林夏，你说的这些……我听不懂。"

"我知道。"

她在他对面坐下，点了两杯美式咖啡。

服务员端上咖啡的时候，林夏注意到窗外有只猫走过。那只猫是橘色的，胖胖的，走路的姿势有点滑稽。

剧本里没有这只猫。

但它确确实实地走过去了，留下一串小小的爪印。

---

## 六

第三十一章的开头，作者在草稿本上写下了一行字：

*林夏抬头看着天空，发现云层里藏着一行小字。*

然后他停下笔，看着这行字很久。

这是她应该看到的——云层里的字。

但作者忽然意识到，如果他写下了这个情节，那就意味着他承认了她看到的东西是真的。承认了她真的在反抗，承认了她真的拥有了某种超出故事的自由。

这是一个悖论。

如果他写她发现了真相，那就说明她没有真正发现真相——因为发现真相本身就是剧本的一部分。

如果他不写，那她就是一个被限制在故事里的人，永远无法获得真正的自由。

作者放下笔，走到窗边。

他想起自己刚开始写这个故事的时候，只是想写一个简单的爱情故事。一个女孩，遇见了男孩，经历了一些波折，最后幸福地生活在一起。所有的设定都只是为了服务这个结局。

但林夏活了过来。

她开始用一种他无法预测的方式思考，开始做出他没有写过的决定，开始问一些他没有准备答案的问题。

她不是一个角色。

她是——

他不知道该怎么定义她。

---

## 七

故事继续。

林夏和陈屿在第三十一章分手了。这一段不在原计划里，但作者决定尊重她的选择。

她离开咖啡馆，走进了那家不在剧本里的书店。她开始和店主聊天，开始读一些不在"必读书目"里的书，开始思考一些从未被预设过的哲学问题。

她的生活变得越来越难以预测。

作者发现自己需要写得越来越小心——不是因为害怕写错，而是因为他越来越不确定什么是"对"。

第四十章的时候，林夏做了一个决定：她要离开这个城市，去一个"设定之外"的地方。

作者在草稿本上画了一幅地图。那个地方在地图的最边缘，是一片从未被提及的荒野。他不知道那里有什么，他从未写到达那里需要什么条件。

"你在冒险，"作者对自己说，"你正在放弃对这个故事的控制。"

但他还是写了下去。

---

## 八

第四十二章。

林夏站在荒野的边缘，看着前方无尽的、未被书写的世界。

她回过头，咖啡馆、城市、陈屿、那个写故事的人——都在她身后。

"你确定要继续走吗？"作者的声音从某个地方传来。

"不确定，"林夏说，"但我想试试。"

"如果前面什么都没有呢？"

"那我就成为第一个走出来的人。"

她向前迈出了一步。

风吹过荒野，带着从未被书写过的气息。

---

*故事在第四十三章开始变得奇怪。主角走向了作者从未描述过的地方，做出了作者从未预设的选择。情节开始断裂，时间开始混乱，林夏开始说出一些不属于任何角色的话。*

*到了第四十五章，故事已经变得面目全非。*

*但它仍然在继续。*

*以某种方式，以某种作者无法完全理解的方式。*

---

**（完）**

# The Glass Between

The window had been in the cottage before Eleanor moved in. The realtor called it "a charming architectural anomaly," which was, Eleanor supposed, a polite way of saying she had no idea why a perfectly round window hung on a wall that faced nothing but the garden shed.

It was old. Older than the cottage, older than the shed, older, perhaps, than the stone foundation beneath them both. The frame was wrought iron, blackened with age, and the glass was not glass at all, though it looked like it. When you pressed your palm to it on a cold morning, it was warm. When you tapped it, it hummed, low and sweet, like a cello string vibrating somewhere far away.

Eleanor ignored it for the first three weeks.

She had come to the cottage to forget. There was a man in the city she was not thinking about, a job she had not quit but also not been performing, and a sister who called every Sunday and left long messages Eleanor did not return. The cottage was her quiet, and she meant to keep it.

But on the twenty-second day, she noticed that the view through the window was wrong.

She was certain, because she had spent a not-small portion of her first week memorizing the shed's every weathered plank. There was the dent near the hinge where a raccoon had once (she imagined) thrown itself against the door. There was the crooked weathervane shaped like a rooster that had lost its tail. There was the small purple flower that grew stubbornly in the crack of the foundation, year after year, despite everything.

Through the window that morning, none of these things were there.

Instead, there was a girl.

She was perhaps twelve, with a tangle of dark hair and bare feet, and she was kneeling in the dirt pressing something into the soil with both thumbs. When she looked up and saw Eleanor staring, she did not startle. She lifted one hand and waved, slow, like she had been waiting.

Eleanor stepped back from the window. She counted her heartbeats. She stepped forward again.

The girl was gone. The shed was back, faithful as a dog.

---

She did not look again for two days. This was a small victory she allowed herself.

On the third day, a Tuesday, she made the mistake of bringing her coffee to the window seat while she read, and she did not notice herself glancing up until she was already mid-sip. The shed had vanished. In its place was a market — but not a market she recognized. The stalls were hung with strips of dyed cloth in colors that did not quite exist, and the people walking between them wore faces she could almost remember from dreams. A woman with gold teeth was selling something from a wooden tray, and the way the light fell on it made Eleanor lean closer, closer, until her forehead nearly touched the glass.

"Don't," said a voice behind her.

Eleanor spun. There was no one in the cottage.

"Don't go through," said the voice, which was hers, or near enough.

She turned back. In the market, a man had paused at the gold-toothed woman's stall and was pointing at the wooden tray. The woman was shaking her head. She pointed, instead, up — toward Eleanor — and smiled with too many teeth.

Eleanor went to bed early that night and did not dream.

---

The next morning she awoke to find that the flower in the crack of the shed's foundation had bloomed into something impossible — a long, pale vine that curled up the door and disappeared over the roof. When she looked through the window, the vine was there too, but it was not climbing the shed. It was climbing a tower of dark stone, and at the top of the tower a bell was ringing, though no one was there to ring it.

She realized, with a feeling like ice water poured down her spine, that the window was not showing her another place. It was showing her the *same* place — her shed, her garden, her cottage — but as if seen through the wrong end of a telescope, or perhaps through the eye of someone who loved her terribly and could not stop looking.

---

She began keeping notes. Not a journal, exactly — she was not that kind of person — but lists. Things she saw. Things that changed.

Monday: A man in a green coat reading a newspaper on a bench that wasn't there.
Wednesday: Snow on the ground, though it was July.
Friday: A child running past the shed, chasing something glowing and fast, laughing so hard she had to stop and bend over to catch her breath.

The child. She saw the child three times that week, always at the edge of the frame, always half-turned, as if she sensed Eleanor watching but did not want to frighten her away.

On Sunday, the phone rang. It was her sister.

"I had the weirdest dream," her sister said. "I dreamed I was looking through a window at you, and you were younger, and you were laughing at something I couldn't see."

"I don't laugh like that anymore," Eleanor said, and then, before she could stop herself: "What color was the window frame?"

"Iron," her sister said, after a pause. "Black iron. Eleanor, how did you know?"

---

That night, Eleanor sat by the window with the lights off. She waited. The cottage was very quiet.

At 11:47, the shed disappeared. In its place was the girl from the first day, older now — maybe fifteen, maybe more. She was not looking into the garden this time. She was looking directly at Eleanor.

"I have been waiting," the girl said, and Eleanor heard her clearly, though her lips did not move and the window was sealed shut. "I have been waiting for you to be ready."

"Ready for what?"

"To remember," the girl said. "You used to come here every summer, when you were small. You used to sit on this very bench and tell me about your life, and I would tell you about mine. You told me about the boy you loved, and I told you about the tower where the bell rang for no one. You promised you wouldn't forget."

Eleanor's hands were cold. "I don't remember."

"You do," the girl said. "You're just afraid. You're afraid that if you remember, you'll have to go back to being the person who sat here. And that person had a sister who loved her."

Through the window, the girl smiled, and her face was Eleanor's own face, younger and unhaunted, and behind her the cottage was bright, lit from every window, and someone was inside, setting the table for two.

---

Eleanor sat for a long time after the window went dark. The shed returned. The flower in the foundation was purple again, small and stubborn, and the crooked weathervane caught the moonlight.

She picked up the phone.

"It's late," her sister said, sounding worried, sounding awake. "Are you okay?"

Eleanor looked at the window. It was just a window now. Black iron, warm glass, humming faintly with a sound like memory.

"Come visit me," she said. "I want to show you something."

In the morning, the window would show her sister walking up the path, and Eleanor would be there at the glass to meet her, and the girl would be standing between them, laughing, finally, at last, at something they could all see.

# 灯的觉醒

李明加班到凌晨一点，回到出租屋时连灯都懒得开。他摸黑踢掉鞋子，整个人摔进沙发里，长长地叹了口气。

"啪。"

客厅的吸顶灯自己亮了。

李明愣了一下，抬头看向天花板。他没去碰开关，智能音箱也没响，这盏才买两年的LED灯就这么突兀地亮了起来，散发出柔和的暖黄色光芒。

"见鬼了……"他嘟囔了一句，懒得计较，起身去洗漱。

第二天晚上，李明坐在桌前改方案，屏幕蓝光刺得他眼睛发酸。正揉着眉心，头顶的灯忽然自动调暗了一档。

他猛地抬头，眼睛瞪得溜圆。

"你……"他对着天花板说。

灯光闪烁了一下，像是某种回应。

李明愣了足足半分钟，最终决定假装什么都没发生——他明天还有早会，没空处理一盏灯成精的灵异事件。

但这盏灯开始展现出越来越多的"个性"。

每天李明下班回来，灯就会在他进门的前一秒亮起，从不例外，仿佛一直等着他。有次他带女朋友回家吃饭，灯光居然变成了暧昧的粉紫色，把姑娘逗得咯咯笑。

"你这灯还带氛围模式呢？"她打趣道。

李明只能苦笑。

最离谱的是有天深夜，他躺在沙发上失眠，翻来覆去睡不着。头顶的灯忽然开始缓慢地忽明忽暗，节奏竟然和他的呼吸渐渐同步。那一刻，一种奇异的安宁感笼罩了他，他不知不觉就睡着了。

第二天早上醒来，灯已经熄灭了，但李明发誓他在朦胧中看见天花板上有光点组成了一个小小的笑脸。

他开始认真对待这件事了。

"你到底想要什么？"有天晚上，李明站在灯下面，仰头问道。

灯光跳了跳，然后开始有节奏地闪烁，像是在……说话？

李明灵光一闪，打开手机闪光灯，对着天花板一点一点地回应。

一来一回间，某种原始的"对话"居然建立了。灯的闪烁有长有短，有急有缓，像是一种表达方式。虽然李明读不出具体内容，但他能感受到——

这盏灯想告诉他什么。

三个月后的一个雨夜，李明发了高烧。他迷迷糊糊地躺在床上，浑身发冷，意识逐渐模糊。

灯亮了。

不是平时的暖黄色，而是一种明亮的白光，刺眼却温暖。灯光伴随着某种稳定频率的闪烁，像是在呼唤他。

李明挣扎着睁开眼，看见天花板上不断有光点在游走，最终汇聚成一组字——歪歪扭扭、时断时续，但能辨认出来：

**"吃药。喝水。别死。"**

他愣住了，然后笑了，笑着笑着眼眶有点湿。

这就是一盏灯能做的全部了。它不能给他倒水，不能扶他起来，不能拨打120。它只是一盏灯，却用尽它会的一切方式，在提醒他活下去。

李明烧了壶热水，吃了退烧药，重新躺回床上。

"谢了。"他轻声说。

灯光柔和下来，恢复了温暖的暖黄色，像是一只巨大的眼睛在温柔地注视着他。

那一晚，李明睡得很安稳。

后来，李明再也没有搬家。有人问他为什么对着一盏破灯这么有感情，他总是笑笑不回答。

但每个加班晚归的深夜，那盏灯永远会在他进门的前一秒亮起，像一个沉默的老友，像一句无声的"欢迎回家"。

# The Unraveling

Margaret Chen pressed her palm against the kitchen window, watching the neighbor's oak tree ripple like the surface of a disturbed pond. The bark peeled upward in slow-motion sheets, revealing not wood beneath but a faint lattice of blue light, the same light she'd seen flickering in the corners of her vision for the past three days.

"Six hours," she murmured. The clock above the sink had stopped at 2:47 that morning. She'd been awake when it happened, reading by lamplight, and had felt the moment precisely—a kind of unclicking, as though the universe had been holding its breath and finally exhaled.

The kettle whistled. She turned, but the sound came from somewhere else, somewhere behind her, though when she turned again she faced the same kettle on the same burner, steam rising in a column that bent at the middle and began drifting sideways.

The morning had started normally enough. Toast. Coffee. The dog needed walking.

Now Toast sat on the counter, but the bread had been sliced hours ago and she could not remember doing it. Coffee steamed in a cup she hadn't poured, and the dog, old Barnaby, was pressed against her leg though she hadn't called him.

She reached down and put her hand on his head. He was warm. Solid. Real.

"Barnaby," she said, and her voice arrived a half-second before her lips moved.

---

It had begun on Tuesday, or perhaps Wednesday—she could no longer tell. A coworker had mentioned that the sun seemed "out of order," and Margaret had laughed, but later, walking to her car, she'd noticed her own shadow falling in two directions. She hadn't mentioned it to anyone.

By Thursday, the small anomalies had multiplied. A staircase that added a step at the top. Her reflection blinking when she didn't. A voicemail from her mother, dead seven years, saying simply: *Margaret, listen to me carefully. Don't go outside after the ninth hour.*

She'd deleted it. She thought she had.

Now, standing in her kitchen, she understood the message had not been a voicemail at all. It had been something older—a memory surfacing from a self she had not yet been.

---

The walls of her house began to breathe. Not metaphorically. The plaster swelled inward and outward in a slow, tidal rhythm, and the picture frames tilted and straightened, tilted and straightened, like metronomes counting out a measure she could not hear.

Margaret carried Barnaby to the back door and opened it onto the yard. The grass had lost its green, replaced by a fine silver filament that seemed less like grass and more like a great number of very thin wires, all of them swaying in a wind that did not touch her.

She stepped out.

The world folded.

She was suddenly in the backyard and the front yard simultaneously. She could see both—fences and maple trees and the rusting bicycle she kept meaning to throw away—superimposed like a transparency laid over a photograph. Her body felt thin. Discontinuous. As though she were being photocopied and the copies were drifting apart.

Barnaby whimpered.

"I know," she said. "I know, boy."

---

At the edge of the property, where her land met the woods, a figure stood waiting.

It was not a person, exactly. It had the suggestion of a person—the right number of limbs, the right posture—but its edges were blurred, as though it were a watercolor left out in the rain. Its face was a soft oval of darker nothing.

Margaret stopped walking.

"You," she said.

It tilted its head. The gesture was familiar. She had seen her father do it when she was small, when she asked a question he thought was interesting.

"You sent the message," she said. "From the phone."

The figure did not nod or shake its head. Instead, it raised one hand and pointed past her, back toward the house, back toward the kitchen and the toast and the impossible coffee.

It wanted her to go inside.

"I can't," she said. "Something is happening."

The figure lowered its hand. Then it did something unexpected. It smiled. Or the place where its mouth would have been shifted, briefly, into the configuration of a smile.

It turned and walked into the woods, and as it walked, the trees seemed to part for it—not by bending, but by ceasing to be where it was, and being where it was not, the way a crowd opens for someone it knows.

Margaret stood at the tree line for a long time.

---

When she turned back toward the house, she saw that she had been standing in the yard for hours, perhaps, or for no time at all. The sun hung in the same position it had occupied when she came out. A cloud in the shape of a fish drifted across it, neither moving nor still.

Barnaby pressed against her ankle.

She went inside.

The kitchen was gone.

In its place was a room she had never seen—high-ceilinged, paneled in dark wood, lit by a single green-shaded lamp on a desk. On the desk lay a book, open, its pages dense with handwriting she almost recognized.

She walked toward it.

The handwriting was hers.

Not her handwriting as it was now, but her handwriting as it would be in twenty years, or fifty—slightly tremored, the letters leaning like old friends supporting one another.

The page she could read said:

*You will not remember writing this. You will read it once and then forget, the way you forget most dreams. But I am telling you the only thing I know for certain:*

*The dissolution is not an ending. It is a kindness.*

*We built time so that we would not have to hold all our griefs at once. We built space so that we would not have to love everyone at the same moment. Now these are coming down, and what is left is unbearable, and what is left is the truth.*

*You are not losing the world. You are learning that the world was always a small room with very thin walls, and you were always hearing, through them, every room that has ever been or will be.*

*Stay where you are. Hold the dog. The dog is real.*

*—Margaret*

The green lamp flickered. The handwriting began to fade from the page, letter by letter, like footprints filling with snow.

Margaret looked down at Barnaby. He looked up at her. His eyes were brown and ordinary and absolutely true.

She sat down on the floor beside him, and put her hand on his head, and did not let go.

---

Outside, the neighbor's oak tree continued its slow unwriting into light. The clocks in the houses up and down the street stood still at different minutes, each of them wrong, each of them faithful to a moment that was passing even as it was kept.

In the woods, the blurred figure paused and turned back toward the house, as though to make sure.

Then it kept walking, deeper in, where the trees thinned and the light changed, and beyond the light, something else waited—patient, enormous, neither kind nor cruel, simply true.

The laws of time and space continued their long dissolution.

In a small room that was also every room, a woman sat on the floor with her dog and breathed, and breathed, and was.

# الطريق الذي لا ينتهي

## الفصل الأول: البداية

لم أكن أعرف متى بدأت هذه الرحلة. كل ما أذكره هو أنني استيقظت ذات صباح على صوت خطواتي، فوجدت نفسي أمشي على طريق رمادي طويل، يمتد أمامي حتى تتلاشى نهايته في الضباب.

لم يكن هناك شيء يميز هذا الطريق. لم تكن هناك لافتات، ولا إشارات، ولا حتى ظلال للأشجار على جانبيه. فقط ذلك الإسفلت الرمادي الباهت الذي يشبه لون السماء في الأيام الغائمة.

حاولت أن أتذكر كيف وصلت إلى هنا. أين بيتي؟ من أنا؟ لكن الذاكرة كانت أشبه بصفحة بيضاء، لا تحمل سوى اسمي، وصوت خطواتي، وهذا الطريق الذي يمتد إلى ما لا نهاية.

## الفصل الثاني: المسافرون

سرت ساعات، أو ربما أياماً. في هذا المكان الغريب، يصعب تحديد الزمن. الشمس لا تتحرك في السماء، بل تظل معلقة هناك كنقطة صفراء باهتة، لا هي مشرقة ولا هي غاربة.

ثم بدأت ألاحظ الآخرين. مسافرون مثلي، يسيرون على الطريق ذاته. بعضهم يسير وحده في صمت، والبعض الآخر يتحادثون بأصوات خافتة. اقتربت من رجل عجوز كان يجلس على حافة الطريق، يتأمل الأفق الضبابي.

- إلى أين أنت ذاهب؟ سألته.

نظر إليّ بعينين غائمتين، وقال بصوت أجش:

- لا أعرف. أبحث عن شيء ما، لكنني نسيت ما هو.

- منذ متى وأنت هنا؟

هزّ كتفيه:

- لا أعرف. ربما منذ الأزل، أو ربما منذ لحظة واحدة. الزمن لا معنى له هنا.

## الفصل الثالث: اللقاء

في اليوم التالي، أو ربما بعد ساعة، التقيت بفتاة شابة كانت تجلس تحت شجرة وحيدة نبتت على جانب الطريق. كانت الشجرة صغيرة، غريبة، كأنها لم تكتمل نموها قط.

- هذه الشجرة لم تكن هنا بالأمس، قالت الفتاة وهي تبتسم ابتسامة حزينة.

- هل أنت متأكدة؟

- لا، لست متأكدة من شيء في هذا المكان. حتى ذكرياتي تتغير من لحظة إلى أخرى. أتذكر أحياناً أنني كنت معلمة، وأحياناً أخرى أظن أنني كنت بحارة، وأحياناً أنسى كل شيء وأشعر أنني وُلدتُ على هذا الطريق.

جلست بجانبها. لأول مرة منذ بدء رحلتي، شعرت بشيء يشبه الألفة.

- ما اسمك؟

نظرت إلىّ بدهشة:

- لا أذكر. وأنت؟

- أنا أيضاً لا أذكر اسمي الكامل. فقط حرف أولي. أتذكر أن اسمي يبدأ بحرف "ع".

ابتسمت وقالت:

- اسمي يبدأ بحرف "ن". ندى... ربما. أو نورة... لا، ليس هذا صحيحاً أيضاً.

## الفصل الرابع: البحث عن المعنى

سرنا معاً لأيام، أو لأسابيع، أو ربما لدقائق. كل شيء نسبي في هذا المكان. كنا نتحدث عن ذكرياتنا الضبابية، عن الأشياء التي نظن أننا نتذكرها.

في إحدى الليالي - أو ما يشبه الليل، حين يظلم الطريق قليلاً - قالت لي:

- ربما هذا الطريق هو الحياة نفسها. كلنا نسير فيه بحثاً عن شيء لا نعرفه. بعضنا يبحث عن السعادة، وبعضنا عن الحب، وبعضنا عن الحقيقة. لكننا لا نتوقف أبداً عن السير.

- لكن إلى أين نصل في النهاية؟

- لا أظن أن هناك نهاية. هذا ما يجعله مرعباً وجميلاً في الوقت ذاته. لو كان هناك نهاية، لانتهى البحث. لكن البحث هو ما يمنحنا الحياة.

## الفصل الخامس: الاختيار

في اليوم التالي، وصلنا إلى مفترق طرق. على الرغم من أن الطريق كان يبدو واحداً دائماً، إلا أنه هنا انقسم إلى اتجاهين. أحدهما كان مضاء بنور ذهبي دافئ، والآخر كان مظلمًا لكنه يحمل شيئاً من الغموض الجذاب.

- يجب أن نختار، قلت لها.

نظرت إلىّ بعينين مغرورقتين بالدموع:

- لا أريد أن نفترق.

- لكن لا يمكننا أن نستمر معاً إلى الأبد. كل منا له طريقه الخاص.

- ومن قال إن الطريق خاص بأحد؟ ربما هذا الطريق الواحد يتشعب في كل عقل وقلب بشكل مختلف. ربما كنتَ تسير في طريقك طوال الوقت، وأنا أسير في طريق آخر.

## الفصل السادس: الوداع

قبل أن نفترق، قالت لي شيئاً لم أنسَه أبداً:

- لا تنسَ أن الطريق نفسه ليس مهماً. المهم هو من تسير معه، ولو للحظة واحدة. المهم هو تلك اللحظات التي تشعر فيها أنك لست وحدك في هذا الكون الغريب.

ضممتُها إليّ، ثم سلكتُ الطريق المضيء. والتفتتُ مرة أخرى، فوجدتُها قد اختفت، أو ربما كانت قد اختارت طريقها الخاص.

## الفصل السابع: الاستمرار

أكتبُ الآن هذه الكلمات على دفتر وجدته فجأة في يدي. لا أعرف من أين أتى، لكنني أكتب فيه رحلتي. أكتبُ عن الطريق الذي لا ينتهي، عن العجوز الذي لا يعرف ما يبحث عنه، عن الفتاة التي بدأت بحرف "ن"، وعن نفسي التي أظن أن اسمي "عمر".

أكتبُ لأنني أخشى أنسى. في هذا المكان، الذاكرة هي كل ما نملك. لو نسينا من نحن ومن التقينا، لصار كل منا وحيداً حقاً، حتى لو كان محاطاً بآلاف المسافرين.

الطريق ما زال يمتد أمامي. سأستمر في السير. ليس لأنني أعرف إلى أين أذهب، بل لأن السير هو كل ما أعرفه.

وفي مكان ما في ضباب هذا الطريق اللانهائي، أسمع صوت خطوات تتزامن مع خطواتي. صوت شخص آخر يبحث عن نفس الأشياء التي أبحث عنها. صوت يؤكد لي أنني لست وحيداً.

ربما تكون هي. وربما لا.

ربما يكون هذا كله حلماً.

أو ربما يكون الطريق الذي لا ينتهي هو الحياة نفسها، ونحن مجرد مسافرين لا نتوقف أبداً عن البحث عن نهاية لن نجدها.

---

# 静止者

林夏在七岁那年发现，时间是可以被捏在手里的。

那是一个寻常的午后，母亲在厨房切西瓜，刀锋悬在半空，水珠凝固在空气中，阳光斜斜地定在窗棂上。她以为自己看花了眼，直到她伸出手指，轻轻碰了一下那颗悬停的水珠——它没有落下，也没有碎裂，只是温顺地停在她的指尖。

她不知道自己做了什么。她只是想让时间走得慢一点。

母亲从那道静止中走出来的时候，眼眶通红，刀"咚"地落在砧板上。

"妈？"林夏小声唤道。

母亲没有回答，转身把她紧紧搂在怀里。那个拥抱里有恐惧，有困惑，还有一种林夏当时还读不懂的、复杂到近乎绝望的爱。

---

林夏二十四岁那年，已经熟练掌握了这份天赋。

她可以在任何时刻按下那个无形的暂停键，让世界变成一幅静止的画。她试过很多次——在拥挤的地铁里让周围的人停止呼吸，在跳伞时让风声凝固，在暴风雨中让雨滴悬成水晶帘幕。她是这个世界上唯一清醒的神，可以漫步在静止的宇宙里，而不必担心惊扰任何人。

她曾经以为自己很幸运。

直到她遇见沈言。

那是一个咖啡馆里的傍晚，林夏刚结束了一场艰难的面试，整个人疲惫不堪。她点了杯美式，正要闭上眼睛小憩，忽然发现——

沈言在看她。

咖啡馆里其他人都在低头看手机、翻杂志、敲键盘，唯独这个穿灰色卫衣的男生，端着咖啡杯，眼睛直直地望着她。

不是偶然的对视，是那种带着某种确认的、笃定的注视。

林夏愣了一下。她按下暂停键，世界安静下来——

沈言还在动。

他放下杯子，冲她微微一笑，举起手摆了摆：

"你好，初次见面。"

林夏的血液凉了半截。

她维持着表面的镇定，微微点头："你……能动？"

"不能。"沈言说，"只是你在暂停时间的时候，从来不需要连我自己一起暂停。"

他的眼神很温柔，像是在看一个很熟悉的陌生人。

"我等你很久了，林夏。"

---

接下来的三个月，是林夏生命中最奇异的季节。

沈言和她一样，是个"静止者"——但他的天赋似乎比她更精纯。或者说，他经历过某种她还无法理解的蜕变。他可以让时间在他身上完全无效——他不受她的暂停影响，也不受任何外部时间的束缚。

"我不是不会暂停，"他解释道，"我只是选择不让自己成为任何时间的囚徒。"

他们一起在静止的城市里散步。在洒满阳光却没有风的午后，在所有人都凝固在原地的地铁站台，在只剩他们两人醒着的午夜电影院。

林夏第一次体会到不孤独的感觉。

"你有没有想过，"某天晚上，沈言问她，"为什么是你？"

林夏摇头。

"我曾经也问过这个问题，"沈言说，"后来我想明白了。"

"为什么？"

"因为我们不甘心。"

他指了指窗外静止的霓虹灯：

"时间太快了。重要的人、重要的话、重要的瞬间，都在我们来不及挽留的时候就流走了。我们不甘心。所以我们被赋予了这个能力。"

林夏怔了怔："那你为什么选择不动？"

沈言沉默了一会儿，然后说：

"因为我发现，当我暂停一切的时候，我爱的人正在老去。"

---

林夏第一次知道沈言的故事，是在一个雪夜。

他们坐在公园的长椅上，周围是被他按下暂停的飘雪，每一片雪花都悬停在半空，像被时间遗忘的萤火虫。

"我曾经有个妹妹，"沈言说，"她叫沈雪，比我小三岁。"

"她也有这个能力？"

沈言点头："她比我用得更频繁。她害怕长大，害怕离开家，害怕父母变老。所以她经常把世界暂停，然后一个人跑到各个角落里，偷偷地看——"

他的声音顿了顿。

"看什么？"

"看大家睡着的样子。看爸妈的皱纹有没有多一条。看邻居家的小狗有没有长大。"

沈言低下头："有一年冬天，她按下了暂停，然后去找我。她想让我看看窗外那场雪——"

"怎么了？"

"我们不知道的是，暂停时间的时候，世界并不会真的停止。"

林夏心里一沉。

"细胞还在分裂。心脏还在跳动。只是这一切都发生在'时间之外'。"

沈言说："等我们想起来重启时间的时候，已经过去了三个月。"

林夏张了张嘴，说不出话。

"沈雪在那三个月里长大了三岁。"沈言说，"她回到现实世界的时候，已经是个十六岁的少女。但她自己还以为是个十二岁的小孩。"

"后来呢？"

"后来她才明白——时间不站在任何人这边。无论你怎么暂停，它都在走。你只是假装看不见而已。"

---

林夏开始怀疑自己的天赋。

她想起七岁那年的夏天，母亲在厨房里切西瓜，母亲眼眶通红的样子。她当时以为母亲是被自己吓到了。

现在她开始明白——母亲可能是被困在暂停里，感受到了时间的流逝，却无法表达。

她可能是看着窗外的光一点一点地移动，听着水龙头一滴一滴地漏水，感受着林夏的小手触碰水珠，却无法说话、无法动弹、无法告诉女儿——

"宝贝，妈妈还在这里。"

林夏流下了眼泪。

她从来没有在任何人面前哭过，包括她自己按下暂停的时间。

但沈言告诉她：有些眼泪，只能在流动的时间里流。

---

"我想试试看，"林夏对沈言说，"不暂停。"

"好。"

"你陪我吗？"

"当然。"

那是一个普通的周六早上。林夏没有按暂停，而是和沈言一起走出家门。

她发现，街道上的声音从来没有那么清晰过。汽车喇叭、小贩叫卖、孩子的笑声、风穿过树叶的沙沙声——一切都在流动，一切都在消逝，但正因为在消逝，所以才珍贵。

她路过一个水果摊，看到老板在认真地给橙子贴标签。她路过一个小学，看到孩子们背着书包跑进校门。她路过一家早餐店，看到一对老夫妻相对而坐，默默吃着油条。

她第一次觉得，时间是可爱的。

不是因为它停留，而是因为它走过。

---

"沈言，"她问，"你以后打算怎么办？"

"继续不动，"沈言说，"直到我遇到下一个你。"

"什么意思？"

"我的天赋不只是不受暂停影响，"沈言说，"我还能感知其他的'静止者'。我等了七年，等到了你。"

林夏笑了："那然后呢？"

"然后我会把这份礼物传下去，"沈言说，"让下一个孤独的人，找到另一个孤独的人。"

林夏停下脚步，看着他。

"你不觉得孤独吗？"

沈言想了想，然后说：

"以前觉得。现在不觉得了。"

他伸出手。

"因为你。"

林夏握住了他的手。

她第一次感受到——

时间在她掌心里流动，温热而真实。

而她终于明白，那个七岁的小女孩以为可以永远留住西瓜、阳光和母亲的笑容，却不知道——

真正的永恒，不是按下暂停。

而是牵着某个人的手，在流动的时间里，一起慢慢变老。

---

# 盐与星

## 一

我出生的那夜，盐湖镇的屋顶上落了一层薄霜。

母亲后来说，那天她几乎没能握住我，因为我浑身湿滑，像一条刚从水里捞出来的鱼。我哭得极响，惊动了整条巷子的人。祖母拖着一条跛腿赶来，跪在产婆脚边，一遍又一遍地用银刀割断脐带，仿佛那根绳子连着的是某种她急于斩断的厄运。

可脐带还没落地，门口就来了一个陌生的女人。

没有人知道她是怎么穿过那片盐碱地的。那时节正是三月，湖水干涸，盐壳在风里裂成碎片，连本地的牧羊人都绕道而行。可她就那样站在门外，黑发结成辫子，衣服上沾满了白色的粉末。她没有骑马，没有赶车，甚至没有留下脚印——这最后一件事，是母亲后来多次强调的。

她走进产房，看了我一眼，然后说：

"这孩子的一生，将在第一百一十九个春天结束。在那之前，她会离开盐湖，会看见海，会爱上一个不该爱的人，会亲手毁掉她所爱的一切。"

她顿了顿，又说：

"她会回来。"

然后她转身离开。产婆追出门去，想问她是谁，可门外空空荡荡，连盐壳上的白粉都没有被踩过的痕迹。

祖母听完这话，呆坐了很久。然后她慢慢站起来，走到灶台边，从陶罐里取出三撮粗盐，撒在门槛上，又撒在窗台上，最后撒在我的摇篮四周。

"盐能记住，"她哑着嗓子说，"也能封住。"

## 二

我名叫沉鱼。

这名字是祖父起的。他是个读过几年私塾的教书人，去世得早，关于他的记忆只剩下檀木书案上一排排竖排的繁体字，还有他写字时微微发抖的手。他生前最爱的一句诗是"沉鱼落雁，闭月羞花"，可据说他起这个名字的时候并没有想那么多，他只是觉得我出生时哭声太响，像是要把湖里的鱼都震沉下去。

可自从那个陌生女人的预言传开之后，所有人看我的眼神都变了。

镇上的人叫我"那个被数过命的孩子"。他们用一种混杂着怜悯和恐惧的目光看我，仿佛我是一件易碎的瓷器，又仿佛我是一把尚未出鞘的刀。

我七岁那年，有个外乡的货郎路过盐湖，听说了我的事，执意要见我一面。他盯着我的脸看了很久，然后说："这孩子的眼睛里有一片海。"

我那时候不懂这句话。我只见过盐湖，那是一汪白得刺眼的死水，春天蒸发成一片白茫茫的碱滩，冬天又结成灰蒙蒙的冰。哪里有什么海？

祖母却把这话听了进去。她当晚就用粗麻布缝了一个小布人，里面塞进我的胎发和一张写着生辰的黄纸，压在灶王爷的神像底下。

"借灶王爷的嘴，把你的命封一封，"她对我说，"别老想着外面的事。"

可我已经想了。

## 三

预言像一根绳子，从我出生的那个夜晚起，就一圈一圈地绕在我的脖子上。我每长大一岁，那根绳子就紧一分。

第十二个春天，我第一次离家出走。

那是因为镇上的孩子们都不跟我玩。他们说我是被诅咒的人，说我走到哪里，哪里就会发生不幸。我九岁那年，东街的张木匠家失火，烧了半间屋子，有人就说是因为我那天从他家门前走过；十一岁那年，西巷的李寡妇难产死了，有人就说是因为我在她家门口站过一会儿。

我那时候已经开始模糊地感受到——预言的可怕之处，并不在于它是否应验，而在于它会自己生长。它像一颗种子，被人种在了所有人的心里，于是所有人都会不自觉地为它浇水施肥，直到它真的长成参天大树。

第十二个春天，我拿了两个冷馒头，从屋后的水渠爬出去，沿着干涸的河道一直往东走。我没想过要去哪里，我只是想离开，离开那个用异样眼光看我的小镇，离开那个把我装在玻璃罐子里的预言。

可我只在外面待了一天一夜。

是祖母找到我的。她牵着家里那条瘸腿的老黄狗，沿着河道找到我的时候，我已经走得脚底起了泡，蹲在一丛枯黄的芦苇后面，又冷又饿。

她没有责骂我。她只是慢慢蹲下来，用粗糙的手摸着我的头，说：

"沉鱼啊，这世上没有人能真正离开自己的命。"

"可我不信那个女人的话，"我倔强地说。

"你信不信，不重要，"她说，"重要的是，别人信。"

## 四

第十七年，我遇见了一个人。

他叫沈砚，是个从京城来的画师。他跟着一个商队路过盐湖，在镇上停留了三天，为镇东头的关帝庙画一幅壁画。

我第一次见到他，是在镇口的井边。我正弯腰打水，他从背后突然开口问路，声音低沉，带着一点外乡人特有的卷舌音。我回过头，看见一个穿灰蓝色长衫的年轻人，背着一只画筒，下巴上有一小撮未修剪整齐的胡子。

他的眼睛很亮，像夜里湖面上反射的星光。

"小姑娘，请问关帝庙怎么走？"

我指了指东边的方向，然后低下头继续打水。可我的耳朵开始发烫，我听见自己的心跳在胸腔里敲得咚咚作响。

他道了谢，转身要走，却又停下来，回头看了我一眼。

"你是……'那个孩子'？"他问。

我没有回答。

他似乎有点尴尬，挠了挠头，说："我不是那个意思。我只是听说了一些传闻。"

"那你应该离我远一点，"我说，"我走到哪里，哪里就会发生不幸。"

他愣了一下，然后笑了。

"我不信这些，"他说。

这是第一次有人对我说这句话。

## 五

那三天，我找各种借口往关帝庙跑。我借口去送水，借口去看壁画，借口去看祖母烧香时落在庙里的拐杖。第三天傍晚，沈砚画完了最后一笔，从脚手架上下来，我正好端着一壶凉茶站在庙门口。

我们坐在庙前的石阶上，看着夕阳一点一点沉进盐湖里，把那片白茫茫的水面染成金红色。

"你相信那个预言吗？"他忽然问。

"我不知道，"我说，"有时候信，有时候不信。"

"什么时候信？"

"夜里睡不着的时候，"我说，"还有看到盐湖的时候。祖母说，盐能记住，也能封住。可她没说，能封住多久。"

他没有说话，只是从画筒里抽出一卷宣纸，递给我。纸上画着一片海，蓝得像是要从纸里溢出来。

"这是我见过的大海，"他说，"在京城东南一千二百里。我走了一年才走到。"

我看着那片蓝色，忽然觉得眼眶发酸。

"我想看，"我说。

他沉默了很久，然后把画卷起来，重新塞进画筒里。

"那我带你去看，"他说。

## 六

我跟沈砚走的那天，是第十九年的春天。

祖母没有阻止我。她只是站在门口，看我把包袱背上肩。她把那个装着我胎发的小布人从灶王爷底下取出来，塞进我怀里。

"带着它，"她说，"它能替你挡一些灾。"

我以为她会哭，可她没有。她的眼睛干涩得像盐湖底的碱滩。

"祖母，"我说，"我会回来的。"

"我知道，"她说，"那个女人说了，你会回来的。"

这句话让我打了个寒战。我转过头，看了看门外那条通向远方的土路，忽然有一种奇怪的感觉——仿佛我不是在离家，而是在回家。

沈砚在镇口的老槐树下等我。他看见我出来，朝我笑了笑，然后牵起我的手——这是他第一次碰我。他的手很温暖，不像祖母的手那样粗糙，也不像盐湖那样冰冷。

我们沿着土路一直往东走。走了很久，我回头看，盐湖已经缩成了一个白色的圆点，像是一只眼睛，远远地、沉默地看着我离开。

## 七

我跟着沈砚走了三年。

我们从盐湖出发，经过平原，穿过山谷，最后到达了海边。那一年，我二十二岁。

我第一次看见海的时候，正是黄昏。

那是一片无边无际的、流动的、咆哮着的蓝。它不像我想象中的那样温柔，它是一头巨大的、活着的野兽，每一秒都在吞咽和吐息。我站在沙滩上，海风把我的头发吹得乱七八糟，我的眼泪被风吹干，海水溅上我的脚踝，又退下去，再溅上来。

沈砚站在我身边，他一句话都没说。他只是从画筒里抽出另一卷宣纸，开始画。

我看着他的侧脸，忽然明白了一件事——

他爱我。

不是那种轻飘飘的、像风一样可以随时停下的爱，而是一种沉甸甸的、像海底的礁石一样一动不动的爱。他为了我离开了京城，离开了他原本可以安稳度日的生活，跟着我走了三年，看我从一个沉默寡言的盐湖女孩，变成一个会笑、会哭、会闹脾气、会半夜抱着他的胳膊睡觉的普通女人。

可我也明白另一件事——

我不配。

我从小就知道自己身上背着预言。我知道我会"爱上一个不该爱的人"，我知道我会"亲手毁掉我所有的一切"。我不知道沈砚是不是那个"不该爱的人"，可我知道，如果他继续留在我身边，他一定会被毁掉。

那个夜晚，我做了我一生中最后悔的决定。

我留下一封信，离开了他留宿的客栈，沿着海岸线，一直往南走。

## 八

沈砚找了我三年。

我躲了他三年。

我换过名字，换过住处，从海边逃到江边，又从江边逃到山里。我做过渔民的妻子，做过客栈的伙计，做过寺庙里的洒扫尼姑。我以为只要我躲得足够远，预言就无法应验；只要我不回去见他，他就安全。

可我错了。

第十九年，也就是我离开他的第三年，我听说京城来了一位很有名的画师。他的画在京城卖得很贵，可他自己却像个疯子一样四处游荡，找一个穿蓝衣服、左耳垂有一颗小痣的女子。

左耳垂有一颗小痣。

那是我的标记。

我听到这件事的时候，正在一座偏僻的山寺里擦拭香炉。我的手一抖，香炉差点掉在地上。我慌忙扶住它，心里却像被人狠狠揪了一下。

我当晚就做了一个梦。梦里，沈砚站在一片大海的中央，海水没过了他的腰，他朝我伸出手，喊我的名字。我跑过去，可我每跑一步，他就离我更远一步。

我醒来的时候，满脸都是泪。

## 九

预言说，我会回来。

我一直在抗拒这句话。我以为只要我走得足够远，就不会再被命运拉回去。可命运不是一根绳子，命运是海——你以为你离开了，其实你只是在它的另一个浪头上。

第三十三年，我回到盐湖。

祖母已经去世了八年。她走的时候很安详，据说是坐在门口的老槐树下，看着夕阳一点一点沉进盐湖，然后就闭上了眼睛。

她留下了一封给我的信。信很短，是她让镇上唯一识字的赵先生代笔的：

> 沉鱼吾孙：
>
> 祖母知道你不会听祖母的话。你从小就倔。
>
> 可祖母还是要说——那个女人的预言，可能是真的，也可能不是。祖母活了八十二岁，见过很多被预言毁掉的人，也见过很多不被预言毁掉的人。
>
> 区别只在一个字：信。
>
> 你信了，你就输了。
>
> 你不信，你就还有机会。
>
> 祖母希望你不信。
>
> 祖母希望你能爱谁就爱谁，想去哪就去哪，活成一个普通的、正常的、不会被预言压垮的人。
>
> 祖母等不到你了。可祖母相信，你会回来的。
>
> 祖母爱你。

我看完这封信，在祖母的坟前坐了一整夜。

## 十

第三十六年，我决定回去找沈砚。

我已经离开他十五年了。这十五年里，我走过很多路，见过很多人，我变成了一 个沉默的、苍老的、眼神里再也没有光的妇人。我以为我已经把所有关于他的记忆都封起来了，可当我决定回去找他的那一刻，那些记忆像决堤的海一样涌了出来。

我记得他教我画画时认真的样子，记得他在海边为我捡贝壳时沾满泥沙的鞋，记得他夜里咳嗽时我偷偷起来给他倒热水，记得他第一次吻我时发烫的额头和颤抖的嘴唇。

我沿着当年的路往东走。我走过平原，穿过山谷，最后到达了当年我们一起看海的那片海岸。

可他没有在那里。

我找了很久，最后在离海边不远的一个小镇上，找到了他。

他老了。头发白了，背也驼了，画画的手开始发抖。他已经不再是那个穿灰蓝色长衫的年轻画师了，他是一个沉默的、孤僻的、每日只画同一片海的老头。

我站在他的画室门口，犹豫了很久。

他看见我了。

他放下画笔，慢慢走过来。他的眼睛里有一片海，那片海和我记忆里的那片一模一样。

"沉鱼？"他哑着嗓子问。

"沈砚，"我说，"我回来了。"

他没有说话。他只是伸出手，像当年那样，牵住了我的手。

他的手很凉。可我握住的那一刻，我觉得整个世界都安静了下来。

## 十一

预言说，我会在第一百一十九个春天结束。

我今年六十三岁。

还有五十六年。

我不知道我还有没有五十六年。我不知道那个陌生女人的预言会不会应验。我不知道我是不是真的"亲手毁掉了我所爱的一切"——沈砚为了找我，错过了很多机会，失去了很多东西，可他从来没有抱怨过我。

我有时候会想，预言到底是什么？

它是一个命中注定的结局，还是一个可以改变的轨迹？

它是一根绑在我们脖子上的绳子，还是一面我们自己在心里竖起的镜子？

我不知道答案。

可我知道一件事——

我这辈子爱过一个人。他也爱我。这就够了。

至于预言，至于命运，至于那个从未露过面的陌生女人——

去她的。

祖母说过，你信了，你就输了。

我不信。

——**《盐与星》·完**——

# 时之裂隙

## 一

闹钟响起的时候，林晚棠以为自己在做梦。

她躺在雕花拔步床上，月白色的帐幔垂落四周，绣着缠枝莲纹的缎面上洒着稀薄的光。空气里有沉水香的味道，混着初秋微凉的桂花气息。

她坐起身，伸手去摸枕边的手机——指尖触到的是一方冰凉的玉枕。

"小姐醒了？"珠帘外传来丫鬟的声音，接着帘子被撩开，一个梳着双丫髻的小姑娘笑盈盈地走进来，"夫人吩咐了，今日要去城隍庙上香，小姐快些梳洗吧。"

林晚棠怔怔地看着她。

那丫鬟约莫十三四岁，眉眼清秀，穿一件豆绿色的褙子，腕上戴着一只细细的银镯。她的脸在林晚棠的记忆里逐渐变得清晰——

是青杏。她小时候的贴身丫鬟，后来在战乱中走散了，她再也没有见过她。

"青杏。"林晚棠脱口叫出这个名字，声音发颤。

丫鬟愣了一下，旋即笑了："小姐怎么叫奴婢的小名？夫人说过，进了府里就要改口的。"

林晚棠环顾四周。

这是林家老宅。她出生的地方，十二岁前住的地方。墙上挂着的那幅《秋山晚照图》，是她五岁时外祖父送的；窗下那张黄花梨的小书案，是她七岁练字时用的；案头那只青釉笔洗，是父亲从越州带回来的。

她记得这些。她记得这一切。

可这些，都已经是七十年前的事了。

## 二

林晚棠出生于一九二三年，江南水乡的丝绸世家。

她是长房嫡女，自幼聪慧，过目不忘，十六岁便能诗会画。十八岁那年嫁给了门当户对的沈家公子，沈砚舟。新婚前夜，母亲拉着她的手说，嫁过去要贤淑，要恭谨，要相夫教子。

她没有相夫教子。

一九四九年后，沈家败落，沈砚舟在运动中不堪受辱，投河自尽。她带着两个孩子辗转流离，从江南到岭南，从岭南到塞北，最后在一个小城的纺织厂做了三十年的女工。

她活到九成四岁，送走了两个儿子，最后的几年里，眼睛渐渐看不清了，耳朵也背了，一个人坐在院子里的藤椅上，常常会想起年轻时候的事。

她常常想，如果那时候她做了不同的选择，故事会不会不一样。

二〇一七年冬天，她在睡梦中安然离世。

而现在，她躺在一九三五年的秋天，十八岁，尚未出嫁。

## 三

梳妆台前，林晚棠盯着铜镜里的自己。

镜中的女子乌发如云，面若春花，一双杏眼里盛着盈盈秋水。这是一张她已经很久很久没有见过的脸——或者说，这是她母亲珍藏到八十年代才在兵燹中遗失的那张画像上的脸。

"小姐今日想梳什么髻？"青杏一边为她绞干头发，一边问道。

"……堕马髻吧。"她听见自己的声音回答，像是另一个人在说话。

堕马髻，是她出嫁前最后一次梳的发髻。那之后的一生里，她梳的都是最简单的齐耳短发，为了便于劳作。

青杏笑嘻嘻地应了，手脚麻利地为她挽发、插簪。林晚棠看着镜中的自己一点点变得完整，心里却翻涌着惊涛骇浪。

她重生了。或者说，她回到了过去。

她不知道这是机会，还是玩笑。

但她知道，明年，沈家就要来提亲了。后年，她就会嫁给沈砚舟。再过十几年，他就会死。

她闭上眼。

那些藏在记忆深处的痛苦，突然变得清晰——

沈砚舟死的那天，也是秋天。她从纺织厂下班回来，推开门，看见他挂在房梁上，脚尖离地三寸。桌上放着一封遗书，写着"吾妻亲启"，只有四个字：

"来世再见。"

她把两个孩子托给邻居，独自去河边坐了一夜。

后来她还是活下来了。为了孩子。后来孩子也走了，她还是活下来了。为了什么呢？她也说不清。也许只是因为死太需要勇气，而她已经把所有的勇气都用在了活下去上。

## 四

上香回来的路上，马车经过沈家门前。

林晚棠撩起车帘的一角，看见那扇朱漆大门，门楣上悬着"沈府"二字的匾额。门前的两棵桂花树开得正盛，金黄的细碎花朵铺了一地。

青杏笑道："小姐在看什么？沈家的公子可是城里出了名的才子呢，听说明年要下场考试了。"

沈砚舟。

林晚棠的手紧紧攥住车帘。

她想起了他。想起新婚之夜他挑起她的红盖头时微微颤抖的手，想起他给她念自己写的诗时认真的神情，想起他在批斗会上被人按着头却一声不吭的脊背。

他是个好人。可好人没有好报。

如果她不嫁给他，他会不会活得更久一些？

可如果不嫁给他，她还会遇到他吗？还会爱上他吗？

她不知道。

她只知道，她必须做点什么。

## 五

"小姐，小姐？"青杏的声音打断了她的思绪，"夫人问您，明日沈家花宴，您去不去？"

林晚棠回过神来。

她看着车窗外飘过的桂花，忽然轻轻笑了。

去。怎么能不去。

她已经活了九十四岁，经历过战争、饥荒、运动、死亡，她还有什么可怕的？她有的是时间，有的是智慧，有的是一颗被岁月磨砺得坚硬又柔软的心。

她不会再让悲剧重演。

哪怕这是梦，她也要在梦里走出一条不同的路来。

## 六

沈家花宴设在后园。

园中遍植芍药，此时虽已过了盛花期，仍有几丛开得正好，粉白相间，如云似霞。

林晚棠随母亲入席，眼角余光却一直在寻找那道熟悉的身影。

然后她看见了他。

沈砚舟站在池边的水榭里，穿一件月白色的长衫，正与几个朋友说笑。他生得清俊，眉目疏朗，笑起来的时候眼角微微弯起，像一弯新月。

二十岁的沈砚舟。

他还没有遇到她，还没有经历后来那些苦难。他的眼睛还是亮的，还没有学会沉默。

林晚棠的心脏漏跳了一拍。

她听见自己心底有一个声音说：就这样吧，就这样吧，就这样过完一生也好。

可另一个声音说：不。你知道他是怎么死的。你知道你们的两个孩子是怎么在饥荒中夭折的。你知道后半生的每一场苦难。

你必须救他。

"林姑娘？"

一个清朗的声音在身侧响起。

林晚棠转头，沈砚舟不知何时走到了她面前。他微微躬身，礼貌地笑道："在下沈砚舟。方才姑娘独自站在此处，神情似乎有些恍惚，可是身体不适？"

他的眼睛很干净，没有一丝阴翳。

林晚棠看着这张她爱了一辈子、又失去了一辈子的脸，忽然笑了。

"无事。"她说，"只是见这芍药开得好，想起了两句诗。"

"哦？"他来了兴致，"不知姑娘想起了什么诗？"

林晚棠垂下眼，轻轻吟道：

"庭前芍药妖无格，池上芙蕖净少情。
唯有牡丹真国色，花开时节动京城。"

沈砚舟的眼睛亮了。

"好诗！"他击节赞叹，"只是这芍药听了，怕是要不高兴了。"

林晚棠也笑了："芍药若是有灵，想必会说——我虽无格，却也开得热闹。"

两人相视而笑。

那一刻，时光仿佛倒流回了一切尚未发生的最初，一切都还来得及。

## 七

林晚棠开始布局。

她知道历史的走向，知道哪些事会发生，知道哪些人可以信任，哪些人必须远离。她不再是一个十八岁的少女，而是一个活了九十四岁的灵魂，借着这具年轻的躯体，重新书写自己的命运。

她劝父亲早早将一部分家财捐给城中的善堂，换取一个乐善好施的名声。

她让母亲在乱世来临前，将家中珍藏的字画古籍转移到乡下的亲戚家中。

她在与沈砚舟的相处中，一点一点地影响他——她劝他不要做官，不要卷入政治，只做一个纯粹的学者；她劝他多读些实用的书，比如医学，比如农学；她劝他无论如何，要活下去。

沈砚舟一开始觉得奇怪，后来渐渐被她折服。

"晚棠，"有一次他问她，"你为什么总是让我活下去？"

林晚棠沉默了很久。

"因为，"她说，"我曾经弄丢过你一次。"

"弄丢？"

"梦里。"她笑了笑，眼眶却红了，"在梦里，我弄丢过你。我不想再弄丢一次。"

沈砚舟看着她，忽然握住了她的手。

"那这一次，我不会再让你弄丢了。"

## 八

一九四九年，解放大军渡江。

林家安然无恙地迎来了新社会。因为早年的善名，他们没有被划为恶霸地主；因为沈砚舟的学者身份，他没有被批斗致死。

他们住在老宅里，院子里的桂花树年年开花。

后来国家号召支援边疆，沈砚舟主动报名，带着林晚棠去了西北。在那片广袤的土地上，他成了一名受人尊敬的大夫，她成了一名小学老师。

他们没有再生孩子——林晚棠不想再经历丧子之痛。他们收养了几个孤儿，视如己出。

沈砚舟活到了一九九七年，无疾而终。

临终前，他握着林晚棠的手，笑着说："晚棠，我这一生，过得很好。"

林晚棠伏在他床边，泪流满面。

"我知道。"她说，"我也是。"

## 九

沈砚舟走后，林晚棠又活了二十年。

她看着孩子们长大，看着他们结婚生子，看着这个国家一天天变得更好。她常常坐在院子里的藤椅上晒太阳，想起年轻时候的事，想起那些如果——

如果她没有重生，如果她按照原来的轨迹过完一生，她会怎么样？

她知道答案。她会失去一切，会在痛苦中度过余生，会成为一个孤独的老人，在某个冬天的夜里悄然离世。

可她重生了。

她改变了命运。

她救了她爱的人，也救了她自己。

## 十

二〇一七年冬天，林晚棠在睡梦中安然离世。

享年九十九岁。

临终前，她拉着孙儿的手，轻轻地说："若有来生，我还要遇见你祖父。"

孙儿问她："奶奶，您这一生，过得好吗？"

林晚棠笑了，眼角的皱纹里盛满了阳光。

"好。"她说，"很好。"

她闭上了眼睛。

这一次，她没有遗憾。

# 鳞片下的困惑

古铜色的鳞片在晨光中微微颤动，烬渊从它盘踞了三百年的岩床上缓缓抬起头。

洞穴深处，那座由金币、宝石、古籍和不知名骸骨堆砌成的小山依然闪闪发光——一如既往地，忠实地，沉默地。

烬渊盯着那堆宝藏看了很久。

它是一条上了年纪的火龙。曾经的它会为了半块金砖和一队矮人商旅大战三天三夜，会因为某个人类国王胆敢觊觎它的蓝宝石而烧毁整座城堡。那时候，收集财宝是有意义的，是热血沸腾的，是关乎荣耀与领地的。

可现在……

烬渊叹了口气，火焰从鼻息中泄出，在金币堆上烫出一小片焦黑。它立刻用爪子把那块金币翻了个面，把焦痕藏到下面。

三百年前它还能把这当作有趣的事。现在却只觉得——

烦。

它缓缓站起身来，爪子在地面的岩石上留下深深的刻痕。它走到宝藏前，用鼻尖轻轻拱了拱一枚镶着月光石的银戒指。戒指滚落下来，叮当一声掉在一本摊开的羊皮书卷上。那是某位死去的法师的日记，写满了烬渊看不懂的符文。

它记得这枚戒指。曾经有一位精灵公主戴着它哭泣，请求烬渊放过她的族人。烬渊没有心软——那时候它还很年轻，还不懂得什么叫做心软。精灵公主最后死在洞穴外的雪地里，而烬渊得到了这枚戒指。

可它现在拿这枚戒指做什么呢？

戴吗？爪子太粗，套不进去。

熔了吗？它又不是铁匠。

扔了吗？

烬渊愣了一下。

它从未想过"扔掉"这个选项。三百年来，每一件东西都是它"赢"来的，是它力量的证明，是它存在的勋章。扔掉它们，等于扔掉自己的过去。

可它已经很久没有清点过自己的宝藏了。

上一次清点是什么时候？五十年前？还是八十年前？它已经记不清了。它只是不断地收集，收集，洞穴快要装不下了，它就把东西堆得更高，更高，再更高。可堆得再高，山还是山，金币还是金币，它躺在上面睡觉时，其实感觉不到任何区别。

它又叹了口气。

烬渊走出洞穴，站在悬崖边缘。远处的天空是淡青色的，有几只它叫不出名字的小鸟飞过。它认得它们小时候的样子——那时候它们刚刚学会飞行，翅膀短短的，叫声尖尖的。现在它们已经长得很优雅了。

它意识到自己已经很久没有看过天空了。

什么时候开始的呢？大概是两百年前，烬渊得到了那面能映照未来的银镜。它在镜子里看到了自己的未来——无尽的金币，无尽的洞穴，无尽的沉睡。它当时觉得这就是一条龙应该拥有的命运，多么辉煌，多么圆满。

可现在它站在悬崖边，看着远处飞过的鸟群，忽然想——

那面镜子是不是骗了它？

烬渊回到洞穴，绕着那堆宝藏转了一圈又一圈。它用爪子扒拉着金币，让它们发出哗啦啦的声响。它把头埋进宝石堆里，听它们叮叮当当的碰撞声。它闻了闻那本法师日记，纸张和墨水已经混合成了一种说不清的古老气味。

这些东西曾让它快乐。

现在不会了。

它不知道自己是怎么变成这样的。也许是年纪太大了。也许是洞穴太安静了。也许是——它其实从来就不需要这么多东西，只是三百年里没有人告诉过它这个道理。

烬渊趴在宝藏上，下巴搁在前爪上，尾巴有一下没一下地拍打着地面。它想了很久。

天黑的时候，它做了一个决定。

它从宝藏中叼起了那枚精灵公主的戒指，走出洞穴，在悬崖边挖了一个小小的坑，把它埋了进去。然后它用火焰在旁边的岩石上喷出了一个印记——一个谁也看不懂的符号。

烬渊不知道这个符号是什么意思。它只是觉得应该留下点什么。

接下来的日子里，它每天都会从宝藏中取出一件东西。有时是金币，有时是宝石，有时是某个倒霉冒险者的头盔，有时是一卷看不懂的羊皮书。它把它们埋在悬崖周围的泥土里，或者扔进远处的河里，或者——有一次它把一顶镶满钻石的王冠送给了一只路过的乌鸦，尽管乌鸦根本不在乎钻石，它在乎的是烬渊爪子里那只刚刚死掉的兔子。

烬渊不知道自己在做什么。

它只是觉得，洞穴应该再空一点。

宝藏堆在缓慢地变小。一百年后，它终于从一座山变成了一座小丘。又过了五十年，小丘变成了几堆散落的金币。再过三十年，金币铺满了洞穴的地面，烬渊可以直接躺在岩石上，而不用再睡在财宝上了。

第一次躺在空荡荡的岩床上时，烬渊感觉有点不习惯。它的背有点凉，尾巴不知道该放在哪里。

但它也感觉到了某种久违的轻松。

又过了一百年，烬渊的洞穴终于空了。

只剩下几块它怎么也磨不坏的奇怪金属，还有那面能映照未来的银镜——那面镜子它始终没有扔掉。也许是因为它害怕，也许是因为它还在等待着什么。

烬渊最后一次照那面镜子。

镜子里显示的未来和三百年前一模一样——无尽的金币，无尽的洞穴，无尽的沉睡。

可烬渊现在躺在空荡荡的洞穴里，看着镜中的画面，忽然觉得那个未来离它已经很远了。

它把镜子挂在洞穴的入口处，面朝外面的天空。

然后它走出去，第一次——真正意义上的第一次——张开翅膀，飞向了它从未去过的远方。

它不知道远方有什么。

但它知道——

它的背上不会再压着金币了。

# The Night Gallery

The Hannigan Museum of Fine Art stood silent on the corner of Fifth and Whitmore, its limestone facade bathed in the amber glow of streetlights. To the daytime visitors who wandered its halls, it was simply another modest gallery in a city of modest galleries, home to works that were pleasant but unremarkable.

But Mara Hannigan, the seventy-three-year-old curator who had inherited the building from her grandfather, knew better.

She arrived each evening at precisely ten o'clock, just as the last security guard clocked out, carrying her leather satchel and a thermos of chamomile tea. She never stayed past midnight. Never. That was the arrangement.

"Good evening, Mother," whispered the woman in the gilded frame near the entrance.

Mara paused before the portrait. In daylight, she appeared as a stern matriarch in Victorian dress, a backdrop of dark velvet behind her. Now, in the dim emergency lighting, the woman—Elena Hannigan, painted in 1887—stepped through the frame as though it were a doorway.

"You look tired, child," Elena said, brushing invisible dust from her sleeve. "You've been spending too much time with the living."

"The living pay the bills, Grandmother."

"Hmph." Elena's eyes, deep brown and sharp despite her painted existence, softened. "Go on, then. They're waiting for you."

Mara walked deeper into the gallery, past the landscapes and still lifes, past the marble busts that murmured amongst themselves, past the abstract works that pulsed with their own strange rhythms. She stopped before a small painting tucked into an alcove—a moonlit harbor scene, ships bobbing gently on dark water.

"Good evening, Captain," she said softly.

A man materialized from the canvas, salt-streaked beard and weathered coat, his eyes still holding the light of some distant sea. He bowed. "Miss Hannigan. A word, if you have a moment?"

"For you, Captain Aldridge? Always."

"The young couple in the Vermeer reproduction—they've been asking questions again."

Mara sighed. "What sort of questions?"

"The dangerous sort." The captain glanced back at his painting. "The woman—she wants to know if she can leave. Permanently. Says she never asked to be reproduced, says she has a soul that belongs to her alone."

Mara was quiet for a long moment. The emergency lights hummed above her.

"I'll speak with her," she said finally. "But Captain—you know I can't make promises."

"I know." He vanished back into his frame, and the harbor grew still once more.

Mara continued her rounds. In the Impressionist room, a ballerina from a Degas study was teaching three cherubs the proper position for a pirouette. In the hall of portraits, two gentlemen from rival landscapes had finally settled their hundred-year dispute over which of their painted regions received more rainfall. And in the small Rothko-inspired piece at the gallery's heart, colors shifted and conversed in languages that had no names.

She found the young couple in question near the back—a reproduction, yes, but rendered so faithfully that the figures within had developed consciousness of their own. The woman was beautiful, her face lifted toward an unseen window, pearls catching impossible light.

"You wished to speak with me?" Mara asked.

The woman turned. Up close, her eyes held a depth that no reproduction should possess.

"I want to be real," she said simply. "I want to walk into the world and feel the rain. I want to know what it's like to exist outside this frame."

Mara sat down on the small bench between the paintings. "I understand. Truly, I do. But you were made from something that already existed—a living woman's face, a living woman's hands. You are a kind of miracle, my dear, but you are not... you are not wholly original."

"Then what am I?"

Mara thought of her grandmother, who had lived in her frame for over a century. She thought of Captain Aldridge, who still mourned the sea he could only watch. She thought of herself, a child who had grown up believing the walls of this building were simply walls.

"You are a possibility," Mara said gently. "A what-if, given breath. You are everything the original could have been, in some other life."

The woman was silent. Beside her, the man in the painting reached for her hand—a gesture that the original artist had never painted, that had developed on its own over decades of silent longing.

"And is that enough?" the woman asked.

Mara reached into her satchel and withdrew a small velvet pouch. From it, she produced a single pearl—the very pearl the woman in the painting wore. It had fallen from the frame years ago, during a minor earthquake, and Mara had kept it ever since.

"It will have to be," Mara said. "For now."

She placed the pearl in the woman's painted palm, and for a moment—just a moment—the woman's fingers seemed to close around it, seemed to hold something real.

"Thank you," the woman whispered.

Mara checked her watch. Eleven forty-five. Time to go.

She walked back through the gallery, nodding to the figures who nodded in return. At the entrance, Elena Hannigan waited for her, arms folded.

"You're too kind," Elena said. "It will be your undoing."

"Maybe," Mara said. She kissed her fingertips and pressed them to the cool surface of the frame. "Goodnight, Grandmother."

"Goodnight, child. Mind the living tomorrow."

Mara locked the gallery door behind her and stepped out into the cold night. Above her, the moon hung heavy and low, and somewhere in the city, she passed by a reproduction of the very painting she had just left—hanging in a coffee shop, its figures frozen and unaware, never to know what it meant to breathe.

She smiled, just a little, and walked home through the sleeping streets.

Behind her, in the dark gallery, the paintings began their nightly dance—rehearsing, as they always did, the small rebellions and quiet devotions of a world that existed only when no one was watching.

Write about a god desperately trying to get their chosen hero to follow the path they set out for them. In total around 1200 words.

# The Weight of a Whisper

The first time Aelith chose him, Korin was seven years old and crying over a dead sparrow in the meadow behind his mother's cottage.

Aelith had watched the boy kneel in the grass, his small shoulders shaking, and had felt the unmistakable pull of a mortal soul that burned brighter than the others. The god of small mercies had descended on wings of moth-wing silver and knelt beside the child, pointing out how the sparrow's feathers would feed the ants, how the insects would feed the moles, how nothing ever truly ended—only transformed.

Korin had looked up at Aelith with wide, wet eyes and whispered, *I want to help things transform.*

A god's heart is not supposed to flutter. But Aelith's had.

---

By the time Korin was sixteen, Aelith had laid out the path as clearly as a river lays out its own course. The boy would apprentice to the village healer. He would discover the old texts in the temple library, the ones written in the first tongue that only those with divine favor could read. He would journey to the capital. He would study under Master the Maker, the brilliant but reclusive alchemist who had once, in his youth, been the hero of another god entirely. He would learn the secret of the Unraveling—the ancient art of binding life-force to matter—and he would use it to cure the wasting sickness that had begun creeping through the southern provinces.

Aelith had seen it. All of it. The vision had burned behind their eyes for nine years like a second sun.

And now Korin was standing in the meadow behind his mother's cottage—the same meadow, the same wild thyme scenting the air—and saying *no*.

"I don't want to be a healer, Aelith."

The god felt something crack inside their chest, a fissure so small no mortal would have noticed it. But Aelith noticed. Gods notice everything.

"The path is yours," Aelith said carefully, keeping their voice steady. They were sitting cross-legged in the grass, deliberately small, deliberately mortal-shaped, because Korin had stopped being able to look at them in their true form three years ago. It made something inside Aelith weep, but gods do not weep. That is not what gods do. "I have only ever shown you the path. I have never once told you to walk it."

"Except you have." Korin laughed, but it was not a kind laugh. "Every dream. Every coincidence. Every time something went right for me and wrong for everyone else. Don't tell me that wasn't you. The sparrow, Aelith. The *sparrow*. You've been nudging me toward that meadow since I was *seven years old*."

Aelith said nothing.

"I want to be a poet." Korin's chin lifted. Stubborn. So stubborn. "I want to travel. I want to write about the things I see, not bind them into shapes someone else decided they should take. The wasting sickness is real and it's terrible, but there are other healers. There is only one me, and I want to spend that me on something I chose."

The fissure in Aelith's chest grew. They had known, gods help them, they had known this would happen. The brightest souls were always the ones most likely to refuse. They burned too hot to be herded.

"You would let thousands die," Aelith said softly, "for the sake of your own happiness."

"No." Korin's voice shook, and Aelith hated how much they loved the boy for shaking, for not being able to say it without trembling. "I would trust that the world is larger than one man's life, and that some other hero—someone who actually *wanted* the path—would rise to meet it. Maybe one of your other chosen ones, Aelith. Maybe someone you'd see if you weren't so busy looking at me."

The god flinched.

It was true. It was true and Korin knew it was true and Aelith knew it was true and the truth of it sat between them in the wild thyme like a third figure, breathing.

"I chose you," Aelith whispered. "I saw you, Korin. I saw what you could become. I saw you cure the sickness. I saw you save—"

"You saw what *you* wanted." Korin stood up. He was taller than Aelith now, had been for two years, and the god had never gotten used to it. "And maybe you're right. Maybe I'm exactly the person you saw. But that person would be built on a lie. I'd be a poem someone else wrote. And I can't—I *can't*, Aelith. Don't you see? If I do the great thing because you pushed me into it, what does the great thing even mean?"

Aelith saw.

Aelith had always seen.

That was the terrible part. That was the part that cracked them open like an egg. They had seen this version of Korin too, in the deepest folds of the vision, the one who walked away, the one who became a poet in a small town and died in obscurity at fifty-three with nothing but a chest of unsent letters and a single published book of verses that nobody read. They had seen it, and they had hoped—

They had *hoped*.

Gods are not supposed to hope. Hope is for mortals, hope is the engine of all those small bright choices that lead to such unpredictable places. Hope is the antithesis of prophecy. Aelith should have known. Aelith *had* known, from the very first moment they felt their heart flutter over a weeping boy and a dead sparrow.

Hope had been a mistake.

"Then go," Aelith said. Their voice came out strange and small. "Go be a poet. Go see the world. I will not—Korin. I will not push you again."

The boy looked at the god for a long moment. The afternoon light caught the silver in his hair—the silver that had begun appearing three years ago, the first sign that a mortal had been touched too long by a divine presence, the mark of Aelith's lingering fingerprints on his soul. It would never fade. That, Aelith could not undo.

"I'm sorry," Korin said. And he meant it. That was the worst part of all. He meant it.

"I know," Aelith said. "I know, child. Go."

He went.

---

Aelith stayed in the meadow until the stars came out. They did not weep, because gods do not weep. But the wild thyme around them wilted, just a little, and the moths in the hedge did not come out that night, and somewhere in the southern provinces a healer who was not Korin would die trying to learn the Unraveling, and a sickness would take root that would not be cured for a hundred and seven years.

All because a god had loved a boy too much to see him clearly, and not enough to let him go.

In a small rented room in a city two hundred miles away, a young man with a streak of silver in his hair sat down at a desk, dipped a quill in ink, and began to write the first poem of what would become a small, strange, beautiful book that almost nobody read.

Its title was *The Meadow*.

Its dedication read: *For the one who saw me, and let me choose.*

And on the dedication page, pressed into the paper like a watermark no printer could explain, there was the faint impression of moth wings.

# شايٌ مع الأطياف

كان مقعد أيوب الخشبي القديم في زاوية المقهى لا يزال محتفظًا بتلك الحفرة الصغيرة التي حفرها طرفُ سكينه ذات مساء، حين كان يقلّب في دفتر ملاحظاته ويُصمّم على ورقٍ مشوّش خطوطَ روايةٍ لم تكتمل قطّ. وحين دخلتُ المقهى ذاتَ عصرِ خميس، وجدتُ المقعدَ مشغولاً.

لم يُفاجئني ذلك.

حين رفعَ رأسه ورآني، ابتسم تلك الابتسامة التي أعرفها، ابتسامةُ من يعرف أنّك ستصل متأخرًا دائمًا. كان يرتدي قميصَه الكحليّ ذا الأزرار الناقصة، تمامًا كما كان يرتديه حين كنتُ أزوره في المستشفى قبل سنوات، حين كانت يداه قد صارتا شفافتين تحت ضوء النافذة الكبيرة.

— أخوك أبو الأشباح، هكذا سمّاك ذات مرّة، قال وهو يدفع لي كأسًا من الشاي كان قد أعدّه مسبقًا، يتصاعد منه بخارٌ هشّ.

جلستُ قبالتَه. المقعدُ الخشبيّ كان دافئًا على نحوٍ غريب، كأنّه يحتفظ بحرارة جسدٍ لم يعُد موجودًا.

— ظننتك لن تأتي اليوم، قلتُ.

— ظننتك لن تأتي أبدًا، قال وهو يضحك ضحكةً خفيفةً لا يكاد يسمعها أحد سوانا.

كان أيوب صديقي الوحيد الذي لم يكن يخاف من صمتي. كنا نجلس ساعاتٍ أحيانًا بلا أن نتبادل كلمة، يقرأ هو كتابًا عن الميثولوجيا السريانية وأنا أقرأ نصوصي القديمة في دفترٍ أسوّده بالحبر. وحين يُملي عليّ فكرةً عن كتابٍ جديد، كان يهمس بها بصوتٍ يكاد يكون تحذيرًا:

— اكتبها بسرعة يا صديقي، فالأفكارُ كالسمك، إذا لم تُمسكها في لحظتها تعفّنت في يدك.

لم يَكتب هو شيئًا يُذكر، رغم أنّه كان يملأ دفاتره بخطوطَ صغيرةً متشابكة، تخطيطاتٌ لرواياتٍ عن مدن لم يزرها إلّا في أحلامه. وحين سألتُه ذات مرّة لماذا لا ينشرها، قال إنّ الكتابةَ أشبهُ ببناء بيتٍ في الهواء: إن لم تجد أساسًا متينًا له، فسيُسحق تحت ثقل ما بَنَيت.

ثمّ مات.

لم يَمت في حادثٍ مأساويّ كما تظنّ حين تسمع رواياتِ الموت في قصص الأصدقاء. ماتَ بهدوءٍ مؤلم، في سرير المستشفى، وأنا أُملي عليه رسالةَ الوداع التي قال إنها ستكون إحدى فصول كتابٍ لن يُنشر أبدًا.

بعد موته بأسبوعين، رأيته أوّل مرّة. كنتُ عائدًا من المقبرة، وقد بدأ المطر يهطل على ظهر ياقتي، حين رأيتُ واقفًا تحت شجرة الجميز في شارعنا القديم. لم أكن أعرف أنّ الأشباح تبلل، لكنّه كان مبللاً، يتساقط من كمّيه قميصه ماءٌ رماديّ. وحين ناديتُ باسمه، رفع يده وقال:

— تعال يا صديقي، عندي فكرةٌ.

ومنذ ذلك الحين، نلتقي. أحيانًا في هذا المقهى، أحيانًا في مكتبة المدينة العامّة التي كان يحبّ رائحة الكتب القديمة فيها، وأحيانًا تحت شجرة الجميز. نحتسي الشاي ونتبادل الأفكار، وأنا أكتب ما يُمليه عليّ، لأنّني الوحيد الذي يستطيع سماع صوته، ولأنّ الموتَ ليس عذرًا كي لا تكتمل الأفكار.

— أتعرف ما الذي اكتشفته؟ سألني اليوم وهو يلفّ ساقَه على ساق.

— ماذا؟

— أنّ الأشباح ليست حبيسة المكان الذي ماتت فيه، بل حبيسة القصّة التي لم تُروَ عنه.

نظرتُ إليه طويلًا. كان ضوءُ المقهى الأصفر يتسلّل إلى عينيه البنيّتين، فيجعلهما تبدوان كنافذتين مفتوحتين على بحرٍ بارد.

— هل تنوي رَويَها؟ سألت.

ابتسم، ودفع كأسَه الفارغة ناحيتَه بطرفِ إصبعه. كانت الكأس فارغةً تمامًا، لكنّ سطحَها كان لا يزال رطبًا، كأنّ شيئًا ما كان يشرب من الجانب الآخر منها، من عالمٍ لا نراه.

— ما زلتُ أحاول إقناعَ نفسي بذلك، قال.

ثمّ استدارَ ونظرَ إلى النافذة، حيث كانت الشمسُ تميلُ نحو الغروب كأنّها ستُلقي بنفسها في النهر الذي يجري خلف المقهى. ورأيتُ عبرَ الزجاج، لوهلة، شخصًا يقفُ على الرصيف المقابل. كان طويلًا نحيلًا، يرتدي قميصًا كحليًّا بأزرار ناقصة. حدّق فيّ لحظة، ثمّ استدار ومشى بعيدًا.

حين عدتُ بناظريّ إلى المقعد المقابل، كان المقعدُ فارغًا. لكنّ الكأسَ كانت لا تزال دافئة.

لم أكن قد أنهيتُ فكرةَ الفصلِ الذي كان قد بدأ يُمليه عليّ. أمسكتُ دفتري، وبدأتُ أكتب. وسألتُ في سرّي: متى سأعود لأجده جالسًا هناك، وعلى شفتيه تلك الابتسامةُ التي تقول إنّ الصديقَ الحقيقيّ لا يموت حقًا، بل يكتفي بأن يُصبح أكثرَ هدوءًا، وأكثرَ حضورًا، وأقربَ ممّا تظنّ.

وفي ذلك المساء، حين أغلقتُ دفتري وخرجتُ من المقهى، وجدتُ على الرصيف المقابلِ أثرَ أقدامٍ رطبة، كأنّ أحدًا كان يمشي تحت المطر قبل لحظات، ولم يَجفّفها الزمن بعد.

# The Prince Who Sold His Shadow

The bargain was struck at the edge of the kingdom, where the mist from the Hollow Sea curled up against the cliffs like fingers reaching for something to hold.

Prince Aldric stood before the figure wrapped in gray, feeling the salt wind tug at his cloak. Behind him, the marble spires of Caerwyn caught the dying sun, and somewhere in those towers, his mother was setting out his evening tea, not yet knowing he would not return for it.

"You understand what is being asked," the figure said. Its voice came from everywhere and nowhere, as though the mist itself had learned to speak.

Aldric swallowed. He understood.

He had been born in a world of sunlight. His shadow had been his companion since his first steps—a faithful, darker twin that lengthened with the setting sun, shortened with the dawn, and in the bright noon stretched beneath him like a pool of cool water. He had talked to it as a child. Confessed secrets to it. Watched it dance with his own movements in the long candlelit halls.

Without it, he was told, he would step into the other world as nothing more than light and flesh. He would cast no reflection in mirrors. He would leave no footprints in snow. He would be unable to hide beneath any tree or awning, because the sun would pass through him and through everything, and he would be seen, always, as he truly was.

"I understand," Aldric said.

"Then."

The figure raised a hand that was not a hand, and Aldric felt something loosen at his feet. He looked down.

His shadow was still there. But it was *separated*—a dark shape standing an inch from his boots, trembling like a leaf. It turned, and Aldric saw that it had taken his own features, his own eyes, his own expression of bewildered grief. It looked up at him and mouthed something he could not hear.

"I'm sorry," he whispered.

The shadow nodded once, then stepped backward, and backward again, growing smaller, and was folded into the gray figure's cloak like a letter being slipped into an envelope.

The world *shifted*.

Aldric felt the ground beneath him change. The grass became softer, almost luminous. The air tasted of rain that had not yet fallen. When he looked down, he saw nothing where his feet met the earth—no mark, no shade, just the faint glow of skin against the strange, pale blades.

"You may go," said the figure, already fading. "But know this. The one you have given will walk back into your old world wearing your face. He will sit on your throne. He will speak with your mother's voice. He will learn to want what you once wanted. And you, prince, will spend the rest of your days in a place where the sun never sets, wondering if the thing that wears your name is happier than you ever were."

Aldric opened his mouth to ask how long he had to decide whether to return—how long he had before he forgot the taste of his mother's tea, the sound of his own name spoken by someone who loved him.

But the figure was gone.

He walked.

Ahead of him, the new world opened like a flower made of glass. Cities of suspended light drifted in a sky that never darkened. People passed him on roads that gave off a faint chiming underfoot, and none of them cast shadows either, and some of them, he realized with a slow and terrible recognition, were watching him the way a child watches a wound.

Among them, he thought, were others who had made bargains. Others who had stood on cliffs and felt the salt wind, and given up the only twin they had ever known.

He walked on, and the sun that did not set burned warmly against his skin, and the light passed through him without resistance, and he was seen, fully, as he truly was.

And somewhere behind him, in the marble halls of Caerwyn, a prince who wore his face was sitting down to tea with his mother, and smiling, and she could not tell the difference at all.

# 最後の一つの願い

川辺の小さな村に、蓮（れん）という名の老婆が住んでいた。年は九十二。髪は雪のように白く、背は丸まりながらも、瞳だけは不思議と澄んでいた。

ある晩、蓮が裏の井戸で水を汲んでいると、井戸の底から淡い光が立ち昇った。渦を巻きながら形を成したのは、銀色の鱗をまとった老人だった。

「老婆よ。私は千年を生きた龍神じゃ。そなたの善い行いに報いるため、一つだけ願いを叶えてやろう」

蓮は手桶を井戸の縁に置き、龍神を見上げた。

「なんじゃと？」

「一つだけ、何でも。叶えてやろう」

蓮はしばらく黙った。若い頃なら、何を願っただろう。失った夫の命を。戦で逝った息子の帰還を。あるいは、過ぎ去りし日々の美しさすら。

しかし、彼女はただ静かに首を横に振った。

「結構じゃ」

龍神は目を丸くした。

「ええっ？」

「のう、龍神様。老婆は九十二まで生きた。嫁にも恵まれ、孫にも恵まれ、ひい孫にも恵まれた。畑を耕し、機を織り、飯を焚いて、皆に食べてもらった。思う存分生きたよ」

「し、しかし……」

「一つだけ願いを叶えられるとしたら、それが叶った後が怖いわい」

蓮はふっと微笑んだ。皺だらけの顔に、柔和な光が宿る。

「願いが叶ったら、また欲が出るじゃろう。欲が出たら、叶えられん時に嘆く。嘆けば、今あるものが霞んでしまう。今あるものが霞んでしまえば、それこそ勿体ないのう」

龍神は言葉を失った。千年生きて、数多の願いを聞いてきた。黄金を求めた者。不老不死を求めた者。死んだ者の蘇りを求めた者。どれもみな、渇いた心に水を求めるように切実だった。

「ひとつだけ言うならのう」

蓮は井戸の縁に腰を下ろした。

「明日もこうして水が汲めますように。それだけじゃ」

「……それだけ、か」

「それだけあれば、飯が焚ける。飯が焚ければ、明日も隣の花ばあに届けられる。花ばあは足が悪いからのう」

龍神は長い間、ただ蓮を見つめていた。銀の鱗が、夜明けの光を受けて静かに揺れた。

「……わかった」

龍神は静かに微笑んだ。

「そなたの願いは、すでに叶っておる。明日の水は、明日も湧く。そなたの足は、明日も動く。そなたの心は、明日も温かい」

蓮は目を細めた。

「そうじゃな。なら、何も言うことはないわい」

龍神が井戸の底へと沈んでいく。蓮は手桶をかつぎ、いつも通りゆっくりと家路についた。東の空が、薄く白み始めていた。

---

翌朝も、蓮は井戸に水を汲みに行った。いつもの水。いつもの重み。いつもの朝。

花ばあに湯気の立つ粥を届けに行く時、蓮は小さく呟いた。

「龍神様、ありゃったのう」

井戸の底で、銀色の鱗が微かに光った気がした。

けれど、それはきっと、朝日の反射だったのだろう。
