# **Những Lớp Của Câu Chuyện**

Tôi đã viết rất nhiều câu chuyện trong đời mình, nhưng chưa bao giờ tôi kể cho ai nghe câu chuyện này. Có lẽ vì nó bắt đầu vào một đêm mưa cách đây đã lâu, khi tôi còn là một cô gái mười tám tuổi ngồi co ro trong quán cà phê cuối phố, chờ một người không bao giờ đến.

Người đó gửi cho tôi một lá thư, viết trên giấy ngà vàng ố, với nét chữ run rẩy của một bàn tay già nua:

*"Con gái của ta ơi, nếu con đọc được những dòng này, hãy tìm cuốn sách trong hộp gỗ dưới gầm giường bà ngoại con. Trong đó có câu chuyện mà ông cố của con đã kể cho ông nội con, ông nội đã kể cho bà con, và bà con đã hứa sẽ kể lại cho con. Bây giờ, nó thuộc về con."*

Tôi đã tìm thấy cuốn sách đó. Bìa da bong tróc, trang giấy đã ố vàng, nhưng câu chuyện bên trong thì vẫn sống động như ngày đầu tiên nó được viết ra. Và đây là câu chuyện đó:

---

**Phần thứ nhất — Câu chuyện của ông cố tôi**

Ngày xửa ngày xưa, có một ngôi làng nằm sâu trong rừng, nơi những cây cổ thụ cao vút che kín cả bầu trời. Trong làng có một chàng trai tên Thiện, với đôi mắt buồn như đáy giếng sâu.

Một đêm trăng, Thiện ngồi bên bờ suối và nghe thấy tiếng hát từ dòng nước. Một tiên nữ đang tắm dưới ánh trăng, mái tóc đen dài xõa trên mặt nước như rừng tảo đen. Thiện nín thở, sợ làm kinh động nàng. Nhưng rồi nàng quay lại, và đôi mắt nàng — ôi, đôi mắt nàng sáng hơn cả ánh trăng.

"Ta biết ngươi ở đó," nàng nói, giọng trong veo như suối. "Ngươi đã nhìn ta, vậy ngươi phải chịu lời nguyền: mất đi giọng nói cho đến khi tìm được người yêu ngươi bằng cả tâm hồn."

Thiện mở miệng, nhưng không còn âm thanh nào phát ra. Nàng biến mất, chỉ còn sương đêm và tiếng suối rì rầm.

Thiện đi khắp nơi, gặp gỡ bao cô gái. Nhưng không ai yêu anh — họ chỉ yêu sự im lặng của anh, sự bí ẩn, sự lạ lùng. Không ai yêu *anh*.

Một ngày, anh gặp một bà lão sống trong túp lều trên núi. Bà nhìn anh, và bà khóc.

"Ta nhìn thấy bên trong ngươi," bà nói. "Ngươi mang một vết thương cũ, từ kiếp trước. Ngươi đã từng là người yêu của nàng tiên đó, nhưng ngươi đã phản bội lời thề. Vì vậy, nàng nguyền rủa ngươi. Nhưng ngươi không thể tự phá giải lời nguyền — chỉ có chính nàng mới có thể làm điều đó."

"Làm sao tôi tìm được nàng?" Thiện hỏi trong lòng, biết rằng không ai nghe thấy.

"Hãy kể câu chuyện của ngươi," bà lão đáp. "Kể cho người khác nghe. Và khi câu chuyện đi đủ xa, đến tai ai đó yêu ngươi vì chính ngươi — họ sẽ tìm đến ngươi, và lời nguyền sẽ tan."

Thiện không hiểu, nhưng anh bắt đầu kể. Anh vẽ những bức tranh về nàng tiên, về nỗi buồn của mình. Người ta nhìn tranh, nhưng không ai hiểu. Họ chỉ thấy một người đàn ông câm vẽ về một người tình trong mơ.

Năm tháng trôi qua. Thiện già đi. Rồi một ngày, có một cô gái trẻ đến gần anh. Cô không nhìn tranh, cô nhìn *anh*.

"Anh đang tìm ai vậy?" cô hỏi.

Và Thiện, lần đầu tiên sau ngàn năm, mở miệng, và giọng anh cất lên:

"Tôi đang tìm em."

Lời nguyền tan biến. Nhưng cô gái không phải nàng tiên. Cô chỉ là một người bình thường, đi ngang qua, và bằng cách nào đó, cô đã nghe thấy tiếng nói của một người đàn ông mà không ai khác nghe thấy.

"Em không hiểu câu chuyện của anh," cô nói. "Nhưng em yêu anh."

Và đó là cách lời nguyền được phá giải.

---

**Phần thứ hai — Câu chuyện của ông nội tôi**

Ông nội tôi đọc câu chuyện của ông cố tôi, rồi ông kể cho tôi nghe một câu chuyện khác, mà ông nói là phần tiếp theo:

Nàng tiên kia, sau khi Thiện rời đi, đã khóc rất nhiều. Nàng không muốn nguyền rủa ai. Nàng chỉ muốn được yêu, nhưng vì là tiên, nàng không biết cách yêu của người trần.

Nàng bơi xuống đáy suối, ở đó có một cung điện bằng ngọc. Trong cung điện có một ông lão — vua của loài cá. Ông lão nhìn nàng và nói:

"Con ơi, con đã yêu một người trần, nhưng con không biết yêu đúng cách. Hãy nghe ta kể một câu chuyện."

Ông lão vua cá kể:

*"Ngày xưa, có một con cá vàng bơi trong dòng suối. Nó yêu một bông hoa mọc trên bờ. Mỗi ngày, nó nhìn bông hoa, và bông hoa cũng nghiêng mình về phía nước. Chúng yêu nhau, nhưng không bao giờ chạm được vào nhau.*

*Một ngày, bông hoa rơi xuống nước, và dòng suối đưa nó đi xa. Con cá vàng bơi theo, nhưng không kịp. Nó buồn bã cả đời.*

*Nhưng bông hoa không chết. Nó trôi đến một vùng đất khác, mọc lên thành một cây hoa mới. Và con cá vàng, khi già đi, cũng trôi đến vùng đất đó. Chúng gặp lại nhau, nhưng dưới dạng khác — cá thành đá, hoa thành rêu. Và chúng vẫn ở bên nhau."*

Nàng tiên nghe xong, và hiểu ra: yêu không phải là chiếm hữu, yêu là để người mình yêu được tự do. Cô đã sai khi nguyền rủa Thiện. Cô đã sai khi muốn anh chỉ thuộc về mình.

Vì vậy, cô bơi lên mặt nước, tìm Thiện. Nhưng Thiện đã già, và cô vẫn trẻ. Cô đứng bên anh, nhìn anh nắm tay người vợ mới, và cô mỉm cười.

Cô nói: "Cảm ơn anh đã kể câu chuyện của chúng ta. Nhờ anh, em đã hiểu tình yêu là gì."

Rồi cô biến mất, và không ai nhìn thấy cô nữa.

---

**Phần thứ ba — Câu chuyện của bà ngoại tôi**

Bà ngoại tôi nói: "Câu chuyện chưa kết thúc đâu."

Bà kể tiếp:

Nàng tiên không biến mất. Cô ở lại, nhưng dưới dạng một dòng suối nhỏ chảy qua ngôi làng. Ai uống nước suối đó sẽ nghe thấy tiếng cô cười trong gió.

Một ngày, có một cô gái đi ngang qua suối, dừng lại uống nước. Cô không nghe thấy tiếng cười, nhưng cô cảm thấy bình yên. Cô ngồi bên suối, viết vào sổ tay:

*"Hôm nay tôi uống nước suối, và tôi nhớ về một người tôi từng yêu. Anh ấy đã đi xa, và tôi đã buông tay. Tôi nghĩ mình đã thua, nhưng bây giờ tôi hiểu: tôi không thua, tôi chỉ đang trên đường đi đến một cuộc gặp mới."*

Nàng tiên đọc được dòng chữ đó. Và nàng khóc — lần đầu tiên trong đời tiên, nàng khóc vì hạnh phúc.

Có một cô gái ở dưới phàm trần đã hiểu được điều mà nàng đã mất ngàn năm để hiểu: buông tay không phải là mất, mà là mở ra cánh cửa cho điều mới.

Từ đó, dòng suối chảy mạnh hơn. Và ai uống nước suối đều cảm thấy nhẹ nhõm, như vừa đặt xuống một gánh nặng mà họ mang theo từ lâu lắm rồi.

---

**Phần thứ tư — Câu chuyện của tôi**

Tôi đóng cuốn sách lại. Tôi không tìm thấy hộp gỗ dưới gầm giường bà ngoại — nó đã không còn ở đó. Có lẽ ai đó đã lấy mất, có lẽ nó chưa từng tồn tại, có lẽ tôi đã mơ cả lá thư và cuốn sách này.

Nhưng tôi nhớ từng câu chữ. Và tôi hiểu rằng:

Mỗi người kể câu chuyện của mình, và trong câu chuyện đó có câu chuyện của người khác, và trong câu chuyện của người khác lại có câu chuyện của những người chưa từng gặp. Cứ thế, lớp này chồng lớp khác, như những vòng sóng trên mặt suối.

Có lẽ cuốn sách không nằm dưới gầm giường bà ngoại. Có lẽ nó nằm ở đâu đó — trong tiếng cười của một đứa trẻ, trong nỗi buồn của một người lạ, trong ánh mắt của một người tôi chưa gặp nhưng sẽ gặp.

Tôi đặt bút xuống. Tôi không viết thêm.

Vì tôi biết: câu chuyện này sẽ không bao giờ kết thúc. Ai đó sẽ đọc nó, rồi kể lại, rồi trong câu chuyện của họ sẽ có câu chuyện của tôi, và tôi sẽ lại sống, dù chỉ là trong vài dòng chữ trên giấy.

Và có lẽ — chỉ có lẽ thôi — một ngày nào đó, có ai đó sẽ đọc câu chuyện này, và sẽ đi tìm hộp gỗ dưới gầm giường bà ngoại họ. Và họ sẽ thấy một cuốn sách khác, có câu chuyện khác, nhưng giống y hệt.

Và vòng xoáy ấy sẽ tiếp tục.

---

*Và đây, bạn của tôi, là nơi câu chuyện tạm dừng. Không phải kết thúc — chỉ là dừng lại, để bạn thở, rồi tiếp tục kể câu chuyện của chính bạn.*

# 불의 대지: 외로운 늑대의 귀환

## 제1장: 재가 된 고향

카시미르 산맥의 눈보라가 잦아든 뒤, 코도 마을은 마치 거대한 손바닥에 눌린 것처럼 평지에 누워 있었다. 반쯤 무너진 목장栅栏, 그리고 하늘을 향해 벌려진 검은 굴뚝들. 삼백 년 전 이곳은 제국 전쟁의 피난처였고, 전쟁이 끝난 뒤에는 변방의 개척지로서 사람들을 불러들였다. 그러나 그 이름 ‘코도’는 더 이상 누구의 입에서도 나오지 않았다.

‘몰락자’라고 불리는 자들이 나타나기 시작하면서부터였다. 마법이 마력을 잃어가는 시대, 마력은 검과 화약으로 대체되었다. 그러나 마력에 의존해 살아온 노른빛 마족의 후예들은 마력의 감소와 함께 점점 야위어 갔고, 마지막에는 ‘몰락자’라 불리며 변방 마을을 습격해 약탈했다.

나는 카스—모든 걸 잃은 외로운 늖대. 무녀(武女)로서 이름을 날렸던 어머니 ‘레나 코도’의 외아들이다. 어머니는 몰락자 토벌의 선봉에 섰고, 마지막 전투에서 사라졌다. 마을 사람들은 어머니를 영웅이라 불렀지만, 나는 그녀가 돌아오지 않을 거라는 걸 알고 있었다.

“형, 이거 가져가.”

마을 어귀에서 손을 흔드는 꼬마 ‘도리’. 어머니가 사라진 뒤 나를 돌봐준 목동의 아들이다. 호주머니에서 꺼낸 건 낡은 권총—어머니가 쓰던 것. 어머니의 무덤 앞에 놓여 있던 것을 도리가 몰래 챙겨 온 것이다.

“돌려놓아.” 나는 낮게 말했다.

“돌려놓으면 또 거기 묻힐 거잖아.” 도리의 눈이 붉었다. “형이 없으면 난 어떡해?”

대답 대신, 나는 망토를 뒤집어쓰고 말을 몰았다. 서쪽, 해가 지는 방향—몰락자들이 마지막으로 목격된 곳.

---

## 제2장: 노른빛의 무녀

카시미르 평원을 가로지르는 동안, 하늘은 점점 붉은색을 띠었다. 마력의 잔재가 옅게 떠다니는 지역에선 늘 이런 현상이 벌어졌다. 붉은 하늘 아래, 거대한 나무 한 그루가 보였다. 그 나무에는 검은 천이 매달려 있고, 그 천에는 ‘코도’란 글씨가 새겨져 있었다.

‘어머니의 푯말.’

말을 세우고 푯말 앞에 섰을 때, 숲 속에서 인기척이 들렸다.

“혼자 온 거냐, 늖대 씨?”

숲의 그늘에서 나타난 자—노른빛 피부를 가진 ‘몰락자’였지만, 피부를 제외하면 평범한 인간의 모습이었다. 검은 로브, 허리에는 낡은 검 한 자루. 그리고 눈—그 눈에는 광기가 아닌, 슬픔이 서려 있었다.

“마족의 후예.” 나는 손잡이에 손을 얹었다. “무기가 있군.”

“이건 어머니의 유품일 뿐이야.” 그가 검을 뽑지 않았다. 대신, 품에서 낡은 봉투를 꺼냈다. “레나 코도님이 남긴 것이 있다. 너에게 전하라고.”

‘어머니가?’

봉투를 뜯자, 손글씨가 적힌 종이가 나왔다.

> *‘카스에게. 어머니는 너에게 해줄 말이 많아. 하지만 시간이 없어. 외로운 늖대는 무리를 찾아야 해. 노른빛을 두려워하지 마라. 그들도 다만 살아남으려 할 뿐이니.’*

“뭐야, 이게?” 나는 고개를 들었다.

몰락자는 어깨를 으쓱했다. “레나 코도님은 우리와 함께 싸우셨어. 마력으로 문을 열어 우리가 머물 곳을 마련하셨지. 네가 모르는 것들이 있어, 늖대야. 어머니는 영웅이 아니었어—어머니는 역사가 잊어버린 존재였을 뿐이야.”

“뭐라고?”

“코도 마을의 진짜 역사를 알려줄게.” 그가 숲을 가리켰다. “온다면.”

나는 망설였다. 내 어머니가 몰락자와 함께 싸웠다니? 어머니는 항상 “마족의 후예는 위험하다”고 했는데. 하지만 종이를 내려다보며, 어머니의 손글씨를 만지작거렸다. 따뜻했다.

“앞질러 가라.”

몰락자는 씩 웃고, 숲으로 사라졌다.

---

## 제3장: 잊혀진 전쟁의 기억

숲 깊은 곳, 커다란 동굴 입구가 나타났다. 동굴 안은 희미한 빛으로 가득했다—마력의 빛이었다.

“여긴 ‘마력의 보고’라 불리는 곳이야.” 몰락자가 말했다. “삼백 년 전 전쟁 당시, 마족과 인간이 함께 싸웠다. 마족은 마력으로 문을 열어, 인간 군대가 통과할 수 있게 했어. 그 공로로 인간들은 마족에게 ‘변방의 땅’을 약속했다. 그게 바로 카시미르 평원이야.”

“그런데 왜 몰락자가 생겼지?”

“마력이 사라졌으니까.” 그의 목소리가 낮아졌다. “마력에 의존하던 마족은 점점 쇠약해졌고, 인간들은 약속을 잊은 채 마족을 밀어냈어. 그래서 우리는 ‘몰락자’가 됐고, 약탈을 시작했다.”

동굴 안, 벽에는 그림들이 그려져 있었다. 마족과 인간이 함께 싸우는 장면, 서로의 손을 잡는 장면. 그리고 마지막에는—돌아서서 등을 보이는 장면.

“어머니는 이걸 바꾸려 했어.” 몰락자가 말했다. “코도 마을은 마족과 인간이 함께 사는 마을이 되도록 했어. 하지만 어머니가 사라진 뒤, 마을 사람들은 마족을 다시 밀어내기 시작했고.”

나는 벽의 그림을 만지작거렸다. 어머니의 얼굴이 떠올랐다. 어머니가 늘 “무리는 강하다”고 했던 게 기억났다. 어머니는 혼자가 아니었다—어머니는 늘 함께였다.

“네 이름이 뭐지?”

“…‘하루’라고 불러.”

---

## 제4장: 외로운 늖대와 무리

하루와 함께 코도 마을로 돌아왔을 때, 마을은 아비규환이었다. 마을 광장에 사람들과 마족들이 뒤엉켜 싸우고 있었다. 노인들의 비명, 아이들의 울음소리.

“멈춰!” 내가 외쳤다.

하지만 아무도 듣지 않았다. 한 남자가 도끼를 들어 마족 아이를 내려치려는 순간, 나는 권총을 꺼내 그의 앞에 섰다.

“카스?” 남자가 눈을 크게 떴다. “네가 왜—”

“어머니는 너희에게 이렇게 하라고 한 게 아니야.” 나는 말했다. “어머니는 ‘무리를 찾아라’고 했어.”

“무리라니, 마족을 말하는 거냐?”

“그렇다.”

마을이 조용해졌다. 사람들의 표정에는 의문이 가득했다. 하지만 하루가 앞으로 나서며 말을 이었다.

“우리는 적이 아니야. 우리가 필요한 건 이 땅이야. 너희가 필요한 건 우리야. 마력은 사라졌지만, 우리는 너희와 함께 살 수 있어.”

긴 침묵이 흘렀다.

그때, 도리가 광장으로 뛰어 들어왔다. “형! 큰일 났어! 동쪽에서 ‘검은 코도’라 불리는 마족 무리가 오고 있어! 코도 마을을 또 습격하려고!”

검은 코도. 마족 중 가장 광적인 자들. 마력의 감소로 미쳐버린 자들.

“몇 명이냐?”

“백이 넘어요.”

하루와 나는 서로를 바라봤다. 그리고 동시에 웃었다.

“백이면 좋지.” 하루가 검을 뽑았다. “우리도 백을 모을 수 있으니까.”

나는 돌아서서 마을 사람들을 향해 외쳤다.

“듣거라, 코도 마을의 사람들아! 나는 카스 코도다. 어머니 레나 코도의 아들. 어머니는 늘 말했어—‘무리는 강하다.’ 오늘, 그 무리를 만들다. 나와 함께 적을 맞서 싸울 자는 모두 내 뒤에 서라!”

사람들의 표정이 변했다. 망설이는 자들도 있었지만, 도리가 먼저 내 옆에 섰다. 그리고 마을의 노인, 젊은이, 어머니를 잃은 아내들—하나둘씩 내 뒤에 섰다.

하루는 숲을 향해 소리쳤다.

“형제들이여! 나오너라!”

숲에서 노른빛 피부의 마족들이 모습을 드러냈다. 어제까지 우리의 적이었지만, 오늘부터는 우리의 동료.

---

## 제5장: 불의 대지

검은 코도의 무리가 코도 마을로 몰려왔다. 그들은 검은 기운을 두르고, 눈에는 광기가 서려 있었다. 그 중 한 명이 앞장서서 소리쳤다.

“인간이여! 너희는 우리의 땅을 훔쳤다! 오늘 그 대가를 치르겠다!”

하지만 나는 앞으로 나서며 말했다.

“훔친 게 아니야. 나눈 거다. 이 땅은 마족과 인간이 함께 만든 거다. 너희도 그걸 잊었나?”

검은 코도의 두목이 비웃었다. “인간의 혀가 늘어났군. 칼로 증명하라!”

전투가 시작되었다. 마족과 인간이 나란히 섰다. 권총과 검이 부딪히고, 마력과 화약이 뒤엉켰다. 처음에는 우리가 밀렸다. 하지만 하나씩, 둘씩, 서로의 등을 맡기 시작했다.

마족의 마력이 약해졌어도, 그 마력으로 인간의 화약 무기를 강화할 수 있었다. 인간의 화약이 마족의 빠른 몸을 보호해줄 수 있었다. 서로의 약점을 서로가 채웠다.

전투의 한복판에서, 검은 코도의 두목이 나에게 달려들었다. 그의 검은 검에 검은 기운이 실려 있었다. 하지만 나는 어머니의 권총을 들어 그의 검을 막아섰다.

“어머니는 ‘무리를 찾아라’고 했어.” 나는 외쳤다. “난 찾았다!”

권총이 불을 뿜었고, 두목은 쓰러졌다.

전투가 끝났을 때, 코도 마을은 절반이 무너져 있었지만, 살아남았다. 그리고 무엇보다—마을에는 새로운 무리가 살고 있었다.

하루가 내 어깨에 손을 얹었다. “고맙다, 늖대야.”

“난 카스라고.”

“알고 있어.” 그가 씩 웃었다. “네가 외로운 늖대인 건 이제 그만이다.”

나는 하늘을 올려다봤다. 붉은 하늘은 여전히 붉었지만, 이제 그 붉은색이 다르게 보였다. 불의 대지가 아니라, 노을의 대지.

서쪽, 해가 지고 있었다. 하지만 내일은 또다시 떠오를 터였다.

**— 끝 —**

---

*“무리는 강하다. 혼자가 아닌, 함께일 때.”*
*— 레나 코도의 마지막 말*

# 苔痕与猫影：卫城之灵

雅典卫城的石灰岩在正午的烈日下泛着刺目的白光。游客们三三两两地从帕特农神庙的廊柱间穿过，快门声此起彼伏，却没有任何人注意到，在厄瑞克忒翁神庙北侧一道不起眼的裂缝里，一双琥珀色的眼睛正安静地注视着这一切。

那是一只灰白相间的猫，没有人知道它在这片废墟中生活了多久。它的左耳缺了一个小角——那是去年冬天与一只狐狸争夺领地时留下的勋章。它的皮毛不如家猫那般光滑柔顺，而是带着风霜磨砺后的粗粝质感，四只爪子上总沾着干燥的尘土。

它叫阿索斯。至少，塞浦路斯来的考古学家玛利亚是这样叫它的。

---

玛利亚第一次遇见阿索斯是在三年前的春天。

那天她独自留在工地整理陶片，直到夕阳将神庙的柱影拉得极长。她蹲在卡里亚提斯女神柱廊旁，忽然听见一阵细碎的声响。一只瘦小的灰猫从石缝中钻出来，嘴里叼着一只还在挣扎的蜥蜴。

"你这小强盗。"玛利亚轻声说，伸手想要抚摸它。

猫停下脚步，警惕地打量着这个蹲在地上的人类。它歪了歪头，然后——也许是因为这个女人蹲着的姿势不那么具有威胁性——它竟没有逃走。它放下口中的猎物，坐了下来，用那双琥珀色的眼睛直直地望向她，仿佛在审视一个入侵者，又仿佛在打量一位老友。

"阿索斯。"玛利亚脱口而出，"你长得像塞浦路斯山里的那些野猫。我叫玛利亚。我叫……阿索斯。"

猫打了个哈欠，转身消失在石缝之中。但从那天起，每当玛利亚出现在卫城，它便会出现。

---

卫城的猫并非稀客。这片古迹是雅典城中最大的野猫庇护所，志愿者们每日带来清水和猫粮，猫咪们在廊柱间追逐嬉戏，在石阶上慵懒地打着盹。然而阿索斯与众不同。

它几乎从不去游客众多的区域。它偏爱那些被围栏隔开的修复区，是那些正在被科学家用激光清洗的浮雕所在的安静角落。它会在考古学家们低头研究残片时悄然出现，跳上一块千年古石，蜷缩起来，将下巴搁在前爪上，半闭着眼睛，尾巴尖偶尔轻轻摆动。

工人们起初想赶走它——野猫在古迹中并非总受欢迎，它们的粪便和抓痕可能损害脆弱的石质表面。但玛利亚替它说话了。

"它是这里最古老的居民，"她说，"比我们所有人加起来都更属于这片土地。"

这话半是玩笑，半是真心的敬畏。

---

考古学家们渐渐注意到了一件奇怪的事。

那座正在修复的厄瑞克忒翁神庙，门廊的檐口有一处古代工匠留下的隐秘刻痕——一个简单的几何符号，象征着"守护"之意。这个符号的位置极其刁钻，被后来加建的支撑结构遮挡了数百年，直至最近清理工作时才重现天日。

然而就在发现它的前一天晚上，阿索斯曾在那根石柱顶端坐了很久。值夜的保安用手机拍下了照片——月光下的猫影与那只灰白色的猫融为一体，宛如一个守着秘密的哨兵。

"它不会就是这只符号的化身吧？"玛利亚开玩笑说。但那天夜里她做了一个奇怪的梦，梦见古希腊的工匠们举着火把，在月光下雕刻那只符号，而一只猫就坐在他们脚边，仰头注视着，瞳孔中倒映着火光。

醒来时，她发现窗外真的有一只猫坐在窗台上。阿索斯。它的琥珀色眼睛在黎明中闪烁，尾巴悠然摆动，仿佛在说：你梦见的，正是我记住的。

---

春天来临时，阿索斯消失了整整一周。

玛利亚在卫城四处寻找，在它常去的每一处石缝、每一根廊柱旁放下猫粮，却始终不见它的踪影。她开始担心——野猫的寿命本就不长，这只年岁不明的猫是否终于走到了尽头？

第七天傍晚，她坐在雅典娜胜利神庙的废墟旁，几乎要放弃寻找时，草丛中响起了熟悉的窸窣声。

阿索斯出现了。它的嘴里叼着一只刚出生的、毛茸茸的小猫。

它小心翼翼地将小猫放在玛利亚面前，抬头望向她，发出一声低沉的"喵"。那声音里有一种罕见的郑重，仿佛在托付什么珍贵的东西。

小猫的花色与母亲一般无二，只是更小，眼睛还未完全睁开。它在玛利亚的掌心里蠕动，发出细弱的叫声。

"你当妈妈了？"玛利亚惊讶地低声说。她小心地将小猫捧起，发现它的后腿上有一道旧伤——或许是难产时留下的。

阿索斯没有反对人类的触碰。它只是蹲坐着，看着玛利亚，眼神中有一种说不清的东西——像是感激，又像是解脱。

---

那只小猫被取名为"涅瑞伊德斯"——海洋女神的名字，象征着生命的起源。

它被带到了玛利亚的公寓，在温暖的毯子上度过了最初的几个月。然而每周，玛利亚都会带它回到卫城，让它与母亲相见。阿索斯总会在老地方等待，看见女儿便凑上去，嗅闻，轻舔，然后并肩坐在石阶上，望着雅典的天空。

涅瑞伊德斯渐渐长大了。它继承了母亲对古迹的亲近，却比母亲更亲人，更愿意靠近人类。它会在游客面前摆姿势合影，也会在考古学家的小腿边蹭来蹭去讨要抚摸。但它从不离开卫城范围太远，仿佛有一条无形的线，将它系在这片土地上。

一年后，它自己也有了孩子。三只小猫，毛色深浅不一，在帕特农神庙的廊柱间追逐嬉戏。

---

许多年过去了。

雅典娜胜利神庙在一次小型地震中受损，三根廊柱出现了裂缝，整片区域被围起来进行紧急修复。游客们从卫城的其他入口进出，那里依旧熙熙攘攘。

阿索斯已经很老了。它的眼睛有些浑浊，皮毛失去了往日的光泽，整只猫瘦得只剩一把骨头。但它依然固执地出现在工地上，蜷在那根刻着"守护"符号的石柱脚下，半眯着眼睛注视着来来往往的人们。

有一天，玛利亚在清理一处新发现的铭文时，忽然听见了微弱的叫声。

她放下刷子，转头望去——阿索斯正躺在那块古老的石板上。它的呼吸很浅，眼睛却睁得很大，琥珀色的瞳孔中倒映着雅典的天空、神庙的廊柱、以及正在落下的夕阳。

玛利亚跪下身，轻轻将它抱起。阿索斯没有反抗，只是用尽最后的力气，将头靠在她的臂弯里。

"你这一生，守护了什么？"玛利亚低声问，眼眶有些湿润。

猫看了她一眼，发出一声长长的、低沉的"喵"。那声音穿越了数不清的世纪，仿佛在说：我守护了记忆。我守护了那些被遗忘的角落。我守护了你们的文明。

然后，它的眼睛缓缓闭上，尾巴最后轻轻摆动了一下，像是在说再见。

---

阿索斯被埋在了卫城脚下的橄榄林中。玛利亚没有立碑，只在它常睡的那块石板上，用她考古用的细笔，悄悄描了一个符号——

那个古代工匠刻下的"守护"符号。

涅瑞伊德斯继承了母亲的领地。它如今是卫城中最年长的猫，也是最神秘的一只。偶尔，志愿者会带来新的猫粮和清水，而它只是静静地坐在那块石板上，望着雅典城的灯火渐次亮起。

游客们从它身边走过，看着这只端坐如雕像的灰猫，常常会忍不住驻足，赞叹它的优雅与安宁。没有人知道它的来历，更不会有人想到，在遥远的过去，曾有一只更为古老的猫，怀着同样的姿态，守护过这片土地。

但月亮知道。

每当满月升起，月光洒在帕特农神庙的廊柱上，洒在那块刻着"守护"符号的石板上，洒在卫城所有的猫身上——年老的、年轻的、刚出生的——那些琥珀色的眼睛都会一同亮起，像是某种古老的回响。

它们记得。

那些人类已经遗忘的，关于守护的记忆。

---

*帕特农神庙的猫，至今仍在雅典的星空下打盹。如果你某日去到那里，在夕阳西下时静静坐在厄瑞克忒翁神庙旁，或许你会看见一只灰白相间的猫，从石缝中悠然走出，在古老的廊柱间伸一个长长的懒腰。*

*它不会走近你，也不会躲开你。它只会与你对视一眼——琥珀色的、清澈见底的眼睛。*

*在那一瞬间，你或许会忽然明白：有些守护者，从不言语。*

**The Cartographer of Forgotten Things**

Eleanor Vance had a name that belonged to other people's history books.

It wasn't her fault, of course. Her mother had been a librarian in a small town in Vermont, and her father had been the sort of man who kept a framed photograph of his grandmother on his desk until the day he died. Eleanor was named for a great-aunt who had crossed the Atlantic in 1923 with nothing but a suitcase and a talent for languages. That Eleanor had translated poetry in a smoky café in Paris, had loved a man she couldn't keep, and had written letters every week of her life until the morning she didn't.

Our Eleanor—the younger one, the living one—had inherited none of these talents, or so she believed. She was a cartographer. Specifically, she made maps for a regional park service in western Massachusetts, the kind of maps that no one would ever frame. Trails in yellow. Elevation in pale green. Tiny symbols for the outhouses.

She was forty-three when her mother died.

It was the letters that undid her.

They were in the attic, in a trunk lined with cedar, wrapped in tissue paper that had gone the color of old lace. Seven hundred and forty-two of them, bound in ribbons by year. Her great-aunt Eleanor had written them to her grandmother, and her grandmother had kept every one.

That winter, our Eleanor read them all.

She read them in the order they had been written, starting with the crossing, with the small boat pitching in the harbor at Halifax, with the young woman's handwriting slanting against the wind. She read about the café on the rue de Tournon, about a man named Étienne who played the violin and said things that made her laugh until she cried. She read about the war coming, about the letters from Étienne that stopped arriving, about the small apartment in the sixth arrondissement where Eleanor lived for thirty more years and never stopped waiting for the post.

The last letter was dated a Tuesday in October. It said only: *There will be no more letters. I have run out of things to tell you. But I wanted you to know that someone read every one of yours.*

Our Eleanor read that line three times.

Then she put the letters back in the trunk, drove home, and sat for a long time in her kitchen with the lights off. Outside, the snow was beginning. She thought about all the maps she had drawn, all the trails she had marked for other people to follow. She thought about how a map was a kind of promise: *This path will lead you somewhere.*

She thought about how some paths did not lead anywhere.

In the spring, she took a leave of absence.

She told no one where she was going. She packed a small bag, bought a ticket at the airport, and flew to Paris.

The café was still there. It had been repainted, twice, and the owner was a man who did not speak English. But the counter was the same oak, and the stool by the window was the same height, and when Eleanor sat on it, she felt something loosen in her chest, like a stitch finally giving way.

She did not know what she had come looking for. She had imagined that she might find something—an address, a building, a street corner where her great-aunt had once stood and waited. But Paris did not give up its ghosts so easily. The city was too full of its living, too busy with its present tense.

On her third day, she wandered into a museum she had not planned to visit. It was small and warm and smelled of wood polish. She wandered from room to room until she stopped, suddenly, in front of a glass case.

Inside the case was a violin.

It was old, and the wood had darkened to the color of tea. The strings had been removed. There was a card beside it, hand-lettered, in French. Eleanor did not read French well. But she could make out the name on the card.

*Étienne. Circa 1924. Believed to have belonged to a musician who emigrated from Lyon.*

She stood there for a long time.

When she left the museum, she walked without direction, the way her great-aunt must have walked, the way all lonely people walk when they have stopped pretending they have somewhere to be. She walked until she found a small park, and then she sat on a bench, and then she began to cry.

Not for Étienne. Not even for the great-aunt Eleanor.

For herself. For all the years she had spent drawing lines on paper that led nowhere in particular. For the small, tired, careful life she had mistaken for a life. For the woman she had not yet become.

When she stopped crying, the light had changed. It was the color of late afternoon, the color of the letters she had read, the color of the violin in its case. She sat very still and let it fall across her hands.

Then she stood up, brushed off her coat, and began to walk back toward the hotel.

She did not know yet what she would do next. She did not have a map.

But she had, for the first time in a long time, somewhere to begin.

Write about a character who was considered a prodigy when they were young. Aim for roughly 800 words.

# El peso de un número

A los seis años, Julián resolvió la ecuación que el doctor en física del pueblo tenía clavada en la pizarra desde hacía una semana. A los ocho, ganó el primer premio nacional de matemáticas con una demostración propia del teorema de los cuatro colores que los jueces adultos apenas lograron seguir. A los diez, ya hablaba cuatro idiomas, componía sonatas al piano que dejaban sin aliento a profesores de conservatorio y había aprendido más sobre el universo que la mayoría de los adultos que lo rodeaban.

La palabra *prodigio* se quedó pegada a él como una etiqueta en una maleta. Su madre, Marta, la usaba con orgullo cuando hablaba con las visitas, mientras servía café en la sala oscura de aquella casa antigua. Su padre, un hombre callado y algo decepcionado de la vida, sonreía con esfuerzo cada vez que alguien le decía que tenía un hijo excepcional. Los vecinos hablaban de él en susurros: *el niño que no es como los demás*. Los periódicos locales publicaron varias notas, e incluso una cadena nacional le dedicó un reportaje breve donde Julián aparecía mirando a la cámara con esos ojos demasiado serios para su edad.

Nadie le preguntó qué quería él.

A los catorce, Julián seguía siendo delgado, casi transparente. Ya no sonreía con la cámara. Había aprendido que las entrevistas se parecían todas y que las preguntas siempre eran iguales: *¿Cómo lo logras? ¿De dónde viene tu talento? ¿Qué sientes al ser tan especial?* Él respondía con frases ensayadas que complacían a su madre. Por dentro, sentía algo parecido al vacío.

En secreto, Julián escribía. Pequeñas notas que escondía entre las páginas de sus libros de cálculo. Dibujaba mapas de ciudades imaginarias, inventaba nombres para estrellas que aún no habían sido descubiertas. Esas cosas no interesaban a nadie. No eran prodigiosas, no servían para ganar premios, no aparecían en los reportajes.

Su madre seguía hablándole del futuro como si fuera un tren con horario fijo. La universidad a los dieciséis, el doctorado a los veintidós, el premio Nobel quizás a los treinta. Todo estaba trazado, todo estaba decidido. Julián no recordaba haber elegido nada.

Fue a los diecisiete cuando empezó a desmoronarse.

No de manera dramática, no con gestos que alguien pudiera notar. Fue algo más silencioso, más parecido a una gotera en un techo antiguo. Dejó de estudiar durante semanas enteras. Se quedaba en la cama mirando el techo. Perdió un examen de matemáticas por primera vez en su vida y, cuando su madre le preguntó qué había pasado, él solo dijo:

—No fui.

Ella no entendió. *No fui* no era una respuesta posible para alguien como Julián. Las personas como Julián siempre van, siempre brillan, siempre entregan lo que se espera de ellas.

Una tarde, mientras la casa estaba vacía y la lluvia golpeaba los ventanales, Julián se sentó frente al piano. Hacía meses que no lo tocaba. Puso los dedos sobre las teclas, frías como mármol, y en lugar de interpretar a Chopin o a Rachmaninoff, tocó lo que le salió. Tres notas repetidas. Un ritmo lento, casi torpe. Melodía de alguien que no sabía componer, de alguien que por fin no estaba intentando impresionar a nadie.

Sonó el teléfono. Era una universidad europea interesada en su perfil. Julián escuchó la voz al otro lado con el auricular separado del oído, como si el sonido le llegara desde muy lejos.

—Tengo que pensarlo —dijo, y colgó antes de que terminaran la frase.

Esa noche, su madre lo encontró dormido sobre las partituras. Había estado escribiendo otra vez, en un cuaderno nuevo. Cuando Marta lo abrió, esperando quizás ecuaciones o notas eruditas, encontró algo distinto:

*Hoy vi una lagartija en la pared del jardín. Se quedó quieta mucho rato, como si entendiera algo que yo no entiendo. Luego se fue.*

Marta cerró el cuaderno con cuidado y se quedó de pie en el pasillo oscuro, con el papel temblándole entre las manos. Tal vez fue la primera vez que comprendió que su hijo, el niño prodigio que había sido suyo y del mundo entero, estaba intentando ser alguien más. Alguien sin nombre todavía, alguien que aún no sabía quién era pero que, por primera vez, estaba buscándolo.

A la mañana siguiente, Julián se despertó tarde. El sol entraba oblicuo por la ventana y dibujaba una franja dorada sobre el suelo. Encontró a su madre en la cocina, sentada con una taza de café entre las manos, mirándolo como si lo viera por primera vez.

—¿Quieres desayunar? —le preguntó.

Y Julián, que llevaba años esperando una pregunta tan sencilla, tan pequeña, tan humana, se sentó frente a ella y respondió que sí.

---

*Hay dos tipos de prodigio, dicen algunos. El que deslumbra al mundo y el que necesita toda una vida para comprenderse a sí mismo. A veces, afortunadamente, coinciden en la misma persona, y entonces basta una mañana cualquiera, una taza de café, una pregunta sin trampa, para que algo empiece a cambiar.*

Write about someone rediscovering something old they thought they’d lost. Total: ~400 words.

# The Pocket Watch

The attic smelled of cedar and forgotten summers. Eleanor climbed the last three stairs with a flashlight in one hand and a chipped mug of cold tea in the other. She hadn't set foot up here in nearly eleven years, not since the funeral.

She had come looking for her mother's wedding album, something she wanted to show her niece next weekend. The dust lay thick over everything, but she eventually pried open the trunk she'd been avoiding.

Folded quilts. A stack of yellowed letters tied with kitchen twine. Her father's old army cap, still holding the shape of his head. She dug deeper, past porcelain figurines and a cracked music box that, for once, did not play.

Near the bottom, beneath an old cashmere sweater she used to steal in high school, her fingers closed around something cold.

She pulled it out slowly, and her breath caught.

It was the pocket watch.

Her grandfather had carried it every day of his life until his hands grew too stiff to wind it. She'd been given it at twenty-three, the summer after college, and lost it somewhere between then and now—a broken dresser drawer in an apartment she'd long since left. She had assumed it vanished into a landfill, swallowed by time.

She pressed the crown. It resisted, then gave. The mechanism shuddered, gears clicking like an old man clearing his throat, and then the second hand began to move.

Eleanor sat back on her heels. She could hear the rain start on the roof above her, and somewhere down the hallway, the clock in the kitchen chimed the hour. She held the watch to her ear and listened to the tiny heartbeat inside it, steady as a promise.

She thought of her grandfather teaching her to tell time when she was six—*the big hand is the minutes, the little hand is the hours, and the second hand is everything you're too impatient to wait for*. She thought of how, when she was nine, he had let her wind it herself, standing behind her with his weathered hands over hers, showing her the gentle pressure it needed.

She had not thought about any of this in over a decade.

The watch ticked on in her palm, indifferent to the years it had missed. The rain picked up. Eleanor closed the trunk, picked up the flashlight, and walked back down the stairs—slowly this time, one step at a time, the way her grandfather used to climb them near the end, when each stair was a small summit he refused to be defeated by.

She put the kettle on. She would call her niece tomorrow and tell her she had found something important to bring with the album. Something that still kept time, after all this while. Something that had been waiting for her, patient as a grandfather, in a place she had been afraid to look.

Write about someone stuck in an endless cycle who finally manages to break free. Approximately 700 words.

# The Clockmaker's Apprentice

Every morning at 5:47 AM, not 5:46 or 5:48, but precisely 5:47, Edmund Wren woke to the sound of his father's pocket watch chiming from the nightstand. He opened his eyes to the same water stain on the ceiling shaped like a question mark. He swung his legs over the same bed, wore the same frayed slippers, and walked the same seven steps to the window where the same grey light greeted him through the same crooked curtain.

For thirty-eight years, Edmund had been the apprentice at Wren & Sons Clockworks. Thirty-eight years of winding springs, replacing gears, oiling mechanisms. His father, Harold, had been the master clockmaker for every one of those years. And his father before him. And his father before that. The Wren family had wound the town's clocks for four generations, which would have been a proud legacy if Edmund had ever once wanted to wind a clock.

He hadn't.

Not since he was nine years old and his mother had placed a tiny brass movement in his palm and asked him what he heard. Other boys would have heard ticking. Edmund had heard something else—a soft, secret music beneath the ticking, like the town itself breathing in its sleep. He had told his mother this, and she had smiled and said, "Good. Now forget it."

He had spent twenty-nine years trying to forget.

But the morning his mother died, everything changed. She had been sick for a long time, fading the way a clock fades when its mainspring slowly uncoils. In her final hour, she pressed something into his hand. A key. Not a clock key—too small, too ornate, its handle carved with spirals that seemed to move when Edmund wasn't looking directly at them.

"Bring this to the chapel," she whispered. "Behind the old grandfather. You know the one."

She was gone before Edmund could ask which grandfather, but he knew. Of course he knew. The massive oak clock in the abandoned chapel at the edge of town, the one no Wren had been permitted to touch for a hundred years. The one that had stopped the day his great-great-grandfather had first heard the music and tried to play it back.

Edmund had never told anyone about the music. He had assumed it was madness, or weakness, or both.

That night, for the first time in thirty-eight years, Edmund did not go home after work. He walked instead to the chapel on the hill, the key burning in his pocket like a coal. The doors creaked open at his touch, though they had been sealed for decades. Moonlight fell through the broken rose window and pooled around the grandfather clock, which stood taller than a man, its face carved with the phases of moons no living person had ever seen.

Edmund fitted the key into the clock's heart.

He turned it.

And the music came back.

Not the frantic mechanical music of a wound spring, but something older. Something that sounded like every morning he had ever lived, played at once and yet separately, each one distinct. He heard the morning he learned his mother was sick. The morning he decided to stay. The morning he decided to leave, and the morning after that, and the morning after that, looping and looping through decades of silent surrender.

He understood then what the cycle had been. Not punishment. Preservation. The town had needed someone to hear it, to remember it, to be ready.

Edmund turned the key again, and this time he wound. He wound for thirty-eight years. He wound for every morning he had swallowed his songs, every evening he had polished brass instead of writing poetry, every night he had lain awake listening to the music and telling himself it wasn't there.

The clock began to chime. Not the hour—something else. Something that sounded like a name. His name. The one his mother had given him before he became his father's apprentice, before he became the keeper of other people's time.

When the chiming stopped, the chapel was no longer abandoned. It was full of people he had known and forgotten, and they were waiting for him to speak.

Edmund Wren, who had not said an unscripted word in decades, opened his mouth.

And what came out was not silence.

It was song.

---

In the morning, the townspeople found the chapel doors thrown open and the great clock running smoothly for the first time in a century. Edmund was sitting beneath it, his father's pocket watch still ticking in his pocket, but no longer chiming.

He had wound it down himself.

Some clocks, he understood now, are meant to be stopped. So that the person carrying them can finally, truly, begin.

Write about someone who is stuck between two opposing sides and can’t decide which one to choose. Length: about 3100 characters.

# 棋盘上的独行者

林深站在老宅的门槛上，手里攥着两封信。

信封已经泛黄，边角被汗水浸润得有些发软。一封来自远在京都的兄长，信封上的火漆印是林家大房的徽记；另一封来自岭南的母亲，寄信人是二房的私章。两封信他读了不下百遍，几乎能闭着眼背诵出每一个字。

"深儿，速归京都。你父亲临终前有遗愿未了，大房需要你。"

"阿深，娘想你。岭南虽苦，但总归是家。"

十年前那场分家产的风波，至今仍是林家上下讳莫如深的禁忌。父亲本是林家嫡长子，却因祖父偏心，将家业尽数传给二房。父亲一气之下带着妻儿远赴岭南谋生，却在去年郁郁而终。临终前，他握着林深的手，反复念叨着"京都""祖宅""该拿回来的"。

母亲却总是摇头："你爹争了一辈子，到头来呢？人没了，才拿回来有什么用？"

大伯母的信写得更漂亮——什么"血浓于水"，什么"落叶归根"，什么"你是我看着长大的"。字里行间却透着一股森冷的算计。林深在商海沉浮多年，怎会看不出那字句背后的意味？大房唯一的男丁三年前病故，大伯母膝下无子，正是青黄不接的时候。

"二叔家的林砚堂倒是年轻有为，"大伯母写道，"只是他毕竟姓林不姓……"

信到这里戛然而止，林深却读懂了潜台词。大伯母需要的是一个可以继承香火、打理家业的傀儡，而林砚堂虽是林家人，却从小养在二房身边，未必肯乖乖听话。

母亲那边就简单得多。岭南的日子清苦却安稳，林深靠着自己的本事置下了一份不大不小的家业。母亲只盼着他娶妻生子，平安终老。

"争那些做什么？"母亲总是这样说，"你爹争了一辈子，争到最后连命都搭进去了。"

林深将两封信叠好，塞进怀里。他抬头望着天边翻滚的乌云，知道暴风雨就要来了。

……

他决定在老宅住一晚。

老宅是祖父留下的祖产，分家时被大房占去。如今林深以"祭祖"为由回来暂住，倒也没人敢拦他。只是住进来之后，他便察觉到了无数双暗处的眼睛。

夜里，林深梦见父亲。

父亲穿着一身白衣，站在祖宅的庭院里，背景是那棵百年老槐。梦中的父亲不像记忆中那样愁苦，反而神情平静，带着一丝若有若无的笑意。

"深儿，"父亲说，"你可想好了？"

"爹，"林深跪在地上，"儿子不知该如何抉择。"

父亲沉默良久，忽然问道："你可还记得这老宅的院门朝哪边开？"

林深一愣。他当然记得——院门朝南，正对着那条通往京都的官道。可分家之后，大房嫌风水不好，改成了朝北，对着后山。说是"聚财"，其实是断绝与南方的往来。

"你祖父说，院门朝南，是因为林家起于南方，不可忘本。"父亲的身影渐渐模糊，"可你大伯说，朝南的风水养不了富贵。深儿，这院门的事，你想明白了吗？"

林深从梦中惊醒，窗外正下着大雨。

……

第二天清晨，大伯母派人来请他去花厅用膳。

花厅里坐着大伯母，以及一个意想不到的人——林砚堂。

林砚堂是二房的嫡孙，今年刚满二十，眉目间与林深有几分相似。他是来参加乡试的，顺道拜访大房。两人目光相接，林砚堂微微颔首，算是见礼。

"深哥儿来得正好，"大伯母笑容可掬，"砚堂这孩子也是来祭祖的。难得我们林家子孙都在，不如今日就把祖产的事议一议？"

林深不动声色地坐下。他知道，正戏要开场了。

林砚堂却皱了皱眉："大伯母，这事是不是该等乡试过后再议？"

"乡试？"大伯母掩嘴一笑，"砚堂啊，你二房那边早就没落了，你父亲那点家底，还不够你赴京的盘缠呢。何必舍近求远？你大伯母做主，只要你肯回来，这祖产——"

"大伯母，"林深忽然开口，打断了她的话，"我记得林家的规矩，祖产传承需得三房到场方可议定。我母亲还在岭南，没接到信之前，这事恐怕议不了。"

大伯母的脸色微微一变。林砚堂却抬眼看向林深，目光中多了几分兴味。

……

消息传到岭南时，已是半月之后。

母亲没有回信，只是让人捎来一句话："你爹的坟前还缺一炷香。"

林深沉默了许久。他忽然想起一个细节——分家那年，父亲带着他们离开祖宅，母亲却独自折返回去，在祖宅的影壁后站了整整一个时辰。没有人知道她在做什么。

他唤来老仆阿福。

"阿福，分家那年，我娘在影壁后做什么？"

阿福犹豫了一下，终于道出实情："老太太……在影壁上刻了一行字。"

"什么字？"

"'林氏子孙，永不分离'。"

阿福压低声音："可那字第二天就被大房的人铲掉了。老太太当时就吐了血。"

林深感觉有什么东西在心底轰然崩塌。

……

他决定去见母亲。

岭南的路途遥远，林深快马加鞭，整整走了十日。沿途他不断想起父亲临终前的眼神，想起母亲的叹息，想起大伯母那滴水不漏的笑脸。

他想，自己或许从一开始就想错了。

这不是大房与二房的对峙，也不是京都与岭南的抉择。这是一个更古老、更深沉的问题——

林家，到底是什么？

是那座占地百亩的祖宅？是堆积如山的金银？是朝南还是朝北的院门？还是……

还是那行被铲掉的字？

……

母亲在村口的老槐树下等他。

她苍老了许多，头发几乎全白了。林深翻身下马，跪在她面前。

"娘，儿子不孝。"

母亲没有说话，只是伸出手，轻轻摸了摸他的头发。

"进屋吧，"她说，"你爹的牌位前，有东西给你。"

……

父亲牌位前放着一只檀木匣子。打开，里面是一封信，以及一份泛黄的契书。

信是父亲写的，时间是父亲去世前一个月。字迹颤抖，可见写信时已是病入膏肓。

> 深儿：
>
> 你看到这封信时，爹大概已经不在了。有些事，爹必须告诉你。
>
> 分家那年，你祖父其实是给我留了东西的。祖宅里有一间密室，藏着你祖父一生的心血。那不是金银，也不是地契，而是一批古籍善本、一套林家祖传的制茶工艺，还有一份你曾祖父留下的手书。
>
> 你祖父临终前对我说："这些才是林家的根。宅子可以分，金银可以散，唯独这根不能断。你若能守住它，林家便在；守不住，林家也就散了。"
>
> 我争了一辈子，争的从来不是宅子和金银。是你祖父那句话。
>
> 深儿，你是大房还是二房，是去京都还是留岭南，爹都不在乎。爹在乎的是，你能不能守住那间密室。
>
> 你祖父说，密室的钥匙分成两半，一半在大房，一半在二房。合在一起，才能打开。
>
> 爹把二房这一半交给了你娘。你若要去找大房那一半，得自己去拿。
>
> 深儿，林家的根不在京都，也不在岭南。林家的根在那间密室里，在那些古籍里，在那份手书里。
>
> 你明白了，爹就放心了。
>
> ——父 林远山

林深抬起头，看向母亲。

母亲缓缓从怀中取出一枚铜制的钥匙，递给他。

"你爹一辈子争的不是家产，"她说，"是我误会了他整整十年。"

她轻轻叹了口气："深儿，去吧。京都也好，岭南也好，把那间密室找出来。那才是林家的根。"

……

林深回到京都祖宅时，已是三个月后。

他没有去见大伯母，而是径直找到了林砚堂。

两人在一间茶楼里对坐。林砚堂听完林深的讲述，沉默了很久。

"所以，"林砚堂说，"祖父留的那间密室，才是林家的真正根基？"

"是。"

"大伯母知道吗？"

"她若是知道，就不会费尽心机想让我回去当傀儡了。她要的只是这座祖宅和那份家产，至于祖父留下的东西，她根本不在乎。"

林砚堂苦笑："二房这边也一样。我父亲只知道祖宅里有值钱的东西，却不知道那间密室的存在。"

"你愿意帮我吗？"

林砚堂看着林深，目光中闪过复杂的情绪。两人虽同属林家，却从未有过深交。他的父亲被林深的父亲夺去了继承权，他从小听着"都是大房的人害的"长大。

"深哥儿，"林砚堂说，"我凭什么信你？"

林深从怀中取出那枚铜钥匙，轻轻放在桌上。

"就凭这个，"他说，"这是二房的钥匙。你若不信，可以现在就拿走。"

林砚堂没有动。他盯着那枚钥匙，良久，忽然笑了。

"深哥儿，你比我想象的要有意思得多。"

他从怀中取出另一样东西——也是一枚铜钥匙。

"大伯母不知道我有这个，"林砚堂说，"这是我从祖父的遗物里偷偷找到的。我一直不知道它有什么用，现在我知道了。"

两枚钥匙合在一起，咔哒一声，严丝合缝。

……

密室在祖宅的最深处，被一堵假墙遮掩了数十年。

推开门的瞬间，林深和林砚堂同时怔住了。

密室不大，四壁皆是书架。架上整齐排列着数百册古籍善本，从先秦诸子到明清笔记，涵盖经史子集。角落里有一套精巧的制茶工具，旁边是一份详细的工艺手札。

而在密室正中央，供奉着一尊牌位。

牌位上写着——"林氏先祖云崖公之位"。

牌位前放着一份泛黄的手书，是林家曾祖父亲笔所写：

> 林氏起于微末，世代以读书传家、以手艺立身。后世子孙若争宅产，便是舍本逐末；若能守此密室，便是守住林家之根。
>
> 宅产可分，根脉不可断。
>
> 切记，切记。

林深跪倒在地，泪如雨下。

林砚堂也跪了下来。两人对视一眼，忽然都笑了。

"深哥儿，"林砚堂说，"我觉得祖父他们当年分家的时候，就已经知道会有今天了。"

"是啊，"林深擦去眼泪，"他们把钥匙分成两半，一半给大房，一半给二房。只有我们联手，才能打开这扇门。"

"可大伯母那边……"

"她会明白的，"林深站起身，望向那尊牌位，"如果我们让她明白的话。"

……

尾声

大伯母最终还是没有明白。

但那已经不重要了。

林深和林砚堂将密室中的古籍和工艺手札整理出来，在祖宅中开辟了一间书斋。他们以林家先祖的名义，将古籍捐赠给了朝廷的藏书阁，将制茶工艺传授给了当地的茶农。

祖宅的院门，被他们重新改回了朝南。

母亲从岭南赶来，看着那扇朝南的院门，老泪纵横。

"你爹若是在天有灵，"她说，"该有多高兴。"

林深扶着母亲，缓缓走过庭院。

他想起那个雨夜做的梦，忽然明白了父亲最后那个问题的答案——

院门朝南还是朝北，从来不是问题的关键。

关键在于，院门里的人，是否还记得自己从哪里来，要往哪里去。

（全文完）

# 最后的电报员

陈德山还记得电报时代的辉煌。

那是1958年，他十八岁，刚从邮电学校毕业，被分配到县邮电局。那时的电报大楼日夜灯火通明，"滴滴答答"的莫尔斯电码声此起彼伏，像一首永不停歇的金属交响曲。

"有急事就打电报。"这是那个年代的口头禅。

陈德山的手指能在按键上敲出每分钟一百二十个字的速率，耳朵能在嘈杂的电流声中分辨出最细微的差别。他闭着眼睛都能背出所有的电码表，三千多个汉字，每一个对应的"嘀嗒"组合，都刻在了他的肌肉记忆里。

后来有了电话，再后来有了传真，电子邮件，互联网，智能手机。世界变化得比他预想的快得多。

2000年，邮电局通知他，电报业务将在年底正式停办。那天，陈德山在值班室里坐了一整夜，最后一次敲响那台老式电报机。

"滴答滴答滴——"

他发送的是最后一份电报，来自一位远方的母亲，内容只有四个字：**儿啊，归来。**

---

三十年后。

陈德山已经九十三岁，独自住在老城区的一间平房里。他的儿女在省城工作，多次劝他搬过去同住，他都拒绝了。

他的房间里，最显眼的是那台保养得锃亮的老式电报机。

每天清晨，陈德山都会戴上老花镜，端坐在电报机前。他戴上手指套——那是用细铜丝编织的，专为电报员设计——然后开始敲击。

"滴答，滴滴——滴答答——"

没有人接收这些电报。

或者说，曾经接收过。

二十年前，陈德山的老伴去世了。她叫秀英，是他的发报员搭档，两个人在电报大楼里并肩工作了三十多年。他们相识于一次电码考核，她的手法比他还要快，他输给了她，心甘情愿。

"老头子又在发报了？"隔壁的老王偶尔会来串门，看着陈德山专注的侧脸说，"发给谁呢？"

陈德山笑了笑，不说话。

他发给谁？

他发给那个叫秀英的女人。发给那些年轻的同事——小赵、老李、阿芳。发给那个总是让电报大楼充满笑声的周师傅。发给所有那些在时代洪流里渐渐远去的人们。

他相信，在某个遥远的地方，有一台电报机还会在深夜轻轻响起。

---

清明节那天，陈德山的儿子陈建国从省城回来，发现父亲坐在电报机前，姿势和往常一样，只是头微微垂下。

手还搭在按键上。

手指套还戴着。

电报机的屏幕还亮着，最后一行电码静静地躺在那里：

**我爱你，秀英。等我。**

陈建国这才明白，父亲一辈子发的，不是电报，是情书。

---

如今，县城的旧邮电局已经改造成了博物馆。展柜里陈列着发报机、电码本，还有一些泛黄的电报底稿。其中一份被放在最显眼的位置，上面写着：

**儿啊，速归。母。**

讲解员会告诉每一位参观者：这是某个年代的电报，曾经是人们传递思念最快的工具。

但没有人知道，在这座城市里，曾经有一位电报员，用一辈子在发送一份永远得不到回复的电报。

那是他写给整个旧时代的，寄往时间深处的，最后一封信。

# The Boy Who Listened to the Stars

## Part One: The Quiet Before

The storm that shattered the Calderón household arrived not on a Tuesday in October, as Eliana always insisted, but on a Wednesday in early November. She would insist on this small inaccuracy for the rest of her life, because memory, she would one day write, is a country we build from the bricks of feeling rather than the mortar of fact.

She was seven years old when her father came home with a strange machine balanced in his arms. It looked, to her young eyes, like a turtle that had eaten a smaller turtle and regretted the decision. Wires spilled from its cracked belly. A single glass eye, amber and unblinking, protruded from its top.

"This," her father announced with the theatrical gravity of a man who had just been fired from the sanitation department after seventeen loyal years, "is a radio."

In the village of San Mateo del Oro, nestled in the dry bones of a forgotten province in a country no one in the wider world bothered to name, radios were luxuries. They were owned by the priest, by the mayor's wife, and by the man who ran the only store, who kept his in a cabinet of dark wood and would not let the village children touch it on pain of being told the story of the boy who touched it and grew hair on his palms.

Tonight, her father explained, the radio would be theirs.

## Part Two: The Thief

The radio had been stolen. This Eliana learned later, when the word traveled through the village the way wildfires travel through dry grass. Her father, drunk and desperate, had taken it from the back of a repairman's truck. The repairman, a man named Octavio who had thick glasses and kind hands, was the only person in three villages who could fix such things. He was also, inconveniently, the brother of the mayor's wife.

For two months, the secret lived happily in their small adobe house. Her father, in the cool dark of evenings, would wind the radio with a silver key and the static would come alive, crackling like the sound the ocean made in the seashells Eliana had never seen. And then, miraculously, voices. Music. The news from cities that sounded made-up, where the streets were paved with something harder than dirt and the people ate meat every day of the week.

Eliana learned to be still. She learned to lean her ear close to the speaker, to close her eyes, to let the sounds wash over her like bathwater. She memorized the names of places she would never see: Paris. Cairo. Tokyo. She repeated them under her breath like prayers.

Then came the night the mayor's men came.

## Part Three: The Lessons

What happened next would become the first paragraph of her first published essay, fourteen years later, in a journal printed in a city on another continent. She would write it in a language her father could not read, and she would win an award for it, and the award would sit on a shelf in an office she would come to own.

But that is later. That is the after.

In the before, there was this: her father was taken. Her mother wept in a way that frightened Eliana, because she had never seen her mother's face do that before, the way it crumpled like paper held too close to a flame. Her younger brother, barely three, cried because everyone was crying and he did not understand the reason. And Eliana stood in the doorway of their small house and watched the men take her father into the dark.

In the morning, she went to find Octavio.

She found him in his workshop, surrounded by the carcasses of machines. He looked at her over his thick glasses. He knew. Of course he knew. Everyone knew.

"Why?" she asked. She was seven. She did not yet know how to ask the harder questions, so she asked the easiest one. "Why did he take it?"

Octavio considered her for a long moment. Then he knelt down, slowly, his knees cracking, until his face was level with hers.

"Your father," he said, "wanted to hear the world."

This was not an answer. It was also, she would realize decades later, the only answer that mattered.

## Part Four: The Father, Returned

Her father came home eleven days later. He was thinner. He would not speak of where he had been. He would not speak of many things for many years. But he would look at Eliana sometimes, when he thought she was not watching, with an expression she could not read. She would not understand that expression until she was much older, until she herself had children who watched her from doorways.

The radio was gone. Confiscated, perhaps. Returned to Octavio, perhaps, though he would never say. What remained was the memory of the sound, and that was not nothing.

Eliana began, in secret, to build her own radios.

She started with crystals wrapped in wire, hidden in a cigar box under her bed. They did not work. She tried again. And again. By the time she was ten, she had built a device that could pick up, faintly, a single station broadcasting from three hundred kilometers away. She listened to it every night, pressing her ear to the box, learning the cadences of a language she could not yet understand but felt, somehow, was meant for her.

By the time she was fifteen, she had taught herself to read in three languages, using books salvaged from the trash behind the school. By the time she was eighteen, she had won a scholarship to a university in the capital. By the time she was twenty-two, she had published her first paper on the mathematics of signal propagation in mountain terrain, a field so obscure that no one in her country had thought to study it, and so practical that it would change the way information traveled through her entire region.

By the time she was thirty, she had built the first low-cost communication network capable of reaching the most remote villages of her country, using technology adapted from principles she had begun to discover as a child, hunched over a cigar box, listening for voices.

## Part Five: The Award

At the ceremony, when they handed her the medal that had been carried across an ocean by a man who had flown through the night, they asked her the question they always asked. They asked it in four languages, because they did not know which one she dreamed in.

"What," they asked, "inspired you?"

She thought of her father. She thought of the turtle-machine cradled in his arms. She thought of Octavio, kneeling in his workshop, telling her that her father had wanted to hear the world.

She thought, briefly, of saying this. But there were cameras, and the world was watching, and the truth was too small and too large at once, the kind of truth that does not survive translation.

She said instead: "I learned, very young, that there are voices everywhere, if you are quiet enough to hear them."

The audience applauded. They thought they understood.

## Part Six: The Return

Many years later, when the world had learned her name and forgotten it and learned it again, Eliana Calderón returned to San Mateo del Oro. She came in a car that could not fit down the village's single narrow street, so she walked the last kilometer, as she had walked it every day of her childhood, kicking up the same pale dust.

Her father was gone by then. Her mother was very old. Octavio, she learned, had died the year before, and his workshop had been locked since.

She went to the workshop. She had a key now. She had bought the building from Octavio's nephew, who had been glad to sell it, not understanding what it was.

Inside, among the dust and the silence and the patient skeletons of broken machines, she found what she had come for.

A radio. Small. Old. Its amber eye still intact.

She picked it up. She carried it outside. She set it on a stone in the plaza, where the village children gathered, curious about the stranger with the silver hair and the kind face.

"This," she said, "is a radio."

She wound the key. The static crackled, and the children leaned in, their eyes wide, and somewhere in the warm dark of the machine, a voice began to speak.

And Eliana Calderón, who had once been a small girl standing in a doorway watching the world take her father away, sat down among them, and listened.

# The Last Light of Auriga

The horizon bled amber.

Elara pressed her palm against the cool glass of the observation deck, watching as the sun of Auriga IV began its slow descent behind the silver towers of the capital. The light fractured into a thousand pieces across the clouds, turning the sky into a cathedral of gold and rose. She had watched this sunset seventeen times now—seventeen rotations of this pale, watery star—and she had never once grown tired of it.

Back on Earth, sunsets had been rare things. Filtered through pollution, choked by the dust of a dying world, they had appeared as smudged afterthoughts on the horizon. Here, on the colony world, the sky still remembered how to perform.

"You're out here again."

She didn't turn. She knew the voice—had memorized it over seventeen cycles, along with the way footsteps sounded on the metal grating, the particular rhythm of his breathing when he was worried versus when he was amused.

"The sunsets here are different," she said. "Different from what we had."

Kael stepped up beside her, close enough that she could feel the warmth of him even through the thin climate suit. He was holding two steaming cups of something that passed for coffee this far from home. He handed her one without a word.

They stood in silence as the sun sank lower. The towers of Auriga City caught the light and held it, glowing like embers in a dying fire. Below, the streets were filling with the evening shift, people moving between domes with the determined rhythm of those building something new.

"Today's the day," Kael said finally.

Elara's grip tightened on her cup. She had known he would say it. She had known it since she woke, since she walked here, since she felt the first brush of evening on her face.

"I know."

"The expedition leaves at dawn. Three years, maybe more, before we reach the next viable system. You could still change your mind. Stay here. Help build."

"I can't build something I'm not willing to live in."

He looked at her then, really looked, and she saw in his eyes the reflection of the dying sun. They had had this conversation before, in the small hours, in the mess hall, in the dark of their shared quarters. They had never resolved it. She suspected now that they wouldn't.

"You think the ship will make it?"

"No." She smiled, surprising herself. "But I think we'll try anyway. That's the point, isn't it? Trying. Even when the math says no."

The last sliver of sun vanished below the horizon, and the sky shifted from gold to violet to the deep, endless blue of coming night. The first stars appeared—familiar constellations, seen from a new angle.

Elara finished her coffee and set the cup on the railing. She had packed everything that mattered into a single bag. The rest she would leave behind: the small apartment with its window facing west, the garden she had started in the hydroponics bay, the view she had learned by heart.

She turned to Kael, and for a long moment they simply looked at each other. There were no words left. They had spent them all in seventeen cycles of trying.

"Walk me to the launch field?"

He nodded.

They moved through the corridors of the colony together, past the murals painted by first-generation children, past the memorial wall with its seven hundred names, past the mess hall where someone was playing a guitar and singing in a language that hadn't existed a century ago. The colony was still awake, still alive, still building. It would go on without her. That was the point of a colony—that it outlasts the people who planted it.

At the edge of the launch field, the *Vanguard* waited. A long, silver needle against the darkening sky, bristling with antennae and prayer. Tomorrow it would rise on a column of fire and push toward the black between stars, carrying the last of Earth's dreamers to whatever waited on the other side of impossible.

Kael stopped at the boundary line. Beyond it, the suits would be required, and his work was here, in the soil and the steel, in the slow patient labor of roots.

Elara turned back one last time. The sky behind the colony was fully dark now, stars thick as scattered salt. But to the east—impossibly, beautifully—the sky was beginning to lighten. The first faint blush of dawn, hours early, a trick of atmosphere and light that happened sometimes on this world.

Two skies at once. Sunset and sunrise, ending and beginning, held in the same breath.

She had never seen anything so human.

"Goodbye, Kael."

"Goodbye, Elara."

She walked toward the ship without looking back. The airlock hissed open, and the dark interior swallowed her whole. Somewhere behind her, the dawn was breaking over a world she had loved, and somewhere ahead, a star she had never seen was waiting to be born.

The door sealed shut.

The *Vanguard* began to sing.

"Você veio pelo selo do Yeti?"

Otomar Girardi ergueu os olhos da vitrine onde organizava sua coleção de itens sovietizados da estação Vostok. Diante dele estava uma mulher magra, de óculos grossos, com um crachá que dizia **Dra. Beatriz Cordeiro — Instituto Antártico Brasileiro**.

Otomar riu — um riso curto, quase reverente. Era assim que se falava naquele lugar: em sussurros, em meio-murmúrios, como se a paixão fosse algo a ser protegido do vento.

---

A convenção se espalhava por três salões. No primeiro, as mesas de negociação — longas filas de filatelistas curvados sobre lupas de mesa, discutindo a posição de uma dobra, o ângulo de uma goma, a procedência de uma sobrecarga. Homens velhos, em sua maioria. Mulheres, poucas, mas presentes — e respeitadas, porque aqui, dizia-se, *a falta de colecionador é maior que a falta de coleção*.

No segundo salão, as palestras: **"A Perícia Forense do Selo: Detectando Falsificações da Tchecoslováquia Socialista"**, **"O Mistério dos Selos sem Valor Declarado da Patagônia de 1947"**, **"Cartas Hiperbólicas: A Correspondência do Almirante Byrd com sua Esposa"**.

No terceiro, o coração do evento — a Exposição Competitiva. Os três jurados eram alemães, vindos de Frankfurt, e falavam inglês com sotaque de quem já perdeu a conta de quantas competições julgou. Um deles, o Dr. Reinhard Köhler, era considerado pelos filatelistas polares uma espécie de sumo sacerdote.

---

Otomar estava nervoso.

Há trinta e dois anos colecionava os selos emitidos em ocasiões de expedições polares. Começara com uma coleção de presente do pai — um carimbo da Operação Naval Brasileira para a Antártica, 1982. Aos poucos, o hobby engolira a vida: as economias, o quarto de hóspedes (que virou arquivo), o casamento (que acabou, com a esposa levando o cachorro, mas deixando a coleção, por uma estranha misericórdia conjugal).

Agora, pela primeira vez, ele submetia uma página competitiva. Apenas uma. O suficiente, dizia a si mesmo, para saber.

Era a história do **Selo do Regresso** — uma emissão experimental norueguesa de 1971, projetada pelo artista gráfico Harald Damsleth, que mostrava um urso polar solitário sob uma aurora boreal estilizada. O selo havia sido emitido em quantidade limitada — 12.000 unidades — e depois recolhido por supostamente conter um erro de impressão: o urso tinha seis dedos em uma pata. Ou talvez o recolhimento tivesse sido por outro motivo. Ninguém sabia ao certo.

Otomar não tinha o selo original.

Em vez disso, tinha um **fragmento de carta** — uma carta real, datada de 12 de março de 1971, escrita por um estudante de biologia de Tromsø para a mãe em Bergen. Na carta, o rapaz mencionava ter recebido "o selo do urso" pelo correio, e descrevia em detalhes sua reação. A carta estava carimbada com o selo — não inteiro, mas com um pedaço significativo.

Era a única peça conhecida que continha aquele selo em uso postal, com a dobra, o carimbo, a goma natural dos anos.

Para os filatelistas, era uma relíquia.

Para Otomar, era a prova de que coisas belas podiam existir por breves instantes antes de desaparecerem.

---

Na noite anterior à premiação, Otomar estava no bar do hotel, o único bar aberto àquela hora em convenções tão obscuras. Tomava um Campari com soda — uma bebida de velho, dizia ele mesmo — quando viu a Dra. Beatriz Cordeiro sentada sozinha numa das mesas, olhando fixamente para uma foto ampliada de uma paisagem antártica.

"Posso?" — perguntou.

Ela assentiu.

"Você está olhando para a foto como quem procura alguém", disse ele.

"Estou procurando o lugar onde o meu pai esteve em 1978. Ele era oceanógrafo. Ficou quatro meses na estação chilena de Frei. Nunca mais foi o mesmo."

Otomar não disse nada por um longo momento. Depois, lentamente, tirou do bolso uma pequena lupa de bolso e ofereceu.

"Quer ver o selo do Regresso com mais detalhe?"

Ela aceitou. E, por um instante, sob a luz amarela do bar de hotel, dois adultos sérios se inclinaram sobre um pedaço de papel envelhecido, buscando juntos algo que talvez não existisse — um erro de impressão, um sexto dedo, uma graça escondida.

---

No dia seguinte, antes do anúncio dos vencedores, o Dr. Köhler pediu a palavra. A sala inteira silenciou — oitocentas pessoas, mais ou menos, que em qualquer outro lugar do mundo seriam consideradas excêntricas, e ali dentro eram apenas *colegas*.

"O hobby da filatelia polar", disse o alemão, em seu inglês difícil, "É talvez o hobby mais raro do planeta. Não por causa do número de praticantes — embora seja pequeno. Mas porque exige uma combinação absurda: o frio como tema, o papel como material, o tempo como substância, e uma paciência tão grande que beira a loucura."

Ele pausou.

"Nós, que colecionamos os selos dos confins do mundo, sabemos que existem lugares que ninguém alcança. E que existem coisas que só existem para os que sabem olhar de perto. Vocês são, em certo sentido, o último clube de gentlemen do planeta — não porque sejam refinados, mas porque escolheram amar algo que ninguém ama com vocês."

Otomar sentiu o ar tremer. Ao seu lado, Beatriz apertou o copo de papel do café entre os dedos.

O prêmio de ouro foi para um paulista de oitenta e três anos, por uma coleção sobre os correios antárticos argentinos — uma apresentação impecável, digna dos museus de Buenos Aires.

O prêmio de prata foi para Otomar.

Ele subiu ao palco. As mãos tremiam. Recebeu o diploma emoldurado — um papel com o brasão da Federação Internacional de Filatelia Polar — e apertou as mãos dos três juízes alemães.

Quando voltou ao seu lugar, Beatriz colocou a mão no ombro dele.

"E o sexto dedo?" — ela perguntou.

"Não existe", disse Otomar, sorrindo pela primeira vez em trinta e dois anos. "Nunca existiu. Foi recolhido por outro motivo. Talvez por vaidade. Talvez por medo."

"E o urso?"

"O urso continua lá. Em algum lugar. Andando no gelo."

---

À saída do hotel, quando a convenção já se dispersava, Otomar parou na calçada. A chuva de Curitiba tinha parado. O ar estava limpo, frio, austral de alguma forma.

Ele abriu a carteira e, no compartimento de cédulas onde caberia dinheiro, guardava outra coisa — um pequeno envelope com o fragmento da carta do estudante de Tromsø. Era o seu ímã de prótons, o ponto para o qual todas as bússolas de sua vida apontavam.

Ele não precisava mais provar nada a ninguém. Não precisava mais de uma esposa, ou de reconhecimento, ou de público. Precisava apenas continuar existindo, como o urso polar, em sua solidão escolhida.

Beatriz apareceu ao lado dele, com sua mala pequena e seu crachá de pesquisadora.

"Vou ao aeroporto", disse ela. "Mas antes — você vai voltar no próximo ano?"

Otomar pensou. Pensou nas noites em claro olhando para o catálogo, na paciência de quem espera o lote certo no eBay, na conversa com os três juízes, no sexto dedo que nunca existiu.

"Vou", disse.

E os dois, sem combinarem nada, foram andando lado a lado em direção à estação de ônibus, em silêncio — o tipo de silêncio que só é compreendido por quem já viu de perto um urso polar atravessando o gelo.

# The Quiet Hour

The bar on Clover Street had no name on its awning. There was a painted wooden sign above the door—just a small chalkboard easel that Margaret rotated each morning. Today's read: *Good evening. We are listening.*

Henry pushed through the heavy oak door at 8:47 p.m., carrying the weight of a day that had gone sideways around noon and never righted itself. He expected the usual: dim lighting, a long mahogany counter, the clink of glass on glass. He'd been told about the place by a colleague who said it had helped him, though he'd never explained what *helped* meant.

What Henry found was darker than expected and quieter. No jukebox. No television glowing blue above the bottles. Behind the counter, instead of rows of whiskey and gin, there were rows of small ceramic pots—each one labeled in neat handwriting. *Grief. Regret. Longing. Fatigue. Joy (complicated).* And dozens more he couldn't read from the doorway.

The bartender was a woman in her sixties with silver hair pulled back in a low knot. She didn't ask what he wanted. She simply placed a small linen napkin in front of him and waited.

"I don't understand," Henry said.

"What did you bring with you tonight?"

He almost laughed. "I don't know. A bad day. My marriage, maybe. The feeling that I'm forty-four years old and I still don't know what I'm doing."

She nodded and reached for one of the pots. It was labeled *Uncertainty*, and from it she poured something into a small crystal glass—not liquid, exactly, but something that moved like smoke trapped in water. She set it before him.

"You don't have to drink it," she said. "You can just sit with it. Most people stay an hour. Some stay three."

Henry took a seat on the stool. Around him, others sat in the low booths, some alone, some in pairs. A young man in a paint-stained hoodie was crying quietly into his hands while a ceramic pot labeled *Failure* sat unopened beside him. Two elderly women in the corner were laughing, sharing something from a pot marked *Winters Past*.

No one looked at Henry. No one asked him anything. He realized, after a few minutes, that this was the point.

He lifted the glass. The smoke inside it shifted, settling into something that almost resembled a memory—the way his wife's face had looked that morning when she'd asked him, gently, if he was ever going to be happy.

He didn't drink it. But he looked at it for a long time.

When he left at 9:53 p.m., the bartender placed a small card on the counter. *Same time tomorrow?* it asked.

Henry slid it into his coat pocket. Outside, the city hummed with its ordinary chaos—sirens, traffic, the laughter of strangers who had somewhere else to be. He stood for a moment on the sidewalk, breathing.

Then he turned, and walked toward home, where his wife was waiting, and where—maybe, tomorrow—the conversation he'd been avoiding for three years might finally begin.

"别哭了，"他轻声说，"你不会再被卖出去了。我保证。"

哭泣声渐渐平息。

林书白忽然明白祖母为什么一辈子守着这家不怎么赚钱的书店了。这里不只是一个卖书的地方，更是无数灵魂的庇护所。

"莫兰，"他回到那本蓝色书前，"我有个请求。"

*"说。"*

"教我怎么做这家书店的主人。教我听书说话，教我守护它们。"

书页上浮现出两个字：

*"成交。"*

然后，书店里所有的书都发出了轻微的沙沙声，像是无数声音在同时说："欢迎回家，新主人。"

窗外的最后一缕夕阳消失了，书店的灯光亮起来，温暖而柔和。林书白知道，从今天起，他的人生将翻开全新的一页。

而在那些书架深处，无数故事正等待着被发现，无数秘密正等待着被倾听。

墨痕书坊的故事，永远不会落幕。

# 深夜食堂的最后一位客人

城东那家"老周小厨"，是整个清河镇评分最低的餐厅。

大众点评1.2分，136条差评，几乎每一条都写着"难吃"、"态度差"、"再也不会来"。可奇怪的是，它每天晚上十一点准时亮灯，凌晨三点才熄，从不歇业。

我第一次推门进去，是因为喝多了。

"老板，来碗面。"

吧台后面站着一个五十多岁的男人，头发花白，系着一条洗得发白的围裙。他抬头看了我一眼，没说话，转身进了厨房。

十五分钟后，一碗清汤面端上来。

汤是清的，面条是手擀的，卧着一个煎得焦边的荷包蛋。我喝了一口汤，忽然愣住了——

是葱油味。和我妈做的一模一样。

我眼眶发酸，埋头把面吃完，放下二十块钱。

"多了。"老头数出五块递回来。

"不用找了。"

他看了我一会儿，把钱收了。

---

后来我常来。

每次都点清汤面，每次都不多说话。老周也不问，坐在吧台后面擦他的搪瓷杯，听着收音机里咿咿呀呀的戏曲。

慢慢地，我知道了他的故事。

二十年前，他儿子高考前夜，非要吃一碗葱油拌面。老周嫌他添乱，骂了几句。儿子赌气摔门出去，再也没回来。

后来在城北的河里找到人，捞上来时手里还攥着手机，屏幕碎了，最后一条消息是发给老周的："爸，面不吃了，我去同学家。"

老周从那以后就开了这家店，只卖夜宵，只做葱油面。

"差评就差评吧，"他有一次喝了点酒，跟我说，"我也不是做给别人吃的。"

"那是做给谁的？"

他没答，拿起搪瓷杯，对着空气举了举。

---

那晚之后我再去，店门紧锁。

门上贴着一张纸条，字迹颤抖：

**"店转让，厨具留下。汤底配方在第三个罐子里。"**

我问了街坊才知道，老周上个月查出来胃癌晚期，不肯治。

顺着纸条留下的地址，我找到老周租的房子。屋里没什么家具，桌上放着一个旧相框，里面的男孩穿着校服，笑得灿烂。

老周躺在床上，瘦得脱了相，却还认得我。

"来了啊。"他说。

"老板，您……"

"别叫我老板，"他笑了笑，"叫老周就行。"

我从口袋里掏出一个本子——是我这几个月偷偷记下的他的配方和做面手法。

"您看看，我学得像不像。"

他接过去翻了翻，手抖得厉害，却笑了。

"学得像。"

"那您放心，我会替您把店开下去。"

他摆摆手。

"不用，"他看着我，眼神清亮，"我那店评分太低，留着害人。你要是真想学，就去做给别人吃。"

"做给谁？"

老周望向窗外，夜色很深，什么也看不见。

"做给那些，"他说，"晚上睡不着的人。"

---

我离开清河镇的时候，把那碗葱油面的做法教给了镇上一个开早餐铺的胖大姐。

她听完愣了一下，然后笑了："行，那我早上也卖这个。"

"记得汤要清。"

"知道啦，小老板。"

多年以后我偶尔回去吃早饭，胖大姐的葱油面已经成了清河镇的招牌。

有人问她为什么做这个，她说是跟一个老先生学的。

"那老先生人呢？"

她擦着围裙，笑了笑。

"走啦。走得挺安详的。"

**—— 完 ——**

# The Curve of Baker Street

Margaret had walked past it every morning for thirty-seven years.

The iron railing on the corner of Baker and Wexford had become so familiar that her hand knew its bumps the way a tongue knows the ridges of a favorite spoon. She'd gripped it crossing the road, leaned against it waiting for buses, tapped it impatiently during long phone conversations with her mother in 1987. She'd run her gloves along its scrollwork the morning of David's funeral, and again, fourteen years later, the morning she'd scattered his ashes in the garden behind their flat.

It was, she supposed, just a railing. Wrought iron, painted black every few years by some borough worker she never saw. The paint peeled in little curls she could pick at with her thumbnail if she let herself. She'd watched pigeons land on it in every season, watched a fox sniff along its base one winter night at three in the morning, watched a child bounce a ball off it once, repeatedly, while his mother scolded in a language Margaret didn't speak.

She had not, until this morning, ever really *looked* at it.

She was late, as usual, for the corner shop. She'd forgotten the sugar, or the milk, or some small errand that sent her back out into the gray October air. The light was doing something strange—a low, amber slant through the clouds that made the wet pavement look like poured bronze. And the railing, suddenly, was not a railing at all.

It was a vine. A climbing thing, frozen mid-reach by some Victorian blacksmith who had understood, with a patience Margaret had never credited him with, that iron could grow. The scrolls unfurled like ferns uncurling in spring. The finial at the top—she had never really looked at the finial, she realized, never once in nearly four decades—bloomed into a tight, perfect rose, its petals layered just so, each one a small triumph of hammered metal.

She put her hand on it. The iron was cold, of course. Iron was always cold. But this morning it felt like a pulse.

Margaret thought of David, who had once spent an entire Sunday afternoon sketching a single dandelion in the garden, saying *look at the architecture of it, Meg, look at the engineering*. She had thought he was being fanciful. She had not understood that he was being precise.

She thought of her mother, gone now twelve years, who had kept a small glass dish on the kitchen windowsill for "special buttons"—buttons that fell off coats, buttons that came in jars, buttons of no particular value, gathered only because her mother had decided they were worth looking at. Margaret had rolled her eyes at the dish. She had not understood that her mother was building a museum, one button at a time, of the world's small perfections.

She thought of herself, at seven, pressing her nose to the front window and watching rain fall in slanted silver threads against the streetlamp, thinking the world was a place of wonders, every one of them.

She had lost that. Somewhere between seven and sixty-four, she had lost that. And the railing, she understood now, had been waiting for her. Patient as a saint. Patient as iron. It had bloomed there, quietly, every single morning, and she had walked past it with her head full of sugar and milk and grief and weather.

A blackbird landed on the rose finial. It tilted its head at her, gave a single bright call, and flew away.

Margaret stood there for a long time. The shop could wait. The sugar could wait. She had finally, after all these years, somewhere to be.

# 一盆绿萝

苏晚是在搬家公司离开后的第三个小时，才意识到屋子里有多空。

三十七平的一居室，客厅和卧室之间只隔了一道半截墙。她站在窗前，看着对面阳台上别人晾的床单被风吹成一个鼓起来的气球，又慢慢瘪下去。茶几上放着她刚泡的速溶咖啡，纸箱还没来得及拆完，最上面那个写着"书籍"的箱子里，露出一截多肉植物的旧花盆边缘。

那是她养了三年的桃蛋，死在了去年冬天。

苏晚在原来的出租屋住了五年，房东是个六十多岁的大爷，从不涨租，每到过年还会给她塞一袋自己包的饺子。苏晚在那间屋子里学会了自己做饭、学会了换灯泡、学会了在深夜加班回来后对着空气说"我回家了"。后来大爷的儿子要把房子收回去给孙子做婚房，提前两个月通知她搬家。

她找了两周的房子，最后选了现在这间。租金便宜，采光还行，离地铁站步行八分钟。签合同那天她在小区门口的小饭馆吃了碗牛肉面，庆祝乔迁之喜，面汤里放了很多醋，酸得她直皱眉头。

搬家公司的工人走后，她坐在纸箱堆里发了会儿呆，然后出门了。

小区北门外那条街新开了不少店，奶茶店、打印店、房产中介，还有一家花店。花店不大，门头上挂着一串塑料绿藤，招牌上写着"青藤园艺"。苏晚路过时脚步慢了一下，然后走了进去。

店里灯光暖黄，空气里有泥土和植物混合的气味。她不懂花，只认识几种最常见的，绿萝、吊兰、发财树。老板是个二十出头的姑娘，正蹲在地上给一盆什么植物换土，抬头看了她一眼："随便看啊，有喜欢的可以问我。"

苏晚在一排绿色里走了个来回，最后停在一盆绿萝前面。

它长在一个白色的陶盆里，叶子很绿，有几片叶尖发黄，但整体还算精神。她想起小时候家里的阳台上，奶奶也养过一盆绿萝，用的是搪瓷缸子，里面的土总是湿的。奶奶去世后那盆绿萝没人管，最后枯成了一捆干柴。

"这盆多少钱？"

"二十五。"

苏晚付了钱，提着那盆绿萝往回走。路过便利店时她又买了一袋营养土和一个小喷壶。进小区的时候，保安大爷在门岗室里看电视，朝她点了点头。她也点了点头。

回到屋里，她把绿萝放在窗台上。

夕阳正好照过来，在白色的墙面上投下一个摇晃的影子。她站在那里看了它很久，叶子边缘有一圈淡淡的金色。

苏晚忽然想，这盆绿萝以后也会长出很长的藤，垂到地上，或者爬上窗框。她会定期给它浇水，偶尔搬到阳台上晒晒太阳。也许明年春天它会开一次花，也许不会。但无论怎样，它都会在这里。

她在这个城市里又有一个地方，可以放一盆植物了。

苏晚从纸箱堆里翻出一个杯子，倒了点水，慢慢浇在绿萝的根部。水渗进土里，发出轻微的声响。

窗外的天色暗下来，她没有开灯，就那么站在原地，看着那盆绿萝的轮廓在暮色中一点点模糊，又慢慢和整间屋子融为一体。

她终于觉得，这个家开始有点像家了。

# The Album in the Attic

Dust motes swirled in the slanted light as Eleanor lifted the album from the trunk. The leather cover was cracked and brittle, its gilt edges worn to pale threads. She hadn't opened it in fifteen years—hadn't been able to. Not since the funeral.

The first pages were formal portraits. Her great-grandparents, stiff-backed and unsmiling in turn-of-the-century sepia. Then photographs that grew looser, freer: picnics on summer lawns, children with sunburned noses, a dog that appeared in four consecutive Christmases.

Eleanor turned the pages slowly, her fingertip tracing the curling corners. Here was her mother at twenty-three, laughing at something off-camera, her whole face lit up. Eleanor had never seen that laugh. By the time Eleanor was old enough to remember, grief had already settled into the lines around her mother's mouth.

A loose photograph slipped from between the pages. Eleanor caught it before it hit the floor and held it up to the light.

Two girls stood on a dock, arms around each other's shoulders, the lake behind them impossibly blue. Her sister Margot, and another girl Eleanor didn't recognize. On the back, in handwriting she knew as well as her own, was written: *M. and C., summer of '61.*

Margot had died in 1987. Eleanor had been twenty-four. In all the years since, she'd never heard anyone mention a "C."

She sat with the photograph in her lap for a long time, listening to the old house settle around her. Then she carried it to the desk, pulled out a piece of paper, and began a letter she had no one to address.

*Dear C.,*

*You knew my sister. I would very much like to know you.*

Outside, the first snow of November began to fall, soft and slow, covering the steps she hadn't yet swept.

# The Weight of Silence

The morning light cut through the dusty blinds of Marcus's living room, illuminating the chess set that had been his constant companion for the past three years. At sixty-two, his wife Eleanor had stopped asking him to join her book club, stopped suggesting dinners out, stopped filling the silence that had grown between them like ivy on a forgotten wall.

"It's your move," Marcus said, though he was alone. He moved his knight, captured an invisible bishop, and sighed.

When the doorbell rang, he ignored it. It rang again. And again.

"I'm not buying anything," he muttered, shuffling to the door in his threadbare slippers.

But it was his granddaughter Lily, sixteen and vibrating with the particular energy of someone who refused to accept the word "no."

"Grandpa." She pushed past him without invitation, a battered tackle box under one arm. "We're going fishing."

"We are absolutely not going fishing."

"Grandpa." She set the tackle box on his coffee table, right next to his chess set, and fixed him with eyes that were Eleanor's eyes, that were his daughter's eyes, that were somehow every stubborn woman in this family condensed into one pointed stare. "Grandma called me."

"Eleanor called you about what?"

"About how you haven't left this apartment in two weeks. About how you talk to your chess pieces. About how you—" Her voice cracked, just slightly, before she steeled it again. "She asked me to try. So I'm trying."

Marcus looked at the tackle box. Looked at his granddaughter. "I don't fish."

"You used to." Lily pulled out a worn photograph from her back pocket—him at thirty-five, holding up a trout almost as long as his arm, grinning like he'd won the lottery. "You taught me when I was eight. Remember? You said fishing wasn't about catching anything. It was about—" she squinted, pretending to remember, "—'being still enough to hear what the world is trying to tell you.'"

"I said that?"

"You said a lot of things. Then you stopped."

He wanted to argue. He wanted to retreat back to his chair, his chess set, his careful solitude. But there was something in Lily's face that reminded him of himself, once, before the silence had become a country he lived in rather than a sea he crossed.

"One hour," he said. "One hour, and then I'm coming home."

Lily's smile broke like sunrise. "Deal."

---

They drove to Lake Harmon in her beat-up Civic, the tackle box rattling between them like a metronome. Marcus hadn't been outside in weeks, and the wind through the open window felt like a question he didn't know how to answer.

"I don't even know if the fish are biting," he grumbled.

"Grandpa." Lily parked and killed the engine. "The fish don't have to bite. We just have to show up."

She said it with such simple certainty that he almost laughed.

They found a spot on the old wooden dock, the one he'd fished from as a boy, as a young man, as a father. The wood was weathered now, silver-grey, and he wondered if he looked the same to it as it looked to him.

Lily set up his rod with practiced hands, threading the line, tying a knot he didn't recognize. "Dad taught me the new knots," she said. "The old ones were falling apart anyway. Like a lot of things."

She baited his hook without him asking. Cast his line without him asking. Handed him the rod with a gentleness that made his throat tight.

"Now what?" he asked.

"Now we wait."

Waiting. He was good at waiting. Had spent three years waiting for Eleanor to fill the silence, for his daughter to call back, for sleep to come without dreaming. But this waiting was different. This waiting had Lily beside him, kicking her feet in the water, humming something off-key.

"An hour's up," she announced forty-five minutes later.

"I didn't say stop."

"I know." She smiled at the water. "I was giving you the option."

He pulled his line in. Empty hook. Threw it back.

They stayed until the sun began its slow slide toward the trees, until the sky turned the color of a healed bruise, until Eleanor texted to ask if they wanted dinner.

"She knew you'd say yes," Marcus said, looking at his phone.

"She always knows," Lily said. "Grandmas are like that."

On the drive home, with the windows down and the evening settling around them like a blanket, Marcus reached over and squeezed his granddaughter's hand.

"Same time Thursday?"

"Every Thursday," she said, like it was the most obvious thing in the world. "Until you don't need me anymore."

He watched the road unspool before them, and for the first time in three years, he didn't feel like he was driving away from something.

He felt like he was coming home.

The kettle whistled, a thin, familiar sound that had punctuated Miriam's mornings for forty-three years. She lifted it off the burner before the whistle could sharpen into a scream and poured the steaming water over the pale gold leaves in her favorite chipped mug—the one with the faded blue forget-me-nots that her daughter had given her when she first moved into the small apartment above the laundromat.

It was not her apartment, of course. It belonged to Mr. Petrakis, who lived downstairs and who charged her very little rent in exchange for her keeping an eye on the building, watering his plants when he visited his sister in Thessaloniki, and pretending not to notice when his grandson came around at odd hours. Miriam suspected the grandson was selling something that was not baked goods, but she had learned, in her years, that some things were better left unobserved.

She carried the mug to the window and looked down at the street. It was early still—the kind of early where the light had not quite committed to being light, where the cars parked along the curb still wore a faint dusting of dew. A woman she did not recognize was walking a dog she did recognize: the small brown terrier that belonged to the new tenants on the third floor. The couple fought often, but the dog seemed happy enough.

Miriam wrapped both hands around the mug and thought about nothing in particular. This was, she had come to believe, the closest thing to happiness available to a person: a warm cup in your hands, a window to look through, and no particular reason to do anything else.

She was just lifting the mug to her lips when she heard the footsteps on the stairs.

They were hesitant footsteps, the kind that pause on every other step, as if the person climbing them were having second thoughts. Miriam knew the rhythm of everyone in the building. Mr. Petrakis's shuffle. The young couple's quick, simultaneous tread. The mail carrier's heavy boots. These were not any of those.

She set the mug down on the windowsill and waited.

There was a knock at her door—soft, almost apologetic.

"Coming," she called, though she wasn't. She liked to make people wait a moment. It gave her time to arrange her face into something welcoming, and to decide, based on the smallest clues, who it might be.

She opened the door.

The girl on the landing could not have been more than nineteen or twenty. She had dark hair cut short and unevenly, as if she had done it herself in a bathroom mirror, and she wore a coat that was too large for her—men's, by the look of it, the kind of wool coat that had once been respectable and was now tired. Her eyes were red-rimmed, and her hands, Miriam noticed, were trembling.

"I'm sorry," the girl said. "I don't—I don't know where else to go."

Miriam studied her for a long moment. She had seen enough of the world to know the particular posture of someone who had been walking all night, of someone who was trying very hard not to cry, of someone who had knocked on this door specifically because it had looked like the kind of door that might open.

"You're cold," Miriam said. It was not a question.

"Yes," the girl said.

"Well. Come in, then. I just put the kettle on."

She stepped aside, and the girl came into the apartment as carefully as if she were entering a temple, or a dream. Miriam closed the door behind her and went back to the stove, where she set about making a second cup of tea with the same unhurried movements she had used for the first.

"The milk is in the door of the fridge," she said over her shoulder. "Help yourself if you'd like. And there's bread, if you're hungry."

The girl stood in the middle of the small kitchen, still wearing her coat, still trembling slightly. "I don't have any money," she said.

"I didn't ask you for any."

"Why are you being kind to me?"

Miriam considered this. She poured the hot water into a second mug—this one plain white, chipped at the rim—and set it on the table in front of the girl.

"Because," she said, "the tea is better when it's shared. That is the only reason. And perhaps because you looked like you needed somewhere to be for a little while."

The girl sat down. She pulled the coat tighter around her shoulders, and then, slowly, as if remembering how, she reached for the mug.

Outside, the sun had finally committed to rising. The light came through the window and lay across the table in a long, warm stripe, touching the girl's hands, the chipped mugs, the steam that rose from both of them in curling, parallel columns.

"Thank you," the girl whispered.

Miriam sat down across from her with her own mug cradled in her hands. She did not ask the girl's name. She did not ask where she had come from or where she was going. There would be time for questions later, or there would not; either way, the tea was best drunk while it was still hot, and the morning was best met in the company of someone, even a stranger, even someone who had appeared on your doorstep like a bird blown in from a storm.

She sipped. The girl sipped. And for a little while, in the small apartment above the laundromat, neither of them said anything at all.

林夏把藤编野餐垫铺开的时候，手机显示下午两点十三分。三月的阳光像稀释过的蜂蜜，懒洋洋地淌过法租界梧桐树的枝桠，在草地上烙出一片斑驳的金色。

她把三明治从棉布袋里取出来——火腿芝士的，是男友陈屿最爱的口味。旁边的玻璃罐里装着她今早亲手煮的柠檬茶，柠檬片还带着冰箱的凉意。还有一盒马卡龙，粉色的草莓味，淡绿的开心果味，摆成两排小队列兵似的。

"你真把这场野餐当回事啊。"陈屿到的时候，西装革履还没来得及换，手里拎着笔记本电脑。

"你上周答应我的。"林夏没有抬头，把番茄酱瓶子摆正了一点点。

陈屿在她身边坐下，扯松了领带，但还是把电脑搁在了膝盖上。"等一下，我把这份报表发掉，就半小时。"

林夏没说话。她看着法租界的梧桐树，看着草地上追逐的白色萨摩耶，看着远处一个女孩正往天上放风筝。她想，她已经三十二岁了，不应该再为这种事情生气。

可她还是生了气。

---

风是在三点零七分刮起来的。

起初只是树叶沙沙地响，然后野餐垫的一角被掀起来，像有人扯住了一角在抖动。林夏赶紧按住那盒马卡龙——粉色的那只已经滚了出去，滚到了草地里，沾了一身绿色的草屑。

"陈屿！"

陈屿头也不抬地说："你按一下。"

风变大了。野餐垫被整个吹翻，三明治飞出去，柠檬茶瓶子倒了，琥珀色的液体从棉布袋里渗出来。林夏扑过去抢救那盒马卡龙——草莓味的那只先落地了，碎成几瓣粉色的尸骸。

"陈屿！电脑！"

她喊的时候，陈屿正盯着屏幕皱眉。他慢了半拍，合上电脑的时候，屏幕上已经溅了几滴柠檬茶。

"你怎么不早说！"陈屿吼了一声。

"我——"

"我这报表还没保存呢！"

林夏站在风里，头发贴在脸上，手里还捏着那盒幸存的马卡龙。她突然觉得这一切都荒谬极了。她想笑，可眼眶却开始发热。

---

后来的事情像被按了快进键。

陈屿去公司处理"被毁掉的文件"，留下林夏一个人在公园里收拾残局。她蹲在草地上，把碎掉的三明治扔进垃圾袋，把打湿的棉布叠起来，把那些完好的马卡龙一只只放回盒子。

阳光依旧很好。放风筝的女孩已经收线了，那只风筝挂在远处的树枝上，像一只受伤的鸟。

林夏坐在空荡荡的野餐垫上，打开手机。朋友圈里有人在晒下午茶，有人在晒新买的包。她想发点什么，可又觉得没有什么好发的。

她打开和陈屿的对话框。最后一条消息还是两天前的，她说"明天野餐别迟到"，他回了一个"嗯"。

她把手机扔到一边，仰面躺在草地上。

---

蚂蚁是在这个时候出现的。

她感觉有什么东西在手腕上爬，抬手一看，一只黑色的小蚂蚁正沿着她的生命线跋涉。她没有拂掉它，只是看着。

蚂蚁爬到了她的中指指尖，停下来，触角动了动，像在思考什么。然后它掉头，往回走。

林夏突然想，她是不是也应该掉头。

---

五点半的时候，她给陈屿发了条消息：

"我们谈谈。"

发完她就把手机关了机。她知道陈屿会在半小时后回过来，问她"怎么了"，问"是不是还在生气"。他会道歉，但那种道歉像一块补丁，缝在裂痕上，下一次还会裂开。

她站起身，拍了拍裙子上的草屑。

夕阳把法租界的梧桐影子拉得很长，像一根根细瘦的手指，指向她来的方向。

她没有回头。

---

走出公园的时候，她的手机震了一下。她没有看，只是把那盒还剩两只的马卡龙扔进了路边的垃圾桶。

粉色的草莓味。淡绿的开心果味。

她忽然想起来，这两种口味，陈屿都不爱吃。

这是她自己喜欢的。
