# Der alte Pendel und das neue Herz

Die 3 im Hofcafé an der Eichenstraße rostete seit drei Jahren an ihrem Platz. Niemand wusste mehr genau, wer sie hingestellt hatte – vielleicht der alte Petersen, vielleicht der Hausmeister, vielleicht ein Student, der längst in eine andere Stadt gezogen war. Sie trug die Patina einer kleinen Ewigkeit, hatte Risse im Plastik und einen Fleck auf dem Sitzpolster, der aussah wie eine verblasste Landkarte.

Mira sah die 3 jeden Morgen, wenn sie das Café betrat. Sie war vor sechs Wochen aus Hamburg gekommen, in eine Wohnung drei Häuser weiter, und hatte sich noch immer nicht daran gewöhnt, dass die Leute hier „Moin" sagten, selbst um vier Uhr nachmittags, und dass der Bäcker sie beim dritten Besuch mit Namen kannte.

An diesem Dienstag – es war der Dienstag, an dem alles begann – saß bereits jemand auf der 3.

„Ist der Platz frei?", fragte Mira.

Die Frau auf der 3 blickte auf. Sie war vielleicht sechzig, trug eine viel zu große Jacke und einen Schal in der Farbe von trockenem Moos. „Für Sie immer."

Mira setzte sich auf die 2. Sie bestellte ihren Kaffee, schlug ihr Buch auf und las drei Seiten, ohne ein Wort zu verstehen. Die Frau ihr gegenüber las auch, ein Taschenbuch mit einem abgegriffenen Einband. Sie trank keinen Kaffee, sondern heiße Schokolade mit viel zu viel Schlagsahne.

Sie sprachen nicht miteinander.

---

Es wurde eine Gewohnheit.

Manchmal saß die Frau schon da, manchmal kam Mira zuerst. Sie grüßten sich, sie nickten, sie lächelten manchmal über dieselbe Sache – den Kellner, der ständig mit dem Tablett gegen die Tür stieß, den Vogel, der jeden Morgen versuchte, durch die Glasscheibe zu fliegen. Sie redeten nicht. Es war eine Freundschaft, die sich nicht anhörte wie eine.

Eines Nachmittags – es war Donnerstag, und es regnete so dicht, dass die Welt hinter den Scheiben zu Tinte wurde – legte die Frau plötzlich ihr Buch hin.

„Sie lesen gerade *Die Vermessung der Welt*", sagte sie.

Mira blickte auf. „Ja."

„Ich auch. Zum dritten Mal." Die Frau strich über den Einband. „Ich finde, es ist ein Buch über zwei Sorten von Einsamkeit. Humboldt konnte unter Menschen nicht atmen. Gauss konnte es nur unter Menschen."

Mira lachte. „Das ist die klügste Rezension, die ich je gehört habe."

Die Frau hob ihre Tasse. „Ich heiße übrigens Margit."

„Mira."

„Wissen Sie, Mira, ich bin erst seit sechs Wochen hier. Ich bin aus Köln. Ich bin hier, weil meine Tochter mich eingeladen hat, und meine Tochter weiß nicht, dass ich eigentlich nur gekommen bin, weil ich mich von meinem Mann getrennt habe und nicht wusste, wohin."

Mira schwieg. Dann sagte sie: „Ich bin hergezogen, weil mein letzter Freund gesagt hat, ich würde mich hinter Büchern verstecken. Also bin ich in eine Stadt gezogen, in der ich niemanden kenne, um zu beweisen, dass ich das nicht tue."

Margit sah sie an. „Und? Funktioniert es?"

„Ich sitze gerade mit einer Fremden in einem Café und rede über Alexander von Humboldt. Das fühlt sich nicht wie ein Versteck an."

Margit lachte – ein kleines, warmes Lachen, das ein bisschen wie Regen klang. „Gut. Dann sind wir quitt. Ich heiße Margit, ich bin sechzig, und ich habe gerade erfahren, dass ich anscheinend hysterisch bin."

„Wer sagt das?"

„Mein Mann. Er hat es in einem Brief geschrieben, der eigentlich ein Abschiedsbrief war. *Liebe Margit, du machst alles hysterisch.* Ich habe den Brief fünfmal gelesen. Ich glaube, ich bin nicht hysterisch. Ich glaube, ich bin nur eine Frau, die weint, wenn sie weinen muss."

---

Von diesem Tag an änderte sich die 3.

Sie redeten jetzt. Nicht viel. Nicht laut. Aber sie redeten.

Sie redeten über Humboldt und über Gauss, über Kölner Dom und Hamburger Hafen, über das Wetter in dieser neuen Stadt, das sich anfühlte wie das Wetter in keiner anderen Stadt – zu weich für September, zu grau für Mai.

Margit erzählte von ihrer Tochter, die so beschäftigt war mit ihrem Leben, dass sie manchmal drei Tage vergaß, anzurufen. Mira erzählte von ihrem Ex-Freund, der in ihrer Wohnung in Hamburg noch eine Zahnbürste hatte, die sie jetzt symbolisch nicht vermisste.

Eines Morgens kam Margit nicht.

Mira wartete eine Stunde. Sie bestellte zwei Kaffees, dann trank sie beide. Sie las das Buch nicht. Sie schrieb Margit eine SMS, die sie sofort wieder löschte.

Am nächsten Tag kam Margit nicht. Und am übernächsten.

Am vierten Tag setzte sich jemand Fremder auf die 3. Ein junger Mann mit Kopfhörern und einem Laptop. Er bemerkte nicht, dass Mira ihn anstarrte, als hätte er einen Diebstahl begangen.

---

Mira erfuhr zwei Wochen später, was passiert war. Margits Tochter erzählte es im Café – einer Freundin, die es ihrer Mutter erzählte, die es Mira erzählte. Margit hatte einen Schlaganfall gehabt, nicht schwer, aber schwer genug. Sie war jetzt in einer Reha-Klinik in der Nachbarstadt, und sie kam erst in zwei Monaten zurück, wenn überhaupt.

Mira schrieb ihr einen Brief. Sie schrieb drei, dann riss sie sie alle auf.

Sie schrieb den vierten:

*Liebe Margit,*

*ich sitze auf der 3, und es ist kalt. Die 2 ist auch da, aber die 2 ist nicht dasselbe ohne Sie. Ich habe heute übrigens herausgefunden, dass Humboldt einmal in Freiberg eine silberne Treppe hinuntergefallen ist und sich den Schädel gebrochen hat. Er war danach ein halbes Jahr krank und schrieb trotzdem fünf Bücher. Ich glaube, das ist ein bisschen wie das, was Ihnen gerade passiert.*

*Ich vermisse Sie.*

*Ihre Mira*

Den Brief steckte sie nicht ein. Sie faltete ihn zusammen und schob ihn zwischen die Seiten von *Die Vermessung der Welt*, das sie nicht mehr las.

---

Drei Wochen später, an einem Montag, setzte sich jemand auf die 3.

Es war nicht Margit. Es war Margits Tochter. Sie war jünger, als Mira sie sich vorgestellt hatte – Mitte dreißig, müde, freundlich.

„Sie sind Mira, oder?", sagte sie.

„Ja."

„Meine Mutter hat mir von Ihnen erzählt. Sie hat in der Reha viel von Ihnen erzählt. Sie hat mir gesagt, ich soll Ihnen das hier geben."

Sie legte einen Umschlag auf den Tisch. Mira öffnete ihn nicht sofort. Margits Tochter trank einen Kaffee, dann stand sie auf.

„Sie hat übrigens gesagt, ich soll mich bei Ihnen entschuldigen."

„Wofür?"

„Dafür, dass ich in den letzten Jahren nicht angerufen habe. Sie hat gesagt, Sie hätten ihr das beigebracht – dass man manchmal zu beschäftigt ist mit dem eigenen Leben, um zu merken, dass man jemanden verliert."

Sie ging. Mira blieb sitzen. Sie öffnete den Umschlag.

Darin war ein Foto von der 3, auf der Rückseite in Margits krakeliger Schrift:

*Wir haben uns ein Café geteilt. Das ist mehr, als die meisten Menschen jemals bekommen.*

Mira faltete das Foto zusammen und schob es in ihre Jackentasche. Sie bestellte einen Kaffee und eine heiße Schokolade mit extra Schlagsahne. Sie trank beides.

---

Margit kam nicht zurück.

Nicht nach zwei Monaten. Nicht nach drei. Irgendwann rief Margits Tochter an und sagte, ihre Mutter sei in ein Heim in der Nähe von Köln gezogen, näher bei ihrer alten Heimat, näher bei den Erinnerungen, die sie brauchte. Mira sagte, sie verstehe das.

Sie verstand es nicht.

Sie ging weiter in das Café. Sie saß auf der 2, weil die 3 war noch immer von Fremden besetzt, immer von anderen, die nicht wussten, dass dieser Stuhl jemandem gehörte. Sie las *Die Vermessung der Welt* zu Ende und legte das Buch dann auf den Tisch, mit dem Brief an Margit noch immer zwischen den Seiten.

Eines Tages – es war ein Jahr später, ein Dienstag im Oktober – sagte der Kellner:

„Sie wissen schon, dass der Stuhl Ihnen gehört, oder? Seit einem Jahr reserviere ich ihn für Sie. Der alte Stammgast neben Ihnen hat gefragt, ob er ihn haben kann. Ich habe gesagt, der ist vergeben."

Mira lächelte. „Von wem?"

„Von Ihnen. Von der Dame, die nicht mehr kommt."

Mira dachte nach. „Stimmt", sagte sie dann. „Von der Dame, die nicht mehr kommt."

Sie ging nach Hause und schrieb Margit einen letzten Brief. Diesen steckte sie in einen Umschlag, und diesen Umschlag schickte sie an das Heim in Köln.

Sie schrieb:

*Liebe Margit,*

*Sie haben mir einmal gesagt, Sie seien hysterisch. Ich glaube, Sie sind nicht hysterisch. Ich glaube, Sie sind die mutigste Frau, die ich je in einem Café getroffen habe. Sie haben sich hingesetzt und sind geblieben. Sie haben mit einer Fremden über Humboldt geredet, obwohl Sie das nicht mussten. Sie haben mir beigebracht, dass Freundschaft nicht bedeutet, dass man immer da ist. Sie bedeutet, dass man da war.*

*Ich sitze weiter auf der 2. Ich trinke meinen Kaffee und Ihre heiße Schokolade. Ich denke an Sie.*

*Ihre Mira*

Sie bekam nie eine Antwort. Drei Wochen später kam ein Brief aus dem Heim. Margits Tochter schrieb, ihre Mutter habe den Brief gelesen und dann lange geweint, und dann habe sie gesagt:

*Sag ihr, sie soll nicht aufhören zu lesen. Und sie soll nicht aufhören, mit Fremden zu reden. Es lohnt sich.*

Mira faltete den Brief zusammen und schob ihn in das Buch. Sie ging am nächsten Tag wieder ins Café. Sie setzte sich auf die 2. Die 3 war leer.

Sie bestellte zwei Getränke. Sie trank beide. Dann stand sie auf, legte einen Zwanzig-Euro-Schein auf den Tisch und sagte zum Kellner:

„Für die 3. Für falls jemand kommt."

Sie ging nach Hause, und draußen war es Herbst, und die Blätter fielen, und sie dachte: Das ist das Seltsame an Freundschaften – sie beginnen mit einem Satz und enden mit einer Geste, und dazwischen ist alles das wirkliche Leben.

Sie öffnete die Tür zu ihrer Wohnung. Sie hängte ihre Jacke an den Haken. Sie nahm *Die Vermessung der Welt* aus der Tasche und legte es auf den Tisch neben ihrem Bett.

Sie würde es noch einmal lesen. Morgen. Mit anderen Augen.

Draußen wurde es dunkel. In Köln war es auch dunkel. Und irgendwo zwischen diesen beiden Dunkelheiten saß eine alte Frau in einem Heim und dachte an eine 3 in einem Café und an eine Fremde, die sie einmal geliebt hatte, ohne es zu wissen.

Freundschaft, dachte Mira, ist nichts, was man besitzt. Sie ist etwas, was man weitergibt. Sie ist ein Stuhl, den man für jemanden freihält. Sie ist ein Brief, den man nicht schickt, weil man weiß, dass er angekommen ist.

Sie machte das Licht aus.

Sie schlief ein.

Und in ihrem Buch, zwischen den Seiten 184 und 185, faltete sich das Foto von der 3 ein bisschen, als würde es atmen, als würde es sich erinnern, als würde es wissen, dass alles, was jemals zwischen zwei Menschen wirklich gewesen ist, nie aufhört, auch wenn die Stühle leer werden und die Städte sich verändern und die Jahre vergehen wie Regen über einer Glasscheibe.

Es hört nicht auf.

Es hat nie aufgehört.

# The Wrong Sort of Trouble

The rain in Ashford had been falling for three days, and Mira Voss had decided she was finished being patient with it.

She stood in the doorway of her rented cottage, arms crossed, watching the storm flatten her garden. Mud had crept up the flagstone path, and the rosemary she'd planted that spring was looking drowned and sorry. Inside, a kettle whistled. Outside, the world was a grey smear. And somewhere, she suspected, the universe was laughing at her.

A knock came at the door—three sharp raps that had no business being so confident on such a wretched day.

Mira opened it.

The man on her step was the sort of person she avoided in cities: too tall, too rumpled, with a coat that had clearly been through several lifetimes. His hair was dark and pushed back without ceremony, and there was a smear of something on his jaw—ink, she thought, or possibly jam. He had the look of a man who had not slept well and was not interested in discussing it.

"Miss Voss?" he said, as though confirming a suspicion he'd rather not have confirmed.

"Yes."

"I'm from next door." He did not smile. "The fence. The one your chimney fell on."

"It was the wind."

"The wind." He looked at the sky as if asking it to back him up. The sky offered no assistance. "My greenhouse is in twelve pieces. My seedlings are in the back field. My insurance is in the post."

Mira felt her spine stiffen. She had come to this village to be left alone. She had come to be a quiet woman in a quiet place, writing her quiet books, minding her quiet business. The last thing she required was some damp, accusatory stranger telling her about his seedlings.

"The wind," she repeated, and began to close the door.

He put out a hand. Not roughly—more like a man stopping a swinging gate. "I'm Theo. Theo Marsh."

"I know who you are."

"You do?"

"The villagers talk." *About you*, she didn't add, because what they said was none of her business and almost certainly untrue. They said he was odd. They said he kept strange hours and stranger company. They said he had once, years ago, done something nobody could quite name, and that the village had never quite forgiven him for it. Mira didn't believe most of what people said. She also didn't intend to find out.

"I see," said Theo. His eyes were very blue and very tired. "Then you'll know I don't want trouble."

"You've come to the wrong cottage for that, then."

She closed the door. The kettle screamed, the rain drummed, and Mira went to make her tea with the firm belief that she would never speak to Theo Marsh again.

---

Theo stood on the step for a moment after the door closed. He looked at the wet stone, the downtrodden rosemary, the small cottage with its chimney slightly askew. He had come expecting—an apology, perhaps. A discussion. Some adult exchange about fences and weather and the basic responsibilities of homeownership.

He had not come expecting *that*.

The woman behind the door had been tall and precise, with dark hair cut to her jaw and a face that suggested she had stopped being surprised by the world some years ago. Her voice had been cool, her eyes colder, and the look she'd given him—the *look*—had been the particular brand of polite contempt he had come to Ashford to escape.

He pulled his collar up and walked home through the rain.

The greenhouse was indeed in twelve pieces, though he'd exaggerated. It was in nine. The seedlings were mostly fine, being a hardy sort. The insurance was, in fact, in the post.

Theo Marsh had not always been a man who grew seedlings and avoided his neighbours. Ten years ago, he had been a barrister in London, the sort that newspapers wrote about. He had worn good suits. He had won cases. He had had a wife, briefly, and a reputation, longer.

Then there had been a case. A young woman. A man who should not have been defended, defended too well. And afterward, a silence Theo could not get out of, no matter how many rooms he filled with plants.

He came to Ashford to learn how to be small. To be a man who mended fences and lost arguments about chimneys and was not, in any way, important.

This woman, with her sharp mouth and her closed door, was the first person in three years to make him feel like he was still the man he'd been.

He didn't like it.

---

Mira spent the next morning re-reading a chapter of her manuscript and finding nothing in it she liked. The trouble with writing a novel was that you had to spend time inside your own head, and her head, today, contained nothing but the memory of those blue eyes on her doorstep. It was infuriating. She had closed that door for a reason. She had closed every door for a reason.

She had come to Ashford eight months ago, after the affair with David, after the book tour that had been a kind of public flaying, after the long and quiet unraveling she did not care to name. She had told her publisher she needed space. Her publisher had said, *Of course, darling, take all the time in the world, just don't take too much*. Mira had taken a cottage, installed herself in it, and announced to the village that she was a reclusive writer who did not wish to be disturbed.

The village had respected this about as much as villages ever respect such things, which is to say, not at all. People left vegetables on her step. People waved. People asked about the weather and, when she said *fine*, said *is it?* and stood in her garden.

But no one had stood on her step and looked at her the way Theo Marsh had. As if he could see the part of her she had been so careful to bury.

She went out at noon to walk off the feeling. The rain had stopped, leaving the village in a rinsed and gleaming quiet. She passed the church, the pub, the pond where the ducks were conducting some kind of meeting. She did not intend to walk past Theo's cottage. The lane simply bent that way.

He was in the wreckage of his greenhouse, of course, sorting through glass. He had the look of a man who had decided that if the world would not leave him alone, he would at least make it tidy. He was, she noted with irritation, wearing the same coat.

He saw her. He straightened. He did not wave.

She walked past without speaking. She made it six steps.

"Your rosemary," he said, to her back.

She stopped. Turned, slightly. "What about it?"

"It's not dead." He wiped his hands on a rag. "Rosemary likes wet. You're overthinking the drainage."

Mira stared at him. She had been overthinking the drainage for a week. She had consulted three books. She had considered writing to the Royal Horticultural Society.

"I'm fine," she said, in the tone of voice that meant she was not fine and resented the question.

"Of course," said Theo. He picked up a piece of glass and held it to the light. "Just trying to be neighbourly."

"Then be neighbourly from a distance."

She walked on. She did not look back. She absolutely did not think about the way he'd said *neighbourly*, as if the word tasted of something he didn't entirely trust.

---

The third time they met, it was not a meeting so much as an ambush by circumstance.

Mira was at the post office. The post office was run by a woman named Peggy, who was seventy-four and had opinions about most things and all people. Mira was attempting to post a manuscript to her editor when the door opened and Theo Marsh walked in, holding a small package and looking, if possible, more exhausted than the last time she had seen him.

"Ah," said Peggy, in the tone of a woman who has been waiting all morning for exactly this. "Mr. Marsh. And Miss Voss. Both here. Together."

"Peggy," said Mira, warningly.

"I was only saying," said Peggy, with the wounded dignity of the entirely unbothered. "How nice. Two of my favourite people. In one place. At one time."

Theo looked at Mira. Mira looked at the ceiling. Outside, a car passed. The post office, which was roughly the size of a generous closet, suddenly felt like a confessional.

"I've come about the fence," said Theo.

"The fence is fine."

"My insurance assessor is coming Thursday."

"Your insurance assessor can come to your house. Why are you telling me this?"

"Because part of the damage is on your side."

The silence that followed was of the variety that could be cut into slices and served at funerals.

"The chimney fell on *my* greenhouse," said Theo, carefully, as if explaining something to a child. "It would be helpful if you were there. To confirm. That the chimney is yours."

"My chimney is on my cottage."

"Yes. The one that fell on my greenhouse."

"Peggy," said Mira, turning. "Tell this man whose chimney that is."

Peggy, who had been enjoying the show with the air of a woman at the theatre, blinked. "Well," she said. "I really couldn't say. I'm not a chimney expert."

"You are the postmaster."

"I am the *postmistress*," said Peggy, with dignity. "And chimneys are not my department."

Theo, to his credit, did not laugh. He turned to Mira with an expression of such weary patience that she had to look away.

"Thursday," he said. "Ten o'clock. Your cottage. I'll bring tea."

"I don't drink tea."

"Everyone drinks tea."

"I don't."

He looked at her for a long moment. "What do you drink?"

"Strong coffee. Black. No sugar."

He nodded, as if she had told him something important. "Thursday. Ten o'clock. No sugar."

He paid for his package and left. The bell above the door rang after him like a small accusation.

Peggy watched Mira with the bright eyes of a woman filing something away for later use. "He's not what people say, you know."

"What do people say?"

"Oh, the usual. Terrible things. Mostly untrue." Peggy stamped a letter with great ceremony. "He's just a man who did a job too well and didn't know how to forgive himself after."

Mira said nothing. She paid for her postage. She left.

She did not, however, stop thinking about it.

---

Thursday came. Mira spent the morning arranging and rearranging things in her cottage. She moved a stack of books. She dusted a shelf. She put the kettle on, took it off, put it on again.

At ten o'clock precisely, there was a knock.

He had brought coffee. He had, in fact, brought a small French press and a paper bag of beans and a little enamel pot of milk, in case she had changed her mind. He set these on her kitchen table with the quiet efficiency of a man who had thought about it.

"Sit," he said. "I'll make it."

She sat. She didn't know why. There was something about him today, in her kitchen, that was different. He moved carefully, as if the cottage were a place he was not sure he was welcome, and yet he moved in it like he understood it. He knew where the cups were without asking. He knew which drawer had the spoons. He had, she realized with a small shock, been paying more attention than she had thought.

"Milk?" he said.

"You brought milk."

"In case."

She let him put a little in. She didn't usually take milk. She didn't mention this. The coffee, when he poured it, was better than any she had made herself in eight months.

The insurance assessor arrived at half past ten. He was a small, dry man named Mr. Albright who examined the chimney, the greenhouse, the fence, and Mira's face with equal gravity. He asked her several questions. She answered them. She was, to her own surprise, polite.

When he left, Theo stood in her garden with his hands in his pockets.

"Thank you," he said.

"I didn't do anything."

"You confirmed the chimney was yours."

"It *was* mine. I wasn't lying."

"No," he said. "You weren't."

They stood there, in the damp garden, with the rosemary looking more alive than it had in days, and neither of them said anything for what felt like a long time.

"You write, don't you," he said, at last.

"Who told you that?"

"Peggy."

"Peggy talks too much."

"Peggy is a national treasure. Don't tell her I said so." He looked at the cottage, at the small window where her desk sat. "I used to read, a lot. Before."

"Before what?"

"Before I stopped." He paused. "I read your book. The first one. I was in London, then. I was in a bad way. It—it helped."

Mira felt something inside her chest go very still. Her first novel had been about a woman who could not forgive herself. She had written it during a long winter when she herself could not forgive herself, and she had not known, all these years, that it had done for anyone what it had done for her.

"It was a different book, then," she said. "I'm not that person anymore."

"Neither am I." He met her eyes, and there was something in his that she had not seen before. Not the cool appraisal of the doorstep, not the weariness of the greenhouse. Something open. Something that had been closed for a long time and was, with effort, being opened. "But I think the books we wrote back then still know things we haven't learned yet."

She wanted to laugh. She wanted to say something cutting. She wanted, very much, to send him away.

Instead, she said, "Do you want to see the rosemary?"

He looked surprised. Then he smiled. It was a small smile, and a little rusty, as if it had not been used in a while and was not entirely sure of itself. But it was real.

"Very much," he said.

---

They stood in the garden, looking at the rosemary. He told her about drainage. She told him about the Royal Horticultural Society. He laughed, properly, and the sound of it was so unexpected in that quiet place that she laughed too, and they stood there for a moment, two people who had come to this village to be small, discovering that they were not yet finished being something else.

It was, she thought, a beginning. The wrong sort of beginning, perhaps. The sort that began with a fallen chimney and a closed door and the wrong impression, every wrong impression, made and then slowly, slowly, unmade.

But a beginning, nonetheless.

She picked a sprig of rosemary and held it out to him. He took it. Their fingers brushed, and neither of them pulled away.

"Theo," she said.

"Mira."

"I was rude to you. On the doorstep."

"You were."

"I'm sorry."

He looked at her. "I deserved it. I was rude back."

"You weren't."

"I was." He tucked the rosemary into his coat pocket. "I'm not very good at the first meeting. I'm better at the second."

"There's only one of those, usually."

"Then I suppose I'll have to make the first one count, next time."

She didn't answer. She didn't need to. He smiled again—that small, rusty, real smile—and walked back through the gate to his own garden, and the wreckage of his greenhouse, and the quiet life he had been building out of the pieces of the one he had lost.

Mira stood in her doorway and watched him go.

She had come to Ashford to be left alone. She had come to write her quiet books and bury her past and be a woman with no story worth telling.

She had not, she thought, accounted for the rosemary.

Or for him.

# The Best Year Ever

The first time I noticed it, I thought maybe I had done something wrong.

The Big One was still in the kitchen when the sun came up. Normally, he rises with the darkness and disappears for what feels like forever. But today, he was right there, his feet on the floor, his eyes half-open, making the warm-water drink in his hand. He made that noise he makes sometimes, the low rumble from his chest, and when he saw me, he smiled.

I wagged so hard my whole back end joined in.

The Door That Doesn't Open was closed all day. Every day. For so many days in a row that I stopped counting, because counting is hard and also because the Big One was RIGHT THERE. He was in the chair. He was on the floor with me. He was making the yummy butter smell on the bread. Every single moment I wanted him, he was there.

This was the best thing that had ever happened.

At first, I thought perhaps I was sick. When good things happen, sometimes the small one takes me to the place with the cold table, so I worried. But no one was putting me in the car. The Big One just kept being *here*, in all the places, at all the times. When he left to do the outside work, he came back. He always came back. This had never happened before, not in my whole life.

I decided I had been a very good dog. This was my reward.

I was going to be the best dog. The BEST dog. I would protect him from everything. The squirrel that runs on the fence. The mail carrier with the loud box. The scary robot that moves across the floor on its own. I would put myself between him and all of them. He would know he was safe. He would know I was worthy of him being home forever.

The Small One was home too, which was confusing because the Small One usually disappears at the same time as the Big One. The Small One moved to a different room sometimes, where the bright squares float in the air, but she would come out. And sometimes she would sit on the soft place with me and rub my ears in the way that makes my leg go thump-thump-thump against the floor.

I made a nest between their two rooms. From there, I could hear if either of them moved. I could leap up and follow if they went to the kitchen, or to the other soft place, or to the outside part. I slept with one eye open, because what if they needed me? What if they tried to leave and I missed it?

The Big One started doing something strange. He would sit in the chair for a long time, and then he would sigh. The sigh was a long, slow breath, and his shoulders would go up and down. Sometimes he would look out the window for a very long time, even though there was nothing to see except the yard and the sky. His face was doing the thing I don't like, the lines across his forehead, the eyes that look smaller.

I put my head on his knee.

He always does the right thing when I put my head on his knee. He remembers I am here. His hand comes down on my head, or behind my ears, and the face softens. The lines go away. He says my name, the long version of it, and I thump my tail.

I think he is sad about something. I don't know what. I wish I could know what. I would fix it if I could. I would bring it to him in my mouth if it was small enough. I would chase it away if it was big. I would bark at it until it left. But I don't know what it is, so I just keep my head on his knee.

Every day, I think maybe today he will put on the shoes. Every day, he doesn't. The shoes sit by the Door That Doesn't Open, all in a row, and they wait. I wait with them. I am ready for when he finally leaves, because he always leaves eventually. I will be brave. I will watch him go.

But for now, for now, he is here. He is on the floor. He is throwing the small round thing and I am getting it and bringing it back, and he is saying "good boy, good boy," and the Small One is laughing in the other room. The sun is moving across the floor and I am lying in the warm spot, and my people are RIGHT THERE.

I hope this lasts forever. I don't know what forever is, exactly. I think it might be a very long time. I think the Big One might know what forever is, because he is the one who knows about things like the Door That Doesn't Open and the outside and the long stretches when he is gone.

But I think maybe forever is not about time at all.

I think forever is this. Right now. The warm spot. The people in the next room. The shoes that don't move. The hand that comes down on my head.

I put my chin on my paws. I close my eyes. I listen to them breathing in the other room.

I am the luckiest dog in the world. I have been for a whole year now.

And I'm going to be a good boy, the best boy, for every single day that I get to have them here, so that maybe, just maybe, I can make the lines go away from the Big One's face.

Because that's what dogs are for.

And right now, I have never been more sure of anything in my life.

Write a story in which two people who know each other are introduced — but neither person admits to knowing the other. Target length: ~2800 characters.

# 雨季的真相

## 一

苏蔓第一次在咖啡馆看见陆辞的时候，手里的拿铁差点洒出来。

他坐在靠窗的位置，窗外的雨丝顺着玻璃往下淌，像极了三年前他们在苏州分别时的那个黄昏。他的头发比从前短了些，下颌线条更加硬朗，正低头翻看一本精装书——封面她看不清，但那个微微蹙眉的习惯，她再熟悉不过。

苏蔓在门口站了三秒钟，强迫自己移开视线。

她今天约了人。一个在业内颇有声望的建筑设计师，据说性格古怪，从不接小项目。她投了三次方案才换来这次见面机会。她不能让过去的人扰乱现在的事。

她深吸一口气，整理好表情，径直走到吧台点了一杯美式，然后不经意地扫了一眼那个方向——陆辞依旧低着头，像是没有注意到她。

也好。

苏蔓找了一个离他最远的位置坐下，打开笔记本电脑，开始做最后的准备。

十分钟后，咖啡馆的风铃响了。

一个男人推门走进来，带着一身潮气，手里拎着一把还在滴水的黑伞。他环顾四周，目光掠过苏蔓的时候，没有任何停留。

然后他径直走向了靠窗的那个位置。

"陆老师，久等了。"

苏蔓的指尖在键盘上僵住了。

陆辞抬起头，合上书，微微点头："周助理，坐。"

那个被称作周助理的男人坐到陆辞对面，从公文包里取出一沓文件："这是委托人刚发来的资料，她说如果方案合适，可以现场签约。"

"委托人？"

"对，苏蔓女士。做独立花艺师的，好像很年轻。"

苏蔓坐在三米之外，听见自己的名字从别人嘴里说出来，那种荒诞感几乎让她想笑。三年前，她和陆辞一起做建筑与景观设计的联合项目；三年后，她改了行，做了花艺师，而他是她请都请不动的设计师——命运的玩笑未免太拙劣了些。

她看到陆辞接过文件，翻开第一页。

当他的目光落在委托人名字上的时候，翻页的动作停顿了大约半秒。然后他若无其事地继续往下看，表情没有任何变化。

苏蔓突然意识到：他知道。

他从一开始就知道她是谁。刚才她进门时，他一定认出了她。他只是没有抬头。

## 二

接下来的二十分钟，苏蔓一直盯着屏幕上的方案，眼睛却没有看进去一个字。

她听见周助理在那边介绍项目背景——某个私人庭院改造，预算不高，但委托人很有诚意。陆辞偶尔问一两句，语气专业而疏离，听不出任何私人情绪。

"这个项目的设计师，陆老师有人选吗？"周助理问。

"需要现场看过再定。"陆辞答。

"那委托人那边……"

"我会亲自去。"

苏蔓听到这句话，心跳漏了一拍。

三年前，他们也一起去看过现场。在杭州西湖边的一个茶园改造项目，他们在山上走了整整一天，傍晚时找了家民宿住下。那天晚上下了很大的雨，她说怕打雷，他就坐在走廊里陪她聊了一夜。

第二天早晨，雨停了，山上起了雾。她看着他说："以后再也不接联合项目了。"

他笑着说好。

后来那个项目做完，他们就再也没有见过面。

苏蔓至今不知道那算不算分手。他们没有吵过架，没有说过任何重话，只是慢慢地、默契地、不再联系了。她删了他的微信（他大概也删了她的），换了一个城市，开始新的生活。

她以为他也会一样。

但她错了。

"苏女士？"

一个声音在她面前响起。她抬起头，看见陆辞站在她桌边，手里拿着那沓文件。他穿着深灰色的休闲西装，气质比从前沉稳了很多。

"你的方案，周助理已经发给你了。"他说，语气像是面对一个完全陌生的客户，"如果方便的话，我想这周去看现场。"

苏蔓站起来。她比他矮半个头，要仰起脸才能和他对视。她控制着自己的表情，让它尽可能显得职业化。

"好。"她说，"时间你定。"

"那周六上午？"

"可以。"

他点了点头，转身要走。走了两步，又停下来。

"苏女士。"

"嗯？"

他背对着她，声音很轻："从前的事，我以为你已经不在意了。"

苏蔓的手指在桌沿上收紧了。

她看着他僵直的背影，忽然不知道该说什么。

他以为她不在意——这是什么意思？她发了那么多条没有回复的微信？她在苏州等了他三个月？她在每一个下雨天都会想起他？

还是说，他以为"不在意"的那个人，是他？

"陆先生。"她听见自己说，"我确实不在意了。"

她不知道为什么要说这句话。或许是为了维护那点可怜的自尊，或许是为了让他不要看出她此刻的失态，又或许——是为了测试他。

陆辞转过头，看着她。

他的眼睛里有一种她读不懂的神情。三年前她也常常看不懂他，所以最后才选择了放弃。

"那就好。"他说。

他走了。

苏蔓站在原地，看着他推开咖啡馆的门，走入雨里。她忽然发现，刚才整个过程里，他们谁都没有承认认识对方。

他们装作是陌生人，装作是第一次见面，装作三年前的一切都没有发生过。

但他们都知道。

## 三

周六上午，苏蔓在私家庭院门口等陆辞。

这是她一个朋友的家，主人常年旅居海外，托她帮忙打理庭院。她想改造一下，作为自己花艺工作室的样板，顺便给陆辞看看她的审美——不对，是看看设计师是否合她的意。

她心里清楚，这只是借口。

天空阴沉沉的，像是要下雨，又一直没有下。

陆辞准时到了。他换了一辆深蓝色的车，下车时手里拿着一把伞。他看了她一眼，点点头，然后径直走进了院子。

整个上午，他都在认真地查看院子的每一处细节——建筑结构、排水系统、采光条件、植物生长的现状。他偶尔会用手机拍照，偶尔在笔记本上记一些东西，偶尔问她一些专业的问题。

苏蔓回答得体，态度配合，像一个称职的委托人。

中午时分，他们坐在院子里的石凳上，吃她带来的便当。雨终于落下来了，打在芭蕉叶上，发出沉闷的声响。

"方案我可以做。"陆辞说。

苏蔓愣了一下。她原本以为他只是在敷衍，没想到他真的要接。

"预算不高。"她说，"你可以拒绝。"

"我知道。"

"为什么不接？"

陆辞没有立刻回答。他看着院子里的雨，像是在想什么。

"三年前，"他忽然开口，"你说以后再也不接联合项目了。"

苏蔓的心跳停了一拍。

她没想到他会在这个时候提起这件事。她更没想到的是，他的声音听起来，竟然有一丝……疲倦。

"我记得。"她说。

"我那时候答应了你。"他说，"但后来我发现，我错了。"

"哪里错了？"

"我以为不联系就是尊重。我以为让你开始新生活就是对你好。我以为……"

他停顿了一下，看着她。

"我以为你真的不在意了。"

苏蔓的鼻子突然有点酸。

她想说点什么，但她发现自己的喉咙被什么东西堵住了。

雨越下越大，打在芭蕉叶上的声音变成了哗哗的白噪音。她看着陆辞的侧脸——三年了，他老了一些，瘦了一些，但眼睛还是她记忆里的样子。

"我等了三个月。"她终于说，"在苏州。"

陆辞转过头，看她。

"后来我想，"她继续说，"也许你真的不想再见到我了。也许我应该识趣一点。所以我走了。"

"我也等了三个月。"他说。

"在哪儿？"

"苏州。"

他们对视了一下，然后同时移开目光。

雨声填满了他们之间的沉默。

## 四

后来的事情发展得顺理成章。

陆辞接下了这个项目，每周来一次现场。他们开始讨论方案，讨论植物，讨论材料和细节。一切都像三年前在杭州那个项目一样，专业而默契。

只是中间多了一些说不清的东西。

他们会在讨论结束后一起喝一杯咖啡，会在院子里散步，会在某个黄昏的窗前站很久，看着天色一点点暗下去。但他们始终没有承认认识对方。

在周助理眼里，苏蔓是一个新客户；在苏蔓的朋友眼里，陆辞是一个新请的设计师。他们之间没有任何故事。

只有他们自己知道，每次见面时那种小心翼翼的克制，背后藏着多少东西。

方案完成的那一天，陆辞把最终的图纸交给她。她翻了一遍，很满意。然后她合上图纸，看着他。

"陆辞，"她说，"我很感谢你。"

这是三个月来，她第一次叫他的名字。

他愣了一下。

"不客气。"他说。

"但我还是有一个问题想问你。"

"什么？"

"三年前，你为什么不联系我？"

陆辞沉默了很久。

"因为我怕，"他说，"我怕一旦联系你，我就会忍不住告诉你，我从来没有同意过分手。"

苏蔓的眼泪忽然就下来了。

她哭得毫无预兆，像是一个憋了三年的孩子终于找到了出口。她一边哭一边说："你为什么不早说？你为什么从来不说？你让我以为你根本不在乎……"

陆辞站起来，走过去，把她拉进怀里。

他拍着她的背，像三年前在杭州的那个雨夜一样。只是这一次，是他主动的。

"我错了。"他说，"以后不会了。"

苏蔓埋在他怀里，哭得更厉害了。

窗外，雨终于停了。

## 尾声

后来苏蔓问陆辞："那天在咖啡馆，你为什么不当场认我？"

他想了想，说："我怕你尴尬。"

"那你为什么不拒绝这个项目？"

"因为我不想再错过你了。"

苏蔓没有再问下去。

她知道，有些问题的答案，其实他们彼此都心知肚明——他们都是那种不擅长说出口的人。他们都在用自己的方式沉默地爱着，也沉默地错过。

只是这一次，他们都不想再错过了。

他们再也没有假装不认识对方。

（全文完）

# 《雨季的客人》

那是一个被梅雨泡软的夏天。

我刚搬到这间临河的老房子，屋顶会漏雨，墙角会发霉，唯一的好处是房租便宜得可笑。搬家那天雨下得很大，我一个人把纸箱搬进屋，累得瘫在地板上喘气，忽然听见窗台上有"嗒嗒嗒"的声响。

一只青蛙。

不，准确地说，是一只拇指大的树蛙，通体翠绿，肚皮雪白，眼睛圆得像两颗黑曜石。它蹲在窗沿上，歪着脑袋看我，喉囊一鼓一鼓的，仿佛在打量这位新来的邻居。

"你好。"我有气无力地说。

它眨了眨眼睛。

"你也来躲雨？"

它又眨了眨眼睛。

我笑了，把它当成这间破屋子给我的第一个欢迎仪式。那晚我给它找了个小碟子盛了点水，它竟然真的跳过来，蹲在水边，用前爪一下一下地拨弄着水面，溅起细碎的水花。

我给它起了个名字，叫"小绿"。

---

小绿就这样住了下来。

它喜欢蹲在我书桌的台灯罩上，听我敲键盘写稿子。有时候写到凌晨，我会听见它跳到键盘边上，用冰凉的小肚子贴着我的手背。我停下动作，它就跳到我手心，蹲下来，安安静静的，像一颗温凉的翡翠。

雨季漫长，整个七月我都没怎么出门，靠着写稿和泡面过日子。小绿成了我唯一的同伴。我给它讲我写的小说情节，它听不懂，但它从不走开。后来我习惯了自言自语地对着它说话——反正也没有别人可以倾诉。

有一回我感冒发烧，躺在床上迷迷糊糊的，醒来时发现小绿蹲在我枕头边。它的肚皮贴着我的脸颊，凉凉的，很舒服。我不知道它是不是真的在"照顾"我，还是只是凑巧路过。但那一刻我鼻子一酸，差点哭出来。

原来被人惦记着，是这种感觉啊。

---

八月中旬，雨季终于结束了。

我坐在窗边发呆，看见小绿蹲在窗台上，望着外面被阳光晒得发白的世界。它的喉囊快速地鼓动着，眼睛里倒映着外面的树和云。

它该走了。

我没有拦它。我打开窗户，它跳到窗框上，回过头看了我一眼，然后轻轻一纵，消失在河边的草丛里。

那天晚上我写了一段文字："有些陪伴，短暂得像是借来的。但借来的光，也是光。"

后来我再也没有见过小绿。

但每年梅雨季节，我都会在窗台上放一小碟清水。有时清晨醒来，会看见碟子里的水被拨弄得乱七八糟，溅得窗沿上到处都是。

我猜，是它回来看我了。

我也总是对着空气说一声：

"你好，小绿。"

# Resident 3B

The permit had been taped to Clara's refrigerator for six months before she finally used it. Yellow paper, blue border, the official city seal embossed in the corner. RESIDENT PARKING, ZONE 4. Her name printed in thin block letters: C. HOLLAND, APT 3B.

She'd found it in the mail on a Tuesday in March, tucked between a grocery store flyer and a bill. Her landlord had added it without comment, as if every apartment came with one. As if Clara had ever lived anywhere with designated parking.

For twenty-three years, she hadn't. She'd moved twelve times, always to neighborhoods where the sidewalks disappeared into cracked asphalt and the nearest thing to a parking spot was a patch of grass behind a dumpster. Her cars had been dinged, stolen, set on fire once. She'd learned to park in driveways that weren't hers, to move her vehicle at three a.m. when the street sweepers came, to carry quarters for meters that didn't exist.

Now she lived on Elm Court, where the trees were young and the streetlights actually worked.

She hung the permit on the fridge and walked to the bus stop.

---

On a Thursday in September, her Civic made a sound like a cat being stepped on. Clara was on Birch Avenue, three blocks from the mechanic she'd been meaning to visit for a year. The car shuddered to a stop in front of a hydrant.

She sat for a moment, listening to the engine tick. Then she got out and looked at the street. Empty. No signs. No meters. Just a quiet residential block with maple trees dropping their first yellow leaves.

She could leave it here. Probably fine.

But she'd been meaning to test the permit.

Back at the apartment, she retrieved it from the fridge—sticky residue from the tape leaving a faint rectangle on the door—and carried it to the Civic. She placed it on the dashboard, smoothing it flat.

The ticket came eleven minutes later.

She found it tucked under her wiper blade when she returned from the mechanic on the bus. $87. PARKED IN VIOLATION—NOT A PERMITTED VEHICLE.

Clara read the ticket three times. Then she called the number on the back.

"Ma'am," the clerk said, after she'd explained, "the permit is registered to you. It should be fine."

"It is fine."

"And the vehicle is registered to you?"

"Yes."

"Then I don't see the problem."

Clara looked at the ticket, then at the permit on her dashboard, then at the small print at the bottom of the permit she'd never read. *Permit must be displayed in conjunction with valid vehicle registration matching the address on file.*

"I just moved here," Clara said. "I haven't updated my registration."

A pause. "That's, uh, that's the issue, then."

She mailed the check that afternoon.

---

The DMV was a beige building with a beige soul. Clara took a number, 47, and sat among the other residents of Zone 4 and the zones adjacent. A man reading a newspaper. A teenager with headphones. An older woman feeding her grandchild puffs from a plastic container.

Clara had brought a book, but she found herself watching the permit in her lap instead. RESIDENT PARKING, ZONE 4. The first official document she'd ever held that said *you belong here.*

When her number was called, she approached the counter with the permit in one hand and her old registration in the other. The clerk—young, tired, a lanyard that said *TREVOR*—typed without looking up.

"Address change?"

"Yes."

"New address?"

Clara told him. He typed.

"Vehicle?"

The Civic's details. He typed.

"Out-of-state transfer?"

"No. Same state."

"Good. That'll be forty-six dollars."

She paid. Trevor printed something. She signed something. He handed her a new registration and a stack of carbon copies she didn't know what to do with.

"Anything else?"

Clara hesitated. "The permit—was it, I mean, did it have an expiration?"

"December thirty-first." Trevor glanced at the screen. "You renewed your lease?"

"Yes."

"Then you'll get a new one in the mail." He was already looking past her. "Next."

---

She didn't park on Birch Avenue again that fall. Not because she was avoiding it—she simply didn't have reason to go there. The mechanic, once she'd gotten the Civic back, had fixed the belt and the thermostat and a thing she'd forgotten the name of. The car ran quieter now.

But she kept the permit on the dashboard. Habit, maybe. Or something else.

In October, someone sideswiped her in the grocery store lot—a hit and run, no note, just a fresh scrape along the passenger door. Clara stood looking at it for a long time, the autumn light catching the bare metal. She'd had this car for nine years. It had been with her through two apartments and a divorce and a move across the state. She knew every scratch, every stain on the upholstery.

This one would scab over and become part of the pattern.

She drove home carefully, watching the mirrors. Parked in her spot—her actual spot, the one that belonged to 3B—and sat for a moment with the engine off. The permit glowed yellow in the late afternoon light.

---

The renewal came in December. Same yellow paper, same blue border. RESIDENT PARKING, ZONE 4. C. HOLLAND, APT 3B.

Clara held it for a long time before taping it to the fridge. She stood in her kitchen, looking at the old rectangle of sticky residue where the first one had been, and then at the new permit in her hand. A year. She was still surprised by how fast it had passed.

She thought about the first apartment she'd rented, at twenty-two, in a city she didn't live in anymore. How the landlord had collected cash and never given a receipt. How she'd slept on a mattress on the floor and parked on a street where the lamps were always out.

She thought about all the cars. The one that had been stolen from outside a laundromat. The one her ex had taken and never returned. The one that had burned—somebody's cigarette, the fire department had said, though Clara had her doubts.

She thought about how strange it was to have a thing that said *you belong here* and to have it feel, still, like a miracle.

Clara taped the new permit to the fridge, over the old residue. Then she made tea. Then she sat on her couch with the book she'd been trying to read for three months, and this time, she read.

# 墙那边的秘密

老周的茶馆开在巷子深处，青砖灰瓦，门脸不大，却有三十年的老茶客。店里只有六张桌子，每张桌子之间隔着一扇雕花木屏风，既是装饰，也方便各桌客人说话不被旁人听见。

这天午后，店里来了个奇怪的客人。

那是个五十出头的男人，穿一件洗得发白的灰布夹克，进门就要了最里面那张靠墙的桌子。"老规矩，一壶碧螺春。"他压低声音说。

老周给他续了三次水，那人也不喝，只是侧着耳朵，像在听什么。第三次续水时，他忽然开口："老周，你这墙隔壁，是不是住着一户人家？"

"是啊。"老周点头，"张婶，一个人住。她儿子在外地打工。"

"她每天下午都跟人说话？"男人眼睛亮了起来，"我路过几次都听见她屋里有人声，可她明明一个人住。"

老周笑了笑，没接话。这话他听了几十年了，每隔一段时间就有人问起。张婶的丈夫二十年前就去世了，她一个人拉扯大了儿子。丈夫走后，她常常自言自语，老周起初也觉着奇怪，后来听习惯了，也就当成了白噪音。

那男人却上了心。

第二天，他又来了。这回他特意要了隔壁那张桌子，离墙只有一尺的距离。他侧耳贴着雕花屏风，眼睛微闭，像是在听一场大戏。老周给他续水时，看见他嘴角勾起一抹笑。

"老周，"他压低声音，"你听听，隔壁是不是有人在说'阿珍'？"

老周愣了一下。张婶确实叫阿珍，但他从没听清过她自言自语的具体内容。他侧耳听了听，墙那边传来张婶模糊的说话声，像是在跟人聊天，又像是在念叨。

"她在跟谁说话？"男人问。

"不知道。"老周摇头，"可能是她丈夫。"

男人皱眉，似乎不太相信。老周没再多说，转身回柜台擦杯子去了。

第三天，男人又来了。这回他来得更早，几乎是茶馆开门就来了。他又要了那张靠墙的桌子，点了茶，然后就那么侧耳听了一上午。中午张婶的声音停了，男人也起身离开，走到门口时，他回头问老周："老周，我能在你这墙上凿个小洞吗？"

"不行。"老周一口回绝。

男人有些失望，但也没再坚持。临走前，他从口袋里掏出一沓钱，压在茶杯下，说："老周，你要是能帮我打听打听隔壁阿珍跟谁说话，这钱就是你的。"

老周没动那钱。

"你到底想知道什么？"他问。

男人沉默了一会儿，说："我年轻时在这巷子里住过。隔壁那家，男主人叫张明德。"

老周心里咯噔一下。

"他是我师傅。"男人接着说，"二十年前他走了，我以为他病死了。前几天我路过，听见张婶屋里有人说话，那声音……像我师傅。"

老周沉默了很久。

"你师傅走了二十年了。"他说，"人死不能复生。"

"我知道。"男人苦笑，"可那声音，分明就是他。我师傅说话有个习惯，每句话末尾都要带个'嗯'。我刚才听了一上午，他说了十七句话，每一句后面都带着'嗯'。"

老周心里一震。张婶的丈夫张明德，活着的时候他确实见过几面，说话确实有这个习惯。

"你……听了几十年的墙？"老周问。

男人点了点头："我搬到城里后，每年清明都回来给师傅上坟。这几年腿脚不好，就来得少了。前几天路过，想进去喝杯茶，就听见了那声音。"

他顿了顿，眼眶有些红了："我想知道，是不是师傅还在。他是不是有什么未了的心愿。"

老周叹了口气。他想了很久，最后说："你明天再来，我带你去见见张婶。"

---

第二天，男人如期而至。老周领着他穿过茶馆，来到后面的小院。张婶正坐在院子里的藤椅上晒太阳，看见老周带着个陌生人来，愣了一下。

"张婶，"老周开口，"这位客人说他认识张师傅。"

张婶的目光落在男人身上，愣了几秒，然后忽然笑了："你是……小李吧？明德以前总提起你，说你学徒的时候笨手笨脚，有一次把模具都敲坏了。"

男人——小李——愣住了，眼眶一下子红了："师娘，您还记得我？"

"怎么不记得。"张婶笑着站起身，"你师傅走之前还念叨你，说你虽然笨，但是心眼实。"

小李抹了抹眼睛，问出了那句话："师娘，您屋里……是不是有人在跟您说话？"

张婶沉默了一会儿，慢慢地说："你听见了？"

小李点头。

张婶转身进屋，半晌，拿出一个小录音机，按下播放键。一个苍老的声音从录音机里传出来：

"阿珍，今天太阳好，记得出去走走，嗯。"
"阿珍，柜子上的药按时吃，嗯。"
"阿珍，小李那孩子最近怎么样了，嗯。"

小李呆住了。

"这是明德走之前录的。"张婶说，"他知道自己时间不多了，就录了这个播放器，说怕我一个人太闷，让我听着解闷。"

她顿了顿，声音有些哽咽："这播放器我听了二十年。前几天不小心把线碰断了，我让隔壁小王帮我修好的。"

小李沉默了很久，忽然跪下来，朝屋里张明德的遗像磕了三个头。

"师傅，"他哽咽着说，"徒弟来看您了，嗯。"

张婶愣住了，然后笑了，眼泪也跟着流下来。

---

那天晚上，老周关店的时候，小李已经走了。他走到那张靠墙的桌子前坐下，侧耳听了听。墙那边，张婶的声音轻轻的：

"明德，小李来过了，嗯。"
"他说你教得好，嗯。"
"你听到了吗，嗯。"

老周笑了笑，起身关了灯。

有些秘密，是不需要偷听的。

# The Detour

The morning Marcus told me he could take me to the airport, I almost said no.

"It's an hour out of your way," I said, standing in his doorway with my suitcase already balanced on its wheels. "I'll just grab a rideshare."

"Don't be ridiculous." Marcus waved a hand, already reaching for his jacket. He'd already lost ten pounds in the last month—the grief carved into the hollows of his cheeks—and I knew he needed something to do with his hands. "It's nothing. I want to."

He wanted to feel useful. I understood that. After Laura, everything that had once felt easy between us now felt like a debt.

"Okay," I said. "Thank you."

The car was an old Accord, something he'd been meaning to replace since before the funeral. He backed out of the driveway carefully, the way he always did, and we pulled onto the road just as the sun broke through the trees. For a while neither of us spoke. I watched the familiar neighborhoods slide past and tried not to think about why I was going.

"You didn't have to do this," I said finally. "The job thing."

"You did."

"I'm serious. It looks bad enough that I'm leaving so soon. People are going to say—"

"People are going to say whatever they want to say." He glanced at me. "You need this, June. We both know you do."

I didn't argue. Outside, the highway was already thickening with morning traffic. We merged, and Marcus settled into the middle lane, settling into the comfortable silence of two people who had once been so close that words were almost redundant.

That was before.

About thirty minutes in, somewhere past the last of the suburbs, the Accord made a sound I'd never heard before. A kind of grinding hiccup, followed by a shudder that ran through the whole frame. Then the check engine light blinked on, and the RPM needle began to dance.

"Oh no," Marcus said quietly.

"No no no."

He pulled onto the shoulder, and we sat there for a moment listening to the car wheeze. I could smell something hot and vaguely electrical. He turned the key once, twice, and the engine made a sound like a cat trying to cough up a bone.

"It's not—" I started.

"No," he said. "It's not."

The silence that followed was enormous. We were still forty minutes from the airport. My flight was in ninety minutes. I could already feel the math closing in.

"Call someone," I said, though he was already reaching for his phone.

He called roadside assistance. Forty-five minutes, minimum, the woman said. Could be longer. He called a taxi company. No cars available. He called me a rideshare, but the nearest driver was twenty-five minutes away, and surge pricing had made the fare astronomical.

"I can pay—" I started.

"No," he said. "Absolutely not."

"Marcus."

"I said no." He was gripping the steering wheel with both hands, staring straight ahead. "This is my car. My problem."

"People are going to say I'm an ungrateful—"

"June." He turned to look at me, and there was something in his eyes that I hadn't seen in weeks. Something almost like life. "Stop. Please. Just let me try to fix this."

He popped the hood and got out. I followed, standing on the shoulder in my good coat while he bent over the engine, muttering. He wasn't a mechanic. He'd never been a mechanic. But he was the kind of man who tried things, who couldn't sit still when he felt responsible.

I watched him and felt something twist in my chest. He'd been like this at the hospital too. Bargaining with the vending machine, bringing Laura too many blankets, calling every specialist he could find on his phone during the long nights. He'd tried so hard. He'd tried until there was nothing left to try.

Two hours later, we were still on the shoulder.

The tow truck had come and gone. The mechanic had looked at the engine, then looked at Marcus, then quoted a number that made us both wince. The rideshare had finally arrived, only to cancel when the driver saw how far the trip was. My flight had departed without me. I had missed it.

Marcus was sitting on the guardrail, head in his hands.

"I should have just let you take a cab," he said.

"It wasn't your fault."

"It was my car."

"And it could have been any car. It could have been a thunderstorm. It could have been anything." I sat down beside him. The late morning sun was warm on my face. Somewhere far away, a plane cut a white line across the blue. "It just was."

He laughed, but it was a broken sound. "You were supposed to be gone by now. You were supposed to be starting over."

"I know."

"I'm sorry, June. I'm so sorry."

I thought about Laura. About the way she'd laughed when I'd come over with the wrong kind of flour. About the way she'd taken my hand at the wedding and said *you're going to be okay, you two, I can tell.* About the way she'd held on at the end, even when it didn't make sense to hold on.

I thought about how she would have teased us mercilessly for this. *Marcus,* she would have said, *you couldn't break a car any more perfectly if you tried.*

"It's okay," I said.

"It's not."

"I know." I put my arm through his, the way I used to. "But it will be."

He didn't pull away. We sat on the guardrail for a long time, watching the cars stream past, neither of us going anywhere at all.

# 숨바꼭질

---

주방에서 그릇이 깨지는 소리가 났다.

유진은 숨을 멈추었다. 식칼이 식탁 위를 미끄러지는 소리, 냉장고 문이 열리는 소리, 그리고 어머니가 숨을 들이쉬는 소리까지 들렸다. 평일 저녁, 여덟 시. 유진이 제 시간에 돌아오지 않은 날의 어머니는 항상 이러했다.

유진은 세탁실 바구니 속에 웅크리고 있었다. 빨래 더미가 코를 간지럽혔지만, 꾹 참았다. 어머니의 발소리가 복도를 지나갔다. 안방 쪽. 아니, 현관 쪽으로 다시 돌아왔다. 현관문이 열리고 닫혔다. 현관 밖으로 나간 것이다.

유진은 바구니에서 나왔다. 세탁실 문을 열면 바로 부엌이었다. 부엌에서 주방 문을 밀면 뒤뜰로 나갈 수 있었다. 어머니는 몰랐다. 유진이 뒤뜰의 담장 밑에 뚫어놓은 작은 구멍을 알고 있다는 것을.

구멍을 빠져나가자 골목길의 차가운 공기가 폐를 찔렀다. 열한 살의 유진에게 이 동네는 이미 지형이었다. 편의점 뒤, 폐건물 2층, 놀이터 그네 아래, 교회 지붕 위까지. 어디로 가야 할지 골라야 했다.

유진은 골목을 돌다가 멈추었다.

골목 끝, 가로등 아래에 한 소녀가 서 있었다. 손전등을 들고 있었지만 불을 켜지 않았다. 그저 어둠 속에서 가만히 유진을 기다리고 있듯이.

"태리."

소녀가 고개를 돌렸다. 이름이 불린 순간, 손전등 불이 켜졌다. 눈이 너무 환해 빛에 눈이 부셨다.

"오빠, 또 엄마한테 도망쳤어?"

유진은 대답하지 않았다. 대신 걸어가서 태리 옆에 섰다. 둘은 어깨를 나란히 하고 골목을 걸었다.

---

이것은 세 번째 여름이었다.

첫 번째 여름, 유진은 다른 동네에서 이사를 왔다. 어머니의 새 남자 친구 때문이었다. 태리는 그 남자 친구의 딸이었다. 같은 아파트, 같은 복도, 다른 방.

"같이 숨자." 태리가 말했다. 첫 여름의 어느 날이었다. "오빠가 숨으면 내가 찾을 거야. 진짜 숨바꼭질처럼."

유진은 이상한 아이라고 생각했다. 하지만 태리는 진심이었다. 매일 저녁, 식탁에서 어머니와 남자 친구가 소리를 지르는 소리가 들릴 때쯤, 태리가 복도에서 손전등을 흔들었다. 그게 신호였다. 유진이 문을 열면, 태리는 이미 달리고 있었다. "하나, 둘, 셋."

그렇게 둘은 아파트 옥상까지, 주차장 지하까지, 뒷산 둘레길까지 숨어 다녔다. 태리는 정말 잘 찾았다. 어디에 숨든 금방이었다. 유진이 숨은 곳을 골라야 하는 이유가 그것 때문이었다. 태리가 찾을 수 있는 곳으로. 그래야 끝이 났다. 그래야 다시 집으로 돌아갈 수 있었다.

두 번째 여름, 태리의 아버지가 어머니와 헤어졌다. 태리는 친척집으로 돌아갔다. 유진은 혼자 숨었다. 세탁실 바구니 안에서, 어머니가 발소리를 멈출 때까지. 하지만 어머니는 멈추지 않았다. 점점 더 멀어졌다. 유진이 숨을 곳도 점점 깊어졌다. 빨래 바구니에서 옷장 안으로, 옷장에서 지붕 아래 다락방으로, 다락방에서 집 밖으로.

유진은 한 번도 찾지 못했다. 스스로를. 그게 무서웠다. 그래서일까, 세 번째 여름, 태리가 다시 나타났을 때 유진은 울었다.

"오빠, 울지 마."

"나 숨을 곳이 없어졌어."

태리는 대답하지 않았다. 대신 손전등을 꺼서 유진의 손에 쥐어 주었다. 불이 꺼진 손전등이었다. 켜지도 않는. 그냥 유진의 손에 쥐어진 차가운 금속.

"그래도 난 찾을 거야."

---

세 번째 여름, 지금.

둘은 골목을 지나 작은 공원에 도착했다. 공원은 비어 있었다. 그네가 바람에 흔들리고, 모래밭에는 고양이 발자국이 있었다.

"여기서 할까?" 태리가 물었다.

유진은 고개를 끄덕였다. 손전등이 주머니에서 무거웠다. 열두 살의 유진은 열일곱이었고, 태리는 열여섯이었다. 둘 다 숨을 곳이 필요한 나이였다.

"하나, 둘, 셋."

태리가 돌아서서 벽을 향했다. 유진은 뛰었다. 공원을 벗어나, 골목을 지나, 낡은 아파트 단지로 들어갔다. 3동. 4층. 끝 방 창문이 열려 있었다. 알았다. 그 집은 오래 비어 있었다. 태리가 알려준 것이 아니라, 유진이 스스로 알게 된 것이었다.

유진은 창문으로 들어갔다. 까만 방 안에서 숨을 곳을 골랐다. 옷장 안은 너무 좁았다. 침대 밑은 너무 얕았다. 천장 위 다락은... 유진은 올라갔다. 다락은 좁고 더웠지만, 꼭 맞았다.

숨을 쉬지 않았다. 발소리를 들었다. 계단을 올라오는 소리. 4층. 끝 방. 문이 열리는 소리. 발소리가 멈추었다.

"유진아."

태리의 목소리가 천장 바로 아래에서 들렸다.

"나 여기 있어."

"...알아."

"어떻게 알았어?"

"몰라. 그냥 알았어."

태리가 웃었다. 희미한 웃음이었다. 다락 아래, 까만 방 안에서, 유진에게 들리는 것처럼.

"오빠, 이제 내려와."

유진은 내려가지 않았다. 대신 물었다.

"왜 날 찾아?"

태리가 대답했다.

"안 찾으면 어떻게 돼? 네가 거기서 썩어? 천장에서? 옷장에서? 엄마 목소리 안 들리는 데서?"

유진은 입을 다물었다.

"내려와. 내려오면 보일 거야. 네가 숨은 게 아닌 게 뭔지."

유진은 천장에서 내려왔다. 까만 방 안, 창가에 태리가 서 있었다. 가로등 불빛이 창으로 들어와 태리 얼굴 반쪽을 비추었다.

"찾아줘서 고마워."

"또 도망갈 거잖아."

"...응."

"그래도 찾을 거야. 항상."

유진은 고개를 끄덕였다. 이번에는 울지 않았다. 대신 손전등을 꺼내 태리에게 건넸다. 이번에는 불이 켜졌다.

"불 켜진 걸로 바꿔줄게."

태리는 손전등을 받았다. 불빛이 둘 사이에 떨어졌다. 환하게. 너무 환해서 눈을 감을 수밖에 없게.

---

그렇게 둘은 또 걸었다. 어깨를 나란히 하고, 골목을 지나, 아파트 단지를 지나, 작은 공원으로 돌아왔다. 그네에 앉았다. 태리가 그네를 밀었고, 유진이 그네를 탔다. 하늘에는 별이 떠 있었다. 도시의 별은 적었지만, 그래도 있었다.

"오빠."

"응."

"우리 엄마가 그러는데, 도망치는 건 숨는 게 아니라 쫓기는 거래."

"...그럼 숨는 건 뭔데?"

"모르겠어. 그래서 찾는 거야. 숨는 게 뭔지."

유진은 그네에서 내려왔다. 땅에 발이 닿았다. 차가웠다. 단단했다. 숨을 곳이 아니었다. 사는 곳이었다.

"태리야."

"응."

"나 내일 또 엄마한테 도망칠 거야."

"알아."

"그때도 찾을 거야?"

"그럼."

"왜?"

태리는 고개를 들어 별을 보았다. 도시의 별을.

"오빠가 없으면, 나도 숨을 곳이 없으니까."

유진은 아무 말도 하지 않았다. 대신 손을 내밀었다. 태리가 잡았다. 두 손이 차가웠다. 잡고 있으니까 조금 따뜻해졌다.

둘은 그렇게 서 있었다. 별 아래, 빈 공원 안에서. 숨는 아이와 찾는 아이. 도망치는 아이와 기다리는 아이. 어느 쪽이든 같은 편이었다.

가로등이 꺼졌다. 어둠이 내려왔다. 하지만 둘은 여전히 서 있었다. 잡은 손이 이끄는 대로.

내일, 유진은 또 도망칠 것이다. 빨래 바구니에서, 옷장에서, 다락방에서, 아파트 옥상에서. 어디든. 하지만 태리가 찾을 것이다. 항상. 그게 약속이었다.

어둠 속에서 손전등이 한 번 깜박였다. 그리고 다시 켜졌다.

---

*끝*

Write about a character looking for a sign. Length: about 500 words.

**The Sign**

Mara pressed her forehead against the cold glass of the bus shelter, watching the rain stitch the city into grey ribbons. Forty-seven days. She had been counting, though she told herself she wasn't.

Forty-seven days since Daniel left a note on the kitchen counter—a single line in his careful handwriting—and disappeared behind the closing front door.

*I need to find out who I am without you. Don't look for me.*

She hadn't looked. Not once. She had stayed in the apartment, watered the fern he'd named Gerald, and waited. For what, she could not have said. An explanation. An apology. A sign.

The bus shelter's advertisement behind her flickered: a woman's face mid-laugh, teeth white as piano keys, selling something Mara would never buy. A teenager slumped on the bench, earbuds leaking tinny music, eyes half-closed. A man in a damp coat argued quietly into his phone about loading docks.

Normal life. The ordinary machinery of people getting somewhere.

Mara's phone buzzed. Her sister, again. *Please, Mare. Come for dinner. He wasn't right for you. You deserve*— She had stopped reading after that. The sentences stacked up like bricks, building a wall she didn't want to stand behind.

She was about to give up on the bus when she saw him.

No—not him. Someone. A man across the street, the right height, the right slope of shoulders, wearing the kind of dark wool coat Daniel used to wear in winter. He walked with his hands in his pockets, head slightly bowed against the rain.

Her heart took off like a startled bird.

She stepped out from under the shelter without thinking. Rain struck her hair, her face, the shoulders of her thin jacket. The man turned left at the corner. She followed, keeping her distance, telling herself she was only crossing the street, only walking home.

At the corner she stopped. A bookshop she didn't remember, wedged between a laundromat and a shuttered bakery. The lights inside were warm and yellow, and through the rain-streaked window she could see a cat asleep on a stack of hardcovers.

A sign in the window, hand-painted, slightly crooked: **New Chapters.**

Mara laughed—a real laugh, startled out of her—and pressed her hand to her mouth.

It wasn't a sign about Daniel. She knew that. It was just a bookshop, opening after a renovation, a small brave thing in a city that swallowed small brave things daily. But standing there in the rain, with her sister's unanswered texts and the fern he had named and the note folded in her pocket like a paper wound, she felt something shift.

Not an answer. A question, asked gently, in a voice that might have been her own.

*What do you want to become, now that you are becoming?*

She wiped her face with the back of her hand—it could have been rain, it could have been more—and walked into the bookshop. The cat lifted its head. The man behind the counter looked up and smiled as if she had been expected.

"First customer in the rain," he said. "That's lucky."

"Maybe," she said. "Or maybe it's just weather."

He laughed. She laughed. Somewhere behind her, the rain kept falling, and the city kept turning, and the man in the wool coat walked on toward whatever he was becoming too.

Mara ran her finger along the spines of the books, and did not look back.

# The Recipe She Never Wrote Down

The kitchen smelled of rosemary and something Mira couldn't name—something that lived only in the space between memory and muscle. She moved through it with the certainty of long practice, her hands remembering even as her mind drifted to other rooms in the house, other years.

She was making her mother's stew.

Not her mother's recipe, exactly—her mother had never written anything down, had measured with pinched fingers and poured olive oil in shining arcs from the bottle. *A little more,* she'd say. *Now stop. Now a little more again.* Mira had learned by watching, the way children learn language, without ever knowing they were learning.

The onion went into the pot first. She liked to let it brown at the edges, to listen for the moment the sizzle deepened. The kitchen window was open, and outside she could hear the wind moving through the lilac bushes her mother had planted thirty years ago. They had grown leggy and wild since then, but they still bloomed every May, defiant and purple, leaning against the fence like old women gossiping.

The carrots she cut on a bias, the way she'd been taught. *Always on the bias,* her mother had insisted. *It looks like you're trying, even when you're not.* And then she'd laughed, that particular laugh she had, the one that made her whole face crinkle up, and Mira had laughed too without understanding why.

She added the potatoes. She added the small, pale mushrooms her mother had loved. She stood at the stove for a long moment, watching the liquid come to a simmer, the steam rising to fog the window above the sink. In the fogged glass she could almost see her own face, younger, looking back.

He would be home soon. Her son. Forty-three years old and still, somehow, the boy who came in hungry from school, who dropped his book bag by the door and filled the kitchen with his noise. She had made this stew a hundred times for him, and he had never once asked for the recipe. Perhaps he didn't want it. Perhaps he understood, the way she had finally understood, that recipes weren't the point. That what she was giving him was not a list of ingredients but a kind of proof—proof that she remembered, proof that she was still here, proof that love had a taste, and this was it.

She stirred the pot once, gently, and tasted from the wooden spoon. Closed her eyes.

It was right. It was exactly right.

She set the spoon aside and went to set the table—two places, as always, though one of them had been empty for a long time now.

Write about a character who decides to give themselves, or someone else, a fashion makeover. Total: ~1200 words.

# The Reassembly of Eleanor Vance

The scissors hovered an inch from the first lock of hair, trembling almost imperceptibly in Eleanor Vance's grip. In the mirror, she caught a flicker of herself—not the woman she saw every morning, but someone younger, someone who still believed that change was possible.

She had told herself this was about Maria. Her younger sister, visiting from Phoenix for the first time in three years, who had called last Tuesday sounding like she was gargling gravel. "I'm coming," Maria had said. "But El—don't let me look like I've been living in a desert tomb. Do something."

Eleanor had agreed before she realized she'd have to figure out what "something" actually meant.

Now, standing in the pale morning light of her Brooklyn apartment, she studied her reflection with the clinical detachment she usually reserved for other people's problems. The hair: long, brown, parted in the middle like a sleepwalker. The clothes: whatever had been clean. The face: kind, she supposed, but absent. A face that had stopped trying.

Maria arrived on Friday with two suitcases and a single high-wheeled suitcase containing, she announced, her "ashes." Not literal ashes—just everything that had burned down. The job. The apartment. The boyfriend of four years who had, it turned out, been running a parallel life with a woman in Scottsdale named Brittany who kept appearing in his tagged photos.

"He didn't even block her," Maria said, dropping onto Eleanor's couch. "That's how little he thought of me."

Eleanor looked at her sister and saw someone who had been beautiful once and was now simply *visible*—gray sweats, no makeup, hair that hadn't seen a proper washing in days. Maria was thirty-four. She looked fifty.

"Okay," Eleanor said. "Get up."

"What?"

"Get up. We're going out."

"To where?"

"To everywhere."

---

They started at a vintage shop in Williamsburg, because Eleanor remembered Maria, at twenty-two, spending an entire Saturday trying on 1960s cocktail dresses. Maria wandered the racks like a ghost until Eleanor physically removed three items and held them up to her body.

"These are not your size," Maria said flatly.

"They will be."

They weren't. But they were close enough to see something else—the shape of a woman who had curves, not just weight. Eleanor paid for a cranberry silk blouse, high-waisted dark trousers, and a leather belt that Maria refused to touch.

"I can't afford—"

"You're not buying. I'm buying. Consider it an early inheritance."

Maria's mouth opened, then closed. "El."

"Don't. Just try them on."

In the cramped fitting room, Maria emerged transformed by fabric. Not beautiful—not yet—but *assembled*. Like a sentence that finally had verbs.

In the mirror, Maria touched the collar of the blouse. "I look like my mother."

"You look like yourself. The you that hasn't had to beg anyone to love her in a long time."

Maria's eyes filled, and Eleanor steered her quickly toward the register before either of them could cry in public.

---

They walked to a small salon Eleanor had passed a thousand times but never entered. A woman with magenta hair and silver earrings looked up from her appointment book.

"Walk-ins?"

"For a resurrection," Eleanor said.

The woman—her card said *Cleo*—laughed and gestured them in.

It was Maria's hair that needed the most work. Cleo studied it with the focus of a diagnostician. "When did you last come in?"

"Grad school."

"Jesus." Cleo turned to Eleanor. "You want to watch, or do you want to participate?"

Eleanor looked at Maria. Maria looked back with the wary eyes of someone who had stopped trusting kindness.

"Participate," Eleanor said.

Cleo handed her a pair of shears—not the nervous pair Eleanor had wielded that morning, but heavier, professional, certain. "Cut when I say cut. Trust your hands."

She wasn't sure why she agreed. But she did.

For the next ninety minutes, Eleanor watched auburn lengths fall to the floor, and with them, the heavy curtain Maria had been hiding behind. Cleo talked the entire time—not gossip, but a running commentary on shape, on why certain faces needed shorter lengths, on the architecture of a good cut.

"Most people cut hair," Cleo said. "I sculpt what's already trying to emerge."

Eleanor thought of the past five years of her own life. The job at the nonprofit. The apartment she'd chosen because it was convenient, not because she loved it. The relationship with David, who was kind but who she'd chosen because he'd asked, and she'd forgotten how to want.

She cut a final lock, and Maria turned in the chair.

The woman in the mirror was not the one who had arrived that morning. There were cheekbones now. There was a jaw. There were eyes that looked, for the first time in a long time, like they might consider the future.

"Oh," Maria said softly. "Hi."

Cleo beamed. "Now makeup. Do you trust me?"

Maria looked at Eleanor. "I trust you."

"No," Eleanor said. "You trust yourself. I'm just here to remind you that I'm seeing you."

---

They walked out into the late afternoon, and the light fell differently on Maria. Not better—just *differently*. Eleanor watched her sister look at her own reflection in a storefront window, then again, and again.

"It's just clothes," Maria said, but she was smiling.

"It's never just clothes," Eleanor said. "It's a decision. About who gets to take up space."

Maria stopped walking. "Are you talking about me?"

Eleanor considered lying. Then she thought of the woman in the mirror that morning. The sleepwalker.

"I'm talking about me," she said.

Maria studied her sister's face—the same face she'd known her whole life, but suddenly more legible. The same brown hair, parted in the middle. The same gray sweater Eleanor had owned for six years.

"When's the last time someone did this for you?" Maria asked.

Eleanor opened her mouth. Closed it. Tried to remember.

"Come on," Maria said, and took her hand. "I want to do your hair."

"Maria—"

"I mean it. Sit down. Let me try."

---

They went back to the apartment, and Maria pulled out a small bag of cosmetics she hadn't used in a year. She sat Eleanor down at the kitchen table and, with the same quiet intensity she'd once brought to her accounting work, began to study her sister's face.

"You're tired," Maria said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm fine."

"El. You're *tired*."

The word landed somewhere deep. Eleanor felt something shift—the same tectonic shift she'd felt earlier, holding the shears, watching auburn hair fall.

"I don't know who I am anymore," Eleanor said, and it was the first time she'd said it aloud.

Maria nodded. She didn't offer platitudes. She just picked up a brush.

"Then we're going to find out."

She did Eleanor's makeup slowly, carefully. She didn't try to make her look younger or different—just *present*. A little color on the cheeks. A defined brow. A lip that had something to say.

When she finished, Eleanor looked in the bathroom mirror and saw, for the first time in years, her own eyes looking back.

"Oh," she said, echoing her sister.

Maria leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed. "So what do you want to wear? To the dinner? To your life?"

Eleanor laughed—a real laugh, surprising them both. "I don't know yet."

"Good," Maria said. "That means we're starting."

《檐下客》

深秋的风从北方刮过来，裹挟着黄沙和寒意，把行人的衣角掀得猎猎作响。沈青萝裹紧了身上那件洗得发白的蓝布棉袄，背着一只破旧的藤箱，站在岔路口，抬头望着天上翻涌的乌云。

她已经走了三天了。

三天前，娘咽气前拉着她的手，说去临州找你舅舅，他总归会收留你的。她爹走得早，家里再没有一个亲人，娘把她托付给十几年没见面的舅舅，便撒手去了。

从清平镇到临州，本该两天的路程。可她带的盘缠在第二天夜里被人偷了。她蹲在破庙里哭了半夜，天亮时擦干眼泪，继续往前走。

脚上的布鞋已经磨穿了底，寒气从脚底直往心里钻。她不得不把稻草裹在脚上，用布条缠紧，走起路来像个蹩脚的稻草人。

傍晚时分，雨落下来了。先是零星的几滴，接着便是瓢泼大雨，天地间一片白茫茫。她慌不择路地跑进一个村子，想找个屋檐避避雨。

村口有一户人家，篱笆墙围着一座茅屋，炊烟正从烟囱里袅袅升起。她犹豫了一下，还是上前敲了门。

开门的是个五十来岁的妇人，穿着青布衣裳，头上挽着纂儿，看见一个浑身湿透的小姑娘站在门外，先是一愣。

"大娘，我、我是个过路的，下了大雨，想借贵处避一避雨。"沈青萝怯怯地说。

妇人上下打量了她一眼，看她衣裳虽旧却干净整齐，眼神也清亮，便侧身让开："进来吧。"

堂屋不大，收拾得井井有条。灶上烧着一锅红薯稀饭，热气腾腾的。沈青萝站在门口不敢进去，怕自己一身泥水弄脏了人家干净的地。

"愣着干啥？进来烤烤火。"妇人指了指灶边的一条矮凳，"我家那口子去了镇上，家中就我一个婆子，没什么讲究。"

沈青萝小心翼翼地在矮凳上坐下。妇人给她倒了一碗热水，又翻出一双旧布鞋："先换上这个，别冻坏了脚。"

她接过鞋子，眼眶一热，差点掉下泪来。

妇人自称姓周，村人都叫她周婶。她一面往灶里添柴，一面问沈青萝从哪里来，到哪里去。沈青萝把家中的变故一五一十地说了，说到母亲过世时，忍不住抽泣起来。

周婶叹了口气："也是个苦命的孩子。"

雨越下越大，没有要停的意思。天色渐渐暗了下来，沈青萝站起身想要告辞，周婶拉住了她："这雨一时半会儿停不了，你一个姑娘家，夜里走路也不安全。今晚就在我家歇了吧，柴房里有张旧床，我给你铺上被褥。"

"这……"沈青萝不知道说什么好。

"别这那的了，先进屋喝碗热粥暖暖身子。"

那一晚，沈青萝喝了三碗红薯稀饭，胃里暖烘烘的。她躺在柴房的旧床上，听着外面的雨声，想起了小时候娘给她唱的童谣，眼泪不知不觉地流湿了枕头。

第二天，雨停了。沈青萝起来时，周婶已经在灶边忙活。她煮了杂粮粥，还煎了两个鸡蛋。

"吃完再走吧。"周婶把粥端到她面前，"路上还有二十多里地呢，饿着肚子怎么走得动？"

沈青萝小口小口地喝着，眼泪又掉进了粥里。

吃完饭，周婶又包了几个杂粮饼给她路上吃，还硬塞给她几十个铜板："拿着，路上应急。到了临州，找到了你舅舅，往后的日子会慢慢好起来的。"

沈青萝要给她磕头，被周婶拦住了。"快走吧，趁着天晴。"她说。

沈青萝背着藤箱走到篱笆门口，回头望了一眼。周婶站在门口，一手扶着门框，朝她挥了挥手。

她转过身，深一脚浅一脚地往前走。走了很远，再回头时，那个篱笆小院已经缩成了一个小点，渐渐地，消失在了视野里。

后来的路上，她又借住过很多地方。有好心的老农让她睡在稻草堆里，有逃荒的妇人分了半个馒头给她，有素不相识的货郎给她指了路。这些人她大多不知道名字，可她都记在心里。

到了临州时，已经又过去了三天。她辗转找到了舅舅的住处，那是一座三进的大宅院，门楣上挂着灯笼，朱漆大门敞开着。可门房告诉她，主人一家上个月去了京城，不在家中。

沈青萝站在那扇朱漆大门前，身上的棉袄已经破了好几个洞，藤箱上沾满了泥点。她忽然想起娘的话——"他总归会收留你的"。可眼前，朱门深似海，舅舅又不在家。

她站在那儿，不知过了多久。

最终，她转过身，沿着来时的路，慢慢地往回走。

她没有回清平镇，而是凭着记忆，回到了那个小村子，那个篱笆小院。

周婶看见她又回来了，先是一愣，然后笑着说："没找着你舅舅？"

沈青萝点点头。

"那就先在我家住下吧。"周婶说，"我家虽然穷，可多你一双筷子还是添得起的。"

沈青萝"扑通"一声跪在地上。

"傻孩子，快起来。"周婶把她拉起来，"进了这个门，就是自家人了。"

那天晚上，周婶的男人老赵从镇上回来，看见家里多了个人，也没多问，只是多添了一副碗筷。后来，沈青萝就住在了这个篱笆小院里，她管周婶叫"干娘"，管老赵叫"干爹"。

三年后，她嫁给了邻村一个姓陆的后生。成亲那天，周婶哭得像个泪人，拉着她的手说："闺女，往后要好好的。"

沈青萝抱着周婶，哭得说不出话来。

很多年后，沈青萝做了母亲，做了祖母。她常常给儿孙们讲起那个深秋的傍晚，那场大雨，那碗热粥，那双旧布鞋。

"我这辈子，"她说，"多亏了那些在檐下收留过我的陌生人。"

# The Cloud Keeper

Eleanor had a name for every cloud.

She didn't tell anyone about it—that was her secret, kept folded neatly between the pages of her life like a pressed flower. From the window seat of her third-floor apartment, she watched the sky the way other people read novels, finding stories in the slow migration of vapor across an endless blue page.

There was the bread cloud that appeared most mornings, golden-edged and reliable, puffing up over the bakery three blocks east. There were the rabbit clouds of spring—fleeting, nervous, always dissolving before she could name them properly. And once, on the day she turned forty-three, a dragon had unfurled across the entire western sky, smoke curling from nostrils made of thunderheads, and she had laughed until her tea went cold in her hands.

Most people thought she was a little odd. Eleanor knew this because she'd heard them whispering at the post office, seen the polite confusion on her neighbor's face when Eleanor cancelled plans because *the clouds are too good today, you have to see them.* She didn't mind. The clouds had been there before any of those people, and they would be there after. The clouds, she felt certain, understood her.

Her apartment was small and filled with light. She had no television, no pets, no children. Her shelves held books of poetry she'd underlined twice and a collection of pressed leaves she hadn't looked at in years. What she had, instead, was the window seat—a deep, worn velvet thing she'd found at an estate sale—and a thermos that she filled with different teas depending on season. In summer, cold mint. In winter, something dark and smoky that tasted like the clouds looked.

She had worked as a librarian for thirty-one years, and she had retired on a Wednesday. That was four years ago. On Thursdays, she had begun to notice the clouds.

At first, she thought it was grief—something to do with the sudden emptiness of her mornings, the absence of small tasks that had once structured her days. But the clouds had their own kind of presence, their own kind of demand. They asked nothing of her. They simply arrived.

She learned their moods. She learned that certain clouds meant rain and others only threatened it, that some carried wind in their bellies and others drifted like sleepwalkers. She learned that clouds at dawn were different animals than clouds at dusk—the morning ones pale and tentative, the evening ones dramatic, bruised purple and rose. The clouds of late afternoon were her favorites, when the light went long and golden and everything looked like a memory of itself.

She began to sketch them. Not because she was any good at drawing—she wasn't, not really—but because she wanted to remember. She filled notebooks with cloud shapes: the ship cloud, the cathedral cloud, the one that looked like her grandmother's hands. Sometimes she wrote little notes beside them. *The day the robins returned.* *The afternoon I finally called Margaret.* *Today the sky looked like someone had been crying, beautifully.*

It was the clouds that brought her to Elias.

He was sitting on the bench below her window one Tuesday in October, looking up. She almost didn't notice him—people rarely sat on that bench—but then she saw the way he was watching the sky, his head tilted back, his whole body still in a way that reminded her of herself.

She went downstairs.

"You're cloud-gazing," she said, before she'd thought about whether she should say anything at all.

He looked up at her, surprised. "I was, wasn't I? I didn't know there was a word for it."

"There should be," she said. "It deserves one."

He smiled. His name was Elias, and he was a widower, and he had just moved into the building across the street. He told her he'd spent forty years looking at the ground—at ledgers, at invoices, at the worried faces of clients. He was done with all that now.

"I don't know what to look at instead," he said.

Eleanor sat down beside him. Above them, a long procession of clouds was crossing the sky, white and slow and impossibly patient.

"I do," she said.

That was three years ago. Now they have tea on the bench most afternoons when the weather permits, two retired people with nothing in particular to do except notice. They've seen a thousand clouds together. They've named the regulars—the cauliflower one that appears on Tuesdays, the lonely one that always seems to be lagging behind. They've watched storms roll in and roll out. They've seen clouds that looked like heartbreak and clouds that looked like joy, and once, on their second anniversary of meeting, a cloud that looked exactly like two old people sitting on a bench, looking up.

Eleanor still doesn't tell most people about her cloud-gazing. Some things, she has learned, are better when they're small. When they're a folded thing kept between the pages of an ordinary life. When they're the kind of secret that turns out, sometimes, to be waiting for someone else to share.

The clouds understand her. They always have.

But these days, when the light goes long and golden, she finds it's nicer to be understood by a person too.

# O Segredo de Dona Cida

Dona Cida estava morrendo de vontade de contar. Não era uma vontade comum, dessas que a gente sente e esquece no dia seguinte. Era uma coceira na ponta da língua, um formigamento nos lábios, uma pressão no peito que só aumentava a cada hora que passava sem que ela pudesse abrir a boca.

Ela já tinha acordado três vezes naquela noite. Às uma, levantou para beber água e ficou parada na frente da janela da cozinha, olhando para a rua deserta, imaginando como soltaria a bomba. Às três, foi ao banheiro e ficou se olhando no espelho, ensaiando frases. Às cinco, desistiu de dormir de vez e foi fazer café, porque aquele dia exigia coragem, e coragem, ela sabia, precisa de uma xícara bem cheia.

O segredo não era dela. Esse era o problema. Se fosse, teria contado na hora, sem pestanejar, para quem quisesse ouvir — para o entregador de gás, para a moça do caixa do mercado, para o padre, para o cachorro. Mas o segredo pertencia à sua melhor amiga, Marlene, que lhe contara tudo na terça-feira passada, com os olhos vermelhos e as mãos tremendo, depois de três copos de vinho barato.

"Não conta pra ninguém, Cida. Pra ninguém. Juro por Deus."

E ela tinha jurado. Com a mão no peito, com a mão na Bíblia, com a mão onde ela quisesse. Mas agora, seis dias depois, o segredo estava fazendo ninho dentro dela, crescendo, inchando, empurrando as paredes do seu estômago. Ela se sentia como uma panela de pressão com o pino prestes a saltar.

Foi caminhar no parque para tentar se distrair. Comprou um picolé de uva. Sentou no banco da praça. Leu uma revista velha. Nada ajudava. A cada pessoa que passava, ela pensava: "Será que essa pessoa já sabe? Será que o marido dela já contou? Será que todo o bairro está comentando pelas minhas costas enquanto eu fingo que não sei de nada?"

Na padaria, a fila parecia propositalmente longa. A senhora da frente comentou qualquer coisa sobre o tempo, e Dona Cida quase deixou escapar. "Ah, tempo? Se eu te contasse o que eu sei sobre o tempo que a Marlene passou no motel com o irmão do prefeito..." Mas mordeu a língua. Literalmente. Sentiu o gosto de sangue se misturar com o de pão de queijo.

Tentou a velha técnica de escrever para não falar. Pegou o caderno, a caneta, e começou: *Eu, Cidalva Martins de Oliveira, não posso contar o que sei sobre...* Parou. Rasgou a folha. Se alguém encontrasse aquele papel, estaria tudo perdido.

Ligou para a sobrinha. A moça era boa de fofoca, daquelas que escuta, anota mentalmente e nunca esquece. Mas Dona Cida desligou no segundo toque. Não podia. Era sério demais. Era o tipo de coisa que, se saísse, destruiria uma família, um casamento, uma reputação construída em trinta e sete anos de casamento aparentemente feliz.

À noite, não aguentou mais. Foi até a casa de Marlene. Bateu na porta com força. A amiga atendeu, pálida, de robe, com olheiras que mais pareciam hematomas.

"Cida, pelo amor de Deus, o que foi?"

Dona Cida entrou, sentou no sofá, e ficou em silêncio por um longo momento. Marlene esperou, nervosa, retorcendo a barra do robe.

"Marlene", disse ela, finalmente, com a voz grave, solene. "Você precisa contar para o seu marido."

Marlene arregalou os olhos. "O quê? Cida, você prometeu!"

"Eu sei o que prometi. E eu não vou contar pra ninguém. Mas você precisa. Olha, minha amiga, eu te amo mais do que à minha própria vida, mas eu tô ficando doente. Não durmo, não como, não consigo olhar pro seu marido na missa sem sentir que vou explodir. Você precisa resolver isso. Eu tô morrendo, Marlene. Tô morrendo pra contar, e se você não contar, eu juro que não sei o que eu faço. Então conta logo, antes que eu conte por você."

Marlene caiu no choro. Dona Cida chorou junto. As duas ficaram ali, abraçadas no sofá da sala, chorando como se o mundo estivesse acabando, até que, entre soluços, Marlene disse:

"Tá bom. Eu conto. Amanhã."

"Melhor que seja", disse Dona Cida, enxugando os olhos com a barra da blusa. "Porque se você não contar, eu não me responsabilizo."

Saiu da casa da amiga com o coração apertado, mas a alma leve. Na esquina, deu uma risadinha sozinha. A coceira na língua finalmente havia cedido. Ela não tinha contado nada, não tinha quebrado a promessa, mas tinha feito a coisa certa.

E isso, Dona Cida sabia, era muito mais difícil do que qualquer fofoca.

# 迟来的冬至

"苏阿姨真的来吗？"

林栀蹲在玄关，一只手里攥着给苏阿姨织了一半的围巾，另一只手无意识地揪着自己洗得发白的毛衣下摆。她十二岁了，已经懂得分辨大人话里的虚虚实实，可关于"苏阿姨今年能来"这件事，她还是想从妈妈嘴里听到一个确切的答案。

妈妈正在厨房里切葱花，砧板笃笃地响。她头也没抬，只是"嗯"了一声。

林栀知道这个"嗯"的分量。

她打开手机，翻到那个叫"小院子"的群聊。最后一条消息停留在三个月前——苏阿姨发的：栀栀，阿姨这边走不开，元旦再去看你。

元旦过了，春节过了，清明也过了。苏阿姨的"再来"像是被风吹散的蒲公英，年年都飞，年年都落不到地上。

---

苏阿姨全名苏茉，是妈妈二十多年前在福利院一起长大的姐妹。

林栀从小听妈妈讲她们的故事：两个没人要的小女孩挤在一张铁架床上，苏茉总把饭里的肉拨给妈妈，而妈妈偷偷把作业借给她抄。十八岁那年她们先后被领养，一个去了南边的海岛城市，一个留在了这座北方小城，从此天各一方。

后来她们通过福利院留下的旧地址重新联系上，便有了那个叫"小院子"的群。后来妈妈生了林栀，再后来苏阿姨离婚、再婚、移居、再离婚、再移居——群里的人来来去去，最后只剩下她们三个。

"为什么不打电话？"小时候的林栀问过。

妈妈笑了笑，摸了摸她的头："大人有大人忙的理由。"

林栀长大后慢慢明白，那些"理由"多半是：苏阿姨每次说要来，不是孩子生病就是工作调动，要么是新找的男朋友出了岔子；妈妈这边呢，爸爸走之后这间二十平米的小店就成了她全部的生活，她出不去，也不敢出，怕苏阿姨白跑一趟。

就这样一拖十几年，拖到林栀都上了初中。

---

冬至前一天，苏阿姨终于在群里发了一条语音。

林栀放学回来，是妈妈先听见的。她把手机举到耳边，脸上的表情像春天的冰河，慢慢地、一点一点地裂开。

"她说什么？"林栀问。

"她说她明天晚上的火车。"妈妈的声音有一点抖，"让咱们包饺子。"

那一晚妈妈破例没看店。她从柜子深处翻出那块已经干硬的老面肥，用温水泡开，加了面粉揉成团，盖上湿布醒在暖气旁边。林栀帮着剁馅，是猪肉白菜的，妈妈一边剁一边絮絮叨叨说苏阿姨不爱吃姜，小时候在福利院，每次肉里有姜她都偷偷吐在碗底。

"那她爱吃什么？"

"玉米。"妈妈说，"但现在牙不好了，得切碎点。"

---

冬至那天傍晚，下了今年的第一场雪。

林栀趴在窗台上看，等火车经过铁桥时那一声鸣笛。她听见妈妈在厨房里轻轻哼起一首歌，是福利院里阿姨常放的那首《送别》。

鸣笛声响了。

她从窗台上跳下来冲到玄关，回头看妈妈——妈妈从厨房里探出半个身子，手上还沾着面粉，愣在原地。

"妈，你不去开门吗？"

妈妈没说话。她把围裙慢慢解下来，叠好，搭在椅背上，又抬手理了理头发。然后她才走过去，走得很慢，像是要去赴一个等了很多年的约。

门开了。

门外站着一个烫着卷发的女人，瘦，个子不高，眼角有很深的纹。她一只手里提着一个鼓鼓囊囊的塑料袋，另一只手——林栀看见了——是空的，悬在半空，颤着，像是想去握什么，又怕握不住。

"茉莉。"妈妈先开口。

"......阿瑜。"

就两个字，可林栀觉得她听见了某种东西碎掉的声音。是那种很旧很旧的伤口，终于等到了缝合的针。

她们在门口站了大概三秒钟——三秒，对于等了二十多年的人来说，实在太短了。

然后苏茉把手里的塑料袋往前一递："玉米，我从老家背来的，能煮一大锅。"

妈妈就笑了。笑着笑着眼泪掉下来，她赶紧用袖子去擦，又笑："进来进来，饺子要煮破了。"

---

那一晚的饺子煮得确实过了火，皮都有点烂。

可三个人围着那张小小的折叠桌，吃得比过年还热闹。苏阿姨尝了一口，皱了皱眉——"白菜太多了，肉少。"——然后又夹了第二个，第三个。

林栀把自己织了一半的围巾拿出来，递给苏阿姨看。

"才起了个头，"她说，"等阿姨下次来，我就能织完了。"

苏阿姨摸着那几寸织好的米白色毛线，眼圈又红了。她从随身的包里掏出一只小盒子，打开，里面是一枚很细的银戒指，戒面上刻着一朵栀子花。

"给你的。"她把盒子推过来，"你出生那年我就买好了，一直没机会送。"

林栀愣住了。

她转头看妈妈，妈妈也愣着，最后才轻声说："茉莉，这是......"

"我给栀栀的。"苏阿姨说，"我做不了别的，这点心意总得有。"

林栀低头把戒指套在右手小指上——大了一点，但刚刚好。

---

那晚苏阿姨住在了林栀的小房间里。

她们三个挤在一张一米五的床上，林栀睡中间，左边是妈妈，右边是苏阿姨。窗户外的雪下得越来越大，落在防盗窗上簌簌地响。

"栀栀睡着了？"苏阿姨小声问。

"没呢。"林栀闭着眼说。

"那她听见了，"妈妈的声音也轻轻的，"茉莉，你明年还来吗？"

很长的沉默。

"......不知道。"苏阿姨说，"我想来的。我一直想来的。"

"那就好。"妈妈说，"来不来都行。知道你一直想，就够了。"

林栀把被子往上拉了拉，盖住自己翘起的嘴角。她右手小指上那枚松松的银戒指，在黑暗里泛着一点极微弱的、被雪映亮的光。
