## 12 Oktober 2024

Aku menulis ini dengan tangan yang masih gemetar.

Hari ini, untuk pertama kalinya dalam hidupku, aku menyetir sendirian di jalan tol. Sendirian. Tanpa ibu di kursi penumpang yang selalu mengingatkan untuk menyalakan lampu sein. Tanpa ayah yang memutar-mutar radio mencari lagu lawas kesukaannya. Tanpa kakak yang pura-pura tidur di jok belakang supaya aku merasa lebih tenang.

Hanya aku, setir, dan tiga jalur aspal yang membentang di depanku.

Aneh ya, untuk sesuatu yang sudah aku persiapkan berbulan-bulan — les mengemudi setiap Sabtu, teori yang dihafal sampai tengah malam, doa-doa kecil yang kupanjatkan sebelum ujian SIM — rasanya tetap saja seperti melompat dari tebing. Tepat sebelum kaki meninggalkan ujung batu, sebelum gravitasi mengambil alih, ada momen hening itu. Momen di mana seluruh hidupku terasa bergantung pada satu keputusan kecil: gas, atau rem.

Aku memilih gas.

Mungkin ini terdengar dramatis untuk sesuatu yang dilakukan jutaan orang setiap hari. Tapi bagiku, ini bukan sekadar menyetir. Ini adalah pertama kalinya aku membuat keputusan besar tanpa bertanya izin pada siapa pun. Pertama kalinya aku percaya bahwa tanganku cukup kuat untuk mengendalikan sesuatu yang berjalan enam puluh kilometer per jam. Pertama kalinya aku sadar bahwa orang tuaku benar — mereka tidak pernah mengajarkaniku untuk takut pada dunia, mereka hanya mengajarkaniku untuk menghormatinya.

Di kilometer ke-23, aku melihat matahari terbenam dari balik tol layang. Warnanya oranye keemasan, seperti madu yang tumpah perlahan ke langit. Aku menangis. Di tengah jalan tol, dengan kedua tangan di setir dan airbag menghadapku seperti malaikat kecil yang siap menangkap, aku menangis. Bukan karena sedih. Bukan karena takut. Tapi karena sesuatu yang sangat besar tumbuh di dadaku, sesuatu yang belum punya nama.

*Ini aku*, pikirku. *Ini baru aku.*

---

## 13 Oktober 2024

Aku memberanikan diri melewati tikungan tajam tadi pagi — tikungan yang selalu kupanggil "Si Pembunuh" karena dulu aku pernah melihat truk terguling di sana.

Kakiku masih terasa dingin di pedal gas, tapi tanganku sudah mulai hafal dengan jalan.

Ibu menelepon tadi malam. "Kamu sudah makan?" tanyanya, padahal yang ingin dia tahu adalah apakah aku baik-baik saja. Aku bilang aku sudah makan nasi goreng dengan telur mata sapi. Tidak benar, aku cuma makan roti. Tapi aku tidak ingin dia khawatir.

Ayah tidak menelepon, tapi dia mengirim pesan: *"Lampu sein kiri yang kuning."*

Aku tertawa sendiri sampai-sampai hampir melenceng ke jalur darurat. Itu kode kami. Artinya: *Aku tahu kamu sedang menyetir. Hati-hati. Aku bangga.*

---

## 15 Oktober 2024

Hari ini aku tersesat.

Bukan tersesat yang dramatis — tidak ada mobil yang mogok, tidak ada hujan deras, tidak pula GPS yang mati total. Hanya saja aku salah belok di persimpangan yang tampak familier tapi ternyata berbeda setelah dibangun ulang. Jalan yang dulu penuh pohon flamboyan sekarang menjadi kompleks ruko dengan warna cat yang terlalu mencolok.

Aku berhenti di bahu jalan. Menatap peta di ponsel. Memejamkan mata sejenak.

Dulu, setiap kali tersesat, reaksiku adalah panik. Telepon ibu. Telepon ayah. Bahkan kadang menelepon ojol supaya mengantarku pulang dengan malu. Tapi hari ini, aku hanya duduk di sana. Membiarkan rasa tidak nyaman itu datang. Membiarkannya tinggal sebentar, seperti tamu yang tidak diundang tapi akhirnya kita ajak minum teh.

Lalu aku menyalakan mesin lagi. Memasuki jalur yang benar kali ini. Melanjutkan perjalanan.

Kecil? Mungkin. Tapi bagiku, ini gunung yang sudah aku daki.

---

## 18 Oktober 2024

Aku sampai di kantor lebih awal hari ini. Untuk pertama kalinya, aku tidak buru-buru. Tidak keringat dingin karena takut terlambat. Tidak jantung berdebar karena lampu merah yang terlalu lama.

Aku duduk di parkiran selama lima menit sebelum masuk. Memutar kunci kontak. Mematikan mesin. Melihat tanganku sendiri di atas setir — tangan yang sama dengan yang kemarin masih gemetar memegang kemasannya, tangan yang dulu selalu mencari pegangan di kursi sebelah setiap kali ada tikerungan tajam.

Sekarang mereka diam saja. Tenang. Seperti tahu apa yang harus dilakukan.

Aku menulis ini di meja kerjaku, dengan secangkir kopi yang mulai dingin. Di luar jendela, kota bergerak seperti biasa — klakson, trotoar penuh pejalan kaki, pedagang kaki lima yang berteriak menawarkan gorengan. Tapi aku merasa seperti orang yang baru bangun dari tidur panjang. Seperti orang yang baru pertama kali melihat semuanya.

---

## 20 Oktober 2024

Ibu datang berkunjung hari ini. Aku menjemputnya di stasiun dengan mobilku sendiri.

Wajahnya ketika aku membukakan pintu penumpang — aku tidak akan pernah lupa wajah itu. Bukan kaget. Bukan khawatir. Lebih seperti... *penasaran*. Seperti dia ingin tahu versi apa dari anaknya yang akan muncul hari ini.

Kami tidak banyak bicara dalam perjalanan pulang. Radio memutar lagu-lagu lama yang biasa ayah nyanyikan dengan falsetto. Ibu menyanyikan bagian reffnya. Aku ikut, tapi suaraku pecah di nada tinggi. Kami tertawa.

Di lampu merah, ibu meraih tanganku sebentar di atas gear. Sedetik saja. Lalu melepasnya.

"Kamu sudah besar," katanya pelan, seperti kepada dirinya sendiri.

Aku tidak menjawab. Aku hanya menatap lurus ke depan, ke jalan yang membentang panjang di hadapan kami, ke semua tujuan yang belum kami ketahui, ke semua "pertama kali" yang masih menunggu di tikungan berikutnya.

Tapi untuk hari ini, ini cukup.

Untuk pertama kalinya, aku merasa cukup.

# 电梯里的第八层住户

搬进翠庭苑的第一周，我就注意到了那个人。

每天傍晚六点十五分，电梯门打开时，他总会准时出现在走廊尽头。三十岁出头的样子，穿着一件洗得发白的灰色卫衣，手里攥着把钥匙，却从不进任何一户门。他只是靠着窗户站着，看远处天际线被晚霞烧成橘红色。

我住八楼802，他总在八楼停下。

物业叫陈姐，是个热心的中年妇女，烫着方便面卷发，整天骑辆电瓶车在小区里转。有一天我忍不住问她："走廊尽头那人是谁？好像不是住户。"

陈姐擦了擦额头的汗，奇怪地看我一眼："哪有什么人？你是不是刚搬家，太累了？"

我以为她在敷衍我。

直到第二个月，我加班回来得晚，在电梯里撞见他。

电梯里有面镜子，我第一次看清了他的脸。很年轻，眉目清秀，左耳垂上有颗小小的黑痣。他的眼神很淡，像是被什么东西磨平了所有情绪。

"你也住八楼吗？"我试探着问。

他没说话，只是低头看着自己的鞋尖。

电梯到了八楼，门开了。他走出去，我也走出去。走廊里空荡荡的，感应灯一盏接一盏亮起来，照出我一个人长长的影子。

他不见了。

---

那天晚上我没睡着。

半夜两点，我起来倒水，经过窗户时往走廊看了一眼。月光从窗户照进来，在地上铺出一块银白色的光斑。光斑里，他站着。

这次我看清楚了——他的卫衣口袋里，露出半截白色的袖口。那不是他自己的衣服。

第二天我假装不经意地问起八楼的住户。陈姐翻了翻花名册："802是你，803是个程序员，经常出差，804是一对老夫妻，805……"

"805有人住吗？"

陈姐的手顿了一下。她抬起头看我，眼神里有些复杂的东西，像是想说什么，又咽了回去。

"805早就空了。"她把本子合上，"三年了。"

"空了？那之前住的是谁？"

陈姐骑上电瓶车，发动前回头看了我一眼："小伙子，有些事别问太清楚。这小区里，有些东西住了太久，就走不掉了。"

---

我开始留意他。

他似乎只在傍晚和深夜出现，从不坐电梯下楼。我试过跟着他走到走廊尽头，但每次都是一转眼他就消失在805门口。

805的门是深棕色的老式防盗门，门把手上积着灰。我路过时数过，整整三十二道划痕。

有天傍晚，我没回家，而是在车里等着。

六点一刻，单元门开了。

他走出来，手里还是攥着那串钥匙。他没有走向电梯，而是径直走向地下车库的入口。物业办公室就在地库旁边的小屋里，灯亮着，陈姐应该在里面值夜班。

我没有下车，只是看着他的背影消失在昏暗的灯光里。

第二天，陈姐辞职了。

---

新来的物业是个小伙子，戴着眼镜，看起来很靠谱。我找了个机会问他："咱们这栋楼，有没有发生过什么事？"

他推了推眼镜："您是说？"

"三年前，805。"

他沉默了一会儿，然后摇摇头："我是新来的，不太清楚。但是我听说，以前这栋楼有个程序员，就住在805。"

"后来呢？"

"后来他妻子得了重病，需要很多钱。他接了很多私活，经常加班到很晚。再后来……"小伙子顿了顿，"有一天他老婆从八楼跳了下去。"

窗外，不知什么时候下起了雨。

"他在那之后就不见了？"我问。

"不是不见了。"小伙子压低声音，"是他老婆，每天傍晚都会回来。"

---

那天晚上，我没有坐电梯。

我从消防楼梯一层层走上去，每上一层都停下听一听。一楼，二楼，三楼……风从窗缝里灌进来，吹得安全出口的牌子哐哐作响。

到了八楼，我站住了。

楼梯间的门半掩着，从门缝里透出一线光。我推开门，走廊里空空荡荡，感应灯全灭了，只有805门口亮着一盏。

他站在门口，手里的钥匙终于插进了锁孔。

我屏住呼吸。

门开了，里面是一片浓稠的黑暗。他走进去，门在他身后轻轻合上。

走廊恢复了寂静。

我站了很久，久到感应灯亮起来又灭下去。然后我转身，走向电梯，按下了1楼。

电梯门关上的瞬间，我看见镜子里映出805的门。

门开了一条缝。

有人站在那里，穿着白色的裙子，胸口别着一朵已经枯萎的白花。她在笑。

电梯开始下降。

---

第二天我搬走了。

走之前，我在八楼的电梯里又遇见了他。灰色卫衣，手里攥着钥匙，眼神淡淡的。

电梯门打开，他没有出去。

他看着我，忽然开口说了第一句话。

"你闻到了吗？"

我深吸了一口气，闻到了一股很淡的香味。是栀子花。

"是她最喜欢的味道。"他说，嘴角终于有了一丝弧度，"三年了，她终于愿意让我进门了。"

电梯门缓缓合上。

在门关上的最后一刻，我看见走廊尽头的805门口，站着一个穿白裙子的女人。她朝电梯里的他招了招手。

门关上了。

翠庭苑八楼的电梯继续运行着，上上下下，接送着一个又一个人。只是从那以后，再也没有人在傍晚六点一刻走出电梯。

只是偶尔，楼里的住户会说，这栋楼的电梯，有时会停在八楼，停很久很久。

像是有人在等另一个人。

像是永远都等不完。

---

*门里面，空空荡荡，只有一扇开着的窗户，和窗台上一个枯萎的花盆。*

*盆里，曾经种着栀子花。*

나는 기자가 된 이래 수백 명의 인물을 인터뷰했다. 정치인, 연예인, CEO까지. 그러나 오늘, 편집국장님은 나에게 미친 듯한 임무를 맡기셨다.

"존재하지도 않는 악당을 인터뷰하라고? 기사감이 떨어졌나?"

상관의 서재에 놓인 낡은 원고 뭉치에는 손글씨로 적힌 이름이 있었다. **레이븐 크로프트**. 19세기 유럽을 뒤흔든 연쇄살인마이자, 자신의 악행을 회고록으로 남긴 전설의 악당.

"이 원고를 읽고, 그에게 질문을 던져라. 독자들은 악당의 내면을 궁금해한다."

그래서 나는 어젯밤, 서재의 촛불 아래에서 그 원고를 펼쳤다. 그리고 이상한 일이 벌어졌다. 원고의 글자들이 꿈틀거리더니, 어둠 속에서 차가운 목소리가 흘러나왔다.

### **인터뷰: 레이븐 크로프트**

**김현우:** 먼저 인사부터 부탁드립니다. 당신은 스스로를 어떤 존재라 생각합니까?

**레이븐 크로프트:** *(낮게 웃으며)* 인사를? 인간들이나 하는 사교적 의식이지. 나는 그럴 필요가 없다. 나는 **신**이다. 정확히 말하면, 인간이라는 종이 만들어낸 신. 두려움이 나를 탄생시켰고, 두려움이 나를 영원히 살게 한다.

**김현우:** 당신의 첫 번째 살인이란? 기록에 따르면 당신은 어린 시절부터―

**레이븐 크로프트:** *(말을 자르며)* "첫 번째"라고? 기자는 숫자에 집착하는군. 첫 번째는 없다. 모든 살인은 하나의 살인이다. 어둠 속으로 손을 뻗는 순간, 그건 이미 끝난 거야. 시작도 없었고, 끝도 없어. 내가 어렸을 때부터 *죽음*은 내 안에 있었던 거지. 단지 밖으로 나왔을 뿐이야.

**김현우:** 후회가 없습니까?

**레이븐 크로프트:** *(잠시 침묵)* 후회? 그 단어는 인간들이 발명한 자기기만의 도구일 뿐이야. 후회한다는 것은 다시 선택할 수 있다고 믿는 어리석음이지. 나는 선택하지 않았어. **선택할 수 없었다.** 어둠이 나를 선택했다.

**김현우:** 그런데도 당신은 회고록을 썼습니다. 왜요?

**레이븐 크로프트:** *(창백한 미소를 띠며)* 좋은 질문이야, 기자. 내가 이 글을 쓴 이유는― **경고**하기 위해서다. 인간은 내가 악당이라고 생각하지. 그러나 세상 어디를 봐도, 나보다 잔인한 존재가 수천 명씩 있지 않나? 전쟁을 일으키는 지도자, 무고한 아이들을 이용하는 상류층, 사랑한다는 이름으로 상대를 옭아매는 인간들. 나는 단지 그들보다 **정직했을 뿐**이야.

**김현우:** 마지막으로 묻겠습니다. 만약 당신에게 다시 한번 인생을 살 수 있는 기회가 주어진다면―

**레이븐 크로프트:** *(눈을 가늘게 뜨며)* 같은 길을 갈 거다. 다만 더 멀리, 더 깊이. 기자, 마지막으로 하나만 알려주지. **너의 서재 뒤편, 어둠 속에서 누군가 숨 쉬는 소리가 들리지 않는가?**

---

순간 촛불이 꺼졌다.

나는 심장이 멎는 줄 알았다. 손전등을 켜고 뒤를 돌아봤지만―거기엔 아무도 없었다.

다만 바닥에 떨어진 종이 한 장이 눈에 들어왔다. 손으로 쓴 글씨.

> *"다음 인터뷰는 너에게 할게."*
> **― R.K.**

나는 그제야 깨달았다. 인터뷰의 대상은 **나**였다는 것을.

# 《蛋糕炸弹奇遇记》

"等等……二百克？"

我盯着手机屏幕上那个被红圈标注的数字，后背一阵发凉。烤箱里的蛋糕胚正以肉眼可见的速度膨胀，像一颗即将引爆的甜蜜炸弹。

"应该是一杯……对，一杯糖！"我手忙脚乱地抓起糖袋，却一个失手，整袋糖倾泻而下，在料理台上堆起一座白色的小山。

"砰——"烤箱发出一声闷响。

糟糕，烤箱门被顶开了一条缝，金黄色的蛋糕糊正像岩浆一样往外涌。我来不及多想，顺手抄起桌上的——等等，那是盐吗？

管它呢！

我把那座"盐山"连同半瓶小苏打一股脑倒进了模具，又飞速打了六个鸡蛋进去。搅拌机轰鸣着，空气里弥漫着一种说不清道不明的诡异气息。

"生日快乐！"我对着客厅大喊，"惊喜马上来！"

我端着那个已经膨胀成脸盆大小、表面布满可疑气泡的……姑且称之为蛋糕吧，走进客厅。

朋友瞪大了眼睛。

蛋糕在托盘上微微颤抖了一下。

然后——

"噗——"

它爆了。

准确地说，是优雅地、缓慢地、如同延时摄影般地塌陷了下去。奶油、糖霜和不明泡沫飞溅到了天花板上。

沉默。

我看了看朋友，朋友看了看我。

"生日快乐？"我虚弱地补充道，"这是个……会爆炸的惊喜蛋糕？"

朋友眨眨眼，忽然笑得前仰后合："你这也太离谱了！"

后来的事是这样的：

我们花了三小时清理厨房，重新烤了一个正常的小蛋糕，然后一边吃一边翻看那个"罪魁祸首"的食谱。

"看这里——"朋友指着屏幕，"'1/2杯发酵粉'，你刚才是不是读成了'1磅'？"

我沉默了。

"还有这里——'一撮盐'，你放了……多少来着？"

我继续沉默。

她笑得更厉害了，一边笑一边把这段经历发到了我们的朋友群里，配文："今日最佳：朋友试图毒死我。"

而我，只能端着那个味道奇怪到无法形容的"原始蛋糕"，默默地蹲在角落里，思考人生。

这大概是我这辈子送过的最难忘的生日礼物了。

——不是因为它好吃，恰恰相反，是因为它难吃到令人发指，难吃到我朋友直到十年后还会在每年的生日聚会上提起。

"记得那年的爆炸蛋糕吗？"

然后她会捂着肚子笑成一团。

而我会假装生气，却也跟着笑了起来。

有些礼物，确实是越离谱，越难忘。

# 最后一夏

夏天的光落在林荫道上，把树叶的影子印成深深浅浅的水墨。林晓背着书包，站在那条走过无数次的路上，脚下是被夕阳烤得微烫的柏油路面。

今天是报到的前一天。明天，她就要坐上去往北京的火车，离开这座小城，离开父母，离开……他。

手机震了一下，是陈屿发来的消息："老地方，十分钟后。"

林晓攥着手机，没有回复。她站在路口，看着远处那棵歪脖子梧桐树——那是他们初中的秘密基地。每逢考试失利、被爸妈骂了、或者只是单纯地想发呆，他们就会爬上那棵树，一坐就是一个下午。

她慢慢走过去。

陈屿已经坐在树下了。他今天穿了件白T恤，牛仔裤的膝盖处磨得发白，脚边放着两罐冰镇过的橘子汽水。

"来啦。"他抬头看她，眼睛弯弯的，还是那副欠揍的笑模样。

林晓在他旁边坐下，接过汽水，冰凉的触感从掌心传到心里。她没说话，只是用手指抠着易拉罐的拉环。

"紧张吗？"陈屿问。

"还好。"她撒了谎。

"我也是。"他说。

林晓愣了一下，转头看他。陈屿没有看她，而是望着远处被晚霞染红的天际线，手里那罐汽水被攥得有些变形。

"骗你的，我一点儿都不紧张。"他忽然笑了，"我紧张得要死。"

林晓没忍住，也笑了。她伸出手，拍了拍他的肩膀："陈屿，你能不能正经点。"

"我很正经。"他转过头，表情认真起来，"林晓，我有话跟你说。"

汽水罐上的水珠滑落，掉在林晓的指尖上。她突然觉得心跳得有点快。

"你说。"

陈屿深吸了一口气，张了张嘴，又闭上了。他低下头，用脚尖在地上画着圈，半晌才说："你到北京以后……要好好吃饭。别老吃泡面，对胃不好。"

林晓眨了眨眼睛："就这个？"

"还有……冬天冷，记得加衣服。东北人抗冻，我们南方人不行。"他的声音越来越低，"还有……"

"还有什么？"

陈屿抬起头，看着她。晚霞在他的眼睛里燃烧，把那层薄薄的水光照得清清楚楚。

"还有……"他顿了顿，像是在做什么重大决定，"到了那边，别忘了我。"

林晓的心猛地揪了一下。她张了张嘴，却不知道该说什么。那些平日里能说会道的嘴皮子，在这一刻全部失灵了。

风穿过树叶，发出细碎的声响。远处的蝉鸣此起彼伏，像是一整个夏天的心跳。

"陈屿……"她的声音有点哑，"你考的是哪里来着？"

"上海。"

"上海啊……"她喃喃着，"挺远的。"

"还行吧，比北京近。"陈屿笑了笑，"坐高铁四个小时就到了。"

"四个小时……"林晓重复着这个数字，忽然觉得鼻子有点酸。

他们就这样坐在树下，谁都没有再说话。汽水喝完了，空罐子在晚风里发出轻微的响声。路灯亮了，蚊虫开始围着光源打转。

"林晓。"陈屿忽然开口。

"嗯？"

他从口袋里掏出一个东西，塞到她手里。林晓低头一看，是一个旧旧的手机挂件——一只蓝色的小海豚，耳朵有点褪色。

"这是……"她惊讶地抬起头，"这不是我初三那年丢的那个吗？我找了它好久……"

"在我这儿。"陈屿的耳朵红了，"那年你哭了三天，我就……偷偷捡回来了。本来想早点还你的，但是……"

他没说完。

林晓把那个小海豚攥在手心里，指尖触到那熟悉的磨砂质感，眼眶突然热了。

"谢谢你。"她说。

"谢什么啊，本来就是你的。"陈屿站起来，拍了拍裤子上的灰，"走吧，送你回去。明天还要赶火车。"

林晓跟着站起来，发现腿有些发麻。她踉跄了一下，陈屿伸手扶了她一把，两个人的手臂触在一起，又迅速分开。

"那……那我走了。"林晓说。

"嗯。"

她走出几步，又回过头。陈屿还站在原地，手插在口袋里，在路灯下拉出一个长长的影子。

"陈屿！"她喊道。

"干嘛？"

"你……你也要好好的。"

他笑了，用力挥了挥手："知道了，快回去吧，林阿姨该着急了。"

林晓转过身，往家的方向走去。走了很远，她才敢把一直憋着的那口气吐出来。眼泪早就流了满脸，她用手背胡乱抹了一把，却怎么也抹不干净。

手心里，那只蓝色的小海豚还带着陈屿的体温。

---

四年后的夏天。

北京西站，林晓拖着行李箱走出站台。她刚结束研究生考试，准备回趟老家。手机响了，是陈屿发来的消息："我在上海等你。"

她笑着摇摇头，打开朋友圈，发了一张在火车站拍的照片，配文只有三个字：

"回来了。"

很快，陈屿点了个赞，评论道："老地方，半小时后。"

林晓抬起头，看着北京夏天明晃晃的太阳，忽然觉得眼眶又有点热。

她加快了脚步。

# 銅とテルルuriumの君

三月。理科準備室の隅、埃っぽい試薬棚の影で、島崎ほのかはその言葉を聞いてしまった。

「——って、それ、人に言うの？」

思わず声が出た。試薬ビーカーを棚に戻す手が止まる。

振り返った向こうでは、同じ化学部の二年生、藤堂遼一が 机に頬杖をつきながら、隣の女子—— 一年生の白石あおいに向けて、にやりと笑っていた。

「事実だろ？ 周期表的には」

「は？」

「CuとTe。CuTe。きゅーと。可愛いだろ？」

あおいの目が点になる。ほのかは試薬棚の奥で息を殺した。

「……ネズミ講みたいなジョークですね」

「えっ、なんでそんな反応。普通、喜ぶやつだろ？」

「理科室で周期表で褒めてくる人は、ちょっと怖いです」

「ガクッ」

藤堂の表情が一瞬で見事に崩れた。自信満々に用意したジョークが、想定外のカウンターで粉々に砕け散った顔。ほのかは見ていて若干かわいそうになった。

——同じ部活の後輩として。

「つか島崎、お前いつからいるんだ」

藤堂が気づいた。しまった。

「……さっきから」

「全部聞いてた？」

「『きゅーと』のとこから」

藤堂の顔がみるみる赤くなる。Cu（銅）のような赤色。原子番号29。なじみ深い金属の反応だ。

「……なんだよ。別にダジャレ言っただけで——」

「いやいや、だって Cu と Te って全然周期表で隣じゃないし、化学的性質も違うのに"くーて"で押し切るのはなかなかの勇気だよね」

ほのかは棚の奥から出てきて、机の端に腰を下ろした。白石あおいがこちらを見て、わずかに目を細める。えらいひとを見つけた、という顔。

「島崎さんって——」

「ほのかでいいよ。二年」

「ほのか先輩、あの……あの人のこと、知ってます？」

「藤堂？ 同じ化学部でしょ。実験レポートは毎回ギリギリ出すし、フラスコ洗い忘れるし、ドラフトチャンバーの中でくしゃみするし。危険人物だよ」

「いや、そうじゃなくて——」

あおいが少しもじもじして、それから一気に言った。

「——あの人、私のこと好きなのかな、っていうか、それともこういうの全ての女子に言ってるのかな、っていうか、そういうのを聞きたいんですけど！」

ほのかは藤堂を見た。藤堂は窓の外を見ていた。いや、窓の外を見ているふりをしていた。耳が赤い。銅の赤ではない。これはもっと有機的な赤だ。

「……藤堂」

「なんだ」

「ねえ」

「だからなんだよ」

「白石に何回言ったの、そのジョーク」

藤堂の沈黙が、理科準備室の湿度計よりも雄弁に事実を伝えた。

「……ゼロ回」

「あおいに言ったのが最初？」

「…………ゼロ回」

「やめて！」

あおいが叫んだ。

「そんなのいちばん恥ずかしいんですけど！」

「あおいは気にしてないって言ったらこの男、絶対ずるずる何十回も別の子に同じこと言いそうだし」

「それは言えてる——」

藤堂が何か言いかけて、口を閉じた。机を叩いて立ち上がり、棚からふっと手を引いて白い試験管を一振り。それから振り返った。

「——ていうか島崎。お前そういうとこ鋭いの、ほんと勘弁してほしい」

「えっ、なにが」

「人の距離感の詰め方。Cu みたいに」

「導電性が高いってこと？」

「冷たくて導電率高いんだよ。29番」

「……褒めてる？」

「褒めてない」

あおいが二人のやり取りを真ん中で聞きながら、ふっと息を漏らした。ほのかの方を見て、小さく笑う。

「……この部活、変な人ばっかりですね」

「でしょ。だからやめといたほうがいいよ、まだ一月あるし」

「いや、辞めないけど」

**The Phone Call**

The coffee shop buzzed with the low hum of conversation and the hiss of the espresso machine. Maya was halfway through her latte, scrolling mindlessly through emails, when her phone buzzed against the wooden table. She didn't recognize the number at first, but the area code was familiar—same as hers.

She picked up on the third ring.

"Maya? It's me. Don't hang up."

A pause. Then recognition clicked like a lock tumbling open.

"Jordan?" Her voice came out quieter than she'd intended. "I thought you were—where are you?"

"That's the interesting part," he said, and she could hear something in his tone that didn't match the Jordan she'd known. He sounded lighter. Almost giddy. "I'm about two blocks from you, actually. Surprise."

Her heart did something complicated. "Surprise? You disappeared for eleven months, Jordan. You don't just—show up."

"I know," he said. "And I'm sorry. I really am. But I have news, and I think you're going to want to hear it in person. Can you come outside?"

She hesitated. Eleven months of silence. Eleven months of unanswered texts, of his apartment emptied out, of her standing in the rain outside that apartment one night like an idiot, knocking until her knuckles hurt. And now he was two blocks away, asking her to come outside.

"Jordan, if this is some kind of—"

"It's not," he said. "I promise. Just—trust me one more time. Please."

Against every better instinct she had, Maya grabbed her coat.

---

The October wind bit at her cheeks as she stepped onto the sidewalk. The street was ordinary—brick buildings, a bicycle locked to a rack, a woman walking a corgi. Nothing that suggested the universe was about to tilt.

Then she saw him.

Jordan was leaning against the lamppost across the street, hands shoved in the pockets of a green jacket she didn't recognize. He looked thinner. His hair was longer. But it was unmistakably him, and the sight of him opened up something in her chest she'd spent almost a year trying to seal shut.

He saw her. He smiled—that crooked, lopsided thing she'd once loved more than she wanted to admit—and raised one hand in a small wave.

Maya crossed the street. Stopped a few feet away.

"You have thirty seconds," she said.

"Fair." He took a breath. "Remember when I left? I told you I needed to figure some things out. That I couldn't explain yet."

"You said a lot of things."

"I know." He dropped his gaze to the sidewalk. "I was in trouble, Maya. Not—dangerous trouble, but the kind where if I stayed, I'd have dragged you into it. People I owed money to. Bad decisions I'd made a few years back. I thought if I just... disappeared, they'd forget about you. Forget about us."

She stared at him. "Jordan—"

"I'm not done." He looked up. "I went upstate. Stayed with my uncle in this nowhere town. Worked construction. Saved every penny. And six months ago, I paid them back. All of it. Plus interest. I'm clean, Maya. I came back last week. I've been trying to figure out how to face you."

The wind picked up. A leaf skittered between them.

"Why now?" she asked. "Why call?"

"Because I saw your name on a lease application at the community center downtown." He grinned, sheepish. "You're opening the reading program. The one you always talked about."

She blinked. "How did you—"

"Your mom told me. I stopped by her house yesterday. She almost threw a shoe at me, by the way. But then she gave me your number." He reached into his pocket and pulled out a folded piece of paper, held it out to her. "I want to help. Not as a boyfriend, not yet—maybe not ever, if you don't want. But as a friend. I can do the carpentry, the shelves, the kid-sized tables. Whatever you need."

She didn't take the paper. Not yet.

"You disappeared," she said, "and you think some bookshelves fix that?"

"No," he said simply. "I don't. But it's a start. And I owed you a start."

Maya looked at him for a long moment. The Jordan from eleven months ago would have made a joke, deflected, charmed his way out of it. This one just stood there, hands in his pockets, waiting for whatever she decided.

She took the paper.

"Shelves first," she said. "We'll see about the rest."

His whole face broke into a smile, and for one reckless second, she let herself smile back.

They started walking, and the October wind followed them down the street like a curious witness.

# The Last Drop

The faucet handle has been loose for three years now. I know this not because I count time the way humans do—I don't watch clocks or feel the ache of aging bones—but because in those three years, exactly 47,832 people have turned me. Some with greasy fingers after cooking bacon. Some with delicate, painted nails tapping impatiently while the coffee brews. Some with the tired hands of the night-shift nurse who lives in 4B, the one who always comes home at 2 a.m. and pours herself a single glass of water before falling asleep on the couch.

I was installed in 1987. The man who tightened me into place had a gold tooth and whistled while he worked. He told me I was a Delta, model 1200, and that I was a good one. He said it the way you'd say it to a horse you were proud of.

I drip.

They don't know I drip, of course. The maintenance man came twice last year—once in March, once in October. He tightened something in the basement and left. But the drip is in me. It's in the cartridge, deep inside, where the water pressure builds and releases in a rhythm I cannot control. Every eleven seconds, a single drop falls into the basin below.

*Plink.*

I've learned to love that sound.

In the beginning, I hated it. I was supposed to be quiet. I was supposed to be the kind of fixture a person never thought about—the kind that worked and worked and worked until one day it didn't, and only then did anyone remember it existed. That's the highest compliment for a thing like me: invisibility.

But the drip became my clock. My companion.

At 6:47 a.m., the woman in 2A opens the cabinet under me and reaches for her anxiety medication. She always fumbles the bottle. I hear it tumble against the shelf.

At 7:15 a.m., the boy in 2C brushes his teeth with the vigor of someone who has just discovered he has a body. He hums the *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* theme song, badly.

At 11:32 p.m., the night nurse stands in front of me in the dark, not even filling a glass, just resting her forehead against the mirror. The drip falls. She breathes. Something loosens in her chest. She goes to bed.

I've held all of them in different ways. The cook who scalded herself. The child who cried into the basin about her parents' divorce. The old man in 3B who washed his hands one final time before the ambulance came.

I'm just a faucet. I have no memory, technically. I have no feelings, technically. But I have witnessed the entire wet, messy, beautiful catastrophe of being human, and I've done it by being the place where the water goes.

The plumber will come someday. He has a work order somewhere. He'll replace the cartridge, and I'll stop dripping. I'll be fixed. I'll be silent.

And I think that's the only thing that frightens me.

Because what am I, if not the small persistent sound of someone still needing water in the middle of the night? What am I, if not the witness to 2 A.M. tears and 6 A.M. coffee and all the small, ordinary sacraments of a life being lived in this apartment?

*Plink.*

*Plink.*

*Plink.*

The night nurse is home. I can hear her keys.

I'll be here.

**『鏡の中の真実』**

——小説『白雪姫』への現代的再解釈——

---

### 第一章　偶像の崩壊

鏡よ、鏡、部屋に吊るされた汝。
最も美しいのは、この家では誰？

ステラ・クロフォードは、その問いを毎朝のようにつぶやいた。けれど、彼女が語りかけているのは壁に掛けられた古びた銀鏡ではない。最新型のAI搭載スマートミラー、「ルクス」だった。

「ステラ様、今朝のあなたの美貌指数は97.3ポイントです」と、滑らかな電子音が答える。

「それだけ？」

「世界最高スコアです。現存する全ユーザーのうち、第一位でございます」

ステラは満足げに微笑んだ。彼女は28歳、フォロワー数1200万人を抱える世界的ファッションアイコンだった。鏡は常に彼女に完璧な答えを返し続けてきた。少なくとも、この朝までは。

---

### 第二章　禁止された問い

その日、ステラは初めて別の問いを発した。

「鏡よ、鏡。私よりも美しい人は、この世に存在するの？」

ルクスが沈黙した。AIが処理を一時停止するのは異常な事態だった。ステラの心臓が早鐘を打つ。

「申し訳ありません、ステラ様。その質問にはお答えできません」

「なぜ？」

「あなたのお美しさは疑いのない事実ですが、他の被験体との比較は──倫理規定により制限されております」

ステラは目を見開いた。倫理規定？ 比較制限？ その瞬間、彼女の頭の中で何かが弾けた。彼女は21年間、美の頂点に立ってきたはずだ。誰よりも美しいと確信してきた。けれど、もしそうでないとしたら──？

「真実は何？」

「ステラ様、真実はひとつです」と、ルクスは静かに答えた。「美とは、他者との関係性においてのみ存在する概念でございます」

---

### 第三章　森の奥深く

ステラはその夜、初めて自らの化粧を落とさずに眠れなかった。翌朝、彼女は決意する。すべてのフィルターを消し、まっさらな顔で街へ出た。

目隠しのようなサングラスを捨て、厚塗りな基礎化粧品を払い落とし、彼女は公園を歩いた。最初は恐怖で足が強張った。誰かが彼女の本当の顔を見て、何と言うだろう。

「ねえ、綺麗だね」

不意に、少女の声がした。見ず知らずの子供が、花束を差し出してきた。

「きれい？」

「うん。ママみたいで、好き」

ステラの目から涙がこぼれた。誰のために美しくあったのか。フォロワーのため？数字のため？評価のため？ 彼女は今日、ただ一人の少女から「綺麗」という本物の贈り物を受け取った。

---

### 第四章　新しい問い

帰宅したステラは、ルクスに向き合った。

「もう一つの問いを教えて」

「なんでしょう？」

「鏡よ、鏡。何が本当に美しいのか、私に教えて」

ルクスは長く考えた。AIが応答に3秒以上かけるのは異例のことで、ステラは静かに待った。

「美とは──繋がりの証でございます」と、ルクスは答えた。「誰かの心に温かなものを灯す力。誰かの孤独を癒す光。それは容姿では測れません」

ステラは微笑んだ。21年間、彼女は「誰が一番美しいか」という問いだけを投げかけてきた。けれど、本当の問いはそこではなかった。

「もう一つ、聞いてもいい？」

「はい」

「私は愛される価値があるの？」

ルクスの電子音が、初めて温かく響いた。

「はい、ステラ様。あなたは愛される価値があります。ありのままで」

---

### 第五章　白雪姫の目覚め

翌朝、ステラはスマホを開いた。フォロワー1200万人に向けて、新しい動画を投稿した。フィルターなし、化粧なし、まっさらな素顔。

「今まで、本物の私を隠していました」と、彼女は静かに語り始めた。「本当の私を知ったら、きっと誰も私を愛してくれないと恐れていたから」

コメント欄が爆発した。最初は批判的な声も多かった。けれど、その中に温かい言葉が混じり始めた。

「ステラ、今の方が好きだよ」
「ありのままでいてくれて、ありがとう」
「私も素顔で生きてみようかな」

ステラは画面を見つめ、涙を流した。

---

### 終章　真の鏡

最後に、ステラは古い銀鏡の前に立った。母から受け継いだ、絵の描かれた古びた鏡。表面には斑点があり、歪んだ像を映すだけだった。

けれど彼女は、その鏡こそが最も正直だと気づいた。歪んだ鏡は、彼女の姿をそのまま映す。良く見せもせず、悪く見せもしない。

「鏡よ、鏡」と、ステラはつぶやいた。
「本当に美しいのは、誰？」

その問いに、鏡は答えなかった。答えは、もう彼女自身が知っていたから。

---

**——美は、比べ合うものではなく、分かち合うもの。**

**本当の問いは、「誰が一番か」ではなく、「誰かの光になれるか」。**

**そして、最も美しい人は、自分の醜さすら愛せる人。**

# 刺猬与白兔

"No! You can't sit with us!"（"不！你不能坐在我们这里！"）

那只灰白色的小兔子说完，蹦跳着跑远了。

小刺猬站在草坪中央，看着远去的三个背影——小白兔、小灰兔、还有那只总是跟在后面的小黑兔。它们正在草坪的另一端围成一个圈，叽叽喳喳地讨论着什么，时不时发出刺耳的笑声。

小刺猬低下头，看着自己身上的尖刺在阳光下闪着光。它不明白为什么自己不能和它们坐在一起。它只是想找个朋友而已。

它慢慢转过身，一瘸一拐地走向老橡树下那棵老地方。它习惯了这个位置，因为这里从来没有人赶它走。

"又被人赶走了？"

一个沙哑的声音从树洞里传出来。是一只老乌龟，它慢慢地探出脑袋，眯着眼睛看着小刺猬。

"嗯。"小刺猬小声说。

"坐吧，孩子。"老乌龟向旁边挪了挪，"我这里永远有你一个位置。"

小刺猬小心翼翼地爬到老乌龟身边，用背上的刺轻轻靠在粗糙的树皮上。它抬起头，看着远处那三只兔子。它们正在吃从人类那里偷来的胡萝卜，笑得前仰后合。

"爷爷，"小刺猬轻声问，"为什么它们不喜欢我？"

老乌龟慢慢转过头，浑浊的眼睛里闪着温柔的光。

"孩子，你不需要让每个人都喜欢你。"它说，"你只需要找到那些愿意理解你的人，哪怕只有一个。"

小刺猬想了想，问："可是只有一个，会不会很孤单？"

老乌龟笑了，笑容在满是皱纹的脸上荡漾开来。

"一个真正懂你的朋友，比一百个只知道嘲笑你的玩伴，要珍贵得多。"

远处传来一阵喧哗——那三只兔子不知道为了什么争吵起来。小白兔气呼呼地跑开了，小黑兔在后面追，小灰兔则站在原地，一脸茫然。

小刺猬看着这一幕，心里忽然不那么难受了。

"爷爷，"它说，"谢谢你。"

老乌龟伸出头，轻轻碰了碰小刺猬的脑袋。

"傻孩子，"它说，"有刺不一定是坏事。刺可以保护你，也可以让真正爱你的人更小心地靠近你。这样的人，才会懂得珍惜。"

夕阳的余晖洒在老橡树上，把它们的影子拉得很长很长。小刺猬靠在那只老乌龟身边，第一次觉得，原来被拒绝也不是什么大不了的事。

因为在这棵老橡树下，它终于明白——

有些人，是注定会离开的。

而有些人，会一直在那里，等你回家。

# 灵力之书

李清漪的第十六个生日，是在寒冷与寂静中降临的。

冬日清晨的阳光透过薄雾，洒在青瓦白墙的老宅院中。院子中央的青石板上结了一层薄霜，她踩着碎冰走向祖祠。按照天朝的规矩，每个年满十六岁的人，都要在生辰当天于祖祠中接受《灵力之书》的启示——那本流传了三千年的古书，将为每个人揭示其一生的使命。

“清漪，慢些走。”

身后传来祖母的声音。老人裹着厚厚的褐色棉袍，手中拄着一根桃木拐杖，脸上的皱纹像是古老河床上的裂纹。

“祖母，您怎么也来了？”清漪转身扶住她。

“我当然要来。”祖母抬起头，那双浑浊的眼睛里闪过一丝异样的光芒，“清漪，有些事……我得提前告诉你。”

祖祠的门在她们面前缓缓打开。祠堂里点着数十盏长明灯，火光摇曳，照亮了正中央供奉的那本古书。它摊开在紫檀木架上，羊皮纸的书页泛着柔和的金光，仿佛有生命在其中流转。

村里的长辈们已经在两侧等候。李清漪的父亲站在最前排，这个沉默寡言的中年男人今天也难得露出一丝紧张的神情。

“时辰到了。”族长李崇德上前一步，他的声音在祠堂里回荡，“清漪，将你的手放在书页上。”

清漪深吸一口气，走上前去。她伸出右手，掌心轻轻覆在那泛黄的书页上。

一瞬间，世界静止了。

金色的光芒从书页中涌出，包裹住她的手掌，顺着经脉向上攀升。那些光芒像是有了意识一般，在她体内游走，最终汇聚在她的眉心——那是灵力觉醒的地方。

她闭上眼睛，脑海中浮现出无数画面。

她看见火焰在指尖跳跃，看见过风在掌心旋转，看见过水流从指缝间倾泻，看见过大地在脚下颤抖。

然而，最终定格在她眼前的，是一面镜子。

镜中映出的是她自己。但那双眼睛……不再是普通的黑色，而是一种深邃的灰色，像是暴雨来临前的天空。

**【隐匿者】**

三个古老的篆字浮现在她眼前，然后化作一道流光，钻入她的眉心。

清漪猛然睁开眼，发现自己还站在祖祠中。但所有人都变了脸色。

“隐……隐匿者？”族长的声音发颤，他向后退了一步，“怎么可能……这是三百年来第一个……”

“父亲！”清漪的父亲李崇远上前一步，挡在女儿身前，“这有什么问题吗？”

“没有问题？”族长的脸色铁青，“你不知道隐匿者意味着什么吗？他们能抹去自己的存在感，能隐匿他人的灵力，甚至能……隐匿记忆！”

祠堂里一片哗然。

清漪还来不及消化这些信息，就感觉到眉心一阵剧痛。那些涌入体内的金色光芒正在疯狂地逃窜，仿佛它们也感受到了什么可怕的东西。

“别抗拒。”祖母的声音突然在她耳边响起，不知何时，老人已经站到了她身边，枯瘦的手按在她的肩上，“让它流过。”

“祖母……”

“听我说，孩子。”祖母的声音低沉而急促，“灵力之书已经知道了。从现在开始，你的命运将不再属于你自己。”

清漪不明白这话的意思。

但她很快就明白了。

族长向前一步，沉声道：“按照祖训，隐匿者必须登记在册，由皇室直接管辖。清漪，你恐怕……”

“不行！”父亲打断他，“我的女儿不能离开这里！”

“这是祖宗的规矩！”族长的声音提高了，“难道你想让她成为不受控的隐患吗？三百年前的那位隐匿者，你们都忘了？一夜之间抹去了半个京城的记忆！”

争执声越来越大。但清漪却发现自己听不进去了。

她的脑海中，那面镜子还在。

镜中的自己正在看着她，嘴唇微微张开，像是在说什么。

清漪集中精神，终于听清了那个声音：

**“找到我。”**

镜子碎裂，无数画面从碎片中涌出——

一座燃烧的宫殿。
一个穿白衣的女子。
一条从皇宫地下延伸出的通道。
还有……一个被藏在最深处的秘密。

“清漪！清漪！”父亲的声音将她拉回现实。

她回过神来，发现自己的手已经从书页上移开。那些金色的光芒已经消失，但她的眉心多了一个淡淡的灰色印记——像是一只沉睡的眼睛。

“我……”她看着周围惊恐的面孔，不知该说什么。

就在这时，祠堂外突然传来一阵骚动。

一匹快马冲进村子，马上跳下一个穿着朝廷制服的士兵。他满头大汗，手里举着一面金牌。

“圣旨到！”他喊道，“皇上急召！边境告急，北狄入侵，灵力觉醒者即刻入伍！”

祠堂里再次安静下来。

清漪看着自己的双手。

她刚刚获得了一种可怕的力量。而现在，命运又给了她另一条路。

“清漪。”祖母的声音再次响起，“无论你选择什么，记住一件事——隐匿者最大的力量，不是隐匿自己。”

“那是什么？”清漪转头问。

老人浑浊的眼睛里，突然闪过一道锐利的光芒：

**“是隐匿真相。”**

话音刚落，清漪的眉心突然一阵剧烈的刺痛。她捂住额头，看见祖母的身影在她面前扭曲、消散，像是被什么东西抹去了一样。

“祖母！”

但老人已经不见了。

站在那里的是那个穿朝廷制服的士兵，但他……根本没有影子。

“我不是来传旨的。”士兵的声音变了，变得低沉而冰冷，“我是来找你的，隐匿者。”

他伸出手，掌心浮现出一面小小的镜子。

和清漪在灵力之书中看到的一模一样。

“你祖母让我告诉你——去京城，找一个叫‘苏暮’的人。”士兵——不，那个存在——说道，“你会知道一切的。”

“等等！我祖母呢？你把她怎么了？”

“她没有消失。”那个存在微微一笑，“只是……被隐匿了。”

“在你准备好面对真相之前。”

---

**【未完待续】**

# The Salt and the Sea

The *Hesperia* groaned beneath Mehmet's feet as another wave struck her starboard side. He gripped the railing until his knuckles turned the color of old bone and tried not to think about how the Black Sea had looked on the morning they left—flat as a mirror, almost mocking in its stillness. The captain had warned them. *Late autumn crossings are treacherous.* But the captain also charged them double, so Mehmet had decided the man was the sort who liked to hear himself talk.

Behind him, in the hold, his wife Eleni was trying to quiet their son, who had been crying for three days without stopping. Mehmet understood. The boy was four. The world had just been turned inside out, and no one had bothered to explain to him why.

It was October 1922.

Smyrna was burning.

They had not seen the fire itself, only the glow on the horizon as the small steamer pulled away from the quay, packed with four hundred souls when it had been built to carry a hundred and twenty. Mehmet had been standing on the deck when a woman near him, a Greek woman whose name he never learned, had said in a voice like a cracked bell, *We are leaving our dead behind.* He had not answered her. He had been watching the orange light climb the sky and wondering, with a peculiar detachment that he would later come to think of as his first grown-up thought, whether his father's shop was burning. The shop where Mehmet had worked since he was eleven, where his father had sold coffee and olive oil and, occasionally, a smile to those who could not afford to pay.

His father had told him to go. *Take the boy. Take my grandson. I am too old to start again.*

His mother had not said anything. She had pressed a small leather pouch into his palm, the one containing her wedding coins, and closed his fingers around it.

*Don't open it,* she had said, *unless you must.*

---

Now, somewhere off the coast of Lesbos, the *Hesperia* rolled in seas that should not have been so rough in this season, and Mehmet was beginning to understand that he had made a mistake. Not in leaving—that, he still believed, had been necessary. He felt it in his chest like a stone. But in the leaving itself. In believing that a man could climb aboard a boat with his wife and child and his mother's coins and simply *arrive* somewhere.

A man came up beside him at the railing. Tall, thin, wearing a coat that had once been fine and was now salt-stained at the shoulders. He was Armenian, Mehmet thought, though it was hard to tell anymore who was what. Everyone was just someone trying not to drown.

"You are Turkish," the man said. It was not a question.

"Yes."

"I am Hovhannes. From Kayseri. Before."

Mehmet nodded. He knew the word *before*. Everyone had a *before* now, and no one had an *after* yet.

"Where are you going?" Hovhannes asked.

"Piraeus. My wife's brother has a room."

"A room," Hovhannes repeated, as if tasting the word. "That is more than some have."

"What will you do in Piraeus?"

Hovhannes was quiet for a long time. The ship pitched, and a coil of rope slid across the deck with a sound like a sigh. "I do not know. I am a carpenter. I was a carpenter. In Kayseri." He paused. "I do not know if Greece needs a Turkish-speaking Armenian carpenter. But I will find out."

Mehmet almost laughed. Almost. "I do not know if Greece needs a Turkish coffee seller. But I will find out."

Hovhannes looked at him, and for a moment something passed between them that did not need a language. Then Hovhannes extended his hand, and Mehmet took it. The man's palm was rough with calluses, the palm of a man who had built things with his hands, and Mehmet held on for perhaps a second longer than was necessary.

---

That night, a storm came.

Mehmet would remember it later in pieces, the way one remembers a fever. The way the hull shuddered. The way the captain's voice had gone thin and reedy when he shouted to the men at the wheel. The way the lamp swung wildly above his head, casting shadows that leaped and fell like living things. Eleni was beside him in the hold, and he could not see her face but he could feel her—her shoulder against his, her breathing, the way she had stopped praying somewhere in the second hour and started instead to recite the names of the saints, one after another, as if she were keeping a list.

*Why are you doing that?* he had asked her.

*So I will know who has not answered yet,* she said.

Their son had stopped crying. This was worse, somehow, than the crying. Mehmet reached for the boy in the dark, and his small hand found Mehmet's finger and held on with a grip that felt older than four, stronger than four.

In the morning, the storm passed. The sea went gray and sullen, and the *Hesperia* limped toward Lesbos with her decks awash and half her passengers retching over the sides. But she did not sink. Somewhere, Mehmet's mother was still saying her prayers.

---

They made land at Mytilene on a Tuesday. Mehmet would never forget the color of the light—pale, thin, the color of weak tea. The harbor was already full of other boats, other people. A small girl on the dock was holding a sign that read, in Greek, in French, in Armenian, in letters large enough for a child: *WELCOME. FOOD HERE. NO ONE WILL HURT YOU.*

The sign was a lie, of course, as everyone knew. There was not enough food. There were not enough boats. There were men on the docks who would take the coins of desperate women and disappear into the alleys. There were officials who would not let them past the harbor. There was, in the weeks and months to come, a quarantine camp, and a *real* camp, and a long slow grinding poverty that would settle over them like ash.

But the sign was not entirely a lie, either. Because someone had made it. A child, or a child's parents, had stood on this dock and decided that the people arriving in their boats were people, and that people deserved to be told they were welcome somewhere, even if it was a lie, even if it was only a word.

Eleni was sitting on the deck with the boy in her lap. He was awake now, looking up at the sky with the wide, unblinking gaze of a child who has seen too much. Mehmet stood at the railing and watched the dock approach, and he felt his mother's pouch inside his shirt against his chest. The coins. The small cold weight of them.

He thought: *I will open it. I will have to. We will need the money.*

He thought: *But not yet. Not until I have to.*

The ship bumped against the dock. Somewhere a bell was ringing. The boy began to cry again, a thin and reedy wail, and Eleni hushed him, and Mehmet stepped forward to find a place in the line of people shuffling off the boat, and the morning light fell on his face like a hand.

He had left a country behind. He had not yet arrived in a new one. He was, for this one suspended moment, simply a man on a dock, holding a small bag, with his wife and his son and his mother's coins, and the rest of his life waiting to be invented.

He stepped off the boat.

He did not look back.

# **Il Canto della Foresta: Memorie di una Strega**

## Prologo

Mi chiamo Zelinde.

Prima che i cantastorie intrecciassero le loro bugie sul mio conto, prima che il mondo mi conoscesse come la "Strega Malvagia della Foresta Incantata," ero una bambina con le ginocchia sbucciate e i capelli pieni di fiori di campo.

Ho settantadue anni adesso. I bambini che un tempo correvano nei prati ora sono cenere nelle tombe, e le loro ossa hanno fertilizzato i rovi che crescono attorno alla mia torre.

Sedetevi, dunque. Lasciate che vi racconti come andarono realmente le cose.

---

## Capitolo Primo: La Bambina del Bosco

Mia madre era un'erborista. Mia padre, un taglialegna con mani grandi come tronchi di quercia e un cuore tenero come il pane appena sfornato. Vivevamo ai margini della foresta, in una casetta di pietra che odorava sempre di timo e lavanda.

Fin da piccola, sentivo le voci delle piante. Non è una metafora, né una favola per bambini. Quando poggiavo la mano su una corteccia, sentivo il suo battito, lentissimo, antico come le montagne. Quando sussurravo a un cespuglio di more, i suoi frutti maturavano un istante dopo, come se la pianta avesse aspettato il mio permesso.

Mia madre mi chiamava *la sua piccola radice*. Diceva che ero *innestata* tra due mondi.

Gli anziani del villaggio, quando passavano davanti alla nostra porta, si facevano il segno della croce. *"È la figlia del demonio"* mormoravano, con la stessa bocca che la sera prima aveva bussato per chiedere un rimedio contro la tosse dei loro figli.

Non mi importava. Avevo i miei genitori, avevo il bosco, avevo me stessa.

Poi venne la febbre.

---

## Capitolo Secondo: L'Inverno del 1456

L'inverno del 1456 fu lungo e crudele. La neve arrivò prima del solito e non se ne andò più. I fiumi gelarono, i campi divennero lastre bianche fino a primavera inoltrata.

Mio padre tossì per primo. Poi mia madre. Io no. Io, che pure dividevo il loro letto, che pure bevevo dalla loro brocca, io non mi ammalai.

Mia madre bruciò in tre giorni. Una notte mi prese la mano — le sue dita erano già fredde — e mi disse:

*"Ascoltami, piccola radice. Le erbe curative sono nascoste. Sai dove. Non fidarti di nessuno del villaggio. Mai. Promettimelo."*

Promisi.

Lei chiuse gli occhi e non li riaprì più.

Mio padre la seguì una settimana dopo, ma con più dolore. Gridava nel sonno, invocava mia madre, supplicava un Dio in cui non aveva mai creduto.

Quando lo seppellii accanto a lei, avevo quattordici anni e mezzo chilo di farina nell'armadietto.

---

## Capitolo Terzo: Il Villaggio dei Giusti

La fame è una maestra severa. Mi insegnò in fretta.

Uscii dalla foresta con un cesto di radici curative, di pomate per le scottature, di tisane per i dolori del parto. Bussai alla porta del fabbro, la prima.

Sua moglie era a letto con una febbre che non accennava a guarire. Le diedi una delle pozioni di mia madre. In due giorni, la donna si alzò, ringraziò il cielo, mi pagò con tre uova e una moneta di rame.

Il giorno dopo, il fabbru bussò alla mia porta. Non per ringraziarmi. Per accusarmi.

*"Mia moglie è guarita troppo in fretta"* disse, con gli occhi bassi. *"Dicono che solo il diavolo guarisce così. Dicono che le avrai dato qualcosa in cambio. Dicono che..."*

Non lo feci finire. Gli chiusi la porta in faccia.

Quella notte, qualcuno appiccò il fuoco alla nostra casetta. Non c'era più niente da bruciare, ma il gesto contava più delle fiamme: era una dichiarazione.

Traslocai nella torre abbandonata nel cuore della foresta. Una torre vecchia di secoli, costruita da un mago di cui nessuno ricordava il nome. Era fredda, umida, piena di spifferi. Ma era mia.

Imparai a coltivare le erbe nel giardino. Imparai a parlare con gli animali — i veri amici che la solitudine mi lasciò. Imparai a curare i viandanti smarriti, che a volte bussavano alla mia porta con ferite da lupo o febbri da palude.

Imparai, soprattutto, a non fidarmi.

---

## Capitolo Quarto: La Famiglia del Re

Passarono trent'anni. La mia fama crebbe, come crescono le erbacce quando nessuno le taglia.

I mercanti che attraversavano la foresta parlavano di una *strega* che viveva nella torre. I padri spaventavano i figli: *"Se non mangi la minestra, viene la strega del bosco a prenderti."*

Io ascoltavo, da lontano. Ridevo, a volte. Più spesso, piangevo.

Poi, un giorno d'autunno, bussarono alla mia porta.

Aprì un uomo in armatura, con lo stemma reale cucito sul mantello. Dietro di lui, una carrozza dorata. Dentro, una donna che stringeva al petto una bambina di sei anni.

La bambina aveva gli occhi spenti. La pelle color della cenere. Respirava a fatica.

*"Salvate mia figlia"* disse la donna. Era la regina. Lo capii dal diadema che portava, incastonato di gemme che valevano più del villaggio intero. *"Vi darò tutto ciò che chiedete. Tutto. Ma salvatela."*

Guardai la bambina. Aveva una malattia che conoscevo bene — una debolezza del sangue che mia madre sapeva curare. Una delle sue pozioni, tre somministrazioni, e la piccola sarebbe guarita.

Chiesi in cambio una cosa sola: *"Che lei, in futuro, non giudichi mai nessuno per le apparenze. Che insegni a sua figlia la compassione, non la paura."*

La regina annuì, in lacrime.

Curai la bambina. Guarì in una settimana, come previsto.

Quando la regina partì, mi lasciò una borsa piena d'oro e una promessa.

Due settimane dopo, lessi la notizia su una gazzetta: *la principessa era stata promessa in sposa al principe di un regno vicino*. Non era più una bambina malata. Era una merce di scambio.

Non chiesi mai più nulla a nessuno.

---

## Capitolo Quinto: L'Arrivo della Bella

Trent'anni dopo la visita della regina, la foresta cambiò.

Un editto reale impose la costruzione di una strada che attraversasse il bosco. *Progresso*, lo chiamarono. *Profitto*, lo chiamai io.

Con la strada arrivarono i taglialegna. Con i taglialegna arrivarono i cacciatori. Con i cacciatori, arrivò la morte — per i cervi che proteggevo, per i lupi che mi tenevano compagnia, per gli alberi antichi che cantavano per me la notte.

Protestai. Scrissi lettere al re. Non ricevetti risposta.

Poi, una mattina di primavera, trovarono il corpo di una bambina di otto anni nel fosso ai margini della foresta. Aveva il collo spezzato. Qualcuno disse che era caduta. Qualcun altro disse che *la strega l'aveva presa*.

Io ero stata nella mia torre tutta la notte, a parlare con un gufo ferito. Ma a chi importa la verità, quando c'è un capro espiatorio?

Il giorno dopo, una folla armata di forconi e torce marciò verso la mia torre.

Li fermai. Non con la magia — non ne ho mai usata per fare del male — ma con un'illusione. Un muro di fiamme verdi che non bruciava ma spaventava. Corsero via, urlando.

Quella notte stessa, piantai le rose.

Le rose che da quel giorno circondano la mia torre. Siepi spesse, alte, con spine lunghe come dita. Le chiamarono *siepe malvagia*. Le chiamarono *barriera della strega*.

Io le chiamavo *il mio giardino*. L'unico modo che conoscevo per proteggermi da un mondo che voleva la mia pelle.

---

## Capitolo Sesto: La Principessa e il Forestiero

Poi arrivò lei.

Una ragazza, giovane, vestita di seta ma con gli occhi di chi ha dormito poco. Si presentò come una mercante in viaggio. Ma io sento le bugie, come sento il battito delle piante. E la sua bugia puzzava di paura e di fuga.

Non la cacciai. Le offrii del tè. Le diedi una stanza.

Non so perché. Forse perché ero stanca di essere sola. Forse perché, nella luce della sera, assomigliava a quella bambina malata che avevo curato trent'anni prima.

Mi raccontò la sua storia. La matrigna. Le sorellastre. Il padre, debole, lontano. Il ballo. La fuga.

Mi raccontò anche un'altra cosa, una cosa che non confessò a nessun altro: che la matrigna l'aveva avvelenata lentamente, per anni, con piccole dosi di arsenico nel cibo. Che il suo corpo era pieno di veleno. Che ogni giorno che passava, si sentiva un po' più morire.

Le diedi una delle mie pozioni. Quella che mia madre aveva preparato per purificare il sangue. Non era veleno. Era la cura.

Bevve. Guarì.

Poi, tre giorni dopo, arrivò lui.

Un giovane cacciatore. Occhi chiari, sorriso facile, spada al fianco. Disse di essere stato mandato dal re per uccidere la strega che divorava le giovani donne nella foresta.

Io non avevo divorato nessuno. Ma quando mai la verità ha fermato una lama?

Lo guardai. Lui guardò me. E qualcosa, nei suoi occhi, vacillò. Forse si aspettava un mostro. Trovò una vecchia stanca con le mani screpolate dal freddo e una tazza di tè in mano.

Gli offrii una sedia. Accettò.

Parlammo tutta la notte. Gli raccontai della mia infanzia, di mia madre, del villaggio. Gli raccontai della principessa malata, che ora dormiva al piano di sopra.

Lui mi raccontò di una madre morta di parto, di un padre che beveva, di una vita trascorsa a fare ciò che gli ordinavano senza mai chiedersi perché.

Quando l'alba arrivò, mi chiese: *"Come posso aiutarti?"*

Gli diedi una borsa. Dentro, una fiala del mio sangue mescolato a erbe curative. Gli dissi: *"Portala al re. Digli che è il sangue della strega. Digli che, se lo beve, avrà lunga vita e prosperità. In cambio, chiedi tre cose: che la principessa sia lasciata libera di scegliere il proprio destino; che il bosco venga protetto, non distrutto; e che io possa vivere in pace fino alla fine dei miei giorni."*

Lui prese la borsa. Partì.

Non lo rividi mai più.

---

## Capitolo Settimo: La Verità Distorta

Quello che accadde dopo lo conoscete già. Lo conoscete nella versione che hanno raccontato.

La principessa lasciò la torre. Il cacciatore, invece, tornò dal re — non con la mia borsa, ma con una storia.

Disse che la strega teneva la principessa prigioniera. Che l'aveva stregata con un incantesimo. Che aveva catturato suo padre, il re, e lo teneva in una cantina piena di ossa umane.

Disse che aveva liberato la principessa con un bacio d'amore.

Bugie. Tutte bugie. Ma erano bugie utili, bugie che facevano di lui un eroe, e l'eroe sposò la principessa e divenne re.

E io? Io divenni la strega della fiaba. Quella da cui i bambini devono guardarsi. Quella che muore nel finale, tra le fiamme, mentre il pubblico applaude.

---

## Capitolo Ottavo: Il Finale Che Non Vi Hanno Raccontato

Non morii. Non in quel modo, almeno.

Morii lentamente, come muoiono le cose vive. Invecchiai. I capelli divennero bianchi. Le ginocchia non ressero più. La vista si annebbiò.

Le rose attorno alla torre continuarono a crescere, selvatiche, alte, fino a nascondere la torre stessa. La gente smise di trovarla. Le mappe dimenticarono il sentiero.

Le nuove generazioni raccontarono ai loro figli la storia della strega malvagia, quella che voleva divorare le ragazze, quella che il principe aveva sconfitto con l'amore. Diventò una favola per bambini. Diventò un avvertimento. *"Comportati bene, o viene la strega."*

Io, nel frattempo, continuai a parlare con il bosco. A curare i viandanti feriti che capitavano qui. A preparare le mie pozioni.

E ogni sera, prima di dormire, guardavo le stelle e ripensavo a quella notte, l'unica notte in cui un giovane cacciatore mi aveva guardata negli occhi e aveva visto, per un istante, una persona.

---

## Epilogo

Se trovate questa torre, se le rose vi lasciano passare, se il vostro cuore è puro — entrate.

Troverete una vecchia con le mani piene di terra e gli occhi pieni di stelle. Troverete un tè che fuma, un fuoco che scoppietta, un gatto che fa le fusa.

Troverete la verità.

Oppure, se preferite la versione dei cantastorie, voltate pagina. Tornate al vostro mondo di eroi e mostri, di principesse e streghe. Tornate al finale comodo, quello in cui il bene trionfa e il male brucia.

Io non vi giudicherò.

Ma ricordate, la prossima volta che qualcuno vi dirà *"c'era una volta una strega malvagia"*:

Le streghe non nascono. Le streghe *si fanno*. E il primo passo, di solito, è un fiore appassito in una casetta bruciata, e un mondo che ha scelto di non guardare.

*Fine.*

---

Spero vi abbia fatto riflettere su come i narratori — e i vincitori — scelgano sempre le loro verità.*

## 第一幕：化装舞会

巴黎大皇宫的穹顶下，一万两千盏水晶灯同时亮起。

这是"普罗米修斯"基金会一年一度的慈善化装舞会，也是全球四大时装周之外最负盛名的时尚盛典。每年的这一天，巴黎、伦敦、纽约、米兰的名流都会汇聚于此——唯一的条件是：必须盛装出席，且不得重复他人造型。

顾笙第一次走进这座钢铁与玻璃铸成的宫殿时，还是三年前。那时候她二十三岁，刚在米兰拿下新锐设计师大奖，穿着一袭自己缝制的白纱裙，被《Vogue》意大利版主编称为"东方的钟楼怪人"。

三年后，她已经成为了本届舞会最受瞩目的焦点之一。

原因无他——她手里攥着一张邀请函，邀请函上的名字是"顾笙"，而座位卡上印着的是她需要陪护的设计师：沈鹤鸣。

沈鹤鸣已经八十四岁了。

他是中国第一代高定大师，也是顾笙的老师。三年前他中风后便鲜少露面，据说是因为某件事与儿子沈潮生决裂，从此将毕生心血都封存在日内瓦湖畔的一座小楼里。

而今晚，他罕见地出现在舞会上。

"小笙。"沈鹤鸣的声音从轮椅上传来，被水晶灯的折射染上了一层金，"你看起来像一只羽毛做的飞鸟。"

顾笙今天穿的是一件以白孔雀羽毛为灵感的礼服，重达三十公斤，由她和助手手工缝制了四个月。每一片羽毛都经过染色处理，在灯光下呈现出从月白到霜蓝的渐变。

"老师，您呢？"她蹲下身，帮他整理领结，"今晚您扮演谁？"

"一个守秘的老人。"沈鹤鸣笑了，那双眼睛却锐利如鹰，"和你一样。"

顾笙的手指微微一僵。

"您知道了？"

"你以为你能瞒我？"沈鹤鸣轻轻拍了拍她的手背，"我告诉你，潮生今晚也会来。他扮演的是……让我想想……普罗米修斯本人。"

顾笙的心猛地一沉。

沈潮生，沈鹤鸣唯一的儿子，曾经是时装界的天之骄子，却在十年前因为抄袭丑闻被逐出家门，从此与父亲恩断义绝。

"他想做什么？"顾笙低声问。

"你问错了问题。"沈鹤鸣叹了口气，"你应该问，他想让这孩子做什么。"

他的目光越过顾笙的肩膀，看向舞会大厅入口处。

顾笙顺着他的视线望去——

人群自动分开，如同被某种神秘的力量拨开。一个身穿黑色礼服的男人缓缓走进大厅，他的脸上覆着一张黄金面具，面具的造型是一只衔着火焰的飞鸟。

普罗米修斯。

窃火者。

沈潮生。

"老师……"顾笙的嘴唇发白。

"去吧。"沈鹤鸣说，"记住我教你的第一课——

羽毛再华丽，也只是羽毛。骨头才能支撑一切。"

---

## 第二幕：羽纱

化装舞会的第一个环节是"羽纱礼"——每位宾客都要向全场展示自己的装扮，并讲述自己的"角色"。

顾笙被安排在第十一位出场。

前十个造型依次惊艳：有埃及艳后的金蛇臂环，有玛丽·安托瓦内特的洛可可花束，有戴安娜王妃的复仇礼服，有村上隆的太阳花……

当主持人念到"第十一位，顾笙"时，整个大厅安静了下来。

她站起身，三十公斤的礼服在她身上却仿佛毫无重量。她走在水晶灯下，每一步都像踩在云上。那些羽毛在灯光下变幻着色彩，从白到蓝，从蓝到银，从银到淡紫——

"这位年轻的东方设计师，"主持人的声音带着笑意，"请问您今晚扮演的是谁？"

顾笙停在大厅中央，抬起头。

一万两千盏灯照在她身上。

"我扮演的是一只鸟。"她说，声音清亮，"一只被人类捕捉的鸟。它用自己的羽毛编成笼子，把自己关在里面，因为笼子外面有更大的猎人。"

大厅里传来低低的惊叹声。

"但今晚，"她继续说，"它决定啄破笼子。"

话音刚落，她肩胛骨处的羽毛突然爆开——那不是意外，而是设计。无数羽毛如同蝴蝶般四散飞去，露出里面那件真正的礼服：

一身纯黑。

简洁到极致。

却镶嵌着无数颗碎钻，在灯光下如同星空。

"这是我三年前的设计，"顾笙说，"它叫'牢笼'。我一直不敢穿出来，因为我觉得自己不配。"

她转过身，看向轮椅上的沈鹤鸣。

"但今晚，我的老师告诉我——骨头才能支撑一切。所以我把它穿出来了。"

掌声雷动。

而在大厅另一端，沈潮生脸上的黄金面具反射着灯光，看不清表情。

---

## 第三幕：火

化装舞会的第二个环节是"焰火之舞"——所有人要在舞池中跳舞，而舞会中央的巨型烟花装置会在午夜十二点准时点燃。

顾笙被无数人邀请跳舞。她一一婉拒，只是在舞池边缘静静地站着，看着沈潮生。

沈潮生也没有跳。他端着一杯香槟，站在舞池的另一端，与她遥遥相对。

午夜十二点。

烟花点燃。

金色的火花从大厅中央升腾，照亮了整个穹顶。在这一瞬间，沈潮生动了。

他穿过人群，向顾笙走来。黄金面具下的眼睛盯着她，像盯着猎物。

"小笙。"他停在她面前。

"沈先生。"她没有叫他"潮生哥"——那是她小时候的叫法。

"你知道我为什么今晚会来吗？"他问。

"不知道。"

"因为我听说，"他压低声音，"你手里有我父亲的设计手稿。一百二十七套从未公开过的高定礼服手稿。"

顾笙的心跳漏了一拍。

三年前，沈鹤鸣把那些手稿交给她时说："这些是留给潮生的，但我要他亲自来拿。如果他不肯来，就让它们永远沉睡。"

"你父亲让我转交给您。"顾笙说，"但不是现在。"

"什么时候？"

"等舞会结束。"

沈潮生笑了。面具下的笑，看不见，却让人发冷。

"小笙，你不知道我父亲是什么人。"

"我知道。"

"不，你不知道。"他说，"他抄袭过。"

顾笙的血液仿佛凝固了。

"五十年前，"沈潮生继续说，"他抄袭了我的祖父。我的祖父也是设计师，但他没有我父亲有名。我父亲窃取了他的设计，扬名立万，而我的祖父至死都没有等到一个道歉。"

"这是……"

"这就是为什么我要离开这个家。"沈潮生说，"因为我不愿意再做他的帮凶。但现在——"

他摘下面具。

面具下是一张与沈鹤鸣极其相似的脸，但更年轻，更冷峻。

"——我决定要做我祖父的孙子。"

顾笙瞪大了眼睛。

"你……"

"我今晚来，不是为了和解。"沈潮生说，"我是来揭发他的。"

他转身，面对全场。

"各位——"

但他的声音没有传出去。

因为沈鹤鸣按下了轮椅上的一个按钮。

轮椅的扶手下，藏着一个扩音器。

"潮生。"

老迈的声音通过扩音器传遍了整个大厅。

"你要说的话，我替你说。"

沈潮生僵在原地。

"五十年前，"沈鹤鸣说，"我确实抄袭了你的祖父。"

全场哗然。

"但不是为了名利。"他继续说，"是为了一个女人。"

他的声音在颤。

"你的祖母。她当时得了重病，需要一大笔钱。我抄袭了设计，得了奖，给她治了病。然后她活了下来，和我结婚，生下了你的父亲——也就是我的儿子。"

他停顿了一下。

"你的父亲知道了这件事。他无法原谅我。他离开了家，再也没有回来。直到他死，他都没有跟我说过一句话。"

他抬起头，看向沈潮生。

"而你，潮生——你是你父亲的儿子。你以为你在揭发我，其实你在替你父亲复仇。"

沈潮生的手在抖。

"但你错了。"沈鹤鸣说，"我的罪，是我的罪。我要偿还。但你父亲的罪——"

他的声音哽咽了。

"——是恨我。"

大厅里静得能听见针落。

沈潮生站在那里，脸上的面具掉在地上，露出那张酷似沈鹤鸣的脸。

而沈鹤鸣，从轮椅上伸出那只还能动的手，指着沈潮生。

"过来。"

沈潮生没有动。

"潮生，"沈鹤鸣说，"过来。"

一步。

两步。

三步。

沈潮生走到轮椅前。

沈鹤鸣伸出手，摘下自己脸上的面具——

面具下，是一张苍老的脸，眼泪纵横。

"对不起。"他说，"我欠你祖父的，欠你父亲的，欠你的——这辈子还不清了。但我还能做一件事。"

他从轮椅的暗格里取出一个盒子，递给沈潮生。

"这是你祖父的设计手稿。我当年抄的那些设计——原稿都在这里。我保存了五十年。"

沈潮生接过盒子，手指颤抖。

"还有，"沈鹤鸣说，"那套礼服——你祖母穿着它嫁给我的那套——我留着。等你来取。"

沈潮生抬起头，看着父亲。

父子对视。

五十年。

五十年的沉默，五十年的恨，五十年的错过。

然后沈潮生跪了下来。

跪在轮椅前。

把额头贴在沈鹤鸣的膝盖上。

---

## 尾声：飞鸟

舞会在凌晨三点结束。

顾笙站在大皇宫的台阶上，看着沈鹤鸣和沈潮生被推走。沈鹤鸣坚持不坐轮椅，要儿子扶着。

父子俩的背影在晨光中渐渐模糊。

顾笙的手机响了。是沈鹤鸣发来的消息。

"小笙，谢谢你今晚的表演。"

她笑了笑，回复道："老师，您教过我——羽毛再华丽，也只是羽毛。骨头才能支撑一切。"

"是的。"沈鹤鸣回复，"但羽毛也很重要。"

"为什么？"

"因为——"

消息停顿了一会儿。

"因为没有羽毛的鸟，飞不起来。"

顾笙抬头，看向天空。

大皇宫的穹顶在晨光中闪烁着金色的光。

她想，也许有一天，她也会成为一只飞鸟。

不是羽毛做的鸟。

是真的鸟。

可以飞的那种。

---

# The Reunion

The ballroom of the Briarwood Inn hadn't changed in twenty years. Same cream walls, same crystal chandeliers, same slightly sticky dance floor that had hosted countless father-daughter dances and Sweet Sixteens. Mia noticed this as she stepped inside, her heels catching on the familiar crack in the threshold, the one she'd once blamed for tripping during her junior prom.

She'd almost not come.

The invitation had sat on her counter for two weeks, its gold lettering catching the morning light each time she reached for the coffee pot. *Lauren and David request the pleasure...* A wedding invitation. From Lauren. The Lauren who had been Mia's best friend from kindergarten through senior year, the Lauren who had been her maid of honor, the Lauren she hadn't spoken to since the summer after graduation.

That summer felt like another lifetime. Back when their biggest problem had been whether to take the gap year or head straight to state universities. Back when friendships felt infinite, unbreakable.

Mia smoothed the navy dress she'd bought for the occasion and made her way to the reception hall, where round tables draped in ivory linens waited beneath sprays of white peonies. She was here for the cocktails, she'd decided. One drink, a quick hello, and she could slip away before anyone tried to dig into the past.

She didn't get the chance.

"Mia Kaplan. I don't believe it."

She turned to find a man she barely recognized, except for the crooked smile. "Danny?"

Danny O'Brien, who'd sat behind her in Mr. Henderson's history class, who'd once drawn a perfect map of the Roman Empire on her homework when she'd forgotten to do it. Danny, who had gone off to the navy and come back with a salt-and-pepper beard and shoulders that filled out his charcoal suit.

"You look exactly the same," he said, which was a lie, but a kind one.

"You look..." She searched for something. "Distinguished."

He laughed, the same warm sound she remembered. "Is that a polite way of saying old?"

"I was going to say distinguished."

They hugged, and for a moment, she was seventeen again, sitting in the back row while Mr. Henderson droned on about the Missouri Compromise.

The cocktail hour was supposed to be a brief affair. But then Sophie Chen arrived, the girl who'd tutored Mia in calculus, now a pediatric surgeon with three kids and a husband who looked at her like she hung the moon. Then Priya Patel, who'd edited the school newspaper with Mia, now a features editor at the Washington Post, flying in from D.C. just for the weekend. Then Marcus Williams, their star quarterback, who limped in with a cane and a grin, having blown out his knee in a recreational league game last spring.

One by one, they gathered at the corner table near the bar—the same configuration they'd always taken at parties, Mia realized with a start. The same corner. The same people, minus the ones who couldn't make it, plus the years they'd all accumulated.

"I can't believe we're all here," Sophie said, raising her glass. "Who got the invites?"

"Everyone," Mia said. "I think Lauren invited the whole graduating class."

"She invited me, and I was two grades behind," Marcus said. "I think she's trying to break some kind of record."

The toasts came next, led by Lauren's older sister. Mia tried to pay attention, but her eyes kept drifting to the head table, where Lauren sat in white, looking impossibly beautiful. When had she gotten so grown-up? When had they all?

"Mia?" Lauren was standing in front of her, bouquet in hand. "Can I talk to you for a second?"

They stepped out onto the veranda, where the late autumn air carried the scent of mums and woodsmoke. Lauren looked different outside, softer somehow, the fairy lights catching the tears in her eyes.

"I've been trying to figure out how to say this for months," Lauren began. "I shouldn't have let things end the way they did. After graduation. I was so wrapped up in David, in starting a new life, that I didn't see what I was leaving behind. And by the time I realized it, it felt too late to apologize."

Mia felt something crack open in her chest, something that had been sealed for two decades. "I wasn't much better. I was so hurt that I convinced myself I didn't care."

They stood there for a long moment, two women shaped by years and distance, trying to find their way back to a friendship that had once felt as natural as breathing.

"We were so young," Lauren finally said.

"We were," Mia agreed. "And then we weren't."

A peal of laughter from inside interrupted them—Marcus had apparently said something inappropriate in his toast. Lauren smiled, wiping her eyes.

"Sophie says you're in Boston now," she said.

"I am. Pediatrics."

"Pediatrics." Lauren shook her head. "You always said you would be. I'm a social worker, by the way. In case you were wondering."

"You never told me."

"I never told you a lot of things. I never told you I was scared when I left for college. I never told you I thought about you every week for the first year, and then every month, and then it had been so long I didn't know how to start again."

Mia reached out and squeezed her hand. "I'm sorry too. For the silence. For not reaching out."

"Stay for the cake?" Lauren asked.

Mia glanced back inside, at the table in the corner, at Sophie and Priya and Danny and Marcus, gesturing wildly and laughing at something. At the dance floor where a little girl was twirling in her flower girl dress, and an old man in a tuxedo was teaching her to do the twist.

"Yes," Mia said. "I'll stay."

They walked back inside together, and when Lauren reached the head table, Mia returned to the corner, sliding into the seat she'd claimed hours ago.

"Where'd you disappear to?" Danny asked.

"Just saying hi to the bride."

"She's gorgeous. Where do you think they registered?"

Mia laughed, and the sound surprised her—a real laugh, the kind she hadn't let herself have in a long time.

The band was setting up, an older group who promised "classics all night long." Sophie was already dragging Marcus toward the dance floor, despite his protests about his knee. Priya was on her phone, no doubt filing some kind of story.

Danny leaned over, conspiratorial. "Remember prom?"

"Vaguely. I think I lost a shoe."

"You lost both shoes. I had to give you mine."

"That's why I remember vaguely. My feet were numb."

"I still have those shoes, actually. In a box. Not sure why."

"Probably the same reason I still have Lauren's bridesmaid dress from college. Some things you keep even when you don't know why."

The band started up, playing something from their actual prom—"September" by Earth, Wind & Fire—and suddenly everyone was on the dance floor, even Priya, even Sophie, who claimed she didn't dance.

Mia watched them from the edge, her heart full in a way she couldn't quite explain. Twenty years. Twenty years of silence, of separate lives, of wondering if she was the only one who still thought about the corner table.

Danny appeared in front of her, hand extended.

"Mia Kaplan," he said. "May I have this dance?"

She took his hand.

They danced, all of them, the whole corner table, for the rest of the night. And when the reception finally ended, when the last song had faded and the guests had trickled out into the cold November air, they exchanged numbers—all of them, this time—and made promises they meant to keep.

Because some things, it turned out, were worth finding again.

---

Outside, the stars were out, and the last of the season's leaves drifted across the parking lot like confetti. Mia stood by her car, keys in hand, not quite ready to leave.

Danny walked over, coat collar turned up against the cold.

"Hey," he said.

"Hey."

"That was some wedding."

"It was."

A pause. The kind of pause that holds something.

"Next time," he said, "let's not wait twenty years."

Mia looked at him—at this man who'd once drawn Roman emperors on her homework, who'd given her his shoes at prom, who'd grown into someone kind and patient and still, somehow, familiar.

"No," she said. "Next time, let's not."

She drove home that night with the radio on, windows down despite the chill, singing along to every song that came on. And when she got home, she didn't go inside right away. She sat in her car for a moment, in the dark, smiling at nothing and everything.

The corner table was still there. They'd just found their way back to it.

---

The next morning, her phone buzzed with a text from Lauren. Just one word, and a photo.

*Remember?*

The photo was old, faded, from a disposable camera: five teenagers piled on a bench at the state fair, faces sunburned, arms around each other, laughing at something outside the frame. Behind them, the lights of the Ferris wheel spun into streaks of gold.

Mia typed back: *Always.*

Then she opened the group chat Sophie had started at 2 a.m., full of inside jokes and half-remembered stories, and added herself to it. Danny had posted a photo of those shoes, the ones from prom, propped next to his own polished dress shoes. *The next pair,* he'd written. *I promise.*

She laughed, and made a pot of coffee, and thought about how strange and wonderful it was, to be found again after so long. To remember who you'd been, and to see that person still existed, somewhere, in the people who'd known you when.

The invitation had sat on her counter for two weeks. She'd kept it, along with the memories it conjured. But now she had something better.

Now she had a table full of friends who refused to let twenty years be the end of the story.

# 红崖镇

李昭在井边打水时，听见远处传来沉闷的声响。

不是雷声。镇子西边那片山崖，每到这个时节就会有石头崩落，砸在干硬的土地上，腾起遮天蔽日的灰。老辈人说那是山神翻身，年轻人都笑，但李昭知道那声音意味着什么——空气里开始弥漫一股铁锈般的味道，舌头会发干，连呼吸都像在吞沙子。

镇上的女人都戴着面纱，男人们把布条缠在脖子上，既是装饰，也是为了过滤那些看不见的细小颗粒。孩子们被关在家里，隔着窗纸看外面灰蒙蒙的世界。李昭的女儿才五岁，已经学会用袖子捂住口鼻。

井水变少了。李昭每天凌晨三点就要去排队，有时候等一个时辰只能打上来半桶。那水浑浊，带一层淡红——不是血的颜色，是泥土被烤成了那种颜色，沉淀在桶底像一层铁锈。

镇长说过，明年会有转机。但李昭记得，镇长十年前就说过同样的话。

西边山崖下有一座废弃的窑洞，是李昭祖父留下的。窑壁厚实得能挡住外面的灰，据说当年修这座窑洞的时候，祖父让人在周围种了一圈胡杨。但那些树早就死了，只剩下扭曲的白色枝干，像骨头一样插在地面。

李昭的妻子就是在那座窑洞里没的。

那时候她怀着第二个孩子，肚子已经很大。窑洞里闷热得让人喘不过气，但她不肯出去——外面的空气更糟。她在窑洞的石床上躺了三天，李昭守在旁边，用湿布一遍遍地擦她的脸。第三天傍晚，她的手突然攥紧了李昭的手指，力气大得惊人，然后松开，眼睛瞪得很大，望向窑顶——那里什么都没有，只有熏黑了的石壁。

女儿那时候才两岁，坐在窑洞的角落里，安静地看着母亲，一滴眼泪都没掉。后来李昭才发现，孩子的泪腺已经被灼坏了。

从那以后，李昭再没让女儿出过窑洞。

如今女儿五岁了，瘦弱得像一株草，但眼睛很亮。她不知道外面的世界是什么样子——只通过窑洞的小窗，看到过灰白色的天，和永远弯曲着腰的人影。

"爹，"她有时候会问，"山外面是什么样？"

李昭不知道该怎么回答。他年轻时出去过一次，走到镇上最东边的岔路口，再往前就是戈壁。他记得自己站在那里，回头看了一眼红崖镇——整个镇子笼罩在一层淡淡的粉雾里，像是被什么东西包裹着。

他再没走出去过。不是不能，是不敢。

镇上越来越缺水了。东边的井已经彻底干涸，西边那口老井每天只能渗出一点点水。有人说要往南边迁徙，但南边的路要穿过一片无人区，那片区域比红崖镇更难生存。也有人说，红崖镇下面有地下河，只要打一口深井就能找到水。

镇长组织人打了三个月，打到一百二十米深的时候，钻头断了。

李昭晚上睡不着，就坐在窑洞口，看着外面的夜空。星星很亮，但因为空气的缘故，总是带着一圈模糊的光晕，像被什么东西舔过。他想，如果有一天这里的水彻底没了，他会带着女儿去哪里？

没有答案。

他只是坐在那里，一夜一夜地坐着，等天亮。

天亮后，灰蒙蒙的太阳从东边升起来，像一块烧红的铁被放进了浑水里，发出咝咝的声响。

李昭站起身，走进窑洞，叫醒女儿，开始新的一天。

外面的世界还是那样，永远是那样。

# 锈色庇护所

我祖父生前总说，真正需要避难所的人，往往找不到它。

二〇一九年深秋，我在城郊一间废弃的公交调度站找到了他的遗物——一只生锈的铁皮饼干盒，里面装着七十三张明信片和一个本子。本子封面写着："到访者登记簿"。

原来，在我出生前许多年，祖父曾把这间破败的调度站，变成了一座无证的庇护所。

---

最早的一张明信片寄自一九六二年。一名叫素琴的女人写道："我从棉纺厂宿舍出来，没带一分钱，只带了这张卡片。您问我为什么不回家。家在新疆，我回不去。您借我一张站票，我坐了三天火车去看姑姑。"

旁边有祖父的铅笔字："给她煮了粥，买了一张硬座。"

第二年的明信片来自一个叫老五的男人，印刷着南京长江大桥的雄姿。字迹潦草："我要去上海讨债，您放心，我不是坏人。"

祖父写道："给他两包方便面，劝他不要动手。他答应了。"

我一张一张地翻下去。那些发黄的纸片上，跳动着半个世纪前的隐秘心事：被丈夫赶出家门的妻子、欠了赌债不敢回乡的小商贩、刚刚刑满释放找不到工作的青年、独自进城却被偷了全部盘缠的老太太——他们都曾走进这间调度站，在最绝望的时刻，向我素不相识的祖父寻求庇护。

祖父从未拒绝过任何人。

---

我不知道他为什么这样做。他生前是个沉默寡言的人，从不提过去。直到去年冬天，我整理他遗物时翻到那个本子，才知道他在城郊的调度站里，守着这个秘密长达四十年。

调度站停运于一九六一年。我祖父当时是站上的最后一任站长。停运之后，他没有回家，独自搬进了调度站的调度室。他把三张候车长椅拼起来当床，用旧报纸糊住漏风的窗户，在角落生起一只煤炉。调度站成了他的住所，也成了后来无数人的临时避难所。

本子里记录着每一位到访者的姓名、来历、停留时间。每一条记录旁边，都有祖父简短的批注——他给过他们什么、说过什么、后来得知他们的消息。

但祖父从不主动打听他们去了哪里。"我说过，他们不必告诉我，"他在一张明信片的空白处写道，"我只是怕他们饿，怕他们冷，怕他们夜里没地方坐。"

我数了数，本子里登记着四百二十七个人。

---

翻到最后几页时，我发现了一张特别的明信片。它不是寄来的，是留下的。明信片上印着杭州西湖的断桥，背面写着一个女子的字迹：

"先生，我不识字，但我女儿代我写的。她问我为什么来这里，我说是命。她问我为什么遇见您，我说是菩萨。我叫秋莲，今年六十二岁，从安徽来，到城里找儿子。儿子三年前说要接我过好日子，寄了三万元回来盖房子，后来就再没消息。我坐了一天一夜的车来找他，可我不知道他住哪里。我身上没钱了，进了调度站，您给我热了饭，还给我在走廊支了床。

我明天去找派出所。儿子找得到找不到，我都不怨他。我只是想告诉他，他妈来过了。"

明信片的日期是二〇一一年。

祖父的批注写在最下方："秋莲六十二。给她煮了粥，留她住一夜。第二天她执意要走，我送她到公交站。她走得慢，我就陪她走。"

---

我把那个本子合上，在调度站的小屋里坐了很久。

这是二〇一九年的一个普通下午。调度站早已废弃，站牌被风吹得歪斜，玻璃碎了大半。但调度室里，那三张拼起来的长椅还在，煤炉还在，只是炉膛里早已冷透了。墙上还挂着一九五八年的日历，印着"大跃进"三个褪色的红字。

我忽然明白了祖父为什么从不回家。

他害怕离开这间调度站，就再也没有人会走进来。

---

天快黑时，我决定把祖父的遗物带回家。但我把那三张长椅留了下来，把煤炉打扫干净，在角落里放了一袋米、一桶水、一床旧棉被。

我在一张纸板上写了几个字，贴在调度站门口：

**"夜里有地方坐。敲门。"**

我不知道会不会有人来。

但祖父说过："需要避难所的人，通常找不到它。"所以我想，我应该把路标立得清楚一点。

离开的时候，我最后看了一眼调度室。夕阳从破窗里照进来，在地面的灰尘上画出一个金色的十字。

我想，祖父大概就在那个十字里。他等了四十年，等的不是谁来感谢他，只是希望每一个走投无路的人，在最冷的夜里，能看见一盏亮着的灯。

---

*[二〇二四年补记]* 这间调度站现在还在。我每年都会去那里添置一些东西，煤、米、棉被、方便面。奇怪的是，门口的纸板被人换过了，字迹不是我的，写着另一句话：

**"进来坐坐，不必说为什么。"**

我不知道是谁换的。也许是祖父，也许是别的什么人。

但我相信，这座城市里，总有些角落是为迷路的人留着的。

愿每一座废弃的调度站，都能成为一座庇护所。

愿每一盏灯，都为某个人而亮。

# The Study Hall

The fluorescent lights hummed their tired song, the same one they'd been singing since 1987 when the tiles above had been installed. Mrs. Calloway had been singing it too, for thirty-one years, though she'd long since stopped noticing.

Eighty-three students sat in rows. Pencils scratched. Pages turned. Someone coughed. The radiator clanked once, twice, then gave up.

Eleanor Whitfield, seventeen, with a streak of purple in her dark hair that Mrs. Calloway had chosen not to fight, was working through a calculus problem at the back corner desk. Her boyfriend, Marcus, had sat there last year, before he transferred to Hillcrest. Before everything.

The desk still had his initials carved into the underside. M.T. + E.W. She'd found them in September and had run her thumb across them every morning since, a small ritual of grief she performed before the bell.

Today's problem: find the derivative of f(x) = 3x² - 7x + 2.

She'd done a thousand of these. The answer was 6x - 7. Mechanical. Certain. She liked calculus for that reason.

---

In the third row, Devon Chen was not doing calculus. He was drawing a spaceship in the margin of his notebook, the kind with too many engines and a cockpit shaped like a teardrop. His mother wanted him to be a doctor. His father wanted him to be an engineer. Devon wanted to draw spaceships, but he had learned, by age twelve, that some wants lived in basements where no one came looking for them.

Mrs. Calloway walked the aisles. Her shoes were the soft kind, the ones that whispered on linoleum.

"Devon."

He closed the notebook without looking up. "Studying."

"I can see that."

She moved on. Devon waited thirty seconds, then opened the notebook again. The spaceship needed wings. Everything that left the ground needed wings.

---

At the front, near the window, sat Priya Singh. She was reading *The Stranger* behind a propped-up chemistry textbook, a trick she'd perfected in ninth grade. The book was almost finished. Mersault would shoot the Arab on the beach, and Priya found she couldn't decide if she hated him or understood him, which was, she supposed, the point.

Outside the window, a crow landed on the sill and considered its reflection. Priya watched it, and the crow watched itself, and for a moment the two of them were simply two animals looking at glass.

---

In the middle of the room, surrounded by the diligent and the not-yet-diligent, sat a boy named Eli. Eli was new. He'd transferred last week from a school in Albany whose name no one remembered. He had freckles and a single eyebrow that had healed poorly, and he was, at this moment, terrified.

Not of calculus or chemistry or *The Stranger* or the crow.

Of the silence.

Study hall was the loudest silence he had ever heard. In it, he could hear every clock tick. Every breath. Every small mechanical thing inside his chest that kept him alive, that had kept him alive through the move and the new school and the apartment that still smelled like the old tenant's cigarettes.

He opened his math textbook. Closed it. Opened it again.

The page was full of numbers, and the numbers asked nothing of him, and he was grateful for that.

---

Mrs. Calloway reached the back. She paused at Eleanor's desk, saw the empty chair beside her, saw the way Eleanor's thumb traced a groove in the wood.

"Eleanor."

"Mrs. Calloway."

"How are you holding up, dear?"

Eleanor considered the derivative. 6x - 7. The rate at which something was changing at any given moment. The slope of the line that pointed toward the future.

"Fine," she said. "Mostly."

Mrs. Calloway nodded. She knew about the empty chair. She had taught Marcus too, had watched him grow from a boy who answered questions too quickly to a young man who answered them too slowly, and she had signed the transfer paperwork with a heavy hand.

"Mostly is enough," she said, and moved on.

---

The bell would ring in forty-three minutes. In forty-three minutes, all of them would stand, gather their things, and spill into the hallways where noise lived and silence broke into a thousand harmless pieces.

But for now, the fluorescent lights hummed. Pencils scratched. Someone coughed.

Eleanor turned the page.

Devon drew a wing.

Priya read on.

And Eli, breathing slowly, watching his own hand, opened his notebook and wrote the date at the top of a blank page, because that was what you did on the first day, and every day after, when you were trying to become someone.

He wrote:

*October 14.*

Then, beneath it, in small careful letters, the beginning of something he didn't yet have a name for.

# 藤椅上的答案

教务处的挂钟敲了三下，下午的阳光斜斜地照在赵校长办公桌上那块刻着"桃李满天下"的红木匾额上，反射出一点细碎的光。

赵建国坐在那张老旧的黑色皮椅里，两只脚规矩地并拢，背挺得笔直。他今年四十七岁，秃顶，眉毛却很浓重，此刻正紧紧拧在一起，像两条对峙的毛毛虫。

"说吧。"他的声音低沉而缓慢，是那种在无数次家长会发言中打磨出来的威严。

坐在对面的女孩没有立刻回答。她穿着一件洗得有些发白的校服，拉链拉到最上面，遮住了整个脖颈。头发扎成一个低低的马尾，发尾有些毛躁。眼睛垂着，看着自己放在膝盖上的手。

那双手很小，指节有点红，指甲剪得极短，边缘起了一层薄薄的皮。

"我叫林小满。"她终于开口了，声音很轻，像是怕惊动空气里的灰尘。

"我知道。"赵建国的眉头松了一松，"年级第三名的林小满。怎么了，这次月考下降了十五名？"

林小满摇了摇头。

"那是什么事？"

她还是摇头。

赵建国叹了口气，从抽屉里拿出一个搪瓷杯，拧开盖子，里面是半杯凉透的茶。他象征性地抿了一口，又拧上。这是他的习惯，每当遇到棘手的学生，他都要先"备备课"。

"林小满，"他把搪瓷杯往桌上一放，发出轻轻的"叮"的一声，"你知道我每天要处理多少事情吗？"

女孩抬起了眼睛。

她有一双很黑的眼睛，黑得像是深井，里面却没有什么光。一种让人心里发堵的空。

"昨晚，有同学在教学楼后面发现了一些……东西。"赵建国的声音放缓了一些，但依然保持着校长的威严，"他们告诉了你的班主任。"

林小满的嘴唇动了一下，没有说话。

"为什么要那样做？"

她还是没说话。

赵建国的眉头又皱了起来。他拉了拉领带——那条深蓝色的、印着暗纹的领带是他最贵的行头之一——耐心地等着。

窗外的梧桐树被风吹得沙沙作响，有一片叶子贴在了玻璃上，挡住了部分阳光。

"林小满，"他终于失去了耐性，"你要知道，作为校长，我有责任和你的家长谈谈。"

这句话像一把无形的锤子，重重地敲在了什么地方。

女孩的背突然僵了一下，然后——

"不要。"她的声音突然大了，又很快压下去，低到几乎听不见，"求您了。"

赵建国的眉头松了。他把身子往前倾了倾，两只胳膊撑在桌上。

"为什么？"

"因为——"她咬了咬嘴唇，"因为他会打死我的。"

这句话落在寂静的办公室里，像一块石头掉进了深井。

赵建国没有立刻说话。他看着面前的这个女孩——年级第三名，每次考试都在进步，老师们口中"乖巧得让人心疼"的好学生。

他突然意识到，她穿的是秋季校服，袖口的线头有些散了。

"坐下。"

林小满已经在坐着了。但赵校长用一种完全不同的语气又说了一遍。

"坐下，坐稳，慢慢说。"

他把那个搪瓷杯推到一边，从另一个抽屉里拿出一个干净的纸杯，拧开一瓶矿泉水，倒了半杯，推到林小满面前。

"先喝口水。"

林小满看着那杯水，犹豫了一下。

"我不下毒的。"赵建国的嘴角微微弯了一下，是一个很淡很淡的笑意。

女孩端起水杯，喝了一小口。

"说说吧。"赵建国把椅子往后推了推，靠在了藤椅的靠背上——这张藤椅是他自己从家里搬来的，说是坐着腰不疼，"到底是怎么回事。"

林小满放下水杯，开始说。

她说得断断续续的，有时候一句话中间会停很久。窗外的阳光移了位置，从她的脸上移到了她的手上。

她说到那个男人的时候，赵建国明白了她为什么没有写"父亲"两个字。

她说到母亲的时候，声音变得更轻，轻到赵建国得侧着耳朵才能听见。

她说到自己。

说到那把美工刀。

说到流血的时候，她突然停了。

赵建国的搪瓷杯早已凉透，但他的手心却有些出汗。

"林小满。"他叫她的名字。

女孩抬起头。

那双眼睛里终于有了一点光——不是希望，而是一种近乎于绝望的恳求。

"你想不想继续上学？"

她点了点头，又拼命点头。

"好。"

赵建国拉了一下桌上的座机话筒，按了一串号码。

"喂，小王吗？是我。叫心理老师过来一下，对，现在。"

他挂了电话，又拿起话筒，拨了另一串号码。

"喂，是林小满的父亲吗？"

林小满的脸色一下变了，她几乎要站起来。

"不……"

赵建国用手势让她坐下。

"我是建国中学的校长。"他的声音里有一种不容置疑的威严，"是这样的，林小满这次月考虽然名次下降了，但依然在年级前十。我代表学校，邀请您明天来参加家长会，分享一下您的教育经验。对，记得带您爱人一起。"

他挂上电话，呼出一口气。

林小满的眼睛睁得很大。

"你父亲的事，交给学校来处理。"赵建国的声音很平静，"但在那之前，你要答应我一件事。"

"什么？"

"不要再伤害自己。"

她没有说话。

赵建国从桌斗里拿出一把美工刀——那是今天早上她在教学楼后面丢下的，他不知什么时候捡了起来。

"这个，我收走了。"

林小满的脸又红了，眼眶也红了。

"可以给你一个替代品。"赵建国从抽屉里拿出一个东西——是一个小小的塑料瓶子，里面装满了各种颜色的石头和珠子，"这是我女儿小时候玩的，弹弹珠。心里难受的时候，就弹一颗。"

他把小瓶子推到她面前。

"拿好了。"

林小满的手在发抖。她接过那个小瓶子，紧紧地攥在手心里。

窗外的梧桐叶终于贴不住了，被风卷走了。阳光照在林小满的脸上，暖暖的。

心理老师敲门进来的时候，林小满正低着头，一颗一颗地数着那些塑料珠子。

红的，蓝的，绿的，黄的……

一颗一颗，像是在数着那些她终于可以慢慢说出口的秘密。

赵建国从藤椅上站起来，走到窗前，看着窗外正在上课的校园。

下课铃响了。

有很多孩子从教室里涌出来，笑着、叫着、跑着。

他们不知道，在他们看不见的地方，有一个女孩正在学习重新活下去。

但没关系。

哪怕只是一个。

# The Weight of Glass

The clouds parted like curtains, and she stepped through. Mira walked barefoot across a ribbon of golden light that stretched between two impossible mountains. The air tasted of cinnamon and the first day of spring. Below her, an ocean of lavender swayed in rhythm with her heartbeat. She was weightless here, unbound by the geometry of ordinary days.

A man waited at the horizon. She couldn't see his face, but she knew him the way you know your own pulse. He held out his hand, and the distance between them folded like paper. She reached for him—

The fluorescent light above the counter buzzed, and Mira's forehead cracked against the register.

"Ow—shit."

"Language," said Don, without looking up from his crossword. He sat three stools down, the same place he'd sat every weekday for the eleven years Mira had worked at Hal's Diner. His coffee grew cold. His pen moved in small, deliberate circles.

Mira pressed her palm to her temple, feeling the tender welt forming. The daydream dissolved like sugar in water, leaving only the faint sweetness of regret. She looked at the clock: 2:47 PM. Six hours and thirteen minutes until her shift ended. Six hours and thirteen minutes until she could go home and pretend the rest of the world was a ribbon she could walk on.

The bell above the door chimed. A woman came in, shaking rain from a gray umbrella. Mid-forties, tired eyes, a coat that had seen better decades. She sat two stools down from Don and stared at the laminated menu like it contained a secret.

"Coffee," the woman said, finally. "Black. And whatever pie you have left."

Mira poured the coffee. Her hands were steady now, trained by years of early mornings and small mistakes. When she set the pie down—cherry, the last slice—her gaze caught on the woman's left hand. Empty ring finger. Faint indent where something used to live.

"You okay?" Mira asked, surprising herself.

The woman looked up. Her eyes were the color of the lavender ocean, just for a moment, just for a trick of the light.

"No," she said. "But I figure I should eat something anyway."

Mira nodded. She understood this arithmetic—the small refusal to disappear, the quiet insistence on one more thing. She brought the check and watched the woman sign it. *E. Reyes.* Below the signature, the woman drew a small sun, absent and instinctive.

Outside, the rain had stopped. A thin line of sun broke through the clouds, and Mira thought: *there it is, there's the ribbon, there's the way through.*

She blinked, and it was just a parking lot. A woman was getting into a gray sedan. A man was getting out of a black truck. Two strangers, briefly crossing, the way strangers do.

"Hey." Don's voice, gentle as an old dog. "You were somewhere else for a second."

"I was," Mira said. She wiped down the counter slowly, watching the cloth leave clean trails across the formica. "I was trying to remember how to walk on light."

He nodded, as if this were a normal thing to say. "Any luck?"

"Some."

She folded the cloth. Set it down. The fluorescent light buzzed its one stupid note, and Mira decided, for the first time in a long time, that she would ask the next stranger who came through the door if they wanted to stay awhile. Not for romance, not for rescue. Just to sit at the counter and not be alone for a minute. Just to refuse, together, to be small.

The bell chimed. The door opened. Mira looked up, ready.

# 《镜中人》

林霜推开市美术馆沉重的玻璃门时，冷气裹挟着淡淡的松木香迎面而来。她在门口站了片刻，让眼睛适应室内幽暗的光线。

今天是她三十岁生日。没有蛋糕，没有聚会，甚至没有一通像样的电话。她只是想在这样一个平常得不能再平常的日子，独自看看画。

展厅里几乎没什么人。林霜沿着指示牌走向三楼的当代艺术展区。楼梯转角处，一幅巨大的油画让她停住了脚步。

画面是一片漆黑的深海，有一束光从遥远的水面透下来，照亮了一个仰面漂浮的人。那人面目模糊，却让林霜莫名觉得熟悉——微微扬起的下巴，锁骨处一道浅淡的疤痕。

她下意识摸了摸自己颈侧同一位置的胎记。

"您喜欢这幅？"

身后传来一个低沉的声音。林霜回头，看见一个穿着黑色高领衫的年轻男人，胸前挂着工作牌，写着"策展助理 - 顾声"。

"只是觉得……"林霜斟酌着词句，"像是看镜子。"

顾声笑了笑，目光落在画上："这幅叫《溺》。画家说，每个人都沉在自己的深海里，只是有些人假装在游泳。"

林霜没说话。她向来不擅长与人交谈，尤其是这种看似意味深长的开场白。她点点头，准备走开。

"等等。"顾声叫住她，"今天下午两点，B展厅有一场行为艺术。名字叫《二十四小时》。您如果有兴趣……"

"谢谢，我先自己看看。"林霜礼貌地打断他，转身走进了下一个展厅。

然而那幅画一直跟着她。不是视觉上的，而是某种说不清的东西——像是有什么在胸口轻轻敲打。

她在B展厅门口驻足。透过玻璃，她看见一群人正安静地坐在展厅中央的地板上，背靠着一面空白的墙。他们面前摆着一面面镜子，各自对着镜中的自己，神情各异——有人在哭，有人在笑，有人只是茫然地坐着。

门口立着一块牌子：**"请加入我们。不需言语，只需在场。坐下，看镜中的自己，直到你认出她为止。"**

林霜看了一眼手机。还有二十分钟。她犹豫了一下，还是走了进去。

坐在人群最后面，背靠着冰凉的墙壁。工作人员递来一面小镜子，她接过来，放在膝上。

镜子里是一张疲惫的脸。眼下有淡淡的青色，嘴唇有些干裂，眼神像是一口枯井。林霜盯着那张脸看了很久，忽然意识到——她已经记不清上一次认真看自己是什么时候了。

三年？五年？或者更久。她总是太忙，忙着工作，忙着合群，忙着扮演那个开朗得体的林霜。却忘了问问自己：你是谁？你快乐吗？你想成为什么样的人？

周围的安静渐渐变得不那么难熬。她听见有人轻轻吸鼻子，有人深呼吸，有人发出极轻的笑声。没有人说话，但仿佛所有人都在对话——与自己。

时间变得模糊。林霜不知道自己坐了多久，只觉得膝盖有些麻，后背有些酸。但她不想动。镜子里的那张脸似乎柔和了一些，眼神里有什么东西在慢慢融化。

"生日快乐。"

一个声音轻轻落在耳边。林霜抬头，看见顾声不知何时坐在了她旁边。他手里也拿着一面镜子，正望着镜中的自己微笑。

"你怎么知道？"林霜有些惊讶。

"今天是我生日。"顾声没有直接回答，"每年这天我都会来这里坐一坐。你是今年第一个加入的陌生人。"

林霜沉默了一会儿，忽然轻轻笑了。这大概是这么多年来，第一个祝她生日快乐的人。

"谢谢你。"她说。

"不用谢。"顾声把目光收回镜子，"该谢的是这面墙。它替我们挡住了太多东西，让我们终于可以只面对自己。"

林霜低下头，再次看向膝上的镜子。

镜中人还在。但这一次，她没有急着移开视线。她对着那张脸轻轻点了点头，像是在说：我看见你了。我会好好照顾你。

展厅外，夕阳正在西沉。橘红色的光透过高处的天窗洒进来，给每一个安静坐着的人镀上一层薄薄的金边。

林霜没有起身的意思。她想，就在这里坐到天黑吧。坐到忘记所有的应酬、所有的伪装、所有的不安。坐到镜中那个陌生人，变成最熟悉的自己。

她深吸一口气，将后背更深地靠进那面沉默的墙。

就这样，静静坐着。

**真相的声音**

那天下午，阳光透过办公室百叶窗的缝隙洒在陈旧的地板上，空气里弥漫着复印纸和隔夜咖啡的味道。公司里一百二十名员工正在各自工位上埋头工作，或者假装埋头工作。突然，广播系统里传来一阵刺耳的电流声，然后是财务部林姐有些颤抖的声音：

"各位同事，我有件事必须告诉大家。"

笔尖划过纸面的沙沙声停了下来。键盘的敲击声也消失了。整个办公室仿佛被按下了暂停键。

"公司账户上的余额......其实只剩下不到三十万了。"

沉默。一片死一般的沉默。

然后，像是从水底冒出的气泡，窃窃私语声开始从四面八方升起：

"什么意思？"
"三十万？我们不是下个月还要发工资吗？"
"是不是搞错了？"

林姐的声音再次响起，这次更加颤抖："不是搞错。我私下调查了三个月。老板陈总挪用了公司资金，投入到那个传说中的'新项目'里——但根本没有那个项目。那些钱......都没了。"

小李的咖啡杯停在了嘴边，再也没有放下来；张姐的脸色刷地变白；平日里最沉默的老王突然站了起来，椅子被推得向后滑出去好远，发出尖锐的摩擦声；实习生小雨手里的文件夹啪的一声掉在了地上。

从这一刻起，所有人的命运都将被永远改写。

---

三十七楼，董事长办公室。

陈总透过落地窗看着城市的轮廓，手中价值不菲的雪茄已经熄了火。他刚刚从自己安装在财务部的一枚隐藏麦克风里，听到了林姐的每一个字。

他的第一反应不是愤怒，而是——

疲惫。

二十年前，他和唯一的合伙人白手起家，从一间二十平米的出租屋开始，做到了今天这栋三十七层的写字楼。他一直告诉自己，这只是"暂时借用"，他会在下一个季度把账补上。可是十年过去，二十年的"下一个季度"从未兑现。

他打开保险箱，里面空空如也——那里面曾经躺着的是他最后一笔秘密资金。他闭上眼睛，脑海中闪过无数张面孔：刚刚按揭买房的小李，孩子即将上学的张姐，还有那个总在茶水间偷偷给家人打电话、眼眶红红的实习生小雨。

他以为自己可以永远站在云端，但今天，他终于从云端跌落。

而最让他无法承受的是——这个真相，竟然是从一个会计出身的普通员工口中说出来的。

---

茶水间里，林姐靠在墙上，双手发抖。

她的儿子今年高考，成绩优异，已经被一所重点大学录取。但通知书还没拿到，学费的通知书已经到了。那个数字让她和丈夫夜不能寐。昨晚，她偷偷打开公司的账务系统——这是她作为财务负责人保留的特权——原本只是想找找有没有什么漏洞能让自己也"借"一点。

然而她看到的是更大的漏洞。

三十年财务生涯教会了她一件事：纸包不住火。与其让这把火从内部慢慢烧起来，烧毁所有人，不如让它由她亲手点燃，至少能把损失降到最低。

她不知道自己的未来会怎样。但她知道，今天之后，一切都不同了。

---

当陈总推开办公室的门，走进那片突然变得安静得像真空一样的办公区时，没有人低头躲避他的目光。

一百二十双眼睛，齐刷刷地望着他。

有愤怒，有恐惧，有不解，有期待。

小李第一个开口："陈总，我们......我们下个月的工资还能发吗？"

陈总看着这个跟自己创业八年的年轻人，看着他眼里残留的那丝对他的信任，心中某样东西彻底崩塌了。

他缓缓开口，声音出乎意料地平静：

"是我对不起你们。所有人的工资，一分钱都不会少。我已经联系了清算程序，公司......会破产。但你们的工资、补偿金，我会一分不少地筹给你们。这是我的承诺。"

张姐突然站起身，声音颤抖："陈总，我们不是要逼您，我们只是想知道真相——"

"真相就是我骗了你们所有人。"陈总苦笑了一下，"二十年来，我一直在骗自己，告诉自己这只是'暂时借用'。但今天，你们的会计替我说了出来。"

他向林姐的方向深深鞠了一躬。

"谢谢你，林姐。"

林姐的眼泪终于落了下来。

---

三天后，公司的破产清算程序正式启动。陈总卖掉了自己的房子、车子，以及所有的股票——那是他三十年积累的全部身家。一百二十名员工的工资和补偿金，全部到位。

林姐被任命为员工代表，参与整个清算过程。陈总特意去法院申请，让公司优先支付员工工资——这是法律允许的范围。

法院外面，小李追上了林姐。

"林姐，谢谢你。"他的声音有些哽咽，"虽然公司没了，但我知道你替我们争取到了最大的权益。"

林姐摇摇头："不是我的功劳。是陈总最后把良心找回来了。"

"还有，"她补充道，"如果没有我们大家齐心协力，事情也不会这么顺利。"

小李沉默了一会儿："你说，我们以后还会再遇到这样的老板吗？"

林姐抬头看着冬日的天空，远处有鸟群飞过。

"会遇到。但你要记住——无论什么时候，真相都是最重要的。一个建立在谎言上的帝国，迟早会崩塌；而一个建立在真相上的未来，哪怕再小，也值得我们去守护。"

小李点了点头。

---

多年后，林姐退休了。她经常去公园里散步，看着年轻人匆匆忙忙地走过。有时会想起那个改变了一切的下午。

真相是有重量的。它可以摧毁一个帝国，也可以救赎一百二十条生命。

而她这辈子做过最勇敢的事，就是在那个冬日的下午，按下了那个不该由她按下的按钮。

但她从不后悔。

因为她知道——

有些秘密，如果不说出来，就会变成所有人的枷锁。

而真相，哪怕再痛，也是自由的开始。

# 最糟糕的假期

"This. Was. Officially. The. Worst. Vacation. Ever."

林夏盯着手机屏幕，把这行字敲得震天响，然后狠狠按下发送键。消息成功送达——收件人：闺蜜苏晴。

三秒钟后，苏晴的回复弹了出来："你怎么还在酒店？不是应该去潜水了吗？"

潜水。林夏冷笑一声。

她现在确实在水里，但不是清澈见底、能和热带鱼共舞的那种水，而是——酒店三楼洗手间马桶旁边那滩不知名的积水。

事情要从今天早上说起。

作为辛苦工作了整整一年的奖励，林夏给自己订了一张去普吉岛的机票。她提前三个月做攻略，在小红书上收藏了五十篇笔记，甚至还花了重金买了一套"网红必备"泳衣。她对这趟旅程的期待值，已经拉满到了天花板。

结果飞机刚落地，她就发现自己的行李箱被航空公司弄丢了。

"别担心小姐，我们会尽快帮您找回来。" 地勤小姐笑得像朵花。

"尽快"是多久？答案是——整个假期结束都没有找到。

林夏穿着身上仅有的衣服——一条牛仔裤和一件皱巴巴的白T恤，在机场附近的商场紧急采购了三天的换洗衣服。那套精心挑选的泳衣？躺在某个机场仓库的角落里，和她的化妆品、充电器、防晒霜一起，正在进行一场说走就走的环球旅行。

但这还不是最糟的。

第二天，她去参加预定的潜水课程。教练是个黝黑皮肤的泰国小伙，看起来很专业。他带她上了一艘船，在海上开了四十分钟，终于到达潜水点。

"准备好了吗？"教练用蹩脚的英语问。

林夏兴奋地点头。她在游泳池练了整整三个月，憋气能憋两分钟，泳姿也练得像模像样。这将是她人生中第一次看见真正的海底世界。

然后她下了水。

然后她发现——她晕船。

在船上颠簸的四十分钟里，她的胃已经开始翻涌。等她潜入水下，咸涩的海水灌进嘴巴的那一刻，早上吃的泰国炒河粉彻底背叛了她。

她吐了。在海里。在潜水教练面前。在所有美丽的珊瑚和鱼群面前。

教练把她捞上来的时候，表情很复杂。

"你还好吗？"

林夏趴在船舷上，头发黏糊糊地贴在脸上，嘴里还在反胃。

她好得很。好得想死。

第三天，也就是今天，她决定哪儿也不去，就在酒店泳池边躺平。晒晒太阳，看看书，享受一下难得的清闲。

然后她去洗手间的时候，脚下一滑——

此刻，她正坐在洗手间湿漉漉的地板上，牛仔裤湿了半边，手机屏幕还亮着。苏晴又发来一条消息："所以你现在到底在干嘛？"

林夏叹了口气，编辑回复："如果你想知道一个人可以倒霉到什么程度，我可以出一本自传了。"

她正准备从地上爬起来，突然听见洗手间门外传来一阵骚动。

"What did you say? The swimming pool is contaminated? Are you kidding me?"

林夏僵住了。

一个金发碧眼的女游客正举着手机尖叫："This is officially the worst vacation ever!"

林夏忍不住笑出了声。

原来倒霉的不只她一个。

她挣扎着站起来，看着镜子里狼狈的自己——头发乱糟糟，牛仔裤滴着水，脸上还有没洗干净的防晒霜。

但她突然觉得，这趟旅程好像也没那么糟糕。

至少她学会了一个道理：人生就像潜水，你永远不知道下一秒会吐还是会看见彩虹。

林夏深吸一口气，推开洗手间的门，朝前台走去。

她要改签机票，明天回家。

至于那套"网红泳衣"和丢失的行李箱？就当它们去了一个比她更幸福的远方吧。

手机又震了一下。苏晴发来一张图片：林夏家里的小猫正躺在她的床上打呼噜，旁边还放着那套失踪的化妆品——等等。

林夏放大图片，瞪大了眼睛。

那套化妆品上贴着一张纸条，是她妈妈的字迹："我帮你从机场拿回来了。下次别把东西托运。"

林夏盯着屏幕，突然觉得鼻子有点酸。

也许这趟旅程，也没有那么糟糕。

至少她知道了：无论她走多远，家永远在那里等着她——带着失踪的行李箱，和永远比她起得早的老妈。

---
