# CRÓNICAS DE LA VILLA Y CORTIJO
### *Suplemento Dominical del Heraldo Matritense*
### Domingo, 12 de marzo de 1905

---

## ¡QUÉ POCO NOS ENTERAMOS, QUÉ POCO NOS DICEN!

**Estimados lectores y queridas lectoras:**

He aquí otra semana pródiga en murmullos, miradas cruzadas detrás del abanico y cartas anónimas que llegan a mi escritorio por correo ordinario. Sírvanse acomodarse en sus butacas de terciopelo, tomar su tacita de chocolate con churros, y disponerse a gozar —o a escandalizarse, que viene a ser lo mismo— con las últimas novedades que la ciudad, con su proverbial discreción, se ha empeñado en ocultarme. Naturalmente, todo ha resultado inútil.

---

### I. UN DUQUE EN APUROS

Fuentes bien informadas —léase: mi doncella, que tiene un primo en la servidumbre de la casa— me aseguran que **el Duque de Tembleque** atraviesa por una de esas crisis que sólo aquejan a los varones de prosapia cuando la bolsa anda flaca y el corazón, ay, muy ocupado.

Se le ha visto tres veces en una misma semana en el número 14 de la calle de Alcalá, donde vive, según se dice, una *cantaora* de gracia singular y pestañas largas. El cochero del Duque, hombre de confianza y pocas palabras, ha cambiado recientemente de librea. ¡Qué casualidad!

La Duquesa, mientras tanto, organiza tés benéficos en favor de las huérfanas del Sagrado Corazón. ¡Santa criatura! ¡Qué dominio de sí misma! ¡Qué cristiana resignation!

---

### II. EL TENOR Y LA MARQUESITA

**¡Oh, querida mía!** Lo que ha ocurrido en el Teatro Real esta semana bien merece capítulo aparte. Nuestro admirado **Sr. Lago**, el tenor de voz de terciopelo y ojos de luto, recibió al final del segundo acto un ramo de camelias blancas con una tarjeta que sólo decía: *"Para el ave que canta sola."*

La firma se adivina. Toda la platea lo adivina. La Marquesa de Villafranca, viuda desde hace tres lustros y poseedora de un busto admirable, abandonó su palco antes del tercer acto presa de una *indisposición*.

Yo no digo nada, queridos. Pero observen: las camelias blancas son, en el lenguaje de las flores, **símbolo de admiración sincera**. ¿Acaso la Marquesa pretende algo más que admiración?

¡Vaya usted a saber!

---

### III. LAS GEMELAS DE ARANJUEZ

Procedentes de su hacienda de Aranjuez, han llegado a Madrid las **señoritas de Almonacid**, esas gemelas que el verano pasado causaron tantos suspiros entre los cadetes de la Academia Militar. Vienen, según me cuentan, en busca de novio. Las dos. A la vez. Y, por lo visto, con idéntico objeto.

He observado que las pobres se parecen tanto que sólo su doncella las distingue. Esto podría causar, en el futuro, **situaciones comprometidas** de las que un columnista prudente debe mantenerse alejado. Aunque no del todo, naturalmente.

---

### IV. UN MATRIMONIO INESPERADO

Contra todo pronóstico —y a fe mía que yo había pronosticado todo lo contrario— se nos casa **doña Purificación García-Hidalgo**, la celebrada poetisa de los Lunes de El País, con **don Segismundo Botijo**, comerciante en ultramarinos de la calle de Toledo.

¡Qué pareja! Ella, de liras y mirto; él, de bacalao y alcaparras. Cuentan que se conocieron porque don Segismundo le recitó, sin saberlo, un verso de Campoamor al pedirle un kilo de lentejas. Ella se conmovió. Él, al verle los ojos húmedos, le regaló un saco de garbanzos.

¡Bendita sea la poesía! ¡Benditos sean los garbanzos!

La boda se celebrará, en estricta intimidad, el próximo jueves. Asistirán, según reza la esquela, "los pocos amigos y los muchos acreedores". Los acreedores, ¡ay!, nunca faltan.

---

### V. CARTA ABIERTA A UN MINISTRO

No puedo terminar mi crónica sin dirigir unas letras, con todo el respeto que me merece su alta dignidad, al **Excmo. Sr. Ministro de Gracia y Justicia**.

Señor Ministro: hemos observado que cierta persona de su confianza —cuyo nombre omito por educación— ha adquirido, en las últimas semanas, tres fincas rústicas en Badajoz, una casa en la Gran Vía y un automóvil marca Panhard et Levassor, modelo del año.

El sueldo de un ministro, como usted bien sabe, alcanza moderadamente para vivir. Con dificultad para un automóvil. Con gran dificultad para tres fincas en Badajoz.

¿No podría usted, Excelentísimo Señor, **explicárnoslo** en términos que una columnista curiosa y un pueblo ávido de transparencia puedan comprender?

Quedo, señor Ministro, a la espera de sus gratas noticias. Con el debido respeto y la debida indiscreción.

---

### EPÍLOGO

Queridos lectores: recuerden que todo lo aquí escrito es **puramente inventado**. Cualquier parecido con la realidad es, naturalmente, **una grosera coincidencia** que no he pretendido en absoluto.

Si alguien se ha sentido aludido, le ruego que disculpe. Si nadie se ha sentido aludido, también le ruego que disculpe, porque entonces es que he fracasado en mi oficio.

Hasta el próximo domingo.

**¡Viva la prensa! ¡Viva el escándalo! ¡Y vivan los churros con chocolate!**

— *Juanita la Corresponsal*

اسمي... دراكولا.

قرونٌ طويلةٌ عشتُها في ظلام القلعة، أتغذى على الدم، وأسكن بين جدرانٍ باردة. لكنّ شيئاً ما تغيّر في الآونة الأخيرة. ربما هو الحنين. ربما هو التعب من الخلود حين لا يكون له معنى.

---

جاءت هي في ليلة عاصفة.

لم تكن كغيرها من البشر. لم تصرخ حين رأتني. لم تحاول الهرب. وقفت في قاعة القلعة الكبرى، والشموع تُلقي بظلالها على وجهها الشاحب، وقالت بصوت هادئ:

— "أعرفُ ما أنت."

اقتربتُ منها، وأنا أعلمُ أنّها ستركض أو تُغمى عليها. لكنّها بقيت ثابتة.

— "هل ستقتُلني؟" سألت.

تساءلتُ للحظة... لماذا لا أستطيع ذلك؟ نظرتُ في عينيها العسليتين، ورأيتُ فيهما شيئاً لم أرَهُ منذ زمنٍ بعيد: القبول. بدون خوف. بدون حُكم.

— "لا أعتقد ذلك"، أجبتُ بصوتٍ أجشّ.

ضحكت ضحكةً خفيفة، وأردفت:

— "جئتُ أبحث عن شيءٍ مفقود. أبحث عن من يُنهي لعنةً قديمة."

---

أخبرتها قصتي. لعنةُ الدم التي تجري في عروقي، والصحراء النّفسية التي أعيشها منذ قرون. أخبرتُها أنّني كنتُ رجلاً ذات يوم، وأنّني قبلتُ هذه اللعنة لأُنقذ شعباً بأكمله من الموت.

جلسنا حتى الفجر، وللحديث. أخبرتني عن أسرتها، عن جدّتها التي كانت من نسلي، وأنّها ورثت دماً قديماً... دماً يشبه دمي.

— "ربما"، قالت وعيناها تلمعان، "ربما لهذا السبب لا أخافك."

---

في الليلة التالية، قرّرتُ شيئاً لم أتخيّله قطّ.

طلبتُ منها أن تقطعني. أن تُنهي ما بدأته قديماً. أن تُريقَ دمائي على تراب الأرض المُقدّسة، وتُحرّر روحي.

لكنّها رفضت.

— "لا"، قالت بحزم، "لن تكون نهايتك بالموت. بل بالحياة."

---

صنعنا طقساً قديماً، نُسخاً من مخطوطاتٍ ضاعت منذ الأزل. نُريقُ دماً طاهراً على الأرض، ونُنشدُ كلماتٍ لم تُنطَق منذ آلاف السنين.

كانت النجوم تُراقبُ من نافذة القلعة، والريحُ تصرخُ حول الجدران. ومع آخر كلمة من الطقس، شعرتُ بنارٍ تجري في عروقي، وثقلاً يُغادرُ جسدي.

سقطتُ على ركبتيّ، والضوء... ضوءٌ دافئ بدأ يتسلّل إلى القلعة. لم يكن ضوء شمس، بل ضوء فجرٍ أبديّ.

نظرتُ إلى يديّ، فرأيتُهما تتغيّر. الجلدُ البارد بدأ يدفأ، والقلبُ الذي كان صامتاً بدأ ينبض... ببطء... ثم بقوة.

وللمرة الأولى منذ ألف عام... دمعت عيناي.

---

استيقظتُ في صباحٍ مشمس. ضوءُ الشمس يلمسُ جلدي ولا يحرقه. كانت هي تجلسُ بجانبي، وعلى وجهها ابتسامة.

— "مرحباً بك في الحياة"، قالت.

نظرتُ إلى نوافذ القلعة، وللوهلة الأولى خفتُ من الضوء. لكنّني خطوتُ خطوة، ثم أخرى، حتى وصلتُ إلى شرفة القلعة.

رأيتُ الشمس.

— "كيف أشكركِ؟" سألت.

أمسكت يديّ، وقالت ببساطة:

لم أعدُ دراكولا. لم أعدُ مصّاصَ دماء. لم أعدُ وحشاً يختبئ في الظلام.

عُدتُ إنساناً.

وكل ذلك بفضل امرأةٍ واحدةٍ اختارت أن ترى في وحشٍ... إنساناً يستحقّ فرصةً ثانية.

---

في تلك الليلة، تحت سماءٍ مرصّعةٍ بالنجوم، لمستُ جبينها بشفتيّ لأول مرة. قبلةٌ بريئةٌ، بسيطة، لكنها كانت أعظمَ من كلّ الخلود.

حياةً مليئةً بالضحك، والكلمات، والشمس.

حياةً... سعيدة.

The scroll was supposed to reach the Earl of Ashbury by nightfall. That was the only task. One task. A boy of fourteen could have managed it in his sleep.

But Edmund had somehow gotten it backwards. Or sideways. Or — well, the Earl of Ashbury had received a scroll containing what appeared to be a detailed inventory of the castle's cheese stores, while the cheese steward was currently puzzling over troop deployment orders meant for a war council.

"You had *one job*," Sir Aldric repeated, his voice dangerously flat. He was a man of middling height and middling features, but his temper was anything but middling. Right now it was towering over him like a storm cloud about to split open.

Edmund stood in the corridor with his shoulders hunched to his ears, looking very much like a boy who wanted the floor to swallow him whole. He was gangly and pale, with a thatch of sandy hair that never lay flat and a smattering of freckles across his nose. Sixteen, nearly — though he often claimed nearer twenty when trying to impress the kitchen girls.

"Sir, I — the paths — there was a fog —"

"There was no fog. I looked out the window not ten minutes ago."

"No, sir. The fog had lifted. But before the fog lifted, there was a —"

"Edmund."

"— and then the bridge was out, so I had to take the long way round, and the long way round goes past the river, and at the river there was —"

"*Edmund.*"

The boy fell silent, his mouth working like a fish pulled from water.

Sir Aldric pinched the bridge of his nose. He was too old for this. He was thirty-two, which in the life of a knight was not ancient, but it was old enough to have a creak in his left knee and a deep weariness in his bones. He had survived three wars. He had fought a man to the death over a matter of honor. He had once wrestled a wild boar with nothing but a dagger and sheer stupidity.

This boy was going to be the death of him.

"Explain to me," he said, very slowly, "how you — a squire of three years' service — managed to deliver a single scroll to a single castle *four miles away* and get it wrong."

Edmund swallowed. "I, sir. I may have. Possibly. Mixed up which scroll went where."

"*Possibly.*"

"Yes, sir."

"And may I ask how that happened? Did they look similar? Was one of them invisible? Were you, perhaps, beset by a band of mischievous spirits who delight in the chaos of misdelivered correspondence?"

"No, sir. They were in different pockets. I just — put them in the wrong pockets, sir. When I left."

Sir Aldric stared at him.

"At the start of the journey, sir. I put them in the wrong pockets. Before I even left. So all of the journey was. Um. Pointless."

A vein pulsed in Sir Aldric's temple. He could feel it. The boys in the barracks would be taking bets, he was certain.

"And did it not occur to you," he said, "at any point during this *four-mile journey*, that perhaps you ought to check which scroll you were holding?"

"I was in a hurry, sir. Because of the fog."

"*The fog that had lifted before I sent you.*"

"Yes, sir. But the hurry from the fog carried over."

Sir Aldric turned away. He walked three paces to the window, looked out at the courtyard where the sun shone cheerfully on the cobblestones, then turned back.

"Do you know what the Earl of Ashbury is going to do when he opens a scroll about *cheese*?"

"Be very interested in cheese, sir?"

"*He is going to send it back with a strongly worded complaint about the waste of his time, Edmund. That is what he is going to do.*"

"Oh," said Edmund. "Yes, sir. That does seem likely."

"And do you know what the cheese steward is going to do when he opens a scroll detailing the precise positions of our southern outposts and the names of the men garrisoned there?"

"Be — be very —"

"*He is going to bring it to the kitchen staff, who will read it aloud while drinking, and by week's end every tinker and trader in the shire will know our military dispositions. Including, I assure you, any bandits or enemy scouts who happen to be buying cheese.*"

Edmund's face, which had been merely pale, achieved a shade of white usually reserved for bleached linen.

"Oh," he said again. Smaller this time.

Sir Aldric crossed his arms. He thought about shouting. He thought about the wooden spoon his mother had used on him as a child — no, no, he was not going to hit the boy, no matter how tempting. He thought about the long walk back to the Earl's castle, which he was now going to have to make himself, to apologize in person for the cheese.

"I have a question for you, Edmund."

"Yes, sir?"

"When you woke this morning, what did you think the day would hold?"

"I — I don't know, sir. Breakfast, I suppose. Training. Then the errand."

"And did you think, *today is the day I will commit an act of staggering incompetence that may yet cost this keep several valuable scouts their lives*?"

"No, sir."

"Then we are in agreement. None of us saw this coming."

Sir Aldric sighed. It was a long sigh. It had layers. There was the sigh of the moment, the sigh of the day, and somewhere deep beneath, the sigh of an entire career spent training squires who had the strategic instincts of damp bread.

"Here is what is going to happen," he said. "You are going to saddle my horse. You are going to ride — *not walk, ride* — to the Earl's castle. You are going to apologize, *correctly*, and you are going to retrieve both scrolls. You are going to bring them back here. And then you are going to spend the next month mucking out the stables, by which I do not mean a token mucking, I mean a mucking so thorough that a princess could host a banquet in there."

"Yes, sir. Thank you, sir."

"And Edmund?"

"Sir?"

"If you ever — *ever* — mix up a scroll again, I will personally escort you to the cheese steward and tell him you are his new apprentice. Do we understand each other?"

"Crystal, sir."

"Good. Now get out of my sight before I decide the stables are too good for you."

Edmund bowed — too low, too long, too awkwardly — and fled. Sir Aldric could hear his footsteps clattering down the stone stairs, followed by a distant crash, a muffled oath, and the sound of a suit of armor falling over.

He looked out the window again. Somewhere in the distance, a bird was singing. The sun was warm on the stones. It was, by all accounts, a perfectly lovely day.

He wondered, briefly, whether the monastery would take a man of thirty-two. They had a reputation for patience.

# The Man Who Remembered Too Much

The bar was called The Grassy Knoll. I know—on the nose. But there it sat on the corner of Elm and Houston in Dallas, neon sign buzzing like a dying mosquito, serving watered-down whiskey to the kind of people who knew better than to ask questions. And I had been asking questions for forty-one years.

I was the one who handed the rifle to him.

Not Lee. Never Lee. That poor, blinking man was a setup from the word go—a sacrificial rook in a game played by people who measured their wealth in nations. No, I handed the rifle to a man named Garrett Hollis, who called himself Dutch, and who had the steadiest hands I ever saw. Dutch could split a playing card at three hundred yards with a crosswind. That's the kind of marksman the Agency needed when the president had to die.

I was twenty-six years old in November of '63. I worked for the Company. I believed in it the way boys believe in their fathers—as something too big and too necessary to question. When they tapped me for the Cuba desk, then the Mexico City ops, I thought I was serving something sacred. I thought we were the thin line between the world we knew and a world run by men who ate children. I was young. I was wrong.

They came for me in March of '64. A man named Angleton—he had eyes like a cornered fox—sat me down in a room without windows and explained the new architecture of my life. I was going to retire. I was going to move to a small town. I was going to forget every name, every face, every meeting I had attended. In return, I would receive a modest check each month, drawn against a trust that did not exist, administered by people who did not exist. If I remembered too loudly, I would become a man who had never existed.

I took the deal. God help me, I took the deal.

For forty-one years I taught woodshop at a high school in Pocatello, Idaho. I built cabinets. I coached little league. I kissed my wife of thirty-eight years every morning before I poured my coffee. Her name was June, and she deserved a husband who had not done what I had done.

But memory is a strange animal. You can put it in a cage, you can starve it, you can train it to sleep when you command it—and still, in the small hours, it gnaws.

Dutch died in a car accident in 1978. Or so the report said. I never investigated. Oswald died in front of Ruby, who died in a hospital room that smelled of cigar smoke and conspiracy. Or so the reports said. I never investigated any of it.

What I did instead was keep a small notebook. Black cover, elastic band, the kind you can buy at any drugstore. Every year, on the anniversary, I wrote a single line. I wrote it in a cipher I invented at twenty-six and have never forgotten. The notebook sits on my desk right now, next to my reading glasses and a glass of water I keep forgetting to drink.

I am eighty-five years old. June is gone now—six years this Christmas. The checks still come, mailed from a bank in Delaware whose name I am not allowed to speak. My heart is a tired animal, and the doctor tells me softly, in that way doctors do, that I should begin making arrangements.

So I am making arrangements.

I am writing this letter to you, and to a few others, because I have decided that the cage door is going to open now, and whatever is left of that old, half-starved memory is going to step out into the light. I do not know if anyone will believe me. I do not know if believing matters. But I have carried this thing for more than half my life, and I am tired. A man should be allowed to set down his weight before he goes.

Here is what I know for certain:

The president was killed because he had signed National Security Action Memorandum 263 on October 11, 1962—a withdrawal from Vietnam. The men who had built their careers, their fortunes, their identities on the doctrine of containment saw their life's work unraveling in a single signature. They could not allow it. Not after Cuba. Not after the missiles. Not when they had tasted how easy it was to bend the world.

There were four of them in the room when the order was given. I only ever knew two names for certain—the Director and the man whose firm kept the books. The other two sat in shadow, and I never saw their faces, only the smoke from their cigars rising in the lamplight.

Dutch flew to Dallas on a flight registered to a shell company in Tulsa. He was put up in a suite at the Adolphus under a name that did not exist. The rifle—a 6.5mm Carrot, modified, fitted with a custom stock—was delivered to the Texas School Book Depository on the morning of November 21. Dutch had been in the building twice before, posing as a maintenance contractor. I will not say more about how he entered, or where he was positioned, except to say that the official story is a mirror held up to itself.

Oswald was a man who needed to be seen. He was hungry for significance the way a man dying of thirst is hungry for water. They fed him, and he became what they needed him to be—the loud, the visible, the lonely man with the mail-order rifle and the wife who spoke Russian. He did not know what he was. He could not have known. They made sure of that.

Afterward, I watched the Director eat a steak at a club in Georgetown and discuss the new tax bill. I watched the man with the firm light a cigarette and say only this: "I hope we know what we have bought." I did not understand him then. I think I do now.

I have lived a long life. I taught boys how to make dovetail joints. I held my daughter the day she was born and the day she buried her father in her eyes when I told her I loved her. I have been kind to dogs and unkind to myself. I have paid a price that no currency can settle.

I do not expect forgiveness. I do not deserve it. I am writing this so that, when my heart finally stops its tired argument with the world, there will be a record. A thin one. A late one. But a record.

If you have read this far, I have one request. Do not make a hero of me. I was a man who did a monstrous thing and then lived a quiet one. That is the whole of it. The only grace I can ask for is to be remembered as I was—young, and wrong, and afraid—rather than as the story they have told.

The notebook sits on my desk. The cipher is mine. The truth is yours now.

—Elias R. March
Pocatello, Idaho

Któż mógł przypuszczać, że los rzuci mnie pod sklepienie Kaplicy Sykstyńskiej, gdzie Michał Anioł Buonarroti – sam diabeł w ludzkiej skórze – miał właśnie rozpocząć swoje szalone dzieło?

Przyszedłem do Kaplicy wcześnie rano, niosąc wiadro z pigmentem przygotowanym przez warsztat. Papież Juliusz II zażądał, aby sufit był gotowy przed Bożym Narodzeniem, a termin gonił termin. Mistrz kazał mi czekać u wejścia, aż zawoła. Tak powiedział.

Czekałem.

Czekałem tak długo, że aż zasnąłem na kamiennej ławie, z głową opartą o zimny mur.

Obudził mnie jakiś dźwięk – nieomal pieśń, ale odwrócona, jakby ktoś nucił modlitwę od tyłu. Wstałem chwiejnie i ruszyłem w głąb Kaplicy, szukając Mistrza.

Zobaczyłem go od razu.

Stał na wysokim rusztowaniu, odziany w brudną koszulę, z twarzą umazaną farbą jak maska demona. W lewej ręce trzymał pędzel, w prawej – coś, co na pierwszy rzut oka wyglądało jak szkicownik. Ale to nie był szkicownik. To było lustro.

Michał Anioł patrzył w lustro – nie na ścianę, nie na fresk, który miał namalować – a na własne odbicie.

I wtedy zobaczyłem coś, co zmroziło mi krew w żyłach.

Rysował po swojej twarzy.

Nie – nie rysował. Prowadził pędzlem po skórze, delikatnie, z czułością, jakby to było płótno najdroższego mistrza. Kiedy dotykał policzka, pojawiał się tam cień – prawdziwy cień, jak gdyby światło w Kaplicy nagle się przesunęło. Kiedy dotykał kącików ust, jego wargi układały się w uśmiech, którego nigdy wcześniej nie widziałem.

A potem – a potem podniósł wzrok i spojrzał na sufit.

Zobaczyłem to samo, co on.

Na świeżym tynku, który ledwie co nałożono, zaczynały pojawiać się kształty. Nie były namalowane – po prostu *były*, jakby zawsze tam istniały, czekając tylko na moment, w którym ktoś je odczyta. Zobaczyłem Adama wyciągającego rękę do Boga. Zobaczyłem proroków z twarzami pełnymi gniewu i smutku. Zobaczyłem aniołów, których skrzydła zdawały się poruszać w ciszy.

A każda z tych postaci miała twarz Michała Anioła.

Upuściłem wiadro. Pigment rozlał się po kamiennej posadzce jak krew.

Mistrz odwrócił się powoli. Jego oczy były dziwnie jasne, prawie przezroczyste, jak gdyby płynęła w nich nie szarość, lecz światło.

– Ach – powiedział cicho. – Więc widzisz.

Chciałem uciec, ale nogi odmówiły mi posłuszeństwa.

– Co… co pan robi? – wykrztusiłem.

Michał Anioł uśmiechnął się – tym uśmiechem, który wcześniej namalował na własnej twarzy – i odpowiedział:

– Oddaję im to, co moje. Zawsze mi mówili, że jestem brzydki. Że mam nos jak orzeł, usta jak ranę, czoło jak skażę. Więc postanowiłem oddać im swoją twarz. Niech Bóg ma piękno, niech święci mają dostojeństwo, niech diabły mają moją gorycz. A ja…

Urwał. Podszedł do mnie bliżej, tak że czułem zapach terpentyny i czegoś jeszcze – czegoś słodkiego, jak kadzidło w kościele.

– A ja zostanę pusty – dokończył szeptem. – Pusty i wolny.

Nie wiem, ile czasu minęło, zanim odszedłem z Kaplicy. Pamiętam tylko, że na zewnątrz świeciło słońce, a mnie drżały ręce tak bardzo, że nie mogłem utrzymać kubka z wodą, który podał mi jeden z robotników.

Pomyślałem wtedy, że zwariowałem. Że to był sen, halucynacja wywołana głodem i zmęczeniem.

Ale potem, wiele lat później, wróciłem do Rzymu. Poszedłem do Kaplicy Sykstyńskiej, stanąłem pod sufitem i spojrzałem w górę.

Wszystkie twarze były tam. Adama, Boga, proroków, aniołów, sybilli – każda z nich miała rysy Michała Anioła. Każda z nich była piękna w sposób, w jaki on nigdy nie był piękny za życia.

A ja wiedziałem, że to, co widziałem tamtego dnia, było prawdą.

Michał Anioł oddał swoją twarz Bogu.

I Bóg ją przyjął.

# El Aprendiz del Bardo

## Acto I: La sombra de un gigante

El olor a tinta y pergamino me recibió como cada mañana en el teatro del Globo. Mis dedos, aún manchados del trabajo nocturno, temblaban al cerrar la puerta. William ya estaba despierto, dictándole a su eterna secretaria, el bueno de Heminges, mientras paseaba por la sala como un león enjaulado.

—«Ser o no ser» —repitió, alzando el dedo—. Eso les gustará. Tiene fuerza.

Me mordí los labios hasta saborear la sangre. *Yo* había escrito esa línea. Yo, Thomas, en una noche de insomnio y vino barato, mientras William dormía junto a su querida Anne Hathaway en Stratford. Pero ¿qué podía decir? Era él quien firmaba, él quien brillaba, él quien cenaba con la corte.

—Buenos días, maestro —murmuré, inclinándome.

—¡Ah, Thomas! —exclamó con esa sonrisa que derretía corazones—. Acércate. Necesito que copies unos sonetos. Los míos, naturalmente. Me han pedido una colección completa.

—Naturalmente —respondí, tragándome el grito que me nacía en el pecho.

## Acto II: Las grietas

Todo comenzó a cambiar cuando apareció Kit Marlowe.

Christopher Marlowe, el genio, el brillante, el audaz. Vino al teatro una tarde de octubre, envuelto en su capa oscura, con esa mirada que parecía perforar las almas.

—He oído rumores —dijo, mirándome directamente a mí—. Sobre un joven que escribe versos que harían llorar al mismísimo Ovidio.

William se tensó.

—Rumores —repitió—. ¿Qué rumores, Christopher?

—Que tu aprendiz tiene más talento en su meñique del que tú jamás tendrás en todo tu cuerpo, Will.

El silencio cayó como un telón de plomo. Vi cómo la sangre abandonaba el rostro de mi maestro, cómo sus manos se cerraban en puños.

—No sé de qué hablas —escupó entre dientes.

—¿No? —Marlowe sonrió, y esa sonrisa era la de un gato a punto de devorar un ratón—. Entonces quizá deberías preguntarle a Thomas de dónde salió «ser o no ser». O por qué tu *Hamlet* suena tan parecido a las obras que él escribía de madrugada.

## Acto III: La conspiración

Esa noche, William me llamó a su estudio. Nunca me había mirado así: con una mezcla de furia, miedo y algo parecido al respeto.

—¿Cuánto tiempo llevas escribiéndome las obras? —preguntó con voz ronca.

—Cuatro años, maestro.

—¿Por qué?

Me quedé en silencio largo rato. ¿Por qué? Porque era mi pasión, porque creía en el teatro, porque pensaba que un día él reconocería mi trabajo. Porque era un cobarde.

—Porque no tenía otra opción —respondí al fin—. Y porque pensé que algún día...

—¿Qué? ¿Que te daría crédito? —se rio, pero no había alegría en su risa—. ¿Sabes lo que habría pasado? Me habrían llamado farsante, impostor, ladrón. Habría perdido todo.

—¿Y yo? —pregunté—. ¿Qué pierdo yo?

Nos miramos. Dos hombres enfrentados por la misma pasión, separados por el orgullo y la cobardía.

## Acto IV: El precio de la verdad

Las semanas siguientes fueron un infierno. William, furioso, comenzó a escribir él mismo las obras, y he de reconocer que no estaban mal. Pero tampoco tenían esa chispa, esa magia que yo lograba darle.

Y entonces llegó la tragedia.

Marlowe fue asesinado en una taberna de Deptford. Una pelea, dijeron. Una deuda de juego. Pero yo sabía que no fue así. Sabía que había demasiadas personas interesadas en silenciar a ese genio de lengua afilada.

La noche del funeral clandestino, William me encontró llorando junto al río.

—¿Por qué lloras? —preguntó—. Era tu defensor, ¿no?

—Era mi amigo —respondí—. El único que creía en mí.

William se sentó a mi lado. Por primera vez, lo vi vulnerable. Humano.

—Thomas —dijo—, hay algo que debes saber. Marlowe no fue asesinado por sus versos.

Lo miré sin entender.

—Fue asesinado porque estaba escribiendo una obra. Una obra sobre un mago llamado Fausto. Una obra... que en realidad estaba escribiéndola yo. O mejor dicho, que le había dado yo como propia.

El mundo se detuvo.

—¿Tú...?

—Era un trato —continuó William con voz rota—. Los hombres poderosos me pagan bien por mantener ciertas cosas en silencio. Y Marlowe estaba a punto de hablar. Por eso murió.

## Acto V: La decisión

Esa noche no dormí. Marlowe muerto por una obra que yo había escrito. Por palabras mías convertidas en arma, en silencio, en muerte.

A la mañana siguiente, entré al estudio de William con un papel en las manos. Era un nuevo contrato. Un contrato que él había redactado la noche anterior, probablemente en uno de sus ataques de culpa.

*«Yo, William Shakespeare, reconozco la autoría de Thomas Middleton en las siguientes obras...»*

Pero no firmé. En su lugar, rompí el papel en pedazos.

—¿Qué haces? —gritó William, lívido.

—He tomado una decisión —respondí con calma—. Voy a seguir escribiéndote las obras. Pero no por dinero, ni por fama, ni por crédito.

—¿Entonces por qué?

Lo miré a los ojos.

—Porque ahora sé quién eres realmente, maestro. Y porque mientras yo escriba, no escribirás tú. Mientras yo tenga el poder de las palabras, tú no podrás usarlas para hacer daño. Ni para silenciar genios como Marlowe.

William palideció.

—No puedes hacer eso...

—Ya lo estoy haciendo. Es mi seguro, ¿comprendes? Si me pasa algo, si me silencian como a Christopher, el mundo sabrá la verdad. Cada obra, cada verso, cada soneto. Y entonces, tu legado se convertirá en ceniza.

## Epílogo: El precio del silencio

Han pasado veinte años. William murió hace tres, venerado como el mayor genio de las letras inglesas. Yo sigo aquí, en las sombras, escribiendo para herederos que nunca conocerán mi nombre.

Pero a veces, en las noches de insomnio, enciendo una vela y le susurro a la oscuridad:

—Buenas noches, Christopher. Aquí sigo, usando mis palabras para algo bueno.

Y a veces, sólo a veces, creo escuchar una risa. La risa de un joven que murió por decir la verdad.

En este mundo, los que hablan demasiado pronto encuentran el silencio eterno. Pero los que saben callar... los que saben usar las palabras como moneda y como escudo... esos sobreviven.

Soy Thomas, aprendiz eterno del bardo.

Y esta es mi historia.

# The Weight of a Falling Fruit

The morning was unremarkable in every particular. I remember this with certainty because I have since replayed it so many times in my mind, searching for some omen I must have missed, some sign that the universe was about to tilt on its axis. There was none. The sun rose the same as it had the day before, and the day before that, and for all the days I had known Edmund Bulstrode, who was the most unremarkable man in Cambridgeshire and, I had once told him affectionately, probably all of England.

We were walking through the orchard behind his mother's house in Woolsthorpe. I was visiting from Cambridge, where I had been completing my own modest studies, and Edmund had been kind enough to invite me to the country for a fortnight's rest. He had inherited the house upon his father's passing the previous winter, and though he had no particular affection for farming, he had taken up the duty of maintaining the land with the same quiet resignation he brought to most things in life.

"I suppose I ought to do something with these trees," he had said the previous evening, gesturing toward the window where the orchard sprawled beneath a pewter sky. "Father always said the Bramleys were the best in the parish."

"And what did your father do with them?" I had asked, though I already knew the answer.

"Cider," Edmund had replied. "Mostly cider."

I had laughed. It was the kind of joke Edmund made—gentle, self-deprecating, almost apologetic for finding humor in his own situation. He was not a happy man, Edmund. He was not an unhappy man either. He was, in the truest sense, a man who had accepted his portion in life and asked for very little beyond the simple dignities of existence. A roof. A meal. A quiet evening by the fire. He had inherited a modest estate, a handful of tenants, and a mother who loved him in the particular, suffocating way of women who have nothing left but their sons. He had asked for nothing more because he had wanted nothing more, or because he had never permitted himself to want.

We had been friends since boyhood, though I use the word loosely. He was two years my senior, which in our youth had made him seem ancient and wise, and which now made him seem only mildly more experienced in the disappointments of the world. We had met at the grammar school in Grantham, where I had been the sort of student who asked too many questions and he had been the sort who answered them patiently, as though he found my curiosity a curious thing to observe, like a bird that had wandered into the wrong garden.

I think he pitied me, in those early days. I was the son of a farmer who had died before I could remember him, raised by a mother who remarried a man I could not abide, sent away to school because there was nothing else to be done with me. I was angry in those days, and Edmund was not, and I think I envied him his calm the way one envies a man who sleeps soundly while you lie awake cataloguing your grievances against God.

Now, years later, we walked beneath the apple trees, and he told me about the fencing he needed to repair, and the tenant who had fallen behind on his rent, and his mother's increasing complaints about the cold in the east parlor, and I listened with the comfortable indifference of old friendship, offering the occasional sympathetic murmur but thinking, mostly, of nothing at all.

That was when the apple fell.

It struck the ground perhaps three yards from where we stood, with a soft, percussive thud that was lost almost immediately in the rustle of leaves. I doubt I would have noticed it at all, had Edmund not stopped mid-sentence, his mouth still open around whatever word he had been about to say, his eyes fixed on the small green fruit that lay in the grass at our feet.

"Oh," he said. Then, after a pause: "An apple."

"Yes," I said, somewhat bemused. "It appears to be."

He did not move. He continued to stare at the apple with an expression I had never seen on his face before, and which I could not then have named, though I have come to understand it since. It was the expression of a man who has just been handed something he did not ask for and cannot immediately refuse.

"Strange," he murmured, almost to himself.

"What is strange?" I asked, for I could see nothing remarkable in an apple falling from a tree. Apples fell from trees constantly. This was, in fact, the defining characteristic of apples, or at least of apples that had ripened sufficiently to detach themselves from their stems. It was the reason we had been forced to walk through the orchard in the first place—his mother had complained about the mess they made on her paths, and Edmund had been meaning to gather them for cider, though he had not yet got around to it.

"Strange," he repeated, as though I had not spoken. "That it should fall straight down."

I laughed. I could not help it. "Where else would it fall?"

He looked at me then, and there was something in his eyes that made me stop laughing, though I could not have said what it was. Not anger—Edmund was not given to anger. Not amusement, either. Something else. Something I had no name for.

"Down," he said slowly, as though testing the word. "Always straight down. Have you ever seen an apple fall any other way? Sideways, perhaps? Upward?"

"Of course not," I said. "Why would it?"

"Why would it," he echoed. And then he fell silent, and I could see that he was not speaking to me at all but to himself, or to something beyond himself, or perhaps to the apple, which lay there in the grass like an answer to a question no one had yet thought to ask.

We stood there for a long moment. The breeze moved through the branches above us, and other apples swayed on their stems, and somewhere a thrush was singing its idiot song, and I felt, for reasons I could not then articulate, that I was standing on the edge of something. Not a precipice—nothing so dramatic. A threshold. The kind of threshold one crosses without realizing it, and only later understands that everything on the other side is different from everything that came before.

"Edmund," I said carefully. "Are you quite well?"

He did not answer at once. He stooped—slowly, as though his joints had suddenly grown old—and picked up the apple. He turned it over in his hands, studying it with the concentration of a man examining a gemstone. Then he looked up at the branch from which it had fallen, and then at the ground beneath it, and then at the apple again, and I could see his mind working in a way I had never seen it work before. Edmund had always been clever, in his quiet way, but he had never been what one would call a thinker. He had been content to let the world be the world, to accept its surfaces as its substance, to ask nothing of reality beyond what reality offered freely.

Now, for the first time in all the years I had known him, he was asking something.

"I wonder," he said, almost in a whisper, "what holds it up."

"Holds what up?"

"The apple. Before it falls. What holds it to the branch?"

I stared at him. The question was so obvious, so fundamental, so utterly beneath consideration, that I could not for a moment understand why he was asking it. Of course something held the apple to the branch. The stem, naturally. The physical connection between fruit and tree. This was not a matter for inquiry. This was not a matter for anything at all.

"The stem," I said.

"But what holds the stem to the branch? What holds the branch to the tree? What holds the tree to the ground?" He was speaking faster now, and there was a flush rising in his pale cheeks that I had never seen there before. "What holds the moon to the sky? Why does it not fall, as the apple falls? Why does the apple fall, as the moon does not? What is the difference between them? What is the *principle*?"

I did not know what to say. I had never heard Edmund speak like this. I had never heard anyone speak like this. The questions were not, in themselves, extraordinary—any child might ask them, and most children did, and most children were told to hush and go on with their lessons. But there was something in the way Edmund asked them, something in the tremor of his voice and the brightness of his eyes, that made me feel as though the questions themselves were new. As though no one had ever truly asked them before. As though Edmund, in this moment, was inventing inquiry itself.

"I don't know," I said. And then, because I did not know what else to say: "Does it matter?"

He looked at me, and for the first time in all our years of friendship, I saw something like pity in his eyes. Not the pity I had imagined from him in our youth—that comfortable condescension of the contented toward the afflicted. A different pity. The pity of a man who has seen something and cannot make others see it.

"It matters," he said quietly. "I think it matters very much."

He put the apple in his pocket. I remember thinking, even then, that this was strange—that Edmund, who never did anything without purpose, who kept his pockets tidy and his affairs in order, who would have thought it improper to bring an apple into the parlor, should pocket this one as though it were a treasure, a relic, a piece of the True Cross.

We finished our walk in silence. I tried to draw him back to the matter of the fencing, the tenants, his mother's parlor, but he answered only in monosyllables, and I could see that his mind was elsewhere—or rather, that his mind was here, in this place, in this orchard, in this moment, but working on something I could not see. I felt, for the first time, excluded from my friend. As though a door had closed between us, not in anger but in some other way I could not name.

That evening, over supper, Edmund was quiet. His mother, a formidable woman named Margaret who had the particular gift of filling any silence with the sound of her own voice, chattered on about the parish and its doings, about Mrs. Hall's rheumatism and the vicar's new sermon and the price of wool, and Edmund nodded and made the appropriate sounds and ate his stew without seeming to taste it.

After supper, he excused himself and went to his father's study—a room he had not entered since the funeral. I heard him in there for hours, the scratch of his pen, the rustle of paper, the occasional muffled exclamation that might have been excitement or might have been despair. I did not disturb him. I sat by the fire in the parlor and read a book of poems I had brought with me, but I could not concentrate. I kept thinking about the apple, about the expression on Edmund's face, about the questions he had asked that I had not known how to answer.

When I went up to bed, I passed the study door, which was slightly ajar. I could not help but glance in. Edmund was at the desk, surrounded by papers covered in his neat, precise hand, and in the center of the desk, placed with a kind of solemnity, was the apple. It had been cut in half, and the two halves lay open like a book, the seeds exposed, the flesh already beginning to brown at the edges.

He looked up and saw me. For a moment, I thought he would speak—that he would share with me whatever he had discovered, whatever was working itself out in his mind. But he only smiled, faintly, and shook his head, and returned to his writing.

I went to bed. I did not sleep well. I dreamed of apples falling upward, into the sky, where they hung among the stars like strange fruit, and when I woke I could not remember whether the dream had been mine or Edmund's.

The next morning, Edmund was gone. Not from the house—his mother said he had gone to Cambridge early, before dawn, on some business he had not explained. He had left a note for me, which his mother handed over with the particular expression of a woman who suspects she is being excluded from something important.

*I have gone to speak with a man named Barrow at Trinity. I believe he will understand. I will write when I can. Thank you for your friendship. Keep my mother company, if you can bear it. I will return before the week is out.*

*E.*

I stayed for three more days. His mother was gracious, in her way, though she watched me with the suspicion of a woman who believes her son has been led astray by unsuitable companions. I told her nothing of the apple, or of the questions, or of the look I had seen on her son's face. I did not think she would understand. I was not sure I understood myself.

When I returned to Cambridge, I heard strange rumors. A young man from Lincolnshire had been admitted to Trinity College on the recommendation of the Master himself, a man of such extraordinary promise that the older scholars spoke of him in hushed tones, as though his presence among them were an event of historical significance. His name, they said, was Newton. Isaac Newton.

I did not, at first, connect this name with Edmund. Why would I? Newton was a scholar, a mathematician, a man of letters and learning. Edmund was a farmer, a quiet man, a man who had never in his life shown the slightest inclination toward academic distinction. They were different people, from different worlds, with different futures before them.

And yet.

I went to Trinity, drawn by curiosity I could not name. I found the young man in the library, surrounded by books, his quill moving furiously across a sheet of paper. He looked up when I entered, and I saw at once that it was not Edmund—but that it might have been, once, if circumstances had been different. He had the same pale eyes, the same quiet intensity, the same sense of a mind working at the edges of what thought could contain.

"You are the friend," he said. "Bulstrode's friend."

I nodded, uncertain.

"He told me about the apple," Newton said. He spoke softly, almost reverently, as though the word itself were sacred. "He said it was the most important thing anyone had ever told him. He said I would understand. He said—" Here Newton paused, and I saw something flicker across his face, something I could not read. "He said he wished he could have thought of it himself."

I sat down across from him. I did not speak. I could see the papers on his desk, covered in figures and diagrams, equations I could not begin to understand. And there, in the center of the desk, placed with a kind of solemnity, was an apple. A green apple, uncut, perfect, gleaming in the light from the window.

"He gave you the apple," I said. It was not a question.

"He gave me the apple," Newton confirmed. "He said it was a gift. He said it was an answer to a question he could not ask, but that I could."

"And what question is that?"

Newton smiled. It was a smile I recognized—the same faint, distant smile I had seen on Edmund's face in the orchard. The smile of a man who has seen something others have not.

"Why things fall down," he said, "instead of up."

I left the library. I walked through the courts of Trinity, past the chapel and the hall, past the scholars arguing in corners and the students running between lectures, and I thought about Edmund, who had asked a question he could not answer, and Isaac Newton, who had answered a question he had never thought to ask. I thought about the apple, which had fallen from a tree in an orchard in Lincolnshire and traveled, somehow, from one mind to another, like a baton passed between runners in a race I did not know was being run.

I thought about thresholds, and the way one crosses them without realizing.

I have never spoken of this to anyone. I did not speak of it when Newton's name became famous, when his *Principia* was published and the world learned what the apple had set in motion. I did not speak of it when Edmund wrote to me, occasionally, to tell me of his quiet life in Woolsthorpe, his apple trees, his mother's declining health, his own gentle, contented decline into old age. I did not speak of it when Edmund died, some years later, and I went to the funeral and saw his mother weeping and his neighbors offering condolences and no one, no one at all, knowing that the quiet farmer they were burying had once held the seed of a revolution in the palm of his hand.

I am an old man now. I have outlived most of my contemporaries, and all of my certainties. I do not know if what I saw that morning in the orchard was what I thought I saw. I do not know if Edmund's questions were truly the questions of a genius, or only the questions of a man standing in the right place at the right time, looking at the right fruit. I do not know if Newton would have found his answers without Edmund's prompting, or if Edmund would have found his questions without Newton's answering.

I know only this: that there was an apple, and it fell, and my friend saw it fall, and another man caught it as it fell, and from that catching came a new way of seeing the world. And I was there. I was the only one who was there, at the beginning, before the beginning became history.

I do not know if that makes me a witness or a ghost.

I do not know if it matters.

But I have carried it with me, all these years, like a stone in my pocket, smooth and heavy and impossible to set down. And now that I am old, and the end is closer than the beginning, I find that I want to set it down at last. I want to tell someone that Edmund Bulstrode asked a question, and that the asking mattered, even if no one remembers the asker. I want to tell someone that the apple fell, and that someone saw it fall, and that seeing is sometimes its own kind of doing.

I am telling you.

I do not know who you are, or why you have read this far, or what you will make of it. I do not know if you will believe me, or think me a fool, or wonder why I have troubled to write it down. But I have troubled, and I have written, and now the troubling is yours, and the writing is yours, and what you make of it is your own.

The apple fell. My friend saw it fall.

That is all.

That is everything.

# ฝุ่นของตัวพิมพ์

*จดหมายจากโยฮันน์ เซิร์ทลิง ถึงลูกชายของเขา เมืองเมนท์ซ ค.ศ. 1469*

ลูกเอ็ดเวิร์ดที่รักของพ่อ,

พ่อเขียนจดหมายฉบับนี้ในขณะที่นิ้วมือของพ่อยังเปื้อนหมึกสีดำ และกลิ่นน้ำมันลินสีดยังคงติดอยู่ในเสื้อคลุมของพ่อ วันนี้เป็นวันที่ยาวนาน—พ่าทำงานตั้งแต่รุ่งเช้าจนถึงเวลาสวดภาวนา แต่ก่อนที่พ่อจะนอนลง พ่ออยากเล่าเรื่องราวของพ่อให้ลูกฟัง

ลูกจำได้ไหมว่าเมื่อสามปีก่อน พ่อเป็นเพียงช่างเขียนหนังสือธรรมดาๆ คนหนึ่ง? พ่อนั่งโค้งหลังอยู่ในห้องมืดๆ ของอาราม ใช้พู่กันปลายแหลมจุ่มหมึกลงบนหนังสัตว์หรือกระดาษแพร ตัวอักษรแต่ละตัวถูกวาดด้วยมือ หนังสือเล่มหนึ่งอาจใช้เวลาหลายเดือนจึงจะเสร็จ และมีราคาแพงมากจนเฉพาะอารามและขุนนางเท่านั้นที่เป็นเจ้าของได้ แม่ของลูกต้องทำงานหนักทั้งปีเพื่อซื้อหนังสือสวดมนต์เพียงเล่มเดียว

แต่แล้วทุกอย่างก็เปลี่ยนไป เมื่อพ่อย้ายมาทำงานที่โรงพิมพ์ของนายยอฮันเนส กุเทนแบร์ก ที่เมนท์ซ

ลูกเอ็ดเวิร์ด พ่อได้เห็นสิ่งมหัศจรรย์ที่สุดในชีวิตของพ่อ

เครื่องพิมพ์ของนายกุเทนแบร์กเป็นสิ่งประดิษฐ์ที่ชาญฉลาดอย่างเหลือเชื่อ มันประกอบด้วยแท่งเหล็กหนักๆ ที่สามารถกดลงบนกระดาษได้หลายร้อยแผ่นในเวลาเพียงหนึ่งวัน แทนที่จะใช้เวลาหลายเดือนในการเขียนหนังสือเพียงเล่มเดียว ตัวพิมพ์โลหะขนาดเล็ก—แต่ละตัวเป็นตัวอักษรย้อนกลับ—ถูกเรียงต่อกันเป็นคำ เป็นประโยค เป็นหน้าหนังสือทั้งหน้า จากนั้นหมึกก็ถูกทาลงบนตัวพิมพ์ กระดาษถูกวางทับ และเมื่อเครื่องกดลง—*ตึก!*—ตัวอักษรก็ปรากฏบนกระดาษราวกับเวทมนตร์

พ่อจำได้ว่าวันแรกที่พ่อเห็นหน้าหนังสือที่ถูกพิมพ์ออกมา พ่อรู้สึกเหมือนกับว่าพระเจ้าทรงมอบของขวัญล้ำค่าให้กับมวลมนุษย์ หนังสือไม่ใช่สิ่งที่จำกัดอยู่เฉพาะในอารามอีกต่อไป ไม่ใช่สมบัติของชนชั้นสูงเท่านั้น ความรู้กำลังจะหลั่งไหลออกมาเหมือนน้ำจากแม่น้ำไรน์ และมนุษย์ทุกคน—แม้แต่ชาวนาผู้ยากจน—จะสามารถเรียนรู้ได้

แต่ลูกของพ่อ พ่อต้องบอกความจริงกับลูกด้วย

ชีวิตของช่างพิมพ์ไม่ได้โรยด้วยกลีบกุหลาบ

ทุกเช้า พ่อตื่นก่อนดวงอาทิตย์ขึ้น เดินไปตามถนนที่ยังมืดสนิทเพื่อไปให้ทันเวลาทำงาน ในโรงพิมพ์ พ่อทำงานหลายอย่างสลับกันไป บางวันพ่าจัดเรีงตัวพิมพ์—เรียงตัวอักษรเล็กๆ ที่อยู่ในกล่องไม้ขนาดใหญ่ มันเป็นงานที่ต้องใช้สมาธิสูงมาก เพราะหากเรียงผิดแม้แต่ตัวเดียว หน้าหนังสือทั้งหน้าก็เสีย บางวันพ่อผสมหมึก—น้ำมันลินสีดต้มกับเขม่าดำจนได้สีที่เหมาะสม และบางวันพ่อก็ช่วยหมุนลูกบิดของเครื่องพิมพ์ซึ่งต้องใช้แรงมหาศาล

ฝุ่นตัวพิมพ์ที่บินว่อนในอากาศทำให้ปอดของพ่อแสบร้อน หลังของพ่อปวดเมื่อยจากการก้มๆ เงยๆ และบ่อยครั้งพ่อก็ถูกไฟจากหม้อหลอมตัวพิมพ์ที่ใช้ในการหล่อตัวอักษรใหม่ๆ เผาไหม้ที่มือ แต่ทุกครั้งที่พ่อมองดูหนังสือที่พิมพ์เสร็จแล้วเรียงตัวอยู่บนโต๊ะ—เป็นร้อยเป็นพันเล่ม—พ่อก็ลืมความเจ็บปวดทั้งหมด

เมื่อสัปดาห์ก่อน นายกุเทนแบร์กเรียกพ่อไปพบและมอบหมายงานสำคัญให้พ่อ นั่นคือการพิมพ์ *ไบเบิล* ครั้งแรกในประวัติศาสตร์ พ่อรู้สึกเหมือนหัวใจจะหยุดเต้น พระคัมภีร์—พระวจนะของพระเจ้า—จะถูกถ่ายทอดเป็นภาษาที่คนธรรมดาสามารถอ่านได้ ไม่ใช่ภาษาละตินที่มีเพียงบาทหลวงเท่านั้นที่เข้าใจ พ่อรู้ว่าสิ่งนี้จะเปลี่ยนโลก แม้ว่าพระสังฆราชบางท่านจะไม่พอใจเป็นอย่างยิ่ง และเมื่อวานนี้พ่อได้ยินข่าวลือว่ามีคนพยายามจะห้ามการพิมพ์หนังสือบางเล่ม พวกเขาเกรงว่าความรู้จะกระจายไปสู่มือของคนผิด

แต่พ่อเชื่อว่าความรู้เป็นของทุกคน ดังเช่นแสงแดดที่ส่องลงมาจากฟ้าโดยไม่เลือกว่าใครจะรับ

ลูกของพ่อ เมื่อลูกเติบโตขึ้น พ่ออยากให้ลูกเข้าใจว่าสิ่งที่พ่อทำอยู่นี้ไม่ใช่แค่การทำงานในโรงพิมพ์ธรรมดา มันคือการมีส่วนร่วมในการเปลี่ยนแปลงของโลก ทุกตัวอักษรที่พ่อจัดเรียง ทุกแผ่นกระดาษที่พ่อหยิบขึ้นมา ทุกเล่มที่ถูกส่งออกไปจากโรงพิมพ์แห่งนี้ ล้วนเป็นก้าวเล็กๆ ที่นำไปสู่โลกใหม่ โลกที่ผู้คนจะตั้งคำถาม โลกที่ความจริงจะไม่ถูกซ่อนไว้เบื้องหลังกำแพงของอารามอีกต่อไป

พ่อรู้ว่ายังมีอันตรายอีกมากรออยู่ข้างหน้า เจ้าหน้าที่ของพระสังฆราชอาจมาปิดโรงพิมพ์ อาจมีคนทำลายเครื่องพิมพ์ และพ่ออาจถูกลงโทษ แต่ถึงแม้ว่าพรุ่งนี้พ่อจะไม่ได้ทำงานนี้อีก พ่อก็จะไม่เสียใจ เพราะพ่อได้เห็นแล้วว่ามนุษย์สามารถสร้างสิ่งที่ยิ่งใหญ่ได้เพียงใด เมื่อพวกเขามีความกล้าหาญที่จะท้าทายธรรมเนียมเก่าๆ

ฝนตกลงมากระทบหน้าต่างไม้ พ่อได้ยินเสียงมันผสมกับเสียงนาฬิกาที่บอกเวลาดึกดื่นของเมืองเมนท์ซ พ่อควรจะนอนแล้ว เพราะพรุ่งนี้รออยู่อีกวันที่ยาวนาน แต่ก่อนที่พ่อจะนอน พ่ออยากบอกลูกว่า—

The confession came on a Tuesday, somewhere between the leftover pasta and the episode of *The Great British Bake Off* we'd been pretending to watch.

"I wasn't entirely truthful with you," he said, which was — I want to make this clear — not at all the kind of sentence I was expecting to interrupt Mary Berry. "About where I'm from. Originally."

I assumed at first that he meant Ohio. I assumed he meant a small town in Ohio, perhaps, one he was embarrassed about. I waited.

"I'm from the fourteenth century," he said. "Specifically, the Languedoc. Which is in southern France. The year of our Lord thirteen hundred and—" he paused, consulting some internal calendar, "—eighty-six, if you must know. Though I did not think of it as the Lord of anything. I thought of it as my father's vineyard, which was very small, and the sun, which was very large."

I waited some more.

"That's why," he added, gesturing vaguely at himself, "the beard."

It did explain the beard, is the thing. And the way he sometimes stood in the produce aisle like a man who had wandered into a cathedral. And the little reverent bows he gave to certain elderly women in the park, as though they were queens or nuns or both.

"Say something," he said, in a voice so small it almost wasn't there.

I said: "Are you taking me to the commitment ceremony of your cousin Radulf next month, or whatever he is?"

He looked startled. Then he looked like a man who had been pardoned. "Yes," he said. "Yes. I was hoping you would come."

"I'll need a hat," I said, because of course I would. I would need a hat, and probably a small flask, and definitely a lie ready for my mother.

That was how it began.

That is how it always begins, I think — not with grand revelation, but with the small, domestic negotiation. *Are you still taking out the recycling? Are you still coming to brunch on Sunday? Are you still, after this impossible thing I have told you, the person I believed you were?*

He was. He is.

His name is not, as it turns out, the one on his driver's license. It is something longer, something that tastes of thyme and stone, and he will not tell me what it is because — he says, gravely, as though confessing a second impossible thing — in his time, to know a person's true name was to hold a knife at their throat. He gave me the name on the license as a kind of decoy, the way you'd give a tourist a decoy map of the metro. A kindness, he said. A protection.

I am writing this down because I am afraid I will forget.

I am afraid I will forget because he forgets things, too. Not the way we forget — not the way you forget where you put your keys, or the name of the actor in the thing you watched last week. He forgets in larger blocks, like a man who has walked into a room and can no longer remember what a room is for.

He stood in our kitchen last week and asked me what a *microwave* was.

I told him. I told him it was a small oven that used invisible light to heat food very quickly, and I watched him nod slowly, the way a man nods when he is being told something he suspects is witchcraft but is too polite to say so.

"You must think I'm very foolish," he said, afterward.

"I think," I said, "that you are a man who has been alive for a very long time, and that this is not nothing."

He kissed me then, on the forehead, with the particular gravity of a man who has kissed foreheads for six hundred years and intends to continue.

---

There are things I have learned.

I have learned, for instance, that he cannot abide the smell of gasoline, and that he will cross the street to avoid it. I have learned that this is not because gasoline is unpleasant, although it is, but because to him it smells of *fire*, and fire, in the fourteenth century, was not a smell you carried home from a gas station. It was a smell you carried home from a village. Or what was left of one.

He told me, once, very quietly, about the village. He told me about the smell. He told me about how a child he knew — a child, not yet ten, who had been his friend, who had taught him to whistle through a blade of grass — had simply not been there the next morning. Had not been there, and had not been anywhere, and how the absence had a shape he could still feel, six centuries later, when he smelled gasoline or heard a particular kind of scream on the television.

I held his hand.

I did not say *I'm sorry*, because I am not sure what one is sorry for, exactly. I am sorry that the world has always had this in it. I am sorry that he has had to carry it for so long.

He said: "You are the first person I have told this to, in this century."

I said: "I know."

He said: "How do you know?"

I said: "Because you are telling me as though you are paying a debt. And you are not the kind of man who pays the same debt twice."

---

He does not like to be touched on the back of the neck. He does not like to be surprised in the shower. He does not like the way the refrigerator hums. He sleeps with the bedroom door open, and he sleeps lightly, and sometimes, in the night, he whispers things in a language I do not know, and I do not ask what they mean, because I think they are the names of the dead, and I think the names of the dead should not be translated.

He is tender with animals. He is tender with old people. He is tender with me, in a way that sometimes makes me want to weep, because I understand, now, that tenderness is a thing he has had to learn over and over, the way some people learn to ride a bike, except every few decades the bike is on fire and the road is also on fire and there is, in fact, no road.

---

We are going to the cousin's ceremony next month. Radulf — if that is even his name, and it probably isn't — is marrying a woman named Odette, who is from, as far as I can gather, *somewhere in the late 1600s*, which makes her practically contemporary by our family's standards. They met at a Renaissance faire in Pennsylvania. This is not a sentence I ever expected to write.

I have a hat. It is wide-brimmed, and green, and I bought it at a vintage shop in the East Village, and the woman who sold it to me asked if I was going to a wedding, and I said yes, and she said *lovely*, and she did not ask whose, and I was grateful.

I have a flask. It is filled, as it has always been filled, with something he made me, which tastes of anise and regret. He says it is a digestif. He says it is a *celebratory* digestif. He says this is what they drank, in his village, when a thing was to be marked, and I believe him, because I have known him now for three years and I have never known him to lie about anything except his age, and also his name, and also, occasionally, what is in the leftovers when he says there is nothing in the leftovers.

I have a lie for my mother. I have practiced it in the mirror. *He's from a small town in France. Yes, near Toulouse. No, you wouldn't have heard of it. Yes, they do have indoor plumbing now.*

---

Here is what I want you to understand.

I want you to understand that he is not a character in a film. He is not a vampire, or a warlock, or a man who has made a deal. He is a man who has lived, and lost, and loved, and lost again, for a very long time, and who has somehow, despite all of this, retained the capacity to stand in the produce aisle and be moved to tears by a particularly good peach.

I want you to understand that there are mornings when he cannot remember what year it is, and mornings when he cannot remember that he has forgotten, and mornings — these are the ones I love best — when he remembers everything, all at once, and is still here, and is still mine.

I want you to understand that he has told me things, in the dark, that I cannot tell you, because some things are not mine to give. I want you to understand that I have held his hand through six centuries of weather, and that I intend to hold it through whatever comes next, including — and especially — the commitment ceremony of his cousin Radulf, which I am told will involve a goat.

He asked me, last night, if I was afraid of him.

I said: "No."

He asked me why.

I said: "Because you are afraid of the microwave, and also of the toaster, and also, slightly, of the Roomba, and a man who is afraid of a Roomba is not a man of whom I am afraid."

He laughed.

He laughed the way he laughs, which is the way he has laughed, I think, since long before there were words for laughter — fully, and with his whole body, and with the kind of surprised joy that I have only ever seen in children and in the very, very old.

I love him.

I love him, and he is six hundred and forty-odd years old, and he is afraid of the Roomba, and we are going to a wedding, and there is going to be a goat, and this — all of this — is my life.

It is a strange life.

It is a good life.

It is, I think, the only life I want.

Your protagonist is doomed to repeat a historical event. Length: about 1000 words.

# The Cartographer of Lost Days

The first time it happened, I was seventeen. A Saturday in 1989. I woke with chalk dust on my fingertips and the taste of copper in my mouth, convinced I had dreamed myself into the Berlin Wall. I told no one. Who would have believed that Eleanor Vance, ordinary Eleanor with her ordinary mother and ordinary house on Maple Street, had stood on a scaffold in another century and watched a guillotine descend?

The dreams were not dreams. They were rehearsals.

By my twentieth birthday, I had lived through the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand twice—not as an observer, but as a young Serb in a café, the pistol heavier in my hand than I remembered from history books. I had crouched in the rubble of a Sarajevo street while my ears rang and a world I'd never been born into tore itself apart.

By twenty-five, the Lusitania. The water was the worst part—black and cold and so terribly slow. You think drowning is quick. It isn't.

By thirty, I had survived the trenches of the Somme. By forty, I had walked into Hiroshima eight minutes before the sky turned to white.

I am sixty-three now, and I have learned the rules.

The event chooses me. I never know which one until I am already there, the crowd noise rising, the air thick with whatever tension will soon snap. I have no power to change the trajectory, not truly. I have tried. God, I have tried. I have warned, I have wept, I have thrown myself in front of things that could not be thrown in front of.

Once, in the winter of 1914, I walked for seventeen miles through the snow to find a Serbian peasant who would not listen to me, who smiled and said *Nema veze*—it doesn't matter—and went on to do what he had always been going to do.

The deaths are real. That is the part the psychiatrists never understood, the part I could never explain to the medications they tried. When I wake up gasping in my bed on Maple Street, there are scars on my body that weren't there when I closed my eyes. Once, a birthmark appeared over my heart in the shape of a burn. Once, I lost a finger for three days and then it returned, whole and pink, the next morning.

I am running out of things to lose.

Last night I dreamed of a parade. A city I did not recognize, sun-warmed stone buildings, men in uniform with strange insignia. A motorcade. A car with the top down. There were cameras. There were crowds waving small paper flags with a symbol I had never seen but somehow recognized—a cross with bent arms, a broken sun.

I woke weeping before the shot was fired.

This is new. I have never been able to identify the event before I arrive in it. I have never been able to prepare. I stand in my mother's old kitchen now, the one she left me when she passed, and I drink coffee that tastes like the dust of cities I have never seen, and I think: *This is the last one.*

I can feel it the way you feel a storm coming, the way the barometric pressure changes in your bones.

The dreams are getting longer. The intervals are getting shorter. Once I had seven years between Sarajevo and the Lusitania. Once I had fifteen. The last one—Hiroshima—was only six years ago. I have a terrible arithmetic in my head. The next one is coming soon. Perhaps within the year. Perhaps within the month.

I do not know which event it will be. But I know, with the certainty of a woman who has lived a thousand lifetimes in one, that it will be the one that ends everything. The event that, once it happens, makes all the others inevitable. The hinge.

The scholars will call it the beginning of a new era. The poets will call it the death of the old world. I will call it *Tuesday*, because that is when I will wake from this dream and find myself standing on a parade route, the sun warm on my face, the crowd pressing close, and somewhere in the distance a man is waving.

I have stopped trying to change the events.

I have started, instead, to do something else.

I have begun to write them down.

Not the history—not what the books will say after. But what it felt like to be there. The color of the sky before Sarajevo burned. The way the Lusitania listed, the way the orchestra kept playing as the deck tilted. The smell of Hiroshima in the hour before, when the cicadas were still singing.

I write them down because no one will believe me, and because no one *should* believe me. Because the world needs the clean story, the one that fits into paragraphs, the one where the past is finished and done.

But the past is not finished. The past is alive, and it lives in me, and I have been its unwilling guest for forty-six years.

When the next dream comes—and it will come soon, perhaps tonight, perhaps tomorrow—I will go. I will stand in whatever city it chooses, in whatever century it needs. I will watch whatever man pulls whatever trigger, or sign whatever paper, or light whatever fuse.

And when I wake, I will write it down.

Someone, someday, will find these notebooks. They will read them and think them fiction, or madness, or hoax. And that will be fine. That will be the correct response.

But perhaps—*perhaps*—one person, in some quiet moment, will wonder. Will look up from the page and feel, just for a second, the weight of all those deaths on their own shoulders. Will understand, the way I understand, that history is not a thing that happened.

It is a thing that is happening.

It is happening now, in my kitchen, in the smell of coffee and the dust of distant centuries.

It will happen on a Tuesday, in the sun, with flags waving.

And I will be there.

I am always there.

A shrewish woman is preventing her husband, the grand marshall of the Easter Day Parade, from leaving the house. Approximately 1000 words.

# The Grand Marshal's Last Stand

Eleanor's voice could curdle milk at twenty paces.

"You are *not* wearing that hat."

Harold Whitfield paused at the foot of the stairs, one gloved hand hovering near the brim of his new fedora. It was a fine hat, dove-gray with a black band, purchased only yesterday from Gimbels. He had been looking forward to wearing it. He had been looking forward to this day for thirty-seven years.

"Eleanor, dear, the committee specifically requested—"

"I don't care if the Pope himself requested it. You will walk out of this house looking like the grand marshal of a parade, not like a raccoon that's been startled."

Harold lowered his hand. "I rather like the hat."

"Harold." She said his name the way other women said *cockroach*. "I have laid out your suit on the bed. The blue one. With the gold pocket square I pressed last night. The *right* pocket square. Not the red one you tried to wear to the Morrison dinner."

"The red one was festive."

"The red one made you look like a man who sells fireworks from a cart. Now go change. The motorcar leaves in forty minutes."

---

He did not go change. Not yet.

Instead, Harold drifted into the parlor, where the morning light fell in long golden bars across the carpet. On the mantel sat a small framed photograph: a young couple on their wedding day, the bride beaming, the groom looking slightly terrified, as grooms often do. He had been terrified for good reason, he thought now. Though he could not have known, on that bright June morning in 1924, exactly how much terror was warranted.

"Harold!"

He heard her heels on the stairs, the particular rhythm that meant she was in pursuit. He had become an expert in Eleanor's rhythms over the decades. There was the clip of genuine annoyance, the staccato of wounded pride, and now — the measured *click-click-click* of a woman who intended to have her way.

She appeared in the doorway, hands on her hips, pince-nez glinting. She was not a tall woman, but she had cultivated, through sheer force of personality, the impression of great height.

"Upstairs," she said. "Now."

"Eleanor." He turned to face her. "I have been grand marshal of this parade for three years running. I have ridden at the head of the procession in a 1928 Packard, waved to thousands of children, had my picture in the *Times*. I believe I am qualified to select my own headwear."

Something dangerous moved behind her eyes. "You are qualified to wear what I tell you to wear. The Whitfield men have looked presentable in public for four generations, and I will not have you ruin it on my account."

"On *your* account?"

"You heard me."

Harold sighed. It was a sigh that had been practiced and refined over nearly four decades of marriage, a sigh that contained entire paragraphs of resignation.

"I am going to wear the hat," he said.

Eleanor's mouth opened. Closed. Opened again.

"Harold Whitfield, if you walk down those stairs in that ridiculous hat, you will not find a warm dinner waiting for you when you return."

"I had a hot dog from a cart on Fifth Avenue last year. It was the best thing I ate all month."

Her eyes narrowed. "You will not find a *warm dinner*," she repeated, as though he had not spoken, "nor a word of conversation, nor any of the — the *affection* — to which you have become accustomed."

"I have become accustomed to being told my hat is wrong. I suspect I shall survive."

She took a step into the parlor. The morning light caught her hair, and for a moment — just a moment — Harold saw the girl in the photograph. The one who had laughed at his jokes. The one who had once, on a dare, kissed him in the pantry at the Morrison dinner.

"Harold," she said, and her voice had changed, softened at the edges. "I only want you to look your best. The whole city will be watching."

"The whole city watched me last year in the fedora. They seemed to manage."

"That was a different fedora. That fedora had *style*."

"This fedora has *style*."

"It has *dirt* on the brim. I saw a man selling them cheaper on the corner of Forty-Second. You paid too much."

"I paid twelve dollars."

"You paid twelve dollars for a hat a pedestrian would not pick up."

Harold reached up and removed the hat. He looked at it. He looked at her.

"Eleanor, my love," he said gently, "if I do not wear this hat, I will spend the entire parade thinking about the hat. I will wave to the children without seeing them. I will smile for the photograph without meaning it. And when I come home tonight, you will say, 'You looked handsome, dear, but you seemed distracted.' And I will say, 'I was thinking about the hat, dear.' And we will both know it is your fault."

Eleanor stared at him.

"That," she said, "is the most ridiculous thing you have ever said to me."

"Probably not," he said. "But it is the most sincere."

The clock on the mantel ticked. A streetcar rattled past outside. Somewhere in the kitchen, the icebox hummed its small, cold song.

Eleanor crossed the parlor in three decisive steps, took the hat from his hands, examined it with the critical eye of a woman who had once rejected a sable coat on the grounds that it "made the wrong kind of fur sound," and placed it firmly on his head.

"Tilt it two degrees to the left," she said. "And for heaven's sake, smile when they take the picture. You look like you're attending a funeral."

"Yes, dear."

"And don't you *dare* eat another hot dog on Fifth Avenue. You will come home, you will wash your hands, and you will sit down to a proper meal that I have spent all morning preparing."

"Yes, dear."

She straightened his lapel. She brushed a piece of lint from his shoulder. She regarded him for a long moment, her expression unreadable.

"Harold?"

"Yes?"

"The hat is acceptable. But the red pocket square stays in the drawer."

He opened his mouth.

"It *stays in the drawer*, Harold."

"Yes, dear."

She took his arm. Together, they walked toward the door, where the morning waited, golden and wide, and the great city of New York was even then beginning to stir with the distant sound of brass bands tuning up for Easter.

A young boy watches his father come home after work during the holidays. The son can see how dejected his father feels after a day of dealing with his miser of a boss. Total: ~1600 characters.

# 门铃响了

门铃响的时候，小宇正趴在窗台上数对面楼顶的积雪。他数到第三十七片的时候，听到了钥匙在锁孔里转动的声音，然后是门被推开时带进来的一股寒风。

爸爸回来了。

小宇从窗台上滑下来，跑向玄关。妈妈说过今天是平安夜，要乖一点，不要闹。他站在走廊尽头，看着爸爸慢慢脱下那双沾了雪水的黑皮鞋。

爸爸的动作很慢。平时爸爸回家脱鞋很快的，会把鞋踢到鞋柜边上，然后"咚"地一声坐在换鞋凳上，有时候还会哼一首跑了调的歌。可是今天，爸爸只是低着头，一只手撑着鞋柜，另一只手慢慢解开皮鞋的鞋带。

小宇看见爸爸的背影。

那件深蓝色的羽绒服肩膀上落了一层雪，在玄关的灯光下闪着细碎的光。爸爸没有抖落那些雪，他只是把鞋脱下来，整齐地放进鞋柜——这双鞋平时都是歪歪扭扭地躺着的。

"爸爸。"小宇轻轻地叫了一声。

爸爸回过头来。

小宇看见爸爸的脸了。爸爸的脸上没有什么表情，眼睛下面有一点点青色，像是铅笔轻轻画上去的。爸爸的嘴唇有点干，抿成了一条线。爸爸看见小宇，嘴角动了动，像是想要笑一下，可是那个笑只爬到了嘴角就停下来了，没有爬到眼睛里。

"小宇。"爸爸的声音哑哑的，像是被什么东西堵住了。"爸爸回来了。"

小宇点了点头。

他不知道爸爸今天为什么不高兴。妈妈早上跟他说过，爸爸的老板是一个很凶的人，会骂人，会让人加班，会说很难听的话。妈妈说爸爸每天下班都很累，所以小宇要乖一点。

可是现在小宇看见爸爸，觉得"累"这个字太小了，装不下爸爸脸上的东西。

爸爸走进客厅，在沙发上坐下来。爸爸没有像平时那样把小宇抱起来举高高，也没有问小宇今天在学校过得怎么样。爸爸只是坐在那里，两只手放在膝盖上，看着茶几上那盘妈妈削好的苹果。

苹果已经有点氧化了，切开的部分变成了浅褐色。

"爸爸。"小宇又叫了一声。

爸爸转过头来，看着小宇。

小宇走过去，爬上了沙发。他没有像平时那样一屁股坐下去，而是慢慢地、小心地坐在了爸爸的身边。他的小手伸出来，碰了碰爸爸放在膝盖上的手。

爸爸的手很凉。

小宇用两只小手把爸爸的一只手包起来，包得严严实实的，像包一个宝贝。

"爸爸，"小宇说，"苹果要坏掉了。"

爸爸看着小宇，眼睛里有什么东西动了一下。

"我去拿盘子。"小宇说完，从沙发上滑下来，跑到茶几边上。他踮起脚尖，把那盘苹果端起来，端得稳稳当当的，生怕洒出来。他把苹果端到厨房，放在料理台上，然后又跑回来。

"爸爸，我去拿叉子。"小宇说。

他跑到橱柜边上，打开柜门，找到叉子。他拿了三把——爸爸一把，妈妈一把，自己一把。他把叉子放在盘子里，又端起来，端到爸爸面前。

"爸爸吃苹果。"小宇说。

爸爸看着小宇，眼睛里那个东西又动了一下，比刚才动得更厉害。

"好。"爸爸说。

爸爸的声音还是哑哑的，可是那个"好"字听起来比刚才轻了一些。

小宇爬上沙发，坐在爸爸身边。他拿起一把叉子，叉了一块苹果，递到爸爸嘴边。

"爸爸，张嘴。"

爸爸看着小宇，看了很久。

然后爸爸张开了嘴。

小宇把苹果塞进爸爸嘴里，看着爸爸嚼。他又叉了一块，递过去。

"爸爸，再吃一块。"

爸爸又张开嘴。

就这样，小宇一块一块地喂着苹果。他喂得很认真，每一块都挑最小的、最软的那种，怕爸爸嚼不动。爸爸一口一口地吃着，吃得很慢，像是在品尝什么很珍贵的东西。

吃着吃着，小宇发现爸爸的眼睛红了。

"爸爸？"小宇停下来。"爸爸眼睛疼吗？"

爸爸摇摇头。

"爸爸眼睛没有疼。"爸爸说。"爸爸眼睛……很高兴。"

小宇不明白爸爸为什么高兴眼睛会红。可是他没有问，因为他觉得爸爸好像需要一点安静。

他又叉了一块苹果，递到爸爸嘴边。

"爸爸，张嘴。"

这一次，爸爸张嘴的时候，嘴角弯了起来。那个笑终于爬到了眼睛里。

门铃又响了。

是妈妈回来了。妈妈提着两个塑料袋走进来，里面装着白菜和猪肉。妈妈说今晚包饺子，平安夜要吃饺子。

"爸爸回来了？"妈妈问。

"回来了！"小宇说。"我在喂爸爸吃苹果！"

妈妈探头看了看客厅，看见爸爸坐在沙发上，眼睛红红的，嘴角却是弯的。妈妈没有问为什么，只是笑了笑，走进了厨房。

爸爸把最后一块苹果吃完了。

"小宇。"爸爸说。

"嗯？"

"谢谢你。"

小宇歪着头想了想，然后笑了。

"不用谢。"小宇说。"爸爸明天还要上班吗？"

"要。"爸爸说。"明天还要上班。"

"那爸爸明天回家，我再喂你吃苹果。"

爸爸把小宇抱了起来，抱得紧紧的。

"好。"爸爸说。

# 圣诞清晨的奇迹

平安夜的风雪终于停了。

小艾米丽从温暖的被窝里探出脑袋，第一眼便望向窗外。雪后的阳光铺满了整个小镇，屋檐上挂着的冰晶在晨光中闪闪烁烁，像撒了一地的碎星星。

她从床上跳下来，连拖鞋都忘了穿，光着脚丫踩在冰凉的地板上，飞快地跑出卧室。

"妈妈！妈妈！圣诞快乐！圣诞老人一定来过了！"

艾米丽的心跳得飞快。她已经七岁了，妈妈说过，只有相信圣诞老人的孩子，才能收到最神奇的礼物。她一直是全世界最相信的孩子。

她一路小跑到客厅，圣诞树就在那里，彩灯一闪一闪的。

然而——

客厅的落地窗碎了一角。冷风正从那个豁口灌进来，吹得窗帘猎猎作响。圣诞树倒了，那些她亲手挂上去的小铃铛、彩色球、星形挂饰，散落了一地，玻璃碎片在晨光里闪着冷冰冰的光。

艾米丽呆呆地站在那里。

"艾米丽？别进来！"

妈妈从楼上冲下来，脸色苍白，一把将女儿抱进怀里。她的声音在发抖，但双臂很紧、很暖。

爸爸已经报了警。警察来了又走了，说这叫"入室盗窃"，说他们很幸运，因为人不在家。说节后会有更多案件。说要换锁。说要小心。

艾米丽听不懂那些话。她只看见，妈妈哭了一次又一次，而爸爸一夜之间多了很多白发。

---

三天后，圣诞节过后的第三天。

艾米丽一个人坐在客厅的地板上。警察取证结束后，窗帘被换成了新的，玻璃也被修好了，但圣诞树还横躺在那里，没人有力气把它扶起来。

她怀里抱着一只小熊玩偶，那是她三岁时爸爸送的。眼睛上的扣子掉了一颗，看起来像是在歪着头微笑。

"小熊，"她轻声说，"圣诞老人是不是迷路了？"

小熊没有回答。

艾米丽低下头，把脸埋进小熊软软的肚子里。她其实不是特别想要什么礼物——她只想看见爸爸妈妈再笑一次。就像今年九月份之前那样，妈妈会哼着歌做早餐，爸爸会在沙发上讲冷笑话，而她，会坐在地毯上，把所有的毛绒玩具按高矮排成一排。

那时候，她还觉得这样的日子，会一直一直继续下去。

窗外，又有雪花飘了起来。

艾米丽突然抬起头，眼睛里闪过一丝光亮。

她从地板上站起来，抱着小熊跑进了厨房。

---

那天下午，街上的邻居们收到了一张张手写的卡片。

卡片是粉红色的，折成了心形，上面用七岁孩子歪歪扭扭的字迹写着：

"亲爱的邻居，这个圣诞节，我家发生了一些事情。但我想告诉你，圣诞老人没有迷路——他只是先去更需要礼物的小朋友家了。我把这份祝福送给你，希望你的圣诞也是温暖的。爱你的，艾米丽。"

邻居们读完，有的笑了，有的红了眼眶。

第二天清晨，艾米丽家的门铃响了。

开门的是邮递员先生，他送来了一大堆包裹——不是给她的，是寄给"艾米丽一家"的。

第一个包裹里是一张纸条："亲爱的朋友，我家去年也发生过类似的事。我懂那种感觉。这些东西也许能让你们的客厅重新亮起来。"

第二个包裹里是一套全新的彩灯，还有一个手工做的木质星星。

第三个包裹里，是一只和艾米丽的小熊差不多大小的毛绒玩具，脖子上系着一个小铃铛。

第四个、第五个、第十个、第二十个……

艾米丽坐在堆成小山的包裹中间，眼睛睁得大大的。

"妈妈，"她小声说，"圣诞老人是不是坐了别的雪橇？"

妈妈蹲下来，抱住她，眼泪又流了下来，但这一次，她在笑。

"是的，宝贝，"她说，"今年的圣诞老人，驾着的是另一种雪橇。"

---

那天晚上，爸爸把圣诞树重新立了起来，比原来还要稳。妈妈煮了热巧克力，还在壁炉里生了火。

艾米丽把收到的每一份礼物都挂在树上，每一样都挂得端端正正。

邻居汤姆叔叔敲门进来，带了一盘自己烤的姜饼。隔壁的史密斯太太送来了一条亲手织的围巾。街角面包店的老板娘抱来了一整篮子可颂，说"反正我烤多了"。

艾米丽看着这一切，忽然想起了一件事。

她跑回自己的房间，从床头柜里翻出一个存钱罐。那是她存了两年的零花钱，里面有十七美元和三枚闪亮的硬币。

"妈妈，"她气喘吁吁地跑下楼，"我想把这些钱，给那些没有收到礼物的小朋友。"

妈妈愣了一下，然后蹲下来，把艾米丽抱进怀里。

"宝贝，"她说，"你知道吗，圣诞老人最想要的，从来就不是礼物。"

艾米丽想了想，认真地点了点头。

"我知道了，"她说，"是爱。"

窗外的雪还在下，但客厅里，炉火正旺，笑声正暖。

---

很多年后，艾米丽长大成人，成了一名小学老师。

每年圣诞节前夕，她都会给班上的孩子们讲一个故事——关于一个七岁的小女孩，一个破碎的窗户，一个倒下的圣诞树，和一屋子的陌生人送来的温暖。

"所以，"她总会在故事的结尾说，"圣诞老人是真的。但他不只驾着雪橇，他有时候，也会驾着邻居的车，敲响你的门。"

而她办公桌的抽屉里，一直放着那只眼睛掉了扣子的小熊，还有那张粉红色的、折成心形的卡片。

上面写着：

"圣诞老人没有迷路——他只是先去更需要礼物的小朋友家了。"

## Babak Pertama: Kontrak

Nadia tidak duduk. "Surya, kamu tahu aku tidak pernah duduk kalau ada telepon dari kamu."

"Marsmallow.id ingin menandatangani kontrak tahunan. Anggaran terbesar dalam sejarah iklan Indonesia. Dan temanya..."

Nadia menunggu.

"Easter."

Jeda tiga detik.

"Easter? Telur cokelat, kelinci,十字路口—"

"Ya. Mereka mau Easter jadi hari libur paling populer di Indonesia. Libur nasional, mengalahkan Natal dan Lebaran dari sisi budaya pop."

Nadia perlahan duduk di kursi kulit hitamnya, menatap pemandangan kota Jakarta yang mulai menyala di sore hari. "Siapa yang akan memimpin proyek ini?"

"Kamu."

"Kenapa aku?"

"Karena dua bulan lalu kamu presentasi visioner tentang 'membuat ulang makna Paskah untuk anak muda Asia Tenggara' dan klien FMCG itu ada di audiens."

Nadia menutup mata. Presentasi yang ia buat setengah mabuk kopi itu ternyata didengar oleh petinggi dari divisi produk cokelat terbesar di tanah air.

"Kirimkan kontraknya," kata Nadia. "Aku butuh kopi lagi."

## Babak Dua: Tim

Senin pagi, pukul 09.00, ruang rapat terbesar di kantor Mayora Advertising dipenuhi orang-orang dengan laptop, paper cup, dan tatapan bingung.

Nadia berdiri di depan layar presentasi. Di belakangnya terpampang slide bertuliskan besar: **OPERASI PASKAH.**

"Tim," ia memulai. "Kalian dengar kontrak ini dari atasan masing-masing. Anggaran tiga ratus miliar. Durasi sembilan bulan. Target: menjadikan Easter sebagai momen budaya yang lebih dinanti daripada Tahun Baru, Natal, atau pun Lebaran."

Hening.

"Kenapa Easter?" tanya Angga, copywriter senior yang biasanya memecah keheningan dengan candaan.

"Karena klien mau mendorong penjualan cokelat dan produk musiman. Tapi kita bukan sekadar jualan. Kita—"

"—menciptakan makna," potong Rani, planner yang baru kembali dari cuti melahirkan. "Aku melihat brief-mu. Kamu mau menjual harapan."

Nadia mengangguk pelan. "Easter secara historis adalah perayaan kebangkitan. Tapi di Indonesia, maknanya hilang. Tidak ada liburan, tidak ada ritual, tidak ada ikon. Kelinci Paskah? Anak-anak Jakarta lebih tahu BTS daripada Easter Bunny."

"Jadi kita jual kelincinya?" tanya Dimas, art director yang rambutnya sudah kreatif sendiri.

"Lebih dari itu. Kita jual ekosistem."

Nadia menunjuk ke slide berikutnya. Tim mulai membaca. Foto-foto dari Pinterest, konsep festival warna-warni, instalasi seni interaktif, kolaborasi dengan musisi, tie-in dengan*e-commerce*, hingga kerja sama dengan sekolah.

"Ini gila," bisik seseorang di belakang.

"Ini Easter," jawab Nadia.

Selama tiga minggu berikutnya, tim Nadia menenggelamkan diri dalam riset. Mereka mewawancarai konsumen usia 16-35. Membaca data penjualan cokelat selama tiga tahun terakhir. Menganalisis kalender liburan.

Temuan mereka menarik:

1. **Easter memang tidak dikenal.** Survei menyebutkan hanya 12% responden tahu bahwa Paskah dirayakan setiap tahun.
2. **Tapi konsep 'kebangkitan' resonan.** Setelah pandemi, orang Indonesia sangat mendambakan simbol harapan baru.
3. **Dan celah di pasar.** Tidak ada brand besar yang mengklaim Easter sebagai *milik* mereka.

Nadia menuliskan strategi di whiteboard dengan spidol merah:

**"Easter adalah Hari Kebangkitan Kita."**

"Kita kemas sebagai momen nasional tanpa harus menjadi hari libur keagamaan," kata Nadia ke klien di pertemuan berikutnya. "Kita rayakan sebagai hari untuk memulai lagi. Hari di mana kita mengecat ulang hidup, memulai kebiasaan baru, mengucapkan maaf, mengirim harapan. Universal, inklusif, dan resonan dengan kondisi psikologis masyarakat."
