# 初日の出と、新しい椅子

---

正月の朝、海沿いの温泉旅館の大広間は、すでにざわめいていた。

まどかは廊下を歩きながら、自分の心臓の音を意識的に数えた。 one、 two、 three。それでも靴下の下のつま先が冷たい。旅館の廊下は、ことりと古い木の香りを纏っている。突き当たりにある宴会場の襖一枚の向こうに、家族が待っている。

——新しい、家族が。

まどかが二十七の夏、父は再婚した。相手は父の中学からの友人だったという女性、紗英（さえ）。母を亡くしてから四年。父はようやく「誰かのために、味噌汁をもう一椀よそおう」と思える人を見つけたらしい。紗英には連れ子がいた。結人（ゆいと）、二十一歳の大学生。年の離れた兄と妹。父はそれを「家族が増えた」と言ったが、まどかにとっては、何かが壊されたのではなく、何かが「もうひとつ、増えた」感覚だった。増えすぎたコップを食器棚にしまい直すような、どこか収まりきらない手触り。

「まどか、起きているの」

背後から、紗英の穏やかな声。旅館の浴衣の上にダウンジャケットを羽織った姿は、どこかお母さんのようでもあった。まどかは「うん」とだけ答える。紗英はそれに頓着せず、まどかの隣に並んで歩き出した。

「結人がね、今朝は結人とお父さんの二人で初日の出を見に行くって、張り切ってるの」

「はいはい」

「一緒に来なかったら怒ると思うよ、まどかにも」

「怒るって。二十一のお兄さんに」

「もう、意地なのよ、あの人は」

紗英が小さく笑う。笑い方を真似したわけではないのに、目が細くなるカーブだけはなぜか似ていた。まどかはそれに気づかないふりをして、襖に手をかけた。

---

宴会場には丸い卓がひとつ。旅館側が「ご家族団らん用」と用意してくれたのだろう。十人は余裕で座れる大きな輪だった。

すでに父がいた。浴衣に半纏をはおった、いつもの「父さんの正月」。結人は隣にいて、フードのついたパーカーをごく自然に着込んでいる。色は大晦日の夜に初詣に行ったときと同じ、深い緑。紗英が「新しい家族に新しい色を」とその時に買ってくれたものだった。

「まどか、おはよう」

父が顔を上げた。その声のトーンが、去年までと少しだけ違う。声というより空気に、誰かがもう一人いることが前提として織り込まれているような。

「おはようございます」

まどかは円卓を半周して、父の向かいに座った。父の右手が紗英、左手は空いている。空いている左手の隣が、まどかのいつもの位置だった。紗英と結人の間にもう一脚、椅子がある。

——あ、ここが私だったの。

そういうことが、空間ごと入れ替わったような気がした。

「で、結人が張り切ってね」父が結人のことを口にする時、少しだけ語尾が柔らくなる。「日の出、見えるかって」

「見えるよ、ここ」結人は窓の外を指さした。旅館は崖の上に建っていて、真正面に太平洋が広がっている。「朝五時四十二分、日の出。スマホの天気予報で見た」

「え、もうそんな時間？」

まどかが壁の柱時計を見る。五時三十五分。卓の上には既に、旅館の女将さんが運んでくれたお節が並んでいた。黒豆、数の子、紅白なます、慈姑（くわい）、田作り。蓋付きの重箱の蓋を取ると、湯気が白い息のように立ちのぼった。

「さあ、食べる前に」父が重箱のふたを持ち上げて、じっと見つめた。「今年初の乾杯、しようか」

「お屠蘇（とそ）でしょう」紗英が小さな徳利を取り上げた。「旅館の方が、ちゃんと用意してくれてたの」

「母さんの頃は」結人が何気なく言いかけて、口を噤んだ。

卓の上の空気が、一瞬だけ張り詰めた。

「……うん」

父が、静かに頷いた。母さんは、屠蘇ではなくワインを一杯だけ舐めるのが正月だった。好きだったぶどうのスパークリングを、父が毎年買ってきて、仏壇に少しだけ注いだ。

「紗英が今年は——」父が言い淀んだ。「ぶどうのスパークリングも買ってきたんだよ。一本」

紗英が小さく目を伏せた。結人の箸がぴたりと止まった。まどかは自分の掌を見ている。

「……一緒に出してもいい？」

父が聞いた。声は震えてはいなかった。ただ、探っていた。

「いいよ」

最初に答えたのは、結人だった。

「いいよ。母さんの分も、紗英さんの分も、ってことでしょ」

「——うん」

「ぼく、お酒飲めないけど、ぶどうジュースでいいなら混ぜてもらっていい？」

結人が笑った。少しだけ照れたような、でもどこか誇らしげな笑みだった。

紗英がふっと息を吐いて、結人の頭をくしゃくしゃと撫でた。結人は「やめて」と言うけれど避けなかった。

まどかはそれを見ていた。母さんが結いをほどくとき、くしゃくしゃと髪を撫でていたのを思い出した。違う手だ。違う人だ。でも温度は、たぶんそんなに遠くはなかった。

「まどかは」

紗英がこちらを見た。

「まどかは、どうする？」

「……」

まどかは、父と紗英の顔を見比べ、それから結人を見た。結人はぶどうジュースのグラスを高く掲げていた。

「……同じにする。ぶどうの、混ぜてもらう」

「いいね」

紗英が立ち上がって、小さなワインボトルからスパークリングを注いだ。泡が立ちのぼる。結人の分と、まどかの分。父には屠蘇が注がれ、紗英の分はうっすらと色づいたお茶だった。

「それじゃ」父がグラスを掲げた。「今年、初の、家族の、乾杯を」

四つのグラスが、円卓の上で小さな音を鳴らした。

---

日の出は、予定通りだった。

結人が「来た！」と叫んだときには、水平線の向こうがもう白く割けていた。紗英が目を細めて、父が黙って手を合わせて、まどかは水平線の端を見つめていた。日の出は一人ずつ違う色を連れてくる。今朝は薄い山吹色から少し濃い蜜柑色へと変わっていった。

「きれいだね」紗英が言った。

「うん」

まどかは答えた。

結人がスマホで写真を撮っている。父と紗英の横顔、後ろ姿、それから水平線だけ。シャッター音が四回鳴って、結人はそれからくるりと振り返った。

「まどかも、入るよ」

「え」

「ほら」

結人がスマホを旅館の女将さんに渡している。女将さんは慣れた手つきで頷いて、スマホを受け取った。「はい、はい、並ばれて」

紗英がまどかの肩にそっと手を置いた。「行きなさい」と囁く。

まどかは、父の隣に立った。紗英が反対側に立ち、結人が真ん中に入った。シャッターが鳴る。

「もう一枚」結人が言った。「まどか、笑って」

「笑ってるけど」

「目だけで笑ってる。口も笑って」

「うるさいな」

「はい、はい、もう一枚」女将さんが笑った。

シャッターが鳴る。今度は、たぶん笑えていた。

---

朝食は、そこからだった。

お節をつつき、雑煮を啜る。旅館の雑煮は白味噌仕立てで、里芋と鶏肉が入っていた。母さんの実家が出身だった北の土地は、白味噌にすこしだけ塩気が効いた汁だった。紗英は箸を止めて、結人の椀にそっと餅を足してやった。結人は「自分で取れる」と小声で言うが、受け取る。

父が雑煮を啜る音は昔と同じだった。すこし音を立てるのを母さんに怒られていたのを、まどかも結人も紗英も知っている。

「あのさ」

結人が、お重の蓋をそっと閉じながら言った。

「さっき、ぶどうのスパークリング。ぼく、最初ちょっと — っとなったんだけど、おいしかった。母さんの味なのかは、ぼくには正直わからない。でも」

結人は父を見た。

「お父さんが、嬉しそうだったから、ぼくもうれしかった」

「……」

父は何も言わなかった。ただ、箸を置いた。

紗英が結人の膝をぽんと叩いた。「もう、変なこと言って、泣かせないで」

「泣いてない」

「泣いてる」

「泣いてない！」

父が笑った。こらえきれないような笑い方で、目元を指の甲で拭った。

まどかは自分の椀を見つめている。白味噌の湯気が、まだ細く立ち昇っていた。

——たぶん、私もだ。

思ってもみなかった言葉が、自分の内で静かに形になっていた。

母さんが好きだったぶどう。母さんが亡くなったあとも、毎正月に父が注いできたぶどうのスパークリング。母さん一人分の死者への手向けだったそれがいま、父、紗英、結人、まどかの四人の間で巡っている。母さんが知らない味の隣に座る誰かのために。

これは「置き換え」ではないのだ、と思う。ぶどうはぶどうのままだし、屠蘇は屠蘇だ。ただ卓がひとつ大きくなり、椅子がひとつ増え、誰かが「混ぜてもいい？」と聞いて、それを誰かが「いいよ」と返す。そういうことだ。

「紗英さん」

まどかは口を開いていた。自分でも少し驚いていた。

「来年の正月は、お節に何が入ってる？」

紗英は少し目を見開いた。

「え？ 来年？」

「うん。紗英さんのお実家では、何か入れるの。うちは母さんの頃は——」

まどかは一度言葉を切った。

「——うん、なんでも教えて」

紗英は、少しだけ目を細めた。泣きそうな、でも笑おうとしているような顔だった。

「うちはね、関西だからね。たつくり——って言うの、ごまめ。あと、たたきごぼう。入れるのよ」

「たたきごぼう」結人が繰り返した。「それ、おいしいの？」

「おいしいわよ。紗英が作る？」紗英は父に聞いた。

「え、ああ」父が驚いたように言った。「僕が？ 作るか」

「そうよ。来年は、まどかと紗英と三人でお節作りましょう」

「ぼくは？」

「結人は、数の子の薄皮むき」

「え——」

紗英が立ち上がって、結人の肩をぽんと叩いた。

「いいじゃない、家族でしょう」

結人は困った顔をして、まどかを振り返った。まどかは思わずにやっと笑った。口の端まで、ちゃんと。

---

食事の後、みんなで旅館の廊下を歩いた。父と紗英が先に、結人とまどかがその後ろ。

廊下の突き当たりに、神棚があった。旅館の守り神さま。紗英が立ち止まって、小さく手を合わせた。結人も倣った。父はそれを見て目を細めていた。

「あのさ」結人が言った。「紗英さん、お祈りしてたの、何をお願いしてたの」

紗英は少し考える顔をした。「さあ、なんでしょうね。教えないわ」

「ずるい」

「あなたに教えたら、お賽銭が足りないでしょう」

紗英が笑った。結人も笑った。

「まどかは？」結人が聞いた。「ぼくのことも教えて」

「教えない」

「え——」

「みんなそうよ。神さまだけ教えてあげられるの」

結人が不満そうに鼻を鳴らした。でもそのあとに、小さく呟いた。

「紗英さんのそういうとこ、お母さんに似てる」

紗英は目を丸くした。

「……そう？」

「うん。意地悪なところ」

「意地悪じゃないでしょう」

「意地悪だよ。ぼくたちのこといじわるするくせに、嫌いになれないとこ」

紗英は何も言わなかった。ただ、廊下の窓の外を見ながら、静かに目を細めていた。

父と紗英が先に廊下の角を曲がる。結人はそれに続いた。まどかは、少しだけ取り残されて、自分の足音に耳を澄ませた。

——お祈り、何にしよう。

母さんの仏壇は、旅館の部屋にもあった。紗英が気を利かせて、小さなお盆を用意してくれていた。旅館側が、とは思えなかった。水向けの花と、線香の香りと、ぶどうのスパークリングがほんの少し残った小さな瓶。

まどかは神棚にむかってではなく、旅館の自室に戻る廊下で、自分の足元に手を合わせた。

来る年も、ぶどうのスパークリングが注がれますように。
結人兄さんが、お節の薄皮むきを、来年も文句を言いながらくれますように。
父さんが、白味噌の雑煮を、変わらず音を立てて啜れますように。
紗英さんが、「意地悪」だと笑われますように。

まどかは目を閉じた。

——そして、来年の正月に、あの円卓に、私たち四人がまた、座れますように。

---

旅館の中庭に出ると、風が少し冷たくなっていた。太平洋の水平線はもう白く光っている。

父が、紗英の手をそっと取った。紗英は少し驚いて、でもすぐにその手を握り返した。

結人が後ろから小さく口笛を吹いた。「おーい、おい」

「何」父が振り返った。

「いやなんでもない」結人はパーカーのポケットに両手を突っ込んだ。

「もー、からかわないの」紗英が窘めた。

「ぼくはからかってない」

「からかってるでしょう」

「紗英さんのそういうとこ、お母さんに似てる」

「もう、結人！」

笑い声が、潮風に紛れていった。

まどかは少しだけ遅れて、彼らの後ろを歩いた。指先は、相変わらず冷たかった。 でもそれはもう、怖いからではなく、朝の海風に当たったせいだけだった。

円卓は、明日には片付けられて、また違う家族のものになるだろう。けれど、椅子は四脚だった。その四脚の上に座るそれぞれの人の重みは、もう、ちゃんとここに在る。

それは、喪失の置き換えではなかった。
それは、喪失のうえに積み上げられた、新しい時間だった。

まどかは、水平線を背にして、家族の後ろ姿を見つめた。

「おい、まどか！」結人が振り返った。「お父さんが、おみくじ引こうって！」

「はいはい、今行く」

まどかは駆け出した。

四人の足音が、旅館の石畳に、やがて重なる。

# The Night the Lights Came Back

The Wellingtons' annual Christmas party was supposed to be the event of the season. Fourteen years running, their townhouse on Maple Lane had drawn the neighborhood like clockwork—warm mulled wine, twinkling lights, the mayor's wife handing out homemade cookies that everyone pretended not to fight over.

This year, everything was perfect. Too perfect, perhaps, for the universe to allow.

It started with the tree. Margaret Wellington had spent three hours stringing twelve hundred lights across a twelve-foot Douglas fir, and her husband Harold had stood on the ladder handing them up like surgical instruments. Then, just as the first guests began arriving—old Mr. Pemberton from three doors down, the young Hendersons with their new baby, the cantankerous Mr. Cho who never came to anything but somehow came to this—Margaret reached for the plug.

And the entire block went dark.

A transformer had blown somewhere on the street. Not just their house—the whole neighborhood, stretching three blocks in every direction. The oven full of hams, the mulled wine warming on the stove, the baby monitor Mrs. Henderson had plugged in downstairs—all dead. People stood in the Wellington foyer holding casseroles and wine bottles, looking at each other in the dim glow of a single flashlight Harold had found in the junk drawer.

"Well," said Mr. Pemberton, who was eighty-four and had seen worse, "this is awkward."

Mr. Cho, who was standing by the door with his coat still on, muttered something that sounded like "I knew I shouldn't have come."

The baby started crying. The smoke alarm, somehow disturbed by the power surge, began its dying, intermittent beep. Someone's cell phone rang, muffled, in a coat pocket.

Margaret Wellington looked at her husband. Harold looked at the tree. The tree looked back, dark and silent, no longer the centerpiece of the season but a twelve-foot monument to their bad luck.

"We're not going to let this ruin everything," Harold said, in the voice of a man who had absolutely no idea how to prevent that.

And then, quite softly, the doorbell rang.

No one was at the door.

Harold opened it anyway, because that was the sort of thing you did when nothing else was working. Standing on the welcome mat was a woman he had never seen before—small, perhaps seventy, wrapped in a coat the color of cranberries, with a face like a dried apple and eyes that seemed to have a candle behind them.

"Well now," she said, looking past him into the dim foyer. "You're in a bit of a state, aren't you?"

"I'm sorry," Harold began, "I don't think we've—"

"No, we haven't met." She stepped inside without being invited, which Margaret would normally have minded, but the smoke alarm chose that moment to give a particularly mournful wail, and Margaret had bigger problems. "I'm Alma. I live on Birch Street."

"The street with the transformer," Mr. Pemberton said darkly.

"The very one." Alma unbuttoned her coat. Beneath it, she wore what could only be described as an extremely festive sweater, featuring a reindeer whose antlers appeared to be made of actual twigs. "I thought you might need a hand."

"We need a utility crew, is what we need," Mr. Cho said.

"Oh, we don't need anything of the sort," Alma said pleasantly. She reached into her enormous bag—bigger on the inside than it looked on the outside, which Margaret noticed but decided to file away—and produced a candelabra. Not an electric one. A candelabra with actual candles in it.

She set it on the entryway table. She struck a match. She lit all five candles at once, which Margaret would have struggled to do with a long fireplace match.

And the foyer came alive with warm, golden light.

The smoke alarm stopped beeping. Nobody mentioned this. Everyone was too busy staring.

"There," Alma said. "Better."

Margaret felt the strange compulsion to apologize. "I'm sorry, I don't mean to be rude, but—how did you do that?"

"Years of practice." Alma was already moving toward the kitchen, where she began opening drawers with the confidence of a woman who had owned the house. She found matches, more candles, a pack of birthday candles for the cake Margaret had not yet gotten to frost. She lit them all. She set them in jars, on plates, in a gravy boat. She arranged them on the dining table like a constellation.

Harold, who had gone very quiet, finally spoke. "Are you, by any chance, some sort of—?"

"Magical?" Alma smiled. It made her look younger, though not young. "Oh, heavens. No. I'm a retired librarian. I just pay attention."

"To what?"

"To the small things," Alma said. She handed him a candle in a mason jar. "Here. Go light the hallway."

And so it began.

By the time Alma had made her way through the ground floor, the party had found its second wind. People who had been standing in awkward clusters were now sitting on the floor, on the stairs, in the bay window seat. They passed around cookies and wine, which someone had thoughtfully brought, and told stories they wouldn't have told with the lights on.

Mr. Pemberton, it turned out, had once been a chorus boy. He stood up—slowly, with Margaret's help—and sang a snippet of something from a 1962 musical that no one in the room had ever heard of, but everyone loved. Mrs. Henderson passed the baby around, and the baby, who had been screaming for an hour, fell peacefully asleep in the arms of Mr. Cho, who held him as if he had been doing it his whole life.

The young couple from the second floor—the ones who always came late and left early—sat by the tree in the candlelight and whispered to each other in a way that suggested a small announcement was coming.

And Alma moved through it all, lighting candles, straightening garlands, smiling her apple-face smile. She poured wine for people. She found the matches in Mr. Pemberton's coat pocket that he had been searching for. She pulled a perfect sprig of holly from her bag and pinned it to Margaret's collar without asking.

"I don't understand," Margaret said, finding her in the kitchen an hour later. "The smoke alarm. You just—you just looked at it, and it stopped."

"Did I?" Alma seemed honestly surprised. "Oh. Well. I suppose I did."

"Who are you?"

Alma considered this. "I'm a woman who has had a very long time to learn that the lights going out is not the worst thing that can happen at a party. In fact, it might be the best."

"But—"

"Shh." Alma pressed something into Margaret's hand. It was a small, smooth stone, warm as if it had been sitting in the sun. "Keep that in your pocket. Whenever the power goes out—and it will, eventually, it always does—you'll find you have everything you need."

Margaret looked at the stone. When she looked up, Alma was gone. Her cranberry coat hung over the kitchen chair. Her enormous bag sat empty by the door. Outside, snow had begun to fall—fat, lazy flakes that seemed to glow in the candlelight from every window on Maple Lane.

The power came back at 11:47 p.m., just as Harold was telling the story of how he had proposed to Margaret, which he told every year and which never got less embarrassing or less sweet. The lights snapped on, the tree blazed to life, the oven began to hum.

The party cheered. The baby woke up and started crying again. Mr. Pemberton sat down with great dignity and accepted a cookie.

And Margaret Wellington, standing in her suddenly bright kitchen, reached into her pocket and felt the smooth, warm stone.

It was still there. It was still warm.

She didn't tell anyone about Alma. Harold would have thought she was being fanciful. The Hendersons would have worried. Mr. Cho would have said something grumpy.

But the next year, when the lights went out—because of course they did, a squirrel in the transformer this time—Margaret lit the candles herself. And the year after that. And the year after that.

And every year, on the night of the party, there was a sprig of holly on her collar that she had not put there.

And every year, the stone in her pocket was warm.

And every year, the lights came back just in time to see the magic.

Write about someone who goes to great lengths to avoid being pranked on April 1st, only to realize they had the date wrong and it’s already April 2nd. Roughly 1800 characters in length.

# 愚人节的迟到者

李明从凌晨三点就开始了准备工作。

闹钟还没响，他就蹑手蹑脚地爬起来，把卧室门用胶带封了一圈，又在门缝里塞了一根细线——线的另一端系着一只空罐头盒。任何试图推门而入的"不速之客"，都会先被这简陋却有效的警报系统出卖。

厨房里，他把所有瓶瓶罐罐都贴上了标签："这不是盐""这不是糖""这不是可乐"。冰箱门上贴着一张A4纸，用加粗的红笔写着：**今日任何可疑的邀请、告白、突发事件，均视为恶作剧。**

五点半，他在客厅的各个角落安装了"陷阱"——地板上撒了些面粉作为足迹探测器，茶几上摆了一杯"水"（其实是白醋），并在显眼处放了一个假手机，屏幕永远定格在"妻子来电"。这是他的钓鱼陷阱——谁要是忍不住偷看，那泛白的屏幕后面绝对藏着让他社死的视频。

"咖啡机坏了。"室友张伟揉着眼睛走出房间，"你怎么起这么早？"

"今天是愚人节。"李明头也不抬地说，继续往门把手上系铃铛。

张伟愣了一下，然后笑出声来："就为了这个？你也太——"

"太什么？"李明警惕地盯着他。

"太认真了。"张伟耸耸肩，"兄弟，去年你被骗了接个饭？"

"两次。"李明竖起两根手指，表情严肃得像在陈述战败史，"一次是'老板让你去会议室'，我在里面站了二十分钟才发现是空的。一次是'你女朋友在楼下等你'，我穿着拖鞋冲下楼，结果——"

"结果根本没有女朋友。"

"……所以今年，"李明戴上头盔，凝视着门口，"我要让所有的阴谋诡计都失败在萌芽状态。"

---

上午九点，李明纹丝不动地坐在沙发上，像一只过度警觉的猫头鹰。

室友的每一次走动，他都要问"你要干什么"；同事发来的每一条微信，他都要在心里分析三遍语义；外卖小哥敲门时，他坚持让对方先把外卖举过头顶，原地转一圈，再从门缝底下递进来。

"你疯了。"张伟中午回来时，看到门口堆着的"消毒"过的外卖盒，瞪大了眼睛。

"谨慎。"李明纠正他。

下午三点，李明的手机收到一条短信："您的快递已被放置在门口，请注意查收。"

他没有动。

这条短信可疑得如此明显，简直是在侮辱他的智商。

但二十分钟后，真正的快递员打电话来了。

"先生，您的包裹就在门口，您能下来取一下吗？"

"你给我拍照证明。"

"……什么？"

"拍你自己的脸，举着我的快递，拍一张合影发给我。"

电话那头沉默了几秒，然后快递员挂断了电话。

十五分钟后，门铃响起。快递员站在门口，脸上带着职业性的微笑，但眼睛里明显写着"这人有病"。

李明用他提前准备好的假手（其实就是一只橡胶手套塞在袖子里）接过快递，全程没有暴露真身。

"你是李先生？"快递员看着那只从门缝伸出来的橡胶手，问。

"有证据吗？"

快递员把快递放下，转身走了。

---

傍晚六点，李明接到了妈妈的电话。

"明明啊，今天加班吗？怎么没给我打电话？"

"妈，今天愚人节，我——"

"我知道，我知道，"妈妈笑着说，"所以我没有相信你爸说他中了五百万的彩票。"

李明愣了一下："爸说他中彩票了？"

"是啊，早上就说了，我还以为是愚人节玩笑，结果他去买了五注同样的号码，还说晚上要请全家吃饭。"

"……妈，爸平时会买彩票吗？"

"从来不买。"

李明沉默了三秒。

"妈，你等着，我给爸打个电话。"

挂断妈妈的电话后，李明立刻拨给爸爸。电话响了六声才接通。

"儿子啊，今晚记得来吃饭！爸爸要请你们吃大餐！"

"爸，"李明深吸一口气，"你是不是在开玩笑？"

"开什么玩笑？五百万啊儿子！爸爸终于可以——"

"爸。"李明的声音冷静得像一盆冰水，"今天愚人节。"

电话那头沉默了一会儿。

"……几号？"

"四月一号。"

又是漫长的沉默。

然后，李明听到爸爸用一种生无可恋的声音说：

"儿子，我买了五注。"

"我知道。"

"还是同号的。"

"……"

"你妈刚才把家里的旧沙发扔了，说反正要买新的。"

李明闭上眼睛，深深地叹了口气。

---

晚上九点，李明终于允许自己解除警戒。

他疲惫地坐在沙发上，看着电视上播出的综艺节目。张伟在旁边打游戏，时不时发出笑声。

"你知道吗，"张伟突然开口，"你这样防着别人整你，有没有想过……"

"想过什么？"

"想过其实根本没有人在整你？"

李明转过头，看着室友。

"什么意思？"

"我的意思是，"张伟放下手柄，认真地看着他，"我们部门今天没有人策划任何整蛊活动。我本来想告诉你，但又觉得看你这样还挺有意思的，就没说。"

"……"

"你的那些陷阱、那些检查、那些假手……"张伟忍不住笑出声来，"兄弟，你整蛊的对象只有你自己。"

李明呆住了。

就在这时，他的手机震动了一下。是一条来自日历的提醒：

**📅 4月1日 愚人节已过。**

不对。

李明瞪大了眼睛，看向手机顶部的日期。

**4月2日。**

他猛地抬起头，看向墙上的日历——那张他三个月前买的、上面印着卡通猫咪的日历，此刻清清楚楚地显示着：

**4月2日 星期三。**

"今天是……"李明的声音有些发抖。

"二号啊，"张伟看了看手机，"愚人节昨天就过完了。"

李明的大脑一片空白。

他想起了妈妈的电话——

想起了那个说他中彩票的爸爸——

想起了一切。

"那我爸他……"

"他应该是认真的吧。"张伟拍了拍他的肩膀，"恭喜你，你可能真的有个中了彩票的爸爸，也可能有个被吓到心脏骤停的爸爸。"

"……"

李明缓缓地把头埋进了双手里。

门外传来汽车引擎熄火的声音。

然后是爸爸兴奋的声音："儿子！儿子！你快出来！爸爸真的要请你吃大餐！——对了，先帮我跟你妈解释一下，我中彩票这件事是真的，不是什么愚人节玩笑……她今天已经把家里两个柜子扔了。"

李明站起身，走到门口，拉开门。

他看着眼前激动得满脸通红的爸爸，又看了看手机上的日期。

然后，他慢慢地关上了门。

"你们整我。"

"我们没有。"爸爸和室友异口同声。

李明盯着他们两个人看了五秒钟。

然后，他把头盔重新戴好。

"从现在起，"他严肃地宣布，"每一天，都是潜在的危险日。"

爸爸和室友对视一眼，默默地后退了一步。

Write about someone who hates pranks and spends April Fools’ Day doing good deeds instead. Aim for roughly 2800 words.

# El Día de los Falsos Favores

Marcos Gutiérrez odiaba el primero de abril con la misma intensidad con la que amaba el silencio de las mañanas de domingo. Para él, aquella fecha no representaba ninguna gracia: era una jornada decepción, una celebración de la mentira disfrazada de tradición. A sus treinta y cuatro años, podía recordar con precisión quirúrgica cada broma que le habían gastado y el sabor agridulce que dejaban en su pecho.

A los siete, su primo Adrián le hizo creer que su tortuga, Doña Esperanza, había escapado del jardín. Marcos lloró durante tres horas hasta que su madre encontró al reptil tomando el sol detrás del rosal, indiferente a la tragedia.

A los quince, su mejor amigo le envió una carta falsa de la universidad de sus sueños, rechazándolo. Marcos pasó una semana entera sin dormir, repasando mentalmente cada error de su vida académica, antes de descubrir que el sello era de un sello cómico que vendían en el kiosco de la esquina.

A los veintidós, su novia le organizó una cena romántica en la azotea de su edificio para después confesarle que llevaba seis meses viendo a otro. También era una broma, le dijo, riendo. No lo era.

Por eso, cuando abril asomaba cada año en el calendario, Marcos se preparaba como un general se prepara para una guerra silenciosa. No respondía llamadas de números desconocidos. Revisaba tres veces cada mensaje antes de reaccionar. Y desde hacía cinco años, había convertido el Día de los Inocentes en su propia contracorriente: el Día de los Falsos Favores, como él lo llamaba.

---

La mañana del primero de abril amaneció con un cielo despejado, como si el universo quisiera cooperar con su cruzada personal. Marcos se levantó a las seis, preparó un termo de café bien cargado y revisó la lista que había elaborado la noche anterior en una libreta de tapas azules.

*1. Ayudar a doña Carmen con las bolsas del mercado.*
*2. Llevar el coche al taller de los Ramírez sin que me lo pidan (hoy el aceite, la semana pasada los frenos).*
*3. Dejar un paquete anónimo de galletas en la puerta de la señora del tercero.*
*4. Llamar a mamá. Solo para decirle que la quiero.*

Salió de su apartamento en el tercer piso del edificio de la calle Álamo, en el barrio de Las Flores, y bajó las escaleras con pasos tranquilos. La ciudad empezaba a despertar y él quería adelantarse a las primeras bromas del día.

En el rellano del segundo piso, se topó con el pequeño Bruno, de seis años, que subía corriendo las escaleras con una sonrisa enorme. El niño llevaba un globo rojo atado a la muñeca y una hoja de papel en la mano.

—¡Don Marcos! —gritó el pequeño, deteniéndose frente a él—. ¿Sabe qué día es hoy?

—El primero de abril —respondió Marcos, con una media sonrisa que intentaba ocultar la incomodidad.

—¡Sí! Y tengo una broma para usted. —Bruno levantó la hoja de papel, donde había dibujado un monstruo con muchos dientes—. ¡Es un león! ¡Le voy a comer!

Marcos miró el dibujo. El león, más que吓人, parecía un perro con paperas.

—Es muy feroz —dijo, con absoluta seriedad—. Creo que me voy a desmayar del miedo.

—¿Verdad que sí? —Bruno soltó una carcajada y salió corriendo escaleras arriba, dejando a Marcos con la hoja en la mano.

El hombre miró el dibujo un momento, lo dobló con cuidado y se lo guardó en el bolsillo del abrigo. Había algo en la risa de los niños que siempre desarmaba un poco su armadura. Quizás porque todavía no habían aprendido que las palabras podían cortar más que los dientes de cualquier bestia imaginaria.

---

La panadería de don Eligio abría a las siete menos cuarto, y Marcos llegó cuando el dueño estaba colocando los panes en la vitrina. Don Eligio tenía setenta y dos años, las manos llenas de harina y unos ojos que siempre parecían estar a punto de contar un chiste.

—¿Y hoy qué toca? —preguntó el panadero al verlo entrar—. ¿Vienes a advertirme de que me vas a cambiar la sal por el azúcar?

—Hoy vengo a comprar, don Eligio. Y a pagar lo suyo.

—¿Lo mío?

—Los bollos de la semana pasada. Y los de la anterior. Y los de la anterior a esa.

El panadero se quedó con la bandeja a medio camino del mostrador. Marcos había ido comprando bollos durante semanas, siempre "para la vecina del segundo" o "para la señora del tercero", pero pagaba solo los suyos. El resto lo cargaba a la cuenta de los vecinos, que no siempre podían permitirse el lujo de un bollo de chocolate en el desayuno.

—No sé de qué me hablas, muchacho.

—De la cuenta que lleva usted en ese cuaderno negro. Sé que lo hace. No se lo digo para que deje de hacerlo, sino para que sepa que lo sé. Y que merece cobrar.

Don Eligio dejó la bandeja sobre el mostrador y se limpió las manos en el delantal. Por un momento, sus ojos parecieron los de un niño al que descubren haciendo algo vergonzoso y bonito al mismo tiempo.

—Eres un buen hombre, Marcos.

—No. Solo soy alguien que sabe lo que cuesta ganarse el pan.

Marcos pagó todo lo que debía, dejó veinte euros extra y salió antes de que el panadero pudiera protestar. En la calle, el sol empezaba a calentar los adoquines y el barrio se llenaba de los primeros aromas de pan tostado y café con leche.

---

La siguiente parada fue el taller de los hermanos Ramírez, un negocio familiar de coches que sobrevivía en la esquina de la calle Mayor con la placita de la iglesia. Mateo y Lucía habían heredado el taller de su padre, y aunque la economía no les sonreía últimamente, seguían atendiendo a los vecinos con una honestidad que ya no se estilaba.

Marcos conocía el coche de los Ramírez mejor que el suyo propio. Les había llevado el suyo un martes cualquiera, hacía ya tres meses, para una "revisión rutinaria" que no era sino una excusa para que Mateo pudiera comprarle los medicamentos a su madre, enferma de algo que él mismo no terminaba de entender. En las visitas siguientes, Marcos siempre encontraba alguna avería nueva: los frenos, el aceite, la correa del alternador, la suspensión que hacía un ruido extraño. Todo mentira. Todo pagado por él.

—Vengo por el coche —dijo al entrar al taller.

Mateo levantó la vista del motor de un Citroën viejo y se limpió las manos con un trapo negro.

—¿Otra vez? Pero si te lo revisamos hace quince días. ¿Qué le pasa ahora?

—Algo me dijo mi instinto. Ya sabes, el coche a veces habla.

Mateo lo miró con suspicacia. Era un hombre de pocas palabras y muchas sospechas, pero también de un código de honor que no le permitía rechazar un cliente. Asintió lentamente.

—Déjamelo hasta la tarde. Le echo un vistazo.

Marcos se marchó antes de que pudiera negarse a cobrarle.

---

A las diez de la mañana, Marcos se encontraba en el mercado de la plaza San Andrés, ayudando a doña Carmen a cargar sus bolsas de naranjas. La mujer, de ochenta y tres años, vivía sola en un quinto sin ascensor y cada miércoles y viernes bajaba al mercado como si fuera una peregrinación a tierra santa.

—Pero muchacho, ¿tú no tienes que trabajar? —protestó ella, mientras Marcos le sujetaba la bolsa más pesada.

—Soy dueño de mi tiempo, doña Carmen. Y hoy decidí que mi tiempo es suyo.

La anciana lo miró por encima de las gafas, con esa mirada que tienen las personas que han vivido lo suficiente como para distinguir la verdad del cumplido vacío.

—Eres raro, Marcos Gutiérrez. Raro y bueno. Una combinación peligrosa en estos tiempos.

—Ya me lo han dicho.

La ayudó a subir las bolsas hasta su casa, se tomó el café que ella le ofreció a regañadientes y se marchó con una bolsa de naranjas de regalo que no había pedido.

---

El paquete anónimo de galletas fue más complicado. Marcos había comprado la caja de galletas artesanales en la tienda de la señora Marga, la del tercero, que tenía las rodillas tan gastadas que apenas podía subir las escaleras. Pero no quería que supiera que el regalo era de él, porque entonces ella insistiría en devolverle el favor y los favores entre vecinos se convertían a veces en cadenas imposibles de romper.

Dejó la caja en el felpudo, llamó al timbre y se escondió detrás de la esquina del rellano. La puerta se abrió, una mano temblorosa recogió el paquete y una voz suave dijo, hacia el vacío del pasillo:

—Gracias, quien quiera que seas. Que Dios te bendiga.

Marcos bajó las escaleras con una sonrisa que le dolía en las mejillas de lo poco acostumbrada que estaba.

---

La llamada a su madre fue la más difícil de todas.

No porque no la quisiera —la quería con la devoción silenciosa de los hijos que han aprendido tarde a decir lo que sienten—, sino porque cada vez que hablaba con ella, su madre aprovechaba para recordarle que "ya iba siendo hora de sentar la cabeza", que "su prima Patricia acaba de tener otro niño" y que "el vecino del quinto ha comprado un piso más grande, ¿tú no podrías ahorrar algo?".

Pero ese día, Marcos decidió que ninguna de esas frases lo iba a afectar. Respiró hondo, marcó el número y esperó.

—¿Sí?

—Hola, mamá. Soy yo. Solo llamaba para decirte que te quiero.

Silencio al otro lado de la línea. Un silencio largo, de esos que pesan como plomo.

—¿Quién es? ¿Es una broma? Porque hoy es primero de abril, ¿eh? No me vas a gastar una broma a mí, ¿verdad, Marcos?

—No, mamá. No es una broma. Te quiero. Solo eso.

—Ay, hijo, me has asustado. Creí que me ibas a decir que te mudabas al extranjero o algo así. Bueno, te quiero yo también. ¿Has comido? ¿Estás comiendo bien?

Marcos sonrió. Algunas cosas nunca cambiaban, y no estaba mal que fuera así.

---

La tarde la pasó en una asociación de vecinos que organizaba una merienda para los ancianos del barrio. Llevó pasteles que había comprado por la mañana, ayudó a servir el chocolate y se sentó a escuchar las historias de quienes ya no tenían a nadie que quisiera escucharlas. Aprendió que doña Asunción, de noventa y un años, había sido profesora de latín en un instituto de jóvenes que ya estaban muertos. Que don Eduardo, su vecino de sillón, había sido torero durante un verano, hacía ya sesenta años, y guardaba todavía la muleta en el fondo de un armario. Que la soledad de los viejos no era sino el eco de todas las conversaciones que ya no tenían a quién dirigir.

A las seis de la tarde, cuando la merienda se terminó y los últimos voluntarios recogían las mesas, Marcos salió a la calle con las manos vacías y el pecho lleno.

---

Fue entonces cuando lo vio.

En la esquina de la calle Mayor, un grupo de adolescentes reía alrededor de alguien. Marcos se acercó, porque había aprendido que las risas de los jóvenes en grupo a veces esconden cosas que no son risa en absoluto.

Lo que encontró fue a un chico de unos catorce años, sentado en el suelo, con la mochila abierta y los libros desparramados. Tenía los ojos rojos y la nariz mocosa, y uno de los adolescentes —el más grande, con una sudadera roja y una risa que le sonó a Marcos inmediatamente como algo conocido y repugnante— le estaba diciendo:

—No llores, tontorrón. Era una broma. ¿No sabes qué día es hoy? Anda, levántate.

El chico del suelo intentó recoger sus libros con manos temblorosas. Uno de ellos cayó de nuevo, abriéndose por una página donde había anotaciones hechas con esfero azul, con la pulcritud de quien todavía cree que estudiar sirve para algo.

—No te preocupes —dijo Marcos, acercándose—. Yo te ayudo.

Se arrodilló junto al chico y empezó a recoger los cuadernos. El adolescente de la sudadera roja lo miró con una mezcla de sorpresa y fastidio.

—Eh, abuelo, no te metas donde no te llaman. Es una broma. ¿No ves que es una broma?

—Claro que es una broma —respondió Marcos, sin levantar la vista—. Una broma. Como la que me gastó mi primo cuando tenía siete años, haciéndome creer que mi tortuga se había escapado. O como la broma de mi amigo de la universidad, que me envió una carta falsa de rechazo. O como la broma de mi ex novia, que me dijo que me dejaba por otro y luego me dijo que era broma, aunque no lo era.

El chico de la sudadera roja parpadeó, confundido. Los otros tres adolescentes que lo acompañaban se miraron entre sí, incómodos.

—¿Tú sabes lo que pasa cuando le gastas una broma a alguien y ese alguien se la cree? —continuó Marcos, por fin levantando la vista—. Que esa persona se queda sola con su dolor. Y cuando descubres que era mentira, no te sientes mejor. Te sientes idiota. Por haberlo creído. Por haber permitido que alguien entrara en tu cabeza y moviera los hilos de lo que sientes.

El chico de la sudadera roja abrió la boca, pero no dijo nada. Por primera vez en su vida, quizás, se quedó sin respuesta.

—Y lo peor —añadió Marcos, poniéndose de pie con los libros del chico en la mano—, es que aprendes a no confiar. Y a veces, esa lección se queda contigo más tiempo del que la broma duró.

Hubo un momento de silencio espeso, de esos que pesan como plomo. Luego el adolescente de la sudadera roja murmuró algo incomprensible, dio media vuelta y se fue. Los otros lo siguieron, algunos sin mirar atrás, otros mirando a Marcos con expresiones que iban del arrepentimiento a la confusión.

Marcos se agachó junto al chico del suelo, que ya se había limpiado las lágrimas con la manga de la sudadera.

—¿Estás bien?

—Sí —dijo, con la voz todavía temblorosa—. Gracias.

—De nada. ¿Cómo te llamas?

—Hugo.

—Hola, Hugo. Yo soy Marcos. ¿Quieres que te acompañe a casa?

—No hace falta, ya está cerca.

—De acuerdo. Pero llévate esto. —Marcos sacó un paquete de pañuelos de papel del bolsillo y se lo ofreció—. Para las próximas veces que alguien intente hacerte llorar con una broma. Que serán muchas, me temo.

Hugo sonrió, una sonrisa pequeña y todavía húmeda, pero auténtica.

—¿Y usted? ¿No le gastan a usted bromas?

—A mí ya no. Aprendí a esquivarlas hace tiempo. Y aprendí algo mejor: a devolver, en lugar de una broma, algo que merezca la pena.

Hugo asintió, como si acabara de aprender algo que no iba a olvidar. Se guardó los libros en la mochila, se puso de pie y se fue corriendo, con la mochila saltando a su espalda.

Marcos lo vio desaparecer por la esquina y luego miró al cielo, que empezaba a teñirse de naranja. El primero de abril se acababa. Mañana sería un día cualquiera, y la ciudad seguiría girando como siempre, con sus bromas y sus verdades, con sus crueldades y sus pequeños gestos de bondad.

Pero hoy, al menos, Marcos había ganado. Había convertido el día de las mentiras en el día de las verdades silenciosas. Había llenado una jornada de falsedades con actos pequeños, imperceptibles para la mayoría, pero que para él significaban algo que las palabras no alcanzaban a decir.

Caminó hacia su casa con las manos en los bolsillos y la libreta azul en el bolsillo del abrigo, donde la lista ya estaba tachada, pero donde añadía, con letra pequeña, una nueva línea:

*5. Recordar que las mejores bromas son las que no le hacen daño a nadie.*

Y al llegar a la puerta de su edificio, se encontró a Bruno, el niño del segundo, esperándolo con un nuevo dibujo en la mano. Esta vez era un dragón con muchos dientes, todavía más feroz que el león de la mañana.

—Don Marcos, ¿le hago la foto al dragón?

—Hazle dos. Una para mí y otra para mi refrigerador.

El niño sonrió, y Marcos también, porque algunas batallas contra la seriedad del mundo se ganan simplemente aceptando que un dragón de papel puede ser la mejor compañía de una tarde de abril.

Entró en su casa, preparó otro café, se sentó en el balcón y miró cómo la ciudad encendía sus luces. En algún lugar del barrio, alguien recibía galletas anónimas, un anciano dormía con el pecho lleno de chocolate, una madre hablaba con su hijo por teléfono, un mecánico revisaba un coche que no necesitaba revisión, y un adolescente llamado Hugo quizás, solo quizás, estaba pensando en que las palabras pueden cortar o pueden curar, y que la diferencia entre una cosa y la otra no estaba en lo que se decía, sino en el corazón de quien las decía.

Marcos cerró la libreta azul, tomó un sorbo de café y, por primera vez en mucho tiempo, se permitió sentir que el día de los inocentes había sido, en realidad, un día de los sabios.

*FIN*

# 十二月の雛鳥

---

十二月、街はイルミネーションで彩られていた。会社勤めの水野あかりは、帰省する妹家族のためのプレゼントを抱えて、実家の玄関をくぐった。ミントグリーンの小さな箱。中からは微かな羽ばたきと、ちいさく、ちいさく、くちばしが何かを突く音。

「なに、それ」

母が台所から顔を出した。エプロン越しに覗きこむ目。いつもは優しい母の目が、今日に限って少しとがっている気がした。

「インコ。文鳥ってやつ。妹が子供に、って」

「生き物を、電車で二時間も」

「大丈夫だって、サイトに書いてあった」

母は何も言わなかった。ただ、台所に戻り、みじん切りの包丁の音だけを大きくした。あかりは箱を居間に置き、手のあいた妹の子供——三歳のひなたに、中を見せることにした。

「ひーちゃん、見てみて。とりさん」

ひなたは目を丸くした。甲高い声を上げ、箱の中の白い小さな生き物を指差した。セキセイインコ。二ヶ月。性別はまだわからない。名前すら、決めていない。

「とりさーん、ちっちゃーい！」

翌朝、あかりが目を覚ますと、鳥はすでに目を覚ましていた。止まり木の上で、頭を左右にゆっくり傾け、あかりを見つめている。黒い目玉。ボタンみたいに丸い。

「……おはよう」

返事はない。当然だ。あかりは身の振り方を考えた。エサは昨日ペットショップでもらった小さな袋。水は与えなければならない。温度は、二十度は保たないと、よくない——と、どこかで読んだ気がする。暖房。実家の居間は、石油ファンヒーターが主で、隙間風が多い。

母親がノックもせずに入ってきた。

「朝ごはん、食べたの」

「うん。あのさ、鳥って、朝になったらこうやって、動くのね」

「生きてるんだから」

「うん。そうだよね」

母はまた何も言わずに去った。あかりは爪切りを取り出し、爪を切らなければならない、と思ったが、やり方がわからない。YouTubeを開いたが、通信が重い。結局、鳥かごの中の小鳥をただ眺めて、一日が過ぎた。

三日目の朝、ひなたがインコに向かって「ワンワン！」と叫んだ。犬だと思っているらしい。インコはびくりと羽を膨らませた。くちばしがパキパキと音を立てる。怒っているのか、喜んでいるのか、あかりにはわからない。

「ひなたちゃん、ちいさな声でね」

「えー」

ひなたの声は、ちいさくならなかった。

五日目の夕方、父親が帰ってきた。工場勤め。大きな手のひらが、鳥かごの金網に触れた。

「なんだこれ。ジャマになるな」

「プレゼント……」

「生き物のプレゼントってのは、どうなんだ」

父親はすぐに自室にこもった。母は黙々と夕飯の支度をし、あかりはインコのフンを掃除した。ちいさな丸い粒が、新聞紙の上に落ちている。一日二回。思ったより多い。

七日目の朝、インコが羽を震わせた。くちばしを開け、くぐもった声を出す。何かを訴えているのかもしれない。あかりは鳥かごの前にしゃがみこみ、目を合わせた。

「どうしたの」

インコは答えなかった。当然だ。

あかりは、この一週間、何ひとつ正しくできていない気がした。名前をつけてやれない。爪も切れない。さえずりの意味もわからない。ただ、時々やってきては水を換え、エサをつぎ足し、フンを取る。それだけのことをしている。

それでも、インコは死ななかった。

九日目の朝、インコがはじめて、鳴いた。はっきりとした、鈴のような音。「ピィッ」と、短く、一度だけ。あかりは不意打ちをくったように驚いた。インコは止まり木の上で、ふたたび小さな目をこちらに向けていた。

「……鳴いたね」

母が台所から声をかけた。

「鳴いたねえ」

あかりは、こみあげるものがあり、鳥かごに顔を近づけた。インコは、くちばしを金網にこすりつけた。

十二日目の夜、妹が子供を迎えにきた。ひなたはインコにバイバイをせず、靴もはかずに帰っていった。妹が何か言うのを、母が制した。「いいから」。

残ったのは、あかりと、鳥かご一台。

「持っていきなさいよ」

母が言った。

「東京に、持って帰るの」

「しかたないでしょ。あなたの選んだのよ」

あかりは、段ボール箱を押し入れから出してきた。インコを移し替え、駅まで歩いた。十二月の風は冷たい。インコは箱の中で、くちばしを動かしている。何を食べようとしているのか。何を考えているのか。あかりにはわからない。

ただ、一緒に帰る。

ホームのベンチに座り、箱を膝に抱えた。横を通る人々。マスク越しの咳。どこかの子供が母親にだだをこねている。日常の切れ端が、ゆっくりと過ぎていく。

電車が来た。乗り込み、箱を網棚に上げた。インコが微かに鳴いた。「ピィッ」と。

あかりは、目を閉じた。名前をつけてやれていない。でも、明日、帰ったら、考えよう。エサのこと、温度のこと、爪のこと、いろいろ。わからないことばかりだ。間違えるかもしれない。でも、インコは鳴いた。あかりに向かって鳴いた。それだけで、なんか、良かった。

汽車の窓の外を、夜の街が流れていく。十二月の飾りつけが、光の線になって、瞬きもせず飛び去る。

あかりは、箱にそっと手を添えた。温かかった。

「これから、よろしくね」

インコは、答えなかった。当然だ。

でも、あかりは知っていた。たぶん、この子も、少しだけ、嬉しかったのだと。

---

# The Best April Fool's Day Prank I Could Ever Pull

I've always believed that the perfect prank isn't about humiliation or chaos. It's about crafting a moment so surreal, so perfectly executed, that for one shining instant, the entire world tilts on its axis—before gently, delightedly, righting itself with laughter.

Here's how I would pull it off.

---

**Six Months of Preparation**

The prank would begin not on April 1st, but the previous October. I would start a small, exquisitely designed magazine called *The Interim*. It would feature essays, poetry, short stories, and interviews with respected public figures. The production quality would be impeccable—letter-pressed covers, embossed spines, the kind of object you'd find in the back rooms of independent bookshops.

I would hand-deliver these magazines, one by one, to the doorsteps of literary editors, podcasters, and book reviewers across the country. No accompanying note. No return address. Just the magazine, wrapped in plain brown paper.

By spring, *The Interim* would have developed a small but devoted following. People would wonder who was behind it.

---

**The Day Before**

On March 31st, I would release one final issue. This one would contain a single, extraordinary piece: a "lost" manuscript by a famously reclusive author—one whose work is studied in universities, whose absence from public life has become legend. The piece would be called "The Cartographer's Confession," and it would be, by every measure, a masterpiece. Twenty-two pages of prose so startling in its beauty that it would make the literary world gasp.

I had, of course, written it myself, over the course of years.

---

**April 1st, 8:00 AM**

At eight o'clock in the morning, my phone would begin to ring.

It would not stop ringing.

Editors at major outlets. Producers at morning shows. The author's estate. An actual academic who had been searching for this manuscript for two decades. Twitter would be on fire. Substack would be on fire. The literary internet would be having a collective experience.

I would say nothing. I would simply watch.

---

**The Reveal**

At noon, I would post a single message across all my quiet channels:

*"The Cartographer's Confession" was written by me. It was written for you. There is no lost manuscript. There is only the question: what would you have believed, if you had wanted to believe it badly enough?*

*Happy April Fool's Day.*

*"A lie may take us halfway around the world before the truth has a chance to put on its trousers."—Winston Churchill (probably).*

---

**Why This Would Be the Best**

Because the prank would never quite end.

Long after the laughter, people would still be asking: *Was it real? Did I read something beautiful, or was I fooled?*

And the answer would be: *Yes. Both.*

---

The best prank, I've come to think, is the one that leaves behind something true. A real piece of writing. A real moment of wonder. A real question about belief, longing, and the stories we are so desperate to receive that we sometimes forget to ask where they came from.

That is the prank I would pull.

And then I would disappear—quietly, gracefully, perhaps with a smile—into the long, ordinary months between next October and next April.

# 🎅 Affaire n° 2024-SANTA-001 : *Le Peuple contre Nicholas Kringle*

## ⚖️ TRIBUNAL DE PREMIÈRE INSTANCE DU COMTÉ DE L'ESPRIT GÉNÉRAL

---

**Le Juge :** Mesdames et Messieurs du jury, veuillez vous lever.

*(Le prétoire s'installe. Un homme âgé, à la barbe blanche fournie et au costume rouge élimé, est assis à la barre des accusés. Son sourire ne faiblit pas malgré la gravité du moment.)*

**Le Juge :** L'audience est ouverte. Monsieur le Greffier, veuillez lire l'acte d'accusation.

**Le Greffier :** *"Le 24 décembre 2023, dans le comté de l'Esprit Général, un individu se présentant sous le nom de Nicholas Kringle, alias Père Noël, alias Santa Claus, alias Saint Nicolas, aurait pénétré dans plusieurs dizaines de millions de foyers sans autorisation légale, consommé des quantités industrielles de lait et de biscuits non déclarées au fisc, et opéré un attelage de rennes volants en violation du code de l'aviation civile."*

**Le Juge :** Monsieur Kringle, comment plaidez-vous ?

**Kringle :** *Ho ho ho*, Votre Honneur, non coupable. Et pour cause : je *suis* le Père Noël. Je n'ai rien à plaider, puisque mes actes sont, par définition, licites.

**Le Juge :** Tout le problème est là.

---

## 📜 EXPOSÉ DES FAITS

La défense repose sur une prémisse singulière : l'accusé *est* réellement Santa Claus. Il ne s'agit donc pas d'une usurpation d'identité, mais d'une **revendication ontologique**.

La couronne, pour sa part, soutient que :
1. Aucun registre d'état civil ne reconnaît une telle identité.
2. L'existence d'un seul Père Noël n'est pas prouvée — il pourrait s'agir d'une légende collective.
3. L'accusé refuse de divulguer l'emplacement de son "atelier", ce qui constitue un obstacle à toute vérification.

La défense, menée par Maître Holly Evergreen, argue que :
1. L'absence de preuve n'est pas la preuve de l'absence.
2. Plusieurs milliards d'enfants peuvent témoigner de la matérialité de ses visites.
3. Le sourire de l'accusé est, à lui seul, une preuve suffisante.

---

## 🧑‍⚖️ AUDITION DES TÉMOINS

**Le Juge :** Appelons le premier témoin.

*(Un enfant de sept ans s'avance, tenant un ours en peluche.)*

**Le Juge :** Petit, comment sais-tu que le Père Noël existe ?

**L'Enfant :** Parce qu'il m'a apporté une locomotive l'année dernière.

**Le Juge :** Et tes parents ?

**L'Enfant :** Mes parents disent que c'est eux. Mais je ne les crois pas. Ils n'ont pas de traîneau.

**Le Juge :** *Note pour le dossier : témoin partial mais sincère.*

*(Le Procureur, Maure Misletoe, se lève, l'air grave.)*

**Le Procureur :** Votre Honneur, si je puis me permettre… La défense fonde son argumentation sur du vent. Littéralement. Aucun élément matériel n'a été présenté. Pas de traîneau, pas de rennes, pas de hotte — rien. Où sont les preuves ?

**Maître Evergreen :** Monsieur le Procureur, peut-on prouver l'amour ? La foi ? Le sourire d'un enfant le matin de Noël ?

**Le Procureur :** Nous ne sommes pas à confesse, Maître. Nous sommes au tribunal.

**Le Juge :** Maître Evergreen, je vous suggère de rester dans le domaine du juridique, si vous voulez bien. L'émotion est l'opium des magistrats fatigués — et je ne suis pas encore fatigué.

---

## 🦌 LE MOMENT CLÉ : L'audition de Rudolph

**Le Juge :** Appelons le témoin surprise de la défense : Rudolph le Renne.

*(Un renne au nez rouge s'avance à la barre. La salle murmure.)*

**Le Juge :** Rudolph, êtes-vous doué d'un nez bioluminescent ?

**Rudolph :** …

**Le Juge :** Très bien. Est-ce que l'accusé vous maltraite ?

**Rudolph :** …

**Le Juge :** Maître Evergreen, votre témoin est muet.

**Maître Evergreen :** Il est *réservé*, Votre Honneur. Il faut comprendre son silence comme une forme de respect pour la procédure.

**Le Procureur :** Ou peut-être que c'est un renne ordinaire !

**Le Juge :** Monsieur le Procureur, les rennes ordinaires ne témoignent pas devant les tribunaux. Je note que celui-ci a un comportement procédural étrangement civilisé. Ça mérite réflexion.

---

## 🎄 LE TÉMOIGNAGE DE MADAME CLAUS

**Le Juge :** Appelons Mme Claus à la barre.

*(Une femme chaleureuse, au châle rouge, s'assoit.)*

**Le Juge :** Madame, confirmez-vous que votre époux est bien le Père Noël ?

**Mme Claus :** Je l'ai épousé en 1732. Il avait déjà la barbe blanche à l'époque. À vrai dire, je ne sais pas trop quel âge il a. Mais je vous confirme qu'il part chaque nuit du 24 décembre, et qu'il rentre avec une indigestion de biscuits au gingembre.

**Le Juge :** Et la neige sur ses bottes ?

**Mme Claus :** Vous m'en demandez trop, Votre Honneur. J'ai arrêté de poser des questions il y a deux siècles.

**Le Juge :** *Soupir.* Bien. Témoin suivante.

---

## ⚖️ PLAIDOIRIE FINALE

**Maître Evergreen :** Votre Honneur, mesdames et messieurs du jury, je vous le demande : peut-on condamner un homme pour être exactement ce qu'il prétend être ? Si mon client est bien le Père Noël, alors ses actes ne sont pas des crimes — ce sont des miracles. Et si mon client n'est *pas* le Père Noël, alors il est simplement un vieillard bienveillant qui distribue des cadeaux. Dans les deux cas, où est le crime ?

**Le Procureur Misletoe :** Votre Honneur, la défense nous invite à un raisonnement circulaire. L'accusé est innocent parce qu'il est le Père Noël, et il est le Père Noël parce que nous devons le croire innocent. C'est une pétition de principe ! Mais la justice ne fonctionne pas à la foi. Elle fonctionne à la preuve. Et je n'en vois aucune.

*(Silence.)*

---

## 📜 JUGEMENT

**Le Juge :** Ce tribunal a longuement délibéré. Nous sommes saisis d'une question d'une difficulté inouïe : peut-on juger un homme pour des actes qui, par hypothèse, n'auraient pu être commis que par lui ?

Considérant que :
- L'accusé a été vu par des milliards d'individus, ce qui constitue un faisceau de témoignages sans précédent dans l'histoire judiciaire ;
- L'accusé n'a causé de tort à personne, bien au contraire ;
- Rudolph le Renne a effectivement un nez rouge, ce qui, convenons-en, est statistiquement improbable ;
- L'accusé a coopéré avec la justice, n'a fui aucune convocation, et s'est même présenté volontairement, ce qui est cohérent avec l'idée qu'il n'a rien à cacher ;
- Le parquet n'a pas réussi à démontrer que les actes en cause avaient été commis *par quelqu'un d'autre* ;

**Le Tribunal, statuant publiquement et en premier ressort :**

1. **Déclare que Nicholas Kringle est, selon la balance des probabilités émotionnelles, bien le Père Noël.**
2. **L'acquitte de l'ensemble des charges retenues contre lui.**
3. **Ordonne toutefois**, conformément au principe de précaution, que l'accusé soumette son attelage à un contrôle technique annuel, et qu'il dépose un état prévisionnel de biscuits et de lait, à titre indicatif, à des fins statistiques.
4. **Rappelle**, à l'attention du parquet, que la magie n'est pas un casier judiciaire.

*(Coup de marteau.)*

**Le Juge :** La séance est levée. Joyeux Noël à toutes les parties.

---

*Fin de l'audience.*
*Le tribunal souhaite à l'accusé, à la défense, au parquet, au jury, et aux rennes, d'excellentes fêtes de fin d'année.*

You are the Ghost of Christmas Past. You receive an unexpected visit from someone. Around 1500 words.

The candle on my windowsill had been burning for a very long time. I had stopped counting the years. Time moves strangely for those of us who exist outside of it—sometimes a single night stretches longer than a century, and sometimes centuries fold into the space between breaths.

I had grown accustomed to being summoned.

Every Christmas Eve, I rose from whatever quiet reverie held me, answered the call of whatever mortal needed reminding of what they had forgotten. Lost loves. Wasted chances. The small kindnesses that had slipped through their fingers like sand. I showed them these things because I remembered them when they could not, and because someone had to.

Tonight, however, the summons did not come from a living heart.

It came from a place I did not recognize—a doorway that should not have existed, opening onto a room I had never seen. And standing in the threshold, looking as though he had walked through a snowstorm without the benefit of a coat, was a young man.

No. Not young. He had once been young, perhaps. But there was something old in his eyes, something that recognized me before I had even fully materialized.

"Ghost," he said. His voice was hoarse. "I need to speak with you."

I blinked into fuller visibility, letting my robes settle around me like fog remembering it was once a cloud. "You are not Scrooge."

"No."

"You are not any of my charges. I have no business with you."

"I know." He stepped inside. The doorway did not close behind him, but neither did the cold follow him in. That was wrong. Everything about him was wrong. "That's why I came. You're the only one who might remember."

I studied him more carefully now. He was perhaps thirty, with the kind of face that had once been handsome and was now simply tired. His clothes were anachronistic—not quite of one era or another, as though he had dressed in the dark from a wardrobe that belonged to several lifetimes at once.

"Remember what?" I asked.

"My name."

I felt something I had not felt in a very long while. Surprise. The dead do not forget their names. It is one of the few comforts we have, that the syllables our mothers gave us stay with us into whatever comes after. For a man to forget his own name was for a star to forget how to burn.

"Who are you?" I asked, because that was, I realized, the proper question.

"I don't know." He laughed, and the sound was hollow. "That's rather the problem. I woke this morning, and I knew I was dead—I know what I am now, I know the rules of this place—but my name was gone. Like a tooth that falls out while you're sleeping. I reached for it, and there was just... nothing."

"And you came to me."

"You're the Ghost of Christmas Past." He looked at me as though this explained everything, and perhaps to him it did. "I thought, if anyone would remember a Christmas I lived, it would be you."

I have been asked many things, in my long tenure. To show mercy. To show grief. To show men the boys they used to be, the loves they used to hold. But I had never been asked to remember for someone else. It was, I confess, an unusual request.

"What was your favorite Christmas?" I asked, because one must begin somewhere.

He closed his eyes. For a long moment, he was silent. Then: "I don't know. I don't remember any of them. I remember the shape of them—the feeling of having had Christmases, the way you remember having dreamed without knowing what the dream was about—but the details are gone. The faces. The gifts. The food."

This was very strange. Very wrong. Memories can fade, of course—they fade for the living every day—but for the dead, they should be crystalline. We are made of memory, in a way. It is the only substance we possess.

"Tell me," I said slowly, "what do you remember about yourself?"

"I remember that I was kind," he said. "I think I was kind. I remember learning to ride a bicycle. I remember the smell of pine needles. I remember—" He stopped. "I remember being loved. I know I was loved. I remember that, even though I cannot remember a single face."

"And what year did you die?"

He shook his head. "I don't know that either. I don't know how long I've been here. The place where I exist is... it doesn't have time. Not really."

This was troubling. A ghost without a name, without a death-date, without memories—it was as though someone had reached into a library and torn out a single book, leaving only the empty space where it had been.

"Sit down," I said, gesturing to a chair that had appeared beside him without my intending it. "I will try."

I closed my eyes, which for a ghost is a strange thing to do, because we have no need to close them. But I closed them anyway, and I reached out with the part of me that knows Christmas Past, the part that has witnessed every Yuletide since the first one was celebrated in a stable two thousand years ago.

And I found him.

I found a small boy opening a wooden train on Christmas morning, his father watching from the doorway with a cup of coffee. I found a teenager sulking through midnight Mass, his coat still on, thinking about a girl who hadn't said yes. I found a young man proposing on Christmas Eve, the ring trembling in his hand, her answer lost in the snow. I found a father, years later, assembling a bicycle at two in the morning because his daughter had grown impatient. I found a grandfather, holding a newborn on Christmas Day, weeping without quite knowing why.

I found him everywhere. In every Christmas, he was there. A background figure in other people's joy, but there. Present. Loved.

I opened my eyes.

"You were called William," I said.

He looked up at me. His expression did not change, but something behind his eyes did—a light, faint but unmistakable, as though a candle had been lit in a room that had been dark for a very long time.

"William," he repeated, as though testing the word. As though it were a key he hadn't used in years and was trying in a lock.

"Yes."

"Will. Will... what?"

"Your surname was Ashford." I said it carefully, and as I did, I watched his face fill in, the way a photograph develops in solution. Lines returning. Expression returning. The boy I had seen in the memories becoming the man sitting before me now. "William Ashford. You were born in 1947. You died on Christmas morning, 2019, in a hospital bed, holding your wife's hand."

"Mary," he breathed. "Her name was Mary."

"Yes."

He wept. It was not a dramatic weeping—there were no sobs, no sounds at all. The tears simply fell from his eyes, and I understood that he had not cried since he arrived in whatever place he had arrived in. He had not remembered how.

"I remember now," he said. "I remember everything. The train. The bicycle. Mary." He laughed, and this time the laughter was real. "Oh, I remember. I remember it all."

"You were a good man, William Ashford."

"I tried to be."

"That is the same thing."

He stood. The chair beside him vanished, as it had come. The strange doorway through which he had entered began to glow softly, as though it had grown impatient.

"I didn't know where else to go," he said. "I didn't know who else to ask."

"You came to the right place."

He smiled at me—a real smile, the kind that uses the whole face. "Will I remember this? When I go back to... wherever I am. Will I remember being here?"

"I don't know," I admitted. "That is not my province. I am only the Past."

"Well." He drew himself up. He looked, for a moment, like the young man who had proposed on Christmas Eve, nervous and hopeful and entirely unaware of what the next sixty years would hold. "Then I suppose I should go."

"Yes."

He turned toward the door, then paused. "Ghost?"

"Yes?"

"Thank you. For remembering me."

"It was my pleasure, William Ashford."

He walked through the doorway, and the doorway closed behind him, and the room I had not known I was in dissolved back into the nothing from which it had come.

I stood alone in my window, watching the snow fall past, and I thought about the strangeness of the evening. I had shown a thousand Scrooges their pasts. I had shown a thousand Tims their futures, a thousand present-crouches their present wrongs. But this was the first time I had simply remembered for someone who had forgotten themselves.

It felt, I confess, rather like Christmas.

The candle on my windowsill flickered once, then burned steadily on, and I waited for the next summons, whatever it might be.

# The Only One

The parking lot was empty when I pulled in at 7:14 AM, my headlights cutting through the thin November mist. I counted four cars total—mine and three belonging to the security guard, the maintenance guy, and probably someone in management who never learned how to use an out-of-office reply.

I sat in my car for a moment, engine idling, watching the clouds of my breath merge with the fog through the windshield. *Public holidays are for family,* my mother had said that morning, holding my half-packed lunch like a small accusation. *People who love you.*

I loved her too. I also loved paying rent.

The lobby was tomb-silent. My footsteps echoed off the marble floors as I crossed to the security desk, where Dennis was already halfway through a thermos of coffee that smelled like it had been brewed sometime during the previous administration.

"Morning, kid," he said, not looking up from his phone. "You're early."

"It's almost seven-fifteen."

"Early for a holiday." He finally glanced at me. "Floor seven?"

"Six."

"Huh." He shrugged as if I'd said something deeply philosophical. "Whole building's got the heat turned down. Maintenance is in the basement complaining about it."

"Of course they are."

The elevator chimed. I stepped inside and watched the doors close on Dennis, who had already returned to whatever he was watching. Probably a cat video. Definitely a cat video.

Floor six was the way I'd left it Friday night—empty desks, dark monitors, a half-eaten granola bar someone had abandoned on the kitchen counter and which I now eyed with deep suspicion. I set my bag down at my desk, and the office felt less like a place I'd chosen to spend my life and more like the set of a moderately successful horror film.

I had work to do. That was the thing, wasn't it? There was always work. A report due Wednesday that I could finish today, a project that needed my "unique perspective" (read: willingness to read forty pages of legal jargon no one else would touch), a meeting I was supposedly preparing for, though I suspected no one on the other end of that meeting knew I existed half the time.

I turned on my monitor. It hummed to life, filling the room with that particular blue glow that made everything look like it was taking place underwater.

An hour passed. Then two.

At 9:47 AM, my phone buzzed. A text from my coworker Priya: *Hope you're not actually there. Go home.*

I typed back: *I am actually here. Hello.*

*Oh god. Why?*

*Because someone has to.*

*You're a better person than me.* Then, a moment later: *There's leftover cake in the breakroom fridge from Jenny's thing. Just saying.*

I went and got the cake. It was red velvet. Jenny had good taste, even if her "thing" had been a going-away party for someone who, as far as I could tell, had not actually gone away.

I ate the cake at my desk and watched the fog lift outside the window, revealing the city below in that strange, soft way it had on mornings when everyone else was still asleep. From up here, you couldn't see the traffic or the crowds or any of the things that made Monday mornings feel like a personal vendetta against your will to live. You could just see rooftops, and the river, and the way the light came down.

I kept working.

Around lunch, I heard the elevator. Dennis's voice, then another voice—Jim from maintenance, who appeared in my doorway with a wrench in one hand and a sandwich in the other.

"Elevator's making a noise," he said, by way of greeting. "Figured I'd come up and tell someone who could put in a work order."

"I can't put in a work orders. I'm in marketing."

"Oh." He considered this. "You could try anyway."

"I could try anyway."

"Yeah." He took a bite of his sandwich. "You want half? My wife made too much."

I took half.

At 2 PM, the building HVAC system made a sound like a dying whale, and the temperature on floor six dropped from sixty-eight to approximately the surface of Mars. I considered my options: go home, or put on the cardigan I kept in my bottom drawer for exactly this kind of emergency. I put on the cardigan.

At 3:15, I finished the report. I read through it once, twice, three times. It was good. It was, if I was being honest with myself, the best work I'd done in months. Something about the silence, maybe. Something about not having anyone to perform for.

At 4 PM, I shut down my computer.

The building was already darker when I walked back through the lobby, the emergency lights casting everything in that dim, underwater glow. Dennis was on the phone now, his voice low and serious, though he waved at me as I passed.

"Have a good one," he called.

"You too."

"Whole building to yourself again tomorrow?"

I paused at the door, hand on the handle. "No. Tomorrow's Tuesday. Tuesday's a real day."

He laughed—a short, surprised bark—and I pushed out into the late afternoon, where the sun was just starting to think about setting, and the city was still and quiet in that particular way it only ever was on days when almost no one was watching.

I got in my car. I sat for a moment.

Then I drove home.

---

My mother called at six. *How was your day, sweetheart?*

*Good,* I said. *Quiet. I got a lot done.*

*Did you eat?*

*Yes.*

*That's my girl.*

I didn't tell her about the cake, or Jim's sandwich, or the way the light had come through the windows in the afternoon, or how I'd worn my cardigan like armor against the dying of the暖气. Some things you keep for yourself. Some things are better when they're just yours.

I made tea. I sat on the couch. Outside, the city hummed on without me, and for once, I didn't mind.

I had been the only one there. And it had been, in its strange and quiet way, exactly enough.

"You know what this is, right?" Dave said, wiping his eyes. "This is a bit. You're going to do this for like a week and then forget."

"I am not."

"You absolutely are."

"Fine," I said. "I'll prove it. By New Year's *next* year, I'm going to stand on that balcony—" I pointed toward the sliding glass door "—and whistle 'Danny Boy' through a blade of grass so pure it'll make you cry."

Maya raised her glass. "To delusions of grandeur."

"I'll take it."

I smiled into my drink.

I had a year.

I just needed to find the right grass.

## 1장: 평범한 동네

리처드슨 가의 주민들은 크리스마스를 좋아했다. 12월이 되면 각 집 앞마당에는 화려한 조명이 걸리고, 굴뚝からは 연기가 피어올랐다. 특히 23번지부터 41번지까지 늘어선 집들은 하나같이 장식에 공을 들이는 집주인들이었기에, 거리 전체가 마치 거대한 카드 병설을 보는 것 같았다.

제인 콜린스는 25번지에 사는 은퇴한 교사였다. 그녀는 27년 동안 이 동네에서 산 사람으로서, 이웃들이 휴가를 떠나면 우유와 신문을 받아두고, 쓰레기통을 밖에 내놓아주는 등 친절한 이웃이었다.

"올해는 정말 어디 안 가시나이까, 맥카시 부인?"

12월 둘째 주, 그녀는 옆집의 맥카시 부인을 만났다. 부인은 장갑을 낀 손으로 트렁크에 짐을 싣고 있었다.

"플로리다에요. 1월 둘째 주까지." 맥카시 부인이 미소 지으며 말했다. "앤디 시어러 부부도 어제 출발했고, 윌슨 가족은 다음 주에 가요."

그녀가 생각하기에, 이 동네의 장점이자 단점은 바로 이웃들의 여행 성향이었다. 12월만 되면 절반 이상의 집이 비었고, 그녀는 늘 빈 집들이 신경 쓰였다. 하지만 27년간 한 번도 도난 사건이 없었기에 크게 걱정하지 않았다.

적어도, 지금까지는.

The boy stood at the edge of the lot, hands shoved deep in his pockets, his sneakers too thin for the December cold. He couldn't have been more than nine or ten. His coat was two sizes too small, the sleeves ending halfway down his forearms, and his cheeks were the kind of raw-red that spoke of more than just the weather.

He walked between the rows of balsams and frasers slowly, almost reverently, running his fingers along the needles as if greeting old friends. Then he stopped. In the very back, half-hidden behind a dumpster and a stack of forgotten tree stands, sat the smallest tree I had. It was a Charlie Brown special if I'd ever seen one—sparse, lopsided, with a bald patch near the bottom that I'd been meaning to throw away for a week.

He crouched down and studied it the way a jeweler studies a stone.

"I'll take this one," he said.

I looked at the tree. I looked at him. I looked back at the tree.

"Kid, that one's not for sale."

"Why not?"

"Because it's—look at it. It barely qualifies as a tree. Your mother would come back here and have my head."

Something flickered across his face. Just for a moment. Then the mask came back down, the careful, too-old blankness that kids wear when they've learned too early not to let anything show.

"My mom died last March."

I felt the words land in my chest like a fist.

"I—" I started. "I'm sorry. I didn't—"

"It's okay." He shrugged, a tiny, practiced motion. "I'm picking it for my little sister. She's four. She doesn't know about trees dying and getting cut down. She just thinks they come from heaven with sparkles still on them."

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a crumpled five-dollar bill, holding it out to me like a peace offering.

"That's all I got," he said. "Is it enough?"

I took the money from his hand. His fingers were ice cold.

"Hold on a minute," I said.

I walked to the back of my truck and pulled out the roll of twine I keep for wrapping purchases. Then I went to my best tree, a tall, fat, perfectly symmetrical Douglas fir—the kind families fight over and photograph in front of. I dragged it next to the scrawny one.

"Alright," I said. "Here's the deal. The little one's three dollars. But the big one's only two if you buy them together."

He looked at me. For a long moment, he just looked at me.

"Sir, that's—that's not how it works."

"I'm the boss. I say how it works."

His lower lip trembled, just once, before he bit down on it. "Does it come with a stand?"

"Comes with everything you need."

I tied both trees to the roof of his mother's old sedan—the car I'd noticed parked crookedly across two spots—and showed him how to adjust the straps. He wrote down my address on a scrap of cardboard.

"Your sister's name?" I asked.

"Claire."

"Claire's going to have the best Christmas in the state," I told him. "You make sure of that."

He nodded, then climbed into the driver's seat—*the driver's seat*, of a car, at ten years old, because no one else was left to drive it—and cranked the engine. It rattled twice before catching.

As he pulled away, I saw him glance in the rearview mirror. Not at the road. At the trees strapped to the roof, their branches swaying against the gray December sky.

I closed up the stall early that night. Drove home with a strange warmth in my chest that the heater couldn't account for.

Christmas Eve, there was a card in my mailbox. Construction-paper red, folded in half, decorated in wobbly crayon. On the front, in a child's careful print:

*THANK YOU MR. TREE MAN*

Inside, in slightly larger handwriting—the sister's, presumably:

*Claire says the trees have sparkles. Claire is right.*

I stood at the mailbox for a long time, holding that piece of red paper against the cold.

Then I went inside and called my own kids.

# The Return

The fluorescent lights of Hargrove & Sons Accounting hummed their usual indifferent hymn when the door to my office swung open at 4:47 PM on December 19th.

I didn't look up right away. December was our busiest month—tax prep, year-end audits, the usual pre-holiday panic of small business owners who had ignored their bookkeeping all year.

"Mr. Hargrove?"

The voice was young. Uncertain. Male.

"Mr. Hargrove, my name is Elliot. I'm—I'm looking for Thomas Hargrove. Are you him?"

I set down my pen. Looked up.

He was maybe nineteen. Tall, though he had that gangly quality of someone who hadn't quite finished growing into his frame. Dark hair, a little too long. Brown eyes—God, those eyes. My mother's eyes. My eyes, looking back at me from a face I'd never seen.

"Can I help you?" I asked, because that's what you say, isn't it? What you always say.

"I'm your son."

The pen I'd set down rolled off my desk and hit the carpet. I didn't hear it land.

"I think you have the wrong office," I said. My voice sounded far away. "I'm an accountant. I don't—I'm not married. I don't have any children."

He swallowed. I watched his Adam's apple bob, and I thought: *that's something I would do.*

"My mom is Catherine Bell. She worked at a diner in Portland, Oregon, in the fall of 2000. She says you came through town for about three weeks. A consulting job, I think. She was nineteen. You were twenty-three."

The world tilted. I gripped the edge of my desk.

"I have a picture," he said, reaching into his jacket pocket. His hands were shaking. "Of you. From back then."

He slid it across my desk. A Polaroid, edges yellowed. A young woman with red hair and a nervous smile. And me—younger, thinner, with a different face but the same eyes. Same chin. I was sitting on a porch somewhere, looking at her like she was the only person in the world.

Because she had been.

"I didn't know," I whispered. The words came out broken. "I didn't know she was pregnant. I swear to you, I didn't—"

"She believes you," Elliot said quickly. "She's never said otherwise. She just—she kept me. Raised me. She did her best."

The office was very quiet. Outside my window, the city was beginning to glitter with early holiday lights, and I thought about how I had spent nineteen Christmas Eves alone in this very building, working late, eating takeout over spreadsheets, telling myself I preferred it that way.

"Why now?" I asked.

He looked down at his shoes—scuffed Converse, one lace untied. "I'm going to college in the fall. Bioengineering. My mom didn't want me to find you until I was older, but I—I'm not doing it for money or anything. I just wanted to see you. Once. Before I became a person, I guess. I wanted to know where I came from."

I stood up. Sat back down. My hands were trembling now too.

"Sit down, Elliot. Please. Sit down."

He sat.

I looked at him for a long time, trying to find myself in his face, trying to understand how I had missed nineteen years of someone who existed because of me. The mole on his left cheek—I had that same mole. The way he held his shoulders, slightly hunched, as if apologizing for taking up space—I had done that my whole life until I learned to stop.

"I don't have anything," I said, and hated myself for it. "No family to speak of. No wife. Just this office. Just me. I'm not—I'm not what you came looking for, probably."

"I'm not looking for anything," he said. "I just wanted you to know I existed."

The clock on my wall ticked. 4:52 PM. Outside, a siren wailed somewhere, distant and fading.

"Do you want to get dinner?" I heard myself ask. "There's a place downstairs. It's not much, but—"

"Yeah," he said, and smiled. It was my smile. My mother's smile. It was a smile I had never seen before but recognized immediately, the way you recognize your own handwriting.

"Yeah, I'd like that."

I grabbed my coat. Turned off the desk lamp. Walked toward the door with a stranger who was not a stranger, who had my blood and my mother's eyes and a Polaroid of a past I thought I had buried.

"Elliot," I said, pausing at the threshold.

"Yeah?"

"Merry Christmas."

He laughed—a startled, joyful sound, the kind of laugh that belongs to someone young and hopeful.

"Merry Christmas, Dad."

We walked out together into the cold December evening, and for the first time in as long as I could remember, I did not feel like the last person left in the world.

# The Loop That Wasn't Punxsutawney

The first time the alarm went off, it was blaring "Jingle Bell Rock" and I knew immediately something was wrong.

Not because of the song. Because I was waking up in my childhood bedroom, in my parents' house, on December 23rd, and my mother was shouting up the stairs that breakfast was ready and would I *please* come down before the cinnamon rolls got cold.

I went downstairs. The cinnamon rolls were not cold. My mother kissed my forehead. My father was reading the paper. My little brother was thirteen again and complaining about his homework.

I had not been thirteen in fifteen years.

I spent the first loop in a kind of fog. I ate. I watched television. I helped my brother with his math. At 4:00 PM, my mother began preparing the Christmas Eve appetizers, and at 6:00 PM, my father poured the eggnog, and at 8:00 PM, my brother and I opened *one* present each, as was tradition, and at 11:00 PM, I went to bed, and at 6:00 AM the alarm went off, and it was December 23rd again, and my mother was shouting up the stairs about cinnamon rolls.

The second loop, I panicked.

I tried to break things. I broke a lamp. I broke a plate. I broke my brother's retainer. Each time, the broken thing was fixed by morning. Each time, my mother shouted about cinnamon rolls.

By the fifth loop, I had stopped breaking things.

By the tenth loop, I had stopped panicking.

By the twentieth loop, I was starting to enjoy myself.

This was the part I didn't expect. I had heard the stories — had watched the movie, even, twice — and I knew that time loops were supposed to be existentially devastating, that they were supposed to grind you down into a fine psychological dust. But mine wasn't like that. My loop was *warm*. My loop had cinnamon rolls and bad Christmas movies and my father falling asleep in his recliner and my mother humming "O Holy Night" while she did the dishes. My loop was the best version of a holiday I had stopped bothering to come home for, repeated forever, a small snow globe of a world that I never had to leave.

I should have been suspicious.

---

It was on the forty-third loop that I noticed the cat.

She was sitting on the kitchen counter when I came down for breakfast. Gray tabby. Green eyes. Watching me with an expression I can only describe as *evaluative*.

"Whose cat?" I asked my mother.

She looked at me like I had said something strange. "She's always been here, sweetheart. Don't you remember?"

I did not remember. I had never seen this cat in my life.

The cat's name, I learned over breakfast, was Hazel. She had been with us since I was five. She had died when I was twelve, the summer before we moved away. I had not thought about her in twenty years.

I reached out to pet her. She bit me.

---

The next loop, Hazel was waiting for me on the stairs.

The loop after that, she was sitting in my childhood desk chair, watching me brush my teeth.

The loop after that, she was lying on my pillow.

"She doesn't usually like people," my mother said, puzzled. "She must really love you being home."

Hazel stared at me. Her green eyes held something I could not read. Something almost like *intent*.

"You don't exist," I told her, on the seventy-first loop, whispering, in case my mother could somehow hear. "You died when I was twelve. You're not supposed to be here."

Hazel yawned. She had very sharp teeth.

---

I tried ignoring her. She followed me. I tried locking her out of my room. She materialized inside. I tried carrying her outside. She was too heavy, and also, she didn't seem to care about the outside.

On the eighty-sixth loop, I sat down on the kitchen floor at 3:00 AM and waited. There was no rule that I had to sleep. There was no rule about anything, really. That was the strange thing about my loop. There were no rules. No lessons to learn. No moral at the end. Just an endless, perfect Christmas Eve, repeated and repeated and repeated, with a dead cat that wouldn't leave me alone.

Hazel appeared beside me. She did not purr. She just sat.

"What do you *want*?" I asked her.

She looked at me. Then she walked, unhurried, to the basement door, and sat in front of it.

---

I had not been in the basement since I was twelve. My father had taken it over as a workshop when we moved back here for college, and later as a storage space, and now it was full of old furniture and broken exercise equipment and a freezer that hummed too loudly. It was not a place I went.

I opened the basement door.

The stairs creaked. The light did not work. I used my phone.

The basement was exactly as I remembered it. The same cardboard boxes. The same cobwebs. The same hum from the freezer. Hazel was sitting at the bottom of the stairs, her eyes reflecting my phone light like two green coins.

I followed her.

She led me to a corner behind the freezer, where a sheet was draped over something tall and angular. I had no memory of this sheet. I had no memory of anything behind the freezer.

I pulled the sheet away.

---

It was a mirror. Old, wooden-framed, the kind you might find at a flea market. The glass was clouded with age. Hazel sat at my feet, watching.

My reflection was not my reflection.

My reflection was *me* — but the me from before the loops. The me with the real job and the real apartment and the real life I had stopped bothering to come home for. That me was staring back at me with an expression I recognized, because it was the expression I had worn in the airport, two weeks ago, when I had decided, very calmly, that I wasn't going to fly home for Christmas this year.

I had been too busy. There had been too much work. I would come next year. There was always next year.

"Hi," I said.

My reflection did not smile. My reflection opened its mouth, and what came out was not my voice. It was the voice of the cat.

"*You said there was always next year,*" the reflection said.

I stepped back. Hazel wound between my ankles.

"*But you never came,*" the reflection said. "*Not next year. Not the year after. Not any year. You kept saying you would. You kept meaning to. And then there was no more next year, and you never came at all.*"

I was shaking. The basement was very cold.

"*So I am giving you next year,*" the reflection said. "*I am giving you every next year. I am giving you the chance to have this, over and over, forever. The cinnamon rolls. The bad movies. The brother who still has his retainer. The mother who is still alive. Take it. Take it forever. Why would you ever leave?*"

I looked at Hazel. Hazel looked at me.

"*She isn't even a cat,*" the reflection said. "*She is what I left to show you the way. She is the part of you that still remembered the stairs.*"

The hum of the freezer was very loud.

---

I woke up on December 23rd.

The alarm was playing "Jingle Bell Rock." My mother shouted about cinnamon rolls.

I went downstairs. I ate. I watched television. I helped my brother with his math.

At 4:00 PM, my mother began preparing the appetizers. At 6:00 PM, my father poured the eggnog. At 8:00 PM, my brother and I opened one present each. At 11:00 PM, my mother kissed my forehead, and I went to bed.

At 6:00 AM, the alarm went off.

It was December 24th.

---

I sat up in bed.

I sat up in bed for a very long time.

My mother shouted up the stairs. Breakfast was ready. The cinnamon rolls were getting cold.

I went downstairs. I ate two. My brother complained about his homework. My father fell asleep in his recliner. My mother hummed "O Holy Night."

I did not go to the basement. I did not look for Hazel. I did not look for the mirror.

At 4:00 PM, my mother began preparing the appetizers. At 6:00 PM, my father poured the eggnog. At 8:00 PM, my brother and I opened one present each. At 11:00 PM, my mother kissed my forehead, and I said, "Mom?"

"Yes, sweetheart?"

"I love you."

She laughed. She said, "I love you too, honey. Now go to bed, you have a long drive tomorrow."

I went to bed.

At 6:00 AM, the alarm went off.

It was December 25th.

---

I packed my things.

I kissed my mother goodbye. I shook my father's hand. I hugged my brother until he squealed.

"See you next year," my mother said, waving from the porch.

"See you next year," I said.

I got in my car. I started driving.

On the radio, "Jingle Bell Rock" came on. I turned it off. I turned it back on. I left it on.

I have not come back to that loop. I have not tried to. I think about it sometimes — the cinnamon rolls, the bad movies, the mother who is still alive, the brother with the whole rest of his life ahead of him. I think about how easy it would be to go back. How warm it was.

But there is a rule, I have decided, even if no one ever told me the rule.

You don't get to keep the snow globe.

You get to visit.

And then you have to go home.

---

*This Christmas, my mother is alive, and I am going to see her. That is the whole story. That is the only miracle I needed.*

# 午夜钟声

## 楔子

那座房子矗立在橡树岭的尽头，像一截烧焦的指骨指向灰蒙蒙的天空。镇上没人叫它"鬼屋"，而是用更古老的说法——"那座收钱的地方"。因为每年深秋，都有人从外地来，揣着孤注一掷的绝望，走进那扇生锈的铁门。

## 第一章 邀请函

林深把那张烫金请柬翻过来时，后厨的油烟正呛得他睁不开眼。请柬上只有一行字：

*"待一晚，十万。勿带火，勿开灯，勿答话。"*

落款是一朵用红蜡封的玫瑰，背面印着一串GPS坐标——正是他每天骑车路过都会绕开的那栋维多利亚式老宅。

他犹豫了三秒。三十五岁，前妻带着孩子消失在省城，餐馆合伙人卷款跑了，他连下个月的房租都交不起。老板娘今天已经第三次暗示他"再赊账就别来了"。

当晚，他给那串号码发了条短信：**我去。**

## 第二章 规则

来接他的是一辆黑色加长轿车，司机面无表情地递过一个皮质手提箱。林深打开，里面是十叠崭新的百元钞——和一把生了铜绿的钥匙。

"定金。"司机终于开口，声音像砂纸擦过铁皮，"午夜十二点进门，明早六点日出离开。其间无论听到什么、看到什么，**不要回应**。"

林深问："如果违反了？"

司机从后视镜里看他一眼，那眼神让林深想起殡仪馆的冰柜。"那就不是钱的事了。"

## 第三章 第一个声音

房子比他想象的更大。一楼客厅铺着厚厚的灰尘，壁炉里残留着某种烧焦的羽毛气味。二楼有七扇门，林深选了最靠楼梯口的那间，锁上门，靠着床头坐下。

手表指针划过十二点整。

"……林深。"

一个女人的声音，温柔得像妻子从前哄孩子入睡时的语调。但他的前妻从不会这样叫他的全名——她总是喊他"阿深"。

他攥紧拳头，把嘴唇咬出血。**不要回应。**

"你为什么不来找我们？"声音从墙角渗出来，像水汽一样弥漫，"妈妈等你很久了。"

林深的眼眶发热。他想起了儿子那张五岁时拍的照片，被前妻一并带走了。**不要回应。**

声音消失了。壁炉里的灰烬却忽然无风自动，飘出一道微弱的弧线，像一只无形的手在招手。

## 第四章 午夜三点

最可怕的不是鬼，是寂静中的**缺席**。

凌晨三点，林深发现自己忽然听不见任何声音——不是安静，而是声音本身被抽走了。连自己的呼吸都变成了默片。他看见自己的胸腔在起伏，嘴唇在动，却发不出一丝声响。

然后壁炉亮了。

不是火，是一种冰冷的蓝白色光芒。一个身影从光芒中走出来——是个穿西装的男人，五官模糊得像一张失焦的照片。但林深认得那身西装。那是他父亲的寿衣。

父亲伸出手，指向林深的胸口，嘴唇开合。

这一次，声音回来了。

"……你口袋里那张照片。"

林深浑身僵硬。他下意识摸向衬衫口袋——那里确实有一张折叠的照片，是他今天从餐馆更衣室捡到的，是父亲年轻时的黑白照。他已经二十年没见过这张脸了。

"把它烧给我。"父亲说，"像小时候那样。"

林深想起七岁那年的清明，他和父亲在山上烧纸钱，火苗舔着天空，父亲说：*"烧给看不见的人，他们就能看见了。"*

他差点开口。**差点。**

但在最后一秒，他想起了司机的话——*那就不是钱的事了*。

他把照片按回口袋，转身面向墙壁。

身后传来一声长长的叹息，像风穿过空旷的走廊。然后，蓝光熄灭，房间重新陷入死寂。

## 第五章 黎明

早上六点，第一缕阳光刺破窗帘时，林深发现自己站在大门外。

他不记得自己是怎么下楼的。铁门在他身后缓缓合上，锈迹斑斑的门锁发出一声沉闷的咔嚓。

司机依然在车里等着。手提箱空了，里面多了一张纸条：

*"谢谢你的沉默。明年见。"*

林深的手在抖。不是因为恐惧，是因为他忽然意识到——

他口袋里那张照片，**不见了**。

他低头看自己的手，掌心有一道浅浅的灼烧痕迹，正好是照片大小的椭圆。

## 尾声

三个月后，林深在老宅附近的镇上开了一家小面馆。他再也没有回过省城，也没有去找前妻和孩子。

但每年秋天，他都会在门口的信箱里收到同样的请柬。

今年那张请柬上，多了一行小字：

*"令尊问好。"*
