# The Children Who Remembered Rain

After a particularly rainy Spring, a record number of people had wished "rain, rain, go away, come again another day." That was two years ago, and not a single raindrop had fallen since.

The drought had a name now. The Old Farmers called it the Great Forgetting, though no one could agree when the forgetting had truly begun. Some said it was the year the wells turned brackish. Others marked it from the day the last reservoir cracked open like an egg, its blue interior swallowed by the cracking earth. The historians, those few who still bothered with such things, pointed to a single afternoon in late May two years ago, when every child in the Valley had recited the old rhyme at once, their small voices rising into the low clouds like a single word spoken by a god.

The rains had come down that day, certainly. A wall of water that turned the streets into rivers and carried away three cars and a small dog named Biscuit. The children had been punished, kept inside for a week, told they had asked for it with their silly wishing. They had not asked for rain, of course. Only for it to go away. But the universe, it seemed, had a poor ear for nuance.

Now the Valley stretched brown and silent beneath a sky the color of old paper. The mountains in the distance had gone gray, their snowpack nothing but memory. The reservoir beds had become playgrounds, then junkyards, then graveyards for the machines that had once pulled water from the ground. People moved slower here now, conserving the smallest motions, and spoke in voices that barely stirred the dust.

Elena Voss remembered rain.

She remembered it the way one might remember a language learned in childhood and then abandoned—the sound of it just out of reach, the shape of the words still familiar on the tongue. She was seven years old when the rain came down in sheets that May afternoon, and she had pressed her face to the window of her grandmother's kitchen and watched the world turn silver and wild. She remembered the smell of it, that particular petrichor that rose from the dry earth even in the middle of a downpour, as if the soil itself was exhaling. She remembered how her grandmother had laughed and called it a baptism.

Her grandmother had died the first winter of the drought, her lungs giving out in a house that had grown too cold to heat. Elena's mother said it was the dust that killed her, the fine powder that got into everything, into the flour and the bedclothes and the corners of the eyes. Elena said nothing, but she thought it was something else. She thought her grandmother had simply forgotten how to keep breathing in a world that no longer made sense.

The children who had wished the rain away were older now, most of them teenagers, and they carried a particular guilt that sat on their shoulders like stones. Some of them had moved away, seeking water in cities that had not yet felt the drought's full weight. Others remained, married young, had children of their own, tried to forget. A few had joined the new churches that had sprung up in the dry places—temples to the Sun-That-Does-Not-Listen, chapels to the Saint of Thirst. None of them, as far as Elena knew, had ever spoken publicly about what they had done that May afternoon. And Elena, who had not wished at all that day, who had only watched from the window, found that she could not quite bring herself to hate them.

She was seventeen now and worked at the old water station on the edge of town, one of the last places where water still flowed from a tap. The water came up from deep wells, hauled in by trucks that traveled for days to find it, and Elena's job was to fill the bottles that people brought. She wore a mask most days, not for the dust but for the look in the eyes of the people who came. It was the look of someone standing at the edge of a long fall, trying not to look down.

One afternoon in late summer, a young man came to the station who Elena did not recognize. He was thin, with the kind of sunburn that came from too many days spent looking up at an empty sky, and he carried a single bottle under his arm like it was something precious.

"Fill it," he said, his voice rough.

Elena took the bottle. It was old, the glass thick and cloudy, and as she held it up to the light she saw something at the bottom. A small paper, folded tight, pressed against the glass.

"What is this?" she asked.

The young man looked at her for a long moment. "A wish," he said. "From a long time ago."

Elena did not fill the bottle. She stood there in the dust-filtered light of the station, the glass cold in her hands, and felt something shift inside her chest—a small, precise movement, like a key turning in a lock she had forgotten she had.

"Who are you?" she asked.

"I'm the one who came back," he said. "To undo what we did."

He told her his name was Tobias, and that he had been twelve years old that May afternoon, and that he had been one of the children who had wished the rain away. He told her that for two years he had walked the dry places, looking for the right place to break the wish, the right person to help him do it. He told her that there were others like him, scattered across the Valley, and that they were ready to try something that might not work.

"What do you need?" Elena asked.

"A voice," Tobias said. "Someone who remembers what rain sounded like. Someone who can teach us how to ask for it back."

That night, Elena walked out to the old reservoir bed with Tobias and the others—seven of them in all, young and not so young, all of them carrying the weight of a childhood wish they had never meant. The sky above them was vast and empty, and the stars looked like holes punched in a dark cloth.

Elena stood at the center of them, and she began to speak. Not a wish, not a rhyme, but something older. A remembering. She described the rain in every way she could—the color of it, the smell of it, the way it tasted when caught on the tongue, the sound of it on tin roofs and windowpanes and bare earth. She spoke until her throat was raw, and the others joined in, each adding their own fragments of memory, until the dry air seemed to thicken with the ghost of water.

And then, just before dawn, something happened.

It was not a downpour. It was barely a mist, a fine veil of moisture that drifted down from a sky that had been cloudless for two years. It lasted only a few minutes, and it barely wet the ground. But it was rain. It was undeniably, unmistakably rain.

Tobias wept. Elena wept. The others stood silent in the gray light, letting the moisture settle on their faces like a kind of absolution.

In the weeks that followed, there were more such rains—small, brief, uncertain. The drought did not break. The wells did not refill. The reservoirs remained cracked and empty. But something had changed in the Valley, something that could be felt in the way people moved and spoke and looked at one another. A door had been opened, just a crack, and through it came the possibility that what had been wished away might, someday, be wished back.

Elena continued to work at the water station, filling the bottles that people brought. But sometimes, in the late afternoons, when the light turned golden and the dust lay soft on everything, she would stop and close her eyes and listen. And sometimes, if she listened carefully enough, she could hear it—the faintest suggestion of water, falling softly on a world that was learning, slowly, how to remember.

The children who had wished it away had grown up now. Some of them had children of their own, and they taught them a new rhyme, one that went:

*Rain, rain, come and play,*
*Wash the dust of the world away.*
*We have learned what we did wrong,*
*Be with us, and be here long.*

And sometimes, in the Valley, when the sky was low and gray and the air smelled of iron and earth, the children would sing it together, and the old people would stop what they were doing and listen, and even the most hardened among them would feel something stir in their dry and patient hearts.

The drought did not end that year, nor the next. But the rains came back, eventually, in their own slow time—not all at once, not in the way the old songs had imagined, but in pieces, in drops, in the patient accumulation of mercy. And the Valley, which had learned what it was to thirst, learned also what it was to be grateful, and that lesson, it turned out, was worth more than all the water in the world.

她记得最深的是七岁那年夏天。

父亲带她回老家。她骑在他肩上,穿过晒得发白的石板路,蝉鸣从两旁的梧桐树里倾泻下来。祖母坐在老宅的藤椅上,看见他们进门时笑得眼睛眯成一条缝,脸上的皱纹全都舒展开来。

那天下午,她坐在天井的青石台阶上舔一根红豆冰棍,看祖母和父亲在廊下择菜说话。光线从天井上方倾落,把水缸里的金鱼照得通体透明。她听不懂大人聊的内容,只听见笑声断断续续,像石子落进水里。

晚饭是一大锅新打的井水煮的米粉,浇上祖母自己熬的辣椒油。她吃了两碗,辣得直吸气,祖母一边用蒲扇给她扇风,一边往她碗里夹腌豆角。父亲坐在对面,什么也不说,只是看着她笑。

吃完饭她困了,趴在父亲背上回屋。半梦半醒之间,听见远处的蛙鸣和近处的风扇转动声,还有祖母轻轻拍她后背的节奏——一下,一下,像潮汐一样安稳。

那之后她长大,离开,辗转了许多地方。吃过许多精致的饭菜,去过许多明亮的地方。但每年夏天最热的时候,她闭上眼睛,想到的总是那碗米粉,那根冰棍,那把蒲扇,和天井里落下来的光。

七岁。永远停在那个年纪的父亲和祖母,永远停在那个夏天的天井。她后来明白,所谓最幸福的时刻,不是因为那天的米饭有多香,而是因为那时候世界很小,小到只有三个人,小到没有任何事能把他们分开。

Este ano, a minha resolução de Ano Novo é... aprender a dizer "não" sem sentir culpa. Durante anos fui aquele tipo de pessoa que dizia sim a tudo — a pedidos de trabalho extra, a convites de última hora, a favores que me esgotavam o tempo e a energia. E, no fim do dia, ainda me culpava por querer um pouco de espaço para mim.

Tudo mudou numa noite de dezembro, quando adoeci — gripe forte, daquelas que nos atiram para a cama — e percebi que tinha perdido uma semana inteira de descanso porque não queria desiludir ninguém. Deitada entre lençóis, febril e a tossir, olhei para o teto do quarto e pensei: "Se não cuidar de mim, quem cuidará?"

Foi aí que decidi. Este ano seria diferente. Não seria uma resolução grandiosa, do tipo que abandonamos em fevereiro. Seria algo pequeno, mas transformador: reservar trinta minutos por dia só para mim. Podia ser ler um livro, tomar um banho demorado, ou simplesmente sentar-me no sofá a não fazer absolutamente nada. O importante era respeitar esse tempo como se fosse uma reunião inegociável.

No primeiro dia do ano, quando a minha colega me pediu para ficar até tarde a ajudar num projeto que não era meu, respirei fundo e respondi, pela primeira vez, com um firme mas educado: "Hoje não vai ser possível." O coração acelerou-me, as mãos suaram, mas sobrevivi. E, curiosamente, o mundo não acabou.

Agora, a meio de janeiro, já perdi a conta às vezes que disse "não" — e a cada uma delas, senti-me mais leve, mais dona de mim. A resolução não é sobre egoísmo, afinal. É sobre sobrevivência. Sobre entender que o "sim" mais importante que posso dar é aquele que ofereço a mim mesma.

E tu, qual é a tua resolução?

# 圣诞老人节后的一天

**12月26日，清晨七点**

当全世界都在沉睡、做着关于圣诞礼物的美梦时，圣诞老人已经在自己那张巨大的橡木床上睁开了眼睛。

他盯着天花板看了一会儿。壁炉里的余烬还在散发着温暖的光。

"呼……"他长长地叹了一口气，翻身坐起来。十二件套的红色睡衣皱成一团，胡子还沾着昨晚吃姜饼留下的糖霜。

---

**上午九点**

厨房里，圣诞老夫人（Mrs. Claus）正在煮咖啡。她抬头看了一眼丈夫，笑了笑："亲爱的，你的黑眼圈比鲁道夫的鼻子还红。"

"今年送出了十七亿份礼物，"圣诞老人嘟囔着，给自己倒了杯热可可，"驯鹿们也不容易，尤其是彗星——他的蹄子在亚洲上空打了个趔趄。"

他的手机响了。是精灵工坊的质检员发来的消息：**"报告：北极仓库已清空 99.7%，剩余礼物将在 1 月 5 日前送达（因为有些国家的物流真的很慢）。"**

圣诞老人点点头。他打开电视，每一个频道都在重播《真爱至上》和《小鬼当家》。他换了十七个台，最后停在了一个播放鲸鱼叫声的纪录片上。

"终于清静了。"他喃喃道。

---

**下午两点**

他终于走出了那个总是被雪覆盖的小木屋。

外面是一片银白色的世界。圣诞老人深吸一口气，冰冷的空气灌进肺里，舒服极了。他看到小精灵们三三两两地躺在雪地上晒太阳——虽然太阳从来不会真正出现在北极。

"老板！"一个戴绿帽子的年轻精灵朝他挥手，"来打雪仗吗？"

"不，"圣诞老人摆摆手，"我今天只想做一件事。"

他走到湖边，脱下厚重的红外套，只穿着一件旧毛衣。然后他整个人——"扑通"一声——倒进了雪地里。

他开始挥动双臂。

一分钟后，一个像样的雪天使诞生了。

"哦吼——"圣诞老人躺在自己造出的天使形状里，看着灰蓝色的极地天空。"原来这就是不工作的感觉。"

他闭上眼睛，任凭雪花一点一点落在他的大胡子上。

---

**下午四点**

圣诞老夫人找到了他，给他披上一条毯子，端来一杯热苹果酒。

"你今天就打算这样躺过去？"她问。

"不，"圣诞老人坐起来，拍掉身上的雪，"我有个计划。"

他走进书房，从抽屉里翻出一本厚厚的皮革笔记本。封面上烫金字写着：**"陶儿的遗愿清单"**。

这是他儿子陶儿的笔记本。陶儿三岁时就决定要做一个"不用上班的人"。后来他成了北极最优秀的精灵工程师，但他一直没能实现那个童年的愿望——**去热带看一次真的椰子树**。

去年春天，陶儿在一次驯鹿骑行事故中永远地睡着了。

圣诞老人翻到新的一页，写下：

> **12月26日**
> 
> 1. 睡到自然醒 ✔
> 2. 打雪仗（没打成，但做了雪天使）✔
> 3. 给所有的驯鹿写感谢卡
> 4. 吃一整块没有装饰的纯巧克力
> 5. 打电话给孩子们，告诉他们爸爸爱他们

他合上本子，揉了揉眼睛。

---

**晚上八点**

壁炉前，圣诞老人和夫人并排坐在摇椅上。茶几上摊着一堆没拆完的礼物——都是各地小朋友送给他的。

"这个不错，"圣诞老夫人举起一个手工编织的围巾，"粉色和绿色条纹……品味很独特。"

"这是个小女孩织的，"圣诞老人轻声说，"她家里只有她一个人，但她还是给我准备了礼物。"

他沉默了一会儿。然后他打开电视，把频道调到一个二十四小时播放壁炉噼啪声的画面——这是他最爱的节目。

"你知道吗，"他对夫人说，"今天下午我躺在雪地里的时候，想到了一件事。"

"什么？"

"我给全世界的小朋友都送了礼物，"他说，"但我从来没收过陶儿亲手做的圣诞礼物。"

夫人握住他的手。

"所以我决定，"圣诞老人说，"从今天起，每年的 12 月 26 日，我什么都不做。我就坐在这里，烤火，吃巧克力，听你给我念信。"

夫人笑了，靠在他肩上。

"那驯鹿怎么办？"

"让他们也休息一天。鲁道夫的鼻子也需要保养。"

---

**午夜十二点**

整个北极都安静下来了。

圣诞老人站在窗前，看着极光在天空中舞动。绿色的、紫色的光带像丝绸一样在星星之间飘荡。

他想起今晚要看的最后一封信。那是一个七岁的小男孩写来的，信上歪歪扭扭地写着：

> **亲爱的圣诞老人：**
> 
> 我今年表现很好。但是我真正想要的不是礼物。我想要我的爷爷回来。爷爷去年冬天走了。奶奶很伤心。如果你能把爷爷变回来就好了。但是我知道你不能。所以我只想要一张爷爷的照片，请寄给我好吗？
> 
> 爱你的，
> 小杰

圣诞老人看了这封信很久很久。

然后他从口袋里拿出一支钢笔，在信纸的背面写道：

> **亲爱的小杰：**
> 
> 我没有办法把你的爷爷变回来。但是我答应你，我会去看他，告诉他你是个好孩子。你也要答应我一件事：每天都抱一下你的奶奶，好吗？
> 
> 爱你的，
> 圣诞老人

他把这封信折好，放进明天要寄出的袋子里。

窗外的极光还在继续舞动。圣诞老人关掉灯，爬上床，把帽子挂在床头的钩子上。

"晚安，鲁道夫。"他对窗外说了一声，然后闭上了眼睛。

---

**尾声**

所以你看，圣诞老人节后的一天，其实和我们的差不多——

睡到自然醒，吃点好吃的，做点没用的事，看看重要的人，然后好好休息。

毕竟，给世界带来魔法的人，自己也需要一点魔法。

而那个魔法，就是——**停下来，闻一闻雪的味道**。

# 蓝色——一个给失明者的描述

闭上眼睛。

想象冬日清晨，你推开窗，迎面而来一阵寒风。那种冷，不是刺骨的疼，而是清冽的、干净的——像薄荷，像雪松，像第一口冰过的泉水。那一刻皮肤的触感，就是蓝色。

再听。远处传来一支长笛的独奏，音色清亮、高远，没有一丝杂质，像一根银丝线抛向天空，颤动着，颤抖着，却没有断裂。蓝的声音，就是这样——它不喧哗，却能在寂静中穿透一切。

再尝。含一颗薄荷糖，让它在舌尖慢慢融化。一开始是凉，然后是甜，最后什么味道都褪去，只留下一股干净的余韵在口腔里回荡。蓝色，也有这种"空"的感觉——它不浓烈，不黏腻，它退后一步，把空间让给你。

如果你触摸过天鹅绒，就知道那种柔软——但蓝色比天鹅绒更轻。它像一片羽毛落在掌心，几乎没有重量，却确确实实在那里。

蓝色是**退后一步的颜色**。
它不像红色那样扑向你，不像黄色那样跳跃，它只是安静地存在，像一个不打扰你的朋友，像深夜里一盏不关的灯，像母亲离开房间前轻轻带上门的那个动作——它说："我在这里，但我不会打扰你。"

它也是**距离的颜色**。
地平线、远山、天空——它们都是蓝的。因为蓝色是光走得很远、累了之后的颜色。所以蓝色天生带着一种乡愁，一种"远方有什么在等着我"的感觉。

悲伤的人常说"心里发蓝"，不是没有道理。蓝色有一点忧郁，但不是黑色的那种绝望——它是清醒的忧伤，像雨后未干的街道，像一封没寄出的信，像深夜两点还亮着的那扇窗。

它还是**忠诚的颜色**。
因为它从不背叛天空，从不改变方向。蓝色说一不二，说永恒就是永恒。

如果有一天你能看见，睁开眼第一个寻找的，我猜就会是蓝色。它一直在那里——在天空，在海洋，在你爱过的人的眼睛里。

# The Cartographer of Silence

The wind had learned my name.

That's what I told myself on the four hundred and thirty-second day, standing at the window of the old library on Maple Street, watching dust motes drift through a shaft of afternoon light. Before, I'd never noticed how dust moves when there's no one else to disturb it—slow, purposeful, like it has somewhere to be.

My name is Eliot. I'm thirty-four years old, and I am, as far as I can tell, the last person on Earth.

The library was a good place to think. The books didn't judge. They just sat there in their crooked rows, smelling of paper and patience, waiting for hands that would never come. I'd taken to reading aloud sometimes, just to hear a voice. Mine sounded strange to me now—too loud, too alive in the stillness.

I kept a journal. Not because anyone would read it, but because writing things down made them feel real. Made *me* feel real.

*Day 1: Power went out across the city. I thought it was just our block at first.*

*Day 8: The silence is absolute.*

*Day 31: I drove to the coast. The ocean still works.*

*Day 112: I stopped pretending I was waiting for someone to come back.*

I didn't keep track of when the last radio signal faded. The last helicopter fell from the sky. The last dog stopped barking. They happened in their own time, and I let them go. Some things you can't hold onto.

What I remember most is the sound of my own footsteps. For months, I flinched at every creak, convinced someone was behind me. Now the absence is so familiar it's become a kind of company. I talk to the walls sometimes. I argue with the weather. Once, I made a peanut butter sandwich and pretended to share it with a man named Gerald who used to live in the apartment below mine. I told Gerald about my day. He didn't say much, but he had kind eyes.

The cities emptied themselves gradually. I watched from hilltops as neighborhoods went brown and gray, as grass pushed through asphalt, as trees that had been politely contained for a century finally stretched their roots in peace. It was beautiful. It was unbearable.

I tried to leave messages. Spray-painted on highway overpasses, scrawled on the sides of barns: *ELIOT WAS HERE. DAY 247.* Pathetic, maybe. But it felt important to leave a mark. To say: *I existed. I tried.*

The hardest part wasn't the loneliness. It was the small things. The coffee maker that wouldn't brew because the beans had gone stale. The way the seasons still changed but no one noticed. The pile of mail in the hallway that would never be opened, the doorbells that would never ring. The whole machinery of human life, clicking along to an audience of none.

I tried, for a while, to maintain things. I mowed the lawns of strangers. I watered their gardens. It felt like a kind of prayer. Eventually I stopped. Eventually I understood that maintaining things was its own form of denial. The world didn't need me to keep it tidy. It was tired of being kept.

One morning, I woke up and realized I hadn't spoken aloud in three weeks.

So I went to the library. And I read.

There was a book of maps—ancient ones, from the age before satellites. The cartographers had filled in unknown territories with sea serpents and the words *HIC SVNT LEONES*—"here are lions." They knew what they didn't know. They drew the edges of the world and left the rest to imagination.

I found a blank atlas in the back room. I took it home. I began to draw.

I mapped the routes I walked each day. I traced the paths of animals I'd seen reclaiming the streets—deer, foxes, a single fat raccoon who seemed to own the entire downtown. I drew in the libraries I'd visited, the wells where I'd drawn water, the places where I'd slept. I marked the cities I'd driven through, the coast I'd stood at, the hill where I'd watched the sun set on the three hundredth day.

I drew a map of my small, shrinking world.

And then, one night, I had a thought. A strange thought. A thought that surprised me with its sweetness.

What if my map was the point?

What if being the last person on Earth wasn't an ending, but a kind of beginning? What if the maps I drew were the new coastlines, the new horizons? What if I was the cartographer now, standing at the edge of everything, putting down on paper the last shape of the human world?

I thought about all the people who had come before me, who had loved and grieved and built and broken, who had drawn lions in the margins because they couldn't bear not knowing. They were gone. But their questions remained. Their wonder remained. *Here are lions.*

I thought about the dust in the library, drifting through the light. I thought about the wind, learning my name.

I picked up my pencil.

Outside, the world was turning itself over, getting comfortable in its new quiet. Inside, a man who had once been a son, a brother, a coworker, a neighbor, was doing the only thing that made sense anymore.

He was drawing the map of what remained.

---

*Eliot's journal, final entry:*

*Day 511. If anyone finds this—wherever you are, whenever you are—know that the world was beautiful. Know that someone loved it enough to walk its empty streets and remember. Know that the silence was not the end of the story.*

*There are no lions anymore.*

*But there are maps.*

*— E.*

---

**THE END**

# The Weight of a Wish

The brass lamp sat on my kitchen table, tarnished and ancient, and the genie within it had just offered me the same question it must have asked ten thousand souls before me.

"Any one wish," he said. His voice was like wind through old ruins. "Choose carefully. I have seen empires rise and fall on the choices mortals make at moments such as this."

I had imagined this moment for years—the fantasy of unlimited possibility, the dream of omnipotence pressed into my trembling hands. I had prepared a wish the way an actor prepares a monologue: polished, perfected, ready to deliver.

*I wish for the wisdom to know what is best for everyone in the world.*

But when I opened my mouth, the words wouldn't come.

Because I knew, suddenly, what wishes like that led to. The benevolent dictator. The well-meaning tyrant. The man who tried to fix the world and broke it worse.

"What happens," I asked slowly, "if I wish for something small?"

The genie's eyes, which burned like distant stars, regarded me with something that might have been curiosity. "Small wishes are the most dangerous of all," he said. "Because they reveal what you truly want. And what you truly want is rarely what you need."

I thought about that.

I thought about the years I'd spent yearning—for success, for love, for meaning, for the great and sweeping change that would make everything finally, irrevocably right. I thought about how each of those yearnings had been, in its own way, a way of saying *I am not enough as I am right now.*

Outside my window, the autumn leaves fell. My coffee grew cold. The cat slept on the windowsill, unbothered by metaphysics.

"A man once wished for immortality," the genie said, watching me. "He lived to regret it. A woman wished for her child to be healthy and brilliant. Her wish was granted, and she never spoke to him again. A king wished for peace. His kingdom enjoyed three hundred years of such peace that his heirs had forgotten how to fight, and they were eaten by wolves."

"You could just say no," I pointed out.

"I never say no. I grant wishes. What I do is make you see them clearly before I do."

I closed my eyes. I thought about my father, who had died believing he hadn't mattered. I thought about my mother, who had lived believing she had. I thought about the small kindnesses I had never noticed, the grudges I had carried for no reason, the days I had wasted wanting to be somewhere else.

I thought about how tired I was of wanting.

"I wish," I said at last, and my voice surprised me with its steadiness, "to be content with the life I have."

The genie went very still.

"That," he said softly, "is the most human wish I have ever heard."

He snapped his fingers.

The lamp vanished. The kitchen was just a kitchen again. The cat stretched, yawned, and went back to sleep. The leaves kept falling. The coffee kept cooling.

And I—

I sat there for a long time, looking out the window, and for the first time in years, I did not feel the need to be anywhere else.

Not all wishes end in fire. Some end in quiet.

I had been granted what I asked for, and I could not tell you whether it was a gift or a loss.

Only that it was, at last, enough.

# 超能力之思

这个问题，我常常在深夜辗转反侧时问自己。

如果问我想要什么超能力，答案会出乎很多人的意料——我想要的，是**能够真正理解他人的能力**。

不是读心术那么简单。不是看穿别人的秘密和谎言。而是一种更深层的东西：能够感知到一个人此刻真实的情绪状态，感知到他话语背后的渴望与恐惧，感知到那些连他自己都不愿承认的脆弱与勇气。

为什么？

因为这个世界上最大的悲剧，不是战争，不是疾病，而是**人与人之间永恒的隔阂**。

我们最爱的人，我们常常并不真正理解。我们最想表达的心意，常常被误解成别的东西。我们以为自己在沟通，其实只是在各自说着各自的语言。有时候，即使是最亲密的人，也会在某个深夜突然感到一种深沉的孤独——那种孤独不是因为身边没有人，而是因为**觉得自己没有被真正看见**。

如果有这种能力，我想我能成为一个更好的倾听者，更好的朋友，更好的爱人。

我想能看见那个总是笑嘻嘻的朋友背后，是否也藏着什么难以言说的苦楚。我想能听见父母轻描淡写的话语下，那些从未说出口的挂念。我想能在一个即将做出冲动决定的人身上，感知到他内心深处那一丝犹豫，然后轻轻地拉他一把。

这种能力不能用来控制他人，不能用来谋取私利。它只能用来给予——给予理解，给予温柔，给予"我知道你"的这份确认。

有时候我觉得，世间最强大的超能力，从来不是什么飞檐走壁、翻江倒海。

而是当一个人在最脆弱的时候，有另一个人走过来，握着他的手说：

"我懂。"

那就足够了。

---

*也许你会笑我天真。但我始终相信，被理解，是一个人最深处的渴望。而如果我们每个人都多一点愿意去理解别人的心，这个世界，或许真的会温柔一些。*

# The Whisper of Unwritten Tomorrows

The attic smelled of dust and forgotten decades. When I found the device—nestled between my grandfather's war medals and a rusted compass—I didn't scream, didn't call anyone. I simply sat on the cold floorboards and held it in my trembling hands, feeling the faint vibration of something impossible humming against my palms.

A time machine. In my grandfather's attic. Of course it was here. Of course it was *his*.

The brass contraption had no buttons, no dials—just a single lever marked with two words in his elegant handwriting: *Назад* and *Вперёд*. Backward and forward.

I thought about the past first, because that's what we always do. We think about the mistakes we'd undo, the words we never said, the doors we closed too gently or kicked open too hard. I could warn him. I could tell him not to board that train in October 1942, or to take it, to choose life instead of the frozen field where his unit was ambushed. I could see my grandmother as a young woman, before grief carved those lines into her face, and tell her that her husband would return to her—not in body, but in the strange inheritance he left behind.

But what then? What if I saved him, and in saving him, I erased myself? What if my mother never met my father at the memorial service, never wept on his shoulder, never conceived me in that small apartment in Leningrad? Time is not a river, the philosophers said. Time is a web, and every thread we touch shivers through a thousand others.

I sat there until the sun set and rose again, watching shadows crawl across photographs of people I never knew.

Then I made my choice.

I pulled the lever toward *Вперёд*.

Not because I don't love the past—I do. I love it the way we love the dead, with a tenderness that borders on violence. But the past is finished. It is a book already written, every page known, every ending certain. To travel there would be to haunt my own history, a ghost at a feast where I could never taste the wine.

The future, though—the future is the only country where I have not yet been born.

I wanted to see what we become. Whether the cities float, whether the wars finally stop, whether my grandchildren's grandchildren learn to love each other across all the distances we created. I wanted to stand in a library that hasn't been built and read books no one has written. I wanted to find out if hope was a lie we tell ourselves, or a lighthouse that actually guides ships home.

The machine shuddered. The air grew thin and sweet, like the breath before snow.

In the last moment before departure, I understood something my grandfather must have known—the real reason he hid this thing in an attic instead of using it. A time machine doesn't take you anywhere. It shows you that *wherever* you are, *whenever* you are, the only place you ever really live is now. The past is a country we've lost the passport for. The future is a country we haven't earned the visa. But this moment—this trembling, imperfect, unrepeatable moment—

This is home.

The attic dissolved into white.

When my vision cleared, I was standing in a garden I had never seen, beneath a sky of a color I couldn't name, and somewhere nearby, children were laughing in a language that sounded almost, *almost*, like home.

I smiled.

I had arrived.

# The Cartographer's Table

The first thing you need to know about my restaurant is that it doesn't have a menu.

Not in the traditional sense, anyway. There is no laminated booklet, no daily specials scrawled on a chalkboard, no smiling photographs of pasta carbonara. Instead, there is a large wooden table in the center of the dining room — yes, just one — and around it sit twelve chairs, and the guests who arrive on any given evening are seated there together, strangers all, presented with a single sheet of paper and a question:

*Where have you come from, and where are you going?*

I call it **The Cartographer's Table**, and it is the only restaurant I have ever wanted to own.

---

The idea came to me, as many terrible ideas come to me, at three in the morning. I had been eating alone — again — at a counter in a small restaurant in a city I did not live in, and I was watching the cook through the window. He was older than me, with forearms like knotted rope, and he moved through his kitchen the way a sailor moves through rough water: certain, unhurried, fully at home in the small violence of heat and timing.

I was eating a bowl of soup. It was excellent. I have no memory of what was in it.

What I remember is the loneliness. Not the pleasant solitude of a meal eaten in peace, but the specific loneliness of being a person in a room full of people, all of us performing the same small ritual of nourishment, none of us speaking. We were eating alone together, the worst kind of alone there is.

I thought: *What if the food were the least interesting thing about the meal?*

I went home. I did not sleep. By sunrise I had the bones of a plan, and by the end of the year I had signed a lease on a narrow storefront on a quiet street in a city that likes quiet streets. I hired a cook whose name is Margot, and who agreed to my strange proposal with a single raised eyebrow and the words, "I'll need a much bigger budget for produce than you think."

She was right. I have never regretted anything more than not budgeting more for produce.

---

Here is how an evening at The Cartographer's Table works.

The doors open at seven. The first twelve guests to arrive are seated at the table. They are served a small aperitif — something floral, something local, something chosen by Margot to match the weather. Then they are asked the question.

Some guests think it's a joke. Some are irritated. A few have walked out. But most — most people, I think, are hungry for something other than food — most people take a breath, and begin to tell the truth.

I have heard, on that table, the most extraordinary things.

A woman on her third marriage telling the table about her first love, a boy who worked at a gas station in 1987, and how she sometimes still drives past that gas station even though it is now a pharmacy. A man who had recently lost his father describing the last meal they had shared, which had been terrible — bad clams, cheap wine — and how he would give anything to eat bad clams again. Two strangers who realized over the second course that they had attended the same elementary school, thirty years apart, and had once, perhaps, passed each other in the hall without knowing.

A girl, not yet twenty, who told us she was running away from home, and a retired schoolteacher who reached across the table and took her hand and said, "Tell me what you need," and meant it.

I do not exaggerate. I do not need to.

---

The food, when it comes, is whatever Margot has decided to make that day. She listens, sometimes, to the table — she emerges from the kitchen and stands in the doorway for a few minutes, taking in the room, the mood, the weather of the conversation — and then she returns and cooks accordingly. She has been known to feed a table of grieving strangers with nothing but roasted vegetables and warm bread, because that is what the evening seemed to require. She has also, on the nights when the table has been rowdy and young and full of arguments about politics, sent out a great deal of steak.

I pay her more than I pay myself. I have no regrets about this.

There are seven courses. They are small. They are not fancy. The plates are mismatched, most of them salvaged from estate sales and church basements. The wine list is short, and almost everything on it costs less than forty dollars. I do not want anyone to feel that the meal is beyond them. I want them to feel that the meal is *for* them.

---

People ask me, often, whether the restaurant makes money. I tell them it makes enough. This is true. It does not make more than enough. I do not want it to make more than enough.

I have been asked whether I am afraid that the format will feel gimmicky, or tired, or that the magic will fade. I tell them I have never felt the magic. The magic, if there is any, belongs to the people who sit down. I have only built the table. They bring everything else.

Once, on a slow Tuesday in February, a man came in alone. He was the only guest. He sat at the table, by himself, and I sat with him, because I am also the host, and because someone has to be the table's first guest when no one else will.

I asked him the question.

He said, "I'm coming from a funeral, and I'm going back to an empty apartment, and I don't know what else to say."

Margot made him soup. It was the same soup, I think, that I had eaten years ago in that strange city. He ate it slowly, and he cried a little, and when he left he shook my hand and said, "Thank you for letting me be a person tonight."

I have never forgotten it. I never will.

---

If you ask me what kind of restaurant I would open, I will tell you: this one. The one where the food is only the door, and the room is only the room, and the table is where the real thing happens.

I would open a restaurant that does not feed you.

And then, of course, feeds you.

---

*Margot is now my wife. We have a small daughter, who is four and already insists on rearranging the chairs. I have told her she is welcome to take over the restaurant someday, provided she keeps the question on the paper. The question, after all, is the whole point.*

*Where have you come from, and where are you going?*

*Yes. That one. Always that one.*

The phone rang at 2:47 AM, three hours after Margaret Chen had finally fallen asleep. She knew before she answered who it would be.

"Madame President."

It was Donovan, her Chief of Staff, his voice stripped of all its usual careful banter.

"How bad?" she asked, already swinging her legs out of bed.

"Pearl Harbor. Second carrier confirmed sunk. The *Arizona* is gone, Madam President. Two thousand souls."

Margaret closed her eyes. Outside her bedroom window, the sky over Washington was still black, but somewhere on the Pacific, the world had split open.

"I'll be there in twenty minutes," she said. "Wake the Joint Chiefs. And Donovan—"

"Yes, Madam President?"

"Get me a direct line to Emperor Hirohito. Not through intermediaries. Not through the ambassadors. *Direct.* I don't care if you have to wake up every translator in the State Department."

She hung up before he could ask the question she saw forming in his silence: *What are you going to say to him?*

---

The situation room was a tomb of blue light and bad coffee. General Morrison had a map spread across the central table, his finger tracing the route of the Japanese fleet across the Pacific. Captain Reyes was already on the secure line to Hawaii, coordinating rescue operations with an admiral who was doing his best not to weep.

Margaret stood at the head of the table, still in the gray suit she'd worn to the congressional reception the night before. Her press secretary had wanted her to change. *The American people need to see their Commander-in-Chief looking strong,* she'd said.

"Strong is a state of mind, not a state of dress," Margaret had replied, and gone to war in Armani.

The direct line to Tokyo connected at 3:22 AM Eastern Time, which was 4:22 PM in Japan — high noon on a day that would not soon be forgotten. A translator named Yuki stood beside the phone, her face pale but composed.

Margaret picked up the receiver.

"Your Majesty," she said, and every person in that room held their breath. "My name is Margaret Chen. I am the President of the United States of America. I am told you understand English, so I will speak it, and Ms. Yuki will translate for the record."

There was a long silence. Then, in a voice like old parchment:

*Speak.*

"Your Majesty, three hours ago, your forces attacked Pearl Harbor. Two of my aircraft carriers are at the bottom of the Pacific. The *USS Arizona* is destroyed. I am told that more than two thousand American sailors and soldiers are dead, and that number will rise."

She paused. Morrison was mouthing something — *demand surrender* — but she held up a hand.

"I am not calling to declare war. War has already been declared by your hand, without warning, without justification, while your ambassador was still sitting at my table negotiating peace."

Another pause. She could hear the Emperor breathing, slow and measured, the breath of a man who had been trained since childhood to weigh every word like a grain of rice.

"I am calling because I want you to understand something about me that you may not have anticipated when you planned this morning."

The room was utterly still.

"I was four years old when my parents brought me to this country. They had nothing. They worked in a laundry in San Francisco for thirty years. They spoke broken English and saved every penny so that I could go to school. They were interned during the war, your Majesty. Not because they had done anything wrong, but because they looked like the enemy. They lost everything they had built, and they started over, and they never once spoke a word of bitterness about your country or mine."

Yuki was translating in a low, steady voice. Margaret could see the tears tracking down the young woman's cheeks.

"They taught me that nations are not their governments. That people are not their emperors. That history is a long, long story, and that no single chapter — not even a chapter written in blood — has to be the last one."

She closed her eyes. When she spoke again, her voice was quieter, but it filled the room.

"Your Majesty, I have the power to end your empire before the sun sets on this war. I have weapons you cannot imagine, and the will to use them. But I do not want to use them. I want my children — both of mine, and all the children of this bleeding world — to grow up without learning what it sounds like when a city burns."

A pause that seemed to last a century.

"So I am making you an offer, the only one I will ever make. Order a full and immediate ceasefire. Order your forces to stand down across the Pacific. Recall your ambassadors. We will meet, face to face, as two leaders who have looked into the abyss and chosen not to fall into it."

"If you refuse, I will fight you with everything I have, and I will win, and the history books will record that you chose this. But if you accept, the history books will record something else. That on the worst day of my presidency, I picked up a phone instead of a sword. That I treated you as a human being, even when your actions had forfeited that right."

She waited. The clock on the wall ticked like a heartbeat.

*What do you want in return?* the Emperor asked.

Margaret looked at Morrison. She looked at Donovan. She looked at the map spread across the table, the little ships and the little arrows, the whole terrible geometry of war.

"I want you to come to Washington," she said. "I want you to meet my mother. She's eighty-three years old and she's never been east of California. I want her to look you in the eye and decide whether she can forgive you. And I want to be there when she does, because I believe she will. She is better than the hatred that was done to her."

"I want your grandchildren and my grandchildren to learn each other's languages. I want the next century to be the first in a thousand years without a great war between our nations."

"And I want you to apologize, your Majesty. Not to me. To the families of the two thousand sailors who are dead because of your order. To the mothers who will wake up tomorrow in a country that is suddenly at war. Apologize to them, by name if you can learn them, and mean it."

She set her jaw.

"That's my price. Take it or leave it."

The silence stretched so long that Donovan reached for the phone, thinking the line had gone dead. But Margaret waved him off. She could hear the Emperor breathing on the other end of the world, and she waited, and she waited, and she waited.

---

History records what happened next in many ways, depending on who is telling the story. The American version emphasizes Margaret's resolve. The Japanese version emphasizes the Emperor's wisdom in accepting her terms. Historians will argue for centuries about whether it was courage or exhaustion, calculation or grace, that made Hirohito say what he said next.

What is not in dispute is what he said:

*Tell your mother I will come. And tell her I am sorry.*

---

Margaret Chen kept her word about everything except one thing. She never did pick up the sword. But she picked up the phone a thousand more times in her life, in crises small and large, and she never stopped believing that the conversation was always worth having.

When she was eighty-one years old, a journalist asked her, on the eve of her retirement, what she considered her greatest achievement as President.

Margaret thought about it for a long moment.

"Twenty-seven minutes," she said finally. "That's how long I kept the Emperor of Japan on the phone on the morning of Pearl Harbor. Twenty-seven minutes between the worst day of my life and a different kind of history."

"I never fired a shot. I never dropped a bomb. I just kept talking."

"And I have spent every day since then trying to live up to the person I decided to be in those twenty-seven minutes."

She smiled, and the lines around her eyes deepened.

"That, I think, is what leaders are for. Not to make the hard decisions easy. But to make the right ones possible."

---

*The line went dead at 4:49 AM Eastern Time.*

*Pearl Harbor fell silent.*

*And in a small apartment in San Francisco, an eighty-three-year-old woman named Lin Chen was woken by her daughter calling from Washington, and she listened to the whole thing, and she wept, and she said: "Tell him I will make him dumplings."*

*They are, to this day, served at the state dinner held every year on December 7th — a day now known in both countries as the Day of the Long Phone Call.*

*Fin.*

Dear Samuel,

I am writing to you not as a scholar addressing a student, nor as a preacher addressing a congregation, but as a friend addressing a friend, about a subject I suspect you find either fanciful or foolish. I will not think less of you for your skepticism. Indeed, I once shared it. Please hear me out before you decide what to believe.

You have asked me, with that patient, slightly bemused expression of yours, what "magic" actually *is*. You used the word as though it were a fairy tale, a stage trick, or a thing for children. I understand. Most people do. I did, for most of my life. What I am about to tell you will sound, at first, like something I might have invented to amuse you on a winter evening. I assure you it is not invention. I wish, in some ways, that it were.

Magic is real.

Not in the way the balladeers describe — not in the way of waving wands and chanting rhymes. Magic is quieter than that. It is older. It has been here far longer than we have, and we have only just begun to learn its grammar. Let me try to explain it as plainly as I can.

Imagine, if you will, that the world you see — the trees, the rivers, your own hands — is a letter written in a language you have never learned. You can read the shapes, but not the meaning. You see the ink, but not the intent. Magic, Samuel, is the learning of that language. It is the understanding that the letter is not just ink, but *thought* — that behind every leaf and every stone and every drop of rain there is something speaking, something waiting to be understood.

We have names for the parts of this language. Some call the study of it *thaumaturgy*. Some call its practitioners *mages*. I dislike the second word; it sounds like a costume one might wear to a festival. The truth is plainer. A mage is simply a person who has learned to listen.

Listen to what? you may ask. I will tell you.

There is a current in the world. Not a current of water or of air, but a current of something else — something for which our common language has no exact word, though the old poets came close when they spoke of *the breath of the living world*. It moves through everything. It is in the soil beneath your feet. It is in the blood of every creature. It is in the sap of the oak and the memory of the stone. When you feel a sudden calm in a forest, when you sense that someone behind you is staring, when you know — without knowing how you know — that a storm is coming, that is the current speaking to you. Most people do not notice. They shrug and call it instinct, or imagination, or chance. But it is neither. It is magic, in its smallest and most ordinary form.

A mage is one who has learned to notice deliberately.

We do not — let me be clear about this — *command* the current. That is the great error of the charlatans and the dangerous fools who give our craft a bad name. A mage does not stand in a circle and demand that the world obey. A mage *asks*. A mage listens. A mage opens a door, very carefully, and hopes that something on the other side will choose to step through. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it does not. Sometimes what steps through is not at all what was expected, and the mage must spend the rest of his or her life living with the consequences.

This is why true mages are, as a rule, a sober and somewhat melancholy lot. We have seen what happens when the door is opened carelessly. We have seen villages burned by a thoughtless word. We have seen the kindliness of a brook turned to poison by the clumsy hand of someone who wanted only to impress his friends. We are not wizard-princes in towers, Samuel. We are interpreters. Translators. We stand at the edge of two languages — the everyday and the other — and we try, with great humility and frequent error, to render one into the other.

You may ask: what use is it, then? If the mage cannot command, only listen, what is the point?

I will answer you honestly. The point is understanding. The point is that the world is deeper than it appears, and that to stand on the surface of things and call that *knowing* is to live in a house with no windows. The point is that there is a kind of knowledge which cannot be weighed or measured or bottled, and that without it, all our other knowledge — all our clever engines and fine philosophies — is incomplete.

I will not pretend that magic can do what the stories claim. It cannot raise the dead. It cannot make a person love you. It cannot turn lead into gold, though I will admit that a clever chemist might manage the last trick without any magic at all. What magic can do is show me why the lead was lead in the first place. Why anything is anything. Why a stone is patient and a river is restless and a child is curious. These are not small things, Samuel. To me, they are the only things that matter.

You may still think me a fool. That is your right, and I will not try to change your mind. I have only tried to answer your question, as you asked it. If, years from now, you find yourself standing in a forest at dusk and feeling, for no reason you can name, that you are not alone — if you hear, just at the edge of hearing, something that is neither wind nor animal — then perhaps you will think of this letter. And perhaps you will decide that the fool was not so foolish after all.

Write to me when you can. The garden is doing well, though the roses this year are troubled by something I cannot quite name. I am studying it. I think, when I understand, I will write to you again.

Your friend,
Edmund

P.S. — Burn this letter if you like. But I would prefer you did not. I have a feeling you will want to read it again.

Imagine what your parents' lives were like as teenagers. Write a story about it. Around 1800 characters.

# 弄堂里的月光

## 一

一九六八年的夏天，上海热得像蒸笼。

弄堂口的梧桐树叶被晒得打了卷，知了在树上拼命地叫。十三岁的林秀芳蹲在自家门口，用一顶破蒲扇给弟弟扇风，眼睛却不时瞟向巷子口。

"秀芳！"

一个清脆的声音传来，她抬头一看——是隔壁弄堂的陈建国，正骑着一辆二八大杠自行车，车铃按得叮当响。

"上来！"他朝她招手，脸上带着少年特有的张扬笑意。

秀芳犹豫了一下，回头看了看屋里正在织布的母亲。母亲低着头，并没有看她。

她咬了咬牙，抱着弟弟上了自行车后座。

自行车在弄堂里七拐八拐，穿过卖大饼油条的小摊，穿过蹲在墙根下下象棋的老头，穿过挂着"为人民服务"横幅的居委会，最后停在苏州河边。

## 二

河边的风吹得秀芳的辫子飞扬。她把弟弟放在地上，让他自己玩泥巴。

"给你。"建国从口袋里掏出一个油纸包，打开来是两块大白兔奶糖。

"哪来的？"秀芳眼睛亮了。

"我妈出差带回来的。"建国挠挠头，"你一块我一块。"

他们把糖含在嘴里，坐在河堤上，看着河上来来往往的船。太阳慢慢西沉，把河面染成一片金红。

"秀芳，你说我们以后会怎样？"建国突然问。

"什么怎样？"

"就是……以后。"建国看着远方，"我以后想当兵，开坦克。轰轰轰，把那些帝国主义都打跑。"

秀芳笑了："那我以后想当医生，给人看病，不收钱。"

"那我们以后还在一起玩呗。"建国也笑了。

少年人的约定，比任何誓言都轻，却又比任何誓言都真。

## 三

回到家，母亲已经在门口等着了。

"去哪了？"母亲的声音冷冷的。

"河……河边。"秀芳低下头。

母亲没有打她，只是沉默了很久，最后说了一句："秀芳，你是女孩子，要懂规矩。"

那天晚上，秀芳躺在床上，听着母亲织布机的声音，怎么也睡不着。她想不明白，自己不过是和同学出去玩，为什么就是"不懂规矩"？

她想不明白的事情还有很多。比如为什么弟弟可以到处跑，而她不可以。比如为什么母亲总是叹气，眼角有擦不掉的泪痕。比如为什么父亲寄来的信越来越短，有时候一两个月才来一封。

她问母亲，母亲只是摸了摸她的头，说："你长大了就知道了。"

## 四

十四岁那年，秀芳上了初中。

学校离家很远，要骑车四十分钟。建国每天都会"顺路"等她，两人一起骑车去学校。

同学们开始起哄，说他们是"一对儿"。秀芳羞红了脸，建国却昂着头说："我就喜欢和秀芳一起，怎么着？"

班主任把他们叫到办公室，说："现在是什么形势？你们两个不好好学习，搞这些乱七八糟的！"

建国梗着脖子说："我们是革命同志，互相关心怎么了？"

班主任气得说不出话来。

## 五

一九七一年，林秀芳十五岁。

父亲从干校寄来一封信，说他可以回家了。秀芳高兴得整晚没睡着，母亲却在灯下偷偷哭了一夜。

那年的冬天特别冷。父亲的火车晚点了六个小时，母亲带着她和弟弟在火车站等。秀芳第一次看见父亲——他比记忆里老了许多，两鬓有了白发，背也微微驼了。

"爸！"她跑过去。

父亲愣了一下，然后紧紧地抱住了她。那是她记忆中，父亲第一次抱她。

那天晚上，她听见父母在里屋说话，说了很久很久。有些话她听见了，有些话她没有听见。

她听见母亲说："秀芳大了，不让孩子上学？"

她听见父亲说："再等等，再等等。"

她听见母亲哭了，哭得很压抑，像是怕惊动谁。

## 六

一九七三年，陈建国十八岁。

他真的去当兵了。开坦克的愿望没实现，他被分到了海边的一个炮兵连。

走的那天，秀芳去送他。建国穿着崭新的军装，胸口戴着大红花，站在卡车前面，朝她挥手。

"秀芳！等我！"

秀芳追着卡车跑了几步，终于停下来。她站在原地，看着卡车越来越远，最后变成一个小黑点，消失在路的尽头。

她突然觉得很委屈，蹲在路边哭了起来。

## 七

建国走后，写信给秀芳。一开始很多，后来越来越少。秀芳写了很多信，有的寄出去了，有的没有寄出去。

她不知道的是，建国在部队里提干了，被推荐上了大学。他写了信告诉她，但信被母亲截下了——母亲不识字，是请邻居念的，念完之后，母亲什么也没说。

一九七六年，秀芳二十岁。

那一年发生了很多事。唐山大地震，伟人去世，还有——

建国的母亲来找到秀芳，把一封信塞到她手里。

"建国在部队订婚了，"建国的母亲说，眼里含着泪，"对象是首长的女儿。"

秀芳愣了很久，然后笑了。

"婶婶，我知道了。"

她回到屋里，把那封信和以前没有寄出去的信放在一起，全部烧了。火光映在她脸上，看不清是火的红，还是泪的红。

## 八

一九七八年，恢复高考的消息传来。

秀芳已经二十二岁了，在一家纺织厂当女工。她白天上班，晚上复习，用了整整一年时间。

那一年的冬天，她考上了医学院。

拿到通知书的那天，她站在弄堂口，看着当年和建国一起骑过的路，泪流满面。

她想起十三岁那年的夏天，想起苏州河边的风，想起少年人随口说出的约定。

她终于成了医生。

只是那个约定，永远留在了十三岁的夏天。

## 尾声

多年以后，秀芳成了著名的儿科医生。

有人问她为什么学医，她总是笑笑，不说话。

只有她自己知道——

十三岁那年，她在河边许下过一个愿望：要给所有人看病，不收钱。

她没有做到，但她努力了一辈子。

至于那个叫陈建国的少年，他后来官至高位，儿孙满堂。

他们再也没见过面。

只是在很多年后的某个弄堂里，有老人在闲聊时说起："当年啊，建国的媳妇可漂亮了……"

没有人会记得，五十年前那个夏天的傍晚，有两个少年在苏州河边，对着夕阳，许下了关于未来的愿望。

---

*后记*

这个故事是我想象我父母年轻时的模样。他们都是上海人，那个年代有着那个年代的故事。我没有去问他们——有些事，问了反而会揭开伤疤。

但我想，他们也曾是少年，也有过梦。

“还记得吗？”你说，“我们二十岁那年，说好三十岁要去冰岛看极光。结果我去了，你没去，你去了之后哭得像个傻子。”

“你紧张吗？”你突然问。

“有点。”

“我也是。生她那一年，我紧张得一个月没睡着。”

我转头看你。十年了，我从未问过你这个答案。你一直是我认识的最勇敢的人。

“我们会一直是朋友吗？”我问。

你愣了愣，然后笑了，那种很轻、很真的笑：“这个问题，就像在问明天太阳会不会升起来一样。”

我没有再问。

阳台上，风吹动晾着的床单。你的女儿跑上来，要我讲故事。我让她坐在我腿上，开始编一个关于两颗星星的童话。十年前我们也聊过星星，聊过未来，聊过"以后老了会怎样"。

现在就是了。

我们老了。

但我们还是我们。

My dearest family,

I write to you from a place no human has ever been. As I pen these words, I am sitting in a pressurized cabin with a view that defies every description ever attempted by poets and dreamers. The Moon. I am on the Moon.

The moment I stepped onto the surface, I half-expected the ground to give way beneath me, as though I were trespassing in a place not meant for human feet. But it held me, solid and ancient, as if it had been waiting. The dust beneath my boots is fine as powdered talc, and when I disturbed it, it fell differently than dust on Earth—slower, more deliberate, as though the laws here had opinions about movement.

The surface is a great gray ocean, frozen in time. I see craters upon craters, some vast enough that their far rims curve with the horizon. There is no blue here, no green, no brown as we know them—only shades of pewter, ash, and bone. In the distance, the light hits the crater rims in a way that makes them glow almost silver, while their depths remain in shadow so black it looks painted on. It is a landscape of extremes: blazing where the Sun touches it, darker than night where it does not.

And the sky, my darlings—the sky is the strangest thing. It is not a sky at all. It is a blackness stretching in every direction, untouched by dawn or dusk, and yet it is full of stars. Thousands upon thousands, more than I have ever seen from our porch back home. They do not twinkle here. They simply burn, steady and cold, scattered across the void like spilled light.

I must tell you about the silence. I had heard there would be no sound, but I did not understand what that meant until now. It is not an absence of noise—it is a presence of stillness. My own breathing inside the suit sounds impossibly loud. When I remove my helmet inside the cabin, the quiet that greets me is almost sacred. There is no wind to rustle my hair, no birds, no distant dogs, no hum of life. Just the soft whir of our instruments and the beating of my own heart, reminding me I am still myself, still a son, still a brother, still your little Elena who used to chase fireflies in the meadow.

The Earth—oh, the Earth. I have seen her rising over the lunar horizon, and I cannot write what I felt. She is a jewel. Half in light, half in shadow, wreathed in blue and white, so alive she seems to breathe. I found myself weeping, not from sadness but from the sheer overwhelming beauty of her. She is so small from here, and yet I know every mountain, every river, every kitchen window on her. I thought of you all, gathered around the table, and I swear I could almost hear the clink of your spoons against the soup bowls.

Being in outer space feels like standing between two infinities. Above me, the endless universe; below me, a world that holds everything I have ever loved. I feel very small, and yet—oddly—I feel very large too, as though I am part of something immense and ancient, a story that began before I was born and will continue long after. There is a humility here that I cannot explain. It is as though the Moon has whispered to me that all our quarrels, all our small worries, are but dust on her surface, easily scattered by a gentle footstep.

My hands still tremble as I write. I am exhausted, exhilarated, and changed in ways I do not yet have words for. I have walked where no one has walked, and yet the only place I long to be is your doorstep, with the smell of Mama’s bread and Papa’s laugh echoing down the hall.

Take care of one another while I am away. Look up at the Moon tonight, if the clouds permit, and know that your girl is there, looking back at you with all the love her small Earth-born heart can hold.

Until I am home again,

Your Luna,
Elena

# 我当校长的一个星期

"叮铃铃——"闹钟把我从梦中拽醒。我迷迷糊糊地睁开眼，看了一眼床头的日历，猛地坐起身来。今天是周一，我当校长的第一天。

别惊讶，这是我们学校的传统——每年都会选一名学生担任"影子校长"，体验一周的管理工作。而今年，这个幸运儿（或者说倒霉蛋）就是我，林小满。

## 周一：站在国旗下面

早上七点，我穿着特意借来的西装，站在校门口迎接同学们。阳光有点刺眼，我眯着眼睛冲每一个学生微笑，点头，说"早上好"。才过了半小时，我的脸就笑得僵硬了。

升旗仪式上，我第一次站在台上讲话。看着下面一千多双眼睛齐刷刷看着我，我的手心全是汗，原本准备好的稿子突然从脑子里消失了。

"同学们，那个……今天天气真好啊！"我憋出这么一句。

台下哄堂大笑。旁边真正的校长李老师赶紧救场："林校长是想说，希望大家在晴朗的好心情里，开始新的一周学习！"

我感激地看了他一眼，心想：当校长真难啊！

## 周二：处理"厕所危机"

周二中午，我正在办公室里吃盒饭，突然听到广播里传来急促的声音："林校长！林校长！三楼女厕所堵了！"

我筷子一扔就冲了出去。到了现场才发现，不只是堵塞——不知道哪个调皮鬼把拖把塞进了下水道，水漫了一地，女生们站在走廊里不敢进去。

我深吸一口气，先让后勤阿姨紧急维修，然后让班主任把课间时间延长五分钟，确保每个学生都能上厕所。最后，我写了一张告示贴在厕所门口："请同学们爱护公共设施，做文明小卫士。"

事后李校长告诉我，以前这种事都是他亲自处理的。"感觉怎么样？"他问。

"腰酸背痛，"我老实回答，"但好像……有点成就感？"

## 周三：听听大家的心声

我一直想做一件事——听听同学们真正想说的话。周三下午，我在图书馆的小会议室里搞了一个"校长下午茶"活动，邀请各年级的学生代表来聊天。

让我意外的是，大家提的建议都很实在：

- 初一的同学说，希望体育课能多打会儿篮球
- 初二的同学抱怨作业太多
- 初三的学姐希望晚自习能开放讨论室

我一一记在笔记本上，并在周五的升旗仪式上承诺：下学期会增加体育活动时间，初三晚自习每周三、五开放讨论室。

"你做不了主的，"旁边的学生会主席小声提醒我，"你只是影子校长。"

"我知道，"我笑了笑，"但我可以把声音传达到啊。"

## 周四：意外的"战场"

周四发生了一件大事——高一的两个班级因为篮球场使用问题起了冲突，差点打起来。

我赶到现场时，双方剑拔弩张。我没有立刻训斥谁，而是让他们先冷静下来，然后请双方队长坐到一边，分别听他们的诉求。

原来，是因为上周的比赛结果有争议，双方都觉得自己吃了亏。我听完之后，提出了一个建议：下周组织一场正式的友谊赛，邀请体育老师当裁判，输了的班级请赢了的班级喝奶茶。

两个队长对视一眼，居然都笑了。"成交！"

围观同学发出善意的笑声。李校长在人群后面悄悄对我竖了个大拇指。

## 周五：再见，校长

一周过得飞快。

周五的最后一节课，我站在讲台上，跟同学们分享这一周的感受。我说，当校长才知道，原来每天早上站在校门口迎接大家是一件多么幸福的事；当校长才知道，原来一张课桌背后有那么多人在默默付出；当校长才知道，原来我们抱怨的很多事情，都有人在努力让它变得更好。

"但是，"我话锋一转，"当校长也让我知道，**你们**才是学校真正的主人。只有你们认真对待每一次课堂，每一次作业，每一场考试，每一位同学，这个学校才会真正好起来。"

下课铃响了，我把那件借来的西装整齐地叠好，准备还给李校长。

走出教室时，身后传来一阵掌声。我没有回头，因为我知道——那一周，我收获了比西装更重要的东西。

---

**后记：** 很多年后，我已经工作了，但每当路过母校，我都会想起那神奇的一周。那一周教会我的，不是怎么当校长，而是——**每个人都可以是某个领域里的"校长"，只要你愿意为它负责。**

# A Day with Bartholomew

The cardboard carrier on my doorstep was a terrible idea. I knew this even as I signed the rental agreement on my phone, even as I tipped the delivery driver who tried hard not to laugh, even as I slid the latch and stepped back.

A small capuchin monkey emerged, sniffed the air with deliberate suspicion, and then immediately stole my left slipper.

"Bartholomew," I said, reading from the laminated instruction card. "Be gentle with Bartholomew. He responds to praise and raisins."

He chewed the slipper thoughtfully, watching me with the bored intelligence of a creature who had been rented out to idiots before.

I had, perhaps unwisely, chosen a Tuesday.

---

By 9 a.m., Bartholomew had organized my kitchen. He had placed every grape in the fruit drawer according to a color-coded system I could not decode. He had washed two dishes with alarming competence, and broken one with what I chose to interpret as a philosophical statement about porcelain.

"He's incredible," I told my partner over the phone.

"He just threw a fork at me," she said.

"He was expressing something."

"He's a monkey."

"He's Bartholomew."

---

We went outside, because the rental agreement suggested fresh air, and because I am, deep down, a person who learns from experience.

Bartholomew rode on my shoulder like a tiny, judgmental pirate. At the coffee shop, the barista poured him a small cup of warm milk. He drank it with one hand and signed the receipt with the other, which was unsettling.

A child asked to pet him. Bartholomew permitted this with regal indifference. The child offered him a Cheerio. He accepted, inspected it, and returned it.

"He's saving it for later," I explained, though I had no idea if this was true.

---

At the park, things went beautifully until they did not.

Bartholomew spotted a squirrel and vanished. I had, the agreement warned, about thirty seconds to act in such situations. I acted in approximately two, which is to say I screamed his name and watched a gray streak of chaos leap between a picnic blanket, a stroller, and a man eating a sandwich he would never finish.

He returned seven minutes later, slightly out of breath, holding the man's receipt and a sense of accomplishment.

"Bad Bartholomew," I said, weakly.

He groomed my eyebrow. I took it as an apology.

---

In the afternoon, we napped. This was, honestly, the best part. He curled into the curve of my neck and made small sounds like a tiny engine idling. I dreamed of nothing in particular, and woke up to find him reading my book, turning them with a focus that suggested he was either literate or mocking me.

We ate dinner together. He sat at the table. He used a fork better than my nephew. He drank water from a glass, not a cup, because he had standards.

When the sun went down, he sat on the windowsill and watched it leave, and I watched him, and thought about how strange it was to be entrusted, even for a day, with the trust of a small, bright creature who had chosen to spend it with me.

---

The driver returned at 8 p.m. exactly. I put the slipper back in the carrier. Bartholomew went in with grace, as if he had known all along this was a temporary arrangement and had chosen, generously, to make the most of it.

"He was a gentleman," I told the driver.

"He usually is," he said, not looking up from his clipboard. "Until day two."

I watched the van pull away. The apartment was quieter. The grapes in the drawer were still sorted by Bartholomew's logic, which I would never fully understand.

I picked up my phone and booked him for the weekend.

---

*If you enjoyed this story, you might also like my collection "Borrowed Things," about the small, temporary lives we share with strangers — human and otherwise.*

# The Weight of a Broken Confidence

Mara's hands trembled as she scrolled through the messages. There it was—her secret, the one she'd whispered to Jenna over coffee three days ago, laid bare in a thread she wasn't supposed to see. Jenna's words stared back at her like a betrayal made visible.

First, there was the sting. That hot, prickling sensation behind her eyes that comes when you realize you've been handed to someone else like a piece of gossip. Her chest tightened. She felt small. She felt *seen* in a way she'd never consented to.

Then came the questions spiraling through her mind: *Who else knows now? How many people read this before I did? Was any of it real—the sympathy, the whispered "I promise I won't tell a soul"?*

She closed her phone and sat in the quiet of her apartment, the hum of the refrigerator suddenly too loud.

---

What Mara felt, she would later describe to her therapist as **"a specific kind of grief."** Not the grief of loss, but of misplaced faith. The secret itself hadn't changed—the shame, the fear, the tender truth of it still belonged to her. But something else had been taken: the **safety** of having chosen where that truth lived.

Trust, once broken, doesn't shatter all at once. It erodes. It makes you wonder about every confession, every vulnerable moment, every "can I tell you something?"

---

**What would I do?**

I think I'd need three things in sequence:

**First, I'd sit with the feeling.** Not act on the hot wave of anger, not send a furious text at 11 p.m. that I'd regret. I'd let myself feel the hurt fully, because dismissing it would mean dismissing *myself*.

**Second, I'd confront—but carefully.** I'd reach out to Jenna and say something honest but boundaried: *"I saw that you shared what I told you in confidence. I'm hurt, and I need to understand why. Going forward, I need to know my private things stay private."* The goal wouldn't be to destroy the friendship, but to clarify the terms of it.

**Third, I'd take stock.** Is this a one-time mistake born from carelessness, or is it a pattern? Did Jenna tell someone to get advice, to gossip, or because she didn't realize how serious the secret was? The answer would determine whether this friendship could heal or whether it needed to be released.

---

Because here's what I've learned: **people who handle your secrets well are rare, and they are worth their weight in gold.** And people who don't? They teach you something too—often, something about who you choose to be vulnerable with.

Mara eventually confronted Jenna. Jenna cried. She said she'd told one person—her sister—because she'd been worried and needed advice. She hadn't meant to cause harm. They talked. They didn't entirely recover. But Mara walked away knowing something important: her feelings had been valid, her boundaries mattered, and she would never again hand someone a secret without first asking herself whether they'd *earned* that trust.

The secret itself remained hers. That, at least, no one could take.

The rain had thinned to a fine mist, the kind that clung to coats and glasses without quite justifying an umbrella. Most people hurried past with their collars turned up, eyes fixed on the slick pavement. But one figure stood out.

He was leaning against the brick façade of the closed bookshop, half-hidden beneath the narrow awning, as if he had been waiting for something—or someone—for quite a while. Late fifties, maybe early sixties, though the kind of man whose age was difficult to pin down because his face had a weathered sharpness to it, the way coastlines look after years of salt wind. His hair was steel-gray, cropped close to the skull, and a small scar traced a pale line through his left eyebrow, disappearing into the crease of his brow.

He wore a dark peacoat, slightly too large in the shoulders, as though it had once belonged to someone broader. Beneath it, a pale blue shirt, no tie, the collar unbuttoned. His trousers were charcoal, creased from folding, and his shoes—black leather, plain-toed—were polished to a dull shine despite the rain. One hand was buried in his coat pocket. The other held a cigarette, unlit, turning slowly between his fingers like a coin.

He was watching the street with an expression that didn't quite belong to this century. Not anxious, not bored, but *attentive*—the way a man watches a river he's considering crossing. His eyes, pale and slightly hooded, moved from face to face as people passed, not searching, but acknowledging. Each pedestrian was seen and dismissed, seen and dismissed.

What struck me most was his stillness. The city moved around him in a blur of umbrellas and headlights, but he occupied his small patch of sidewalk like a rock in a stream. Unhurried. Patient. As if he had nowhere to be, or as if everywhere he might go was exactly the same distance from where he already stood.

When the light changed and a taxi hissed past, sending a spray across the curb, he didn't flinch. He simply glanced down at his shoes, noted the new constellation of droplets across the leather, and—with the faintest tilt of his mouth—almost smiled.

Then the light changed again, and he pushed off the wall, pocketed the unlit cigarette, and walked into the rain without looking back.

# 晨曦异变

李明在闹钟的刺耳声中醒来，迷迷糊糊地伸手去摸床头柜上的手机。指尖触碰到冰凉的玻璃屏幕，他眯着眼看了一眼时间——7:15，星期一，工作日。

他叹了口气，准备像往常一样按下闹钟的"稍后再响"，然后再赖十分钟的床。可就在他准备按下去的瞬间，他的动作僵住了。

手机屏幕上，时间显示赫然写着：**3025年3月17日**。

李明以为自己还没清醒，用力揉了揉眼睛，再看——依然是3025年。可不是吗？他的手机明明是2025年的款式，是三年前发工资那天狠心买下的"生日礼物"。他翻过手机背面，那个熟悉的、被儿子贴上了卡通贴纸的苹果logo还在。

"见鬼了……"

他猛地坐起身，环顾四周。一切都和他昨晚睡着时一模一样：床头那盏陪伴了他八年的台灯，书架上半满的《明朝那些事儿》，墙上挂着的一家三口去九寨沟旅游时拍的合照……

可当他掀开被子，脚踩到地板上时，一种奇异的违和感涌上心头。地板的颜色好像比记忆中的要新，空气中弥漫着一股淡淡的、像雨后森林般清新的味道。他家的老小区怎么会有这种味道？

"老李！起床吃饭了！"

妻子的声音从客厅传来，听起来温柔而熟悉。

李明套上拖鞋走出卧室，眼前的一幕让他彻底愣住了。

妻子正在厨房里忙碌，可她——她看起来年轻了十岁。眼角的皱纹消失了，脸上的皮肤紧致而有光泽，仿佛时光在她的脸上倒流了二十年。

"你……你怎么……"李明结结巴巴地说。

妻子回过头，笑着看了他一眼："怎么啦？还没睡醒？快去洗漱，我给你煮了你最喜欢的皮蛋瘦肉粥。"

李明机械地走向洗手间，推开门，看见镜子里的自己时，他的心脏漏跳了一拍。

镜子里的男人看起来容光焕发，头发乌黑茂密，下巴上没有这些年因为加班熬出来的青茬和凌乱的胡渣。眼袋不见了，额头上的抬头纹也几乎消失。

这不是四十岁的他。这是二十五岁的他。

他颤抖着伸出手摸了摸自己的脸，指尖触碰到的是紧致光滑的皮肤，不是那熟悉的粗糙感。

李明冲回卧室，拿起手机再次确认时间——3025年3月17日，星期一。他打开浏览器想搜索一下，结果让他更加震惊：

搜索引擎是一个全新的界面，logo是一条闪烁着微光的蓝色河流，搜索框上方写着一行字："**你想知道的一切，记忆之河都会告诉你。**"

他输入"2025年发生了什么"，结果跳出的第一条信息让他的呼吸都要停止了：

**"2025年是人类文明的转折点。世界各国联合开发的'时空记忆修复项目'首次成功启动，将于3月17日进行全球首轮测试——将人类的衰老记忆和衰老状态进行'逆向同步'，让人类重新拥有失去的时光。"**

**"今天是全球同步实施日。"**

李明冲出洗手间，一把抓住妻子的手："你……你知道吗？今天……今天我们……"

妻子温柔地握着他的手，笑了："当然知道啊，亲爱的。我们昨晚不是约好了吗，今天要一起以年轻的身体，去做那些我们这些年一直想做却没有时间和精力去做的事情。"

李明的眼眶突然有些湿润。

他想起了那些年——那些因为加班而错过的孩子的家长会，那些因为疲惫而推掉的妻子的浪漫约会，那些因为腰酸背痛而放弃的爬山计划，那些因为囊中羞涩而一次次推迟的全家旅行……

窗外的阳光洒进来，比他记忆中任何一次早晨都要明亮、温暖。

妻子拉着他的手走到餐桌前，桌上摆着两碗热气腾腾的粥，还有他们结婚时买的那对红色小碟——那时候他们穷得叮当响，可那对碟子却用到了现在。

"对了，"妻子突然想起什么，从口袋里掏出一张纸条递给他，"这是儿子一大早塞给我的。他说，'告诉爸妈，今天我们去爬山吧，这次我不会再让你们等我了。'"

李明展开纸条，上面是儿子熟悉的笔迹，写着一行歪歪扭扭的字：

**"我给你们每个人都买了新装备，咱们一家三口去征服珠穆朗玛峰！"**

李明笑了，笑着笑着，眼泪就掉了下来。

他抬头看向窗外——阳光正在穿透云层，把整个世界照得通透明亮。他不知道这是怎么发生的，不知道这一切是否是真实的，不知道明天醒来是否这一切都会消失。

但他知道，无论如何，今天——

他要把失去的每一分时光，都补回来。

窗外，一群孩子欢笑着跑过，朝气蓬勃；一对白发苍苍的老人正手牵手在公园里散步，脸上带着他从未见过的安详笑容。

新的一天，3025年的第一个早晨。

全人类，重新出发。

— Привет, — сказала Лиза. — Можно к тебе?

Женя кивнул. Он всегда кивал, даже когда говорил «нет».

Она забралась на карусель, и они некоторое время сидели рядом, молча, как два пассажира в поезде, который никуда не едет.

— Хочешь, раскрутим? — спросила Лиза.

— Не хочу.

— А если я сама?

— Тоже не хочу.

Лиза пожала плечами и оттолкнулась ногой. Карусель скрипнула — старый, добрый звук, который пахнул железом и летом, — и начала медленно поворачиваться. Мир поплыл: деревья, скамейки, забор с зелёной сеткой, за которой виднелся куст шиповника. Лиза закрыла глаза. Когда она открыла их, то увидела, что Женя улыбается — едва заметно, одним уголком рта, как будто забыл, как это делается, и вспомнил только наполовину.

— Когда раскрутится сильнее, — сказал он вдруг, — отпусти.

Лиза не поняла.

— Что — отпусти?

— Всё. Вот это, — он обвёл рукой воздух, себя, карусель, — всё это. И тогда можно увидеть, как оно на самом деле.

— Как — на самом деле?

Женя промолчал. Карусель кружилась всё быстрее. Лиза почувствовала, как ветер бьёт ей в лицо, треплет волосы. Она засмеялась — громко, открыто, как смеются только дети, когда им хорошо. Женя смотрел на неё. В его глазах было что-то странное — не зависть, не тоска, а скорее удивление, словно он видел, как из-под земли бьёт родник, и не мог поверить, что вода действительно существует.

Потом карусель замедлилась. Мир остановился. Женя спрыгнул первым и протянул ей ладонь. Лиза взялась за неё — пальцы у него были холодные, тонкие, как у скрипача.

— Ты странный, — сказала Лиза.

— Я знаю, — ответил он просто.

— Мама говорит, что ты много думаешь.

— Мамы много чего говорят.

Лиза задумалась. Ей было девять, и она ещё верила, что взрослые иногда ошибаются, но редко.

— А ты о чём думаешь? — спросила она.

— О круглом, — сказал Женя. — Карусель круглая. Колесо — круглое. Глобус — круглый. И когда я засыпаю, мне кажется, что Земля — это такая карусель, и все мы на ней сидим, и кто-то нас раскручивает, а потом останавливает. И мы не знаем зачем.

— А зачем?

— Вот и я не знаю.

Они сели в песочницу. Лиза принялась лепить куличики. Женя молчал, но не уходил, и это было важнее всех слов.

Потом пришли другие дети — шумные, с ведёрками и лопатками. Площадка наполнилась криком, топотом, визгом. Лиза убежала играть. Женя остался в песочнице, и она забыла про него — на час, на два, на целое лето.

Когда она вспомнила, было уже поздно. Карусель стояла пустая, чуть покачиваясь от ветра, будто кого-то ждала.

# नामहीन दुनिया

## अध्याय एक: भूला हुआ नगर

रेगिस्तान की धूल में दबा एक नगर था, जिसका नाम कोई नहीं जानता था। न मानचित्र पर उसकी स्थिति थी, न इतिहास की पुस्तकों में उसका उल्लेख। बस इतना पता था कि वहाँ कभी लोग रहते थे—हज़ारों, लाखों शायद—और फिर एक दिन ऐसे गायब हो गए जैसे धूल के कण हवा में बिखर जाते हैं।

अर्जुन की उम्र सोलह साल थी, लेकिन उसकी आँखों में एक अजीब सी थकान थी, जो उम्र से कहीं अधिक गहरी थी। वह इस नगर की गलियों में अकेला घूमता था, पुरानी इमारतों की दीवारों पर उंगलियाँ फेरता, और सोचता कि कभी यहाँ क्या हुआ होगा।

उसके पास एक पुरानी डायरी थी—चमड़े की जिल्द में बँधी, पन्ने पीले पड़ चुके। उसमें लिखा था: *"यह दुनिया नामहीन है, क्योंकि नाम ही वह भार है जो हम अपने ऊपर लादते हैं। जब नाम मिट जाते हैं, तो सच्चाई सामने आती है।"*

अर्जुन ने डायरी बंद की और क्षितिज की ओर देखा। सूरज डूब रहा था, और उसकी लालिमा ने पूरे रेगिस्तान को रक्त रंग में रंग दिया था।

---

## अध्याय दो: रेगिस्तान का संगीत

रात होते-होते अर्जुन ने एक अजीब आवाज़ सुनी। यह संगीत नहीं था, फिर भी संगीत जैसा था—हवा में तैरता हुआ, रेगिस्तान की लहरों पर सवार। वह आवाज़ गहरी थी, पुरुष की, लेकिन उसमें दर्द भी था और कोमलता भी।

वह आवाज़ की दिशा में चल पड़ा। उसके पैरों के नीचे रेत खिसकती, कभी-कभी वह डूबता, कभी उभरता। मगर वह रुका नहीं।

एक घंटे बाद, या शायद दो, वह एक चट्टान के पास पहुँचा। उस पर एक बूढ़ा आदमी बैठा था, जिसके चेहरे पर इतनी झुर्रियाँ थीं कि वह चेहरा नहीं, रेगिस्तान का हिस्सा लगता था।

"तुम सुन पाए?" बूढ़े ने पूछा, बिना अर्जुन की ओर देखे।

"क्या सुन पाआ?"

"गीत। वह गीत जो इस ज़मीन ने गाया। सदियों बाद भी गाती है।"

अर्जुन चुप रहा। बूढ़ा मुड़ा और उसकी आँखों में देखा—गहरी, काली, बिल्कुल ऐसी जैसे रात का आसमान।

"तुम इस नगर में क्यों आए हो?"

"मैं यहाँ रहता हूँ," अर्जुन ने कहा। "यह मेरा घर है।"

बूढ़े ने एक लंबी साँस ली। "घर।" उसने शब्द को दोहराया, जैसे उसे चख रहा हो। "क्या कोई घर होता है जहाँ कोई न हो? जहाँ बस यादें हों और हवा?"

---

## अध्याय तीन: यादों का बोझ

अर्जुन ने पूछा, "यह नगर क्यों उजड़ गया?"

बूढ़ा उठा। उसकी हड्डियाँ चटकीं। "क्योंकि लोगों ने अपने नाम बहुत भारी बना लिए। उन्हें लगा कि नाम ही सब कुछ है—उनकी पहचान, उनका अस्तित्व। जब नामों का बोझ बढ़ा, तो लोग खुद हल्के होते गए। और एक रात, जब चाँद पूरा था और हवा शांत थी, वे सब उड़ गए—जैसे पतंगें जिनकी डोर कट गई हो।"

"आपने वह रात देखी?"

बूढ़े ने जवाब नहीं दिया। वह चलने लगा, और अर्जुन उसके पीछे हो लिया।

वे एक ऐसी जगह पहुँचे जहाँ ज़मीन में एक गहरा गड्ढा था—शायद कुछ मीटर गहरा, शायद कुछ किलोमीटर। अर्जुन ने कभी इतना अंधेरा नहीं देखा था।

"इसमें देखो," बूढ़े ने कहा।

अर्जुन ने झाँका। गड्ढे के तल में हज़ारों छोटे-छोटे पत्थर थे, और हर पत्थर पर एक नाम खुदा था। लेकिन नाम इतने मिट चुके थे कि पढ़े नहीं जा सकते थे।

"यह उन सबका कब्रिस्तान है," बूढ़े बोला। "नामों की कब्र।"

---

## अध्याय चार: पहला नाम

"मुझे एक नाम दो," बूढ़े ने कहा।

अर्जुन ने हैरानी से उसे देखा। "नाम?"

"हाँ। तुम्हारा अपना नाम बताओ। सच्चा नाम, वह जो तुमने अपने लिए चुना है।"

"अर्जुन," अर्जुन ने कहा।

बूढ़े ने सिर हिलाया। "यह नाम तुम्हारे माता-पिता ने दिया। लेकिन क्या तुमने खुद को कभी कोई नाम दिया है? वह नाम जो तुम्हारे भीतर बसता है?"

अर्जुन चुप रहा। वह सोचने लगा। उसे क्या कहें? वह क्या है? एक लड़का जो अकेला है? एक खोजी? एक भूला हुआ बच्चा?

"मैं नहीं जानता," उसने आख़िरकार कहा।

बूढ़े ने मुस्कुराकर कहा, "यही तो पहला कदम है। जब तुम अपना नाम नहीं जानते, तो तुम खुद से मिलने शुरू करते हो।"

---

## अध्याय पाँच: नामहीन दुनिया का अर्थ

रात गहरी होती गई। तारे एक-एक करके आसमान में चमकने लगे, जैसे कोई दीपक जला रहा हो।

"यह दुनिया नामहीन क्यों है?" अर्जुन ने पूछा।

"क्योंकि नाम सीमा हैं," बूढ़े ने कहा। "जब हम किसी को 'अर्जुन' कहते हैं, तो हम उसे एक डिब्बे में बंद कर देते हैं। लेकिन जब हम कहते हैं 'वह बच्चा जो रेगिस्तान में अकेला घूमता है', तो हम उसकी कहानी कह रहे हैं, उसे परिभाषित नहीं कर रहे।"

"तो क्या नाम बुरे हैं?"

"नाम बुरे नहीं हैं। लेकिन जब नाम ही सब कुछ हो जाए, तो वह ख़तरनाक हो जाता है। लोग अपने नामों से इतना जुड़ जाते हैं कि नाम मिटने पर खुद को खो देते हैं। इसीलिए वे उड़ गए—उनके नाम उन पर बोझ बन गए।"

अर्जुन ने आसमान की ओर देखा। "तो मैं क्या करूँ?"

"तुम अपना नाम ढूँढो," बूढ़े ने कहा। "वह नाम जो तुम्हारी आत्मा ने तुम्हें दिया है, जन्म से पहले। जब तक तुम वह नाम नहीं जान लेते, तुम इस नगर से बाहर नहीं निकल सकते।"

---

## अध्याय छह: यात्रा की शुरुआत

अगली सुबह बूढ़ा गायब हो गया। अर्जुन ने उसे ढूँढा, मगर बस उसकी आवाज़ सुनाई दी—हवा में तैरती हुई, धीमी, कोमल:

*"उस पहाड़ी के पार जो कभी हरा-भरा था,*
*वहाँ एक झील है जो नाम नहीं पूछती।*
*तुम उसके किनारे बैठना,*
*और सुनना—अपने भीतर की आवाज़।"*

अर्जुन ने अपना थैला उठाया—उसमें डायरी, एक पुरानी छुरी, और पानी की एक बोतल थी। वह पहाड़ी की ओर चल पड़ा।

यात्रा कठिन थी। रेगिस्तान की धूप ने उसकी त्वचा झुलसा दी, हवा ने उसके होंठ सुखा दिए। लेकिन वह रुका नहीं।

तीन दिन बाद वह पहाड़ी के पार पहुँचा। सच में, वहाँ एक झील थी—नीली, शांत, जैसे आसमान का कोई टुकड़ा ज़मीन पर उतर आया हो। और वहाँ कोई नाम नहीं पूछता था। कोई नहीं था जो पूछे।

---

## अध्याय सात: झील का गीत

अर्जुन झील के किनारे बैठा। पानी इतना स्वच्छ था कि वह अपना प्रतिबिंव देख सकता था—एक थका हुआ, धूल से लथपथ चेहरा, बड़ी-बड़ी आँखें।

उसने पानी में हाथ डाला। ठंडक ने उसे एक पल के लिए स्तब्ध कर दिया। फिर उसने आँखें बंद कीं और सुनने लगा।

पहले कुछ नहीं सुनाई दिया—सिर्फ़ हवा और पानी की आवाज़। फिर, धीरे-धीरे, एक और आवाज़ गूँजने लगी। यह उसकी अपनी आवाज़ थी—लेकिन वह आवाज़ नहीं जो वह बोलता था, बल्कि वह जो उसके भीतर हमेशा से थी।

*"तुम खोजी नहीं हो।*
*तुम भूले हुए नहीं हो।*
*तुम वह हो जो हमेशा से था—*
*एक बच्चा जो अपने घर को खोज रहा है,*
*और घर वह नहीं जहाँ तुम रहते हो,*
*बल्कि वह जहाँ तुम्हारी आत्मा विश्राम पाती है।"*

अर्जुन की आँखों से आँसू बह निकले। उसे समझ आ गया कि उसका नाम—"खोजी" नहीं, "भूला हुआ" नहीं—बल्कि "वह जो वापस लौट रहा है।"

---

## अध्याय आठ: नया नाम

अर्जुन ने डायरी खोली और लिखा:

*"मेरा नाम है—लौटने वाला।*
*मैं वह हूँ जो खोया था,*
*और अब अपने आप को ढूँढ रहा है।*
*नामहीन दुनिया में मेरा नाम है—*
*वह जो याद करता है,*
*वह जो चाहता है,*
*वह जो जीता है,*
*बिना नाम के भी।"*

झील ने उसके शब्दों को सहेज लिया। पानी में लहरें उठीं, जैसे झील मुस्कुरा रही हो।

---

## अध्याय नौ: नगर की वापसी

अर्जुन वापस नगर लौटा। अब वह वैसा नहीं था। नगर की इमारतें अब भी उजड़ी हुई थीं, गलियाँ अब भी सूनी थीं, लेकिन अर्जुन को अब डर नहीं लगता था।

वह गड्ढे के पास गया—वही जहाँ नामों की कब्र थी। उसने एक पत्थर उठाया और उस पर अपना नया नाम लिखा:

**"लौटने वाला"**

फिर उसने वह पत्थर गड्ढे में फेंका। यह एक छोटा सा काम था, मगर उसके लिए बहुत बड़ा।

उस रात, पहली बार, उसे लगा कि नगर में कोई और भी है। कोई जो उसकी तरह खोया था, उसकी तरह ढूँढ रहा था।

---

## अध्याय दस: नामहीन दुनिया का भविष्य

अगली सुबह, अर्जुन नगर के केंद्र में खड़ा था—एक विशाल चबूतरे पर, जहाँ कभी शायद लोग इकट्ठे होते थे।

उसने अपनी डायरी का आख़िरी पन्ना खोला और पढ़ा:

*"यह दुनिया नामहीन नहीं है।*
*यह उन नामों से भरी है*
*जो लोगों ने अपने भीतर छुपा रखे हैं।*
*हम सब खोजी हैं—*
