# 失语的钟表匠

## 一、遗物

柏林夏洛滕堡区的一条老巷深处，有一间从不开灯的钟表店。招牌上写着"霍夫曼父子"，油漆斑驳得像一张被雨水反复冲洗过的旧脸。

苏晚晴第一次推开那扇门时，是在一个深秋的黄昏。她手里捧着一只老旧的怀表——她刚去世的外祖母留下的唯一遗物。

"表针停了。"她说。

柜台后坐着一位白发老人，戴着一副厚厚的圆框眼镜，镜片后的眼睛像两颗被遗忘了很久的玻璃珠。他抬起头，看了苏晚晴一眼，又低头看了看那只怀表。

"它不会走的。"老人的声音像生锈的齿轮，"它到了该停的时候。"

"我想让它走。"

老人沉默了很久。然后他从柜台后站起来，佝偻的背影像一把折叠了太久的尺。他从苏晚晴手里接过怀表，拇指在表盖上摩挲了一下。

"您祖母叫什么名字？"

"苏锦瑟。"

老人的手微微一颤。他把怀表还给苏晚晴，转身走向店铺最深处，从一架积满灰尘的落地钟后取出一个木盒。

"您来得比我预想的晚了二十年。"他说，"您祖母让我把这个交给她的外孙女——如果她来的话。"

木盒里躺着一张对折的羊皮纸，已经发黄发脆。苏晚晴展开它，上面只有一行字，用她熟悉的、略带颤抖的笔迹写着：

**"当这封信被你读到的时候，去找霍夫曼先生，请他带你去看那座停了七十三年的钟。但不要在雨夜去。"**

苏晚晴抬起头，却发现老人已经不见了。

店铺深处，落地钟的钟摆突然开始晃动——它明明停了七十年，却在这一刻，发出了沉闷的、当当作响的声音。

## 二、不要在雨夜

苏晚晴在外祖母的葬礼上哭干了眼泪。她从小是外祖母带大的，父母长年在海外做生意，只在生日时寄来昂贵的礼物和短暂的视频通话。外祖母教她念唐诗、画水墨、在夏夜的院子里数星星，给她讲那些从未在任何书本上出现过的故事——关于一座停了七十三年的钟，关于一个会修时间的钟表匠，关于一场必须等待的相遇。

"等你长大了，替外婆去做一件事。"外祖母最后一次清醒时对她说，手指冰凉，"但要记住——不要在雨夜去。"

苏晚晴以为那只是老人糊涂了。

直到此刻，她握着那张羊皮纸，站在昏暗的钟表店里，听着七十年未响的落地钟轰鸣如雷。

"霍夫曼先生？"她朝店铺深处喊道。

没有回应。

她向前走了几步。落地钟的钟摆晃得越来越剧烈，每一下都像在敲击她的心脏。在钟的背后，她看到了一扇暗门——准确地说，是一面被刻意做旧的墙，中间有一条几乎不可见的缝隙。

苏晚晴把手伸进去。

暗门无声地打开了。

门后是一条向下延伸的石阶，消失在黑暗里。一股带着机油、铁锈和某种她无法辨认的气味的凉风扑面而来。

她回头看了一眼店铺——夕阳的最后一线光正从橱窗里撤退。她想起了羊皮纸上的话。

**不要在雨夜去。**

她看了眼手机。天气预报显示，今天是晴天。

苏晚晴走了下去。

## 三、地下

石阶尽头是一个出乎意料的宽敞空间。数百座钟表挂在四面墙上，大小不一，形态各异——怀表、座钟、挂钟、布谷鸟钟、沙漏，甚至还有几座她叫不出名字的、像是来自另一个时代的机械装置。它们全都静止着，像一片由时间凝固成的森林。

空间中央，是一座她从未见过的钟。

它大约有两人高，青铜的外壳上布满了看不懂的铭文和符号。钟面是空白的——没有刻度，没有指针，只有一个巨大的、缓缓旋转的齿轮在表盘后面若隐若现。最奇特的是，这座钟并没有"停"——它在运转，发出的却是反向的声音，像是在把什么东西往回拨。

"您来了。"

苏晚晴猛地转身。老人不知什么时候出现在了她身后，手里端着一盏煤油灯。灯火在他镜片后面跳动，像两只不安分的眼睛。

"这……这是什么？"苏晚晴问。

"时间本身。"老人说，"或者说，时间被遗留下来的一小块碎片。"

苏晚晴听不懂。

老人叹了口气，把煤油灯放在地上。他解开外套的扣子，苏晚晴这才注意到，他的左胸上别着一枚徽章——那是一个由齿轮和玫瑰组成的图案，她在外祖母最珍藏的旧相册里见过。

"我叫汉斯·霍夫曼。"老人说，"我的父亲叫埃里希·霍夫曼，他的父亲也叫埃里希·霍夫曼——我们家族每一代人，都使用同一个名字。我们是这座钟的守护者，已经守了七十三代。"

"守护什么？"

"守护一个秘密。"老人抬起手，指向那座青铜巨钟，"这座钟，可以回到过去——但只能回到一个人一生中最重要的一天。那一天被封存在齿轮里，等待着被解锁。"

苏晚晴的呼吸急促起来。

"我祖母……她来过这里？"

"她不仅来过。"老人说，"她把她的那一天，锁在了这座钟里。"

## 四、那一天

煤油灯的火苗跳了跳，像是听懂了什么。

老人从口袋里取出一枚钥匙——不是金属的，是用某种透明的、像冰又像玻璃的材料制成的，在灯光下折射出淡淡的彩虹。

"你祖母是 1953 年的春天来到这里的。"老人说，"那年她十八岁，和你一样的眼睛——黑色，但里面装着星星。"

苏晚晴的鼻子一酸。

"她爱上了一个不该爱的人。"老人继续说，"一个德国青年，一个钟表学徒，名字叫埃里希——我的祖父。"

苏晚晴愣在那里。

"那个时代，那条边界，两个相爱的人，注定无法在一起。"老人的声音变得极轻，"她在离开的那个早晨，把她一生中最重要的一天交给了我祖父——那是一个夏天的清晨，他们在菩提树下告别，蝉鸣很响，她说她永远不会忘记他看她的眼神。"

"我祖父用毕生的时间，把那一天刻进了这座钟。"

"然后他等了一辈子。等到他的儿子、他的孙子，替他继续等下去。"

"等到你。"

苏晚晴觉得自己的眼眶像是被什么烫了一下。

"可是……"她哽咽道，"她已经去世了。我再也见不到她了。"

"你不必见到她。"老人说，"但你可以回到那一天——她最珍贵的一天，回到那一刻，回到菩提树下。你会看到她，也会看到那个年轻的德国青年。你不会改变任何事，因为那一天已经被封存了，不会再被书写。"

"你只是去看一眼。"

苏晚晴握紧了那枚冰凉的钥匙。

"可是羊皮纸上说，不要在雨夜去。"

"因为在雨夜，时间会哭。"老人说，"眼泪会打湿齿轮，那一天就会被冲走。"

他抬起头，看向头顶那片看不见的天空。

"今天是晴天。"他说，"但明天，会下雨。"

## 五、选择

苏晚晴在巨钟前站了很久。

她想起了外祖母在她七岁那年的一个雨夜，独自坐在窗前，背对着她，肩膀微微颤抖。她走过去，问外婆怎么了。外婆转过身，笑着对她说"没事"，但眼睛是红的。

那是一个她从未问出口的问题。

"如果我回去，"她问老人，"我能和她说话吗？"

"不能。"老人说，"你是旁观者。那一天已经发生过了，你不能参与。"

"那我能做什么？"

"看她。"老人说，"好好看她。把她记在心里。"

苏晚晴点了点头。她伸出颤抖的手，把钥匙插进了巨钟背后一个她之前没有注意到的锁孔。

"等等。"老人突然说。

苏晚晴停下动作。

"你祖母还留下了一样东西。"老人说，"她说如果你决定去，就把这个给你。"

他从怀里取出一个陈旧的小铁盒。苏晚晴打开它，里面是一张泛黄的照片——年轻的祖母穿着素色旗袍，站在一棵巨大的菩提树下，微微笑着，眼睛却看着画面之外，像是在看着什么她再也看不到的人。

照片的背面，有一行小字：

**"替我问他一声：那天，你后悔吗？"**

苏晚晴的眼泪终于落了下来。

## 六、雨前

苏晚晴深吸一口气，把钥匙转动了一圈。

巨钟开始轰鸣，那些刻在青铜上的铭文和符号同时亮了起来，发出一种温柔的、像母亲哼唱摇篮曲一样的光。空白钟面上，齿轮的旋转突然加快，整个地下室开始震动。

她闭上眼睛。

当她再次睁开眼时，她站在一条铺满落叶的街道上。阳光明媚，空气里有菩提花的清香。远处传来钟声——不是整点，是那种轻快的、跳跃的报时声。

她面前是一棵巨大的菩提树。树下站着一个穿着素色旗袍的少女，和一个金发的德国青年。

少女的脸——那是外祖母的脸。年轻的，没有皱纹的，眼角没有泪痕的外祖母。她正仰着头，对那个德国青年说什么。德国青年低下头，看着她，眼睛里装着整个夏天的阳光。

苏晚晴站在几步之外，看着他们。她想走过去，想抱住那个少女，想告诉她："外婆，我来了，我长大了，我没有忘记你教我的诗。"

但她不能。她只是站在那里，看着这一刻，像看着一颗遥远的星星。

德国青年突然抬起头，越过少女的肩膀，看向了苏晚晴的方向。

他的眼睛里闪过一丝惊讶，然后是了然，最后是一种几乎可以被称为"感谢"的神情。

他微微点了点头。

然后他低下头，对少女说了什么。少女的脸红了，眼眶却湿了——但她笑了，笑着流下了眼泪。

那一刻，时间仿佛凝固了。蝉鸣、钟声、落叶、阳光，全都在那一刻定格成了一幅永远不会褪色的画。

苏晚晴明白了。

她明白了外祖母为什么一辈子都爱听钟声，为什么总是在某个夏天的清晨独自坐在院子里发呆，为什么她给孙女起的名字里，有一个"晴"字。

她也明白了，那个德国青年——那个她从未谋面的"外公"——那一天并不后悔。

他从来没有后悔过。

## 七、雨落

苏晚晴睁开眼睛时，她已经站在了钟表店的地下室里。

她的脸上全是泪水。

煤油灯已经快要燃尽，火焰虚弱地跳动着。老人站在原地，看着她，眼神里有七十三代人的重量。

"我看到了。"苏晚晴哽咽道。

老人点了点头。

"他……他看到我了。"她说，"他对她笑了。"

"那是他最后能为她做的事。"老人说，"他在等这一刻，等了七十三年。等到有人来见证他们的告别。等到那个人——你，告诉他：那一天，不后悔。"

苏晚晴握紧了手中的照片。

巨钟的轰鸣渐渐平息，钟面上的齿轮恢复了缓慢的旋转。但这一次，苏晚晴看到钟面上出现了一个极淡的、像是水印一样的图案——菩提树的轮廓，和两个并肩站立的身影。

"这是……"

"那是她留给你的礼物。"老人说，"从今以后，这座钟会为你转动一次。你可以选择你一生中最重要的一天，封存进去。等你老了，或者等你准备好了，再把它交给那个应该来的人。"

苏晚晴愣在那里。

"但要记住——"老人补充道，"不要在雨夜去。"

他转身朝石阶走去，背影佝偻得像一把被时间折叠过太多次的尺。

"等等。"苏晚晴喊道，"这座钟……会一直在这里吗？"

老人停下脚步，没有回头。

"只要你记得它，它就会在。"他说，"时间这东西，最怕的不是被遗忘——而是被记得。"

他的身影消失在了石阶尽头。

## 八、后记

苏晚晴走出钟表店时，天空已经飘起了细雨。

她站在檐下，看了看手机。天气预报说，这场雨会下一整夜。

她摸了摸怀里那张照片，照片上的少女依然微微笑着，眼神温柔。

**"替我问他一声：那天，你后悔吗？"**

苏晚晴在心里回答了她从未谋面的外婆：

"不后悔。"

"他从来没有后悔过。"

她撑开伞，走进雨里。

身后，那间从不开灯的钟表店安静地立在巷子深处。但在某一个瞬间——只有她能看到的瞬间——橱窗里亮起了一盏煤油灯的微光，照亮了一个白发老人的侧脸。

他在对她微笑。

苏晚晴也对他笑了笑，然后转身，消失在雨里。

她不知道的是，在那座停了七十三年的钟的钟面上，此刻正浮现出一行极淡的字：

**"第七十四代守护者：苏晚晴。"**

雨继续下着。

钟继续走着。

而那个关于等待与告别的故事，会在下一个七十三年的某一天，由某个她爱的人，继续讲下去。

# The Hour of Silence

The plateau overlooking the valley had not seen this many people in living memory. They came in caravans of RVs and dented sedans, on tour buses and motorcycles, on foot from the nearest trailhead two miles below. They spread blankets on the rocky ground and set up folding chairs, raised binoculars and long-lens cameras. Children were shushed. Phones glowed like a sea of tiny moons.

Tonight, for the first time in four hundred and twelve years, the comet Aethon would cross the sky in perfect alignment with the seven sister stars of the Pleiades. Astronomers had promised a spectacle unlike any in recorded history—a celestial collision of light that would pour across the heavens like spilled honey. A once-in-a-lifetime natural phenomenon. The words had been printed on T-shirts and coffee mugs. The town below had sold out of every room.

Mara sat near the edge of the bluff, her knees drawn up, a thermos of lukewarm tea cooling between her palms. She had driven up alone from the city, eight hours through the night, because her daughter had wanted to see it. Her daughter was seven. Her daughter was not here.

The sky deepened. The first stars pricked through. A murmur ran through the crowd as a greenish smear appeared above the eastern ridge, faint as a memory.

Then Aethon came.

It rose slow and terrible, trailing a tail that split the dark like a wound. The Pleiades glittered ahead of it, and when the comet's leading edge touched the cluster, the light did something that light was not supposed to do.

It stopped.

The blaze held, suspended, neither moving nor fading. The crowd drew a collective breath. Children pointed. A man with a telescope swore softly under it.

And then the sound went out of the world.

Not silence—silence is the absence of sound. This was the *removal* of it. The wind that had been tugging at hats and hair simply ceased to exist. Insects vanished mid-chirp. The distant highway noise, the murmur of thousands of people, the beat of Mara's own heart—all of it plucked away like threads from a tapestry, leaving behind a hole shaped exactly like hearing.

Mara saw mouths open around her. She saw the panic on faces, the hands rising to ears. She felt her own lips part in a scream that never came.

The light in the sky began to move downward.

It slid from the heavens in ribbons, pale and luminous, pooling on the plateau like fog made of moonshine. Where it touched the ground, the rocks shimmered. Where it touched people, they went still.

Mara looked down at her hands. They were glowing, faintly, at the edges. She watched the glow climb her wrists, her forearms, painting her in the color of starlight. It did not hurt. It felt like being remembered.

Around her, forty thousand people stood frozen, eyes open, faces tilted toward the sky. No one fell. No one ran. The light held them upright the way a hand holds a candle—gently, because it could.

In the absence of sound, something else arrived.

She could not call it thought. It was larger than thought, older than language. It pressed against the inside of her skull with the patience of water against a dam. It carried with it the impression of distance—enormous, unmeasurable distance, the kind that exists between stars and the things that watch them.

*We have heard you,* the impression said. *For so long, we have heard you.*

Mara tried to speak. There was no throat to speak with. There was no air.

*You call into the dark,* it went on, *and the dark carries your calls farther than you know. We are the things on the other side. We are the listeners.*

She understood, then, with a clarity that did not belong to her, that the comet was not a comet. The Pleiades were not stars, or were not only stars. They were an ear, pressed against the sky. They had been listening to Earth for four centuries since the last alignment, waiting, cataloguing every shout and whisper and song that had risen into the night.

And now they had answered.

The light reached her chest. She felt it pool there, warm and strangely familiar, like the hand of someone she had loved a long time ago. She thought of her daughter. She thought of the small cold hand she had held at the hospital, and the way the machines had beeped in the long afterward. She thought of all the nights she had stood outside afterward, looking up, saying nothing, because there was nothing left to say.

*We have come to take you with us,* the impression said, *so that you may continue your songs where we can hear them always.*

Mara looked out across the plateau. The faces around her were peaceful in the light. Some were smiling. Some were weeping without tears. A young man held his phone above his head, screen cracked, but still recording—recording what, she could not imagine. There would be no one to play it back for.

She thought of all the things she had meant to do. The book she had not finished. The apology she had not made. The name she had not spoken.

She thought of how small these things were, in the end. How the universe did not keep ledgers. How even a life as brief and cluttered as hers had still sent its voices into the dark, and the dark had answered, and the answer was not cruelty.

It was only attention.

The light reached her throat. Her eyes. The last thing she saw, before the seeing left her, was the sky above—still and glittering, the Pleiades burning steady, the place where the comet had been now empty, the long tail already fading into the dark behind the mountains, on its way back out, back through the silence, back to wherever it had come from.

And in that last moment, Mara understood that the comet would return, in four hundred and twelve years, and the listening would begin again, and that somewhere, on some other plateau, other people would gather with blankets and thermoses and broken hearts, and look up, and be heard.

The plateau went still. The light pooled, and thinned, and finally withdrew, slipping back into the sky in pale ribbons that stitched themselves into the dark. The stars resumed their ancient, indifferent burning. The wind came back first—a sigh through the grass. Then the insects, hesitant. Then the distant hum of the highway, where cars were still driving, unaware.

Only the people were gone.

Forty thousand blankets remained. Forty thousand empty chairs. A single sock in the dirt, a child's, bright yellow, slowly losing its warmth in the night air.

Below, in the town, the lights of the inns and diners still glowed. A waitress wiped down a counter. A dog barked, once, at nothing.

Above, the sky went on without them, vast and unhurried, carrying its new songs into the deep, where someone, or something, was already listening.

# 锈色月光

张伟第三次试图撬开那把生锈的挂锁时，铁皮墙外传来了脚步声。

他屏住呼吸，整个人蜷缩在角落那堆发霉的旧报纸后面。储藏室里堆得满满当当——落灰的纸箱摞到了天花板，一架缺了琴弦的吉他斜靠在墙角，三个行李箱像叠罗汉似的堆在一起，中间的那个开着口，露出半截毛茸茸的玩偶耳朵。空气里弥漫着一股陈旧的、混合了樟脑丸和旧皮革的味道。

脚步声停在了门外。

"三号仓这个月的租费又没交。"是个女人的声音，听起来很年轻。

"那就贴封条呗，下个月再清理。"另一个声音，男的，打了个哈欠。

张伟的心跳到了嗓子眼。他从昨晚藏进来之后，已经在这间不到十平米的铁皮箱子里待了整整二十个小时。手机没电了，他不敢发出声音，甚至不敢开灯——虽然那盏坏了很久的日光灯早就没什么意义。

脚步声渐渐远去。

他慢慢松了口气，后脑勺磕在了身后的纸箱上。箱子晃了晃，最上面那个没封口的倒了下来，几本泛黄的相册散落在地。他随手翻开一本，黑白照片里，一个扎着羊角辫的小女孩抱着一只塑料娃娃冲镜头笑。照片背面有人用钢笔写着：*小婷三岁生日，1987年。*

他忽然意识到，这间储藏室里堆着的，是别人的人生。

那个缺弦的吉他属于谁？中间那个行李箱为什么敞着口，是主人匆匆离去忘了关上，还是根本就没打算回来？那些发霉的报纸里，是不是藏着某个已经没人记得的故事？

张伟来这里，原本是为了藏身。他欠了一屁股债，债主放话说要卸他一条腿。朋友给他介绍了这地方——说是郊区一家废弃的仓储公司，老板欠了朋友的人情，答应让他免费躲几天。

但他没料到的是，这里会让他想起这么多东西。

他继续翻看那本相册。小女孩慢慢长大，上了小学，初中，高中，戴上了眼镜，学会了骑自行车，脖子上挂着一串贝壳项链。最后一张照片是在一个码头上，她穿着白色的连衣裙，头发被风吹乱，身边站着一个穿白衬衫的年轻男人，两人都在笑。

照片背面没有字。

"她后来怎么样了？"张伟喃喃自语。

没人回答他。储藏室里静得能听见自己的呼吸。

他靠着那堆纸箱坐下来，发现自己并不害怕了。债主、追债、断腿——那些事情忽然变得很遥远。此刻他关心的，是照片里那个叫小婷的女孩，那个穿着白衬衫的男人，还有那串再也不会被戴上的贝壳项链。

他翻遍了所有散落的相册，想找到更多关于她的线索。最后在一张照片的背后，他看到了一行字，是用铅笔写的，笔迹稚嫩：

*希望我永远不会忘记他。*

张伟忽然想哭。

他也曾有过那样的希望。希望永远不会忘记某个人，希望某段时光永远不会结束，希望自己永远是码头上那个会笑的人。

但后来，那些希望都不见了。

门外又响起了脚步声。这次不是工作人员，是有人在踹门。铁皮门板震得哐哐响，几片铁锈簌簌地落在他肩头。

"张伟！老子知道你在里面！"

是债主的声音。

他死死地抱住那本相册，整个人缩在行李箱和纸箱之间的缝隙里。月光从门缝里挤进来，落在那架缺弦的吉他上，像撒了一层薄薄的银粉。

他想，如果要死在这里，至少可以死在这堆别人的人生中间。至少可以让自己的故事，混进那些已经没人在意的旧时光里。

"张伟！你再不开门，老子就点了它！"

他从纸箱后面站了起来。

门被踹开的那一刻，月光涌了进来。站在外面的男人逆着光，看不清脸，但张伟看见了他手里的打火机。

"等等。"张伟说。

男人愣了一下。

"我想让你看张照片。"张伟把相册递了过去。

"你他妈耍什么花招？"

"就一眼。"

男人莫名其妙地接过相册，低头看了一眼。照片里，一个穿白裙子的女孩站在码头上，笑着，身边站着一个穿白衬衫的年轻男人。

"看完了。"男人说，语气软了一点。

"你知道她后来怎么样了吗？"张伟问。

"关我屁事。"

"对，"张伟说，"关你屁事。关我屁事。关这世上大多数人都屁事没有。可她还是把照片留下了，藏在这堆破烂里，希望有人能看见。"

男人沉默了几秒，把相册扔还给他。"少他妈废话。钱呢？"

"没有。"

"那腿呢？"

张伟闭上眼。他忽然明白了一件事——这间储藏室里堆着的，不只是别人的人生，也是他自己的。这些年他一直在逃避，逃避债务，逃避责任，逃避所有让他觉得窒息的东西。他以为自己是在逃离生活，其实他只是把自己塞进了一个又一个储藏室里，落灰，发霉，被遗忘。

就像这些纸箱。

就像那架缺弦的吉他。

就像那串再也不会被戴上的贝壳项链。

"我跟你走。"张伟说。

男人又愣了一下。"你说什么？"

"我说我跟你走。腿也好，手也好，你随便。但你得等我做一件事。"

"什么事？"

张伟蹲下身，把散落的相册一页页捡起来，整齐地叠好，重新放回纸箱里。然后他合上那个敞着口的行李箱，把玩偶的耳朵塞回去，拉上拉链。

他站起身，走到那架缺弦的吉他前面，轻轻拨了一下弦。没有声音。

"好了。"他说，"走吧。"

男人盯着他看了好一会儿，最后收起打火机，从鼻子里哼了一声。"算你识相。"

他们一前一后走出储藏室。张伟回头看了一眼那扇敞开的铁门，月光把里面照得亮堂堂的，那些纸箱、吉他、行李箱，都镀上了一层银色的光。

"关门吗？"男人问。

张伟想了想。"关吧。"

铁门合上，发出一声沉闷的响。

那个叫小婷的女孩，她的相册、她的吉他、她的贝壳项链，又被重新锁进了黑暗里。

但至少，有人记得她笑的样子。

张伟转过身，跟着男人走进了夜色里。他不知道自己将面对什么，但他知道，从今晚开始，他不会再逃了。

有些储藏室，是用来存放东西的。

而人生，不是。

她仰头把壶里最后一口酒倒进嘴里，喉结滚动一下，然后把空壶往身后一抛。铜壶落在床板上，发出一声闷响，在寂静中格外刺耳。

"出来吧。"她说，声音不高，却笃定得很，"跟了我三天了，不累么？"

窗外的老槐树上，一片叶子晃了晃，然后一道黑影无声落在院中青石板上，是个穿夜行衣的瘦削男人，单膝跪地，抱拳道："沈姑娘，我家主人想请您去府上喝杯茶。"

"喝茶？"沈七娘笑了一声，月光下那张脸白得有些透明，"你家主人是阎王爷么？这时候请人喝茶。"

黑衣人没动，依旧垂着头："主人说，今夜月圆，有些旧账，该算一算了。"

沈七娘垂下眼睫，看着自己腰间那柄落了层薄灰的长刀。三年了，她没再碰过这东西。

"什么旧账？"她问，语气淡得像在谈别人的事。

"青州，沈家。"

短短五个字，像五根针，钉进她耳朵里。

沈七娘沉默了很久，久到黑衣人开始不安地微微抬头。她忽然笑了，笑得眉眼弯弯，却让那黑衣人脊背一凉。

"行。"她说，跳下窗台，赤足踩在冰凉的木地板上，伸手握住刀柄。三年没拔出的刀，出鞘时竟没有半点滞涩，刀光映着圆月，像一弯冷到骨子里的眉月。

"带路吧。"她抬脚往门外走，经过黑衣人时顿了一下，"对了，告诉你家主人——沈七娘三年前就死了。今夜来的，是讨债的鬼。"

院外，月亮悬在中天，清辉如霜。

这一夜，注定有人要还债。

The Dust on the Shelf

Mara found it wedged between a rusted pair of binoculars and a box of tarnished compasses in her grandfather's attic. It was a disc, about the size of her palm, made of some iridescent material that shifted between deep violet and burnt orange depending on how she tilted it. There was no seam, no obvious mechanism, no brand name. Just a smooth, weighty disc that felt almost warm against her skin, as if it had been sitting in the sun.

She wiped a layer of grime from its surface with the hem of her sweater. Beneath the dust, a thin spiral pattern emerged, etched so fine it looked like a single hair coiled a thousand times.

"Grandpa?" she called down the narrow staircase. "What's this?"

No answer. The house below her was silent in that particular way that old houses are silent—not empty, but full of the memory of sounds.

She turned the disc over. On the back, in her grandfather's careful, spidery handwriting, a single word: *PLAY*.

Mara smiled. He had been a magician, her grandfather. Not the kind with rabbits and cards, but the kind who told you that the laws of physics were merely suggestions, and who could spend an entire afternoon explaining why a spoon could not possibly be bent, and then bend one in his bare hands. He had filled her childhood with wonder and left behind a house full of strange, beautiful things that didn't quite work the way things were supposed to work.

She had come to sort through his belongings. He had died three weeks ago, in his sleep, at ninety-two, with a smile on his face. The doctors said it was peaceful. Mara believed them. He had been ready. He had told her so, the last time she saw him, with that twinkle in his eye that meant he knew something she didn't.

*When I go,* he had said, *look for the things I left you. Not the things you think you want. The things that find you.*

She had thought he meant the old photographs, the watches, the pocketknife. But the disc was what had found her, slipping out from between the binoculars as she pulled the box from the shelf.

She pressed her thumb to the word *PLAY*.

For a moment, nothing. Then the spiral on the front began to move, slow at first, then faster, the iridescent colors blooming outward like ripples in a pond. The disc hummed—not with sound, exactly, but with vibration, the way a cat purrs against your hand.

And then, impossibly, the attic filled with the smell of pipe tobacco and cedar.

Mara froze.

The attic was still dusty, still cluttered, still her grandfather's. But the light coming through the small round window had turned golden, the way it did only in late September, and she could hear, very faintly, the sound of a phonograph needle settling into the groove of a record, that soft *shhhh-shhhh* of expectation.

She looked down at the disc. The spiral had stopped moving. In its center, a tiny image had appeared, like a reflection in a drop of water: a room, a chair, and a man sitting in the chair, watching her.

He was old. Ninety-two, maybe. White-haired, sharp-eyed, with a pipe between his teeth and a smile that was somehow both sad and delighted.

He raised one hand and waved.

Mara's breath caught. She knew that wave. She had seen it a thousand times, at the end of every visit, from the porch, as she drove away.

*Hello, my dear,* he said. His voice came not from the disc, but from everywhere—from the walls, the rafters, the dust in the air. *I wondered if you'd find that one first.*

"Grandpa," she whispered.

*I'm not really here, you understand.* He shifted in the chair. *I'm a memory, mostly. The last bit I had in me before I left. I put it in the disc because I knew you'd come up here eventually, and I knew you'd press the button, because you were always the curious one.*

She sat down on the dusty floor, cross-legged, the disc cradled in her hands. The little image of him was no bigger than a thumbnail, but she could see every line in his face, every glint in his eye.

*There are other discs,* he said. *Hidden in the house, in the shop, in places you haven't found yet. They'll play other things. Other memories. Some of them are mine. Some of them are older.*

"Older than you?"

He chuckled. The sound was warm. *Much older, my dear. This house was here before I was. Before your grandmother was. Before any of us. The discs were here too, waiting. I found my first one when I was nineteen. I spent the rest of my life trying to understand them.*

He leaned forward, and the image grew slightly larger, as if he were coming closer. *I never did, you know. Not fully. But I learned to listen. And I learned that some things aren't meant to be understood. They're meant to be sat with.*

The phonograph sound grew louder, and a melody drifted in—something old, something sweet, something she almost recognized. It smelled of autumn, of woodsmoke, of her grandmother's kitchen.

*You can play this one as many times as you like,* he said. *It won't wear out. It won't change. I'm right here, the way I was, the way I am.*

Mara felt the tears come, hot and unexpected, sliding down her cheeks and dropping onto the disc. The tears seemed to vanish into the iridescent surface, absorbed without trace.

*Don't cry, sweetheart.* His voice was gentle. *I'm not gone, you know. I'm just... elsewhere. The kind of elsewhere I can send you postcards from.*

He winked. *And the discs are the postcards. Keep looking. There's more to find. There's a whole world in this house you haven't met yet.*

The image began to fade, the colors softening at the edges.

*Wait,* Mara said. *I have questions. I have so many—*

*I know you do. You'll find your answers. Some of them, anyway. And the rest...* He smiled, and the smile was the same one she had seen a thousand times, the one that meant he was keeping a secret he would someday tell. *The rest, you'll have to figure out for yourself. That's the fun part.*

The attic dimmed. The smell of tobacco faded. The phonograph needle lifted.

*Be brave, my girl. Be curious. And don't forget to—*

The disc went still.

Mara sat for a long time in the golden light, holding the disc, feeling its strange warmth. Outside, a sparrow sang from the eaves. Somewhere in the house, a floorboard creaked.

She looked around the attic, at the boxes and the dust and the long shadows of the afternoon. Somewhere in here, she thought, were more discs. More memories. More postcards from her grandfather, and from whoever had come before him.

She stood up, brushed the dust from her jeans, and began to search.

# The Photograph in the Drawer

The photo was tucked between two mismatched envelopes, the kind that had no address but still held the weight of something unsaid. Eleanor had found it while searching for her father's death certificate—a task that felt both urgent and impossible to begin.

She held it up to the lamp, though the light had always been bad in this corner of the spare room. The colors were off, slightly yellowed at the edges, as if the photograph itself were embarrassed to exist.

In it, a child stood at the edge of a lake. Not Eleanor. Not any of her siblings, as far as she could tell. The child was turned away from the camera, looking out at the water, one hand lifted as if pointing at something—or someone—just out of frame. The child's hair was the color of wheat in late summer. Their clothes were old-fashioned in a way that Eleanor couldn't quite place, though they looked new.

She didn't remember taking the picture. She didn't remember the lake, or the child, or the particular slant of light that made the water look like hammered tin.

She turned it over. On the back, in handwriting she didn't recognize—her mother's, perhaps, though her mother's hand had been shaky near the end—were three words:

*Before everything changed.*

Eleanor set the photograph down on the desk. She sat in the chair her father had used to write his letters, the one that smelled faintly of pipe tobacco even now, years after the pipes had been given away. Outside, a car passed, its headlights sweeping briefly across the curtains.

She picked the photo up again. The child at the lake. The pointing hand.

She was beginning to suspect that her entire life—the house, the town, the slow accumulation of years she thought she remembered—had been built on top of something else. Something that had happened before her, or perhaps because of her. Something the photograph remembered, even if she could not.

The clock in the hallway ticked on, indifferent.

Eleanor reached for the phone. She thought of calling her sister, but her sister would say it was nothing, a picture from a trip they'd taken as girls, don't you remember? She thought of calling the doctor instead, but the doctor would ask questions she wasn't ready to answer.

Instead, she went to the window and looked out at the street. A man was walking a dog, slow and purposeful, as if he had nowhere to be. The streetlight flickered once and held.

When she turned back to the desk, the photograph was face-down again. She was almost certain she had left it the other way. Almost certain, though not quite.

She reached for it.

*Before everything changed.*

Eleanor began, very carefully, to remember.

《尘封的笔谈》

林夏的指尖沿着图书馆东侧的书架缓缓滑过，指腹沾上了一层细密的灰尘。这排书架位于馆内最深处的角落，灯光常年照不到这里，仿佛被整个图书馆遗忘了。

她原本只是想找一本绝版的《诗经》注疏，却在书架与墙壁的夹缝间，触碰到了一处异常的凹陷。

"这是……"

林夏屏住呼吸，俯身细看。书架的底板与墙根之间，有一道细细的缝隙，若非刻意寻找，绝难发现。她用力推了推，书架竟发出一声沉闷的吱呀，向内滑开了半尺。

一股陈旧的、混杂着墨香与霉味的气息扑面而来。林夏心跳加速，掏出手机打开手电筒，小心翼翼地侧身挤了进去。

那是一间不足十平米的暗室，没有窗户，只有从门缝透进的一线微光。四面墙壁嵌着直达天花板的木架，架上整齐地码放着数十个牛皮纸袋，每个纸袋上都用毛笔写着年份——从一九五三到一九七九，跨越了整整二十六年。

林夏随手取下一九六五年的纸袋，解开系着的棉绳。里面是一沓泛黄的信笺，抬头写着：

"致未来的读者："

她的手指微微颤抖。

信笺上的字迹清秀端庄，署名是"中文系三年级 周淮安"。信中写道，他与同窗好友沈若棠共同发起了"笔谈"计划——在那个特殊的年代，许多话不便明说，他们便将思想、困惑、争论、鼓励写在纸上，存入这间只有他们知晓的暗室，期待有朝一日被后人发现。

"若你读到这些文字，"周淮安写道，"请相信，无论身处何种时代，总有人愿意为思想保留一炬微光。"

林夏一页页翻阅。纸袋里不仅有周淮安与沈若棠的通信，还有许多其他学生的笔谈记录。他们讨论诗歌、争论哲学、分享读书心得，甚至记录了某个深夜食堂里的诗会，某个雨天的即兴辩论。

在一九七二年的纸袋中，林夏读到一封未署名的信：

"今日听闻沈若棠老师已下放，离别前他将这个秘密托付给我。他说：'这些纸张比我们活得长久。'"

她翻到最后一页，愣住了。那张信笺上写着：

"我叫林秋白，是沈若棠的学生。二零一八年，我在整理图书馆旧籍时发现了这间暗室。我今年八十三岁，恐怕时日无多。现在，我将这个秘密记入档案，期待下一个发现它的人——希望是百年之后，希望那时的人们依然相信，文字有穿越时光的力量。"

信笺末尾盖着一枚旧印章，刻的是"守灯人"三字。

林夏缓缓坐在布满灰尘的地板上，手电筒的光束在信笺上微微晃动。她想起自己正在为毕业论文焦虑，为找不到选题而彷徨，为那些看似无法言说的困惑而苦闷。

此刻她忽然明白，有些话不必说给当下的人听，也可以说给时间听。

她从背包里取出一个新本子，拧开钢笔，在第一页郑重地写下：

"致未来的读者：我是第——位发现这里的人。现在是二零二五年，我叫林夏。从今天起，我愿意接过这盏灯……"

窗外，图书馆的闭馆铃声悠悠响起。而在这间无人知晓的暗室里，灯火已悄然传递了半个多世纪。

# 双重迷局

---

陈默推开那扇生锈的铁门时，门轴发出一声尖锐的呻吟。

雨已经下了三天。整座城市像是被泡在灰色的墨水里，连空气都带着一股潮湿的铁锈味。他站在废弃工厂的走廊里，手电筒的光束在斑驳的水泥墙上划出一道惨白的痕迹。

第三名受害者。

和前两个一样——死者仰面倒在地上，双手交叉放在胸前，脸上带着一种奇异的、近乎安详的微笑。没有挣扎的痕迹，没有外伤，甚至连衣服都整整齐齐。

"又是这样……"

陈默低声自语，蹲下身查看尸体。死者的瞳孔已经浑浊，但嘴角那抹笑容仿佛被定格在了某个永恒的瞬间。

这不是普通的凶杀案。他从第一个受害者开始就知道。

---

三天前，市中心的公寓里发现了第一名死者。林雪，女，32岁，心理咨询师。

两天前，河滨公园的长椅上发现了第二名死者。周明远，男，45岁，大学教授。

现在，仓库里的第三名死者。王芳，女，28岁，记者。

三个毫无关联的人，三种完全不同的社会身份，却被同一种手法杀害——或者更准确地说，被同一种"仪式"终结。

陈默站起身，从口袋里掏出手机。

"喂，是我。查一下王芳最近一周的通讯记录，所有通话和短信都要。还有她的社交媒体账号，从注册到现在，每一条动态都不要漏掉。"

挂断电话，他环顾四周。仓库很大，堆满了废弃的机械零件和生锈的铁桶。手电筒的光扫过地面，在灰尘中留下一道移动的阴影。

突然，他停住了。

地上有脚印。

不是受害者的——她穿着平底鞋，鞋印清晰。而这一串脚印是男式皮鞋，尺码大约42，而且……

陈默皱起眉头。

脚印不是从门口延伸过来的，而是从仓库深处走出来的。也就是说，有人从里面走到了尸体旁边，然后……又走回去了？

他顺着脚印的方向走去。仓库的最深处是一堵墙，看起来和其他墙壁没什么两样。但当他仔细查看时，发现墙根处有一道细微的缝隙。

暗门。

陈默没有贸然行动。他退后几步，掏出手机拍了几张照片，然后转身离开了现场。

---

"你确定？"

市公安局刑侦支队的办公室里，队长李建国盯着陈默，眼神复杂。

"确定。凶手有同伙，或者至少有一个内应在现场。而且这个内应很可能是故意留下脚印引我过去的。"

"什么意思？"

"那道暗门太明显了。"陈默靠在椅背上，双手交叉放在胸前。"我从事刑侦十二年，见过各种隐蔽的暗格。那道暗门的边缘没有任何磨损的痕迹，说明它很少被使用。一个谨慎的凶手，不会把一个不常用的逃生通道留在受害者死亡现场。这不合理。"

李建国沉默了片刻。

"你的意思是，有人想让你发现那道门？"

"或者，有人想把我引到某个地方去。"

陈默站起身，走到窗边。窗外的雨还在下，模糊了远处的街景。

"这个案子有三个奇怪的地方。第一，受害者的表情。三个人死前都面带微笑，这不符合常理。除非他们在死前看到了什么让他们感到安慰的东西。"

"第二，作案手法。三名受害者没有任何外伤，也没有中毒迹象。法医说他们的死亡时间几乎完全相同——都是在凌晨三点十七分。这太巧了。"

"第三，也是最重要的——三名受害者之间没有任何关联。不同的性别、年龄、职业、社交圈。他们唯一的共同点是……"

陈默顿了顿。

"他们都在三个月内报过警。"

李建国的眼神变了。

"你是说，凶手在报复报警的人？"

"不是报复。是阻止。"陈默转过身，目光锐利。"三名受害者报警的内容分别是——林雪报警说有陌生人跟踪她；周明远报警说有人半夜闯入他家；王芳报警说有人给她寄恐吓信。三起报警都被以'证据不足'为由驳回。"

"等等……"李建国皱起眉头，"这三起案子我都没有印象。"

"因为经手的人不是我们。"陈默的声音冷了下来。"是另一组人。市局有个叫周晏的督察，你听说过吗？"

李建国愣了一下："周晏？听说过，他负责的案件结案率很高，在局里口碑不错。怎么了？"

陈默没有回答。他走到办公桌前，从抽屉里拿出一个文件夹，扔到李建国面前。

"看看这个。"

---

文件夹里是厚厚一叠资料。陈默花了三天时间，从市局的旧档案里挖出来的。

过去两年里，全市共有七起"微笑死亡案"。七名受害者，死亡时间全部是凌晨三点十七分，死前表情安详，没有外伤，没有中毒迹象。死因被统一判定为"心脏骤停"。

但让陈默真正警觉的是另一组数据。

这七个人，在死前三个月内，全部报过警。而经手他们报警案件的人——

全部是周晏。

"这个人……"李建国的声音有些发干，"他在阻止报警人？"

"不只是阻止。"陈默的声音很轻，但每个字都像钉子一样扎进空气里。"他在杀人。每一次有人报警，报警内容就会被记录在案。如果报警内容涉及到某些……敏感的事情，报警人就会'意外死亡'。而经手案件的督察，会顺理成章地把案件压下来，不予立案。"

"但为什么？什么人会这么做？周晏图什么？"

陈默摇了摇头："我不知道。但我知道一件事——"

他看向窗外，眼神幽深。

"周晏今天早上向支队长递交了申请，要求接手'微笑死亡案'的调查工作。"

---

雨终于停了。

陈默站在市局大楼的门口，看着灰蒙蒙的天空。他知道自己现在应该做什么——把证据交给上级，申请对周晏进行调查。

但他没有动。

因为他突然意识到一件事。

如果周晏真的是凶手，那他为什么要主动申请接手这个案子？一个聪明到能策划完美犯罪的人，不会犯这种低级错误。

除非——

他根本不是凶手。

或者，他不是唯一的凶手。

陈默的思绪被一阵脚步声打断。

他转过身，看到一个穿着风衣的男人正向他走来。男人大约三十五六岁，面容清秀，眼神锐利，嘴角挂着一丝淡淡的笑意。

"陈默警官？"男人在他面前停下，伸出手。"我是周晏。久仰大名。"

陈默没有握手。

"周督察有什么事？"

周晏收回手，并不显得尴尬。他的笑容反而更深了。

"我来是想告诉你一件事。"他压低声音，眼神忽然变得锐利如刀。"你查的那些档案，我三天前就查完了。你今天看到的所有东西——那七起案件、那些报警记录、我经手的所有案件——都是我想让你看到的。"

陈默的心沉了一下。

"你什么意思？"

"意思是，从一开始，我就知道你会查到这个案子。"周晏的声音很轻，但每一个字都像锤子一样砸在陈默的耳朵里。"你以为你在追查凶手，其实你在追查的每一步，都在我的计划之内。"

陈默后退一步，手悄悄摸向腰间的配枪。

"你在承认自己是凶手？"

周晏笑了。

"陈警官，你为什么会觉得我是凶手？"

"因为所有的证据都指向——"

"所有的证据？"周晏打断他，"那七起微笑死亡案，受害者的死亡时间、死亡地点、死亡方式，全部公开在案卷里。任何人都可以查到。而我经手他们的报警记录，也是有据可查的事实。你把这些串连起来，就得出我是凶手的结论——这不就是典型的'相关不等于因果'吗？"

陈默愣了一下。

"你在狡辩。"

"不，我在陈述事实。"周晏的语气平静得可怕。"你有没有想过，为什么你会把这些事情联系在一起？为什么你一看到'周晏'这个名字，就会立刻联想到'凶手'？"

陈默没有说话。

"因为有人在引导你。"周晏的眼神忽然变得意味深长。"陈警官，你有没有想过，在这场游戏中，你不是猎人——"

他顿了顿，嘴角的笑意愈发深浓。

"你也是猎物。"

---

陈默用了三秒钟消化这句话。

然后他笑了。

"周督察，你的意思是说，有第三个人在操控我们两个？"

"不是第三个人。"周晏摇了摇头。"是同一个凶手。他杀了那七个人，然后故意留下线索，让我们两个互相怀疑。他知道你会查到这个案子，也知道我会比你先一步。他想要的，是让我们两个自相残杀——或者，至少让其中一个人彻底毁掉另一个人。"

"那你为什么来找我？"陈默盯着他。"你可以躲起来看戏。"

"因为我不想让凶手得逞。"周晏的眼神忽然变得认真。"陈警官，我知道你不信任我。但在这一点上，我们的目标是一样的——找出真正的凶手。"

陈默沉默了很长时间。

雨后的空气里弥漫着一股清冷的气息。远处，一只乌鸦从树梢飞起，发出一声沙哑的鸣叫。

"好。"陈默终于开口。"我姑且相信你。但如果你骗我——"

"你不会有这个机会的。"周晏伸出手，这一次，陈默握了上去。

两只手在雨后的阳光里交握，像是某种古老的契约。

---

接下来的一周，陈默和周晏开始合作调查。

这是一件奇怪的事情。两个人互相提防，互相试探，但同时又必须依赖彼此。陈默负责现场调查，周晏负责档案分析。他们交换信息，但也保留关键线索。

第七天，他们终于有了突破。

"找到了。"周晏把一份档案扔到陈默面前。"七名受害者虽然看似没有关联，但他们有一个共同点——他们都曾在三个月内去过同一家心理诊所。"

陈默翻开档案。

诊所的名字叫"心灵港湾"，主治心理医生叫孙雅芝。

"孙雅芝……"陈默念着这个名字，突然想起了什么。"等等，林雪也是心理咨询师。她和孙雅芝是同行，会不会——"

"她们不只是同行。"周晏打断他，眼神闪烁。"她们是师徒关系。林雪是孙雅芝的学生，五年前从她那里出师，然后自立门户。"

陈默的心跳漏了一拍。

"你的意思是——"

"我查了孙雅芝的过去。"周晏的声音低沉。"二十年前，她曾卷入一起医疗事故。一名患者在她的治疗下死亡，家属起诉了她。最后案子以证据不足为由撤诉，但孙雅芝的职业生涯也毁了。她关了原来的诊所，搬到这座城市，改名换姓，重新开始。"

"而那七名受害者……"

"都曾在她的新诊所就诊过。"周晏的眼神变得锐利。"陈警官，我有一个推测——但说出来之前，我需要你做好心理准备。"

"说。"

周晏深吸一口气。

"凶手可能不是外人。是孙雅芝本人。"

---

"心灵港湾"心理诊所位于市中心的一栋写字楼里。

下午三点，陈默和周晏敲开了诊所的大门。

开门的是一个五十多岁的女人，头发花白，面容慈祥，眼神里带着一种让人安心的温柔。

"两位警官，有什么事吗？"

陈默出示了证件："孙雅芝医生？我们是市公安局的，有些问题想请教您。"

孙雅芝的表情没有任何变化。她侧身让开门口："请进。"

诊所的装修很温馨，墙上挂着几幅风景画，角落里摆着几盆绿植。空气中弥漫着一股淡淡的薰衣草香味，让人不由自主地放松下来。

陈默和周晏在沙发上坐下。孙雅芝给他们倒了茶，然后坐在对面的椅子上，神态自若。

"孙医生，我们想了解一下最近去世的几位患者的情况。"周晏开门见山。

孙雅芝端着茶杯的手顿了顿。

"林雪是我的学生，周明远是我的老患者，王芳是新患者。"她的声音平静，但眼神里闪过一丝复杂的光。"他们的死……我很难过。"

"您最后一次见他们是什么时候？"

"林雪是一周前，周明远是两周前，王芳是三天前——就在她死的前一天。"

陈默和周晏交换了一个眼神。

"孙医生，您能谈谈他们的治疗情况吗？"

孙雅芝放下茶杯，沉默了一会儿。

"林雪有严重的焦虑症，她总觉得有人在跟踪她。周明远有被迫害妄想，总说有人要闯入他家。王芳……"她顿了顿，"她收到了恐吓信，精神状态非常不稳定。"

"他们都报警了。"周晏说。

"是的。"孙雅芝的眼神忽然变得深邃。"他们报警的内容，我都看过。但警察告诉他们证据不足，无法立案。"

"您怎么看？"

孙雅芝没有立刻回答。她站起身，走到窗边，背对着他们。

"警官，有些事情，警察不会相信。但我会相信。"她的声音很轻，像是在自言自语。"他们不是疯了。他们是真的看到了某些东西。"

陈默的心跳加速："您什么意思？"

孙雅芝转过身，眼神忽然变得锐利。

"我的意思是——有人在跟踪他们，闯入他们家，给他们寄恐吓信。而那个人，就是我。"

---

空气仿佛凝固了。

陈默和周晏同时站起身，手摸向腰间的配枪。

"别紧张。"孙雅芝的声音依然平静。"我不是要伤害你们。我只是在陈述事实。"

"你承认跟踪、骚扰那七名受害者？"周晏的声音发紧。

"是的。"孙雅芝慢慢走回椅子边，重新坐下。"他们来找我看病，说他们看到了一些东西。我一开始以为他们是在描述梦境或者幻觉。但后来我发现，他们说的都是真的。"

"什么意思？"

"有一个组织。"孙雅芝的声音变得低沉。"他们专门寻找那些能看到'某些东西'的人。然后……除掉他们。"

陈默皱起眉头："什么东西？"

孙雅芝没有直接回答。她从口袋里掏出一张照片，递给陈默。

照片上是七名受害者的合影——但照片里还有一个人，站在他们身后，穿着一件黑色的风衣，脸被阴影遮住了。

"这是……"

"这张照片是我在每个受害者的遗物里找到的。"孙雅芝的声音开始发抖。"他们每个人都在死前收到了这张照片。他们以为这是恐吓信，但实际上……这是真相。"

"什么真相？"

孙雅芝抬起头，眼神直视陈默。

"那个人站在他们身后。拍下这张照片的时候，那个人就在他们身边。他们能看到这个人——因为他们能看见我们看不见的东西。"

"你是说……幽灵？"

"不是幽灵。"孙雅芝摇了摇头。"是另一种存在。它们存在于人类意识的边缘，只有极少数人能感知到它们。而那个组织——他们负责清除那些能感知到它们的人。"

陈默和周晏面面相觑。

"孙医生，您在说些什么？"陈默的声音有些发干。"这听起来像是……"

"像是疯话？"孙雅芝苦笑了一下。"我知道。你们不会相信的。没有人会相信的。"

她站起身，走到办公桌前，从抽屉里拿出一个信封。

"这是我给你们的最后一样东西。"

信封里是一叠照片和一份文件。陈默翻开文件，瞳孔骤然收缩。

那是一份组织架构图。最上方写着两个字——"守夜人"。

下面列着十几个名字，其中一个名字旁边标注着红色的叉号：周晏。

"这是……"

"周警官，你确实是守夜人的成员。"孙雅芝看向周晏，眼神复杂。"但你不知道，对吗？你不知道自己效忠的组织到底在做什么。"

周晏的脸色苍白如纸。

"不可能……我加入守夜人，是因为我相信他们能保护普通人免受超自然存在的侵害……"

"你保护的只是大多数人。"孙雅芝的声音变得冰冷。"那些能感知到异象的人，在守夜人眼里是'异常'。他们必须被清除，因为他们的存在会让普通人产生恐慌。"

"所以你杀了他们？"

"不。"孙雅芝摇了摇头。"我没有杀他们。跟踪他们、骚扰他们，只是为了让他们报警，让守夜人知道他们的存在。但我没有想到……守夜人会直接动手。"

陈默握紧了拳头："那真正的凶手是谁？"

孙雅芝看向窗外，眼神里带着深深的悲伤。

"守夜人的高层。他们决定清除所有能感知到异象的人——不管这些人是否会造成恐慌。我试图阻止，但失败了。"

"所以你来告诉我们这些？"

"因为我快死了。"孙雅芝的声音忽然变得平静。"我能感觉到它们。它们就在附近。守夜人知道我背叛了他们，今晚——"

她的话还没说完，诊所的灯突然熄灭了。

黑暗中，陈默听到了一个声音。

一个不属于这个房间的声音。

一个冰冷的、没有温度的声音。

"时间到了。"

---

# The First Day

The first day you opened your own office as a private investigator, you didn't expect it to be busy. You were wrong.

The sign above the door read MORGAN & ASSOCIATES PRIVATE INVESTIGATIONS. You'd added "Associates" even though you had no associates, no employees, not even a plant to make the place look lived-in. The building was a converted tailor's shop on Archer Street, sandwiched between a laundromat that smelled of fabric softener and a pawn shop whose window display hadn't changed since 1987.

You were three hours into your first day, watching dust motes drift through the bars of sunlight that fell across your empty desk, when the door chimed.

The man who walked in was not what you'd expected. You kept a mental file of your first clients—you'd imagined nervous housewives, desperate husbands, maybe a gruff businessman with a photograph of his wayward daughter. Instead, you got a woman in her seventies wearing a lavender cardigan, clutching a plastic bag from a discount grocery store.

"Mr. Morgan?" she asked, peering at you through glasses held together at the bridge by a Band-Aid.

"That's me." You stood too quickly, knocking a pen onto the floor. "Please, have a seat. Can I get you coffee? I don't actually have coffee yet. Water?"

"Water would be lovely, dear."

She sat in the client chair—a secondhand leather thing you'd found on a neighborhood app. She arranged the plastic bag beside her like a small, loyal pet.

You poured her tap water into a paper cup from the bathroom dispenser and tried to look professional. You had a suit on, purchased at a thrift store two days before, and you'd polished your shoes with the wrong kind of polish, so they had a slightly sticky, glazed look that you were hoping came across as purposeful.

"My name," the woman began, "is Mrs. Edna Pruitt. I live three blocks from here, on Larkspur Lane. I've been married for fifty-two years to a man named Arthur Pruitt, and I have come to tell you, Mr. Morgan, that I believe my husband is trying to kill me."

She said it the way someone might announce the weather. You waited for her to smile. She did not smile.

"Kill you," you repeated.

"That's right."

"Okay." You pulled a notebook toward you. You hadn't decided yet whether you actually used a notebook or whether that was just something people did on television. You decided today was the day to commit. "Tell me about Arthur."

Mrs. Pruitt opened her plastic bag and withdrew a folder, the kind with the brads in the middle, and set it on your desk with a satisfying thump.

Inside were forty-three pages. You counted.

"Suspect behavior," she said, tapping the first page. "He's been buying strange things at the hardware store. Rope, though I grant you some rope is normal. But also bungee cords, which he has no use for. We don't own a boat. We don't own anything that requires a bungee cord. Last week I caught him reading a book about Antarctica, which I thought was innocent until I saw that he'd underlined a passage about frostbite."

"That's—" You cleared your throat. "That's certainly suspicious."

"I haven't even gotten to the antifreeze."

"There's antifreeze?"

"He says it's for the car. We don't have a car, Mr. Morgan. We sold our car in 2014."

You wrote *ANTARCTICA. FROSTBITE. NO CAR* in your notebook. The pen ran out halfway through NO CAR. You opened your desk drawer and discovered that you owned exactly one pen, and it was now dead.

"Hold on," you said, standing. "I just need to—there's a stationery place down the block—"

"Take your time," Mrs. Pruitt said pleasantly. She was looking around your office with an air of polite evaluation. "I like what you've done with the place. Very Hemingway."

You did not know what to do with that.

---

By the end of the first day, you had three more clients.

The second was a man named Gerald Hoff, who believed his neighbor was running an illegal dog-fighting ring out of his garage. The evidence, he admitted freely, was that the neighbor owned three pit bulls. "But the *way* they bark," Gerald said, leaning forward with the intensity of a man who had rehearsed this speech, "it's not normal barking. It's *organized* barking. Like a chant."

You wrote that down in pencil, because you had not yet located a pen.

The third client was a teenager named Brittaney, who had walked in on roller skates and sat on your client chair in such a way that her skates stuck straight out into the room like a challenge. She was looking for her father, who had left when she was two and who, according to her mother, was dead, and according to her aunt, was living in Reno, and according to a psychic she had visited on YouTube, was "somewhere with water."

"I have one hundred and forty-two dollars," she announced. "I was thinking fifty now and the rest when you find him."

"I'm going to need—" You gestured vaguely. "More than that. Probably."

"That's all I have."

"It's a really good first offer," you said, because you had decided today was a day of honesty. "Let me think about it."

The fourth client came at 4:47 PM, just as you were starting to wonder how one actually closed an office for the day. Did you flip a sign? Lock a door? Make a speech?

He was a tall man, mid-fifties, in a coat that had seen better days. He didn't sit down. He stood in your doorway, hat in hand, and looked at you with the kind of eyes that made you glad you weren't the sort of person who had secrets.

"You Morgan?"

"I am."

"I was told you do favors."

"I do investigations."

"Same thing." He smiled, but it was the kind of smile that didn't reach the rest of him. "I need you to find a girl. She worked for me, once upon a time. Smart girl. Too smart, maybe. She took something that didn't belong to her, and now she's gone, and I want her back before certain people find her first."

You felt the room get slightly smaller.

"Find her," he said. He put a card on your desk. The card had no name on it, only a phone number in small, precise numerals. "Don't find her. Either way, I'll be in touch. You have a week."

He left. The door chimed.

You sat there for a long time. Outside, the laundromat churned. The pawn shop glittered with its permanent display. Mrs. Pruitt's folder sat on your desk, forty-three pages of a husband's suspicious purchases. Gerald Hoff's organized barking waited in your inbox. Brittaney's hundred and forty-two dollars and her father somewhere with water. And now a man with no name and a girl who had stolen something.

You looked at the clock. 5:02 PM.

You thought: *this is my first day.*

You thought: *tomorrow it will be different.*

You were wrong about that, too, but you didn't know it yet.

You picked up the dead pen, remembered it was dead, set it down. You pulled a fresh pencil from the mug you had optimistically labeled *OFFICE SUPPLIES* and opened a fresh page of your notebook.

At the top, you wrote:

**THINGS TO DO TOMORROW**

Below it, after some thought, you added:

1. Buy a pen.

You locked the door, turned off the light, and stood for a moment on the sidewalk in the blue early evening, listening to the city hum its patient, complicated hum.

Then you went home, and you slept the uneasy sleep of a man who had just realized that the job he had chosen had, possibly, also chosen him.

And somewhere out there—maybe three blocks away on Larkspur Lane, maybe in a garage with organized barking, maybe on roller skates heading toward Reno, maybe in a room with no name—a case was already waiting.

Your second day was going to be even busier.

**Underneath**

There's something underneath my bed — and it's not a monster.

I've checked. I've checked twice, three times, more times than I can count. I crouched down with a flashlight at midnight and shone the beam into the dark, the way my mother taught me when I was five and convinced the boogeyman lived in the closet. Nothing. Just dust bunnies and one rubber band I'd lost in July and a single sock with no mate.

But it's there.

It doesn't make sounds. It doesn't breathe. It doesn't drag itself across the floorboards at 3 AM like the stories say. No. It's quieter than that. It's the kind of presence that sits beneath you like a held breath — patient, certain, unmoving.

I first noticed it the night I moved in.

The apartment on Linden Street was a steal — too much of a steal, my sister said, with that wrinkle in her nose she gets when she thinks I'm doing something stupid. The landlord was an old man with tired eyes who handed me the keys without even checking my credit. "It's been empty a while," he said. "Most people don't last."

I didn't ask what he meant by that.

The first week was fine. Boxes everywhere, the smell of fresh paint and old radiators. I'd come home from work, drop my bag by the door, and collapse onto my new mattress — still on the floor, frame not yet assembled. I'd stare at the ceiling. I'd fall asleep.

But somewhere in the second week, I started waking up at exactly 2:17 AM. Every night. Not groggy, not in that half-sleep way where you're not sure if you're really awake. Awake awake. The kind of awake where your heart is already going.

I'd lie still. I'd listen.

The radiator ticked. A car passed outside. The neighbor's cat yowled from somewhere down the hall.

But underneath me — below the mattress, below the plywood I'd laid down because the bed frame was still in a box — there was something else. Not a sound. A *weight*. A pressure that wasn't quite physical but wasn't quite imagined, either. Like the apartment itself was heavier at that exact spot. Like gravity had decided to concentrate.

I started setting my alarm. 2:15. I'd lie in wait.

Nothing visible. Nothing audible. But at 2:17, the pressure would arrive — settling in like fog, like something leaning against the other side of a very thin wall. It would stay for exactly eleven minutes. Then lift. Then I'd sleep again, dreamless, until morning.

I told no one. What would I say? *There's something under my bed but I can't see it or hear it or touch it, but I know it's there because the universe feels slightly different at that one specific spot between 2:17 and 2:28 AM?*

People would think I was crazy.

Maybe I was.

The fourth week, I started leaving things underneath. Notes. Small objects. A marble my father had given me. A paperclip. A receipt from the diner on 5th where I eat eggs every Sunday. In the morning, I'd check. They were always there. Undisturbed. But sometimes — sometimes — the marble was in a slightly different position. Turned, maybe. Or the receipt was folded at a different crease.

I'd tell myself: *It's the vibrations from the floor. It's settling. It's nothing.*

But I kept leaving things anyway.

The fifth week, I stopped eating. Not on purpose — I just forgot. I'd come home and sit on the mattress and stare at the wall and realize hours had passed and I hadn't had dinner. My clothes hung looser. My sister called and said I sounded thin. I said I was fine. I said I was busy.

At night, I'd lie down and wait for 2:17.

It became the only thing I looked forward to.

The pressure was different now. Warmer. Closer. Like whatever was down there had grown used to me — or I to it. Once, I swear I felt something shift. Not a sound. A *thought*. Like someone trying very hard not to disturb you while they slept.

I don't know why I started talking to it.

The first night, I whispered *hello* into the dark, and my own voice sounded insane. I laughed — a short, sharp thing that bounced off the walls. I rolled over. I went back to sleep.

The second night, I said, *I'm not going to ask what you are.*

The third night, I said, *I think I know why the landlord said people don't last.*

I never heard it. It never answered. But after that third night, I woke up and found the marble I'd left underneath — on my pillow. Just sitting there, plain as anything. I held it in my palm and it was warm.

Warm like something had been holding it.

I should have been frightened. I should have moved out, called someone, slept with the lights on. Instead, I moved the mattress aside. I lay down on the bare floorboards, cheek against the wood, and I waited.

2:17 came.

The pressure arrived — but from above this time, pressing down on me, all around me, like being held. Not crushing. Cradling. Like something vast and very tired had finally been given permission to rest.

I closed my eyes.

*I know what you are,* I whispered.

It wasn't a monster. Monsters are hungry, and this was nothing like hunger.

It was grief.

Old grief. The kind that settles into the foundations of a place and stays. Someone had loved here once — truly loved — and lost, and the loss had soaked so deep into the floorboards that it had become a kind of presence. A residue. A echo that didn't know how to fade.

The landlord's tired eyes. *Most people don't last.* Because people felt it. Because people woke at 2:17 with an emptiness they couldn't name, and they thought they were losing their minds, and they left.

But I didn't have anyone. Not anymore. My mother, three years gone. My father before her. Friends scattered to cities that might as well be countries. I'd been empty for so long that when the grief downstairs reached up to meet mine, it didn't feel like haunting.

It felt like company.

I lay on the floor all night. I didn't sleep — not really — but I wasn't awake, either. I was somewhere in between, drifting in a dark warm place that smelled like old wood and lavender and the faintest trace of someone else's perfume.

In the morning, I felt rested for the first time in years.

I called my sister. *I think I'm going to stay in the apartment.*

She was quiet for a long moment. *Are you okay?*

*I think so.*

*You don't sound okay.*

I looked out the window at the street below — the cracked sidewalks, the broken streetlight, the old brick building across the way with its boarded-up windows. *I sound better,* I said. *I sound like I'm somewhere I belong.*

She didn't understand. That's okay.

Most people wouldn't.

That night, I left something different underneath the bed. Not a marble, not a receipt. A photograph. My mother, young, laughing at something off-camera. I slid it carefully under the mattress and lay on top and waited.

2:17.

The pressure came — and with it, something new. A tremor. A wave. Like tears, if grief could cry.

I pressed my hand flat against the mattress.

*I know,* I said. *I know.*

And somewhere underneath my bed — not a monster, never a monster — something that had been holding its breath for God knows how long finally, finally, let go.

I woke the next morning to find the photograph back on my pillow. But there was something behind it now. A small, faded photograph of my own — one I'd never seen. A woman in a kitchen, holding a cup of coffee, smiling like she had all the time in the world. On the back, in handwriting I didn't recognize but somehow understood:

*Thank you.*

I put it in a frame. I put it on my nightstand.

The apartment is quiet now. I still wake at 2:17 some nights — old habits, I guess — but the pressure is gone. The weight has lifted. Whatever lived beneath my bed has moved on, or finally rested, or found whatever it was waiting for.

I like to think we helped each other.

I like to think that's what homes are for.

# The Last Frame

They say a picture is worth a thousand words, but you knew the one you'd just taken was worth a million.

Maybe more.

The camera felt heavier in your hands than it had a moment ago, as though the image itself carried weight. Your thumb still hovered over the review button, afraid to look again. Afraid that looking would make it real. But you already knew it was real—you'd heard the crack of bone, the wet gurgle, the silence that followed.

You should run. That was the smart thing to do. But your legs had forgotten how, and the streetlamp above you buzzed and flickered like it was trying to remember how to be a streetlamp.

The man on the ground wasn't moving.

He'd been running. You remembered that much. Coat flapping behind him like the wings of some panicked bird, briefcase swinging. He hadn't seen the car. You had. You'd raised your phone almost without thinking, the way people do now, capturing tragedy like tourists at a cathedral.

The flash hadn't gone off. Small mercy.

Your phone buzzed. A notification. Then another. Then a cascade.

*The algorithm*, you thought distantly. *The algorithm likes a good disaster.*

You finally looked down at the screen. The image was sharp—too sharp. You could count the droplets of blood spattered across the asphalt, see the individual fibers of his tie, the way his glasses had flown off and landed three feet away, lenses still miraculously intact.

You could see his face.

You knew that face.

Not from TV. Not from a wanted poster or a missing persons flyer. From somewhere deeper. Somewhere the brain keeps things it doesn't want you to forget but can't quite throw away.

A birthday party, maybe. Or a funeral. You couldn't tell anymore. The memory was a photograph itself—faded at the edges, overexposed in the middle.

The phone buzzed again. **+10,000 shares.**

Your hands were shaking now. The man on the ground made a sound—small, pitiful, the kind of sound a bird makes when it hits a window. You should call 911. You should drop the phone and run to him, press your hands against the wound, whisper *it's going to be okay* even if you knew it wasn't.

You did neither.

You took another picture.

And another.

And the algorithm, that great hungry god of the modern age, began to feed.

---

By morning, the image had circled the globe three times. By noon, it had a name. By evening, a backstory—a cheating husband, a disgruntled employee, a man who deserved what he got, according to the comments. The theories multiplied like bacteria in a petri dish, each one more confident than the last.

You watched it all from your apartment, curtains drawn, phone charging on the nightstand like a small, patient predator.

The knock came at midnight.

You knew who it would be before you opened the door. The same face. The same coat, though cleaner now. The same tie, though the knot was different.

He looked at you the way a man looks at a grave he didn't expect to visit.

"You took those pictures," he said. Not a question.

You wanted to deny it. You wanted to say *I don't know what you're talking about*, slam the door, call the police, pretend the last twelve hours had been a fever dream. But your mouth had gone dry, and your hands had found your phone again, and the camera was open, and his face filled the viewfinder once more.

"I did," you whispered.

He stepped inside. The door closed behind him. The lock clicked with the finality of a coffin.

"Then you'll take one more."

He handed you an envelope. Inside was an address, a time, and a single sentence: *The man who did this to me will be there.*

You looked up at him. He was smiling, but only with his mouth.

"You wanted a picture worth a million words," he said. "I'm going to give you one worth ten million. But first, you're going to help me balance the ledger."

The phone was still in your hands. The camera still open. The algorithm still hungry.

Outside, the city hummed with the indifferent music of eight million lives, none of them knowing what was about to be set in motion by a single tap of a shutter button.

You looked at the screen.

You looked at him.

You thought about what they say—a picture being worth a thousand words—and wondered, for the first time, who *they* were, and why they thought pictures were worth anything at all.

A picture doesn't speak.

It only shows.

And what it shows, sometimes, is the shape of your own damnation, frozen forever in light.

# 租客

李明哲搬进这间公寓时，房价便宜得令人起疑。

中介是个戴金丝眼镜的中年男人，说话时眼珠不断往旁边瞟。他说这房子之所以便宜，是因为上一个租客"出了点事"。但具体什么事，他又支支吾吾说不清楚，只是不停地强调"价钱"和"机会难得"。

明哲当时刚和女朋友分手，急着搬出他们共同租的房子，根本没心思细想。他只想找个便宜、安静、离公司近的地方。

这间公寓恰好满足所有条件。

---

头几天，什么事都没发生。

公寓在七楼，一室一厅，朝南，采光不错。家具老旧但齐全，热水充足，Wi-Fi信号满格。明哲觉得自己捡了个大便宜，甚至开始规划要在阳台上种些绿植。

第七天夜里，他被一阵声音吵醒。

"嗒、嗒、嗒——"

是高跟鞋踩在地板上的声音，从客厅传来。明哲迷迷糊糊看了眼手机——凌晨三点十七分。

他翻了个身，心想也许是楼上的邻居。他这栋楼隔音不算太好，之前也偶尔能听到拖动家具的声音。

"嗒、嗒、嗒——"

高跟鞋声走到了卧室门口，停了。

明哲睁开眼，盯着紧闭的房门。月光从窗帘缝隙里透进来，在地板上画出一道银白色的线。

门把手缓缓转动。

明哲一下子坐起来，心跳得厉害。他盯着门把手——它确实在转，非常慢，非常轻，像是有什么东西正在小心翼翼地试探。

"谁？"他喊了一声。

声音在空荡荡的卧室里显得有点单薄。

门把手停止了转动。

高跟鞋声响起，由近及远，"嗒、嗒、嗒——"，走到客厅，然后消失了。

明哲在黑暗中坐了很久，没有再睡着。

---

第二天，他去问物业。

物业是个胖胖的中年妇女，听了他的描述，脸色有点微妙。

"高跟鞋？"她重复道，手指不自觉地绞着抹布。

"对，高跟鞋。从客厅走到卧室门口。"

"您……确定是从客厅传来的？"

明哲点头。

物业妇女的抹布绞得更紧了。她往四周看了看，压低声音说："先生，我建议您换个地方住吧。这房子……不太干净。"

"什么意思？"

她欲言又止，最后只说："反正不干净。您去找别的房子吧，我们把押金退给您。"

明哲想追问，但她已经转身进了办公室，把门关上了。

---

那天晚上，明哲特意没睡，坐在客厅里看书。

午夜十二点，什么都没发生。

凌晨一点，还是什么都没有。

他开始觉得昨晚可能只是自己太累，产生了幻觉。他打了个哈欠，关上灯准备去睡觉。

就在他起身的瞬间，客厅的灯自己亮了。

明哲僵在原地。

灯光下，客厅和平时没什么两样——沙发、茶几、电视柜。茶几上放着他喝了一半的水，水杯里的水在微微晃动。

"嗒。"

一声轻响。

明哲低头——茶几底下伸出一只手。

那是一只女人的手，皮肤苍白，指甲涂着鲜红的甲油。它从茶几底下慢慢伸出来，贴着地板，像是想要够什么东西。

明哲连呼吸都不敢了。

那只手在地板上摸索了一会儿，忽然停住，像是抓住了什么。然后，慢慢缩了回去，消失在茶几的阴影里。

"嗒、嗒、嗒——"

高跟鞋声响起，由客厅走向卧室。

明哲腿一软，跌坐在地上。等他回过神来时，灯已经灭了，客厅又陷入了黑暗。

他连夜收拾东西，打车去了朋友家。

---

三天后，明哲去找那个中介退钱。

中介推三阻四，说合同上没写"无鬼"条款。明哲气得不轻，最后撂下狠话："不退钱也行，但我要去看看这房子到底怎么回事。"

中介的脸刷地变了："你、你去看什么，房子已经租出去了——"

"租出去了？"明哲愣住，"才三天就租出去了？"

中介没回答，转身想走。

明哲一把拉住他："说清楚，到底怎么回事？"

中介挣扎了几下，最后泄了气，压低声音说："那个房子……每任租客都住不长。"

"为什么？"

"他们都说有'东西'。"中介的眼珠又开始乱瞟，"但奇怪的是，没几个能说出具体是什么。有的说是高跟鞋，有的说是小孩哭声，有的说是唱歌的女人——"

他顿了顿，声音更低了："每个人看到的都不一样。"

明哲脑子里忽然闪过一个念头——物业妇女当时的表情。

她问的是："您确定是从客厅传来的？"

她为什么这么问？

"我去查查上一个租客的事。"明哲说。

中介的脸白了："别、别查了——"

"为什么？"

"因为上一个租客……"中介咽了口唾沫，"没走成。"

---

明哲动用了点关系，查到了一些事。

上一个租客是个年轻女孩，独居，白天上班晚上回来。大约三个月前的一个深夜，邻居听到这间公寓传出剧烈的争吵声，然后是玻璃碎裂的声音，再然后是重物落地的声音。

第二天早上，女孩被发现在卧室里，已经死了。

死因是坠楼。

但诡异的是——

她住七楼。窗户是那种老式的铝合金推拉窗，只能打开半扇，而且有防盗网。一个成年女性，根本不可能从这种窗户"意外坠落"。

警察调查了很长时间，最后的结论是"自杀"。

但明哲查到了另一些东西。

女孩死后，这间公寓被紧急清理过。房东亲自处理了所有遗物——衣服、化妆品、鞋子。但明哲在社区的垃圾回收站找到了一些东西：

一双红色高跟鞋。

那是女孩的鞋。她死的时候穿着的就是这双鞋——但警察说，她坠落时，鞋子留在了窗台上。

这双鞋，是房东清理遗物时扔掉的。

也就是说——

女孩坠落的时候，穿着一双高跟鞋，鞋子却留在了窗台上。

那她是怎么穿着鞋坠楼的？

除非——

她坠落的时候，并没有穿鞋。

这双鞋，是她自己脱下来，放在窗台上的。

然后，她光着脚，从那扇不可能坠楼的窗户，跳了下去。

---

明哲站在公寓门口，手里拎着那双红色高跟鞋。

他不知道自己为什么要来这里。也许是想确认什么，也许是想找到答案，也许只是想给自己一个交代。

门开了。

屋里一片漆黑。他摸到开关，按下去，灯没亮。

他掏出手机，打开手电筒。

光柱扫过客厅——茶几、沙发、电视柜。一切都和他记忆中一样。

他走向卧室。

卧室门虚掩着。他用手电筒照进去——

床上坐着一个人。

一个女人。

她穿着白色的睡裙，赤着脚，头发披散在肩上。她低着头，看不清脸。

明哲的手电筒照在她身上，她慢慢抬起头。

是那个女孩。

她的脸苍白得像纸，眼睛是两个黑黑的洞，嘴唇是诡异的紫红色。她的脖子上有一道深深的勒痕——不对，那不是勒痕，那是一道伤口，从左到右，贯穿了整个脖颈。

她看着明哲，嘴角忽然裂开，露出一个笑容。

那个笑容太宽了，咧到了耳根后面。

"你找到我的鞋了。"她说。

声音像是从很深的地方传来，带着空洞的回响。

明哲往后退了一步，后背撞上了什么。

他回头——

另一个她站在那里。

穿着同样的白裙子，同样的赤脚，同样的披散头发。但这个她的脸是正常的——就是那张曾经在照片里看到过的年轻的脸，清秀，安静，甚至有点忧伤。

"别听她的。"这个她说，声音轻柔，像是正常人。

"你在找什么？"另一个她问，那个笑容的女人。

两个"她"，一个在床前，一个在他身后。

明哲终于明白了。

中介说过，每个人看到的都不一样。

高跟鞋。小孩哭声。唱歌的女人。

不是房子里有什么。

是房子里——不止一个。

---

明哲后来没和任何人说起那天晚上的事。

他只说，押金要不回来了，算自己倒霉。

至于那双红色高跟鞋，他找了个没人的地方，挖了个坑，埋了。

他再也没去过那栋楼。

直到半年后，他偶然路过那条街。

他抬头看了一眼七楼的那扇窗。

窗户开着。

窗台上坐着两个人。

一个在笑。

一个在哭。

两个都穿着白裙子。

两个都赤着脚。

她们同时低下头，看向明哲。

明哲转身就走，再也没有回头。

---

**尾声**

后来明哲在网上查到了更多关于那间公寓的事。

那栋楼建于上世纪七十年代，最早是一个工厂的职工宿舍。九十年代工厂改制，房子被卖给了私人。

但有一个传言一直没断过——

建这栋楼的地皮，原先是一片乱葬岗。

乱葬岗上埋的，都是女人。

没人知道她们是谁，为什么会被埋在那里。

但她们——

好像从来没走。

## 一、雾中来客

陈墨舟提着旧皮箱踏入青螺镇的那一刻，浓雾便吞没了来路。

他本是省城《晨光报》的一名校对员，业余爱好写些不入流的推理小说。此番收到叔父遗书，言及有急事相商，却不想在路上便得知叔父陈墨池已于一日前暴毙于青螺客栈。

镇子坐落在云岭深处，四面环山，常年雾气弥漫。镇上的人走路轻得没有声音，说话低得仿佛怕惊动什么。陈墨舟站在客栈门口，看着那块褪色的"青螺客栈"木匾，总觉得那四个字像是在哭丧着脸。

"陈先生，令叔父的丧事尚未操办，"镇长方如海迎上来，是个矮胖的中年人，笑起来眼睛眯成一条缝，"您请节哀。有什么需要帮忙的，尽管吩咐。"

"我叔父是怎么死的？"陈墨舟直接问道。

方镇长的笑容僵了一瞬。"官府说是……心疾暴发。"

"我不信。"

方镇长看了他一眼，那眼神里有些难以捉摸的东西。"陈先生初来乍到，恐怕不知青螺镇的规矩——有些事，不问为好。"

## 二、镜中人影

陈墨池的遗体停放在客栈后院的冰窖里。当陈墨舟掀开白布时，倒吸一口凉气。

叔父面色铁青，双目圆睁，死不瞑目。脖颈处有一道细细的红痕，像是被人用丝线勒过，又像是被什么锐利的东西划过。

"这叫'雾锁喉'，"身后传来一个苍老的声音。

陈墨舟转身，看见一个白发苍苍的老妇人拄着拐杖站在门口。她叫叶婆，是青螺镇最老的居民，据说活了一百二十岁。

"雾锁喉？"陈墨舟皱眉。

"青螺镇有五大奇案，皆非人力所为。"叶婆的声音像是从地底传来，"令叔父不是第一个，也不会是最后一个。"

"什么奇案？"

叶婆伸出枯瘦的手指，点了点冰窖的石壁。陈墨舟凑近一看，只见石壁上刻着五个名字：

**雾锁喉、镜中人、纸轿夫、水底灯、山中影。**

每一个名字后面，都跟着一个日期和一个死亡的符号。

"这是近三十年来，青螺镇所有离奇死亡的记录，"叶婆说，"你的叔父，是第五个'雾锁喉'。"

## 三、客栈的镜子

陈墨舟决定暂住青螺客栈，等待真相浮出水面。

客栈一楼大堂里，挂着一面巨大的铜镜。据掌柜说，这镜子已有一百五十年历史，照过无数人的脸。陈墨舟望着镜中自己的倒影，忽然发现——

镜中的他，正在朝他微笑。

而他自己，明明没有笑。

"你也看到了？"一个清脆的女声从楼梯上传来。

陈墨舟抬头，看见一个穿着素白长裙的年轻女子缓缓走下。她约莫二十出头，眉眼清冷，却有种说不出的诡异气质。

"我叫柳烟，是这客栈的住客，"她说，"已经住了三年。"

"三年？"陈墨舟愕然，"客栈住三年？"

"因为，"柳烟指了指那面铜镜，"我出不去。"

陈墨舟顺着她的手指望去，镜中除了他自己的倒影外，竟还有另一个身影——一个身穿红衣的女子，正站在柳烟身后，长发垂地，面容模糊。

柳烟却浑然不觉。

## 四、纸轿夫

第二天夜里，陈墨舟被一阵唢呐声惊醒。

他推开窗户，只见浓雾中，一顶红色纸轿正从街心穿过。四个轿夫身形佝偻，面无表情，脚步却整齐划一。轿帘掀起一角，露出里面坐着的一个纸人——

那纸人的脸，竟与他叔父一模一样。

陈墨舟冲出客栈，跟在纸轿后面。纸轿穿过长街，绕过后山，最终停在一座荒废的祠堂前。轿夫们将纸人抬进祠堂，然后——

纸人站了起来。

它转过头，看向陈墨舟，嘴角微微上扬。陈墨舟想跑，双腿却像灌了铅一般沉重。纸人一寸一寸地走近，每一步都带起地上的灰尘。

就在纸人伸手要触碰他的一刻，一道剑光闪过——

柳烟不知何时出现在他身旁，手中握着一柄泛着幽光的青铜短剑。

"还不快跑！"她低喝一声。

陈墨舟回过神，拉着柳烟狂奔。身后传来纸人撕裂般的咆哮，震得屋瓦簌簌落下。

## 五、水底灯

他们逃到镇外的青螺湖边时，天色已经微明。

柳烟靠着柳树喘息，那柄短剑还握在手里，剑身上的幽光已经黯淡。

"谢谢你，"陈墨舟说，"那是什么？"

"'纸轿夫'，五大奇案之一，"柳烟说，"它们每逢月圆便会出来，带走一个人。令叔父……我猜便是那夜被带走的。"

"被带去哪里？"

"镜子里。"柳烟指了指湖面，"你看。"

陈墨舟低头，只见平静的湖面下，竟有一点灯光在闪烁。越看越亮，越看越清晰——那是一盏古朴的宫灯，灯下站着一个模糊的人影。

那人影缓缓抬起头，竟是陈墨池的脸。

"叔父！"陈墨舟扑向湖边，却被柳烟一把拉住。

"你下去，就回不来了，"柳烟说，"那叫'水底灯'，是五大奇案之一。它会诱骗活人下水，让他们永远留在镜中世界。"

"镜中世界？"陈墨舟怔住。

"青螺镇有一个古老的传说，"柳烟望着湖面，"说这里有一面巨大的镜子，镜中有一个与现实一模一样的世界。每隔一段时间，现实里的人就会被镜中的'他们'取代。而被取代的人，会被关进镜中，永远出不来。"

"你……也是被关进去的？"

柳烟沉默了片刻。"三年前，我发现了这面镜子的秘密。我看到了镜中的自己，想要逃出去，却发现自己已经回不去了。我的肉身还在现实里走动，但我的魂魄，已经留在了镜中。"

她转过身，那双清冷的眼睛里，有着深深的悲凉。

"你叔父，是镜中的'它'们派出来的奸细。他想取代现实中的某个活人——"

"谁？"

柳烟没有回答，只是望着湖面。

水底的灯光，越来越亮。

## 六、最后的谜题

叶婆找到陈墨舟时，他正坐在客栈大堂里，对着那面铜镜发呆。

镜中，他看见了自己的倒影。但那倒影的眼睛里，闪烁着与陈墨池临死前一模一样的红光。

"你明白了吧？"叶婆在他身旁坐下，"令叔父不是被杀死的，而是被'取代'了。镜中的他出来了，现实的他被关进去了。"

"可方镇长说，叔父是心疾暴发……"

"方如海是镜中的'它'们的傀儡，"叶婆冷笑一声，"五大奇案从未真正破过，因为每一次'它们'都能找到替身，掩盖真相。而新的镇长、新的客栈掌柜——都是'它们'的棋子。"

"那要怎么阻止？"陈墨舟攥紧拳头。

叶婆递给他一张泛黄的纸条，上面写着四行字：

*雾锁喉，喉中血，镜中影，影中穴。*
*若要破，需问心。心若明，路自现。*

"这是三十年来，所有想要破解谜题的人留下的，"叶婆说，"他们全都失败了。"

"我叔父为什么要来青螺镇？"陈墨舟忽然问。

叶婆沉默良久。"因为他发现了这面镜子的秘密，想要毁掉它。他以为他能成功……"

"我能见他吗？"陈墨舟指了指镜中那微弱的灯光，"在镜子里？"

"能。但你进去，就未必出得来。"

陈墨舟望着镜中的自己，深吸一口气。

"我想试试。"

## 七、雾散时分

月圆之夜，陈墨舟独自站在铜镜前。

柳烟、叶婆、还有客栈里所有住客都聚在大堂里，望着他。叶婆手中拈着一张符咒，柳烟握着那柄青铜短剑，所有人神情凝重。

"记住，"叶婆说，"镜中的世界与现实相反。白为黑，真为假，活为死。你必须找到你叔父，问他三个问题，才能带他出来。"

"哪三个问题？"

"只有你叔父知道。"

陈墨舟点了点头，伸手触碰镜面。那冰凉的触感渐渐变得温热，镜面如同水面一般荡起涟漪。他深吸一口气，踏了进去。

——

镜中世界一片混沌。

没有雾，没有镇子，只有一片无边的黑暗。陈墨舟摸索着前行，脚下踩到柔软的东西——那是落叶，已经腐烂了不知多少年。

远处有一点微光。陈墨舟循光而去，渐渐看见了熟悉的街景：青螺客栈、长街、后山、青螺湖……但一切都是倒过来的。

湖在天上，山在脚下，房子倒悬在半空。

陈墨舟在倒悬的客栈前停下，看见门口站着一个身影。

"叔父？"

那人转过身。的确是陈墨池，但他的脸色苍白如纸，眼神空洞。

"墨舟，你不该来的。"他说。

"我来带你回去。"

陈墨池苦笑。"回不去了。我犯了一个错误——我想毁掉这面镜子，却低估了它的力量。它把我关在这里，永远出不去。"

"那我陪你。"陈墨舟说。

陈墨池望着他，眼中闪过一丝光芒。"你真的想救我？"

"当然。"

"那你要回答我三个问题——如果答错，我们都会永远留在这里。"

## 八、三个问题

**第一问："你为何而来？"**

陈墨舟沉默片刻。"为了真相。"

"错。"陈墨池摇头，"你来，是为了名利。你想写一篇独家报道，让所有人知道青螺镇的秘密，让你自己一举成名。"

陈墨舟怔住。他想说不是，但看到叔父洞悉一切的眼神，知道撒谎无用。

"再来。"陈墨池说。

陈墨舟深吸一口气，重新组织语言。"我来，是因为你是我叔父。我不能看着你不明不白地死去。"

陈墨池的眼中有了笑意。"过。"

**第二问："你见何为真？"**

"所见即真，"陈墨舟答。

"错。镜中的世界，你所见皆为虚妄。"

陈墨舟想了想。"不见为真。我用心去感受，不被表象迷惑。"

"半对半错。"陈墨池摇头，"再想。"

陈墨舟闭上眼，良久。"真不在所见，也不在心。真的是——我所做的一切，问心无愧。"

陈墨池点了点头。"过。"

**第三问："你愿以何换？"**

陈墨舟毫不犹豫。"一切。"

"错。"陈墨池叹息，"你太年轻，不懂得'一切'的分量。"

陈墨舟沉默。他开始思考这个问题。叔父想听什么答案？

"你愿以何换？"叔父再问。

"我愿以我的命换你的命，"陈墨舟说。

陈墨池久久地望着他，眼中竟有泪光。"过。"

镜中世界开始剧烈震动。陈墨池伸出手，抓住陈墨舟的手腕。

"墨舟，记住——出去后，不要相信任何人。"

"包括你？"

陈墨池笑了笑，那笑容里有着说不出的苍凉。"我早已不是我了。但你要记住一件事——"

他的身影开始碎裂。

"镜子要碎了——小心！"

## 九、雾散

陈墨舟猛然惊醒。

他发现自己站在客栈大堂的铜镜前。镜面已经碎成无数片，每一片里都映着他不同的倒影。叶婆、柳烟、还有所有住客都围在他身边，神情紧张。

"我叔父呢？"陈墨舟四下张望。

没有人回答。

陈墨舟低头，看见地上有一缕青烟缓缓升起——那是陈墨池留在这世间的最后一缕魂魄，在晨光中渐渐消散。

"叔父！"陈墨舟想伸手去抓，却只抓到虚空。

"他回不来了，"叶婆说，"但他给了你机会。"

"什么机会？"

叶婆指向碎裂的铜镜。"镜子碎了，封印解除了。但镜中的'它们'也出来了。青螺镇，从今以后，不再是那个被隐藏的秘境——"

她望着窗外，只见浓雾正缓缓散去。

三十年来笼罩着青螺镇的大雾，在这一刻，终于散尽。

远处传来嘈杂的人声。省城的官府终于找到了进镇的路，第一批记者也蜂拥而至。青螺镇的故事，很快就会传遍全国。

陈墨舟站在客栈门口，望着那些涌进来的人，忽然明白了叔父最后那句话的意思——

"不要相信任何人。"

因为这些涌进来的人里，不知有多少，是镜中的"它们"派出来的。

## 尾声

陈墨舟离开青螺镇的那天，柳烟也消失了。

有人说她在镇外的小溪边被人看见过，有人说她跳进了青螺湖。陈墨舟找遍了整个镇子，都没有找到她。

但在他离开镇子的最后一刻，他回头望去——

在客栈那面碎裂的铜镜前，有一个白裙女子的身影，正朝他挥手。

她微笑着，嘴唇无声地动了动。陈墨舟看不清她说了什么，但他隐约觉得，那是三个字——

"谢谢你。"

陈墨舟攥紧了口袋里的一张纸条。那是叶婆临别时塞给他的，上面只写着四个字：

**镜中有人。**

他没有告诉任何人，包括自己最亲密的朋友。因为他知道，从踏入青螺镇的那一刻起，他就已经不再是原来的自己了。

而镜中的"它们"，也从未放弃过寻找下一个替身。

陈墨舟回头望了最后一眼那已经散去迷雾的青螺镇，转身踏上了回省城的路。

他知道，故事还没有结束。

在某个雾气弥漫的夜晚，那面碎裂的铜镜，或许会重新拼合。

而镜中的"它们"，会再次派出新的纸轿夫、新的水底灯、新的镜中人——

寻找下一个迷途的来客。

# 错位的影子

## 一

凌晨两点四十七分，沈砚秋接到电话时，正独自坐在书房里擦拭那把跟了他二十年的左轮手枪。

电话是刑侦大队的老周打来的，案情重大，语气急促得像连珠炮：城西"听雨轩"茶馆，老板娘柳如烟死在二楼的雅间里，死因是氰化物中毒，现场没有任何打斗痕迹，门窗从内部反锁——典型的密室。

沈砚秋赶到现场时，天边已经泛起鱼肚白。

柳如烟的尸体斜倚在红木圈椅里，姿态近乎优雅，仿佛只是小憩片刻。她的右手边是一只青花瓷杯，杯壁上残留着淡淡的苦杏仁味——那是氰化物的标志。她的左手搭在椅子扶手上，手指修长，指甲修剪得体，腕上戴着一只老式的翡翠镯子，成色极好。

老周凑过来，压低声音说："沈哥，初步排查，茶馆里当晚一共五个人——柳如烟自己，还有她的茶艺师小棠、帮厨阿福、送货司机老马，以及当晚唯一的外来客人，茶叶商人陆鹤年。"

"陆鹤年？"

"对，杭州来的，说是要谈一批明前龙井的收购。柳如烟和他以前就认识，算是老主顾了。"老周翻着笔记本，"我们查了他的背景，干净得很，正经生意人，没案底。"

沈砚秋没说话，蹲下身，盯着那只青花瓷杯看了很久。

杯底有一圈淡淡的水渍，形状不规则，像是被人端起又放下过。茶叶舒展得很好，说明泡茶的人手艺不错。他又看了一眼柳如烟的手——右手食指和中指之间，有一道极浅的、被茶汤浸润过的痕迹，像是握笔的姿势。

"她死前在写字？"沈砚秋问。

老周愣了一下："没……没发现纸笔啊。"

沈砚秋没有回答。他站起身，环顾整个雅间。博古架上摆着各式茶具，墙上挂着一幅水墨山水，角落里立着一架古琴。窗户是传统的花梨木雕花窗，月光透过雕花洒进来，在地砖上投下斑驳的影子。

"这窗户，是从里面反锁的？"他问。

"是，插销是死的，没人动过。"

"那凶手是怎么离开的？"

"这……"老周挠了挠头，"我们正在排查。可能是茶馆里的人配合的。"

## 二

沈砚秋花了一整天时间，分别询问了那四个人。

茶艺师小棠，二十出头，圆脸，说话时眼神闪烁，像一只受惊的小鹿。她说柳如烟对她很好，像亲姐姐一样，她不可能杀人。说这话的时候，她的手指不停地绞着衣角。

帮厨阿福，三十多岁，木讷寡言，问一句答一句，从不多说一个字。他说当晚他一直在厨房备料，没上过二楼。问谁能证明，他摇了摇头。

送货司机老马，五十来岁，满脸风霜，眼神浑浊但透着精明。他说柳如烟是他看着长大的，这孩子命苦，男人死得早，她一个人撑着茶馆不容易。说这话的时候，他的声音哽咽了。

陆鹤年，四十出头，文质彬彬，谈吐得体，穿一件藏青色的棉麻长衫。他说自己是来谈生意的，没想到会发生这种事。他主动交出了自己的行程单、身份证、名片，甚至愿意配合任何调查。他说得很诚恳，沈砚秋看他的眼神，也确实不像凶手。

但沈砚秋的目光最终停在了某处。

"老周，"他问，"柳如烟的翡翠镯子，平时都戴吗？"

"戴的，我们走访过她的邻居，都说几乎没见她摘下来过。"

"那她死的时候，镯子在左腕还是右腕？"

"左腕。"

沈砚秋皱起了眉。柳如烟是右利手，他看过她握杯的姿势，习惯用右手端茶。一个右利手的人，翡翠镯子通常戴在左手——这是对的。但问题在于，柳如烟长期戴镯子的左腕，按理说应该比右腕细一些，因为镯子会有一种"塑形"作用，让手腕适应它的形状。

可是现场的照片里，左腕和右腕的粗细，几乎一样。

"这只镯子，是她自己戴上去的，还是死后被人戴上去的？"沈砚秋喃喃自语。

老周没听清："沈哥，你说啥？"

沈砚秋摆摆手，没再说什么。

## 三

第三天，沈砚秋带着小棠、阿福、老马和陆鹤年，重返案发现场。

"我想再看看那个雅间。"他说。

四个人表情各异。小棠低着头，阿福面无表情，老马眉头紧锁，陆鹤年微微一笑："沈警官需要我们配合什么？"

沈砚秋没有回答，径直上了楼。

雅间还是老样子，只是尸体已经被移走，空气里残留着一丝若有若无的苦杏仁味。沈砚秋走到窗前，伸手摸了一下雕花窗棂。

"老周，"他说，"你过来看。"

老周凑过去。沈砚秋指着窗棂的一处雕花——那是一朵镂空的梅花，花瓣之间有一个微小的缺口。

"这个缺口，是新茬还是旧痕？"

老周仔细看了看，脸色变了："新茬。"

"也就是说，有人从这里动过。"

沈砚秋转过身，环视着四个人。他的目光，从左到右，依次扫过每个人的脸。

小棠的脸最白，阿福的脸最僵，老马的脸最沉，陆鹤年的脸……最平静。

"凶手就在你们四个人中间。"沈砚秋说。

雅间里安静得可以听见心跳声。

"我已经知道是谁了。"

这句话像一颗石子投进平静的水面，激起一圈圈涟漪。小棠的呼吸急促起来，阿福的手指微微颤抖，老马的喉结动了动，只有陆鹤年，依然保持着那副文质彬彬的微笑。

"沈警官，"陆鹤年温和地说，"愿闻其详。"

沈砚秋走到博古架前，拿起一只青花瓷杯——和杀死柳如烟的那只杯子，是同一套。

"陆先生，你是杭州来的茶叶商人，对吧？"

"是。"

"你说你和柳如烟是老主顾，但今晚是你第一次来'听雨轩'谈生意，对吗？"

"是的，怎么？"

"那你怎么知道，二楼雅间的窗户雕花里，有一朵梅花？"

陆鹤年的笑容僵了一瞬。但只是一瞬，他很快恢复了镇定："沈警官，你这话什么意思？我不明白。"

"我的意思是，"沈砚秋一字一顿地说，"你知道那朵梅花，是因为你事先踩过点。你知道柳如烟的镯子常年戴在左腕，知道她的茶杯握法，知道她习惯把门窗反锁。你对她了如指掌，但你们今晚才第一次见面——除非，你们之前就已经认识。"

"我……"陆鹤年刚要开口，沈砚秋抬手打断了他。

"还有一个证据。柳如烟死的时候，镯子在左腕。但一个常年戴镯子的人，左腕应该比右腕细。我量过尸体的腕围，几乎一样。这说明，镯子是死后才戴上去的——或者说，是被人从右手腕摘下来，又戴到左手腕的。"

"这能说明什么？"陆鹤年的声音冷了下来。

"这说明，凶手在伪造现场。他想让我们以为，柳如烟是正常死亡，镯子也戴在正常位置。但实际上，他太刻意了，反而露出了破绽。"

陆鹤年沉默了几秒钟，然后叹了口气。

"精彩，沈警官。"他说，"你比我想的要厉害。"

他伸手，从袖口里滑出一样东西——是一把小巧的竹制飞刀，尖端泛着幽幽的蓝光。

"但你还是错了。"

沈砚秋的瞳孔骤然收缩。

"我不是凶手。"

陆鹤年手腕一翻，飞刀脱手而出，擦着沈砚秋的耳边飞过，钉在了身后的门框上。老马和阿福几乎同时动了——不是冲向沈砚秋，而是冲向陆鹤年。

"动手！"老马大喝一声。

## 四

混战中，沈砚秋被阿福扑倒在地。他这才看清，阿福和老马都是练家子，身手极好，三两下就把陆鹤年制住了。

"你们……"沈砚秋愣住了。

"沈警官，"老马擦了擦额头的汗，"对不起，瞒了你。但我们是柳如烟的人。"

"柳如烟的人？"

"她男人死得早，但生前是江湖上有头有脸的人物。她接手茶馆，不只是为了做生意。"阿福低声说，"今晚的事，是有人要灭口。柳如烟查到了不该查的东西。"

沈砚秋缓缓站起身，看向被制住的陆鹤年："那他……"

"他是来保护柳如烟的。"老马说，"我们是他的后援。"

"保护？可他……"

"他发现凶手要动手，想阻止，但晚了一步。"阿福说，"凶手用的是氰化物，下在茶水里，陆先生赶到时，柳如烟已经……他只能做一件事——伪装现场，把嫌疑引到自己身上，让我们有足够的时间追查真凶。"

沈砚秋愣住了。

他想起了陆鹤年那双平静的眼睛，想起了他说"你错了"时那丝如释重负的表情。

"那真凶是谁？"

老马和阿福对视了一眼，然后——

"是我。"

小棠的声音，从门口传来。

## 五

沈砚秋转过头。

小棠站在门口，圆脸上挂着泪痕，眼神却出奇地平静。

"小棠？"沈砚秋难以置信，"你才二十出头……"

"我十三岁就被柳姐姐收养了。"小棠轻声说，"她对我很好。但我亲生父母，是被她男人害死的。"

雅间里死一般的寂静。

"我等了七年。"小棠说，"七年，足够让一个人学会很多东西。比如，怎么配出无色无味的氰化物溶液，怎么在茶水里让人喝不出来，怎么在密室里杀人——"

"怎么伪造不在场证明。"沈砚秋接口。

小棠苦笑了一下："是的。我甚至知道你会来，知道你会查那只翡翠镯子——那是我故意戴反的。我以为会拖住你更久，没想到……"

她抬起手。沈砚秋这才看见，她的袖口里，也藏着一把竹制飞刀。

"别动！"老马和阿福同时扑了上去。

但小棠没有攻击。她只是把那把飞刀，递给了沈砚秋。

"这是我爹的遗物。"她说，"他说，江湖人，死也要死得明白。沈警官，我认罪。"

沈砚秋接过飞刀，手有些发抖。

他想起了昨晚，他在书房里擦的那把左轮手枪。他当了三十年刑警，见过无数凶手，但从未见过一个——

——把复仇藏了七年、把杀意伪装成感恩、把死亡演绎得像一场梦的女孩。

"带走。"他听见自己的声音，陌生而疲惫。

## 尾声

案子结了，但沈砚秋没有结案。

他反复回想那个夜晚，想象着另一种可能——如果他没有注意到镯子的细节，如果他没有追问那朵梅花的雕花，如果他没能识破陆鹤年的伪装……

结果会怎样？

小棠会逍遥法外？柳如烟会白死？老马和阿福会继续追凶，而真凶会一直藏在"乖巧女孩"的面具下？

他不知道答案。

但他知道一件事——

他差点就抓错了人。

那个文质彬彬、谈吐得体的陆鹤年，那个主动交出身份证和行程单的"嫌疑人"，那个在最后一刻承认"我不是凶手"的茶商……

才是他应该感谢的人。

而他，差点把感谢送进了监狱。

沈砚秋点了一支烟，在书房里坐了很久。

窗外，天快亮了。

# The Curious Case of the Missing Cohorts

Detective Vivian Pratt had been staring at the case board for so long that the pushpins had started to blur into constellations. Five years. Twenty-three retirees. Zero leads. The folks of Sunnybrook Estates didn't just vanish into thin air—they vanished into absolutely nowhere, with their shoes neatly aligned by their beds and their televisions still tuned to *Matlock*.

The department had long since given up. Pratt hadn't.

On a humid Tuesday in August, Pratt found herself in the community's clubhouse, staring at the floral wallpaper and trying not to scream. The janitor, a man named Gerald who smelled vaguely of mothballs and resignation, was mopping the floor in slow, contemplative loops.

"Gerald," Pratt said, "you've worked here twenty years. You must have noticed something."

Gerald leaned on his mop. "I notice lots of things, Detective."

"Like what?"

"Like how Mrs. Henderson from 4B orders exactly three Werther's Originals every afternoon, then puts one in her pocket for later. Like how Mr. Pellington waters his lawn at 3 a.m. in his bathrobe, talking to it. Like how every Tuesday at noon, the back room fills up with people who weren't here a second ago."

Pratt froze. "The back room."

"Oh yes." Gerald mopped thoughtfully. "Big purple door at the end of the hall. They file in, file out, and then we never see them again. I assumed it was some kind of mahjong tournament."

Pratt drew her weapon. She had not drawn her weapon in three years.

The purple door, when they reached it, had a small gold plaque: **REINCARNATION NOW: EST. 1987**.

Inside, a cheerful man in a turtleneck sat behind a desk made entirely of recycled yogurt containers. A banner behind him read: *Your Next Chapter Starts Here!*

"Ah," said the man, beaming, "Detective Pratt! We've been expecting you. You're three minutes late for your own appointment."

Pratt stared. "My what?"

"Your transition! Paperwork's all set. You'll be reborn as a particularly ambitious barnacle on the hull of a container ship passing through the Strait of Malacca. Excellent career trajectory."

"The *missing retirees*," Pratt managed.

"Oh, them." The man waved a hand. "Wonderful clients. Very eager. Mr. Kowalski became a heron—gorgeous plumage. Mrs. Pell chose to come back as her own granddaughter's childhood imaginary friend. Very touching, honestly."

"But they just—*left*. Without telling anyone. There were searches. Candlelight vigils. Their families—"

"Look," the man said, and for the first time his smile dimmed. "Have you *met* their families? Half of them were going to be Mr. Pellington's cat. The cat had a better diet. Some of them wanted to start over entirely—no more bridge club, no more Phyllis with her opinions about Medicare. Phyllis alone drove three of them in."

Gerald raised a tentative hand. "If everyone's reincarnating, who's left to play mahjong?"

The man tilted his head. "We did try to tell the families. We sent brochures. Very tasteful, watercolor of a sunrise on the front." He slid a sample across the desk. It featured a cartoon cloud giving a thumbs up.

Pratt sat down slowly on a beanbag shaped like a lotus flower. She had trained at Quantico. She had once disarmed a suspect while eating a calzone. She had *no framework for this*.

"The police chief," she said. "Does he know?"

"He was our first client. He's a very happy sea otter now. Slightly anarchic, but very happy."

Pratt looked at Gerald. Gerald looked at Pratt.

"Tell you what," the man said brightly. "I'll pencil you in for Thursday. We'll get you into the system before the rush."

Pratt handed in her badge that afternoon. Gerald handed in his mop. The families, when told the truth, were mostly relieved, with the exception of the Kowalskis, who had been holding a seat at the Thanksgiving table for four years.

Phyllis, when she heard, went immediately to schedule her own appointment. Even Phyllis, it turned out, had somewhere better to be.

**미제 사건의 마지막 식탁**

2013년의 어느 비 오는 화요일, 서울 광화문 네거리에서 사라진 양승호 씨의 행방은 12년 동안 대한민국 경찰史(사)상 가장 골치 아픈 떡밥이었다. 승호 씨가 마지막으로 등장한 것은 당시 신설된 AI 기반 CCTV ‘아이즈(SH-7)’의 모니터링실. 승호 씨는 모니터를 한참 응시하다가 “이거… 내 얼굴이 왜 저래?”라고 중얼거린 뒤, 그대로 액정에 머리를 박고 실종되었다.

이 사건은 모든 CCTV가 ‘정상 작동 중’이라고 뻔뻔하게 보고했지만, 정작 승호 씨의 마지막 발자국은 기록되지 않았다. SBS 그것이 알고싶다에서는 “양승호 씨는 디지털 세계로 건너갔을지도 모른다”는 음모론을 제기했고, MBC 그것이 알고싶다에서는 “양승호 씨는 절대 디지털 세계로 건너가지 않았다”라는 반박을 제기해 시청률이 역대급으로 치솟았다. 양승호 씨는 그사이 유튜브 채널을 개설해 “나는 살아 있다”라는 영상을 3년간 매일 업로드했으나, 알고리즘은 그를 ‘반복 콘텐츠 크리에이터’라며 노출을 끊었다.

---

2025년 가을, 사건은 우연히 — 그리고 매우 우스꽝스럽게 — 해결된다.

서울중앙지검 검사 박지수는 승진 욕구에 사로잡혀 미제사건 클리어링 프로젝트에 자원했다. 그의 첫 번째 타깃은 양승호 사건. 박 검사는 “CCTV 데이터 1테라바이트, 형사 5명, 예산 3억 원이면 양승호 정도는 잡는 건 일도 아니죠. 못 잡는 건 의지 문제죠.”라고 코트를 여미며 출근했다.

그러나 데이터는 말썽이었다. SH-7 시스템은 ‘광화문 광장 CCTV 정밀 데이터셋’이라면서 폴더 안에 ‘광화문은_빛이_들어오는_곳.txt’라 적힌 텍스트 파일 하나만 딸랑 들어 있었다. 박 검사는 AI 수사관 ‘오로라-3’에게 데이터를 던졌다.

오로라-3는 박 검사에게 이렇게 답했다.

> “사용자. 해당 데이터셋에는 사람의 얼굴이 0.0% 포함되어 있습니다. 단, 모니터 액정에 비친 얼굴 1점이 ‘비정규 좌표계(프랙털 차원)’ 상에 존재합니다. 이는 ‘누군가 모니터 속에 들어가 살고 있다’는 매우 희박한 가설을 지지합니다. 추천 행동: 모니터를 부숴서 구조신고를 합니다.”

박 검사는 오로라-3의 제안대로 모니터를 부수려다 멈칫했다. 모니터는 예산 때문이다. 그러던 중 광화문 청사 경비원 노인이 양승호 씨의 왼쪽 신발 한 짝을 들고 나타났다. “청소하다가 화단 밑에서 찾았어요. 이거 12년 된 거 같은데, 주인한테 좀 갖다 달라고요.” 노인은 신발 안에 손수건을 말아 넣고 있었는데, 손수건에는 깨알 같은 글씨가 적혀 있었다.

— 「김 과장에게 전함. 나는 여기 있다. SH-7 관리자 메뉴, 비밀번호는 ‘mother1234’. 죽은 줄 알았지? 전역 후에도 월세 받으러 와라. 11월 23일, 새벽 2시, 광화문 분수대 정면 0.5m 앞, 내가 있을 거다」

박 검사는 한숨을 쉬었다. ‘mother1234’… 그것은 대한민국 공공기관 비밀번호 선정 통계 1위인 ‘password1234’의 자매품이었다.

자정, 광화문 분수대. 박 검사는 잠옷 바람 차림의 중년 남성과 눈이 마주쳤다. 그 남성은 정확히 “양승호”가 맞았다. 다만 살이 23kg 찐 모습이었고, 셔츠에는 ‘나는 디지털 인간입니다 V2.0’이라 적혀 있었다. 옆에는 버려진 모니터 다섯 개가 쌓여 있었는데, 그 안에서 누군가가 자판을 두드리고 있었다.

“아, 검사님 오셨습니까. 어서 오세요.”

승호 씨는 박 검사에게 ‘진실의 도시락’을 권했다. 도시락에는 12년치 CCTV 기록이 SD 카드 모양으로 정렬되어 있었다. “전부 제가 모니터 안에서 작업한 겁니다. 밖에서 일하면 월세 내야 하니까. 모니터 안은 광장 정문에서 반경 7m 안에 있으니까, 주소지 인정돼서 전역 처리됐어요. 광화문 일대 전체가 제 셋방입니다.”

박 검사는 어이없다는 표정을 지었다.

“그럼… 왜 돌아나오지 않으셨어요?”

승호 씨는 미묘하게 웃었다. “검사님, 모니터 안의 삶이 더 안전하더라고요. 밖에서는 매일 아침 7시에 알람이 울리고, 월세를 내야 하고, 회사에서 ‘이게 맞아요?’라는 슬랙을 받아야 하잖아요. 모니터 안에서는 그냥 화면 밝기만 관리하면 됩니다. 그리고 가장 큰 이유 — 모니터 안의 저승호 씨는 ‘사회적으로 죽은’ 상태가 아니라 ‘전역한’ 상태로 인정받거든요. 모니터 밖의 세상은 저를 죽었다고 우기고 있었지만, 모니터 안은 저를 입대 처리해 준 거예요. 거기다 셋방은 무료고요.”

“그럼… 지금 CCTV는요?”

# The Inheritance

Margaret found the envelope on a Tuesday morning, tucked between the pages of her grandmother's old photo album. The handwriting was unmistakably her grandmother's—those careful, slanted letters Margaret had learned to read as a child.

*For Margaret, on her forty-fifth birthday. Do not open until then.*

She checked the calendar. Her birthday was in three weeks.

Margaret did not open it. She carried it to the kitchen, placed it on the counter, and tried not to look at it while she made coffee. She failed. The envelope sat there like a small, patient animal, and by Wednesday, she had moved it to her nightstand. By Friday, it was in her purse. By Sunday, she was taking it out at traffic lights just to feel the weight of it.

The house grew quieter each day. She was used to quiet—her grandmother had passed six months ago, and Margaret had inherited not just the photographs and the china, but the stillness of a life interrupted. Her grandmother at 89, gone in her sleep, leaving behind a son who never called and a granddaughter who visited every Sunday for seventeen years.

On her birthday, Margaret sat at the kitchen table with a cup of tea that had gone cold. She slid her finger under the flap.

Inside was a letter, and inside the letter was a key.

*Dear Margaret,*

*If you are reading this, I am gone, and you have done me the honor of waiting. The key opens a safe deposit box at the First National on Maple Street. Inside, you will find everything I never knew how to say.*

*There is also a second envelope. Please do not open it yet. Give it ten years. If you have children, give it to your firstborn on their twentieth birthday. If you do not, open it yourself when you are ready to understand.*

*Thank you for the Sundays.*

*All my love,*
*Grandma*

Margaret drove to the bank. The teller, who had known her grandmother, smiled sadly. The box was small and heavy.

Inside were three things: a stack of letters tied with a faded ribbon, a worn wedding ring, and a photograph of a young man in a military uniform she had never seen before.

She read the letters first. They were love letters, written in her grandmother's hand, addressed to someone named *Eli*. They spanned from 1948 to 1954. They were tender, desperate, beautiful.

Then she read the date on the back of the photograph.

*1953.*

Her grandmother had been married to Harold in 1953. Margaret had always known her grandfather Harold—a stern, quiet man who died before she was born. The family history was simple: a long marriage, one son, decades in the same house.

Her grandmother had had another life. A whole one. With Eli.

Margaret read the letters again. She cried. She drove home.

She put the second envelope in her nightstand drawer. She did not open it.

Ten years, her grandmother had said. *If you have children, give it to your firstborn on their twentieth birthday.*

Margaret was forty-five. She had never married. She had never wanted children.

She thought of the second envelope, sealed and waiting, somewhere in her future. She thought of her grandmother, who had loved twice and told no one, who had left her whole secret life in a safe deposit box and trusted her granddaughter with it.

*If you do not, open it yourself when you are ready to understand.*

Margaret sat at the kitchen table for a long time.

Then she took out a pen and a piece of paper.

*Dear Eli,* she wrote, in her grandmother's slanted hand, practicing carefully. *I never knew you. But I think I would have liked you.*

She stopped. She thought about the second envelope. She thought about what her grandmother had been willing to wait for, and what she had been willing to tell.

Then, very slowly, Margaret opened the drawer and lifted the second envelope to the light. She turned it over in her hands. It was heavier than it looked.

She had waited three weeks. Her grandmother had waited fifty years.

The phone rang. Margaret jumped, then laughed at herself. It was probably her aunt, calling to wish her happy birthday.

She let it ring. She had decided.

She would wait.

---

*Margaret waited.*

She did not open the second envelope that year, or the next. She moved it from the nightstand to a shoebox, then to a small lockbox she bought specifically for the purpose. She traveled. She took up painting. She fell in love, briefly, with a woman named June, who understood about waiting for things.

At fifty-five, she reread her grandmother's letters. They were different now. Less romantic, more melancholy. She understood things about them she hadn't understood before.

At sixty, she opened the lockbox. The envelope was still there. The paper had yellowed. The handwriting on the front, which she had memorized, looked like a stranger's.

*For the firstborn,* it said. *Or for you.*

June had died two years before. Margaret lived alone now, in a small house with a garden. She had never regretted not having children, but she sometimes wondered what her grandmother had imagined, all those years ago, when she wrote those words. Had she pictured a great-granddaughter? Had she pictured Margaret alone at sixty, holding an envelope, deciding?

She had not opened it yet.

She was not sure she ever would.

The thing about the second envelope, Margaret understood now, was that her grandmother had not left her a secret. She had left her a question. *Are you ready?* it asked. *Are you finally ready to know what I could not tell you when I was alive?*

And the answer, Margaret realized, was that she might never be ready. She might carry this envelope to her grave. She might pass it on to a niece, or a friend, or a stranger. She might let it outlive her.

That was okay, too.

She put the envelope back in the lockbox. She went out to the garden. She weeded the tomatoes and thought about Eli, whoever he had been, and about her grandmother's long life, and about all the things people carry with them, unopened, until the end.

The tomatoes were coming in well.

She had time.

---

# The Twist

And so, when Margaret died at eighty-three, peacefully, in her sleep, the way her grandmother had, the lockbox was found by her nephew's wife, a kind woman named Rebecca, who sorted through the belongings with care.

Inside the lockbox was the second envelope, still sealed, and a note in Margaret's hand:

*To whoever finds this. I never opened it. I think that's okay. I think that's what she wanted.*

Rebecca, curious, opened the envelope. Inside was a single piece of paper, and on it, in her great-grandmother's slanted hand, were the words:

*Hello, future. I hope you are happy. I hope you have loved someone. I hope you have told them.*

*Thank you for waiting.*

*—E.H., 1979*

Rebecca stared at it for a long time. Then she folded the letter carefully, placed it back in the envelope, and put it in her own drawer.

She would wait too.

# Poranek pod sufitem

Kornel otworzył oczy i przez ułamek sekundy pomyślał, że wciąż śpi. Sufit nad nim był zielony. Nie jakiś tam zgniłozielony, nie szpitalny, nie wyblakły – tylko intensywnie, kosmicznie zielony, jak wnętrze liścia w powiększeniu albo ekran w trybie pełnej saturacji.

Przetarł oczy wierzchem dłoni. Zielony.

Usiadł na łóżku, które – co dopiero teraz zauważył – stało na środku trawnika. Nie jego trawnika. Nie żadnego znanego mu trawnika. Trawa sięgała mu do kolan, mokra od rosy, pachnąca jak początek wakacji nad jeziorem. Wokół, we wszystkich kierunkach, rozciągał się ten sam zielony ocean, a wysoko nad nim wisiał ten sam zielony sufit, tyle że bez ścian.

Zsunął nogi z łóżka, ale zanim zdążył dotknąć trawy, zobaczył, że jego piżama zmieniła się w coś miękkiego, puszystego, w kolorze soczystej pomarańczy. Wyglądał jak wielki owoc mandarynki z ludzkimi kończynami.

– To się nie dzieje – powiedział na głos, bo zawsze tak robił, kiedy coś się działo.

Głos brzmiał normalnie. To go trochę uspokoiło.

Wtedy z trawy wyskoczył chrząszcz wielkości psa. Miał na grzbiecie maleńki melon, a z czułków zwisały dwie miniaturowe, idealnie okrągłe okulary przeciwsłoneczne.

– Dzień dobry, panie Kornelu – odezwał się chrząszcz melodyjnym głosem, lekko zniekształconym, jakby mówił przez słoik. – Melon jest świeży, rano zerwany. Mam też dla pana instrukcję.

Kornel zamrugał.

– Jaką instrukcję?

Chrzączszcz wyciągnął odnóże. Trzymał w nim zwinięty rulonik, który zaczął się sam rozwijać w powietrzu, zawisając przed twarzą Kornela jak transparent. Widniał na nim napis:

*„INSTRUKCJA DNIA: 1. Nie panikuj (już za późno). 2. Zjedz melon (to ważne). 3. Idź tam, gdzie trawa jest nieco jaśniejsza. 4. Nie pytaj dlaczego.”*

– Punkt czwarty jest chyba najtrudniejszy do wykonania – mruknął Kornel.

– Och, nie taki trudny – odparł chrząszcz, poprawiając okulary. – Ludzki umysł jest zaskakująco chętny do akceptacji absurdów, jeśli tylko ma przy sobie świeży melon.

Kornel, nie wiedząc czemu to robi, wziął melona. Był zimny, ciężki i pachniał latem. Ugryzł.

Smak był dokładnie taki, jakiego oczekiwałbyś od melona – słodki, wodnisty, odrobinę mdły w tym szczególny sposób, w jaki bywają mdłe melony. To go jakoś zakotwiczyło. Jeśli melon smakował normalnie, może reszta też była prawdziwa.

– Dalej – powiedział do chrząszcza.

– Oczywiście.

Chrząszcz ruszył pierwszy, przedzierając się przez trawę z godnością turysty z plecakiem. Kornel szedł za nim, a trawa szeleściła mu o puszystą pomarańczową piżamę. Po kilku minutach zauważył to, o czym mówiła instrukcja – w oddali, mniej więcej tam, gdzie powinien być horyzont, trawa rzeczywiście stawała się jaśniejsza, prawie żółto-zielona.

– Kornel – odezwał się nagle chrząszcz, nie odwracając się. – Mogę zapytać, co panu się śniło?

– Nie pamiętam.

– To dobrze. To znaczy, że sen się jeszcze nie skończył, tylko się zmienił.

Kornel chciał zapytać, co to ma znaczyć, ale wtedy trawa pod jego stopami zaczęła się rozrzedzać. Pojawiły się drobne, białe kwiatki, a potem nagle podłoże zaczęło się wznosić łagodną pochyłością. Na szczycie pochyłości stał maleńki drewniany domek, z którego komina unosił się dym w kolorze indygo.

Drzwi domku otworzyły się i stanął w nich ktoś, kto wyglądał jak Kornel sprzed trzydziestu lat – tyle że miał skrzydła ważki i nosił cylinder.

– Nareszcie – powiedział tamten Kornel. – Mleko już ostygło, ale herbata jest świeża.

Chrząszcz zatrzymał się, odwrócił i spojrzał na Kornela swoimi złożonymi oczami.

– To pański dzień, panie Kornelu. Nie pytaj dlaczego. Proszę wejść.

Kornel spojrzał na melona w swojej ręce. Spojrzał na domek. Spojrzał na sufit wciąż wiszący wysoko nad nim, zielony, cierpliwy, niewzruszony.

Zrobił to, o co nigdy by się nie podejrzewał – uśmiechnął się.

Wszedł do domku.

A za nim, w trawie, która odzyskiwała już swój zwykły, poranny kolor, chrząszcz wielkości psa poprawił melonowe okulary, westchnął z ulgą i ruszył w stronę swojego następnego zadania – gdzieś dalej, w czyimś innym śnie, który właśnie zaczynał się od absurdalnego sufitu.

---

*Kornel obudził się ponownie o 7:14. Sufit był biały. Za oknem padał deszcz. Na stoliku nocnym leżał nie zjedzony do końca melon, a obok niego – maleńkie, okrągłe okulary przeciwsłoneczne.*

*Nie zapytał dlaczego.*
