# The Cartomancer's Confession

The brass bell above the door chimed its familiar two-note song, and Mira didn't need to look up from shuffling her tarot deck to know who had arrived. She knew the cadence of his boots on the warped wooden floor, the soft sigh he always gave when he sat, the particular way he exhaled when he laid his palm face-up on the velvet cloth.

Four months. He had been coming for four months, every third Tuesday, like clockwork.

"You're early," Mira said, still not looking up.

"Traffic was light."

"Liar. The 7 train has been delayed all week."

A soft laugh. "You know I hate the subway."

"I know many things." She finally raised her eyes and met his gaze across the small table. Daniel Reeves. Thirty-four. Architect. Recently divorced—or finalizing, the messy kind. He had come to her in September with grief pressing between his shoulder blades and questions knotting his brow. *Will I be okay? Will I ever love again?*

She had read his palm and told him what she told everyone: *The lines suggest possibility. The future is unwritten.*

But with him, she had wanted to say more. With him, she had felt the cards lean toward her like conspirators, whispering things she couldn't quite translate.

"Show me," she said.

He extended his left hand. His fingers were callused at the tips from sketching, the nail of his index finger permanently smudged with graphite. She took his hand in both of hers, as she did every month, and felt the small shock of it—the way her pulse answered his, the way her thumb memorized the topography of his lifeline.

She traced the creases. Long life line. Deep heart line, recently fractured. A fate line that curved strangely toward the base of his thumb, suggesting unusual circumstances,">something she had noted before but never explained.

"You're going to take a trip," she murmured, reading the new wrinkles. "Not far. Upstate, maybe. There's a cabin in your future."

"I don't know any cabins."

"You will."

He watched her face, as he always did, with that expression of half-belief, half-desire to believe. He was the only client who looked at her like that. The others came skeptical and left skeptical; he came grieving and stayed curious.

She turned his palm upward and pressed her thumb into the center, feeling the warmth of him.

"Your heart line has changed," she said softly. "It's... reaching."

"Reaching toward what?"

She looked up. The candles guttered. Somewhere outside, a car honked, and the radiator clanked its winter complaints.

"Toward someone who was waiting," she said.

The words hung between them. She felt their weight, the gravity of them pulling at something inside her chest.

"Mira."

"Don't." She released his hand and reached for the deck. "Let's do a three-card spread. Past, present, future."

But he caught her wrist. Not roughly—gently, the way one might catch a falling leaf.

"Is it you?" he asked. "The one waiting?"

She should have laughed. She should have pulled her hand away and shuffled her cards and read him some nonsense about a new beginning or a stranger bearing gifts. She had done it for twenty years. She had read palms in carnivals, at parties, in her tiny rented shop on Bedford Street. She had built walls so thick she sometimes forgot there was anything behind them.

"I'm the fortuneteller," she said. "I don't appear in the reading."

"That's not true, though, is it? You're in the room."

"I'm always in the room."

"Then you're in the reading."

She met his eyes. The candles seemed to burn brighter.

"You're a client," she said. "I don't—I can't—"

"I know," he said. "I know the rules."

She did not know why she had rules. She had invented them herself, years ago, after a man in Atlantic City had wanted her to read him every week and she had realized, slowly, that she was waiting for him. After he stopped coming, she had promised herself she would never wait again.

"You could come every week," he said, as if reading her. "Every day. I'd pay whatever—"

"That's not the point."

"Then what is?"

She looked at his palm again. The reaching line. The strange fate line. The future, written there in skin and time.

"You don't fall in love with the fortuneteller," she said. "It's rule one."

"Maybe I already have."

The bell above the door chimed. Neither of them had heard anyone enter. A woman stood in the doorway, looking lost, clutching a purse strap with both hands.

"Excuse me," the woman said. "Are you open? I need—I need to know if I should keep hoping."

Mira withdrew her hand from Daniel's. Slowly, she gathered the cards. Slowly, she arranged her face into the pleasant neutrality she had worn for decades.

"Yes," she said to the woman. "Come in. Sit."

The woman came forward, sat in the chair Daniel had vacated. He had stepped back, his hands in his pockets, watching Mira with those eyes that saw too much.

"Daniel," Mira said, without looking at him. "Same time next month?"

There was a pause. A long one.

"Yes," he said finally. "Same time."

He left money on the counter—more than the reading cost, as he always did—and left. The bell chimed twice. The woman across from her unfolded her hands and laid them on the cloth, palms up, begging for a glimpse.

Mira took a breath. She touched the woman's lifeline and began to speak of futures.

But in the center of her own chest, a line was being drawn. A new crease, deepening with each passing month, each returning Tuesday, each time he walked through her door and sat across from her and waited for her to tell him what she could not say:

That the cards had stopped lying to her years ago. That the only future she could see now was the one where he came back.

She read the woman's palm and did not look at the door.

Outside, snow had begun to fall.

# The Margins We Left Behind

The smell of old paper hit Eleanor like a benediction the moment she pushed open the door of Abernathy & Vale, the used bookshop wedged between a vintage record store and a florist on Hartwood Lane. It was the kind of place that existed in defiance of e-readers and algorithms—a warren of leaning shelves and forgotten volumes, where the floorboards groaned and dust motes drifted through slanted beams of afternoon light.

She had forty-five minutes before she needed to be anywhere, and forty-five minutes was exactly the right amount of time to disappear.

Eleanor ran her fingertips along the spines in the poetry section—Millay, Plath, Rilke, Dickinson—before her hand paused on a battered copy of *The Prophet* by Kahlil Gibran. She pulled it free, noting the price in pencil on the inside cover: three dollars. Someone had underlined a line in fading ink: *Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself.*

She carried it to the back of the shop, where a faded velvet armchair waited beneath a window. The chair had a tiny brass plaque she had read a hundred times: *In memory of Arthur Abernathy, 1942-2019, who believed a good book was its own destination.*

She had barely opened the first page when a man rounded the corner of the aisle and stopped short, a stack of hardcovers balanced against his chest.

"Oh," he said, blinking behind wire-rimmed glasses. "I didn't realize anyone was—"

"The chair's free," Eleanor said, though she didn't move.

"That's not—" He glanced toward the front of the store, then back at her. "I was looking for a book. For my mother. She likes mysteries, the kind with—" He made a vague gesture. "—cozy villages and murders that don't involve too much blood."

"There's a section in the back, past the atlases," Eleanor said. "Second shelf from the top."

He hesitated. "Thank you."

She nodded, and he disappeared.

---

Eleanor came back the next Saturday.

And the next.

It became a quiet ritual: the walk down Hartwood Lane, the bell chiming as she pushed the door open, the velvet chair, the Gibran she was reading in pieces, as if savoring it. She was halfway through when he appeared again, this time holding a paperback of *Rebecca* by Daphne du Maurier.

"You're back," he said.

"So are you."

He smiled, a small, careful thing. "I'm Theo."

"Eleanor."

"I know." He looked embarrassed. "There's a sign-up sheet by the register. For the loyalty program. I saw your name."

"Every time you check out?"

"I check out a lot." He lifted the du Maurier. "My mother reads them faster than I can find them. I'm running out of small English villages."

Eleanor laughed, surprising herself. "Have you tried the Yorkshire ones? *The Woman Who Went to Scotland*—that whole series."

"I didn't know there was a whole series."

"Oh, there is. Twelve books. No blood."

"I like the sound of that." He nodded toward the armchair. "Is that seat saved?"

"It is now."

He pulled up a stool from behind the poetry shelf and sat across from her, and they talked—about nothing, about everything—until the light outside the window turned amber and Theo checked his watch and swore softly.

"I have to go. My sister will worry."

Eleanor nodded. Theo paused, then reached into his bag and pulled out a slim paperback. He held it out.

"Here. I found this in the donation bin this morning. It's a little water-stained."

Eleanor took it. *The Summer Book* by Tove Jansson.

"You can borrow it," she said. "When I'm done."

"Okay." He smiled, that small, careful thing again. "See you next Saturday?"

"Maybe."

He left, and the bell chimed behind him, and Eleanor pressed her hand against the cover of the book and tried not to smile too hard.

---

The weeks folded into one another. They learned each other in increments, the way one learns a new city—slowly, by accident, through small repeated explorations.

Theo was an architect who drew buildings the way other people wrote journals. He had a cat named Brontë who liked to sleep on his drafting table. He had a sister with Down syndrome, Mara, whom he helped care for on weekends, which was why he always had to leave by five. He had once read *Crime and Punishment* in one sitting and felt sick for a week.

Eleanor was a freelance editor who worked from home and rarely left it. She had moved to Hartwood after a bad breakup and a worse year, and the bookshop had become her way of feeling human again. She was afraid of birds, a fact she had confessed only to her dentist, and now, she discovered, to Theo.

"You don't like birds?" he had asked.

"I'm *afraid* of them. There's a difference."

"Most birds are smaller than you."

"That's not the point."

"What *is* the point?"

"They're watching you. Always."

He had thought about this very seriously. "The penguins at the aquarium?"

"Terrifying."

He had laughed until his coffee almost came out his nose.

In return, she learned that he had a dimple on his left cheek that only appeared when he really meant a smile. That he twisted a paperclip between his fingers when he was thinking. That he smelled faintly of cedar and paper, which she tried very hard not to think about.

They did not, strictly speaking, date. They met, every Saturday, and then on some Wednesdays too, when Eleanor could not stand her apartment one more minute. They sat across from each other and read and talked and sometimes didn't talk, and once, when Theo was halfway through a description of a problem with a client's roofline, Eleanor realized she had stopped listening entirely and was simply watching the way his hands moved in the air.

It occurred to her, then, that she was in trouble.

---

"Why do you always read *The Prophet*?" Theo asked one Saturday in late October. Outside the window, the trees on Hartwood Lane had turned the color of fire, and Eleanor had brought two mugs of tea from the café next door, and they were sharing a scone.

"It's the one my mother used to read at bedtime," she said. "When I was small. Before she got sick."

Theo was quiet for a moment. "Is she—"

"She's gone. Five years."

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be. She read me this book until I was twelve. By the time I was thirteen, I had half of it memorized. *Then Almitra spoke again: Speak to us of Love.*"

She hadn't meant to say it. The words came out before she could catch them.

Theo set down his scone. "Read it to me?"

"What?"

"The line. Read it."

Eleanor swallowed. "It's not very—"

"Please."

She closed her eyes. She had not spoken it aloud in five years.

"*Then Almitra spoke again: Speak to us of Love.*"

She opened her eyes. Theo was watching her, the light from the window catching the edge of his glasses.

"She loved you very much," he said softly.

Eleanor laughed, but it came out wrong, cracked in the middle. "How do you know?"

"Because you still read it like she's listening."

---

It happened in November.

The shop was closing early—the owner, Mr. Vale, had a doctor's appointment—and Theo and Eleanor were the last ones inside. The light was thin and gray, and the radiators were ticking, and they had been talking about the architecture of memory, which had somehow turned into a conversation about their fathers, which had somehow turned into Eleanor admitting that she had not spoken to her own in eight years.

"I don't want to talk about it," she said quickly. "I just—I don't know why I said it."

"You don't have to know why."

"It's embarrassing. I'm a thirty-four-year-old woman who hasn't spoken to her father in almost a decade."

"That's not embarrassing. That's survival."

She looked at him. "What do you mean?"

"I mean—I think there are some people we have to stop speaking to in order to keep speaking at all." He paused. "I'm sorry. That sounded like a fortune cookie."

Eleanor laughed, wetly, and put her hands over her face. She was crying. She hadn't cried about it in years.

Theo hesitated, then reached across and gently took her wrists. "Hey. Hey."

She let him pull her hands down. He was closer than she had ever seen him, the lines of his face very clear, the gray in his eyes very blue.

"Can I show you something?" he asked.

She nodded, not trusting her voice.

He pulled a small, worn paperback from his bag. *Persuasion* by Jane Austen. He opened it to the inside cover. There, in pencil, in a slanting, girlish hand, was a name: *Margot Bellows, 1962.*

"My grandmother," he said. "She wrote her name in every book she owned. Hundreds of them. My mother kept them all in a box after she died. When I was little, I used to sit and look at her handwriting and try to imagine her as a girl."

Eleanor looked at the inscription. "She was nineteen."

"Nineteen." He closed the book carefully. "I think about her sometimes, when I'm reading. What she'd think of it. If she'd like the same parts I like." He paused. "I think she'd like you."

Eleanor's breath caught. "You do?"

"Yeah." He smiled, the small one, with the dimple. "I do."

---

Outside, the sky had gone the color of a bruise, and the streetlamps on Hartwood Lane were flickering on one by one.

They stood outside the bookshop, both pretending they were about to say goodbye. The bell chimed behind them as Mr. Vale locked the door.

"I had a good time," Eleanor said.

"Me too."

Pause.

"Theo—"

"Eleanor—"

They both stopped. They both laughed.

"You first," she said.

"No, you."

"I don't actually have anything. I just didn't want you to leave."

Theo looked at her for a long, quiet moment. Then he stepped forward, slowly, giving her time to pull away, and pressed his lips to her forehead—softly, the way one might kiss a child, or a prayer, or a page of a beloved book.

"I'm not going anywhere," he said.

---

They walked. They walked all the way to the end of Hartwood Lane, past the record store and the florist and the closed bakery, until they reached the small park by the river. There were no birds there, thank god, and they sat on a bench and watched the water go dark.

"I need to tell you something," Eleanor said.

"Okay."

"I've been in love with you since the third Saturday."

Theo turned his head. "The third Saturday?"

"You brought me the *Summer Book*."

"I remember."

"I went home and read the first paragraph and I thought, *Oh. There you are.*"

He was quiet for a moment. Then he reached into his coat pocket and pulled out a folded piece of paper. He handed it to her.

Eleanor unfolded it. It was a sketch—a small, careful drawing of a velvet armchair, and a window, and a woman reading. The woman had her hair tucked behind one ear and her legs curled beneath her.

She looked up.

"I drew that the first day I saw you," he said. "Before I knew your name. Before the loyalty card."

Eleanor pressed the paper against her chest.

"I love you too," he said. "In case that wasn't clear."

She kissed him. Not like a prayer this time, but like a person, clumsy and laughing, her hands in his coat, his hands in her hair, the river moving past them, indifferent and eternal.

---

Years later, when they had a flat above a print shop on a street that was not Hartwood Lane but close enough, Eleanor would sometimes take down her copy of *The Prophet* from the shelf and open it to the underlined line, and read it aloud to the small, quiet person they had made together, who liked the sound of words even before she understood them.

*"Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself."*

And Theo, in the doorway with two mugs of tea, would smile his small, careful, dimpled smile, and Eleanor would look up, and they would look at each other, and the world would be, for a moment, exactly the size of the room they were in.

# The Photo in the Wallet

The twenty-dollar bill was the first thing Marcus noticed when he bent to retrieve the wallet from where it had skidded into the curb. He almost left it—everyone had their own problems—but then he saw the driver's license tucked into the clear sleeve and felt the civic duty nag at him.

He waited at the corner of 5th and Maple, the agreed meeting spot. The address on the ID was local. He expected someone middle-aged, maybe a little harried, the kind of person who loses wallets while juggling coffee and car fobs.

He did not expect the photo.

Inside the laminate was a face that stopped his breath. Dark eyes, a serious mouth, a scattering of freckles across a nose that seemed made for laughing. The name read: ELI VASQUEZ. The address was an apartment three blocks from his own.

At 4:47, three minutes early, Marcus saw someone approaching. His heart did something embarrassing.

The man walking toward him was tall, broad-shouldered, with a neatly trimmed beard and kind eyes that crinkled at the corners. He wore a faded band t-shirt and jeans that had clearly seen better decades. He was maybe forty, definitely not the person in the photo.

"Hi," the man said, slightly out of breath. "You found my wallet? I'm so sorry—I must have dropped it getting out of the Uber. I’m Eli’s dad. Daniel. He asked me to come since he’s stuck at work."

Marcus's stomach dipped in a way he tried very hard not to examine.

"Oh," he managed. "Of course. Here you go."

He handed over the wallet, and Daniel took it with a grateful smile, thumbing through to make sure everything was there. "Cards, cash, all good. You didn't have to do this. Most people would've just kept it."

"I'd want someone to return mine," Marcus said, which was true, but not the whole truth. The whole truth was that he'd been hoping to see the face in the photo and was now standing in front of its apparent father, which felt like a comedy of errors he hadn't signed up for.

Daniel laughed, a warm rumble. "Let me give you something for your trouble—"

"No, really—"

"At least let me give you Eli's number. He'd want to thank you himself. He hates owing people."

Marcus wanted to say *that's unnecessary.* What he said was, "Sure. That'd be nice."

Daniel scrawled a number on the back of a receipt from his pocket and pressed it into Marcus's hand. Their fingers brushed. "He's a good kid," Daniel said, almost defensively, as though Marcus had asked. "Just got promoted. Busy. Good head on his shoulders."

"I'm sure he is," Marcus said.

Daniel nodded, gave one last grateful wave, and headed back down the street, and Marcus stood there holding a scrap of paper like it was a winning lottery ticket, which—depending on how things went—maybe it was.

---

He waited two days before texting. That felt reasonable. Not eager. Not desperate. Just polite.

*Hi, this is Marcus. I returned your wallet to your dad at 5th and Maple. Hope everything's still in it.*

The reply came eleven minutes later.

*Oh my god YES. Dad told me. I cannot believe someone actually returned it. I was so sure I'd have to cancel everything. Thank you so so much. Seriously. Can I buy you a coffee?*

Marcus, who had been staring at his phone from the couch for the better part of those eleven minutes, typed back immediately and then pretended he hadn't.

*Only if you're buying something stronger than coffee.*

*Ha. Deal. Saturday?*

*Saturday works.*

---

The coffee shop was one Marcus knew well—he'd been going there for years, which meant he'd never seen Eli Vasquez there, which seemed statistically impossible now that he was looking for him.

Eli arrived exactly on time, which Marcus had not expected from someone who lost wallets and got promoted and was apparently busy enough to send his father to retrieve his belongings. He was wearing a green button-down with the sleeves rolled to the elbows and he looked, in person, exactly like his photo except more—the freckles more present, the eyes more present, the slight nervous energy more visible in the way he shifted his weight from foot to foot while scanning the room.

Then he saw Marcus and his face did something complicated. Surprise, then a quick assessment, then a small, pleased smile.

"Marcus?"

"Eli."

He slid into the booth across from him. "Okay, so my dad said you were a nice guy, but he undersold it. He also said you were 'tall' but that feels like a weird thing to lead with." He grinned. "He liked you. He doesn't like anyone."

"I have that effect," Marcus said, and Eli laughed, and the laugh was better than the photo, better than anything, and Marcus thought, *Oh, this is going to be a problem.*

They ordered coffee. Then, somehow, two hours later, they ordered dinner.

---

Three weeks in, lying on Marcus's couch with the TV murmuring something they weren't watching, Eli turned his head and said, "So are you going to admit you kept the wallet because of my license photo, or do I have to keep pretending that's not what happened?"

Marcus groaned and covered his face with a pillow. "We agreed never to discuss this."

"We did not."

"We absolutely did. It was in the fine print. Second date."

"There was no fine print." Eli tugged the pillow away. His hair was a disaster and his eyes were bright and he looked ridiculous and perfect. "You saw the photo and you were curious. Admit it."

"I was *civically minded.*"

"You were *horny.*"

"I was—" Marcus started, and then gave up, because Eli was grinning at him with the full force of every freckle, and lying had never been his strong suit. "Fine. Yes. The photo was— look, it was a very good photo."

"It was a terrible photo. I had a cold."

"It was a *very good photo.*"

Eli kissed him, then, soft and slow, the kind of kiss that made Marcus forget what they were arguing about. When he pulled back, he said, "For the record, I would have come to meet you myself, but I had a deadline, and my dad has been desperate to live vicariously through me since I turned twenty-six, and I think you two would've hit it off."

"I like your dad."

"Everyone likes my dad. He's a problem that way." Eli settled back against his chest, and Marcus wrapped an arm around him and thought about how a wallet had skidded into a curb and rolled into his life.

"You should lose your wallet more often," he said.

"If I do, will you keep coming to find me?"

"Every time."

Eli smiled into his collarbone. "Deal."

# 59小时7分钟

## 一、空场

下午两点十七分，我站在时代广场的IMAX影院门口，手里攥着两张连座票，感觉自己像个傻瓜。

"要不打给他们？"小雯把奶茶吸得滋滋响，眼睛却在扫街。

我掏出手机，群里最后一条消息停留在昨晚十一点——阿杰发的"明天见"，后面跟了六个OK的手势。然后是今早九点整，群主林哥那条被撤回的、只剩下"抱歉兄弟，我——"的残骸。

"林哥说要带孩子去医院。"

"阿杰说他女朋友从深圳杀过来了。"

"小雨和男朋友去长滩岛了，昨晚在机场发的朋友圈你没看？"

我当然没看。我昨晚在剪辑视频，为了今天能准时出现在这里，把手机调成了勿扰模式。

我们订的是漫威全系列连映，从下午三点开始，一直放到后天凌晨两点十七分结束——59小时7分钟，一共二十三部电影。小雯提前三个月抢的票，还特意买了能量饮料、润喉糖、眼罩和颈枕，塞满了两个登山包。

现在，只剩我们两个人，扛着两个登山包，站在这个据说全国最大的IMAX银幕前，像两个误入漫展的外星人。

"退票吧。"小雯说。

"退不了，"我说，"买的时候写着不退不换。"

她看着我，我看着她。

"那……就看？"

"那就看。"

我们走进了几乎空无一人的影厅。三号厅，428个座位，工作人员给了我们中间偏后的最佳观影位，银幕大得能装下一整个宇宙。

灯暗下来的那一刻，我忽然有一种荒诞的预感：接下来的59小时7分钟，我们这两个被全世界放鸽子的人，要独自面对漫威宇宙的所有生离死别。

## 二、铁罐

《钢铁侠》的片头字幕滚过去的时候，小雯从包里掏出一包辣条，撕开，往我这边递。

"不吃。"

"你就当这是托尼·史塔克的应援物。"

我接过来，咬了一口。

我们看的是全新修复版，亮度比家里下载的资源好太多，托尼在山洞里敲出第一块方舟反应堆的电路板时，我能看见他手指上的油污和汗珠。

"你知道吗，"小雯压低声音，"我第一次看这个片子，是高三那年，在网吧包夜。"

"然后呢？"

"然后我英语考了39分，被我妈打了一顿。"

我差点把辣条喷出来。

电影演到托尼在记者会上说"I am Iron Man"的时候，小雯忽然不说话了。我侧头看她，发现她在擦眼睛。

"喂。"

"没事，"她吸了吸鼻子，"每次看到这儿我都哭。"

"你到底看哭过几次？"

"记不清了。反正我哭过的那些年，我的同学们都还跟我一起。"

我听懂了。她没说出口的那句话是——这一次，陪她看的人，缩成了我一个。

## 三、美队

凌晨四点，《美国队长：冬日战士》放到神盾局母舰从天上砸下来的那一幕，我终于彻底醒了。

小雯已经靠在座椅上睡着了，颈枕歪到一边，嘴巴微张。我轻轻帮她把颈枕扶正，她哼了一声，又睡过去了。

这个时间段的影院只剩我们两个人和两个工作人员。一个保洁阿姨在最后排打瞌睡，一个保安小哥站在门口刷抖音，外放的声音压得很低，是那种很古早的搞笑视频。

我看着银幕上史蒂夫·罗杰斯从河里被打捞上来，又想起很多年前，自己第一次看这个场景，是在大学宿舍的电脑前，室友们挤在一张床上，爆米花撒了一地。

那时候我们真的相信，英雄不会死，死去的只是肉体，灵魂会变成新的人，回到我们中间。

我什么时候开始不信的？

可能是工作的第二年，那个和我一起熬夜写代码的同事突发心梗走了。可能是第三次搬家，把所有的漫威手办扔进垃圾桶的时候。可能是上个月，群里约这次活动，最先说"一定到"的那个兄弟，最后一条消息停留在一个没头没尾的"我可能……"，然后再也没有出现过。

银幕上的史蒂夫在跳伞前对娜塔莎说了一句"在我跳之前，你还有别的指令吗"，娜塔莎没有回答。

我忽然很想知道，那个没说完"我可能"的人，他现在到底怎么了。

## 四、复联

第二天下午，《复仇者联盟3》开始的时候，小雯带来了一瓶红酒。

"哪来的？"

"在隔壁便利店买的，"她晃晃瓶子，"喝吗？"

"在电影院？"

"反正没人管我们。"

我们用瓶盖当酒杯，一人一口，轮着喝。红酒很涩，配上爆米花更涩，但谁在乎呢。

灭霸打完响指的那一幕，整个影厅忽然亮了一下——是银幕的反光，小雯手里的红酒洒了一些在裤子上，她浑然不觉，只是盯着银幕，眼泪啪嗒啪嗒地掉。

"你知道我最怕什么吗？"她轻声说。

"什么？"

"我最怕有一天打开手机，发现我想联系的人，全都不在了。"

我没说话，只是把纸巾递给她。她接过去，没擦眼泪，先擦了擦洒在裤子上的红酒。

"小雯。"

"嗯？"

"我也在。"

她看了我一眼，没明白。

"我说，就算全世界都放了我们鸽子，我也还在。"

她笑了一下，眼泪还挂在脸上。

"你这话说得跟托尼·史塔克似的。"

"我可不是亿万富翁。"

"但你是我的人。"

这句话太重了，我一时不知道该怎么接。

## 五、终局

第三天凌晨一点四十五分，距离结束还剩32分钟。

《复联4》的最后，托尼·史塔克打完了响指，躺在一片废墟里，彼得·帕克扑过去喊他。

小雯已经哭不出来了，只是呆坐着。

我也没哭，只是觉得胸腔里有什么东西堵着，很沉。

"我一直在想，"小雯说，"托尼那么有钱，那么聪明，为什么还会死？"

"因为编剧要他死。"

"不是，"她摇头，"是因为他本来就快死了。他胸口那个方舟反应堆一直在毒他，从第一部就开始了，他一直在倒计时。"

我愣了一下。

"所以，"她继续说，"他每一次穿上战甲，都是在和死神抢时间。每一次拯救世界，都是在透支自己的命。我们以为他在做英雄，其实他只是在做选择——在所有他想保护的人里，选一个他愿意为之赴死的。"

"你想说什么？"

"我想说，"她转过头看我，眼睛里映着银幕的光，"我们这群人，一直在假装自己还有很多时间。总觉得明天还能约，下周还能聚，下个月还能一起做点什么。一直到现在——直到我们被放鸽子，直到我们发现，承诺来的那些人，有一半其实根本不会来。"

她顿了顿。

"我其实很庆幸。"

"庆幸什么？"

"庆幸今天坐在这里的，是我和你。"

## 六、灯亮

凌晨两点十七分，《复联4》的最后一行字幕滚完，灯缓缓亮起。

工作人员走过来，说"两位，结束了"。

我们走出影厅，时代广场的夜风很冷，街上几乎没人。小雯走在前面，影子被路灯拉得很长。

"你饿不饿？"我问她。

"饿。"

"想吃什么？"

"热干面。"

"武汉？"

"嗯。我想我爸了。"

她爸去年走的，她当时没赶回去，是她妈打电话告诉她的。她说"你爸走得很安详，你别担心"，电话那头还传来她爸生前养的那只猫的叫声。

那之后她就再也没提过她爸。我们也不敢提。

"走，"我说，"我请你吃热干面。"

"这附近有吗？"

"导航说三公里外有一家。"

"那就走。"

我们走了三公里，到了那家店。老板是个武汉人，看见我们进来，眼睛亮了——"你们也是武汉的？"

"我是，她不是，"我说，"但她爱吃热干面。"

老板笑了，给我们下了两碗面，多加了酸豆角，还送了两杯豆浆。

小雯吃了一口，眼泪又掉下来了——这次我没问她为什么哭。

有些眼泪不需要原因。

## 七、回程

吃完面，我们在路边等网约车。凌晨三点半的城市，出租车很少，等了二十分钟才来一辆。

车里很安静，小雯靠在车窗上，看着外面的街灯一盏一盏地往后退。

"诶，"她忽然开口。

"嗯？"

"你说，我们以后还会不会这样？"

"这样什么？"

"这样——被全世界放鸽子，然后发现，最后陪在自己身边的人，其实只有那么几个。"

我想了想，说："可能会越来越多。"

"为什么？"

"因为大家都在长大，都在忙，都在变成自己不想变成的大人。"

"你呢？"

"我也一样。"

"那你会不会有一天，也不来？"

"不会。"

"为什么？"

"因为，"我说，"我答应过托尼·史塔克，要做你的钢铁侠。"

她愣了一下，然后笑了，笑得眼泪又掉下来了。

"你可真不要脸。"

"彼此彼此。"

车子驶过跨江大桥，江面上有雾气，远处的城市灯火像漫威宇宙里那些发光的星星，明灭不定。

我们都知道，明天醒来，我们会回到各自的格子间里，继续加班，继续应付客户，继续在群里发"下次一定"。我们可能会慢慢失去联系，可能很多年都不会再见面。

但至少今晚——

至少在过去的59小时7分钟里——

我们是彼此的超级英雄。

这就够了。

# A Prova da Alma Gêmea

## Capítulo 1: O Anúncio

O mundo parou numa terça-feira cinzenta de março.

A Dra. Helena Vasconcelos, neurocientista portuguesa do Instituto Karolinska de Estocolmo, ajustou os óculos sobre o nariz e pigarreou diante das câmaras. Atrás dela, num ecrã gigante, brilhava a palavra que iria mudar a humanidade para sempre: **ALMA GÉMEA**.

— Durante séculos — começou ela, com a voz trémula —, a humanidade acreditou que a ideia de almas gémeas era apenas poesia, romanticismo, superstição. Hoje, posso afirmar, com base em dez anos de investigação e em estudos com mais de vinte mil casais —, que **existe uma base neurológica e quântica para este fenómeno**.

A conferência de imprensa foi transmitida em directo para 192 países. O hashtag **#AlmaGémeaProvada** trending topic mundial em menos de quatro minutos.

No pequeno apartamento da Rua de Santa Catarina, no Porto, Inês Ferreira, trinta e dois anos, professora de primária, deixou cair a chávena de café. O líquido escorreu pela mesa enquanto ela fitava o ecrã do telemóvel com os olhos arregalados.

— Impossível — murmurou.

---

## Capítulo 2: A Teoria

Nas semanas que se seguiram, o artigo da Dra. Vasconcelos foi publicado na revista *Nature Neuroscience*. Intitulava-se **"Acoplamento Ressonante de Padrões Neurais em Pares Românticos: Uma Nova Perspectiva sobre a Alma Gémea"**.

A teoria, embora complexa, podia ser resumida assim:

Cada cérebro humano emite um padrão único de ondas electromagnéticas — uma espécie de "frequência de consciência". Segundo a investigação, certas pessoas emitem frequências que, ao encontrarem a frequência compatível, entram num estado de **ressonância harmónica**, produzindo efeitos mensuráveis: batimentos cardíacos sincronizados, dilatação pupilar mútua, e até, segundo os casos mais extremos, a capacidade de sentir a dor física do outro.

A Dra. Vasconcelos introduziu um novo conceito: o **Índice de Compatibilidade Ressonante (ICR)**. Um número de 0 a 100 que mediava a probabilidade de duas pessoas serem almas gémeas.

— Não estamos a dizer — aclarou ela numa entrevista — que todos temos uma alma gémea. Muitos casais maravilhosos têm ICRs de 60, 70. Estamos a dizer que, em casos raros — talvez 3% da população —, existe um encaixe quase perfeito. Uma assinatura cósmica, se quisermos usar linguagem menos científica.

A humanidade dividiu-se em dois campos: os que quiseram fazer o teste imediatamente, e os que acharam tudo uma fraude colossal.

---

## Capítulo 3: Inês

Inês pertencia ao segundo campo.

Filha de uma mãe que acreditara piamente em horóscopos e que casara com o pai por "sentir uma energia especial", e que acabara num divórcio amargo aos catorze anos de casado, Inês crescera com uma desconfiança visceral de tudo o que cheirasse a destino. Tinha vinte e sete anos quando terminou a primeira relação séria. Trinta quando terminou a segunda. Trinta e dois quando jurou a si mesma que nunca mais sofreria por amor.

Era uma mulher bonita, de um modo quieto e resistente. Cabelo castanho-escuro quase sempre preso num rabo-de-cavalo, olhos verdes que pareciam guardar uma piada que ninguém tinha contado, e uma predilecção por livros usados e por caminhadas ao domingo na Foz.

Tinha uma aluna especial na sua turma do segundo ano: uma menina chamada Beatriz, sete anos, que desenhava princesas a combater dragões e que escrevia cartas ao "menino invisível" que vivia, segundo ela, dentro do armário da sala.

— Professora — disse Beatriz numa sexta-feira, muito séria —, o menino diz que a senhora vai chorar hoje.

Inês riu-se.

— Ele está enganado, Beatriz.

Não estava enganado.

Quando Inês chegou a casa nessa noite, encontrou um envelope no chão do corredor. Tinha sido empurrado por baixo da porta. O seu nome estava escrito numa caligrafia antiquada, quase gótica. Dentro, uma única folha de papel:

*"Há uma porta que ainda não abriste. Procura a biblioteca dos Lóios, na segunda-feira, às 15h. Vem sozinha. Traz luvas."*

Inês releu o bilhete três vezes. Depois quatro. Pôs o café a ferver, sentou-se à mesa, e decidiu que ignoraria tudo.

Na segunda-feira, às 14h55, estava à porta da biblioteca.

---

## Capítulo 4: A Biblioteca dos Lóios

Era um edifício esquecido, encostado à Igreja dos Lóios, no coração do Porto. Tinha sido uma livraria antiquária no século XIX, depois um arquivo municipal, e agora estava praticamente abandonada, embora ainda figurasse nos mapas como "biblioteca pública em reestruturação".

Inês empurrou a porta de carvalho. Rangia como se estivesse a despertar.

O interior cheirava a pó e a tempo. Estantes de madeira escura subiam até ao tecto. No centro da sala, havia uma única mesa com uma cadeira de cada lado. Numa das cadeiras, estava sentado um homem.

Tinha talvez trinta e cinco anos. Cabelo grisalho nas têmporas, barba aparada, óculos redondos. Vestia um fato escuro, simples, e tinha à sua frente um livro aberto e um relógio de bolso que parecia ter parado há décadas.

— Inês Ferreira — disse ele, sem se levantar. Não era uma pergunta.

— Quem é o senhor?

— O meu nome é Tomás Aragão. Sou o último bibliotecário desta casa. E sou o guardião de um segredo que os seus colegas cientistas não descobriram, porque ainda não tinham procurado no sítio certo.

Inês cruzou os braços.

— Ouvi a conferência da Dra. Vasconcelos — disse ela. — Sou uma de muitas pessoas que acha tudo isso ridículo.

Tomás sorriu.

— Não é ridículo. É incompleto. A Dra. Vasconcelos descobriu o **como**. Falta-lhe o **porquê**. E o porquê está guardado nesta biblioteca há duzentos e cinquenta anos.

Ele apontou para o livro aberto diante de si.

— Aproxime-se, Inês. Trouxe as luvas, como o bilhete pedia?

Ela tinha trazido. Tinha ido buscá-las ao fundo de uma gaveta, sem saber bem porquê.

— Trouxe.

— Óptimo. Então venha ver o que nenhuma máquina alguma vez digitalizou.

---

## Capítulo 5: O Manuscrito

O livro era um manuscrito encadernado em couro verde, sem título na capa, sem data, sem autor. As páginas estavam escritas à mão, em latim e português arcaico, com ilustrações que pareciam diagramas neurais — embora fossem anteriores ao nascimento da neurociência.

— Este manuscrito — disse Tomás, com o cuidado de quem manuseia relíquias —, é chamado **Codex Animarum**. Foi escrito por um frei beneditino português em 1764, frei Mateus da Ascensão. Era neuroanatomista antes de a palavra existir. Disseccionava cérebros de criminosos executados e acreditava ter descoberto uma estrutura invisível a olho nu, mas visível em certas condições de luz e de espírito. Chamava-lhe **o nó da alma**.

Inês arregalou os olhos.

— Isso é anatomicamente possível?

— Tudo é anatomicamente possível até alguém o descobrir oficialmente. Frei Mateus acreditava que este nó, quando activado por experiências-limite — quase-morte, êxtase místico, parto, amor correspondido —, libertava uma espécie de projecção de si mesmo. Algo que hoje chamaríamos um campo. E que duas pessoas cujos campos fossem compatíveis poderiam, em condições raras, encontrar-se.

— E encontrou provas disso?

Tomás virou uma página. Mostrava um desenho: duas silhuetas humanas, uma de cada lado de uma folha. Entre elas, uma teia de linhas finas, como raízes entrelaçadas. No centro, um pequeno ponto luminoso.

— Frei Mateus — continuou Tomás —, deixou uma lista. Os nomes das pessoas que, na sua época, tinham ICRs superiores a 95. Algumas, segundo ele, tinham-no encontrado. Outras, tinham morrido sem nunca o encontrar.

— E agora?

— Agora — disse Tomás, e a sua voz tremeu pela primeira vez —, há uma nova lista. Eu mantive-a durante vinte anos. Pessoas que apareceram aqui, vindas de todo o mundo, atraídas por motivos que não sabiam explicar. Todas com a mesma assinatura neural que a Dra. Vasconcelos descreveu. E o nome dela — apontou para um ponto do livro — está nela há dezassete anos, Inês. Eu esperei. Disse a mim mesmo que estava enganado. Que era coincidência.

Inês sentiu o chão fugir-lhe debaixo dos pés.

— Como sabe o meu nome?

— Frei Mateus deixou instruções muito específicas sobre como encontrar almas gémeas. E uma delas — olhou para ela com uma intensidade nova — é que, quando duas estão perto uma da outra, **a biblioteca chama-as**. Eu apenas ouvi o chamamento.

O relógio de bolso dele começou, inexplicavelmente, a funcionar.

---

## Capítulo 6: O Outro Lado da Mesa

— Onde está ele? — perguntou Inês, com um fio de voz.

Tomás indicou a cadeira vazia diante de si.

— Não sei ainda. O manuscrito diz que a alma gémea aparece no momento exacto em que a primeira está pronta. Mas há um problema.

— Que problema?

— Frei Mateus errou numa coisa. Ou talvez estivesse certo, e nós é que ainda não percebemos. As almas gémeas não se encontram por acaso. **Escolhem**. E essa escolha tem um custo. Uma delas — a que chega primeiro à biblioteca —, tem de atravessar uma porta interior. Tem de abandonar uma versão de si mesma. Tem de deixar de ser quem era.

Inês sentou-se, porque as pernas já não a aguentavam.

— Que tipo de porta?

— Daquelas que não têm maçaneta, mas que abrem quando se está pronto a perder tudo o que se conhece.

A biblioteca ficou em silêncio. As estantes pareciam respirar.

— E se eu não estiver pronta?

— Então o relógio parará outra vez — disse Tomás. — e nenhum de nós virá a saber o que poderia ter sido.

Inés fechou os olhos. Pensou em Beatriz, no "menino invisível" do armário. Pensou na mãe, que ainda esperava um sinal do marido que a tinha abandonado. Pensou em si mesma, aos vinte e sete anos, a chorar na casa de banho de um restaurante enquanto o primeiro namorado lhe dizia que precisava de "espaço".

— Há outra coisa — disse Tomás, muito baixinho. — Frei Mateus escreveu que, na hora do encontro, a alma gémea que chega primeiro tem de dizer o seu nome completo. E a outra responde. Se houver silêncio — ou se houver mentira —, o encontro falha. E nunca mais há segunda tentativa.

Inês abriu os olhos.

— Estou a perceber que isto tudo é uma loucura — disse ela, com uma calma que surpreendeu até a si mesma. — Estou a perceber que provavelmente vou sair daqui, ir ao médico, dizer que ando a ter alucinações, e levar medicação. Mas eu já vivi trinta e dois anos a fingir que o amor era uma coisa razoável. Que se escolhia com listas de prós e contras. E isso nunca funcionou. — respirou fundo. — Estou pronta.

A porta da biblioteca rangeu.

Alguém entrou.

---

## Capítulo 7: Tiago

Era um homem alto, de ombros largos mas gestos contidos. Tinha o rosto de quem ri com facilidade mas que ultimamente tem rido pouco. Olheiras fundas, como se não dormisse há dias. Vestia calças de ganga e uma camisa branca que parecia ter sido vestida às pressas.

Parou a três metros da mesa. Olhou para Inês. Olhou para Tomás. E depois, lentamente, sentou-se na cadeira vazia.

— Demorei — disse ele, com um sotaque de Lisboa. — Estava em Madrid. Tinha um voo às seis da manhã, mas o táxi não apareceu, e depois pensei que era loucura, e depois pensei outra vez, e depois percebi que o que me tinha puxado para o aeroporto não era a cabeça.

— Como se chama? — perguntou Tomás, com a formalidade de um ritual.

— Tiago Salgueiro Mendes de Almeida. Engenheiro civil. Trinta e seis anos. E vim porque ouvi uma voz dentro de mim que disse "vai ao Porto, à biblioteca dos Lóios, segunda-feira às três". E eu nem sabia que havia uma biblioteca dos Lóios.

Inês olhava para ele. O coração dela batia de um modo estranho — não depressa, mas em ondas, como o mar a entrar numa gruta. Sentia a respiração dele como se fosse a sua. E havia uma coisa nas mãos dele, pousadas sobre a mesa, que pareciam exactamente do tamanho das suas.

— O seu nome completo? — perguntou Tiago, voltando-se para ela.

Inês engoliu em seco.

— Inês Maria de Lourdes Ferreira Pinto. Professora. Trinta e dois anos. E não sei porque é que vim — disse ela, e a voz dela tremeu —, mas agora sei que tinha de vir.

O relógio de bolso de Tomás acelerou.

— Está feito — disse o bibliotecário, e lágrimas lhe escorriam pelo rosto sem que ele fizesse nada para as esconder. — Em vinte anos, é a primeira vez que vejo o encontro completo.

Tiago estendeu a mão direita, com a palma virada para cima, no centro exacto da mesa. Inés pôs a mão esquerda sobre a dele. Não se tocaram. Ficaram a um milímetro de distância. E nesse milímetro, naquele instante suspenso em que o ar pareceu cristalizar, Inês sentiu — não viu, **sentiu** — uma faísca. Não metafórica. Uma faísca real, com cheiro a ozono, que saltou da mão dele para a dela e que lhes percorreu o corpo inteiro como uma corrente eléctrica suave.

As luzes da biblioteca tremeram.

Beatriz, no seu quarto em Matosinhos, a oitocentos metros dali, acordou do seu sono de sete anos e disse à mãe, sonolenta:

— Mãe, o menino do armário disse que a professora já não vai estar triste.

---

## Capítulo 8: O Que Vem Depois

Na semana seguinte, a Dra. Helena Vasconcelos recebeu um relatório anónimo. Tinha apenas uma linha:

*"A assinatura neural é real. Mas é só o envelope. O conteúdo é mais antigo do que nós."*

Ela releu o relatório várias vezes. Na margem, escreveu a lápis: *"Codex Animarum? Biblioteca dos Lóios?"*

Depois guardou o relatório numa gaveta e foi fazer café.

Nessa noite, Inês e Tiago jantaram juntos num restaurante da Ribeira. Ela falou-lhe do medo que tinha do amor. Ele falou-lhe do medo que tinha de partir. Falaram de Lisboa e do Porto, de tios excêntricos e de verões em Tavira. Falaram de tudo menos do instante na biblioteca.

Quando se despediram à porta do restaurante, Inês disse:

— Posso ver-te amanhã?

Tiago sorriu pela primeira vez naquela noite.

— Podes. Eu vou estar onde precisares de mim.

---

## Capítulo 9: Epílogo — Um Ano Depois

No dia do casamento deles, na Igreja dos Lóios — não por acaso, embora tenham mentido a todos sobre o motivo —, o padre que celebrou a cerimónia ficou estranhamente comovido. Depois disse à sacristã:

— Sabe, padre Lopes, nunca vi dois noivos tão calmos. Parecia que já se conheciam há séculos.

Na primeira fila, Beatriz, agora com oito anos e um laço azul no cabelo, sussurrou à mãe:

— Mãe, a professora encontrou o menino do armário.

A mãe riu-se.

— Que menino, Beatriz?

— O que vivia escondido. Agora está cá fora.

E pareceu à mãe, por um instante, que uma sombra suave do lado esquerdo da Beatriz se movia. Mas foi só um instante. Depois desapareceu.

Na biblioteca dos Lóios, fechada ao público, o relógio de bolso de Tomás Aragão continuava a funcionar. Já não parava desde aquele dia de março. E no livro verde, à página 247, em caligrafia minúscula, frei Mateus da Ascensão tinha deixado uma nota que só agora fazia sentido:

*"Quando duas almas gémeas se encontram, a biblioteca não fecha. Apenas muda de guardião. E começa a esperar as seguintes."*

Die schweren Holztüren schließen sich mit einem leisen Klicken hinter uns, und der vertraute Geruch von Lavendel und altem Leder steigt mir in die Nase. Dr. Hellgrubs Praxis. Wie immer.

Nora bleibt abrupt stehen. Ihr Blick wandert zur bronzenen Türklinke, dann zu mir.

„Couples' therapy — what a nice way to spend your anniversary“, sagt sie.

Ich atme aus. Schwer.

„Du hast den Termin gemacht“, erinnere ich sie leise.

„Ich weiß.“ Sie streicht sich eine Haarsträhne hinters Ohr, die längst perfekt liegt. Eine Geste, die ich kenne. Dreizehn Jahre. Und ausgerechnet am dreizehnten Hochzeitstag sitzen wir in einem Wartezimmer, das nach den Tränen anderer Leute riecht.

„Ich will es“, sage ich. Meine Stimme klingt rauer, als ich beabsichtige. „Aber ich will auch ehrlich sein. Ich habe Angst, Nora. Angst, dass sie etwas sagt, was ich nicht hören will. Angst, dass du ihr recht gibst. Angst, dass ich…“

Ich breche ab. Sie legt ihre Hand auf meine. Kühl. Wie immer.

„Dass du was?“, fragt sie sanft.

„Dass ich gar nicht mehr weiß, wie ich dich erreichen soll. Dass ich es verlernt habe. Oder nie gelernt habe. Ich weiß es nicht.“ Ich schlucke. „Und das nach dreizehn Jahren. Was sagt das über mich?“

Sie antwortet nicht sofort. Ihre Augen wandern zum Fenster, hinaus in den Regen, der seit dem Nachmittag gegen die Scheiben peitscht. Ein Tropfen sucht seinen Weg die Scheibe hinunter, zögert, beschleunigt.

„Es sagt, dass du ehrlich bist“, sagt sie schließlich. „Es sagt, dass dir das hier nicht egal ist.“ Eine Pause. „Und das ist mehr, als ich letzte Woche gedacht habe. Nach dem Abend mit deiner Mutter. Nach dem, was sie gesagt hat, über — “

„Nora. Bitte. Nicht jetzt. Nicht —“

„Doch, jetzt.“ Sie dreht sich zu mir, und ihre Augen funkeln. Nicht wütend. Entschlossen. „Wenn wir das hier machen, dann richtig. Dann fangen wir genau hier an. Genau mit dem, was uns kaputtmacht.“ Ihre Stimme zittert leicht. „Denn wenn wir das nicht tun, dann sitzen wir nächstes Jahr wieder hier. Oder wir sitzen gar nicht mehr zusammen. Und dann war es das. Mit allem, was wir hatten. Mit allem, was wir *sein* könnten, wenn wir nur —“

Sie bricht ab. Presst die Lippen zusammen. Eine Träne löst sich, läuft über ihre Wange. Sie wischt sie weg, fast wütend.

„Entschuldige“, flüstert sie.

„Nein.“ Ich nehme ihre Hand fester. „Nein, du entschuldigst dich nicht. Nicht dafür. Nie dafür.“ Ich stocke. „Nora, hör zu. Ich habe letzte Nacht nicht geschlafen. Ich habe an die Hochzeit gedacht. Daran, wie du aussahst, als du auf mich zugelaufen bist. Dieser kleine nervöse Schritt, bevor du losgelaufen bist. Als wüsstest du nicht, ob ich wirklich stehen bleibe.“ Ich lächle schwach. „Ich wusste nicht, ob ich stehen bleiben würde. Das war ich nicht. Das war ich nicht wert. Aber ich bin stehen geblieben. Und das ist das Einzige, was ich richtig gemacht habe in meinem ganzen Leben. Und ich will nicht, dass das umsonst war. Ich will nicht, dass *wir* umsonst waren.“

Sie lächelt uns an — dieses warme, leicht schief geratene Lächeln, das mich jedes Mal daran erinnert, dass sie wahrscheinlich schon alles gesehen hat. Alles, was zwei Menschen sich antun können.

„Kommen Sie rein“, sagt sie nur.

Nora sieht mich an. Ich sehe sie an. Dreizehn Jahre in einem Blick. Unser Hochzeitstag. Regen. Lavendel.

Sie steht auf. Ich stehe auf. Unsere Finger verschränken sich — nicht perfekt, ein bisschen zu fest, ein bisschen zu feucht — aber sie halten einander.

„Zusammen?“, frage ich.

„Zusammen“, sagt sie.

# Der Schuss des Amor

Die Wiese lag im Zwielicht der Abenddämmerung, getränkt von jenem seltsamen Gold, das nur der Übergang zwischen Tag und Nacht hervorbringen kann. Mücken tanzten über dem hohen Gras, und irgendwo in der Ferne sang eine Amsel ihr letztes Lied.

Niemand hätte an diesem Ort einen Gott vermutet. Und doch stand er dort, mit nackten Füßen auf der feuchten Erde, den schlanken Bogen aus dunklem Holz lässig über die Schulter gelegt. Ein Knabe, der aussah wie sechzehn, mit Locken, die ihm ins Gesicht fielen, und Augen, die älter waren als die Berge hinter ihm.

Amor. Cupido. Der Schütze der Herzen.

Er musterte mich mit einem Ausdruck, der zwischen Amüsiertheit und leichter Verachtung schwankte – als wäre ich ein lästiges Insekt, das sich in seine Sphäre verirrt hatte.

„Du hast gerufen“, sagte er, und seine Stimme klang wie Wind, der über eine Wasserfläche streicht. „Oder besser: Du hast gewünscht. Sehr stark gewünscht. So stark, dass ich es hörte, obwohl ich eigentlich beschäftigt war. Sehr beschäftigt. Ich war gerade dabei, eine Königin in einen Schäfer zu verlieben, was, kann ich Dir sagen, eine *höchst* undankbare Aufgabe ist, wenn man bedenkt –“

„Bitte“, unterbrach ich ihn. Meine Stimme zitterte.

Er verdrehte die Augen. Götter haben keine Geduld für Sterbliche, die nicht auf den Punkt kommen.

„Also gut. Du liebst jemanden. Du möchtest, dass diese Person Dich liebt. Standard. Routine. Ich könnte das im Schlaf, und das tue ich buchstäblich auch. Ein Schuss, ein Treffer, fertig. Die Geschichte ist so alt wie –“

„Es gibt eine Bedingung“, presste ich hervor.

Amor hob eine Augenbraue. Es war eine kleine, aber bedeutsame Bewegung – die Bewegung eines Wesens, das unsterblich war und daher vergesslich, aber niemals überrascht.

„Ich höre“, sagte er.

Ich schluckte. „Die Person, die ich liebe, hat mich bereits gern. Nicht… nicht so. Nicht auf diese Art. Aber sie mag mich. Es ist… es ist ein Anfang. Eine Wärme, wenn sie mich ansieht. Ein Lächeln, das nur mir gilt. Manchmal, wenn wir uns verabschieden, zögert sie, als wollte sie noch etwas sagen, und dann lacht sie über sich selbst und geht doch. Ich weiß nicht, was es ist. Aber es ist *etwas*. Und ich möchte nicht, dass dieses Etwas verschwindet, nur weil –“

„Weil ich meinen Pfeil abschieße“, vollendete Amor trocken. Er hatte innegehalten. Die Mücken tanzten weiter, aber die Luft schien dichter geworden zu sein. „Du verstehst nicht, wie das funktioniert, Sterblicher. Du verstehst es nie. Ihr seid so damit beschäftigt, *zu wollen*, dass Ihr nie fragt, *was* Ihr wollt. Oder *warum*."

Er trat einen Schritt näher. Seine Augen waren nicht braun, wie ich zuerst gedacht hatte, sondern von einem unbestimmbaren Farbton, der zwischen Gold und Grün und etwas Dunklerem schwankte.

„Mein Pfeil macht nicht ‚Liebe‘. Er macht *Leidenschaft*. Verlangen. Dieses brennende, alles verzehrende Gefühl, das Euch nachts wach hält und Euch morgens wie betrunken aufstehen lässt. Die große, zerstörerische, göttliche Liebe. Kennst Du das Gedicht von dem Mann, der sich vor seinen Wagen wirft? Kennst Du die Frau, die ihr Königreich verrät? Das bin ich. Das ist mein Werk."

„Aber die andere Zuneigung – die kleine, warme, alltägliche –“

„Die gehört nicht mir“, sagte Amor. „Die gehört den Menschen. Sie wächst langsam, wie Moos auf einem Stein. Sie ist…“, er suchte nach einem Wort, und zum ersten Mal sah ich Unsicherheit in seinem göttlichen Gesicht, „…sie ist vielleicht das Ehrlichere, was Ihr hervorbringt. Ich bin nur der Blitz. Sie ist das Feuer, das danach bleibt."

Ein Schweigen trat zwischen uns, schwer wie Blei.

„Was passiert“, fragte ich langsam, „wenn ich ablehne?"

Amor lächelte. Es war kein freundliches Lächeln.

„Dann passiert nichts. Deine Angebetete wird Dich weiterhin mögen – auf ihre kleine, warme Art. Ihr werdet Freunde sein. Vielleicht mehr, eines Tages, auf jene Weise, die keine Götter braucht. Vielleicht auch nicht. Du wirst weiterträumen, und die Träume werden Dir genügen müssen, denn die Wirklichkeit wird immer ein wenig blasser sein als das, was ich hätte schenken können. Das ist der Preis der Vorsicht."

Er spannte den Bogen. Ohne hinzusehen, zog er einen Pfeil aus dem Köcher an seiner Hüfte. Die Spitze glänzte im schwindenden Licht – nicht golden, wie ich erwartet hatte, sondern von jenem unbestimmbaren Schimmer, den seine Augen hatten.

„Aber wenn ich schieße", fuhr er fort, „dann wird diese kleine Zuneigung vergehen. Wie Tau vor der Sonne. Was bleibt, ist… *mehr*. So viel mehr, dass Du es Dir jetzt nicht vorstellen kannst. So viel mehr, dass es manchmal wehtut. Die große Liebe ist kein Geschenk, Sterblicher. Sie ist ein Sturm. Du kannst danach nicht mehr derselbe sein."

Er hielt mir den Bogen hin.

„Nein", sagte ich. „Ich meine – das ist nicht – Du sollst ihn mir geben. Ich soll schießen?"

Amor lachte. Es war ein kurzes, spöttisches Geräusch, wie das Brechen eines dünnen Zweigs.

„Du willst, dass *ich* schieße. Auf wen? Du hast mir keinen Namen gesagt. Du hast mir nicht einmal ein Gesicht gezeigt. Du hast nur von ‚dieser Person‘ gesprochen, als wäre sie ein Konzept und kein Mensch."

Ich öffnete den Mund. Schloss ihn wieder.

Er hatte recht. Ich hatte kein Gesicht genannt. Keinen Namen. In meinem Kopf gab es ein Bild – Haare im Wind, eine bestimmte Art, den Kopf zu neigen, ein Lachen, das klang wie – aber nichts Konkretes. Nur das Gefühl, nur die Sehnsucht.

„Das", sagte Amor sanfter, und zum ersten Mal klang er nicht spöttisch, sondern traurig, „ist es, was ich meine. Du liebst eine Vorstellung. Eine Projektion. Ein Bild, das Du Dir gemacht hast, weil das wirkliche Bild zu kompliziert ist, zu widersprüchlich, zu *menschlich*. Wenn ich schieße, dann wirst Du das Bild lieben – mit der ganzen Gewalt, die mein Pfeil entfesselt. Aber das Bild wird antworten. Und dann wirst Du erkennen, dass es nicht zurückliebt. Nicht so. Nicht in der Form, die Du Dir erträumt hast. Und dann wirst Du zerbrechen. Oder sie wird zerbrechen. Oder beide."

Er ließ den Bogen sinken.

„Geh nach Hause, Sterblicher. Trink einen Tee. Schlaf darüber. Und morgen – morgen schau dieses Wesen an, das Du zu lieben glaubst, und frage Dich, ob Du es kennst. Wirklich kennst. Nicht die Version, die Du in Deinen Träumen erschaffen hast, sondern die, die morgens müde ist und vergisst, die Zähne zu putzen, und bei Regen schlechte Laune hat und manchmal Dinge sagt, die sie nicht meint."

Er wandte sich ab. Bereits zu gehen.

„Warte", rief ich.

Er hielt inne. Drehte sich nicht um.

„Was, wenn ich es trotzdem will? Trotz allem? Den Sturm. Die Zerstörung. Das Brennen."

Ein langes Schweigen. Die Amsel war verstummt. Irgendwo ging der Mond auf, blass und gleichgültig.

„Dann nenne mir einen Namen", sagte Amor leise. „Einen wirklichen Namen. Den Namen der Person, wie sie auf ihrer Geburtsurkunde steht. Nicht ‚meine Angebetete‘, nicht ‚die, die ich liebe‘. Sondern *sie*. Mit ihrer ganzen Häßlichkeit und Widersprüchlichkeit. Und dann sag mir: Kennst Du sie? Bist Du bereit, sie zu lieben, auch wenn sie Dich nicht so liebt, wie Du es Dir wünschst? Auch wenn sie Dich eines Tages verlässt? Auch wenn der Sturm, den mein Pfeil entfacht, sie verbrennt statt Dich?"

Ich öffnete den Mund.

Und erkannte, dass ich ihren Namen nicht kannte. Nicht wirklich. Ich kannte die Form ihrer Lippen, den Klang ihres Lachens, die Art, wie sie die Stirn runzelte, wenn sie nachdachte – aber nicht ihren Namen. Nicht ihre Geschichte. Nicht das, was sie ängstigte. Nicht das, was sie hoffte, wenn sie nachts wach lag.

Amor ging. Seine Schritte hinterließen keine Spuren im taufeuchten Gras.

Der Bogen lag noch da, wo er gestanden hatte. Ich starrte ihn an, lange. Dann bückte ich mich und hob ihn auf. Er war warm, wie lebendige Haut. Der Pfeil im Köcher vibrierte leise, als wartete er.

Ich schulterte den Bogen und ging nach Hause.

Am nächsten Morgen wachte ich auf und wusste: Ich würde sie fragen. Ihren richtigen Namen. Ihren Kindheitsnamen. Ihre größte Angst. Ihren geheimsten Wunsch. Alles, was sie nicht auf der Straße zeigte, alles, was unter der Oberfläche schlummerte.

Ich würde sie kennenlernen.

Und dann – vielleicht – würde ich entscheiden, ob ich den Schuss wagen wollte.

Vielleicht würde ich den Bogen behalten, für Jahre. Vielleicht für immer. Vielleicht würde ich eines Tages zurückkommen auf diese Wiese, in diesem Zwielicht, und rufen: *Amor! Ich bin bereit!*

Oder vielleicht – und das war der Gedanke, der mich am meisten ängstigte und am meisten tröstete zugleich – vielleicht würde ich feststellen, dass ich den Bogen gar nicht brauchte.

Dass die kleine, warme Zuneigung, die sie bereits für mich empfand – das Lächeln, das nur mir galt, das Zögern beim Abschied – dass *das* genug war.

Dass die größte Liebe keine Göttin braucht.

Dass die größte Liebe ein Moos ist, das langsam wächst.

Dass die größte Liebe ein Name ist, den man wirklich kennt.

Ich stellte den Bogen in die Ecke meines Zimmers, wo er im Morgenlicht schimmerte wie etwas aus einem Traum, der zu Ende geht.

Und ging hinaus, um sie zu treffen.

Richtig zu treten.

Zum ersten Mal.

# The Last Clockmaker of Avenport

The clocktower of Avenport had not chimed in eighty-three years.

This was a problem, because it was New Year's Eve, and Mayor Hollis had been promising the townsfolk a restored tower for nearly a decade. Now, with midnight thirty minutes away, he stood in the cobwebbed belly of the great clock, wringing his hands at the man crouched before the frozen gears.

"Can you do it or not, Mr. Calloway?"

Eli Calloway, last in a line of clockmakers stretching back to the town's founding, did not look up. His fingers, stained with oil and decades of solitary work, traced the hairline fracture in the mainspring.

"I can," he said. "But you won't like the cost."

Hollis sputtered. "I've already paid you—"

"Not with coin." Eli finally lifted his gaze. His eyes were the pale blue of winter dawn, and he was younger than Hollis expected—mid-thirties at most, though something in his face suggested a much longer exhaustion. "The tower stopped for a reason, Mayor. My grandfather stopped it on purpose, the year my grandmother died. He said some clocks shouldn't keep measuring time when the people we love fall out of it."

"That's superstition—"

"That's truth." Eli rose to his feet, and the lamplight caught the silver threading his temples. "I've spent fifteen years studying the mechanism. The gears aren't broken. They're *waiting*. The whole tower is wound around a promise my grandfather made, and I would need to break it to make the bells ring tonight."

The mayor's face reddened. "I don't care about your family promises. There are ten thousand people in the square expecting—"

"Eleven thousand," Eli said quietly. "I counted the lanterns."

Down below, through the open window, the gathered crowd hummed with cold and champagne. Eli could see the banners stretched across the square, the brass band tuning their instruments, the enormous paper numerals waiting to drop at midnight. And he could see, at the edge of the crowd near the chestnut vendor, a woman in a green coat, her dark hair tucked behind her ears.

Mira. Who had loved him once. Who had stopped writing when he stopped coming down from the tower.

"It will only chime once," Hollis said. "That's the legend, isn't it? One strike, and the year turns. Surely that's not too high a price—"

"You don't know what it costs because you don't know what it *gives*." Eli's voice sharpened. "If I wind it, the tower will ring, and the year will turn, and I will lose—"

He stopped.

*Lose the only hour I have left with her.*

That was the secret of the Calloway clocks. They didn't just measure time. They kept it. Eli had lived in the tower for fifteen years, never aging past his real years, because the broken mechanism had trapped him in a single long minute—the moment before his grandmother died, when his grandfather had wound the clock for her final time. Every day, he lived that same minute a thousand times over. He had grown used to the loneliness. He had grown used to the silence.

But once, seven years ago, Mira had climbed the tower stairs with a basket of bread and a frown on her lovely face, demanding to know why Eli had vanished on her.

He had told her about the clocks. About the frozen moment. About his grandfather's bargain—that if the tower ever chimed again, the trapped minute would release, and whoever lived inside it would have to live, truly live, whatever remained of their life.

She had kissed him then, in the dusty heart of the tower, with the silent bells above them. She had kissed him, and said, *Then we have all the time in the world.*

She had not understood. Not really. Because she could leave the tower and grow older, while he stayed the same. And one day, she would be old, and he would still be thirty-five, and the frozen minute would feel less like a gift and more like a theft.

She stopped coming two years later.

Eli watched her now, in her green coat, buying chestnuts from a vendor who did not know her name. She was thirty-eight. There were lines at the corners of her eyes he had not put there. She was beautiful in a way that ached, because it was the beauty of someone who had continued to live without him.

"You have ten minutes," the mayor said, and then, perhaps because even politicians sometimes know when to leave a man alone, he descended the stairs.

Eli was alone with the clock.

He thought of his grandfather's hands, gnarled and trembling, winding the great spring for the last time. *Don't ever let it ring, boy. Some sounds are meant to be heard only once, and once you let them out, you cannot call them back.*

He thought of Mira, at twenty-three, climbing the spiral stairs with her boots in one hand, refusing to believe the tower had no elevator.

He thought of Mira, at thirty, writing a letter he had never received, because the postman could not find a man who did not officially exist.

He thought of Mira, at thirty-eight, standing in the cold with her chestnuts, and he understood, suddenly, what it meant that she had come.

*She came back.*

For the bells. For the new year. For the chance that, once in her life, she might hear the tower chime.

He put his hand on the mainspring.

Below, the band struck up "Auld Lang Syne." The crowd began to sing, off-key and joyful. The paper numerals began their slow descent.

*Five minutes.*

Eli turned the key.

The gears groaned. They had not moved in fifteen years, and they resisted him, fighting every tooth and pinion, whispering *stay, stay, stay.* He thought of his grandmother's face. He thought of his grandfather's tears. He thought of Mira's hand in his, seven years ago, warm and certain.

*Then we have all the time in the world.*

She had been wrong, he knew that now. They had not had all the time in the world. They had had only one frozen minute, stretched across fifteen years, and now he was spending it.

He turned the key harder.

The mainspring tightened. The first gear caught. The second. The third. The whole mechanism shuddered to life, gears spinning, pendulums swinging, and Eli felt the trapped minute begin to slide out of him like a held breath.

It hurt. God, it hurt. He felt the years he had not lived pour back into him—thirty-six, thirty-seven, thirty-nine, forty—and he staggered, catching himself on the iron railing.

The bells above him began to sway.

*One minute.*

Eli looked down from the tower window. Mira was looking up. He could not see her face from here, but he knew her face. He knew every line of it. He had memorized it across a thousand frozen afternoons, and he could find it now, in any crowd, in any weather, for the rest of whatever life he had left.

He climbed out onto the ledge. The wind was knife-sharp and smelled of woodsmoke and snow.

*Thirty seconds.*

He did not know if she could hear him. He shouted anyway.

"MIRA!"

Below, she looked up. The crowd gasped. Someone shouted for the police.

She knew his face.

*Ten seconds.*

"STAY THERE!" he shouted. "I'M COMING DOWN!"

*Five.*

The bells began to ring.

It was not one strike, as the legend promised. It was every bell in the tower, every bell his grandfather had silenced, ringing out together in a great cascading chord that shook the snow from the rooftops and the tears from Eli's eyes. The sound rose into the sky, and the sky answered, and for one impossible moment, Avenport was not a town but a bell, ringing with the pure bright joy of a year finally turned.

The crowd cheered. The numerals dropped. Confetti flew.

And Eli Calloway, aged now by every year he had borrowed, ran down the spiral stairs of the clocktower as fast as his forty-three-year-old legs could carry him.

She met him at the bottom.

She was crying. He was crying. They stood in the snow in the square, surrounded by strangers kissing strangers, and for a moment neither of them moved.

"You idiot," she said. "You absolute idiot. You could have just come down."

"I couldn't," he said. "I couldn't leave the minute."

"Then why did you?"

He looked at her—at the lines at her eyes, at the gray threading her dark hair, at the mouth that had kissed him seven years ago in a silent tower and then left him to the silence.

"Because you came back."

She made a sound that was half laugh, half sob, and then her hands were on his face, and her mouth was on his, and they were kissing in the snow at midnight, in the wreckage of the legend, in the first minute of the rest of their lives.

Above them, the tower bells rang on.

# The Shoulder Tap

The Friday night crowd at Élan had that particular electricity that only existed between October and December—students back from break, locals returning from summer travels, all crammed into the converted warehouse like they needed the warmth to survive. I was three drinks deep and counting, my roommate Dani long gone with some guy from her chemistry seminar, when I saw *her*.

She stood at the bar with her back to me, dark hair twisted up in a clip, posture that suggested either good genes or a lifetime of dance classes. The way she tilted her head when she laughed at something the bartender said—the bartender who was clearly flirting—made my stomach do something irresponsible.

I was halfway across the room before my brain caught up with my feet.

My cousin Margot has the same silhouette from behind. Same height, same way of standing with weight on one hip. We'd played this exact game since we were kids—sneaking up, tapping shoulders, watching each other jump. It had become reflex. Pavlovian, really.

I tapped her shoulder.

She turned around, and oh.

Not Margot.

Definitely, spectacularly, *not* Margot.

Her face was all sharp angles and warm eyes, cheekbones that caught the amber light of the hanging bulbs. She wore a small silver necklace that dipped just below her collarbone, and her expression when she looked at me was one of polite confusion that I wanted to spend the rest of the night replacing with other things.

"Sorry," I started, already backing up, already dying. "I thought you were my—sorry. My cousin. You have the same—" I gestured vaguely at her entire existence.

Her confusion melted into amusement. One eyebrow lifted. "My same *what*, exactly?"

"Just—hair. Build. I have a cousin who looks like you from behind. Bad lighting. My mistake."

"Mhm." She picked up her drink—something clear with lime—and took a sip, watching me over the rim. "And did your cousin teach you to apologize by complimenting her?"

"I—what?"

"You said 'sorry' and then something about how I looked. From behind." The corner of her mouth twitched. "That's usually how these things work, right? Tap a stranger, insult them, then spend ten minutes explaining it away?"

Heat crawled up my neck. "No, I—God. I'm making this worse."

"You are," she agreed cheerfully. "But it's entertaining, so keep going."

I should have walked away. I should have laughed it off, ordered another drink, found Dani in the back room and made a complete fool of myself to her instead. But the woman in front of me had this *patience*, this willingness to watch me flounder that felt like an invitation, and I was three drinks deep and counting and had apparently lost all survival instincts somewhere around the door.

"Alright," I said. "Honest version?"

"Please."

"From behind I thought that you were my relative, which is why I tapped you on your shoulder. But honestly, you're much hotter."

The silence lasted maybe two seconds. Then she laughed—a real one, surprised out of her, head tipping back—and the sound was better than any song the DJ had played all night.

"That's *much* worse," she said.

"I know."

"You're aware that's not a compliment, right? You're essentially saying I look like your cousin but in a sexy way. That's—there's math that doesn't work there."

"I have a very hot cousin."

"You don't."

"I might."

"You absolutely don't, because you wouldn't be this awkward if you had anyone to practice on."

I stared at her. "Are you—a bartender? Are you *trained* for this?"

"Sophomore," she said. "Pre-law."

"Of course you are."

"Take a guess why."

"You enjoy watching people suffer?"

She raised her glass to me. "Give this one a prize."

I was smiling. I hadn't realized I was smiling until my face started to hurt from it.

"Can I buy you a drink?" I asked. "As penance for the shoulder thing? And the cousin thing? And the math thing?"

"You can try," she said. "But I'm Sloane, and I don't usually let strange women buy me things after they've confessed to ogling my ass."

"That's fair."

"It's very fair."

"What if I confessed I was also ogling your face? Plural. Both, even."

She considered this. Behind her, the bartender—who had given up on flirting the moment he'd noticed Sloane was otherwise occupied—was already pouring something amber and expensive-looking.

"One drink," Sloane said. "And you have to let me critique your entire opening strategy. I'm taking notes."

"For what?"

"Evidence. In case I have to testify against you someday."

"You'd look great on the stand."

"Oh my god."

"Sorry. Sorry, that was—I'm going to stop talking."

"Probably for the best."

She moved aside, and I slid up to the bar beside her, suddenly aware of exactly how much space existed between our shoulders—how easy it would be to close it, how easy it would be to do exactly what I'd done moments before.

I didn't.

But I thought about it.

"You know," Sloane said, not looking at me, "if I *were* your cousin, I'd be very flattered."

"You'd be the only one."

"By the way." She turned then, finally, and her eyes in the amber light were darker than I'd expected. Softer. "I never actually saw you ogling anything. I just liked the part where you panicked."

"That's—"

"Relatable," she said. "I panic too. Sometimes I just do it with better posture."

I bought her two drinks after that. Three, actually. We stayed until last call, until the bartender stopped pretending he wasn't listening to our increasingly unhinged debate about whether shoulder-tapping strangers should be legal in all fifty states or just the reasonable ones.

She gave me her number, written on a napkin in handwriting that was somehow both elegant and chaotic, and walked out into the October night without looking back.

I called Dani at two in the morning, drunk and vibrating.

"I think I'm in love," I said.

"With the bartender?"

"No. With the woman I mistook for our cousin and accidentally called hot."

A long pause. Then: "Oh, you absolute disaster. Tell me everything."

I did.

I told her about the shoulder, the laughter, the way Sloane had looked at me like I was a particularly interesting exhibit. I told her about the napkin, which I'd carefully unfolded and re-folded seventeen times since getting home. I told her about pre-law and cocktails and how Sloane had said, right before she left, *"You should try that opener on someone whose family you're not related to. See if it works."*

"She sounds perfect for you," Dani said.

"She's mean to me."

"You like that."

"I *really* like that."

"Then text her, you disaster. Before you convince yourself it was a fever dream."

I didn't text her that night. I waited until morning, until I'd sobered up and showered and written three drafts I deleted.

What I sent, finally, was this:

*Hi Sloane. This is the woman from the bar who tapped your shoulder. I wanted you to know that I went home and thought about what you said, and you're right—my opener needs work. However, I refuse to accept that my cousin isn't objectively attractive. She is. Separately from you. In a different way. Mostly.*

*Also, are you free Saturday? I promise not to touch you, stand near you, or make prolonged eye contact with the back of your head.*

*This is Olive, by the way. From the bar. The disaster.*

*You said to give you my number too, if I wanted. I want.*

Her reply came four minutes later:

*Olive. I remember. You smelled like gin and bad decisions.*

*Saturday works. Wear something with a tag. I want to make sure I can identify you next time.*

*In case I'm looking for someone to tap.*

I laughed so hard I woke up my roommate on the other side of the wall.

**THE END**

*Oh, tidak.*

"Kenapa kamu melihatku begitu?" tanya Rangga, alis terangkat.

"Ap—tidak! Aku tidak melihatmu begitu!" Kinan memalingkan wajah, pipinya memanas. "Dan presentasiku biasa saja."

Rangga terkekeh pelan. "Kinan, kalau aku boleh jujur—aku selalu memperhatikan caramu berpikir. Itu yang membuatku sulit berhenti berdebat denganmu."

Kinan membeku. *Apa?*

"Aku rasa," lanjut Rangga, suaranya melembut dengan cara yang tidak pernah Kinan dengar sebelumnya, "kita ini sebenernya bukan musuh. Kita cuma... dua orang yang terlalu bangga untuk mengakui kalau kita saling *menghormati*."

Dan saat itulah Kinan tahu bahwa ia sudah kalah. Bukan dalam debat. Bukan dalam perang akademik tiga tahun ini. Tapi dalam perang yang jauh lebih berbahaya—perang yang ia lawan di dalam dirinya sendiri.

"Iya," bisik Kinan, akhirnya jujur pada dirinya sendiri. "Aku rasa aku sudah jatuh cinta dengan musuh bebuyutanku."

Rangga tersenyum lagi. Kali ini lebih lebar, lebih hangat, seolah-olah ia sudah tahu sejak lama.

"Aku juga."

Hujan masih turun di luar. Tapi di dalam lorong itu, untuk pertama kalinya, Kinan tidak ingin pulang.

Hijau.
