# San Valentino al Villaggio dei Glicini

Il sole di febbraio filtrava timido attraverso le tende di lino bianco della sala comune, dipingendo rettangoli dorati sul pavimento di marmo consumato. Fuori, i giardini della Casa di Riposo Villaggio dei Glicini erano ancora avvolti nella brina, ma dentro, qualcuno si era dato un gran daffare.

Strisce di carta rossa pendevano dal soffitto. Cuori di feltro decoravano ogni angolo. E al centro della sala, troneggiava un enorme albero di San Valentino improvvisato, i cui rami spogli erano stati abbelliti con palline rosa, nastri e bigliettini scritti a mano.

"Ecco, vede, signora Ferrari, l'ho appeso proprio accanto alla foto di suo marito," disse Lucia, l'animatrice trentenne con i capelli raccolti in una treccia disordinata, sistemando un cuore di cartoncino sul ramo più alto.

L'anziana signora sollevò lo sguardo, gli occhi lucidi. "Grazie, cara. Il mio Anselmo sarebbe contento di vedere tutta questa confusione. Lui diceva sempre che l'amore non ha età."

Lucia sorrise, stringendole la mano con delicatezza. "E aveva ragione, signora."

In un angolo della sala, seduto accanto alla finestra, il signor Tommaso osservava la scena con aria scettica. Ottantasette anni, due guerre vissute, una fabbrica gestita per quarant'anni, e ora eccolo lì, costretto a festeggiare San Valentino come un bambino delle elementari.

"Secondo me è tutta una montatura," borbottò al suo vicino di poltrona, il signor Ettore, che sonnecchiava beatamente con un bavaglino macchiato di sugo.

"Una montatura?" mormorò Ettore, aprendo un occhio. "Tommaso, vecchio mio, dovresti uscire di più. L'aria ti fa bene al cervello."

"Allora dimmi, filosofo, perché dovremmo festeggiare l'amore? Io ho amato mia moglie per cinquantadue anni, e non avevo bisogno di un albero rosa per dimostrarglielo."

Ettore ridacchiò piano. "Ah, ma il fatto che tu sia ancora qui a lamentarti dopo che la tua Margherita è morta da tre anni, la dice lunga, caro mio."

Tommaso aprì la bocca per rispondere, poi la richiuse. Si voltò verso la finestra, ma il suo riflesso nel vetro tradì un sorriso fugace.

---

Nel frattempo, al tavolo dei lavoretti manuali, la signora Adelina, novantatré anni portati con fierezza regale, stava dipingendo un acquerello. I suoi pennelli danzavano sulla carta con una grazia che tradiva l'artista che era stata, un tempo, prima che l'artrite le irrigidisse le dita.

"Posso?" chiese una vocina timida.

Adelina alzò lo sguardo. Una bambina di sette anni, con due trecce bionde e un vestitino a fiori, la fissava con i grandi occhi marroni.

"Certo, tesoro. Come ti chiami?"

"Sofia. Sono venuta a trovare la nonna."

"E chi è la tua nonna?"

Sofia indicò verso l'angolo opposto, dove una donna anziana stava giocando a tombola.

"È la signora Carla. Mi ha detto che qui oggi è San Valentino."

Adelina annuì lentamente. "Sì, è San Valentino. Sai cosa significa?"

Sofia scosse la testa.

"Significa che bisogna dire alle persone che amiamo quanto sono importanti. Lo fai con la mamma e il papà?"

Sofia rifletté, seria. "Con la mamma sì. Papà è un po' difficile. Dice che lui l'amore non lo sa dire."

Adelina rise, una risata cristallina che attirò gli sguardi di tutti nella sala. "Tanti uomini sono così, bambina mia. Ma il cuore parla anche quando la bocca tace."

La bambina la guardò con aria solenne. "E lei? Chi ama, signora Adelina?"

La vecchia artista posò il pennello. Il suo sguardo si perse oltre le tende di lino, oltre i giardini brinati, oltre il tempo stesso.

"Amavo un uomo che si chiamava Vittorio," disse con voce morbida. "L'ho amato per settant'anni, anche se lui è morto nel 1962."

"Così tanti anni!" esclamò Sofia, impressionata. "E non l'ha dimenticato?"

"Ci ho provato, bambina. Ma certi amori sono come l'inchiostro sulla pelle. Sbiadiscono, ma non scompaiono mai del tutto."

Sofia sembrò riflettere profondamente su quelle parole. Poi, con un gesto deciso, tirò fuori dalla tasca un bigliettino sgualcito e una matita. Scrisse qualcosa, lentamente, con la lingua che sporgeva tra le labbra per la concentrazione.

"Questo è per lei," disse, porgendole il biglietto.

Adelina lo prese con mani tremanti. Lesse: *Cara signora Adelina, buon San Valentino. La sua storia mi piace. Sofia.*

Gli occhi dell'anziana signora si riempirono di lacrime. "Grazie, tesoro," sussurrò. "Lo conserverò per sempre."

---

L'ora di pranzo arrivò con il suo carico di minestrina, purè e cotoletta. Nella sala da pranzo, gli ospiti si sistemarono ai tavoli assegnati, e un mormorio di voci riempì l'aria.

Il signor Tommaso si ritrovò seduto di fronte alla signora Giuseppina, una nuova arrivata che aveva sostituito la sua Margherita ai pasti. Settantanove anni, capelli argentati raccolti in un elegante chignon, occhi verdi come il vetro di Murano.

"Mi sembra di conoscerla," disse Tommaso, più bruscamente di quanto intendesse.

Giuseppina alzò un sopracciglio. "Davvero? E da dove?"

"Non lo so. Forse da un'altra vita."

Lei rise, una risata calda e inaspettata. "Sa che è la cosa più romantica che mi abbiano detto negli ultimi vent'anni?"

Tommaso arrossì, cosa che non gli succedeva dal 1985. "Non intendevo... io non sono un tipo romantico."

"Lo so. Ho sentito che si lamenta dell'albero di San Valentino."

Lui la guardò, sbalordito. "Chi glielo ha detto?"

"Le mura hanno orecchie, signor Tommaso. E in questa casa, le orecchie sono la nostra principale fonte di intrattenimento."

Tommaso non poté fare a meno di sorridere. Margherita gli mancava, certo. Ma forse, forse, la vita aveva ancora qualche carta da giocare.

---

Il pomeriggio trascorse lento, come solo i pomeriggi nelle case di riposo sanno essere. Lucia organizzò una tombolata, e le urla di "Tombola!" riecheggiarono per i corridoi. Il signor Ettore vinse un cesto di cioccolatini, che divise immediatamente con la signora del tavolo accanto. La bambina Sofia insegnò alla nonna a fare gli origami. E il signor Tommaso, con grande sorpresa di tutti, si offrì di leggere una poesia di Neruda alla sala riunita.

La sua voce, roca e stentorea, riempì il silenzio:

*"È così breve il tempo dell'amore,*
*che solo un'ora può sembrare un anno,*
*un solo giorno può sembrare un'ora,*
*se l'amore è perfetto..."*

Quando finì, la sala era in silenzio. Poi, lentamente, partì un applauso. Tommaso si schermì, ma i suoi occhi cercarono quelli di Giuseppina, che lo guardava con un sorriso che diceva più di mille parole.

---

La sera calò sul Villaggio dei Glicini. Gli ospiti furono accompagnati nelle loro stanze, gli animatori sparecchiarono la sala, le infermiere fecero l'ultimo giro di controllo.

Nella sua stanza, il signor Tommaso si sedette sulla poltrona accanto alla finestra. La foto di Margherita, in cornice d'argento, lo guardava dal comodino.

"Lo so cosa stai pensando," disse piano. "Ma non ti preoccupare. Il mio cuore è abbastanza grande per due. Per te, che sei stata la mia vita. E per questa nuova signora, che forse è solo un'amicizia. O forse no. Non lo so ancora."

La foto non rispose, naturalmente. Ma a Tommaso sembrò che il sorriso di Margherita fosse luminoso, quella sera. Approvatore, persino.

In un'altra stanza, la signora Adelina ripose il biglietto di Sofia nel cassetto del comodino, accanto a una lettera ingiallita del 1961, scritta da un uomo che si chiamava Vittorio.

"San Valentino," mormorò tra sé. "Che sciocchezza commerciale. Eppure..."

Eppure, per una volta, le sciocchezze commerciali le sembravano contenere una verità profonda. L'amore non aveva età, non aveva tempo, non aveva confini. Soprattutto, non aveva fine.

Dalla finestra, la luna piena di febbraio illuminava i giardinieri addormentati, dove i primi bucaneve facevano capolino tra la brina, annunciando una primavera che, come sempre, sarebbe arrivata.

Perché l'amore, in fondo, è la primavera del cuore.

E non smette mai di fiorire.

# The Space Between Floors

The fluorescent light hummed its one-note song overhead, and Marcus had to resist the urge to rip it from the ceiling.

"So," Anika said, arms crossed, leaning against the far wall. "This is awkward."

Marcus laughed, sharp and humorless. "Understatement of the year."

The elevator shuddered, then stilled. Somewhere below them, cables groaned in protest. He pressed the emergency button three times for good measure. Nothing.

"Of course it's not working," he muttered. "Of course."

Anika checked her watch—a nervous habit, he'd noticed over the years of shared conference rooms. "We're between fourteen and fifteen. Probably a power surge."

"Probably."

Silence filled the small box, heavy as the stale air. They'd been at the Crosswell & Associates annual partners' retreat, trading barbs across the breakfast table just two hours ago. He remembered her comment about his "reckless" merger strategy. He remembered the way he'd suggested her "penny-pinching" tendencies were why she'd never made managing partner.

All the things they'd said. All the things they meant.

"You're wondering how long we'll be stuck," she said, not looking at him.

"I'm wondering why I let David talk me into this partnership track at all."

Her head turned. In the harsh light, he could see the dark circles beneath her eyes, usually hidden beneath makeup. "You? I thought you loved it."

"I love winning. I hate the rest."

She considered this. "Same, actually."

The admission surprised him. Anika Patel, who'd clawed her way to senior partner by age thirty-eight. Anika Patel, who treated every quarterly review like a chess match.

"Why do you think we do this to ourselves?" she asked.

"Do what?"

"Hate each other."

He was quiet for a moment, watching the indicator lights blink uselessly above the doors. "I don't know. It felt easier. You were the enemy, so I didn't have to—"

The words caught in his throat.

"Didn't have to what?"

"Didn't have to admit I was terrified of not being good enough."

She didn't laugh. She didn't mock. She just nodded slowly, as though she'd been waiting for him to say it.

"I'm forty-three years old," she said softly. "I have a mortgage and a mother with Alzheimer's and a cat that I'm pretty sure hates me more than you do."

"I don't hate you."

"I know."

The elevator swayed slightly, just enough to make them both reach for the handrails. Their knuckles brushed. Neither pulled away.

"I shouldn't have said what I said at breakfast," he offered.

"Which part?"

"All of it. The thing about your father."

She went very still. In all their years of rivalry, he'd never gone there. Not until the chardonnay had loosened his tongue and the old resentments had come pouring out.

"No," she agreed quietly. "You shouldn't have."

"I'm sorry."

She looked at him then, really looked, and he saw something he hadn't expected. Not anger. Not forgiveness, either. Something more like recognition.

"You didn't know," she said. "About any of it. But you should have asked before you assumed."

"Yeah." He swallowed. "I should have."

Somewhere above them, footsteps crossed the lobby. Muffled voices debated something. Neither of them called out.

"What are you thinking?" she asked.

"I'm thinking we're both too stubborn for our own good."

"Probably."

"And I'm thinking"—he let out a breath he'd been holding for what felt like years—"that I've spent a decade making you the villain of my story. And it's exhausting."

She was quiet for a long moment. Then she crossed the small space and sat down on the floor, her back against the wall. After a beat, she gestured for him to join her.

He did.

They sat shoulder to shoulder, watching the numbers above the door that refused to change.

"My mother sometimes remembers me," Anika said. "On the good days. On the bad ones, she asks where her daughter went."

He didn't say anything. Just let her talk.

"I built walls," she continued, "because I thought if I was hard enough, sharp enough, no one could get close enough to hurt me."

"Me too."

"The thing about walls, Marcus, is they keep everything out. Including the good stuff."

He thought about that. About the loneliness of his corner office. About the way he'd celebrated every one of his wins alone, with takeout and a podcast.

"I don't want to be your enemy anymore," he said.

She tilted her head back against the wall. "Then don't be."

Above them, the lights flickered. The elevator groaned. And somewhere in the building, someone was probably working on getting them out.

But for now—just for now—the space between fourteen and fifteen felt like exactly where they were supposed to be.

# The Countdown

The rooftop of the Bellweather Hotel buzzed with laughter and the clink of champagne flutes. Somewhere below, Times Square was already glowing, a sea of upturned faces watching the digital ball slowly descend. But up here, in the velvet-roped VIP section, the world felt smaller. More intimate. Like the universe had drawn a curtain around just the two of us.

"You know," I said, turning to you, "I've never actually been kissed at midnight on New Year's."

You raised an eyebrow, that crooked smile I'd been staring at all night finally getting the better of me. "Never?"

"Not once. I'm tragically uncoupled every December 31st." I gestured at the glittering skyline. "It's becoming a tradition at this point."

"Lucky for you," you said, stepping closer, "I have a habit of fixing traditions."

The countdown started somewhere across the room—ten, nine, eight—and I should have been watching the fireworks, the confetti cannons, the couples around us leaning in like it was choreographed. But I was watching you. The way the city lights caught the edge of your jaw. The way your hand found the small of my back like it had always belonged there.

Three. Two. One.

You kissed me like the world was ending and beginning all at once. Like you had been waiting all year, all *life*, to do exactly this. The champagne on your lips tasted like futures I hadn't dared imagine. Somewhere behind us, someone popped a cork and shouted, and the band struck up "Auld Lang Syne," and I remember thinking, absurdly, *so this is what all the songs are about*.

When we finally broke apart, breathless and grinning, you pressed your forehead to mine.

"Happy New Year," you whispered.

"Happy New Year," I answered.

And I knew—I *knew*, with the certainty of someone watching a door swing open onto a room they've been searching for their whole life—that I would never uncouple again on December 31st.

Not ever.

# The Cartography of Us

Margaret found the map on a Tuesday.

It was tucked between the pages of his high school yearbook, yellowed and brittle at the folds, the kind of road atlas no one printed anymore. She recognized his handwriting instantly—that impatient slant, the way he crossed his T's like tiny anchors. The route was traced in blue ballpoint, snaking from their hometown in Ohio to a stretch of beach in South Carolina neither of them had ever seen.

Beside the starting point, in a sixteen-year-old's scrawl, he had written: *Someday.*

That was fifty-three years ago.

---

She was fifteen when she first noticed him—really noticed him—not as the boy who mowed her father's lawn or delivered the Sunday paper, but as a person with the kind of face that made you want to know what he was thinking. He had a habit of squinting into the middle distance, as though he were watching something no one else could see.

"Stop looking at me like that," he'd said one afternoon, catching her. They were sitting on the tailgate of his father's pickup, eating peaches so ripe the juice ran down their wrists. "Like you're trying to figure something out."

"I'm not looking at you."

"You were."

"Was not."

She was. She still was, sixty-eight years later, though now he looked more like a paper crane someone had folded carefully and set on a windowsill—thin, angular, translucent in certain light. His squint had deepened into something permanent. His hair, once as black as a wet stone, had gone the color of a November sky.

But he was still looking into the middle distance.

She still wanted to know what he was thinking.

---

They married at nineteen and twenty-one, in a church so small the choir had to stand in the vestibule. Her mother wept. His father, a man of few words, shook his hand once, firmly, and that was that.

The honeymoon was that trip to South Carolina. They drove all night in a Chevrolet with a faulty heater, stopping at diners where the coffee came in thick ceramic mugs and the waitresses called them honey. He had saved for two years to afford it. She had sewn her own sundress.

They stayed in a motel with green carpet that smelled like other people's vacations. They walked along the shore at dawn, their shadows stretching ahead of them like long-held promises. The Atlantic was bigger than either of them had imagined.

"We could stay," he'd said. "Forget about going back."

"We'd starve."

"I'd learn to fish."

"You'd get bored."

"I'd learn to fish *and* not get bored."

She laughed so hard she had to sit down in the sand. He sat beside her, and they watched the tide come in, and he put his arm around her, and she leaned her head against his shoulder, and that was the whole of it—that was the whole beginning.

---

They came back, of course. There were mortgages and children and the long, ordinary slog of building a life. His father died the year after. Her mother followed not long after that. There were jobs he loved and jobs he didn't, winters that never ended, a furnace that broke the week the second baby came.

There were also good things. So many good things they sometimes blurred. The way he always remembered the anniversary of her father's death and brought her a white flower without saying why. The way she learned to make his mother's pot roast even though she'd never liked it, because she knew it made him feel like a boy again, safe and warm and known.

There were two children, a boy and a girl, who grew up and moved away and came back and moved away again. There were grandchildren now, teenagers themselves, who looked at their grandparents the way Margaret had once looked at him—curious, a little in awe, trying to figure something out.

---

The trouble started the year he turned seventy.

It was small at first. He forgot where he put his keys. He repeated a story about a fishing trip that Margaret had heard thirty times. Once, in the grocery store, he called her by his sister's name.

She told herself it was nothing. Aging. The ordinary erosion of time.

But it kept happening, and then it kept happening more, until the days took on a new shape—one shaped around what he could no longer remember, what he could still hold onto, what she had to quietly absorb for him.

He was diagnosed in the spring, the kind of diagnosis no one wants to hear.

They sat in the neurologist's office, the paper crinkling beneath her as she leaned forward to hear every word. He reached for her hand, and she gave it, and for a moment they were the kids in the pickup again, the world suddenly enormous and not quite real.

"What do we do?" she asked, after.

He looked at her, and for a moment she saw the boy clearly, squinting into the middle distance, watching something none of them could see yet.

"We keep going," he said. "We keep going until we can't."

---

And they did.

She learned to be patient in ways she hadn't known she needed to learn. She learned to answer the same question three times in an hour without sighing, though some days she did sigh, and then she went into the bathroom and pressed her palms against her eyes and breathed until the bad feeling passed. She learned to laugh at the things that weren't funny anymore—his coat on in summer, the way he sometimes forgot which grandchild was which—because he could tell when she was afraid, and fear made him worse.

He learned to be afraid.

He had been many things in his life—a son, a husband, a father, an engineer, a man who once fixed everything that broke in the house. Now he was becoming something else, something without a name, a country he was being slowly exiled from. Some days he woke up and didn't know where he was. Some days he didn't know who she was, and those were the worst days, the days she went into the kitchen and stood very still until the trembling stopped.

But there were also good days. Days when he looked at her and she could see him in there, the real him, the boy with the peaches and the pickup and the dream of the sea. On those days, he sometimes reached for her face and traced her features like a man reading braille, as though he were memorizing her, as though he were saying the things he would not be able to say later.

"I know you," he whispered once. "I don't know your name, but I know you."

She kissed his palm. "That's enough," she said. "That's enough."

---

On their fiftieth wedding anniversary, their daughter arranged for them to go back to South Carolina.

Margaret didn't know if it was a kindness or a cruelty until they got there. The motel was gone, replaced by condominiums. The beach was the same, though—the same long stretch of sand, the same wild and patient sea.

She helped him down to the water. He moved slowly now, one hand on her arm, the other on the cane. They stood at the edge of the surf and let the waves come in, cold and bright, foaming around their ankles.

He closed his eyes.

"I remember this," he said.

She almost couldn't speak. "What do you remember?"

"The sand. The way you laughed. You laughed at something I said." He opened his eyes and looked at her, and there it was—the look she'd been chasing her whole life. "I think I made you laugh."

"You did."

"I think I still do. Sometimes."

"You do," she said. "You do."

---

He died on a Wednesday.

There was no drama to it. She woke up and he was beside her, and he was not breathing, and the room was very quiet. The light through the curtains was the color of a peach, and for a moment—just a moment—she thought she could hear him breathing.

But she could not.

She lay beside him for a long time. She did not call anyone. She did not weep, not yet. She just lay there, her hand on his chest, feeling the absence of him like a tide that had gone out and would not come back.

Eventually, she got up. She washed her face. She made coffee. She called their son, and then their daughter, and she answered their questions in a voice that sounded almost normal.

Later—much later—his daughter found the map.

She brought it to Margaret, who had been sitting in his chair, in his shirt, holding a photograph of them on their wedding day.

"He kept it all this time," her daughter said.

Margaret smoothed the brittle paper. The blue line, the starting point, the word.

*Someday.*

---

She is eighty-three now.

She lives alone in the house they bought together, the house where their children took their first steps, where he taught her to make pancakes on Sunday mornings, where they argued about politics and made up in the hallway and said things they did not mean and took them back.

She is learning a new language—the language of without. She goes to the grocery store and buys only what she can carry. She turns the thermostat up because no one is here to remind her to save money. She eats at the kitchen table instead of in front of the television, because there is no one to eat in front of the television with.

She keeps his sweater in the closet. She cannot wear it. She cannot give it away.

On his birthday, she drives to the cemetery. The headstone is small and plain, the way he would have wanted it. She brings a white flower—she has done this for so many years that the florist knows her, and now sets one aside without being asked.

"Hello, my love," she says, and sits on the bench beside his plot, and tells him about the grandchildren, about the cat that adopted her, about the way the neighbor boy shoveled her walk without being asked.

Sometimes, if the light is right, if the wind is gentle, she swears she can feel him there, just behind her shoulder, watching her with his head tilted, squinting into the middle distance, trying to see what comes next.

---

She still goes to the beach, sometimes.

There is a stretch of coast she returns to, year after year, the same stretch where they stood in the surf on their fiftieth anniversary. She walks slowly now, with a cane of her own. She does not swim. She just walks, and looks, and listens.

The Atlantic is bigger than either of them had ever imagined.

Some nights, when the moon is up and the water is silver, she takes off her shoes and wades in. The cold takes her breath away. She stands there, ankle-deep, looking out at the horizon where the sky meets the sea and the world seems to go on forever.

She thinks of him then—of the boy he was, the man he became, the long years of love and trouble and laughter that wove them together like a single thread.

She thinks of the map, and the word he wrote at the beginning of it.

*Someday.*

She had spent a whole life waiting for someday. Now she understood that someday wasn't a place on a map. It was the walking itself. It was the going. It was the long and patient act of loving someone, year after year, until the loving was the destination and the road was home.

The waves come in.

The waves go out.

She watches them for a long time, and then she turns, and walks back up the beach, and goes on.

# Осколки зимнего солнца

Анна впервые увидела его в библиотеке старого Петербурга — среди пыльных томов по архитектуре, забытых читателями. Он сидел у окна, и свет февральского солнца очерчивал его профиль золотой линией. Высокий, чуть сутулый, с тёмными волосами, небрежно упавшими на лоб.

Он поднял глаза, и она почувствовала, как земля уходит из-под ног.

— Вы ищете Достоевского? — спросил он голосом, похожим на далёкий колокол.

— Я ищу... — она замялась, — я ищу потерянное время.

Он улыбнулся. Эта улыбка решила всё.

---

Марк оказался реставратором. Он восстанавливал старинные здания, возвращал им утраченную красоту. Его руки, шершавые от известки, были самыми нежными руками, которые Анна когда-либо знала.

Они гуляли по зимнему городу, и он показывал ей дома так, словно читал стихи:

— Видишь этот карниз? Восемнадцатый век. Он пережил наводнение, революцию, войну. А теперь смотрит на нас.

Анна смотрела на карниз, но видела только его глаза — серые, как петербургское небо, и такие же глубокие.

Через месяц она переехала к нему.

---

Их квартира была на пятом этаже, без лифта. Каждый вечер он носил её на руках по лестнице, и она смеялась, а он говорил:

— Ты моя главная реставрация. Я собираю тебя по кусочкам.

Она не понимала тогда, что он говорил это не ради красивой фразы.

В марте он стал другим. Не сразу — постепенно, как трещина идёт по стене. Сначала перестал приходить вовремя. Потом — отвечать на звонки. Потом Анна нашла в его кармане чужой женский платок.

— Это ничего не значит, — сказал он, и его голос звучал так, как звучит треснувшее стекло.

— Это значит всё.

Но она простила. Потому что любила. Потому что боялась пустой квартиры. Потому что за окном был город, который они вместе открывали, и казалось — без него она ослепнет.

В апреле она узнала точно: у него есть другая. Жена. Ребёнок. Целая жизнь, о которой Анна ничего не знала.

---

Она сидела на подоконнике их — теперь уже её — квартиры и смотрела на Невский. Фонари зажигались один за другим, словно город пытался ей что-то сказать.

Она вспоминала его слова о карнизе: *«Он пережил наводнение, революцию, войну. А теперь смотрит на нас.»*

Карниз пережил. А она?

На столе лежал его подарок — старинная брошь в виде снежинки. Он нашёл её при раскопках фундамента. *«Для тебя, — сказал он тогда. — Ты мой осколок зимнего солнца.»*

Анна сжала брошь в кулаке.

Она думала о том, что реставратор возвращает зданиям прежний облик, но никогда не спрашивает, какими они были до разрушения. Он решает за них. Он выбирает, что должно быть видно, а что — скрыто под слоем штукатурки.

Марк тоже так поступал. Скрывал жену под слоем штукатурки. Скрывал ребёнка. А она — она принимала его работу, не заглядывая глубже.

За окном начал падать снег — редкий для апреля, нежданный. Город замер, как на старой открытке.

Анна встала, надела пальто. Она не знала, куда идёт. Но она знала, что остаться не может.

На пороге она обернулась. Квартира смотрела на неё пустыми глазами окон. Она вспомнила его руки, его голос, его смех — и впервые поняла, что всё это было лишь узором на фасаде.

Красивым. Обманчивым. Чужим.

Она вышла на лестницу и тихо сказала — так тихо, что услышали только стены:

— Я сделала огромную ошибку.

---

*Снег падал на Петербург, как будто город хотел всё исправить. Но ошибки, как и старые здания, не всегда можно восстановить. Иногда их нужно просто оставить позади.*

# 最后的春天

## 一

灰烬落下来的那一年，季野七岁。

他记得那天是星期四，妈妈让他去便利店买盐。他走到半路，天忽然暗了下来，像谁把一块脏兮兮的灰布蒙在了太阳上。他抬头看，看见天空裂开一道口子，白色的光从里面涌出来，烫得他眼泪直流。

后来他才知道，那是旧世界最后的尖叫。

等他从昏迷中醒来，便利店已经塌了一半，街上横七竖八躺着人，有的还在动，有的已经不动了。妈妈从家里跑出来找他的时候，摔倒在路中间，再也没有起来。

七年过去了。

## 二

今年是第三年。

所谓"第三年"，是人们从废墟里爬出来后，给这个新世界起的名字。没有国家，没有城市，只有大大小小的据点。人们不再问"你是哪里人"，而是问"你是第几年活过来的"。

季野今年十四岁，是一个拾荒者。

他住的地方叫"灯塔"，是旧世界一座消防站的残骸。站长是个独眼的中年男人，绰号叫"老海"，因为他的左眼像蒙了一层海。老海在消防站的顶上架了一盏探照灯，每晚都亮着，让方圆十里的人知道这里有人。

每天天亮，季野就和其他拾荒者一起出去，翻找废墟里的食物、药品、还能用的工具。天黑之前必须回来，因为晚上是另一种东西的天下——他们管那种东西叫"锈兽"，不知道是什么变异来的，只知道它们的眼睛像两团锈水，见什么啃什么。

## 三

季野是在一个雨天的废墟里遇见她的。

那天的雨下得奇怪，雨点落在皮肤上不是凉的，是温的，像旧世界电视剧里那种浪漫的桥段。他在一座塌了一半的图书馆里翻找，意外发现了一本没有烧毁的书，封面是个女人，眼睛很大，笑着。

然后他听到了声音。

很轻，像老鼠，又像婴儿。是从书架后面传来的。他握紧了手里的铁管，慢慢绕过去——

是一个女孩。

比他小一点，瘦得像根豆芽菜，裹在一件破烂的成人外套里，缩在墙角。她看见季野，没有尖叫，只是用一双过分安静的眼睛看着他。

"你是谁？"季野问。

女孩没有说话，只是指了指自己的嗓子，摆摆手。

她不会说话。

## 四

老海看见季野带回一个哑巴女孩，皱了皱眉。

"我们养不起闲人。"他说。

"她不是闲人。"季野说，"她可以干活。"

老海看了女孩一眼。女孩站在灯塔的火光里，安静得像一截影子。

"叫什么？"老海问。

女孩摇摇头。

"就叫你影儿吧。"老海说，"影儿，留下来可以，但丑话说前头——你得干活，得听话，得守规矩。"

影儿点了点头。

就这样，灯塔多了一个人。

## 五

影儿真的不是闲人。

她学东西很快，跟着其他拾荒者出去两三次，就学会了怎么找食物、怎么避开危险。她最厉害的本领是认路——在那些迷宫一样的废墟里，她永远知道哪条路通哪里，从来不迷路。

而且，她很安静。

灯塔里的人大多是经历过旧世界的成年人，身上带着各种创伤。有的暴躁，有的麻木，有的整夜整夜地睡不着，对着墙说话。影儿从来不打扰任何人，她就默默地干活，默默地吃饭，默默地找一个角落睡觉。

季野有时候会偷偷观察她。他发现影儿有个习惯——她喜欢把捡到的东西整整齐齐地摆成一排。有一次她摆的是七颗石子，从大到小，排得很整齐。

那天季野忍不住问她："这代表什么？"

影儿想了想，用树枝在地上画了七个小人，一个挨一个站成一排。

季野愣了一下。

"你家里有七口人？"

影儿摇摇头，又点点头，最后指了指自己，画了一个圈，然后画了一个大大的叉。

"只剩你一个了。"季野说。

影儿低下头。

## 六

他们熟起来，是在季野受伤之后。

那是一次很糟糕的拾荒。他们遇上了一群流浪者，流浪者比锈兽更可怕，因为锈兽只是想吃你，流浪者是想夺走你的一切。季野为了掩护同伴撤退，被铁管砸中了后背。

他被抬回灯塔的时候，已经昏了过去。

醒来的时候，影儿坐在他床边。

她的眼睛红红的，像是哭过。她手里端着一碗稀粥，用勺子舀起来，吹凉了，送到他嘴边。

"我自己能吃。"季野说。

影儿固执地不肯放下勺子。

季野只好张了嘴。

就这样，一勺一勺，季野把那碗粥吃完了。影儿的表情这才松下来，像是完成了一件大事。

那天晚上，季野睡不着，因为后背疼得厉害。他听见影儿也睡不着——她在角落里轻轻地翻身。

"影儿。"他小声叫。

影儿立刻坐了起来。

"谢谢你的粥。"他说。

影儿在黑暗中摆摆手。

"还有，"季野说，"谢谢你陪我。"

影儿愣了一下。

然后，在季野看不见的黑暗里，她轻轻地笑了。

## 七

伤好了之后，季野开始带着影儿一起出去。

他发现影儿其实很勇敢。有一次他们在废墟里遇上一只落单的锈兽——那是一只变异的狗，体型大得像小牛，眼睛是两团浑浊的锈水。其他人吓得转身就跑，影儿却拉住了季野，指了指另一边。

他们从另一条路绕了过去。

"你怎么知道？"事后季野问。

影儿指了指自己的鼻子。

"你能闻到它？"

影儿点点头。

季野突然明白了——影儿不只是认路厉害，她对危险的感知也比别人敏锐。她靠的是一种说不清道不明的本能。

"以后，"季野认真地说，"你就是我的鼻子。"

影儿歪着头想了想，然后笑了。

## 八

第三年的冬天，来得特别早。

十月的天就开始飘雪，十一月河水就结了冰。灯塔里的食物储备开始告急，出去拾荒的人越来越多，但能找到的东西越来越少。

老海把大家召集起来，说要做一件事——派一支队伍去南边的"绿洲"。据说南方有一个地方，那里的变异植物结出了可以吃的果子，还有一条没被污染的河。

"路很远，要走二十多天。"老海说，"我不勉强，想去的报名。"

季野报了名。

影儿也报了名。

老海看了他们一眼，叹了口气："你们两个小的，凑什么热闹。"

"我不小了。"季野说，"我十四了。"

"我也——"影儿张了张嘴，发出了一个沙哑的音节。

所有人都愣住了。

这是影儿第一次发出声音。

老海沉默了一会儿，说："行。你们两个，跟着大部队走。但是——"他顿了顿，"我丑话说前头，路上出了事，我顾不上你们。"

"不用你顾。"季野说，"我们互相顾。"

他说这话的时候，看了影儿一眼。影儿的脸红了一点——在末世的灰烬里，那种红显得格外明亮。

## 九

他们走了二十三天。

这二十三天里，他们穿过荒废的城市，越过结冰的河流，走过空无一人的平原。夜里他们挤在一起取暖，轮流守夜。白天他们边走边找吃的，有时候能找到一点，有时候一整天都只能喝雪水。

第十四天的时候，他们遇上了一场大雪。

那场雪下了整整三天，队伍走散了。等雪停的时候，季野发现身边只剩下影儿一个人。

"怎么办？"他问。

影儿指了指前方。

"你确定？"

影儿点点头，眼神很坚定。

季野决定相信她。

他们又走了六天。饿了啃树皮，渴了吃雪。季野的脚冻伤了，影儿用破布给他包起来。她的手很凉，但包扎的时候很认真。

"影儿。"季野在某个寒冷的夜晚说。

影儿抬起头。

"等到了绿洲，"他说，"我们种点东西吧。"

影儿歪着头。

"种土豆。"季野说，"听说旧世界的人就是靠土豆活过来的。等土豆熟了，我给你烤着吃。"

影儿的眼睛亮了。

"还有，"季野说，"等到了绿洲，我想——我想一直跟你在一起。"

影儿的脸在火光里红了起来。

她点了点头。

## 十

他们是在第二十一天的黄昏看到绿洲的。

那是一片绿——真正的绿。在灰蒙蒙的世界里待久了，那种绿显得那么不真实，像是一幅画，像是一个梦。

他们站在山坡上，看着那片绿。

影儿的眼泪流了下来。

季野也哭了。

他们抱在了一起，在风里，在黄昏里，在末世的废墟与希望之间。

很久以后，季野在绿洲的小屋里醒来，看见影儿正在窗边摆弄那些捡来的石子。她还是把石子排成一排，从大到小。

但这一次，石子的旁边多了一颗小小的土豆。

"这是什么？"季野问。

影儿指了指窗外的地，地上已经冒出了一小片绿芽。

"你种的？"季野惊讶地问。

影儿点点头，笑了。

季野也笑了。

他走过去，从背后抱住了影儿。

"谢谢你，"他说，"谢谢你陪我找到这里。"

影儿靠在他怀里，抬头看着窗外的绿芽。

在第三年的末尾，在末世的某个角落，最后的春天，终于来了。

Write a romance that involves one partner saving the other from a fire. About 1500 words long.

# Embers of You

The first time Owen saw Eliza Marsh, she was standing in the parking lot of the station, arguing with a tree.

Not literally a tree, but the man dressed in full forestry gear, who was waving a clipboard like he was conducting an orchestra. Eliza's hands flew through the air in sharp, precise gestures—stop, go, wait, now—and Owen found himself slowing the truck, just to watch her a moment longer.

"Lieutenant Daniels! Stop daydreaming." Chief Howler leaned out of his window. "We've got a controlled burn going sideways up at Pine Ridge."

Owen nodded, pulling forward. But his eyes caught Eliza's one more time—dark hair escaped from her ponytail, dirt smudged across her cheek, eyes fierce as she fought the wind. He smiled. He was in trouble.

---

The fire crew worked the Pine Ridge burn for three days. Owen worked beside Eliza, learning the way she moved through a fire line, the way she listened to a tree before she cut it, the way she hummed old country songs when she thought no one was listening.

"You're staring again," she said one evening, passing him a canteen.

"Hard not to. You hum when you're thinking."

She laughed—a real laugh, surprising them both. "That's classified information, Daniels."

"Consider it safe with me."

Three weeks of controlled burns turned into a summer of evening campfires, of borrowed flannels and mosquito-bitten shoulders, of quiet conversations under canopies of pine. Eliza was fire in human form—sharp-tongued, warm-hearted, terrifyingly brave—and Owen fell so hard he stopped noticing the ground beneath him.

They moved into a drafty old house at the edge of town that November. The wiring was a disaster. Owen knew it. He'd added it to the list of things to fix, somewhere below *replace porch railing* and above *finally fix the hall door*.

He never made it down the list.

---

February was cruel that year, the kind of cold that made wood splinter and pipes groan. Eliza had been gone for a week on a job in the southern district—prescribed burn for a state park, important enough to pull her away mid-winter. Owen had the house to himself, a stack of paperwork on the kitchen table, and a dog named Buddy who thought he was a lap-sized animal.

The night it happened, Owen was asleep by ten. He'd worked a sixteen-hour shift—two-car accident, a chimney fire, a kid who'd climbed a tree and gotten stuck. The kind of day that hollowed a man out.

He woke to the smell.

It was subtle at first—the way a forgotten loaf of bread in the oven announces itself. Then thicker, sharper. His eyes flew open.

Smoke curled along the ceiling of the bedroom like a slow, gray river. The hallway beyond was a tunnel of black, and at the far end, where the old wiring ran, orange light licked up the wall.

The fire had been waiting for him. Waiting for the draft, the cold, the night it thought he wouldn't wake.

Owen didn't think. He moved.

The hallway was already gone. He pressed his face into his shirt, slid along the wall—don't breathe, don't breathe, don't breathe—and made it to the kitchen. The flames were in the walls, racing through the bones of the house faster than he could track. The kitchen table was smoking. The curtains were blooming into red flowers.

He dialed 911 with shaking hands.

"What is your emergency?"

"House fire. 17 Linden. I'm inside." His voice didn't sound like his own.

"Sir, you need to exit immediately."

"I can't. Hallway's gone." He coughed. The smoke was pooling near the floor now, thick and black. "Second floor bedroom window. Send someone."

He hung up before she could tell him to stay on the line. He knew the rules. He broke them anyway.

He crawled to the pantry, found a rag, wet it under the sink. The water came out tepid—he could hear it sizzling as it hit the sink. He wrapped the rag around his face and made for the stairs, but the second floor was a furnace above him. Heat pressed down through the ceiling like a hand.

He was going to die in his own kitchen, and Eliza was going to come home to ashes.

*Not yet. Not like this.*

He pulled a chair to the counter, climbed onto it, and threw himself onto the roof of the small back porch. The shingles were hot under his palms but not yet burning. He crawled, gasping, his lungs full of cinders, and made it to the edge of the porch roof.

The drop was maybe nine feet. Buddy was below, whining, circling.

Owen jumped.

---

The ladder came before he could crawl to the front of the house. He looked up, blinking through the smoke in his eyes, and there she was.

Eliza.

She was on the ladder, in jeans and boots and his old fire-resistant jacket, her hair whipping around her face in the winter wind. She was supposed to be three hundred miles south. She was supposed to be in a motel, sleeping. But she was here—*she was here*—because she'd felt something wrong, she'd told him later, like a hand around her throat.

"Lieutenant Daniels," she said, and her voice cracked on his name. "If you ever do that again—"

"Ma'am," he croaked, "this is highly irregular."

She reached down, gripped his collar, and pulled him up the ladder like he weighed nothing. He slumped against her when he reached the top rung, and she wrapped both arms around him, hard. He could feel her shaking. He could feel her heart against his chest, hammering like a trapped bird.

The house burned behind them. They didn't watch. They sat on the frozen ground, the truck's headlights cutting the dark, and held onto each other like the world was ending.

Which, in a way, it was. Their world, anyway.

The one they'd built—the borrowed flannels, the campfires, the morning coffee, the plans for spring—all of it, gone. A box of photos. Her grandmother's quilt. The ring he'd been carrying in his sock drawer for two months, waiting for the right moment.

When the fire crew arrived, they found Owen wrapped in a blanket, Eliza refusing to let go of his hand. Chief Howler took one look at them and wrote the incident report in pencil so he could erase the parts that made him cry.

---

They lived in a motel for three weeks. Then a rental. Then a tiny house on the edge of town that Eliza found first—a place with good bones and new wiring, with a porch big enough for two chairs and a dog.

The night they moved in, they sat on the porch steps with Buddy between them. The sky was full of stars and the air smelled like woodsmoke from a distant chimney, and Owen reached into his jacket pocket.

"Eliza."

She looked at him.

"I'm going to say something, and I need you to let me finish before you call me an idiot."

She raised an eyebrow but nodded.

"I bought a ring before the fire. I was going to give it to you on our anniversary. Then the house burned, and I thought—well, I thought a lot of things. Mostly that I'd waited too long, that I should have asked you sooner, that we—"

"Owen."

"—that we don't have to wait for the right moment because there isn't one. There never is. There's just—us. And whatever's left after the fire."

He opened the box.

The ring was simple. A thin gold band, a small diamond. Nothing grand. Everything real.

Eliza stared at it for a long time. Then she looked at him, and her eyes were bright.

"You absolute *disaster* of a man," she whispered, and kissed him so hard the stars spun.

---

They were married in the spring, in the backyard of the new house, under an arbor Eliza had built herself. Chief Howler officiated. Buddy was the ring bearer. The vows they wrote were short and imperfect and exactly right.

*I will love you through the smoke.*
*I will find you in the dark.*
*I will build you a house and never let it burn.*

Years later, when people asked how they met, Eliza would tell them about the parking lot and the tree, and Owen would tell them about the fire, and they'd disagree about who saved whom, and they'd laugh, and they'd kiss, and Buddy would bark at nothing in particular.

Some loves begin with a spark.
Theirs began with a flame.

And every year, on the anniversary of the fire, they would sit on the porch of their house—the *new* house, the *real* house—and toast the life they'd almost lost, and the one they'd found.

Because the truth was this: Owen had pulled Eliza from the wreckage of a burning house, and she had pulled him from the wreckage of himself, and neither of them had ever let go.

They didn't plan to, either.

Not in this life. Not in any.

Write a romance where the characters pretend to be dating each other in order to win a reality show. Length: about 1800 words.

# Hearts on Camera

The fluorescent lights of the casting room hummed like an angry hive. Maya Delacroix shifted her weight in the plastic chair, her vintage band tee—Radiohead, 1992 tour—suddenly feeling like a costume. Across from her, twenty other hopefuls sat in various states of practiced indifference.

A production assistant with a clipboard and the energy of a caffeinated squirrel paced the rows. "Okay, listen up. If you're here, you've already made it through the first round, which means you already know the premise." She paused for effect, as though she were announcing the winner of the lottery rather than explaining the worst idea anyone had ever pitched to a network. "So, if you'll turn to page three of your contracts, you'll see—"

"Page three?" A guy near the front laughed. "I've never made it past page one of any contract."

Maya glanced over. He had dark curly hair escaping a backwards baseball cap, a crooked smile, and the kind of jawline that should have come with a warning label. He also had a vintage Pac-Man backpack slung over his chair, which immediately redeemed him in her eyes.

"The part you really want to know," the assistant continued, tapping her clipboard, "is that we need to make a few adjustments to the format."

---

Later, at the coffee shop across the street, Maya found herself sitting across from the Pac-Man guy. His name, according to his contract, was Eli Whitfield. Twenty-eight. Writer. He'd been working on a novel for six years and had recently quit his barista job after his agent convinced him he needed "life experience" to finish it.

"So," Maya said, wrapping both hands around her chai latte. "They want us to pretend to date."

"I got that part." Eli stirred his cold brew. "What I don't get is *why* they're telling us upfront. Reality shows usually make the contestants figure out who's pretending and who's genuine, right? It's the whole gimmick."

"Yeah, but this is different." Maya had read the format brief twice on the subway. "It's not about falling in love. It's about whether a fake relationship can survive public scrutiny for ten weeks. They want to see how it affects us. Whether we catch feelings. Whether we crash and burn."

Eli's eyebrows rose. "So we're lab rats in a relationship experiment."

"Cuddly lab rats." Maya shrugged. "They're offering us each fifty thousand dollars. I have sixty-three dollars in my bank account right now and a rent payment due in nine days."

He whistled low. "That's a lot of rent."

"That is *a lot* of rent."

They sat in silence for a moment, the hiss of the espresso machine filling the gap.

"So," Eli said slowly, "what do we need to make this work?"

---

**Week One: The Foundation**

They met every day for two weeks before filming began. Not because the contract required it—Maya had checked—but because they needed a backstory, and good lies were built on good truths.

Maya told him about her mother's funeral. About the dress she hadn't worn to her father's wedding to a woman she'd only met twice. About why she'd moved to New York with two suitcases and a dead dream of being an illustrator.

Eli told her about the novel. About the protagonist he'd been writing toward for six years and who kept changing on him. About the night his college girlfriend had told him she loved him and he'd panicked and said, *"That's a really strong draft of an emotion,"* and how he'd learned the hard way that not everything needed editing.

By the end of two weeks, they knew each other in the particular way that strangers sometimes did: deeply in places, completely unknown in others.

"Quick," Eli would say when they passed in the hallway of their shared brownstone. "Favorite color."

"You'd think I'd remember that."

"Favorite food."

"Pad thai, obviously. Yours?"

"Anything my grandmother made."

"Favorite movie."

"*Amelie*."

"*Amelie*?"

"Don't judge me. Yours?"

"*When Harry Met Sally*."

He groaned theatrically. "Meg Ryan."

"I will end this fake relationship before it begins."

"You'd miss me."

"I really, really wouldn't."

She would, and they both knew it.

---

**Week Three: The Cameras**

The crew was smaller than Maya had expected. Two camera operators, a sound tech, and a producer named Becca who wore cat-eye glasses and seemed to find everything delightful.

"Just be yourselves," Becca said on day one, which Maya thought was the most ridiculous piece of direction she'd ever received. Be yourself, but in front of cameras. Be yourself, but for an audience of millions. Be yourself, but knowing that every micro-expression was being analyzed by relationship experts who would appear on talk shows the next morning to discuss whether your eye contact indicated genuine intimacy or merely good acting.

She'd told Eli once, on their third pre-filming meeting, "I don't know how to be myself when I'm being watched."

"I don't think anyone does," he'd said. "Maybe that's the point."

The first night, the producers paired everyone off and let them meet on camera for the first time. Maya and Eli had been given a "first date" at a rooftop bar, complete with fairy lights and a string quartet playing Top 40 hits.

"You look nervous," Eli said, the moment they sat down. The cameras circled them like hungry birds.

"I'm not nervous."

"Your leg is bouncing."

"That's caffeine."

"You don't drink caffeine."

She laughed despite herself, and one of the cameras zoomed in on her smile.

---

**Week Five: The Cracks**

The trouble started with a kiss.

Not *the* kiss—that came later, in week eight, on a balcony at sunset, captured by a drone that had definitely not been in the contract—but the first kiss, which happened in the middle of an argument about whether Eli's character on the show should be more "outgoing."

"I just don't think I can be someone I'm not," he said.

They were in the confessional, the tiny interview room where cast members talked directly to camera about their feelings. Becca had specifically told them to use this space to be honest.

"I'm not asking you to be someone you're not," Maya said, aware that the camera was capturing the way her jaw tightened. "I'm asking you to be a version of someone you're not. There's a difference."

"That's such a writer thing to say."

"What's that supposed to mean?"

"It means you're using precision to avoid having an actual emotion."

The words hung in the air between them. Maya could feel the camera operator shifting uncomfortably outside the door.

"You're right," she said quietly. "I'm scared."

"Of what?"

"Of doing this wrong. Of people watching me fail at something else." She paused. "My dad used to watch all those dating shows with his new wife. Commenting on the contestants. Saying how easy it looked. How he couldn't understand why anyone would struggle with love when the rules were so simple."

Eli didn't say anything for a long moment. Then he reached across and took her hand.

"I think," he said carefully, "we just did something honest."

They didn't kiss. But they both looked at each other like they wanted to.

---

**Week Eight: The Balcony**

The balcony scene was filmed six times.

The first take, Eli forgot his line. The second, a pigeon landed on Maya's shoulder. The third, the light was wrong. The fourth, someone in the background started laughing.

The fifth take, Maya got teary for real and they had to cut because the producers wanted the kiss to be "joyful, not emotional." The sixth take, she thought her heart might actually explode.

"You ready?" Eli asked, between takes, his forehead pressed against hers.

"I was born ready."

"Liar."

"The biggest."

He smiled, and she felt it in her chest.

When they actually filmed the scene—the real one, the one that would later be replayed on every clip show and meme account and Twitter thread—they didn't have to act. They just had to stop pretending they weren't feeling what they were feeling.

The kiss was soft. Slow. The kind of kiss that says, *I see you, I see me, I see us.*

Somewhere in the editing bay, Becca would later say, "That's the take. That's the one. Don't even look at the others."

---

**Week Ten: The Finale**

The final episode was filmed live in front of a studio audience. Maya stood on stage in a dress she'd borrowed from a friend, holding Eli's hand, trying to remember how to breathe.

The host—a man named Greg who had the smile of someone who had never questioned a single life choice—asked them the question Maya had been dreading for ten weeks.

"Maya, Eli. The question everyone wants to know." Greg paused for dramatic effect. "Was it real?"

The audience held its breath.

Maya looked at Eli. He looked back at her. In his eyes, she saw the boy who'd panicked at his college girlfriend's confession. She saw the man who'd spent six years writing toward a character he couldn't quite reach. She saw someone who had been just as scared as she was, and just as hopeful, and just as confused about what they were doing here.

She thought about saying *no*. About being honest about the contract and the cameras and the fifty thousand dollars. About protecting herself from the inevitable heartbreak of being on a stage and realizing that the person you loved might not love you back in quite the same way.

Instead, she said: "I came here to pretend to be in love. I didn't expect to actually do it."

The audience erupted. Greg beamed. Eli made a sound that was half-laugh, half-sob.

"Maya," Greg said, "that's a beautiful answer. But I have to ask—is it the answer you rehearsed, or the answer that's true?"

"It's the answer that's true," she said, and even though she was looking at Greg, she was really looking at Eli. "Which is scarier."

Then she kissed him, and somewhere in the audience, Becca was crying into her cat-eye glasses.

---

**Epilogue: Six Months Later**

The novel was published in the spring. Eli dedicated it to "M.D., who taught me that some drafts don't need editing."

Maya saw it for the first time when she picked up her advance copy from the bookstore on Atlantic Avenue. She'd been living in Eli's apartment for three months, which was a thing that had happened, gradually and then all at once, like most important things did.

*Some drafts don't need editing.*

She took a picture of the dedication and sent it to him. He responded with a string of heart emojis and then, immediately after, a message that said: *"Actually, can you grab oat milk on your way home? We're out."*

And Maya, who had once moved across the country with two suitcases and a dead dream, who had once pretended to fall in love on national television, who had once believed that love was something you performed for an audience—

Maya smiled.

And went to get the oat milk.

---

*THE END*

Write a romance where your character falls in love with the last person they expected to. Plan for about 2000 words.

# The Last Person I Expected

The first time I met Hattie Boudreaux, she threw a wrench at my truck.

Not *at* me, technically—just at the hunk of rusted metal I'd been trying to coax down the back roads of Grand Marais for the better part of an hour. But it landed with a clang that made my teeth ache, and when I looked up from the engine block, she was standing in the middle of the dirt road with her arms crossed and murder in her eyes.

"You gonna sit there all day, or you gonna move it?"

I blinked. "It's broken down."

"Clearly." She wore paint-spattered overalls and a shirt that had seen better decades. Her hair was pulled back in a knot so tight it looked punitive. "This is a private road."

"This is a public road. It's been a public road since—"

"It's been *my* road since my family built this place in 1942. You block it, you're gonna hear about it."

I stared at her. She stared at me. Somewhere behind her, a rooster crowed like it had opinions.

I was not in the mood. I'd driven six hours from Minneapolis to get away from a life that had imploded in slow motion—my fiancée sleeping with my best friend, my business partner bleeding our accounts dry, my sister calling every two hours to check if I'd eaten. The last thing I needed was a feral woman with a wrench and a grievance.

I moved the truck. She watched me the whole way, arms still crossed, like I might try something.

"You lost?" she called as I passed.

"I'm looking for a rental."

"Then you're lost. Closest rental's forty minutes that way." She pointed back toward the highway I'd come from.

I closed my eyes. Breathed. "Any chance there's anywhere closer?"

"No."

"You're sure."

"Positive."

I parked the truck and turned off the engine. She watched me get out, get my bag from the back, start walking.

"Where are you going?"

"Forty minutes that way."

She laughed. It wasn't a nice laugh. "It's gonna rain."

I looked up. The sky was a bruise color, fat clouds rolling in off the lake. I kept walking.

It rained, of course. It rained so hard I was soaked within five, my suitcase dragging through the mud, my sneakers squelching like they were trying to escape. I made it maybe a mile before I heard the sound of an engine behind me.

A battered pickup pulled up beside me. The window rolled down.

She didn't say anything. Just unlocked the passenger door.

I stood there, dripping, for what felt like an eternity.

"I'm not going to apologize," she said.

"I didn't ask you to."

"Good."

I got in. The cab smelled like sawdust and dog. She had a dog, actually—a huge gray thing that sat in the space between us, panting heavily.

"His name is Chester," she said, unprompted.

"Hi, Chester."

"He's friendly."

"Great."

We drove in silence. The wipers beat a frantic rhythm. I was shivering by the time she turned off the road, up a gravel drive, and parked in front of a sprawling, ramshackle house with a porch that wrapped around it like a hug.

"I have a guest room," she said, not looking at me. "You can stay the night. One night. Then you leave."

"Why?"

She finally looked at me. Her eyes were a startling green, like new leaves, and for the first time I noticed the small scar that ran through her left eyebrow.

"Because you're pathetic and you're gonna get pneumonia and die in a ditch, and I'd rather not have that on my conscience."

---

I didn't die in a ditch. I spent the night in a small bedroom that smelled like cedar and old books, listening to rain on the roof and the soft snoring of Chester, who'd decided to sleep at the foot of my bed without asking.

In the morning, I went downstairs to find Hattie at the kitchen table, reading a book and drinking coffee out of a mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST MECHANIC.

"There's coffee," she said, not looking up.

"Thank you."

"I didn't make it for you."

"I know."

She went back to her book. I poured myself a cup and sat across from her. She had a stack of books beside her—paperbacks with cracked spines and dog-eared pages. I recognized some of them. Mystery novels, mostly. Old ones.

"You read a lot," I said.

"You don't."

"How would you know?"

"You haven't stopped talking since you got here."

I shut up. She turned a page. The dog was eating out of his bowl in the corner, making a tremendous noise.

After a while, she said, "There's a town meeting tonight. At the VFW. They're voting on whether to tear down the old theater."

"Why?"

"Because nothing lasts, that's why."

I looked at her. She was staring at her book, but I had the sense she wasn't reading.

"I could fix your truck," I said.

"I don't need my truck fixed."

"It's making a noise."

"Every truck on this road makes a noise."

"This one sounds expensive."

She looked up then. Studied me. I had the feeling of being measured.

"You a mechanic?"

"I ran a restoration business. Cars, mostly. Vintage stuff."

"And now you don't."

"And now I don't."

"Why?"

I took a sip of coffee. It was the best coffee I'd had in months. "Long story."

She went back to her book. "I don't like long stories."

"Then you'll like this one. It's short. I got robbed by my best friend, betrayed by my fiancée, and decided to drive to the end of the world until I ran out of gas."

She didn't laugh. But she didn't not laugh, either. Something around her mouth softened, just barely.

"There's a part in the distributor cap," she said. "If you can find it."

I went out to the truck. It took me twenty minutes. The part was indeed shot—I could see why it was making the noise—and I had a spare in my toolbox. I was tightening the last bolt when she came out and stood over me.

"You didn't have to do that."

"I know."

"Why did you do that?"

I sat up. She was backlit by the sun, and her hair had come loose from its knot, and she looked—for the first time—like someone who hadn't been angry in a while. Someone who maybe wanted to stop being angry but didn't know how.

"I don't know," I said.

She held out her hand. I took it. She pulled me to my feet and didn't let go right away.

"Stay for dinner," she said. "One night."

"Okay."

---

One night became two. Two became a week. A week became a month, and somewhere in there, without either of us really noticing, it became something else.

She taught me how to fix things—not just cars, but everything. The screen door that wouldn't close right. The pump that groaned when you primed it. The henhouse roof that leaked in six different places. I had been a person who made things beautiful again, in my old life. She was a person who made things *work*. I realized, slowly, that I had been fooling myself. Beauty without function was just decoration.

She let me help with the animals. She let me drive the truck into town for supplies. She let me sit beside her on the porch in the evenings, watching the light go out of the sky, drinking beer she didn't like but kept for guests who never came.

She didn't let me touch her. Not yet. Not for a long time.

But she let me stay.

---

The night of the theater vote, we drove into town together. The VFW was packed—everyone in a fifty-mile radius seemed to be there, arguing about taxes and progress and what it meant that the young people kept leaving.

Hattie sat in the back, her arms crossed, watching the proceedings like they were a personal insult.

"They're going to tear it down," she said.

"You don't know that."

"Yes, I do."

"Why does it matter?"

She looked at me like I'd said something stupid. "It was built in 1938. By hand. By people who had nothing. It's the only thing in this town that means anything."

"You mean something."

"Don't be sweet. I can't stand it."

"I'm not being sweet. I'm being accurate."

She looked away. But I saw her mouth do the thing it did when she was trying not to smile.

They voted to tear it down. Hattie stood up in the middle of the announcement, walked out of the building, and didn't speak to me on the drive home. I parked the truck and went to the guest room. I lay awake for hours, listening to her pace above me.

In the morning, she was gone. There was a note on the kitchen table.

*Came to town. Don't wait up.*

I waited up. She came home at midnight, smelling like sawdust and old wood.

"I bought it," she said.

"What?"

"The theater. The bank was selling it. I bought it."

"With what?"

"My savings."

"Hattie—"

"Don't." She was standing in the doorway, arms crossed, like she was bracing for a blow. "Don't tell me I'm crazy. Don't tell me I can't afford it. Don't tell me I should have talked to you first."

"I wasn't going to say any of that."

"What were you going to say?"

I walked over to her. She didn't move.

"I was going to say," I said, "that I've never met anyone braver than you. And that I think I've been in love with you since you threw that wrench at my truck."

She stared at me. Her eyes were wet, which I would learn, over time, was the only sign of tears she ever allowed herself.

"You don't know what you're saying."

"I do."

"I'm difficult. I'm stubborn. I'm mean to strangers."

"I know."

"I've been alone for a long time. I don't know how to do this."

"Neither do I."

She looked at me for a long moment. Then she reached up—slowly, like she was expecting me to flinch—and put her hand on the side of my face.

"If you leave," she said, "I'll break your heart."

"I know."

"You might leave anyway."

"I might."

"You might wake up one day and decide I'm too much."

"I won't."

"You don't know that."

"I know me," I said. "And I'm not going anywhere."

She kissed me. It was the first time. It was not the last.

Outside, the rain had started again, beating on the roof like it had somewhere to be. Chester barked once, from somewhere in the house, then settled. And I stood there in the doorway of a woman I'd known for six weeks, in a town I'd never heard of, in a life I couldn't have imagined, and I felt—for the first time in years—like I'd finally come home.

---

Years later, when people ask me how we met, I tell them the truth.

I tell them she threw a wrench at my truck.

I tell them she called me pathetic.

I tell them I spent the night in her guest room, and woke up the next morning to the smell of coffee, and the sound of a dog eating, and the quiet company of a woman who didn't know yet that she was going to save my life.

And I tell them this: that love, real love, the kind that lasts—it doesn't come when you expect it. It doesn't come when you're ready. It comes when you're broken down on a dirt road in the rain, and a stranger with a wrench pulls up beside you, and you make the choice to get in.

It comes in the last person you'd ever choose.

And it turns out to be the only one that matters.

# The Algorithm of Us

Maya Okonkwo was late, which was ironic because she had spent her entire career optimizing other people's schedules. As a productivity consultant, she had once reorganized a bakery's entire inventory system during a croissant shortage, and now she couldn't find her own car keys.

"They're on the counter," said her roommate, Devon, not looking up from his laptop.

"I know that."

"You've said 'I know that' three times this week about things that were on the counter."

Maya found the keys. They were, predictably, on the counter. She grabbed her bag and paused.

"What time is my 2 PM again?"

"Your 2 PM is at 2:30 now. You moved it."

"I—what?"

"You moved it. You have notes. You did this."

"I did not move my—Devon, you have to stop listening to my appointments."

"You leave your calendar open on the shared screen, Maya."

She left before he could finish the sentence, which was probably for the best because she had a lot of them and he had opinions about all of them.

---

The client meeting was at a co-working space called The Nest, which Maya had always thought sounded like either a startup incubator or a Hitchcock film. She was here to restructure the daily operations of a small dating-app company called Alignr, whose tagline was "Real Connections, No Games."

She hated it immediately.

The CEO, a former couples therapist named Eleanor Chen, met Maya in the lobby with a handshake that communicated both warmth and an unreasonable number of push notifications.

"Welcome to chaos," Eleanor said cheerfully.

"I prefer to call it 'untapped potential,'" Maya replied, which was something she'd said to a candle company last week.

Eleanor gave her a tour. There were beanbags. There was a kombucha tap. There were seventeen motivational posters and only two of them were ironic.

"And this is our analytics team," Eleanor said, gesturing toward a glass-walled room where four people sat hunched over laptops like they were solving a murder that only they knew about.

One of them looked up.

His name was Sam Park, and he was the lead data scientist, which meant he spent his days trying to mathematically prove that love existed. He had a PhD in statistics and a habit of pausing mid-sentence when he realized he was about to say something embarrassing, which happened more often than you'd think.

He looked up, registered Maya's presence, and immediately returned to his screen.

"Was that rude?" Eleanor asked.

"No," Maya said. "That was efficient. I respect efficient."

---

Sam was not avoiding Maya.

He was simply very focused on his work, which happened to be in the opposite direction of wherever she was.

Their first meeting was in a conference room called The Aviary, which Maya noted had no windows, possibly by design.

"Thank you for coming in," Eleanor said. "We need your help. Our matching algorithm is failing."

"Failing how?" Maya asked.

"It's matching people too well."

Maya set down her pen.

"I'm sorry. Too well?"

"They're going on dates," Eleanor said, as if this were a pest problem. "Real dates. In person. Having conversations. We have a 94% message-to-meeting ratio, and our users are forming genuine attachments. It's a disaster."

Maya looked at Sam. Sam looked at the table.

"Our investors want a hookup app," Eleanor continued. "They want dopamine hits, not depth. They want matches that fizzle in three days, not relationships that last three decades. We have a meeting in six weeks to present a new direction, and I—"

She stopped. Composed herself.

"I built this company on the belief that people deserve better. Not better in the shallow sense. Better in the *soul* sense. And now I have to pretend I don't believe that, or I'll lose the funding that lets me keep believing it."

The room was quiet.

"I'm not asking you to build something fake," Eleanor said. "I'm asking you to help me figure out how to build something honest that also doesn't get me fired."

Sam finally looked up. "She cried in the last pitch meeting," he said quietly. "The investors thought she was being dramatic. She's allergic to dishonesty."

"Sam."

"It's relevant context."

Maya looked at both of them.

"Okay," she said. "I think I can help."

---

Working with Sam turned out to be the most infuriating experience of Maya's professional life.

Not because he was difficult. Because he wasn't.

He was thoughtful. He was careful. He sent his work in clean, clearly labeled documents with no typos and no nonsense. He asked questions that made her rethink assumptions she'd held for years. When she pushed back, he didn't get defensive; he got curious.

It was awful.

The first time they disagreed, it was about user feedback forms.

"We should ask 'What are you looking for?'" Maya said.

"We shouldn't," Sam replied.

"People want to be asked."

"People want to be asked what they already think. They don't want to be asked what they don't know they want."

"That's pretentious."

"That's literally my job."

She stared at him. He met her eyes. Neither of them blinked.

"You're right," she said.

"I know."

"That was annoying."

"Sorry."

He didn't look sorry at all.

---

They fell into a routine.

Coffee at 8:30. Standup at 9:00. Work in the same room until lunch, then separate until 3, then back together until Eleanor kicked them out at 7.

They did not, Maya noticed, have any chemistry.

This was a problem, because Maya had been hired to *optimize* things, and somewhere along the way she had stopped optimizing their workflow and started optimizing their proximity.

She recognized the signs. She'd seen them in clients.

The "accidental" touches when passing laptops. The way she laughed too long at his statistics jokes, even when they weren't funny (they were sometimes funny). The fact that she had started wearing the blue sweater he once complimented, which she would admit to no one, especially Devon, who would absolutely never let her live it down.

She was, to her horror, developing feelings for someone who communicated clearly.

It was the most inconvenient thing that had ever happened to her.

---

"Maya," Devon said one evening. "We need to talk."

"We absolutely do not."

"You're wearing the blue sweater."

"I wear a lot of sweaters."

"You own three sweaters. You have rotated them since 2019. That is new."

"It's not new. I bought it. Months ago."

"It's got the tag still on."

Maya looked down. It did, in fact, still have the tag on.

"He's a data scientist," she said, in lieu of explanation.

"Is that good?"

"He uses words like 'longitudinal' and 'confound' and he knows what they mean."

"And?"

"And he told me my framework for client intake was elegant."

Devon sat down slowly.

"Maya. That's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about your work."

"I know."

"Go for it."

"I can't go for it. I *work* with him."

"Like half the population."

"Like people who have to see each other on Monday."

Devon considered this. "You see each other every day now."

"I know."

"You see each other *here*."

"I KNOW, Devon."

He raised an eyebrow. She threw a cushion at him.

---

The breakthrough came on a Tuesday.

They had been arguing about the algorithm for three hours. Maya wanted to incorporate emotional intelligence metrics; Sam said quantifying emotions was a fool's errand.

"You're reducing people to numbers," she said.

"I'm not reducing them. I'm *finding* them. There's a difference."

"There's not."

"There is. The numbers are already there. I'm just reading them."

"That's what stalkers say."

Sam stopped. He looked at her, really looked at her, and Maya realized with a start that he was hurt.

She sat down.

"Sam."

"It's okay."

"It's not. I shouldn't have said that."

"No, you shouldn't have."

"I was trying to win the argument."

"I know."

"I do that."

"I know."

She took a breath. "I'm scared," she said.

"Of what?"

"Of being wrong. Of building something that doesn't work. Of caring about something and having it fail."

Sam was quiet for a moment. "I'm scared of the same thing," he said. "I run statistics all day because if I can find the pattern, I can control the outcome. And I know that's not how life works, but it's how I cope."

Maya felt something shift in her chest. It was small, like a key turning in a lock.

"Can we try again?" she asked.

"Please."

---

They tried again.

The new version of the algorithm didn't try to predict who you'd fall in love with. It asked better questions: What kind of person do you want to become? What kind of person do you want to spend a hard day with? What kind of person would you want to call when you got good news?

It was messier. The matching was less precise. The users complained, at first.

Then they didn't.

Eleanor cried in the second pitch meeting, but this time the investors were crying too.

"We want to invest more," one of them said.

"You said this was a bad direction," Eleanor replied, wiping her eyes.

"It is a bad direction. It's also the right direction. We're confused."

"Good," Eleanor said. "Confusion is the first step."

---

After the meeting, Maya and Sam sat on the roof of the co-working space, legs dangling over the edge of a city that did not care about their algorithm.

"We did it," Sam said.

"We did."

"You were right, by the way."

"About which part?"

"The emotional intelligence metrics. They made the algorithm better."

"I know."

"That was annoying."

"Sorry."

He smiled. She smiled back. It was the kind of moment that people write songs about, except the songs are usually a little more dramatic and don't involve two tired people with laptops.

"Maya," Sam said.

"Sam."

"Can I take you to dinner?"

"Yes."

"Just yes? Not 'let me check my calendar'?"

"My calendar is clear."

"It is not."

"How do you know that?"

"I may have looked."

She turned to look at him fully. "Sam Park. Did you look at my calendar?"

"You leave it open."

"On the shared screen?"

"It was right there."

She stared at him. "Take me to dinner."

"Where?"

"Anywhere. I don't care. I've been optimizing my whole life. I just want someone who shows up."

He took her hand.

"I can do that," he said.

---

Two years later, at their wedding, Eleanor gave a toast.

"When I hired Maya, I thought I was hiring a consultant," she said. "When I hired Sam, I thought I was hiring a data scientist. What I actually did was introduce two people who would spend six weeks arguing about whether emotions could be quantified, fall in love over the disagreement, and then build a company based on the principle that they shouldn't be."

She raised her glass.

"To the algorithm of us. May it always be slightly inefficient, deeply human, and full of terrible, beautiful questions."

Everyone cheered.

Maya looked at Sam. Sam looked at Maya.

They did not blink.

---

**THE END**

# The Cartographer of Joy

Margaret spent three Saturdays in the antique district before she gave up on clocks. Her partner, Elliot, was a man who already owned three watches he never wore, claiming he preferred to feel the day rather than count it.

She moved on to books. She lingered in the poetry section of Holloway & Sons, running her fingers along spines, searching for a collection that might speak to him the way Neruda had once made him weep on their third date. But the more she read, the more she realized she was searching for a moment rather than a book.

By the fourth week, Margaret had become a regular at seven different shops. The woman at the leather goods store knew her coffee order. The man at the vintage map shop saved things in the back for her. She had a small notebook now, and she wrote in it constantly—not lists, but observations. Things Elliot said. Things that made him pause.

*"I always wondered what the coast of Portugal sounds like in October."*
*"Do you think stars get lonely?"*
*"I'd like to learn something useless and beautiful."*

On a rainy Tuesday, she found it.

The map shop had a corner she hadn't explored, up a narrow staircase that creaked like an old ship. There, on a table by the window, was a blank journal. Not a notebook exactly—more like a field guide with no species listed. The pages were thick and cream-colored, meant for watercolor or ink, and the cover was soft green leather that smelled like libraries.

She thought of Elliot immediately. Not the journal, but the empty space inside it.

That evening, she wrapped it in brown paper and tied it with twine. She wrote on a small card: *For the places you'll go and the things you'll learn to love, useless and beautiful.*

When Elliot unwrapped it, he was quiet for a long time. He opened the first page. He opened the last. He ran his thumb along the spine the way he sometimes did with books he wanted to remember.

"Margaret," he said finally. "I don't have a thing for this."

"I know."

"I've never had a journal. I don't know what I'd even—"

"You don't have to know." She touched the cover. "That's the point. It's not finished yet."

He looked at her then, really looked, the way he had that first night when she'd told him about her grandmother's garden and how the tomatoes always tasted like something remembered rather than something eaten.

"You saw me," he said.

"I always see you."

He held the journal like a small, green door, and Margaret understood at last that she had not been searching for a gift at all. She had been searching for a way to say: *I have been paying attention. I have been listening. Here is a place to put all the things you are, and all the things you are still becoming.*

The perfect gift, she decided, was never an object.

It was evidence.

And Elliot, who preferred to feel the day rather than count it, opened the journal that very night and began to write.
