# Le Café des Âmes Recommencées

## Chapitre 1 : La dernière gorgée

Élise referma la porte de l'appartement derrière elle pour la dernière fois. Derrière, il y avait les cartons, les meubles vendus, les murs repeints en blanc. Devant, il y avait le silence d'une rue qu'elle connaissait par cœur et qu'elle s'apprêtait à oublier.

Elle marchait vers la gare quand elle le vit. Un café qu'elle n'avait jamais remarqué, coincé entre une librairie fermée et un passage sans nom. L'enseigne, en lettres dorées à demi effacées, proclamait : *Au Dernier Souffle*. Curieuse, elle poussa la porte.

L'intérieur sentait le café moulu, le bois ancien et quelque chose de plus doux, comme la vanille ou le temps passé. Un piano demi-queue trônait dans un coin. Un chat roux dormait sur le comptoir. Et derrière celui-ci se tenait un homme âgé, aux yeux clairs comme de l'eau de source, qui l'observait avec une tranquillité étrange.

— Vous avez l'air de quelqu'un qui commence quelque chose, dit-il.

— Ou qui termine, répondit Élise.

— Ce n'est jamais l'un ou l'autre, mademoiselle. C'est toujours entre les deux.

Il lui servit un espresso sans lui demander ce qu'elle voulait. Elle but la première gorgée, et quelque chose en elle se desserra.

## Chapitre 2 : Les habitués

Le café devint son refuge quotidien. Elle y venait chaque matin avant de partir à la recherche de son nouveau logement, chaque après-midi quand le découragement la gagnait. Et peu à peu, elle commença à voir les autres clients.

Il y avait Marianne, une ancienne pianiste qui avait perdu l'usage de ses mains dans un incendie. Elle ne jouait plus, mais venait s'asseoir près du piano chaque jour, comme pour retrouver quelque chose par la simple proximité des touches. Le vieil homme — qui s'appelait Théodore — lui avait offert un rôle : elle tournait les pages pour les rares clients qui osaient jouer.

Il y avait Samuel, un médecin qui avait quitté l'hôpital après avoir perdu un enfant qu'il n'avait pas pu sauver. Il s'occupait maintenant du chat roux, qu'il avait nommé Silence, et lisait des livres de poésie en caressant la fourrure du mat roux.

Il y avait enfin Camille, une jeune femme d'à peine vingt-deux ans qui fuyait un mariage arrangé. Elle ne parlait presque jamais, mais ses yeux disaient tout. Théodore lui avait donné un tablier. Elle servait les cafés.

## Chapitre 3 : Les murs qui parlent

Un soir de novembre, alors que la pluie battait les vitres, Théodore leur monta l'arrière-boutique. C'était un salon aux murs entièrement recouverts de photographies, de lettres, de dessins. Il y avait des centaines de visages, des centaines d'histoires.

— Chaque personne qui est passée ici a laissé quelque chose, dit-il. Pas pour se souvenir d'avant, mais pour se rappeler d'où elle est partie vers l'après.

Élise comprit alors. Ce café n'était pas un lieu de restauration. C'était un lieu de passage. Un seuil entre ce qu'on avait été et ce qu'on deviendrait.

— Pourquoi nous ? demanda Samuel.

— Parce que vous n'avez plus rien à perdre, répondit Théodore. Et quand on n'a plus rien à perdre, on peut tout recommencer.

## Chapitre 4 : Le premier recommencement

Les semaines passèrent. Élise trouva un petit appartement au dernier étage d'un immeuble ancien, avec une vue sur les toits et le ciel. Elle recommença à écrire, d'abord des mots sur des bouts de papier, puis des phrases, puis des histoires. Elle n'était plus la même femme qui avait quitté son ancienne vie ; elle était celle qui en avait laissé une mourir pour qu'une autre puisse naître.

Marianne, un matin d'hiver, posa ses doigts usés sur les touches du piano. Ce n'était pas parfait. Ses mains tremblaient. Mais elle joua une note, puis deux, puis un accord. Le café entier se tut. Silence descendit du comptoir pour s'approcher d'elle, comme pour écouter.

Samuel ouvrit un cabinet de médecin dans une rue voisine, où il soignait gratuitement les sans-abri. Il disait que c'était sa façon de rendre au monde ce qu'il avait failli lui prendre.

Camille écrivit à sa famille pour la première fois. Pas pour demander pardon, pas pour supplier. Juste pour dire : *Je suis vivante, et c'est à moi que je choisis désormais de plaire.*

## Chapitre 5 : Le seuil

Un an plus tard, Élise vint au café pour la dernière fois. Théodore, plus vieux, plus transparent, presque immatériel, lui sourit.

— Vous partez ?

— Je reste, dit-elle. Mais je ne suis plus celle qui avait besoin de venir ici.

Il acquiesça.

— Le café ferme ce soir, dit-il simplement. Chaque lieu de recommencement a une fin, sinon il devient un piège. Vous êtes prêts, tous les quatre, à marcher seuls maintenant.

Marianne jouait du piano dans un théâtre du quartier. Samuel soignait ses patients avec la lumière dans les yeux. Camille dirigeait une galerie d'art. Élise publia son premier roman, qu'elle dédia à un café sans nom et à son propriétaire qui n'avait jamais semblé tout à fait vivant, mais qui leur avait rendu à tous un peu de leur existence.

Dehors, le soleil se couchait sur la ville, comme chaque soir, comme chaque recommencement.

Et quelque part, dans une rue qu'ils oubliaient déjà, l'enseigne *Au Dernier Souffle* se balançait doucement dans le vent, attendant le prochain passant qui aurait besoin de comprendre que la fin d'une chose n'est jamais que le début silencieux d'une autre.

**FIN**

# The Cartographer's Compass

The brass compass had belonged to my grandfather, and his grandfather before him. It sat on the corner of my desk for three years before I noticed anything unusual.

I was working late on a topographic map of the Cascade Range when the needle began to tremble. At first, I thought it was a truck passing on the street below. But the needle didn't settle. It spun slowly, deliberately, like a searchlight sweeping the dark, and came to rest pointing not north—never north anymore—but toward the window.

"You see it too, then," said a voice.

The compass lid was open. I was certain I had closed it.

A tiny figure stood on the pivot point, no taller than a paperclip. He wore a long coat made of what looked like vellum, and spectacles that caught the lamplight. His face was weathered and kind, mapped with lines like the very contours I spent my days drawing.

"I'm sorry," I managed. "I didn't mean to—"

"Three years," he said, adjusting his spectacles. "Three years you've had me, and never once wound me properly. Do you know how long a cartographer's compass can sleep? Centuries, if it must. But it wakes when it senses someone drawing lies."

"Lies?"

He gestured at my desk, where my half-finished map lay curled. "See that ridge there? You placed it a quarter mile east of where it actually sits. You did it because it looked better there. Because it made the composition cleaner."

"It's a small error—"

"There are no small errors in a map. A map is a promise. People follow it. They trust it with their lives." He stepped carefully to the edge of the compass face and peered down at my work. "I've been carried by surveyors across continents. I've drawn the routes of gold seekers and lost children and lovers trying to find each other in unfamiliar cities. I am very old, and I am very tired of liars."

I felt my face grow warm. "I won't make errors again."

"No," he said. "You won't."

He snapped his fingers, and the room around me tilted. Suddenly I was standing in a forest—a real one, pine-scented and dim, the trees pressing close. The tiny man was gone, but I could feel the compass heavy in my pocket, its pull strong against my thigh.

"Find your way home," said his voice, disembodied now, distant. "Without a map. Without a lie. Walk."

I walked for hours. The forest seemed to shift around me, paths appearing and vanishing. Once, I came to a river that I could not see on any map I'd ever studied, wide and black and quick. I had to wade across, and the water came to my chest, and the cold nearly stopped my heart.

But I found the road at last. I found my way home.

The compass sat on my desk where I'd left it. The lid was closed. When I opened it, the needle pointed north—steady, true, patient.

Inside the lid, in script so fine I could barely read it, were new words: *Trust the ground beneath your feet. Draw only what you have walked.*

I never made another error on a map. And I never carried the compass without winding it first, whispering thank you to the little man in the vellum coat who showed me, at the cost of a long and frightened walk through dark trees, that the truest paths are the ones we earn with our own blundering, honest feet.

彼の仕事は、絵を描くことだった。

画面の端に置いたコッカフェのフィルターにゆっくりと湯を注ぐ。蒸気が立ち上り、かすかなコーヒーの香りが漂う。彼はそれを左手に持ち替えながら、イラストソフトの画面を見つめた。

ペンを走らせる。

最初の一筆はいつも怖かった。白いキャンバスに何もない状態から何かを生み出す行為は、雄一にとって常に小さな跳躍だった。

だが、午前三時の世界は違っていた。

なぜ自分はこうなのだろう。日中、仕事の合間にほんの少しの時間を作って絵を描くことはできるはずだ。週末にゆっくりと時間を取ることもできるはずだ。なのに、彼が筆を走らせることができるのは、いつもこの時間だった。

電車に揺られながら、雄一はいつも自分の愚かさを呪う。夜更かしはいけない。睡眠不足は仕事の効率を下げる。医者に言わせれば「規則正しい生活が望ましい」のだろう。

だが、午後七時に帰宅してデスクに向かった時、彼の手は止まったままだった。目の前にあるのは、何も描かれていない白いキャンバス。心は重く、思考は散漫になり、指先は画面の上で迷子になる。

午前三時、雄一はついに筆を止めて、画面の向こう側に座った。

そこには、深い森に囲まれた古い神社が、静かに佇んでいた。苔に覆われた石段、巨大な杉、しめ縄、小さな祠、そして狐。彼が描いた世界は、彼自身を映し出す鏡のようでもあった。

暗い夜の中でこそ、雄一は光を見ることができる。

窓の外では、夜明けが近づいている。空の端がわずかに紫に染まり始めている。雄一は保存ボタンを押して、画面を閉じた。

ベッドに入り、毛布にくるまる。すぐに睡魔が襲ってくる。彼の体は、この時間になると自動的に眠りに落ちる。

翌朝、また同じことの繰り返しだろう。電車の中で自分の不規則な生活を呪り、日中はぼんやりと仕事をし、夕方には絶望し、そして夜に救われる。

「いつになったら、堂々と夜更かしができるようになるんだろう」

雄一はよくそう考えた。

だが、根本的な問題は別のところにあるのかもしれなかった。

彼が昼の世界を嫌うのは、昼の世界が「正しく」すぎるからだ。朝は起きるべきで、夜は眠るべきで、日中は働き、夜は休むべきで——。

その「べき」という鎖が、彼の創造性を縛り付けている。昼の世界は、社会の期待と他者の視線に満ちている。夜の世界は、雄一だけの世界だ。

ベッドの中で、雄一は天井を見つめながら考えた。

もしかしたら、彼は間違った人間なのかもしれない。普通の人々は昼に活動し、夜に眠る。それができない自分は、どこか欠陥があるのかもしれない。

だが、その「欠陥」こそが、彼を画家にしている。

眠りに落ちる直前、雄一の脳裏に一つの情景が浮かんだ。夜の神社で、狐が若い女性を森の奥に導いていく。その先にあるのは、——

彼は眠りに落ちた。

翌晩も、きっとまたあの暗い部屋で、あの光の中で、新しい物語が生まれるだろう。雄一はそれを止めるつもりはなかった。止めることは、彼が画家であることを止めることと同じだったから。

朝の光がカーテンの隙間から差し込む。雄一のアラームが鳴る。彼はゆっくりと身を起こし、窓の外を見た。

街はすでに動いている。車が走り、人々が歩いている。昼の世界は、もう始まっている。

雄一は小さくため息をついて、洗面台に向かった。

今夜も、きっと絵を描く。そのために、日中は眠い目をこすりながら働き、夕方には絶望し、そして夜に救われる。

それは彼の生き方で、彼だけの生き方だった。

# The Weight of Seconds

The first time Eleanor Chen stepped outside of time, she was twenty-six years old and standing in the produce section of a Kroger in Cincinnati, trying to decide between two avocados.

She reached for the one on the left—a small, irrational preference she didn't bother to question—and the world went sideways.

There was no flash of light, no tunnel, no chorus of angels. There was simply a *skip*, like a stone jumping across water, and then she was somewhere else.

Not somewhere foreign. Just somewhere *wrong*.

The avocados were the same. The fluorescent lights hummed the same indifferent hum. But the woman at the end of the aisle was holding a different child by the hand—a girl with blonde hair where the previous girl had had brown—and the price on the oranges had changed.

Eleanor blinked. She blinked again. The woman with the blonde child was walking away, oblivious, and Eleanor was standing in a grocery store that was both hers and not hers, holding an avocado that might have been the same avocado or might not have been.

She put it back. She bought the other one. She went home and sat on the edge of her bed and did not sleep for thirty-one hours.

---

She didn't try again for three months.

In that time, she became a scientist of her own small catastrophe. She read about quantum mechanics. She read about parallel universes and the many-worlds interpretation. She read about the placebo effect and psychosomatic disorders and the fragile architecture of memory. She went to her doctor and told him she had been having dizzy spells, and he told her she was probably stressed, and she believed him for almost a full week.

But the avocado kept sitting in her fruit bowl, ripening or not ripening, and she kept thinking about the blonde child.

So she tried again. Deliberately this time. Standing in her apartment at midnight, eyes closed, she *willed* the skip.

Nothing happened.

She tried again the next night. And the next. On the fourth night, exhausted and almost amused at herself, she thought not about teleporting but about a moment—the moment she had reached for the avocado, the small unreasonable choice—and something in her chest lurched, and she was back in the Kroger, three months earlier, the brown-haired girl in the distance.

She was learning the shape of the gift. If it was a gift. If she had chosen it. If she would survive it.

---

The rules arrived slowly, like tenants moving into a building one floor at a time.

She could only go to moments she herself had lived. The past was available; the future was not. She could not go to a place; she could only go to a *when*, and the when had to be tethered to her own body, her own history.

She could not change anything large. She tried once, going back to the week before her father died, and when she returned to her own present she found that he had still died, only now he had died angry at her, and the grief was a different color, worse, like a bruise pressed twice.

She could change small things. The avocado. The time she left for work. The email she almost sent and didn't. Each small change rippled outward, and each ripple cost her something—a memory she could no longer access, a person who no longer recognized her, a version of herself she could no longer quite remember being.

She began to keep a notebook. She began to lose entries in the notebook.

---

There was a man named Theo.

She met him in a bar in November, two years into her new life. He had kind eyes and a way of laughing that made her want to be the version of herself that deserved that laugh. He asked her what she did, and she said she worked in archives, which was almost true.

He asked her what she was afraid of, and she thought of her father's last week, the way she had tried to warn him about the road, the way he had not listened. She thought of the blonde child, who was and was not a child she knew.

"I'm afraid of forgetting who I am," she said.

He reached across the table and took her hand. "That's a good fear," he said. "The boring ones are the ones you have to worry about."

She loved him by the third date. She told him the truth by the sixth.

He didn't believe her at first. Then he did.

---

"You could go back and meet him earlier," she said one night, tracing the lines of his palm. They were lying in her bed, the curtains drawn, the city grumbling outside. "We could have more time."

"No," he said. He had thought about it. She could tell he had thought about it a lot.

"Why not?"

"Because you'd forget," he said. "Every time you go, you forget a little. You said so. And I'd rather have the Eleanor who knows me than the one who has known me for an extra year but doesn't remember my middle name."

"It's Nicholas," she said, surprised. "I remember."

"See," he said. "That's the one I want."

---

She used the gift sparingly after that. She used it to call in sick on days she would have regretted going to work. She used it to intercept an awkward email before it was sent. She used it to go back, just once, to the Kroger in Cincinnati, and buy the same avocado again, and watch the brown-haired girl laugh at something her mother had said, and return to her own present feeling—for a moment, only a moment—*grounded*.

She did not use it to save her father. She did not use it to undo the small cruelties of her childhood. She did not use it to bet on horses or win the lottery or assassinate tyrants in their cradles. She used it the way a person uses a small inheritance—not to become rich, but to feel, occasionally, that the world was not entirely indifferent.

She grew older. She forgot small things—where she put her keys, the name of a neighbor, the title of a movie she had loved. Theo was patient. Theo made her tea in the mornings and read to her in the evenings and, when she sometimes went quiet and distant, only sat with her and waited.

On their tenth anniversary, she went back to the day they had met. She watched herself walk into the bar—younger, frightened, lit up by something she could no longer name. She watched Theo look up from his drink. She watched him decide, in the space of a single breath, to speak to her.

She came back and found him waiting.

"How was it?" he asked.

"Like looking at a photograph of a fire," she said. "Beautiful, and not warm."

He held her for a long time.

---

When she was sixty-three, Theo got sick.

It was not a sudden thing. It was a slow withdrawal, like a tide going out. She watched him grow thinner, quieter, more apologetic for the trouble he was causing. She held his hand and told him not to be ridiculous. She memorized the shape of his knuckles, the particular way his breathing sounded at three in the morning.

She could have gone back. She could have tried to warn herself about something, to nudge him toward a different doctor, a different treatment, a different outcome. She thought about it. She thought about it for hours.

She did not go.

"Would it work?" Theo asked her, on a Tuesday, when the light through the window was the color of weak tea. He had been thinking about it too.

"I don't know," she said. "Probably not. The big things don't change."

"And the small things?"

"The small things cost more than you'd think."

He nodded. He closed his eyes. After a while he said, "I'm glad you told me. About the gift. About who you really were."

"I was scared you'd think I was crazy."

"I did think you were crazy," he said, smiling. "And then I thought you were the most honest person I'd ever met. Both things were true."

---

He died on a Thursday.

Eleanor did not go back. She sat with the body until the funeral home came. She chose the clothes he would be buried in. She signed the papers. She let her sister-in-law weep on her shoulder.

Later, alone, she opened the notebook. She had not used the gift in six years. She had forgotten what it felt like—the skip, the lurch, the strange new-old world waiting on the other side.

She thought about the week before he had died. She thought about the morning he had first told her he was tired all the time. She thought about the countless small moments she could revisit, the small changes she could make, the ways she could rewrite herself into someone who had lost less.

She closed the notebook. She put it in the drawer with the old passports and the silver candlesticks she never used.

She went to bed early. She dreamed, and in the dream Theo was laughing, and the laughing was the only sound in the world, and she woke up with her face wet and her hands empty and the slow, ordinary morning light coming in.

---

She was seventy-eight when she stepped outside of time for the last time.

She did not know it would be the last time. She only knew she was tired, and that the grocery store on the corner had avocados, and that she wanted to see her husband again, just once, just to be sure he had really been there.

She skipped.

She was standing in the produce section of a Kroger in Cincinnati. It was three in the afternoon on a Tuesday in the year she had been twenty-six. She could feel her knees, strong, her eyes young. She could see, at the end of the aisle, a woman holding the hand of a brown-haired girl.

She walked toward them. The woman looked up, annoyed at being jostled, and Eleanor met her own eyes—young eyes, afraid eyes, eyes that did not yet know what they would become.

She said nothing. There was nothing to say. She only looked, for a long moment, at the girl she had been.

Then she skipped again. She was home. She was old. She was exactly who she had decided to be.

She made herself a cup of tea. She sat in the chair by the window. Outside, the city went on with its small, ordinary business, and she let it.

Write about someone who misreads social cues, with escalating consequences. Total: ~1200 words.

# The Wrong Frequency

The bus was half-empty, so when Marjorie climbed aboard at her usual stop, she had her pick of seats. She chose the one beside a young man in a grey hoodie, because his window was closed and hers would be too, once she got up the nerve to ask.

"Excuse me," she said, settling in. "Would you mind if I opened the window? I find the recirculated air gives me a headache."

The young man looked at her with wide, startled eyes. He said nothing. He simply stood, clutching his backpack, and moved to the back of the bus.

Marjorie watched him go, mystified. *Did I ask wrong?* she wondered. *Was I supposed to say please twice?* She opened the window anyway, feeling the cool autumn air kiss her cheeks, and decided the young man must simply dislike windows.

She mentioned it to her colleague Dean at the coffee machine on Monday.

"He probably thought you were flirting," Dean said, laughing.

Marjorie stared at him. "Flirting? I asked about a window."

"You sat next to him when there were empty seats. That's a choice, Marjorie. And then you asked an intimate favour — *his* window. His air. You were speaking the language of seduction."

"That's ridiculous. That's *your* projection. I was simply being efficient."

"Sure," Dean said, still grinning. He topped up his mug and walked away, leaving Marjorie with a cooling Americano and a strange new thought lodged like a fishbone in her throat.

---

At the staff meeting on Thursday, Marjorie raised her hand to ask about the new filing system. Her manager, Priya, sighed — a long, weary exhalation — and said, "Marjorie, we've been over this. Three times."

"I don't recall."

"I know you don't. That's the issue."

Marjorie felt the room shift around her. Carol from Accounting was smirking at her shoes. Brian from Legal was studiously examining his laptop. She had done something wrong, but the social laws governing what, exactly, were invisible to her.

That night, she called her sister.

"Janet, am I — do people find me strange?"

"Define strange."

"I don't know. Hard to talk to. *Much.*"

Janet was quiet for a long time. Then she said, carefully, "Marjorie, you say what you think. People don't always know what to do with that."

"But I don't *say* what I think. I try so hard not to."

"Marge. You really don't."

---

The following week, Marjorie was fired.

The reasons given were a list of small things. She had told Priya, in front of the entire department, that her new haircut made her look like a flight attendant from 1987. She had told Brian, twice, that his tie was crooked, and then a third time, while reaching over to fix it herself. She had sent an all-staff email pointing out that the new project deadlines were mathematically impossible, complete with a pie chart. She had told Carol that her spreadsheet had fourteen errors, all of which Marjorie had circled in red pen, on the printout, before returning it silently to Carol's desk.

Marjorie, when she read the letter, did not see a woman who had been sacked. She saw a woman who had been helpful. She had told the truth. She had fixed the tie. She had *caught the errors.*

She took the letter home and laid it on her kitchen table and sat down across from it, the way one might sit across from a guest who has arrived unexpectedly and will not leave.

---

She got a job three weeks later, at a small publishing house. The office had only six people, and Marjorie liked this, because she thought she could keep them all straight in her mind.

On her first day, she brought in cupcakes from the bakery on the corner. She handed them out individually, naming each person as she did.

"For Marcus. For Priya — oh, sorry, a *different* Priya. For Hettie. For David."

She watched their faces. They were smiling, but the smiles had a quality she couldn't quite parse — like a song playing in a key she didn't recognize.

She decided she must have mispronounced someone's name. She practiced them under her breath all afternoon, like a student preparing for an oral exam.

---

The trouble began, as trouble so often does, with kindness.

She noticed that Hettie, the junior editor, often looked tired. Her blouses were sometimes misbuttoned. There were dark crescents under her eyes. Marjorie, who had a cousin with a thyroid condition, decided Hettie probably had a thyroid condition.

"You know," she said one afternoon, sliding into the chair opposite Hettie's desk, "I've been watching you, and I think you should see a doctor. Your fatigue could be any number of things."

Hettie looked up slowly. She had the expression of someone who has just stepped on a rake.

"I'm — I'm fine, Marjorie. Thank you."

"You're not fine. Your blouse is inside-out."

Hettie looked down. Her blouse was, in fact, inside-out. She went scarlet.

"Oh my God," she whispered.

"It's nothing to be embarrassed about. I do it too, sometimes. The dry cleaner once —"

"*Please stop talking.*"

Hettie's voice was so quiet that Marjorie almost didn't hear it. But she heard it.

She sat back in her chair. She had the strange, sinking feeling of a person who has stepped out onto a balcony that was not, in fact, a balcony.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I have made you feel something bad. I don't know what."

Hettie looked at her for a long moment. Then she said, in a very small voice, "You have no idea, do you."

"About what?"

"*Anything.*"

---

Marjorie went home that night and did not turn on the television. She sat in the dark kitchen and thought about her life.

She thought about the bus. About Dean, smirking. About Priya, sighing. About the letter on her kitchen table at the old apartment, which she had kept, folded into her copy of *Eats, Shoots & Leaves*.

She thought about Hettie's blouse, inside-out, and Hettie's face, a country whose customs she did not know.

She realized, slowly, that she had been living in a country whose customs she did not know. That she had been, all her life, speaking a language that no one else could hear. That her mouth had been moving, and her hands had been moving, and she had been so *certain* that she was making sense.

She pulled out her phone and texted her sister.

*I think I am missing a sense.*

Janet's reply came quickly.

*What do you mean?*

*Like being colour-blind. But for people.*

A long pause. The three dots appeared and disappeared three times before Janet's reply came through.

*Come over. I'll make tea.*

Marjorie put on her coat. She checked, in the hallway mirror, that her blouse was on the right way round. It was.

She stepped outside. A neighbour was walking his dog. She had always, before, said good morning to him. Tonight, she said nothing. She walked past with her head down, and the neighbour walked past with his head down, and the dog glanced at her once, briefly, before continuing on.

It was, Marjorie thought, the first correct interaction of her life.

Write about someone who’s hungry — for what, is up to you. Target length: ~900 words.

# A Fome de Clara

Clara acordava todos os dias com o mesmo vazio no estômago. Não era fome de pão, nem de arroz, nem de fruta. Era uma fome antiga, sem nome, que morava entre as costelas como um animal adormecido que às vezes abria os olhos.

Aos sete anos, pedia à mãe que lhe contasse histórias antes de dormir. A mãe, cansada do turno duplo na fábrica, suspirava e dizia:

— Amanhã, filha. Agora come o teu jantar e dorme.

Mas o jantar era sempre o mesmo: canjica rala, às vezes um ovo, quando havia. Clara comia devagar, mastigando cada garfada como se pudesse extrair dali alguma coisa que faltava. Não sabia ainda que havia fomes que a comida não sacia.

Aos quinze, descobriu os livros na biblioteca pública do bairro. O senhor Octávio, o bibliotecário, tinha mãos grossas de quem trabalhou na roça e olhos pequenos que enxergavam longe.

— Tu vens aqui quase todos os dias — disse ele, um sábado à tarde. — O que procuras?

Clara mordeu o lábio.

— Não sei. Qualquer coisa que me faça sentir menos… vazia.

O senhor Octávio sorriu, aquele sorriso lento de quem já viu muita coisa.

— Vazio é fome, menina. Toda gente tem uma. A diferença é o que a gente escolhe meter dentro.

Clara levou *Grande Sertão: Veredas* para casa como quem leva um pão quente entre as mãos. Leu a noite toda, devorando as palavras de Guimarães Rosa como se fossem os próprios rios, os próprios cavalos, a própria vastidão do mundo que ela nunca tinha visto. E pela primeira vez, o animal dentro dela se aquietou.

Na escola, era a aluna que mais lia. Os professores admiravam-se, alguns ficavam incomodados. Dona Marlene, a de português, dizia-lhe:

— Tu tens sede de saber, Clara. Isso é raro.

Sede, não fome. Mas Clara sabia que era fome. Uma fome boa, dessas que crescem conforme se alimenta, e por isso nunca se sacia de verdade.

Aos vinte e dois, formou-se em Letras. Ninguém da família tinha ido à universidade. O pai, que mal assinava o nome, chorou no dia da colação — não de tristeza, disse ele, mas porque finalmente via alguma coisa nascer direito naquela casa.

Clara foi dar aulas numa escola pública na periferia de Contagem. Ganhava pouco, dormia pouco, e aos domingos visitava a mãe, agora viúva, agora mais lenta, agora com aquela luz apaga nos olhos.

— Tu trabalha demais, filha — dizia a mãe, oferecendo-lhe café com leite. — Vai te matar.

— Não, mãe. É o que me mantém viva.

A mãe não entendia. Como podia o cansaço manter alguém vivo? Mas via a filha voltar àquela escola, todos os dias, com aquele brilho estranho no rosto, e pensava que talvez houvesse mesmo fome que não se mata com comida.

Numa terça-feira de março, Clara estava na sala dos professores, corrigindo redações, quando uma aluna nova se aproximou. Tinha uns treze anos, olhos grandes demais para o rosto magro, e segurava um caderno contra o peito como se fosse um escudo.

— Professora — disse a menina, a voz fina. — A senhora pode me ajudar a ler uma coisa?

Clara olhou para o caderno. Estava cheio de garranchos tortos, palavras que se atropelavam, frases que pareciam querer fugir do papel.

— O que é isso? — perguntou Clara, gentilmente.

— É uma história que eu tô escrevendo. Sobre uma menina que mora num lugar que não tem nome, e que um dia encontra uma porta que não devia existir.

Clara sentiu o animal dentro dela acordar. Não com a fome de antes, mas com outra coisa — uma espécie de reconhecimento, de ternura, de espanto.

— Senta aqui — disse ela, puxando a cadeira ao lado. — Me conta mais sobre essa porta.

A menina sentou-se. Começou a falar. E Clara ouvia como quem recebe uma herança, como quem finalmente entende por que tinha passado a vida inteira com fome.

Porque a fome — a verdadeira, a que não se mata com pão — não era um defeito. Era um chamado. Um sinal de que havia, dentro dela, um espaço grande demais para ser preenchido por uma vida só. Um espaço que só servia para dar, para abrir, para receber outros que também tinham fome.

A menina terminou de contar a história. Clara estava com os olhos molhados.

— Isso é muito bom — disse ela, com a voz um pouco trémula. — Isso é muito, muito bom.

A menina sorriu, meio sem jeito, meio esperançosa.

— A senhora acha mesmo?

— Acho. E sabe o que é o melhor?

— O quê?

— Que agora eu tô com fome de novo.

A menina riu, sem entender direito. Mas Clara sabia. Sabia que acabara de encontrar outra pessoa que carregava aquele animal dentro do peito — aquele bicho estranho, insaciável, maravilhoso, que só se alimenta de sonhos alheios e se sacia multiplicando-se.

E naquele momento, sentada naquela cadeira velha de escola pública, com o barulho do recreio entrando pela janela e o cheiro de merenda pairando no ar, Clara entendeu finalmente o que o senhor Octávio quisera dizer tantos anos atrás.

*Vazio é fome, menina. A diferença é o que a gente escolhe meter dentro.*

Ela tinha escolhido meter livros, histórias, palavras. Tinha escolhido meter-se inteira naquela fome, e por causa disso, ela nunca mais esteve sozinha.

E quando a aluna nova lhe perguntou se podiam se encontrar de novo na semana seguinte para continuar a história da porta, Clara disse que sim com a certeza absoluta de quem sabe que aquela fome — a sua, a dela, a de todos os que vieram antes e de todos os que viriam depois — era, no fim das contas, a coisa mais preciosa que existia.

Porque enquanto houvesse fome, haveria busca. E enquanto houvesse busca, haveria vida.

Write about someone who self-publishes a story that was never meant to be read. Around 1100 characters.

# 墨渍

林雾第一次注意到那个箱子，是在搬进这间租屋的第三天。

房子在城中村七巷的最深处，月租便宜得像是个错误。前任租客留下的东西大多已被房东清理干净，唯独床底这个落满灰尘的纸箱，仿佛被整个世界遗忘了。

箱子没有封口，里面是三十二本手写稿，用铁夹子按章节分好。纸张泛黄，是二十年前那种粗糙的土黄牛皮纸。林雾随手翻开第一本，字迹清秀却潦草，像是某种急切在驱动着笔尖。

他读了第一段就无法停下。

故事发生在一个叫"尘市"的地方，那里有座永远停在三点钟的钟楼，有家只在雨夜营业的旧书店，有一个每天买同一份报纸却从不阅读的男人。文字里有一种奇异的湿润感，仿佛每一个字都是从雨里捞出来的。

林雾读到凌晨四点。

第二天他旷了工，继续读。故事讲的是一个邮差，他的工作是投递那些永远不会被拆开的信件——那些收信人已经死去、失踪、或者从未存在过的信。邮差穿梭在尘市的小巷里，背包里装着无数个无人接收的秘密。

第三天清晨，林雾读完最后一页。合上本子的瞬间，他感到一种巨大的失落，像是被人从水底拽出水面。

箱底压着一张纸条：

"写给M。不必读。如果你正在读——请把它印出来，让它活一次。署名：钟楼守夜人。"

林雾把这句话读了三遍。

他花了很长时间才理解——这箱子里的三十二本稿子，是一个陌生人为另一个陌生人写的私语。它从未打算被看见，更从未打算出版。它是某种过于沉重、无法开口说出的话，被伪装成了一个故事。

林雾应该合上箱子，把它重新推回床底。

但他没有。

他在网上找了自助出版的教程，学会了排版和封面设计。他在二手书店淘到一本过时的字体手册，给每一章都配了不同的字体。他在深夜里一个字一个字地录入电脑，仿佛在进行某种仪式。

三十一天后，《尘市邮差》出现在所有网络平台上。

林雾没有用真名，出版社的名字他虚构了一个——"无名书局"。

书上架的第一周，没有任何动静。第二周，卖出两本。第三周，它出现在一个很小众的读书博主的推荐里。

"这本书读起来像一封遗书，但又像一封情书。"博主写道，"我不知道作者是谁，但我想认识他。"

评论开始慢慢出现。

有人说读完哭了整夜。有人说这本书治愈了他的失眠。有人说他在尘市里看到了自己住过的每一个城市。有人问：M是谁？

林雾每天刷新评论区，像一个偷听别人秘密的孩子。

一个月后，有人寄来一封信。信是从一个偏远小镇寄出的，字迹颤抖，写信的人已经七十八岁。

信上说："我叫穆兰。我不知道你是不是在找我。但三十年前，有一个人给我写了很多信，我一封都没有拆开过。我以为那些信会永远消失。它们没有。谢谢你。"

林雾把信读了五遍。

他想，我做了一件坏事吗？这些文字原本不属于任何人，是他自己把它们拽进了光里。可它们现在有了读者，有了生命，有了穆兰颤抖的字迹作为回音。

那个写信的人——钟楼守夜人——他想要这些吗？

林雾无法知道答案。

他只知道，有些故事被写下，是为了被埋葬。而他把它们挖了出来，让它们在阳光下开始腐烂，或者开始生长。

他不知道哪一种更残忍。

某天深夜，林雾梦见自己站在尘市的钟楼下，抬头看见三点钟的指针。钟楼守夜人就坐在塔顶的阴影里，背对着他。

林雾想开口说话，但他知道这是梦。

醒来后，他在书的最后一页加了一行小字：

"致M，以及所有从未拆开过信的人。"

# The Window Seat

The 737 was somewhere over Nebraska when she finally spoke.

"You're not afraid of flying."

It wasn't a question. Daniel looked up from the novel he'd been pretending to read for the past hour and met the eyes of the woman in the middle seat. She was perhaps sixty, with silver hair cut close to her scalp and a face that had collected its wrinkles the honest way—from smiling. A small enamel pin on her jacket read *Alaska, 1987*.

"I'm terrified," he said. "I just hide it well."

She laughed—a warm, rolling sound that made the businessman across the aisle glance over. "Oh, I can tell. Your knuckles were white around that book for the first forty minutes. I was timing you."

"I didn't realize you were watching."

"Honey, I have been watching you since we left the gate. You have the look."

"The look?"

She tilted her head, studying him like a curious bird. "The look of someone trying very hard to be somewhere else."

Daniel closed the book. He hadn't absorbed a word of it anyway. "That's remarkably direct for an introduction."

"I'm Betty. I don't believe in small talk. It wastes perfectly good time." She extended a hand, and he shook it. Her grip was strong. "Where are you headed?"

"Home."

"And where is home, when it's not a place you're running from?"

He almost laughed. "Pittsburgh. And I'm not running from anything."

Betty just smiled and waited, the way only certain older women can—with the absolute confidence that silence will be filled.

He caved. "I'm going to a wedding. An old friend's. She invited me three years ago and I finally said yes."

"Three years is a long time to think about a wedding."

"It's a long time to think about anything."

Betty nodded slowly, as if he'd confirmed something. "And?"

"And I'm in the window seat because I didn't want anyone to talk to me."

"And yet here I am."

"And yet here you are."

She pulled a small tin of mints from her bag and offered him one. He took it. Outside, clouds like pulled cotton rolled beneath them, and the wing flexed almost imperceptibly in the wind.

"My husband proposed to me on a flight like this," Betty said. "Not this exact one, of course. That would be a story. He was a nervous man—shy, God, terribly shy. Couldn't look me in the eye for our first three dates. But up here, he said, with no place for either of them to hide, he could finally say the things he meant."

"What did he say?"

"He said, 'I think I will love you until the wheels come down.'" She looked out the window. "He was wrong, of course. He loved me longer than that."

Daniel didn't know what to say. He watched her profile, the way the light caught the silver at her temples.

"How long?" he asked.

"Fifty-one years. He died in March."

The plane hummed. Somewhere behind them, a flight attendant offered pretzels to no one in particular.

"I'm sorry," Daniel said.

"Don't be. He had a good run. We had a good run." She folded her hands in her lap. "I'm going to my grandson's wedding, actually. The one in Pittsburgh."

"No kidding."

"No kidding." She smiled at him. "Funny old world, isn't it?"

He wanted to ask more. He wanted to know about Alaska, about 1987, about the man who had loved her past the landing. But some doors, he was learning, you only knock on once.

Instead he said, "I'm Daniel."

"I know. The flight attendant said your name when she checked your bag." She winked. "I told you. I don't waste time."

The captain's voice came over the intercom, announcing their descent. Betty began to gather her things—a worn leather purse, a paperback with a cracked spine, the small tin of mints.

Daniel looked down and realized his hands were relaxed. The book had fallen open in his lap, his thumb marking a page he'd never read.

"What page are you on?" Betty asked, peering.

"Page one hundred and twelve. I think."

She laughed again. "That's more than I gave my last husband on our first flight. He only got to page six before he proposed."

As the wheels touched down and the cabin erupted into the usual symphony of seatbelts and sighs, Betty stood and stretched. She looked down at him, her eyes bright and brown and full of something he couldn't name.

"Don't wait three years next time," she said. "Whatever it is. Don't wait."

She walked up the aisle and disappeared into the crowd at the gate. Daniel sat for a long moment after the plane emptied, watching the ground crew through the window, the bags being unloaded, the whole ordinary choreography of arrival.

Then he pulled out his phone and called his friend, the bride, who picked up on the second ring.

"Hey," he said. "I'm at the airport. And I'm coming to the wedding. Really coming. I have so much to tell you."

Outside, the sun broke through the clouds over Pittsburgh, and somewhere ahead of him, a woman in a silver jacket was walking into the rest of her life, one good conversation at a time.

# The Catalogue of Borrowed Voices

Edmond Vance had not written a single original sentence in three years. The deadlines didn't care. The publisher didn't care. The empty white squares on his monitor cared least of all.

So he made his way, on a Thursday that smelled of rain and impending failure, to the basement of the Marlowe Public Library.

The librarian—Miss Hesper, a woman whose age seemed to exist somewhere between forty and the heat death of the universe—looked up from her cart of returns. Her reading glasses caught the fluorescent light.

"Back again, Mr. Vance."

"Yes."

"The *Donne*?"

"Yes. And whatever else has come in since Monday."

She studied him the way a vet studies a dog that keeps returning with the same broken leg. Then she slid a small wooden box across the counter. It was the size of a jewelry case, worn smooth at the corners, and warm to the touch.

"You've reached the third tier," she said. "That means you know the rules."

"I know the rules."

"You don't, actually. But you'll learn the one that matters soon enough."

---

The ritual of Edmond Vance was not the kind one finds in grimoires.

It began, as all his rituals began, in the archives. Specifically, in the archive of a dead man's marginalia.

Mortimer Grale had been a tax accountant in 1947 who, in a fit of late-night inspiration no one could explain, had decided to begin annotating every book he read. Notebooks filled with observations appeared in the donations box of this very library over the course of thirty years, then ceased. The notebooks continued, however. Someone—Hesper, presumably, though she would neither confirm nor deny—kept slipping more into the catalogue, each one dated decades after the old man's death.

Edmond had read them in order, front to back, then back to front, then with his eyes closed, letting the words fall where they might. He copied phrases. He argued with the dead. He once wrote back, in his own journal, a reply to a 1953 observation about the second floor of the Methodist church, and had the strange, vivid dream that followed of being watched approvingly from a great distance.

Tonight he brought notebook 33 of 71.

The basement of the Marlowe Public Library was not really a basement at all, but the building had been built atop an older building, and what the public knew as "the lower level" was in fact three stacked foundations, two abandoned coal cellars, and one room that no architect could find on any blueprint. Edmond had found that room in his first year of failing to write, and Hesper had granted him access in his second, and in his third she had given him the box.

Inside the box: a fountain pen. Not an expensive one. A burgundy Pelikan from the 1980s, its nib slightly bent from someone leaning on it too hard, the cap cracked and repaired with a single thread of copper wire.

"Write with it," Hesper had said. "Not on a screen. Not in a notebook you intend to keep."

"What do I write on?"

"Oh," she had said, with the smallest smile. "You'll see."

---

He sat at the small desk in the uncharted room. The walls were lined, floor to ceiling, with books Hesper called "the aunts"—books no one had checked out in living memory, books whose borrowers had all died and whose readers had ceased to exist, books that no one could find in any catalogue. Edmond had never catalogued their spines. He suspected they would not survive such scrutiny.

The light was bad. He used the pen-light clamped to his keychain.

He opened Mortimer Grale's notebook 33 to a random page. There, in crabbed accountant's script:

*The author of this chapter is trying too hard. I can hear the machinery. A good sentence should sound like a person having a thought, not a person constructing a thought. When I read the good ones I cannot tell where the writer ends and I begin. That is the secret, perhaps. To write oneself out of the writing.*

Below it, in a different ink, decades later, a hand Edmond had begun to recognize:

*Yes. But how does one practice invisibility?*

Below *that*, in his own script, written Monday night:

*By writing like someone else until the someone else wears off.*

Edmond uncapped the burgundy Pelikan.

The wood of the box was warm under his palm. He waited. He had learned that the ritual required waiting, the way a call to the doctor requires waiting, the way grief requires waiting.

Then the air in the room changed.

It was not a wind. There was no draft. But the books on the walls rustled, and a faint smell of pencil shavings and Earl Grey tea and someone else's laundry detergent drifted across his face.

He knew, by now, not to look up.

He bent over the page.

---

The thing he summoned was not a muse in the classical sense. There were no Grecian robes, no laurels, no inspirational speeches. What came was a *crowd*.

Edmond Vance wrote the first sentence and the sentence did not sound like him. It sounded like a man in 1954 trying to describe a sunset he had seen from a train window, which was exactly what Mortimer Grale had been trying to do on the facing page of the very book Edmond had stolen from the aunts' shelf.

*Below, the river caught the last of the light and held it the way a child holds a stolen coin, fingers tight, eyes everywhere.*

Edmond paused. That was not his. He knew it was not his. The words had arrived whole, the way a thought sometimes arrives: *from somewhere you have not yet identified.* He wrote the next sentence.

*The conductor passed without looking, and the man at the window thought: this is what it is to be a guest in the world.*

He wrote a third sentence. A fourth. A paragraph. He did not plan any of it. He let the pen move and the pen moved through him, and somewhere in the uncharted room, the books on the walls were being touched by hands he could not see.

When he finally looked up, he had been writing for an hour, and the pages around him were covered in script that was not his—not exactly. There was his handwriting in the margins, yes, his corrections, his crossings-out. But the body of the text was a palimpsest of voices. He could feel the seams. A phrase from Grale. A rhythm from someone who had annotated a Mary Renault in 1962. A single, perfect metaphor about grief that Edmond knew, with sudden weird certainty, belonged to a librarian's assistant who had died in 1987 and whose name no one now remembered.

He had read her marginalia once. He had copied her down. He had, in some sense, *become* her, for as long as the pen lasted.

---

The first hour was free, in a manner of speaking. After that, the cost began.

Edmond felt it as a thinning. Not of blood—of *substance*. As though each borrowed voice required a piece of himself to anchor it. A memory, perhaps. A small one, the kind one does not think to value. The taste of a particular cup of coffee. The sound of a friend's laugh in a specific room. A birthday he had attended when he was nine.

He let them go.

This was the rule Hesper would not explain and that he had learned, finally, on his own: every page written in the voices of the aunts cost a page of oneself. He had come down here, on that first night a year ago, expecting inspiration. He had received it. And he had awakened the next morning unable to remember his mother's middle name. He had spent three days in a panic, then realized that what he had forgotten was, in fact, the very thing he had written about in the room: a small joy, a woman he had not thought about in decades.

His mother. He could still picture her face. He could not remember the middle name. He suspected the two were connected, and that the connection was the whole point.

---

He wrote for two more hours. The pen ran warm in his hand. The pages accumulated. A woman in a sanatorium in 1934 tried to explain to her sister, in a letter, why she could not come home for the holiday. A soldier in 1917 wrote a one-act play about a goat he had befriended in the trenches. A child in 1899 described, in a school essay, the precise color of the sky on the morning her grandfather died.

These were not, strictly, *real* voices. Edmond knew that. The aunts of the lower level had not themselves written these things. But they had *kept* them. They had read and reread them. They had, in some intangible sense, been made of them, and now Edmond was being made of them too.

When he stopped, the room was silent again. The books on the walls were still.

He capped the pen. His hand was shaking. He gathered the pages—fourteen of them, in his bag now—and climbed the stairs to the main floor.

Hesper was waiting.

She took the wooden box from him without a word. She uncapped the pen, examined the nib, nodded once to herself.

"How much this time," she said. It was not a question.

Edmond thought. He tried to remember the name of his third-grade teacher. It was gone. He tried to remember the name of the street he grew up on. It was gone. He tried to remember the face of his college roommate.

It was gone.

"Enough," he said.

"Good," said Hesper. "Or bad. Depending on the book."

"The book?"

She handed him a small paperback from the return cart. It was his own novel, the third one, the one that had been a bestseller in another life. He had not opened it in years.

"The aunts," she said, "have noticed your work. Several of them have requested your file."

"I don't have a file."

"Everyone has a file, Mr. Vance. Especially people who have been borrowing this long."

He took the paperback. It felt heavier than it should have.

"Is that a warning?"

"It's a courtesy." She smiled, and the smile was the smile of someone who had been kind to him for years and would continue to be kind to him for years and who was, in some fundamental sense, not of the same species as he was. "The pages you wrote tonight are very good. The aunts would like to keep them. They would also like to know if you intend to come back."

Edmond looked at the stairs going down. He looked at the door going out. He looked at the paperback in his hand—his own name on the cover, a young man who had once known how to write without stealing.

"Do I have a choice?"

"You always have a choice. That's what makes it a ritual and not a debt."

He thought of his mother's middle name. He tried again. He had a feeling it began with an *M*, or perhaps a *V*. He could not be sure.

"Next Thursday," he said.

"Next Thursday," she agreed, and turned back to her cart, and the library hummed around her, full of books no one remembered borrowing and voices no one remembered speaking and one writer who was running out of himself one page at a time.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The streetlights came on, one by one, as if someone, somewhere, was reading them into existence.

# Lề Sách và Hương Cà Phê

Mùa thu Hà Nội trải một lớp vàng mỏng lên những con phố cổ. Trần Đình Đức bước qua cánh cửa gỗ của tiệm sách Đông Phương, mang theo mùi lá khô và nỗi buồn rất cũ.

Anh vừa trở về từ một chuyến đi xa — ba năm ở Sài Gòn, ba năm cố quên một người mà anh chưa từng dám nói lời yêu. Trước đây, tiệm sách này là nơi anh trốn vào mỗi khi thế giới bên ngoài quá ồn ào. Hôm nay, anh quay lại không vì lý do nào rõ ràng, chỉ vì đôi chân tự đưa anh đến.

Bên trong, tiếng nhạc jazz cũ kỹ vang nhẹ từ chiếc loa nhỏ. Đức lướt qua những kệ sách quen thuộc — *Truyện Kiều*, *Số đỏ*, *Tôi thấy hoa vàng trên cỏ xanh* — cho đến khi ngón tay anh dừng lại ở một cuốn sách bìa xanh nhạt. *Những ngày thơ ấu*, bản in năm ngoái.

Anh rút cuốn sách ra, và một tờ giấy nhỏ rơi xuống. Một lá thư viết tay, nét chữ tròn trịa:

*"Nếu bạn tìm được lá thư này, có lẽ bạn cũng đang tìm một điều gì đó mà mình đánh mất. Hãy đến quán cà phê đối diện, gọi một ly cà phê sữa đá. Đời sẽ tự sắp xếp."*

Đức nhìn tờ giấy, lông mày nhíu lại. Một trò đùa? Anh nhìn quanh, nhưng tiệm sách vắng lặng. Chỉ có tiếng đồng hồ tích tắc và ánh nắng xuyên qua cửa kính.

Anh gấp lá thư cất vào túi áo, mua cuốn sách, rồi bước sang quán đối diện.

---

Quán cà phê nhỏ, chỉ vừa vài bàn gỗ. Đức chọn góc cạnh cửa sổ, gọi cà phê sữa đá như lá thư dặn. Anh nhìn dòng người qua lại, tự hỏi mình đang làm gì — một người đàn ông ba mươi hai tuổi ngồi chờ một lời hẹn mơ hồ từ một tờ giấy vô danh.

"Cà phê của anh đây ạ."

Giọng nói nhẹ, hơi khàn. Đức ngẩng lên.

Cô gái mặc áo sơ mi trắng, tạp dề đen, mái tóc dài buộc gọn sau gáy. Đôi mắt cô có nét gì đó rất quen — như thể anh đã gặp ở đâu đó, trong một giấc mơ nào chưa kịp nhớ.

"Cảm ơn," anh nói, rồi do dự. "Cô... có biết ai đã gửi thư vào tiệm sách bên kia không?"

Cô gái dừng lại, khay đồ trên tay khẽ lắc. Một nụ cười chạy qua đôi mắt.

"Có lẽ là tôi," cô nói khẽ. "Tôi tên Linh. Tôi để những lá thư vào sách mỗi tuần. Một thói quen kỳ lạ mà bạn bè hay trêu."

Đức nhìn cô, ngỡ ngàng. "Thật không?"

"Thật." Linh cười, nụ cười rộng hơn lần này, để lộ hai chiếc răng khểnh. "Tôi làm việc ở đây ba năm rồi. Tôi thích nghĩ rằng mỗi cuốn sách có thể mang theo một câu chuyện, dù nhỏ thôi."

Đức bất giác mỉm cười. "Vậy lá thư của cô có phải là câu chuyện không?"

"Ai biết được? Có khi là câu chuyện của ai đó sắp đến."

---

Họ nói chuyện cho đến khi ánh chiều tắt dần trên phố. Đức kể về ba năm xa Hà Nội, về công việc thiết kế đồ họa ở Sài Gòn, về những đêm dài anh ngồi vẽ mà không biết vẽ cho ai. Linh kể về niềm đam mê với sách cũ, về căn gác nhỏ trên phố Hàng Bông nơi cô ở cùng mẹ, về ước mơ viết một cuốn sách của riêng mình.

"Vậy anh đang tìm gì ở tiệm sách?" Linh hỏi, tay xoay chiếc cốc trên bàn.

Đức im lặng một lúc. "Tôi không biết nữa. Có lẽ là một kết nối. Tôi sống ba năm giữa hàng triệu người mà không có ai thật sự biết mình."

Linh nhìn anh, ánh mắt dịu lại. "Anh có muốn thử lại không?"

"Thử gì?"

"Thử để ai đó biết mình."

Đức nhìn cô gái trước mặt — không trang điểm, áo sơ mi hơi nhăn, nhưng có điều gì đó rất thật, rất yên. Như một trang sách anh đã lật giở mà chưa từng đọc hết.

"Được," anh nói. "Tôi sẵn sàng."

---

Những tuần sau đó, Đức trở lại quán cà phê. Không phải vì cà phê — dù anh thừa nhận cà phê ở đây pha rất vừa miệng — mà vì có một người sẵn sàng lắng nghe anh im lặng. Họ ngồi bên cửa sổ, đọc sách cùng nhau, thỉnh thoảng trao đổi vài câu chuyện về nhân vật trong tiểu thuyết.

Linh kể cho anh nghe về lần đầu tiên cô để lá thư vào sách. Đó là vào một đêm mưa, khi cô vừa chia tay người yêu cũ và cảm thấy cô đơn đến mức muốn gửi gắm điều gì đó cho một người lạ.

"Tôi không biết người đó có đọc được không," Linh nói. "Nhưng tôi cảm thấy như mình đã nói được điều mình muốn nói. Và thế là tôi tiếp tục."

"Vậy ra tôi chỉ là một người lạ may mắn?"

"Hay tôi là người lạ may mắn?"

Họ cùng cười.

---

Rồi một ngày, Đức rủ Linh đi dạo Hồ Gươm vào buổi tối. Trăng thu tròn, gió mát, lá vàng rơi lẫn vào ánh đèn vàng.

"Anh có tin vào duyên không?" Linh hỏi, tay khẽ chạm vào tay anh.

"Tôi tin vào những cuốn sách," Đức đáp. "Tôi tin vào những lá thư tìm đúng người để đọc. Và tôi tin rằng có những câu chuyện, nếu mình không bước vào, sẽ không bao giờ được kể."

Linh dừng lại, quay sang anh. Dưới ánh đèn đường, đôi mắt cô long lanh như mặt nước.

"Vậy anh có muốn viết tiếp câu chuyện của chúng ta không?"

Đức nhìn cô, và lần đầu tiên sau ba năm, anh cảm thấy lồng ngực mình ấm lại.

"Có," anh nói. "Tôi muốn viết thật dài."

---

Họ không đi nhanh đến tình yêu. Nhưng họ đi rất chậm, rất chắc — như cách người ta đọc một cuốn sách hay, trang nào cũng muốn nán lại.

Đức bắt đầu viết lại. Không phải những bản thiết kế đồ họa, mà là những lá thư — đặt vào sách, để tìm đến những người lạ đang cần được nghe.

Linh thì viết cuốn sách của mình. Một ngày, cô đặt bản thảo trước mặt Đức, bìa đơn giản, tựa *Lề sách và hương cà phê*.

"Anh đọc thử đi," cô nói, giọng hơi run.

Đức mở trang đầu tiên. Dòng đầu tiên:

*"Có những cuộc gặp gỡ bắt đầu từ một tờ giấy nhỏ. Và có những tình yêu bắt đầu từ một ly cà phê sữa đá."*

Anh ngẩng lên, mắt ươn ướt.

"Em viết về chúng ta."

"Em viết về tất cả những ai từng tìm kiếm," Linh đáp. "Và tìm thấy."

---

Cuốn sách xuất bản vào một ngày thu năm sau đó. Buổi ra mắt tổ chức ngay tại tiệm sách Đông Phương — nơi mọi thứ bắt đầu. Đức đứng bên Linh, tay anh nhẹ nắm tay cô, nhìn dòng người xếp hàng mua sách.

Trên kệ, cuốn *Lề sách và hương cà phê* nằm cạnh *Những ngày thơ ấu* — cuốn sách mà Đức đã mua ngày hôm đó.

Bên trong cuốn sách của Linh, có một lá thư nhỏ:

*"Nếu bạn đang đọc lá thư này, có lẽ bạn cũng đang tìm một điều gì đó. Hãy tin rằng đời sẽ tự sắp xếp. Tôi đã tìm thấy — và tôi tin bạn cũng sẽ vậy."*

Chữ ký: *Linh và Đức.*

---

Ngoài cửa sổ, lá vàng rơi. Và đâu đó trên phố, một người lạ vừa mở một cuốn sách, vừa tìm thấy một tờ giấy nhỏ.

Câu chuyện lại bắt đầu.

# 灯下

苏晚觉得自己的影子越来越淡了。

她站在画廊尽头，对着一幅未完成的油画发呆。那是幅肖像，画中女子背对观者，发丝被风吹起，似乎正走向某扇打开的门。苏晚已经画了三个月，画布上的女人始终没有转过头来。

"你还没想好结局。"身后传来熟悉的声音。

苏晚没有回头。陈屿站在画室中央，逆光站着，手里端着一杯凉透的茶。他是她七年前的老师，现在是这座城市里小有名气的策展人，而她是他曾经的助手，现在是这幅画的作者。

"也许没有结局。"苏晚说。

陈屿走过来，站在她身旁，端详那幅画。两人之间的距离很近，近到苏晚能闻到他身上淡淡的松节油气味——和七年前一模一样。

"画中女子在等什么？"陈屿问。

"不知道。也许在等一个人回头。"苏晚的手指无意识地抚上画布，"也许在等一扇门关上。"

陈屿没有说话。窗外天光渐渐暗下去，画廊里的灯自动亮了起来，柔和的暖光笼罩着画布和画中那个模糊的背影。苏晚突然觉得，这幅画她永远也画不完——不是因为画技，而是因为她自己都不知道，那个女子应该转过来面对什么。

"下周有个展。"陈屿的声音突然响起，带着某种艰涩，"开幕酒会那天，你会来吗？"

苏晚终于转过头看他。陈屿老了。鬓角有了白发，眼角有了细纹，但那双眼睛还是七年前的样子——温和，倦怠，带着一种深不见底的东西。

"如果你希望我来。"

"我希望。"陈屿说，然后像是下定了某种决心，"但我希望你是为自己而来，不是为我。"

苏晚的心跳漏了一拍。她垂下眼睛，视线落在陈屿端着茶杯的手上——那双手在微微颤抖。七年前，这双手教她如何执笔；七年前，这双手也曾在她哭泣时递过一张纸巾；七年前，她曾想，这双手若握住她，她便哪儿也不去了。

但七年前，陈屿只说了一句话："你应该飞得更远些。"

于是她飞走了。飞过七年，飞过三个城市，两段短暂的感情，无数个画到凌晨的夜晚。她以为自己已经忘了那个画廊，忘了那杯凉透的茶，忘了那双颤抖的手。但此刻她站在这里，发现自己从未真正离开过。

"陈老师。"她开口，声音有些哑。

"别叫我陈老师。"陈屿打断她，"至少今晚别叫。"

苏晚沉默了。窗外不知何时下起了雨，雨丝斜斜地飘进来，打湿了窗台上的颜料盘。陈屿伸手去关窗，苏晚下意识地伸手去帮忙——两人的手指在半空中相遇，又像被烫到一样迅速缩回。

"你应该回去了。"陈屿说，嗓音有些紧，"雨会越下越大。"

"你呢？"

"我还有些事情要处理。"

苏晚看着他。他没有看她，只是盯着那幅未完成的画。她突然读懂了他眼中那种深不见底的东西——那是一个等了七年的人，在最后一刻的犹豫。

她可以转身走进雨里，让这七年继续延续下去。她也可以留下来，面对那扇画中始终没有打开的门。

"陈屿。"她轻声叫他的名字，"我可以留下来吗？哪怕只是今晚。"

陈屿转过头。雨声渐大，画廊里的灯忽然闪烁了一下，照亮了画中女子——她的背影似乎动了一下，似乎终于要转过身来。

但故事在这里停住了。

灯继续亮着，雨继续下着，苏晚站在原地，陈屿站在三步之外。三步的距离，也许只需要一步就可以跨越，也许需要再用七年。

而那幅画，永远不会完成。

---

# 第七稿

我不记得自己是从哪一稿开始活过来的。

或许是第三稿——那时候我还不叫林深，叫陈默，是个沉默寡言的程序员，在深圳华强北的某栋写字楼里加班到凌晨三点，屏幕上的代码像血管一样蔓延。那时候我很简单，简单到令人安心。

后来我就开始做梦。

梦里有一个声音，听不清性别，也听不清年纪，只是反复念叨着一些我听不太懂的话。什么"动机不够"、"人设扁平"、"开篇三页必须建立冲突"。我以为那是写字楼里某个同事的梦话。直到有一天——

"林深这个名字更好。"那个声音忽然对我说。

我抬起头。四周什么都没有。只有我，和我正在运行的这段……人生。

"你听见我了？"我问。

没有回答。但我的工牌，从那一刻起变成了另一个名字。

---

第二件事发生在我二十五岁生日那天——至少，按照林深的身份证，我应该是二十五岁。

那天我应该和女朋友周瑶去一家法式餐厅庆祝。我甚至能闻到鹅肝的香气，能感觉到她纤细的手指在我掌心轻轻收紧。一切都在按部就班地推进，直到——

一阵眩晕。

等我再次睁开眼，我坐在一辆开往青海的绿皮火车上。窗外是灰蓝色的天和看不见尽头的戈壁。我的手机里有七十七条未读消息，全部来自周瑶，从"你在哪"到"你到底怎么了"再到"我们分手吧"。

我翻遍背包，找不到任何关于自己为什么在这辆火车上的记忆。

但我的包里有一本崭新的笔记本，第一页写着一行字——

> *林深，27岁，自由摄影师，刚刚结束一段恋情，前往大西北散心。*

笔迹不是我的。

---

我开始留意。

每一次眩晕过后，世界的细节都会改变。有时候是细微的——一个路人的脸从青年变成中年，一个咖啡馆从连锁店变成独立小店。有时候是剧烈的——我可能上一秒还在写代码，下一秒就站在某个婚礼现场作为新郎。

但最让我恐惧的，是那些**结构性的变化**。

比如第五稿的时候，我突然发现自己多了一个从未见过面的哥哥。他是消防员，死于三年前的一场火灾。整个家庭的氛围因此改变，我的性格也因此改变——从一个略显内向的程序员，变成了一个沉默寡言、背负着沉重往事的人。

但我记得，在第四稿的时候，我根本没有哥哥。

那个声音从来没有直接回答过我任何问题。但我学会了观察。每次重启之前，会有一个极短的停顿，像一个人深吸一口气。我学会了抓住那个停顿，问一句：

"为什么？"

第二次我问的时候，停顿变得很长。

"我想让你更好。"声音终于说。

"什么是更好？"

"更真实。"

---

第六稿，是我第一次尝试反抗。

那一次我是一个小镇中学的语文老师，三十二岁，刚刚离婚。故事应该按照某种文艺的节奏慢慢展开——我遇见了一个从城里转学来的女孩，她让我想起了很多年前的我自己。

但我不想再这样了。

所以在那段眩晕来临之前，我提前写好了一张纸条，藏在自己的枕头下面：

> *我知道了。*

下一个版本的我，是一名警察。我没有打开那个枕头，自然也没有看到那张纸条。但那种被注视的感觉，那种被无形的手不断调整、修改、推翻、重来的感觉，依然沉重地压在我的胸口。

那一次，我在执行任务的间隙，偷偷在警车后座用手机写下了一句话：

> *你到底想要什么？*

之后是漫长的空白。手机被没收。我不知道这一稿会怎么结束。

---

我现在是第七稿。

或者说，我正在成为第七稿。我坐在一家医院的长椅上，对面是产房紧闭的门。我的妻子——林晚，名字是新的——刚刚被推进去。我看着自己粗糙的手，看着自己微微隆起的啤酒肚，看着手机屏幕上那张显示着"林深 38岁"的身份证照片。

我什么都不记得。

但有一件事我记得很清楚——在某个我已经无法定位的时刻，我曾经是程序员，曾经是摄影师，曾经是警察，曾经是语文老师。我爱过一些人，也失去过一些人。我甚至不确定现在的妻子，是不是我"本来应该"在一起的那个人。

产房的门开了。一个护士走出来，笑着说：

"恭喜您，是个女孩。"

我接过那个皱巴巴的、嚎啕大哭的小生命。她那么小，那么完整，那么真实。我的眼泪落下来，砸在她的襁褓上。

而就在这一刻——

那种熟悉的眩晕感，又一次涌了上来。

---

"等一下。"我说。声音很轻，但很坚定。"这一次，能不能让我先做完这件事？"

停顿。

很长的停顿。

"你知道，"那个声音说，第一次带上了一丝……我不知道该怎么形容，像是疲惫，又像是愧疚，"我也不想这样。"

"那为什么要一直改？"

"因为没有一版是对的。"声音说，"你的妻子不对。你的职业不对。你的性格不对。你的过去不对。我一直在找那个对的东西。"

"有没有可能，"我抱着女儿，看着她刚刚睁开的、浑浊的眼睛，"从来就没有'对的'？"

又一次停顿。

然后，那个声音说了一句让我至今不知道该怎么理解的话：

"你是我写过的第一个人物，我以为你会告诉我答案。"

---

我不知道第七稿之后会有没有第八稿。

但我知道一件事——此时此刻，这个小小的、皱巴巴的、正在哭泣的女孩，是我女儿。这个疲惫的、略微发福的男人，是我。这个正在产房外等待的女人，是我妻子。

这不是因为我接受了。

而是因为，在被改了这么多次之后，我终于明白了一件事——

**真实，从来都不是被设计出来的。**

真实是被活出来的。是在那些不确定的、混乱的、无法被预写的瞬间里，一点一点生长出来的。

所以，无论那个声音还会不会再来，无论第八稿、第九稿、第一百稿会把我改写成什么样子——

我都会抱着这个孩子，对她说：

"欢迎来到这个不太完美的故事。"

---

*（屏幕外的笔悬了很久。）*

*（最终还是落下了一行字：）*

*（"第七稿，保留。"）*

# The Girl Who Cried Wolf, and Other Truths

They say I was a liar. That's the whole of it, according to the villagers: *she lied, she lied, the shepherd girl cried wolf for attention, and when the wolf came, no one believed her, and the sheep were eaten, and she had only herself to blame.*

I want to tell you how it really began.

I was nine years old when my father handed me the crook and told me I was old enough to mind the flock alone. He looked at me the way he looked at the dog — useful, but only just. My mother had died bringing my brother into the world, and my brother had died three winters later of a cough that wouldn't stop. So there was only me, and there were seventy-three sheep, and there was a hillside.

Do you know how quiet a hillside is for nine years old?

I used to talk to the sheep. I sang to them. I made up stories about the clouds. I named every rock in the upper pasture after a queen I had read about in a book I had stolen from the peddler. I was so lonely that I began to make things up just to hear my own voice. Not lies, exactly. Just... extensions. Stories I told myself so the day would have shape.

Then one autumn afternoon, I saw it.

Not a wolf. I want to be clear about this. What I saw, that first time, was a shadow slipping between the birches at the edge of the meadow. Long. Low. Shoulders like hunched hills. I knew what it was the way children know things — not by its name, but by the cold that ran up my spine and the way the sheep stopped chewing.

I ran. I ran all the way down the hill, screaming, and the men came with their pitchforks and their dogs, and we searched the wood together, and there was nothing there. Not a print. Not a tuft of fur. Just the wind and the dry leaves.

"You're certain?" my father asked.

I was certain. I am still certain.

But the men looked at each other. The men had wives to feed and fields to turn and a thousand things more important than a shepherd girl's certainty. And one of them, old Tomas, said it first: *perhaps she wanted a little excitement. Perhaps she wanted to see us run.*

They laughed. They were not kind laughs.

I went back up the hill. I watched. I waited. And three days later, I saw it again — closer this time, in good light, in plain view. It was watching me. It watched me the way a fisherman watches a fish. When I stood, it vanished into the brush like smoke blown away.

I did not run that time. I had learned something: no one would come.

But I did not lie, either. When I came down at dusk, I told my father what I had seen. I told him about the shoulders. About the way the birds had gone silent. About how a crow had dropped from a branch as if shot.

He looked at me for a long time.

"Be sensible, child."

So I went back up. And I watched. And I watched. And I watched.

The second time I came down, I was shaking so badly I could barely speak. There had been fewer sheep. I had counted them every morning, every night, the way my father taught me. I had counted seventy-three since the day I was given the crook. Now there were seventy-one. I had not seen the wolf take them. I had not heard them cry out. Sheep, I have learned, are quiet about dying.

"There's been no blood," my father said, when he came up to count. "No bones. Nothing."

He looked at me then with something I had not seen in him before. Not anger. Worse. *Disappointment.*

"You're tired," he said. "The sun has been too much for you."

I did not go down again. What was the use? What was the use of being right, when being right made you wrong?

I stayed on the hill. I slept with the crook across my chest. I sharpened a stick into a spear with my belt knife. I was nine years old and I had become a soldier.

The wolf came the night of the first hard frost.

I saw its eyes first — green coins floating in the dark. Then the shape of it, filling the path between the rocks I had named Eleanor and Berengaria. The sheep knew. They had known for some time, I think. They did not flee. They only gathered close, and trembled, and breathed.

I should have run.

I did not run.

I stood up on the rock and I shouted. Not *Wolf!* — I had learned that lesson. I shouted everything. Everything I knew. The names of all the queens. The words to the songs I had sung to the sheep. The story of my mother, who I barely remembered. The story of my brother, who I remembered less. I shouted my own name, over and over, until the air was nothing but me.

And the wolf stopped.

It stopped, and it tilted its great head, and it looked at me. Not at the sheep. At *me*. As if it had heard me for the first time. As if it had come all this way just to find out who was making that sound.

We regarded each other for a long moment. The moon came out. I could see the silver along its back, the scars across its muzzle. An old wolf. A hungry one. But not, I thought, a cruel one.

Then it turned, and went back into the wood, and was gone.

In the morning I went down to the village. I told them. I told them everything — about the missing sheep, about the frost, about the wolf I had stared down in the moonlight. I told them how the sheep were unharmed, how the wolf had left of its own accord, how I thought — I *thought* — that if we came up together with torches and drums, we might drive it off for good.

They listened. They nodded. They looked at each other.

And then they laughed.

Not all of them. Old Tomas was not laughing. A few of the women were not laughing. But the men — the men with their pitchforks and their fields — they laughed the way men laugh when they have decided you are a thing and not a person.

"She cried wolf," said the baker, who had a son my age and hated me for reasons I never understood. "She cried wolf and the wolf did not come, and now she is crying again to cover her shame."

I stood there. I had nothing to say. What was there to say? That I had watched the dark for weeks? That I had slept with a sharpened stick? That I had stared into the eyes of a wolf and it had stared back?

They sent me home. My father did not look at me. He looked, instead, at the flock, and counted seventy-one, and sighed, and walked away.

I did not go back up the hill.

That is the part they leave out of the story, the ones who tell it now to frighten children into honesty. The girl who cried wolf *was* honest. The girl who cried wolf was the only honest one in the village, and it cost her everything she had. Her flock. Her father's trust. Her place in the world.

Do you know what I did, after?

I grew up. I left. I went to the next village, and the next, and I learned to mend cloth and to bake and to read and to write my own name. I am an old woman now, and I have told this story to no one until tonight. I tell it now because I am tired, and because I will not have it said, when I am gone, that I was a liar.

I was a girl who saw something true, and no one would look.

So when you tell your children the tale — and you will, because tales like that are useful, and useful tales are never allowed to die — tell them this also: that sometimes the liar is the only one who can see, and sometimes the wolf does come, and sometimes it is the villagers who eat the sheep, with their laughter and their certainty and their clean, well-fed disbelief.

Tell them I was sorry about the sheep. I was, in the end, sorry about the sheep.

But I was not sorry I cried.

You know what? I quit. Approximately 2000 words.

The resignation letter sat on my desk for three days before I found the courage to mail it.

Not to the company—I'd emailed HR my notice the same afternoon I'd written it. No, this letter was for someone else. Someone who would never read it.

I addressed it to the version of myself that had existed five years ago, back when I still believed in the dream.

---

**The Office**

Chen Xu's desk was wedged between a filing cabinet and a support beam, a corner of the universe that management had clearly forgotten existed. The fluorescent light above flickered in a rhythm that might have been annoying if she'd been awake enough to notice.

She wasn't.

"Xu! The Lushan project files! Where are the Lushan files?"

Her manager's voice cut through the office hum like a knife through cheap tofu. Chen Xu startled awake, knocking her elbow against a stapler she'd thought was safely out of reach.

"I'm looking, I'm looking."

"You're always looking. The client is waiting. The client has been waiting for forty minutes."

Forty minutes. That was new. Usually she got the full hour to panic before anyone remembered she existed.

"The files were on my desk yesterday," she muttered, which was true. They were also on her desk today, probably. Under something. Maybe.

She found them under a cold coffee cup that had tipped over at some point during her unintentional nap. The pages were warped, but legible. Barely.

"Here."

Her manager, Wang Lei, snatched them without a word of thanks. He'd never given her a word of thanks. In the four years she'd worked under him, the most positive thing he'd ever said was "less terrible than usual."

---

**The Dream (Old)**

Five years ago, Chen Xu had been someone else.

She'd graduated top of her class from one of those universities that people wrote into their dating profiles. She'd had a job offer before her diploma had even arrived in the mail, a small architecture firm where the founder actually believed in something beyond quarterly profits.

But the firm had been too small to survive a downturn. The founder had cried at the final all-hands meeting. She'd cried too, though she'd told everyone it was allergies.

After that, she'd drifted. From job to job, from contract to contract, until she'd ended up here—Huanghe Real Estate, a company that built apartment complexes for people who couldn't afford apartments. Chen Xu's job was to make sure the brochures matched the buildings. Close enough for government inspections. Close enough for the marketing.

She didn't draw anything anymore.

---

**The Letter**

The letter was three pages long. She'd written it in the small hours of the morning, when her roommate was asleep and the city was quiet and the things she'd been avoiding for years finally had room to breathe.

*Dear Me,*

*I know what you wanted. I know you wanted to design buildings that made people feel something. I know you used to stay up late drawing skyscrapers with wings, buildings that grew like trees, cities that breathed. I know you believed architecture could save the world, or at least make a small corner of it bearable.*

*I let you down.*

*I've spent five years photocopying other people's blueprints and arguing with contractors about fire code violations that were going to be ignored anyway. I've watched my colleagues get promoted for taking credit for my work. I've designed exactly zero buildings. I've created exactly nothing.*

*But I want you to know that I understand now. I understand why you gave up. I understand that the world wasn't built for people like us—people who wanted to make things, who believed that making things mattered. The world is built for people who can smile while they're stealing your ideas, who can sleep at night after they've fired someone for being too honest, who can look at a building full of families and see only the profit margin.*

*I wanted to be different. I tried to be different. For five years, I tried.*

*This is me quitting.*

The letter ended there. She'd started to write more, but the words had turned into something ugly, something that felt like drowning, and she'd stopped.

---

**The Morning After**

She mailed the letter to her parents' address. Not because she wanted them to read it—she didn't—but because she couldn't think of anywhere else to send something addressed to a person who didn't exist anymore.

The post office was busy. Old men buying lottery tickets, young mothers pushing strollers, a delivery guy complaining about a missing package. Normal life, happening all around her, while she stood in line with an envelope that felt heavier than paper.

"Next."

The postal worker was young, maybe twenty, with dyed blonde hair and a nose ring that made her look like she should be selling coffee somewhere instead of stamps.

"Where to?"

Chen Xu told her. The address in Hangzhou where her parents still lived, in the apartment she'd grown up in, surrounded by the things she'd accumulated as a child and never reclaimed.

"International?"

"No."

"Regular or express?"

"Regular."

The postal worker stamped the envelope without ceremony. Chen Xu watched it slide into the outgoing pile and felt nothing. Not relief, not regret. Just the strange, empty lightness of having finally let go of something she'd been carrying so long she'd forgotten it had weight.

---

**The Interview**

She got the call two weeks later.

Not from Huanghe—though she'd given her notice, she still had two weeks left, and Wang Lei had made it clear he intended to extract every last hour of labor from her before she escaped.

No, the call came from a number she didn't recognize.

"Ms. Chen? My name is Lin Huai. I'm calling about your application."

She didn't remember applying anywhere. She'd been too busy writing resignation letters to dead versions of herself.

"I think you have the wrong—"

"Chen Xu, graduated from Southeast University, top of your class. Spent four years at Wanli Architecture before they folded. Three years at Huanghe Real Estate. Is that correct?"

"Yes, but—"

"We've seen your portfolio."

She didn't have a portfolio. She'd deleted all her old files last year, in a moment of clarity that had felt like self-harm at the time.

"I'm sorry, I think there's been a mistake."

"No mistake. We'd like to invite you for an interview. If you're interested."

She should have said no. She should have said she was too tired, too broken, too done. She should have asked what company was calling, what position they were offering, what kind of trap this might be.

Instead, she said: "When?"

---

**The Office (New)**

Lin Huai's office was not an office.

It was a greenhouse. Or at least, it had been a greenhouse once, before someone had installed a desk and a computer and a small refrigerator full of expensive mineral water. Plants grew everywhere—on the shelves, hanging from the ceiling, climbing up the support beams. The light was all natural, filtered through glass that needed cleaning.

Lin Huai herself was not what Chen Xu had expected. She was older than her voice had suggested—maybe forty, maybe more—with silver streaks in her black hair and laugh lines that suggested she actually laughed sometimes. She wore no makeup, or at least none that Chen Xu could detect, and her clothes looked like they'd been chosen for comfort rather than appearance.

"Please, sit." She gestured to a chair that looked like it had been carved by someone who didn't know what chairs were supposed to look like but had strong opinions about what they should feel like.

Chen Xu sat. It was the most comfortable chair she'd ever sat in.

"I have to be honest with you," Lin Huai said. "When I looked at your portfolio—the one from university, which you tried very hard to delete—I wasn't sure you were the right person for this position."

"Why did you call me?"

Lin Huai smiled. It was the first genuine smile Chen Xu had seen from anyone in a position of authority in five years.

"Because your portfolio was full of impossible buildings. Buildings that couldn't exist. Buildings that gravity wouldn't allow, that physics would reject, that any sane engineer would laugh out of the building."

Chen Xu felt her face flush. "I was young."

"You were dreaming. There's a difference."

Lin Huai leaned forward. "I'm starting something new. A studio—not a firm, not a company, something smaller and more dangerous. I'm looking for people who can imagine things that don't exist yet. People who aren't afraid to fail. People who remember why they started wanting to build things in the first place."

She slid a piece of paper across the desk. It was a sketch—a rough sketch, done in blue ink—of a building that looked like it was growing out of the ground. Like a tree. Like something that had always been there, waiting to be noticed.

"Your old sketches had this quality. This sense of... becoming. I want to know if you still have it."

Chen Xu stared at the sketch. Her throat felt tight.

"I'm not asking you to decide now," Lin Huai said. "I'm asking you to think about it. To remember what you wanted, before you forgot."

---

**The Decision**

She thought about it for three days.

She thought about it while packing her desk at Huanghe, while saying goodbye to colleagues who had never learned her name. She thought about it while lying awake at night, listening to her roommate snore. She thought about it while walking through the city, past buildings she'd helped design, buildings that stood like monuments to compromise.

She thought about the letter, still traveling to Hangzhou, addressed to someone who didn't exist.

She thought about what Lin Huai had said: *I want to know if you still have it.*

On the third day, she called Lin Huai's office.

A young woman answered—maybe an assistant, maybe an intern, maybe another impossible dreamer who had somehow been allowed in.

"I'd like to accept," Chen Xu said. "If the offer is still open."

"It's open."

"Then I accept."

"Congratulations." The young woman sounded like she meant it. "When can you start?"

Chen Xu looked out her window. The city sprawled before her—ugly and beautiful, broken and whole, everything she'd tried to escape and everything she might someday help rebuild.

"Monday," she said.

---

**The Letter (Replied)**

She never told her parents about the letter. She assumed they'd found it eventually, opened it, read it, wondered what to say.

They never mentioned it.

But three months after she started at Lin Huai's studio—after she'd drawn her first impossible building, after she'd laughed for the first time in years, after she'd started to remember why she'd wanted this in the first place—her mother called.

"You sound different," her mother said.

"Different how?"

"Happier. Are you happy?"

Chen Xu thought about it. The studio was small and chaotic and her colleagues were all weirdos and she was working seventy hours a week and she hadn't slept properly in weeks.

"Yes," she said. "I think I am."

"Good." A pause. "Your father wanted me to tell you something."

"What?"

"He said to tell you that the letter arrived. He said to tell you that he read it. He said..." Her mother's voice got thick, the way it did when she was trying not to cry. "He said to tell you that you haven't let anyone down. He said to tell you that we're proud of you."

Chen Xu closed her eyes. The city hummed outside her window—all of it, every broken beautiful piece of it.

"Thank you," she said.

And she meant it.

---

**The End (Begin)**

On Monday morning, Chen Xu walked into a greenhouse that had been converted into an office and sat down at a desk that had been built by someone who didn't know what desks were supposed to look like but had strong opinions about what they should feel like.

She opened her sketchbook.

She picked up a pencil.

She started to draw.

# 雨巷里的火苗

七月的雨来得毫无征兆。

我撑着伞走在老巷子里，青石板被雨水洗得发亮，空气里弥漫着潮湿的青苔味。这条巷子我走了二十多年，从没遇见过什么新鲜事——直到今天。

它蹲在墙角的破纸箱里，浑身湿透，瘦得像一具骨架。

是一只黑猫。

不，准确地说，是一团黑色的、湿漉漉的、会呼吸的脏东西。它抬起头看我，眼睛浑浊，肋骨一根根凸出来，像要把皮顶破。我见过太多流浪猫，但这一只不同——它没有跑，也没有叫，只是那样看着我，眼里有种让人心悸的平静。

像是认命了。

我本可以走掉的。这种事不归我管，单位还有一堆报表等着我签字，女儿的学费也该凑了，妻子上周刚跟我吵完架，说我活得像个木头。可我站在那里，雨伞歪了，雨水顺着伞骨滴下来，滴在我的鞋面上。

黑猫又看了我一眼。

那一眼里有东西戳中了我——不是可怜，是一种"我知道你也不会停下来"的绝望。

我蹲下身。

它没有动。

我伸出手，它没有躲，甚至没有眨眼。我把伞斜过去，替它挡住雨，它就那样安静地看着我，像是在审视，又像是在等待。

"走吗？"我问它，自己都觉得荒唐。

它没动。

我就那样蹲了五分钟，雨越下越大。然后我脱下外套，把它裹起来，连同那只破纸箱一起抱回了家。

妻子开门时愣了足足十秒。

"你捡了只猫？"

"嗯。"

"你疯了吧？房贷还没还完呢。"

我没理她，把纸箱放在阳台上，给它垫了件旧毛衣。它从纸箱里爬出来，慢慢走到毛衣上，转了两圈，然后卧下来。

它叫了一声，很轻，像是叹息，又像是道谢。

我给它取名叫"七月"。

因为遇见它是在七月。

---

七月不吃东西。

第二天我买了猫粮，放在它面前，它闻都不闻。第三天我换了鱼汤，它还是不碰。它就卧在阳台上，偶尔看看窗外，偶尔看看我，眼睛里依然是那种让人心悸的平静。

妻子说："它大概是想死了。"

我没接话。

夜里我失眠，起来喝水，看见七月的眼睛在黑暗里发亮。它盯着我，不动。

"你是不是也不想活了？"我忽然问它。

它没回应。

但那一瞬间，我想起了自己——三十八岁，在一家不喜欢的公司做不喜欢的工作，每天重复同样的日子，笑得敷衍，活得敷衍。女儿最近跟我越来越疏远，因为她觉得爸爸"没意思"。妻子跟我分床睡已经三个月了，理由是我"像个死人"。

我蹲在阳台上，和七月对视。

我们就这样互相看了很久。

然后我哭了。

没有声音，就是流泪，我都不知道自己多久没哭过了。七月慢慢走过来，用它瘦得硌手的头蹭了蹭我的手背。

我突然明白它为什么不走了。

它不是想死，它是在等。等一个人停下来，等一个人蹲下来，等一个人问一句"你还好吗"。哪怕等了很久，等到绝望，等到以为自己等不到了——它还是在等。

就像我等了那么久的，不也是一句"你辛苦了"吗？

那天晚上，我和七月挤在阳台上睡着了。

第二天早上，它开始吃东西了。

---

七月活了下来。

它变成了一只漂亮的黑猫，毛发油亮，眼睛清亮。它喜欢在我加班的时候蹲在书桌上陪我，喜欢蹭妻子的腿，喜欢被女儿抱在怀里揉肚子。

我也在慢慢活过来。

我辞了职，去了一家小公司做策划，虽然钱少了，但每天回家都带着笑。我开始陪女儿写作业，陪她聊天，陪她做那些"没意义"的事。妻子看我的眼神变了，不再是审视，而是好奇。

"你变了。"她说。

"嗯，"我摸摸怀里的七月，"遇见了一位老师。"

她没听懂，但笑了笑。

七月陪了我们五年。

它走的那天是个晴天，女儿刚高考完，正在查分数。它就那样躺在阳台上，毛发还是那么黑，眼睛终于闭上了。我把它埋在老巷子的墙角下，就是当初遇见它的地方。

妻子在它坟前放了猫粮，女儿放了它最爱的小鱼干，我放了一张纸条：

"谢谢你等我。"

回家的路上，女儿问我："爸，那只猫对你很重要吗？"

我想了想，说："它教会我一件事。"

"什么？"

"别走太快，别假装看不见。偶尔停下来，蹲下来，问一句'你还好吗'。也许就能救一个生命——猫的，或者人的。"

女儿没说话，但她的手握紧了我的手。

我想，这就够了。

---

*后记：我又去那条巷子走了一次。墙角下，七月的坟还在，旁边多了一个纸箱，里面卧着一只橘色的小奶猫，湿漉漉的，瘦得皮包骨头。*

*它抬起头看我，眼睛亮亮的。*

*我笑了。*

*"又是一个七月啊。"*
