Giọt nước đầu tiên rơi xuống mái hiên, lách tách, như một lời chào rụt rè của trời đất sau ba tháng hạn hán kéo dài. Bà Lan ngẩng đầu lên, đôi mắt đã mờ đục bỗng sáng lên một tia lấp lánh. Bà đặt chiếc quạt mo xuống bậu cửa, bước ra hiên nhà đón những giọt mưa còn lác đác.

"Ông ơi, mưa rồi," bà nói nhỏ với khoảng không phía trước, nơi chiếc ghế trống kê sát lan can.

Hai mươi năm rồi, cứ mỗi mùa mưa đến, bà đều nói câu ấy. Hồi ông còn sống, ông ngồi trên chiếc ghế đó, hút điếu thuốc lào, nhìn trời nhìn đất, rồi quay sang cười với bà: "Mưa rồi thì trồng rau, bà ơi."

Mưa bắt đầu nặng hạt hơn. Nước chảy thành dòng trên mái ngói cũ kỹ, rơi xuống mảnh sân lát gạch tàu đã bạc màu. Bà Lan không vội vào nhà. Bà đứng đó, hai bàn tay chai sần đan vào nhau trước ngực, để mưa phả vào tóc, vào vai chiếc áo bà ba nâu đã sờn.

Đứa cháu nội tên Thư, mười hai tuổi, từ trong bếp chạy ra.

"Bà ơi, mưa to rồi, vào trong kẻo ướt!"

Bà Lan quay lại, nụ cười hiền hậu nở trên gương mặt nhiều nếp nhăn. "Bà nhớ hồi xưa, hồi mới cưới ông nội con, cũng một cơn mưa như thế này. Ông ấy cởi áo tơi của mình ra đội lên đầu bà, rồi hai người chạy từ ngoài đồng về. Ướt như chuột lột mà vui lắm."

Thư cười toe toét. Con bé thích nghe bà kể chuyện ngày xưa, dù nhiều câu chuyện bà đã kể đi kể lại đến mức Thư có thể thuộc lòng.

"Bà kể tiếp đi!"

"Ngày xưa," bà Lan ngồi xuống ghế, kéo Thư vào lòng, "con đường làng mình chưa có xi măng, mưa xuống thì lầy lội lắm. Bà và ông nội con phải đi vòng qua cái đồng sau nhà. Mà cái đồng ấy hồi đó trồng lúa, nước ngập đến bụng. Ông nội con bế bà đi, bà ôm cổ ông ấy, vừa đi vừa cười. Hai người ướt nhẹp mà thấy lòng vui như được ai cho vàng."

Thư tựa đầu vào ngực bà, nghe tiếng mưa rơi bên ngoài. Mùi đất ẩm tràn vào hiên nhà, mùi quen thuộc của mỗi mùa mưa về.

"Bà ơi, bà buồn không khi ông nội mất?"

Câu hỏi bất chợt khiến bà Lan im lặng một lúc. Bà nhìn ra ngoài sân, nơi mưa đã tạnh, và những đám mây đen đang dần trôi qua để lộ khoảng trời xanh phía xa.

"Bà không buồn, con à," bà nói chậm rãi. "Ông nội con vẫn ở đây. Trong mỗi cơn mưa, trong mỗi mùa lúa, trong con đường làng mình đã đi qua. Bà chỉ giận ông ấy thôi."

Thư ngẩng đầu lên, ngạc nhiên. "Giận ông nội? Giận vì sao hả bà?"

Bà Lan cười, một nụ cười vừa buồn vừa dịu dàng. "Vì ông ấy đi trước bà. Bà tưởng hai ông bà sẽ cùng nhau đón cơn mưa cuối cùng của đời mình. Ai dè ông ấy hấp tấp, đi một mình."

Thư im lặng. Con bé chưa hiểu hết nỗi buồn trong câu nói của bà, nhưng con bé hiểu rằng tình yêu giữa ông bà là một thứ gì đó rất đẹp, rất bền, như cái cây đa trước cổng nhà đã đứng đó hàng trăm năm.

Mưa lại bắt đầu rơi, nhẹ nhàng hơn. Bà Lan đứng dậy, cầm chiếc chổi tre quét lại hiên nhà cho khô ráo.

"Thư ơi, con ra vườn xem mấi giúp bà. Mưa đầu mùa rồi, đất mềm, phải gieo hạt ngay kẻo trễ."

Thư lon ton chạy theo bà ra vườn sau. Mảnh vườn nhỏ của bà Lan bỏ hoang đã lâu, từ ngày ông mất. Nhưng hôm nay, bà quyết định sẽ trồng lại rau.

Hai bà cháu cùng nhau cuốc đất, gieo hạt. Bà Lan vừa làm vừa kể cho Thư nghe về những giống rau ngày xưa ông bà hay trồng, về mùa nào trồng cây gì, về cách chăm sóc để rau xanh tốt. Thư nghe say sưa, hai bàn tay nhỏ bám đầy đất đen.

Mặt trời dần lên cao. Mưa tạnh hẳn. Hơi nước bốc lên từ mặt đất, tạo thành một làn sương mỏng bay lơ lửng giữa vườn. Mùi đất tươi mới, mùi lá cây ướt, mùi của sự sống đang trỗi dậy.

Bà Lan đứng giữa vườn, nhìn những luống đất mới cuốc. Bà nghĩ đến ông, đến câu nói quen thuộc "mưa rồi thì trồng rau, bà ơi". Nụ cười lại nở trên môi bà.

"Bà ơi, hôm nay bà vui hả?"

"Vui lắm, con ơi," bà Lan nói, giọng nhẹ như gió. "Mưa đầu mùa rồi. Mọi thứ lại bắt đầu."

*"Mưa rồi thì trồng rau, bà ơi."*

This year's spring showers are as frequent as ever, except for one big difference — the sky is showering money. Roughly 900 words in length.

# The Rain of a Different Sort

The first coin landed on Widow Marple's tomato seedlings with a soft *tink*, and she nearly jumped out of her skin.

"Walter! Walter, come quick!" She pressed her face to the kitchen window, fogging the glass. "Something's falling from the sky!"

Walter shuffled in from the parlor, his reading glasses perched on his nose. "Probably hail. Though I suppose in April—"

But it wasn't hail.

By the time he reached the window, the garden was shimmering. Pennies, mostly. A few nickels. One suspicious-looking button that Walter swore was from his old army coat.

"Well, I'll be damned," he whispered.

---

By noon, the town of Cresswell had turned upside down.

Folks ran through the streets with upturned buckets, pillowcases, even the children's wading pool. Old Man Geddings stood in his yard in a rain hat and galoshes, mouth open to the heavens, catching quarters on his tongue like a man who'd finally found religion.

Mayor Pruitt declared a state of what he called "Precautionary Jubilation," which nobody was quite sure was a real thing but sounded important enough to close the schools.

The bank tellers worked through lunch, converting soggy bills into dry ones, their fingers pruny with cash.

And the rain kept falling.

---

"It's a miracle," said Reverend Lyle from his porch, clutching a fistful of dimes. "The Lord has provided."

At the diner, Betty-Lou snorted into her coffee. "The Lord has provided, huh? Then where was He when my transmission blew in '09?"

A silence fell over the counter. Betty-Lou was known for her mouth, but today nobody seemed to mind.

"It doesn't feel right," muttered Jack Harmon, staring at the wet pavement where a twenty-dollar bill had landed moments before. "Money just... falling out of the sky. Like manna or something."

"Manna fell from heaven because the Israelites were starving," said his wife, Ellen, not looking up from her coffee. "We're not starving, Jack. We just want more."

---

That night, the rain came harder.

Coins beat against rooftops like a metallic symphony. Dollar bills plastered themselves to windshields. A single hundred-dollar note drifted down and stuck, trembling, to the crossing sign at Elm and Main.

And something else came with it.

Walter Marple found it at dawn, resting on the tomato seedlings like an accusation. A small glass vial, no bigger than his thumb, stoppered with black wax. Inside was a slip of paper, rolled tight.

He carried it to the kitchen table. Widow Marple leaned over his shoulder, the smell of breakfast bacon between them.

"What does it say?" she whispered.

Walter unrolled the paper. The handwriting was precise, old-fashioned, the ink a deep rust-red he didn't want to think about.

*FOR EVERY GIFT, THERE IS A LEDGER. MIND WHAT YOU KEEP.*

---

They told no one, of course. Who would believe them? The town was drunk on fortune. By the second week, people had stopped working. Why bother, when the sky provided? Garden plots went untended. The diner saw only a few customers a day; Betty-Lou started sleeping through her shifts.

The money was real. The money spent. The bank vaults overflowed.

But strange things began to happen.

Old Man Geddings, who'd caught the most coins of anyone, couldn't sleep. He said he heard jingling in his walls. Jack Harmon woke one night to find his mattress pinned to the ceiling by a single golden dollar, vibrating slightly, refusing to be reached.

The children stopped laughing. They sat in their yards and counted their treasures with the solemnity of accountants.

And still the rain fell.

---

On the twenty-third day, the clouds parted for the first time since the rains began.

The town square gathered, blinking in the sudden sunlight, pockets bulging with damp bills. Mayor Pruitt raised his hands to speak, but the words caught in his throat.

Because standing at the edge of the square was a figure none of them recognized. Tall. Gaunt. Dressed in a long coat that seemed to drink the light around it. In one hand, he held a ledger. In the other, a pen.

"Citizens of Cresswell," he said. His voice was the sound of coins dropping into a deep well. "Your accounts are settled. The balance has been paid."

He opened the ledger. The pages were blank.

"The books are empty," he said, almost gently. "You have given all that you had. Every unbought thing you might have made. Every unworked hour. Every word you didn't say to the people you love."

He closed the book with a sound like a sigh.

"There will be no more rain."

He turned and walked into the cornfield, and was not seen again.

---

The money did not disappear. It lay in piles and drifts across the town, perfectly preserved, perfectly worthless.

Because the rain had taken something else with it. Something none of them could name but all of them could feel. The hum of purpose. The small, stubborn pride of making do. The quiet dignity of being broke but trying.

Betty-Lou reopened the diner the next morning. She served free coffee to anyone who walked in. Nobody had coins, anyway.

Walter Marple stood in his garden, the ruined tomato seedlings at his feet. He knelt and began pulling weeds. Widow Marple brought him a glass of water and sat beside him in the dirt.

"Suppose we'll have to replant," she said.

"Suppose we will," he said.

Above them, the sky was clear and empty and very, very blue.

And somewhere far away, over the next town, the first clouds were beginning to gather.

Wait, you think to yourself. Something's wrong. It's April, and the leaves haven't grown back on the trees yet. Plan for about 200 words.

The absence gnawed at you like a splinter under the skin. You stood at the kitchen window, coffee cooling in your hands, watching the bare branches scratch against a pale morning sky. It was April. The crocuses should have pushed through the soil weeks ago. The maples down the street should have been blushing, at least, their tight buds swelling with the promise of green.

But the trees were stark. Not just bare—*stripped*. Their branches looked like they'd been scalded, like some invisible frost had come in the night and burned everything off. The neighbor's dogwood was the worst. Its usually delicate silhouette was reduced to something cruel and angular, as though the tree had been caught mid-scream and frozen there.

You remembered last spring. The explosion of life, the way the world had seemed to sigh with relief after the long gray of winter. You remembered pressing your palm against the rough bark of the old oak at the end of your driveway, feeling the hum of sap rising beneath the surface.

No hum now. Nothing.

The news had been quiet about it. Something about a delayed season, climate cycles, an unusually stubborn cold snap. But you'd driven past the state park last weekend and seen the rangers posting signs on the trailheads. *Area Closed. Habitat Concerns.* And your daughter had called from college, her voice small and strange. "Mom, the trees here too. All of them. Even the evergreens."

The coffee had gone cold. You poured it down the sink and watched it spiral away, dark and ordinary.

Outside, a robin landed on a branch that should have been teeming with insects by now. It sat there, head tilted, listening for something that wasn't coming.

Margaret had been awake since five, the way she always was when spring came to the valley. She pulled on her patched canvas jacket and stepped out onto the porch, her breath making small clouds in the cool air. The world was still blue with the last of the night, and somewhere down by the creek, a wood thrush was rehearsing its flute-song.

Her garden waited at the bottom of the slope, behind the old stone wall her husband had laid forty years ago. Most of it had gone wild in the years since, but the bones were still good—raised beds of weathered cedar, paths of crushed granite, the iron arch where the climbing roses had swallowed everything in their path. She walked down slowly, her knees complaining on the uneven ground.

The first thing she did, as always, was pull up a single chair and sit.

People didn't understand this, her daughter especially. *Mom, are you going to actually do anything out there today?* But Margaret knew that sitting was part of it. You had to listen to a garden before you worked in it. You had to let it tell you what it needed.

Today, it seemed to want attention at the back bed, where the lamb's ear had spread beyond its bounds and was bullying the columbine. The hose had frozen again at the spigot, so she filled her old galvanized watering can from the rain barrel, the water shockingly cold against her wrists.

She weeded slowly, methodically, dropping the green offenders into a bucket she would later empty onto the compost. Her hands knew this work the way an old dog's legs knew the path to the door. She didn't need to think about it. Her mind wandered to her granddaughter, who was getting married in June, and to whether the white peonies would be open in time. Probably not. Probably just the buds. Still beautiful, though. Even the promise of a thing could be beautiful.

Around seven, the sun cleared the ridge and the garden went from silver to gold. A bumblebee, enormous and drowsy, blundered into the lamb's ear and lay there, drunk on whatever early morning there was to drink. Margaret watched it breathe for a long moment.

When her joints had stiffened past usefulness, she went inside and put the kettle on. She stood at the kitchen window, looking out at the garden she had not finished and would never finish and did not need to finish, because it was not hers, really. She was just borrowing it for a little while, the way she had borrowed everything else—the house, the husband, the children, this slow, particular life.

The kettle whistled. She poured the water over tea leaves and sat down at the table where no one else was coming.

It was enough. It had always been enough.

Write a simple slice of life piece about a Spring evening by a lake. Plan for about 400 words.

# Le Soir au Bord du Lac

Le ciel se découpait en tranches de couleur — d'abord le bleu dur du jour, puis un rose presque timide, et enfin cette teinte orangée qui n'appartient qu'au printemps. Camille retira ses chaussures et sentit l'herbe humide sous ses pieds. La rosée montait déjà, traître comme chaque soir.

Elle s'assit sur le banc de bois grisé, celui qui faisait face au lac. Les planches craquèrent doucement sous son poids, un son familier qu'elle associait désormais à ce moment précis de la journée. Celui où la ville se taisait.

Un héron décolla depuis la rive opposée, lentement, comme à contrecœur. Ses ailes immenses battirent l'air en silence. Camille le suivit des yeux jusqu'à ce qu'il ne soit plus qu'une ligne sombre contre le ciel mauve.

Quelque part, un enfant rit. Puis plus rien.

Les nénuphars fermaient leurs corolles pour la nuit, se repliant sur eux-mêmes avec la pudeur de ceux qui ont trop montré d'eux dans la journée. L'eau, lisse comme un drap froissé, renvoyait les couleurs du couchant en versions tremblantes. Camille pensa qu'elle aimerait peindre ça, un jour. Puis elle pensa que non, finalement. Certaines choses perdent leur magie une fois attrapées.

Une libellule se posa sur son genou. Elle y resta une seconde, peut-être deux, ses ailes transparentes vibrant imperceptiblement. Puis elle s'envola vers les roseaux, et Camille eut l'impression d'avoir reçu une visite.

Le lac était son secret. Ou plutôt, son confident muet. Elle ne venait pas ici pour réfléchir — ça, elle pouvait le faire n'importe où. Elle venait pour ne rien faire. Pour laisser le silence entrer par tous les pores et chasser le bruit de la journée. Les e-mails, les conversations inutiles, les sourires forcés. Tout cela glissait sur elle comme l'eau sur les plumes du canard qui passa à cet instant, indifférent et souverain.

Son téléphone vibra dans sa poche. Elle ne le regarda pas.

Le printemps avait cette qualité particulière : il promettait tout sans rien garantir. Les arbres bourgeonnaient, mais un gel tardif pouvait encore tout détruire. Les jours rallongeaient, mais les soirées restaient fraîches. C'était une saison de peut-être, et Camille aimait ça. Elle aimait cette fragilité qui faisait que chaque belle soirée semblait dérobée au temps.

Le soleil toucha l'horizon. Le lac devint brièvement incandescent, puis s'assombrit d'un coup. Les premiers réverbères s'allumèrent sur la promenade, dessinant des chemins de lumière sur l'eau noire.

Camille resta encore un moment. Elle remit ses chaussures, lassa ses lacets. Avant de partir, elle jeta un dernier regard au lac — il ne lui renvoyait plus rien maintenant, sinon son propre reflet, flou, incertain.

Elle sourit.

Demain, elle reviendrait.

Write a story about a rainy day spent indoors. Roughly 600 words in length.

# The Sound of Rain

The rain had been falling since Tuesday. By Thursday, Elena had stopped counting the hours and started listening to the drops instead.

She sat cross-legged on the worn corduroy armchair by the bay window, a chipped mug of chamomile balanced on the armrest. The tea had gone cold three cups ago, but she hadn't moved. Outside, the world had blurred into watercolor—greens and grays melting together, the old maple in the yard bowing under the weight of the water, the gravel path becoming a shallow river.

She had meant to go out. There were errands to run, a letter to post, the new bookshop that had opened on Maple Street. But when she woke that morning and pulled back the curtain, the rain had looked so committed, so certain of itself, that she had simply sat back down.

And that was how the day began.

---

By noon, she had built a nest on the living room floor. Two quilts from the linen closet, the good one with the faded cabbage roses that her grandmother had made. Three pillows from the sofa. The novel she'd been ignoring for months—a hardback about a lighthouse keeper—and a fresh notebook, still in its shrink wrap.

She made a second cup of tea. This time, Earl Grey, with a spoon of honey. She ate a slice of buttered toast standing at the counter, watching the rain stripe down the kitchen window, and thought about nothing at all.

---

In the afternoon, she found things to do with her hands.

She mended a cardigan whose buttons had been threatening mutiny for a year. She sorted through a cardboard box of photographs she hadn't opened since the move—her mother as a young woman, laughing at something off-camera; her father with his arm slung around a man she couldn't quite place; a Polaroid of herself at maybe seven, missing two front teeth, holding a frog by its legs.

She didn't cry. She had expected to, and waited for it, the way you wait for a bus that never comes. Instead, she simply looked, and looked again, and slid the photographs into a new album she'd bought months ago and never opened.

---

Around four o'clock, the light began to soften. The rain had gentled to a murmur. Elena lit a candle on the mantel, then another, and put on a record she hadn't played since college—a cellist she had loved at twenty-two and somehow forgotten at thirty-four.

The music filled the room the way the rain filled the gutters, slowly and without asking.

She thought about calling her sister. She thought about writing an email. She thought about all the people she should have been checking on, all the conversations she'd postponed, all the small braveries she kept meaning to perform.

Instead, she wrote a list in the new notebook. *Things that are soft*, she titled it.

- Rain on a tin roof.
- Wool sweaters out of the dryer.
- My mother's hands when she was sleeping.
- The belly of a cat when it stretches.
- This, she wrote at the bottom. *This.*

---

By dusk, the rain had slowed to a fine mist that clung to the windows like breath. Elena hadn't put on shoes. She hadn't checked her email. She hadn't done anything, really, except be where she was, in a room she loved, on a day that asked nothing of her.

She made one last cup of tea—this one peppermint—and carried it to the window. The world outside had gone dark and silver at once, the streetlights just beginning to glow, the puddles holding pieces of sky.

She thought: *I will remember this.*

Not the tea, exactly, or the chair, or even the rain. But the feeling of having allowed herself to stop. Of having spent an entire day without becoming anyone other than the woman sitting here, listening to the drops fall, one after another, like a long letter being read aloud, slowly, in a language she was only now beginning to understand.

Write a story about a late bloomer. About 1200 words long.

# The Weight of Petals

Eleanor Mireille Ashworth was forty-seven years old before she painted anything worth keeping.

She had been painting, of course, for as long as she could remember. Watercolors mostly, the kind of careful, studied work that her mother had approved of—pastel still lifes of fruit in porcelain bowls, landscapes lifted dutifully from postcards, all of it technically correct and absolutely bloodless. By thirty, she had a tidy collection of canvases stacked in the hall closet of the apartment she shared with her sister. By forty, she had stopped showing them to anyone.

She worked at a dental office in Hartford, scheduling appointments and filing insurance claims. The fluorescent lights buzzed there in a way she had grown to find almost companionable, the way one grows fond of a low, persistent ache. Her coworkers called her Ellie, though she had asked them not to. She ate her lunch at her desk and read used paperbacks from the library sale. In the evenings, she painted in the small bedroom her sister had given over to her, the one with the view of the brick wall.

Her sister, Margot, was the kind of person who bloomed early and often. She had married at twenty-three, divorced at twenty-six, remarried at thirty, and was now, at fifty-two, in what she called her "lemon phase," having just published a cookbook focused entirely on the fruit. She hosted dinner parties. She went to Greece. She posted photographs of herself on the internet, laughing, always laughing, in places Eleanor had never been.

"You should come out of your room more," Margot said one Tuesday in April, standing in the doorway with a glass of wine. "You have so much to offer, Ellie."

Eleanor said nothing. She was holding a brush that was, she realized, still dry.

The change, when it came, was not dramatic. It was not the kind of moment one would have noticed, had one been watching. It came on a Wednesday in May, the day after a patient at the dental office—a woman of about seventy with a magnificent face, all hollows and angles—had died unexpectedly in the chair during a routine cleaning.

Eleanor had been the one to call 911. She had been the one to hold the woman's hand, which was still warm, and then to cover her face with the small white sheet from the cabinet. Afterward, she had gone home and sat in her room for a long time. She did not turn on the light. The brick wall outside the window turned from gray to lavender to black.

When she finally stood, she did not go to her usual shelf of watercolors. She went instead to the closet in the hall, the one that held the old canvases, and she pulled them out one by one, examining them in the dark. They were, she thought, paintings of someone who had never been in the room. Beautiful paintings, perhaps. But not hers.

She carried them to the kitchen one by one and set them out on the floor, and she began, methodically, to paint over them.

Margot came home from her book club at ten and found her sister on her knees, brushes in a jar of murky water, the kitchen smelling of oil and turpentine.

"Ellie." Margot's voice was careful. "What are you doing?"

"Painting."

"You're painting *over* them?"

"Yes."

"May I ask why?"

Eleanor considered the question. She had been working on the same canvas for several hours—a thing that might once have been a bowl of pears and was now something else, something darker and more urgent, a smear of red and black that seemed to pulse under her gaze. She did not know what it was. She had not known, when she started, that this was what she would make.

"Because no one died in them," she said.

Margot sat down slowly on the kitchen floor, her wine glass balanced on her knee. "Tell me about the woman," she said.

And so Eleanor told her.

She did not paint quickly, and she did not paint often. She worked at the dental office by day and came home to her small room and stood for an hour, sometimes two, before she touched the brush. Often she did not touch it at all. She ruined canvases. She ruined many. The kitchen floor became a permanent gallery of failed beginnings, and Margot learned to step over them with the ease of long practice.

But the paintings that survived were unlike anything she had ever made. They were not beautiful in the way that her mother would have approved of. They were full of things her mother would not have approved of at all—teeth, mostly, and hands, and the strange interior light of a waiting room. They had a weight to them that surprised even her. She looked at them in the mornings before work and felt, for the first time in her life, that she had been somewhere.

It was Margot who, without telling Eleanor, photographed the paintings and sent the images to a small gallery in Provincetown she had once visited. The woman who ran the gallery wrote back within a week. She used the word *unflinching*. She used the word *late*. She asked if Eleanor would be interested in a show.

Eleanor said no, at first. Then she said maybe. Then she said yes.

The show opened on a cold evening in November. Eleanor wore the only dress she owned that was not from a thrift store, a green velvet thing that had belonged to their mother. Margot came and brought seventeen people, including the woman from the gallery and a man from the *Boston Globe* who later wrote a small piece that described Eleanor as "a startling new voice in American painting" and "an artist who has, against all odds and at great personal cost, finally arrived."

Eleanor did not read the review. She stood by the window of the gallery and watched the people look at her paintings and thought about the woman in the dental chair, whose name she had never learned. She thought about how strange it was that a life could end so quietly, in a place designed to be ordinary, while someone was looking at a magazine.

On the drive home, Margot was silent for a long time. Then she said, "I never knew you were like that."

"Like what?"

"Like *that*." Margot gestured vaguely at the dark road ahead. "So full of things."

Eleanor turned to look at her sister. Margot's face in the dashboard light was a thing she had seen a thousand times and never seen at all—the small scar near her eyebrow, the lines at the corners of her mouth, the way her hands gripped the wheel as if she were always, even now, afraid of something.

"I think I was always like this," Eleanor said. "I just didn't know how to get it out."

"How did you learn?"

Eleanor watched the road. Somewhere ahead of them, the sun was coming up, though it was too early to see.

"I didn't," she said. "A woman died, and it fell out."

Margot did not ask any more questions. They drove the rest of the way home in silence, and when they pulled into the driveway, the sky was the color of a thing just beginning.

Eleanor carried her small box of paints into the house. She had a great deal of work to do.

Write a story set in a dog park on a spring day. Around 800 words.

# Il Parco dei Segreti

La luce del mattino filtrava tra i rami dei tigli, tingendo di un verde dorato il vasto prato del Parco dei Segreti. Era una di quelle mattine di aprile in cui l'aria sembra lavata, e ogni respiro porta con sé il profumo dell'erba nuova e della terra che si risveglia.

Margherita si sedette sulla solita panchina di legno, quella vicina alla fontanella che nessuno sembrava mai usare. Tolse il guinzaglio a Brando, il suo golden retriever di cinque anni, e lo guardò partire come un fulmine giallo verso il prato.

— Vai, vai pure — mormorò, con un sorriso che le illuminò il viso.

Brando non era il suo cane. Non davvero. Era stato di suo marito, Tommaso, scomparso due inverni prima in un incidente che ancora faticava a nominare. Brando era il filo sottile che la legava a lui, l'unico essere al mondo che sapeva riconoscere il suono dei suoi passi, l'odore delle sue mani.

---

Sulla panchina opposta, un uomo anziano con un cappello di feltro verde teneva al guinzaglio un piccolo bassotto che sembrava più nervoso del padrone. L'uomo aveva un quaderno aperto sulle ginocchia e una matita corta tra le dita. Non scriveva. Disegnava.

— Si chiama Otto — disse l'uomo, senza alzare lo sguardo, come se Margherita gli avesse fatto una domanda. — Ha otto anni. Otto anni esatti, li abbiamo contati.

Margherita si avvicinò con cautela.

— Io sono Margherita. E lui è Brando.

L'uomo finalmente alzò lo sguardo. Aveva occhi chiari, di un azzurro quasi trasparente, e una barba bianca ben curata.

— Felice di conoscerla, Margherita. Io sono Corrado. Un tempo facevo il veterinario.

— Un tempo?

— Ora disegno cani. È l'unica cosa che mi riesce bene, ormai.

---

Brando e Otto si incontrarono al centro del prato con la cerimoniosità tipica dei cani che si studiano. Brando, con la sua mole, si abbassò in un invito al gioco che sembrava quasi un inchino. Otto gli girò intorno tre volte, annusando, prima di decidersi a seguirlo in una corsa pazza attorno a un cespuglio di lavanda.

— Sembra che vadano d'accordo — disse Corrado.

— Sembra di sì — rispose Margherita, e nella sua voce c'era qualcosa di rotto che non sapeva come nascondere.

Corrado non chiese. Non lo faceva mai. Aveva settantanove anni e aveva imparato che le storie importanti arrivano solo quando qualcuno è pronto a condividerle.

---

Le settimane successive diventarono un rituale. Ogni mattina, alle nove in punto, Margherita arrivava con Brando. Corrado era già lì, con Otto e il suo quaderno. Sedevano sulla stessa panchina, guardavano i cani giocare, parlavano del vento, del tempo che cambiava, delle nuvole che sembravano navi.

Corrado le raccontò di sua moglie Elsa, mancata da tre anni. Le raccontò del loro laboratorio pieno di fiale e microscopi. Le raccontò di come, dopo la sua morte, avesse iniziato a vedere cani ovunque: nei sassi, nelle nuvole, nelle pieghe delle lenzuola.

— Forse perché i cani sono le creature più vicine all'amore incondizionato — disse una volta, con quella sua voce pacata. — E io, invecchiando, ho bisogno di guardarli spesso per ricordarmi come si fa.

Margherita non rispose, ma quella sera, per la prima volta dopo mesi, pianse senza vergogna.

---

Un martedì di maggio, Corrado non venne.

Margherita aspettò un'ora, poi due. Otto non c'era. Il prato era pieno di cani, ma il piccolo bassotto dal mantello color cioccolato non si vedeva da nessuna parte.

Quando tornò il giorno dopo, trovò la panchina vuota. E il giorno dopo ancora. E quello dopo.

Il sabato, una donna sconosciuta si sedette accanto a lei con un cocker spaniel al guinzaglio.

— Lei cercava Corrado? — chiese la donna.

Margherita sentì il cuore fermarsi.

— È mancato lunedì notte. Nel sonno. Voleva che le dicessi una cosa, se l'avessi incontrata. Mi ha fatto giurare.

La donna tirò fuori dalla borsa un pacchetto avvolto in carta kraft.

— Mi ha detto: "Dì a Margherita che Brando non è solo il ricordo di Tommaso. È anche il suo futuro. E che Otto sarà felice di aspettarlo dall'altra parte del prato."

Margherita aprì il pacchetto con mani tremanti. Dentro c'era un disegno: Brando e Otto che giocavano nel parco, e dietro di loro, sedute su una panchina, due figure sfocate — una donna dai capelli castani e un uomo con un cappello di feltro verde.

---

Brando le mise il muso in grembo, come faceva sempre quando la sentiva triste. Margherita lo accarezzò, guardando il prato dove i cani correvano liberi.

— Hai un amico che ti aspetta — sussurrò al cane. — E anche tu, Otto, hai un amico che non ti dimentica.

Il vento di maggio sollevò i petali dei tigli, facendoli danzare nell'aria come coriandoli dorati. In lontananza, due cani che non si conoscevano ancora iniziarono a giocare insieme, ignari che il loro incontro fosse stato, in qualche modo, già scritto.

---

Margherita tornò al Parco dei Segreti ogni mattina, per molti anni. Non era più triste, non proprio. Aveva imparato che i legami veri non si spezzano mai del tutto: cambiano forma, si spostano, diventano disegni su un quaderno, ricordi in un parco, promesse che attraversano il tempo.

E ogni tanto, nelle mattine di primavera, le sembrava di sentire una voce pacata che le sussurrava: *"Il segreto più grande è questo — l'amore non finisce. Si trasforma. E aspetta, sempre, su una panchina al sole."*

Write a story set in an arboretum as the season changes from winter to spring. Around 900 words.

# Le Souffle des Saisons

Le jardinier s'appelait Émile, mais tout le monde — ou plutôt, tout le monde de peu qu'il croisait — le surnommait « le veilleur ». Cela lui convenait. Passer ses journées dans un arboretum, à l'orée d'une petite ville de province, c'était un peu comme veiller sur un sommeil. Les arbres dormaient encore, en ce matin de février où le gel dessinait des dentelles sur les vitres du pavillon d'accueil.

Émile poussa la porte vermoulue et respira l'air glacé. L'arboretum s'étendait devant lui, vaste de vingt hectares, silencieux comme une page blanche. Les chênes pédonculés dressaient leurs branches noueuses vers un ciel couleur d'ardoise. Les hêtres pourpres gardaient leurs feuilles mortes, recroquevillées et rousses, derniers vestiges d'un automne qui semblait s'être accroché bien plus longtemps que de raison. Partout, la terre durcie attendait.

*Encore un peu de patience*, pensa-t-il en enfonçant ses bottes dans le sentier gelé.

Il avait soixante-trois ans, les mains gercées, le dos un peu voûté, mais le cœur obstinément tendre. Trente-deux ans qu'il travaillait ici. Trente-deux ans à observer les bourgeons éclater en avril, à compter les oiseaux migrateurs, à parler aux troncs comme on parle à de vieux amis. Il connaissait chaque arbre, ou presque. Il y avait le grand cèdre bleu près de l'étang, le tilleul centenaire auprès duquel on mariait les enfants du village, le jeune gingko planté par sa filleule Léa le jour de sa naissance — dix-sept ans déjà.

Ce matin-là, il avait rendez-vous avec personne, et c'était très bien ainsi. Il aimait ces heures suspendues où l'arboretum n'appartenait qu'à lui. Il marchait lentement, s'arrêtant parfois pour caresser l'écorce d'un platane, pour écouter le craquement discret de la glace sur la mare. Un merle s'envola à son approche, traçant un arc noir dans la blancheur.

Les jours suivants furent semblables, en apparence. Émile taillait, nettoyait, réparait ce qui pouvait l'être. Il nourrissait les mésanges, vérifiait les protections des jeunes plants contre les cerfs. Son travail était lent, patient, comme celui des saisons elles-mêmes.

Mais quelque chose changeait, imperceptiblement. Le soleil, d'abord, montait un peu plus haut chaque jour. Les ombres s'allongeaient différemment sur les allées. Et puis, un matin — Émile s'en souvint toute sa vie —, il sentit une odeur. Infime, presque insaisissable. Celle de la terre qui se réchauffe, de la sève qui commence à monter, de la promesse.

Il s'arrêta net au milieu du sentier, les yeux clos. C'était si ténu qu'il aurait pu l'imaginer. Mais non. Il connaissait ce parfum par cœur, après trente-deux hivers. C'était le printemps qui s'annonçait.

Les jours qui suivirent furent une lente explosion. D'abord les perce-neige, petites clochettes blanches surgies de nulle part au pied des charmilles. Puis les crocus, violets, jaunes, orange, éclaboussant les pelouses comme des taches de peinture fraîche. Les bourgeons des marronniers gonflèrent, devinrent poisseux, puis, un matin d'une clarté presque insoutenable, s'ouvrirent sur des chandelles vert tendre.

Émile assistait à chaque étape. Il photographiait les chatons du noisetier, comptait les premiers bourdons, saluait les premiers papillons — un paon du jour, un peu étourdi par la douceur nouvelle. Il nommait chaque apparition comme on nomme un enfant qui vient au monde.

Un samedi, le public revint. L'arboretum rouvrait officiellement ses portes pour la saison. Des familles avec enfants, des retraités, des amoureux. Un brouhaha doux, joyeux, qui contrastait avec le silence de l'hiver. Émile, posté près de l'entrée, répondait aux questions, indiquait les sentiers, racontait l'histoire du tilleul centenaire.

Une jeune fille s'approcha de lui, un peu hésitante. Grande, brune, les yeux verts. Il lui fallut quelques secondes pour la reconnaître — dix-sept ans, ça change une enfant. Mais le sourire, surtout, était le même.

— Bonjour, parrain.

— Léa.

Elle se jeta dans ses bras, et il sentit contre son épaule le rire d'une jeune femme qu'il avait tenue bébé dans cette même lumière, sous ces mêmes arbres en bourgeons.

— Je suis venue voir le gingko, dit-elle en se reculant. Il a poussé, hein ?

— Comme toi.

Ils marchèrent ensemble dans les allées, et Émile lui montra les perce-neige, les crocus, les premiers narcisses. Il lui fit écouter le chant d'un pouillot véloce, perché haut dans un chêne. Il lui parla du merle de février, qui revenait chaque année nicher près du pavillon.

— Tu leur parles, à tes arbres ? demanda-t-elle en riant.

— Bien sûr. Et eux aussi, ils me parlent. Il suffit de savoir écouter.

Elle leva les yeux vers la frondaison encore clairsemée, où la lumière du printemps filtrait en lames dorées. Elle comprenait, maintenant, pourquoi son parrain avait consacré sa vie à ce lieu. Ce n'était pas un travail. C'était une manière d'aimer.

Plus tard, quand le soleil commença à descendre, ils s'assirent sur un banc face à l'étang. L'eau, libérée de sa gangue de glace, renvoyait le ciel mobile. Un héron cendré traçait son ombre sur la rive opposée.

— Promets-moi quelque chose, dit Émile.

— Tout ce que tu voudras.

— Quand je ne serai plus là, veille sur eux. Sur chaque arbre, chaque fleur, chaque oiseau. Ils t'ont vue naître. Ils te verront vieillir. À ton tour de les accompagner.

Léa ne répondit pas tout de suite. Elle regardait le grand cèdre bleu, dont les aiguilles frémissaient dans la brise légère. Elle pensa à toutes ces années à venir, aux printemps qui se succéderaient sans que son parrain soit là pour les guetter. Sa gorge se noua.

— Je te le promets, dit-elle enfin.

Émile sourit. Il posa sa main ridée sur la sienne, et ils restèrent ainsi jusqu'à ce que le soir vienne, que les premières étoiles s'allument au-dessus de l'arboretum, et que le printemps, enfin, s'installe tout à fait.

---

*Fin*

# 《四月之约》

四月，学校礼堂被装饰成了星空。

彩色纸灯笼悬在半空，像是被摘下的星星；银色的锡纸被剪成细丝，缠绕在每一根柱子上，风一吹，便发出细碎的声响。音响里放着轻柔的舞曲，操场上的篮球架被推到墙角，取而代之的是一圈圈折叠椅和临时搭建的小舞台。

苏念站在礼堂门口，手里捏着一张皱巴巴的纸条。

那是上周三，她偷偷塞进陆辞书包里的。纸条上写着：*"放学后，我在操场那棵槐树下等你。"*

陆辞没有来。

苏念等了一个小时，看着夕阳一点一点落下去，看着那只野猫从墙头跳下来又跳走，最后自己一个人回了家。她以为他没看见那张纸条，或者看见了，却根本不在意。

但今天，陆辞居然主动来找她了。

"苏念。"他站在她面前，耳朵有点红，"你的纸条我看到了。"

"那你为什么——"

"因为那天我妈突然来接我，说我爷爷住院了。"陆辞低下头，"我给你发过消息，你没回。"

苏念愣住了。她掏出手机，翻到那一天——三条未读消息，都是陆辞的：*"我爷爷住院了"*"我可能要回老家"*"回来看我吗？"*

她的眼泪一瞬间就涌了上来。

"对不起，"她小声说，"我那时候把手机调静音了，在生你的气。"

陆辞没有说话。他从口袋里掏出一张叠得整整齐齐的纸，递给她。

苏念展开。

是她那张纸条。背面，是陆辞的字迹，工整得像是抄课文：

*"四月春假，我回来看你。届时，请你做我的舞伴。"*

她抬头看他，眼眶还是红的，但嘴角已经弯了起来。

"那现在，"陆辞伸出手，掌心向上，"苏念同学，你愿意吗？"

音乐正好换成了新的曲子。是《四月之春》，旋律缓慢而悠长，像春天本身。

苏念把手放上去。

她的手指有一点凉，但陆辞的手心是暖的。

他们走进礼堂。人群自然地为他们分开，又在他们身后合拢。有人在吹口哨，有人在鼓掌，有人举着手机拍照。

苏念有点不好意思，想要抽回手，陆辞却握得更紧了一些。

"别动，"他低声说，"我爷爷已经出院了。"

"那还挺好的。"苏念说。

"嗯，"陆辞说，"他也想见见你。"

苏念没听懂："见谁？"

陆辞没有回答。他带着她转了一个圈，裙摆在灯光下泛起淡淡的光泽。

一曲终了。

他们在众人的目光中停下，喘息未定。窗外的天已经完全黑了，礼堂里的星星却越来越亮。

苏念忽然想：

原来春天，不只是花开的时候。

春天，还是一个人愿意为你等在原地的时候。

是她愿意伸出手，他也愿意接住的时候。

她握紧了陆辞的手。

"下一首，"她说，"你继续。"

陆辞笑了，眼角的弧度温柔得像是四月的风：

"好。"

---

*窗外，月光正好。*

# **El Jardín de los Recuerdos**

En las colinas olvidadas del pueblo de Valdelirio, donde el viento arrastraba los susurros de generaciones pasadas, existía un jardín que nadie se atrevía a cultivar.

Doña Amparo, una anciana de manos curtidas y ojos profundos como pozos de agua clara, fue la primera en quebrantar el silencio. Cada mañana, antes de que el sol rasgara la neblina, ella caminaba con su regadera oxidada hasta un pequeño terreno baldío cercano a la iglesia abandonada. Allí, con paciencia de relojera, plantaba semillas que guardaba en un saquito de terciopelo ajado.

—¿Por qué cultiva flores en tierra de muertos? —le preguntó una vez el niño Tomás, que la observaba desde detrás del muro de piedra.

La anciana sonrió, arrodillándose con dificultad.

—Porque los muertos, pequeño, tienen más necesidad de belleza que los vivos.

Tomás no comprendió. Tenía nueve años, las rodillas llenas de costras y una curiosidad que lo llevaba a meterse en todos los jardines del pueblo, menos en aquel.

Los años pasaron. Tomás creció y se convirtió en un hombre serio, de manos grandes y corazón cerrado. Partió del pueblo buscando fortuna en la ciudad, dejando atrás a su abuela, a sus hermanas y, sobre todo, aquel jardín misterioso que Doña Amparo cuidaba con devoción casi religiosa.

Una carta llegó en noviembre.

*"Ven, Tomás. Las flores están floreciendo y tengo algo que mostrarte."*

No fue. La segunda carta llegó en febrero.

*"Las margaritas preguntan por ti."*

No fue. La tercera, en mayo, fue diferente.

*"El jardín morirá conmigo. Ven antes de que llegue el invierno."*

Esta vez, Tomás sintió algo despertar en su pecho. Algo parecido al arrepentimiento, pero más dulce. Tomó el primer tren hacia Valdelirio.

Cuando llegó, el pueblo había cambiado. La mayoría de las casas estaban vacías, sus ventanas como ojos ciegos mirando hacia ningún lugar. La iglesia seguía abandonada, y el jardín... el jardín era ahora una explosión de color que dolía mirarlo.

Doña Amparo estaba sentada en una silla de mimbre, junto a un rosal que trepaba por una cruz de hierro oxidado. Tenía noventa y tres años y parecía una flor más entre tantas.

—Llegas tarde —dijo sin abrir los ojos.

—Lo siento, abuela.

Ella abrió los ojos y, por un momento, Tomás vio en ellos a todas las mujeres que la habían precedido. Su madre, su abuela, la madre de su abuela.

—Siéntate —pidió ella—. Quiero contarte el secreto de este jardín.

Tomás obedeció.

—Hace setenta años, cuando la guerra se llevó a mi esposo y a mis dos hijos, quise morirme. La tristeza era tan grande que no cabía en mi cuerpo. Una noche, llorando junto a esta tierra baldía, encontré una semilla en el bolsillo de mi hijo menor. Era una semilla de girasol, la última cosa que tocó antes de partir.

Doña Amparo señaló hacia el centro del jardín, donde un girasol gigante, más alto que cualquier hombre, se inclinaba suavemente con el viento.

—La planté aquí. Y lloré tanto sobre la tierra, que la semilla no solo creció: multiplicó. Cada lágrima se convirtió en una flor diferente. Los lirios blancos eran mis noches de insomnio. Las amapolas rojas, mis días de furia. Los pensamientos morados, mis preguntas sin respuesta. Y los girasoles... los girasoles eran mi esperanza.

—¿Y ahora, abuela? —preguntó Tomás, con la voz quebrada.

—Ahora he dejado de llorar. Pero el jardín sigue creciendo. Mira.

La anciana señaló hacia un rincón donde Tomás nunca había mirado con atención. Allí, entre rosales y margaritas, había un pequeño sector dedicado a flores que él no conocía: flores azules como el cielo de verano, flores negras como la noche sin estrellas, flores transparentes como el cristal.

—¿Qué flores son esas? —preguntó.

—Flores del futuro —respondió Doña Amparo—. Son para los que vienen después de mí. Para ti, si decides quedarte. Para tus hijos, si los tienes. Para todos los que necesiten un lugar donde sembrar su dolor.

Tomás miró el jardín con ojos nuevos. Ya no veía solo flores; veía historias. Cada pétalo era una página, cada color un capítulo. Vio margaritas que eran risas de niños olvidados. Vio violetas que eran promesas rotas. Vio hortensias que eran amores imposibles.

—¿Quién cuidará de esto cuando tú te vayas? —preguntó con voz temblorosa.

—Tú —dijo ella con la certeza de quien ha esperado toda una vida.

Esa noche, mientras dormía en la antigua habitación de su infancia, soñó con el jardín. Soñó que las raíces de todas las flores se conectaban bajo la tierra, formando una red tan compleja como las venas de un corazón gigante. Y en el centro de esa red, como un corazón latiendo, estaba la semilla original: la semilla de su tío, el hijo perdido de Doña Amparo.

Cuando despertó, supo lo que tenía que hacer.

A la mañana siguiente, Doña Amparo lo encontró en el jardín, con las manos llenas de tierra y los ojos llenos de lágrimas que, por primera vez en muchos años, no eran de tristeza.

—¿Qué haces, nieto mío? —preguntó ella.

—Sembrar futuras flores —respondió él—. Para cuando usted ya no esté. Para mis hijos. Para los hijos de mis hijos. Para todos los que vengan a Valdelirio buscando un lugar donde llorar.

Doña Amparo sonrió, y esa sonrisa fue más hermosa que todas las flores del jardín.

—Ahora sí llegaste a tiempo —dijo.

Esa primavera, mientras Doña Amparo yacía por primera vez en mucho tiempo sin poder levantarse, Tomás trabajó el jardín con sus propias manos. Plantó semillas que Doña Amparo le había dado: semillas de flores que aún no existían, híbridos de pétalos con forma de recuerdos y colores con sabor a esperanza.

Un día, cerca del mediodía, Doña Amparo llamó a Tomás desde su lecho.

—Ven, hijo. Quiero ver una cosa.

Tomás la llevó en brazos hasta el jardín, a la silla de mimbre. Ella contempló las flores con ojos cansados pero satisfechos.

—Sabes —dijo—, durante años pensé que este jardín era para honrar a los muertos. Hoy entiendo que siempre fue para despertar a los vivos.

Cerró los ojos. Una brisa suave recorrió el jardín, haciendo que todas las flores se inclinaran en una reverencia silenciosa.

Cuando el sol comenzó a ponerse, las primeras estrellas aparecieron en el cielo. En el jardín, una a una, las flores comenzaron a brillar con una luz tenue, fosforescente, como si cada una albergara un fragmento de alma.

Tomás comprendió entonces el verdadero secreto: las flores no eran lágrimas solidificadas. Eran recuerdos que se negaban a morir, bellezas que se rebelaban contra el olvido.

Esa noche, Tomás no lloró. Pero cuando se acostó, descubrió que su almohada estaba llena de semillas diminutas, como estrellas caídas del cielo del jardín.

Al amanecer, las plantó todas en un nuevo sector del terreno. Y así, el jardín de los recuerdos siguió creciendo, generación tras generación, lágrima tras lágrima, flor tras flor.

Porque mientras alguien recuerde, alguien siembre, alguien llore sobre la tierra con amor... el jardín永远不会 morir。

Y en las noches claras de Valdelirio, si prestas atención, aún puedes ver el brillo tenue de las flores de Doña Amparo, guiando a los perdidos hacia casa.

**FIN**

# The Pear Tree on Hollow Hill

They planted the pear tree the autumn Marcus Reed came home from the war.

The soil up on Hollow Hill was poor—nothing but shale and stubborn clay—but his wife, Esther, had asked for a fruit tree the way other women asked for curtains or a parlor rug. She wanted something that would bloom in spring and give them something to look forward to when the world had given them so much to look back on.

Marcus dug the hole himself. His hands, which had learned to hold a rifle steady in the trenches of France, shook as he set the spindly sapling into the ground. Esther pressed her palm against his back, steadying him the way she had steadied him through everything else.

"For the babies we'll have," she said.

They planted it in 1919. The tree did not bloom that year, or the next. Marcus, who had come home, left again—not for war, but for the bottom of a bottle, and finally for the bottom of a river in March of 1923. Esther found him in the spring, when the pear tree finally dared to flower.

She buried him at the foot of the hill, under the tree, where the white blossoms fell on the grave like small surrenders.

---

Forty years later, a girl named Ada Chen climbed Hollow Hill on a dare.

She was eleven that summer, and her grandmother had sent her from Taiwan to live with relatives in the Appalachian town of Millhaven. The other kids didn't know what to make of her—her broken English, her clothes her mother had shipped from Taipei, the way she always seemed to be listening to something no one else could hear. So when the boys said, *climb the hill and touch the pear tree or you're a chicken*, Ada climbed.

The tree had grown enormous. Its trunk was wider than her arms could span, and its branches bent low under the weight of late-summer fruit. Bees moved through the leaves in slow, golden waves. Ada stood at its base and pressed her hand to the bark, feeling the heat trapped there, the slow patient pulse of sap.

She found the gravestone half-buried in clover. *Marcus Reed, 1893–1923. Beloved Husband.*

Ada, who had lost her own father to a different kind of quiet grief, sat down beneath the tree and cried for a stranger. When she came down the hill, she was no longer a chicken. She was something else—a person who had touched something old and been changed by it.

---

In 1978, a man named Samuel Whitaker bought the property on Hollow Hill.

He was thirty-six and recently divorced, and he had decided, in the way men of a certain age do, that what he needed was land. Specifically, he needed land that nobody else wanted. The old Reed farmhouse had stood empty for decades, the porch sagging into the earth, the paint peeling back to bare gray wood. The pear tree, alone, had flourished. Its roots had cracked the foundation of the old tool shed. Its branches reached over the road like the arms of a tired woman making a bed.

Samuel meant to cut it down.

He walked out one August morning with a handsaw, drunk on the freedom of being answerable to no one. He set the blade against the trunk and began to push.

He stopped when the saw caught on something embedded in the bark. A metal button, tarnished green, the kind that had held a soldier's coat together. Samuel pulled it free and turned it in his fingers. He thought of his own father, who had served in Korea and never spoken of it. He thought of the years he had wasted trying to become someone his ex-wife could love.

He set the saw down and walked back to the house. That afternoon, he called a woman he hadn't spoken to in three years. He asked her how she was. He listened when she answered.

The tree stayed.

---

In the spring of 2019, a woman named June sat beneath the pear tree and watched her daughter take her college graduation photos.

The blossoms were everywhere, falling like snow that didn't melt. The photographer kept telling Mae to look at the camera, but Mae kept looking up, laughing, her face turned toward the petals. June thought: *this is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen.*

She had nearly not come. Her mother, Esther's great-granddaughter, had died in February, and June had spent three months in the particular grief of losing someone who had known you when you were nothing. Now she was here, in the same town her great-grandmother had fled after Marcus was buried, the town her grandmother Ada had been sent to as a child. The family had scattered, but they had scattered along lines that all bent back toward this hill.

Mae walked over and sat beside her. "Mom," she said. "Are you okay?"

June nodded. She thought about how a tree could outlive everyone who planted it. She thought about how love was not a thing you finished—it was a thing you put into the ground, and then you waited, sometimes for years, to see what came up.

"Yeah," she said. "I'm okay."

Above them, a breeze moved through the branches, and the petals kept falling.

---

That night, long after Mae and June had driven away, long after the photographer had packed up his gear and the small town of Millhaven had gone dark, the pear tree stood on Hollow Hill under a moon the color of old bone.

A century of roots held the shale together.

A century of blossoms had fallen and rotted and fed the soil.

A soldier slept beneath it. A girl had wept beneath it. A man had almost killed it and then decided, instead, to keep living. A mother had watched her daughter laugh beneath it, and had understood, at last, that the things we plant outlive us—that they are the only argument we have against the dark.

The wind moved through the leaves.

The tree did not speak.

It did not need to.

# The Wind in the Willows

The river had always been Rat's domain, and he knew every eddy, every sandbar, every whispering reed along its banks. So when Mole came scrambling up the bank one spring morning, breathless and blinking in the unfamiliar sunlight, Rat felt something stir in him that he had not felt in many seasons.

"Sit down," Rat said gently, helping his new friend onto the boat. "You seem You've been busy."

Mole laughed—a strange, rusty sound, as though he hadn't used his voice in a long while. "Indeed I have," he said. "It's wonderful, this world above ground. I'd forgotten there was anything but tunnels."

Rat smiled and pushed off from the bank. He knew, with the certainty of water finding its way to the sea, that this odd, blinking creature was going to change his life.

---

They became inseparable that summer. Rat taught Mole to swim and to punt and to listen to the wind in the willows, whose leaves made a sound like whispered secrets. In the evenings, they sat on Rat's veranda and watched the stars reflect on the dark water, while Rat told stories of otters and lost cities beneath the waves.

For Mole, who had lived his whole life in the dark earth, each day was a revelation. He discovered birdsong and butterflies and the cool rush of water over his paws. He discovered that friendship, like a river, could carry you to places you'd never imagined.

---

But Rat had a friend he had not yet introduced. Toad.

"He is wealthy," Rat warned Mole, as they walked toward Toad Hall one bright morning. "And he is possessed of every virtue except one—moderation."

Toad greeted them at his great doors, resplendent in a driving cap and goggles. "A motorcar!" he exclaimed, seizing Mole by the paw. "The very finest thing that ever was. Come, I'll show you!"

Rat sighed. He had seen this before—many times before. Toad's passions were storms, and they raged and passed, leaving only wreckage.

---

That summer, Toad's obsession with motorcars consumed him entirely. He drove too fast, he drove into the river, he drove into the stable, and at last, driven by his own recklessness, he drove himself into the hands of the police.

Rat and Mole sat in the courtroom and watched their friend sentenced to twenty years in prison. It was, Rat said heavily, the hardest thing he had ever done.

---

But the story of Toad is the story of friendship, too. Rat did not abandon his friend. Neither did Mole. They hatched a plan—reckless, ridiculous, perfectly Toad-ish—and on a stormy night, they broke Toad out of prison.

"You must change," Rat told him, as they hid in a woodcutter's cottage. "You must become Toad again. The Toad we know. The Toad we love."

Toad wept. For the first time in many years, he felt shame—and with it, the first stirrings of a better self.

---

They fought their way back to Toad Hall, for the place had been overrun by weasels and stoats in Toad's absence. It was a great battle, fought with swords and frying pans and sheer stubbornness, and at the end of it, Toad Hall belonged to Toad once more.

But this Toad was a different Toad. He had learned, as all of us must learn, that the things we chase so wildly rarely bring us joy. He had learned to be grateful, to be kind, to be still.

---

And so they lived, in the fullness of time. Rat on his river, Mole in his burrow, Toad in his Hall, Badger in his ancient home in the forest. They quarreled and made up. They feasted and explored. They grew old together, as true friends do.

On summer evenings, when the wind stirred in the willows, they would sit on Rat's veranda and remember—remember the spring when Mole first came up from the earth, the summer they broke Toad out of prison, the winter Badger showed them the secrets of the woods.

"Home," Rat would say, looking out over the water. "There's nothing quite like it."

And Mole, who had once known only tunnels, would smile and agree.

---

*For the river, they say, never forgets its children. And the wind in the willows never stops whispering of the friends who once lived there—brave Rat, gentle Mole, foolish Toad, wise Badger—whose stories are told and retold, season after season, in the golden light of an English afternoon.*

**~ Fin ~**

# 花冢

我叫阿沅，是个花匠。

在这座江南小镇上，我家三代都做花匠。爷爷的爷爷留下了一本发黄的花谱，记着一百七十二种花的脾性。父亲说，花比人通透，懂了花，便懂了天地。

我没那么大的志向。我只守着我家那爿小小的花铺，卖些应季的花草，勉强糊口度日。

直到那个暮春的黄昏，她在花铺门前停下脚步。

她穿一身月白色的衫裙，鬓边别着一朵将开未开的白兰花，目光落在我案上那盆半枯的月季上。

"这花，还有救吗？"她的声音很轻，像怕惊扰了什么。

我抬眼看她，心头莫名一颤。那双眼睛很清澈，却藏着一种说不出的疲惫，像开得太久、即将凋谢的花。

"能救。"我说，"只是需要换土、剪枝，还要移到有月光的地方。"

她点了点头，目光里有光一闪。

"那就劳烦你了。"

她没有问价钱。我也没有提。

她姓苏，单名一个"蘅"字，是从省城来此地养病的。

蘅，本就是一种香草的名字。

我每隔三日去她住处送花、换土、修剪。她住在一座老宅的后院里，院子里空空荡荡，只我送去的那盆月季，渐渐抽出新芽。

她有时站在窗边看我侍弄花草，有时隔着窗纱与我说话。她说她在省城教书，教的是生物学。她说她喜欢花，是因为花比人简单。

我没接话。我心里想，花哪里简单？花的心思，比人深多了。

那年五月，月季开出了第一朵花，是极淡的粉，像少女脸上的红晕。

她看着那朵花，忽然落下泪来。

"我已病了三年，"她说，"医生说我时日无多。"

我手中的剪子停了。

"我没有家人，父母早亡，未曾婚嫁。走的时候，怕是连个收尸的人都没有。"她的声音平静得像在说别人的事，"我想在走之前，看看这世上最好看的花，开满一院子。"

我站在那里，许久说不出话。

后来，我做了一件让镇上人都觉得我疯了的事。

我翻遍了父亲留下的花谱，又托人从省城买来许多珍稀的种苗。我把苏蘅的院子整个改造成了一个花圃，种满了各季的花。

春天有桃花、杏花、海棠；
夏天有栀子、荷花、紫薇；
秋天有桂花、菊花、芙蓉；
冬天有梅花、山茶、水仙。

我日出而作，日落不息。我没有收她一文钱。

镇上的人问我图什么。

我说："不图什么。"

其实我心里想的是——她那么爱花，我怎么忍心让她凋谢时，连一片花瓣都看不见。

那年深秋，桂花满院飘香。

苏蘅坐在花树下，怀里抱着一只猫，是只流浪的橘猫。她说这猫是她捡的，原本要死在她怀里，没想到竟活了下来。

"连猫都活着，"她笑着说，"我倒不好意思死了。"

我鼻子一酸，别过脸去。

那年冬天，雪下得很大，梅花开得极盛。

苏蘅的病却奇迹般地好转了。医生也说不清原因，只说或许是她心境开阔，或许是花香有利于养病。

第二年春天，她能下床走动了。她在花圃里走着，一株一株地看过去，像在检阅她的臣民。

走到那盆月季前，她停下脚步。

月季开得正盛，一朵一朵，粉的、红的、白的，开满了枝头。

"你骗我，"她说，"你说这花很难救。"

"没骗你，"我说，"确实很难。只是救的时候，不知不觉就救活了。"

她愣了一下，然后笑了。

那是我第一次见她笑得那样开怀。眼睛弯弯的，嘴唇弯弯的，整个人像一朵盛开的花。

那年秋天，桂花又开了。

苏蘅站在桂花树下，对我说："我打算回省城了。"

我手里的剪子"咔嚓"一声，剪断了一根枝条。

"病好了，该回去了。"她顿了顿，"这里的事……我会记一辈子。"

我低着头，没说话。

我不知道该说什么。我心里想的是——这一院子花，要怎么办？

"花铺的生意不好，"我说，"我想把这爿花铺关了，到省城去谋个差事。"

她抬头看我，眼睛里有什么一闪而过。

"那……这些花呢？"

"花也要搬去的。"我说，"花离了熟悉的地方，会水土不服。"

她沉默良久。

"你这个人，"她说，"真是被花耽误了。"

我抬起头，看着她。

她低下头，看着地上的桂花。

许久，她说："那你就带着你的花，来省城吧。"

我笑了。

那一年深秋，我关了镇上的花铺，带着一卡车的花，跟着她去了省城。

省城很大，花铺很小。

但那爿花铺有个很好听的名字，叫"蘅沅花坊"。

后来镇上的人说，镇上那家花铺搬走了，听说搬到了省城，跟那个养病的女人一起开了铺子。

再后来，听说他们成了亲。

再再后来，听说省城有家很有名的花铺，掌柜的是个花痴，一年四季花开不败，像一座花园，又像一个梦。

那些花，我也叫不全名字。

但我认得其中一种——

是一盆月季，开得最盛，颜色最正。

花谱上说，月季的花语是"等待"。

我等了三年。

值得。

# The Thaw

The first thing Eleanor noticed was the light.

It crept through the slats of the window shutters in thin, golden blades, landing across her closed eyelids like a question she wasn't ready to answer. She lay still beneath three quilts, listening to the house breathe around her. Somewhere, a radiator clanked. Somewhere else, ice shifted on the river.

Three years.

That was how long she had been asleep. Not the ordinary sleep of nights and weekends and Sunday afternoons, but the long, suspended sleep of a woman who had decided, one gray November, that she was finished. Finished with the world, with grief, with the endless performance of being okay. She had pulled the curtains shut, turned off her phone, drunk broth and eaten crackers for weeks before her body, sensing the futility, simply closed itself down. Neighbors brought casseroles that molded in the refrigerator. Her son Marcus called, once, twice, then stopped calling.

And then, one morning in late February, a robin began to sing outside her window.

She had forgotten birds. She had forgotten that the world made sounds that were not for her, not about her, not requiring her attention. The robin sang three notes, paused, sang them again, as if rehearsing something. As if practicing joy.

Eleanor opened her eyes.

The room came into focus slowly, the way a photograph develops in solution. The dust on the dresser. The vase of dried flowers from a funeral. The stack of unread mail on the floor. Her body felt strange—light and heavy at once, as if it had been emptied out and refilled with something more cautious.

She sat up.

This was harder than she expected. Her arms trembled. Her head swam. She felt like a creature emerging from a long swim underwater, gasping at a different kind of air. She swung her legs over the edge of the bed and looked down at her feet. They were smaller than she remembered. Thinner. She had lost so much weight.

She stood, and the world tilted, and she held onto the bedpost until the world remembered where it was supposed to be.

The first thing she did was open the shutters.

Light poured in—cold and sharp and merciless. She blinked against it. Outside, the world was astonishing. Snow lay across everything like a fresh page, unmarked, waiting. The river was silver. The trees were sculptures of black and white. And the sky—that impossible, indifferent blue—went on forever.

She pressed her hand to the glass and felt the cold coming through.

The second thing she did was find a phone.

She kept one in the kitchen drawer, an old thing she had never disconnected. It had no internet, no apps, only the ability to call and to be called. She sat at the kitchen table, the phone heavy in her hands, and looked at the numbers.

She could call Marcus.

She picked up the receiver and held it to her ear before she was ready. There was no dial tone—just a soft, patient hum, as if the line had been waiting for her all this time.

She dialed.

It rang four times. She was about to hang up, to slip back into the warm water of retreat, when the line clicked.

"Mom?"

His voice. Older. The vowels deeper. She had not heard it in three years, and yet she knew it instantly, the way one knows one's own name.

"Hello, sweetheart," she said. Her voice came out strange, a croak, a thing not used. "It's me."

There was a silence. Then a breath.

"Are you—are you okay?"

She looked out the window. The robin had returned. It sat on the bare branch of the maple tree, its breast rust-colored in the white world, and it looked at her through the glass as if it had been waiting too.

"I'm awake," she said. "I'm finally awake."

She did not know what would come next. She did not know if she was healed or only stirring from one kind of sleep into another. She did not know if her son would come, or what she would say when he did, or whether she could bear the weight of his relief and his anger and his hope.

But she was standing. The light was in the room. The phone was warm against her ear.

It was enough. For now, it was enough.

She breathed in, and the air tasted like snow and iron and something she had forgotten the name of—something that might have been the future.

"Stay on the line," she said. "I'm going to put the kettle on."

And for the first time in three years, she walked toward the kitchen, and the light followed her.

# 種をまく女

---

村の東端、川沿いの小さな畑で、志乃は鍬を振るっていた。

七十の手習いという言葉があるが、彼女が畑仕事を知ったのは、それよりずっと前のことだった。戦後の焼け野原で、母親と二人、焼け石に水を注ぐように作物を育てた。多くは枯れた。それでも種をまき続けた。生きるために。

あれから六十年以上が経った。

「志乃さん、起きとるんか」

向かいの家の勘太が、あぜ道から声をかけてきた。八十を超えた勘太は、村で一番の長老だ。かつては炭焼きを生業としていたが、今では日向ぼっこが日課になっている。

「おはよう、勘太さん。きょうはいい日和だね」

「種まき日和じゃな」

志乃は鍬を止めた。手の中に、大根の種が光っている。小さな、小さな種。指先ほどの命の約束。

「勘太さん、わしはね、今年もまくよ」

「去年もまいとったじゃろ」

「去年も、その前も」

勘太はゆっくりと頷いた。

「わしもじゃ。えのきのほだ木、今年も並べる」

---

志乃の家には、もう誰もいない。

夫は二十年前に、娘は十年前にもうこの世を去った。息子が一人いるが、都会で仕事をしており、帰省は盆と正月だけだ。

畑は、ただの畑ではない。

娘が七つのとき、一緒にまいたひまわりの種が、今も毎年咲く。娘の嫁ぎ先に持っていった朝顔の種は、孫娘が大切に育てていると言う。去年の秋には、息子から電話があった。

「母さん、畑やってるんだな」

「やってるよ」

「俺も、マンションだけど、ベランダでバジル育ててる。母さんの血だ」

彼女は笑った。電話を切ってから、しばらく泣いた。

---

春の土は、黒くて柔らかい。

志乃は掌で土を押し固めた。大根の種を一つ、また一つ。土をかぶせる。水をやる。それだけのことだ。

それだけのことが、どれほどの手間かを知っている。

土を耕し、種をまき、雑草を抜き、虫を払い、肥料をやり、水をやり——そして、待つ。何も起こらない日も、何日も。芽が出るまでは、ただ信じて、待つ。

「婆ちゃん、なぜ種なんかまくの」

三年前の夏、孫娘の結衣が泊まりに来たとき、そう聞いた。

十歳の結衣は、都会っ子だった。虫を怖がり、土を汚いと言い、太陽の下で遊ぶことを知らなかった。

志乃は答えた。

「これはね、未来をたくわえるようなもんだよ」

「未来？」

「この種はね、今年食べられないかもしれない。でも土の中で冬を越して、来年の春になったら芽を出す。お婆ちゃんがいなくなっても、この畑はずっとここにあってね、種をまく誰かがいたら、ずっと続いていくんだよ」

結衣は少し考えた後、小さな声で言った。

「じゃあ、私もまきたい」

志乃は結衣に、一握りの種を渡した。ひまわりの種——娘がかつて愛した花。

---

結衣は、今年の春、中学生になった。

部活は科学部だと言う。顕微鏡で細胞の観察をしているらしい。

春休みに帰省した結衣は、ランドセルではなく、スコップを持っていた。

「婆ちゃん、一緒に種をまきたい。去年のひまわりから取れた種、持ってきた」

志乃は驚いた。あの種を、結衣はとっておいてくれたのだ。遠い街で、中学生になった孫娘が、種を持ち帰るまでに育て、守っていたのだ。

「よく持っとってくれたね」

「だって婆ちゃんの種だもん」

二人は並んで土を掘った。志乃が鍬を、結衣が手で。

種をまき、土をかぶせ、水をやる。

「婆ちゃん」

「なあに」

「私ね、将来、農業やりたいかも」

志乃は目を瞬いた。

「種の研究者？ お婆ちゃん、聞いたことないけど、種にも歴史があるんだよ。同じ種でも、年代によって違う性質を持ってる場合があるの。結衣が種の研究したら、お婆ちゃんみたいな人の役に立てるかも」

結衣の目が輝いた。

「じゃあ、種まきながら研究する！」

志乃は笑った。声を出して笑った。久しぶりだった。

---

夏が来て、畑にひまわりが咲いた。

結衣のひまわりは、背が高かった。志乃が六十年前から毎年まいているひまわりよりも、ずっと背が高かった。品種改良されたせいもあるだろうが、それだけではないような気がした。

二人は、ひまわりの前で写真をとった。結衣がスマートフォンで。

「送るね、お父さんに」

「ああ、送ってやれ。息子も喜ぶよ」

夕方、結衣は帰っていった。駅まで見送りに行くと、彼女は電車の窓から叫んだ。

「婆ちゃん、来年も帰るよ！ 種もってくる！」

「待っとるよ！」

汽車が遠ざかり、ホームに風が吹いた。秋桜の種が、風に運ばれていく。

---

秋。

志乃は畑で、大根を収穫していた。冬を越せる分だけの、たくわえ。

畑の隅に、来年のための種をとるための大根を残してある。

向かいの勘太は、今年の春から体調を崩し、寝たきりになっていた。それでも奥さんに言わせると、あの人の持ち前の性分で、毎日が起き上がるように暮らしていると言う。

「志乃さーん、たまにはわしのとこにも来んか」

奥さんの声。

「ああ、今度行くよ。勘太さんのえのきの話、聞きたいからね」

人間の一生は短い。種が芽を出し、花を咲かせ、実を結び、また種を残すまでのほうが、きっと長い。

志乃は土を踏みしめた。彼女の足跡の上に、来年の春、また芽が出る。

種は、いつも未来のためにまかれる。

今を生きる者の務めとして。

# El primer día de primavera

La alarma sonó a las 6:45, pero Lucía ya estaba despierta. Llevaba horas con los ojos abiertos en la oscuridad, mirando el techo de su habitación en aquel pequeño apartamento de la calle Atocha. El corazón le latía con fuerza, como si hubiera corrido una maratón sin moverse de la cama.

Hoy era el día.

Llevaba tres años diciéndoselo a sí misma. Tres años posponiendo, justificándose, mintiéndose. *El mes que viene*. *Cuando tenga más dinero*. *Cuando esté lista*. Las excusas habían sido tan variadas como convincentes en su momento, pero esta noche ninguna había funcionado. Esta noche, la verdad se había colado entre las rendijas de su fingido optimismo y le había susurrado al oído lo que tanto temía escuchar: que nunca estaría lista, que el dinero nunca sería suficiente, que el "más adelante" era simplemente otra forma de decir "nunca".

Se levantó despacio, como si el repentino movimiento pudiera romper algo frágil en el aire. La luz de la mañana apenas se filtraba por las cortinas, gris y suave, como si Madrid todavía no se hubiera decidido a despertar del todo. Pero ella sabía que era la primera de muchas primaveras que venía buscando. La primavera que había decidido regalarse a sí misma.

Se vistió sin mirarse al espejo. No quería ver el miedo reflejado en sus propios ojos. Guardó en una mochila vieja lo que había preparado la noche anterior: un cambio de ropa, documentos, un cuaderno con una lista que había escrito y reescrito docenas de veces, las llaves del estudio diminuto que había alquilado en un pueblo de la costa valenciana, y un sobre con sus ahorros de dos años. Casi doce mil euros. No era mucho, pero era todo lo que tenía.

Antes de salir, se detuvo frente a la puerta. A su lado, en una pequeña mesita, descansaba una foto enmarcada de ella y su madre, sonriendo en una playa mediterránea hacía ya veinte años. La cogió con cuidado, pasó el pulgar por el borde dorado del marco, y la guardó también en la mochila.

—Perdóname, mamá —murmuró—. Pero no puedo quedarme.

Cerró la puerta con llave, bajó las escaleras del edificio sin hacer ruido, y salió a la calle. El aire fresco de marzo le golpeó el rostro, y por primera vez en meses sintió que respiraba de verdad. No el aire viciado de una oficina donde pasaba ocho horas al día contestando emails que no le importaban. No el aire cargado de un hogar que había dejado de sentirse como tal. Respiraba el aire de una nueva vida que todavía no existía pero que ya podía oler: sal marina, azahar, tierra húmeda.

El tren de cercanías salía a las 8:15 desde Atocha. Tenía el billete comprado desde hacía semanas, disimulándolo entre los gastos habituales para que nadie notara nada. Su novio, Andrés, dormía todavía en su piso de Chamberí, ajeno a todo. Creía que Lucía estaba en casa, que esta noche habían quedado para cenar con sus padres en el restaurante de siempre. No había sido difícil mentirle. Hacía tiempo que Andrés vivía en una realidad paralela, donde todo seguía bien, donde los silencios entre ellos no significaban nada, donde el anillo de compromiso que le había dado hacía seis meses seguía siendo una promesa y no una cadena.

En el tren, Lucía se sentó junto a la ventanilla y apoyó la frente contra el cristal frío. Miró cómo Madrid se alejaba poco a poco: primero los edificios grises del centro, después las naves industriales de los barrios del sur, luego el paisaje seco y polvoriento de La Mancha. Cerró los ojos y pensó en su madre, en cómo le decía siempre que la vida era demasiado corta para gastarla en vivir la vida de otros. *Eres libre, Lucía*, le decía. *Solo tienes que atreverte*.

Había muerto hacía cinco años, un febrero frío y húmedo como este. Cáncer de pulmón, aunque ella nunca había fumado. A veces Lucía pensaba que su madre se había consumido simplemente de haber aguantado demasiado: un marido infiel, una hija que se fue lejos, un trabajo que detestaba, un cuerpo que empezó a fallarle cuando ya no quedaba nada por lo que luchar. Había muerto en un hospital público, conectada a máquinas, diciéndole a Lucía que no llorara, que había vivido lo suficiente, que lo único que lamentaba era no haber sido más valiente.

*Mamá*, pensó Lucía mientras el tren avanzaba hacia el sur, *hoy empiezo a ser valiente por las dos.*

El móvil vibró en su bolsillo. Lo sacó con manos temblorosas. Andrés.

*"Buenos días, cariño. ¿Cómo has dormido? Nos vemos a las 9 en el restaurante, ¿no? Mamá está emocionada. Te quiero."*

Lucía leyó el mensaje tres veces. Sintió una punzada en el pecho, algo parecido a la culpa pero también al alivio. Tecleó una respuesta breve: *"Sí. Hasta luego."* No quería mentir más de lo necesario. Ya habría tiempo para todo. Tiempo para explicaciones, para disculpas, para el dolor que sabía que vendría después, cuando la euforia del primer paso se apagara y tuviera que enfrentarse a lo que había dejado atrás.

Pero eso sería después. Hoy era hoy. Hoy era el primer día de la primavera, y también el primer día de su nueva vida.

A las once de la mañana, el tren se detuvo en una estación pequeña, casi vacía, de un pueblo cuyo nombre había buscado en Google Maps y que ahora aparecía ante ella como una promesa: **Dènia**. Bajó al andén con su mochila al hombro, y el sol le dio de lleno en la cara, cálido y generoso, como si la estuviera esperando. El olor a sal y a flores de almendro llenó sus pulmones, y por primera vez en años, Lucía se permitió sonreír.

Caminó hacia la salida, atravesó el pequeño vestíbulo de la estación, y cuando salió a la plaza, se detuvo un momento. El mundo seguía girando, indiferente a su decisión. Los vecinos cruzaban la plaza camino del mercado, una madre empujaba un cochecito, un grupo de jubilados tomaba el sol en un banco. Nadie sabía quién era ella. Nadie sabía de dónde venía. Nadie sabía que aquella mujer de mirada triste y mochila gastada había cruzado media España huyendo de una vida que no había elegido.

Y eso, precisamente eso, era lo que la hacía sentir más libre.

Se ajustó la mochila, respiró hondo, y empezó a caminar hacia el estudio que había visto en fotos y que ahora iba a ser su hogar. No sabía cuánto tiempo se quedaría. No sabía si funcionaría, si el dinero le alcanzaría, si la soledad la devoraría o la salvaría. No sabía si algún día llamaría a Andrés para pedirle perdón, o si algún día él la buscaría para devolvérselo todo.

Solo sabía una cosa, y era lo único que necesitaba saber en ese primer día de primavera, en esa primera hora de su nueva vida:

Que por fin había dejado de prometerse el mañana y había empezado a caminar hacia él.

Y eso, se dijo mientras el sol le calentaba la nuca y una brisa suave le revolvía el pelo, era más de lo que había hecho en treinta y dos años de vida.

El primer paso estaba dado.

Ahora solo quedaban todos los demás.

# Pollen and Posies

The first bouquet appeared on Monday.

Marigolds, I think. Or maybe daisies—something small and golden that caught the fluorescent office light and made Lena's corner of the bullpen glow like a sunrise. I noticed because I'm always noticing Lena. I'd noticed the way she tucks her hair behind her ear when she's concentrating, the way she hums off-key while waiting for the coffee machine, the way her laugh sounds like wind chimes in a thunderstorm.

I'd also noticed, approximately forty minutes after arriving at work that first Monday, that my sinuses had declared war.

*Gesundheit*, Lena called across the room, waving.

I sneezed into a tissue and smiled.

---

By Wednesday, she'd switched to tulips. Pink ones, fanned out in a chipped mug that read *WORLD'S OKAYEST COWORKER* (a Secret Santa gift from three years ago, according to office legend). I took two antihistamines and a decongestant and told myself I was being romantic.

"You're looking a little puffy," said Derek from accounting, peering at me over his cubicle wall.

"Late night," I said.

"Must've been a good one."

The worst part—the very worst—was that I couldn't stop looking at her. The way she'd angle the flowers just so, tilting the mug until the petals caught the light. The way she'd lean down and breathe them in, eyes half-closed, like she was the protagonist in a perfume commercial.

I wanted to be the protagonist in her perfume commercial. I wanted to be the flowers. I wanted to be anything that got to be that close to her face.

I took a third antihistamine and my heart raced uncomfortably for an unrelated reason.

---

On Friday, I made a decision.

It was unprofessional. It was, possibly, insane. But I had spent ninety-three dollars on a small plant from the nursery on Fourth Street—a peace lily, low-maintenance, lush and green and blessedly, mercifully pollen-free—and I had carried it across the parking lot with the tender care of a person transporting a human infant.

I set it on the edge of her desk, beside the tulips.

Lena looked up from her keyboard. Her eyes, which were the color of coffee with too much cream, went wide.

"Is this—?"

"For your collection," I said. My voice sounded strange. Possibly because my sinuses were approximately ninety percent closed. "I noticed you liked having something alive on your desk. But uh." I rubbed the back of my neck. "Some of us are, you know. Allergy people."

"Are you saying I should stop?" Her brow furrowed. "I can stop. I didn't realize—"

"No! No, I like—" I swallowed. "I like that you like them. I just thought maybe you could like one that's alive and doesn't want to murder me."

Something shifted in her face. A small rearrangement, like a picture being straightened on a wall.

"The peace lily," she said softly.

"The peace lily."

"You bought me a peace lily because you're allergic to the flowers I keep buying myself."

"That's—yes. That's accurate."

Lena tilted her head, studying me the way she studied the bouquets—like she was figuring out the best angle for the light. Then she smiled, and the smile was warm and slow and entirely unguarded, and I forgot, briefly, how to breathe. Which, given the circumstances, may have been a mercy.

"You know what?" she said. She picked up the peace lily and set it directly in the center of her desk, in front of the tulips, like a small green bodyguard. "I think I like this one best."

She looked up at me, still smiling.

"You want to get lunch? There's a place around the corner with a really good soup. And," she added, standing and gathering her jacket, "no flowers. I promise."

I followed her out of the office, sneezing exactly once into my elbow, happier than I'd been in months.

Behind us, on Lena's desk, the peace lily sat in the slanting afternoon light, broad green leaves unfurled like a small, leafy heart.

---
