# The Latitude of Almost

The lighthouse keeper's cottage was the color of unripe apricots and had been leaning slightly east for as long as anyone in Kestrel Cove could remember. Mara had rented it for the summer because it was cheap, because it was far from the marketing department she'd fled in Atlanta, and because she liked the idea of sleeping somewhere that had stood crooked through a century of storms.

She had not expected the garden.

It was tucked behind the cottage, a wild, half-tended sprawl that tumbled down toward the cliffs. Whoever had lived there before had loved roses. They grew everywhere—in cracked washbasins, against the lichen-eaten fence, climbing the rusted iron skeleton of what might once have been a gazebo. They bloomed in colors Mara couldn't name, custard-yellow and coral and a deep, bruised red that looked almost black at dusk.

"And you must be the new tenant."

The voice came from the far side of the hedge. Mara looked up from the watering can she'd borrowed from inside and saw a man stepping through a gap in the overgrown privet. He was carrying a bucket of something that smelled sharply of compost.

"I'm Julian," he said. "The cottage next door. The keeper's daughter still lives in the big house up the lane, but she asked me to keep an eye on the garden. I'm afraid I've neglected it."

"You?" Mara said. "You planted all this?"

"Planted, weeded, pruned, despaired of." He smiled. He had a narrow face, a small mouth, and eyes that crinkled when he smiled so that he looked like a much younger man than his beard suggested. "I'm a bad gardener and a worse neighbor, as you'll discover. I mostly apologize."

She introduced herself, and he nodded and stayed for perhaps fifteen minutes. He showed her where the spigot dripped, where the rosemary had taken over the herb bed, where a fox had been digging under the fence. He left her with the bucket and a wave.

She didn't think about him again until Friday, when she walked down to the village for milk and saw him in the post office, buying stamps with the slow deliberation of a man who wrote letters.

It became a thing, then. Not a pattern, exactly. More like weather.

She would hear him at the fence, the rhythmic snip of his shears, and she would wander out with a glass of iced tea. They talked about books, about the strange behavior of seabirds, about a mutual friend they didn't have but invented—a professor of nautical folklore named Dr. Halloran who corresponded from Helsinki. Julian was a translator, he said. He worked from Dutch and German into English, mostly technical manuals. He said it with a slight shrug, as if confessing to a minor crime.

"You don't look like a translator of technical manuals," Mara said, on her third or fourth visit to the fence.

"What does a translator of technical manuals look like?"

"More glasses. Less beard."

He laughed. "I have two pairs of glasses. One for distance and one for despair. The beard is a separate project."

She went back to Atlanta in the fall, she told herself. She had a job, a lease, a life that didn't include compost buckets and imaginary professors. She was only here until August.

But August was a long time.

One evening in late June, she went out to the garden and found him sitting on the low stone wall at its edge, looking out at the sea. The sun was doing something extravagant with the horizon. He turned when he heard her, and there was a space on the wall beside him that looked like it had been waiting.

She sat down.

The stone was warm.

"I should tell you something," he said, after a while. "I'm not just here for the summer. I live here. I'll be here in October."

"I know," she said. "I figured."

"Okay." He nodded. He seemed relieved, which surprised her, because she'd assumed he understood the situation perfectly. "And you?"

"I'm here until the end of August."

"Right," he said. "That's what I thought."

They sat with that for a minute. A gull wheeled past, very close, and cried out at them.

"I wasn't planning this," she said, though she wasn't sure what *this* was yet. "I came here to be alone."

"I know," he said again. "I can leave the garden to itself, if that's better."

"Don't," she said. "Please don't."

He didn't.

What unfolded between them was not a love affair in any sense she recognized from the self-help aisle of the airport bookstore. It didn't have the urgency of new love or the drama of an affair or the catastrophe of something forbidden. It had the odd, weightless quality of two people who had decided, independently, not to count.

They didn't make plans. They didn't talk about the future. When she asked him once what he was thinking, he said, "I'm thinking that the light on that rock looks like it's been there for ten thousand years and will be there for ten thousand more, and that we are extremely temporary, and that I find this oddly comforting."

"That sounds like a translation of something," she said.

"It is. It's from a Dutch poet. But the original is much sadder."

They went walking on the cliff. They went swimming once, at a small cove where the water was the temperature of a cold bath. He made her a meal of new potatoes and mackerel and a salad that was ninety percent herbs. She read aloud to him on the sofa in her cottage, a novel she found both boring and compelling, while he mended a pair of trousers and occasionally closed his eyes.

She learned the geography of his hands, which were surprisingly rough for a man who spent his days with words. She learned that he hummed when he was concentrating and forgot to finish sentences when he was tired. She learned that he had been married once, very young, to a woman who now lived in Antwerp and sent him a card at Christmas, and that he had a daughter in her twenties who lived in Berlin and rarely answered his letters.

"You can tell me to stop," he said, the first time he mentioned her.

"I won't," she said.

He told her about his daughter. He told her about the translation job he had once had, translating the memoirs of a man who had survived something terrible and wanted the world to know. He told her it had nearly broken him, and that he had decided then to stick to manuals. He told her he was forty-six. She told him she was thirty-three, which still surprised her whenever she said it.

In July there was a heat wave. The roses went mad. The lavender, which had been so polite in June, suddenly erupted. She lay on the grass in the garden with her eyes closed and listened to him read aloud from the Dutch poet, his English slightly accented in a way she could not identify.

In the evenings they sat on the stone wall and watched the boats go out. He pointed out the ones he knew, the lobster boats with their specific rigs, the small sailboats belonging to people whose names he knew.

She didn't ask him to spend the night, and he didn't ask her. They kissed sometimes, leaning against the cottage wall, or sitting on the sofa while her novel waited, neglected. The kisses were unhurried and exploratory, as if they were both learning a new dialect.

In August the light began to change. The evenings arrived earlier. The roses started to look tired.

"I'm going to miss this garden," he said, one morning, standing among the browned stalks with his shears.

"You'll have it all year."

"Yes," he said. "That's true."

On the second to last day, she went up to the village to post a box of books back to herself. He offered to drive her. They had never gone to the village together. She realized, sitting in the passenger seat of his old car, that she had no idea how he behaved in the world. He might be a completely different person at the post office. He might be someone she didn't know.

He wasn't. He was exactly himself, only more so. He said good morning to a woman at the post office counter. He asked about her hip. He bought a newspaper from the rack and folded it under his arm. He was a man who lived here, who had a place here, who would go on living here after she left.

Back at the cottage, he helped her carry the box out of the car. They set it by the gate.

"You'll come back?" he said.

"No," she said. "I mean yes, but not for that."

He nodded.

"What do you mean?" he asked.

"I mean I won't come back to do this over again. I mean this was the thing, and now it's the thing that's been."

He considered this. "Yes," he said. "I think that's right."

She kissed him, there by the gate, with the box of books at their feet. He put his hand on the back of her neck, where the hair was still damp from the shower.

"I should go in," she said.

"Yes."

"You should go home."

"Yes."

Neither of them moved for a long time.

Later, alone in the cottage, she packed the last of her things and stood for a while at the kitchen window, looking out at the garden. The roses were mostly done. The lavender had gone to seed. A single blackbird hopped along the path, very busy, very purposeful.

She thought about the stone wall, and the light on the rock, and the sound of him reading in Dutch. She thought about the way he had said *temporary* as if it were a kind of grace.

She turned off the light and drove away in the dark.

In the rearview mirror, the cottage leaned its small, persistent lean against the dawn.

# 《雾中的灯塔》

林屿在雾中站了整整七年。

最初来到这座小岛时，她以为自己只是暂时迷失。海风裹挟着咸涩的水汽扑面而来，白色的雾像一匹永远扯不开的绸缎，将整个世界裹得严严实实。她在那座废弃灯塔的旧居里安顿下来，靠着修补渔网和给岛上的老人写信度日。

七年间，她没有收到过任何一封回信。

她写给城里的母亲，写给曾经说好要一起去看极地的挚友，写给那个在车站转身离开的恋人。信封在门口的信箱里塞得满满当当，最终被海风吹散，落入潮水。

岛上只有一盏灯还能亮。那是老灯塔最顶层的一盏旧灯，林屿每隔三天就要爬上去擦拭灯罩、添上煤油。雾太浓的时候，那灯光只能照亮眼前三尺的地方。她常常对着那三尺光亮发呆，想象灯塔以外的世界是不是真的存在。

第七年的深秋，一只灰色的信鸽撞在了灯塔的玻璃窗上。

林屿捧着那只奄奄一息的鸽子，发现它的腿上绑着一只小小的铜管。铜管里塞着一张被海浪浸得发皱的纸条，纸条上只有一行字：

*"如果你还愿意走出来，请点燃灯塔最高处的灯。我们会来接。"*

没有日期，没有署名，笔迹却熟悉得让她的心脏猛地抽紧。那是她自己的字迹。是七年前，她出发前写给未来自己的那张纸条，被某个陌生人不知从何处拾起，又辗转寄回了这座小岛。

林屿在旧木箱里翻出那封早已褪色的信——那是母亲在她离开那天寄出的最后一封信。她一直不敢拆开，因为害怕里面写着"不要再回来了"这样的话。

她颤抖着拆开。信纸上只有四个字：

*"家里等你。"*

那晚，林屿第一次不是为了照亮海面而点灯。她将煤油添满，将灯芯拨到最亮，然后站在灯塔的最高处，看那束光穿破七年来从未散去的雾。光柱切开浓雾，像一把利剑，将她与世界隔绝了七年的那堵墙劈开了一道口子。

雾开始消散。

远处的海平线上，露出一艘小船的轮廓。船头站着一位头发花白的老人，怀里抱着一件叠得整整齐齐的红色围巾。那是林屿离家时，母亲坚持让她带上却始终未被想起的东西。

船靠岸的时候，晨光已经从东边透了出来。

林屿跑下灯塔的石阶，踩过七年来被她踏过无数遍的青苔，跑过那扇永远塞满信件却从未被打开的信箱，跑过雾中那条她以为没有尽头的路。

她没有立刻走向船。她先转身，望了一眼那座陪伴了她七年的旧灯塔。灯光在晨曦中显得微弱，却仍倔强地亮着。

她轻声说："谢谢你照亮我。"

然后她转过身，走向沙滩，走向船，走向那个已经等待了她七年的怀抱。

海风最后一次吹过她的发梢，带着的不再只是咸涩，还有阳光晒过的温度。

当她踏上甲板，母亲把那件红色围巾披在她肩上。围巾很轻，却压得她眼眶一酸。她靠在母亲肩头，终于让憋了七年的眼泪落了下来。

船缓缓驶离小岛。林屿站在船尾，看着灯塔在视野里越来越小。她知道，那盏灯会一直亮着，直到下一个需要它的人到来。

船向着太阳升起的方向驶去。

雾气彻底散去的早晨，林屿抬起头，看着天边那道金色的光线铺满海面，铺满整个世界。

她深深地吸了一口气，迈步走下甲板，踏上了码头坚实的土地。周围人来人往，有卖早点的吆喝声，有自行车铃铛的脆响，有孩子跑过时咯咯的笑声。

林屿眯起眼睛，适应着久违的明亮。

然后她抬起头，微微一笑，朝着母亲伸出的那只手走去——

**她一步，踏进了阳光里。**

**The Last Cup of Tea**

The bell above the door of *Slightly Warped Books* jingled, though the shop hadn't seen a customer in three days. Or maybe three weeks. Eleanor had stopped keeping track somewhere between the power outage and the third leak in the upstairs apartment.

She set down her mug—chipped, one of a kind she'd promised herself she'd replace years ago—and shuffled toward the front. Her knees protested. They always protested now.

Behind the counter, a man stood staring at the empty space where the romance section used to be.

"Can I help you?" Eleanor asked.

"I hope so." He turned, and she saw that he was perhaps her age, perhaps older, with the kind of face that had been handsome once and had settled into something more interesting. "I'm looking for a book. I don't remember the title. Or the author. I just remember the cover was yellow, and there was a lighthouse on it, and I think it made me cry when I was twelve."

Eleanor almost smiled. "That's not much to go on."

"No," he agreed. "It's not."

She found herself studying him. The way he held his hands, uncertain. The small bandage on his cheek, fresh. "You've come a long way."

"Further than you'd think."

She led him to the back, where the unsorted orphans lived in leaning towers. Dust motes spun in the light from the single window. They didn't speak as they searched, just the occasional grunt or the soft thud of a book being moved.

She found it first. A slim paperback, cover sun-faded to almost exactly the yellow he'd described. A small lighthouse perched on a cliff, a single figure walking toward it. *The Keeper of the Light*, by someone whose name had been forgotten by everyone except maybe the author herself.

He took it with both hands. "I didn't think I'd ever see this again."

"I didn't think I'd ever sell another book," Eleanor said. "And yet."

He laughed, surprised, and she laughed too, and for a moment they were just two old people in a dusty shop, finding something they'd lost.

He paid in cash. He had no card, he explained, and his phone was dead, and his car was somewhere being towed, and he'd had a morning.

"I gathered," she said.

At the door, he paused. The street outside was the same street it had always been—cracked pavement, a traffic light stuck on yellow, a sky the color of old dishwater—but he looked at it like he was seeing it for the first time.

"My wife used to say that every day was an adventure," he said. "I thought she was being optimistic. Turns out she was being literal."

"Was?"

"She passed. Two years now. Maybe three." He touched the book's cover. "She bought this for me. The day we met. Said she'd read it three times and I should too, and then we could talk about it."

"Did you?"

"Not yet." He looked at Eleanor, and his eyes were bright but steady. "I'm going to now. I'm going to read it, and then I'm going to find someone to talk about it with."

Eleanor didn't know what to say. She nodded.

He nodded back. The bell jingled. He stepped out into the uncertain afternoon.

Eleanor stood in the doorway for a long time after he'd gone, watching the traffic light cycle through its colors—red, yellow, green, red, yellow, green—until she lost count.

She thought about the book she'd sold. She thought about the woman who'd bought it, decades ago, for a man she hadn't yet met, in a shop that hadn't yet been hers, in a year that felt like someone else's memory.

She thought about her own husband, gone these eleven years, and the copy of *East of Eden* still sitting on his nightstand, bookmarked at page two hundred and something, waiting for him to come back and finish it.

She closed the shop early.

She boiled the kettle.

She made herself one last cup of tea, and sat in the window, and watched the world do what it always did—begin, and end, and begin again—without asking anyone's permission.

Outside, somewhere in the city, a man opened a yellow book and started to read.

Eleanor sipped her tea.

"What a day," she said to no one in particular, and meant it in every possible sense of the word.

# The Furnace

The thermostat on the kitchen wall read 110°F. Marcus stared at it, willing the numbers to change. They didn't. A bead of sweat traced a slow path down his temple, dripped off his jaw, and landed on the linoleum with a soft *plap* that was the loudest sound in the house.

The repairman had said it couldn't be fixed until Monday. That was four days away.

Marcus pulled out his phone. The screen flickered with seventeen notifications—neighbors, mostly. *Saw the AC truck. Rough luck, buddy.* He didn't have the energy to respond to any of them. He just stood there in his boxers, a damp towel slung over one shoulder, watching the mercury climb like a curse.

His wife Elena was at her sister's in Tucson. She'd left Sunday morning, kissed him on the cheek, and told him to keep the house cool for when she got back Thursday night.

Thursday night. A lifetime away.

He thought about the dog, Biscuit, a portly beagle who'd taken up residence under the kitchen table, panting so hard his whole body vibrated. The dog looked at Marcus with mournful, betrayed eyes, as if Marcus had personally invented summer.

"Okay, buddy," Marcus said, his voice cracking with dryness. "Okay."

He went to the garage and found what was left of his dignity: a box fan from 2014, a kiddie pool that had belonged to his niece, and a roll of aluminum foil he'd once watched a YouTube video about using to reflect heat. The foil didn't work. The fan sounded like a dying cat. The pool, once filled, became a lukewarm bath that Marcus sat in fully clothed, feeling ridiculous and desperate in equal measure.

At night, he slept on the back porch in a hammock, naked, a wet rag on his chest, watching the stars swim through the heat shimmer rising off the patio furniture. The darkness offered no relief. The air sat on him like a living thing, heavy and close, smelling of dust and sage and something vaguely burnt from the neighbor's yard.

By Tuesday, Marcus had stopped cooking. He'd taken to eating grapes straight from the bunch and drinking ice water until his teeth ached. He showered four, five times a day, standing under the pathetic trickle that passed for cold water in the old pipes, not really getting clean, just *existing* in the brief window of cool before the heat crept back in.

Biscuit refused to leave his spot under the table. Marcus had to put the water bowl directly under him, and even then the dog only lapped at it weakly, his pink tongue barely making contact.

Wednesday. 112°F.

Marcus lay on the tile floor, the coolest surface in the house, and thought about the pilgrims. The pioneers. The early settlers of the Sonoran Desert, who'd somehow figured out how to live here without dying, or at least without *complaining* about dying. He'd never appreciated them. He appreciated them now.

At some point in the afternoon, he stopped sweating. This seemed like a small victory until he realized it probably meant he was approaching heat exhaustion. He forced himself to sit up, drink a glass of room-temperature water, and place a cold compress on the back of his neck. The YouTube video had mentioned the compress. The YouTube video had become his bible.

He called Elena, half hoping she'd tell him to come to Tucson. Instead, she told him he'd be fine. "You're a tough guy," she said, laughing. He could hear the hum of her sister's central air in the background, a sound as distant and beautiful as whale song.

"Easy for you to say," he muttered.

Thursday morning. 108°F. The cloud cover was a gift, like a cruel joke on payday.

Marcus had moved all his operations to the basement, which stayed a relatively civilized 92°F. He sat on an old couch down there, Biscuit in his lap, and watched the dust motes drift through a single shaft of light from the ground-level window.

He thought about his childhood in Oregon, where summers topped out at a friendly 85°F and air conditioning was considered an affectation. He thought about his father, who'd spent thirty years working construction in Phoenix and never complained about the heat, just drank Gatorade and whistled while he worked.

"You're weaker than I thought," he said out loud to the empty basement.

Biscuit thumped his tail once in agreement.

At 4:47 PM on Thursday, the front door opened. Elena came in with her suitcase, her arms full of cold things she'd picked up at the store. Gatorade. Ice cream. A bag of ice.

"How's my desert man?" she asked, smiling.

Marcus stood up from the basement couch, his bones cracking, his hair a disaster, his dignity in tatters.

"I'm never letting you leave again," he said.

Elena laughed. She crossed the house and kissed him on the cheek, her skin cool and dry from the air-conditioned car.

"I had them fix the AC while I was gone," she said. "The guy came out this morning."

Marcus blinked.

"You—" He looked at the wall thermostat. She had already reached over and adjusted it. The unit hummed to life, that beautiful mechanical sigh, and cold air began to pour from the vents like a benediction.

Biscuit scrambled off his lap and ran toward the living room, toenails clicking on the floor, tail wagging in ecstasy.

Marcus sat back down on the couch. He put his face in his hands. He was shaking, he realized—not from cold, not yet, but from the sudden, overwhelming relief of it all.

"Mean," he said, when he could speak again. "That was mean."

Elena crouched in front of him, smiling. "You survived."

"Barely."

"You learned something."

"What's that?"

"That you're a wimp," she said sweetly. "And that you love me."

Marcus looked up at her. He didn't have the energy to argue.

"Both," he said. "Apparently both."

The AC kicked into high gear. The basement began to cool. Marcus sat in the middle of it, finally, *finally* not sweating, and laughed until he cried.

Outside, the sun began its long slow descent toward the horizon. The temperature would drop to a merciful 95°F by midnight. Tomorrow, the repairman would come. The unit would be declared officially fixed.

But for now, in this moment, Marcus had cold air, his wife, and a beagle asleep on his feet, and that was enough. That was everything.

في أحرّ يوم من أيام السنة، حين بدا الهواء يتصاعد من الأرصفة كأنه بخار يخرج من فم تنين خفيّ، توقّف الزمن في قرية "وادي النخيل" الصغيرة. كانت الشمس معلّقة في السماء كقرص نحاسي ملتهب، لا تريم مكانها، كأنها أرادت أن تحرق كلّ أثر للحياة.

لم يجرؤ أحد على الخروج. حتى الكلاب نامت تحت ظلال الجدران، وأخرجت ألسنتها من أفواهها كأنها تلهث بحثاً عن نسمة هواء واحدة. في بيته الطيني القديم، جلس الحاجّ سليم، رجلٌ في الستين من عمره، وجهه محفور كقاع نهر جاف، يتأمّل من نافذته الخربة.

كان يقول دائماً: "في مثل هذا اليوم، اختبأت أمي بي في بئر الماء القديم. كان البرد يسري في عروقنا، وكنا نسمع العالم من فوقنا مكتوماً، وكأنه ينبض في مكان آخر."

على سريرها الخشبي، كانت الجدّة فاطمة تهمس لأحفادها حكايةً يعرفونها عن ظهر قلب، لكنّها ترويها في كلّ صيف كأنها أوّل مرة. "في يوم قائظ كهذا، خرج صيّادٌ اسمه يوسف إلى الصحراء. كان الماء قد نفد، والحيوانات نفقت، لكنه لم ييأس..."

# 숲 속의 불빛

1998년의 어느 여름, 나는 오빠와 함께 영월 산골의 외할머니 댁으로 여름방학을 보내러 갔다. 서울에서 온 열 살짜리 도시 아이였던 나는, 차 안에서 내리는 내내 이마를 유리창에 붙이고 초록빛 숲을 멍하니 바라보았다.

"예준아, 도착했다."

오빠가 내 등을 툭 치자, 차 문이 열리며 무더운 여름 공기가 밀려왔다. 하지만 산골의 더위는 서울과 달랐다. 젖은 흙과 솔잎, 그리고 어디선가 들려오는 개울 소리까지 — 후끈하면서도 시원한, 묘한 냄새가 났다.

## 1장. 외할머니의 산장

외할머니 댁은 숲 깊숙한 곳에 있었다. 초가집은 아니었지만, 처마 밑으로 넝쿨이 기어오른 오래된 나무집이었다. 마당에는 큰 감나무가 하나 있었고, 그 옆에 허름한 오두막이 하나 더 있었다.

"저긴 뭔데?" 내가 물었다.

외할머니가 주걱으로 방향을 가리키며 말했다. *"거긴 산장이다. 밤에는 거기 가지 마라."*

그 말에 오빠가 피식 웃었다. *"외할머니, 산장이 뭐가 무서워요. 귀신 나오는 집이에요?"*

외할머니의 표정이 잠깐 굳었다. 하지만 이내 웃으며 우리 손을 잡고 집 안으로 들어갔다. *"얘들아, 배고프지? 호박죽 해줄게."*

그날 밤, 이불 속에서도 나는 계속 그 오두막을 생각했다. 창문 너머로 달빛이 쏟아지고 있었고, 어디선가 희미한 불빛이 깜빡이는 것 같기도 했다.

## 2장. 빛의 주인

며칠이 지나자 나는 숲이 좋아졌다. 오빠와 함께 개울에서 물고기를 잡고, 산딸기를 따고, 참나무 그늘에서 시원한 바람을 쐬며 놀았다. 하지만 외할머니는 여전히 이상했다.

저녁마다 외할머니는 마당에 작은 상을 차렸다. 밥, 된장찌개, 생선 한 마리. 그리고 맨 앞에 조그만 잔을 놓았다.

"누구랑 밥 먹어요?" 오빠가 물었다.

외할머니는 조용히 웃기만 했다. *"오랜 친구란다."*

그날 밤, 오빠가 이미 잠든 뒤에 나는 혼자 마당으로 나갔다. 소변을 보러 간 척하면서, 외할머니가 차려놓은 밥상을 살짝 들여다보았다. 밥이 줄어들어 있었다. 아니, 누군가 이미 먹고 간 것처럼.

그때, 숲 안쪽에서 희미한 불빛이 깜빡였다. 등불. 누군가가 등불을 들고 서 있었다.

## 3장. 아이의 비밀

다음 날 아침, 나는 외할머니에게 물었다. *"외할머니, 숲에 누가 살아요?"*

외할머니의 손이 잠깐 멈추었다. 그 손에는 호박을 썰던 칼이 들려 있었다. *"너, 어젯밤에 뭘 봤니?"*

나는 고개를 끄덕였다. 외할머니는 한참을 말이 없다가, 이내 나를 무릎 위에 앉히고 말했다.

*"저기 산장에는 오래전부터 한 분이 산단다. 이름은 '산지기'라고 해. 우리네 외갓집이 이 숲을 지킬 때부터, 늘 함께해준 분이지."*

"사람이에요?"

외할머니는 고개를 저었다. *"사람도 아니고, 귀신도 아니야. 그냥… 숲이야. 숲이 된 거지."*

## 4장. 약속

외할머니의 이야기는 이랬다. 수백 년 전, 이 산에는 마을을 지키던 나무꾼이 있었다. 마을에 큰 화재가 났을 때, 나무꾼은 혼자 숲을 헤치고 물을 길어와 마을을 구했다. 그 나무꾼은 그날 밤, 숲 한가운데서 숨을 거두었다.

그 이후로, 숲은 마을을 지켜주었다. 나무꾼은 숲이 되었고, 마을 사람들은 숲에게 음식을 차려 바쳤다.

*"근데 요즘은 사람들이 숲을 잘 안 찾아와."* 외할머니은 쓸쓸하게 말했다. *"도시로 다 떠나서, 산도 마을도 텅 비었어. 산지기도 외로워하고 있을 거야."*

나는 가슴이 아팠다. 어쩌면, 숲이 깜빡이던 그 불빛은 — 단순한 불빛이 아니었을지도 모른다.

## 5장. 마지막 밤

방학이 끝나갈 무렵이었다. 외할머니는 갑자기 열이 나기 시작하셨다. 어머니가 서울에서 내려오셨고, 응급실에 가야 한다고 했다. 떠나는 날, 외할머니는 내 손을 잡으셨다.

*"예준아, 외할머니 댁 자주 놀러와. 그리고 산지기 잘 보살펴줘."*

나는 울음을 참으며 고개를 끄덕였다.

차 안에서 뒤를 돌아봤다. 외할머니의 집이 점점 작아졌다. 그 순간, 숲 안쪽에서 불빛이 깜빡였다. 이번에는 평소보다 길게, 길게 — 마치 인사하듯.

## 에필로그. 서울의 밤

지금도 서울의 밤하늘을 바라보면, 그때의 그 깜빡이던 불빛이 떠오른다. 가끔씩 주말에 부모님을 졸라 영월 외할머니 댁에 놀러간다. 외할머니는 돌아가셨지만, 집은 아직 그대로 있다.

마당에 밥상을 차릴 때면, 옆에서 바람이 솔솔 분다. 그때 나는 생각한다. 누군가 — 아니, 무언가가 여전히 여기 있다고.

숲은 절대 사람들을 잊지 않는다. 우리도 숲을 잊지 말아야 할 것이다.

这栋楼是九十年代建的砖混结构，隔热差得离谱。即便窗帘拉得严严实实，下午三点的阳光依然像某种液态的东西，从窗缝里渗进来，把整个客厅烤成蒸笼。

林深坐在地上，背靠着墙，汗水顺着下巴滴在搬家时剩下的纸箱上，洇出一块深色的印子。

他刚失业。准确地说是被裁，五年青春喂给了一家在他心里永远伟大的公司，最后换来HR一句轻飘飘的"业务调整"。三十一岁，没成家，没房没车，存款勉强够在这座新一线城市再撑三个月。

手机又震了一下。

物业群里有邻居在抱怨："这破楼电路又跳闸了，三楼那户空调外机烧了吧，整层都停电。"

林深没回复。他盯着天花板上一个慢慢移动的光斑——是窗外的树叶在风里摇晃，投下斑驳的影子。风扇吹过来的风是热的，带着一股老房子特有的霉味。

这房子是他临时找的过渡房，押一付三，图的就是便宜。上一任租客是个跑保险的中年大叔，走了大概有半年，屋里还有股淡淡的烟味。

林深打开手机，漫无目的地刷着招聘软件。简历投出去几十份，回复的寥寥无几，就算回复了也是"与岗位匹配度不高"之类客气的废话。

热浪从窗外涌进来，他觉得自己像一条被摆在铁板上的鱼，正在被慢慢煎熟。

外卖是吃不下去的。他煮了一碗白面条，拌了点酱油，勉强吃了几口。汗水顺着筷子滴进碗里，他甚至懒得擦。

晚上九点，热度丝毫没有减弱的意思。林深冲了个凉水澡，换了条短裤，坐在窗边发呆。楼下是烧烤摊的烟火气，几个光膀子的大汉在喝啤酒，声音隔着窗户玻璃传上来，听不清说什么，但笑声很响。

这城市里有几百万人，每个人都有自己的烦恼。而他的烦恼是具体的、精确的——下个月的房租还没着落。

他想起老家。老家这个时候应该也热，但老家有老家的法子——村口的小卖部有台老冰柜，两块钱一根绿豆冰棍，坐在树荫下一口一口咬，凉意能从舌头一直沁到心底。

林深已经十年没回过老家了。

他十八岁那年离开村子，兜里揣着母亲给的八百块钱和一袋自己腌的咸菜，坐了十六个小时的绿皮火车到了这座城市。母亲送他到村口，他没回头。不是不想，是怕一回头就走不了了。

后来他在这座城市扎了根，每年回去一次，待三四天。母亲在电话里从来不问他挣多少钱，只问"吃了没""瘦了没""一个人在外面要吃饱"。

去年母亲走了。胃癌晚期，发现的时候已经是最后三个月。林深从公司请了假赶回去，在医院的走廊里坐了一夜。第二天早上，母亲醒来第一句话是："你瘦了，在外面没好好吃饭吧？"

他想说没有，他想说我有好好吃饭、好好工作、好好活着。但他的眼泪先掉了下来。

母亲走的那天很热，也是七月。老家那个地方没有空调，只有一台落地扇呼呼地转。母亲瘦得像一片叶子，手背上插着针管，眼睛却还是亮的。她让林深把家里那台老冰柜留着，"等你下次回来，给你冻冰棍吃"。

林深没有"下次"了。

那台老冰柜现在还在老家堂屋里，落满了灰。林深的姐姐说要不要处理掉，林深说先放着。

他不知道自己为什么要留着那台冰柜。大概是想留一个念想。大概是想骗自己，母亲还在，还在那个村口的小卖部等他，等他回来吃一根两块钱的绿豆冰棍。

窗外有人放了一颗烟花，"嘭"的一声炸开，在夜空里绽出一朵短暂的花。林深抬头看了一眼，又低下了头。

手机屏幕亮了一下，是条短信：

"林深您好，我是猎头公司的张经理，看到您的简历，觉得您和我们正在招聘的高级运营经理岗位非常匹配，方便明天上午十点电话沟通吗？"

林深盯着这条短信看了很久。

这是三个月来，第一条让他觉得可能是真的招聘短信。前面那些，他一眼就能看出是自动回复或者群发的钓鱼短信。但这条不一样，这条有具体的岗位、有具体的薪资范围——比他上一份工作还高30%。

他躺在床上，心跳得很快。窗外还是热，但那种热好像有了一点重量，压在他胸口，让他有点喘不过气。

他想起母亲的话："一个人在外面要吃饱。"

他想起母亲的冰柜。

他想起很多年前，母亲送他到村口，他没回头。

现在他很想回头。但他知道，他回不去了。

林深闭上眼睛，手机攥在手里，屏幕的微光照在他脸上。汗水又冒了出来，和泪水混在一起，分不清哪个是哪个。

天气预报说，明天还是高温。

最高气温40℃以上。

他决定明天上午十点，等那通电话。

# 蝉鸣

蝉来得比往年早。

七月初，苏望月就听见了那片震耳欲聋的嘶鸣。那时她正蹲在后院给月季浇水，抬头时愣住了——院墙外那棵百年老槐上，黑压压一片，全是蝉蜕。

"怎么这么多？"她喃喃。

母亲在屋里喊："望月，吃饭了。"

她应了一声，起身时忽然觉得脊背发凉。那种凉意说不出所以然，仿佛有什么东西正从地底缓慢地苏醒，正用亿万只眼睛打量着这个世界。

## 第一章

苏望月是市博物馆的文物修复师，二十六岁，未婚，养了一盆快死的茉莉。

日子过得平淡如白水——上班、修文物、回家浇花、睡觉。她住的这片老城区叫"槐安巷"，巷子得名于那棵老槐树。据老人讲，这树是明朝种的，活了快五百年，见证过三场瘟疫、两场兵乱。

今年七月初，蝉突然爆发了。

新闻里说，是气候异常。气象学家说，全球变暖导致蝉的幼虫提前结束地下生活。生物学家说，这是十七年蝉与十三年蝉同时出现的罕见"双爆发"。

苏望月不懂这些。她只觉得这声音太吵，吵得人心烦意乱，吵得她连续三天失眠。

第四天，她顶着一对黑眼圈去上班，发现博物馆也变了样。

院子里那棵老银杏上挂满了蝉，地上落了一层蝉蜕。同事们拿着扫帚在扫，抱怨连连。馆长老周站在台阶上，愁眉苦脸："这玩意儿怎么除？喷药？"

"喷药也没用。"说话的是新来的实习生，叫林深，大学生物系的研究生，二十三岁，戴一副黑框眼镜。他蹲在地上，正翻看着一具蝉蜕，神情古怪。"周馆长，这不对。"

"什么不对？"

"蜕皮的时间。"林深指着那具半透明的壳，"蝉从若虫到成虫，蜕皮一般需要一两个小时。但这具……它的外骨骼已经钙化完成了。而且您看这个——"他翻过来，"背部有一条纵线，正常蜕皮的蝉不会这样。"

苏望月本想绕过去，但鬼使神差地停下了脚步。

那条纵线细如发丝，从头部一直延伸到尾端，隐隐发着不祥的暗红。

"像什么？"她问。

林深抬头看她，推了推眼镜。

"像一道裂缝。"

## 第二章

当晚，苏望月做了个梦。

梦里她站在一片无边的荒原上，脚下是龟裂的大地，天空是一种病态的绛紫色。远处有什么东西在移动，黑压压一片，像潮水。

走近了才发现，那是蝉。

亿万只蝉。

它们不像普通的蝉那样爬行，而是直立行走，用后腿，姿态像人。它们的眼睛不是复眼，而是一只竖瞳，深处有幽幽的光。

领头的蝉比其他都大，有半人高。它停在苏望月面前，开口说话。

声音像千万片蝉翼同时振动：

"时候到了。"

她尖叫着醒来，浑身冷汗。

窗外，蝉声震天。

## 第三章

接下来的日子，事情开始不对劲。

先是新闻。

七月中旬，全国各地陆续报道异常事件：某地惊现百万只蝉聚集；某地铁站被蝉群堵塞；某小区一夜之间爬满了蝉蜕，蜕壳姿态诡异，全都面朝同一个方向——北。

然后是动物。

流浪猫狗开始失踪。动物园报告老虎、狮子焦躁不安，拒绝进食。海洋馆里的鲸豚发出悲鸣。宠物店的金鱼整缸跳出，摔死在地上。

"它们在逃。"林深说。

他拿着一份打印出来的论文给苏望月看，是日本一所大学去年发表的：蝉的振动频率与某些灾害前的地层活动有关。2011 年东日本大地震前，当地蝉鸣出现异常增幅。

"你的意思是……"

"我不确定。"林深摇头，神色凝重，"但我师傅在西北做地质监测，他给我发了些数据。地壳应力在变化，很微弱，仪器都检测不到，但蝉能感知。"

"感知什么？"

林深沉默了很久。

"地层深处……有东西在动。"

## 第四章

七月二十三日凌晨三点，苏望月被一声巨响惊醒。

不是蝉鸣，是另一种声音——一种低沉的、持续的、仿佛来自地心的轰鸣。

手机疯狂震动。她抓起来看，全市地震预警：预计 30 秒后到达，波级 6.2。

她来不及反应，只是本能地冲向母亲的房间。

然后世界开始摇晃。

槐安巷的老房子在尖叫。瓦片坠落，墙体开裂，那棵五百年的老槐在黑暗中轰然倒下，砸在苏家的屋顶上。

她记得的最后一幕，是一片尘土中，无数蝉从地底涌出，铺天盖地，遮住了月光。

## 第五章

苏望月在医院醒来时，是七月二十四日中午。

母亲没事，被压在梁下但没受伤，只是昏迷。同事们陆续探望，带来外面的消息。

地震震中是槐安巷地下十七公里处，震级 7.8，百年罕见。但诡异的是，震源不在任何已知的断层上，地质学家形容那是"凭空出现的一道裂缝"。

更诡异的是地震后的情况。

全市的蝉一夜之间消失了。

不是死亡，是消失。地上的蝉蜕全都不见了，仿佛从未存在过。只有那棵倒塌的老槐上，还残留着一些半透明的壳。

林深来了，眼眶通红。

"我师傅……在震中监测到了一组数据。"他递过来一张打印的波形图，"地震发生前三秒，地层深处传来一个信号。"

"什么信号？"

"不是地震波。"林深的声音在发抖，"是……一种振动。频率、振幅……和蝉鸣完全一致。"

苏望月看着那张图，耳边仿佛又响起梦里那亿万片蝉翼振动的声音：

*时候到了。*

## 尾声

秋天来的时候，苏望月回到了修缮一新的槐安巷。

老宅被列为危房，扒掉了重盖。新槐树种下了，嫩绿的叶子在秋风里摇曳。蝉声消失了，安静得有些不习惯。

她偶尔会站在院子里发呆，看着那片新土，想起那个梦。

林深说得对，蝉是某种信号。

不是预兆，而是……苏醒。

她不知道那东西是什么，来自哪里，要做什么。但她知道它还在。

因为每年七月，当她站在这片土地上，耳边总会隐隐约约听到一点声音——

像蝉鸣，又不像。

像呼吸。

*地底的呼吸。*

# 海风里的不速之客

阿宁在民宿的露台上等了二十分钟，才等到那辆载着周亦的车缓缓驶入。

车窗降下来时，她看见的不是闺蜜周亦一个人。

驾驶座上坐着个陌生男人，副驾上的周亦一脸歉意地冲她挥手。阿宁心头一沉，但还是维持着笑容迎了上去。

"路上捡的，"周亦压低声音解释，"我的车在高速上抛锚，多亏这位陆先生帮忙。"

陆廷昭礼貌地点头，主动伸出手来。阿宁注意到他手指上还有淡淡的机油印。

民宿的老板娘是个热情的中年妇人，硬是多安排了一间房。

晚饭时，三人围坐在小院的石桌旁。陆廷昭话不多，但总能在阿宁抱怨工作、抱怨前任的时候，恰到好处地接上一两句。风趣，又不越界。

周亦悄悄在桌下踢了她一脚，凑过来耳语："人还不错吧？"

阿宁装作没听见，低头喝汤。

---

第二天清晨，阿宁醒来发现周亦已经在阳台上了，对着海景盘头发。

"陆先生一大早就去海边捡贝壳了，"周亦头也不抬地说，"说要给咱们一人做一条项链。"

阿宁皱眉："他不是陌生人吗？你怎么什么都跟人说。"

周亦这才抬头，表情有些复杂。"我没说什么，就是告诉他我们这次出来是为了散心，你刚分手，我刚辞职……"

阿宁心里咯噔一下。

整个上午的行程变得古怪起来。陆廷昭仿佛自带导航，总能恰到好处地出现在她们想要停留的地方；周亦却一反常态地话少，时常盯着手机屏幕发呆。

---

转折发生在第二天的下午。

三人坐在礁石上看日落时，周亦忽然开口："我有一件事一直没说。"

她转过头，看向陆廷昭，眼眶已经红了。"其实我在高速上遇到你，不是巧合。我在等你。"

阿宁呆住了。

周亦深吸一口气："我查过你。你就是我妈当年插足我家庭的那个男人。"

海风忽然停了。

陆廷昭的笑容一点点消失。他没有辩解，也没有愤怒，只是静静地看着周亦，然后说："我一直在找你。"

阿宁这才意识到，她从头到尾都只是这场重逢的旁观者。她不远千里来散心，结果成了别人二十年恩怨的见证人。

她摸了摸手腕，忽然觉得很累。

---

那天晚上，阿宁独自去了民宿后面的小海滩。周亦发来很多消息，她一条也没回。

海浪一遍遍冲刷着礁石。月光冷冷地照着。

不知过了多久，身后响起脚步声。陆廷昭在她旁边站了一会儿，然后蹲下，也看向海面。

"对不起，"他说，"搅了你们的旅行。"

阿宁没接话。

"她这些年过得不好，"陆廷昭继续说，"她妈也是。我以为躲得远远的就行了，没想到她还是查到了我。"

阿宁开口了："那你为什么还要来？"

陆廷昭沉默了很久。

"我想亲眼看看她变成了什么样的人。"他的声音很轻，"当年她妈抱着她离开的时候，她才三岁。她回头看了我一眼。我记了二十年。"

海风重新吹起来，带着盐味。

阿宁忽然明白，这趟旅程真正要散的心，不是她的，是周亦的。而她从头到尾都只是托底的工具。

她应该愤怒。但此刻看着陆廷昭佝偻的背影，她只觉得荒凉。

---

第二天清晨，阿宁独自收拾了行李。

周亦和陆廷昭坐在客厅里，两人之间隔着整整一张茶几。阿宁走过去，把周亦的行李箱也拉了过来。

"周亦，我们回去。"她说，"什么时候要分开说，但别在这里。"

周亦抬头，眼眶里有血丝。"你不问我吗？"

"你想说自然会说，"阿宁拉上行李箱拉链，"走吧。"

周亦忽然哭出声来。陆廷昭站起来，似乎想伸手，最终还是停住了。

阿宁拖着两个行李箱走向门口。周亦在身后哽咽着说了句什么，阿宁没听清，也不想听清。

---

返程的车上，周亦一直在睡。阿宁开着车，窗外是漫长的海岸线。

她在想，二十年的恩怨，怎么就摊在了她和周亦的海边假期里。

又或者，每一个看似普通的假期，都可能在某个转角处，露出生活最深的褶皱。

而朋友的意义，也许就是在那道褶皱里，依然彼此作伴。

# 归途

林舟在西藏待了整整四十天。

四十年的人生里，他从没有离开过那座沿海小城超过一周。妻子笑他，说他像一棵扎根太深的树，连风都吹不动。林舟不反驳，只是笑笑，继续修他的钟表。

可这一次不一样。

他报了旅行社的团，独自一人飞往拉萨。妻子问为什么，他说想去看看布达拉宫。妻子没再问，替他收拾了行李。

在拉萨的第二天，他在八廓街迷了路。

手机没信号，他凭着感觉拐进一条窄巷，阳光被两旁的藏式土墙切割成一块块金色的碎片。巷子深处，一个老阿妈坐在门口转经筒，旁边蹲着一个年轻人，正帮老人修理一台老旧的收音机。

林舟走过去，本想问问路，却被那台收音机吸引住了。

"你也懂这个？"年轻人抬头看他，眼睛很亮，像是高原上空的星子。

林舟蹲下来，仔细看了看那台收音机。"我是修钟表的。"

"钟表？时间？"年轻人笑了，"时间在西藏是最不值钱的东西。"

他叫扎西，在拉萨做流动修理工，修收音机、修手表、修一切会坏掉的东西。

那天他们聊了很久。林舟帮他拧紧了一颗松动的螺丝，扎西教他念了一段六字真言。太阳落山的时候，扎西说："明天我带你去一个地方。"

第三天清晨，扎西骑着摩托车载他驶出城区。路越来越颠簸，海拔越来越高。林舟紧紧抓着后座把手，心跳得像要冲出喉咙。

他们在一片草原上停下来。

远处是连绵的雪山，近处是星星点点的黑色牦牛。风很大，吹得草浪像海一样翻涌。

扎西从背包里拿出一块怀表。

那是一块老旧的瑞士怀表，表盖上刻着一朵雪莲花。扎西说，这是他爷爷留下的，已经停了二十多年。

"我修不好它。"扎西的声音被风吹得断断续续，"我爷爷去世前说，这块表里住着他的时间。我一直想让它重新走起来。"

林舟接过怀表，掂了掂重量。他打开后盖，里面的机芯已经锈蚀。他看了很久，眉头紧锁。

"能修好吗？"扎西问。

林舟摇摇头，又点点头。"要带回去修。我需要一些工具，还有……一些时间。"

扎西笑了，从脖子上取下一条红色的绳子，穿过怀表表链，挂在林舟脖子上。"那就拜托你了。"

那块怀表贴着林舟的胸口，分量不重，却有种奇异的感觉，像揣着一个人的一生。

之后的日子里，林舟跟着扎西在拉萨周边转悠。他们住在简陋的旅馆里，吃糌粑，喝酥油茶。扎西给他讲这片土地的故事，讲每一座山、每一条河的名字从何而来，讲格桑花为什么叫"幸福花"。

"幸福是什么？"有一次林舟问。

扎西想了想，说："幸福就是此刻啊。此刻你在这里，我也在这里，风在吹，太阳在晒，这就是幸福。"

林舟没有说话。他想起妻子，想起那间摆了四十年钟表的店铺，想起自己每天重复的日子。他突然觉得，自己好像已经很久没有真正"在"过任何一个时刻了。

第十五天的时候，他们去了纳木错。

湖面像一面巨大的镜子，倒映着天空和雪山。扎西说，纳木错是念青唐古拉山的妻子，他们世世代代守望着彼此。

"你信这些？"林舟问。

"信不信有什么关系呢？"扎西说，"重要的是，它让我心里有东西可以相信。"

林舟看着那片湖水，忽然有些想哭。他不知道为什么，也许是海拔太高，也许是风太大，也许是别的什么。

第二十八天，扎西病了。

高原反应，加上连日的奔波，他住进了医院。林舟守在病床前，看着他吸氧、输液、昏睡。三天后，扎西睁开眼，对他笑了笑："别担心，我命大。"

第四十天，林舟要回去了。

扎西还在医院里，没能去送他。他们在病床上握了握手，扎西说："把那块表修好，然后给我写封信，告诉我它是怎么走的。"

林舟点头。他想说很多话，最后只说了一句："保重。"

飞机降落在沿海机场的时候，妻子来接他。她看着他晒黑的脸，张了张嘴，什么也没说，只是接过他的行李箱。

回到家里，林舟做的第一件事，是把那块怀表放在工作台上。

他花了一整个星期，把怀表的每一个零件拆下来，清洗，重新组装。表盘上的雪莲花在灯下泛着柔和的光泽。他上了发条，听见齿轮转动的声音，清脆、细小，像一颗心脏重新开始跳动。

第二天，他把怀表放进一个木盒子里，连同一封信，寄往拉萨。

信里他写道：

*扎西：*

*表修好了。*

*它走得很准，和你一样准。*

*你说幸福是此刻。我想了很久，觉得你说得对。但我想补充一点：幸福也是远方，是此刻想念一个人时，心里那块柔软的地方。*

*我以前觉得时间是用来数的，一天一天，一年一年。现在我知道，时间是用来感受的。*

*谢谢你带我去看纳木错，去看雪山，去看格桑花。谢谢你让我知道，时间可以停下来，也可以重新开始。*

*我会好好的。*

*林舟*

信寄出后，林舟走出店铺，沿着海边走了一圈。海风吹在脸上，和高原的风不一样，但同样真实。

回到家，妻子正在厨房里做饭。她听见门响，转过头，问："饿了吧？"

林舟走过去，从背后轻轻抱住她。

"怎么了？"妻子有些意外。

"没什么。"他说，"就是忽然想抱抱你。"

妻子笑了，拍拍他的手："去洗手，吃饭了。"

饭桌上摆着红烧鱼、清炒时蔬、一碗紫菜蛋花汤。林舟吃得比平时多，也比平时慢。妻子看着他，眼睛里有一点湿润。

"你变了。"她说。

"哪里变了？"

"说不上来。"她想了想，"好像……松了。"

林舟笑了。他想起扎西说的话，想起那块怀表重新走起来的声音。

是的，他松了。

四十天的高原，一场相遇，一块怀表。他带回来的不是一块表，而是一颗重新跳动的心。

窗外，海浪轻轻拍打着岸边，发出永恒的声音。

而时间，在他胸口，再次流动起来。

# 雪融之后

林夏第一次觉得自己不喜欢冬天，是在一场葬礼之后。

那是一月的北京，灰蒙蒙的天空像一块永远拧不干的抹布，压在城市的头顶。殡仪馆里暖气开得很足，可她的指尖依然是冰的。奶奶躺在白色的花丛中，穿着她生前最喜欢的藏青色棉袄，表情平静得仿佛只是睡着了。

奶奶是在冬天走的。

从那以后，每年冬天，林夏都觉得寒风像刀子一样往骨头缝里钻。春节的鞭炮声震耳欲聋，可她听见的总是奶奶最后一次咳嗽时喉咙里的杂音。街上的红灯笼喜庆得像另一个世界的事，她裹着厚厚的羽绒服走在人群里，像一截被冻僵的木头。

她开始怀念夏天。

确切地说，是怀念奶奶还活着的那几个夏天。

"奶奶，我回来了！"七岁的林夏背着书包冲进院子，额头上全是汗。

奶奶坐在藤椅上摇蒲扇，看见她进来，笑得眼角的皱纹都舒展开来。"又跑哪儿疯去了？瞧这一脑门的汗。"她从口袋里掏出一方叠得整整齐齐的棉帕子，蘸了凉水，一下一下地擦着林夏的脸。

"奶奶，太热了！"小女孩嘟着嘴。

"傻丫头。"奶奶笑着捏她的鼻子，"夏天热有热的好。你看那荷花——"

院子角落有一口大缸，缸里种着荷花。七月的荷花开得正盛，粉白相间，在绿色的圆叶间探出头来，像一个个害羞的小姑娘。

"出淤泥而不染，濯清涟而不妖。"奶奶念叨着，"做人也要这样，干净、坦荡。"

林夏不懂这些，只觉得荷花的味道很好闻。奶奶会摘几片荷叶，铺在蒸笼里，蒸出来的馒头带着一股清新的香气。她还会用莲子熬粥，放一点点冰糖，甜而不腻。

夏天是漫长的白昼，是蝉鸣，是井水里冰过的西瓜，是奶奶手摇蒲扇时带起的风。

后来奶奶病了。

是夏天查出来的。林夏记得妈妈在医院走廊里哭，奶奶反倒笑着安慰大家："人这一辈子，谁没个头疼脑热的？我这把老骨头，还能撑几年呢。"

那一年的夏天格外漫长。林夏每天放学都去医院，在病床边给奶奶念课文。奶奶总说："夏丫头，你念书的声音好听，像夏天。"

再后来，奶奶就只能在冬天出门了。她裹在厚厚的棉衣里，坐在轮椅上，脸上的笑容却还是那样慈祥。

直到那个冬天。

林夏站在院子里，看着那口大缸。缸里的荷叶早枯了，只剩下几根残茎歪歪斜斜地立在冰水里。

"奶奶走了。"她对自己说，声音很轻。

那年她十六岁。

高三那年夏天，林夏发了疯似地学习。她把所有的悲伤和思念都压在心底，只在无人的时候翻出奶奶的相片看一眼。妈妈说："你这孩子，怎么跟换了个人似的。"

林夏没回答。她只是害怕。害怕冬天，害怕那个季节再次带走她珍视的人。

她考上了北京的大学。离开家乡那天，正是夏天。火车驶过一片片金黄的麦田，她想起小时候奶奶带她去拾麦穗的午后。阳光暖得像一只大手，托着她整个人。

大学毕业后，林夏留在了北京，成了一名小学语文老师。她喜欢给孩子们讲夏天的课文——讲《荷塘月色》，讲《雨的四季》，讲朱自清笔下的绿。

同事们觉得奇怪，这个南方姑娘为什么从不抱怨北京的夏天。"热一点好。"她总是这样说，眼底带着一种说不清的温柔。

又是一年七月。

林夏带着学生们在学校的池塘边写生。荷花开了，开得铺天盖地，像一场盛大而沉默的烟火。

"林老师，荷花为什么能出淤泥而不染呢？"一个小女孩抬头问，眼睛亮晶晶的。

林夏蹲下身，摸了摸她的头。"因为荷花心里是干净的。就像你们一样。"

她顿了一下，又说："我奶奶告诉我，做人要干净、坦荡。不管遇到什么困难，心里都要有一朵荷花。"

小女孩似懂非懂地点点头。

林夏站起身，看着满池的荷花。阳光透过云层洒下来，金色的光芒落在水面上，也落在她的脸上。

她忽然觉得，奶奶就在那些花里。每一朵盛开的荷花，都是奶奶的一个微笑。

远处传来蝉鸣，一阵一阵的，像是大自然在演奏一首关于夏天的歌。

林夏闭上眼睛，微微笑了。

从什么时候开始喜欢夏天的呢？她自己也说不清楚。也许是从那个夏天开始的——那个奶奶握着她的手，告诉她"做人要干净"的夏天。也许是从那口大缸里枯荣交替的荷叶开始的。也许是从她第一次在雪地里哭出声的那个冬天开始的——因为失去，所以更懂得珍惜。

她最喜欢的，是夏天的荷。

也是那个夏天，那个人。

Write a story about a family summer vacation to Europe that… does not go to plan. Approximately 1200 words.

# The Magnificent Disaster

The Berlinski family had been planning their European summer vacation for eleven months, four hundred and sixty-three Pinterest boards, and exactly one argument that nearly ended the marriage. Now, standing in the arrivals hall of Heathrow Airport with a dead phone, a missing suitcase, and three children who were already asking how long until lunch, Eleanor Berlinski allowed herself one small, controlled scream into her palm.

“Okay,” she said aloud, to no one. “Okay. This is fine."

Greg, her husband, appeared around the corner of a café, clutching two coffees and looking like a man who had recently learned something terrible.

"So, good news and bad news," he began.

"No."

"The rental car company has no record of our reservation."

"Greg."

"Apparently their system 'experienced a migration issue' and our booking, along with 'several thousand others,' no longer exists."

The children—Maggie, fifteen and surgically attached to her phone, which was also dead; Theo, twelve, who had recently discovered sarcasm as a personality; and seven-year-old Poppy, who was already crying about something—gathered around. Eleanor looked at the Arrivals board. The next flight to Paris was in six hours. Their hotel in Paris was booked for tonight. Their hotel in Rome was booked for tomorrow. The train they were supposed to take the day after that had specific seats assigned with their names on them.

Greg took a sip of his coffee. "I could call the credit card company?"

"Greg."

"I'm just brainstorming."

Eleanor closed her eyes. She had wanted a *beautiful* vacation. She had wanted their children to remember the way the light fell in the Tuileries, the taste of real gelato, the sound of church bells in a foreign country. She had wanted Greg to finally relax. She had wanted to prove—to herself, to her mother, to the women of the Facebook group "Traveling with Kids (and Sanity)"—that she could pull this off.

"Okay," she said. "New plan. We are going to make a new plan."

---

The new plan was: take the train to London, find a hotel for the night, regroup, and figure out the rest.

The new plan lasted until they reached Paddington Station, where Greg discovered his wallet was missing.

"Maybe in the taxi?" Eleanor said.

"Maybe I left it at home?"

"Gregory."

Theo, without looking up from a sign, said, "Wow, Dad. Really bringing your A-game."

"Theo," Eleanor warned.

"I'm just saying."

Poppy began to cry again, this time because her stuffed rabbit, Mr. Bunns, had apparently been left in the dead suitcase. Maggie, who had been silent for twenty minutes, suddenly announced that she was "not doing this" and sat down on the platform floor with the theatrical finality of a queen abdicating.

Eleanor sat down next to Maggie.

"Get up," Maggie said.

"I will in a minute."

"You're embarrassing me."

"I'm sitting on a floor in London. I think we're past embarrassment."

Maggie looked at her mother. Something shifted, very slightly, in the architecture of her face.

"Mom?"

"Yeah?"

"Why are we even doing this?"

Eleanor thought about it. She thought about the Pinterest boards, the spreadsheets, the twelve thousand dollars they had saved, the fact that her own mother had never been to Europe and Eleanor had wanted, somehow, to do it for both of them.

"I don't know," she said honestly. "I really don't know."

---

They got a hotel. Greg canceled his credit cards. Eleanor bought a phone charger from a man outside a Tesco who was, she was ninety percent sure, not actually a man who worked at Tesco. They ate fish and chips in a pub where the bartender, a woman named Brenda, took one look at the Berlinskis and brought them a round of ciders without being asked.

"You lot look like you've had a day," Brenda said.

"You have no idea," Greg said.

"Try me."

Greg told her. Brenda laughed so hard she had to lean on the bar. Then she told them about a small B&B in Bath run by her sister, about a shortcut through the Cotswolds that tourists never took, about a place in Cornwall where you could see puffins if you went at the right time of morning.

"Why are you telling us this?" Eleanor asked.

"Because you're not going to Paris," Brenda said, as if it were obvious. "No offense. But you lot aren't Paris people. You're *wandering* people. Look at you."

They looked at themselves. They looked, frankly, like five people who had been hit by a small bus.

Brenda slid a napkin across the bar. Her sister's number was written on it, along with the words: *Tell her Brenda sent you. Mention the cider.*

---

They went to Bath.

They did not go to Paris. They did not go to Rome. They did not take the train with the assigned seats.

Instead, they drove a rental car (a new one, paid for with Eleanor's emergency credit card) through the English countryside, and the countryside was so aggressively beautiful that Eleanor had to pull over twice because she was crying. Greg held her hand in a pub in a village whose name neither of them could pronounce. They ate scones with clotted cream. They went to a farm where Poppy held a baby lamb and announced, with the gravity of a Supreme Court justice, that she would be returning to live here.

In Bath, they walked around the Roman Baths and Maggie, who had not smiled in approximately eleven months, smiled. She took a picture with Eleanor's phone, posted it without a filter, and wrote: *here. finally.*

They went to Cornwall, because Brenda had said to go to Cornwall. They saw puffins. Theo, who had been sulking since approximately 2019, looked at a puffin and said, "Okay, that's kind of incredible," and Eleanor wanted to frame the sentence.

In a small bookshop in a town that may or may not have been fictional, Poppy found a stuffed rabbit that was, she declared, Mr. Bunns's *cousin*. She named him Mr. Bunns the Second. She slept with him every night for the rest of the trip.

---

On the last night, in a small inn on the coast, Eleanor and Greg sat on a stone wall and watched the sun go down. The children were asleep. The inn was quiet. The ocean did that thing where it made you feel very small and very lucky at the same time.

"I think we failed," Eleanor said.

"Completely," Greg agreed.

"Our kids are going to be in therapy."

"Expensive therapy."

"Mom is going to ask why we didn't take them to the Louvre."

"She is going to *ask* about the Louvre."

They sat with that for a moment. Then Greg said, "Do you think they'll remember any of this?"

Eleanor thought about Maggie's smile at the Roman Baths. Theo's face at the puffins. Poppy asleep with Mr. Bunns the Second, her face finally peaceful.

"I think they'll remember the cider lady," she said.

"And the dead suitcase."

"And the dead suitcase."

"And whatever that man at Tesco was actually selling."

"He was definitely selling chargers."

"Definitely."

A gull flew overhead. Somewhere inside the inn, a clock chimed.

"Okay," Eleanor said. "Okay. This was fine."

Greg put his arm around her. "This was actually kind of amazing."

"Don't push it."

"I'm just saying."

They sat there a little longer. The sun went all the way down. The stars came out, which they never did in their neighborhood back home. The Berlinskis had not seen Paris. They had not seen Rome. They had seen a dead suitcase, a missing wallet, and the inside of a Tesco Express at midnight.

They had seen England. And England, it turned out, had been there all along.

---

*fin.*

Write a story about a summer afternoon spent in a treehouse. Approximately 700 characters.

# 树屋里的夏日午后

那年夏天，我七岁，表哥十二岁。

我们花了整整一个下午爬到院子后面那棵老槐树上去。不是一般的爬——是那种手脚并用、膝盖蹭破皮、汗水蜇眼睛的爬法。木板在风里晃荡，发出吱呀吱呀的响声，像一只慵懒的猫在打哈欠。

树屋是用几块旧床板和几个木箱搭起来的，歪歪斜斜，却有一种奇异的稳当。表哥用锤子把生锈的钉子敲进树干时，整棵树都会轻轻颤抖，像是大地的脉搏。我坐在里面，看着阳光从槐树叶子的缝隙间漏下来，在木板上画出一圈一圈金色的光斑。

"你说，云是怎么飘起来的？"表哥忽然问。

我想了想，说："因为它们轻。"

"才不是。"表哥把头靠在木箱上，望着头顶那一小块天空，"是因为风托着它们。"

那个夏天的午后特别长，长得像是不会结束。蝉鸣从树下涌上来，密密的、厚厚的，像一床绿色的毯子把我们裹住。空气里弥漫着槐花残留的香气，淡淡的，带着一点甜。

表哥从口袋里掏出一本卷了边的漫画书，是借来的，要三天后还。我们轮流看，看到搞笑的地方就笑，看到热血的地方就挥拳，木板跟着我们的笑声一起颤抖。

"你长大了想做什么？"表哥问我。

"住在树屋里。"我说。

表哥哈哈大笑起来，笑声惊飞了停在树枝上的一只麻雀。我不明白他为什么笑——住在树屋里多好啊，可以整天看着云飘，听着蝉鸣，闻着花香。

后来，我们在树屋里睡着了。

我是被妈妈的声音叫醒的。夕阳已经西斜，把整片天空染成了橙红色。表哥已经爬下去了，站在树下仰头看着我，逆光里他的轮廓像一个剪影。

"快点，"他说，"我妈做了凉面。"

我小心翼翼地爬下梯子，脚踩到地面的时候，土地是温热的。后来我很多次想起那个感觉——从高处回到地面，土地温热，像是大地也晒了一个下午的太阳，正在悄悄打盹。

那碗凉面我吃得很慢。面条筋道，黄瓜丝脆生生的，花生碎香喷喷地落在碗底。表哥吃得很快，三口两口就扒完了，然后端着一碗凉白开蹲在门槛上喝，喝得咕咚咕咚响。

很多年后，表哥离开了小镇去了外地读书，那棵老槐树也被砍掉了——据说是因为根系破坏了邻居家的地基。树屋的旧木板被扔在院子里，下了几场雨之后就成了深褐色的腐木。

但我常常会想起那个夏天的午后。阳光的光斑、槐花的香气、表哥的漫画书、风托着云慢慢飘过那片小小的天空。

那是我人生里最漫长、最轻盈的一个下午。

Write a story about a summer fling. Aim for roughly 1300 words.

# The August Rule

The beach house on Dune Road had been in Mira's family for three generations, but she'd never brought anyone there. Not her college boyfriend of four years. Not the photographer she'd dated through her late twenties. It was her secret place, a weathered saltbox on the edge of the Atlantic where the wifi didn't reach and the nights smelled like woodsmoke and hydrangea.

But Owen didn't know any of that when she agreed to let him come.

They'd met at a Fourth of July fundraiser in the Hamptons—she volunteering for the marine conservation charity, he pouring wine for a vineyard his cousin owned. He'd knocked over a glass of rosé on her feet, and instead of apologizing, he'd laughed and said, "At least it's a good vintage." She'd been annoyed for approximately ninety seconds.

By the end of the night, she knew three things about him: he was visiting from Colorado, his flight left August 18th, and she wanted to see him again.

That should have been the whole story.

---

Their first morning at the beach house, Mira woke to find Owen already on the porch, coffee in hand, watching the light come up over the water. He turned when he heard her footsteps, and something about his expression—the softness there, the unguardedness—made her chest ache in a way she wasn't prepared for.

"You're awake early," she said.

"I couldn't sleep. The quiet is different here. Louder, somehow."

She sat beside him and they didn't speak for a long time. The ocean did its ancient, indifferent thing.

"You know," he said eventually, "I think I understand why people fall in love in summer. It's easier to believe in things when you're not cold."

Mira didn't say anything. She wasn't sure if he was speaking about her or about something else entirely, some private weather she hadn't been invited into.

---

They made a rule, early on.

No pasts. No futures. The August Rule, Owen called it, lifting his beer in a mock toast. Just the present tense.

It wasn't a difficult rule to keep. He didn't ask about her ex-husband, and she didn't ask about the woman in the photograph he'd tucked into the back of his wallet—a woman with kind eyes and a smile that suggested a long history. They didn't talk about what would happen after he left, because neither of them wanted to think about the particular emptiness of a phone screen, the way distance makes strangers of people who once knew each other's breathing.

Instead, they did the things that summer people do.

They swam at dusk and lay on the still-warming sand, tracing constellations with their fingers. They drove to a roadside farm stand in the mornings and bought tomatoes so ripe they tasted like the idea of tomatoes, not tomatoes themselves. They read on the porch in companionable silence, occasionally reading aloud a sentence that struck them, and being pleased when it was the same sentence.

One afternoon, a storm rolled in while they were on the water, and Owen brought the small sailboat back to shore with a competence that surprised her. He had the radio on, some jazz station playing softly, and he was soaked through and grinning, and Mira thought, *Oh. Oh no.*

She didn't say it out loud.

---

Around the second week, Mira caught herself doing something she'd never done before: she was planning ahead. Not in the distant, abstract way she planned her life—in tax quarters, in five-year goals—but in the small, immediate way. What would Owen like for dinner tonight? Should she stock more of the beer he preferred? When the bay scallops came into season next week, would he still be here?

Would he still be here?

She put the thought away. The August Rule. The present tense.

But one night, lying awake listening to him breathe, she realized she was terrified in a way she hadn't been since she was a child. Not of him. Of how thoroughly he had slipped into the architecture of her days. In two weeks, he had become the person she reached for in the dark, the voice she wanted to hear first in the morning, the particular warmth she had been missing without knowing she was missing it.

She had been so careful, she thought. So careful.

---

The night before he left, they walked down to the beach for the last time.

The tide was out, leaving a wide, flat expanse of sand that caught the moonlight and held it. They took off their shoes and walked at the edge of the surf, and Owen, who had been uncharacteristically quiet all day, finally spoke.

"I have to tell you something," he said. "I'm going to break the rule."

Mira's heart, which had been beating steadily all summer, did something complicated.

"I don't want to go back," he said. "I mean—I do. I have to. But I want you to know that whatever happens after this, this wasn't nothing to me. This was a lot. This was more than I knew how to ask for."

She stopped walking. He turned to face her.

"What about the woman in your wallet?" she asked.

He looked surprised. Then he laughed, softly.

"My sister," he said. "She died in March. The photograph is the most recent one I have of her. I keep it there because I'm afraid I'll forget what she looked like, even though I know I never will."

Mira reached up and touched his face. She hadn't known. Of course she hadn't known. The August Rule.

"I'm sorry," she said.

"Don't be," he said. "It made the summer more precious, somehow. Knowing it was finite."

---

The next morning, she drove him to the airport.

They did the things people do at airport drop-offs—standing slightly apart, holding their coffee cups as though the cups were doing important work. He kissed her, finally, properly, and she memorized the exact pressure of it.

"Call me," he said. "When the leaves turn, if you want. If you're lonely. If you're not lonely. Whatever the case is."

"I will," she said, knowing she meant it.

She watched him walk into the terminal, his backpack over one shoulder, his Colorado baseball cap pulled low. She waited until he was out of sight, and then she sat in the drop-off lane for an embarrassingly long time, until a man in a yellow vest politely suggested she move along.

She drove back to the beach house alone.

The porch still smelled like his coffee. The chair he sat in every morning was still warm from the sun, though not, of course, from him.

---

That fall, Mira did not call.

And Owen did not call her.

This is the part of the story that people sometimes don't believe, because they want things to resolve. They want the lovers to find each other, to choose each other, to defy the geography that separated them. They want the August to last.

But some summers are meant to be Augusts. Some people come into it for a reason, and the reason is not forever, and that doesn't make them less. It makes them what they were: a season, a weather, a particular slant of light that you remember long after it's gone.

Mira kept the August Rule, even after he left.

She packed up the beach house in October. She drove back to the city and resumed her life. She didn't Google him, though she wanted to. She didn't send the email she drafted three times and deleted twice.

But sometimes—on the kind of summer evening that makes you nostalgic for a summer you've already lived—she would drive out to Dune Road and sit on the porch alone, watching the light do its thing over the water, and she would think of him. Not with regret. Not with longing, exactly. Just with the quiet recognition of something that had been real.

It had been real.

And in a life made up of small compromises, of half-truths and careful distances, of rules one makes and breaks and makes again—perhaps that was enough.

Perhaps that was a lot.

---

*The end.*

**The Invitation**

The envelope arrived on a Tuesday, cream-colored and stiff as a dried leaf, my name written across the front in emerald ink that smelled faintly of jasmine. I already knew what it was before I broke the seal. There is only one person in this town who still sends proper invitations.

Aunt Vivienne.

I set it on the counter and let it sit there for an hour, willing it to expire. It did not. The gold lettering simply glittered at me more accusingly.

"Darling," the note inside read, in her looping, theatrical hand, "I am hosting a small tea on Saturday at three. You will attend. Do not bring excuses. I've heard them all, and I've invented better ones myself."

She signed it with a single V and a tiny drawing of a teapot that, I swear, looked smug.

I groaned audibly. My cat, Mr. Bingley, lifted his head from the windowsill and gave me the sympathetic look of someone who understood that I had made poor choices in a past life.

---

Saturday came, as Saturdays do, regardless of how I felt about it.

I dressed with the specific kind of care that signals resentment: a navy dress, sensible shoes, my hair pinned up because Vivienne had once commented that I wore it "like a war." I considered bringing a book to read behind a potted fern, but even I knew that was beneath me.

Her house stood at the end of Lilac Lane, the one with the creeping ivy and the door that always looked like it had just been painted that morning, even when it hadn't been painted in years. I had not been inside since I was seventeen, when I had fled a similar tea halfway through the cucumber sandwiches and hitchhiked to the coast.

The door opened before I could knock.

"Finally," said Vivienne.

She was seventy-three and wore it like a coat she could take off if she wished. Her hair was silver, her eyes were sharp, and she smelled, as always, of rosewater and something faintly subversive.

I followed her inside.

---

The sitting room was, predictably, a battlefield of civility. Doilies everywhere, like small surrendered flags. A three-tiered tray of pastries. A silver teapot that I was fairly sure had been in her family since the actual British Empire. And, arranged in careful clusters on the various settees, were six women I half-recognized and fully dreaded.

"Margot!" called Mrs. Pemberton from the corner, waving as if we were old friends and not two people who had once argued for forty minutes about the correct way to fold a napkin.

"Margot, dear," said Cynthia, my mother's oldest friend, patting the cushion beside her like I was a dog being invited onto a sofa.

There was one empty chair. Naturally. In the center of the room. Facing Vivienne, who had arranged the geometry of the afternoon so that there was no escape and no angle from which I could not be observed.

I sat.

Tea was poured. It was, infuriatingly, the exact blend I liked best.

---

The first twenty minutes were a kind of slow-motion torture. Cynthia talked about her colonoscopy. Mrs. Pemberton recounted the price of her new curtains as if delivering scripture. A woman I didn't know, introduced to me twice already as "the one who's moving into the old Carter place," smiled at me with the fixed cheer of someone who had not yet committed to being my enemy.

Vivienne watched me over the rim of her teacup the way a cat watches a mouse it has decided, for now, to let live.

"Tell us, Margot," she said, in a voice like a velvet trap snapping shut, "what have you been doing with yourself?"

The room turned, gently and unanimously, toward me.

I took a sip of tea to buy time. It was perfect. Of course it was.

"Not much," I said. "Reading. Mostly."

"Reading what?" said Cynthia, leaning forward with the gleeful nosiness of someone who had forgotten the concept of boundaries sometime in 1986.

"Books."

"What kind?"

"The kind with pages."

There was a small, scandalized silence. Mrs. Pemberton looked at Vivienne. Vivienne looked at me, and for a moment, the corner of her mouth twitched.

It was going to be a long afternoon.

---

Somewhere between the second pot of tea and the arrival of the scones, something shifted. I am not sure when. It might have been when Cynthia, emboldened by her second glass of sherry, admitted that she had once been in love with a woman in Lisbon and had never told a soul until now. It might have been when Mrs. Pemberton confessed that the new curtains had been a mistake and she was thinking of simply burning the house down. It might have been when the new neighbor, whose name turned out to be June, said quietly, "I moved here because I divorced my husband and I wanted to be somewhere no one knew me to be someone they didn't expect," and the whole room exhaled a little.

Vivienne refilled my cup without asking. I let her.

"You know why I keep doing this," she said later, catching me alone in the hallway while the others argued about whether scones should have jam before cream or after. "Don't you."

"No."

"Liar."

She looked at me, and for a moment, she was not the formidable Vivienne, terror of parish committees and setter of impossible standards. She was just an old woman in a beautiful house who had outlived almost everyone she loved and had decided, in her stubborn, theatrical way, that she would not outlive the habit of gathering them.

"I have you for a few more years, maybe," she said. "I would like them to have scones in them."

I opened my mouth. Closed it.

She patted my cheek, which I would normally have forbidden, and went back to her guests.

---

I stayed until the light went amber, until the sherry was finished and the arguments had softened into laughter. I helped her wash up, though she pretended not to want me to. When I left, she pressed a small paper bag into my hands.

"For tomorrow," she said. "The scones are better the next day. If you warm them."

I walked home down Lilac Lane in the dusk, the bag in my hands, Mr. Bingley waiting for me on the windowsill, the smell of jasmine still clinging to the emerald ink I had not yet thrown away.

I would complain about the next one, too.

I already knew I would go.

Write a story about another day in a heatwave. In total around 900 characters.

# 灼日无休

七月的太阳像一口倒扣的铜锅，把整座城市焖在底下，连空气都发出细微的噼啪声。

李诚蹲在五金店的门槛上，汗水顺着下巴滴在锁头上，砸出一个个深色的小圆点。他已经修了一上午的空调外机，每一台都滚烫得像刚从炉膛里掏出来。徒弟小陈趴在柜台后面，只露出半个脑袋，声音闷闷的："师父，这天热得邪乎，路上连狗都吐舌头。"

"狗吐舌头是散热，人吐舌头那是中暑。"李诚拧紧最后一颗螺丝，把工具袋往肩上一甩，"走，去老周家。他那台柜机据说从昨晚就开始滴水。"

他们骑上电动车，车座晒得能煎鸡蛋。李诚用袖子垫着坐下，刚拧动把手，塑料把手就粘住了手心的汗。

老周住在老城区六楼，没电梯。爬到四楼时，李诚的腿开始发软。小陈跟在后面，脸色煞白，扶着墙喘气："师父，要不……歇会儿？"

"歇什么歇，老周心脏不好，屋里没空调跟蒸笼似的。"李诚咬着牙继续往上走，膝盖骨发出咯吱的响声。

门开了，老周的老伴儿把他们让进去。屋里果然像个蒸笼，老周躺在床上，摇着蒲扇，看见他们来了，眼眶竟有些湿润。

"李师傅，这天没法活了。"老周声音沙哑，"我老伴儿昨晚一夜没睡，给我扇了一宿。"

李诚没说话，打开工具箱就开始干活。狭小的阳台挤不下两个人，小陈站在客厅里递工具，隔着一道门，李诚喊一声，他就递一样。汗水流进眼睛里，杀得生疼，他用袖子胡乱擦一把，继续拧螺丝。

二十分钟后，空调外机终于吐出了第一缕凉风。

老周的老伴儿打开柜机，凉气慢慢弥漫开来。老周闭上眼睛，深深吸了一口气，那表情像是溺水的人终于浮出水面。

"多少钱？"老周问。

李诚看了看那台老旧的柜机，零件都是十几年前的了，换个电容都不容易。他张了张嘴，想报个价，又闭上了。

"算了，这台机器太老了，没什么好收的。您下回要是再坏，就直接换台新的吧。"

"那怎么行——"

"天太热，零件都热胀了，螺丝拧不紧。"李诚打断他，背起工具袋就往外走，"我下次来还得返工，不值当的。"

小陈追上来，欲言又止。到了楼下，他才开口："师父，那电容明明换好了。"

"你小子懂什么。"李诚戴上头盔，声音被闷在里面，"老周儿子在深圳打工，就老两口在家。这种天，空调坏了是要出人命的。"

电动车汇入热浪蒸腾的车流里。李诚眯着眼睛看路，视线被汗水模糊。手机响了一声，是徒弟群里的消息——"师父，七号楼那个老太太打电话来了，说空调不制冷。"

"去。"李诚回了一个字。

小陈从后座探过头来："师父，咱们中午吃什么？"

"凉皮。"李诚说，"多加辣子，出出汗。"

太阳正当顶，没有一丝云。路边的法国梧桐叶子卷成了筒，知了在树上声嘶力竭地叫，叫声像要把这层皮囊一起剥下来。李诚骑着车，穿过一条又一条被晒得发白的街道，心里想着：这单做完，下午还有三单。今晚要是能赶在十二点前收工，就去河边坐坐，听说夜里河边凉快些。

风是热的，但吹在脸上，竟觉得有几分安慰。

他想，这鬼天气，也不知道什么时候是个头。

但活儿总得有人干。

# The Detour

The summer of 1995 stretched out before the four of them like an endless ribbon of asphalt.

Maya gripped the steering wheel of her father's beat-up station wagon, her dark hair pulled back in a messy ponytail. Beside her, Jess navigated through a crumpled road atlas, while their boyfriends, Devon and Theo, argued good-naturedly about music from the backseat.

"We're heading to the Grand Canyon," Maya announced, "and nothing is going to stop us."

"Except maybe this car," Theo muttered, kicking the back of her seat.

Devon laughed. "She's survived worse. My mom drove it through a hailstorm in '92."

The plan was simple: drive from their small town in Ohio to Arizona, see one of the wonders of the world, and make memories that would last a lifetime. They had three weeks, $400 split between them, and a cooler full of snacks that Jess's mother had packed with suspicious intensity.

---

The first sign of trouble came in Missouri.

"Uh, guys?" Devon leaned forward, pressing his face against the window. "Is that smoke?"

Maya's eyes darted to the rearview mirror. A thin gray plume was indeed trailing behind them. She pulled over at a gas station, and the four of them piled out to investigate.

The engine was hot to the touch, and some mysterious fluid was leaking onto the pavement.

"We need a mechanic," Maya said, trying to keep the panic out of her voice.

"In *Hickville, Missouri*?" Theo asked, looking around at the single pump and the dusty building behind it. "Good luck."

But luck, it turned out, was on their side. An old man named Earl emerged from the station's repair shop, wiping his hands on a rag. He took one look at the station wagon, whistled low, and told them he could have it running by morning.

"You're going to need a place to stay," he said, eyeing the four teenagers with a mixture of sympathy and suspicion.

A woman appeared at the door of the station, wiping her hands on an apron. She looked like she'd been cooking for an army.

"You'll stay with us," she said, in a tone that didn't invite argument. "I'm Loretta. Earl, get the spare room ready."

---

That night, they sat around Loretta's kitchen table, eating fried chicken and listening to stories about her children, all grown and gone.

"I always said I'd travel when I was young," she said, her gaze drifting to the window. "But then life happens. You fall in love. You build something. And before you know it, fifty years have gone by."

She looked at them, really looked at them, and something shifted in her expression.

"Don't wait too long, you hear me? Don't let fear or practicality steal your adventures."

Maya felt something tighten in her chest. She thought about her father, who'd always talked about sailing around the world but never did. She thought about her own life, the safe path she'd been planning since childhood.

"We're going to see the Grand Canyon," she said, more to herself than anyone else.

"Then you will," Loretta said firmly. "You'll see it, and it'll change you."

---

Earl fixed the car at dawn, charging them only $80 and a promise to send him a postcard.

"Don't you worry about Loretta's words," he said as they loaded up. "She gets philosophical when she's been cooking."

But Maya was already thinking about the words. *Don't let fear or practicality steal your adventures.*

---

The Grand Canyon was everything they imagined and nothing they expected.

They stood at the South Rim at sunset, the canyon walls burning orange and red below them. The wind was fierce, whipping their hair and clothes, and for a long moment, no one spoke.

"I want to remember this," Jess said, her voice barely audible over the wind. "Forever. Exactly this."

Maya pulled out her disposable camera and started taking pictures, but she knew the truth: the photos would never capture the feeling. The vastness. The strange peace that came from standing at the edge of something so much bigger than yourself.

Devon slipped his arm around her, and she leaned into him.

"What do you want to do?" he asked. "After this. With your life."

It was a question she'd been avoiding for months. The safe answer was: college, then a job, then the slow accumulation of a sensible life.

"I don't know," she said honestly. "I thought I did, but now..."

They stood there until the sun disappeared and the stars came out, more stars than any of them had ever seen.

---

On the drive back, with the Grand Canyon hundreds of miles behind them, Maya made a decision.

She pulled over at a rest stop in New Mexico and gathered everyone around.

"I've been thinking," she said. "About what we saw. About what Loretta said."

She reached into her bag and pulled out four envelopes.

"I'm dropping out of college. I'm going to take a gap year. Travel. Work odd jobs. Figure out what I actually want."

Jess gasped. Devon's eyebrows shot up. Theo just stared at her.

"Maya—" Devon started.

"I'm not asking you to come," she continued. "But if anyone wants to... I'm going to California next week. I found a job at a campground near Yosemite."

The silence stretched out for a long moment.

Then Theo laughed. "You know what? I'm in. I've been dreading starting law school anyway."

Devon looked at Jess. "I can't," he said softly. "I have responsibilities."

Jess nodded, her eyes bright with tears she was trying not to shed. "Neither can I. But Maya—" she grabbed her best friend's hands. "You have to promise to write. Promise to tell me everything."

They hugged for a long time at that rest stop, four friends at the beginning of different paths.

---

Maya and Theo drove west the next morning, leaving Jess and Devon to take the train home.

Three months later, Maya was working at the campground when a letter arrived from Jess. Inside was a postcard of the Grand Canyon, the one they'd promised to send to Earl and Loretta.

On the back, Jess had written:

*Dear Earl and Loretta,*

*We made it. We saw it. And it changed us, just like you said.*

*Maya's gone to California to find her adventures. The rest of us are figuring out our own paths. But we haven't forgotten your kindness, or your words.*

*Don't wait too long.*

*Love,*
*The Ohio Four*

P.S. *The station wagon made it home. Barely. But it made it.*

---

Years later, when Maya would think back on that summer, she wouldn't remember the broken-down car or the long drives or even the breathtaking view from the canyon's edge.

She'd remember the people. Earl and Loretta, who'd given them shelter. Jess and Devon, who'd loved her enough to let her go. Theo, who'd been brave enough to come along.

She'd remember that the best journeys weren't really about the destinations.

They were about the people you met along the way.

Write a story about somebody reminiscing on an event that happened many summers ago. Around 900 characters.

# 那年夏天的萤火虫

奶奶走了以后，我整理她的旧物，在她床底下的樟木箱里翻出了一只玻璃瓶。瓶子里装着几只干瘪的萤火虫，在午后斜照进来的光里，隐隐约约还能看见它们身上残留的微光。

我捧着那只瓶子，忽然就愣了神。

那是二十年前的夏天，我七岁。爸妈工作忙，把我送到乡下奶奶家住一整个暑假。

奶奶家的院子很大，屋后是一片竹林，竹林那边有一条小溪。夏天的傍晚，奶奶会搬两把藤椅到院子里的老槐树下，让我躺在她怀里，给我扇蒲扇，赶走那些烦人的蚊子。

"奶奶，天上怎么有那么多小灯笼？"有一天晚上，我指着竹林那边一明一灭的光点问道。

奶奶笑了笑，把蒲扇放下，牵起我的手："走，奶奶带你去看。"

她领着我穿过院子，走进竹林。月光从竹叶的缝隙里洒下来，在地上印出斑驳的影子。我紧紧攥着奶奶的手，另一只手提着那只玻璃瓶。

等我看见那些萤火虫的时候，我呆住了。

漫山遍野的萤火虫，像是谁打翻了一只装满星子的口袋。它们在空中飞舞，有的停在竹叶上，有的掠过我的鼻尖，有的停在我的肩膀上。我伸出手去，它们就乖乖地落在我的掌心，一闪一闪地亮着，像是在和我说话。

"奶奶，它们在说什么呀？"

奶奶蹲下来，把我抱在怀里："它们在说，小囡囡，欢迎你来到夏天。"

我开心极了，在竹林里跑来跑去，追着那些小灯笼。奶奶站在一旁，笑呵呵地看着我，月光把她的白发照得发亮。她让我把最亮的那几只装进瓶子里，说是要给它们找一个家。

那天晚上，我抱着那只瓶子入睡，梦里有漫天的星光，也有奶奶年轻时候的容颜。

后来我在乡下住了整整两个月。每天傍晚，奶奶都牵着我的手去看萤火虫。我们走遍了村子周围的每一片竹林、每一条小溪、每一块稻田。我装了满满一瓶子的萤火虫，那是我童年最珍贵的宝藏。

暑假结束的时候，爸妈来接我。我抱着那只玻璃瓶，哭得撕心裂肺。奶奶摸着我的头，说："囡囡不哭，明年夏天奶奶还等着你来。"

可是后来爸妈工作越来越忙，我上了各种补习班，再也没有去乡下住过一整个夏天。再后来奶奶搬到了城里，住进了高楼，窗外只有车水马龙和霓虹灯光。

一年又一年，我长大、工作、结婚、生子。奶奶也慢慢老了，她的背越来越弯，头发越来越白，最后她躺在了医院的病床上。

去年夏天，奶奶走了。她走的时候很安详，握着我的手，像是在等什么人。

"囡囡，奶奶要去找你爷爷了。"她艰难地说，"你要是想奶奶了，就看看那些萤火虫，它们会替奶奶陪着你。"

我终于明白，为什么奶奶走的时候是笑着的。

今天我坐在窗前，看着手中的玻璃瓶。夕阳西下，暮色渐浓。不知什么时候，一只真正的萤火虫飞进了我的房间，停在了窗台上，一闪一闪地亮着。

我轻轻地打开瓶盖，那只萤火虫飞了出来，和窗台上的那只一起，绕着那只玻璃瓶飞舞。

我忽然就笑了，泪水却止不住地流下来。

"奶奶，我来看你了。"

# آخر يوم قبل الصيف

في شارعٍ هادئٍ من شوارع القاهرة القديمة، حيث تتشابك ظلال أشجار الجميز مع ضوء الشمس الحاد، وقفت ليلى على عتبة باب بيت جدّتها. كانت قد أتت لتودّع المكان، فبعد يومين، ستسافر عائلتها إلى الإسكندرية، ولن تعود إلى هذا البيت مجددًا.

أخرجت من جيبها ورقةً صفراء بالية، مطويّة بعناية. كانت تلك القائمة التي كتبتها في أول يوم من العطلة الصيفية، حينما أتت إلى هنا مع جدّتها لتقضي الصيف كلّه، كعادتها كلّ عام.

فتحت الورقة وقرأت:  
١- تسلّق شجرة التوت.  
٢- مشاهدة غروب الشمس من سطح البيت.  
٣- جمع خمسين حجرًا ملوّنًا من الحديقة.  
٤- ركوب الترامواي مع جدّتي.  
٥- قراءة ثلاثين كتابًا.  
٦- السباحة في النيل.  
٧- قطف الليمون من الشجرة.  
٨- تدوين سرّ في دفتر.  
٩- الرقص تحت المطر.  
١٠- حفر اسمي على جذع الشجرة.

ابتسمت ليلى حينما تذكّرت كيف كانت تكتب تلك الأحلام الصغيرة بقلم رصاص، والضحكات تعلو وجهها. لكنّها الآن، وبعد أن خطّت القائمة بخطّ أحمر فوق كلّ بند، لم يبقَ إلّا واحد: **كتابة سرّ في الدفتر**.

دخلت البيت. كان الهدوء يغمر الجدران، وكأنّ البيت نفسه يحتفظ بأسراره. صعدت السلّم الخشبيّ الذي يصدر صريرًا تحت قدميها، حتى وصلت إلى غرفتها القديمة. فتحت النافذة، فدخل الهواء المحمل برائحة النعناع والياسمين.

أخرجت دفترًا أسود صغيرًا من حقيبتها. كانت قد اشترته في أول يوم، ولم تكتب فيه شيئًا. جلست على الكرسيّ الخشبيّ، وأمسكت القلم، وبدأت تكتب.

"هذا سرّي الأخير قبل أن أترك هذا البيت للأبد..."

توقّفت قليلًا، ثمّ كتبت:

"لم أكن أعرف أنّ جدّتي ستمرض هذا الصيف. لم أكن أعرف أنّها ستودّعنا بصمت، في ليلة عاصفة، وأنا نائمة في غرفتي. لم أكن أعرف أنّ آخر مرّة رأيتُ فيها ابتسامتها كانت وهي تُخبّئ لي قطعة بسكوت تحت المخدة. الآن أعرف أنّ الصيف لم يكن فقط أيامًا طويلة تحت الشمس، بل كان آخر هديّة من الزمن. لن أعود إلى هذا البيت، لكنّني سأحمله في قلبي. سأحمل رائحة الليمون، وصوت القطار البعيد، وضحكات جدّتي التي كانت تملأ المكان. وسأظلّ كلّ صيف، أعود إليها في الحلم، حتى نلتقي مجددًا في مكانٍ لا ينتهي فيه الصيف."

أغلقت الدفتر، ودمعة واحدة سقطت على غلافه. مسحتها بطرف أصابعها، ثمّ وضعت الدفتر داخل كيسٍ صغير مع أشيائها الأخرى.

نزلت إلى الحديقة. كانت الشمس تميل نحو المغيب، فذهبت إلى شجرة التوت الكبيرة، وحفرت اسمها على جذعها بسكّين صغيرة. ثمّ نظرت إلى البيت للمرّة الأخيرة، وهمست:

"وداعًا يا بيت جدّتي. إلى اللقاء."

خرجت من الباب، وفي يدها حقيبة صغيرة، وفي قلبها سرّ أخيرًا وُلد.

Write a story set in the summer, when suddenly it starts to snow. Around 1800 characters.

# 六月的雪

那年夏天，小渔村的孩子们从未见过这样的天。

七月十五日的中午，天空蓝得像一块刚洗过的绸缎，海面平静得没有一丝皱纹。渔村的孩子们光着脚在沙滩上追逐打闹，王阿婆在榕树下摇着蒲扇打盹，连村里的老黄狗都趴在阴凉处吐着舌头。

然后，就在午后两点左右，天气变了。

起初只是天边飘来一片奇怪的云——不是积雨云那种铅灰色的厚重，而是带着一种不祥的银白色，像是有人把月光剪下来贴在了天空上。云层越聚越多，越压越低，仿佛天空正在缓缓塌陷。

"要下雨了。"王阿婆睁开眼睛，抬头望了一眼，喃喃自语。

但落下来的不是雨。

是雪。

细小的雪花从铅灰色的天空中簌簌落下，在七月的阳光下闪着诡异的光芒。雪落在滚烫的沙滩上，瞬间化成一小滩水；落在孩子们的肩头，带来一阵凉意；落在王阿婆花白的发丝上，转瞬即逝。

"下雪啦！"孩子们先是惊叫，然后欢呼起来，在雪中蹦跳追逐，像一群快乐的小兽。

可大人们的脸色却变了。

老渔民陈伯站在自家门槛上，浑浊的眼睛盯着那漫天飞舞的雪花，嘴唇微微发抖。"六月雪……"他喃喃道，"我活了七十年，头一回见六月下雪。"

雪越下越密。

到了傍晚，沙滩上已经积了薄薄一层白。椰子树叶上挂着晶莹的冰凌，在夕阳下折射出七彩的光芒。整个小渔村像是被施了魔法，变成了一个银装素裹的童话世界。

但没有人觉得美。

村里的祠堂前，人们越聚越多，七嘴八舌地议论着。老村长拄着拐杖，颤巍巍地站在人群中间，脸色比那雪还要苍白。

"我爹在世的时候说过，"老村长清了清嗓子，"我们陈家湾的祖上，有个传说——若六月飞雪，必有沉冤。"

人群静了下来。

陈伯的老伴突然"哎呀"一声，瘫坐在地上，哭了起来："老头子，你到底做了什么孽啊……"

陈伯的脸涨得通红，脖子上的青筋鼓起老高："我陈老三这辈子打鱼为生，从没害过人！"

"那为什么老天爷要在七月下雪？"有人质问。

争论声、哭喊声在暮色中此起彼伏。

就在这时，人群后面响起一个怯生生的声音：

"爷爷，雪是我招来的。"

所有人都转过头去。

说话的是陈伯的孙女小雪，今年刚满八岁，扎着两个羊角辫，圆圆的脸蛋冻得发红，眼眶里含着泪水。

"小雪！你胡说八道什么！"陈伯一把将孙女拉到身后，怒声呵斥。

可小雪却倔强地挣开爷爷的手，从怀里掏出一个布偶——那布偶已经烧去了大半，只剩下一只残缺的手脚和一颗黑乎乎的头颅。

人群发出倒吸凉气的声音。

"三天前，我在后山玩，"小雪抽抽噎噎地说，"看见几个城里来的人在烧什么东西。我问他们烧什么，他们说是旧衣服。我看见这布偶还在烧，就……就想救它……"

她抬起头，泪流满面："我不知道他们是坏人。我不知道他们在烧的是……"

她说不下去了。

老村长的脸色变得铁青。他慢慢走上前，从颤抖的小雪手中接过那只烧焦的布偶，翻过来——布偶的背后，隐约可以看见用针线绣的几个字：

"林秀英之灵位"。

人群中爆发出一阵惊呼。

"林秀英！"王阿婆突然尖叫起来，"那不是……那不是去年跳海的那个女娃娃吗？"

人群再次陷入死一般的寂静。

去年夏天，村里来过几个外地人，说是要在海边建什么化工厂。村里的年轻人们大多反对，可村里的大人们收了人家的钱，便睁一只眼闭一只眼。带头反对最激烈的是一个叫林秀英的城里来的女大学生，她在海边支起了帐篷，绝食抗议，在网上写文章揭露那家公司的黑历史。

一个月后，她被发现死在海边的礁石上。

警方说是自杀。

可村里的人都知道，那几个外地人在她死前一天，去了她的帐篷。

"那几个畜生！"陈伯一拳砸在祠堂的门柱上，"他们现在在哪？"

"今早坐船走了，"有人说，"说是去市里……"

"追！"

不知道是谁喊了一声，人群突然骚动起来。

可就在此时，雪突然变大了。

鹅毛大雪铺天盖地地落下，仿佛天河决了口子。风从海面上呼啸而来，卷起漫天的雪花，让人睁不开眼睛。

"这是老天爷不让啊……"老村长喃喃道，"这是冤魂在拦我们……"

小雪突然挣开人群，朝着大海的方向跑去。

"小雪！"陈伯在后面追，"你要干什么？"

小雪站在海边，浪花打湿了她的裤腿，她张开双臂，对着漫天飞雪大声喊道：

"林姐姐！"

她的声音被风雪撕扯着，却清晰无比。

"我知道你是好人！我知道你死得冤枉！"

"我把你的布偶救回来了！你不要生气了！"

雪似乎小了一些。

小雪从怀里掏出一个东西——是一个用贝壳和小野花编成的花环，是她这几天瞒着大人们偷偷做的。

"我给你戴上！"

她将花环轻轻放在海边的礁石上，然后跪下来，对着大海重重地磕了三个头。

风停了。

雪停了。

太阳不知什么时候从云层后探出了头，金色的阳光洒在海面上，波光粼粼，像是有千万条鱼在跳跃。

花环旁边的礁石上，不知什么时候多了一只海鸥。

它静静地站在那里，黑豆般的眼睛望着小雪，过了好一会儿，才展翅飞向夕阳。

那一晚，陈家湾的渔民们做了一个共同的梦。

梦见一个穿着白裙子的年轻女子，站在海边，对着他们微微鞠了一躬，然后转身走进了大海深处，再也没有回头。

第二天一早，人们发现海边礁石上的花环不见了。礁石上只留下一小片贝壳，在阳光下闪闪发亮。

小雪捡起那片贝壳，紧紧地握在手心里。

那年夏天，陈家湾再也没来过那几个外地人。化工厂的项目也不知怎么就黄了。

每年的七月十五，小雪都会去海边放一个花环。

有人问她做什么，她总是笑笑说：

"去看一个朋友。"

很多年后，小雪成了作家。

她写的第一本书，名字叫《六月的雪》。

扉页上写着：*献给所有沉冤得雪的人。*

Write a story that begins with someone's popsicle melting. Total: ~800 words.

The raspberry popsicle bled down Eleanor's knuckles in long, sticky rivulets. She had bought it from the cart on the corner of Ninth and Maple, the one with the faded umbrella that the old man refused to replace, and she had walked three blocks before she realized she had no intention of eating it. She had bought it out of habit, the way she bought everything now, as though her hands needed to be doing something or they would remember what they had done.

The sun was unforgiving. July in the city turned the sidewalks into griddles and the air above them into something thick and trembling, and Eleanor stood beneath the rusted awning of a laundromat watching her popsicle commit its slow, pink suicide. She should go inside. She should do many things.

A little boy was watching her from behind his mother's leg. He had a face like a peeled peach, all soft and startled, and his own popsicle—grape, by the look of it—was already mostly a memory. He was perhaps four. He looked at her with the grave, considering attention that children sometimes give to strangers, as though they were books one was just learning to read.

Eleanor smiled at him. It surprised her, the smile. She had not known it was coming.

"Your mom's letting it melt," the boy informed her, as though Eleanor were not there at all but a problem to be solved at a distance.

"He's right, you know," the mother said. She was young, tired, beautiful in a way that had nothing to do with rest. "Waste of a good popsicle."

Eleanor looked down at her hand. The popsicle was now a nub, a pale pink afterthought clinging to its stick. The juice had dripped onto her shoe. There was, she realized, no good reason not to eat what was left of it. There was no good reason for anything, but there was also no good reason *against* this particular thing, and the distinction, lately, had become important.

She put the popsicle in her mouth. It was mostly air by then, the flavor faint and sugary, the cold already gone. She finished it anyway, standing on the hot sidewalk with grape-child and his mother, and when the stick was bare she held it up like a small wooden flag of surrender.

"Congratulations," the mother said, and smiled, and tugged her son along.

Eleanor watched them go. The boy looked back once, and she raised her wooden flag again, and he giggled, and then they turned the corner and were gone.

She stood for a long time after that. The laundromat behind her hummed and clicked, the dryers tumbling someone's sheets, someone's shirts, someone's small secret life. The old man at the cart on the corner sold another popsicle to a woman in a red dress. A pigeon landed on the awning and considered Eleanor with one orange eye, then decided she was not worth the trouble and left.

Eleanor looked at the popsicle stick in her hand. It said *RASPBERRY* on it in faded blue ink, and below that, smaller, *Made with real fruit!* She had not known, until this moment, that she was going to do what she did next.

She walked back to the cart.

"One more, please," she said. "Raspberry."

The old man looked at her, and then at her empty hands, and then at the stick she was holding like evidence. He nodded slowly, the way people nod when they understand something without being told what it is, and he pulled a fresh popsicle from the chest of ice. It was the color of a wound, or a sunset, or a thing one might be forgiven for.

"Hot enough for you?" he asked, because that is what people ask.

"Hot enough," she said.

She paid him. She did not walk three blocks this time. She stood right there beside his faded umbrella, and she unwrapped the popsicle, and she ate it slowly, while the city shimmered around her and the old man whistled something tuneless and true. She let it melt a little, even, on purpose, and licked the drips from her fingers, and felt, for the first time in a long while, the small and ridiculous sweetness of being a person who was still here.

When she was done, she kept the stick. She did not know why. She put it in her pocket beside her house keys and the photograph she had been carrying for three months, the one she had not yet been able to look at and had not yet been able to throw away.

She would look at it tomorrow. Or the day after. Or some day that was not today, which was, after all, only the first day she had allowed herself to have a popsicle and mean it.

She thanked the old man and walked home. The sun was lower now, and the shadows were longer, and somewhere a child was laughing about a grape popsicle, and somewhere a mother was young and tired and beautiful, and somewhere Eleanor was going, slowly, in the right direction, even if she could not yet say what *right* meant.

The pocket with the stick made a small, dry sound as she walked, like a wish being made, like a stick being broken to begin something new.
