# The Balloon that Would Not Float

The first balloon of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade lifted off at precisely 9:00 a.m., and Harold Pemberton was already three blocks off course.

He steered his twenty-foot-tall Smokey Bear balloon by a system of ropes and pulleys that he had personally inspected the night before, checking each knot with the reverence most men reserve for wedding vows. The ropes were sound. The knots were true. The wind was behaving. And yet Harold was drifting east, into the soft chaos of Manhattan's upper avenues, where his bear was supposed to be gliding west toward the flags and the cameras and the screaming children bundled in red and gold.

"Pemberton!" crackled the walkie-talkie at his hip. "Pemberton, you are veering. Vee-ering. Do you copy?"

"I copy," Harold said, into the mouthpiece clipped near his collar. "I am aware."

"Awareness is not corrective action, Harold."

"I know, Phil. I know."

He looked up at the bear's enormous face, the wide brim of the ranger hat, the black-nosed smile that had been greeting Americans since 1944. Smokey looked, if Harold had to put a word to it, slightly bemused. As if the bear too were wondering why, after forty-seven Thanksgivings of dutiful parade attendance, his eighty-first year of public service had to be ruined by a sixty-three-year-old man with arthritis in his left shoulder and a stomach that had been bothering him since Tuesday.

The stomach.

Harold did not like to think about the stomach. The stomach, like the wind, was its own creature. The stomach had been making noises. The stomach had opinions.

He tugged the southrope. The bear corrected by two degrees, then resumed its eastward drift.

"Pemberton!"

"I'm working on it, Phil."

"Frank is going to be very unhappy."

Frank was Macy's parade director. Frank was always going to be very unhappy, and yet Harold had somehow, year after year, been allowed to walk beneath his beloved Smokey, holding the ropes that tethered the bear to the city. Harold was not sure why he was allowed to do this. He had asked, once, many years ago, and Frank had looked at him with the exhausted patience of a man who had already answered the question four times that morning and said, "Because the bear likes you, Harold."

Harold had taken this as a metaphor. He had been wrong. Frank had been speaking literally.

Because the bear *did* like him. Smokey Bear, that great inflatable icon, who had been through four manufacturers and three redesigns and one unfortunate incident in 1997 involving a tree branch and a small fire, was a balloon with preferences. The balloons, Frank had explained to him on his first year, were like cats. You could lead them. You could not tell them anything.

"Pemberton, you need to be at the reviewing stand in six minutes. Frank is standing at the reviewing stand. Frank is standing at the reviewing stand with his arms folded."

"I understand, Phil."

"Frank does not have infinite patience, Harold."

"Phil."

"Yes?"

"Frank is going to have to learn to share the city with Smokey today."

He clicked off the walkie-talkie.

Above him, the bear's painted eyes rolled gently in a non-existent breeze. The bear was enormous. The bear was, Harold thought, magnificent. And the bear was going where the bear wanted to go, and the bear wanted to go east, into the side streets, where there were no floats and no bands and no grandstands, where the sidewalks held not the polished crowds of midtown but the smaller, scruffier congregations of the outer avenues.

Harold did not fight the bear. Harold had learned, across the years, not to fight the bear. The bear had taken him down Amsterdam Avenue once, in 2009, when Harold's daughter was eight and riding on her uncle's shoulders and waving so hard she nearly toppled into a hot dog vendor. The bear had pulled him into the Park, briefly, in 2015, and Harold had spent twenty minutes explaining to a park ranger that yes, technically, you were not supposed to bring a giant inflatable bear into Central Park, but the bear was insistent, and Harold was merely the driver.

The bear had taken him, once, to a firehouse. This had been in 1992, Harold's second year, when he was still learning the ropes—literally—and the bear had banked hard left on West 78th and come to rest, gently, against the open bay door of Engine 87. The firemen had come out. The firemen had looked at the bear. The firemen had looked at Harold.

"He wanted to say hello," Harold had said.

The firemen had nodded slowly. They had understood. They were, like Harold, in service. They knew how a creature could want a thing, even a creature made of nylon and helium.

Now, in 2024, the bear wanted the side streets. Harold went with him.

"Excuse me," Harold shouted, to a woman crossing with a stroller. "Excuse me, coming through. Parade balloon."

The woman looked up. Her mouth made a small O.

"My God," she said.

"He's friendly," Harold said.

The bear floated past her, casting a long, bobbing shadow. The woman grabbed her child's hand.

"Pemberton!" Phil was screaming now. "Pemberton, we have lost visual. We have *lost visual*."

"I'm fine, Phil."

"You are not on the route."

"I know."

"You are *not on the route*."

"Phil," Harold said, "I am going to tell you something, and I want you to listen."

A pause. Static.

"...Go ahead."

"I have walked this bear for thirty-two years."

"Yes, Harold."

"And I have fought with him for thirty-two years. And in thirty-two years, the bear has never been wrong."

More static. The kind of static that meant Phil was pinching the bridge of his nose.

"The bear is not wrong *today*, Phil."

"But the route—"

"The route is a thing we made up. The bear is a thing that was given to us."

"Pemberton—"

"In 1944, Harold said, "the Forest Service needed a mascot. They put a hat on a bear. They gave him a name. And they told him to go out and do good. And the bear listened. And now the bear is eighty years old, Phil, and the bear has done more good than you and I and Frank put together, and if the bear wants to go down Amsterdam Avenue on Thanksgiving morning, then I think the bear has earned that."

A very long silence.

"Frank is going to fire you, Harold."

"Maybe," Harold said. "But Frank is going to have to catch me first. And I am moving very fast."

He was not, in fact, moving very fast. Parades, even renegade parades, moved slowly. The bear drifted forward, and Harold drifted with him, and the morning, cold and gold, opened around them like a hand.

They passed a diner. The bear paused, as if considering. Harold paused too. Through the window, a waitress looked up from pouring coffee, and her hand went still on the pot. She stared. The bear stared back, with his painted, benevolent eyes. The waitress raised one finger. She pointed at Harold, then at the bear, then at the ceiling. Harold nodded, slowly. He understood. She wanted to know if he was coming in. He pointed at the bear, and made a sorry face. She nodded, sadly, and raised her coffee pot to the window, in a kind of salute.

The bear moved on.

They passed a playground. The bear stopped again. Harold stopped too. Through the chain-link fence, a handful of children, who had been swinging and sliding and arguing over whose turn it was, stood very still, their mouths open, their mittens forgotten. One of them, a small girl in a yellow hat, pointed. The others looked up. And then, all at once, they began to scream—not in fear, but in the pure, distilled delight that only children and the very old are capable of. They pressed against the fence. They waved. They held up drawings, scribbled in crayon, of turkeys and balloons and other things that had nothing to do with bears.

The bear bowed. Harold would swear, later, to anyone who would listen, that the bear bowed. The bear dipped his massive head, and the little girl in the yellow hat burst into tears of joy, and Harold's eyes stung, suddenly, terribly, and he turned away, because he was sixty-three years old and a man did not cry at his job.

But the stomach.

The stomach.

It clenched, then. A spasm that was not wind, not gas, not the broccoli he should not have eaten the night before. A spasm that was a clenched fist, deep inside him, saying *hello*.

Harold took a breath. He kept walking.

"Pemberton." Phil's voice, now quiet. "We've lost you on the cameras. The commentators are improvising. They are saying you are 'taking an unscheduled detour through the historic Upper West Side.'"

"That's very generous of them."

"Frank is going to need a story, Harold."

"Tell Frank the bear is on a mission."

"What mission?"

"Tell him the bear is visiting his friends."

Another silence. Then, very softly, Phil laughed.

"Copy that, Pemberton. Frank says to take your time."

They went on, the bear and the man. Past the bodega with the faded awning. Past the laundromat, where a man in a Yankees cap stepped outside and simply stared. Past the church, where the doors had been propped open for the early service, and the congregants, spotting the bear through the stained glass, began to sing louder, as if the bear were a kind of benediction.

The stomach clenched again. Harder.

Harold knew, in the way that a body knows things before a mind does, that he was in trouble. He knew, with the same quiet certainty, that the bear knew too. He could feel it, in the way the ropes had gone slack. The bear was no longer pulling. The bear was, for the first time in thirty-two years, accommodating.

"All right, old friend," Harold whispered. "All right."

He steered them, gently, toward the nearest hospital. Mount Sinai West, up on Amsterdam. He had been born there. He had been born there, in 1961, the year after Smokey Bear was given his name by the Advertising Council, and he had been born there with a small defect in his heart that the doctors had patched and patched again, and which had, against all odds, carried him to sixty-three and into the employ of a balloon.

He did not tell Phil where they were going. Phil would have worried. Phil would have called an ambulance. The bear did not need an ambulance. The bear needed to be walked, gently, to where he needed to be.

They arrived at the hospital at 10:47 a.m. Harold could see the clock above the entrance. He guided the bear to a stop in the small plaza in front of the emergency room. The bear came to rest, as gently as a cloud settling, on the clean concrete. The ropes went loose in Harold's hands.

He sat down on the curb.

The stomach clenched, again, and this time Harold let out a small sound, a grunt, that he would not have made in front of Frank. The door of the ER slid open. A nurse came out, pulling on gloves, looking for the patient. She saw the bear. She saw Harold. Her mouth made the same small O.

"Mr. Pemberton?" she said, because she had been reading his chart, because he was expected, because someone had called ahead, because the bear had known.

"Yes," Harold said. "I'm the one with the bear."

She came over. She helped him up. He did not look at the bear, because he could not, because if he looked at the bear he would have to say something, and if he said something he would begin to cry, and he was sixty-three years old and a man did not cry at his job.

"Take care of him," he said, to the nurse. "He gets restless."

"I'll let the doctors know," she said.

She walked him through the glass doors. The doors slid shut behind them. Through the glass, Harold could see the bear, still and patient, in the plaza. Around the bear, a small crowd was gathering. People with phones. People with children. People just walking by, on their way to brunch, who had stopped because something in the morning had called to them.

A little girl, in a yellow hat, was pushing through the crowd. Her mother was behind her, breathless. The girl had a crayon drawing, clutched in her mittened hand. She held it up to the bear.

Harold could not hear what she said. But he could see her mouth, forming the word, plainly, through the glass.

*Thank you.*

Harold closed his eyes.

Above the city, the second balloon of the parade, a giant Snoopy in a flying ace helmet, was lifting off into the cold blue sky. The commentators were speaking. The bands were playing. The floats were moving. The parade, the great American parade, was going on, as it always did, as it would always do, around the small mysteries and quiet heroisms of men and their balloons.

And on the plaza of Mount Sinai West, a bear in a ranger hat held his post, and would not float, and would not be moved, until his friend came out to walk him home.

黑色星期五的早晨五点五十分，鼎盛购物广场外已经排起了长队。这是一年中最魔幻的时刻——数百名消费者裹着羽绒服，手里攥着咖啡，呼出的白气在路灯下升腾，像某种古老的祭祀仪式前最后的祈祷。

队伍的最前排站着林小芳，三十二岁，全职妈妈。她已经在寒风中站了三个小时，只为抢购那台原价的咖啡机。为了这台机器，她让丈夫带女儿去了奶奶家，手机里存着闺蜜发来的"内部价"截屏，眼眶下有明显的黑眼圈，但神情却如同即将奔赴战场的士兵。

六点整，卷闸门准时升起。

人群像开了闸的洪水一样涌入。林小芳被人潮推搡着，脚几乎离了地，身后的背包带被扯断了一只耳朵。她顾不上这些，眼睛死死锁定三楼家电区的方向，那里有一台她心仪已久的咖啡机正在向她招手。

冲到扶梯口时，一个穿着红色羽绒服的女人从侧面斜插进来，撞在林小芳肩膀上。她踉跄了一步，差点摔倒，慌乱中抓住了扶梯的橡胶扶手。

"抱歉啊！"红羽绒服女人头也不回地喊了一句，已经冲上了滚梯。

林小芳揉了揉肩膀，继续往上跑。她跑过了特卖的衣服摊位，跑过了打折的化妆品柜台，耳边是广播里循环播放的"今日特价仅此一天"。她的呼吸变得急促，心跳像打鼓一样敲击着胸腔。

三楼到了。

家电区的货架前已经围了一圈人。林小芳挤到前面，看见那台咖啡机还安静地站在那里。她松了一口气，伸手去拿——

一只手同时抓住了机器的另一端。

林小芳抬头，看见一个头发花白的老太太正死死地盯着她。老太太的眼睛里有一种比黑色星期五更古老的光——那是生存本能的凶猛。

"我先拿到的。"老太太说。

"我排了三个小时的队。"林小芳说。

两个女人的对峙引来了一圈围观者。有人掏出手机准备录像，有人窃窃私语。售货员试图过来调解，但被挤在外面进不来。

林小芳忽然想起了什么。她松开手，拿出手机，打开了一个银行APP，余额显示——两万三千七百六十二元。这是她存了三年的私房钱，原本打算送女儿去夏令营。

她又想起了那个早晨。女儿走的时候，拉着她的手问："妈妈，你今天去干什么呀？"

"妈妈去给你买一个礼物。"她说。

女儿的眼睛亮了："什么礼物？"

她笑了笑，没有回答。

现在，老太太还抓着那台咖啡机，等待着她的反应。林小芳看着老太太的手——那双手枯瘦、青筋暴起，比她更需要一台咖啡机吗？不一定。但那双手里有她不知道的故事，有她无法想象的人生。

"您拿走吧。"林小芳忽然说。

老太太愣住了。周围的人也愣住了。

"您拿走吧，"林小芳又说了一遍，声音平静，"我用不着了。"

她松开手，转身离开。身后传来老太太的声音："姑娘，等等——"

林小芳没有回头。她走出商场的时候，天已经大亮了。十一月的阳光有一种稀薄的温暖，照在她脸上，有一点点像女儿的笑容。

她掏出手机，给女儿发了一条语音：

"宝贝，妈妈今天不买东西了。妈妈带你去公园看树叶好不好？"

发完之后，她看见商场的电子屏幕上滚动的红色大字："今日特价，年度最低，错过再等一年"。

她笑了一下，走向公交车站。

走出三十米后，她忽然停下来，回头看了一眼那座巨大的商业综合体。在那些闪烁的霓虹灯和巨大的促销海报背后，她看见了一个她从未注意过的东西——商场顶楼的窗户里，有一盆绿萝正在阳光下安静地生长。

她继续往前走，脚步轻快了一些。

# Il Giorno del Ringraziamento

"Cosa diavolo avrei da essere grato?"

Elena pronunciò quelle parole fissando il vuoto davanti a sé, con la tazza di caffè ormai fredda stretta tra le mani. Erano le sei del mattino di un giovedì di fine novembre e la luce grigia dell'alba filtrava appena attraverso le persiane del suo appartamento di Brooklyn.

Fuori, il mondo si stava svegliando con un profumo diverso: tacchini che arrostivano, cannella e noce moscata, il suono di risate familiari raccolte attorno a tavole imbandite. Giorno del Ringraziamento. Il primo senza Marco.

Posò la tazza sul davanzale e osservò il proprio riflesso nel vetro: capelli raccolti in una crocchia disordinata, occhiaie profonde, quarantadue anni che all'improvviso sembravano dieci di più. Marco se n'era andato tre mesi prima, un lunedì qualunque, senza preavviso. Un infarto. Aveva cinquantuno anni, faceva jogging ogni mattina, mangiava poco sale. *Non è giusto*, pensava Elena ogni giorno. *La vita non è giusta.*

Si alzò e attraversò l'appartamento evitando specchi e fotografie. Nell'ultimo periodo aveva sviluppato una sorta di mappa mentale dei ricordi da evitare: il corridoio con la foto del loro matrimonio a Positano, la libreria dove teneva i suoi romanzi preferiti, il divano dove la domenica sera guardavano insieme film in bianco e nero.

Il telefono vibrò. Una volta. Due volte. Lo ignorò. Sapeva chi fosse: sua madre, sua sorella, forse Laura, la sua migliore amica. Tutti volevano salvarla, tutti avevano ricette miracolose per il dolore. *Vieni a pranzo da noi. Non restare sola. Devi reagire.* Come se reagire fosse una scelta, come se il lutto avesse una data di scadenza.

Elena si vestì comunque. Un paio di jeans, un maglione grigio, scarpe da passeggiata. Uscì.

Central Park era avvolto in una foschia leggera, quasi irreale. Gli alberi avevano perso quasi tutte le foglie e i loro scheletri si stagliavano contro un cielo color perla. Camminò senza meta, le mani sprofondate nelle tasche, il fiato che formava piccole nuvole nell'aria fredda.

Fu al lago che si fermò.

Una donna anziana era seduta su una panchina, avvolta in un cappotto rosso scuro, con un cestino di vimini accanto. Accanto a lei, un golden retriever anziano dormiva acciambellato, il muso appoggiato sulle zampe. La donna stava lanciando pezzi di pane alle anatre, con gesti lenti e misurati.

Elena si sedette all'estremità opposta della panchina, mantenendo la distanza che aveva imparato a mantenere con tutti.

"Gesù, quest'anno non ho molto di cui essere grata", disse la donna anziana a bassa voce, quasi parlando tra sé.

Elena alzò lo sguardo, sorpresa.

L'altra la guardò e sorrise, un sorriso stanco ma non amaro. "Mi scusi. Non volevo essere scortese. È solo che... beh, lo sa anche lei, vero? Tutti quei discorsi sul Ringraziamento. Quest'anno sembrano... vuoti."

Elena annuì lentamente.

"Io sono Miriam", disse la donna.

"Elena."

Silenzio. Poi Miriam riprese, sempre guardando il lago. "Mio marito è morto a marzo. Sessantadue anni di matrimonio. Non riesco nemmeno a ricordare com'era il silenzio, prima di lui."

Elena sentì qualcosa sciogliersi nel petto, una piccola crepa nel muro che aveva costruito.

"Anche il mio", sussurrò. "Tre mesi fa."

Miriam la guardò. I loro occhi si incontrarono e, per un istante, non servirono altre parole.

Il golden retriever alzò la testa, si stiracchiò, e con passo solenne andò a posare il muso sul ginocchio di Elena. Si chiamava Charlie, disse Miriam. Era stato di suo marito, prima. Adesso era suo, e anche di nessuno, e di tutti quelli che passavano.

Elena accarezzò il pelo morbido. Charlie chiuse gli occhi, sospirando.

"Il Ringraziamento", disse Miriam dopo un po'. "Mio marito odiava il Ringraziamento. Diceva che era una festa ipocrita. I coloni che rubavano la terra ai nativi e poi festeggiavano ringraziando Dio." Scosse la testa. "Ma io gli preparavo sempre la torta di zucca. E lui la mangiava tutta, lamentandosi. *Troppo dolce, Miriam. Sempre troppo dolce.* E poi ne voleva un'altra fetta."

Elena rise. Una risata piccola, arrugginita, che le fece male ai muscoli della gola.

"Anche Marco odiava questa festa", disse, e si stupì di sentir pronunciare il suo nome. "Diceva che era solo buona per il football e i pantaloni della tuta."

"E tu gli preparavi la torta di zucca lo stesso?"

Elena sorrise. "Quella di mele. La faceva sua nonna."

Rimasero in silenzio ancora un po'. Le anatre si avvicinarono, speranzose. Miriam lanciò un altro pezzo di pane.

"Sai cosa mi ha detto mia figlia ieri?" riprese Miriam. "Che dovrei essere grata di averlo avuto per così tanto tempo. Come se il tempo lenisse il dolore. Come se dovessi essere... grata del dolore."

"Lo so", disse Elena. "Me lo dicono tutti. *Devi andare avanti. Lui non vorrebbe vederti così.*"

"Ma chi decide cosa vorrebbe? Come fanno a saperlo?"

Elena guardò l'acqua grigia del lago. Una foglia galleggiava, girando lentamente su se stessa.

"Una volta Marco mi ha detto una cosa strana", disse Elena, quasi parlando a se stessa. "Avevamo litigato, per qualcosa di stupido. E la sera, mentre dormivo, mi ha scritto un biglietto. L'ho trovato la mattina dopo sul comodino."

Miriam la guardò, in attesa.

"C'era scritto: *Sii sono un'isola, ma sono anche il ponte. Scegli tu quando attraversare.* Non l'ho mai capito del tutto."

Miriam annuì lentamente. "Forse non c'è niente da capire. Forse è solo un modo per dire che l'amore è lì, anche quando non si vede."

Charlie emise un piccolo gemito e si accoccolò più vicino a Elena. Lei gli grattò le orecchie.

"Ho paura", confessò Elena. "Di dimenticarlo. Di dimenticare il suono della sua voce. Il modo in cui rideva. Già adesso faccio fatica a ricordare alcuni dettagli, e mi terrorizza."

Miriam posò una mano rugosa su quella di Elena. "Non li dimenticherai. Il tuo cuore non dimentica. Cambiano forma, forse. Ma restano."

Il telefono di Elena vibrò di nuovo nella tasca. Questa volta lo tirò fuori. Era un messaggio di sua sorella: *Spero tu stia bene. Ti voglio bene. La porta è sempre aperta.*

Elena guardò lo schermo, poi Miriam.

"Cosa farai oggi?" chiese Miriam.

Elena ci pensò. Per tre mesi aveva vissuto come in un sonno, evitando tutto e tutti, attraversando le giornate come un automa. Aveva rifiutato inviti, saltato cene, declinato proposte di viaggio.

"Non lo so", disse.

Miriam sorrise. "Io andrò da mia figlia. Mi ha preparato una di quelle torte di zucca disgustosamente dolci che piacevano a Harold. Gliel'ho detto che quest'anno non avevo voglia di festeggiare. Sai cosa mi ha risposto?"

"Cosa?"

"Ha detto: *Mamma, festeggiare non significa che non ti manchi. Significa che nonostante ti manchi, scegli ancora la vita.*"

Elena rimase in silenzio. Il vento sollevò alcune foglie secche dal sentiero, facendole danzare in piccoli vortici dorati.

"Forse ha ragione", disse infine Elena.

"Forse", concesse Miriam. "O forse no. Ma vale la pena provare."

Il sole cominciava a farsi strada tra le nuvole, tingendo il cielo di un grigio più chiaro. Elena guardò Charlie, poi il lago, poi Miriam.

"Venga con me", disse Miriam all'improvviso. "A pranzo da mia figlia. Non deve fare niente, non deve parlare con nessuno se non vuole. Può sedersi in un angolo e basta. Può dare da mangiare alle anatre tutto il giorno se preferisce. Ma... venga."

Elena esitò. C'era ancora quella voce dentro di lei, quella che diceva *non sei pronta, non sei abbastanza, non hai la forza.*

Ma poi guardò Charlie, che la guardava con i suoi occhi marroni e dolci. E guardò Miriam, con il suo cappotto rosso e le sue mani rugose e la sua torta di zucca troppo dolce.

"Sì", disse Elena. "Verrò."

Miriam sorrise, e questa volta il sorriso raggiunse gli occhi.

"Bene. Si chiamerà Hannah, mia figlia. E suo marito Tom fa un tacchino ripieno incredibile. Era il piatto preferito di Harold. Lei lo odiava, ma lo faceva lo stesso. Come me con la torta."

Elena si alzò. Le gambe le tremavano un po', ma si sentiva stranamente leggera.

"Cosa ho da essere grata?", mormorò, quasi tra sé, ripetendo la domanda di quella mattina.

Ma questa volta le parole suonarono diverse. Forse era grata per il pane alle anatre. Per un cane che le aveva scaldato il ginocchio. Per una sconosciuta con un cappotto rosso che le aveva teso una mano senza giudicarla.

E forse, pensò Elena mentre aiutava Miriam ad alzarsi dalla panchina, era grata anche per Marco. Per il suo biglietto sul comodino, per i pantaloni della tuta il giorno del Ringraziamento, per la torta di mele della nonna. Per l'amore che, in qualche modo, aveva scelto di restare.

Il sole uscì finalmente dalle nuvole, inondando il parco di una luce dorata.

Camminarono lentamente verso l'uscita, Miriam ed Elena, con Charlie al guinzaglio corto, e le ombre che si allungavano dietro di loro come vecchie amiche.

# "What are YOU doing here for Thanksgiving?"

The sliding glass door rattled in its frame as Uncle Roy shouldered it open, arms full of grocery bags. He stopped dead when he saw her.

Aunt Margaret froze mid-stir at the stove. Cousin Denise looked up from her phone and gasped.

There, sitting at the head of the table—the seat that had been empty for seven years—sat Great-Grandma Eleanor's china. But it wasn't empty. Seated in the chair, as if she'd never left, was a woman none of them recognized.

She was maybe sixty, with silver hair pinned up neatly and a pearl necklace resting against a dove-gray dress. She looked up from the table she'd been setting—four extra places, Uncle Roy counted, feeling the blood drain from his face—and smiled warmly.

"What are *you* doing here for Thanksgiving?" she asked, her voice light, conversational, as if Uncle Roy were the intruder.

"I... this is my grandmother's house," Roy managed.

"Oh, is it?" She tilted her head. "I just thought it looked cozy. I do hope you don't mind. I'm Edna."

"Edna," Margaret repeated from the kitchen doorway, gripping a wooden spoon like a weapon. "How did you get in?"

"The door was open." Edna gestured vaguely. "I made myself useful. The silver needed polishing, and I took the liberty of starting on the gravy."

Roy's mouth went dry. The gravy was simmering on the stove. The turkey was in the oven. The dining room smelled like rosemary and sage, and he hadn't done any of it. He'd just been trying to unlock the door.

"I think you need to leave," Denise said, standing now, her phone forgotten.

Edna's smile didn't waver, but something in her eyes flickered—a sadness so deep it seemed to pull the light from the room.

"I understand," she said softly. "I always overstay my welcome." She rose, smoothing her dress, and walked toward the door with perfect posture. At the threshold, she paused. "Tell Eleanor I'm sorry I missed her. And tell her—" Her voice caught. "Tell her the cranberry sauce is from her mother's recipe."

She stepped into the gray November afternoon and was gone.

Roy ran outside. The driveway was empty. No car. No footprints in the dead grass.

When he went back inside, Margaret was standing at the table, staring at the extra place settings.

"Roy," she whispered. "Those are the dishes. The ones from the attic. The ones nobody's touched since the funeral."

On the counter, the gravy bubbled. It smelled exactly like his grandmother's.

# The Weight of Wonder

The coffee had gone cold again. Eleanor stared at the mug on her windowsill, the steam long since vanished, and thought about how strange it was that a year ago, she would have microwaved it without hesitation. Now she let it sit. She let it go cold. Because somewhere in the last twelve months, she had learned that some things didn't need to be held onto so tightly.

Her apartment was quiet. The kind of quiet that used to terrify her.

She picked up her journal from the side table and opened it to a fresh page. At the top, she wrote: *Things I have to be grateful for.* Then she set down the pen and began to count.

---

The first thing was the light.

It came through her window every morning around seven, that particular autumn gold that made the wooden floors look like honey. She had lived in this apartment for eleven years and had only just begun noticing it. How had she missed it all this time? She thought of all the mornings she had rushed out the door, late for work, late for the train, late for everything, never once stopping to see what the sun was doing with her floors.

*Light,* she wrote. *For the light.*

---

The second thing was Margaret.

They had met in the oncology waiting room, of all the unlikely places. Margaret had been reading a novel with the cover torn off, and Eleanor had asked what it was, and Margaret had said, "Something terrible. Want it?" They had been friends ever since. Six years now. Margaret was the one who had taught her to sit still.

*Margaret,* she wrote. *For her laugh, which is too loud for small rooms.*

---

The third thing was harder to name, so she sat with it for a while.

It was the absence of something. The absence of the old Eleanor, the one who had spent her whole life building walls out of cleverness, out of sarcasm, out of the careful observation of other people's flaws. That Eleanor had been very tired. She had not realized how tired until she was too sick to keep up the performance, and then, slowly, in the strange suspension of illness, she had let her go.

*For the version of me I had to leave behind,* she wrote. *She kept me alive. I am grateful. I am also free.*

---

The fourth thing was her hands.

She held them up now, turning them over in the morning light. They were thinner than they used to be. The veins stood out like rivers on a map. But they could still hold things: a pen, a cup, a friend's hand in a waiting room. They had held her mother's hand in the hospital at the end. They had held her father's hand the Christmas he forgot who she was. They had held her own face when the news was bad, and again when it was good.

*For my hands,* she wrote. *They are still here.*

---

She wrote for a long time. The list went on and on, not because she had so much, but because she had finally learned to look.

The window the cat liked to sit in. The bakery on the corner that remembered her order. The color of the trees in October. The fact that she had outlived the diagnosis by three years now, which was not a miracle, exactly, but close enough to one that she had stopped arguing with the word.

The pen ran out of ink. She got another one. Then another.

When she finally set it down, the page was full, and the light had moved across the floor and was climbing up the far wall.

Eleanor picked up the cold coffee and drank it anyway.

It tasted like gratitude. Like all the things she had failed to notice for fifty-seven years, finally letting themselves be seen.

She closed the journal. Outside, a sparrow landed on the sill, looked at her once, and flew away.

*For the sparrow,* she thought, smiling. *For everything.*

Then she went to make a fresh cup.

시댁에 처음 온 게 벌써 3년 전이었다. 처음엔 긴장되고 어색했던 이 식탁이, 이제는 익숙하면서도 여전히 긴장되는 공간이 되었다.

"자, 다 왔다. 앉아라."

시아버지의 목소리에 긴장을 한 번 더 삼켰다. 부엌에서 시어머니가 마지막 반찬을 옮겨 오는 소리가 들렸다. 고사리나물, 콩나물무침, 멸치볶음—시댁의 밥상은 언제나 이 정해진 메뉴들로 채워졌다.

"오늘 회사에서 좀 힘들었어."

남편 현우가 자리에 앉으며 말했다. 그의 왼쪽에 나는 자동으로 자리를 잡았다. 맞은편에는 시누이 정민 씨와 그의 아내 유진 씨가 나란히 앉아 있었고, 시어머니와 시아버지가 상좌를 차지했다.

"현우야, 다음 달 승진 시험 잘 봤으면 좋겠다."

시아버지가 입을 열었다. 그분의 말씀에는 언제나 기대와 동시에 일종의 시험 같은 것이 실려 있었다.

"네, 아버지. 열심히 준비하고 있습니다."

나는 현우의 대답을 들으며 국을 퍼담았다. 따뜻한 밥과 함께 올라오는 그 익숙한 향—현미와 검정콩의 냄새. 이 냄새는 이제 어느덧 '집'의 냄새가 되어 있었다.

"유진 씨네 회사가 요즘 좀 힘든 모양이던데?"

시어머니가 갑자기 물었다. 정민 씨와 유진 씨 사이로 시선이 오갔다. 나는 젓가락을 내려놓을까 말까 망설이다가 그냥 반찬을 집었다.

"네, 좀 조정이 있었어요."

유진 씨가 조심스럽게 답했다. 그 목소리에는 한 번도 들어본 적 없는 종류의 피로가 묻어 있었다.

저녁 식사는 늘 그렇듯 중요했다. 그리고 늘 그렇듯 무겁기도 했다. 현우는 아버지의 농담에 맞춰 큰 소리로 웃었고, 정민 씨는 적당히 고개를 끄덕였으며, 나는 밥을 먹는 데 집중했다. 시댁 식탁에서의 나는 늘 그런 식이었다—적당히, 조용히, 눈에 띄지 않게.

"민정 씨, 이거 더 먹어라."

시어머니가 도라지나물을 내밀었다. 새댁인 나를 챙기는 시어머니의 마음—그것은 진심이었다. 다만 그 마음과 함께 따라오는 시선은 언제나 나를 무언가 부족한 사람으로 바라보는 것 같았다.

"네, 어머니. 잘 먹겠습니다."

나는 웃으며 대답했다. 그리고 그 순간, 유진 씨와 눈이 마주쳤다. 아주 짧은 순간이었지만, 우리는 서로를 알아본 것 같았다. 같은 자리에 앉아 있지만, 어느 순간부터 우리는 가족이 아닌 관객이 되어 있었다.

식사가 끝나고 설거지를 도우려 일어섰다.

"앉아 있어, 민정아. 내가 할게."

시어머니가 말했다. 하지만 그 분이 원한 건 정말로 내가 설거지하는 것이 아니라, 내가 거절하는 것이 아니었다. "네, 감사합니다 어머니." 나는 다시 앉았다.

거실로 가서 텔레비전을 켰다. 시아버지와 현우가 뉴스를 보며 경제 얘기를 하고 있었다. 정민 씨는 화장실에 가더니 나오지 않았다.

"유진 씨, 커피 한 잔 드릴까요?"

부엌에서 나오던 유진 씨에게 물었다. 유진 씨는 잠깐 멈칫하더니 고개를 끄덕였다.

커피를 내리며 유진 씨가 낮게 말했다. "민정 씨, 고마워요."

"왜요?"

"여기서 이렇게 말할 수 있는 사람이 있다는 게..."

유진 씨가 말을 잇지 못했다. 나는 컵을 건네며 웃었다. "저도 그런 사람 필요했어요."

사실 나는 이 식탁에서 늘 외로웠다. 말 한마디가 가족 전체의 분위기를 바꿀 수 있는 자리. 그래서 조심스럽고, 그래서 조용하고, 그래서 늘 긴장한다. 가족이 되었음에도 완전히는 아닌, 그 미묘한 경계 위에 서 있는 느낌.

거실에서 큰 웃음소리가 들렸다. 현우가 무슨 농담을 한 모양이었다.

"우리도 가서 앉아요. 너무 오래 있으면 이상해요."

유진 씨가 말했다. 우리는 커피잔을 들고 거실로 향했다.

---

밤, 침대에 누워 현우에게 물었다.

"나, 어머니랑 잘 지내고 있는 것 같아?"

현우는 잠깐 침묵하더니 대답했다. "엄마가 도라지나물 자주 권하는 거 보면 마음에 드신 거야."

"그건 아닐걸."

나는 혼잣말처럼 말했다. 현우는 이미 잠들어 있었다.

나는 천장을 올려다보며 생각했다. 3년 후에도 나는 이 식탁에서 같은 자리에 앉아 있을까. 그때에도 여전히 긴장하며 밥을 먹고 있을까. 아니면, 어느 순간 진짜 가족이 되어 있을까.

도라지나물의 아린 맛이 아직 혀 위에 남아 있었다.

조금 아팠다. 하지만 그 아픔이 싫지는 않았다.

Write a story about a family dinner that includes someone unexpected showing up. Around 1500 characters.

# 一场迟到的团圆饭

周六傍晚，厨房里油烟升腾，妈妈系着那条洗得发白的蓝围裙，在灶台前忙得团团转。红烧肉的酱香、鲈鱼的鲜味、银耳汤的甜润，交织成一种熟悉而温暖的气息。

"小瑜，去看看你爸回来没有！"妈妈头也不抬地喊道。

"知道啦！"我应了一声，放下手中摆弄的筷子，快步走向门口。

今天是奶奶的八十大寿，妈妈一大早就开始筹备。父亲去火车站接从省城赶回来的姑姑一家，这会儿应该快到了。

刚走到门口，就听见楼下传来一阵脚步声，还有父亲爽朗的笑声："妈，您猜谁来了？"

我心里咯噔一下——姑姑一家？不对，姑姑的声音没有这么……嘶哑。

门被推开的瞬间，我愣住了。

站在父亲身后的，是一个五十多岁的男人，穿着件褪色的灰色夹克，头发花白，脸上的皱纹像沟壑一样深。他的眼眶有些红，看见我的那一刻，整个人也愣住了。

"小瑜？"他的声音颤抖着。

我下意识往后退了一步，转头看向父亲。父亲的表情有些复杂，他轻轻叹了口气，说："让他进来吧。"

"谁让他进来的？！"

妈妈的声音从厨房传来，带着压抑的愤怒。她站在厨房门口，手里的锅铲还滴着油，眼神却像刀一样锋利。

"秀莲，"父亲开口，"他是来看妈的。"

"他没资格！"妈妈的声音提高了，"当年他一声不响地走了，把个烂摊子甩给我们，现在倒好，有什么脸回来？！"

"秀莲……"

"别叫我名字！"妈妈的眼眶红了，"二十年，整整二十年！我一个人拉扯小瑜，一个人伺候婆婆，你知道那些年是怎么过的吗？！"

那个男人垂着头，一言不发。他的肩膀微微颤抖，像是在强忍着什么。

奶奶从卧室里慢慢走出来。八十年的人生，在她脸上刻下了无数痕迹，但那双眼睛依然清明。她看着门口的男人，沉默了许久，然后轻轻开口：

"进来吧。"

"妈！"妈妈急了。

"秀莲，"奶奶平静地说，"今天是我八十大寿。"

妈妈咬着嘴唇，眼泪终于掉了下来。她狠狠地把锅铲摔在桌上，转身回了厨房，"砰"地关上门。

客厅里陷入了尴尬的沉默。

那个男人——我的"大伯"，我从未见过的大伯——站在原地，像一棵枯死的老树。

我忽然想起，小时候，妈妈偶尔会提起一个名字，语气里带着恨意。后来奶奶不许她再提，那个名字就成了家里的禁忌。

"坐吧。"奶奶招呼他坐下，又看向我，"小瑜，去给你大伯倒杯茶。"

我机械地走进厨房。妈妈背对着我，肩膀还在微微抖动。我倒了两杯茶，端出来时，看见大伯已经坐在沙发上，正低着头，手指不停地绞着衣角。

"大哥，"奶奶的声音很轻，"你这些年……过得怎么样？"

大伯抬起头，眼眶又红了："妈，我对不住您。当年我……我欠了赌债，怕连累家里，就……就跑出去了。这些年，我在外面打了二十年的工，前几年才把债还清……"

"那你怎么不回来？"奶奶问。

"我没脸回来。"大伯的声音哽咽了，"尤其是听说秀莲一个人撑着这个家，我更不敢回来。我怕回来，给您丢人，给小瑜丢人……"

奶奶沉默了一会儿，忽然问："你吃饭了没？"

大伯愣了一下，然后摇了摇头。

"小瑜，"奶奶站起来，"去叫你妈，多加一副碗筷。"

我迟疑着走进厨房。妈妈还站在灶台前，背对着门，锅铲一动不动。

"妈，奶奶说……"

"我听到了。"妈妈打断我，声音闷闷的。

"妈……"

"你奶奶八十大寿，"妈妈忽然说，"我不应该在这个日子让人难堪。"

她深深地吸了一口气，擦了擦眼角，重新打开火，把锅里已经有些凉的红烧肉又热了起来。

吃饭的时候，气氛依然有些沉重。但奶奶像是没察觉一样，不停地给大伯夹菜："多吃点，你在外面，肯定吃不好。"

大伯的眼泪终于掉了下来。他一边吃一边哭，像个孩子一样。

妈妈始终没有说话，只是默默地吃着饭。

饭后，奶奶把我叫到卧室。她坐在床边，看着窗外的夜色，轻轻地说：

"小瑜，你恨你大伯吗？"

我不知道该怎么回答。

"你大伯当年是混蛋，"奶奶说，"但他也是我儿子。手心手背都是肉啊。"

她顿了顿，又说："你妈这些年苦，我都知道。但有些结，二十年不解开，就会变成一辈子的刺。"

"奶奶，那我该怎么办？"

"什么都不用办，"奶奶摸了摸我的头，"你只要记住——家，永远是家。不管走多远，只要还活着，总要回来的。"

我点了点头。

那天晚上，大伯留了下来。他睡在客厅的沙发上，蜷缩着身子，像一只疲惫的鸟。

我躺在自己的房间里，听着窗外的风声，想着很多事。

二十年，足以让一个少年变成中年，让一个家庭支离破碎。但二十年，也不足以磨灭血脉里的牵绊。

第二天一早，大伯就走了。临走时，他给妈妈鞠了一躬，说了声"对不起"。

妈妈没有说话，只是递给他一个袋子——里面装着昨晚剩的红烧肉。

"路上吃。"她说。

大伯愣了一下，然后重重地点了点头，眼眶又红了。

他走了以后，妈妈站在门口，看了很久。

我走过去，轻轻地握住她的手。

"妈。"

"嗯？"

"我们回家吃饭吧。"

妈妈愣了一下，然后笑了——那是这些天来，她第一次笑。

"好。"她说。

我们转身，走进了那扇熟悉的门。

Write a story about a family gathering to watch the biggest football game of the year. About 900 words long.

# The Last Sunday in February

The Ramirez living room smelled like victory and slow-cooked pork.

Abuela Maria had arrived at four in the morning to begin the pernil, and by the time the first cars pulled into the driveway, the roast had been massaged, marinated, and whispered to with the kind of devotion usually reserved for saints. Now it perfumed the entire house, drifting out to meet anyone brave enough to approach the front door.

"¡Aquí vienen!" Abuela called from the kitchen, though everyone was already inside. She liked the announcement.

Tío Eduardo arrived first, as he always did, carrying a cooler of Modelo and a football-shaped cake from the bakery on Fifth Street. His wife, Tía Carmen, followed with three trays of tostones and a worried expression.

"Mamá, are you sure about the plantains? I could have—"

"I am sure of everything since before you were born," Abuela said, and Tía Carmen retreated to arrange silverware.

The cousins came next—Diego and his girlfriend Priya, who was watching her first Super Bowl and had been briefed extensively on what to expect, though nothing could have prepared her. Then there was Mateo, twenty-two and too cool for everything until the first whistle blew, and little Sofia, eight years old, who had memorized every commercial from last year and intended to hold everyone accountable.

"Where is your father?" Abuela asked, appearing in the doorway with a wooden spoon.

Diego checked his phone. "Ten minutes."

"Every time. Every single time."

The TV glowed blue in the corner, the pregame show already running. A mountain of chips and dips had accumulated on the coffee table like some geological formation. Sofia had claimed the armchair closest to the screen and was draped in a handmade blanket bearing the logo of the team she had chosen for the season based purely on jersey color.

The door opened, and Papá walked in, looking sheepish.

"Mi amor," Mamá said, kissing his cheek.

"Traffic."

"In heaven, there is no traffic. Only here."

He laughed and went to find a beer. The family arranged itself across couches and the floor, a human constellation centered on the television. Priya sat carefully between Diego and Abuela, trying to determine which woman held more authority in the room. (It was Abuela.)

For a while, only the commercials mattered.

Sofia announced each one before it aired, having apparently memorized the entire slate. When the first car commercial showed a truck driving through a frozen lake, Mateo declared it scientifically impossible. Tío Eduardo argued that anything was possible for the right monthly payment. Abuela said she would trust a mule before she trusted a truck, and Tía Carmen shushed everyone because the game was starting.

The first quarter was tense and quiet, broken only by the crunch of plantain chips and Abuela's running commentary in Spanish. She had opinions about every play, every referee, every camera angle. She called the quarterback by his full name each time, as if they were old adversaries.

"My stomach," Priya whispered to Diego around halftime.

"Eat more. It'll help."

"Eat *more?*"

"Trust me."

He led her to the kitchen, where Abuela was assembling plates of food so generous they required structural engineering. The pernil fell apart at the touch of a fork. There were rice and beans, tostones and maduros, a salad no one had asked for but everyone would eat.

"Eat," Abuela told Priya, pressing a plate into her hands. "You are too thin. The wind could carry you."

"She means it lovingly," Diego said.

"I know," Priya said, smiling. She did know.

They returned to the living room with plates balanced on knees. The third quarter was underway, and the family was no longer pretending to be calm. Mateo was pacing. Tío Eduardo had taken off his shoes, a sign of either great comfort or great distress. Sofia was wrapped entirely in her blanket, only her eyes visible.

When the first big play happened—a long pass down the sideline that put one team within striking distance—the room erupted. Diego yelled. Papá yelled. Abuela said something in Spanish that made Tía Carmen cover Sofia's ears.

"This is the best day of my life," Sofia announced.

In the fourth quarter, the game was tied. The kitchen had gone silent. Even Abuela, who had returned to begin dessert prep, emerged holding a single wooden spoon like a scepter, her face drawn with concentration.

With two minutes left, the winning team's kicker lined up for the field goal. The whole family leaned forward. Priya, who had only been a football fan for approximately seven hours, felt her heart in her throat.

The kick was good.

The living room exploded. Mateo threw a cushion in the air. Tío Eduardo hugged Tía Carmen, who tolerated it. Sofia screamed at a pitch that should have been impossible for a human child. Diego kissed Priya, then apologized, then kissed her again. Papá and Mamá held hands, smiling, remembering some other game in some other year.

Abula stood in the doorway and watched them all.

She did not, as it happened, care which team had won. She never really had. The game was an excuse. The food was an excuse. Even the commercials were an excuse.

What she loved—what she had always loved—was the way her family filled a room. The way new people could be folded in, the way Priya was already being passed plates, the way Sofia's joy was uncontainable, the way her son still arrived ten minutes late and her daughter-in-law still worried about plantains.

"Abuela!" Sofia called. "Come watch!"

"I am watching," she said.

And she was.

Write a story about somebody trying to rationalize giving into temptation, even though they know they shouldn’t. About 1100 words long.

# The Weight of a Single Bite

The bakery on Clover Street had always been there, tucked between the laundromat and the boarded-up flower shop. Mira had passed it every morning for seven years on her way to the hospital, where she worked as a cardiac nurse. She knew every pastry in the display case by sight. She knew the owner, a stout Romanian woman named Irina who always waved through the window.

She also knew what was inside the chocolate torte.

Three years ago, after her father's triple bypass, Mira had made a promise to herself. No sugar. Not a crumb. Her father had eaten his way into that operating room with years of butter-laden breakfasts and cream-filled afternoons, and Mira had watched his chest crack open on a table while she held her mother's hand. So she had sworn off the enemy. Sugar was the assassin in a silk dress, and Mira was not going to let it touch her.

For three years, she had kept her promise.

But this morning, something was different.

She had slept badly. Her ex-boyfriend, Daniel, had called at midnight to tell her he was engaged. She had lain awake afterward, watching the ceiling fan rotate in slow, mocking circles, feeling a loneliness so thick she could have choked on it. When her alarm went off at five, she had felt hollowed out, like someone had reached into her chest and removed all the warm things.

By the time she reached Clover Street, the hollowness had calcified into something sharper—a hunger that had nothing to do with food.

The smell hit her before she saw it. Warm butter. Dark chocolate. The faint whisper of vanilla.

Irina was arranging a new torte in the window. She looked up and smiled her usual smile, and Mira's feet simply stopped.

"Just looking," Mira said, even though she was already pushing through the door.

The bell chimed. The warmth enveloped her. She stood before the glass case, hands trembling slightly in her coat pockets, and she looked at the torte.

It was perfect. A single layer of glossy ganache over dense, flourless cake, with a dusting of powdered sugar like fresh snow. *Ridiculous*, she thought. *A heart attack on a plate. Dad's last meal, if he'd had the chance to pick it.*

"I'll have a slice," she said, and her voice sounded far away, like it belonged to someone else.

Irina's knife sliced through the ganache with a sound like a small sigh. Mira watched the piece slide onto a paper plate—small, just a sliver, not even two bites. That was something, wasn't it? A sliver was practically nothing. A sliver was practically medicine.

She carried the plate to the little table by the window. Sat down. Folded her coat over the chair.

*One bite won't kill me,* she thought. She had read the studies, actually. A single indulgence meant nothing in the long run. The body was forgiving. It adapted. Some researchers even said that occasional treats kept the metabolism active, kept the will from cracking under the strain of pure denial. There was science for this. There was logic.

She picked up the tiny fork.

*And anyway,* the voice in her head continued, warming to its work, *you've been so good. Three years. Three whole years without a single slip. That deserves recognition. That deserves a reward. Deprivation is its own kind of damage, you know. The body keeps a ledger, and yours is overdrawn. One bite restores the balance.*

She brought the fork closer.

*Your father ate torte every Sunday and lived to seventy-eight. He just had bad luck. Bad genetics. There's a difference. You could eat torte every Sunday and live to a hundred. Or you could get hit by a bus tomorrow, having denied yourself the only real pleasure left.*

The chocolate gleamed. She could smell the espresso Irina had brushed into the batter. She thought of Daniel. She thought of the empty apartment she would return to tonight. She thought of how, in three years of perfect discipline, she had not felt this close to breaking, and yet how, this morning, the smallest sliver of cake felt like the only warm thing left in the world.

*It's not weakness,* she told herself. *It's wisdom. It's knowing when to bend so you don't break. It's—*

She set the fork down.

Her hand was shaking. She sat very still for a long moment, looking at the torte, and something inside her chest began to ache—not her heart, exactly, but somewhere near it. Somewhere she had been holding very tight for a very long time.

She thought of her father, after the surgery, when he had come home and she had helped him up the stairs. He had stopped halfway up and turned to her, his face pale and damp, and said, "I'd give up every meal I ever ate for one more afternoon in the garden." She had not understood then. She understood now.

The torte sat on the plate, patient and gleaming, asking nothing of her.

Mira pushed the plate to the far side of the table.

"Excuse me," she said to Irina, her voice catching slightly. "I changed my mind."

Irina looked up from her counter, eyebrows raised.

"I just—" Mira began, and then stopped. There was no explanation that would make sense to anyone but herself. "My father had heart surgery," she finally said. "I promised him I wouldn't."

It was the first time she had said it that way. She had always told herself it was a promise to *herself*. But standing there in the warm, buttery smell of the bakery, she realized it had never been about her at all.

Irina nodded slowly. She came around the counter and took the plate away. Then she did something Mira had never seen her do before. She reached beneath the register and brought out a small, paper-wrapped bundle.

"Éclair," Irina said, setting it on the counter. "No sugar. Just egg whites, flour, a little honey. I make them for my husband—he is diabetic."

Mira stared at her.

"On the house," Irina said. "For the girl who is so good every day."

Mira took the éclair. She walked outside into the cold morning. The sky over Clover Street was the color of pewter, and the breath of the city rose around her in white clouds. She bit into the éclair as she walked, and it was good, and it was enough, and she did not look back at the window.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. A text from her mother: *Thinking of you today. Dad would've been proud.*

Mira stopped on the sidewalk. A man hurried past her, briefcase swinging. A taxi honked. Somewhere down the block, a dog barked.

She finished the éclair, folded the paper neatly into her pocket, and kept walking.

Write a story that includes a character using the phrase “swings and roundabouts.” Approximately 500 words.

# Il sentiero dei pro e dei contro

Marco fissava la montagna di scartoffie sulla scrivania del suo ufficio al quinto piano, mentre il tramonto tingeva Torino di sfumature aranciate. Erano passati tre mesi da quando aveva accettato l'incarico di direttore creativo alla Galleria d'Arte Moderna, e il bilancio sembrava un rebus senza soluzione.

"Pro e contro", mormorò tra sé, tamburellando le dita sul piano di legno. "Tutto nella vita è fatto di pro e contro."

La porta si aprì cigolando, e comparve Elena, la segretaria dai capelli raccolti e gli occhi svegli.

"Signor Ferraris, c'è ancora quella telefonata di Parigi. La maison Doucet insiste per la mostra retrospettiva su Modigliani. Ma se accettiamo, dovremo rinviare il progetto educativo per le scuole."

Marco si passò una mano sul viso stanco. "Swings and roundabouts" disse, con un mezzo sorriso che lasciò Elena perplessa. "Letteralmente, 'altalene e giostre'. Un modo inglese per dire che ciò che guadagni da una parte, lo perdi dall'altra. Se prendiamo i fondi dei francesi, avremo meno risorse per i bambini."

"Non la seguo, signore."

"Ci arriverai. Siediti un momento."

Elena obbedì, sistemandosi sulla poltrona di pelle. Marco si alzò e andò alla finestra, osservando le luci della città che si accendevano una dopo l'altra come piccole stelle cadute.

"Mio nonno era un falegname" cominciò. "Mi raccontava sempre che la vita è come un'altalena. Quando sei su, guardi il cielo e tutto sembra possibile. Quando sei giù, vedi solo le scarpe della gente che passa. E nel mezzo, nel punto di equilibrio, capisci che servono entrambe le fasi."

Elena lo osservava in silenzio, notando per la prima volta le rughe sottili attorno ai suoi occhi, i capelli grigi alle tempie.

"Due settimane fa" continuò Marco "ho quasi mandato all'aria un matrimonio. La mia Elena — non tu, un'altra Elena, mia moglie — mi ha accusato di essere sposato con il lavoro. Aveva ragione, probabilmente. Ma ieri sera, quando ho tenuto mia figlia sulle spalle per guardare i fuochi d'artificio, lei ha detto: 'Papà, tu fai volare i sogni della gente'. E ho capito che forse il prezzo che pago non è tutto inutile."

"Si pente di qualcosa?" chiese Elena dopo un momento.

"Di niente. Di tutto. Swings and roundabouts, appunto. Non si può avere tutto. Si può solo scegliere quali perdite sono degne di essere vissute."

Il telefono sulla scrivania cominciò a squillare. Marco tornò alla postazione e rispose, ascoltando per qualche istante.

"Comprendo" disse poi, in un francese stentato. "Merci. À bientôt."

Riattaccò e guardò Elena con un sorriso più luminoso.

"Hanno accettato di co-finanziare il progetto educativo. Swings and roundabouts, Elena. A volte l'altalena si muove da sola."

"Signore?"

"Vieni, ti offro un aperitivo. Stasera festeggiamo, e tu mi insegnerai il tuo vero nome. Perché scommetto che ti chiami diversamente."

Elena arrossì. "Giulia."

Marco rise, una risata piena e liberatoria.

"Bene, Giulia. Allora brindiamo ai pro, ai contro, e a tutte le altalene che ancora non abbiamo provato."

Uscirono insieme nella sera torinese, mentre le stelle vere si mescolavano a quelle artificiali della città, e l'altalena della vita continuava silenziosamente il suo eterno dondolio.

Write a story where a meal or dinner goes horribly wrong. In total around 1200 words.

# The Last Supper at Marrowbone Hollow

Margaret Whitfield had not invited guests to Marrowbone Hollow in eleven years.

The house itself discouraged visitors. It sat at the end of a gravel road that turned to mud in spring and ice in winter, swallowed on three sides by a wood so dense that the property had no proper cell signal. The windows were small, and the chimney stack leaned slightly, as though eavesdropping. Margaret had inherited the place from her great-aunt Edwina, who had died in the upstairs bedroom with her boots on and a look on her face that the coroner, a young man then, had declined to describe.

But tonight was different. Tonight, Margaret had set the long table for six.

She had spent three days preparing. Not cooking—that had taken only the morning—but *preparing*. The polenta had to be stirred in a particular direction, counterclockwise, until it sighed. The radicchio had to be torn, not cut. The wine, a bottle she had been saving since before her husband left her in 1997, had to be uncorked at the exact moment the church bells in the village below struck eight. She did not know why these things mattered. She only knew that they did. That they had been told to her, years ago, in a voice like rain on a tin roof, and that she had finally decided to listen.

Her guests began to arrive as the light failed.

First was Dr. Vincent Pryce, the new general practitioner who had taken over old Dr. Harlow's practice. He was a thin man with careful hands and the unfortunate habit of apologizing for his own breathing. He brought a small pot of forced bulbs, snowdrops, as a gift. Margaret placed them on the windowsill, where they did not seem to belong.

Next came the Carter sisters, Eunice and Helena, spinsters both, who ran the post office and the tearoom and who knew, between them, every scandal in the parish for the last hundred years. They wore matching lavender cardigans and had, Margaret noticed, brought nothing. This was unusual, but she said nothing. The sisters took their seats at the table like birds settling on a wire, watching her with eyes that never blinked quite often enough.

The fourth chair was for Mr. Garrett, the vicar. He arrived last, apologetic, his collar slightly askew. He had walked, he explained, because his bicycle had a slow leak and he had not yet learned to patch it. His shoes were muddy. He smelled, faintly, of wet earth and something older—wormwood, perhaps, or the inside of a coffin. Margaret hung his coat by the door and led him in.

The fifth chair was empty.

The sixth chair was also empty.

"Six place settings," Dr. Pryce observed, with the mild alarm of a man who had been trained to count things. "Are we expecting someone?"

"No," Margaret said. "One of those is for the house."

The sisters exchanged a glance. The vicar smiled his vicar's smile, the one that meant he would be discussing this with someone later, in confidence.

They sat.

Margaret brought out the polenta first. It sat in a shallow dish, golden as a sunset, and as she set it down, every candle in the room guttered at once, as though a door had been opened somewhere.

"How lovely," Eunice said, though she did not reach for her spoon.

"How *golden*," Helena echoed, in a voice that was not quite her own.

They ate.

Or rather, Margaret watched them not eat. Their spoons rose, descended, rose again, but the polenta in their bowls did not diminish. Dr. Pryce chewed with the determination of a man who had once kept a patient alive for six hours on sheer willpower. The vicar made small sounds of pleasure that had no mouth behind them.

The wine, when Margaret poured it, was the color of old blood and did not catch the candlelight.

"Tell us," Eunice said, setting down her spoon with a porcelain click that was too loud, "why you have invited us here, Margaret. After all this time."

Margaret looked at her hands. They were older than she remembered.

"I am dying," she said. "I have known for some time. The doctors—well. The doctors do not know, because I have not told them. But I know. I have known since the spring."

There was a silence. The candles, recovered now, burned very steadily, as though listening.

"And the will," Helena said. "We have all been wondering about the will."

"There is no will."

The vicar made a sympathetic noise. "Perhaps, then, you should—"

"I asked you here," Margaret said, "because the house wanted me to."

The words came out before she could stop them, and she was surprised to find they were true. The house had been whispering to her for weeks. Not in words, exactly. More in the way a dog presses its wet nose into your palm. *Soon*, it had said, in the language of joists and settling stone. *Soon we will be full again.*

"I don't understand," Dr. Pryce said, and the candles guttered again, and the polenta in his bowl gave a small, distinct lurch, as though something beneath it had moved.

The sisters began to laugh. It was a terrible sound, like dry leaves skittering on a pavement, and it did not stop when Margaret asked them to.

"We are hungry, Margaret," Eunice said.

"We have been hungry for a very long time," said Helena.

The vicar stood up. His chair scraped against the floor, and the noise was enormous, filling the room like a held breath.

"I think," he said, "we should perhaps—"

He did not finish. The empty chair at the foot of the table, the fifth chair, scraped out from the table of its own accord, as though someone unseen had risen from it. The sixth chair did the same. They moved together, slowly, with the heavy deliberation of a thing that had been waiting a long time to move at all, and positioned themselves on either side of Margaret, who had not moved, who could not move, whose hands were folded in her lap as though she were at prayer.

"Eat," said a voice that came from nowhere and from everywhere, from inside the walls and beneath the floor and from the chimney that leaned, leaning, to listen. "*Eat with us now, Margaret. We have kept your seat.*"

The polenta in Margaret's bowl had turned, somehow, to a thick black substance that moved like a slow tide. The wine in her glass was full again, though she had not touched it. Around her, the others had stopped pretending; their faces were slack, their eyes fixed on points beyond the room, and they chewed, and chewed, and chewed.

Margaret, who had known all along, who had been preparing for this since the spring, lifted her spoon.

Outside, the gravel road vanished under the first snow of November, and the wood drew itself closer, and the chimney at Marrowbone Hollow, which had leaned for a hundred years, settled at last into a posture of attention.

By morning, the table had been cleared.

By afternoon, the chairs were stacked neatly against the wall, all six of them.

And in the bedroom upstairs, where great-aunt Edwina had died with her boots on, a fresh pair of boots sat by the bed, polished, waiting.

They were Margaret's size, exactly.

## لم يتغير شيء

حين وطئت قدماه أرض المطار، أدرك نادر أن رائحة المكان وحدها كافية لتعيده عشرين عامًا إلى الوراء. نفس الرائحة، مزيج من التراب الرطب بعد المطر، وأوراق الشجر المتحللة، ودخان المدافئ القديمة. حتى سائق التاكسي، نفس النظرة المتعبة في عينيه، ونفس الأسئلة التي لم تتغير منذ طفولته: "كيف الأحوال في المدينة؟" و"متى جيت؟" و"الله يسلمك."

البيت كان ينتظره كما لو أنه لم يغب يومًا. نفس الباب الأزرق الباهت، نفس الشجرة في الحديقة، نفس الكرسي الخشبي تحت شرفة الطابق الأول. أمه فتحت له الباب بابتسامتها المعتادة، تلك الابتسامة التي لا تكبر ولا تصغر مهما مرت السنوات. قالت: "ما تأخرت؟" كأنه عاد من الحي المجاور، لا من قارة أخرى.

دخل إلى غرفته القديمة. نفس السرير، نفس المكتب، نفس الملصقات على الجدران التي لم يطلب من أحد أن ينزعها. فتح الدولاب، فوجد قميصه المدرسي الأزرق لا يزال معلقًا في ركنه، وكأنه ينتظره ليذهب إلى المدرسة صباحًا. على الرف، دفاتره القديمة، وكرته الزرقاء التي لطالما ضاعت ثم عثر عليها، ثم ضاعت، ثم عثر عليها مرة بعد مرة.

في المساء، جلس مع أبيه في الصالة. لم يتغير الأريكة، ولم يتغير التلفاز، ولا القناة التي يتابعها أبوه كل ليلة. الفخار نفسه على الطاولة، والمسبحة في يد أبيه تدور بنفس الإيقاع. أبوه لم يسأله عن عمله، ولا عن مشاريعه، ولا عن الفتاة التي رآها معه في الصورة قبل أشهر. كل ما قاله: "شربت الشاي؟" ونادر، الذي اعتاد على أسئلة المحاسبة والتقارير في المدينة، وجد في هذا السؤال راحة لا يجدها في أي مكان آخر.

خرج في اليوم التالي ليمشي في الشارع القديم. دكان الحاج أبو فادي ما زال يفتح بابه في الثامنة صباحًا، وما زال أبو فادي يجلس خلف طاولته، يمضغ التبغ، ويقرأ الجريدة على ورقها الأصفر. أولاد الجيران كبروا، ثم رحلوا، ثم جاء أولادهم، فكبروا، ثم رحلوا. الشارع وحده بقي ثابتًا، وكأنه يرفض أن يمشي مع الزمن.

زار مقهى الحارة. نفس الطاولات، نفس الكراسي الحديدية، نفس اللوحة المعلقة على الحائط فيها آية الكرسي. النادل الجديد لم يكن يعرفه، لكن النادل القديم ما زال هنا، وقد أصبح الآن أبيض الشعر، لكنه ما زال يبتسم حين يراه، ويقول: "قهوة سادة؟" كأنه سؤال محفوظ عن ظهر قلب منذ ثلاثين عامًا.

اتصل على صديقه القديم، ياسر. أجابه بصوت ناعس: "وينك من زمان يا واد؟" وجدا نفسيهما بعد ساعة في نفس المقهى، يتحدثان عن نفس الأشياء. ياسر تزوج، ثم طلق، ثم تزوج. ياسر اشترى بيتًا، ثم باعه، ثم اشترى غيره. ياسر سافر، ثم عاد، ثم سافر، ثم عاد. في كل مرة يعود، يجد المقهى ينتظره، ويجد النادل يتذكر طلبه، ويجد الآية على الحائط لم تسقط.

في الليل، جلس نادر على شرفة غرفته، يتأمل السماء. من بعيد، سمع صوت أمه تغني في المطبخ نفس الأغنية التي كانت تغنيها له وهو طفل. أغنية عن المسافر الذي يعود، فيجد بيته كما هو، وحبيبته كما هي، وعيناه متعبتان من السفر الطويل. سمع صوت أباه يسعل نفس السعال، وصوت أخته الصغرى تشاجر مع أخيه الأصغر على نفس الأريكة.

وعندئذٍ فهم نادر سرًّا ظل يبحث عنه في كل مكان. ليست المدينة الكبيرة هي التي تمضي، بل هو. هو وحده الذي تغيّر. هو الذي لبس بدلة العمل، وركب المترو كل صباح، وأكل في المطاعم، ونام في شقق صغيرة مؤجرة. هو الذي ظن أنه يكبر، بينما البيت هنا ظل واقفًا في مكانه، ينتظره، كما ينتظر البحر السفن التي تاهت في عرضه. البيت لم يتغير، لأنه لم يكن بحاجة إلى ذلك. التغيير، في الأصل، شأن المسافرين، لا شأن الأوطان.

في الصباح، حزم نادر حقيبته ليغادر. أمه وقفت في الباب، وقالت: "ما تأخرت؟" فابتسم. أبوه جاء ومعه كيس تفاح، وقال: "خذ لأهلك في المدينة." النادل في المقهى، لو رآه، لقال: "قهوة سادة؟" لكنه لم يمر عليه هذه المرة، لأنه أراد أن يبقى في البيت قليلًا قبل أن يركب الطائرة.

وحين أقلعت الطائرة، نظر نادر من النافذة. رأى الحارة الصغيرة، والبيت الأزرق، والشجرة في الحديقة، والمقهى في الزاوية. بدت كلها كنقطة صغيرة على ظهر الأرض، لكنها كانت أثقل من كل المدن التي مرّ بها، وأعمق من كل الشوارع التي مشى فيها، وأقرب إلى قلبه من كل الوجوه التي عرفها.

عاد إلى المدينة. لكن شيئًا في داخله ظل واقفًا في الحارة، تحت الشجرة، على الكرسي الخشبي، ينتظره حتى يعود.

Write about a family with a long-standing tradition, whose members all have conflicting origin stories for it. Aim for roughly 600 words.

# The Recipe

The Holloway family had been making sauce on the last Sunday of every August for as long as anyone could remember. Great-grandmother Ida's recipe card—spattered, faded, and written in a hand that looped and dove like a sparrow in flight—still lived in a zip-lock bag inside a kitchen drawer in the house on Beechwood Lane. Nobody could read it anymore. But every August, three generations gathered around the same battered pot, and every August, somebody lied about where the tradition had come from.

"There were six of us," said Uncle Frank, stirring with a wooden spoon that had darkened over decades. "Six kids in our house, and my mother used to throw a party for the neighborhood at the end of summer. Labor Day weekend, right before we went back to school. All the Italian families on the block would bring something. The sauce was hers."

"That's the Catholic version," said his sister, Aunt Rosa, not looking up from the tomatoes she was coring. "Six kids, one big party. That's not a story. That's just a census."

"The canning," said Frank. "She canned. That's why August. Tomatoes were coming in."

"You are wrong," said Rosa. "She canned in October. She made the sauce in August because of *Nonna* Carmela, who died in August, in the old country, in the heat. The sauce was for her. It was a remembrance."

Their mother, eighty-three years old and folded into a lawn chair at the kitchen doorway so she could supervise without getting underfoot, said nothing for a long moment. Then she said, "In the old country, they made it for the saints. *San Lorenzo*. The feast day. August tenth."

"Uncle Frank, you hear?" Rosa gestured with her knife. "Saints."

"Saints," Frank repeated, as if tasting something bitter. "Sure. Saints."

The grandchildren had learned, over the years, to listen for the little breaks in tone, the moments when the air changed. There was Aunt Rosa's version, which always invoked the dead. There was Uncle Frank's, which always involved a crowd, neighbors, the warmth of belonging. And there was Grandma, who seemed to hold both stories in her hands like two glasses of water, offering neither to anyone.

When their grandmother died, they found in her desk a letter in Italian, the envelope postmarked 1957 and never sent. Her grandson, who was taking Italian in college, sat on the porch for a whole afternoon trying to read it. What he made out, slowly, with the help of an old dictionary, was this:

*My dearest sister,*

*The sauce recipe was yours, and you gave it to me the summer before you left. You said: every year at the end of August, when the tomatoes are bad and the heat is worse, you make this sauce and you think of me. You said it would keep me from being homesick. You said it would keep me from being alone.*

*I have done this every year since. Our children have done it with me. Their children will do it with them. The recipe is yours, but the tradition, I think, was always about you. I wanted to write and tell you. I never knew how to begin.*

*I begin now.*

The envelope had been sealed and re-sealed several times. The letter was never finished.

The following August, the family made the sauce as they always did, with the recipe they still could not read, and for the first time nobody argued about where the tradition had come from. They simply made it, and ate it together, and thought of someone none of them had ever met, who had been loved very much by a woman who had outlived her by sixty years.

It was, in its way, a good recipe. It had kept somebody from being alone for a long time. That was enough.

Write about a Thanksgiving meal from the perspective of someone who is not grateful. About 500 words long.

# Bez wdzięczności

Stół jest pełny. Zawsze jest pełny.

Matka biega między kuchnią a jadalnią z tacą indyka, którego wielkość mogłaby wyżywić małą wioskę. Para unosi się z naczyń jak modlitwa, której nikt nie chce słuchać. Ojciec nalewa wino do kieliszków – dwa dla siebie, jeden dla mnie, chociaż nie mam jeszcze dwudziestu jeden lat. Nikt nie komentuje. Nikt nie patrzy na mnie wystarczająco długo, żeby zauważyć.

Siadam. Sztućce brzęczą o talerze jak kości rzucane przez wieszczkę.

– Za co jesteśmy wdzięczni? – pyta babcia, patrząc na mnie znad krawędzi kieliszka.

Za co.

Jestem wdzięczny za ten dom, który kupił ojciec, sprzedając lata, których nigdy nie odzyska. Jestem wdzięczny za tę rodzinę, która udaje, że jest normalna przez cztery godziny raz w roku. Jestem wdzięczny za farsz, który babcia robi według przepisu prababci, która umarła, zanim zdążyłem ją poznać i zanim ktokolwiek zechciał mi powiedzieć, dlaczego.

– Za rodzinę – mówię, bo tego się ode mnie oczekuje.

Babcia kiwa głową. Matka się uśmiecha, ale oczy ma zajęte sosem żurawinowym z puszki, bo taki lubi ojciec. Ojciec mówi „amen" bezgłośnie i kroi indyka nożem, który jest większy niż moja dłoń.

Jem.

Indyk jest suchy. Ziemniaki za mokre. Sos za słodki. Wszystko smakuje tak, jakby ktoś próbował ugotować wspomnienie, które nigdy nie istniało, i jakoś mu nie wyszło. Wujek Tom opowiada o swoim nowym samochodzie. Ciotka Linda narzeka na pogodę. Kuzynka Megan pokazuje komuś zdjęcia ze swojego telefonu, schylając się, jakby to była tajemnica.

Nikt nie pyta mnie o nic.

Nie, to nieprawda. Ciotka Linda pyta:

– A ty, kochanie, jak twoje studia?

– Dobrze, ciociu. Dziękuję.

– A co studiujesz? Zapomniałam.

– Filozofię.

Cisza. Widelce na chwilę przestają brzęczeć.

– Filozofię? – mówi ojciec, nie podnosząc wzroku. – A co z tym zarabiasz?

– Nic, tato. Jeszcze.

Ktoś się śmieje. Nie wiem kto. Może ja.

Babcia podaje mi dokładkę, zanim zdążę odmówić. Matka pyta, czy chcę więcej soku żurawinowego. Ciotka Linda mówi, że w jej czasach filozofia była dla bogatych. Wujek Tom dodaje, że on w swoim wieku już miał dom i dwa samochody.

Deser.

Ciasto dyniowe, kupione w sklepie, ale z domieszką matczynej pretensji, że nie piecze od trzech lat. Lody waniliowe, bo babcia uważa, że inne są „zbyt wyrafinowane". Kawa czarna, bo w tym domu wszystko jest czarne albo słodkie, nic pomiędzy.

Patrzę na nich.

Na te twarze, które znam od urodzenia, a których tak naprawdę nigdy nie widziałem. Na te ręce, które podawały mi jedzenie, ale nie dotykały mnie. Na te głosy, które mówiły „kocham cię", ale nigdy nie powiedziały „wiem, kim jesteś".

Jestem wdzięczny za ten posiłek.

Za ten idealny, starannie wystylizowany spektakl normalności, który odgrywamy raz w roku, bo tak nakazuje kalendarz i reklama. Za te talerze, które będą zmywane jutro, a których nikt nie pomyje dzisiaj. Za tę wdzięczność, której nikt tu naprawdę nie czuje, ale wszyscy udajemy, bo to wypada.

Nie jestem wdzięczny.

Ale powiem „dziękuję", bo tego się ode mnie oczekuje. Bo matka się postarała, nawet jeśli sos jest z puszki. Bo ojciec przyszedł, nawet jeśli wypił za dużo wina. Bo babcia żyje, nawet jeśli nie zauważa, że ja też.

Nie jestem wdzięczny.

Ale zjem dokładkę.

Bo to wszystko, co mogę zrobić.
