About six years ago, he was turned into a vampire by his best friend. This is the story of everything that happened since. Total: ~2400 words.

# The Last Sunlight

---

The first thing Marcus remembered about being a vampire was how *quiet* the world became.

He'd expected horror. Pain. Some dramatic cinematic awakening in a pool of his own blood. Instead, he woke up in Daniel's basement on a Tuesday in October, and the furnace had been turned off, and he could hear the wallpaper peeling in the bedroom two floors up, and somewhere outside a cardinal was singing its head off, and he was hungry in a way that made his teeth ache.

"Hey," Daniel said from the doorway. He looked exhausted. There was dried blood under his fingernails. "How are you feeling?"

"Hungry," Marcus said. And then: "What did you do to me?"

Daniel sat on the bottom step. He was twenty-four years old and looked twenty-four again, which should have been impossible because Marcus had watched him turn twenty-four last March, watched the candles on the birthday cake his mother baked, watched the small fire Daniel had to blow out three times because his breath was weak. Daniel had been dying. Daniel had been dying for three years, and no one had said it out loud, and then one night Daniel had come to him, shaking, with a question.

*Would you hate me?*

Marcus hadn't known what the question meant. Now he did.

"I did it because I couldn't let you be alone," Daniel said. "I know that sounds backwards. I know."

Marcus sat up. The basement smelled like concrete and old laundry, but underneath it, underneath everything, he could smell Daniel. He could smell the blood moving through him, slow and warm, and something in his throat made a sound he didn't recognize.

"You should go upstairs," Daniel whispered. "Please."

---

The first year was the worst, and also the best, and Marcus would never quite be able to reconcile the two.

He couldn't go home. He called his mother once, in January, from a payphone outside a gas station in Ohio, and when she answered he opened his mouth and what came out was a lie so perfect it surprised him. *I'm fine, Mom. I'm traveling. I met someone.* His voice sounded normal. His voice sounded like his voice. She didn't suspect a thing, and when he hung up he stood in the cold for forty-five minutes, listening to his own heartbeat, which he shouldn't have had but did, thready and strange, somewhere behind his sternum.

He had a heartbeat. Daniel had told him, in those first hazy days, that some vampires did, and some didn't, and no one knew why. A mystery of whatever dark arithmetic governed their new existence. Marcus suspected it was because he was still, somewhere deep down, furious. Hearts beat faster when you were angry.

He moved around. A month here, a month there. He learned the rules the hard way, because Daniel couldn't bear to teach them, and because Daniel was the only other vampire Marcus had ever met.

He learned that hunger was a wave. You could stand in it and let it pass, sometimes, if you were very still and thought about something else. He learned that animal blood worked, in a pinch, but tasted like regret. He learned that he couldn't enter a home without being invited, not even his own childhood home, and he had stood on the sidewalk one September night and looked up at his mother's bedroom window and understood, for the first time, that he was dead.

He learned that sunlight didn't kill him. That was a myth, Daniel said, laughing. It just felt like being skinned. Like every nerve ending in your body decided to report for duty at once. You didn't die from it. You just wished you would.

He learned that he loved Daniel in a way that was complicated now, freighted with something he couldn't name. Resentment, maybe. Gratitude. Terror. The understanding that his best friend had looked at his own death and decided that company was the answer, and that Marcus had not been asked.

---

In the second year, he tried to kill Daniel.

It was March. The anniversary. Daniel had bought a small cake from a bakery in Albany and left it on the kitchen counter with a single candle in it, and Marcus had looked at the candle and thought, *I am going to blow that out with his blood*.

He didn't. He got as far as having Daniel pinned against the refrigerator, his hands around Daniel's throat, Daniel's eyes wide and not fighting, never fighting, *letting* him—and then Marcus heard his own heartbeat, that thready impossible thing, and he stopped.

"I would have let you," Daniel said, after. His voice was hoarse. "You know that, right?"

"I know."

"You should have."

"I know."

They didn't speak for two weeks. Then Daniel came home one night with a bag of blood from a butcher in Schenectady, and they sat on the floor of the living room and drank it cold, and Daniel said, "I'm sorry," and Marcus said, "I know," and that was the year that was.

---

In the third year, he met her.

She was a nurse at a hospital in Boston, and she had a smudge of something on her cheek, and she was on the night shift, and he was there because Daniel had been wrong about something, finally, about something small. Marcus had thought he could go into a hospital, and the smell of all those bodies, all that blood, all those sleeping and waking people, would be manageable.

It was not manageable.

He had fled to the roof. He had sat with his back against an air conditioning unit, breathing through his mouth, trying to think about geometry, about the way leaves unfurled in spring, about anything other than the river of warm life flowing six floors below him. And she had come up through the access door, and she had seen him, and she had said, "You look like you're having a bad night," and he had laughed, which surprised him, because he hadn't laughed in a long time.

Her name was Elena. She had dark hair and a habit of tilting her head when she listened, as if she were trying to hear something underneath the words. She was not beautiful in the way the women Daniel had loved were beautiful, which was to say: easily. She was beautiful in the way that required attention.

He told her his name was Mark. He told her he worked in IT. He told her a lot of things that were not true, and some things that were, and somewhere in the third month of knowing her, he realized he was doing the thing he'd sworn he wouldn't do, which was to love someone who would have to watch him not age.

"You seem older than you look," she said, one night, in his apartment. Daniel was out. She was tracing the line of his jaw with her finger, and he was so still, so terribly still, because if he moved he might hurt her, he might lose control, he might do the thing he was always afraid of doing. "I mean that as a compliment."

"I had a hard year once," he said. "A long time ago."

"Tell me about it."

He didn't. He kissed her instead, and tasted coffee on her lips, and underneath that the bright hot singing of her blood, and thought, *This is what it is to be damned. You get to want what will kill you.*

---

In the fourth year, Daniel disappeared.

It wasn't dramatic. There was no note. There was just one morning Marcus waking up in the apartment they shared in Hartford, and Daniel's coat was gone, and Daniel's shoes were gone, and the small glass jar where Daniel kept the change for the laundromat was empty, and that was it.

Marcus called his phone. Straight to voicemail. He called again. Voicemail. He left a message that was too long and said too much.

He didn't come back. Two weeks. Three. A month.

Marcus got on a train to Albany, to the apartment where they had lived in the second year, and it was empty, the landlord said. They'd moved out in October. Did he have a forwarding address?

He didn't. Marcus sat on the front steps of Daniel's building and watched the sun come up, which was a stupid thing to do, and paid for it in the way you pay for everything, which is later.

He went back to Boston. He went back to Elena. He told her his cousin was sick. He told her he might have to leave for a while. She held his face in her hands and said, "Wherever you go, I'll come find you," and he wanted to laugh, or weep, or both, because she meant it, she meant it in the way only living people could mean things, with their whole doomed stupid brave hearts.

---

In the fifth year, he found out what had happened to Daniel.

He was in a bar in Portland, Maine, not drinking, because he didn't drink anymore, hadn't for two years, and he was watching a baseball game on the television above the bartender's head, and the bartender said, "You look like you've seen a ghost," and Marcus said, "Something like that," and the bartender laughed, and then paused, and said, "Hey. You know there's another one of you, right? I mean. You people."

Marcus went very still.

"You people," he said.

"Whatever you are. The pale ones. There's one who comes in sometimes. Talks like he's from down south. Had a real sad look about him, last time I saw him. Maybe a month ago."

"What did he look like?"

"Tall. Thin. Bald, kind of. Sad eyes. Why?"

Marcus didn't answer. He left a twenty on the bar and walked out into the cold, and stood there, and breathed, and tried to think.

A month ago. Portland, Maine. *Sad.*

He didn't go after Daniel. He stood in the parking lot of the bar for an hour, and then he went home, and he sat in the dark of his apartment, and he thought about the second year, and the third year, and how Daniel had looked at him the morning after the refrigerator incident, with bruises on his throat shaped like Marcus's hands, and how Daniel had said, *I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry,* and how Marcus had said, *I know, I know, I know.*

---

In the sixth year, Elena got sick.

It started small. She was tired. She was always tired, she said. She worked too much. The hospital was short-staffed. She was run down.

It was not run down.

Marcus knew, before the doctors knew, because he could smell it on her. Something wrong in her blood. A kind of whispering wrongness, like a frequency only he could hear. He lay next to her at night, in the dark, and listened to the song of her body, and there was a note in it now that hadn't been there before, a sour note, a wrong note, a note that was getting louder.

He brought her soup. He brought her flowers. He brought her books. He sat with her in the oncologist's office and held her hand, and the oncologist talked about stages and options and statistics, and Elena was brave, Elena was so brave, and Marcus was holding her hand and thinking, *I could fix this. I could fix this. There is a way I could fix this.*

He thought about it for eleven days. He thought about it in the shower, in the car, in the long hours of the afternoon when Elena slept and the sun went past the windows in a slow golden arc that he had to turn his face from.

On the twelfth day, he called Daniel.

The phone rang four times. Five. Six.

"Hey," Daniel said. His voice sounded like a record played too slow. "Mark."

"Daniel."

A long silence. The sound of wind somewhere on Daniel's end. Traffic. A horn.

"How did you get this number?" Daniel said.

"I didn't call to fight."

"I know."

"I need your help."

Another silence. Then Daniel said, very quietly, "Are you going to tell me why?"

Marcus looked at the bedroom door. Behind it, Elena was sleeping. Behind it, Elena was dying.

"I need to know how to do it without killing them," Marcus said. "I need to know if it can be done. I need to know if you can turn someone who's already sick."

Daniel was quiet for a long time.

"I don't know," he said, finally. "I don't know, Mark. I didn't know I could do it the first time. I didn't know if it would work. I just—I couldn't let you be alone. I couldn't."

"Yeah," Marcus said. "I know."

---

That was six months ago.

Elena is still alive. She is in remission, the doctors say, which is a word that means *we don't know, we don't know, we just don't know.* She is thinner than she was. She is tired. But she is alive, and she is here, and on a Tuesday in October, six years to the day after everything changed, she is sitting on the floor of their apartment, sorting through a box of old photographs, and she is holding one up to the light, and she is saying, "Who's this? This guy with you. He looks like you."

Marcus crosses the room. He kneels beside her. He takes the photograph from her hands, and he looks at it, and it is a photograph from before, from a long time ago, from the time when he and Daniel were twenty-two and the world was still made of sunlight and they thought they were going to grow old.

"That's Daniel," he says.

"Your best friend?"

"My best friend."

Elena tilts her head. That listening tilt. "What happened to him?"

Marcus looks at the photograph for a long time. Daniel's face, younger, unlined, grinning at the camera. His own face beside it, squinting in the sun.

"I don't know," he says. And that is the truth, and also it isn't.

Elena puts her head on his shoulder. He can hear her heart. He can hear the blood moving through her, slow and warm, singing its small brave song.

She is alive. He is here. Daniel is somewhere out there in the dark, walking under stars Marcus will never see.

He puts the photograph back in the box. He puts his arm around Elena. He listens to her breathe.

And the world, which is so quiet now, so terribly quiet, goes on.

# Letters in Umber

**A Love Story Told in Correspondence Between Vampires**

---

### Letter One
*From Lirien, in a crumbling manor outside Prague, to an unknown recipient*
*October 14th, 1887*

To Whom It May Concern,

You do not know me. I confess I am uncertain whether I should know you. Your name arrived yesterday, tucked inside a folded deed for a parcel of land I never wished to own, and yet here the deed is, and here is your name at its bottom: *Evariste Marchand, of Lyon.*

I am told I inherited this land from a great-uncle I never met. I am told he was a vampire of considerable age and repute. I am told he died recently, in the manner of our kind, which is to say he simply ceased, and that in his final century he spoke often of me, though I cannot imagine why.

I am twenty-six years old. I have been a vampire for four of those years. I know almost nothing of this world of ours. I know I am lonely in it.

Forgive me if this letter reaches you as an intrusion. I am writing only because I have no one else to write to, and the deed instructs me to inform you of my inheritance, and I find myself, against all good sense, wishing to inform you of more.

Yours in uncertainty,
**Lirien**

---

### Letter Two
*From Evariste, in an apartment above a closed bookshop in Lyon, to Lirien*
*November 2nd, 1887*

My dear Lirien,

You should not write to me. I will explain why, and yet even as I explain, I suspect I shall be unable to stop myself from writing back, which is a poor sort of warning.

Your great-uncle was Lucien Vásárhelyi, who in this world was called Lucien le Vieux. I knew him for ninety-three years. He was, in his fashion, fond of me. In his fashion, he was fond of very few.

The land he left you is not land, properly speaking. It is a hill above the Vltava where, on certain nights of certain years, the soil grows dark with something that is not quite rain and not quite blood, and if one stands in it at the right hour, one hears things one should not hear. I do not recommend standing in it. I do recommend you hire a keeper for the property, one of our kind, and forget the place exists.

You say you are lonely. I am a poor correspondent for loneliness. I am fifty-nine years old, which is to say I am barely more than a youth in our terms, but I have lived those years as if I were trying to outrun something, and I have not spoken to anyone with any honesty in a very long time. I have books. I have a cat who is not a vampire but who tolerates me. I have a small reputation in a city that does not know what to make of me.

If you write again, I will answer. That is the only promise I can make without knowing whether I can keep it.

I remain, against my better judgment,
**Evariste Marchand**

---

### Letter Three
*From Lirien*
*November 19th, 1887*

Dear Evariste,

I find your warning very strange, because it is the first warning anyone has ever given me. I was made into this by a woman who did not stay to teach me, and I have spent four years learning by the very inefficient method of nearly dying. I am pleased to report I have not yet died.

Tell me about the cat. Is he an orange cat? I have a theory that orange cats are the only honest creatures on earth, and I should like to know if the theory holds for French ones as well as Bohemian ones.

Tell me also, if you can bear to, what you are running from. I shall not press. But the night is long, and I find I am hungry for the company of anyone who has chosen to be lonely on purpose.

With unreasonable affection for someone I have never met,
**Lirien**

---

### Letter Four
*From Evariste*
*December 5th, 1887*

Dear Lirien,

His name is Augustin. He is grey, with a small white smudge on his chest, and he has the great misfortune of loving me without reservation, which I do not deserve.

He sits on the letters I am trying to write. I take this as criticism.

You ask what I am running from. This is the question I have been avoiding for fifty-nine years. I shall try, for you, to answer it in pieces.

I was made by a man I loved. I killed him, accidentally, the night he made me. He had warned me that the turning was a kind of death, and I had not understood him. When I woke, I was a murderer and a monster, and I have been trying, since, to figure out which of those I would rather be.

I am running from him, I think. From the version of me that existed before I understood what I was.

Does that answer your question?

Yours in honesty, which is new and uncomfortable,
**Evariste**

---

### Letter Five
*From Lirien*
*December 21st, 1887*

Dear Evariste,

It is the solstice, and the night is the longest of the year. I am writing by candlelight because the gas has gone out and I cannot bring myself to care.

Thank you for telling me about your maker. I have not told anyone about mine, and so perhaps I should try, to make the exchange fair. Her name was Magdalene. She made me because I was dying of a fever and because, she said, she had not made anyone in a very long time and had forgotten what it felt like to be needed. I think she meant it kindly. I think she did not stay because she could not bear to watch me learn what I was.

I think of her sometimes and I am not sure whether I loved her or not. I think she may have been the only person who ever held my hand while I was afraid. I think it is a very strange thing to love and resent someone in the same breath for the rest of eternity.

You are not a monster. I have decided this about you. A monster would not be afraid of being one.

Yours, very stubbornly,
**Lirien**

---

### Letter Six
*From Evariste*
*January 8th, 1888*

Lirien,

I read your letter seven times. I will not tell you which night I read it the most.

I have a confession. The reason I answered your first letter at all is that I recognized your name. Your great-uncle spoke of you often, but he also spoke of *me* in letters I was never meant to see. He wrote, once, that he hoped I would one day meet his great-niece, "who is the only creature of his acquaintance who might love Evariste for what he is rather than what he ought to be."

I thought this was a foolish old vampire's fantasy. I thought he had lost his mind in his last decade.

Now I have a letter on my desk from you, and I am not sure that I am not the one losing my mind.

Will you come to Lyon? I have a room. It is small, and the window does not close properly, and Augustin will hate you at first, which is how he shows approval.

I am asking more than I should.
**Evariste**

---

### Letter Seven
*From Lirien*
*January 22nd, 1888*

Evariste,

Yes.

I will come on the first night of February, by the southern train, if I can find the money for a ticket. I will arrive cold and hungry and probably in a terrible mood. I will knock on your door, or perhaps I will simply stand outside it until you open it, because I do not know what one does when one meets a person one has only ever known through paper and ink.

I should warn you: I do not know how to love someone who is not a memory. I should warn you also: I intend to learn.

Yours, finally, without any uncertainty at all,
**Lirien**

---

### Letter Eight
*From Evariste*
*January 24th, 1888*

Lirien,

I have cleaned the room. I have bought curtains. I have fed, which I had been neglecting. I have tried to teach Augustin to be polite, but he is a French cat and has refused on principle.

When you arrive, I will open the door myself. I will not pretend I am calm.

I have loved you for six weeks, which is a very short time for a vampire, and an eternity for me.

Until February first,
**Evariste**

---

### Letter Nine
*From Lirien, undated, found tucked between the pages of a borrowed book*

Evariste,

I do not need to write letters to you anymore, and so this is the last one, which is a kind of loss.

But I wanted to say — once, in writing, so I could remember it — that you opened the door and I knew you, and you knew me, and we had not yet learned each other's faces.

We have a great deal of time.

I think we should use it.

— *L.*

---

*These letters were found in the estate of Evariste Marchand, who died in 1956 at the age of one hundred and twenty-eight. The last letter was folded into a copy of Rilke's* Letters to a Young Poet, *which he had annotated heavily in the margins. The grey cat, Augustin, was buried in the garden, and lived to the improbable age of twenty-three.*

# Sangre y Estrellas

## Una historia de amor entre inmortales

---

**Verona, Italia. Siglo XVI.**

Las calles empedradas de la ciudad dormían bajo un manto de niebla perpetua, esa bruma espesa que nunca abandonaba el valle. Era como si el cielo mismo supiera el secreto que la nobleza ocultaba tras sus muros de piedra: los Montesco y los Capuleto no eran simples familias rivales. Eran dos antiguas estirpes de vampiros, separadas durante siglos por una guerra de sangre y orgullo.

---

### Capítulo I: La fiesta enmascarada

Romeo Montesco se deslizó entre las sombras del salón de los Capuleto como una exhalación de viento frío. La invitación había sido robada, la máscara, prestada. Su primo Benvolio lo había arrastrado hasta allí con la promesa de diversión, aunque ambos sabían que traspasar esas puertas equivalía a una sentencia de muerte.

—No deberíamos estar aquí —murmuró Benvolio, sus ojos oscuros escaneando la multitud—. Si tu padre se entera...

—Mi padre no debe enterarse de nada —respondió Romeo, y por primera vez en décadas, sintió que su corazón latía con fuerza. Algo había perturbado el ritmo eterno de su sangre.

Entonces la vio.

Capuleta. Hija del enemigo jurado.

Estaba de pie junto a una columna de mármol, vestida de rojo sangre, con el cabello negro cayéndole sobre los hombros como cortinas de seda nocturna. Cuando ella levantó la vista y sus ojos se encontraron a través de las máscaras, Romeo comprendió que estaba perdido.

Julieta no era como las demás de su especie. Había algo cálido en ella, algo vivo. La mayoría de los vampiros perdían todo rastro de humanidad al cabo de un siglo; ella, sin embargo, conservaba una luz interior que parecía negarse a apagarse.

—¿Quién eres? —preguntó ella cuando él se acercó, sin preámbulos, sin juegos cortesanos.

—Alguien que no debería estar aquí.

—Entonces somos dos.

Sus manos se rozaron sobre la copa de cristal tallado, y ambos sintieron el calor imposible de dos pieles frías encendiéndose. Romeo inclinó la cabeza hacia su cuello, no con hambre, sino con reverencia. Percibía su pulso, esa melodía mecánica que delataba la vida que aún residía en ella, quizás el último vestigio de cuando fue humana.

—Bailemos —susurró ella.

Y entre las sombras del salón, donde nadie podía verlos, sus cuerpos se mecieron con la cadencia de algo más antiguo que cualquier vals.

---

### Capítulo II: El juramento del balcón

Aquella noche, Romeo no pudo regresar a la mansión Montesco. Se ocultó entre los cipreses del jardín de los Capuleto, bajo el balcón donde sabía que ella aparecería.

La luna llena derramaba su plata sobre los rosales marchitos cuando Julieta asomó por la balaustrada. Llevaba un camisón blanco que parecía reflejar toda la luz de la eternidad.

—¿Romeo? —llamó ella en voz baja.

—Aquí estoy. Como siempre estaré.

Ella descendió por la enredadera con la gracia de quien ha vivido siglos. Sus pies descalzos no hicieron ruido alguno sobre la hierba húmeda. Cuando llegó hasta él, Romeo cayó de rodillas.

—Julieta, mi sangre y mi destino son tuyos. Si me lo permites, esta noche beberé de tu cuello y te ofreceré el mío. Unidos por la mordedura, jamás la muerte podrá separarnos.

Julieta lo contempló largamente. Sabía lo que significaba aquella propuesta: un vínculo eterno entre vampiros era más fuerte que cualquier juramento humano, más profundo que cualquier matrimonio. Era el pacto que solo las almas gemelas sellaban.

—Y si tu padre lo descubre, te matará.

—Que lo intente.

—Y si el mío descubre que te amo, me condenará al sol.

—Entonces viviremos en las sombras.

Ella se arrodilló frente a él. Sus frentes se tocaron.

—Hazlo —dijo Julieta—. Antes de que amanezca, hazme tuya para siempre.

Romeo le apartó el cabello del cuello con manos temblorosas. Por primera vez en su larga existencia, sintió miedo. No de lastimarla, sino de que este momento terminara. Inclinó la cabeza y, con la delicadeza de quien sostiene algo sagrado, clavó sus colmillos.

Julieta no gritó. Un suspiro escapó de sus labios, y Romeo bebió solo lo suficiente para sellar el pacto. Luego, él se ofreció. Ella mordió su cuello con la dulzura de una primera caricia.

La sangre cantó entre ellos. Un lazo invisible, más fuerte que el acero, los unió para siempre.

---

### Capítulo III: La sangre derramada

El idilio no duró.

Tibaldo, primo de Julieta y vampiro implacable, los descubrió tres noches después. Los encontró en el campanario abandonado de una iglesia en ruinas, abrazados bajo las vigas carcomidas, hablando de huir juntos a tierras donde nadie conociera sus apellidos.

—Traidora —escupió Tiboldo, con los colmillos descubiertos—. Darle tu sangre a un Montesco es peor que morir.

Julieta se interpuso entre ambos.

—Tibaldo, te lo suplico. Lo amo.

—¡El amor es una mentira de los humanos! —rugió él, y se lanzó sobre Romeo.

La pelea fue breve y brutal. Tiboldo era más fuerte, más viejo, más cruel. Cuando Romeo cayó al suelo con una herida abierta en el costado, su sangre —la misma sangre que ahora compartía con Julieta— comenzó a derramarse entre las piedras.

Julieta aulló.

No fue un grito humano. Fue un lamento que hizo temblar los cimientos de la iglesia, un sonido tan antiguo y tan desesperado que las palomas huyeron del campanario en bandada.

—¡Romeo! ¡Romeo, no!

Pero Tiboldo ya había huido, y Romeo yacía en sus brazos, desangrándose.

—Bebe de mí —suplicó ella, acercándose el cuello—. Toma lo que necesites, vive, te lo ruego.

—Julieta... —su voz era apenas un susurro—. Si muero... prométeme que no me seguirás.

—¡No! ¡Jamás te lo prometeré!

—Debes prometerlo. Debes vivir. Debes...

Las palabras se apagaron en sus labios. Los ojos de Romeo se cerraron, y su corazón —ese músculo que ya no necesitaba para vivir— dejó de latir por última vez.

---

### Capítulo IV: El alba

Julieta sostuvo su cuerpo durante horas, meciéndolo, besando sus labios ya fríos. El dolor era tan vasto que apenas cabía en su pecho inmortal.

Cuando el primer rubor del amanecer comenzó a teñir el horizonte, ella comprendió que tenía que tomar una decisión.

Podía cumplir su palabra y vivir, arrastrándose por los siglos con el eco de Romeo en cada rincón de su memoria.

O podía desobedecerle.

Sus dedos recorrieron el rostro de su amado. Aún era bello. Aún parecía dormido.

—Perdóname —susurró.

Lo depositó con cuidado sobre las piedras del campanario. Luego caminó hacia la ventana que daba al este, donde el cielo comenzaba a incendiarse de rosa y oro.

Extendió los brazos.

Y esperó al sol.

---

**Epílogo**

Cuenta la leyenda que en las noches sin luna, cuando la niebla desciende sobre Verona y el mundo contiene su aliento, se puede ver a dos figuras paseando por los jardines de los Capuleto. Él lleva una máscara de plata; ella, un vestido rojo sangre. Se detienen siempre bajo el mismo balcón, donde una vez juraron amarse para siempre.

Y si te acercas lo suficiente, dicen los que se atreven, puedes escuchar el eco de unas palabras que el tiempo no ha podido borrar:

*"Ni el sol, ni la muerte, ni los siglos podrán separarnos. Porque donde tú estés, Romeo, allí habitaré yo. Y nuestro amor será más eterno que las estrellas."*

# 永夜终章

## 一、消息

消息是黄昏时分传进山城的。

彼时我正坐在临街的药铺后院，用石臼研磨着朱砂与雄黄。这两样东西最近涨价涨得厉害——倒不是因为辟邪，纯粹是因为城北王记棺材铺的少东家娶亲，要拿朱砂漆棺材底辟虫。

院墙外忽然传来一阵急促的脚步声，接着是陈四嫂那永远压不低的嗓门："白大夫！白大夫在家么！"

我叹了口气，拍了拍衣襟上的药粉，走到前堂。

陈四嫂是山城出了名的大嘴巴。她男人是城东学堂的厨子，她自己则是整条长乐街最灵通的包打听。她冲进来的时候，一双眼睛亮得像两盏灯笼，气都没喘匀就开了口：

"白大夫，你晓不晓得？北边来的消息——说是、说是那病，能治了！"

我给她倒了杯茶："陈嫂慢慢说。哪门子病？"

"还能是哪门子！"她压低声音，又忍不住提高，"就是那、那夜里的病！吸血的那种！说是洋人的医馆研究出来了，一针打下去就好了！"

我手里的茶壶微微一顿。

"真的？"

"千真万确！我家那口子在学堂听省城来的先生说的！说洋人把这方子印成报纸，发了满天下！不要钱，谁都能看！"

我送走陈四嫂的时候，天已经彻底黑了。

山城依山而建，入夜后街巷昏暗，只有零星的灯笼。我站在药铺门口，看着远处山坡上那座废弃的山神庙，忽然想：这消息传到那里，需要多久？

"白姑娘。"

一个声音从屋檐上落下来，懒洋洋的，带着几分戏谑。

我没有抬头。"你下来。"

"下去做什么？这消息你不也听到了？"

"所以你是来问我打不打算去打那一针的？"

屋檐上沉默了一会儿，然后一阵轻微的风掠过，一个穿着黑色长衫的年轻人落在我面前。他生得很好看——这是所有同族都有的特征——肤色苍白，眉目清隽，只是眼睛里总带着点似笑非笑的意味。

"白蔹，"他叫我名字，"一百年了，咱们打了多少回？这一次，怕是要散伙。"

我没有立刻回答。

我叫白蔹，开这间药铺已经三十七年。在山城，所有人都知道白大夫医术好，专治疑难杂症，却不知道她晚上从不点灯——因为她不需要。

我行医，治病，从不伤人。三十七年来我饮的，都是自愿来我铺子里卖血的穷人的血，每回不过一盏，付足银钱，童叟无欺。

这在同族里是异类。

但此刻，让我心里隐隐作痛的，不是这件事。

## 二、长夜

我认识沈夜亭，是在九十年前。

那时候不叫山城，叫青溪县。我也不是"白蔹"，我有一百三十七岁，正在西北一座破庙里躲雨——那年冬天特别冷，饿殍遍野，连老鼠都被吃光了。

他推门进来的时候，浑身是血，左边胳膊被什么野兽撕掉了一块。我本想赶他走，却发现他身后还藏着一个十来岁的女孩，女孩饿得只剩一把骨头，眼睛却亮得吓人。

"求姑娘救命，"他说，"她还有用。"

后来的事很俗套。我喂了他和那女孩几口血，他们活了下来。女孩叫阿沅，后来跟着我学医，再后来嫁给了县城布庄的少东家，生了三个孩子，七十八岁那年寿终正寝。

沈夜亭却留下来，成了我的……什么呢？

朋友？伴侣？同族？

他说不清，我也说不清。我们一起游历过很多地方，从西北到江南，从塞北到岭南。我们见过太平盛世的繁华，也见过乱世里人命如草芥。他有时候会消失几年，说是去"找乐子"，有时候又突然出现，带着一壶好酒，赖在我药铺里不走。

我开药铺的银钱，有一半是他"找乐子"找来的——他偷富户的，我治穷人的，倒也相安无事。

九十年了。

我看着他，忽然开口："你打算怎么办？"

沈夜亭挑了挑眉："你呢？"

"我是问你。"

"我问的是你。"

我们对视了一会儿。

然后他笑了，笑得很轻："白蔹，你心里早有答案了，何必问我？"

我没有说话。

是的，我有答案。

但我想先听他说。

## 三、各怀心事

接下来的几天，山城热闹得像过年。

北边来的报纸被抄了无数份，满城的识字人都在议论这件事。有人欢喜有人愁，有人信有人疑。但最热闹的，还是城北那座洋人开的新式医院——门口排起了长队，多的是愁眉苦脸的人。

我站在药铺门口，看着那些排队的人，心里明白：他们中的大多数，都不是自愿来的。

是被家人押来的。

是怕一旦发病，亲人变怪物。

是被那个自古以来根深蒂固的恐惧驱赶着来的——恐惧那"非人"的存在。

"白大夫！"

隔壁张屠户的老婆冲过来，眼睛红红的："求你帮帮忙，我家那口子……他要打那个针！"

我一愣："他要打？让他打便是，求我做什么？"

"不是我家那口子！"她哭起来，"是我家大伯！他、他前几天被咬了！还没发病呢，但他婆娘非要他来打！我大伯人好好的，能干活，能吃饭，就是……就是夜里眼睛会亮……"

我沉默了。

"白大夫，求你给句话！那针打了，真的能好么？打了以后，就真的不会变了么？"

我看着她，忽然不知道该怎么回答。

"张嫂，"我慢慢说，"这针……我也不知打了好不好。"

"可你不是……"

她没说完，但她的眼睛看着我，瞳孔里有一种隐秘的恐惧。

我明白她想说什么。

白大夫，你不是夜里也不点灯么？

白大夫，你是不是早就……

我没有承认，也没有否认，只是轻轻叹了口气："张嫂，我只能告诉你，不管打不打针，日子都是自己过的。你家大伯若是愿意，就打；若是不愿意，你也别逼他。"

她哭着走了。

我站在门口，看着她的背影，忽然觉得很累。

晚间，沈夜亭从屋檐上跳下来，手里拎着一壶酒。

"今天又有人来问你了？"

"嗯。"

"你怎么说？"

"实话。"

他在我对面坐下，给我倒了一杯酒。月光下，他的脸苍白如玉，眼底却有一丝不易察觉的青黑——那是饥饿的颜色。

"沈夜亭，"我忽然问，"你多久没进食了？"

他笑了笑，没有回答。

我又问："你打算什么时候去打那一针？"

他还是没有回答，只是举杯冲我遥遥一敬，仰头饮尽。

## 四、表决

消息传开第十天，同族们决定在废弃的山神庙聚一次。

山城周围的同族不多，算上我和沈夜亭，也不过十三人。其中有三个已经老了——不是人类的"老"，是那种形销骨立、行将就木的"老"。他们大约已经活了两三百年，行将"入灭"，不打针也会在几年内化为尘土。

聚会在子时开始。

十三个影子坐在破庙的横梁上、月光里、神台上。气氛凝重得仿佛山雨欲来。

第一个开口的是青衣——一个活了四百年的老妪，在同族中辈分最高。

"这事，你们怎么看？"

没有人回答。

我开口了："我想先问一句：打那一针，真能治好么？"

"北边传来的消息说能。"青衣身边的中年男人说——那是她的孙辈，叫云生，活了一百五十年，说话一向沉稳，"但没人试过。"

"如果打不好呢？"

"那就……"

云生没有说下去，但所有人都明白。

那就死了。

不是人类的"死"，是彻底的、不可逆的消亡。化作尘土，再无来世。

又一阵沉默。

然后一个尖锐的声音响起："我不打！"

是红袖。三百年前是个戏子，性子烈得很。她跳起来，眼睛里燃烧着怒火："打了这一针，我这一百多年算什么？我亲眼看着王朝更迭，看着子孙后代变成一堆白骨，看着这世间沧海桑田——到头来，要我自己把自己了结了？"

"红袖，"青衣缓缓开口，"打了这一针，不是了结。是……新生。"

"什么新生？"红袖冷笑，"变成普通人？活几十年就老死？被人生下来，被人埋进土里——这就是你们想要的新生？"

没有人反驳她。

红袖说得对。

这一针打下去，我们就会变成人。真正的人。会老，会病，会死。

不用再躲躲藏藏，不用再午夜时分才能行走，不用再看着身边的人一代代老去而死我们还活着。

但同时，也再没有那漫长的、几乎无尽的寿命。再没有月光下恣意奔跑的畅快。再没有化血为酒、点石成金的幻术。再没有……

"我也不打。"

又一个声音响起。

是云生。

所有人都看向他。他神色平静，但眼底有一种说不清的东西。

"我活了一百五十年，"他说，"人间的事我见过太多了。我不想再变回人。变回人，就得守人间的规矩，尊人间的礼法——我不想。"

"云生，"青衣问，"人间的规矩，有什么不好？"

"青衣婆婆，您活了一千年，您难道不知道？"云生轻声说，"人间的规矩，最是虚伪。"

红袖忽然笑了起来："说得好！云生！"

但也有人持反对意见。

一个叫寒声的男人——他是本地人，死于两百年前的一场瘟疫——缓缓开口："我倒是……想打。"

"寒声？"红袖惊讶地看着他。

"我想了很久，"寒声低着头，"两百年前，我是被活活烧死的。我的家人、邻居，把我绑在柱子上，点了火。他们以为我是妖孽。我记得火苗舔在皮肤上的感觉，记得肉被烧焦的味道，记得他们往火里扔柴火时脸上的恐惧和厌恶。"

他抬起头，眼眶微红："我不想再被那样对待了。我想……做人。做一个普通的人。可以走在太阳底下，可以被人指着鼻子骂但不会被烧死。"

庙里一片死寂。

然后，所有人的目光都转向了我。

"白蔹，"青衣问，"你呢？"

我沉默了很久。

"我还没想好。"我最终说。

沈夜亭在我身边，一直没说话。但我知道，他也没有想好。

## 五、往事

聚会散后，沈夜亭没有走。

我们并肩坐在庙顶的飞檐上，看着山城的万家灯火。

"白蔹，"他忽然开口，"你还记得阿沅么？"

我的眼眶忽然有些发热。

"记得。"

"她走的时候，"他说，"拉着你的手，对不对？"

"嗯。"

阿沅走的那天，七十八岁，儿孙满堂。她躺在床上，头发全白了，眼睛却还是亮的——六十年前那么亮。

她拉着我的手，说："姐姐，这辈子多谢你。下辈子，我还想跟你学医。"

我笑着说好。

她又说："姐姐，你一个人，会不会寂寞？"

我说不会。有沈夜亭在呢。

她就笑了，放心地闭上了眼睛。

那是我活了两百多年来，唯一一次哭。

"白蔹，"沈夜亭轻声说，"阿沅是人。她只活了七十八年。但她过得很幸福。"

"你想说什么？"

"我想说——"他顿了顿，"我一直很羡慕她。"

我转头看他。

月光下，他的脸苍白如纸，眉目却依然清隽。但我忽然发现，他的眼角有细纹——吸血鬼不该有皱纹的，除非……

"沈夜亭，你怎么了？"

"没什么，"他笑了笑，"老了吧。"

"你才一百六十岁。"

"是吗？"他漫不经心地说，"那也不年轻了。"

我心里忽然涌起一阵恐惧。

"沈夜亭，你是不是……"

"白蔹，"他打断我，"你还记得，我当初为什么被咬么？"

我摇摇头。

他望着远方，目光悠远。

"一百六十年前，我是个书生。进京赶考，路上遇到土匪。他们砍了我一刀，把我扔在路边。我以为自己要死了。然后，遇到了一个女人。"

"她救了你？"

"嗯。她给我喂了血，把我变成了这样。我恨她入骨，发誓要报仇。但后来我发现——她是真心救我。因为她不忍心看着一个年轻人死在路边。"

他顿了顿："白蔹，你知道那女人是谁么？"

我心里忽然有了一个猜测。

"……是我师父。"

他转过头，看着我，笑了："聪明。"

我的师父。白鹿。三百年前圆寂的同族。

她一生救人无数，却从不解释。她临终前把这间药铺传给了我，却没告诉我，她在人间还有这样一个"孙子辈"。

"沈夜亭，"我轻声问，"你恨她么？"

"一开始恨。后来不恨了。"

"为什么？"

"因为她让我多看了很多年的月亮，"他轻声说，"也因为她让我遇见了你。"

我沉默了。

"白蔹，"他忽然说，"我想去打那一针。"

我转头看他。

"但我不是为了变成人，"他说，"我只是想……像阿沅那样，安安静静地老去。"

"为什么？"

"因为我想在一个阳光明媚的下午，像一个普通人那样死，"他轻声说，"而不是在某个阴暗的角落里，无声无息地化为尘土。"

我忽然明白了。

他不是怕死。他是不想再"活"下去了。

活了一百六十年，够了。

## 六、各自的路

第二天，我做出了决定。

我没有去打那一针。

但我也不打算再这样继续下去了。

我关了药铺，把所有的东西——银针、药臼、草药、医书——都送给了隔壁的张大夫。张大夫是个厚道人，我信得过他。

然后，我离开了山城。

沈夜亭打了那一针。

打针那天，我陪着他去医院。洋人的医院干净明亮，到处都是消毒水的味道。护士给他打了一针——其实没什么感觉，就像被蚊子叮了一下。

他在观察室里躺了一天。

傍晚的时候，他睁开眼睛。

他看着我，眼睛里的那种……"光"，没有了。

"白蔹，"他轻声说，"我好像……饿了。"

我笑了："想吃什么？"

"想吃你做的阳春面。"

我扶着他出了医院。夕阳照在他脸上，他有些不适应，微微眯了眼睛。

"太阳真刺眼，"他嘟囔着，"一百六十年没晒过太阳了。"

"习惯就好。"

我们回到药铺——哦，已经是张大夫的了。我在后院的小厨房里，给他做了一碗阳春面。

他吃得很慢，每一口都嚼很久。

"白蔹，"他放下筷子，"你真的想好了？"

"想好了。"

"你不后悔？"

"不后悔。"

他沉默了很久。

"白蔹，"他轻声说，"我打了一针，就不能再陪着你了。"

"我知道。"

"我只有几十年的命了。"

"我知道。"

"你不怕么？"

我看着他，看着他眼睛里那种"光"一点一点消失，看着他从一个近乎永恒的存在，变成一个普通人。

但我还是笑了。

"沈夜亭，"我说，"阿沅只活了七十八年。她过得很幸福。"

他愣住了。

然后，他也笑了。

## 七、尾声

很多年后，山城来了一个游方郎中。

那郎中是个年轻女子，背着一个旧药箱，四处给人看病。她的医术很好，尤其是治一些疑难杂症，几乎药到病除。

有人问她叫什么名字。

她说，叫白蔹。

有人问她从哪里来。

她说，从北边来。

有人问她为什么到处走。

她笑了笑，说："我在找一个人。"

"找谁？"

"一个故人，"她说，"他也是郎中。几十年前，他打了一针，变成普通人了。我不知道他现在在哪里，过得好不好。我想……再见他一面。"

"那他叫什么？"

白蔹想了想，轻声说：

"沈夜亭。"

——

# Darah Terakhir di Dunia

Hujan turun tanpa henti malam itu, mengetuk jendela-jendela tua mansion terbengkalai di pinggiran Praha. Gregor Volkov berdiri di ambang pintu, jas hujan hitamnya basah kuyup, tapi ia tidak merasa dingin. Darah telah mendingin di nadinya sejak lama—sejak malam ketika ia melihat ayahnya dibunuh oleh makhluk yang kini ia buru.

Selama dua puluh tahun, Gregor telah melacak setiap legenda, setiap bisikan, setiap jejak kaki di kuburan. Ia telah membunuh tujuh puluh tiga vampire di empat benua. Tujuh puluh tiga nyawa abadi yang dipadamkan oleh belati peraknya. Tujuh puluh tiga kemenangan yang tidak pernah memberinya kedamaian.

Dan kini, tersisa satu.

Gregor mendorong pintu mansion itu terbuka. Kayunya lapuk, engselnya berdecit seperti rintihan orang sekarat. Di dalam, gelap total. Hanya cahaya bulan yang menerobos melalui celah-celah jendela rusak, menerangi partikel debu yang melayang seperti abu dari dunia lain.

"Aku tahu kamu ada di sini," kata Gregor, suaranya tenang seperti pisau yang diasah. "Aroma darahmu berbeda dari yang lain. Lebih tua. Lebih murni."

Tidak ada jawaban. Hanya keheningan dan tetesan air dari atap yang bocor.

Gregor melangkah masuk. Setiap gerakan adalah perhitungan—tiga puluh tahun berburu telah mengajarinya bahwa vampire terakhir di dunia adalah yang paling berbahaya. Bukan karena kekuatannya, tetapi karena keputusasaannya.

Ia menemukannya di ruang bawah tanah. Sebuah ruangan batu yang lembap, dipenuhi botol-botol berisi darah—ratusan, mungkin ribuan—yang tersusun rapi di rak-rak kayu. Di tengah ruangan, duduk seorang wanita tua. Rambutnya putih seperti salju, kulitnya pucat seperti kertas, tapi matanya—matanya masih berkilat merah, masih hidup, masih lapar.

"Kamu yang terakhir," kata Gregor, mengangkat belatinya.

Wanita itu—yang menyebut dirinya Elisabeth—tersenyum. Sebuah senyum yang membuat Gregor merasa seolah sedang menatap ke dalam lubang hitam yang menelan segalanya.

"Apakah kamu benar-benar percaya aku yang terakhir, pemburu?" tanya Elisabeth, suaranya seperti desau angin di antara tulang. "Bahwa setelah aku mati, tidak akan ada lagi dari jenis kami? Bahwa tidak akan ada yang ketiga, keempat, kelima—bahwa tidak akan pernah ada lagi anak yang lahir dari darah?"

Gregor tidak menjawab. Ia sudah terlalu sering mendengar tipu daya vampire. Kata-kata mereka adalah senjata yang lebih tajam dari taring mereka.

"Selama tiga ribu tahun, kami ada," lanjut Elisabeth. "Sebelum manusiamu menemukan api, sebelum mereka menemukan bahasa, kami sudah ada di sini. Kamu pikir belati kecilmu bisa mengakhiri itu?"

Gregor melihat sekeliling ruangan. Botol-botol darah. Bukan darah biasa—ia bisa melihat label-label kecil yang ditulis dengan tulisan kuno. *Bordeaux, 1348. Konstantinopel, 542. Athena, 429.* Tanggal-tanggal pandemi. Tanggal-tanggal ketika manusia jatuh seperti lalat.

"Aku tidak membunuh jenismu," kata Gregor akhirnya. "Aku membunuh *individu*. Dan kamu adalah individu terakhir."

Elisabeth mengangkat tangannya—tangan yang pernah menggenggam kekuasaan, yang pernah menandatangani条约 yang mengubah sejarah—dan mengarahkannya ke dinding.

Di sana, tergantung foto-foto. Gregor melihat wajah-wajah yang dikenalnya. Alexander yang ia bunuh di Istanbul. Yuki yang ia bunuh di Kyoto. Matthias yang ia bunuh di Berlin. Semua yang pernah ia anggap sebagai target, kini tersenyum dari foto, tampak damai.

"Mereka tidak jahat, Gregor," kata Elisabeth. "Mereka hanya... lapar. Seperti kamu. Seperti aku. Seperti semua makhluk yang pernah hidup."

Gregor merasakan sesuatu yang asing di dadanya. Bukan rasa takut—ia sudah lupa bagaimana rasanya takut. Mungkin keraguan. Mungkin kesedihan. Atau mungkin hanya kelelahan dari tiga puluh tahun perang tanpa akhir.

"Tapi kamu sudah terlalu jauh," bisik Elisabeth, membaca pikirannya dengan kemampuan yang hanya dimiliki vampire tertua. "Kamu sudah membunuh terlalu banyak. Kamu tidak bisa berhenti. Bahkan jika aku yang terakhir, kamu akan terus membunuh—membunuh hantu, membunuh bayangan, membunuh kenangan. Sampai akhirnya, tidak ada yang tersisa kecuali dirimu."

Gregor menggenggam belatinya lebih erat. Ujung peraknya berkilat.

"Lalu biarkan aku menjadi kenangan terakhir," katanya.

Gregor menerjang. Reflex-nya sempurna—tiga puluh tahun latihan tidak pernah ia sia-siakan. Belati menembus jantung Elisabeth dengan presisi bedah.

Elisabeth tidak berteriak. Ia hanya tersenyum, seolah sedang jatuh tertidur setelah tiga ribu tahun terjaga. Darah merah tua—lebih gelap dari darah manusia—mengalir dari lukanya, menggenangi lantai batu.

"Kamu bisa berhenti sekarang," bisik Elisabeth, suaranya semakin lemah. "Atau kamu bisa mencari kami selamanya."

Gregor tidak menjawab. Ia menarik belatinya, dan Elisabeth hancur menjadi abu—abu yang diterbangkan angin dari ventilasi, lenyap begitu saja seolah tidak pernah ada.

Gregor berdiri di ruang bawah tanah yang kosong, dikelilingi oleh botol-botol darah dan foto-foto orang yang telah ia bunuh. Di luar, hujan masih turun. Di suatu tempat di kota, lonceng gereja berdering tiga kali—tengah malam.

*Yang terakhir*, pikir Gregor. *Akhirnya.*

Tapi ketika ia berjalan keluar dari mansion, ia melihat sesuatu yang membuat langkahnya terhenti. Di trotoar basah, di bawah cahaya lampu jalan, ada seorang anak kecil—mungkin delapan atau sembilan tahun—memandangnya dengan mata yang terlalu tua untuk wajahnya.

"Mister," kata anak itu, suaranya lembut seperti bisikan. "Mister, kamu terlihat lelah. Apakah kamu mau ikut dengan saya? Saya bisa membawamu ke tempat yang hangat."

Gregor menatap anak itu lama. Di kedalaman mata anak itu, ia melihat sesuatu—sesuatu yang ia kenali. Sesuatu yang ia buru selama tiga puluh tahun.

*Aku tidak membunuh jenismu*, pikir Gregor lagi. *Aku membunuh individu.*

Tapi bagaimana dengan anak-anak yang belum pernah ia bunuh? Bagaimana dengan mereka yang belum lahir? Bagaimana dengan vampire yang akan ada di masa depan, yang akan menumpahkan darah manusia seperti yang dilakukan pendahulu mereka?

Gregor Volkov—pemburu vampire terakhir—berlutut di trotoar basah, memandang anak kecil di hadapannya.

Dan ketika ia berdiri kembali, ia tidak sendirian.

Mereka berjalan bersama menuju kegelapan, dua makhluk yang sama-sama lapar—satu untuk darah, satu untuk makna—mencari jawaban yang tidak akan pernah mereka temukan di dunia yang semakin gelap.

# Pengembara Senja

Di tepi danau yang permukaannya memantulkan warna jingga matahari terbenam, Dara duduk sendirian. Rumput liar tumbuh di sekitar kakinya, dan angin sore membisikkan melodi yang hanya bisa didengar oleh mereka yang sedang menunggu sesuatu—atau seseorang.

Selama tiga puluh tahun hidupnya, Dara selalu merasa ada kekosongan yang tak bisa dijelaskan. Ia memiliki pekerjaan yang layak, keluarga yang menyayanginya, dan sahabat-sahabat yang bisa diandalkan. Namun, ada satu bagian dari dirinya yang terasa belum pulang.

"Kau datang juga," bisik Dara tanpa menoleh.

Langkah kaki di belakangnya berhenti. Lalu, terdengar suara yang sudah lama tak ia dengar—suara sahabatnya, Lintang, yang telah pindah ke kota lain bertahun-tahun lalu.

"Aku membaca suratmu," kata Lintang, suaranya sedikit bergetar. Ia duduk di samping Dara, membawa sesuatu yang lama tak mereka lakukan bersama: keheningan yang nyaman.

Dara tersenyum tipis. "Jadi, kau ingat."

"Aku ingat segalanya. Perjalanan pertama kita ke danau ini saat masih kecil. Janji kita untuk kembali setiap kali kita merasa hilang." Lintang menatap permukaan air yang beriak pelan. "Kau pikir aku sudah lupa?"

Mereka terdiam, membiarkan senja bekerja dengan caranya sendiri—mengubah langit menjadi kanvas raksasa yang penuh warna.

"Lintang," Dara akhirnya berkata pelan, "aku akan pergi."

Lintang menoleh. "Pergi ke mana?"

"Tempat yang belum pernah aku kunjungi. Tempat yang mungkin tidak ada di peta mana pun." Dara mengeluarkan secarik kertas dari sakunya—surat yang ia tulis sendiri, untuk dirinya sendiri, bertahun-tahun lalu. "Aku ingin menemukan jawabannya. Kenapa aku selalu merasa seperti ini. Kenapa ada bagian dari diriku yang tak pernah puas dengan apa yang ada."

Lintang membaca surat itu dengan perlahan. Air matanya jatuh tanpa suara.

"Aku mengerti," katanya. "Aku selalu mengerti."

Matahari semakin rendah. Langit berubah menjadi ungu tua, dan bintang-bintang mulai bermunculan satu per satu seperti tamu yang terlambat.

"Tapi sebelum aku pergi," Dara berdiri dan mengulurkan tangannya, "aku ingin bertanya padamu. Sebagai sahabat. Sebagai seseorang yang pernah berbagi setiap mimpi bersamaku."

Lintang mendongak, mata mereka bertemu di antara cahaya terakhir hari itu.

# 山间四时

皖南的秋天总是来得静悄悄的。

周家的四兄弟站在老宅的院子里，看着父亲在堂屋里整理那些积了灰的旧物。消息是三天前传来的——父亲决定把这个守了四代人的老宅，连同山后的那片竹林，一起交给镇上的旅游开发公司。

"凭什么？"老二周涛第一个开口，声音里带着压抑不住的怒气，"爸一个人做这么大的主，连商量都不商量一声？"

老三周澜靠在门框上，沉默地抽着烟。老四周泉站在最外圈，手里攥着一部旧手机，那是母亲去世前用过的。

"通知你们回来，不是商量。"父亲的声音从堂屋里传出来，苍老却清晰，"是告别。"

这句话让院子里安静了下来。

---

## 春

周家四兄弟的名字里都有一个水字偏旁。

这是读过私塾的太爷爷定的规矩——山里的孩子，要像水一样活。

周涛是山里长大的。小时候他最怕下雨，因为一下雨山路就滑，他接母亲放学就要多走一个时辰。但母亲总说，慢一点没关系，看清楚脚下的路。

大哥周泽在城里开了公司，每年清明才能回来一次。二哥周涛留在镇上教书，照顾父亲的时间最多。三哥周澜在省城画油画，一年到头见不着几回。四弟周泉最小，刚结婚，在邻市安了家。

母亲走的那年，四兄弟都回来了。

母亲是在春天走的。院子里那棵老梨树开满了白花，风一吹，花瓣落了她一身。

四兄弟跪在床前，母亲拉着每个人的手，最后说的是："你们四个，要好好的。"

谁也没想到，这是遗言。

---

## 夏

处理完母亲后事的那个夏天，四兄弟在老宅里住了一个月。

那是他们成年后相处最长的一段时间。

周泽谈生意，周涛改作业，周澜画画，周泉打游戏。四个房间，四种声音。但每天傍晚，他们都会坐在院子里的石桌旁吃饭。

父亲不让请厨师，自己在厨房里忙活。四个儿子轮流洗碗，轮到谁谁就抱怨，抱怨完又老老实实地洗。

那个夏天，周涛翻出了母亲的日记。

母亲识字不多，日记大多是用图画代替的——一朵花代表心情好，一道斜线代表天气不好，一个圆圈代表一家团圆。

最后一页画着一个圆圈，里面坐着五个人。

四个高矮不一的小人，一个弯着腰的大人。

那是母亲画的"全家福"。

周涛把日记本递给兄弟们看，没有人说话。那天晚上，四个人在院子里坐到了天亮，谁也没提睡觉的事。

---

## 秋

又过了五年，父亲打来电话。

周泽接到电话的时候，正在签一个八位数的合同。他放下笔，让秘书先出去，自己走到落地窗前。

"爸，您说。"

"老宅的事，我做主了。你们回来一趟。"

周泽想说什么，又咽了回去。

四兄弟聚齐的那天，秋雨连绵。山路比母亲走的时候好走多了，政府修了柏油路。

父亲带着他们上山，看了那片竹林。

竹子长得比记忆里更高，更密。父亲说，这片竹林是他年轻时和母亲一起种的，母亲最爱秋天到这里挖笋。

"你们每个人在这里取一棵竹子回去。"父亲说，"种在自己的家里。"

周涛问："爸，您呢？"

父亲笑了笑，没有回答。

---

## 冬

老宅签完交接手续的那天，是冬至。

四兄弟在镇上的小旅馆住了一晚，第二天就要各自回各自的城市。父亲没有跟他们走，说要在镇上多住几天。

临走前，周泽拿出一张银行卡："爸，这是我们四兄弟凑的，您拿着。"

父亲摆摆手："我有钱。你们的孝心我收下，钱你们拿回去。"

"爸——"

"我和你妈商量过了。"父亲打断他，"老宅交出去，但竹林我们要留着。等我走的那天，你们把它种回山里来。"

四兄弟愣住了。

父亲从怀里掏出一封信，是母亲的笔迹，歪歪扭扭的——母亲是后来才学会写字的。

信很短，只有一句话：

**"房子是借住的，山才是家。"**

四兄弟接过来传阅，谁都没说话。

---

## 山间四时

又是一年春天。

四兄弟没有一起回来，但每个人都在自己家的阳台上，种下了一棵竹子。

周泽的那棵种在他办公室的窗外。城里的雾霾重，竹叶上总是灰蒙蒙的，但他每天都让人擦一遍。

周涛的那棵种在学校的后院里。课间的时候，总有学生围过来问，周老师，这是什么树？他就一遍一遍地讲皖南的竹林，讲山里的笋。

周澜的那棵种在画室的天窗下。阳光穿过竹叶，在画布上投下斑驳的影子。他画了一幅油画，名字叫《家书》。

周泉的那棵种在女儿出生的那一年。女儿三岁的时候，会指着竹子问，爸爸，这是什么？他说，这是老家山上的竹子，是奶奶种的。

老宅已经被改造成了民宿，名字叫"四时山居"。但后山的竹林还在，父亲住在镇上的养老院里，每天让护工推他上山看一眼。

护工问他："大爷，您每天都来，不累吗？"

父亲笑着说："这竹林是我和老伴儿种的。她葬在这里，我要看着它长。"

护工不知道的是，父亲的身后，还立着一块小小的木牌。

木牌上是四兄弟的字，每个人写了一句话：

**周泽：山高水长。**
**周涛：此心安处。**
**周澜：归去来兮。**
**周泉：岁岁年年。**

下面还有一行小字，是父亲补的：

**"你们的母亲，周兰英。一九五三——二零一九。爱竹。"**

---

*（全文完）*

# 태양을 등지고

## 1장: 여권 없는 여행자

1893년, 블라디보스톡 항구.

구릿빛 노을이 해수면 위에 천천히 스며드는 시간, 제이콥 블러드머어는 화물선 선창 아래에 웅크리고 있었다. 짐 속에 숨어든 지 사흘째. 짐짝 안의 낡은 양탄자가 체온을 내뱉는 것처럼 미세하게 따뜻했다. 하지만 제이콥의 몸은 차가웠다. 늘 그렇듯이.

선원이 위를 지나갔다. 무거운 군화 발소리가 선체 전체를 울렸다. 제이콥은 숨을 멈췄다. 심장이 뛰지 않는 몸에서 피는 흘러가지 않았지만, 두려움만큼은 여전히 인간과 똑같이 느껴졌다.

「검역 통과하면 곧 출항이야. 다른 건 몰라도 함부로 짐 풀어헤치지는 마.」

선원의 목소리가 멀어졌다. 제이콥은 천천히 입술을 핥았다. 마른 입술에 서서히 붉은 기운이 돌아왔다. 마지막으로 피를 마신 것이 엇그제였다. 아시아 대륙을 가로지르는 긴 항해에 대비해 짐 속에 저장해둔, 짐꾼의 돼지 피.

그것으로 버틸 수 있는 시간은 길지 않았다.

---

## 2장: 검역관의 코

1893년의 국제 검역은 엄격했다. 콜레라가 유럽 전역을 휩쓸던 시기였으므로. 일본으로 향하는 배는 반드시 나가사키 근해의 격리 시설에서 7일을 보내야 했다. 그 7일이 제이콥에게는 지옥과도 같았다.

짐짝 안에서 그는 시간을 죽였다. 기억 속의 것들을 하나씩 꺼내보았다. 1745년, 트란실바니아의 작은 마을. 그곳에서 처음 죽었다가 살아났던 밤. 1812년, 보르디노 전투 뒤의 시체 더미. 1868년, 런던의 어느 빵집 아가씨.

기억은 피처럼 따뜻했다. 하지만 그것만으로는 살아갈 수 없었다.

배가 나가사키에 닿았을 때, 제이콥은 어느덧 짐 밖으로 기어 나와 있었다. 선원들 중 하나가 그를 보았다. 놀란 눈으로 입을 벌리려는 순간, 제이콥의 손이 그의 목을 감았다.

「미안하군.」

영어로 말했지만, 선원은 알아듣지 못했다. 영원한 잠에 들기 전에도.

---

## 3장: 새 여권

1908년, 도쿄.

제이콥은 이제 한국계 일본인 사업가 가와무라 게이조였다. 서류는 완벽했다. 빚을 한 푼도 지지 않는 청결한 신분. 위조가 아니라, 정확히는 한 인간의 정체성을 완전히 흡수한 결과였다.

대상자는 1907년 겨울, 요코하마의 뒷골목에서 쓰러져 있었다. 가와무라 게이조, 34세, 조선 출생. 아버지는 도쿄에서 잡화상을 하던 중 폐결핵으로 죽었다. 본인은 야간 학교를 다니며 도쿄의 한 상사에서 사환으로 일하고 있었다.

제이콥은 그를 내려다보았다. 젊은 얼굴에 삶의 피로가 깊이 배어 있었다.

「부디 편히 가게.」

그는 가와무라의 머리카락 한 올씩 자신의 것으로 만들었다. 목소리도. 지문도. 망막의 패턴까지. 흡수는 정확히 7일 동안 이루어졌다. 어느덧 거울 속에 비친 얼굴은 가와무라의 것이었다.

남은 것은 그의 죽음뿐이었다. 제이콥은 그를 요코하마 항구 깊이 가라앉혔다. 아무도 찾지 않았다. 가와무라에게는 가족이 없었으므로.

---

## 4장: 간판 위의 인간

1912년, 메이지 시대가 끝나고 다이쇼 시대가 시작된 해.

가와무라 게이조라는 이름은 도쿄 상계(商界)에서 조금씩 알려지고 있었다. 그는 잡화상을 물려받아 번창시켰다. 신용은 두텁고, 거래처도 늘어갔다. 단, 그는 늘 야간에만 일했다. 낮에는 어딘가에 숨어 지내고, 해가 떨어진 뒤에야 모습을 드러냈다.

가까운 사람도 그가 어떤 인물인지 정확히 몰랐다. 가와무라 게이조는 불어와 독어에 능통했고, 때때로 서양식 예절을 구사했다. 그러나 그의 얼굴에는 늘 그림자가 있었다. 너무 창백하고, 너무 완벽하게 젊었다.

어느 금융업자는 그에게 말했다.

「게이조 씨, 당신은 마치 피를 빨아먹는 흡혈귀처럼 늙지 않는군요.」

웃으면서 한 농담이었다. 제이콥은 그 자리에서 정중하게 웃어 보였다. 하지만 그의 심장—멈춘 지 167년이 된 심장—이 순간만큼은 뛰는 것 같았다.

---

## 5장: 조선 땅을 밟다

1923년, 관동 대지진.

도쿄는 잿더미가 되었다. 가와무라 잡화상도 예외는 아니었다. 제이콥은 살아남았지만, 신분을 다시 만들어야 했다. 도쿄는 위험했다. 너무 많은 사람이 죽었고, 너무 많은 기록이 소실되었으며, 너무 많은 사람이 사라졌다.

그는 부산으로 향했다. 조선은 그에게 낯선 땅이 아니었다. 1882년의 서울, 임오군란이 한창이던 그때, 그는 조선에 발을 들인 적이 있었다. 그때는 서울의 어느 관료의 신분을 빌려 한양을 누볐다.

이번에는 달랐다. 일본의 패전과 함께 조선을 지배하던 세력은 무너지고 있었고, 새로운 국경선이 그어지고 있었다.

1923년 봄, 부산항.

제이콥은 배 위에서 한국의 국기를 내려다보았다. 태극기. 그의 머릿속에는 200년이 넘는 기억이 흘렀다. 국경은 늘 인류에게 발목을 잡는 것이었다. 하지만 그에게는 발목이 없었다. 맥박이 없었으므로.

부산에 내리자, 어지러운 무더기가 그를 삼켰다. 일본에서 도망쳐 내려온 사람들, 지진의 잔해를 뒤집어쓴 사람들, 그리고 새로운 시대의 시작을 맞이하려는 조선인들. 그 사이에서 제이콥은 자신의 짐을 끌고 사라졌다.

---

## 6장: 박 씨 가문

1945년, 광복.

제이콥은 이제 박윤호였다. 부산의 한 작은 항구 사무소에서 일하는, 40대로 보이는 중년 남자. 그는 결혼했고, 아내가 있었다. 물론 아내의 죽음은 그가 결정했다. 그에게 인간의 시간을 함께하는 것은 언제나 무의미한 일이었다.

박윤호는 부산에서 살아남았다. 한국 전쟁도, 4·19도, 5·18도. 그에게는 정치와 역사의 거센 물결이 일렁이는 한가운데에서도 늘 안전한 지점이 있었다. 그 안전한 지점은 늘 어둠 속에 있었다.

1980년대 후반, 박윤호의 딸이 미국으로 유학을 갔다. 딸은 서신에서 이렇게 적었다.

「아버지, 당신 정말 이상한 분이에요. 살아온 세월이 너무 많은 사람 같아요.」

제이콥—박윤호—은 서울의 작은 아파트에서 그 서신을 읽으며 희미하게 웃었다. 어느덧 늦은 오후였고, 커튼 너머로 노을이 스며들고 있었다.

---

## 7장: 새 천 년의 국경

2024년, 인천공항.

제이콥은 이제 박도현이었다. 박윤호의 외손자. 하지만 박도현의 신분은 이미 1998년에 한 대학생에게서 빌려온 것이었다. 외모는 단정했다. 나이는 서른셋. 국적은 대한민국. 여권에는 출생지가 부산으로 찍혀 있었다.

그는 인천공항 출국장을 서성이고 있었다. 목적지는 뉴욕. 미국은 까다로운 나라였다. 지문, 망막 스캔, 얼굴 인식. 한때는 그 모든 것을 속일 수 있었다. 하지만 이제는 달랐다.

「박도현 씨?」

검은 정장을 입은 직원이 그를 불렀다. 제이콥은 멈췄다. 두려움이 온몸을 훑었다. 기계 학습으로 무장한 국경의 알고리즘은 혈액 순환이 없는 몸을 어떻게 판단할까?

직원이 다가가더니, 가볍게 고개를 숙였다.

「탑승 수속 도와드릴까요? 비즈니스 클래스 손님은 제이드 라운지 이용 가능합니다.」

제이콥은 그를 바라보았다. 직원의 목에서 맥박이 뛰고 있었다. 80회 분당. 건강한 인간의 박자.

「아니요. 괜찮습니다.」

제이콥은 미소를 지었다. 완벽하게 인간다운 미소. 여권에는 사진과 똑같은 얼굴이 찍혀 있었다. 알고리즘은 통과했다.

그는 출국 게이트를 통과했다. 뒤돌아보지 않았다. 한 번도 그래본 적이 없었다.

---

## 8장: 여권 없는 자의 일기

뉴욕 JFK 공항. 2024년 가을.

제이콥은 공항 밖의 어둠 속에 섰다. 도시의 불빛이 하늘을 물들이고 있었다. 279년 전, 그는 트란실바니아의 시체 더미에서 깨어났다. 279년 동안 그는 수많은 국경을 넘었다. 콘스탄티노플의 성벽 아래, 페트로그라드의 눈 위, 상하이의 강변, 도쿄의 차가운 골목, 부산의 피난민 행렬, 서울의 아파트 창문 너머.

언제나 한 가지 원칙을 지켰다.

국경은 인간이 만든 것이다. 그리고 국경 앞에서 우리는 누구나 검열당한다. 하지만 정작 누구도 묻지 않는 것이 있다. 이 피부 아래, 이 몸속에 흐르는 것은 정말 인간의 피인가.

제이콥은 택시를 잡았다. 목적지는 맨해튼의 한 호텔이었다. 그의 가방 안에는 깨끗한 옷가지와 한국 여권이 들어 있었다. 또 하나의 신분. 또 하나의 인생. 또 하나의 100년 후의 도피.

택시가 다리를 건너는 동안, 그는 창밖을 바라보았다. 자유의 여신상이 어둠 속에서 희미하게 빛나고 있었다.

저것은 국경이 아니었다. 다만 인간이 만들어낸 거대한 상징이었다. 제이콥은 그 상징을 바라보며, 279년 전 마지막으로 느꼈던 무언가를 떠올렸다.

배고픔.

그는 그것을 미소 짓는 것으로 덮었다. 택시 안에서, 또 하나의 인간의 박자가 그를 향해 뛰고 있었다.

---

## 에필로그: 2124년의 국경

아무도 제이콥 블러드머어의 정체를 모르리라.

하지만 언젠가, 어떤 역사가가 흥미로운 사실을 발견할지도 모른다. 18세기 후반부터 지금까지, 모든 대륙의 모든 전쟁과 모든 격변 속에서, 한 사람의 인생이 일정한 패턴으로 반복되고 있었다는 사실을.

국경을 넘어가는 자들의 목록에 이름이 없는 자.

여권이 필요 없는 자.

피 대신 기억으로 사는 자.

제이콥은 호텔 방의 커튼을 닫았다. 낮이 오고 있었다. 뉴욕의 하늘이 희미하게 밝아오고 있었다. 그는 창문에서 물러나 어둠 속으로 향했다.

또 하나의 백 년이 시작되려 하고 있었다.

---

# The Weight of Embers

The letter arrived on a Tuesday, tucked between a water bill and a flyer for a yard service. Margaret Holloway almost recycled it without reading it, the envelope was plain manila, her name typed in block letters with no return address. But something, perhaps the weight of it in her hand, heavier than a single sheet of paper ought to be, made her hesitate.

She made tea. She sat in her chair by the window where she had spent the last three years watching the seasons change on Maple Street. The letter waited on the kitchen table, accusatory in its stillness.

Forty-three years ago, Margaret had been twenty-three and in love with a man named Eli Marsh. He had hands like leather and a laugh that started in his chest and climbed up through his throat like something trying to escape. They had been going to marry. She had picked out curtains.

Then came the night in November when Eli's brother, Calvin, came to her apartment with whiskey on his breath and decisions in his head. Margaret still could not say the word for what he did. She had tried, in the early years, to find it, to trap it in language. But it slipped out of every word she held up to it, like smoke through fingers.

Eli never knew. That was the strangest part, or the cruellest. When Margaret, bleeding and ruined, tried to tell him, the words simply would not come. She watched his face for signs, listened for the questions that never arrived. Calvin had simply continued being Calvin, showing up to Sunday dinners with his arm around Margaret's shoulder and his smile as bright as a knife held to the light.

Eli proposed anyway. Margaret said yes, because she did not know what else to do with herself. They married in spring. She wore the white dress and said the vows and felt the cold gold band slide onto her finger like a manacle. She told herself it was penance. She told herself she deserved it.

Eli died in a tractor accident in 1987. Calvin cried at the funeral, real tears, the kind that left tracks in dust. Margaret watched him and understood, for the first time, the precise shape of the thing that had been done to her. She felt it lock into place like a bone setting wrong.

Calvin is dying now, the letter said. Pancreatic. Six months, maybe less. The letter was unsigned.

Margaret sat with her tea going cold and her hands folded in her lap. She thought of all the ways she had imagined this moment. For forty years she had carried a small flame inside her, feeding it when she could, letting it dim when she had to survive. She had pictured confrontations. She had written letters she never sent. She had rehearsed speeches in the mirror until her reflection looked like a stranger.

And now, here it was. The invitation she had never asked for.

She did not go.

---

Three weeks passed. Margaret pruned her roses, paid her bills, watched the news. She told no one. Her daughter, Susan, called on Sundays, and Margaret listened to her complaints about work and her grandson's soccer schedule and felt the tender, worn-through fabric of her love for them.

Then, on a Wednesday, another letter. Same envelope. Same heavy hand.

*Margaret —*

*I know what he did. I have always known. He told me, before he married your sister. He told me because he thought it made him strong. He was wrong.*

*I am not writing to ask you to forgive him. I am writing to ask you to choose.*

*You can go to him. You can let him see your face before he dies. Or you can stay here, and the weight of him dies with him, and you will be free.*

*Either way, the choice is yours. It always was.*

Margaret read it three times. She set it down. She picked it up again. The handwriting, she realized, was not unfamiliar. It belonged to a person she had not thought of in thirty years. Calvin's daughter. Rebecca. A girl who had grown up and moved away and become, by all accounts, someone her father did not deserve.

Margaret sat with the letter for a long time. Then she got up and put the kettle on.

---

She thought about the word *revenge*.

She had always imagined it as an act, a thing done, a wound returned. She had pictured Calvin's face when he understood what he had taken. She had rehearsed the moment until it gleamed in her mind like a coin.

But the letter was asking something else. It was asking her to consider that the coin was already in her hand, and it had been all along. Forty-three years of cold tea and watching the street. Forty-three years of a husband she could not love the way he deserved. Forty-three years of flinching when anyone touched her unexpectedly. The revenge had already happened. She had been the one who paid for it.

This is the strange arithmetic of the long grievance: the person you are punishing has already forgotten, or never knew, or is simply too dull to feel it. The only one still bleeding is you. The only one carrying the debt is you. The fire you have been tending has been burning your own house down for so long that you no longer remember what it was for.

---

Margaret did not go to Calvin's bedside. She did not send a letter. She did not pick up the phone. She sat in her chair and watched the light move across the floor and thought about Eli, about the curtains she had picked out, about the girl she had been before November.

She cried for a long time. Then she stopped.

On Sunday she called Susan and asked about her grandson's game. She listened. She laughed. She told her daughter she loved her, and meant it, and let the words sit in the air without reaching for anything else.

The next morning she drove to the cemetery where Eli was buried. She had not been in years. The grass was wet and her shoes were not right for it. She stood at the headstone and said the things she had been saving, the ones she had never been able to say to anyone else, and when she was done she felt lighter and heavier at the same time.

---

Calvin died on a Thursday in October. Margaret heard about it from her sister, who called crying and confused, who could not understand why Margaret did not cry with her.

"I loved him," her sister said. "He was my husband."

"I know," Margaret said. "I am sorry."

She meant it. That was the thing she had not expected. Somewhere in the long autumn of her anger, the man Calvin had been had calcified into a single act, a single night. The brother who fished with Eli. The uncle who brought her daughter candy. The man who had knelt in church every Sunday and believed, she supposed, that he was forgiven.

She would never forgive him. She understood that now, finally, the way you understand a law of physics. Forgiveness was not hers to give. It had never been. The only thing that had ever been hers was her own life, and she had spent forty-three years giving it away to a fire.

---

She wrote one letter. She did not send it to Rebecca. She did not send it to Calvin, who was past sending. She put it in a drawer in her kitchen, beside the recipe cards and the spare keys, and she did not read it again.

It said: *You took the only years I had. I am asking for them back.*

It was a small, foolish sentence. But she kept it. It was the first true thing she had written in a very long time.

---

In the spring, Margaret planted a new garden in the front yard. Tulips, mostly, and some herbs she did not know how to cook with yet. Susan came over and helped her weed, and they talked about nothing important, and the sun was warm on Margaret's back, and she thought: *this is what is left. This is the whole of it.*

The weight she had been carrying did not disappear. It simply stopped being the heaviest thing in her hands.

She had expected revenge to be a sword. She had carried it for so long. She was surprised to find, in the end, that it was a garden, and that the planting was hers, and that the season, finally, was her own.

# 目击

咖啡馆里弥漫着新鲜研磨的咖啡豆香气，我正准备咬下那块提拉米苏。

然后我看见了他。

坐在角落里的那个男人——大约三十岁出头，苍白的面容，黑色高领毛衣，看起来像个失眠的会计。他对面坐着另一个男人，年纪更大些，灰色大衣，有一种我在博物馆守卫身上见过的从容。

我当时没在意。我只是想在下班后独处一会儿。

我咬下了提拉米苏。可可粉在舌尖散开，然后——

灰衣男人动了。

动作快得不像人。他的手越过桌面，钳住了年轻男人的下巴。年轻男人的眼睛猛然睁大，嘴被强行扳开。

我听见了一个声音。

不是尖叫。是一种湿润的、撕裂的声音，像是有人把丝绒从中间撕开。

灰衣男人俯下身。我看见他的嘴唇贴上了年轻男人的脖颈。我以为那是个变态，一个在公共场所咬人的疯子。

但我看见了年轻男人的脸。

他的表情不是痛苦。是狂喜。那种在婚礼上、在孩子出生时、在彩票中奖时才会出现的神情。

他的身体开始发生变化。我看着他的皮肤变得更白，看着他的眼睛——原本是棕色的——变成了一种深红，像干涸的血。

整个过程不到三十秒。

灰衣男人直起身子，用手帕擦了擦嘴角。他看向年轻男人，年轻男人看向他，两人之间有一种我不理解的东西。

然后他们同时看向我。

我放下叉子。叉子碰到盘子，发出清脆的声响。

"你什么都没看见。"灰衣男人说。他的声音很轻，但每个字都像是刻进空气里。

我想尖叫。但声带不听使唤。我想跑，但双腿像是被钉在地板上。

年轻男人——不，不再是男人了，不再是人类了——露出一个微笑。

"你会忘记的，"他说。他的声音比之前更柔和，像丝绒。"很快。"

我眨眼。

咖啡馆的灯光。提拉米苏的可可粉。窗外是十一月的街道。

我刚才在想什么？

我看着窗外，一个穿灰色大衣的男人正在离开。旁边跟着一个穿黑高领的年轻人。他们消失在人群里。

奇怪。我觉得我应该记住什么。

但我已经忘了。

我又咬了一口提拉米苏，继续看我的报纸。

# The Cartographer and the Tide

The first time Mira saw the creature, she nearly fell off her research skiff.

She had been charting the salt marshes of the eastern inlet for three months, sleeping in a rotting cabin she'd rented from a fisherman who spoke mostly in nods and shrugs. Her grant was small, her equipment older, and her thesis on tidal erosion patterns was the kind of work that nobody read until it was too late to matter. She liked it that way.

The creature surfaced twenty meters from her skiff one foggy morning, when the water was the color of pewter and the world had shrunk to a circle of fifty feet in every direction. It was the size of a large dog, maybe, but shaped like nothing she could name. Its skin was the deep, shifting blue of deep water, and it had eyes — if they were eyes — that regarded her with what she could only describe as polite curiosity.

She wrote in her journal that night: *Local fauna appears more intelligent than initial surveys suggested. Possibly cetacean? No blowhole observed. Did not approach the skiff but did not flee either.*

She named it Solomon, because it seemed to know things.

---

Solomon, as it turned out, did not know things. Solomon was not especially intelligent, by the standards of whatever species it belonged to. But it was curious in a way that Mira had rarely seen in animals. It followed her skiff at a distance of fifteen to twenty meters, never approaching but never leaving, watching her with its dark, depthless eyes.

She talked to it. She told herself this was a scientific observation habit, the kind of thing naturalists had done for centuries. She told herself the creature couldn't understand her. But she talked anyway.

"I mapped another two kilometers of shoreline today," she said one afternoon, sitting on the edge of her skiff with her feet dangling in the cold water. "The erosion is faster than I thought. By the time anyone listens, this whole marsh will be gone."

Solomon surfaced nearby, a smooth dome of dark blue rising from the gray water. It regarded her. She could not prove that it was listening, but she liked to believe it was.

"I grew up near a marsh like this," she said. "In Delaware. My grandmother had a cottage on a bay. It looked just like this. I used to think places like this were infinite. That there would always be more marsh, more mud, more fiddler crabs."

She trailed her fingers in the water. Solomon drifted closer, the smallest of distances.

"I miss her," Mira said, and was surprised to find it true. She had not allowed herself to miss her grandmother in years. The grief had been folded up and put away somewhere, in the way of daughters who had complicated relationships with their mothers and uncomplicated relationships with the women who had raised them.

Solomon made a sound. Not a vocalization, exactly — more like a slow exhalation that left a small constellation of bubbles on the surface.

"Was that sympathy?" Mira asked.

Solomon blinked, if it had eyelids, and sank back beneath the water.

---

She began to look forward to her time on the water.

This was not, she told herself, because of Solomon. She had always loved being on the water. She had always loved the solitude of fieldwork. But she could not pretend that her routes had not subtly shifted, that she did not now find excuses to be in the eastern inlet at particular hours, that her notebooks did not contain more observations of "fauna behavior" than of tidal erosion.

She tried to be a scientist about it. She measured the creature when it surfaced, estimated its size, noted the times and tides of its appearances. She wrote everything down with the clinical precision her advisor would have approved of. She did not write down that she had begun to feel less alone.

Her colleagues emailed. She answered some of them. She had been working on this project for almost a year now, and the grant money was running out, and her advisor was gently asking about preliminary findings. She had preliminary findings. She also had a creature she had named after a king.

"The erosion is accelerating," she wrote in her monthly report. "I am documenting the geomorphology of the inlet and the impact of sea-level rise on the local ecology."

She did not write: *I have made a friend who lives in the salt water and who I believe understands me when I speak.*

---

One morning she found a small fish laid across the bow of her skiff.

She had been anchored near the mouth of a tidal creek, making measurements, when she climbed back aboard. The fish was silver and freshly dead, still cool to the touch, with the kind of clear, blank eye that dead things have.

She looked out at the water. Solomon was twenty meters away, watching.

She picked up the fish. It was a smelt, she thought, or a young herring — some kind of small forage fish, the kind that predators ate. She held it in her hands and felt the strange, irrational prickle of tears behind her eyes.

"That's not how it works," she said aloud. "You're not a dog. I'm not going to throw it for you."

But she put the fish in her cooler anyway, and took it back to the cabin, and ate it for dinner with butter and lemon, and felt less lonely than she had in a long time.

She did not write this down in her journal.

---

In the second year, the erosion got worse.

A storm came through in late autumn, the kind of storm that the old-timers said used to come once a decade and now came every other year. It ripped up a quarter of the marsh she had been mapping. The tidal creeks shifted. The inlet narrowed. She worked eighteen-hour days for a week, taking measurements, mourning what she had lost to the water.

She did not see Solomon for four days after the storm.

She told herself this was fine. The creature had its own life, its own territories, its own reasons for being where it was. She was anthropomorphizing. She was being foolish. She was a scientist.

On the fifth day, she saw him. He surfaced in the late afternoon, when the light was going golden and the water had the strange glassy quality of incoming tide. He came up thirty meters from her skiff, which was farther than usual, and he stayed up longer than usual.

"You survived," she said.

He blinked at her.

"I was worried," she admitted, and the admission felt like something falling out of her, a stone she had not known she was carrying. "I was worried about you."

Solomon drifted closer. Closer than he had ever come. Fifteen meters. Ten. He regarded her with those dark, depthless eyes, and she regarded him, and neither of them moved.

"My grandmother used to say that the marsh was a kind of clock," Mira said. "That you could read the time of the world by what was growing and what was dying. I never understood what she meant. Now I think I do."

Solomon made his bubble sound.

"I'm going to have to leave soon," she said. "The grant's almost up. I have to go back and write the thesis. I have to go back to the university and defend it and get my doctorate and become someone who does important work. I have to leave the marsh."

Solomon sank beneath the water. She watched the place where he had been for a long time.

---

She did not see him the next morning. She did not see him the morning after that. She told herself this was fine. She finished her measurements. She packed her equipment. She drove into the nearby town and mailed boxes of samples back to the university. She cleaned the cabin and left the key with the fisherman, who nodded and shrugged as she had known he would.

On her last morning, she took the skiff out one final time. The water was flat and silver and the fog was just lifting. She anchored in the eastern inlet, near the place where she had first seen him.

She sat on the bow and waited.

An hour passed. The fog burned off. The sun came through and turned the water into something bright and sharp. She watched the gulls. She watched the small crabs on the exposed mud at low tide. She watched her own hands, scarred from fieldwork and rough with salt.

She was about to give up when he surfaced.

He came up twenty meters from her skiff, the smooth blue dome of him rising from the water like a thought. He regarded her. She regarded him.

"I don't know what you are," she said. "I never figured it out. I tried. I really tried."

He blinked.

"I don't know if you understand me. I don't know if any of this has been what I thought it was. But I wanted to say thank you. For the fish. For listening. For being here."

She reached into her pocket and took out the small notebook she had been keeping for him — not the scientific notebook, but the other one, the one with no charts in it, only words. She held it up.

"I'm going to leave this here," she said. "On the bow. You can do what you want with it."

She set it down gently on the weathered wood. She started the engine of the skiff. She turned the bow toward the shore.

She did not look back.

---

Years later, when Mira was an associate professor at a respectable university, she published a paper on tidal erosion in the eastern inlet. It was well-received. It was cited by other researchers. It won a small award from a society she had not heard of before. She was proud of it.

She never returned to the inlet. The marsh was gone by then, anyway, claimed by the rising sea, and the fisherman's cabin had been washed away in another storm. She sometimes thought about the small notebook, left on the bow of a rented skiff. She wondered if it had been found by anyone, if it had been read, if it had mattered.

She did not think this often. She had a life to lead. She had work to do.

But sometimes, on foggy mornings, when the world had shrunk to a circle of fifty feet in every direction, she would feel a sudden, irrational pull in her chest, a kind of homesickness for a place she had never lived. And she would think of Solomon.

And she would smile.

# 血脈の沈黙 ― 吸血鬼一族の興亡

## 第一章：夜明けの血

1607年、冬。トランシルヴァニアの深い森の奥深く、一匹の狼が雪に倒れていた。瀕死の獣の傍らで、跪く男がいた。ラディスラウス・コルヴィン。名を馳せたハンガリー貴族の末裔にして、三十年戦争の敗残者だった。

彼は熱病に冒されていた。戦で受けた傷は癒えど、魂の傷は深く、酒と薬に頼る日々が彼を蝕んでいた。冷たい雪に額を伏せたそのとき、影が射した。

「御前は、まだ死にたくないか」

声は女のものだった。見上げれば、白銀の髪に月光をまとった女が立っていた。名をエラータという。千年の時を生きた血の族の最後の生き残りだった。

「生きる意味など、もうない」

「ならば、もう一度だけ、意味をくれてやろう」

彼女が唇を寄せると、冷たい流れが喉を通り抜けた。心臓が二度、三度と脈打った。死の淵から引き上げられたラディスラウスは、完全なる闇へ足を踏み入れた。

## 第二章：血の契約

エラータの血を受けたラディスラウスは、力を得た。狼の耳が人間のことばを聞き、夜目が森を支配した。エラータは彼を、血の族の復興のための器と定めた。

「一族を建てよ、ラディスラウス。名は『コルヴィン』とせよ。我が血統は、お前の子孫と共に永遠なる眠りから覚める」

ラディスラウスはエラータの血を引く子を設けた。最初の子、ヴィルモシュ。トランシルヴァニアの山岳に城を構え、流浪の血の族を招き入れた。三十年戦争で故郷を失った貴族の子弟、虐げられたジプシー、異端審問を逃れた知識人。彼らを一族の眷属とし、血の絆で結んだ。

十年が過ぎた。コルヴィン一族はトランシルヴァニアの奥地に名を轟かせた。農民は森に踏み入らず、旅人は夜になる前に街道を離れた。ラディスラウスは「夜の長父」と呼ばれ、恐れられた。

## 第三章：栄光の世紀

17世紀の終わり、コルヴィン一族は最盛期を迎えた。ヴィルモシュの子孫たちが枝葉のように広がり、五つの家門が形成された。

**ヴァーナ家** ― 武勇の家門。ラディスラウスの直系。
**エルデシュ家** ― 知の血統。占星術と錬金術に通じた。
**セーケイ家** ― 影の血族。諜報と外交を司った。
**マグヤル家** ― 芸術の家。血の芸術を極めた。
**ラクシャーザ家** ― 異端の家。人間界との交渉役。

一族の血は、時に人間と混じり、稀に「半血」を生んだ。半血たちは完全な力を持たぬ代わりに、昼の世界で生きられた。コルヴィン一族は、政治、芸術、交易を通じてヨーロッパの闇に根を張った。

1700年、ラディスラウスは長眠に入った。彼の心臓は金銀の箱に納められ、城の最深部に安置された。エラータの血統は永遠に続くと思われた。

## 第四章：内なる病

繁栄は、慢心を生んだ。

18世紀、第三代当主ヴァルナヴァ・コルヴィンの時代、一族は内紛を起こす。ヴァルナヴァは人間との混血を禁じる「血の純潔令」を布いた。半血を蔑ろにし、眷属の待遇を引き下げた。

反発したマグヤル家の一団が離反した。彼らはウィーンへ去り、宮廷画家として身を立てた。やがてその子孫の血は皇室の闇に流れ込み、フランス革命の嵐の中で多くが塵と化した。

離反は続き、エルデシュ家も姿を消した。彼らは地中海へ渡り、魔術の書を求めて各地を放浪した。最後に消息を伝えたのは、1753年のマルセイユだった。

## 第五章：人間という災い

19世紀、産業革命の波がヨーロッパを飲み込んだ。都市の光は増え、森は後退した。コルヴィン一族は、移動を余儀なくされた。

第五代当主カタリン・コルヴィンは、時代に適応しようとした。彼女は「狩り」の掟を緩め、犠牲者を慎重に選ぶよう命じた。しかし、これは一族を内部から蝕んだ。

ヴィクトル・コルヴィンという若き血族がいた。人間社会の文化に憧れ、密かに「昼の顔」を作った。最初は僅かな違反だったが、やがて彼は一族を裏切り、人間の狩人に一族の居場所を売った。

1891年の聖金曜日、ドラキュラ城に日の光が入った。

## 第六章：火と灰

侵入者は準備周到だった。聖なる杭、銀の弾丸、そして日の光。コルヴィン一族の結束は緩み、情報漏れを防げなかった。

カタリン当主は、長ヴィクトルと対峙した。

「お前は一族を売った」

「一族？ ああ、古い血の玩具ですよ、母上。僕もあなたも。所詮、人間が恐れる怪物でしかない」

カタリンの杭がヴィクトルの胸を貫いた。しかし侵入者は後を絶たず、地下の聖堂に火が放たれた。ラディスラウスの心臓は、炎の中で灰と化した。

生存者は三分の 一 だった。ラクシャーザ家の残党は東方へ散り、ヴァーナ家の生き残りはバルカン山中に隠れ、セーケイ家はその後二度と姿を現さなかった。

## 第七章：忘却の淵へ

20世紀、二つの大戦が人間世界を揺さぶった。コルヴィン一族の残党は、もはや一族と呼べるものではなかった。個々の血族が、人間社会に溶け込み、生き延びようとした。

2000年、最後の「純血」が死んだ。名前は不明。場所はブカレストの安ホテル。死因は老衰。ただし吸血鬼は老衰しない。誰かが、始末したのだ。

現在、コルヴィンの名は歴史の埃に埋もれている。ドラキュラ城は観光名所となり、ヴァンパイアはハロウィンの仮装にされた。エラータの千年を超える血統は、誰にも知られぬまま静かに途絶えた。

## 終章：沈黙の後

ブカレストの地下に、古い扉がある。錆びた鉄には、かつて紋章が彫られていた。鷲と蛇と、月を啄む狼。今ではそれも苔に覆われ、ほとんど判別できない。

扉の向こうには、何もない。聖堂は崩れ、ラディスラウスの棺は空だった。エラータの血は、どこにも残っていない。

ただ、冬の夜、満月のとき、稀に森で奇妙な目撃談が語られる。銀髪の女が、雪の中に立つ影を。彼女は誰かを待っているのかもしれない。

千年待っても、誰も来ないことを知りながら。

---

*すべての王朝は興り、すべての血は涸れる。夜は明けるためにあるのであり、闇は星を際立たせるための影でしかない。コルヴィン一族の物語は、夜の帳の中でのみ囁かれるべきだったのかもしれない。*

*― 沈黙の書、エルデシュ家の最後の記録より抜粋 ―*

# 镜中人

那是她最后一次看见自己活着的样子。

林晚站在浴室的镜子前，看着镜中那张熟悉的脸。二十六岁，眼下有淡淡的青黑，嘴唇因长期失眠而有些苍白。她伸手摸了摸自己的脸颊，指尖传来的温度真实而冰凉。

镜中的她也抬起了手。

动作完全同步，仿佛在模仿她。林晚没有在意，只是拧开水龙头，准备洗脸。水流哗哗地落下，她俯下身去，让凉水冲刷着面部。

抬起头时，她愣住了。

镜中的自己，嘴角微微上扬，露出一个意味深长的笑容。

林晚僵在原地。她可以发誓，自己的嘴角并没有动。镜中的那个"她"，却笑得愈发诡异，眼睛直直地盯着她，仿佛在打量一只落入陷阱的猎物。

"你……"林晚刚想开口。

镜中的她却抢先一步，伸出一根手指抵在唇边，做了个噤声的手势。然后，那张嘴开始说话——

"从今天起，我就是你。"

声音从镜面深处传来，却清晰地灌入林晚的耳中。她想后退，却发现双脚像是被钉在了地板上，动弹不得。镜中的女人笑着抬起手，一寸一寸地贴上了镜面——

下一秒，一只苍白的手从镜子里伸了出来。

---

## 第一章 替代

林晚记得那种感觉。

像被一股强大的吸力卷入了深渊，四周是无边的黑暗与冰冷。她挣扎着尖叫，却发不出任何声音。她看见自己的身体仍然站在镜子前，却像一具没有灵魂的空壳，眼神空洞地站着。

而镜中那个女人，已经走了出来。

那个女人穿着一模一样的衣服，有着一模一样的脸，却有着截然不同的气质。她从镜框里迈出，就像踏过一道普通的门槛，轻盈而优雅。她转过头，看向悬浮在虚空中的林晚，笑容恬静：

"别怕。我会替你好好活下去的。"

林晚想冲上去质问，想抓住那个冒名顶替者，想把她拖回镜子里面——但她的双手穿过了自己的身体，什么也抓不住。她只是一缕被困在这里的幽魂。

那个女人转身，对着镜面照了照，满意地点点头。然后，她走向浴室的门，拉开门——

门外站着林晚的未婚夫，陈屿。

"晚晚，你洗了好久，没事吧？"他温柔地问，眼里满是关切。

女人笑了，眉眼弯弯："没事，就是有点累。"

她走过去，自然地挽住陈屿的胳膊，声音娇软："今晚吃什么？我饿了。"

陈屿刮了刮她的鼻子："做了你爱吃的糖醋排骨。"

两人说说笑笑地走远了，留下一缕魂魄困在浴室的镜子里。

林晚想哭，却没有眼泪。

---

## 第二章 旁观

镜中世界是一种奇异的存在。

林晚被囚禁在这方寸之间，只能透过镜面观看外面的世界。浴室的镜子连接着卧室的穿衣镜、客厅的装饰镜、玄关的全身镜——她像是一个被关在透明牢笼里的囚徒，只能眼睁睁地看着那个冒名顶替者过着她的生活。

第一周，那个女人表现得堪称完美。

她记得林晚的所有习惯，知道她喜欢把牙膏从中间挤起，知道她睡前一定要喝半杯温水，知道她看恐怖片时会把脸埋进陈屿的肩窝。她完美地扮演着一个温柔体贴的未婚妻，让陈屿满心欢喜。

"晚晚最近状态真好，"陈屿对朋友说，"感觉她整个人都轻松了很多。"

但林晚看得心惊胆战。

因为她注意到一些细节。那个女人做饭时从不尝咸淡——她根本不知道林晚的口味偏好；她与林晚的母亲通话时，总是有意无意地回避某些问题；她看林晚收藏的那些书籍时，眼神里流露的不是怀念，而是……陌生。

她不了解林晚。

她只是在模仿林晚。

更可怕的是，林晚发现自己正在一点点地消失。

起初只是一些细微的变化——她对某些往事的记忆开始模糊，她曾经最爱的歌听起来不再有任何感觉，她想起母亲的脸时，心里泛不起任何波澜。

第七天夜里，她试图回忆陈屿求婚时的场景，却发现脑海里一片空白。

她正在被抹去。

那个女人每多扮演一天"林晚"，真正的林晚就消失一分。

---

## 第三章 真相

第十五天。

那个女人第一次在镜前卸妆时，看见了林晚。

她吓了一跳，随即平静下来。她对着镜中的林晚笑了笑，那笑容里没有恶意，只有一种说不清道不明的情绪。

"你还在啊，"她轻声说，"我还以为你早就消失了。"

林晚看着她，无法言语——在镜中世界，她连声音都无法传达。但她的目光足以传达一切：愤怒、恐惧、绝望。

那个女人叹了口气，在梳妆台前坐下，看着镜中的林晚。

"你想知道为什么吗？"她问，"为什么我要取代你？"

林晚无法回答，只能死死地盯着她。

"因为我就是你啊，"女人笑了，笑容里带着几分苦涩，"或者说，我是你的一部分。"

她开始讲述。

原来，多年前，林晚曾经有过一个双胞胎妹妹。那个妹妹在出生时就因先天不足夭折了——至少，所有人都以为她夭折了。但实际上，那个孩子并没有死。她被困在了某种维度里，就像现在林晚被困在镜中一样，无声无息地存在了二十六年。

"我看着你长大，"女人说，"看着你享受父母的疼爱，看着你被陈屿求婚，看着你拥有我从未拥有的一切。我不恨你——我只是太渴望活着了。"

林晚震惊了。她从不知道自己有这样一个妹妹，更不知道这个妹妹一直在某个角落里看着她。

"所以，"女人站起来，伸出手指抵在镜面上，"让我代替你吧。你已经活够了，而我等了二十六年。"

她开始在镜面上画出一个奇怪的符号，嘴里念念有词。林晚感到一股强大的力量正在撕扯她的灵魂，她的存在感正在飞速消退——

不要！

林晚在心中嘶吼，但她的声音传达不出去。

就在她即将彻底消散的瞬间——

---

## 第四章 选择

"晚晚，你怎么了？"

陈屿的声音从门外传来。

那个女人的动作顿了一下，符号没有画完。

"没事，"她应道，"马上出来。"

她看了林晚一眼，轻声说："下次吧。下次我一定会成功的。"

然后她走出了浴室。

林晚瘫软在镜中世界，大口大口地喘息——如果灵魂也需要喘息的话。她以为自己必死无疑，却在最后关头获得了一丝喘息。

陈屿。

是陈屿无意中救了她。

从那以后，林晚开始思考。她被囚在镜中，无法传达声音，无法与外界交流。但她还有一样东西——

意志。

真正的林晚，正在一点点消失。再过不久，她就会彻底湮灭，连记忆都不会留下。那个女人会彻底取代她，成为新的"林晚"，过上她的人生。

但林晚不甘心。

她不想就这样消失。

于是她开始做一件事：她开始在镜中世界留下痕迹。

每当那个女人照镜子时，林晚就用尽全部意志，在镜面上留下一个微小的符号——那是她们姐妹之间才懂得的语言，是她们在母亲子宫里时曾经用来交流的方式。

那个符号的意思是："我还在。"

起初，那个女人假装没看见。

但到了第二十天，她开始焦虑。她发现自己越来越难以维持"林晚"的形象——某些瞬间，她会忘记林晚的习惯，某些时刻，她会下意识地做出与林晚截然不同的反应。

陈屿开始觉得不对劲。

"晚晚，你最近怎么了？"他问，"感觉你怪怪的。"

"没有啊，"那个女人笑着掩饰，"可能是工作太累了。"

但林晚知道，那个女人的伪装正在崩溃。

而她留下的那些符号，正在一点一点地侵蚀着那个女人的心防。

---

## 第五章 结局

第二十八天。

那个女人终于崩溃了。

她冲进浴室，对着镜中的林晚大吼："你为什么要这样对我？我只是想活下去！我有什么错！"

林晚看着她，第一次在镜中世界发出了声音——那是她用尽全部意志凝聚出的话语，微弱却清晰：

"我理解你。我不恨你。但是——"

"我不想消失。"

那个女人愣住了。

她蹲在地上，捂着脸哭了起来。她哭了很久，哭得妆都花了。她看起来不像是一个窃取别人人生的恶人，而像是一个迷失了很久的孩子。

"我太孤独了，"她哽咽着说，"在那里面，太孤独了……"

林晚沉默了。

她看着这个与自己有着相同面容的女人，心里涌起一种复杂的情绪。她是恨她的——恨她夺走了自己的人生。但她也理解她——二十六年的孤独，足以让任何人疯狂。

"我们……可以共存吗？"林晚问。

那个女人抬起头，泪眼朦胧："什么意思？"

"你不需要取代我，"林晚说，"你可以和我一起存在。我们可以轮流使用这个身体——白天是我，晚上是你。或者平时是我，周末是你。"

"这样……可以吗？"

"我不知道，"林晚诚实地说，"但我们可以试试。总比两败俱伤好。"

那个女人沉默了很久。

最终，她点了点头。

---

她们达成了一个协议。

那个女人不再是镜中的囚徒，而是林晚的一部分。每当夜深人静时，林晚会"睡去"，让那个女人出来。她会用林晚的身体做一些林晚白天没时间做的事——看星星、写日记、在阳台上静静地发呆。

而林晚则会在白天继续她的人生，做那个被所有人认识的"林晚"。

陈屿从未发现异常——他只是觉得未婚妻最近"变得更有深度了"。

林晚的母亲也觉得女儿最近"懂事了很多"。

只有林晚知道，她和她的妹妹，终于不再是孤独的存在。

那天夜里，当那个女人在阳台上看着满天星斗时，她在镜中世界对林晚说：

"谢谢你，姐姐。"

林晚笑了笑："不客气，妹妹。"

镜中的月光洒落下来，照亮了两个相同的灵魂。

她们再也不会孤独了。

---

**【尾声】**

很多年后，林晚和那个女人已经完全融为一体。

当有人问起"林晚为什么有时候会突然发呆"时，她总是笑笑说："在和自己对话呢。"

没有人知道这句话的真正含义。

除了她自己。

和她的妹妹。

*（全文完）*
